Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Dīghanikāye

The Collection of Long Discourses

Sīlakkhandhavaggaṭīkā

The Sub-commentary on the Division of Morality

Ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Introduction

Saṃvaṇṇanārambhe [V 1.0001][M 1.0001][P 1.0001] ratanattayavandanā saṃvaṇṇetabbassa dhammassa pabhavanissayavisuddhipaṭivedanatthaṃ, taṃ pana dhammasaṃvaṇṇanāsu viññūnaṃ bahumānuppādanatthaṃ, taṃ sammadeva tesaṃ uggahadhāraṇādikkamaladdhabbāya sammāpaṭipattiyā sabbahitasukhanipphādanatthaṃ. Atha vā maṅgalabhāvato, sabbakiriyāsu pubbakiccabhāvato, paṇḍitehi sammācaritabhāvato, āyatiṃ paresaṃ diṭṭhānugatiāpajjanato ca saṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ ratanattayapaṇāmakiriyā. Atha vā ratanattayapaṇāmakaraṇaṃ pūjanīyapūjāpuññavisesanibbattanatthaṃ, taṃ attano yathāladdhasampattinimittakassa kammassa balānuppādanatthaṃ, antarā ca tassa asaṅkocanatthaṃ, tadubhayaṃ anantarāyena aṭṭhakathāya parisamāpanatthaṃ. Idameva ca payojanaṃ ācariyena idhādhippetaṃ. Tathā hi vakkhati – “iti me pasannamatino…pe… tassānubhāvenā”ti. Vatthuttayapūjā hi niratisayapuññakkhettasambuddhiyā aparimeyyappabhāvo [V 1.0002] puññātisayoti bahuvidhantarāyepi lokasannivāse antarāyanibandhanasakalasaṃkilesaviddhaṃsanāya pahoti, bhayādiupaddavañca nivāreti. Yathāha –

At the commencement of the exposition, homage is paid to the Triple Gem to make known the origin, basis, and purity of the Dhamma to be expounded. This is also to inspire great esteem among the wise for the exposition of the Dhamma, so that through the right practice to be obtained by the process of learning, retaining, and so on, they may rightly accomplish all welfare and happiness. Alternatively, the act of paying homage to the Triple Gem is performed in this exposition because it is auspicious, because it is a preliminary duty in all undertakings, because it is rightly practiced by the wise, and because it leads to others following the example in the future. Or, paying homage to the Triple Gem is for the purpose of generating the special merit of venerating the venerable. This is for the purpose of producing strength for one’s own kamma, which is the cause of benefits as they are obtained, and for preventing its decline in the meantime. Both of these are for the purpose of completing the commentary without hindrance. This very purpose is intended here by the Teacher. For he will say: “Thus I, with a mind of faith… by its power.” Indeed, the veneration of the three objects, being an unsurpassed field of merit, is a supreme excellence of merit with immeasurable power. Thus, even in a world with many kinds of obstacles, it is able to destroy all defilements that are the cause of hindrances, and it wards off dangers such as fear. As it is said—

“Pūjārahe pūjayato, buddhe yadi va sāvake”tiādi (dha. pa. 1.195; apa. 1.10.1), tathā –

“When one honors those worthy of honor, whether Buddhas or their disciples,” and so on (Dhp. 195; Ap. I.10.1), and likewise –

“Ye [P 1.0002] bhikkhave buddhe pasannā, agge te pasannā. Agge kho pana pasannānaṃ aggo vipāko hotī”tiādi (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90).

“Monks, those who have faith in the Buddha have faith in what is foremost. For those who have faith in what is foremost, the result is foremost,” and so on (AN 4.34; It. 90).

“Buddhoti [M 1.0002] kittayantassa, kāye bhavati yā pīti;

Varameva hi sā pīti, kasiṇenapi jambudīpassa.

Dhammoti…pe… saṅghoti…pe… dīpassā”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.6);

“For one proclaiming ‘Buddha,’ whatever joy arises in the body, that joy is indeed better than the whole of Jambudīpa. For one proclaiming ‘Dhamma’… and so on… for one proclaiming ‘Saṅgha’… and so on… than the island.” (DA 1.6);

Tathā –

And likewise –

“Yasmiṃ, mahānāma, samaye ariyasāvako tathāgataṃ anussarati, nevassa tasmiṃ samaye rāgapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, na dosa…pe… na mohapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hotī”tiādi (a. ni. 6.10; 11.11),

“Mahānāma, at the time when a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, on that occasion his mind is not overcome by lust, nor by hatred… and so on… nor by delusion,” and so on (AN 6.10; 11.11),

“Araññe rukkhamūle vā…pe…

Bhayaṃ vā chambhitattaṃ vā,

Lomahaṃso na hessatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.249) ca

“In the forest or at the foot of a tree… and so on… Fear or dread will not be, nor will the hair stand on end.” (SN 1.249); and

Tattha yassa vatthuttayassa vandanaṃ kattukāmo, tassa guṇātisayayogasandassanatthaṃ “karuṇāsītalahadaya”ntiādinā gāthattayamāha. Guṇātisayayogena hi vandanārahabhāvo, vandanārahe ca katā vandanā yathādhippetappayojanaṃ sādhetīti. Tattha yassā desanāya saṃvaṇṇanaṃ kattukāmo, sā na vinayadesanā viya karuṇāppadhānā, nāpi abhidhammadesanā viya paññāppadhānā, atha kho karuṇāpaññāppadhānāti tadubhayappadhānameva tāva sammāsambuddhassa thomanaṃ kātuṃ taṃmūlakattā sesaratanānaṃ “karuṇāsītalahadaya”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

Herein, wishing to pay homage to the Triple Gem, he spoke three verses beginning with “karuṇāsītalahadaya” to show its connection with the excellence of qualities. For worthiness of homage comes through the connection with the excellence of qualities, and homage paid to one who is worthy accomplishes its intended purpose. Therein, the teaching that he wishes to expound is not, like the Vinaya teaching, predominantly compassion, nor, like the Abhidhamma teaching, predominantly wisdom; rather, it is predominantly both compassion and wisdom. Therefore, to first offer praise to the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, who is pre-eminent in both and is the root of the other gems, the verses beginning with “karuṇāsītalahadaya” were spoken.

Tattha [V 1.0003] kiratīti karuṇā, paradukkhaṃ vikkhipati, apanetīti attho. Atha vā kiṇātīti karuṇā, paradukkhe sati kāruṇikaṃ hiṃsati, vibādhatīti attho, paradukkhe sati sādhūnaṃ [P 1.0003] kampanaṃ hadayakhedaṃ karotīti vā karuṇā. Atha vā kamiti sukhaṃ, taṃ rundhatīti karuṇā. Esā hi paradukkhāpanayanakāmatālakkhaṇā, attasukhanirapekkhatāya kāruṇikānaṃ sukhaṃ rundhati vibandhatīti. Karuṇāya sītalaṃ karuṇāsītalaṃ, karuṇāsītalaṃ hadayaṃ assāti karuṇāsītalahadayo, taṃ karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ. Tattha kiñcāpi paresaṃ hitopasaṃhārasukhādiaparihānicchanasabhāvatāya, byāpādāratīnaṃ ujuvipaccanīkatāya ca sattasantānagatasantāpavicchedanākārappavattiyā mettāmuditānampi cittasītalabhāvakāraṇatā upalabbhati, tathāpi [M 1.0003] dukkhāpanayanākārappavattiyā parūpatāpāsahanarasā avihiṃsābhūtā karuṇā visesena bhagavato cittassa cittapassaddhi viya sītībhāvanimittanti vuttaṃ “karuṇāsītalahadaya”nti. Karuṇāmukhena vā mettāmuditānampi hadayasītalabhāvakāraṇatā vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Herein, `karuṇā` is so called because ‘it scatters’ (kirati); the meaning is that it disperses, it removes the suffering of others. Alternatively, `karuṇā` is so called because ‘it harms’ (kiṇāti); the meaning is that when others suffer, it harms or distresses the compassionate one. Or, `karuṇā` is so called because when others suffer, it causes the good to tremble and their hearts to ache. Alternatively, `kam` means happiness, and `ruṇā` is from the root `rudh`, to obstruct; thus `karuṇā` is that which obstructs it. For this compassion is characterized by the desire to remove the suffering of others; due to the compassionate one’s disregard for their own happiness, it obstructs and binds their happiness. ‘Cooled by compassion’ is `karuṇāsītalaṃ`. One whose heart is cooled by compassion is `karuṇāsītalahadayo`; this is the meaning of `karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ`. Herein, although for loving-kindness and sympathetic joy a cause for the mind’s coolness is also found—due to their nature of wishing for others’ welfare, happiness, and non-decline of prosperity, their being the direct opposite of ill will and aversion, and their proceeding in a way that cuts off the distress in the continuum of beings—nevertheless, compassion, which proceeds by way of removing suffering, has the function of not enduring the affliction of others, and is a state of non-harming, is especially said to be a cause for the cooling of the Blessed One’s mind, just as tranquility of mind is. Or, it should be understood that through the gateway of compassion, the quality of being a cause for the heart’s coolness is stated also for loving-kindness and sympathetic joy.

Atha vā asādhāraṇañāṇavisesanibandhanabhūtā sātisayaṃ niravasesañca sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ viya savisayabyāpitāya mahākaruṇābhāvaṃ upagatā karuṇāva bhagavato atisayena hadayasītalabhāvahetūti āha “karuṇāsītalahadaya”nti. Atha vā satipi mettāmuditānaṃ sātisaye hadayasītībhāvanibandhanatte sakalabuddhaguṇavisesakāraṇatāya tāsampi kāraṇanti karuṇāva bhagavato hadayasītalabhāvakāraṇaṃ vuttā. Karuṇānidānā hi sabbepi buddhaguṇā. Karuṇānubhāvanibbāpiyamānasaṃsāradukkhasantāpassa hi bhagavato paradukkhāpanayanakāmatāya anekānipi asaṅkheyyāni kappānaṃ akilantarūpasseva niravasesabuddhakaradhammasambharaṇaniyatassa samadhigatadhammādhipateyyassa ca sannihitesupi sattasaṅkhārasamupanītahadayūpatāpanimittesu na īsakampi [P 1.0004] cittasītībhāvassaññathattamahosīti. Etasmiñca atthavikappe tīsupi avatthāsu bhagavato karuṇā saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Alternatively, he said, “a heart cooled by compassion,” because the Blessed One’s compassion—which is the foundation for the distinction of his unique knowledge, has attained the state of great compassion by pervading its objects like the superior and complete knowledge of omniscience—is the cause for the exceeding coolness of his heart. Or, although loving-kindness and sympathetic joy are a superior basis for the cooling of the heart, compassion alone is stated to be the cause of the cooling of the Blessed One’s heart, because it is the cause of all the special qualities of a Buddha and is thus the cause of those states as well. For all the qualities of a Buddha have compassion as their source. Indeed, for the Blessed One—whose torment of saṃsāric suffering was extinguished by the power of compassion, who desired to remove the suffering of others, who for many incalculable eons tirelessly accumulated the factors that make a Buddha, and who attained mastery over the Dhamma—there was not even the slightest alteration in the coolness of his mind, even when confronted with signs, produced by the formations of beings, that brought torment to the heart. And in this alternative interpretation, it should be understood that the Blessed One’s compassion is included in all three states.

Pajānātīti paññā, yathāsabhāvaṃ pakārehi paṭivijjhatīti attho. Paññāva ñeyyāvaraṇappahānato pakārehi dhammasabhāvāvajotanaṭṭhena pajjototi paññāpajjoto, savāsanappahānato visesena hataṃ samugghāṭitaṃ vihataṃ, paññāpajjotena vihataṃ paññāpajjotavihataṃ. Muyhanti tena, sayaṃ vā muyhati, mohanamattameva vā tanti moho, avijjā, sveva visayasabhāvapaṭicchādanato andhakārasarikkhatāya tamo viyāti tamo, paññāpajjotavihato mohatamo etassāti paññāpajjotavihatamohatamo, taṃ paññāpajjotavihatamohatamaṃ[V 1.0004]. Sabbesampi hi khīṇāsavānaṃ satipi paññāpajjotena avijjāndhakārassa vihatabhāve saddhādhimuttehi viya diṭṭhippattānaṃ sāvakehi, paccekasambuddhehi ca savāsanappahānena sammāsambuddhānaṃ kilesappahānassa viseso vijjatīti sātisayena avijjāppahānena bhagavantaṃ thomento āha “paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti.

‘One understands,’ thus it is `paññā` (wisdom); the meaning is that it penetrates the true nature of things in various ways. Wisdom itself is a lamp (`pajjoto`), thus `paññāpajjoto` (the lamp of wisdom), because by abandoning the veil over the knowable, it illuminates the nature of phenomena in various ways. ‘Destroyed by the lamp of wisdom’ (`paññāpajjotavihataṃ`) means especially struck, uprooted, destroyed. ‘One is deluded by it,’ or ‘one is deluded,’ or it is merely a state of delusion, thus it is `moho` (delusion), which is ignorance (`avijjā`). Because it conceals the true nature of its object, it is like darkness (`tamo`), thus it is called `tamo`. ‘One for whom the darkness of delusion is destroyed by the lamp of wisdom’ is `paññāpajjotavihatamohatamo`. Although for all whose taints are destroyed—such as disciples liberated by faith or attained to the view, and Paccekabuddhas—the darkness of ignorance is destroyed by the lamp of wisdom, still, for the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas there is a distinction in the abandoning of defilements, which is the abandoning of them together with their latent tendencies. Thus, praising the Blessed One for this superior abandoning of ignorance, he said, “one for whom the darkness of delusion is destroyed by the lamp of wisdom.”

Atha [M 1.0004] vā antarena paropadesaṃ attano santāne accantaṃ avijjāndhakāravigamassa nibbattitattā, tattha ca sabbaññutāya, balesu ca vasībhāvassa samadhigatattā, parasantatiyañca dhammadesanātisayānubhāvena sammadeva tassa pavattitattā bhagavāva visesato mohatamavigamena thometabboti āha “paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti. Imasmiñca atthavikappe “paññāpajjoto”ti padena bhagavato paṭivedhapaññā viya desanāpaññāpi sāmaññaniddesena ekasesanayena vā saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Alternatively, because the utter removal of the darkness of ignorance arose in his own being, apart from the instruction of others, and because he attained omniscience and mastery over the powers, and because through the surpassing power of his teaching, it was rightly established in the successions of others, the Blessed One is especially to be praised for dispelling the darkness of delusion—hence it is said: “the darkness of delusion destroyed by the lamp of wisdom.” In this interpretation, the term “lamp of wisdom” should be understood to include the Blessed One's wisdom of penetration as well as the wisdom of teaching, either through a general description or by way of the ekasesa method.

Atha [P 1.0005] vā bhagavato ñāṇassa ñeyyapariyantikattā sakalañeyyadhammasabhāvābodhanasamatthena anāvaraṇañāṇasaṅkhātena paññāpajjotena sabbañeyyadhammasabhāvacchādakassa mohandhakārassa vidhamitattā anaññasādhāraṇo bhagavato mohatamavināsoti katvā vuttaṃ “paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti. Ettha ca mohatamavidhamanante adhigatattā anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ kāraṇūpacārena sakasantāne mohatamavidhamanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Abhinīhārasampattiyā savāsanappahānameva hi kilesānaṃ “ñeyyāvaraṇappahāna”nti, parasantāne pana mohatamavidhamanassa kāraṇabhāvato anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ “mohatamavidhamana”nti vuccatīti.

Alternatively, because the darkness of delusion that obscures the inherent nature of all knowable things is dispelled by the lamp of wisdom—which is designated as unobstructed knowledge, capable of awakening to the inherent nature of all knowable phenomena since the Blessed One's knowledge encompasses all that is knowable—the Blessed One's destruction of the darkness of delusion is unique. Thus, it is said: 'the darkness of delusion destroyed by the lamp of wisdom.' Here, since unobstructed knowledge is attained upon the destruction of the darkness of delusion, it should be seen, by way of causal transference, as the dispelling of the darkness of delusion in one's own continuum. Indeed, by the attainment of the aspiration, the very abandonment of defilements together with their latent tendencies is 'the abandonment of the obstruction to the knowable.' In the continuum of others, however, since unobstructed knowledge is the cause for dispelling the darkness of delusion, it is called 'the dispelling of the darkness of delusion.'

Kiṃ pana kāraṇaṃ avijjāvigghāto yeveko pahānasampattivasena bhagavato thomanānimittaṃ gayhati, na pana sātisayaniravasesakilesappahānanti? Tappahānavacaneneva tadekaṭṭhatāya sakalasaṃkilesagaṇasamugghātajotitabhāvato. Na hi so tādiso kileso atthi, yo niravasesaavijjāppahānena na pahīyatīti. Atha vā vijjā viya sakalakusaladhammasamuppattiyā niravasesākusaladhammanibbattiyā, saṃsārappavattiyā ca avijjā padhānakāraṇanti tabbigghātavacanena sakalasaṃkilesagaṇasamugghāto vuttoyeva hotīti vuttaṃ “paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti.

What then is the reason that the destruction of ignorance alone is taken as the basis for praising the Blessed One, by virtue of the attainment of abandoning, and not the surpassing and complete abandoning of all defilements? Because by the very statement of its abandonment, since it has the same meaning, the uprooting of the entire mass of defilements is illuminated. For there is no such defilement that is not abandoned by the complete abandonment of ignorance. Alternatively, just as knowledge is for the arising of all wholesome states, ignorance is the primary cause for the production of all unwholesome states and for the continuation of saṃsāra. Therefore, by the statement of its destruction, the uprooting of the entire mass of defilements is indeed stated. Thus it is said: 'the darkness of delusion destroyed by the lamp of wisdom.'

Narā ca amarā ca narāmarā, saha narāmarehīti sanarāmaro, sanarāmaro ca so loko cāti sanarāmaraloko, tassa garuti sanarāmaralokagaru, taṃ sanarāmaralokagaruṃ. Etena devamanussānaṃ [V 1.0005] viya tadavasiṭṭhasattānampi yathārahaṃ guṇavisesāvahato bhagavato upakāritaṃ [M 1.0005] dasseti. Na cettha padhānāpadhānabhāvo codetabbo. Añño hi saddakkamo, añño atthakkamo. Edisesu hi samāsapadesu [P 1.0006] padhānampi appadhānaṃ viya niddisīyati yathā – “sarājikāya parisāyā”ti (apa. aṭṭha. 1.82). Kāmañcettha sattasaṅkhārabhājanavasena tividho loko, garubhāvassa pana adhippetattā garukaraṇasamatthasseva yujjanato sattalokassavasena attho gahetabbo. So hi lokiyanti ettha puññapāpāni tabbipāko cāti “loko”ti vuccati. Amaraggahaṇena cettha upapattidevā adhippetā.

"Narā ca amarā ca narāmarā" means "humans and immortals." "Saha narāmarehīti sanarāmaro" means "together with humans and immortals." "Sanarāmaro ca so loko cāti sanarāmaraloko" means "that world with humans and immortals." "Tassa garu" means "revered by that world," thus "sanarāmaralokagaru." By this, the helpfulness of the Blessed One is shown, which brings about special qualities for devas and humans, as well as for the remaining beings according to their worthiness. Here, the matter of primary and secondary should not be questioned, for the order of words is one thing, and the order of meaning is another. In such compound terms, even what is primary may be indicated as if it were secondary, as in the phrase "with an assembly including its king." Moreover, although the world is threefold—the world of beings, the world of formations, and the receptacle world—since reverence is intended here, the meaning should be taken in terms of the world of beings, as only they are capable of showing reverence. For it is called 'loka' because wholesome and unwholesome deeds and their results are experienced therein. By the term "immortals" here, deities by birth are intended.

Atha vā samūhattho loka-saddo samudāyavasena lokīyati paññāpīyatīti. Saha narehīti sanarā, sanarā ca te amarā ceti sanarāmarā, tesaṃ lokoti sanarāmaralokoti purimanayeneva yojetabbaṃ. Amara-saddena cettha visuddhidevāpi saṅgayhanti. Te hi maraṇābhāvato paramatthato amarā. Narāmarānaṃyeva ca gahaṇaṃ ukkaṭṭhaniddesavasena, yathā – “satthā devamanussāna”nti (dī. ni. 1.157). Tathā hi sabbānatthapariharaṇapubbaṅgamāya niravasesahitasukhavidhānatapparāya niratisayāya payogasampattiyā sadevamanussāya pajāya accantupakāritāya, aparimitanirupamappabhāvaguṇavisesasamaṅgitāya ca sabbasattuttamo bhagavā aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ uttamaṃ gāravaṭṭhānaṃ, tena vuttaṃ – “sanarāmaralokagaru”nti.

Alternatively, the word 'loka' has the meaning of a collection, because it is seen or designated as an aggregate. 'Saha narehīti sanarā,' 'sanarā ca te amarā ceti sanarāmarā,' 'tesaṃ lokoti sanarāmaraloko'—this should be construed in the same way as before. By the word 'immortals' here, pure deities are also included, for they are, in the ultimate sense, immortal due to the absence of death. The inclusion of only humans and immortals is by way of a pre-eminent designation, as in the phrase, "the Teacher of devas and humans." Indeed, the Blessed One, the foremost of all beings, is the supreme object of reverence for innumerable beings in innumerable world-systems, owing to his unsurpassed attainment of practice, which is preceded by the removal of all harm and is dedicated to establishing complete welfare and happiness; owing to his extreme helpfulness to the populace of devas and humans; and owing to his being endowed with special qualities of limitless and incomparable power. Thus, it is said: "revered by the world of humans and immortals."

Sobhanaṃ gataṃ gamanaṃ etassāti sugato. Bhagavato hi veneyyajanupasaṅkamanaṃ ekantena tesaṃ hitasukhanipphādanato sobhanaṃ, tathā lakkhaṇānubyañjana (dī. ni. 2.33; 3.198-200; ma. ni. 2.385, 386) paṭimaṇḍitarūpakāyatāyadutavilambita- khalitānukaḍḍhananippīḷanukkuṭikakuṭilākulatādidosarahitaṃ vilāsitarājahaṃsavasabhavāraṇamigarājagamanaṃ kāyagamanaṃ [P 1.0007] ñāṇagamanañca vipulanimmalakaruṇāsativīriyādiguṇavisesasahitamabhinīhārato yāva mahābodhi anavajjatāya sobhanamevāti.

His going is beautiful, thus he is the Well-Gone (Sugata). For the Blessed One’s approach to those worthy of training is entirely beautiful because it unfailingly brings about their welfare and happiness. Likewise, his bodily movement—his physical form adorned with the major and minor characteristics—is free from faults such as being too fast or too slow, stumbling, dragging the feet, pressing down, squatting, being crooked, or being hurried. His gait—a bodily movement as well as a movement of wisdom—is graceful like that of a royal swan, a noble bull, a noble elephant, or a lion king, and it is accompanied by special qualities such as vast, immaculate compassion, mindfulness, and energy. From his aspiration up to the great enlightenment, his conduct was always beautiful on account of being blameless.

Atha vā sayambhuñāṇena sakalampi lokaṃ pariññābhisamayavasena parijānanto ñāṇena sammā gato avagatoti sugato. Tathā lokasamudayaṃ [M 1.0006] pahānābhisamayavasena pajahanto anuppattidhammataṃ āpādento sammā gato atītoti sugato. Lokanirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikiriyābhisamayavasena sammā gato adhigatoti sugato. Lokanirodhagāminipaṭipadaṃ bhāvanābhisamayavasena sammā gato paṭipannoti sugato. Sotāpattimaggena ye kilesā pahīnā, te kilese na puneti, na pacceti, na paccāgacchatīti sugatotiādinā nayena ayamattho vibhāvetabbo[V 1.0006]. Atha vā sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ sammāsambodhiṃ nibbānameva vā gato adhigatoti sugato. Yasmā vā bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ atthasañhitaṃ vineyyānaṃ yathārahaṃ kālayuttameva ca dhammaṃ bhāsati, tasmā sammā gadatīti sugato, da-kārassa ta-kāraṃ katvā. Iti sobhanagamanatādīhi sugato, taṃ sugataṃ.

Alternatively, having fully understood the entire world through the knowledge of self-enlightenment by means of the penetration of full understanding, he has rightly gone, fully known—thus, the Well-Gone One. Likewise, having abandoned the origin of the world by means of the penetration of relinquishment, bringing it to a state of non-arising, he has rightly gone, transcended—thus, the Well-Gone One. Having realized the cessation of the world, Nibbāna, by means of the penetration of direct experience, he has rightly gone, attained—thus, the Well-Gone One. Having practiced the path leading to the cessation of the world by means of the penetration of cultivation, he has rightly gone, practiced—thus, the Well-Gone One. The defilements that are abandoned by the path of stream-entry, to those defilements he does not return, they do not recur, they do not come back—thus, the Well-Gone One. By this and other methods, this meaning should be elucidated. Alternatively, having gone to the beautiful state—supreme enlightenment or Nibbāna itself—he has attained it, thus, the Well-Gone One. Or because he speaks the Dhamma that is true, factual, beneficial, appropriate to the time, and suitable for those to be trained, therefore he speaks rightly—thus, the Well-Gone One, with the 'd' sound changed to a 't.' Thus, by his beautiful going and so on, he is the Well-Gone One—to that Sugata.

Puññapāpakammehi upapajjanavasena gantabbato gatiyo, upapattibhavavisesā. Tā pana nirayādivasena pañcavidhā, tāhi sakalassāpi bhavagāmikammassa ariyamaggādhigamena avipākārahabhāvakaraṇena nivattitattā bhagavā pañcahipi gatīhi suṭṭhu mutto visaṃyuttoti āha – “gativimutta”nti. Etena bhagavato katthacipi gatiyā apariyāpannataṃ dasseti, yato bhagavā “devātidevo”ti vuccati, tenevāha –

Destinies are destinations to be gone to based on meritorious and demeritorious deeds; they are particular states of existence at rebirth. These are fivefold, such as the hell realm and so on. Through the attainment of the noble path, all kamma leading to existence is turned back, rendered incapable of producing a result. Therefore, the Blessed One is perfectly freed and disjoined from all five destinies—hence he is called 'freed from destinies.' This shows that the Blessed One is not included in any destiny whatsoever, which is why the Blessed One is called 'the deva surpassing devas.' Thus it is said—

“Yena devūpapatyassa, gandhabbo vā vihaṅgamo;

Yakkhattaṃ yena gaccheyyaṃ, manussattañca abbaje;

Te mayhaṃ āsavā khīṇā, viddhastā vinaḷīkatā”ti. (a. ni. 4.36);

"By which there would be rebirth as a deva, or as a gandhabba or a bird; by which I might go to the state of a yakkha, or attain the human state—those taints of mine are destroyed, shattered, and uprooted."

Taṃtaṃgatisaṃvattanakānañhi [P 1.0008] kammakilesānaṃ aggamaggena bodhimūleyeva suppahīnattā natthi bhagavato gatipariyāpannatāti accantameva bhagavā sabbabhavayonigativiññāṇaṭṭhitisattāvāsasattanikāyehi suparimutto, taṃ gativimuttaṃ. Vandeti namāmi, thomemīti vā attho.

Because the actions and defilements that conduce to various destinations have been thoroughly abandoned by the supreme path at the very root of enlightenment, there is for the Blessed One no inclusion in any destination. Thus, the Blessed One is completely liberated from all existences, wombs, destinations, stations of consciousness, abodes of beings, and communities of beings. Him, liberated from destinations, I venerate. 'I venerate' means 'I pay homage' or 'I praise'—such is the meaning.

Atha vā gativimuttanti anupādisesanibbānadhātuppattiyā bhagavantaṃ thometi. Ettha hi dvīhākārehi bhagavato thomanā veditabbā – attahitasampattito, parahitapaṭipattito ca. Tesu attahitasampatti anāvaraṇañāṇādhigamato, savāsanānaṃ sabbesaṃ kilesānaṃ accantappahānato, anupādisesanibbānappattito ca veditabbā. Parahitapaṭipatti lābhasakkārādinirapekkhacittassa [M 1.0007] sabbadukkhaniyyānikadhammadesanāto, viruddhesupi niccaṃ hitajjhāsayato, ñāṇaparipākakālāgamanato ca. Sā panettha āsayato payogato ca duvidhā parahitapaṭipatti, tividhā ca attahitasampatti pakāsitā hoti. Kathaṃ? “Karuṇāsītalahadaya”nti etena āsayato parahitapaṭipatti, sammā gadanatthena sugata-saddena payogato parahitapaṭipatti, “paññāpajjotavihatamohatamaṃ gativimutta”nti etehi catusaccapaṭivedhatthena ca sugata-saddena tividhāpi [V 1.0007] attahitasampatti, avasiṭṭhena, “paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti etena ca sabbāpi attahitasampattiparahitapaṭipatti pakāsitā hotīti.

Alternatively, by 'liberated from destinations,' he praises the Blessed One for attaining the element of Nibbāna without residue remaining. Here, the praise of the Blessed One should be understood in two ways: through the accomplishment of his own welfare and through the practice for the welfare of others. Among these, the accomplishment of his own welfare is understood from the attainment of unobstructed knowledge, the complete abandonment of all defilements along with their underlying tendencies, and the realization of Nibbāna without residue remaining. The practice for the welfare of others is understood from teaching the Dhamma that leads to the cessation of all suffering with a mind free from concern for gain and honor, always intending the welfare of even those who oppose him, and teaching when the time for the maturing of knowledge arrives. Here, the practice for the welfare of others is shown in two ways—by intention and by effort—while the accomplishment of his own welfare is shown in three ways. How? 'With a heart cooled by compassion'—this shows the practice for the welfare of others by intention. The term 'Sugata,' meaning 'one who speaks rightly,' shows the practice for the welfare of others by effort. 'Liberated from destinations, having dispelled the darkness of delusion with the lamp of wisdom'—these words, along with the term 'Sugata' in the sense of penetrating the four truths, show all three aspects of the accomplishment of his own welfare. Moreover, 'having dispelled the darkness of delusion with the lamp of wisdom' shows all aspects of both the accomplishment of his own welfare and the practice for the welfare of others.

Atha vā tīhākārehi bhagavato thomanā veditabbā – hetuto, phalato, upakārato ca. Tattha hetu mahākaruṇā, sā paṭhamapadena nidassitā. Phalaṃ catubbidhaṃ – ñāṇasampadā, pahānasampadā, ānubhāvasampadā, rūpakāyasampadā cāti. Tāsu ñāṇappahānasampadā dutiyapadena saccappaṭivedhatthena ca sugata-saddena pakāsitā honti. Ānubhāvasampadā tatiyapadena, rūpakāyasampadā [P 1.0009] yathāvuttakāyagamanasobhanatthena sugata-saddena, lakkhaṇānubyañjanapāripūriyā (dī. ni. 2.33; 3.198-200; ma. ni. 2.385-386) vinā tadabhāvato. Upakāro antaraṃ abāhiraṃ karitvā tividhayānamukhena vimuttidhammadesanā, so sammā gadanatthena sugata-saddena pakāsito hotīti veditabbaṃ.

Alternatively, the praise of the Blessed One should be understood in three ways: by way of cause, fruit, and benefit. Here, the cause is great compassion, which is shown by the first expression. The fruit is fourfold: the accomplishment of knowledge, the accomplishment of abandonment, the accomplishment of power, and the accomplishment of the physical body. Among these, the accomplishments of knowledge and abandonment are revealed by the second expression and by the word 'Sugata' in its sense of penetrating the truths. The accomplishment of power is indicated by the third expression, while the accomplishment of the physical body is shown by the word 'Sugata' in its sense of the beauty of the body's movement as previously stated, since this would be absent without the complete fulfillment of the major and minor characteristics (dī. ni. 2.33; 3.198-200; ma. ni. 2.385-386). The benefit is the teaching of the Dhamma of liberation through the threefold vehicle, making no distinction between internal and external. This is revealed by the word 'Sugata' in its sense of speaking well; so it should be understood.

Tattha “karuṇāsītalahadaya”nti etena sammāsambodhiyā mūlaṃ dasseti. Mahākaruṇāsañcoditamānaso hi bhagavā saṃsārapaṅkato sattānaṃ samuddharaṇatthaṃ katābhinīhāro anupubbena pāramiyo pūretvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ adhigatoti karuṇā sammāsambodhiyā mūlaṃ. “Paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti etena sammāsambodhiṃ dasseti. Anāvaraṇañāṇapadaṭṭhānañhi maggañāṇaṃ, maggañāṇapadaṭṭhānañca anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ “sammāsambodhī”ti vuccatīti. Sammā gadanatthena sugata-saddena sammāsambodhiyā paṭipattiṃ dasseti, līnuddhaccapatiṭṭhānāyūhanakāmasukhallikattakilamathānuyoga- sassatucchedābhinivesādiantadvayarahitāya karuṇāpaññāpariggahitāya [M 1.0008] majjhimāya paṭipattiyā pakāsanato sugata-saddassa. Itarehi sammāsambodhiyā padhānāppadhānabhedaṃ payojanaṃ dasseti. Saṃsāramahoghato sattasantāraṇañcettha padhānaṃ payojanaṃ, tadaññamappadhānaṃ. Tesu padhānena parahitappaṭipattiṃ dasseti, itarena attahitasampattiṃ, tadubhayena attahitāya paṭipannādīsu (pu. pa. 24, 173) catūsu puggalesu bhagavato catutthapuggalabhāvaṃ dasseti. Tena ca anuttaradakkhiṇeyyabhāvaṃ uttamavandanīyabhāvaṃ, attano ca vandanakiriyāya khettaṅgatabhāvaṃ dasseti.

Here, 'with a heart cooled by compassion' indicates the root of Supreme Perfect Enlightenment. For the Blessed One, motivated by great compassion, resolved to rescue beings from the mire of saṃsāra, gradually fulfilled the perfections, and attained unsurpassed Supreme Perfect Enlightenment—thus compassion is the root of Supreme Perfect Enlightenment. 'Having dispelled the darkness of delusion with the lamp of wisdom' indicates Supreme Perfect Enlightenment. For unobstructed knowledge is the basis of path-knowledge, and path-knowledge is the basis of unobstructed knowledge—this is called 'Supreme Perfect Enlightenment.' By the term 'Sugata,' in the sense of 'speaking rightly,' the practice leading to Supreme Perfect Enlightenment is indicated, through its revelation of the Middle Way, embraced by compassion and wisdom, free from the two extremes of indulgence in sensual pleasures and devotion to self-mortification, as well as from views adhering to eternalism and annihilationism. Through the other terms, the distinction between the principal and secondary benefits of Supreme Perfect Enlightenment is shown. Here, the principal benefit is the rescue of beings from the great flood of saṃsāra, while the other benefits are secondary. By the principal benefit, the practice for the welfare of others is indicated; by the secondary, the accomplishment of his own welfare. Through both, the Blessed One's status as the fourth type of person (pu. pa. 24, 173)—one who practices for his own welfare and for the welfare of others—is shown. Thereby, his unsurpassed worthiness of offerings, his supreme venerableness, and his being a field of merit for acts of veneration are also indicated.

Ettha ca karuṇāggahaṇena lokiyesu mahaggatabhāvappattāsādhāraṇaguṇadīpanato bhagavato sabbalokiyaguṇasampatti [P 1.0010] dassitā hoti, paññāggahaṇena sabbaññutaññāṇapadaṭṭhānamaggañāṇadīpanato sabbalokuttaraguṇasampatti. Tadubhayaggahaṇasiddho hi attho “sanarāmaralokagaru”ntiādinā vipañcīyatīti. Karuṇāggahaṇena ca upagamanaṃ nirupakkilesaṃ [V 1.0008] dasseti, paññāggahaṇena apagamanaṃ. Tathā karuṇāggahaṇena lokasamaññānurūpaṃ bhagavato pavattiṃ dasseti, lokavohāravisayattā karuṇāya, paññāggahaṇena samaññāyānavidhāvanaṃ. Sabhāvānavabodhena hi dhammānaṃ samaññaṃ atidhāvitvā sattādiparāmasanaṃ hotīti. Tathā karuṇāggahaṇena mahākaruṇāsamāpattivihāraṃ dasseti, paññāggahaṇena tīsu kālesu appaṭihatañāṇaṃ, catusaccañāṇaṃ, catuppaṭisambhidāñāṇaṃ, catuvessārajjañāṇaṃ. Karuṇāggahaṇena mahākaruṇāsamāpattiñāṇassa gahitattā sesāsādhāraṇañāṇāni, cha abhiññā, aṭṭhasu parisāsu (ma. ni. 1.151) akampanañāṇāni, dasa balāni, cuddasa buddhañāṇāni, soḷasa ñāṇacariyā, aṭṭhārasa buddhadhammā, (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.305; vibha. mūla. ṭī. ganthārambhavaṇṇanāya) catucattārīsa ñāṇavatthūni, (saṃ. ni. 2.34) sattasattati ñāṇavatthūnīti (saṃ. ni. 2.34) evamādīnaṃ anekesaṃ paññāppabhedānaṃ vasena ñāṇacāraṃ dasseti.

Here, by the inclusion of compassion, the accomplishment of all the Blessed One's mundane qualities is shown, through the manifestation of the uncommon qualities attained in sublime worldly states. By the inclusion of wisdom, the accomplishment of all supramundane qualities is shown, through the manifestation of the path-knowledge that is the basis for the knowledge of omniscience. Indeed, the meaning established by the inclusion of both is elaborated by phrases such as 'teacher of the world with its humans and gods,' and so forth. By the inclusion of compassion, his approach is shown to be free from defilements; by the inclusion of wisdom, his withdrawal. Likewise, by the inclusion of compassion, the Blessed One’s conduct in accordance with worldly convention is shown, since compassion pertains to the sphere of worldly interaction. By the inclusion of wisdom, the non-adherence to convention is shown, for by not comprehending the intrinsic nature of phenomena, one overruns conventions and becomes attached to concepts such as 'a being.' Moreover, by the inclusion of compassion, the abiding in the meditative attainment of great compassion is shown. By the inclusion of wisdom, the unobstructed knowledge regarding the three times, the knowledge of the four truths, the knowledge of the four analytical knowledges, and the knowledge of the four kinds of fearlessness are shown. And since the knowledge of the attainment of great compassion is included by the inclusion of compassion, the range of knowledge is demonstrated through the various divisions of wisdom, such as the remaining unshared knowledges, the six direct knowledges, the unshaken knowledges in the eight assemblies (ma. ni. 1.151), the ten powers, the fourteen kinds of Buddha-knowledge, the sixteen modes of knowledge-conduct, the eighteen unique Buddha-qualities (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.305; vibha. mūla. ṭī. ganthārambhavaṇṇanāya), the forty-four bases of knowledge (saṃ. ni. 2.34), and the seventy-seven bases of knowledge (saṃ. ni. 2.34).

Tathā karuṇāggahaṇena caraṇasampattiṃ, paññāggahaṇena vijjāsampattiṃ. Karuṇāggahaṇena sattādhipatitā, paññāggahaṇena dhammādhipatitā. Karuṇāggahaṇena lokanāthabhāvo, paññāggahaṇena attanāthabhāvo. Tathā karuṇāggahaṇena pubbakāribhāvo, paññāggahaṇena kataññutā[M 1.0009]. Tathā karuṇāggahaṇena aparantapatā, paññāggahaṇena anattantapatā. Karuṇāggahaṇena vā buddhakaradhammasiddhi, paññāggahaṇena buddhabhāvasiddhi. Tathā karuṇāggahaṇena paresaṃ tāraṇaṃ, paññāggahaṇena sayaṃ tāraṇaṃ. Tathā karuṇāggahaṇena sabbasattesu anuggahacittatā, paññāggahaṇena sabbadhammesu virattacittatā dassitā hoti. Sabbesañca [P 1.0011] buddhaguṇānaṃ karuṇā ādi, tannidānabhāvato. Paññā pariyosānaṃ, tato uttarikaraṇīyābhāvato. Iti ādipariyosānadassanena sabbe buddhaguṇā dassitā honti. Tathā karuṇāggahaṇena sīlakkhandhapubbaṅgamo samādhikkhandho dassito hoti. Karuṇānidānañhi sīlaṃ, tato pāṇātipātādiviratippavattito, sā ca jhānattayasampayoginīti. Paññāvacanena paññākkhandho. Sīlañca sabbabuddhaguṇānamādi, samādhi majjhe, paññā pariyosānanti. Evampi ādimajjhapariyosānakalyāṇā sabbe buddhaguṇā dassitā honti, nayato dassitattā. Eso eva hi niravasesato buddhaguṇānaṃ dassanupāyo, yadidaṃ nayaggāhaṇaṃ. Aññathā ko nāma samattho bhagavato guṇe anupadaṃ niravasesato dassetuṃ. Tenevāha –

Thus, by grasping compassion, the perfection of conduct; by grasping wisdom, the perfection of knowledge. By grasping compassion, mastery over beings; by grasping wisdom, mastery over phenomena. By grasping compassion, the state of being a protector of the world; by grasping wisdom, the state of being a protector of oneself. Thus, by grasping compassion, the state of being a benefactor; by grasping wisdom, gratitude. Thus, by grasping compassion, not tormenting others; by grasping wisdom, not tormenting oneself. Or, by grasping compassion, the achievement of the qualities that make a Buddha; by grasping wisdom, the achievement of the state of a Buddha. Thus, by grasping compassion, the deliverance of others; by grasping wisdom, one's own deliverance. Thus, by grasping compassion, a mind of helpfulness towards all beings is shown; by grasping wisdom, a mind of dispassion towards all phenomena. And of all the qualities of a Buddha, compassion is the beginning, because it is their source. Wisdom is the culmination, because there is nothing further to be done beyond it. Thus, by showing the beginning and the culmination, all the qualities of a Buddha are shown. Thus, by grasping compassion, the aggregate of concentration, preceded by the aggregate of virtue, is shown. For virtue has compassion as its source, since it proceeds from the abstinence from killing living beings and so forth, and it is associated with the three jhānas. By the word 'wisdom', the aggregate of wisdom is shown. And virtue is the beginning of all a Buddha's qualities, concentration is the middle, and wisdom is the culmination. In this way too, all the qualities of a Buddha are shown to be excellent in the beginning, in the middle, and in the end, because they are shown by way of method. This indeed is the means for showing the qualities of a Buddha without remainder, that is, the grasping of the method. Otherwise, who indeed would be able to show the qualities of the Blessed One word by word and without remainder? Therefore, it was said:

“Buddhopi buddhassa bhaṇeyya vaṇṇaṃ,

Kappampi ce aññamabhāsamāno;

Khīyetha [V 1.0009] kappo ciradīghamantare,

Vaṇṇo na khīyetha tathāgatassā”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.304; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.141; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 3.425, udā. aṭṭha. 53; bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 4.4; cariyā. aṭṭha. nidānakathāyaṃ, pakiṇṇakakathāyaṃ; apa. aṭṭha. 2.6.20);

"Even a Buddha might speak the praise of a Buddha for an entire aeon, speaking of nothing else; the aeon would be exhausted in that long interval, but the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted." (D.A.I 304; D.A.III 141; M.A.III 425; Ud.A. 53; Bu.A. 4.4; Cariyā.A.Nidānakathāyaṃ, Pakiṇṇakakathāyaṃ; Ap.A.II 6.20);

Teneva ca āyasmatā sāriputtattherenāpi buddhaguṇaparicchedanaṃ pati anuyuttena “no hetaṃ bhante”ti (dī. ni. 2.145) paṭikkhipitvā, “api ca me bhante dhammanvayo vidito”ti (dī. ni. 2.146) vuttaṃ.

For this very reason, when the Venerable Elder Sāriputta was questioned about delimiting the qualities of the Buddha, he too, having rejected it by saying, 'It is not so, venerable sir,' (D.II 145) said, 'But, venerable sir, the sequence of the Dhamma is known to me.' (D.II 146)

Evaṃ saṅkhepena sakalasabbaññuguṇehi bhagavantaṃ abhitthavitvā idāni saddhammaṃ thometuṃ “buddhopī”tiādimāha. Tattha buddhoti kattuniddeso. Buddhabhāvanti kammaniddeso. Bhāvetvā, sacchikatvāti ca pubbakālakiriyāniddeso. Yanti aniyamato kammaniddeso. Upagatoti [P 1.0012] aparakālakiriyāniddeso. Vandeti kiriyāniddeso, tanti [M 1.0010] niyamanaṃ. Dhammanti vandanakiriyāya kammaniddeso. Gatamalaṃ, anuttaranti ca tabbisesanaṃ.

Having thus briefly extolled the Blessed One with all the qualities of the Omniscient One, he now begins to praise the true Dhamma, saying 'buddhopī' and so on. Therein, 'buddha' is a designation of the agent. 'Buddhabhāvaṃ' is a designation of the object. 'Bhāvetvā' and 'sacchikatvā' are designations of prior action. 'Yaṃ' is a designation of the object without specification. 'Upagato' is a designation of subsequent action. 'Vande' is a designation of the action, and 'taṃ' is a specification. 'Dhammaṃ' is a designation of the object of the act of homage. 'Gatamalaṃ' and 'anuttaraṃ' are its qualifiers.

Tattha buddha-saddassa tāva “bujjhitā saccānīti buddho, bodhetā pajāyāti buddho”tiādinā (mahāni. 192; cūḷani. 95-97; paṭi. ma. 1.162) niddesanayena attho veditabbo. Atha vā savāsanāya aññāṇaniddāya accantavigamato, buddhiyā vā vikasitabhāvato buddhavāti buddho, jāgaraṇavikasanatthavasena. Atha vā kassacipi ñeyyadhammassa anavabuddhassa abhāvena ñeyyavisesassa kammabhāvena aggahaṇato kammavacanicchāya abhāvena avagamanatthavaseneva kattuniddeso labbhatīti buddhavāti buddho, yathā “dikkhito na dadātī”ti, atthato pana pāramitāparibhāvito sayambhūñāṇena saha vāsanāya vihataviddhastaniravasesakileso mahākaruṇāsabbaññutaññāṇādiaparimeyya guṇagaṇādhāro khandhasantāno buddho. Yathāha –

Herein, first, the meaning of the word 'Buddha' should be understood by way of the explanation, as in: 'He has understood the truths, thus he is the Buddha; he awakens the populace, thus he is the Buddha,' and so forth (Mahāni. 192; Cūḷani. 95-97; Paṭi.Ma. I.162). Or, because of the complete removal of the sleep of ignorance together with its latent tendencies, or because of the blossomed state of wisdom, he is called 'Buddha'—in the sense of awakening and blossoming. Or, because there is no knowable phenomenon that has not been understood by him, and because there is no grasping of a specific knowable as an object, and because there is no desire for an expression of the object, the designation of the agent is obtained merely in the sense of understanding—thus, 'Buddha' means 'the awakened one,' just as in 'The initiated one does not give.' But in reality, the Buddha is the continuum of aggregates that has been perfected by the perfections, the one with self-originated knowledge whose defilements, along with their latent tendencies, have been struck down, destroyed, and are without remainder, the repository of an immeasurable host of qualities such as great compassion, the knowledge of omniscience, and so on. As it is said:

“Buddhoti yo so bhagavā sayambhū anācariyako pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu sāmaṃ saccāni abhisambujjhi, tattha ca sabbaññutaṃ patto, balesu ca vasībhāva”nti (mahāni. 192; cūḷani. 95-97; paṭi. ma. 1.162).

"The Buddha is that Blessed One who is self-originated, without a teacher, who by himself fully awakened to the truths regarding phenomena unheard of before, and therein attained omniscience and mastery over the powers." (Mahāni. 192; Cūḷani. 95-97; Paṭi.Ma. I.162).

Api-saddo sambhāvane, tena “evaṃ guṇavisesayutto sopi nāma bhagavā”ti vakkhamānaguṇe [V 1.0010] dhamme sambhāvanaṃ dīpeti. Buddhabhāvanti sammāsambodhiṃ. Bhāvetvāti uppādetvā, vaḍḍhetvā ca. Sacchikatvāti paccakkhaṃ katvā. Upagatoti patto, adhigatoti attho, etassa “buddhabhāva”nti etena sambandho. Gatamalanti vigatamalaṃ, niddosanti attho. Vandeti paṇamāmi, thomemi [P 1.0013] vā. Anuttaranti uttararahitaṃ, lokuttaranti attho. Dhammanti yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne apāyato ca, saṃsārato ca apatamāne katvā dhārayatīti dhammo.

The particle 'api' is in the sense of possibility. Thereby, it indicates the possibility regarding the Dhamma with the qualities about to be described, as in: 'Even that Blessed One, endowed with such distinguished qualities...' 'Buddhabhāvaṃ' means Supreme Perfect Enlightenment. 'Bhāvetvā' means having produced and cultivated. 'Sacchikatvā' means having directly realized. 'Upagato' means attained, achieved; this is connected with 'buddhabhāvaṃ.' 'Gatamalaṃ' means devoid of stain, faultless is the meaning. 'Vande' means I venerate or I praise. 'Anuttaraṃ' means without a superior, supramundane is the meaning. 'Dhamma' means that which sustains those who practice in accordance with what is taught, making them not fall into states of deprivation and into saṃsāra—thus it is 'Dhamma'.

Ayañhettha saṅkhepattho – evaṃ vividhaguṇasamannāgato buddhopi bhagavā yaṃ ariyasaṅkhātaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvetvā, phalanibbānasaṅkhātaṃ pana sacchikatvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ adhigato, tametaṃ buddhānampi buddhabhāvahetubhūtaṃ sabbadosamalarahitaṃ attano uttaritarābhāvena anuttaraṃ paṭivedhasaddhammaṃ namāmīti. Pariyattisaddhammassāpi tappakāsanattā idha saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Atha [M 1.0011] vā “abhidhammanayasamuddaṃ bhāvetvā adhigacchi, tīṇi piṭakāni sammasī”ti ca aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttattā pariyattidhammassāpi sacchikiriyāsammasanapariyāyo labbhatīti sopi idha vutto yevāti daṭṭhabbo. Tathā “yaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvetvā, sacchikatvā”ti ca vuttattā buddhakaradhammabhūtāhi pāramitāhi saha pubbabhāge adhisīlasikkhādayopi idha dhamma-saddena saṅgahitāti veditabbā. Tāpi hi vigatapaṭipakkhatāya vigatamalā, anaññasādhāraṇatāya anuttarā cāti. Tathā hi sattānaṃ sakalavaṭṭadukkhanissaraṇāya katamahābhinīhāro mahākaruṇādhivāsapesalajjhāsayo paññāvisesapariyodātanimmalānaṃ dānadamasaññamādīnaṃ uttamadhammānaṃ satasahassādhikāni kappānaṃ cattāri asaṅkheyyāni sakkaccaṃ nirantaraṃ niravasesaṃ bhāvanāpaccakkhakaraṇehi kammādīsu adhigatavasībhāvo, acchariyācinteyyamahānubhāvo, adhisīlaadhicittānaṃ paramukkaṃsapāramippatto bhagavā paccayākāre catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassamukhena mahāvajirañāṇaṃ pesetvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddhoti.

Herein, the concise meaning is this: Thus endowed with various qualities, even the Buddha, the Blessed One, having developed the Dhamma reckoned as noble and having realized that which is reckoned as fruit and Nibbāna, attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. To that very true Dhamma of penetration—which is the cause of Buddhahood even for Buddhas, which is devoid of all faults and stains, and which is unsurpassed due to having nothing superior to it—I pay homage. The inclusion of the true Dhamma of learning should also be understood here, as it serves to reveal that Dhamma of penetration. Alternatively, since it is stated in the commentary, 'Having developed the ocean of the Abhidhamma method, he attained it; he comprehended the three Piṭakas,' the aspect of realizing and comprehending the Dhamma of learning is also obtained. Therefore, it should be understood that this too is stated here. Likewise, since it is said, 'having developed and realized that Dhamma,' it should be known that the trainings in higher virtue and so on in the preliminary stage, along with the perfections that constitute the Dhamma that makes a Buddha, are also included here by the word 'Dhamma.' For these too are devoid of stain because their opposites are eliminated, and they are unsurpassed because they are not shared by others. For indeed, the Blessed One—having made the great aspiration for the release of beings from all the suffering of the cycle; with a disposition amiable and patient due to great compassion; having attained mastery over kamma and so on through developing and directly realizing without remainder, respectfully and continuously for four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand more, the supreme dhammas of giving, self-control, restraint, and so on, which are utterly pure and cleansed by the excellence of wisdom; possessing marvelous, inconceivable great power; having reached the highest summit of perfection in higher virtue and higher mind—sent forth the great diamond-like knowledge through twenty-four trillion approaches to the structure of conditionality and fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.

Ettha [P 1.0014] ca “bhāvetvā”ti etena vijjāsampadāya dhammaṃ thometi, ‘sacchikatvā’ti etena vimuttisampadāya. Tathā paṭhamena jhānasampadāya, dutiyena vimokkhasampadāya. Paṭhamena vā samādhisampadāya, dutiyena samāpattisampadāya. Atha vā paṭhamena khayañāṇabhāvena, dutiyena anuppādañāṇabhāvena. Purimena vā vijjūpamatāya, dutiyena vajirūpamatāya. Purimena vā virāgasampattiyā, dutiyena nirodhasampattiyā. Tathā paṭhamena niyyānabhāvena, dutiyena nissaraṇabhāvena. Paṭhamena vā hetubhāvena, dutiyena asaṅkhatabhāvena. Paṭhamena vā dassanabhāvena, dutiyena vivekabhāvena. Paṭhamena vā adhipatibhāvena, dutiyena amatabhāvena dhammaṃ thometi. Atha vā “yaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvetvā buddhabhāvaṃ upagato”ti etena svākkhātatāya dhammaṃ thometi, “sacchikatvā”ti [V 1.0011] etena sandiṭṭhikatāya. Tathā purimena akālikatāya, pacchimena ehipassikatāya. Purimena vā opaneyyikatāya, pacchimena paccattaṃ veditabbatāya dhammaṃ thometi.

Herein, by “having developed,” the Dhamma is praised in terms of the accomplishment of knowledge, and by “having realized,” it is praised in terms of the accomplishment of liberation. Similarly, by the first, it is praised in terms of the accomplishment of jhāna, and by the second, in terms of the accomplishment of release. Or, by the first, it is praised in terms of the accomplishment of concentration, and by the second, in terms of the accomplishment of attainment. Alternatively, by the first, it is praised in terms of the state of knowledge of destruction, and by the second, in terms of the state of knowledge of non-arising. Or, by the first, it is praised in terms of the simile of lightning, and by the second, in terms of the simile of a diamond. Or, by the first, it is praised in terms of the attainment of dispassion, and by the second, in terms of the attainment of cessation. Similarly, by the first, it is praised in terms of the nature of leading out, and by the second, in terms of the nature of deliverance. Or, by the first, it is praised in terms of the nature of a cause, and by the second, in terms of the nature of the unconditioned. Or, by the first, it is praised in terms of the nature of seeing, and by the second, in terms of the nature of seclusion. Or, by the first, it is praised in terms of the nature of a dominant condition, and by the second, in terms of the nature of the deathless. Or, by the phrase “the Dhamma which, having developed, he attained the state of a Buddha,” the Dhamma is praised in terms of being well-proclaimed, and by “having realized,” it is praised in terms of being visible here and now. Similarly, by the former, it is praised in terms of being immediate, and by the latter, in terms of being inviting to come and see. Or, by the former, it is praised in terms of being leading inwards, and by the latter, in terms of being knowable by the wise, each for themselves.

“Gatamala”nti iminā saṃkilesābhāvadīpanena dhammassa parisuddhataṃ dasseti, “anuttara”nti etena aññassa visiṭṭhassa abhāvadīpanena vipulaparipuṇṇataṃ. Paṭhamena vā pahānasampadaṃ dhammassa dasseti, dutiyena pabhāvasampadaṃ. Bhāvetabbatāya vā dhammassa gatamalabhāvo yojetabbo[M 1.0012]. Bhāvanāguṇena hi so dosānaṃ samugghātako hotīti. Sacchikātabbabhāvena anuttarabhāvo yojetabbo. Sacchikiriyānibbattito hi taduttarikaraṇīyābhāvato anaññasādhāraṇatāya anuttaroti. Tathā “bhāvetvā”ti etena saha pubbabhāgasīlādīhi sekkhā sīlasamādhipaññākkhandhā dassitā honti, “sacchikatvā”ti etena saha asaṅkhatāya dhātuyā asekkhā sīlasamādhipaññākkhandhā dassitā hontīti.

By “gone is the taint,” the purity of the Dhamma is shown by indicating the absence of defilement. By “unsurpassed,” its vastness and completeness are shown by indicating the absence of anything superior. By the first, the accomplishment of abandonment in the Dhamma is shown; by the second, the accomplishment of its power. Alternatively, the state of being free from taint should be connected to the Dhamma as something to be developed, for through the quality of development, it becomes the uprooter of faults. The unsurpassed nature should be connected to the state of being realized, because, arising from the act of realization, there is nothing further to be done beyond it, and thus it is unsurpassed due to its being unique and not shared by others. Furthermore, by “having developed”—together with the preliminary practice of virtue and so forth—the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom of the trainees are shown. By “having realized”—together with the unconditioned element—the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom of those beyond training are shown.

Evaṃ saṅkhepeneva sabbadhammaguṇehi saddhammaṃ abhitthavitvā, idāni ariyasaṅghaṃ thometuṃ “sugatassā”tiādimāha. Tattha sugatassāti sambandhaniddeso, tassa “puttāna”nti etena sambandho. Orasānanti puttavisesanaṃ. Mārasenamathanānanti [P 1.0015] orasaputtabhāve kāraṇaniddeso, tena kilesappahānameva bhagavato orasaputtabhāvakāraṇaṃ anujānātīti dasseti. Aṭṭhannanti gaṇanaparicchedaniddeso, tena ca satipi tesaṃ sattavisesabhāvena anekasatasahassasaṅkhyabhāve imaṃ gaṇanaparicchedaṃ nātivattantīti dasseti, maggaṭṭhaphalaṭṭhabhāvānativattanato. Samūhanti samudāyaniddeso. Ariyasaṅghanti guṇavisiṭṭhasaṅghātabhāvaniddeso, tena asatipi ariyapuggalānaṃ kāyasāmaggiyaṃ ariyasaṅghabhāvaṃ dasseti, diṭṭhisīlasāmaññena saṃhatabhāvato. Tattha urasi bhavā jātā, saṃvaddhā ca orasā. Yathā hi sattānaṃ orasaputtā attajātatāya pitusantakassa dāyajjassa visesena bhāgino honti, evametepi ariyapuggalā sammāsambuddhassa savanante ariyāya jātiyā jātatāya bhagavato santakassa vimuttisukhassa, ariyadhammaratanassa ca ekantabhāginoti orasā viya orasā. Atha vā bhagavato dhammadesanānubhāvena ariyabhūmiṃ okkamamānā, okkantā ca ariyasāvakā bhagavato urovāyāmajanitābhijātatāya nippariyāyena “orasaputtā”ti vattabbataṃ arahanti. Sāvakehi pavattiyamānāpi hi dhammadesanā bhagavato “dhammadesanā” icceva vuccati, taṃmūlakattā, lakkhaṇādivisesābhāvato ca.

Having thus briefly extolled the true Dhamma with all its virtues, now, in order to praise the Noble Sangha, the text begins with “of the Sugata.” Herein, “of the Sugata” is a relational designation, its relation being with “sons.” “True-born” is a specification of the sons. “Destroyers of Māra’s army” is a designation of the reason for being true-born sons, thereby indicating that the very destruction of defilements is acknowledged as the reason for being the Blessed One’s true-born sons. “Eight” is a designation defining the enumeration, and by this it is shown that even though their number is in the hundreds of thousands due to their individual distinctions, they do not exceed this defined enumeration, because they do not go beyond the state of those standing on the path and those standing in the fruit. “Assembly” is a designation of the collection. “Noble Sangha” is a designation of the group distinguished by their virtues, thereby indicating that the state of the Noble Sangha exists even without bodily unity among the noble individuals, since they are united by a commonality of view and virtue. Herein, those born in and grown from the breast are “true-born.” Just as the true-born sons of beings, being born from oneself, are especially entitled to a share of their father’s inheritance, so too these noble individuals, having been born into the noble birth at the conclusion of hearing the teaching of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, are exclusively entitled to the Blessed One’s inheritance of the bliss of liberation and the jewel of the noble Dhamma—thus, they are like true-born sons. Alternatively, the noble disciples who are entering or have entered the noble state by the power of the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, being of a noble lineage generated from the Blessed One’s breast through effort, rightly deserve to be called “true-born sons” without qualification. For even a teaching of the Dhamma delivered by disciples is called “the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma,” because it has him as its root and because there is no difference in its characteristics and so forth.

Yadipi ariyasāvakānaṃ ariyamaggādhigamasamaye bhagavato viya tadantarāyakaraṇatthaṃ devaputtamāro[V 1.0012], māravāhinī vā na ekantena apasādeti, tehi pana apasādetabbatāya kāraṇe vimathite tepi vimathitā [M 1.0013] eva nāma hontīti āha – “mārasenamathanāna”nti. Imasmiṃ panatthe ‘māramārasenamathanāna’nti vattabbe “mārasenamathanāna”nti ekadesasarūpekaseso katoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā khandhābhisaṅkhāramārānaṃ viya devaputtamārassāpi guṇamāraṇe [P 1.0016] sahāyabhāvūpagamanato kilesabalakāyo “senā”ti vuccati. Yathāha – “kāmā te paṭhamā senā”tiādi (su. ni. 438; mahāni. 28, 68; cūḷani. 47). Sā ca tehi diyaḍḍhasahassabhedā, anantabhedā vā kilesavāhinī satidhammavicayavīriyasamathādiguṇapaharaṇehi odhiso vimathitā, vihatā, viddhastā cāti mārasenamathanā, ariyasāvakā. Etena tesaṃ bhagavato anujātaputtataṃ dasseti.

Although at the time of attaining the noble path, noble disciples are not entirely assailed by Māra the deity-son or his army for the purpose of creating an obstacle, as the Blessed One was, yet because the causes for such an attack are destroyed by them, they too are indeed called ‘destroyers’—hence the phrase, “destroyers of Māra’s army.” In this context, though one might say “destroyers of Māra and Māra’s army,” it should be understood that the phrase “destroyers of Māra’s army” is used as a partial representation of the whole. Alternatively, just as there are the Māras of the aggregates and formations, so too for the deity-son Māra, because he becomes an ally in the destruction of virtue, the host of defilements is termed his “army.” As it is said: “Desire is your first army…” (Snp 438; Mahāni. 28, 68; Cūḷani. 47). And that army of defilements, with its fifteen hundred or countless divisions, is specifically struck down, defeated, and destroyed by the noble disciples with the weapons of virtues such as mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, and tranquility. Thus, they are the destroyers of Māra’s army. By this, it is shown that they are the Blessed One’s true spiritual offspring.

Ārakattā kilesehi, anaye na iriyanato, aye ca iriyanato ariyā, niruttinayena. Atha vā sadevakena lokena “saraṇa”nti araṇīyato upagantabbato, upagatānañca tadatthasiddhito ariyā, ariyānaṃ saṅghoti ariyasaṅgho, ariyo ca so, saṅgho cāti vā ariyasaṅgho, taṃ ariyasaṅghaṃ. Bhagavato aparabhāge buddhadhammaratanānampi samadhigamo saṅgharatanādhīnoti assa ariyasaṅghassa bahūpakārataṃ dassetuṃ idheva “sirasā vande”ti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

They are ‘noble’ (ariyā) in an etymological sense because of being far (ārakattā) from defilements, because of not moving (na iriyanato) in a wrong course (anaye), and because of moving (iriyanato) in a right course (aye). Or, they are noble because they are to be gone to (araṇīyato) as a refuge by the world with its gods, and because for those who have gone to them, the goal is achieved. The Sangha of the noble ones is the Noble Sangha; or, it is both noble and a Sangha, hence the Noble Sangha. To show the great helpfulness of this Noble Sangha—since in the period after the Blessed One, even the attainment of the Buddha and Dhamma jewels is dependent on the Sangha jewel—it is said here, “I bow my head in reverence.” This should be understood.

Ettha ca “sugatassa orasānaṃ puttāna”nti etena ariyasaṅghassa pabhavasampadaṃ dasseti, “mārasenamathanāna”nti etena pahānasampadaṃ, sakalasaṃkilesappahānadīpanato. “Aṭṭhannampi samūha”nti etena ñāṇasampadaṃ, maggaṭṭhaphalaṭṭhabhāvadīpanato. “Ariyasaṅgha”nti etena pabhavasampadaṃ dasseti, sabbasaṅghānaṃ aggabhāvadīpanato. Atha vā “sugatassa orasānaṃ puttāna”nti ariyasaṅghassa visuddhanissayabhāvadīpanaṃ, “mārasenamathanāna”nti sammāujuñāyasāmīcippaṭipannabhāvadīpanaṃ, “aṭṭhannampi samūha”nti āhuneyyādibhāvadīpanaṃ, “ariyasaṅgha”nti anuttarapuññakkhettabhāvadīpanaṃ. Tathā “sugatassa orasānaṃ puttāna”nti etena ariyasaṅghassa lokuttarasaraṇagamanasabbhāvaṃ dīpeti. Lokuttarasaraṇagamanena hi te bhagavato orasaputtā jātā. “Mārasenamathanāna”nti [P 1.0017] etena abhinīhārasampadāsiddhaṃ pubbabhāge sammāpaṭipattiṃ dasseti. Katābhinīhārā hi sammā paṭipannā māraṃ, māraparisaṃ vā abhivijinanti. “Aṭṭhannampi samūha”nti etena [M 1.0014] viddhastavipakkhe sekkhāsekkhadhamme dasseti, puggalādhiṭṭhānena maggaphaladhammānaṃ pakāsitattā. “Ariyasaṅgha”nti aggadakkhiṇeyyabhāvaṃ dasseti. Saraṇagamanañca sāvakānaṃ sabbaguṇānamādi, sapubbabhāgappaṭipadā sekkhā sīlakkhandhādayo majjhe, asekkhā sīlakkhandhādayo [V 1.0013] pariyosānanti ādimajjhapariyosānakalyāṇā saṅkhepato sabbe ariyasaṅghaguṇā pakāsitā honti.

Herein, by 'the true-born sons of the Sugata' is shown the excellence of the Noble Sangha's origin; by 'the destroyers of Māra’s army' is shown the excellence of abandonment, as it indicates the complete abandoning of all defilements. By 'the assembly of the eight' is shown the excellence of knowledge, as it indicates their state as those on the path and those who have attained the fruit. By 'the Noble Sangha' is shown their excellence of origin, as it indicates their supreme status among all Sanghas. Alternatively, 'the true-born sons of the Sugata' indicates the Noble Sangha's state of having a pure foundation; 'the destroyers of Māra’s army' indicates their state of having practiced rightly, uprightly, methodically, and properly; 'the assembly of the eight' indicates their state of being worthy of offerings, etc.; and 'the Noble Sangha' indicates their state as an unsurpassed field of merit. Furthermore, by 'the true-born sons of the Sugata' is indicated the Noble Sangha's true state of having gone for refuge in the supramundane. For it is by going for refuge in the supramundane that they are born as the Blessed One’s true-born sons. By 'the destroyers of Māra’s army' is shown the right practice in the preliminary stage, accomplished through the perfection of aspiration. For those who have made the aspiration and practice rightly conquer Māra or Māra's host. By 'the assembly of the eight' are shown the qualities of learners and non-learners, who have vanquished opposing factors, since the path and fruition states are declared with individuals as their basis. 'The Noble Sangha' shows their status as the foremost of those worthy of offerings. And going for refuge is the beginning of all virtues for disciples; the learners' aggregates of virtue, etc., along with the preliminary practice, are the middle; and the non-learners' aggregates of virtue, etc., are the end. Thus, in brief, all the virtues of the Noble Sangha are declared as beautiful in the beginning, beautiful in the middle, and beautiful in the end.

Evaṃ gāthāttayena saṅkhepato sakalaguṇasaṅkittanamukhena ratanattayassa paṇāmaṃ katvā, idāni taṃ nipaccakāraṃ yathādhippete payojane pariṇāmento “iti me”tiādimāha. Tattha ratijananaṭṭhena ratanaṃ, buddhadhammasaṅghā. Tesañhi “itipi so bhagavā”tiādinā yathābhūtaguṇe āvajjantassa amatādhigamahetubhūtaṃ anappakaṃ pītipāmojjaṃ uppajjati. Yathāha –

Having thus paid homage to the Triple Gem in three verses, by way of a brief proclamation of all their virtues, now, directing that reverence toward the intended purpose, he says, 'iti me,' and so on. Herein, 'ratana' (gem) has the meaning of generating delight—namely, the Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha. For when one reflects on their true qualities, as in 'Iti pi so Bhagavā,' etc., abundant joy and gladness arise, which is the cause for attaining the Deathless. As it is said—

“Yasmiṃ, mahānāma, samaye ariyasāvako tathāgataṃ anussarati, nevassa tasmiṃ samaye rāgapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, na dosapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, na mohapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, ujugatamevassa tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ hoti tathāgataṃ ārabbha. Ujugatacitto kho pana, mahānāma, ariyasāvako labhati atthavedaṃ, labhati dhammavedaṃ, labhati dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ pāmojjaṃ, pamuditassa pīti jāyatī”tiādi (a. ni. 6.10; a. ni. 11.11).

"At the time, Mahānāma, when a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, their mind is not overwhelmed by lust, not overwhelmed by hatred, not overwhelmed by delusion. At that time, their mind is quite upright, directed toward the Tathāgata. With a quite upright mind, Mahānāma, the noble disciple gains understanding of the meaning, gains understanding of the Dhamma, gains joy connected with the Dhamma. For one who is joyful, rapture arises," and so on (A. Ni. 6.10; A. Ni. 11.11).

Cittīkatādibhāvo vā ratanaṭṭho. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Or, the meaning of 'gem' is that it is esteemed, etc. For it is said:

“Cittīkataṃ mahagghañca, atulaṃ dullabhadassanaṃ;

Anomasattaparibhogaṃ, ratanaṃ tena vuccatī”ti. (khu. pā. aṭṭha. 6.3; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.33; su. ni. aṭṭha. 1.226; mahāni. aṭṭha. 50);

"Esteemed, of great value, incomparable, rarely seen, Enjoyed by beings of high status— Therefore, it is called a gem."

Cittīkatabhāvādayo [P 1.0018] ca anaññasādhāraṇā buddhādīsu eva labbhantīti. Vandanāva vandanāmayaṃ, yathā “dānamayaṃ, sīlamaya”nti (dī. ni. 3.305; itivu. 60; netti. 34). Vandanā cettha kāyavācācittehi tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇaninnatā, thomanā vā. Pujjabhavaphalanibbattanato puññaṃ, attano santānaṃ puṇātīti vā. Suvihatantarāyoti suṭṭhu vihatantarāyo, etena attano pasādasampattiyā, rattanattayassa [M 1.0015] ca khettabhāvasampattiyā taṃ puññaṃ atthappakāsanassa upaghātakaupaddavānaṃ vihanane samatthanti dasseti. Hutvāti pubbakālakiriyā, tassa “atthaṃ pakāsayissāmī”ti etena sambandho. Tassāti yaṃ ratanattayavandanāmayaṃ puññaṃ, tassa. Ānubhāvenāti balena.

And the qualities of being esteemed, etc., are found exclusively in the Buddha and others. The phrase `vandanāmayaṃ` means 'consisting of homage,' just as in `dānamayaṃ` ('consisting of giving') and `sīlamayaṃ` ('consisting of virtue'). Here, homage is the inclination of body, speech, and mind toward the virtues of the Triple Gem, or it is praise. It is 'merit' (`puñña`) because it generates the fruit of a venerable state, or because it purifies (`puṇāti`) one's own mental continuum. `Suvihatantarāyo` means 'with obstacles well-removed,' that is, thoroughly removed. By this is shown that, due to one's own attainment of confidence and the Triple Gem’s attainment of the state of a field of merit, that merit is capable of removing the destructive disturbances that obstruct the clarification of the meaning. `Hutvā` ('having been') is a verb of prior action, and it is connected with 'I will clarify the meaning.' `Tassa` ('of that') refers to that merit consisting of homage to the Triple Gem. `Ānubhāvena` ('by its power') means by its strength.

Evaṃ [V 1.0014] ratanattayassa nipaccakārakaraṇe payojanaṃ dassetvā, idāni yassā dhammadesanāya atthaṃ saṃvaṇṇetukāmo, tassā tāva guṇābhitthavanavasena upaññāpanatthaṃ “dīghassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha dīghasuttaṅkitassāti dīghappamāṇasuttalakkhitassa, etena “dīgho”ti ayaṃ imassa āgamassa atthānugatā samaññāti dasseti. Nanu ca suttāniyeva āgamo, kassa pana suttehi aṅkananti? Saccametaṃ paramatthato, suttāni pana upādāyapaññatto āgamo. Yathā hi atthabyañjanasamudāye “sutta”nti vohāro, evaṃ suttasamudāye “āgamo”ti vohāro. Paṭiccasamuppādādinipuṇatthasabbhāvato nipuṇassa. Āgamissanti ettha, etena, etasmā vā attatthaparatthādayoti āgamo, āgamo ca so varo cāti āgamavaro, āgamasammatehi vā varoti āgamavaro, tassa. Buddhānaṃ anubuddhā buddhānubuddhā, buddhānaṃ saccapaṭivedhaṃ anugamma paṭividdhasaccā aggasāvakādayo [P 1.0019] ariyā. Tehi atthasaṃvaṇṇanāvasena, guṇasaṃvaṇṇanāvasena ca saṃvaṇṇitassa. Atha vā buddhā ca anubuddhā ca buddhānubuddhāti yojetabbaṃ. Sammāsambuddheneva hi tiṇṇampi piṭakānaṃ atthavaṇṇanākkamo bhāsito, yā “pakiṇṇakadesanā”ti vuccati, tato saṅgāyanādivasena sāvakehīti ācariyā vadanti.

Having thus shown the purpose of paying reverence to the Triple Gem, now, to introduce the Dhamma teaching whose meaning he wishes to explain, the phrase 'of the Dīgha' (`dīghassa`), etc., is stated by way of praising its qualities. Herein, `dīghasuttaṅkitassa` means 'marked by long suttas,' which shows that 'Dīgha' is a designation for this Āgama that is in accordance with its meaning. But are not the suttas themselves the Āgama? By what, then, is the Āgama marked by suttas? This is true in an ultimate sense, but the Āgama is a convention established in dependence on the suttas. For just as the term 'sutta' is used for a collection of meaning and wording, so the term 'Āgama' is used for a collection of suttas. It is 'subtle' (`nipuṇassa`) due to the presence of subtle meanings such as dependent origination. It is an 'Āgama' because one's own welfare, the welfare of others, etc., come (`āgamissanti`) to it (`ettha`), by it (`etena`), or from it (`etasmā`). It is an 'excellent Āgama' (`āgamavaro`) because it is an Āgama and it is excellent (`varo`), or because it is excellent among what is approved as Āgama; 'of that' (`tassa`). `Buddhānubuddhā` means those enlightened after the Buddhas; they are the noble ones, such as the chief disciples, who have penetrated the truth by following after the Buddhas' penetration of the truth. By them it was commented upon by way of explaining its meaning and praising its virtues. Alternatively, `buddhānubuddhā` should be construed as 'the Buddhas and those enlightened after them.' For the sequence of the explanation of the meaning of all three Piṭakas was spoken by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One himself—which is called the 'miscellaneous teaching'—and thereafter by the disciples by way of the councils, etc.; so the teachers say.

Saddhāvahaguṇassāti buddhādīsu pasādāvahasampattikassa. Ayañhi āgamo brahmajālādīsu (dī. ni. 1.5-7, 26-28) sīladiṭṭhādīnaṃ anavasesaniddesādivasena, mahāpadānādīsu (dī. ni. 2.3-5) purimabuddhānampi guṇaniddesādivasena, pāthikasuttādīsu (dī. ni. 3.3,4) titthiye nimadditvā appaṭivattiyasīhanāda nadanādivasena, anuttariyasuttādīsu (a. ni. 6.8) ca visesato buddhaguṇavibhāvanena ratanattaye sātisayappasādaṃ āvahati. Saṃvaṇṇanāsu cāyaṃ ācariyassa pakati, yā taṃtaṃsaṃvaṇṇanāsu ādito tassa tassa saṃvaṇṇetabbassa dhammassa visesaguṇakittanena thomanā. Tathā hi papañcasūdanīsāratthappakāsinīmanorathapūraṇīsu aṭṭhasālinīādīsu ca yathākkamaṃ “paravādamathanassa ñāṇappabhedajananassa [M 1.0016] dhammakathikapuṅgavānaṃ vicittappaṭibhānajananassa tassa gambhīrañāṇehi ogāḷhassa abhiṇhaso nānānayavicittassa abhidhammassā”tiādinā thomanā katā.

'Of that which has the quality of inspiring faith' means of that which has the excellence of inspiring confidence in the Buddha and others. For this Āgama inspires supreme confidence in the Triple Gem: in the Brahmajāla Sutta and others, by way of the exhaustive exposition of morality, views, etc.; in the Mahāpadāna Sutta and others, by way of the description of the virtues of past Buddhas as well; in the Pāthika Sutta and others, by way of crushing the sectarians and roaring the irreversible lion’s roar; and in the Anuttariya Sutta and others, by especially elaborating on the Buddha’s virtues. Moreover, it is this teacher’s custom in the commentaries to praise at the outset, by proclaiming the special virtues of whatever Dhamma is to be commented upon. Thus, in the Papañcasūdanī, Sāratthappakāsinī, Manorathapūraṇī, Aṭṭhasālinī, and others, praises have been made in sequence, such as: 'of that which is the crusher of others’ doctrines, the generator of the divisions of knowledge, the generator of varied and brilliant eloquence for the foremost of Dhamma preachers; of the Abhidhamma, which is immersed in profound knowledge and constantly varied with manifold methods,' and so on.

Attho kathīyati etāyāti atthakathā, sā eva aṭṭhakathā, ttha-kārassa ṭṭha-kāraṃ katvā, yathā “dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho”ti (paṭi. ma. 2.8). Ādito tiādimhi paṭhamasaṅgītiyaṃ. Chaḷabhiññatāya paramena cittavasībhāvena samannāgatattā, jhānādīsu pañcavidhavasitāsabbhāvato ca vasino, therā mahākassapādayo. Tesaṃ satehi pañcahi. Yāti yā aṭṭhakathā. Saṅgītāti atthaṃ pakāsetuṃ yuttaṭṭhāne “ayaṃ etassa attho, ayaṃ etassa attho”ti saṅgahetvā vuttā. Anusaṅgītā [V 1.0015] ca yasattherādīhi [P 1.0020] pacchāpi dutiyatatiyasaṅgītīsu, iminā attano saṃvaṇṇanāya āgamanasuddhiṃ dasseti.

The meaning is explained by this, hence it is called a commentary (atthakathā). That very commentary is also called aṭṭhakathā, by changing the 'ttha' to 'ṭṭha', as in 'suffering has the meaning of oppression' (Paṭi. Ma. 2.8). 'From the beginning' (ādito) refers to the first council. Because they were endowed with the highest mastery of mind through the sixfold higher knowledges, and because they possessed the fivefold mastery in jhāna and other attainments, they were masters (vasino), the elders such as Mahākassapa and others. By those five hundred. That which is the commentary (yā aṭṭhakathā). 'Recited' (saṅgītā) means it was spoken, having been compiled in the appropriate places to explain the meaning, thus: 'this is the meaning of this, this is the meaning of that.' And it was subsequently recited (anusaṅgītā) by elders such as Yasa and others in the second and third councils. By this, he shows the purity of the transmission for his own commentary.

Sīhassa lānato gahaṇato sīhaḷo, sīhakumāro. Taṃvaṃsajātatāya tambapaṇṇidīpe khattiyānaṃ, tesaṃ nivāsatāya tambapaṇṇidīpassa ca sīhaḷabhāvo veditabbo. Ābhatāti jambudīpato ānītā. Athāti pacchā. Aparabhāge hi asaṅkaratthaṃ sīhaḷabhāsāya aṭṭhakathā ṭhapitāti. Tenassa mūlaṭṭhakathā sabbasādhāraṇā na hotīti idaṃ atthappakāsanaṃ ekantena karaṇīyanti dasseti. Tenevāha – “dīpavāsīnamatthāyā”ti. Tattha dīpavāsīnanti jambudīpavāsīnaṃ. Dīpavāsīnanti vā sīhaḷadīpavāsīnaṃ atthāya sīhaḷabhāsāya ṭhapitāti yojanā.

From taking and capturing the lion, [he was called] Sīhaḷa, the lion-prince. Because khattiyas were born in that lineage on the island of Tambapaṇṇi, and because of their dwelling there, the island of Tambapaṇṇi's state as 'Sīhaḷa' should be understood. 'Ābhatā' means brought from Jambudīpa. 'Atha' means afterward. Indeed, in a later period, for the sake of non-confusion, the commentary was established in the Sinhala language. He shows that because of this, its root commentary is not common to all, and therefore this explanation of the meaning must absolutely be done. For that reason he said: 'for the sake of the island-dwellers.' Therein, 'island-dwellers' means the dwellers of Jambudīpa. Or, the construction is: 'for the sake of the island-dwellers' means for the sake of the dwellers of the Sinhala island it was established in the Sinhala language.

Apanetvānāti kañcukasadisaṃ sīhaḷabhāsaṃ apanetvā. Tatoti aṭṭhakathāto. Ahanti attānaṃ niddisati. Manoramaṃ bhāsanti māgadhabhāsaṃ. Sā hi sabhāvaniruttibhūtā paṇḍitānaṃ manaṃ ramayatīti. Tenevāha – “tantinayānucchavika”nti, pāḷigatiyā anulomikaṃ pāḷibhāsāyānuvidhāyininti attho. Vigatadosanti asabhāvaniruttibhāsantararahitaṃ.

‘Having removed’ (apanetvāna) means having removed the Sinhala language, which is like a cloak. ‘From that’ (tato) means from the commentary. ‘I’ (ahaṃ) refers to oneself. ‘Language pleasing to the mind’ (manoramaṃ bhāsaṃ) means the Magadhan language. For it delights the minds of the wise, being the inherent language of expression. Therefore he said, ‘in conformity with the method of the texts’ (tantinayānucchavikaṃ), meaning in accordance with the Pāḷi style, following the Pāḷi language. ‘Free from faults’ (vigatadosaṃ) means devoid of any other language that is not the inherent language of expression.

Samayaṃ avilomentoti siddhantaṃ avirodhento, etena atthadosābhāvamāha. Aviruddhattā eva hi theravādāpi idha pakāsiyissanti. Theravaṃsapadīpānanti thirehi sīlakkhandhādīhi samannāgatattā therā, mahākassapādayo. Tehi āgatā ācariyaparamparā theravaṃso, tappariyāpannā [M 1.0017] hutvā āgamādhigamasampannattā paññāpajjotena tassa samujjalanato theravaṃsapadīpā, mahāvihāravāsino therā, tesaṃ. Vividhehi ākārehi nicchīyatīti vinicchayo, gaṇṭhiṭṭhānesu khīlamaddanākārena pavattā vimaticchedakathā. Suṭṭhu nipuṇo saṇho vinicchayo etesanti sunipuṇavinicchayā. Atha vā vinicchinotīti vinicchayo, yathāvuttavisayaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Suṭṭhu nipuṇo cheko vinicchayo etesanti sunipuṇavinicchayā, etena mahākassapāditheraparamparābhato, tatoyeva ca aviparīto saṇhasukhumo mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ [P 1.0021] vinicchayoti tassa pamāṇabhūtataṃ dasseti.

‘Not violating the doctrine’ (samayaṃ avilomento) means not contradicting the established doctrine; by this, he indicates the absence of fault in meaning. Indeed, because of being non-contradictory, the views of the Theras will also be expounded here. ‘Of the lamps of the lineage of the Elders’ (theravaṃsapadīpānaṃ) means: because they are endowed with steadfast qualities such as the aggregates of morality, etc., they are the Elders (therā), such as Mahākassapa and others. The lineage of teachers that has come down from them is the lineage of the Elders (theravaṃso). Being included in that, and because of their accomplishment in scripture and realization, and because they illuminate that lineage with the lamp of wisdom, they are the ‘lamps of the lineage of the Elders’—the Elders dwelling in the Mahāvihāra; of them. ‘Because it is decided in various ways, it is an analysis (vinicchayo)’; it is the discourse that cuts through doubt, proceeding in the manner of driving a stake into knotty points. ‘Thoroughly skilled and subtle is their analysis,’ hence they are of ‘thoroughly skilled analysis’ (sunippuṇavinicchayā). Or else, ‘because it analyzes, it is an analysis (vinicchayo)’; this is the knowledge regarding the aforementioned subject. ‘Thoroughly skilled and expert is their analysis,’ hence they are of ‘thoroughly skilled analysis’ (sunippuṇavinicchayā). By this he shows that because the analysis of the Mahāvihāra-dwellers is brought down from the lineage of Elders such as Mahākassapa, it is therefore undistorted, gentle, and subtle, thus demonstrating its authoritativeness.

Sujanassa cāti ca-saddo sampiṇḍanattho, tena na kevalaṃ jambudīpavāsīnameva atthāya, atha kho sādhujanatosanatthañcāti dasseti, tena ca tambapaṇṇidīpavāsīnampi atthāyāti ayamattho siddho hoti, uggahaṇādisukaratāya tesampi bahupakārattā. Ciraṭṭhitatthanti ciraṭṭhitiatthaṃ[V 1.0016], cirakālaṭṭhitiyāti attho. Idañhi atthappakāsanaṃ aviparītabyañjanasunikkhepassa atthasunayassa ca upāyabhāvato saddhammassa ciraṭṭhitiyā saṃvattati. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

‘And for good people’ (sujanassa ca): the word ‘ca’ (and) has the purpose of conjoining, indicating that it is not only for the benefit of those dwelling in Jambudīpa but also for pleasing virtuous people. By this, the meaning is established that it is also for the benefit of those living on the island of Tambapaṇṇi, since it is easy to learn and of great help to them too. ‘For the sake of long stability’ (ciraṭṭhitatthaṃ) means for the sake of long-lasting stability, that is, for its endurance over a long time.
