For this exposition of meaning, being a means for the well-placed, undistorted phrasing and for the good method of understanding the meaning, contributes to the long endurance of the True Dhamma. As the Blessed One has said—

“Dveme, bhikkhave, dhammā saddhammassa ṭhitiyā asammosāya anantaradhānāya saṃvattanti. Katame dve? Sunikkhattañca padabyañjanaṃ, attho ca sunīto”ti (a. ni. 2.21).

“Bhikkhus, these two things lead to the stability, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the True Dhamma. What two? Well-placed words and phrasing, and well-understood meaning.”

Yaṃ atthavaṇṇanaṃ kattukāmo, tassā mahattaṃ pariharituṃ “sīlakathā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tenevāha – “na taṃ idha vicārayissāmī”ti. Atha vā yaṃ aṭṭhakathaṃ kattukāmo, tadekadesabhāvena visuddhimaggo ca gahetabboti kathikānaṃ upadesaṃ karonto tattha vicāritadhamme uddesavasena dasseti “sīlakathā” tiādinā. Tattha sīlakathāti cārittavārittādivasena sīlavitthārakathā. Dhutadhammāti piṇḍapātikaṅgādayo (visuddhi. 1.22; theragā. aṭṭha. 2.845, 849) terasa kilesadhunanakadhammā. Kammaṭṭhānāni sabbānīti pāḷiyaṃ āgatāni aṭṭhatiṃsa, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ dveti niravasesāni yogakammassa bhāvanāya pavattiṭṭhānāni. Cariyāvidhānasahitoti rāgacaritādīnaṃ sabhāvādividhānena sahito. Jhānāni cattāri rūpāvacarajjhānāni, samāpattiyo [M 1.0018] catasso arūpasamāpattiyo. Aṭṭhapi vā paṭiladdhamattāni jhānāni, samāpajjanavasībhāvappattiyā samāpattiyo. Jhānāni vā rūpārūpāvacarajjhānāni[P 1.0022], samāpattiyo phalasamāpattinirodhasamāpattiyo.

Wishing to compose a commentary on the meaning, to avoid its great extent, ‘the discussion on virtue’ and so on was said. Therefore he said, ‘I will not examine that here.’ Alternatively, wishing to compose a commentary, while giving instruction to the preachers that the Visuddhimagga should be taken as a part of it, he shows the matters examined therein by way of summary, with ‘the discussion on virtue’ and so on. Therein, ‘the discussion on virtue’ (sīlakathā) is the detailed discourse on virtue by way of conduct, restraint, and so on. ‘The ascetic practices’ (dhutadhammā) are the thirteen practices that shake off defilements, such as the alms-food-eater’s practice. ‘All meditation subjects’ (kammaṭṭhānāni sabbāni) means the thirty-eight that have come down in the Pāḷi and two in the commentary, thus without remainder, all the bases for the proceeding of the development of yogic practice. ‘Together with the classification of temperaments’ (cariyāvidhānasahito) means together with the classification of the nature, etc., of those with lustful temperament and so on. ‘The jhānas’ are the four fine-material jhānas; ‘the attainments’ (samāpattiyo) are the four immaterial attainments. Or, the eight jhānas are those merely attained; the attainments are the mastery in entering them. Or, the jhānas are the fine-material and immaterial jhānas; the attainments are the fruition attainment and the cessation attainment.

Lokiyalokuttarabhedā cha abhiññāyo sabbā abhiññāyo. Ñāṇavibhaṅgādīsu āgatanayena ekavidhādinā paññāya saṅkaletvā sampiṇḍetvā nicchayo paññāsaṅkalananicchayo.

The six higher knowledges (abhiññāyo), with their division into mundane and supramundane, are all the higher knowledges. The determination (nicchayo) made by collecting and summarizing with wisdom in a onefold way and so on, according to the method that has come down in the Ñāṇavibhaṅga and other texts, is the ‘determination by the collection of wisdom’ (paññāsaṅkalananicchayo).

Paccayadhammānaṃ hetādīnaṃ paccayuppannadhammānaṃ hetupaccayādibhāvo paccayākāro, tassa desanā paccayākāradesanā, paṭiccasamuppādakathāti attho. Sā pana ghanavinibbhogassa sudukkaratāya saṇhasukhumā, nikāyantaraladdhisaṅkararahitā, ekattanayādisahitā ca tattha vicāritāti āha – “suparisuddhanipuṇanayā”ti. Paṭisambhidādīsu āgatanayaṃ avissajjetvāva vicāritattā avimuttatanti maggā.

The mode of conditions (paccayākāro) is the state of being the root-condition and so on for dependently arisen phenomena on the part of conditioning phenomena such as the root, etc. The teaching of this is the ‘teaching of the mode of conditions’ (paccayākāradesanā), which means the discourse on dependent origination. And because the analysis of what is compact is extremely difficult, it is subtle and refined, free from confusion with the tenets of other schools, and is examined there together with the method of unity and so on; therefore he said: ‘with a very pure and subtle method’ (suparisuddhanipuṇanayā). Because it is examined without abandoning the method that has come down in the Paṭisambhidāmagga and other texts, it does not deviate from the textual method.

Iti [V 1.0017] pana sabbanti iti-saddo parisamāpane, pana-saddo vacanālaṅkāre, etaṃ sabbanti attho. Idhāti imissā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Na vicārayissāmi, punaruttibhāvatoti adhippāyo.

Regarding ‘iti pana sabbaṃ’: the word ‘iti’ is for conclusion, the word ‘pana’ is a verbal embellishment; the meaning is ‘all this.’ ‘Here’ (idha) means in this commentary. The intention behind ‘I will not examine’ (na vicārayissāmi) is: because it would be a repetition.

Idāni tasseva avicāraṇassa ekantakāraṇaṃ niddhārento “majjhe visuddhimaggo”tiādimāha. Tattha “majjhe ṭhatvā”ti etena majjhebhāvadīpanena visesato catunnaṃ āgamānaṃ sādhāraṇaṭṭhakathā visuddhimaggo, na sumaṅgalavilāsinīādayo viya asādhāraṇaṭṭhakathāti dasseti. “Visesato”ti idaṃ vinayābhidhammānampi visuddhimaggo yathārahaṃ atthavaṇṇanā hoti yevāti katvā vuttaṃ.

Now, specifying the definitive reason for that non-examination, he says, ‘the Visuddhimagga in the middle,’ and so on. Therein, with ‘standing in the middle’ (majjhe ṭhatvā), by this indication of its being in the middle, he shows that the Visuddhimagga is a commentary common especially to the four Nikāyas, not an uncommon commentary like the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī and others. The word ‘especially’ (visesato) is said because the Visuddhimagga is indeed also an explanation of the meaning for the Vinaya and Abhidhamma, as is fitting.

Iccevāti iti eva. Tampīti visuddhimaggampi. Etāyāti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā. Ettha ca “sīhaḷadīpaṃ ābhatā”tiādinā atthappakāsanassa nimittaṃ dasseti, “dīpavāsīnamatthāya, sujanassa ca tuṭṭhatthaṃ, ciraṭṭhitatthañca dhammassā”ti etena payojanaṃ, avasiṭṭhena karaṇappakāraṃ. Sīlakathādīnaṃ avicāraṇampi hi idha karaṇappakāro evāti.

‘Thus indeed’ (icceva) means ‘iti eva.’ ‘That too’ (tampi) means the Visuddhimagga. ‘By this’ (etāya) means by the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī. Here, with ‘having brought it to the island of Sri Lanka’ (sīhaḷadīpaṃ ābhatā) and so on, he shows the occasion for the explanation of the meaning; with ‘for the benefit of the island dwellers, for the satisfaction of good people, and for the long duration of the Dhamma’ (dīpavāsīnamatthāya, sujanassa ca tuṭṭhatthaṃ, ciraṭṭhitatthañca dhammassā), this shows the purpose; and with the remainder, the manner of making. For here, even the non-examination of discourses on virtue and so on is indeed the manner of making.

Ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the introduction to the text is concluded.

Nidānakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Introductory Discourse.

Vibhāgavantānaṃ [V 1.0018][M 1.0019] sabhāvavibhāvanaṃ vibhāgadassanavaseneva hotīti paṭhamaṃ tāva vaggasuttavasena [P 1.0023] vibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ “tattha dīghāgamo nāmā”tiādimāha. Tattha tatthāti “dīghassa āgamavarassa atthaṃ pakāsayissāmī”ti yadidaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmiṃ vacane. Yassa atthaṃ pakāsayissāmīti paṭiññātaṃ, so dīghāgamo nāma vaggasuttavasena evaṃ vibhāgoti attho. Atha vā tatthāti “dīghāgamanissitamattha”nti etasmiṃ vacane. Yo dīghāgamo vutto, so vaggādivasena edisoti attho. Attano saṃvaṇṇanāya paṭhamamahāsaṅgītiyaṃ nikkhittānukkameneva pavattabhāvadassanatthaṃ “tassa vaggesu…pe… vuttaṃ nidānamādī”ti āha. Kasmā pana catūsu āgamesu dīghāgamo paṭhamaṃ saṅgīto, tattha ca sīlakkhandhavaggo ādito nikkhitto, tasmiñca brahmajālanti? Nāyamanuyogo katthacipi na pavattati, api ca saddhāvahaguṇato dīghanikāyo paṭhamaṃ saṅgīto. Saddhā hi kusaladhammānaṃ bījaṃ. Yathāha – “saddhā bījaṃ tapo vuṭṭhī”ti, (saṃ. ni. 1.197; su. ni. 77) saddhāvahaguṇatā cassa dassitāyeva. Kiñca katipayasuttasaṅgahato, appaparimāṇato ca gahaṇadhāraṇādisukhato. Tathāhesa catuttiṃsasuttasaṅgaho catusaṭṭhibhāṇavāraparimāṇo ca. Sīlakathābāhullato pana sīlakkhandhavaggo paṭhamaṃ nikkhitto. Sīlañhi sāsanassa ādi, sīlapatiṭṭhānattā sabbaguṇānaṃ. Tenevāha – “tasmā tiha, tvaṃ bhikkhu, ādimeva visodhehi kusalesu dhammesu. Ko cādi kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ? Sīlañca suvisuddha”ntiādi (saṃ. ni. 5.395). Etena cassa vaggassa anvatthasaññatā vuttā hoti. Diṭṭhiviniveṭhanakathābhāvato pana suttantapiṭakassa niravasesadiṭṭhivibhajanaṃ brahmajālaṃ paṭhamaṃ nikkhittanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tepiṭake hi buddhavacane brahmajālasadisaṃ diṭṭhigatāni niggumbaṃ nijjaṭaṃ katvā vibhattasuttaṃ natthīti.

The discernment of the nature of those with divisions comes about through the very act of seeing divisions. First, to show the division by way of grouped discourses, he begins with, ‘Here, the Long Collection is called…’ (tattha dīghāgamo nāma). Here, ‘here’ (tattha) refers to the statement, ‘I will explain the meaning of the long, excellent collection.’ The meaning is: ‘What I will explain is called the Long Collection, divided in this way by grouped discourses.’ Alternatively, ‘here’ (tattha) refers to the statement, ‘the meaning dependent on the Long Collection.’ The meaning is: ‘What is called the Long Collection is of this kind by way of groups, etc.’ To show the continuity of its transmission, following the arrangement established at the First Great Council for its own exposition, he said: ‘In its groups… the introduction and so on are stated’ (tassa vaggesu…pe… vuttaṃ nidānamādi). But why, among the four Āgamas, was the Dīgha Nikāya recited first, and why, within it, was the Sīlakkhandha Vagga placed at the beginning, with the Brahmajāla as its first discourse? This question does not arise just anywhere, but the Dīgha Nikāya was recited first due to its quality of inspiring faith. For faith is the seed of wholesome qualities, as it is said: ‘Faith is the seed, austerity the rain’ (Saṃ. Ni. 1.197; Su. Ni. 77). Its quality of inspiring faith has already been shown. Moreover, it is easy to grasp, memorize, and retain due to its collection of a few suttas and its limited extent. Indeed, this collection comprises thirty-four suttas and sixty-four recitation sections. Because of the abundance of discussions on virtue, the Sīlakkhandha Vagga was placed first. For virtue is the beginning of the teaching, the foundation of all good qualities. Hence he said: ‘Therefore, monk, here, first purify the beginning of wholesome qualities. And what is the beginning of wholesome qualities? Virtue well purified,’ and so on (Saṃ. Ni. 5.395). By this, the appropriateness of this division’s name is explained. Furthermore, because of its nature as a discourse on dispelling wrong views, it should be understood that the Brahmajāla, which thoroughly dissects all wrong views, was placed first in the Suttanta Piṭaka. For in the Tipiṭaka, there is no discourse in the Buddha’s words comparable to the Brahmajāla—one that uproots and utterly destroys wrong views so thoroughly.

Paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Account of the First Great Council.

Yassā [V 1.0019][P 1.0024] paṭhamamahāsaṅgītiyaṃ nikkhittānukkamena saṃvaṇṇanaṃ kattukāmo, taṃ, tassā ca tantiāruḷhāya idha vacane kāraṇaṃ dassento “paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti…pe… veditabbā”ti āha. Tattha yathāpaccayaṃ tattha tattha desitattā[M 1.0020], paññattattā ca vippakiṇṇānaṃ dhammavinayānaṃ saṅgahetvā gāyanaṃ kathanaṃ saṅgīti, etena taṃtaṃsikkhāpadānaṃ suttānañca ādipariyosānesu, antarantarā ca sambandhavasena ṭhapitaṃ saṅgītikāravacanaṃ saṅgahitaṃ hoti. Mahāvisayattā, pūjanīyattā ca mahatī saṅgīti mahāsaṅgīti, paṭhamā mahāsaṅgīti paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti, tassā pavattikālo paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikālo, tasmiṃ paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle. Nidānanti ca desanaṃ desakālādivasena aviditaṃ viditaṃ katvā nidassetīti nidānaṃ. Sattānaṃ dassanānuttariyasaraṇādipaṭilābhahetubhūtāsu vijjamānāsupi aññāsu bhagavato kiriyāsu “buddho bodheyya”nti (bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. ratanacaṅkamanakaṇḍavaṇṇanā; cariyā. uddhānagāthāvaṇṇanā) paṭiññāya anulomato veneyyānaṃ maggaphalappattīnaṃ hetubhūtā kiriyā nippariyāyena buddhakiccanti āha – “dhammacakkappavattanañhi ādiṃ katvā”ti. Tattha saddhindriyādidhammoyeva pavattanaṭṭhena cakkanti dhammacakkaṃ. Atha vā cakkanti āṇā, dhammato anapetattā dhammañca taṃ cakkañcāti dhammacakkaṃ, dhammena ñāyena cakkantipi dhammacakkaṃ. Yathāha –

Wishing to compose a commentary on the First Great Council in the order it was laid down, and showing the reason for its inclusion in the canonical text here, he says: 'The First Great Council... should be understood.' There, because the scattered Dhamma and Vinaya were taught and designated in various places according to circumstances, the recitation and speaking that gathers them together is called a Council (saṅgīti). By this, the words of the Council-makers, placed at the beginning, end, and intermittently in connection with the training rules and suttas, are included. Due to its vast scope and venerability, a great council is called a Mahāsaṅgīti. The first Great Council is the Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti. The time of its occurrence is the Paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāla; at that time of the First Great Council. The term 'nidāna' also means making known what was previously unknown by explaining the time, place, and so on, of the teaching. Among the various actions of the Blessed One, which exist as causes for beings to attain the unsurpassed vision, refuge, and so on, the action that is the cause for the attainment of paths and fruits for those to be trained, in accordance with the declaration 'The Buddha would awaken' (Bu. Va. Aṭṭha. Ratanacaṅkamanakaṇḍavaṇṇanā; Cariyā. Uddhānagāthāvaṇṇanā), is directly called the Buddha’s activity, as he said: 'Indeed, beginning with the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma.' There, the Dhamma itself, such as the faculty of faith, is called the Wheel (cakka) in the sense of setting in motion; hence, the Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka). Alternatively, 'cakka' means command, and because it is not separate from the Dhamma, it is Dhamma and it is a wheel—thus, the Wheel of Dhamma. Or, it is a wheel by means of the Dhamma, by justice—thus, the Wheel of Dhamma. As it is said—

“Dhammañca pavatteti cakkañcāti dhammacakkaṃ, cakkañca pavatteti dhammañcāti dhammacakkaṃ, dhammena pavattetīti dhammacakkaṃ, dhammacariyāya pavattetīti dhammacakka”ntiādi (paṭi. ma. 2, 39, 41).

"He sets the Dhamma in motion and the wheel, thus it is the Dhamma-wheel; he sets the wheel in motion and the Dhamma, thus it is the Dhamma-wheel; he sets it in motion with the Dhamma, thus it is the Dhamma-wheel; he sets it in motion through the practice of the Dhamma, thus it is the Dhamma-wheel," and so on (Paṭi. Ma. 2, 39, 41).

“Katabuddhakicce”ti etena buddhakattabbassa kassacipi asesitabhāvaṃ dasseti. Nanu ca sāvakehi vinītāpi vineyyā [P 1.0025] bhagavatāyeva vinītā honti, yato sāvakabhāsitaṃ suttaṃ “buddhavacana”nti vuccati, sāvakavineyyā ca na tāva vinītāti? Nāyaṃ doso tesaṃ vinayanupāyassa sāvakesu ṭhapitattā. Tenevāha –

By 'the Buddha's work is done,' this shows that nothing whatsoever of what was to be done by the Buddha was left remaining. But surely, are not even those to be trained by the disciples ultimately trained by the Blessed One, since a discourse spoken by a disciple is called 'the word of the Buddha'? And are those to be trained by disciples not yet trained? This is no fault, because the method for their training was established among the disciples. Therefore, it is said—

“Na tāvāhaṃ, pāpima, parinibbāyissāmi, yāva me bhikkhū na sāvakā bhavissanti viyattā vinītā visāradā bahussutā dhammadharā…pe… uppannaṃ parappavādaṃ saha [V 1.0020] dhammena suniggahitaṃ niggahetvā sappāṭihāriyaṃ dhammaṃ desessa”ntiādi (dī. ni. 2.168; saṃ. ni. 5.822; udā. 51).

"I will not attain final Nibbāna, O Evil One, until my monks are disciples: skilled, trained, confident, learned, upholders of the Dhamma... until, having thoroughly refuted with the Dhamma any opposing doctrines that have arisen, they teach the Dhamma accompanied by wonders," and so on (Dī. Ni. 2.168; Saṃ. Ni. 5.822; Udā. 51).

“Kusinārāya”ntiādi bhagavato parinibbutadesakālavisesadassanaṃ “aparinibbuto bhagavā”ti gāhassa micchābhāvadassanatthaṃ, loke jātasaṃvaddhabhāvadassanatthañca[M 1.0021]. Tathā hi manussabhāvassa supākaṭakaraṇatthaṃ mahābodhisattā carimabhave dārapariggahādīnipi karontīti. Upādīyate kammakilesehīti upādi, vipākakkhandhā kaṭattā ca rūpaṃ. So pana upādi kilesābhisaṅkhāramāranimmathanena nibbānappattiyaṃ anossaṭṭho, idha khandhamaccumāranimmathanena ossaṭṭho nissesitoti ayaṃ anupādisesā, nibbānadhātu. Nibbānadhātūti cettha nibbutimattaṃ adhippetaṃ, itthambhūtalakkhaṇe cāyaṃ karaṇaniddeso. “Dhātubhājanadivase”ti idaṃ na “sannipatitāna”nti etassa visesanaṃ, ussāhajananassa pana visesanaṃ, “dhātubhājanadivase bhikkhūnaṃ ussāhaṃ janesī”ti. Dhātubhājanadivasato hi purimapurimataradivasesu bhikkhū samāgatāti. Atha vā dhātubhājanadivase sannipatitānaṃ kāyasāmaggīvasena sahitānanti attho. Saṅghassa thero saṅghatthero, so pana saṅgho kiṃ parimāṇānanti āha – “sattannaṃ bhikkhusatasahassāna”nti. Niccasāpekkhatāya hi edisesu samāso hotiyeva, yathā – “devadattassa garukula”nti.

“At Kusinārā,” and so on—this indicates the specific place and time of the Blessed One's final Nibbāna, in order to show the falsity of the view, “the Blessed One has not attained final Nibbāna,” and also to show that he was born and grew up in the world. Indeed, for the sake of making the human state very clear, the great bodhisattas in their final existence even undertake such things as taking a wife. That which is clung to by kamma and defilements is “upādi”; this refers to the resultant aggregates and form produced by kamma. That upādi, not relinquished at the attainment of Nibbāna through the crushing of the Māra of defilements and formations, is here relinquished without remainder through the crushing of the Māra of the aggregates and death—this is the Nibbāna-element with no residue remaining. Here, by “Nibbāna-element,” mere extinction is intended, and this is an instrumental designation in the sense of “being of such a nature.” The phrase “on the day of the relic distribution” does not qualify “of those who had gathered,” but rather qualifies the generation of effort, as in: “On the day of the relic distribution, he inspired effort in the bhikkhus.” For the bhikkhus had assembled on the days preceding the relic distribution. Alternatively, it means that on the day of the relic distribution, those who had gathered were united by way of bodily harmony. The elder of the Saṅgha is the Saṅghatthera; as to the size of that Saṅgha, it is said: “of seven hundred thousand bhikkhus.” For in such cases, a compound is indeed used due to constant association, as in “Devadatta’s teacher’s-family.”

Āyasmā mahākassapo puna dullabhabhāvaṃ maññamāno bhikkhūnaṃ [P 1.0026] ussāhaṃ janesīti sambandho. “Dhātubhājanadivase sannipatitāna”nti idaṃ “bhikkhūnaṃ ussāhaṃ janesī”ti ettha “bhikkhūna”nti imināpi padena sambandhanīyaṃ. Subhaddena vuḍḍhapabbajitena vuttavacanamanussarantoti sambandho. Tattha anussaranto dhammasaṃvegavasenāti adhippāyo. “Saddhammaṃ antaradhāpeyyuṃ saṅgāyeyyaṃ…pe… ciraṭṭhitikaṃ tassa kimaññaṃ āṇaṇyaṃ bhavissatī”ti etesaṃ padānaṃ “iti cintayanto”ti etena sambandho. Tathā “yañcāha”nti etassa “anuggahito pasaṃsito”ti etena sambandho. Yaṃ pāpabhikkhūti ettha yanti nipātamattaṃ, kāraṇaniddeso vā, yena kāraṇena antaradhāpeyyuṃ, tadetaṃ kāraṇaṃ vijjatīti attho, addhaniyanti addhānamaggagāmi, addhānakkhamanti attho.

The Venerable Mahākassapa, again, considering the rarity of the opportunity, aroused effort in the bhikkhus—this is the connection. The phrase “On the day of the relic distribution, of those who had gathered” is also to be connected with the word “bhikkhus” in the clause “he aroused effort in the bhikkhus.” Recalling the words spoken by Subhadda, who had gone forth in old age—this is the connection. There, the meaning is that he was recalling with a sense of spiritual urgency concerning the Dhamma. “Lest they cause the true Dhamma to disappear, I should hold a council… so that it may long endure—what other freedom from debt will there be for him?”—these words are connected with “thus thinking.” Similarly, “and that which I” is connected with “supported and praised.” In the phrase “Because wicked bhikkhus,” the word “yaṃ” is merely a particle, or it indicates a reason; the meaning is: the reason by which they might cause it to disappear, that reason exists. “Addhaniya” means one who travels a long road; the meaning is “capable of enduring the journey.”

Yañcāhanti ettha yanti yasmā, yena kāraṇenāti vuttaṃ hoti, kiriyāparāmasanaṃ vā etaṃ, tena “anuggahito pasaṃsito”ti ettha anuggaṇhanaṃ pasaṃsanañca parāmasati. “Cīvare sādhāraṇaparibhogenā”ti ettha “attanā samasamaṭṭhapanenā”ti idha attanā-saddaṃ ānetvā cīvare attanā [V 1.0021][M 1.0022] sādhāraṇaparibhogenāti yojetabbaṃ. Yassa yena hi sambandho dūraṭṭhampi ca tassa tanti atha vā bhagavatā cīvare sādhāraṇaparibhogena bhagavatā anuggahitoti yojanīyaṃ, etassāpi hi karaṇaniddesassa sahayogakattutthajotakattasambhavato. Yāvadeti yāvadeva, yattakaṃ kālaṃ, yattake vā samāpattivihāre, abhiññāvihāre vā ākaṅkhanto viharāmi ceva voharāmi ca, tathā kassapopīti attho. Idañca navānupubbavihārachaḷabhiññabhāvasāmaññena thutimattaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi āyasmā mahākassapo bhagavā viya devasikaṃ catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassasaṅkhyā samāpattiyo samāpajjati, yamakapāṭihāriyādivasena vā abhiññāyo vaḷañjetīti. Tenevāha – “navānupubbavihārachaḷabhiññāppabhede”ti[P 1.0027]. Tassa kimaññaṃ āṇaṇyaṃ bhavissati, aññatra dhammavinayasaṅgāyanāti adhippāyo. “Nanu maṃ bhagavā”tiādinā vuttamevatthaṃ upamāvasena vibhāveti.

Here, in “yañcāhaṃ,” “yaṃ” means “because,” that is to say, “for which reason”; or it is a reference to an action, and thus in “supported and praised,” it refers to the supporting and praising. In “with shared use of the robe,” the word “by myself” should be supplied here and construed as “by myself with shared use of the robe,” meaning “by placing myself on an equal footing with him.” For whatever connection one has with another, even if distant, that is their tradition. Alternatively, it should be construed as “supported by the Blessed One through the shared use of the robe,” for it is possible for this instrumental designation to indicate a co-agent. “As long as” means “for just as long,” for whatever length of time, or in whatever meditative attainments or abidings in higher knowledge I desire, I both dwell and conduct myself; the meaning is that Kassapa does so as well. And this should be seen as merely a statement of praise regarding the commonality of possessing the nine progressive abidings and the six higher knowledges. For the Venerable Mahākassapa does not, like the Blessed One, daily enter into twenty-four hundred-thousand crores of meditative attainments, nor does he employ the higher knowledges by way of the twin miracle, and so on. Therefore, he said: “in the various kinds of nine progressive abidings and six higher knowledges.” What other freedom from debt will there be for him, other than the recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya? This is the meaning. With “Did not the Blessed One...” and so forth, he clarifies this same meaning by way of a simile.

Tato paranti tato bhikkhūnaṃ ussāhajananato parato. Pure adhammo dippatīti apināma dibbati, yāva adhammo dhammaṃ paṭibāhituṃ samattho hoti, tato puretaramevāti attho. Āsanne anicchite hi ayaṃ pure-saddo. Dippatīti ca dippissati. Puresaddasanniyogena hi anāgatatthe ayaṃ vattamānappayogo, yathā – “purā vassati devo”ti.

“After that” means after the inspiring of effort in the bhikkhus. “Before the un-Dhamma shines”—that is, before it can shine, before the un-Dhamma becomes capable of repelling the Dhamma; the meaning is that this should be done even earlier than that. For this word “pure” (before) is used for an imminent and undesirable situation. And “dippati” (it shines) means “it will shine.” Indeed, due to its connection with the word “pure,” this present tense is used with a future meaning, as in the phrase, “Before the god rains.”

“Sakalanavaṅgasatthusāsanapariyattidhare…pe… ekūnapañcasate pariggahesī”ti etena sukkhavipassakakhīṇāsavapariyantānaṃ yathāvuttapuggalānaṃ satipi āgamādhigamasabbhāve saha paṭisambhidāhi pana tevijjādiguṇayuttānaṃ āgamādhigamasampattiyā ukkaṃsagatattā saṅgītiyā bahupakārataṃ dasseti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ saṅgītikkhandhake, (pārā. 437) apaccakkhaṃ nāma natthi paguṇappavattibhāvato, samantapāsādikāyaṃ pana “asammukhā paṭiggahitaṃ nāma natthī”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā) vuttaṃ, taṃ “dve sahassāni bhikkhuto”ti vuttampi bhagavato santike paṭiggahitamevāti katvā vuttaṃ. Caturāsītisahassānīti dhammakkhandhe sandhāyāha. Pavattinoti paguṇāni. Ānandattherassa navappāyāya parisāya vibbhamanena mahākassapatthero evamāha – “na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsī”ti. Tattha mattanti pamāṇaṃ. Chandā āgamanaṃ viyāti padavibhāgo. “Kiñcāpi sekkho”ti idaṃ [M 1.0023] na sekkhānaṃ agatigamanasabbhāvena vuttaṃ, asekkhānameva pana uccinitattāti daṭṭhabbaṃ[P 1.0028]. Paṭhamamaggeneva hi cattāri agatigamanāni pahīyantīti. “Abhabbo chandā…pe… agatiṃ gantu”nti ca dhammasaṅgītiyā tassa yogyabhāvadassanena vijjamānaguṇakathanaṃ. Pariyattoti adhīto.

By the words, “He selected four hundred and ninety-nine… bearers of the entire ninefold teaching of the Teacher,” it is shown that the council was of great benefit. This is because, although there were individuals present up to the limit of Arahants of dry insight who possessed both learning and realization, it was especially due to those endowed with qualities such as the threefold knowledge along with the analytical knowledges, who had reached the pinnacle of accomplishment in learning and realization. This is stated in the Saṅgīti Khandhaka. There is nothing called “not directly perceived” because of its being well-practiced and current. However, in the Samantapāsādikā, it is said, “There is nothing called ‘received without being present.’” That is said by considering that even what was taught to the “two thousand bhikkhus” was indeed received in the presence of the Blessed One. “Eighty-four thousand” refers to the sections of the Dhamma. “Current” means well-practiced. Due to the Venerable Ānanda's agitation in the assembly, which was mostly new, the Venerable Mahākassapa said, “This young man does not know moderation.” Here, “moderation” means measure. “As if coming out of desire” is the word-division. “Although a trainee”—this is not said to imply that trainees are capable of going to wrong paths, but it should be understood that only non-trainees (arahants) were being selected. For the four wrong paths are abandoned by the first path itself. “He is incapable of… going to a wrong path out of desire”—this is a statement of his existing qualities, showing his suitability for the recitation of the Dhamma. “Learned” means studied.

Gāvo [V 1.0022] caranti etthāti gocaro, gocaro viya gocaro, bhikkhācaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ. Visabhāgapuggalo subhaddasadiso. Sattipañjaranti sattikhaggādihatthehi purisehi mallarājūnaṃ bhagavato dhātuārakkhakaraṇaṃ sandhāyāha. Taṃ palibodhaṃ chinditvā taṃ karaṇīyaṃ karotūti saṅgāhakena chinditabbaṃ chinditvā ekantakaraṇīyaṃ karotūti attho. Mahājananti bahujanaṃ. Gandhakuṭiṃ vanditvā paribhogacetiyabhāvatoti adhippāyo. Yathā tanti yathā aññopi yathāvuttasabhāvo, evanti attho. Saṃvejesīti “nanu bhagavatā paṭikacceva akkhātaṃ – ‘sabbeheva piyehi manāpehi nānābhāvo vinābhāvo’”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.183; saṃ. ni. 5.379; a. ni. 10.48; cūḷava. 437) saṃvegaṃ janesi. Ussannadhātukanti upacitadosaṃ. Bhesajjamattāti appakaṃ bhesajjaṃ. Appattho hi ayaṃ mattā-saddo, “mattāsukhapariccāgo”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 290) viya. Dutiyadivaseti devatāya saṃvejitadivasato, jetavanavihāraṃ paviṭṭhadivasato vā dutiyadivase. Āṇāva cakkaṃ āṇācakkaṃ.

"Cows wander here, hence 'gocara' (pasture); 'gocara' is like a pasture, meaning a place for alms-seeking. A person of dissimilar nature is like Subhadda. "The cage of spears" refers to the Malla kings having men holding spears, swords, and the like, guarding the relics of the Blessed One. Having cut off that obstacle, let him accomplish that task—thus, having cut off what should be cut off by the compiler, let him accomplish what is exclusively to be done—this is the meaning. "The great multitude" means many people. Having paid homage to the perfumed chamber, intending it as a shrine of use—this is the purport. "As in the text," and as in other things of the nature described—such is the meaning. "He stirred urgency" by saying, "Indeed, the Blessed One foretold from the beginning: 'All that is dear and pleasing is subject to separation, subject to becoming otherwise.'" "With accumulated humors" means with accumulated faults. "A little medicine" means a small amount of medicine. For this word "mattā" means 'little', as in "the relinquishment of moderate pleasures" and similar phrases. "On the second day" means the day after being stirred by the deity, or the second day after entering the Jetavana Monastery. "The wheel of command" is the command-wheel.

Etadagganti eso aggo. Liṅgavipallāsena hi ayaṃ niddeso. Yadidanti ca yo ayaṃ, yadidaṃ khandhapañcakanti vā yojetabbaṃ. “Paṭhamaṃ [P 1.0029] āvuso upāli pārājikaṃ kattha paññatta”nti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu tassa saṅgītiyā purimakāle paṭhamabhāvo na yuttoti? No na yutto, bhagavatā paññattānukkamena pātimokkhuddesānukkamena ca paṭhamabhāvassa siddhattā. Yebhuyyena hi tīṇi piṭakāni bhagavato dharamānakāle ṭhitānukkameneva saṅgītāni, visesato vinayābhidhammapiṭakānīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Vatthumpi pucchī”tiādi ‘kattha paññatta’ntiādinā dassitena saha tadavasiṭṭhampi saṅgahetvā dassanavasena vuttaṃ. Paṭhamapārājiketi paṭhamapārājikapāḷiyaṃ (pārā. 24), tenevāha – “na hi tathāgatā ekabyañjanampi niratthakaṃ vadantī”ti.

"This is the foremost" means this is the highest. This explanation is due to the inversion of grammatical gender. The phrase "yadidaṃ" should be connected with "yo ayaṃ" or "that which is the five aggregates." "Why is it said, ‘Friend Upāli, where was the first pārājika rule laid down?’? Isn’t it inappropriate for it to be considered first at the time of the recitation?” It is not inappropriate, because the first position is established by the order of the Blessed One’s enactments and the sequence of reciting the Pātimokkha. Indeed, for the most part, the three Piṭakas were compiled following the order maintained during the Blessed One’s lifetime, especially the Vinaya and Abhidhamma Piṭakas—this should be understood. "The question about the incident, etc.," is stated by way of showing, including what remains along with what is shown by "where was it laid down," etc. "The first pārājika" means in the text of the first pārājika (Pārā. 24), therefore he said: "For the Tathāgatas do not speak even a single syllable without meaning."

Jātakādike [M 1.0024] khuddakanikāyapariyāpanne, yebhuyyena ca dhammaniddesabhūte tādise abhidhammapiṭake saṅgaṇhituṃ yuttaṃ, na pana dīghanikāyādippakāre suttantapiṭake, nāpi paññattiniddesabhūte vinayapiṭaketi dīghabhāṇakā “jātakādīnaṃ abhidhammapiṭake saṅgaho”ti vadanti. Cariyāpiṭakabuddhavaṃsānañcettha aggahaṇaṃ, jātakagatikattā. Majjhimabhāṇakā pana “aṭṭhuppattivasena desitānaṃ jātakādīnaṃ yathānulomadesanābhāvato tādise suttantapiṭake saṅgaho yutto, na pana sabhāvadhammaniddesabhūte yathādhammasāsane abhidhammapiṭake”ti jātakādīnaṃ suttantapiṭakapariyāpannataṃ kathayanti. Tattha ca yuttaṃ vicāretvā gahetabbaṃ.

Because it is proper to include in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka the Jātaka and similar texts, which are included in the Khuddaka Nikāya and are for the most part expositions of the Dhamma—but not in the Suttanta Piṭaka like the Dīgha Nikāya and others, nor in the Vinaya Piṭaka, which is an exposition of rules—the Dīghabhāṇakas say: 'The inclusion of the Jātaka and similar texts is in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.' The non-inclusion of the Cariyāpiṭaka and Buddhavaṃsa here is because they are of the Jātaka type. On the other hand, the Majjhimabhāṇakas assert that the Jātaka and similar texts are included in the Suttanta Piṭaka, arguing, "Since the Jātaka and similar texts are taught in terms of events of occurrence, and because their teaching is not in accordance with the natural order of phenomena, they should be included in the Suttanta Piṭaka, not in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, which is in the nature of an exposition of the essential nature of phenomena, according to the true doctrine." In this matter, one should carefully consider and adopt what is appropriate.

Evaṃ [V 1.0023] nimittapayojanakāladesakārakakaraṇappakārehi paṭhamaṃ saṅgītiṃ dassetvā idāni tattha vavatthāpitasiddhesu dhammavinayesu nānappakārakosallatthaṃ ekavidhādibhede dassetuṃ “evameta”ntiādimāha. Tattha vimuttirasanti vimuttiguṇaṃ, vimuttisampattikaṃ vā, aggaphalanipphādanato, vimuttikiccaṃ vā, kilesānaṃ [P 1.0030] accantaṃ vimuttisampādanato. Keci pana “vimuttiassāda”nti vadanti.

Having first shown the initial recitation by means of sign, purpose, time, place, agent, instrument, and manner, now, in order to show the different kinds of skill regarding the Dhamma and Vinaya that were established there, in terms of their divisions beginning with the onefold, he said, "Thus is this," and so on. Here, "the taste of liberation" refers to the quality of liberation, or the accomplishment of liberation, because of accomplishing the highest fruit, or the function of liberation, because of bringing about complete liberation from the defilements. But some say, "the enjoyment of liberation."

Kiñcāpi avisesena sabbampi buddhavacanaṃ kilesavinayanena vinayo, yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne apāyapatanādito dhāraṇena dhammo, idhādhippete pana dhammavinaye niddhāretuṃ “tattha vinayapiṭaka”ntiādimāha. Avasesaṃ buddhavacanaṃ dhammo, khandhādivasena sabhāvadhammadesanābāhullato. Atha vā yadipi dhammoyeva vinayopi, pariyattiyādibhāvato, vinayasaddasannidhāne pana bhinnādhikaraṇabhāvena payutto dhamma-saddo vinayatantividhuraṃ tantiṃ dīpeti yathā “puññañāṇasambhārā, gobalibaddha”nti ca.

Although all the Buddha's word is, without distinction, discipline (vinaya) because it tames defilements, and Dhamma because it protects one who practices as instructed from falling into the states of loss, here, however, in what is intended, he said, "There, the Vinaya Piṭaka," and so on, to distinguish it. The remaining Buddha's word is Dhamma, due to the abundance of teachings on the nature of phenomena like the aggregates and so on. Or, although the Vinaya is also Dhamma, because of its nature as learning and so on, nevertheless, when the word 'Dhamma' is used in proximity to the word 'Vinaya,' it, employed with a separate sense, indicates a text distinct from the Vinaya texts, just as in "merit and knowledge as requisites," and "a cow and a bullock."

“Anekajātisaṃsāra”nti ayaṃ gāthā bhagavatā attano sabbaññutañāṇapadaṭṭhānaṃ arahattappattiṃ paccavekkhantena ekūnavīsatimassa paccavekkhaṇañāṇassa anantaraṃ bhāsitā. Tenāha “idaṃ paṭhamabuddhavacana”nti. Idaṃ kira sabbabuddhehi avijahitaṃ udānaṃ. Ayamassa saṅkhepattho – ahaṃ imassa attabhāvagehassa kārakaṃ taṇhāvaḍḍhakiṃ gavesanto yena ñāṇena taṃ daṭṭhuṃ sakkā, tassa bodhiñāṇassatthāya dīpaṅkarapādamūle katābhinīhāro [M 1.0025] ettakaṃ kālaṃ anekajātisaṃsāraṃ anekajātisatasahassasaṅkhyaṃ saṃsāravaṭṭaṃ anibbisaṃ taṃ ñāṇaṃ avindanto alabhantoyeva sandhāvissaṃ saṃsariṃ. Yasmā jarāvyādhimaraṇamissatāya jāti nāmesā punappunaṃ upagantuṃ dukkhā, na ca sā tasmiṃ adiṭṭhe nivattati, tasmā taṃ gavesanto sandhāvissanti attho. Diṭṭhosīti idāni mayā sabbaññutañāṇaṃ paṭivijjhantena diṭṭho asi. Puna gehanti puna imaṃ attabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ mama gehaṃ. Na kāhasi na karissasi. Tava sabbā avasesākilesaphāsukā mayā bhaggā. Imassa tayā katassa attabhāvagehassa kūṭaṃ avijjāsaṅkhātaṃ kaṇṇikamaṇḍalaṃ visaṅkhataṃ viddhaṃsitaṃ. Visaṅkhāraṃ nibbānaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇavasena gataṃ anupaviṭṭhaṃ idāni mama cittaṃ, ahañca [P 1.0031] taṇhānaṃ khayasaṅkhātaṃ arahattamaggaṃ ajjhagā adhigato pattosmīti. Ayaṃ manasā pavattitadhammānamādi. “Yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā”ti (udā. 1, 2, 3) ayaṃ pana vācāya pavattitadhammānaṃ ādīti vadanti. Antojappanavasena kira bhagavā “anekajātisaṃsāra”ntiādimāha (dha. pa. 153). “Pāṭipadadivase”ti idaṃ “sabbaññubhāvappattassā”ti [V 1.0024] na etena sambandhitabbaṃ, “paccavekkhantassa uppannā”ti etena pana sambandhitabbaṃ. Visākhapuṇṇamāyameva hi bhagavā paccūsasamaye sabbaññutaṃ pattoti.

"Through many a birth in saṃsāra" — this verse was spoken by the Blessed One while reviewing his attainment of arahantship, which was the basis for his omniscient knowledge, immediately after the nineteenth knowledge of reflection. Therefore, it is said, "This is the first utterance of the Buddha." This, indeed, is the exclamation common to all Buddhas. The concise meaning is this: Seeking the maker of this house of existence—craving, the builder—having made the aspiration at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha for the sake of that enlightenment-knowledge by which it is possible to see him, I wandered through saṃsāra for an incalculable length of time, birth after birth, hundreds of thousands of existences, unable to find or attain that knowledge. Because birth, bound up with aging, sickness, and death, is painful to undergo again and again, and because it does not cease until that maker is seen, I wandered in search of it. "Now you are seen" — now, as I penetrated omniscient knowledge, you have been seen. "No more house-building" — no more will you construct this house of existence for me. All your remaining defilement-rafters have been destroyed by me. The ridgepole of this house of existence you built—the pinnacle-circle, which is ignorance—has been dismantled, demolished. My mind has now entered the unconditioned, Nibbāna, as its object, and I have reached, attained, the path of arahantship, which is the destruction of craving. This is the beginning of the Dhamma unfolding in the mind. "When the Dhammas become manifest" (Udāna 1, 2, 3) — this, they say, is the beginning of the Dhamma unfolding in speech. The Blessed One, they say, spoke these words beginning with "Through many a birth in saṃsāra" through inner reflection (Dhammapada 153). "On the first day of the lunar fortnight" — this should not be connected with "the attainment of omniscience," but with "the reflection that arose for one who was reflecting." For the Blessed One attained omniscience at dawn on the full moon of Visākha.

Vayadhammāti aniccalakkhaṇamukhena dukkhānattalakkhaṇampi saṅkhārānaṃ vibhāveti “yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhaṃ, yaṃ dukkhaṃ tadanattā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.15; paṭi. ma. 2.10) vacanato. Lakkhaṇattayavibhāvananayeneva ca tadārammaṇaṃ vipassanaṃ dassento sabbatitthiyānaṃ avisayabhūtaṃ buddhāveṇikaṃ catusaccakammaṭṭhānādhiṭṭhānaṃ aviparītaṃ nibbānagāminippaṭipadaṃ pakāsetīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Idāni tattha sammāpaṭipattiyaṃ niyojeti “appamādena sampādethā”ti. Atha vā “vayadhammā saṅkhārā”ti etena saṅkhepena saṃvejetvā “appamādena sampādethā”ti saṅkhepeneva niravasesaṃ sammāpaṭipattiṃ dasseti. Appamādapadañhi sikkhāttayasaṅgahitaṃ kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ sāsanaṃ pariyādiyitvā tiṭṭhatīti.

“All conditioned things are subject to decay” reveals, through the characteristic of impermanence, the characteristics of suffering and non-self in formations, as stated in the words: “What is impermanent is suffering, and what is suffering is non-self” (Saṃ. Ni. 3.15; Paṭi. Ma. 2.10). And by demonstrating insight meditation having that as its object, through the method of revealing the three characteristics, it should be understood that it proclaims the path leading to Nibbāna—undistorted, unique to the Buddhas, beyond the scope of all other sects, and grounded in the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths. Now, it directs one toward right practice with the words: “Strive on with diligence.” Alternatively, having stirred spiritual urgency with the brief statement, “All conditioned things are subject to decay,” it then presents the entirety of right practice concisely with the words: “Strive on with diligence.” For the term “diligence” stands, having encompassed the entire and complete teaching, which is comprised of the threefold training.

Paṭhamasaṅgītiyaṃ asaṅgītaṃ saṅgītikkhandhakakathāvatthuppakaraṇādi. Keci pana “subhasuttampi (dī. ni. 1.444) paṭhamasaṅgītiyaṃ asaṅgīta”nti vadanti, taṃ pana na yujjati. Paṭhamasaṅgītito [M 1.0026] puretarameva hi āyasmatā ānandena jetavane viharantena subhassa māṇavassa bhāsitanti.

In the First Council, what was not recited were the Saṅgīti Sutta, the Khandhakas, the Kathāvatthu, and other treatises. However, some say that the Subha Sutta (Dī. Ni. 1.444) was also not recited in the First Council, but this is not correct. For it was spoken by the venerable Ānanda to the young man Subha while dwelling in Jetavana even before the First Council took place.

Daḷhikammasithilīkaraṇappayojanā yathākkamaṃ pakatisāvajjapaṇṇattisāvajjesu sikkhāpadesu. Tenāti vividhanayattādinā. Etanti vividhavisesanayattāti gāthāvacanaṃ. Etassāti vinayassa.

The purposes of strengthening and loosening are, respectively, with regard to the training rules concerning what is naturally blameworthy and what is blameworthy by enactment. The word 'tena' (by that) refers to 'by various methods and so on.' The word 'etaṃ' (this) refers to the statement of the verse concerning various distinguishing methods. The word 'etassa' (of this) refers to the Vinaya.

Attatthaparatthādibhedeti [P 1.0032] yo taṃ suttaṃ sajjhāyati, suṇāti, vāceti, cinteti, deseti ca, suttena saṅgahito sīlādiattho tassāpi hoti, tena parassa sādhetabbato parassāpi hotīti, tadubhayaṃ taṃ suttaṃ sūceti dīpeti. Tathā diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaṃ lokiyalokuttarañcāti evamādibhede atthe ādi-saddena saṅgaṇhāti. Attha-saddo cāyaṃ hitapariyāyavacanaṃ, na bhāsitatthavacanaṃ, yadi siyā, suttaṃ attanopi bhāsitatthaṃ sūceti, parassāpīti ayamattho vutto siyā. Suttena ca yo attho pakāsito so tasseva hotīti, na tena parattho sūcito hoti, tena sūcetabbassa paratthassa nivattetabbassa abhāvā atthagahaṇañca na kattabbaṃ. Attatthaparatthavinimmuttassa bhāsitatthassa abhāvā ādiggahaṇañca na kattabbaṃ. Tasmā yathāvuttassa hitapariyāyassa atthassa sutte asambhavato suttadhārassa puggalassa vasena attatthaparatthā vuttā.

One who recites, listens to, repeats, contemplates, and teaches that sutta, the meaning of virtue and so on, included in the sutta, belongs also to him. Since it should be accomplished for another, it belongs also to another. Thus, the sutta indicates and illuminates both. In this way, with the term “ādi,” meanings such as the visible-condition benefit, the future-condition benefit, the mundane, and the supramundane are included. This term “attha” (meaning) here refers to the synonym of benefit, not to the meaning of what is spoken. If it were, the sutta would indicate the spoken meaning for oneself and also for another—this meaning would have been stated. Moreover, the meaning explained by the sutta belongs only to it. It does not indicate a meaning for another, because there is no need to indicate or reject the meaning for another; nor should the grasping of meaning be done. Since there is no spoken meaning devoid of self-benefit or other-benefit, the inclusion of “ādi” should not be done. Therefore, because the synonym of benefit, as stated, cannot arise from the sutta itself, the self-benefit and other-benefit are stated in terms of the individual who retains the sutta.

Atha [V 1.0025] vā suttaṃ anapekkhitvā ye attatthādayo atthappabhedā vuttā “na haññadatthatthipasaṃsalābhā”ti etassa padassa niddese (mahāni. 63; cūḷani. 85) “attattho, parattho, ubhayattho, diṭṭhadhammiko attho, samparāyiko attho, uttāno attho, gambhīro attho, gūḷho attho, paṭicchanno attho, neyyo attho, nīto attho, anavajjo attho, nikkileso attho, vodāno attho, paramattho”ti te suttaṃ sūcetīti attho. Imasmiṃ atthavikappe attha-saddo bhāsitatthapariyāyopi hoti. Ettha hi purimakā pañca atthappabhedā hitapariyāyā, tato pare cha bhāsitatthabhedā, pacchimakā pana ubhayasabhāvā. Tattha duradhigamatāya vibhāvane aladdhagādho gambhīro. Na vivaṭo gūḷho. Mūludakādayo viya paṃsunā akkharasannivesādinā tirohito paṭicchanno[M 1.0027]. Niddhāretvā [P 1.0033] ñāpetabbo neyyo. Yathārutavasena veditabbo nīto. Anavajjanikkilesavodānā pariyāyavasena vuttā, kusalavipākakiriyādhammavasena vā. Paramattho nibbānaṃ, dhammānaṃ aviparītasabhāvo eva vā. Atha vā “attanā ca appiccho hotī”ti attatthaṃ, “appicchākathañca paresaṃ kattā hotī”ti paratthaṃ sūceti. Evaṃ “attanā ca pāṇātipātā paṭivirato hotī”tiādi (a. ni. 4.99, 265) suttāni yojetabbāni. Vinayābhidhammehi ca visesetvā sutta-saddassa attho vattabbo. Tasmā veneyyajjhāsayavasappavattāya desanāya attahitaparahitatādīni sātisayaṃ pakāsitāni hoti tapparabhāvato, na āṇādhammasabhāvavasappavattāyāti idameva ca “atthānaṃ sūcanato sutta”nti vuttaṃ.

Alternatively, independently of the sutta, the various categories of meaning, such as benefit for oneself, etc., are stated: “Not for the sake of killing, stealing, praise, or gain”—in the explanation of this phrase (Mahāni. 63; Cūḷani. 85), “benefit for oneself, benefit for others, benefit for both, visible-in-this-life benefit, future benefit, obvious benefit, profound benefit, hidden benefit, concealed benefit, inferable benefit, directly expressed benefit, blameless benefit, stainless benefit, purified benefit, ultimate benefit”—these indicate the sutta. In this analysis of meaning, the term 'attha' also has the meaning of what is spoken. Here, the first five categories of benefit pertain to welfare, the next six pertain to the divisions of spoken meaning, and the last ones pertain to the nature of both. Among these, 'profound' is difficult to understand due to its depth. 'Hidden' means not openly revealed. 'Concealed' is obscured like roots and water covered by dust, or by the arrangement of letters, etc. 'Inferable' must be made known through deduction. 'Directly expressed' is to be known as heard. 'Blameless,' 'stainless,' and 'purified' are stated figuratively, or in terms of wholesome results and effective actions. The 'ultimate benefit' is Nibbāna, or simply the non-perverted nature of phenomena. Alternatively, “being oneself of few wishes” indicates benefit for oneself, “and being a doer of talk on fewness of wishes for others” indicates benefit for others. Similarly, suttas such as “being oneself abstaining from killing living beings,” etc. (A. Ni. 4.99, 265) should be connected. Moreover, the meaning of the term 'sutta' should be stated by distinguishing it from Vinaya and Abhidhamma. Therefore, in teachings proceeding in accordance with the disposition of the one to be taught, self-benefit, the benefit of others, etc., are revealed especially due to the prominence of that, not in teachings proceeding in accordance with the nature of command and principle. Hence, it is said: “A sutta is that which indicates meanings.”

Sutte ca āṇādhammasabhāvā ca veneyyajjhāsayaṃ anuvattanti, na vinayābhidhammesu viya veneyyajjhāsayo āṇādhammasabhāve. Tasmā veneyyānaṃ ekantahitapaṭilābhasaṃvattanikā suttantadesanā hotīti “suvuttā cetthā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pasavatīti phalati. “Suttāṇā”ti etassa atthaṃ pakāsetuṃ “suṭṭhu ca ne tāyatī”ti vuttaṃ. Attatthādividhānesu ca suttassa pamāṇabhāvo, attatthādīnañca saṅgāhakattaṃ yojetabbaṃ tadatthappakāsanapadhānattā suttassa. Vinayābhidhammehi visesanañca yojetabbaṃ. Etanti “atthānaṃ sūcanato”tiādikaṃ atthavacanaṃ. Etassāti suttassa.

In the Suttas, the nature of command and principle accords with the disposition of those to be trained, unlike in the Vinaya and Abhidhamma where the disposition of those to be trained accords with the nature of command and principle. Therefore, the teaching of the suttas leads solely to the attainment of benefit for those to be trained—hence it is said, “Well spoken here,” and so on. It procreates—it bears fruit. To explain the meaning of 'suttāṇa' (sutta as protection), it is said, “And it well protects them.” Moreover, in the arrangement of meanings such as benefit for oneself, the sutta serves as the standard, and one should connect its role of gathering the meanings for oneself and so on, because the sutta primarily aims at clarifying that meaning. One should also connect the distinction from the Vinaya and Abhidhamma. The word 'etaṃ' (this) refers to the statement of meaning such as “because of indicating the meanings.” The word 'etassa' (of this) refers to the sutta.

Abhikkamantīti ettha abhi-saddo kamanakiriyāya vuddhibhāvaṃ atirekataṃ dīpeti, abhiññātā abhilakkhitāti ettha ñāṇalakkhaṇakiriyānaṃ supākaṭatāvisesaṃ, abhikkantenāti [P 1.0034] ettha kantiyā adhikattaṃ visiṭṭhatanti yuttaṃ kiriyāvisesakattā upasaggassa. Abhirājā abhivinayeti pana pūjitaparicchinnesu rājavinayesu abhi-saddo pavattatīti kathametaṃ yujjeyyāti[V 1.0026]? Pūjanaparicchedanakiriyādīpanato, tāhi ca kiriyāhi rājavinayānaṃ yuttattā. Ettha hi atimālādīsu ati-saddo viya, abhi-saddo yathā saha sādhanena kiriyaṃ vadatīti abhirājaabhivinaya-saddā siddhā, evaṃ abhidhammasadde abhi-saddo saha sādhanena vuḍḍhiyādikiriyaṃ dīpetīti ayamattho dassitoti daṭṭhabbo.

In 'abhikkamanti' (they go forth), the prefix 'abhi-' indicates an increase or excess in the action of going. In 'abhiññātā abhilakkhitā' (well-known, well-marked), it signifies a distinct clarity and excellence in the actions of knowing and marking. In 'abhikkantena' (by one who is attractive), it conveys the surpassing or distinguished nature of attraction. This is appropriate because the prefix serves to specify the action. But how can this be justified in 'abhirājā' (supreme king) and 'abhivinaya' (higher discipline), where the prefix 'abhi-' applies to kings and disciplines that are honored and defined? It is because it indicates the act of honoring and defining, and such actions are fitting for kings and disciplines. Here, just as the prefix 'ati-' in words like 'atimāla' (excessive garland), the prefix 'abhi-' conveys an action along with its means, and so the words 'abhirāja' and 'abhivinaya' are established. Similarly, in the term 'abhidhamma,' the prefix 'abhi-' signifies an action of growth and so on, along with its means—this is the meaning to be understood here.

Bhāvanāpharaṇavuḍḍhīhi [M 1.0028] vuḍḍhimantopi dhammā vuttā. Ārammaṇādīhīti ārammaṇasampayuttakammadvārapaṭipadādīhi. Avisiṭṭhanti aññamaññavisiṭṭhesu vinayasuttābhidhammesu avisiṭṭhaṃ samānaṃ. Taṃ piṭakasaddanti attho. Yathāvuttenāti “evaṃ duvidhatthenā”tiādinā vuttappakārena.

Qualities (dhammas) are also said to be endowed with growth through the increase of development and pervasion. By 'ārammaṇādīhi' (by means of the object, etc.) is meant by means of the object, association, action-door, and practice, etc. 'Avisiṭṭhaṃ' (not distinct) means being not distinct, being the same, among the Vinaya, Suttas, and Abhidhamma, which are distinguished from each other. That is the meaning of the word 'Piṭaka.' By 'yathāvuttena' (as stated) is meant in the manner explained by 'thus with twofold meaning,' and so on.

Kathetabbānaṃ atthānaṃ desakāyattena āṇādividhinā atisajjanaṃ pabodhanaṃ desanā. Sāsitabbapuggalagatena yathāparādhādisāsitabbabhāvena anusāsanaṃ vinayanaṃ sāsanaṃ. Kathetabbassa saṃvarāsaṃvarādino atthassa kathanaṃ vacanapaṭibaddhatākaraṇaṃ kathā. Kathīyati vā etthāti kathā. Saṃvarāsaṃvarassa kathā saṃvarāsaṃvarakathā. Esa nayo itaresupi. Bheda-saddo visuṃ visuṃ yojetabbo “desanābhedaṃ sāsanabhedaṃ kathābhedañca yathārahaṃ paridīpaye”ti. Bhedanti ca nānattanti attho. Sikkhā ca pahānāni ca gambhīrabhāvo ca sikkhāppahānagambhīrabhāvaṃ, tañca paridīpaye. Ettha yathāti upārambhanissaraṇadhammakosarakkhaṇahetupariyāpuṇanaṃ [P 1.0035] suppaṭipatti duppaṭipattīti etehi pakārehi. Āṇaṃ paṇetuṃ arahatīti āṇāraho sammāsambuddhattā. Vohāraparamatthānampi sabbhāvato āha āṇābāhullatoti. Ito paresupi eseva nayo. Pacurāparādhā seyyasakādayo. Ajjhāsayo āsayova atthato diṭṭhi, ñāṇañca. Vuttañcetaṃ –

Desanā (teaching) is the sending forth and awakening of matters to be spoken, on the part of the teacher, through the method of command and so forth. Sāsana (instruction) is the admonishing, training, and disciplining of individuals who should be admonished, according to their faults and so forth. Kathā (discourse) is the speaking of matters concerning restraint and non-restraint, the act of making speech connected to the subject. Or, kathā is that in which something is spoken. The discourse on restraint and non-restraint is the saṃvarāsaṃvarakathā. This is the method for others as well. The word 'bheda' (division) should be applied separately: “He should explain the divisions of teaching, instruction, and discourse as is appropriate.” And 'bheda' means diversity. 'Sikkhāppahānagambhīrabhāvaṃ' means training, abandonments, and profundity, and he should explain that. Here, 'yathā' (as is appropriate) refers to methods such as reproach, escape, the treasury of Dhamma, protection, cause, mastery, good practice, and bad practice. 'Āṇāraho' (worthy of command) means one who is worthy of issuing commands, being a Sammāsambuddha. He speaks of conventional and ultimate truths in their real nature due to the abundance of his command. This is the same method for others as well. Those with many faults are Seyyasaka and others. Ajjhāsaya (inclination) is, in meaning, simply disposition (āsaya), which is view and knowledge. And this was said—

“Sassatucchedadiṭṭhi ca, khanti cevānulomike;

Yathābhūtañca yaṃ ñāṇaṃ, etaṃ āsayasaddita”nti. (visuddhi. ṭī. 1.136);

“The view of eternalism and annihilationism, and forbearance in what is agreeable; And knowledge as it really is—this is called disposition.”

Anusayā kāmarāgabhavarāgadiṭṭhipaṭighavicikicchāmānāvijjāvasena satta anāgatā kilesā, atītā paccuppannā ca tatheva vuccanti. Na hi kālabhedena dhammānaṃ sabhāvabhedo atthīti. Cariyāti cha mūlacariyā, antarabhedena anekavidhā, saṃsaggavasena tesaṭṭhi honti. Te pana amhehi asammohantaradhānasuttaṭīkāyaṃ vibhāgato dassitā, atthikehi tato gahetabbā. Atha vā cariyāti caritaṃ, taṃ sucaritaduccaritavasena duvidhaṃ. Adhimutti nāma sattānaṃ pubbaparicayavasena abhiruci, sā duvidhā hīnapaṇītabhedena. Ghanavinibbhogābhāvato diṭṭhimānataṇhāvasena [V 1.0027] “ahaṃ mamā”ti saññino. Mahanto saṃvaro asaṃvaro. Buddhiattho hi aya’makāro yathā “asekkhā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. 11).

The latent tendencies are seven future defilements, namely, sensual desire, desire for existence, views, aversion, doubt, conceit, and ignorance. Past and present defilements are also called by the same name, for there is no difference in the nature of things based on a difference in time. Practices are the six root practices, which are of many kinds due to intermediate distinctions, and by association they become sixty-three. These have been shown in detail in our subcommentary on the Asammohantaradhānasutta, and those who are interested should take them from there. Alternatively, practice means behavior, which is of two kinds: good behavior and bad behavior. Inclination is the preference of beings based on past habits, and it is of two kinds: inferior and superior. Due to the lack of dispelling compactness, those who perceive 'I' and 'mine' do so by way of views, conceit, and craving. Great is restraint, and great is non-restraint. For this letter 'a' has the meaning of increase, as in 'asekkhā dhammā' (the qualities of those beyond training) (Dh. Sa. 11).

Tīsupi [M 1.0029] cetesu ete dhammatthadesanā paṭivedhāti ettha tantiattho tantidesanā tantiatthapaṭivedho ca tantivisayā hontīti vinayapiṭakādīnaṃ atthadesanāpaṭivedhādhārabhāvo [P 1.0036] yutto, piṭakāni pana tanti yevāti tesaṃ dhammādhārabhāvo kathaṃ yujjeyyāti? Tantisamudāyassa avayavatantiyā ādhārabhāvato. Avayavassa hi samudāyo ādhārabhāvena vuccati, yathā – “rukkhe sākhā”ti. Dhammādīnañca dukkhogāhabhāvato tehi vinayādayo gambhīrāti vinayādīnañca catubbidho gambhīrabhāvo vutto. Tasmā dhammādayo eva dukkhogāhattā gambhīrā, na vinayādayoti na codetabbametaṃ samukhena, visayavisayīmukhena ca vinayādīnaṃyeva gambhīrabhāvassa vuttattā. Dhammo hi vinayādayo, tesaṃ visayo attho, dhammatthavisayā ca desanāpaṭivedhoti. Tattha paṭivedhassa dukkarabhāvato dhammatthānaṃ, desanāñāṇassa dukkarabhāvato desanāya ca dukkhogāhabhāvo veditabbo, paṭivedhassa pana uppādetuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā, tabbisayañāṇuppattiyā ca dukkarabhāvato dukkhogāhatā veditabbā.

In these three, these—Dhamma, meaning, teaching, and penetration—[are found]. Here, the meaning of the text, the teaching of the text, and the penetration of the text’s meaning all pertain to the scope of the text. Thus, it is fitting that the Vinaya Piṭaka and others are the basis for teaching meaning and for penetration, but since the Piṭakas themselves are the text, how can they be the basis for the Dhamma? Because the collection of texts is the basis for its constituent parts. For the collection is called the basis of its parts, just as 'branches [are on] a tree.' And because the Dhamma and so on are difficult to fathom, the Vinaya and so on are profound, and the fourfold profundity of the Vinaya and others has been stated. Therefore, one should not object outright that only the Dhamma and others are profound due to being difficult to fathom, and not the Vinaya and others, because the profundity of the Vinaya and others is stated in terms of their respective objects and that which possesses the object. For the Dhamma is the Vinaya and so on; their object is the meaning; and teaching and penetration have Dhamma and meaning as their object. There, the difficult-to-fathom nature of Dhamma and meaning is to be understood from the difficulty of penetration, and that of teaching from the difficulty of the knowledge of teaching. Moreover, because penetration is impossible to generate, and because the arising of knowledge pertaining to its object is difficult, its difficult-to-fathom nature is to be understood.

“Hetumhi ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā”ti etena vacanena dhammassa hetubhāvo kathaṃ ñātabboti? “Dhammapaṭisambhidā”ti etassa samāsapadassa avayavapadatthaṃ dassentena “hetumhi ñāṇa”nti vuttattā. “Dhamme paṭisambhidā”ti ettha hi “dhamme”ti etassa atthaṃ dassentena “hetumhī”ti vuttaṃ, “paṭisambhidā”ti etassa ca atthaṃ dassentena “ñāṇa”nti. Tasmā hetudhamma-saddā ekatthā, ñāṇapaṭisambhidā-saddā cāti imamatthaṃ vadantena sādhito dhammassa hetubhāvo, atthassa hetuphalabhāvo ca evameva daṭṭhabbo.

“Knowledge in the cause is the analytical knowledge of Dhamma”—by this statement, how is the nature of Dhamma as cause to be understood? Because it is stated as “knowledge in the cause” by one who shows the meaning of the constituent words of the compound word “analytical knowledge of Dhamma.” For here, in the expression “analytical knowledge in Dhamma,” the meaning of “in Dhamma” is shown by the term “in the cause,” and the meaning of “analytical knowledge” by the term “knowledge.” Therefore, the words 'cause' and 'Dhamma' have the same meaning, and so do the words 'knowledge' and 'analytical knowledge'. By stating this meaning, the nature of Dhamma as cause is established, and the nature of the meaning as cause-and-effect should be seen in the same way.

Yathādhammanti cettha dhamma-saddo hetuṃ hetuphalañca sabbaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Sabhāvavācako hesa, na pariyattihetubhāvavācako, tasmā yathādhammanti yo yo avijjāsaṅkhārādidhammo[P 1.0037], tasmiṃ tasminti attho. Dhammānurūpaṃ vā yathādhammaṃ. Desanāpi hi paṭivedho viya aviparītasavisayavibhāvanato dhammānurūpaṃ pavattati, yato ‘aviparītābhilāpo’ti vuccati. Dhammābhilāpoti atthabyañjanako aviparītābhilāpo, etena “tatra dhammaniruttābhilāpe ñāṇaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 718) ettha vuttaṃ sabhāvadhammaniruttiṃ dasseti, saddasabhāvattā desanāya. Tathā hi niruttipaṭisambhidāya [M 1.0030] parittārammaṇādibhāvo paṭisambhidāvibhaṅgapāḷiyaṃ (vibha. 749) vutto. Aṭṭhakathāyañca “taṃ sabhāvaniruttiṃ saddaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā”tiādinā (vibha. aṭṭha. 642) saddārammaṇatā [V 1.0028] dassitā. “Imassa atthassa ayaṃ saddo vācako”ti vacanavacanīye vavatthapetvā taṃtaṃvacanīya vibhāvanavasena pavattito hi saddo desanāti. “Anulomādivasena vā kathana”nti etena tassā dhammaniruttiyā abhilāpaṃ kathanaṃ tassa vacanassa pavattanaṃ dasseti. “Adhippāyo”ti etena “desanāti paññattī”ti etaṃ vacanaṃ dhammaniruttābhilāpaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na tabbinimuttaṃ paññattiṃ sandhāyāti dasseti.

Here, the term 'dhamma' in 'yathādhammanti' encompasses both cause and effect—everything. For it is a term that refers to intrinsic nature, not to the nature of being a cause for scriptural teaching. Therefore, 'yathādhammanti' means 'in accordance with each and every phenomenon, such as ignorance and formations.' Alternatively, 'yathādhammaṃ' means 'in accordance with the Dhamma.' For teaching, just like penetration, proceeds in a manner consistent with the Dhamma, because it clarifies its object without distortion—hence it is called 'undistorted speech.' 'Dhammābhilāpo' refers to undistorted speech that expresses both meaning and phrasing. By this, he explains the statement, 'Here, the knowledge of the language of the Dhamma is the analytical knowledge of language' (Vibh. 718), indicating the natural terminology of phenomena, since teaching has the nature of sound. Indeed, in the Vibhaṅga (Vibh. 749), it is stated that the analytical knowledge of language has limited objects, etc. And in the commentary (Vibh. Aṭṭha. 642), the fact that sound is the object is shown by the passage beginning, 'having made that natural language, which is sound, the object...' For teaching is the sound that proceeds by way of clarifying this or that expressible thing, after having determined the expression and the expressible thus: 'This sound conveys this meaning.' 'Or by speaking in accordance with sequence, etc.'—this indicates the utterance, the speaking, the production of that speech, which is the natural terminology of phenomena. 'Intention'—this shows that the statement, 'Teaching is designation,' is said with reference to the expression of the language of the Dhamma, not with reference to designation apart from it.

Nanu ca “dhammo tantī”ti imasmiṃ pakkhe dhammassa saddasabhāvattā dhammadesanānaṃ viseso na siyāti? Na, tesaṃ tesaṃ atthānaṃ bodhakabhāvena ñāto, uggahaṇādivasena ca pubbe vavatthāpito saddappabandho dhammo, pacchā paresaṃ avabodhanatthaṃ pavattito tadatthappakāsako [P 1.0038] saddo desanāti. Atha vā yathāvuttasaddasamuṭṭhāpako cittuppādo desanā, musāvādādayo viya. “Vacanassa pavattana”nti ca yathāvuttacittuppādavasena yujjati. So hi vacanaṃ pavatteti, tañca tena pavattīyati desīyati. “So ca lokiyalokuttaro”ti evaṃ vuttaṃ abhisamayaṃ yena pakārena abhisameti, yaṃ abhisameti, yo ca tassa sabhāvo, tehi pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ “visayato asammohato ca atthānurūpaṃ dhammesū”tiādimāha. Tattha hi visayato atthādianurūpaṃ dhammādīsu avabodho avijjādidhammasaṅkhārādiatthatadubhayapaññāpanārammaṇo lokiyo abhisamayo, asammohato atthādianurūpaṃ dhammādīsu avabodho nibbānārammaṇo maggasampayutto yathāvuttadhammatthapaññattīsu sammohaviddhaṃsano lokuttaro abhisamayoti. Abhisamayato aññampi paṭivedhatthaṃ dassetuṃ “tesaṃ tesaṃ vā”tiādimāha. ‘Paṭivedhanaṃ paṭivedho’ti iminā hi vacanatthena abhisamayo, ‘paṭivijjhīyatīti paṭivedho’ti iminā taṃtaṃrūpādidhammānaṃ aviparītasabhāvo ca “paṭivedho”ti vuccatīti.

But then, in this view that 'the Dhamma is the text,' since the Dhamma has the nature of sound, would there not be a distinction among Dhamma teachings? No. The Dhamma is a sequence of sounds, known as that which awakens understanding of various meanings and previously established by way of learning and so on. Afterwards, the sound that clarifies that meaning, set forth for the purpose of others' understanding, is the teaching. Alternatively, the mental process that produces the aforesaid sound is the teaching, just like false speech and so on. And 'the utterance of speech' is justified by way of the aforesaid mental process, for it produces speech, and that speech is produced and taught by it. To make clear by what manner one comprehends the comprehension thus stated as 'And that is both mundane and supramundane,' what one comprehends, and what its nature is, he says: 'in the Dhammas, in conformity with the meaning, from the standpoint of the object and from non-delusion,' etc. Herein, mundane comprehension is the understanding in the Dhammas and so on, in conformity with the meaning and so on, from the standpoint of the object, which has as its object the designation of the meaning of phenomena such as ignorance and formations, or of both. Supramundane comprehension is the understanding in the Dhammas and so on, in conformity with the meaning and so on, from the standpoint of non-delusion, which has Nibbāna as its object, is associated with the path, and dispels delusion in the aforesaid designations of Dhamma and meaning. To show another meaning of penetration apart from comprehension, he says: 'of these and those, or...' etc. For by this word-meaning, 'penetrating is penetration,' it is comprehension (abhisamaya). And by this, 'because it is thoroughly penetrated, it is penetration,' the undeviating nature of those various phenomena, such as form, etc., is also called 'penetration.'

Yathāvuttehi dhammādīhi piṭakānaṃ gambhīrabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “idāni yasmā etesu piṭakesū”tiādimāha. Yo cetthāti etesu taṃtaṃpiṭakagatesu dhammādīsu yo paṭivedho, etesu ca piṭakesu tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ yo aviparītasabhāvoti yojetabbaṃ. Dukkhogāhatā ca avijjāsaṅkhārādīnaṃ [M 1.0031] dhammatthānaṃ duppaṭivijjhatāya, tesaṃ paññāpanassa dukkarabhāvato taṃdesanāya, paṭivedhanasaṅkhātassa paṭivedhassa uppādanavisayikaraṇānaṃ asakkuṇeyyattā, aviparītasabhāvasaṅkhātassa paṭivedhassa duviññeyyatāya eva veditabbā.

To demonstrate the profundity of the Piṭakas by means of the aforesaid dhammas and so on, he now says, 'Now, because in these Piṭakas...' Herein, 'yo cettha' should be connected thus: whatever penetration there is into the dhammas and so on found in those respective Piṭakas, and whatever is the undeviating nature of those various dhammas in these Piṭakas. And the difficulty of fathoming is to be understood as due to the difficulty of penetrating the Dhamma-meaning of ignorance, formations, and so on; due to the difficulty of designating them, which is the teaching; due to the impossibility of making an object of the production of penetration, which is designated as 'penetrating;' and due to the difficulty of knowing the penetration, which is designated as 'undeviating nature.'

Yanti [P 1.0039] yaṃ pariyattiduggahaṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Atthanti bhāsitatthaṃ, payojanatthañca. Na upaparikkhantīti na vicārenti. Na nijjhānaṃ khamantīti nijjhānapaññaṃ nakkhamanti, nijjhāyitvā [V 1.0029] paññāya disvā rocetvā gahetabbā na hontīti adhippāyo. Itīti evaṃ etāya pariyattiyā. Vādappamokkhānisaṃsā attano upari parehi āropitavādassa niggahassa pamokkhappayojanā hutvā dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti, vādappamokkhā vā nindāpamokkhā. Yassa catthāyāti yassa ca sīlādipūraṇassa anupādāvimokkhassa vā atthāya dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti ñāyena pariyāpuṇantīti adhippāyo. Assāti assa dhammassa. Nānubhontīti na vindanti. Tesaṃ te dhammā duggahitattā upārambhamānadabbamakkhapalāsādihetubhāvena dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanti. Bhaṇḍāgāre niyutto bhaṇḍāgāriko, bhaṇḍāgāriko viya bhaṇḍāgāriko, dhammaratanānupālako. Aññatthaṃ anapekkhitvā bhaṇḍāgārikasseva sato pariyatti bhaṇḍāgārikapariyatti.

'Yaṃ' refers to what was said concerning the wrong grasping of the scriptures. 'Atthaṃ' refers to both the meaning of what is spoken and its purpose. 'They do not examine' means they do not investigate. 'They do not tolerate deep reflection' means they do not approve of wisdom born of reflection; the intention is that they are not to be accepted after reflecting, seeing with wisdom, and approving. 'Iti' means thus, by this scripture. With the benefit of freedom from disputes—having the purpose of liberation from the censure of accusations placed upon them by others—they learn the Dhamma; or, freedom from disputes is freedom from blame. 'For whose sake?'—for the sake of which fulfillment of virtue, etc., or for the sake of liberation without clinging, they learn the Dhamma; the intention is that they learn it properly. 'Assa' means of this Dhamma. 'They do not experience' means they do not find. For them, those teachings, being wrongly grasped, conduce to long-term harm and suffering, becoming causes for reproach, conceit, hypocrisy, denigration, rivalry, and so on. One appointed to the storehouse is a storekeeper. Like a storekeeper is a storekeeper, a guardian of the Dhamma-treasure. The learning of one who is merely a storekeeper, without regard for any other purpose, is the storekeeper's learning.

“Tāsaṃyevā”ti avadhāraṇaṃ pāpuṇitabbānaṃ chaḷabhiññācatuppaṭisambhidādīnaṃ vinaye pabhedavacanābhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Verañjakaṇḍe (pārā. 12) hi tisso vijjāva vibhattā. Dutiye pana “tāsaṃyevā”ti avadhāraṇaṃ catasso paṭisambhidā apekkhitvā kataṃ, na tisso vijjā. Tā hi chasu abhiññāsu antogadhāti sutte vibhattā yevāti.

'Of those very ones'—this specification is stated with reference to the absence of a detailed statement in the Vinaya concerning the things to be attained, namely, the six higher knowledges, the four analytical knowledges, and so on. For in the Verañja section (Pārā. 12), only the three true knowledges are analyzed. In the second case, however, the specification 'of those very ones' is made in consideration of the four analytical knowledges, not the three true knowledges. For these are included within the six higher knowledges and are thus analyzed in the Sutta.

Duggahitaṃ gaṇhāti, “tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi, yathā tadevidaṃ viññāṇaṃ sandhāvati saṃsarati anañña”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 1.396). Dhammacintanti [P 1.0040] dhammasabhāvavicāraṇaṃ, “cittuppādamatteneva dānaṃ hoti, sayameva cittaṃ attano ārammaṇaṃ hoti, sabbaṃ cittaṃ asabhāvadhammārammaṇa”nti ca evamādi. Tesanti tesaṃ piṭakānaṃ.

He grasps it wrongly, as in: 'As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this very consciousness that runs on and transmigrates, not another,' and so on (MN 38, M I 258). 'Dhammacintā' means investigation into the nature of phenomena, such as: 'Giving occurs by the mere arising of a thought; consciousness itself is its own object; all consciousness has as its object phenomena that are without intrinsic nature,' and so on. 'Tesaṃ' means 'of those Piṭakas.'

Etanti etaṃ buddhavacanaṃ. Atthānulomato anulomiko. Anulomikataṃyeva vibhāvetuṃ “kasmā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ekanikāyampīti ekasamūhampi[M 1.0032]. Poṇikā cikkhallikā ca khattiyā, tesaṃ nivāso poṇikanikāyo cikkhallikanikāyo ca.

'Etaṃ' means this, the word of the Buddha. It is conformable (anulomiko) because it conforms to the meaning. To clarify this very conformity, it is said, 'But why?' and so on. 'Ekanikāyampi' means even a single collection. Poṇikā and Cikkhallikā were khattiyas; their dwelling was the Poṇikanikāya and the Cikkhallikanikāya.

Navappabhedanti ettha kathaṃ navappabhedaṃ? Sagāthakañhi suttaṃ geyyaṃ, niggāthakañca suttaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ, tadubhayavinimuttañca suttaṃ udānādivisesasaññārahitaṃ natthi, yaṃ suttaṅgaṃ siyā, maṅgalasuttādīnañca (khu. pā. 5.2; su. ni. 225) suttaṅgasaṅgaho na siyā, gāthābhāvato, dhammapadādīnaṃ viya, geyyaṅgasaṅgaho vā siyā, sagāthakattā, sagāthavaggassa viya, tathā ubhatovibhaṅgādīsu sagāthakappadesānanti? Vuccate –

Herein, regarding 'of nine kinds,' how is it of nine kinds? For a sutta with verses is Geyya, and a sutta without verses is Veyyākaraṇa. But there exists no sutta that is free from both of these and also lacks a special designation such as Udāna, which could be a Suttaṅga. Furthermore, the Maṅgala Sutta and others could not be included in the Suttaṅga because they are in verse form, like the Dhammapada and other works; or else they would have to be included in the Geyyaṅga because they contain verses, like the Sagāthavagga. And what of the sections with verses in the Ubhatovibhaṅga and other texts? It is said—

“Suttanti [V 1.0030] sāmaññavidhi, visesavidhayo pare;

Sanimittā niruḷhattā sahatāññena nāññato”. (sārattha. ṭī. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā);

'Sutta' is the general category, the others are specific categories; they are distinguished by their characteristics, by being established through usage, by association with another, and not from another.

Sabbassāpi hi buddhavacanassa suttanti ayaṃ sāmaññavidhi. Tenevāha āyasmā mahākaccāno nettiyaṃ – “navavidhasuttantapariyeṭṭhī”ti (netti. saṅgahavāra). “Ettakaṃ tassa bhagavato suttāgataṃ suttapariyāpannaṃ (pāci. 255, 1242), sakavāde pañcasuttasatānī”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā; kathā. aṭṭha. nidānakathā) evamādi ca etassa atthassa sādhakaṃ.

For 'sutta' is the general category for all the Buddha's word. For that reason the Venerable Mahākaccāna said in the Netti: 'the ninefold search for the suttanta.' The statements, 'This much of the Blessed One's teaching has come down as sutta, is included in the suttas,' and 'five hundred suttas in one's own doctrine,' and so on, are evidence for this meaning.

Visesavidhayo [P 1.0041] pare sanimittā tadekadesesu geyyādayo visesavidhayo tena tena nimittena patiṭṭhitā. Tathā hi geyyassa sagāthakattaṃ tabbhāvanimittaṃ. Lokepi hi sasilokaṃ sagāthakaṃ (netti. aṭṭha. 13) cuṇṇiyaganthaṃ ‘geyya’nti vadanti. Gāthāvirahe pana sati pucchaṃ katvā vissajjanabhāvo veyyākaraṇassa tabbhāvanimittaṃ. Pucchāvissajjanañhi ‘byākaraṇa’nti vuccati, byākaraṇameva veyyākaraṇaṃ. Evaṃ sante sagāthakādīnampi pucchaṃ katvā vissajjanavasena pavattānaṃ veyyākaraṇabhāvo āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati, geyyādisaññānaṃ anokāsabhāvato, ‘gāthāvirahe satī’ti visesitattā ca. Tathā hi dhammapadādīsu kevalaṃ gāthābandhesu, sagāthakattepi somanassañāṇamayikagāthāyuttesu, ‘vuttañheta’ntiādivacanasambandhesu, abbhutadhammapaṭisaṃyuttesu ca suttavisesesu yathākkamaṃ gāthāudānaitivuttakaabbhutadhammasaññā patiṭṭhitā, tathā satipi [M 1.0033] gāthābandhabhāve bhagavato atītāsu jātīsu cariyānubhāvappakāsakesu jātakasaññā, satipi pañhāvissajjanabhāve, sagāthakatte ca kesuci suttantesu vedassa labhāpanato vedallasaññā patiṭṭhitāti evaṃ tena tena sagāthakattādinā nimittena tesu tesu suttavisesesu geyyādisaññā patiṭṭhitāti visesavidhayo suttaṅgato pare geyyādayo. Yaṃ panettha geyyaṅgādinimittarahitaṃ, taṃ suttaṅgaṃ visesasaññāparihārena sāmaññasaññāya pavattanatoti. Nanu ca sagāthakaṃ suttaṃ geyyaṃ, niggāthakaṃ suttaṃ veyyākaraṇanti suttaṅgaṃ na sambhavatīti codanā tadavatthā vāti? Na tadavatthā, sodhitattā. Sodhitañhi pubbe gāthāvirahe sati pucchāvissajjanabhāvo veyyākaraṇassa tabbhāvanimittanti.

The others, Geyya and so on, are specific categories established in particular portions by this or that characteristic. For instance, the characteristic for Geyya is its having verses. In the world, too, a prose text with stanzas and verses is called 'geyya.' But when there are no verses, the characteristic for Veyyākaraṇa is the act of giving a reply to a question that has been posed. For a question and answer is called a 'byākaraṇa' (explanation), and Veyyākaraṇa is just that. If so, would texts with verses also become Veyyākaraṇa when they proceed by way of question and answer? They would not, because there is no opportunity for the designations Geyya, etc., and because of the qualification 'when there are no verses.' Thus, for certain specific suttas—such as the Dhammapada and others consisting only of verse compositions; those with verses of joy and knowledge; those connected with statements beginning 'Thus was it said...'; and those connected with wonderful and marvelous phenomena—the designations Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, and Abbhutadhamma are respectively established. Similarly, though they are verse compositions, those that illuminate the Blessed One's conduct and power in past lives receive the designation Jātaka. And though they have a question-and-answer format and verses, certain suttas receive the designation Vedalla because they bring about joy and understanding. In this way, by this or that characteristic—such as having verses—the designations Geyya and so on are established for those specific suttas. Thus Geyya and the others are specific categories apart from Suttaṅga. Whatever here is devoid of the characteristics of Geyyaṅga and so on, that is Suttaṅga, which proceeds by the general designation, having relinquished a specific designation. But is not the objection—'If a sutta with verses is Geyya, and a sutta without verses is Veyyākaraṇa, then Suttaṅga is not possible'—still standing? It is not still standing, as it has been resolved. For it was resolved earlier that the characteristic for Veyyākaraṇa is the act of giving a reply to a question when there are no verses.

Yañca vuttaṃ – “gāthābhāvato maṅgalasuttādīnaṃ (khu. pā. 5.1, 2, 3) suttaṅgasaṅgaho [P 1.0042] na siyā”ti, taṃ na, niruḷhattā. Niruḷho hi maṅgalasuttādīnaṃ suttabhāvo. Na hi tāni dhammapadabuddhavaṃsādayo [V 1.0031] viya gāthābhāvena paññātāni, atha kho suttabhāvena. Teneva hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “suttanāmaka”nti nāmaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Yañca pana vuttaṃ – “sagāthakattā geyyaṅgasaṅgaho siyā”ti, tadapi natthi, yasmā sahatāññena. Saha gāthāhīti hi sagāthakaṃ. Sahabhāvo nāma atthato aññena hoti, na ca maṅgalasuttādīsu kathāvinimutto koci suttapadeso atthi, yo ‘saha gāthāhī’ti vucceyya, na ca samudāyo nāma koci atthi, yadapi vuttaṃ – “ubhatovibhaṅgādīsu sagāthakappadesānaṃ geyyaṅgasaṅgaho siyā”ti tadapi na, aññato. Aññā eva hi tā gāthā jātakādipariyāpannattā. Ato na tāhi ubhatovibhaṅgādīnaṃ geyyaṅgabhāvoti. Evaṃ suttādīnaṃ aṅgānaṃ aññamaññasaṅkarābhāvo veditabbo.

As to what was said—'The Maṅgala Sutta and others could not be included in the Suttaṅga because they consist of verses'—that is not so, because of being established through usage. For the status of the Maṅgala Sutta and others as 'sutta' is established by usage. They are not known as being verses, like the Dhammapada, Buddhavaṃsa, and so on, but rather as being suttas. That is why in the commentary the term 'named sutta' is used. As to what was said—'Because they contain verses, they could be included in the Geyyaṅga'—that too is not the case, because of association with another. For 'sagāthakaṃ' means 'together with verses.' Association occurs with something that is substantially different. But in the Maṅgala Sutta and others, there is no portion of the sutta separate from the discourse that could be said to be 'together with verses,' nor is there any such composite. As to what was said—'The sections with verses in the Ubhatovibhaṅga and others could be included in the Geyyaṅga'—that too is not so, because they are from another. For those verses are indeed 'other,' since they are included in the Jātaka and so on. Therefore they do not confer the status of Geyyaṅga on the Ubhatovibhaṅga and other texts. In this way, the absence of mutual confusion among the Aṅgas—Sutta and the rest—should be understood.

“Ayaṃ dhammo…pe… ayaṃ vinayo, imāni caturāsīti dhammakkhandhasahassānī”ti buddhavacanaṃ dhammavinayādibhedena vavatthapetvā saṅgāyantena mahākassapappamukhena vasigaṇena anekacchariyapātubhāvapaṭimaṇḍitāya saṅgītiyā imassa dīghāgamassa paṭhamamajjhimabuddhavacanādibhāvo vavatthāpitoti dasseti, “evametaṃ abhedato”tiādinā.

By the passage beginning 'Thus this without division,' he shows how the status of this Long Collection as the first, middle, etc., of the Buddha's word was established. This was done by the assembly of masters headed by Mahākassapa, who rehearsed the Buddha's word—'This is the Dhamma… this is the Vinaya, these are the eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma'—having first classified it by way of Dhamma, Vinaya, and so on. They did this at the council, which was adorned with the appearance of many wonders.

Nidānakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the commentary on the introductory story.

1. Brahmajālasuttavaṇṇanā
