1. The Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta

Paribbājakakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Talk with the Wanderers

Evaṃ [P 1.0043][V 1.0032][M 1.0034] paṭhamamahāsaṅgītiṃ dassetvā yadatthaṃ sā idha dassitā, idāni taṃ nigamanavasena dassetuṃ “imissā”tiādimāha.

Having thus shown the First Great Council, now, in order to show by way of conclusion the purpose for which it was shown here, he spoke, beginning with 'of this,' and so on.

1. Ettāvatā ca brahmajālassa sādhāraṇato bāhiranidānaṃ dassetvā idāni abbhantaranidānaṃ saṃvaṇṇetuṃ “tattha eva”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Atha vā chahi ākārehi saṃvaṇṇanā kātabbā sambandhato padato padavibhāgato padatthato anuyogato parihārato cāti. Tattha sambandho nāma desanāsambandho. Yaṃ lokiyā “ummugghāto”ti vadanti. So pana pāḷiyā nidānapāḷivasena, nidānapāḷiyā pana saṅgītivasena veditabboti paṭhamamahāsaṅgītiṃ dassentena nidānapāḷiyā sambandhassa dassitattā padādivasena saṃvaṇṇanaṃ karonto “evanti nipātapada”ntiādimāha. “Metiādīnī”ti ettha antarā-sadda-ca-saddānaṃ nipātapadabhāvo, vattabbo, na vā vattabbo tesaṃ nayaggahaṇena gahitattā, tadavasiṭṭhānaṃ āpaṭi-saddānaṃ ādi-saddena saṅgaṇhanato. “Padavibhāgo”ti padānaṃ viseso, na pana padaviggaho. Atha vā padāni ca padavibhāgo ca padavibhāgo, padaviggaho ca padavibhāgo ca padavibhāgoti vā ekasesavasena padapadaviggahāpi padavibhāga saddena vuttāti veditabbaṃ. Tattha padaviggaho “bhikkhūnaṃ saṅgho”tiādibhedesu padesu daṭṭhabbo.

1. And having thus far shown the external introduction to the Brahmajāla in a general way, now, to explain the internal introduction, it is said, 'Therein, thus...' etc. Alternatively, the explanation should be made in six ways: by connection, by word, by word-division, by word-meaning, by inquiry, and by resolution. Therein, 'connection' is the connection of the discourse, what worldly people call 'the plunge.' This should be understood by way of the Pāli as the introduction to the Pāli, and by way of the introduction to the Pāli as the council. Therefore, since the connection of the introduction to the Pāli has been shown by showing the First Great Council, the commentator, explaining by way of the words, etc., said, beginning with 'evaṃ is a particle-word.' Here, in 'me, etc.', should the status as particles of the intervening words 'antarā' and 'ca' be stated, or not stated? It need not be, since their method is grasped by implication, and because the remaining words, starting from 'āpaṭi', are included by the word 'ādi' (etc.). 'Word-division' means the distinction of words, not word-analysis. Alternatively, 'words and word-division' is 'word-division'; or 'word-analysis and word-division' is 'word-division'. It should be understood that by the principle of ellipsis, even word-analysis is expressed by the term 'word-division'. Therein, word-analysis should be seen in instances such as 'the Sangha of bhikkhus'.

Atthatoti padatthato. Taṃ pana padatthaṃ atthuddhārakkamena [P 1.0044] paṭhamaṃ evaṃ-saddassa dassento “evaṃsaddo tāvā”tiādimāha. Avadhāraṇādīti ettha ādi-saddena idamatthapucchāparimāṇādiatthānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tathā hi “evaṃgatāni, evaṃvidho, evamākāro”tiādīsu idaṃ-saddassa atthe evaṃ-saddo. Gata-saddo hi pakārapariyāyo, tathā vidhākāra-saddā [V 1.0033] ca. Tathā hi vidhayuttagata-sadde lokiyā pakāratthe vadanti. “Evaṃ nu kho, na nu kho, kiṃ nu kho, kathaṃ nu kho”ti, “evaṃ su te sunhātā suvilittā kappitakesamassu, āmuttamālābharaṇā odātavatthavasanā pañcahi [M 1.0035] kāmaguṇehi samappitā samaṅgībhūtā paricārenti, seyyathāpi tvaṃ etarahi sācariyakoti? No hidaṃ bho gotamā”ti ca ādīsu pucchāyaṃ. “Evaṃ lahuparivattaṃ, evaṃ āyupariyanto”ti ca ādīsu parimāṇe. Nanu ca “evaṃ nu kho, evaṃ su te, evaṃ āyupariyanto”ti ettha evaṃ-saddena pucchanākāraparimāṇākārānaṃ vuttattā ākārattho eva evaṃ-saddo ti? Na, visesasabbhāvato. Ākāramattavācako hettha ākāratthoti adhippeto, yathā “evaṃ byākhotiādīsu pana na ākāravisesavācako evañca katvā “evaṃ jātena maccenā”tiādīni upamādīsu udāharaṇāni upapannāni honti. Tathā hi “yathāpi…pe… bahu”nti? Ettha [P 1.0045] puppharāsiṭṭhāniyato manussupapattisappurisūpanissayasaddhammasavanayonisomanasikārabhogasampattiādidānādipuññakiriyāhetusamudāyato sobhāsugandhatādiguṇayogato mālāguṇasadisiyo pahūtā puññakiriyā maritabbasabhāvatāya maccena sattena kattabbāti joditattā puppharāsimālāguṇāva upamā, tesaṃ upamākāro yathā-saddena aniyamato vuttoti evaṃ-saddo upamākāranigamanatthoti vattuṃ yuttaṃ. So pana upamākāro niyamiyamāno atthato upamāva hotīti āha “upamāyaṃ āgato”ti.

‘By meaning’ means by the meaning of the word. Showing first the meaning of the word ‘evaṃ’ by the method of extracting the meaning, he said, beginning with ‘the word evaṃ, in the first place...’ In ‘in affirmation, etc.’ (avadhāraṇādīti), it should be seen that the word ‘ādi’ (etc.) includes such meanings as ‘this matter,’ ‘question,’ and ‘measure.’ For example, in phrases like ‘evaṃgatāni’ (gone thus), ‘evaṃvidho’ (of such a kind), ‘evamākāro’ (of such a nature), the word ‘evaṃ’ conveys the meaning of ‘idaṃ’ (this). The word ‘gata’ is synonymous with manner, and likewise, the words ‘vidhā’ and ‘ākāra’ too. Indeed, worldly people use the word ‘gata’ connected with ‘vidhā’ to denote manner. In questions like ‘Is it so? Is it not so? What is it? How is it?’ and in statements like ‘Are your disciples, good Gotama, thus well bathed, well anointed, with hair and beard trimmed, adorned with garlands and jewelry, dressed in white clothes, indulging in the five strands of sensual pleasures, fully endowed and complete, just as you yourself are now with your teacher? No, good Gotama,’ the word ‘evaṃ’ is used in questioning. In expressions like ‘so swiftly changing,’ ‘so limited is the lifespan,’ it denotes measure. But is it not that in phrases like ‘Is it so?,’ ‘Thus are your disciples...,’ and ‘so limited is the lifespan,’ since the word ‘evaṃ’ is used to express the manner of questioning and the manner of measure, the word ‘evaṃ’ then signifies manner alone? No, because of the existence of a specific difference. Here, ‘in the sense of manner’ is intended to mean ‘denoting mere manner,’ as in ‘thus he explained,’ etc.; but it is not denoting a specific manner. And so, examples from similes and the like, such as ‘thus by a mortal who is born,’ are appropriate. For instance, in the passage ‘just as... much,’ here, the comparison is with a heap of flowers. Because it is stated that many meritorious actions—which are like garlands of flowers on account of possessing qualities like beauty and fragrance, arising from the collective cause of a human rebirth, reliance on good people, hearing the good Dhamma, wise attention, attainment of wealth, and meritorious deeds such as giving—should be done by a mortal being, one who by nature must die, the heap of flowers and the qualities of the garland are the simile. The manner of comparison is expressed indefinitely by the word ‘yathā’ (as); therefore, the word ‘evaṃ’ serves to conclude the manner of the simile. But that manner of comparison, when specified, becomes a simile in meaning; hence it is said, ‘it comes in a simile.’

Tathā evaṃ iminā ākārena “abhikkamitabba”ntiādinā upadisiyamānāya samaṇasāruppāya ākappasampattiyā yo tattha upadisanākāro, so atthato upadesoyevāti vuttaṃ “evaṃ te…pe… upadese”ti. Tathā evametaṃ bhagavā, evametaṃ sugatāti ettha ca bhagavatā yathāvuttamatthaṃ aviparītato jānantehi kataṃ tattha saṃvijjamānaguṇānaṃ pakārehi haṃsanaṃ udaggatākaraṇaṃ sampahaṃsanaṃ, yo tattha sampahaṃsanākāroti yojetabbaṃ. Evamevaṃ panāyanti ettha garahaṇākāroti yojetabbaṃ. So ca garahaṇākāro “vasalī”tiādi khuṃsanasaddasannidhānato idha evaṃ-saddena pakāsitoti viññāyati. Yathā [M 1.0036] cettha, evaṃ upamākārādayopi upamādivasena vuttānaṃ puppharāsiādisaddānaṃ sannidhānatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evañca vadehīti “yathāhaṃ vadāmi, evaṃ samaṇaṃ ānandaṃ vadehī”ti vadanākāro idāni vattabbo evaṃ-saddena nidassīyatīti nidassanattho vutto. Evaṃ noti etthāpi tesaṃ yathāvuttadhammānaṃ ahitadukkhāvahabhāve sanniṭṭhānajananatthaṃ anumatiggahaṇavasena “saṃvattanti, no vā, kathaṃ vā ettha hotī”ti pucchāya katāya “evaṃ no ettha hotī”ti vuttattā tadākārasanniṭṭhānaṃ evaṃ-saddena vibhāvitanti viññāyati, so pana tesaṃ dhammānaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya [P 1.0046] saṃvattanākāro niyamiyamāno avadhāraṇattho [V 1.0034] hotīti āha “evaṃ no ettha hotīti ādīsu avadhāraṇe”ti. Evaṃ bhanteti pana dhammassa sādhukaṃ savanamanasikāre sanniyojitehi bhikkhūhi attano tattha ṭhitabhāvassa paṭijānanavasena vuttattā ettha evaṃ-saddo vacanasampaṭicchanattho vutto, tena evaṃ bhante, sādhu bhante, suṭṭhu bhanteti vuttaṃ hoti.

Likewise, with regard to the accomplishment of conduct befitting a recluse, which is being instructed in this manner with phrases like ‘one should go forward,’ the manner of instruction there is in meaning instruction itself; thus it is said: ‘Thus, you... in the instruction.’ Likewise, in ‘so it is, Blessed One, so it is, Sugata,’ those who understand the meaning as spoken by the Blessed One without distortion rejoice in the qualities present there, expressing delight and upliftment; the manner of rejoicing there should be understood accordingly. In ‘Evamevaṃ panāyanti,’ the manner of reproach should be understood. That manner of reproach is made clear here by the word ‘evaṃ’ due to the proximity of scornful words such as ‘outcast.’ Just as in this case, so too the manner of simile, etc., should be seen from the proximity of words such as ‘heap of flowers,’ which are used by way of simile, etc. In ‘And thus you should speak,’ the manner of speaking, ‘As I speak, so should you speak to the ascetic Ānanda,’ is now indicated by the word ‘evaṃ’; thus it is said to be in the sense of an illustration. In ‘Thus for us’ (evaṃ no), too, for the purpose of producing a conclusion about the fact that the aforesaid things are unconducive to welfare and bring suffering, a question was asked by way of seeking consent: ‘Do they conduce, or not? Or how is it here?’ Since the reply was given, ‘For us (no) it is thus (evaṃ) here,’ the conclusion about that state is clarified by the word ‘evaṃ’. But that manner of conducing to what is not for their welfare and is for their suffering, being specified, becomes the meaning of affirmation. Thus he said: ‘in “For us it is thus here,” etc., it is in the sense of affirmation.’ As for ‘Thus, venerable sir,’ since this was spoken by the bhikkhus who were directed to listen and attend carefully to the Dhamma, by way of acknowledging their own establishment in it, the word ‘evaṃ’ here is said to be in the sense of accepting what was said. By this is meant: ‘Thus, venerable sir; good, venerable sir; excellent, venerable sir.’

Nānānayanipuṇanti ekattanānattaabyāpāraevaṃdhammatāsaṅkhātā, nandiyāvaṭṭa tipukkhalasīhavikkīḷitaaṅkusadisālocanasaṅkhātā vā ādhārādibhedavasena nānāvidhā nayā nānānayā, nayā vā pāḷigatiyo, tā ca paññattianupaññattiādivasena saṃkilebhāgiyādilokiyāditadubhayavomissatādivasena kusalādivasena khandhādivasena saṅgahādivasena samayavimuttādivasena ṭhapanādivasena kusalamūlādivasena tikapaṭṭhānādivasena ca nānappakārāti nānānayā, tehi nipuṇaṃ saṇhasukhumanti nānānayanipuṇaṃ. Āsayova ajjhāsayo, te ca sassatādibhedena, tattha ca apparajakkhatādivasena anekā, attajjhāsayādayo eva vā samuṭṭhānaṃ uppattihetu etassāti anekajjhāsayasamuṭṭhānaṃ. Atthabyañjanasampannanti atthabyañjanaparipuṇṇaṃ upanetabbābhāvato, saṅkāsanapakāsanavivaraṇavibhajanauttānīkaraṇapaññattivasena chahi atthapadehi, akkharapadabyañjanākāraniruttiniddesavasena chahi byañjanapadehi ca samannāgatanti vā attho daṭṭhabbo.

‘Skilled in various methods’ (nānānayanipuṇaṃ): The methods (nayā) are various. They are designated as the nature of being thus, free from concern with unity and diversity; or designated as the investigation similar to the auspicious diagram (nandiyāvaṭṭa), the three-pronged fork (tipukkhala), the lion’s play (sīhavikkīḷita), and the goad (aṅkusa). Or the methods (nayā), the traditions of the Pāli, are of various kinds: by way of concepts and sub-concepts; by way of what is worldly and pertains to defilement; by way of what is mixed with both; by way of what is wholesome, etc.; by way of the aggregates, etc.; by way of inclusion, etc.; by way of the temporarily liberated, etc.; by way of establishment, etc.; by way of the wholesome roots, etc.; and by way of the Paṭṭhāna with its triads, etc. Because it is skilled (nipuṇaṃ)—subtle and fine—in these various methods, it is ‘skilled in various methods.’ ‘Arisen from numerous dispositions’ (anekajjhāsayasamuṭṭhānaṃ): ‘Intention’ (āsaya) is disposition (ajjhāsaya). These are of many kinds, such as eternalism, etc., and therein, by way of having little dust, etc., they are numerous. Or, one’s own dispositions, etc., are the source (samuṭṭhāna), the cause of origin, for this. ‘Endowed with meaning and phrasing’ (atthabyañjanasampannaṃ): It is complete in meaning and phrasing, as there is nothing to be added. It should be understood as being endowed with six aspects of meaning—illuminating, making clear, opening up, analyzing, making plain, and designating—and with six aspects of phrasing: letters, words, syllables, form, grammar, and exposition.

Vividhapāṭihāriyanti ettha pāṭihāriyapadassa vacanatthaṃ “paṭipakkhaharaṇato rāgādikilesāpanayanato pāṭihāriya”nti vadanti. Bhagavato pana paṭipakkhā rāgādayo na santi, ye haritabbā. Puthujjanānampi vigatūpakkilese [M 1.0037] aṭṭhaguṇasamannāgate citte hatapaṭipakkhe iddhividhaṃ pavattati, tasmā tattha pavattavohārena ca na sakkā idha “pāṭihāriya”nti vattuṃ. Sace pana mahākāruṇikassa bhagavato [P 1.0047] veneyyagatā ca kilesā paṭipakkhā, tesaṃ haraṇato “pāṭihāriya”nti vuttaṃ, evaṃ sati yuttametaṃ. Atha vā bhagavato ca sāsanassa ca paṭipakkhā titthiyā, tesaṃ haraṇato pāṭihāriyaṃ. Te hi diṭṭhiharaṇavasena, diṭṭhippakāsane asamatthabhāvena ca iddhiādesanānusāsanīhi haritā apanītā hontīti. “Paṭī”ti vā ayaṃ saddo “pacchā”ti etassa atthaṃ bodheti “tasmiṃ paṭipaviṭṭhamhi, añño āgañchi brāhmaṇo”tiādīsu viya, tasmā samāhite citte, vigatūpakkilese ca katakiccena pacchā haritabbaṃ pavattetabbanti paṭihāriyaṃ, attano vā upakkilesesu catutthajjhānamaggehi haritesu pacchā haraṇaṃ paṭihāriyaṃ. Iddhiādesanānusāsaniyo ca vigatūpakkilesena, katakiccena ca sattahitatthaṃ puna pavattetabbā, haritesu ca attano upakkilesesu parasattānaṃ upakkilesaharaṇāni [V 1.0035] hontīti paṭihāriyāni bhavanti. Paṭihāriyameva pāṭihāriyaṃ. Paṭihāriye vā iddhiādesanānusāsanīsamudāye bhavaṃ ekekaṃ “pāṭihāriya”nti vuccati. Paṭihāriyaṃ vā catutthajjhānaṃ maggo ca paṭipakkhaharaṇato, tattha jātaṃ, tasmiṃ vā nimittabhūte, tato vā āgatanti pāṭihāriyaṃ. Tassa pana iddhiādibhedena visayabhedena ca bahuvidhassa bhagavato desanāya labbhamānattā āha “vividhapāṭihāriya”nti.

Regarding 'varied marvels,' here the meaning of the word 'pāṭihāriya' is explained as 'pāṭihāriya' because it removes what is adverse and gets rid of defilements such as lust. However, the Blessed One has no adversaries such as lust and other defilements to be removed. Even for worldlings, when the mind is free from imperfections and endowed with eight qualities, with adversaries destroyed, the variety of supernormal power operates; therefore, based on the usage there, it is not possible to call it 'pāṭihāriya' here. If, however, the defilements of those to be trained are the adversaries for the greatly compassionate Blessed One, then it is called 'pāṭihāriya' because of their removal; in this case, it is appropriate. Alternatively, the adversaries of the Blessed One and his Dispensation are the sectarians, and their removal is 'pāṭihāriya.' For they are removed and gotten rid of by the marvels of supernormal power, mind-reading, and instruction, by way of removing their views and because of their inability to proclaim their own views. Or, this word 'paṭi' conveys the meaning 'after,' as in such passages as 'after he had entered, another brahmin came.' Therefore, 'pāṭihāriya' is what is to be brought about afterwards by one whose mind is concentrated, free from imperfections, and who has done what had to be done. Or, 'pāṭihāriya' is the removal afterwards when one's own imperfections have been removed by the fourth jhāna and the paths. The marvels of supernormal power, mind-reading, and instruction are to be brought about again for the welfare of beings by one who is free from imperfections and has done what had to be done. And when one's own imperfections have been removed, the removals of the imperfections of other beings become marvels. A marvel itself is 'pāṭihāriya.' Or, in the collection of the marvels of supernormal power, mind-reading, and instruction, each one is called a 'pāṭihāriya.' Or, the fourth jhāna and the path are 'pāṭihāriya' because of their removal of adversaries; or 'pāṭihāriya' is what is born there, or has that as its basis, or comes from that. Since this is obtainable from the teaching of the Blessed One, which is of many kinds due to the distinctions of supernormal power, etc., and the distinctions of its domain, he said 'varied marvels'.

Na aññathāti bhagavato sammukhā sutākārato na aññathāti attho, na pana bhagavato desitākārato. Acinteyyānubhāvā hi bhagavato desanā. Evañca katvā “sabbappakārena ko samattho viññātu”nti idaṃ vacanaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti. Dhāraṇabaladassanañca na virujjhati sutākārāvirajjhanassa adhippetattā. Na hettha atthantaratāparihāro dvinnampi atthānaṃ ekavisayattā, itarathā thero bhagavato desanāya sabbathā paṭiggahaṇe samattho asamattho cāti āpajjeyyāti.

'Not otherwise' means not otherwise than the way it was heard in the presence of the Blessed One; this is the meaning. It does not mean not otherwise than the way it was taught by the Blessed One, for the Blessed One’s teaching is of inconceivable power. This being so, the statement, 'Who is capable of understanding it in every way?' is supported. And the demonstration of the power of retention is not contradicted, because what is intended is non-deviation from the way it was heard. Here there is no exclusion of another meaning, since both meanings pertain to the same subject. Otherwise, it would follow that the elder is both capable and incapable of grasping the Blessed One’s teaching in every way.

“Yo paro na hoti, so attā”ti evaṃ [P 1.0048] vuttāya niyakajjhattasaṅkhātāya sasantatiyaṃ vattanato tividhopi me-saddo kiñcāpi ekasmiṃyeva [M 1.0038] atthe dissati, karaṇasampadānasāminiddesavasena pana vijjamānabhedaṃ sandhāyāha “me-saddo tīsu atthesu dissatī”ti.

Because it occurs with reference to one's own continuity—spoken of thus: 'What is not another, that is the self,' and designated as one's own and internal—although the word 'me' is seen in only one sense, it is threefold. However, referring to the existing distinction by way of indicating the agent, recipient, and owner, it is said: 'The word 'me' is seen in three meanings.'

Kiñcāpi upasaggo kiriyaṃ viseseti, jotakabhāvato pana satipi tasmiṃ suta-saddo eva taṃ tamatthaṃ anuvadatīti anupasaggassa suta-saddassa atthuddhāre saupasaggassa gahaṇaṃ na virujjhatīti dassento “saupasaggo ca anupasaggo cā”ti āha. Assāti suta-saddassa. Kammabhāvasādhanāni idha suta-sadde sambhavantīti vuttaṃ “upadhāritanti vā upadhāraṇanti vā attho”ti. Mayāti atthe satīti yadā mesaddassa kattuvasena karaṇaniddeso, tadāti attho. Mamāti atthe satīti yadā sambandhavasena sāminiddeso, tadā.

Showing that 'although a prefix qualifies the action, since it is merely indicative, even when it is present it is the word suta itself that expresses that particular meaning; therefore, in extracting the meaning of the unprefixed word suta, taking the prefixed form is not contradictory,' he said, 'both with a prefix and without a prefix.' 'Of it' means of the word suta. Because passive and abstract derivations are possible here for the word suta, it was said: 'The meaning is "it was ascertained" or "ascertainment."' 'When there is the meaning "by me"' means when there is an indication of the agent by the instrumental case of the word 'me.' 'When there is the meaning "of me"' is when there is an indication of the owner by way of relation.

Sutasaddasannidhāne payuttena evaṃsaddena savanakiriyājotakena bhavitabbanti vuttaṃ “evanti sotaviññāṇādiviññāṇakiccanidassana”nti. Ādi-saddena sampaṭicchanādīnaṃ pañcadvārikaviññāṇānaṃ tadabhinihaṭānañca manodvārikaviññāṇānaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sabbesampi vākyānaṃ evakāratthasahitattā “suta”nti etassa sutaṃ evāti ayamattho labbhatīti āha “assavanabhāvapaṭikkhepato”ti, etena avadhāraṇena nirākataṃ dasseti. Yathā ca sutaṃ sutaṃ evāti [V 1.0036] niyametabbaṃ, taṃ sammā sutaṃ hotīti āha “anūnādhikāviparītaggahaṇanidassana”nti. Atha vā “saddantaratthāpohanavasena saddo atthaṃ vadatī”ti sutanti asutaṃ na hotīti ayametassa atthoti vuttaṃ “assavanabhāvapaṭikkhepato”ti, iminā diṭṭhādivinivattanaṃ karoti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti. Na idaṃ mayā diṭṭhaṃ, na sayambhuñāṇena sacchikataṃ, atha kho sutaṃ, tañca kho sammadevāti. Tenevāha “anūnādhikāviparītaggahaṇanidassana”nti. Avadhāraṇatthe vā evaṃ-sadde ayaṃ atthayojanā karīyatīti tadapekkhassa suta-saddassa ayamattho vutto “assavanabhāvapaṭikkhepato”ti. Teneva āha [P 1.0049] “anūnādhikāviparītaggahaṇanidassana”nti. Savanasaddo cettha kammattho veditabbo suyyatīti.

It is said that the word 'evaṃ', when used in proximity to the word 'suta', must be an indicator of the act of hearing; thus it is said: ''Evaṃ' is an indication of the function of ear-consciousness and other consciousnesses.' By the word 'etc.,' the inclusion of the five sense-door consciousnesses such as receiving, and the mind-door consciousnesses brought to bear on that, should be understood. Because all the sentences include the meaning of the particle 'eva' (indeed), from the word 'suta' this meaning is obtained: 'it is indeed heard.' Thus he says, 'by the rejection of the state of not-hearing,' showing what is negated by this emphasis. And just as what is heard should be determined as 'indeed heard,' so it is correctly heard. Thus he says: 'an indication of grasping without deficiency, excess, or distortion.' Alternatively, since 'a word expresses its meaning by way of excluding the meanings of other words,' 'heard' means 'not unheard.' This is its meaning. Thus it is said, 'by the rejection of the state of not-hearing.' By this he effects the exclusion of seeing, etc. This is what is said: 'This was not seen by me, nor realized by self-originating knowledge, but it was heard, and that indeed correctly.' For that reason he says: 'an indication of grasping without deficiency, excess, or distortion.' Or, when the word 'evaṃ' has the sense of emphasis, this connection of meaning is made. With reference to that, this meaning of the word 'suta' is stated: 'by the rejection of the state of not-hearing.' For that reason he says: 'an indication of grasping without deficiency, excess, or distortion.' And here the word 'savana' (hearing) should be understood in the passive sense: 'it is heard.'

Evaṃ savanahetusuṇantapuggalasavanavisesavasena padattayassa ekena pakārena atthayojanaṃ dassetvā idāni pakārantarehipi taṃ dassetuṃ “tathā eva”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tassāti yā sā bhagavato sammukhā dhammassavanākārena pavattā manodvāraviññāṇavīthi, tassā. Sā hi nānappakārena [M 1.0039] ārammaṇe pavattituṃ samatthā. Tathā ca vuttaṃ “sotadvārānusārenā”ti. Nānappakārenāti vakkhamānānaṃ anekavihitānaṃ byañjanatthaggahaṇānānākārena, etena imissā yojanāya ākārattho evaṃ-saddo gahitoti dīpeti. Pavattibhāvappakāsananti pavattiyā atthibhāvappakāsanaṃ. “Sutanti dhammappakāsana”nti yasmiṃ ārammaṇe vuttappakārā viññāṇavīthi nānappakārena pavattā, tassa dhammattā vuttaṃ, na sutasaddassa dhammatthattā. Vuttassevatthassa pākaṭīkaraṇaṃ “ayañhetthā”tiādi. Tattha viññāṇavīthiyāti karaṇatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Mayāti katthuatthe.

Thus, having shown in one way the connection of meaning for the three words based on the particulars of the cause of hearing, the person hearing, and the hearing itself, now in order to show it in other ways too, 'just so,' etc., is said. Therein, 'of that' refers to that cognitive series of mind-door consciousness which occurred in the presence of the Blessed One in the manner of hearing the Dhamma. For it is capable of occurring in various ways in relation to an object. And so it was said: 'in accordance with the ear-door.' 'In various ways' means in the various manners of grasping the letter and the meaning of the many things to be explained; by this he shows that in this explanation the word 'evaṃ' is taken in the sense of 'manner' (ākāra). 'Indication of the state of occurrence' means the indication of the existence of the occurrence. ''Heard' is an indication of the Dhamma': this is said because that object in which the aforesaid cognitive series occurred in various ways is Dhamma, not because the word 'suta' itself has the meaning 'Dhamma.' The clarification of what has been said is 'this here,' etc. Therein, 'by the cognitive series' is the instrumental case in the instrumental sense. 'By me' is in the sense of the agent.

“Evanti niddisitabbappakāsana”nti nidassanatthaṃ evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ nidassetabbassa niddisitabbattābhāvābhāvato, tena evaṃ-saddena sakalampi suttaṃ paccāmaṭṭhanti dasseti. Suta-saddassa kiriyāsaddattā, savanakiriyāya ca sādhāraṇaviññāṇappabandhapaṭibaddhattā tattha ca puggalavohāroti vuttaṃ “sutanti puggalakiccappakāsana”nti. Na hi puggalavohārarahite dhammappabandhe savanakiriyā labbhatīti.

“‘Evaṃ’ is an indication of what is to be pointed out”: this is said taking the word ‘evaṃ’ in the sense of an example, because what is to be indicated is necessarily something to be pointed out. Thus he shows that by this word ‘evaṃ’ the entire sutta is referred back to. Because the word ‘suta’ is a verb, and because the act of hearing is connected with a general continuum of consciousness where there is personal designation, it is said: “‘Suta’ is an indication of a person's action.” For the act of hearing is not found in a continuum of dhammas devoid of personal designation.

“Yassa cittasantānassā”tiādipi ākāratthameva evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā purimayojanāya aññathā atthayojanaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha ākārapaññattīti upādāpaññatti eva, dhammānaṃ pavattiākārupādānavasena tathā vuttā. “Sutanti visayaniddeso”ti sotabbabhūto dhammo savanakiriyākattupuggalassa savanakiriyāvasena pavattiṭṭhānanti katvā vuttaṃ. Cittasantānavinimuttassa [V 1.0037] paramatthato [P 1.0050] kassaci kattu abhāvepi saddavohārena buddhiparikappitabhedavacanicchāya cittasantānato aññaṃ viya taṃsamaṅgiṃ katvā vuttaṃ “cittasantānena taṃsamaṅgino”ti. Savanakiriyāvisayopi sotabbadhammo savanakiriyāvasena pavattacittasantānassa idha paramatthato kattubhāvato, savanavasena cittappavattiyā eva vā savanakiriyābhāvato taṃkiriyākattu ca visayo hotīti katvā vuttaṃ “taṃsamaṅgino kattu visaye”ti. Sutākārassa ca therassa sammānicchitabhāvato āha “gahaṇasanniṭṭhāna”nti, etena vā avadhāraṇatthaṃ evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā ayaṃ atthayojanā katāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

“Of which continuity of mind,” etc., is also said to show a different connection of meaning from the previous explanation, taking the word ‘evaṃ’ in the sense of ‘manner.’ Therein, ‘concept of manner’ is just a concept of appropriation (upādāpaññatti), so called because it is based on the appropriation of the manner of occurrence of phenomena. “‘Suta’ is an indication of the object”: this is said on the grounds that the Dhamma to be heard is the place of occurrence for the person who performs the act of hearing, by way of the act of hearing. Although in an ultimate sense there is no agent apart from the continuity of mind, due to linguistic convention and the wish to express a distinction conceived by the intellect, it is spoken of as if it were something other than the continuity of mind, by making it something endowed with it. Thus it is said: “by the continuity of mind of one endowed with it.” The object of the act of hearing, the Dhamma to be heard, is an object for the agent endowed with it, because the continuity of mind occurring by way of the act of hearing is here, in an ultimate sense, the agent; or because the act of hearing is just the occurrence of mind by way of hearing. Thus it is said: “in the object of the agent endowed with it.” And because the manner of what was heard was correctly determined by the elder, he says, “the conclusion of the grasping.” Or it should be seen that this connection of meaning is made by taking the word ‘evaṃ’ in the sense of emphasis.

Pubbe [M 1.0040] sutānaṃ nānāvihitānaṃ suttasaṅkhātānaṃ atthabyañjanānaṃ upadhāritarūpassa ākārassa nidassanassa avadhāraṇassa vā pakāsanasabhāvo evaṃ-saddoti tadākārādiupadhāraṇassa puggalapaññattiyā upādānabhūtadhammappabandhabyāpāratāya vuttaṃ “evanti puggalakiccaniddeso”ti. Savanakiriyā pana puggalavādinopi viññāṇanirapekkhā natthīti visesato viññāṇabyāpāroti āha “sutanti viññāṇakiccaniddeso”ti. Meti saddappavattiyā ekanteneva sattavisayattā, viññāṇakiccassa ca tattheva samodahitabbato “meti ubhayakiccayuttapuggalaniddeso”ti vuttaṃ. Avijjamānapaññattivijjamānapaññattisabhāvā yathākkamaṃ evaṃ-sadda suta-saddānaṃ atthāti te tathārūpapaññattiupādānabyāpārabhāvena dassento āha “evanti puggalakiccaniddeso. Sutanti viññāṇakiccaniddeso”ti. Ettha ca karaṇakiriyākattukammavisesappakāsanavasena puggalabyāpāvisayapuggalabyāpāranidassanavasena gahaṇākāragāhakatabbisayavisesaniddesavasena kattukaraṇa byāpārakattuniddesavasena ca dutiyādayo catasso atthayojanā dassitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The word ‘evaṃ’ has the nature of making clear the form that has been borne in mind, the mode, the indication, or the determination of the meaning and phrasing of the various discourses previously heard, which are known as suttas. It is said, “‘Evaṃ’ is a description of a person’s function,” because it is spoken of in terms of the operation of the continuity of phenomena that is the basis for the designation of a person who bears in mind that mode, etc. But since even for the personalists the act of hearing is not independent of consciousness, it is an operation of consciousness in particular. Thus he said: “‘Sutaṃ’ is a description of consciousness’s function.” Since the word ‘me’ in its occurrence pertains exclusively to the domain of a being, and since the function of consciousness must be comprised therein, it is said: “‘Me’ is a description of a person connected with both functions.” The meanings of the words ‘evaṃ’ and ‘sutaṃ’ have the nature of a non-existent designation and an existent designation respectively. Showing them in terms of the operation of grasping such designations, he said: “‘Evaṃ’ is a description of a person’s function. ‘Sutaṃ’ is a description of consciousness’s function.” And here it should be seen that four applications of the meaning are shown: (1) by way of making clear the distinctions of instrument, action, agent, and object; (2) by way of indicating the sphere of a person’s activity and the person’s activity; (3) by way of describing the distinctions of the mode of grasping, the grasper, and its object; and (4) by way of describing the agent, instrument, operation, and agent.

Sabbassāpi [P 1.0051] saddādhigamanīyassa atthassa paññattimukheneva paṭipajjitabbattā, sabbapaññattīnañca vijjamānādivasena chasu paññattibhedesu antogadhattā tesu “eva”ntiādīnaṃ paññattīnaṃ sarūpaṃ niddhārento āha “evanti ca meti cā”tiādi. Tattha evanti ca meti ca vuccamānassa atthassa ākārādino, dhammānañca asallakkhaṇabhāvato avijjamānapaññattibhāvoti āha “saccikaṭṭhaparamatthavasena avijjamānapaññattī”ti. Tattha saccikaṭṭhaparamatthavasenāti bhūtatthauttamatthavasena. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hotiyo māyāmarīciādayo viya abhūtattho, anussavādīhi gahetabbo viya anuttamattho ca na hoti, so rūpasaddādisabhāvo ruppanānubhavanādisabhāvo vā attho “saccikaṭṭho, paramattha cā”ti vuccati, na tathā evaṃ meti padānamatthoti, etamevatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ kātuṃ “kiñhettha ta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Sutanti pana saddāyatanaṃ sandhāyāha “vijjamānapaññattī”ti. Teneva hi “yañhi tamettha sotena upaladdha”nti vuttaṃ[V 1.0038], “sotadvārānusārena upaladdha”nti pana vutte atthabyañjanādisabbaṃ labbhati. Taṃ taṃ upādāya vattabbatoti sotapathaṃ āgate dhamme upādāya tesaṃ upadhāritākārādino paccāmasanavasena “eva”nti, sasantatipariyāpanne khandhe upādāya “me”ti [M 1.0041] vattabbattāti attho. Diṭṭhādisabhāvarahite saddāyatane pavattamānopi sutavohāro “dutiyaṃ tatiya”ntiādiko viya paṭhamādīni diṭṭhamutaviññāte apekkhitvā pavattoti āha “diṭṭhādīni upanidhāya vattabbato”ti. Asutaṃ na hotīti hi “suta”nti pakāsito yamatthoti.

Since every meaning ascertainable through sound must be approached only through the gate of designation, and since all designations are included in the six kinds of designation, such as ‘existent,’ determining the nature of designations such as ‘evaṃ,’ he says, “‘Evanti ca meti cā,’” etc. Here, because the mode, etc., of the meaning expressed by ‘evaṃ’ and ‘me,’ and phenomena themselves, lack a self-characteristic, they are a non-existent designation. Thus he says: “In the sense of real and ultimate meaning, they are a non-existent designation.” Here, ‘in the sense of real and ultimate meaning’ means in the sense of real meaning and highest meaning. This is what is meant: that meaning which is not an unreal meaning like a magical illusion or a mirage, nor a non-ultimate meaning to be grasped through oral tradition, but which has the nature of form, sound, etc., or the nature of being affected, experienced, etc., is called ‘real and ultimate.’ But the meaning of the words ‘evaṃ’ and ‘me’ is not like that. To make this very meaning clearer, it is said, “‘Kiñhettha tan,’” etc. However, with reference to the sound base, he says ‘sutaṃ’ is ‘an existent designation.’ For this reason it is said: “For that which is apprehended here by the ear.” But if it were said, “apprehended in accordance with the ear-door,” then all meaning and phrasing would be obtained. “It is to be spoken of with reference to this or that” means: with reference to a phenomenon that has entered the path of the ear, by way of reviewing its apprehended mode, etc., one says ‘evaṃ’; with reference to the aggregates included in one’s own continuity, one says ‘me.’ This is the meaning. Although the convention ‘heard’ occurs in relation to the sound base, which is devoid of the nature of the seen, etc., still, like ‘second,’ ‘third,’ etc., it occurs with reference to the seen, sensed, and cognized. Thus he says: “It is to be spoken of by taking the seen, etc., as a basis.” For ‘sutaṃ’ (heard) is explained as having the meaning ‘it is not unheard.’

Attanā paṭividdhā suttassa pakāravisesā “eva”nti therena paccāmaṭṭhāti āha “asammohaṃ dīpetī”ti. “Nānappakārapaṭivedhasamattho hotī”ti etena vakkhamānassa suttassa nānappakārataṃ duppaṭivijjhatañca dasseti. “Sutassa asammosaṃ dīpetī”ti sutākārassa yāthāvato dassiyamānattā vuttaṃ. Asammohenāti sammohābhāvena, paññāya eva [P 1.0052] vā savanakālasambhūtāya taduttarakālapaññāsiddhi, evaṃ asammosenāti etthāpi vattabbaṃ. Byañjanānaṃ paṭivijjhitabbo ākāro nātigambhīro, yathāsutadhāraṇameva tattha karaṇīyanti satiyā byāpāro adhiko, paññā tattha guṇībhūtāti vuttaṃ “paññāpubbaṅgamāyā”tiādi paññāya pubbaṅgamāti katvā. Pubbaṅgamatā cettha padhānabhāvo “manopubbaṅgamā”tiādīsu viya, pubbaṅgamatāya vā cakkhuviññāṇādīsu āvajjanādīnaṃ viya appadhānatte paññā pubbaṅgamā etissāti ayampi attho yujjati, evaṃ “satipubbaṅgamāyā”ti etthāpi vuttanayānusārena yathāsambhavamattho veditabbo. Atthabyañjanasampannassāti atthabyañjanaparipuṇṇassa, saṅkāsanapakāsanavivaraṇavibhajanauttānīkaraṇapaññattivasena chahi atthapadehi, akkharapadabyañjanākāraniruttiniddesavasena chahi byañjanapadehi ca samannāgatassāti vā attho daṭṭhabbo.

The special features of the sutta penetrated by himself are reviewed by the elder as ‘thus’; hence he says, “it illuminates non-delusion.” By “He is capable of penetration in various ways,” he shows the multifaceted nature and the difficulty of penetrating the sutta that is about to be spoken. “It illuminates non-oblivion of what was heard” is said because the mode of what was heard is shown as it really is. “By non-delusion” means by the absence of delusion; or by the wisdom that arose at the time of hearing, there is the accomplishment of wisdom at a later time. The same should be said here for “by non-oblivion.” The mode in which the phrasing is to be penetrated is not very profound; what should be done there is simply to retain what has been heard. Thus the operation of mindfulness is primary, while wisdom is secondary. This is said in the phrase “by that which has wisdom as its forerunner,” taking it as “wisdom is its forerunner.” Here, its being a forerunner is its being primary, as in “mind is their forerunner.” Or, if its being a forerunner is secondary, like adverting in eye-consciousness, etc., then this meaning also fits: “wisdom is the forerunner of this mindfulness.” Similarly, in the case of “by that which has mindfulness as its forerunner,” the meaning should be understood as is suitable according to the method stated. “Endowed with meaning and phrasing” means complete in meaning and phrasing; or the meaning should be seen as endowed with the six items of meaning—indication, making clear, exposition, analysis, making plain, and designation—and with the six items of phrasing—letters, words, phrases, mode, etymology, and description.

Yonisomanasikāraṃ dīpetīti evaṃ-saddena vuccamānānaṃ ākāranidassanāvadhāraṇatthānaṃ aviparītasaddhammavisayattāti adhippāyo. “Avikkhepaṃ dīpetī”ti “brahmajālaṃ kattha bhāsita”ntiādi pucchāvasena pakaraṇappattassa vakkhamānassa suttassa savanaṃ samādhānamantarena na sambhavatīti katvā vuttaṃ. “Vikkhittacittassā”tiādi tassevatthassa samatthanavasena vuttaṃ. Sabbasampattiyāti atthabyañjanadesakapayojanādisampattiyā. Aviparītasaddhammavisayehi viya ākāranidassanāvadhāraṇatthehi yonisomanasikārassa, saddhammassavanena viya ca avikkhepassa yathā yonisomanasikārena [M 1.0042] phalabhūtena [P 1.0053] attasammāpaṇidhipubbekatapuññatānaṃ siddhi vuttā tadavinābhāvato, evaṃ avikkhepena phalabhūtena kāraṇabhūtānaṃ saddhammassavanasappurisūpanissayānaṃ siddhi dassetabbā siyā assutavato, sappurisūpanissayarahitassa ca tadabhāvato.

‘It illuminates wise attention’: the intention is that the meanings expressed by the word ‘evaṃ’—the mode, indication, and determination—have as their object the undistorted good Dhamma. ‘It illuminates non-distraction’ is said because, in the context of the questions such as ‘Where was the Brahmajāla Sutta spoken?’, the hearing of the sutta about to be spoken is not possible without concentration. The words ‘for one with a distracted mind,’ etc., are stated to support this very meaning. By ‘all accomplishment’ is meant accomplishment in meaning, phrasing, teacher, purpose, etc. Just as by wise attention, which is the result, the accomplishment of right aspiration for oneself and of merit formerly done is stated because of its inseparability from them, so by non-distraction, which is the result, the accomplishment of its causes—listening to the good Dhamma and resorting to true persons—should be shown; for one who has not heard and for one who lacks resort to true persons, this is absent.

“Na [V 1.0039] hi vikkhittacitto”tiādinā samatthanavacanena pana avikkhepena kāraṇabhūtena sappurisūpanissayena ca phalabhūtassa saddhammassavanassa siddhi dassitā. Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo yutto siyāsaddhammassavanasappurisūpanissayā na ekantena avikkhepassa kāraṇaṃ bāhiraṅgattā, avikkhepo pana sappurisūpanissayo viya saddhammassavanassa ekantakāraṇanti. Evampi avikkhepena sappurisūpanissayasiddhijotanā na samatthitāva, no na samatthitā vikkhittacittānaṃ sappurisapayirupāsanābhāvassa atthasiddhattā. Ettha ca purimaṃ phalena kāraṇassa siddhidassanaṃ nadīpūrena viya upari vuṭṭhisabbhāvassa, dutiyaṃ kāraṇena phalassa siddhidassanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ ekantena vassinā viya meghavuṭṭhānena vuṭṭhippavattiyā.

But by the supporting statement beginning ‘For not with a distracted mind,’ the accomplishment of listening to the good Dhamma, which is the result, is shown by non-distraction and by resorting to true persons, which are the cause. Here this may be the intended meaning: listening to the good Dhamma and resorting to true persons are not the exclusive cause of non-distraction, because they are external factors; but non-distraction, like resorting to true persons, is an exclusive cause of listening to the good Dhamma. Even so, the demonstration of the accomplishment of resorting to true persons through non-distraction is not fully supported. Yet it is not unsupported, because it is implicitly established that those with distracted minds do not associate with true persons. And here, the former—showing the accomplishment of the cause from the result—should be seen as being like inferring the existence of rain upstream from the flooding of a river. The latter—showing the accomplishment of the result from the cause—should be seen as being like inferring the occurrence of rain from the rising of clouds that will definitely bring rain.

Bhagavato vacanassa atthabyañjanapabhedaparicchedavasena sakalasāsanasampattiogāhanākāro niravasesaparahitapāripūrikāraṇanti vuttaṃ “evaṃ bhaddako ākāro”ti. Yasmā na hotīti sambandho. Pacchimacakkadvayasampattinti attasammāpaṇidhipubbekatapuññatāsaṅkhātaṃ guṇadvayaṃ. Aparāparaṃ vuttiyā cettha cakkabhāvo, caranti etehi sattā sampattibhavesūti vā. Ye sandhāya vuttaṃ “cattārimāni bhikkhave cakkāni, yehi samannāgatānaṃ devamanussānaṃ catucakkaṃ vattatī”tiādi[P 1.0054]. Purimapacchimabhāvo cettha desanākkamavasena daṭṭhabbo. Pacchimacakkadvayasiddhiyāti pacchimacakkadvayassa atthitāya. Sammāpaṇihitatto pubbe ca katapuñño suddhāsayo hoti tadasuddhihetūnaṃ kilesānaṃ dūrībhāvatoti āha “āsayasuddhi siddhā hotī”ti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “sammāpaṇihitaṃ cittaṃ, seyyaso naṃ tato kare”ti, “katapuññosi tvaṃ ānanda, padhānaṃ anuyuñja khippaṃ hohisi anāsavoti ca. Tenevāha “āsayasuddhiyā adhigamabyattisiddhī”ti. Payogasuddhiyāti yonisomanasikārapubbaṅgamassa dhammassavanapayogassa visadabhāvena. Tathā cāha “āgamabyattisiddhī”ti. Sabbassa vā kāyavacīpayogassa [M 1.0043] niddosabhāvena. Parisuddhakāyavacīpayogo hi vippaṭisārābhāvato avikkhittacitto pariyattiyaṃ visārado hotīti.

The manner of the Blessed One’s speech, by way of the distinction and determination of the meaning and the phrasing, is a mode of encompassing all the assets of the teaching and is the reason for the complete fulfillment of the welfare of others without remainder—thus it is said, 'This is an excellent manner.' The connection is: 'Because it is not.' The attainment of the latter two wheels is the pair of qualities designated as right self-direction and merit made in the past. Here, their wheel-like nature is due to their successive operation, or because beings fare on to prosperous existences by means of them. This is what is referred to in the statement, 'Monks, there are these four wheels, possessed of which, gods and humans possess the four wheels,' and so on. The former and latter aspect here should be seen in accordance with the sequence of the discourse. The accomplishment of the latter two wheels is by the existence of the latter two wheels. One with a rightly directed mind and who has made merit in the past has a pure disposition, because the defilements that are the cause of its impurity have been removed—thus it is said, 'Purity of disposition is accomplished.' For it is said: 'A rightly directed mind does for one what is better than that,' and 'You have made merit, Ānanda; apply yourself to the striving, and you will soon be taintless.' Therefore it is said: 'Through purity of disposition, the accomplishment of attainment and competence is achieved.' Through purity of application: by the clarity of the application of listening to the Dhamma, which is preceded by wise attention. Thus it is said: 'The accomplishment of scriptural learning and competence is achieved.' Or, through the faultlessness of all bodily and verbal application. For one whose bodily and verbal application is pure, being free from remorse, has an undistracted mind and becomes expert in the scriptural teaching.

“Nānappakārapaṭivedhadīpakenā”tiādinā atthabyañjanesu therassa evaṃ-sadda suta-saddānaṃ asammohāsammosadīpanato catupaṭisambhidāvasena atthayojanaṃ dasseti. Tattha “sotabbappabhedapaṭivedhadīpakenā”ti etena ayaṃ suta-saddo evaṃ-saddasannidhānato, vakkhamānāpekkhāya vā sāmaññeneva sotabbadhammavisesaṃ āmasatīti dasseti. Manodiṭṭhikaraṇāpariyattidhammānaṃ anupekkhanasuppaṭivedhā visesato manasikārapaṭibaddhāti te vuttanayena yonisomanasikāradīpakena evaṃ-saddena yojetvā, savanadhāraṇavacīparicayā pariyattidhammānaṃ [V 1.0040] visesena sotāvadhānapaṭibaddhāti te avikkhepadīpakena suta-saddena yojetvā dassento sāsanasampattiyā dhammassavane ussāhaṃ janeti. Tattha dhammāti pariyattidhammā. Manasānupekkhitāti “idha sīlaṃ kathitaṃ, idha samādhi, idha paññā, ettakā ettha anusandhiyo”tiādinā [P 1.0055] nayena manasā anupekkhitā. Diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhāti nijjhānakkhantibhūtāya, ñātapariññāsaṅkhātāya vā diṭṭhiyā tattha tattha vuttarūpārūpadhamme “iti rūpaṃ, ettakaṃ rūpa”ntiādinā suṭṭhu vavatthapetvā paṭividdhā.

By the phrase 'by the lamp illuminating the penetration of various kinds,' and so on, the Elder shows the application of the meaning in terms of the four analytical knowledges by illuminating the non-delusion and non-confusion concerning the words 'thus' and 'heard' in the meaning and phrasing. Here, by the phrase 'by the lamp illuminating the penetration of the varieties of what is to be heard,' he shows that this word 'heard,' due to its proximity to the word 'thus,' or in anticipation of what will be said, generally touches upon the specific qualities of the Dhamma that is to be heard. The good penetration through reflection upon the scriptural teachings that are to be made objects of mind and view is especially connected with attention. By connecting those with the word 'thus' by means of the lamp of wise attention in the way described, and by connecting these with the word 'heard' by means of the lamp of non-distraction—since hearing, retaining, and verbal familiarity with the scriptural teachings are especially connected with attentiveness of ear—he shows this, thereby generating diligence in listening to the Dhamma for the sake of the accomplishment of the teaching. Here, 'Dhamma' refers to the scriptural teachings. 'Reflected upon with the mind' means reflected upon with the mind in this way: 'Here virtue is discussed, here concentration, here wisdom; these are the connections here,' and so on. 'Thoroughly penetrated by view' means well-determined and penetrated by a view that has become acceptance through reflection, or by what is designated as full understanding as known, in regard to the material and immaterial phenomena stated here and there, having thoroughly established them thus: 'Such is form, this much is form,' and so on.

“Sakalena vacanenā”ti pubbe tīhi padehi visuṃ visuṃ yojitattā vuttaṃ. Asappurisabhūminti akataññutaṃ “idhekacco pāpabhikkhu tathāgatappaveditaṃ dhammavinayaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā attano dahatī”ti evaṃ vuttaṃ anariyavohārāvatthaṃ. Sā eva anariyavohārāvatthā asaddhammo. Nanu ca ānandattherassa “mamedaṃ vacana”nti adhimānassa, mahākassapattherādīnañca tadāsaṅkāya abhāvato asappurisabhūmisamatikkamādivacanaṃ niratthakaṃ ti? Nayidaṃ evaṃ “evaṃ me suta”nti vadantena ayampi attho vibhāvitoti dassanato. Keci pana “devatānaṃ parivitakkāpekkhaṃ tathāvacananti edisī codanā anavakāsā”ti vadanti. Tasmiṃ kira khaṇe ekaccānaṃ devatānaṃ evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi “tathāgato ca parinibbuto, ayañca āyasmā desanākusalo, idāni dhammaṃ deseti, sakyakulappasuto tathāgatassa bhātā cūḷapituputto, kiṃ nu kho sayaṃ sacchikata dhammaṃ deseti, udāhu bhagavatoyeva vacanaṃ yathāsuta”nti. Evaṃ [M 1.0044] tadāsaṅkitappakārato asappurisabhūmisamokkamādito atikkamādi vibhāvitanti. Attano adahantoti “mameta”nti attani [P 1.0056] aṭṭhapento. Appetīti nidasseti. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthesu yathārahaṃ satte netīti netti, dhammoyeva netti dhammanetti.

'With the entire statement'—this is said because it was previously connected with the three terms, each one separately. 'The plane of an unworthy person' refers to ingratitude, the state of ignoble behavior spoken of thus: 'Here, some bad monk, having learned the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, appropriates it for himself.' That very state of ignoble behavior is the bad Dhamma. But isn't the statement about transcending the plane of an unworthy person and so on meaningless, since Venerable Ānanda had no conceit, 'This is my statement,' and Venerable Mahākassapa and others had no such suspicion? This is not so. For by one who says, 'Thus have I heard,' this meaning too is clarified, because it is shown. Some, however, say that such a criticism is out of place because 'the statement was made in consideration of the thoughts of the deities.' For at that moment, it is said, a thought arose in the minds of certain deities thus: 'The Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, and this venerable one is skilled in discourse. Now he teaches the Dhamma. He is born in the Sakyan clan, the son of the Tathāgata’s paternal uncle. Does he teach a Dhamma he has realized for himself, or is it the Blessed One’s word just as he heard it?' Thus, by dispelling the suspicion that arose in this way, the transcending of the plane of an unworthy person is clarified. 'Not making it his own' means not establishing it in oneself as 'this is mine.' 'He presents' means he indicates. Because it leads beings as is fitting in regard to the meanings pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal, it is guidance (netti); the Dhamma itself is guidance, the Dhamma-guidance.

Daḷhataraniviṭṭhā vicikicchā kaṅkhā. Nātisaṃsappanaṃ matibhedamattaṃ vimati. Assaddhiyaṃ vināseti bhagavato desitattā, sammukhā cassa paṭiggahitattā, khalitaduruttādiggahaṇadosābhāvato ca. Ettha ca paṭhamādayo tisso atthayojanā ākārādiatthesu aggahitavisesameva evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā dassitā, tato parā tisso ākāratthameva evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā vibhāvitā. Pacchimā pana tisso yathākkamaṃ ākāratthaṃ nidassanatthaṃ avadhāraṇatthañca evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā yojitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Doubt (vicikicchā) that is more firmly settled is perplexity (kaṅkhā). Hesitation (vimati) is a mere difference of opinion that does not spread very far. Lack of faith is destroyed because it was taught by the Blessed One, because it was received in his presence, and because there is no fault of grasping what is stumbled upon, badly spoken, etc. Here, the first three applications of meaning are shown by taking the word 'thus' in its meanings of 'manner,' etc., without grasping a specific one. The next three are explained by taking the word 'thus' only in the sense of 'manner.' But the last three should be seen as connected by taking the word 'thus' successively in the sense of 'manner,' in the sense of 'example,' and in the sense of 'emphasis.'

Eka-saddo aññaseṭṭhāsahāyasaṅkhyadīsu dissati. Tathāhesa “sassato attā ca loko ca[V 1.0041], idameva saccaṃ moghamaññanti ittheke abhivadantī”tiādīsu aññatthe dissati, “cetaso ekodibhāva”ntiādīsu seṭṭhatthe, “eko vūpakaṭṭho”tiādīsu asahāye, “ekova kho bhikkhave khaṇo ca samayo ca brahmacariyavāsāyā”tiādīsu saṅkhyayaṃ, idhāpi saṅkhyayanti dassento āha “ekanti gaṇanaparicchedaniddeso”ti. Kālañca samayañcāti yuttakālañca paccayasāmaggiñca. Khaṇoti okāso. Tathāgatuppādādiko hi maggabrahmacariyassa okāso tappaccayapaṭilābhahetuttā. Khaṇo eva [P 1.0057] ca samayo. Yo “khaṇo”ti ca “samayo”ti ca vuccati, so eko vāti hi attho. Mahāsamayoti mahāsamūho. Samayopi khoti sikkhāpadapūraṇassa hetupi. Samayappavādaketi diṭṭhippavādake. Tattha hi nisinnā titthiyā attano attano samayaṃ pavadantīti. Atthābhisamayāti hitapaṭilābhā. Abhisametabboti abhisamayo, abhisamayo atthoti abhisamayaṭṭhoti pīḷana ādīni abhisametabbabhāvena ekībhāvaṃ upanetvā vuttāni. Abhisamayassa vā paṭivedhassa [M 1.0045] visayabhūtabhāvo abhisamayaṭṭhoti tāneva tathā ekattena vuttāni. Tattha pīḷanaṃ dukkhasaccassa taṃ samaṅgīno hiṃsanaṃ avipphārikatākaraṇaṃ. Santāpodukkhadukkhatādivasena santāpanaṃ paridahaṇaṃ.

The word 'one' (eka) is seen in the senses of other, best, alone, number, and so on. For instance, in such passages as 'some (eke) assert thus,' it is seen in the sense of 'other'; in 'unification (ekodibhāva) of the mind,' it is in the sense of 'best'; in 'alone (eko), secluded,' it is in the sense of 'alone'; in 'monks, there is only one (eko) moment and occasion for living the holy life,' it is in the sense of 'number.' Here too, it is in the sense of number, thus he says: '"One" is an indication of numerical determination.' 'Time and occasion' means the suitable time and the convergence of conditions. 'Moment' (khaṇa) means opportunity. For the arising of a Tathāgata and so on is an opportunity for the holy life of the path, as it is a cause for obtaining the conditions for it. The moment is itself the occasion (samayo). The meaning is that what is called 'moment' and 'occasion' is just one. 'Great occasion' (mahāsamayo) means great assembly. 'Occasion' is also a cause for the fulfillment of the training rules. 'Proclaimers of doctrines' (samayappavādakā) means proclaimers of views, for there, seated sectarians proclaim their own respective doctrines. 'Breakthrough to the meaning' (atthābhisamayo) means the attainment of benefit. What is to be fully understood is a breakthrough (abhisamayo); the breakthrough is the meaning (attho), thus 'the meaning of the breakthrough' (abhisamayaṭṭho). Thus, such things as 'oppression' are spoken of by bringing them to unity through their nature of being what is to be fully understood. Or, the state of being the objective field for breakthrough or penetration is 'the meaning of the breakthrough'; thus those same things are spoken of as one. Therein, 'oppression' is a characteristic of the truth of suffering: the afflicting of one endowed with it, the causing of it to be intense. Torment is scorching and consuming, by way of suffering-as-suffering, and so on.

Tattha sahakārīkāraṇaṃ sannijjha sameti samavetīti samayo, samavāyo. Sameti samāgacchati maggabrahmacariyamettha tadādhārapuggalehīti samayo, khaṇo. Sameti ettha, etenava saṃgacchati satto, sabhāvadhammo vā sahajātādīhi, uppādādīhi vāti samayo, kālo. Dhammappavattimattatāya atthato abhūtopi hi kālo dhammappavattiyā adhikaraṇaṃ, karaṇaṃ viya ca kappanāmattasiddhena rūpena voharīyatīti. Samaṃ, saha vā avayavānaṃ ayanaṃ pavatti avaṭṭhānanti samayo, samūho, yathā “samudāyo”ti. Avayavasahāvaṭṭhānameva hi samūhoti. Avasesapaccayānaṃ samāgame eti phalaṃ etasmā uppajjati pavattati cāti samayo, hetu yathā “samudayo”ti. Sameti saṃyojanabhāvato sambandho eti attano visaye pavattati, daḷhaggahaṇabhāvato vā saṃyuttā ayanti pavattanti sattā yathābhinivesaṃ etenāti samayo, diṭṭhi. Diṭṭhisaṃyojanena hi sattā ativiya bajjhantīti. Samiti [P 1.0058] saṅgati samodhānanti samayo, paṭilābho. Samassa yānaṃ, sammā vā yānaṃ apagamoti samayo, pahānaṃ. Abhimukhaṃ ñāṇena etabbo abhisametabboti abhisamayo, dhammānaṃ aviparīto sabhāvo. Abhimukhabhāvena sammā eti gacchati bujjhatīti abhisamayo, dhammānaṃ yathābhūtasabhāvāvabodho. Evaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ atthe samaya-saddassa pavatti veditabbā. Samaya-saddassa atthuddhāre abhisamaya-saddassa udāharaṇaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Assāti samaya-saddassa. Kālo attho samavāyādīnaṃ atthānaṃ [V 1.0042] idha asambhavato desadesakaparisānaṃ viya suttassa nidānabhāvena kālassa apadisitabbato ca.

Herein, because a contributory cause comes together, converges, it is a 'samaya,' a concurrence. Because the path and the holy life come together, assemble, in it through the persons who are their basis, it is a 'samaya,' an occasion. Because a being or a natural phenomenon comes together, converges, here or by means of this with co-nascent things, etc., or with arising, etc., it is a 'samaya,' time. For although time is in reality non-existent, being merely the occurrence of phenomena, it is designated as the basis and as the instrument for the occurrence of phenomena, just as a form established by mere convention is. Because there is an even or a joint going, occurrence, and state of the components, it is a 'samaya,' a collection, as in 'aggregate' (samudāya). For a collection is just the joint state of the components. Because when the remaining conditions come together, the fruit comes, arises, and proceeds from this, it is a 'samaya,' a cause, as in 'origin' (samudaya). Because a connection comes together in the sense of a fetter, and proceeds in its own domain; or because beings, bound, go and proceed by this according to their adherence due to its firm grip, it is a 'samaya,' a view. For beings are exceedingly bound by the fetter of views. Because there is a meeting, a coming together, a conjunction, it is a 'samaya,' an attainment. Because it is the going of what is tranquil, or the right going, a departure, it is a 'samaya,' abandonment. Because it is to be gone to, to be fully understood, by knowledge directly confronting it, it is 'abhisamaya' (full understanding), the unperverted nature of phenomena. Because one rightly comes, goes, and understands in a state of confrontation, it is 'abhisamaya,' the comprehension of the true nature of phenomena. Thus the usage of the word 'samaya' is to be understood in these various meanings. In the extraction of the meaning of the word 'samaya,' the example of the word 'abhisamaya' should be understood in the way that has been stated. Of this word 'samaya,' the meaning is 'time,' because the meanings of concurrence, etc., are not possible here, and because time is to be designated as the introductory setting of the sutta, as for the assemblies of teachers and disciples from various countries.

Kasmā panettha aniyāmitavaseneva kālo niddiṭṭho, na utusaṃvaccharādivasena niyametvāti āha “tattha kiñcāpī”tiādi. Utusaṃvaccharādivasena niyamaṃ akatvā samaya-saddassa vacane ayampi guṇo laddho hotīti dassento “ye vā ime”tiādimāha. Sāmaññajotanā hi visese avatiṭṭhatīti. Tattha diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārasamayo devasikaṃ [M 1.0046] jhānasamāpattīhi vītināmanakālo, visesato sattasattāhāni. Pakāsāti dasasahassilokadhātuyā pakampanaobhāsapātubhāvādīhi pākaṭā. Yathāvuttappabhedesuyeva samayesu ekadesaṃ pakārantarehi saṅgahetvā dassetuṃ “yo cāya”ntiādimāha. Tathā hi ñāṇakiccasamayo attahitapaṭipattisamayo ca abhisambodhisamayo. Ariyatuṇhibhāvasamayo diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārasamayo. Karuṇākiccaparahitapaṭipattidhammikathāsamayo desanāsamayeva.

Why, then, is time indicated here in an unrestricted way, and not fixed by way of seasons, years, etc.? He says: 'Therein, although…' etc. Showing that by not making a restriction by way of seasons, years, etc., this benefit is also obtained in the utterance of the word 'samaya,' he says: 'Or these…' etc. For a general indication stands in the particular. Therein, the time of dwelling happily in this very life is the time of passing the days with the jhānic attainments, especially the seven weeks. 'Manifestations' means made manifest by the quaking, the appearance of a radiance, etc., in the ten-thousand-world-system. To show this by collecting in other ways a portion of the times with the divisions as stated, he says: 'And this…' etc. For the time of the task of knowledge and the time of the practice for one's own welfare is the time of full enlightenment. The time of noble silence is the time of dwelling happily in this very life. The time of the task of compassion, the practice for the welfare of others, and talk on the Dhamma is just the time of teaching.

Karaṇavacanena niddeso kato yathāti sambandho. Tatthāti abhidhammavinayesu. Tathāti bhummakaraṇehi. Adhikaraṇattha ādhārattho. Bhāvo nāma kiriyā, kiriyāya kiriyantaralakkhaṇaṃ bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇaṃ. Tattha yathā kālo sabhāvadhammaparicchinno sayaṃ paramatthato [P 1.0059] avijjamānopi ādhārabhāvena paññāto taṅkhaṇappavattānaṃ tato pubbe parato ca abhāvato “pubbaṇhe jāto, sāyanhe gacchatī”ti, ca ādīsu, samūho ca avayavavinimutto avijjamānopi kappanāmattasiddho avayavānaṃ ādhārabhāvena paññāpīyati “rukkhe sākhā, yavarāsiyaṃ sambhūto”tiādīsu, evaṃ idhāpīti dassento āha “adhikaraṇañhi…pe… dhammāna”nti. Yasmiṃ kāle, dhammapuñje vā kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, tasmiṃyeva kāle, dhammapuñje ca phassādayopi hontīti ayañhi tattha attho. Yathā ca gāvīsu duyhamānāsu gato, duddhāsu āgatoti dohanakiriyāya gamanakiriyā lakkhīyati, evaṃ idhāpi “yasmiṃ samaye, tasmiṃ samaye”ti ca vutte satīti ayamattho viññāyamāno eva hoti padatthassa sattāvirahābhavatoti samayassa sattākiriyāya cittassa uppādakiriyā, phassādīnaṃ bhavanakiriyā ca lakkhīyati. Yasmiṃ samayeti yasmiṃ navame khaṇe, yonisomanasikārādihetumhi, paccayasamavāye vā sati kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, tasmiṃyeva khaṇe, hetumhi, paccayasamavāye ca sati phassādayopi hontīti ubhayattha samaya-sadde bhummaniddeso kato lakkhaṇabhūtabhāvayuttoti dassento āha “khaṇa…pe… lakkhīyatī”ti.

The connection is: 'as the indication is made by the instrumental expression.' 'Therein' means in the Abhidhamma and Vinaya. 'Thus' means by the locative and instrumental. The meaning of 'basis' (adhikaraṇa) is the meaning of 'receptacle' (ādhāra). 'State' (bhāva) means action. The marking of one action by another action is the 'locative absolute' (bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇa). Therein, just as time, though in the ultimate sense non-existent in itself, being defined by natural phenomena, is designated as a receptacle because of the non-existence before and after of things occurring at that moment, as in 'born in the morning, goes in the evening,' etc.; and just as a collection, though non-existent apart from its components, being established by mere convention, is designated as a receptacle for its components, as in 'a branch on the tree,' 'produced in a heap of barley,' etc.; so too here, showing this he says: 'For the basis... of phenomena.' For this is the meaning there: 'At whatever time, or in whatever collection of phenomena, a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen, at that very time, and in that collection of phenomena, contact and the other states also exist.' And just as in 'he went when the cows were being milked, he came when they had been milked,' the action of going is marked by the action of milking, so too here, when it is said, 'at which time... at that time,' this meaning is indeed understood because the meaning of the word is devoid of a being. Thus the action of the arising of consciousness and the action of the occurrence of contact and the other states are marked by the action of the being of the time. 'At which time' means: when, at the ninth moment, or when the cause such as wise attention, or the concurrence of conditions, is present, a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen, at that very moment, or when that cause or concurrence of conditions is present, contact and the other states also exist. Showing that in both cases the word 'samaya' is given a locative indication connected with the state that is the mark, he says: 'The moment... is marked.'

Hetuattho [V 1.0043] karaṇattho ca sambhavati “annena vasati, ajjhenena vasati, pharasunā chindati, kudālena khaṇatī”tiādīsu viya. Vītikkamañhi sutvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātāpetvā otiṇṇavatthukaṃ puggalaṃ paṭipucchitvā, vigarahitvā [M 1.0047] ca taṃ taṃ vatthuṃ otiṇṇakālaṃ anatikkamitvā teneva kālena sikkhāpadāni paññapento bhagavā [P 1.0060] viharati sikkhāpadapaññattihetuñca apekkhamāno tatiyapārājikādīsu viyāti.

The meaning of cause and the meaning of instrument are possible, just as in such examples as: 'he lives by means of food,' 'he lives by means of study,' 'he cuts with an axe,' 'he digs with a spade.' For having heard of a transgression, having had the Saṅgha of bhikkhus assemble, having questioned the person who was the subject of the case, and having reproached him, without letting the time when that case occurred pass by, the Blessed One dwells laying down the training rules at that very time, while attending to the reason for the laying down of the training rules, as in the case of the third pārājika, etc.

Accantameva ārambhato paṭṭhāya yāva desanāniṭṭhānaṃ parahitapaṭipattisaṅkhātena karuṇāvihārena. Tadatthajotanatthanti accantasaṃyogatthajotanatthaṃ. Upayogavacananiddeso kato yathā “māsaṃ ajjhetī”ti.

Continuously from the beginning of the undertaking right up to the conclusion of the teaching, by the abiding in compassion reckoned as the practice for the welfare of others. 'To illuminate that meaning' means to illuminate the meaning of continuous connection. The indication is made by an expression of extent, as in 'he studies for a month.'

Porāṇāti aṭṭhakathācariyā. Abhilāpamattabhedoti vacanamattena viseso. Tena suttavinayesu vibhattibyatayo katoti dasseti.

'The ancients' means the commentary teachers. 'A difference in mere expression' means a difference only in utterance. By this he shows that an interchange of cases has been made in the Suttas and Vinaya.

Seṭṭhanti seṭṭhavācakaṃ vacanaṃ seṭṭhanti vuttaṃ seṭṭhaguṇasahacaraṇato. Tathā uttamanti etthāpi. Gāravayuttoti garubhāvayutto garuguṇayogato, garukaraṇārahatāya vā gāravayutto.

'Best' means the word expressive of the best; it is called 'best' because it accompanies the quality of being best. So too with 'highest.' 'Worthy of reverence' means connected with the state of being venerable because of its connection with the quality of venerableness, or worthy of reverence because of its worthiness to be revered.

Vuttoyeva na pana idha vattabbo visuddhimaggassa imissā aṭṭhakathāya ekadesabhāvatoti adhippāyo.

The intention is that this has already been stated, but it is not to be stated here because the Visuddhimagga is a part of this commentary.

Apica bhage vani, vamīti vā bhagavā, bhage sīlādiguṇe vani bhaji sevi, te vā vineyyasantānesu “kathaṃ nu kho uppajjeyyu”nti vani yāci patthayīti bhagavā, bhagaṃ vā siriṃ, issariyaṃ, yasañca vami khelapiṇḍaṃ viya chaḍḍayīti bhagavā. Tathā hi bhagavā hatthagataṃ siriṃ, catuddīpissariyaṃ, cakkavattisampattisannissayañca sattaratanasamujjalaṃ yasaṃ anapekkho pariccajīti. Atha vā bhāni nāma nakkhattāni, tehi samaṃ gacchanti pavattantīti bhagā, sineruyugandharādigatā bhājanalokasobhā. Te bhagavā vami tappaṭibaddhachandarāgappahānena pajahatīti evampi bhage vamīti bhagavā.

Again, 'bhagavā' is from 'bhage vani' or 'vamīti.' He partook of (bhaji), he served (sevi), the shares (bhage), that is, the qualities of virtue, etc.; or he desired (vani), he requested (yāci), he wished (patthayi) for them in the mental continuities of those to be trained, thinking: 'How indeed might they arise?'—thus he is bhagavā. Or he vomited (vami), that is, he discarded like a ball of phlegm, the shares (bhagaṃ), that is, fortune, sovereignty, and fame—thus he is bhagavā. For the Blessed One, being without concern, abandoned the fortune that had come into his hands, the sovereignty over the four continents, and the fame resplendent with the seven treasures that is the support for the fortune of a wheel-turning monarch. Or else, 'bhāni' are the constellations. The splendors of the receptacle world located in Sineru, Yugandhara, etc., are 'bhagā' because they go and proceed along with them. The Blessed One vomited (vami) them, that is, he abandons them by the abandoning of the desire and lust connected with them. Thus too, 'bhagavā' is from 'bhage vami.'

“Dhammasarīraṃ paccakkhaṃ karotī”ti “yo vo ānanda mayā dhammo ca vinayo ca desito paññatto, so vo mamaccayena satthā”ti vacanato [P 1.0061] dhammassa satthubhāvapariyāyo vijjatīti katvā vuttaṃ.

'He directly experiences the Dhamma-body': this is said on the grounds that, from the statement, 'Ānanda, the Dhamma and Vinaya that I have taught and laid down for you will be your Teacher after my passing,' there exists the alternative of the Dhamma's being the Teacher.

Vajirasaṅghātasamānakāyo [M 1.0048][V 1.0044] parehi abhejjasarīrattā. Na hi bhagavato rūpakāye kenaci antarāyo sakkā kātunti. Desanāsampattiṃ niddisati vakkhamānassa sakalasuttassa “eva”nti niddisanato. Sāvakasampattiṃ niddisati paṭisambhidāppattena pañcasu ṭhānesu bhagavatā etadagge ṭhapitena mayā mahāsāvakena sutaṃ, tañca kho mayāva sutaṃ, na anussavitaṃ, na paramparābhatanti imassatthassa dīpanato. Kālasampattiṃ niddisati “bhagavā”ti padassa sannidhāne payuttassa samaya-saddassa kālassa buddhuppādapaṭimaṇḍitabhāvadīpanato. Buddhuppādaparamā hi kālasampadā. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

His body is like a solid diamond because his body is unbreakable by others. For no one is able to cause harm to the Blessed One's physical body. He indicates the accomplishment of the teaching by the designation 'evaṃ' (thus) for the entire sutta that is about to be spoken. He indicates the accomplishment of the disciples by clarifying this meaning: 'It was heard by me, the great disciple who has attained the analytical knowledges and was placed by the Blessed One at the head in five respects; and it was heard by me myself, not from hearsay, not handed down by tradition.' He indicates the accomplishment of time by showing that the time indicated by the word 'samaya,' used in proximity to the word 'Bhagavā,' is adorned with the arising of a Buddha. For the supreme accomplishment of time is the arising of a Buddha. Therefore it is said:

“Kappakasāye kaliyuge, buddhuppādo aho mahacchariyaṃ;

Hutāvahamajjhe jātaṃ, samuditamakarandamaravinda”nti.

In the stain of the eon, the age of strife, the arising of a Buddha—ah, a great wonder! A lotus with abundant nectar, born in the middle of a sacrificial fire.

Bhagavāti desakasampattiṃ niddisati guṇavisiṭṭhasattuttamagāravādhivacanato.

'Bhagavā' indicates the accomplishment of the Teacher, because it is an appellation of reverence for the supreme being distinguished by qualities.

Vijjantarikāyāti vijjuniccharaṇakkhaṇe. Antaratoti hadaye. Antarāti ārabbha nipphattīnaṃ vemajjhe. Antarikāyāti antarāḷe. Ettha ca “tadantaraṃ ko jāneyya, etesaṃ antarā kappā, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyā, antarantarā kathaṃ opātetī”ti ca ādīsu viya kāraṇavemajjhesu vattamānā antarā-saddā eva [P 1.0062] udāharitabbā siyuṃ, na pana cittakhaṇavivaresu vattamānā antarantarikā-saddā. Antarā-saddassa hi ayaṃ atthuddhāroti. Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo siyā – yesu atthesu antarā-saddo vattati, tesu antarasaddopi vattatīti samānatthattā antarā-saddatthe vattamāno antara-saddo udāhaṭo, antarā-saddo eva vā “yassantarato”ti ettha gāthāsukhatthaṃ rassaṃ katvā vuttoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Antarā-saddo eva pana ika-saddena padaṃ vaḍḍhetvā “antarikā”ti vuttoti evamettha udāharaṇodāharitabbānaṃ virodhābhāvo daṭṭhabbo. Ayojiyamāne upayogavacanaṃ na pāpuṇāti sāmivacanassa pasaṅge antarā-saddayogena upayogavacanassa icchitattā. Tenevāha “antarāsaddena yuttattā upayogavacanaṃ kata”nti.

"Vijjantarikāyāti" means at the moment of a lightning flash. "Antaratoti" means in the heart. "Antarāti" means in the middle of things that have arisen in dependence. "Antarikāyāti" means in the interval. And here, as in such passages as, "Who would know that interval? Between them are eons, incalculable by counting," and "How does he fell them in between?" it is the word antarā occurring in the sense of intervals between causes that should be cited as examples, not the words antara and antarikā occurring in the sense of intervals between moments of consciousness. For this is the extraction of the meaning of the word antarā. Or this might be the intention here: in the meanings in which the word antarā occurs, the word antara also occurs; thus, because they are synonymous, the word antara occurring in the meaning of the word antarā is cited. Or it should be seen that in the phrase "yassantarato," the word antarā itself is stated shortened for the sake of metrical grace in the verse. Or it should be seen that the word antarā itself, when the word is extended with the suffix -ika, is stated as "antarikā." Thus, in this way, the absence of contradiction between the example and what is to be exemplified should be seen. When it is not connected, the locative case is not obtained, since in the context of the genitive case, the locative case is desired through its connection with the word "antarā." Therefore he said: "Because of its connection with the word antarā, the locative case is made."

“Niyato [M 1.0049] sambodhiparāyaṇo, aṭṭhānametaṃ bhikkhave anavakāso, yaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo sañcicca pāṇaṃ jīvitā voropeyya, “netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī” tiādivacanato diṭṭhisīlānaṃ niyatasabhāvattā sotāpannāpi aññamaññaṃ diṭṭhisīlasāmaññena saṃhatā, pageva sakadāgāmiādayo. “Tathārūpāya diṭṭhiyā diṭṭhisāmaññagato viharati, tathārūpesu sīlesu sīlasāmaññagato [V 1.0045] viharatī”ti vacanato puthujjanānampi diṭṭhisīlasāmaññena saṃhatabhāvo labbhatiyeva.

“He is fixed, with enlightenment as his destination. Monks, it is impossible, it is no occasion, that a person accomplished in view would intentionally deprive a living being of life.” From such statements as, “That is not possible,” it is because of the fixed nature of view and virtue that even stream-enterers are united with one another by commonality in view and virtue, how much more so once-returners and others. In accordance with the passage, “He dwells having attained commonality in view through such a view; he dwells having attained commonality in virtue through such virtues,” even for worldlings a state of being united by commonality in view and virtue is certainly obtained.

Suppiyopi khoti ettha kho-saddo avadhāraṇattho “assosi kho”tiādīsu [P 1.0063] viya. Tena addhānamaggapaṭipanno ahosiyeva, nāssa maggapaṭipattiyā koci antarāyo ahosīti ayamattho dīpito hoti. Tatrāti vā kālassa paṭiniddeso. Sopi hi “ekaṃ samaya”nti pubbe adhikato. Yañhi samayaṃ bhagavā antarā rājagahañca nāḷandañca addhānamaggapaṭipanno, tasmiṃyeva samaye suppiyopi taṃ maggaṃ paṭipanno avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, brahmadatto ca vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatīti. Pariyāyati parivattatīti pariyāyo, vāro. Pariyāyeti desetabbamatthaṃ paṭipādetīti pariyāyo, desanā. Pariyāyati attano phalaṃ pariggahetvā pavattatīti pariyāyo, kāraṇanti evaṃ pariyāya-saddassa vārādīsu pavatti veditabbā. Kāraṇenāti kāraṇapatirūpakena. Tathā hi vakkhati “akāraṇameva kāraṇanti vatvā”ti. Kasmā panettha “avaṇṇaṃ bhāsatī”ti, “vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatī”ti ca vattamānakālaniddeso kato, nanu saṅgītikālato so avaṇṇavaṇṇānaṃ bhāsitakālo atītoti? Saccametaṃ, “addhānamaggapaṭipanno hotī”ti ettha hoti-saddo viya atītakālattho bhāsati-saddo ca daṭṭhabbo. Atha vā yasmiṃ kāle tehi avaṇṇo vaṇṇo ca bhāsīyati, taṃ apekkhitvā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Evañca katvā “tatrāti kālassa paṭiniddeso”ti idañca vacanaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti.

In “Suppiyopi kho,” the word “kho” has the sense of emphasis, as in “assosi kho” (he indeed heard) and so on. By this, the meaning is illuminated that he was indeed journeying along the road and there was no obstacle to his journey. Or “tatra” is a reference to time. For it too was previously referred to by “at one time.” For at the time when the Blessed One was journeying on the highway between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā, at that very time Suppiya too was journeying on that road, speaking dispraise, while Brahmadatta spoke praise. Because it turns around (pariyāyati), it is a “pariyāya,” a turn. Because it expounds (pariyāyeti) the meaning to be taught, it is a “pariyāya,” a discourse. Because it proceeds (pariyāyati) having grasped its own fruit, it is a “pariyāya,” a reason. Thus the occurrence of the word “pariyāya” in the sense of “turn,” etc., should be understood. “By means of a reason” means by what has the semblance of a reason. For it will be said: “having said that what is not a reason is a reason.” Why here is the present tense designation used, “he speaks dispraise” and “he speaks praise”? Is it not the case that from the time of the communal recitation that time of speaking dispraise and praise was past? This is true. Just as the word “hoti” in “addhānamaggapaṭipanno hoti” has a past-tense meaning, so too the word “bhāsati” should be seen. Or, it is said thus with reference to the time when dispraise and praise were spoken by them. And by doing so, this statement, “‘tatra’ is a reference to time,” is also supported.

Akāraṇanti ayuttiṃ, anupapattinti attho. Na hi arasarūpatādayo dosā bhagavati saṃvijjanti, dhammasaṅghānañca durakkhātaduppaṭipannatādayoti. Akāraṇanti vā yuttakāraṇarahitaṃ, paṭiññāmattanti adhippāyo[M 1.0050]. Imasmiñca atthe kāraṇanti vatvāti kāraṇaṃ vāti vatvāti attho. Arasarūpādīnañcettha jātivuḍḍhesu abhivādanādisāmīcikammākaraṇaṃ kāraṇaṃ, tathā [P 1.0064] uttarimanussadhammālamariyañāṇadassanābhāvassa sundarikāmaguṇādinavabodho, saṃsārassa ādikoṭiyā apaññāyanapaṭiññā, abyākatavatthubyākaraṇanti evamādayo, tathā asabbaññutādīnaṃ kamāvabodhādayo yathārahaṃ niddhāretabbā. Tathā tathāti jātivuḍḍhānaṃ anabhivādanādiākārena.

“Without reason” means without logic, without basis; this is the meaning. For faults such as tastelessness and the like are not found in the Blessed One, nor are the Dhamma and the Sangha badly expounded or badly practiced. Or “without reason” means devoid of a proper reason; “a mere assertion” is the intention. And in this sense, the phrase “having said it is a reason” means “or having said it is a reason.” Here, the reason for tastelessness and so on is the non-performance of courteous duties such as paying homage to those senior in birth. Likewise, for the absence of the noble knowledge and vision of states beyond the human, the reasons are the new understanding concerning the qualities of the Sundarikā and so on, the assertion that the beginning point of saṃsāra is not discerned, and the non-declaration of undeclared matters, and so on. Likewise, for not being omniscient and so on, the gradual understanding and so on should be determined as appropriate. “In such and such a way” means in the manner of not paying homage to those senior in birth, and so on.

Avaṇṇaṃ bhāsamānoti avaṇṇaṃbhāsanahetu. Hetuattho hi ayaṃ māna-saddo. Anayabyasanaṃ pāpuṇissati ekantamahāsāvajjattā ratanattayopavādassa. Tenevāha –

“Speaking dispraise” means because of speaking dispraise. For this “-māna” suffix has the sense of cause. He will come to ruin and disaster because slander of the Triple Gem is extremely blameworthy. Therefore it is said:

“Yo [V 1.0046] nindiyaṃ pasaṃsati,

Taṃ vā nindati yo pasaṃsiyo;

Vicināti mukhena so kaliṃ,

Kalinā tena sukhaṃ na vindatī”ti.

“He who praises what is blameworthy,

or blames what is praiseworthy,

gathers demerit with his mouth;

through that demerit he finds no happiness.”

“Amhākaṃ ācariyo”tiādinā brahmadattassa saṃveguppattiṃ, attano ācariye kāruññappavattiñca dassetvā kiñcāpi antevāsinā ācariyassa anukūlena bhavitabbaṃ, ayaṃ pana paṇḍitajātikattā na edisesu taṃ anuvattatīti, idāni tassa kammassakataññāṇappavattiṃ dassento “ācariye kho panā”tiādimāha. Vaṇṇaṃ bhāsituṃ āraddho “apināmāyaṃ ettakenāpi ratanattayāvaṇṇato orameyyā”ti. Vaṇṇīyatīti vaṇṇo, guṇo. Vaṇṇanaṃ guṇasaṅkittananti vaṇṇo, pasaṃsā. Saṃññūḷhāti ganthitā, nibandhitāti attho. Atitthena pakkhando dhammakathikoti na vattabbo aparimāṇaguṇattā buddhādīnaṃ[P 1.0065], niravasesānañca tesaṃ idha pakāsanaṃ pāḷisaṃvaṇṇanāyeva sampajjatīti. Anussavādīti ettha ādi-saddena ākāraparivitakkadiṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyo saṅgaṇhāti. Attano thāmena vaṇṇaṃ abhāsi, na pana buddhādīnaṃ guṇānurūpanti adhippāyo. Asaṅkhyayyāparimitappabhedā hi buddhādīnaṃ guṇā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

By “Our teacher,” etc., having shown the arising of Brahmadatta’s sense of spiritual urgency and the arising of his compassion for his own teacher, and that although a pupil should be compliant with his teacher, this one, being of a wise nature, does not follow him in such matters, now, showing the arising of his knowledge of ownership of kamma, he says, “But for the teacher…,” etc. He began to speak praise, thinking: “Perhaps with just this much he might desist from dispraising the Triple Gem.” Because it is praised (vaṇṇīyati), it is praise (vaṇṇo), a quality. The extolling, the proclaiming of qualities, is praise (vaṇṇo), commendation. “Saṃññūḷhā” means woven, bound; this is the meaning.
