It cannot be said, “The preacher of the Dhamma, being himself not satisfied, rushes on,” because the qualities of the Buddha and others are immeasurable, and their complete exposition here is accomplished only by the commentary on the Pāli text. In “by hearsay,” etc., the word “etc.” includes reasoned contemplation, reflection on views, and meditative acceptance. He spoke praise with his own strength, not in a way corresponding to the qualities of the Buddha and others; this is the intention. For the qualities of the Buddha and others are of innumerable, immeasurable, and diverse kinds. For it has been said:

“Buddhopi [M 1.0051] buddhassa bhaṇeyya vaṇṇaṃ,

Kappampi ce aññamabhāsamāno;

Khīyetha kappo ciradīghamantare,

Vaṇṇo na khīyetha tathāgatassā”ti.

“Even a Buddha might speak the praise of a Buddha,

for an eon, speaking of nothing else;

the eon would be exhausted in that long stretch of time,

but the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.”

Idhāpi vakkhati “appamattakaṃ kho paneta”ntiādi.

Here too it will be said, “But this is just a trifle,” and so on.

Iti ha teti ettha itīti vuttappakāraparāmasanaṃ. Ha-kāro nipātamattanti āha “evaṃ te”ti.

In “iti ha te,” “iti” is a reference to the manner that has been spoken of. The syllable “ha” is a mere particle; thus the phrase means “thus to you.”

Iriyāpathānubandhanena anubandhā honti, na pana sammāpaṭipattianubandhanenāti adhippāyo. Tasmiṃ kāleti yasmiṃ saṃvacchare utumhi māse pakkhe vā bhagavā taṃ addhānamaggaṃ paṭipanno, tasmiṃ kāle. Teneva hi kiriyāvicchedadassanavasena “rājagahe piṇḍāya caratī”ti vattamānakālaniddeso [V 1.0047] kato. Soti evaṃ rājagahe vasamāno bhagavā. Taṃ divasanti yaṃ divasaṃ addhānamaggapaṭipanno, taṃ divasaṃ. Taṃ addhānaṃ paṭipanno nāḷandāyaṃ veneyyānaṃ vividha hitasukhanipphattiṃ ākaṅkhamāno imissā ca aṭṭhuppattiyā tividhasīlālaṅkataṃ nānāvidhakuhanalapanādimicchājīvaviddhaṃsanaṃ dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhijālaviniveṭhanaṃ dasasahassilokadhātupakampanaṃ brahmajālasuttantaṃ desessāmīti. Ettāvatā “kasmā pana bhagavā taṃ addhānaṃ paṭipanno”ti codanā visodhitā hoti. “Kasmā ca suppiyo anubandho”ti ayaṃ pana codanā “bhagavato [P 1.0066] taṃ maggaṃ paṭipannabhāvaṃ ajānanto”ti etena visodhitā hoti. Na hi so bhagavantaṃ daṭṭhumeva icchatīti. Tenevāha “sace pana jāneyya, nānubandheyyā”ti.

They were following his physical path, not following the right practice; this is the intention. “At that time” means in whatever year, season, month, or fortnight the Blessed One was journeying on that road, at that time. For this reason, by way of showing the interruption of the action, the present tense designation is made: “he wanders for alms in Rājagaha.” “He” means the Blessed One thus dwelling in Rājagaha. “On that day” means on the day he was journeying on the road. He journeyed on that road desiring the attainment of various benefits and happiness for those in Nāḷandā who were ready to be trained, and also, for the sake of this occasion, intending to teach the Brahmajāla Suttanta, which is adorned with the threefold virtue, which destroys various kinds of deceitful talk and wrong livelihood, which disentangles the net of sixty-two views, and which causes the ten-thousand-world-system to tremble. With this, the objection, “Why did the Blessed One journey on that road?” is cleared up. And the objection, “And why did Suppiya follow?” is cleared up by this: “Not knowing that the Blessed One was journeying on that road.” For he did not wish just to see the Blessed One. Therefore it is said: “But if he had known, he would not have followed.”

Nīlapītalohitodātamañjiṭṭhapabhassaravasena “chabbaṇṇarasmiyo. “Samantā asītihatthappamāṇe”ti tāsaṃ rasmīnaṃ pakatiyā pavattiṭṭhānavasena vuttaṃ. “Tasmiṃ kira samaye”ti ca tasmiṃ addhānagamanasamaye buddhasiriyā anigūhitabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Na hi tadā tassā nigūhane pakkusātiabhigamanādīsu viya kiñcipi kāraṇaṃ atthīti. Ratanāveḷaṃ ratanavaṭaṃsakaṃ. Cīnapiṭṭhacuṇṇaṃ sindhanacuṇṇaṃ.

“The six-colored rays” means by way of blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and brilliant. “In a measure of eighty cubits all around” is said with regard to the natural place of diffusion of those rays. And “At that time, it seems” is said to show the unhidden state of the Buddha’s glory at the time of that journey. For at that time there was no reason at all for its concealment, as there was, for example, on the occasion of Pakkusāti’s approach. “Ratanāveḷaṃ” means a jeweled diadem. “Cīnapiṭṭhacuṇṇaṃ” means powder of Chinese flour; “sindhanacuṇṇaṃ” means powder from Sindh.

Byāmappabhāparikkhepavilāsinī [M 1.0052] ca assa bhagavato lakkhaṇamālāti mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni aññamaññapaṭibaddhattā evamāha. Dvattiṃsāya candamaṇḍalānaṃ mālā kenaci ganthetvā ṭhapitā yadi siyāti parikappanavasenāha “ganthetvā ṭhapitadvattiṃsacandamālāyā”ti. Siriṃ abhibhavantī ivāti sambandho. Esa nayo sūriyamālāyātiādīsupi. Mahātherāti mahāsāvake sandhāyāha. Evaṃ gacchantaṃ bhagavantaṃ bhikkhū ca disvā atha attano parisaṃ avalokesīti sambandho. “Yasmā panesā”tiādinā “kasmā ca so ratanattayassa avaṇṇaṃ bhāsatī”ti codanaṃ visodheti. Itīti evaṃ, vuttappakārenāti attho. Imehi dvīhīti lābhaparivārahāniṃ nigamanavasena dasseti. Bhagavato virodhānunayābhāvavīmaṃsanatthaṃ ete avaṇṇaṃ vaṇṇañca bhāsantīti apare. “Mārena anvāviṭṭhā evaṃ karontī”ti ca vadanti.

And the garland of marks of the Blessed One, resplendent with the surrounding fathom-wide aura, is so called because the marks of a great man are interconnected. By way of conjecture, it says 'like a garland of thirty-two moons strung together,' as if to say, 'if a garland of thirty-two moon-discs were strung together by someone and set in place.' The connection is 'as if overpowering its splendor.' This is the method also in regard to the garland of suns and so on. 'Great elder' refers to the great disciples. The connection is: 'And having seen the Blessed One walking thus, the bhikkhus then looked at their own assembly.' With 'Because this one...,' etc., it clarifies the charge, 'And why does he speak dispraise of the Three Jewels?' 'Iti' means 'thus,' that is, 'in the way stated.' With 'by these two,' it shows the loss of gain and retinue by way of conclusion. Others say: 'They speak dispraise and praise in order to investigate the Blessed One's lack of opposition and compliance.' And some say: 'Possessed by Māra, they act in this way.'

2. Ambalaṭṭhikāya avidūre bhavattā uyyānaṃ ambalaṭṭhikā yathā “varuṇānagaraṃ, godāgāmo”ti. Keci pana “ambalaṭṭhikāti yathāvuttanayeneva ekagāmo”ti vadanti[P 1.0067]. Tesaṃ mate ambalaṭṭhikāyanti samīpatthe bhummavacanaṃ. Rājāgārakaṃ vessavaṇamahārājadevāyatananti eke. Bahuparissayoti bahupaddavo. “Saddhiṃ antevāsinā brahmadattena māṇavenā”ti vuttaṃ sīhaḷaṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Tañca kho pāḷi āruḷhavaseneva, na pana tadā suppiyassa parisāya abhāvato. Kasmā panettha [V 1.0048] brahmadattoyeva pāḷi āruḷho, na suppiyassa parisāti? Payojanābhāvato. Yathā cetaṃ, evaṃ aññampi edisaṃ payojanābhāvato saṅgītikārehi na saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Keci pana “vuttanti pāḷiyaṃ vutta”nti vadanti, taṃ na yujjati pāḷiāruḷhavasena pāḷiyaṃ vuttanti āpajjanato. Tasmā yathāvuttanayenevettha attho gahetabbo. Parivāretvā nisinno hotīti sambandho.

2. Because it was not far from Ambalaṭṭhikā, the park was called Ambalaṭṭhikā, just as 'the city of Varuṇa, the village of Godā.' Some, however, say: 'Ambalaṭṭhikā is a single village in the way already stated.' In their opinion, 'at Ambalaṭṭhikā' is a locative of proximity. Some say the royal rest house was a shrine to the great king Vessavaṇa. 'Fraught with many dangers' means fraught with many perils. 'With his pupil, the young man Brahmadatta' is said in the Sinhala commentary. And that is only by way of its inclusion in the Pāli, not because Suppiya's assembly was absent then. Why is only Brahmadatta included in the Pāli here, and not Suppiya's assembly? Because there was no purpose. Just as this is so, it should be understood that other such instances were not included by the compilers of the canon because there was no purpose. Some, however, say, '“is said” means is said in the Pāli,' but that is not tenable, as it would follow that it is said in the Pāli simply by virtue of its inclusion in the Pāli. Therefore, the meaning here should be taken in the way already stated. The connection is: 'he was sitting surrounded.'

3. Kathādhammoti kathāsabhāvo, kathādhammo upaparikkhāvidhīti keci. Nīyatīti nayo, attho. Saddasatthaṃ anugato nayo saddanayo. Tattha hi anabhiṇhavuttike acchariya-saddo icchito. Tenevāha “andhassa pabbatārohaṇaṃ viyā”ti. Accharāyogganti acchariyanti niruttinayo[M 1.0053], so pana yasmā porāṇaṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgato, tasmā āha “aṭṭhakathānayoti. Yāvañcidaṃ suppaṭividitāti sambandho, tassa yattakaṃ suṭṭhu paṭividitā, taṃ ettakanti na sakkā amhehi paṭivijjhituṃ, akkhātuṃ vāti attho. Tenevāha “tena suppaṭividitatāya appameyyataṃ dassetī”ti.

3. 'The nature of the talk' means the substance of the talk; some say 'the nature of the talk' is the method of investigation. 'That by which one is led' is a method (nayo), a meaning. The method that follows grammar is the grammatical method. There, the word 'wonderful' (acchariya) is intended for what is rarely spoken of. Hence it says, 'like a blind person's climbing of a mountain.' 'Fit for a finger-snap' (accharāyogga) means 'wonderful' (acchariya); this is the etymological method. But because this comes from the ancient commentary, it is called the 'commentarial method.' The connection is with 'how well this has been penetrated.' The meaning is: 'We are unable to penetrate or to declare just how well it has been penetrated by him.' Hence it says: 'By its being well penetrated, he shows its immeasurability.'

Pakatatthapaṭiniddeso taṃ-saddoti tassa “bhagavatā”tiādīhi padehi samānādhikaraṇabhāvena vuttassa yena abhisambuddhabhāvena bhagavā pakato supākaṭo ca hoti, taṃ abhisambuddhabhāvaṃ saddhiṃ āgamanapaṭipadāya atthabhāvena dassento “yo so…pe… abhisambuddho”ti āha. Satipi ñāṇadassana-saddānaṃ idha paññāvevacanabhāve tena tena visesena nesaṃ savisayavisesappavattidassanatthaṃ asādhāraṇañāṇavisesavasena [P 1.0068] vijjattayavasena vijjābhiññānāvaraṇavasena sabbaññutaññāṇamaṃsacakkhuvasena paṭivedhadesanāñāṇavasena ca tadatthaṃ yojetvā dassento “tesaṃ tesa”ntiādimāha. Tattha āsayānusayaṃ jānatāāsayānusayañāṇena. Sabbañeyyadhammaṃ passatā sabbaññutānāvaraṇañāṇehi.

The word 'that' (taṃ) is a reference back to the established meaning. Showing that state of perfect self-enlightenment—by which the Blessed One is established and made manifest, and which is spoken of in apposition with terms such as 'by the Blessed One'—together with the path of its arrival as its meaning, he said: 'He who...pe... has become perfectly self-enlightened.' Although the words 'knowledge' and 'vision' are here synonyms for wisdom, in order to show the occurrence of their specific functions in their respective domains, he connects and shows their meaning by way of various distinctions: by way of the special unique knowledges, by way of the three true knowledges, by way of the true knowledges and direct knowledges and the obstructions, by way of the knowledge of omniscience and the fleshly eye, and by way of the knowledge of penetration and the knowledge of teaching, saying: 'of those...,' etc. Therein, 'knowing their dispositions and underlying tendencies' is by the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies. 'Seeing all knowable things' is by the knowledges of omniscience and unobstructedness.

Pubbenivāsādīhīti pubbenivāsāsavakkhayañāṇehi. Paṭivedhapaññāyāti ariyamaggapaññāya. Arīnanti kilesārīnaṃ, pañcavidhamārānaṃ vā, sāsanapaccatthikānaṃ vā aññatitthiyānaṃ, tesaṃ hananaṃ pāṭihāriyehi abhibhavanaṃ, appaṭibhānatākaraṇaṃ, ajjhupekkhanañca. Kesivinayasuttañcettha nidassanaṃ.

'By past abodes, etc.' means by the knowledges of the recollection of past abodes and the destruction of the taints. 'By penetrative wisdom' means by the wisdom of the noble path. 'Of enemies' means of the enemies that are the defilements, or of the five kinds of Māra, or of the adversaries of the teaching, the sectarians of other schools; their 'slaying' is overcoming them by means of psychic powers, rendering them speechless, and regarding them with equanimity. And the Kesivinaya Sutta is an example here.

Tathā ṭhānāṭhānādīni jānatā, yathākammūpage satte passatā, savāsanānaṃ āsavānaṃ khīṇattā arahatā, abhiññeyyādibhede dhamme abhiññeyyādito aviparītāvabodhato sammāsambuddhena[V 1.0049]. Atha vā tīsu kālesu appaṭihatañāṇatāya jānatā, tiṇṇampi kammānaṃ ñāṇānuparivattito nisammakāritāya passatā, davādīnampi abhāvasādhikāya pahānasampadāya arahatā, chandādīnaṃ ahānihetubhūtāya aparikkhayapaṭibhānasādhikāya sabbaññutāya sammāsambuddhenāti evaṃ dasabalaṭṭhārasāveṇikabuddhadhammehipi yojanā veditabbā.

By one who knows possibilities and impossibilities, etc.; who sees beings faring according to their kamma; an arahant because the taints with their latent tendencies are destroyed; a perfectly self-enlightened one because of his non-inverted understanding of things to be directly known, etc., in their various divisions. Alternatively: by one who knows because his knowledge is unobstructed in the three times; who sees by carefully considering the knowledge that revolves around the three kinds of kamma; an arahant through the accomplishment in abandonment that establishes the absence even of such things as sport; a perfectly self-enlightened one through the omniscience that establishes unimpaired discernment, which is the cause for the non-decline of such things as zeal. Thus the application should be understood also in terms of the ten powers and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

Yadipi [M 1.0054] hīnakalyāṇabhedena duvidhāva adhimutti pāḷiyaṃ vuttā, pavattiākāravasena pana anekabhedabhinnāti āha “nānādhimuttikatā”ti. Sā pana adhimutti ajjhāsayadhātu, tadapi tathā tathā dassanaṃ khamanaṃ rocanañcāti āha “nānājjhāsayatā…pe… rucitā”ti. Nānādhimuttikatañāṇenāti cettha sabbaññutañāṇaṃ adhippetaṃ, na dasabalañāṇanti āha “sabbaññutañāṇenā”ti. Iti ha meti ettha evaṃ-saddattho iti-saddo, ha-kāro [P 1.0069] nipātamattaṃ saralopo ca katoti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “evaṃ ime”ti.

Although inclination (adhimutti) is said in the Pāli to be only twofold, divided into inferior and superior, he said 'diversity of inclinations' (nānādhimuttikatā) because it is divided into many kinds according to its mode of occurrence. That inclination is the element of disposition (ajjhāsayadhātu), and that too is seeing, accepting, and approving in various ways; hence he said 'diversity of dispositions...pe...diversity of preferences' (nānājjhāsayatā...pe...rucitā). Here, by 'the knowledge of the diversity of inclinations,' the knowledge of omniscience is intended, not the knowledge of the ten powers; hence he said 'by the knowledge of omniscience' (sabbaññutañāṇenā). To show that in 'iti ha me,' the word 'iti' has the meaning of the word 'evaṃ' (thus), that 'ha' is a mere particle, and that a vowel has been elided, it is said, 'thus these' (evaṃ ime).

4. Arahattamaggena samugghātaṃ kataṃ, yato “natthi abyāvaṭamano”ti buddhadhammesu vuccati. Vītināmetvā phalasamāpattīhi. Nivāsetvā vihāranivāsanaparivattanavasena. “Kadāci ekako”tiādi tesaṃ tesaṃ vineyyānaṃ vinayanānukūlaṃ bhagavato upasaṅkamadassanaṃ. Pādanikkhepasamaye bhūmiyā samabhāvāpatti suppatiṭṭhitapādatāya nissandaphalaṃ, na iddhinimmānaṃ. “Ṭhapitamatte dakkhiṇapāde”ti buddhānaṃ sabbadakkhiṇatāya vuttaṃ. Arahatte patiṭṭhahantīti sambandho.

4. It has been eradicated by the path of arahantship, which is why it is said among the Buddha's qualities: 'There is no unbusied mind.' Having spent the time with the attainments of fruition. Having dressed, by way of changing the robe worn in the dwelling. 'Sometimes alone,' etc., refers to the Blessed One's approaching and seeing those to be trained in a way suitable for their training. At the time of placing his foot, the ground's becoming level is a natural consequence of his well-planted feet, not a creation of psychic power. 'As soon as the right foot is placed' is said because Buddhas are auspicious in every respect. The connection is: 'they become established in arahantship.'

Dullabhā sampattīti satipi manussattapaṭilābhe patirūpadesavāsaindriyāvekallasaddhāpaṭilābhādayo guṇā dullabhāti attho. Cātumahārājikabhavananti cātumahārājikadevaloke suññavimānāni gacchantīti attho. Esa nayo tāvatiṃsabhavanādīsupi. Kālayuttanti imissā velāya imassa evaṃ vattabbanti taṃtaṃkālānurūpaṃ. Samayayuttanti tasseva vevacanaṃ, aṭṭhuppattianurūpaṃ vā. Atha vā samayayuttanti hetūdāharaṇasahitaṃ. Kālena sāpadesañhi bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti. Utuṃ gaṇhapeti, na pana malaṃ pakkhāletīti adhippāyo. Na hi bhagavato kāye rajojallaṃ upalimpatīti.

'A rare accomplishment': the meaning is that even when one has obtained a human existence, such qualities as residence in a suitable country, completeness of faculties, the obtaining of faith, and so on, are rare. 'The realm of the Four Great Kings' means they go to the empty celestial mansions in the world of the Four Great Kings. This is the method also for the realm of the Tāvatiṃsa gods and so on. 'Connected with the time' (kālayutta) means suitable for the particular time, as when one says, 'At this time, this should be said in this way about this.' 'Connected with the occasion' (samayayutta) is a synonym for that, or it means suitable to the matter that has arisen. Alternatively, 'connected with the occasion' means accompanied by reason and example. For the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma at the right time and with a reasoned basis. The intention is that he makes them grasp the season, but he does not wash away the dirt. For dust and grime do not adhere to the Blessed One's body.

Kilāsubhāvo kilamatho. Sīhaseyyaṃ kappeti sarīrassa kilāsubhāvamocanatthanti yojetabbaṃ. “Buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ voloketī”ti idaṃ pacchimayāme bhagavato bahulaāciṇṇavasena vuttaṃ. Appekadā avasiṭṭhabalañāṇehi sabbaññutañāṇena ca bhagavā tamatthaṃ sādhetīti. “Ime diṭṭhiṭṭhānā”tiādidesanā [P 1.0070] sīhanādo. Tesaṃ “vedanāpaccayā taṇhā” tiādinā [V 1.0050] paccayākāraṃ samodhānetvā. “Sineruṃ [M 1.0055] ukkhipanto viya nabhaṃ paharanto viya cā”ti idaṃ brahmajāladesanāya anaññasādhāraṇattā sudukkaratādassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Etanti “yena, tenā”ti etaṃ padadvayaṃ. Yenāti vā hetumhi karaṇavacanaṃ, yena kāraṇena so maṇḍalamāḷo upasaṅkamitabbo, tena kāraṇena upasaṅkamīti attho, kāraṇaṃ pana “ime bhikkhū”tiādinā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃeva. Kaṭṭhanti nisīdanayogyaṃ dārukkhandhaṃ.

'The state of being not well' is fatigue. It should be connected thus: 'He adopts the lion's posture for the purpose of releasing the body from its state of being not well.' 'He surveys the world with the Buddha-eye': this is said with reference to the Blessed One's frequent practice in the last watch of the night. Sometimes the Blessed One accomplishes that purpose with the remaining powers and knowledges and with the knowledge of omniscience. A teaching such as 'These are the grounds for views' is a lion's roar. Having connected the conditional structure for them with 'with feeling as condition, craving,' etc. 'Like lifting up Mount Sineru and like striking the sky': this is said to show the extreme difficulty of the teaching in the Brahmajāla, on account of its being unique. 'This' (etaṃ) refers to these two words: 'by which' (yena), 'by that' (tena). 'By which' is an instrumental of cause. The meaning is: 'For which reason that assembly hall should be approached, for that reason he approached.' The reason, however, is stated in the commentary as 'these bhikkhus,' etc. 'A piece of wood' means a log suitable for sitting on.

Purimoti “katamāya nu bhavathā”ti evaṃ vutto attho. Kā ca pana voti ettha ca-saddo byatireke. Tena yathāpucchitāya kathāya vakkhamānaṃ vippakatabhāvaṃ joteti. Pana-saddo vacanālaṅkāro. Yāya hi kathāya te bhikkhū sannisinnā, sā eva antarākathābhūtā vippakatā visesena puna pucchīyatīti. Aññāti antarāsaddassa atthamāha. Aññatthe hi ayaṃ antarā-saddo “bhūmantaraṃ samayantara”ntiādīsu viya. Antarāti vā vemajjheti attho. Nanu ca tehi bhikkhūhi sā kathā yathādhippāyaṃ “iti ha me”tiādinā niṭṭhapitā yevāti? Na niṭṭhāpitā bhagavato upasaṅkamanena upacchinnattā. Yadi hi bhagavā tasmiṃ khaṇe na upasaṅkameyya bhiyyopi tappaṭibaddhāyeva kathā pavatteyyuṃ, bhagavato upasaṅkamanena pana na pavattesuṃ. Tenevāha ayaṃ kho…pe… anuppatto”ti. Kasmā panettha dhammavinayasaṅgahe kariyamāne nidānavacanaṃ, nanu bhagavato vacanameva saṅgahetabbanti? Vuccatedesanāya ṭhitiasammosasaddheyyabhāvasampādanatthaṃ. Kāladesadesakavatthudhammapaṭiggāhakapaṭibaddhā hi desanā ciraṭṭhitikā [P 1.0071] hoti, asammosadhammā saddheyyā ca. Desakālakattusotunimittehi upanibandho viya vohāravinicchayo, teneva cāyasmatā mahākassapena “brahmajālaṃ āvuso ānanda kattha bhāsita”ntiādinā desādipucchāsu katāsu tāsaṃ vissajjanaṃ karontena dhammabhaṇḍāgārikena nidānaṃ bhāsitanti tayidamāha “kāla…pe… nidānaṃ bhāsita”nti.

The former means: this is the meaning when it is said, ‘For what talk are you now assembled?’ And in the phrase ‘Kā ca pana vo,’ the particle ‘ca’ is used in the sense of contrast. It thereby illuminates the interrupted state of the talk that was being discussed, which is now being inquired about. The particle ‘pana’ is a verbal embellishment. For that very talk for which those bhikkhus were assembled, that same talk, being an ‘in-between talk,’ was interrupted, and it is this that is now being specifically asked about again. ‘Aññā’ explains the meaning of the word ‘antarā.’ For this word ‘antarā’ is used here in the sense of ‘other,’ as in such expressions as ‘another region’ and ‘another time.’ Or ‘antarā’ means ‘in the middle.’ But was not that talk already concluded by those bhikkhus according to their intention, with such phrases as 'Thus it seems to me'? No, it was not concluded, because it was cut short by the arrival of the Blessed One. For if the Blessed One had not approached at that moment, the talk connected with that topic would have proceeded even further; but because of the Blessed One’s arrival, it did not proceed. Therefore it is said: ‘This... has arrived.’ Why, when the Dhamma and Vinaya were being compiled, was the introductory section included? Should not only the Blessed One’s speech have been compiled? It is said: For the purpose of establishing the stability of the teaching, its freedom from confusion, and its credibility. For a teaching that is connected to the time, place, teacher, subject matter, Dhamma, and recipient endures for a long time, is free from confusion, and is credible. Just as a legal decision is bound by the signs of the speaker, time, agent, and listener, so too, when the Venerable Mahākassapa asked questions about the place, etc., saying, ‘Friend Ānanda, where was the Brahmajāla Sutta spoken?’, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, in answering them, stated the introduction. Thus it is said: ‘The time... the introduction was spoken.’

Apica satthusiddhiyā nidānavacanaṃ. Tathāgatassa hi bhagavato pubbaracanānumānāgamatakkābhāvato sammāsambuddhattasiddhi. Sammāsambuddhabhāvena hissa pubbaracanādīnaṃ abhāvo sabbattha appaṭihatañāṇacāratāya, ekappamāṇattā [M 1.0056] ca ñeyyadhammesu. Tathā ācariyamuṭṭhidhammamacchariyasatthusāvakānurodhābhāvato khīṇāsavattasiddhi. Khīṇā savatāya hissa ācariyamuṭṭhiādīnaṃ abhāvo, visuddhā ca parānuggahappavatti. Iti desakadosabhūtānaṃ diṭṭhicārittasampattidūsakānaṃ avijjātaṇhānaṃ abhāvasūcakehi, ñāṇappahānasampadābhi byañjanakehi ca sambuddhavisuddhabhāvehi purimavesārajjadvayasiddhi, tato eva ca antarāyikaniyyānikadhammesu sammohābhāvasiddhito pacchimavesārajjadvayasiddhīti bhagavato catuvesārajjasamannāgamo[V 1.0051], attahitaparahitappaṭipatti ca pakāsitā hoti nidānavacanena sampattaparisāya ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ ṭhānuppattikappaṭibhānena dhammadesanādīpanato, “jānatā passatā”tiādi vacanato ca. Tena vuttaṃ “satthusiddhiyā nidānavacana”nti.

Furthermore, the introductory statement establishes the Teacher’s authority. For the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the attainment of perfect self-enlightenment is established by the absence of prior composition, inference, tradition, or reasoning. Because he is a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, he has no need for prior composition and the like, on account of the unimpeded range of his knowledge in all things and the single standard of his knowledge regarding all knowable phenomena. Similarly, the attainment of the destruction of the taints is established by the absence of a ‘teacher’s fist,’ of stinginess with the Dhamma, and of favoritism towards disciples. Because his taints are destroyed, he is free from the ‘teacher’s fist’ and the like, and his conduct is pure, proceeding for the benefit of others. Thus, through the indications of the absence of ignorance and craving—which are faults in a teacher that corrupt right view, conduct, and attainment—and through the manifestations of the accomplishment in knowledge and abandonment and the purity of the Enlightened One, the first pair of grounds of self-confidence is established. And from that itself, through the establishment of the absence of delusion regarding obstructive and emancipating phenomena, the latter pair of grounds of self-confidence is established. Thus, the Blessed One’s possession of the four grounds of self-confidence and his practice for his own welfare and the welfare of others are revealed by the introductory statement, through its illuminating the teaching of the Dhamma with a brilliance that arises from the occasion and is appropriate to the disposition of the assembled company, and by such statements as ‘by one who knows and sees.’ Therefore it is said: ‘The introductory statement establishes the Teacher’s authority.’

Tathā satthusiddhiyā nidānavacanaṃ. Ñāṇakaruṇāpariggahitasabbakiriyassa [P 1.0072] hi bhagavato natthi niratthikā pavatti, attahitatthā vā, tasmā paresaṃyeva atthāya pavattasabbakiriyassa sammāsambuddhassa sakalampi kāyavacīmanokammaṃ satthubhūtaṃ, na kabyaracanādisāsanabhūtaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “satthusiddhiyā nidānavacana”nti. Apica satthuno pamāṇabhūtatāvibhāvanena sāsanassa pamāṇabhāvasiddhiyā nidānavacanaṃ. “Bhagavatā”ti hi iminā tathāgatassa guṇavisiṭṭhasattuttamādibhāvadīpanena, “jānatā”tiādinā āsayānusayañāṇādipayogadīpanena ca ayamattho sādhito hoti. Idamettha nidānavacanapayojanassa mukhamattadassanaṃ. Ko hi samattho buddhānubuddhena dhammabhaṇḍāgārikena bhāsitassa nidānassa payojanāni niravasesato vibhāvetunti.

Again, the introductory statement establishes the Teacher’s authority. For the Blessed One, all of whose actions are encompassed by knowledge and compassion, there is no purposeless activity, nor any for his own benefit. Therefore, for the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, all of whose actions proceed solely for the benefit of others, every bodily, verbal, and mental action constitutes the instruction of a Teacher, not a poetic composition or the like. Hence it is said: ‘The introductory statement establishes the Teacher’s authority.’ Furthermore, the introductory statement establishes the authoritativeness of the Dispensation by demonstrating that the Teacher is the standard of authority. Indeed, this point is established by the word ‘by the Blessed One,’ which reveals the Tathāgata’s superior qualities, his state as the supreme being, etc., and by the words ‘by one who knows,’ etc., which reveal his application of the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies, and so on. This is merely a glimpse into the purpose of the introductory statement. For who is able to explain exhaustively the purposes of the introduction spoken by the Treasurer of the Dhamma, who has understood what the Buddha understood?

Nidānavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Introduction is finished.

5. Nikkhittassāti desitassa. Desanāpi hi desetabbassa sīlādiatthassa vineyyasantānesu nikkhipanato “nikkhepo”ti vuccati. Tattha yathā anekasataanekasahassabhedānipi suttantāni saṃkilesabhāgiyādisāsanappaṭṭhānanayena soḷasavidhataṃ nātivattanti, evaṃ attajjhāsayādisuttanikkhepavasena catubbidhabhāvanti āha “cattāro suttanikkhepā”ti. Kāmañcettha attajjhāsayassa, aṭṭhuppattiyā [P 1.0073] ca parajjhāsayapucchāhi [M 1.0057] saddhiṃ saṃsaggabhedo sambhavati ajjhāsayapucchānusandhisabbhāvato, attajjhāsayaaṭṭhuppattīnaṃ pana aññamaññaṃ saṃsaggo natthīti nayidha niravaseso vitthāranayo sambhavati, tasmā “cattāro suttanikkhepā”ti vuttaṃ. Atha vā yadipi aṭṭhuppattiyā ajjhāsayena siyā saṃsaggabhedo, tadantogadhattā pana sesanikkhepānaṃ mūlanikkhepavasena cattārova dassitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. So panāyaṃ suttanikkhepo sāmaññabhāvato paṭhamaṃ vicāretabbo, tasmiṃ vicārite yassā aṭṭhuppattiyā idaṃ suttaṃ nikkhittaṃ, tassā vibhāgavasena “mamaṃ vā bhikkhave”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.5, 6), “appamattakaṃ kho paneta”ntiādinā (dī. ni. 1.7), “atthi bhikkhave”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.28) ca pavattānaṃ suttānaṃ suttapadesānaṃ vaṇṇanā vuccamānā taṃtaṃanusandhidassanasukhatāya [V 1.0052] suviññeyyā hotīti āha “suttanikkhepaṃ vicāretvā vuccamānā pākaṭā hotī”ti.

5. ‘Of what was laid down’ means of what was taught. For the teaching itself is called a ‘laying down’ (nikkhepa) because it lays down in the mental continuities of those to be trained the meaning of such things as virtue, which are to be taught. Here, just as the suttas, though divided into many hundreds and thousands, do not go beyond the sixteenfold classification by way of the establishment of the teaching concerning the side of defilement, etc., so too, with respect to the ways of laying down suttas based on one’s own disposition, etc., they are fourfold. Thus it is said: ‘There are four ways of laying down a sutta.’ Although here a mixed type is possible for one's own disposition, and for the arising of an issue, in combination with another's disposition and with questions—due to the existence of a connection between disposition and question—nevertheless, since there is no mutual combination between one’s own disposition and the arising of an issue, a completely exhaustive method of detailed exposition is not possible here. Therefore it is said: ‘There are four ways of laying down a sutta.’ Or, although there might be a mixed type involving the arising of an issue and a disposition, since the remaining ways of laying down are included within that, it should be understood that only four are shown as the basic ways. This way of laying down a sutta, being a general matter, should be investigated first. When it has been investigated, the commentary being spoken on the sutta passages that were delivered—such as ‘Bhikkhus, whether of myself...’ (DN 1.5-6), ‘But this, bhikkhus, is a small, trivial matter...’ (DN 1.7), and ‘There are, bhikkhus...’ (DN 1.28)—becomes easy to understand by way of the division of that arising of an issue on account of which this sutta was laid down, because it makes it easy to see the respective connections. Therefore it is said: ‘When the way of laying down a sutta has been investigated, what is being explained becomes clear.’

“Suttanikkhepā”tiādīsu nikkhipanaṃ nikkhepo, suttassa nikkhepo suttassa kathanaṃ suttanikkhepo, suttadesanāti attho. Nikkhipīyatīti vā nikkhepo, suttaṃyeva nikkhepo suttanikkhepo. Attano ajjhāsayo attajjhāsayo, so assa atthi suttadesanākāraṇabhūtoti attajjhāsayo. Attano ajjhāsayo etassāti vā attajjhāsayo. Parajjhāsayoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Pucchāya vaso pucchāvaso, so etassa atthīti pucchavasiko. Araṇīyato attho, suttadesanāya vatthu. Atthassa uppatti atthuppatti, atthuppattiyeva aṭṭhuppatti, sā etassa atthīti aṭṭhuppattiko. Atha vā nikkhipīyati suttaṃ etenāti suttanikkhepo, attajjhāsayādi eva. Etasmiṃ pana atthavikappe attano ajjhāsayo attajjhāsayo, paresaṃ ajjhāsayo parajjhāsayo, pucchīyatīti pucchā, pucchitabbo attho. Sotabbavasappavattaṃ dhammappaṭiggāhakānaṃ vacanaṃ pucchāvasikā, tadeva nikkhepasaddāpekkhāya pulliṅgavasena vuttaṃ “pucchāvasiko”ti. Tathā aṭṭhuppattiyeva “aṭṭhuppattiko”ti evampettha attho veditabbo.

In such phrases as ‘ways of laying down a sutta,’ a ‘laying down’ (nikkhepa) is a placing down. The laying down of a sutta (suttanikkhepa) is the speaking of a sutta; the meaning is the teaching of a sutta. Or, a ‘laying down’ is what is laid down; the sutta itself is the laying down, hence ‘suttanikkhepa.’ One’s own disposition is `attajjhāsayo`; it is so called because it exists as the cause for teaching a sutta. Or, `attajjhāsayo` means ‘one who has one’s own disposition.’ The same method applies to `parajjhāsayo` (another’s disposition). Mastery over a question is `pucchāvaso`; one who has this is `pucchavasiko`. The meaning of `attha` is 'from a matter to be undertaken,' the subject matter for the teaching of a sutta. The arising of an issue is `atthuppatti`; `aṭṭhuppatti` is just a variant of this. One for whom this exists is `aṭṭhuppattiko`. Alternatively, `suttanikkhepo` means ‘that by which a sutta is laid down,’ namely, one’s own disposition, etc. In this alternative meaning, one’s own disposition is `attajjhāsayo`; others’ disposition is `parajjhāsayo`; a question (`pucchā`) is what is asked, the matter to be questioned. The speech of the recipients of the Dhamma, which proceeds from a state of readiness to listen, is `pucchāvasikā` (fem.); this same word, in dependence on the word `nikkhepa`, is stated in the masculine gender as `pucchavasiko`. Similarly, `aṭṭhuppatti` itself becomes `aṭṭhuppattiko`. Thus the meaning should be understood here.

Ettha ca paresaṃ indriyaparipākādikāraṇanirapekkhatā attajjhāsayassa visuṃ nikkhepabhāvo yutto. Tenevāha “kevalaṃ attano ajjhāsayeneva kathetī”ti. Parajjhāsayapucchāvasikānaṃ pana paresaṃ ajjhāsayapucchānaṃ [M 1.0058][P 1.0074] desanānimittabhūtānaṃ uppattiyaṃ pavattitānaṃ kathaṃ aṭṭhuppattiyaṃ anavarodho, pucchāvasikaaṭṭhuppattikānaṃ vā parajjhāsayānurodhena pavattitadesanattā kathaṃ parajjhāsaye anavarodhoti na codetabbametaṃ. Paresañhi abhinīhāraparipucchādivinimuttasseva suttadesanākāraṇuppādassa aṭṭhuppattibhāvena gahitattā parajjhāsayapucchāvasikānaṃ visuṃ gahaṇaṃ. Tathā hi dhammadāyādasuttādīnaṃ (ma. ni. 1.29) āmisuppādādidesanānimittaṃ “aṭṭhuppattī”ti vuccati. Paresaṃ pucchaṃ vinā ajjhāsayameva nimittaṃ katvā desito parajjhāsayo, pucchāvasena desito pucchāvasikoti pākaṭo yamatthoti. Attano ajjhāsayeneva kathesi dhammatantiṭhapanatthanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sammappadhānasuttantahārakoti anupubbena niddiṭṭhānaṃ saṃyuttake sammappadhānapaṭisaṃyuttānaṃ suttānaṃ āvaḷi, tathā iddhipādahārakādi. Vimuttiparipācanīyā dhammā saddhindriyādayo. Abhinīhāranti paṇidhānaṃ.

Here, it is appropriate for 'one's own disposition' to be a distinct way of laying down, due to its non-dependence on such causes as the maturation of others' faculties. Hence it is said: 'He speaks solely from his own inclination.' However, one should not raise this objection: For those whose teaching is prompted by another's inclination or a question, which serve as the occasion for the teaching, how are they not included under 'occasion for the teaching'? Or, for those suttas based on a question or on an occasion for teaching, since the teaching proceeds in accordance with another's inclination, how are they not included under 'another's inclination'? For the arising of a cause for a sutta's teaching that is free from others' formal request, repeated questioning, etc., is taken as being an 'occasion for the teaching'; hence 'another's inclination' and 'based on a question' are taken separately. Thus, for suttas like the Dhammadāyāda Sutta (MN 1.29), the occasion for the teaching—such as the arising of material things—is called an 'occasion for the teaching.' A teaching given based on another's inclination without their question is 'another's inclination'; one given based on a question is 'based on a question'—the meaning of this is clear. It should be understood that the statement 'he spoke from his own inclination' is for the purpose of establishing the Dhamma tradition. `Sammappadhāna Suttanta-hāraka` refers to the series of suttas connected with the right strivings in the Saṃyutta Nikāya, arranged in sequence. Similarly, there are sections on the bases of psychic power, etc. The qualities that lead to the maturing of liberation are the faculty of faith, etc. `Abhinīhāra` means aspiration.

Vaṇṇāvaṇṇeti ettha “acchariyaṃ āvuso”tiādinā bhikkhusaṅghena vutto vaṇṇopi saṅgahito, taṃ pana aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā “atthi bhikkhave aññe ca dhammā”tiādinā upari desanaṃ [V 1.0053] ārabhissatīti. “Mamaṃ vā bhikkhave pare vaṇṇaṃ bhāseyyu”nti imissā desanāya brahmadattena vuttavaṇṇo aṭṭhuppattīti katvā vuttaṃ “antevāsī vaṇṇaṃ. Iti imaṃ vaṇṇāvaṇṇaṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā”ti. Vā-saddo upamānasamuccayasaṃsayavavassaggapadapūraṇavikappādīsu bahūsu atthesu dissati. Tathā hesa “paṇḍito vāpi tena so”tiādīsu [P 1.0075] (dha. pa. 63) upamāne dissati, sadisabhāveti attho. “Taṃ vāpi dhīrā muni vedayantī”tiādīsu (su. ni. 203) samuccaye, “ke vā ime, kassa vā”tiādīsu (pārā. 296) saṃsaye, “ayaṃ vā imesaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sabbabālo sabbamūḷho”tiādīsu vavassagge, “na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.154) padapūraṇe, “ye hi keci bhikkhave samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.170) vikappe, idhāyaṃ vikappeyevāti dassento āha “vā-saddo vikappanattho”ti. Para-saddo attheva aññatthe “ahañceva kho pana dhammaṃ deseyyaṃ, pare ca me na ājāneyyu”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.64, 65; ma. ni. 1.281; ma. ni. 2.223; saṃ. ni. 1.172; mahāva. 4, 8) atthi adhike [M 1.0059] “indriyaparopariyattañāṇa”ntiādīsu (paṭi. ma. mātikā 68, 1.111) atthi pacchābhāge “parato āgamissatī”tiādīsu. Atthi paccanīkabhāve “uppannaṃ parappavādaṃ saha dhammena suniggahitaṃ niggahetvā”tiādīsu [P 1.0076] (dī. ni. 2.168). Idhāpi paccanīkabhāveti dassento āha “pareti paṭiviruddhā”ti.

On 'praise and dispraise': Here, the praise spoken by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with such words as, 'It is wonderful, friend!' is also included. However, having made that the occasion for the teaching, he will begin the teaching further on with such words as, 'There are, bhikkhus, other qualities....' For the teaching, 'Or, bhikkhus, if others should speak praise of me,' the praise spoken by Brahmadatta is the occasion for the teaching. Having taken it as such, it is said: 'the disciple's praise. Thus, having made this praise and dispraise the occasion for the teaching....' The particle `vā` is seen in many meanings, such as comparison, conjunction, doubt, determination, expletive, and alternative. For example, in such phrases as 'he is wise thereby' (Dhp 63), it is seen in the sense of comparison, meaning 'similar to.' In such phrases as 'The wise, the sage, also feel that' (Sn 203), it is in the sense of conjunction. In such phrases as 'Who are these, or whose are they?' (Vin Pārā 296), it is in the sense of doubt. In such phrases as 'This one among these ascetics and brahmins is the most foolish, the most deluded,' it is in the sense of determination. In such phrases as 'This boy did not know moderation' (SN 2.154), it is an expletive. In such phrases as 'Whatever ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus...' (MN 1.170), it is in the sense of alternative. To show that here it is in the sense of alternative, he says: 'The particle `vā` has the meaning of an alternative.' The word `para` is found in the sense of 'other' in such passages as: 'I might teach the Dhamma, but others might not understand me' (DN 2.64–65; MN 1.281; MN 2.223; SN 1.172; Mv 4, 8). It is found in the sense of 'superior' in such passages as 'knowledge of the superiority and inferiority of others' faculties' (Paṭisambhidāmagga Mātikā 68; 1.111). It is found in the sense of 'later' in such passages as 'he will come later.' It is found in the sense of 'hostile' in such passages as 'having duly refuted with reason any hostile talk that has arisen' (DN 2.168). To show that here, too, it is in the sense of 'hostile,' he says: '`Pare` means those who are opposed.'

Īdisesupīti ettha pi-saddo sambhāvane, tena ratanattayanimittampi akusalacittappavatti na kātabbā, pageva vaṭṭāmisalokāmisanimittanti dasseti. Sabhāvadhammato aññassa kattuabhāvajotanatthaṃ āhanatīti kattuatthe āghātasaddaṃ dasseti, tattha āhanatīti hiṃsati vibādhati, upatāpeti cāti attho. Āhanati etena, āhananamattaṃ vā āghātoti karaṇabhāvatthāpi sambhavantiyeva. Evaṃ avayavabhedanena āghāta-saddassa atthaṃ vatvā idāni tattha pariyāyenapi atthaṃ dassento “kopassetaṃ adhivacana”nti āha. Ayañca nayo “appaccayo anabhiraddhī”tiādīsupi yathāsambhavaṃ vattabbo. Appatītā honti tenāti pākaṭapariyāyena appaccaya-saddassa atthadassanaṃ, taṃmukhena pana na pacceti tenāti appaccayoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Abhirādhayatīti sādhayati. Dvīhīti āghātaanabhiraddhipadehi. Ekenāti appaccayapadena. Sesānanti saññāviññāṇakkhandhānaṃ, saññāviññāṇaavasiṭṭhasaṅkhārakkhandhasaṅkhātānaṃ vā. Karaṇanti uppādanaṃ. Āghātādīnañhi pavattiyā paccayasamavāyanaṃ idha “karaṇa”nti vuttaṃ, taṃ pana atthato uppādanameva. Anuppādanañhi sandhāya bhagavatā “na karaṇīyā”ti vuttanti. Paṭikkhittameva ekuppādekavatthukekārammaṇekanirodhabhāvato.

Here in `īdisesupi`, the particle `pi` is in the sense of possibility. He thereby shows that an unwholesome course of thought should not be engaged in even with the Triple Gem as the object, still less with worldly and material things as the object. To show that by its intrinsic nature there is no other agent, he explains the word `āghāta` (resentment) in the agentive sense, from `āhanati` (he strikes). There, `āhanati` means he harms, he obstructs, and he torments. 'One strikes with this,' or 'it is merely a striking'—thus `āghāta` can also possibly have the sense of the instrument or the state of being. Having thus explained the meaning of the word `āghāta` by analyzing its components, he now shows its meaning by way of a synonym, saying: 'This is a synonym for anger.' This method should be applied as is suitable to such terms as `appaccayo` (displeasure) and `anabhiraddhi` (dissatisfaction). 'They are displeased by it'—this shows the meaning of the word `appaccaya` by way of a clear synonym. By way of that, however, it should be understood as `appaccayo` because 'one does not trust in it.' `Abhirādhayati` means to propitiate or satisfy. 'By two' refers to the terms `āghāta` and `anabhiraddhi`. 'By one' refers to the term `appaccaya`. 'Of the remaining' refers to the aggregates of perception and consciousness, or to what are designated as the formations aggregate remaining apart from perception and consciousness. `Karaṇa` means production. For the conjunction of conditions for the occurrence of resentment and the like is here called `karaṇa`, but that, in meaning, is just production. It was with reference to non-production that the Blessed One said they 'are not to be done.' It is rejected because of having a single origination, a single basis, a single object, and a single cessation.

Tatthāti [V 1.0054] tasmiṃ manopadose. Tumhanti “tumhāka”nti iminā samānattho eko saddo “yathā amhāka”nti iminā samānattho “amha”nti ayaṃ saddo. Yathāha, “tasmā hi amhaṃ daharā na miyyare”ti (jā. 1.9.93, 99). “Antarāyo”ti [P 1.0077] idaṃ manopadosassa akaraṇīyatāya kāraṇavacanaṃ. Yasmā tumhākaṃyeva ca bhaveyya tena kopādinā paṭhamajjhānādīnaṃ antarāyo, tasmā te kopādipariyāyena vuttā āghātādayo na karaṇīyāti attho. Tena nāhaṃ “sabbaññū”ti issarabhāvena tumhe tato nivāremi, atha kho iminā nāma kāraṇenāti dasseti. Taṃ pana kāraṇavacanaṃ [M 1.0060] yasmā ādīnavavibhāvanaṃ hoti, tasmā āha “ādīnavaṃ dassento”ti. “Api nu tumhe”tiādinā manopadoso na kālantarabhāvinoyeva hitasukhassa antarāyakaro, atha kho taṅkhaṇappavattirahassapi hitasukhassa antarāyakaroti manopadose ādīnavaṃ daḷhataraṃ katvā dasseti. Yesaṃ kesañci “pare”tiādīsu viya na paṭiviruddhānaṃyevāti attho. Tenevāha “kupito”tiādi.

`Tattha` means: in that corruption of mind. `Tumhaṃ` is a single word synonymous with `tumhākaṃ` (of you), just as `amhaṃ` is a word synonymous with `amhākaṃ` (of us). As it is said: 'Therefore our young ones do not die' (Jā 1.9.93, 99). 'An obstacle': this states the reason why corruption of mind should not be engaged in. The meaning is: because through that anger and so on there would be an obstacle for you yourselves to the first jhāna and so on, therefore those states of resentment and so on, spoken of by way of the synonym 'anger,' etc., should not be engaged in. He thereby shows: 'I do not restrain you from that with the lordly power of being "the All-Knowing One," but rather for this reason.' And since that statement of the reason is an explanation of the danger, he therefore says, 'showing the danger.' With 'But do you...?' etc., he shows the danger in corruption of mind more firmly, pointing out that it is not an obstacle only to welfare and happiness that will come to be at a later time, but is an obstacle even to the private welfare and happiness that occurs at that very moment. The meaning is that it is not only towards those who are opposed, as in the case of 'others' for some people. Therefore he says, 'one who is angry,' etc.

Andhatamanti andhabhāvakaratamaṃ. Yanti yattha. Bhummatthe hi etaṃ paccattavacanaṃ. Yasmiṃ kāle kodho sahate naraṃ, andhatamaṃ tadā hotīti sambandho. Yanti vā kāraṇavacanaṃ, yasmā kodho uppajjamāno naraṃ abhibhavati, tasmā andhatamaṃ tadā hoti, yadā kodhoti attho yaṃtaṃsaddānaṃ ekantasambandhibhāvato. Atha vā yanti kiriyāya parāmasanaṃ. Kodho sahateti yadetaṃ kodhassa sahanaṃ abhibhavanaṃ, etaṃ andhakāratamabhavananti attho. Atha vā yaṃ naraṃ kodho sahate abhibhavati, tassa andhatamaṃ tadā hoti, tato ca kuddho atthaṃ na jānāti, kuddho dhammaṃ na passatīti. Antaratoti abbhantarato, cittato vā.

`Andhatamaṃ` (deepest darkness) means that which makes one most blind. `Yaṃ` means `yattha` (where). For this is an accusative used in the sense of the locative. The connection is: 'At what time anger overcomes a person, at that time there is deepest darkness.' Or, `yaṃ` is a word indicating reason. The meaning is: 'Because arising anger overwhelms a person, therefore there is deepest darkness then, when there is anger.' This is because of the invariable correlation of the words `yaṃ` and `taṃ`. Or, `yaṃ` is a reference to the action. The meaning is: 'Anger overcomes'—this overcoming, this overwhelming by anger, is the state of deepest darkness. Or: 'What person anger overcomes, for him there is deepest darkness then.' And because of that, 'the angry one does not know the goal, the angry one does not see the Dhamma.' `Antarato` means from within, or from the mind.

“Idañcidañca kāraṇa”nti iminā sabbaññū eva amhākaṃ satthā aviparītadhammadesanattā, svākkhāto dhammo ekantaniyyānikattā, suppaṭipanno saṅgho saṃkilesarahitattāti imamatthaṃ dasseti. “Idañcidañca kāraṇa”nti etena ca “na [P 1.0078] sabbaññū”tiādivacanaṃ abhūtaṃ atacchanti nibbeṭhitaṃ hoti. Dutiyaṃ padanti “ataccha”nti padaṃ. Paṭhamassāti “abhūta”nti padassa. Catutthañcāti “na ca panetaṃ amhesu saṃvijjatī”ti padaṃ. Tatiyassāti “natthi cetaṃ amhesū”ti padassa. Avaṇṇeyevāti kāraṇapatirūpakaṃ vatvā dosapatiṭṭhāpanavasena nindane eva. Na sabbatthāti kevalaṃ akkosanakhuṃsanavambhanādīsu na ekantena nibbeṭhanaṃ kātabbanti attho. Vuttamevatthaṃ “yadi hī”tiādinā pākaṭaṃ katvā dasseti.

By this, 'For this and that reason,' he shows this meaning: our Teacher is truly the All-Knowing One because he teaches the Dhamma without distortion; the Dhamma is well-proclaimed because it leads exclusively to deliverance; the Saṅgha is of good practice because it is free from defilements. And by this, 'For this and that reason,' the statement 'he is not all-knowing,' etc., is refuted as being unreal and untrue. The second phrase is 'untrue'; this pertains to the first phrase, 'unreal.' The fourth phrase is 'and this is not found in us'; this pertains to the third phrase, 'and this does not exist in us.' 'Only in dispraise': only in censure by way of establishing a fault after stating a semblance of a reason. 'Not in all cases': the meaning is that a refutation should not be made absolutely in cases of mere abuse, reviling, contempt, etc. He makes this same meaning clear and shows it with the passage beginning, 'For if....'

6. Ānandanti pamodanti etena dhammena taṃsamaṅgino sattāti ānanda-saddassa karaṇatthataṃ dasseti[V 1.0055]. Sobhanaṃ mano assāti sumano, sobhanaṃ vā mano sumano, tassa bhāvo somanassanti tadaññadhammānampi sampayuttānaṃ somanassabhāvo āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati ruḷhīsaddattā [M 1.0061] yathā “paṅkaja”nti dassento “cetasikasukhassetaṃ adhivacana”nti āha. Ubbilayatīti ubbilaṃ, bhindati purimāvatthāya visesaṃ āpajjatīti attho. Ubbilameva ubbilāvitaṃ, tassa bhāvo ubbilāvitattaṃ. Yāya uppannāya kāyacittaṃ vātapūritabhastā viya uddhumāyanākārappattaṃ hoti, tassā gehassitāya odaggiyapītiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tenevāha “uddhaccāvahāyā”tiādi. Idhāpi “kiñcāpi tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ubbilāvitameva natthi, atha kho āyatiṃ kulaputtānaṃ edisesupi ṭhānesu akusaluppattiṃ paṭisedhento dhammanettiṃ ṭhapetī”ti, “dvīhi padehi saṅkhārakkhandho, ekena vedanākkhandho vutto”ti ettha “tesaṃ vasena sesānampi sampayuttadhammānaṃ karaṇaṃ paṭikkhittamevā”ti ca aṭṭhakathāyaṃ, “pi-saddo sambhāvane”tiādinā idha ca vuttanayena attho yathāsambhavaṃ veditabbo. “Tumhaṃyevassa [P 1.0079] tena antarāyo”ti etthāpi “antarāyoti ida”ntiādinā heṭṭhā avaṇṇapakkhe vuttanayena attho veditabbo.

6. ‘Ānandanti pamodanti etena dhammena taṃsamaṅgino sattāti’ shows that the word ‘ānanda’ has an instrumental sense: beings endowed with this Dhamma delight and rejoice in it. ‘Sobhanaṃ mano assāti sumano, sobhanaṃ vā mano sumano, tassa bhāvo somanassanti’ means: one who has a beautiful mind is a ‘sumano,’ or a beautiful mind is ‘sumano,’ and the state of that is ‘somanassa’ (gladness). ‘Tadaññadhammānampi sampayuttānaṃ somanassabhāvo āpajjatīti?’: Does the state of gladness also apply to other associated states? ‘Nāpajjati ruḷhīsaddattā’: It does not, because it is a conventional term, just as when explaining ‘paṅkaja,’ it is said: ‘This is a designation for mental pleasure.’ ‘Ubbilayatīti ubbilaṃ, bhindati purimāvatthāya visesaṃ āpajjatīti attho’: ‘Ubbilayati’ means ‘ubbilaṃ’; the meaning is that it breaks with the former state and attains a special condition. ‘Ubbilameva ubbilāvitaṃ, tassa bhāvo ubbilāvitattaṃ’: ‘Ubbilaṃ’ itself is ‘ubbilāvitaṃ,’ and its state is ‘ubbilāvitattaṃ.’ ‘Yāya uppannāya kāyacittaṃ vātapūritabhastā viya uddhumāyanākārappattaṃ hoti, tassā gehassitāya odaggiyapītiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ’: This is a designation for the uplifting rapture based on the household life, by which, when it has arisen, the body and mind become as if inflated like a bellows filled with wind. ‘Tenevāha ‘‘uddhaccāvahāyā’’tiādi’: Therefore it is said, ‘leading to restlessness,’ etc. Here too: ‘Although those bhikkhus have no elation whatsoever, still, in order to prevent the arising of unwholesome states for clansmen in the future in such situations, he lays down a guideline of the Dhamma.’ And in the commentary, concerning ‘the aggregate of formations is stated by two terms, the aggregate of feeling by one,’ it is said that ‘by means of these, the function of the other associated states is also rejected.’ ‘‘‘Pi-saddo sambhāvane’’tiādinā idha ca vuttanayena attho yathāsambhavaṃ veditabbo’: And here the meaning should be understood as is appropriate according to the method stated, as in ‘the particle “pi” is in the sense of possibility,’ etc. ‘‘‘Tumhaṃyevassa tena antarāyo’’ti etthāpi ‘‘antarāyoti ida’’ntiādinā heṭṭhā avaṇṇapakkhe vuttanayena attho veditabbo’: Here too, the meaning of ‘For you, that would be an obstacle’ should be understood according to the method stated below in the section on dispraise, as in ‘“obstacle” means this,’ etc.

Kasmā panetanti ca vakkhamānaṃyeva atthaṃ manasi katvā codeti. Ācariyo “saccaṃ vaṇṇita”nti tamatthaṃ paṭijānitvā “taṃ pana nekkhammanissita”ntiādinā pariharati. Tattha etanti ānandādīnaṃ akaraṇīyatāvacanaṃ. Nanu bhagavatā vaṇṇitanti sambandho. Kasiṇenāti kasiṇatāya sakalabhāvena. Keci pana “jambudīpassāti karaṇe sāmivacana”nti vadanti, tesaṃ matena kasiṇajambudīpa-saddānaṃ samānādhikaraṇabhāvo daṭṭhabbo. Tasmāti yasmā gehassitapītisomanassaṃ jhānādīnaṃ antarāyakaraṃ, tasmā. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā “somanassaṃ pāhaṃ devānaṃ inda duvidhena vadāmi sevitabbampi asevitabbampī”ti (dī. ni. 2.359). “Ayañhī”tiādi yena sampayuttā pīti antarāyakarī, taṃ dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha “idañhi lobhasahagataṃ pītisomanassa”nti vattabbaṃ siyā, pītiggahaṇena pana somanassampi gahitameva hoti somanassarahitāya pītiyā abhāvatoti pītiyeva gahitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā sevitabbāsevitabbavibhāgavacanato somanassassa pākaṭo antarāyakarabhāvo, na tathā pītiyāti pītiyeva lobhasahagatattena [M 1.0062] visesetvā vuttā. “Luddho attha”ntiādigāthānaṃ “kuddho attha”ntiādi gāthāsu viya attho daṭṭhabbo.

And with the words, ‘But why this?,’ he raises an objection, having in mind the meaning about to be stated. The teacher, having acknowledged that meaning by saying, ‘Truly, it is praised,’ answers it with, ‘But that is based on renunciation,’ and so on. Here, ‘this’ refers to the statement that it should not be done by Ānanda and others. The connection is: Is it not what was praised by the Blessed One? ‘With the kasiṇa’ means entirely, with its whole being. Some, however, say: ‘“Of Jambudīpa” is a genitive in the sense of the instrument.’ According to their view, the words ‘kasiṇa’ and ‘Jambudīpa’ should be understood as being in apposition. ‘Therefore’ means: because rapture and gladness based on the household life are an obstacle to jhāna and so on, therefore... For this has been said by the Blessed One: ‘Gladness, O Indra, king of the gods, I say is twofold: to be cultivated and not to be cultivated.’ ‘For this,’ and so on, is said to show with what the rapture is associated when it is an obstacle. Here, it might be said, ‘This is rapture and gladness accompanied by greed.’ But by the mention of rapture, gladness is also included, since there is no rapture devoid of gladness. Thus it should be understood that only rapture is mentioned. Alternatively, from the statement distinguishing what is to be cultivated and not to be cultivated, the obstructive nature of gladness is evident, but not so for rapture; therefore, only rapture is specified as being accompanied by greed. The meaning of the verses beginning ‘The greedy one does not know the goal’ should be understood in the same way as the verses beginning ‘The angry one does not know the goal.’

“Mamaṃ vā bhikkhave pare vaṇṇaṃ bhāseyyuṃ, dhammassa vā vaṇṇaṃ bhāseyyuṃ, saṅghassa vā vaṇṇaṃ bhāseyyuṃ, tatra ce tumhe assatha ānandino sumanā ubbilāvitā, api nu tumhe paresaṃ subhāsitadubbhāsitaṃ ājāneyyāthāti. No hetaṃ bhante”ti ayaṃ tatiyavāro, so desanākāle [V 1.0056] nīharitvā desetabbapuggalābhāvato desanāya anāgatopi tadatthasambhavato atthato āgatoyevāti daṭṭhabbo yathā taṃ [P 1.0080] kathāvatthupakaraṇaṃ vitthāravasenāti adhippāyo. “Atthato āgato yevā”ti etena saṃvaṇṇanākāle tathā bujjhanakasattānaṃ vasena so vāro ānetvā vattabboti dasseti. “Yatheva hī”tiādinā tamevatthasambhavaṃ vibhāveti. Vuttanayenāti “tatra tumhehīti tasmiṃ vaṇṇe tumhehī”tiādinā, “dutiyaṃ padaṃ paṭhamassa padassa, catutthañca tatiyassa vevacana”ntiādinā ca vuttanayena.

‘Bhikkhus, if others were to speak in praise of me, or in praise of the Dhamma, or in praise of the Sangha, and on that account you were to be joyful, glad, and elated, would you be able to know whether what they said was well-spoken or ill-spoken?’ ‘No, venerable sir.’ This is the third section. Although it was not delivered in the discourse because at the time of the teaching there was no person to whom it should be taught after being extracted, it should be seen as having come by way of meaning because its meaning is possible. The intention is that this is like the detailed treatment in the Kathāvatthu. By ‘having come by way of meaning,’ it shows that at the time of commenting, that section should be brought in and stated for the sake of beings who can understand it in that way. By ‘Just as,’ and so on, he clarifies the possibility of that meaning. ‘According to the method stated’ means according to the method stated in such passages as ‘“there by you” means “in that praise by you”’ and ‘the second term is a synonym for the first, and the fourth for the third.’

Cūḷasīlavaṇṇanā

An Explanation of the Minor Morality

7. Nivatto amūlakattā vissajjetabbatābhāvato. Anuvattatiyeva vissajjetabbatāya adhikatabhāvato. Anusandhiṃ dassessati “atthi bhikkhave”tiādinā. Oranti vā aparabhāgo “orato bhogaṃ, oraṃ pāra”ntiādīsu viya. Atha vā heṭṭhāattho ora-saddo “oraṃ āgamanāya ye paccayā, te orambhāgiyāni saṃyojanānī”tiādīsu viya. Sīlañhi samādhipaññāyo apekkhitvā aparabhāgo, heṭṭhābhūtañca hotīti. Sīlamattakanti ettha matta-saddo appakattho vā “bhesajjamattā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.447) viya. Visesanivattiattho vā “avitakkavicāramattā dhammā (dha. sa. tikamātikā 6), manomattā dhātu manodhātū”ti ca ādīsu viya. “Appamattakaṃ, oramattaka”nti padadvayena sāmaññato vuttoyeva hi attho sīlamattakanti visesavasena vutto. Atha vā sīlenapi tadekadesasseva [P 1.0081] saṅgahaṇatthaṃ [M 1.0063] appakatthavācako, visesanivattiattho eva vā “sīlamattaka”nti ettha matta-saddo vutto. Tathā hi indriyasaṃvarapaccayasannissitasīlāni idha desanaṃ anāruḷhāni. Na hi tāni pātimokkhaājīvapārisuddhisīlāni viya sabbaputhujjanesu pākaṭānīti. “Ussāhaṃ katvā”ti etena “vadamāno”ti ettha sattiatthaṃ māna-saddaṃ dasseti.

7. It is settled, because it is baseless and there is no need to answer it. It continues only because there is an abundance of reasons for it to be answered. He will show the connection with ‘There is, bhikkhus,’ and so on. Alternatively, ‘oraṃ’ means the near side, as in ‘wealth on the near side,’ ‘the near shore and the far shore,’ and so on. Or the word ‘ora’ means what is lower, as in ‘the conditions for coming to the near side, these are the lower fetters,’ and so on. For virtue, in relation to concentration and wisdom, is on the near side and is also lower. Regarding ‘a mere matter of virtue,’ here the word ‘matta’ can mean ‘a small amount,’ as in ‘a mere dose of medicine,’ and so on. Or it can mean ‘only,’ for the purpose of exclusion, as in ‘states that are only without applied and sustained thought,’ and ‘the mind-element is only the mind-element,’ and so on. For the meaning generally stated by the two words ‘a trifle, a minor matter’ is stated specifically by ‘a mere matter of virtue.’ Alternatively, the word ‘matta’ in ‘a mere matter of virtue’ is used to mean ‘a small amount’ in order to include only a part of virtue, or it is used to mean ‘only’ for the purpose of exclusion. For the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties and the virtue consisting in the right use of the requisites are not taken up in this discourse. For these are not as evident to all worldlings as are the Pātimokkha restraint and the purification of livelihood. By ‘having made an effort,’ he shows that the suffix ‘-māna’ in ‘vadamāno’ (speaking) has the sense of exertion.

Alaṅkaraṇaṃ vibhūsanaṃ alaṅkāro, kuṇḍalādipasādhanaṃ vā. Ūnaṭṭhānapūraṇaṃ maṇḍanaṃ. Maṇḍaneti maṇḍanahetu. Atha vā maṇḍatīti maṇḍano, maṇḍanajātiko puriso. Bahuvacanatthe ca idaṃ ekavacanaṃ, maṇḍanasīlesūti attho. Paripūrakārīti ettha iti-saddo ādiattho, pakārattho vā, tena sakalampi sīlathomana suttaṃ dasseti. Candananti candanasahacaraṇato candanagandho, tathā tagarādīsupi. Satañca gandhoti ettha gandho viyāti gandhoti vutto sīlanibandhano thutighoso. Sīlañhi kittiyā nimittaṃ. Yathāha “sīlavato sīlasampannassa kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggacchatī”ti [V 1.0057] (dī. ni. 2.150; a. ni. 5.213; mahāva. 285). Pavāyatīti pakāsati. Gandhāva gandhajātā.

Adorning, embellishing, is ‘alaṅkāra’ (adornment); or the preparation of earrings and so on. Filling a deficient place is ‘maṇḍana’ (embellishment). ‘Maṇḍane’ means for the sake of embellishment. Alternatively, one who embellishes is an ‘embellisher,’ a person of an embellishing nature. And this singular is used in a plural sense; the meaning is ‘in those with a nature to embellish.’ Regarding ‘one who fulfills,’ here the word ‘iti’ means ‘and so on’ or indicates the manner; thereby it points to the entire sutta in praise of virtue. ‘Sandalwood’ means the scent of sandalwood because of its association with sandalwood; similarly for tagara, and so on. ‘And the scent of the good’: here, the sound of praise connected with virtue is called ‘scent’ because it is like a scent. For virtue is the basis for renown. As it is said: ‘A fair report of fame goes up for a virtuous person, one accomplished in virtue.’ ‘Spreads’ means shines forth. ‘Fragrances’ means kinds of fragrance.

“Appakaṃ bahuka”nti idaṃ pārāpāraṃ viya aññamaññaṃ upanidhāya vuccatīti āha “upariguṇe upanidhāyā”ti. Sīlañhīti ettha hi-saddo hetuattho, tena idaṃ dasseti “yasmā sīlaṃ kiñcāpi patiṭṭhābhāvena samādhissa bahukāraṃ, pabhāvādiguṇavisese panassa upanidhāya kalampi na upeti, tathā samādhi ca paññāyā”ti. Tenevāha “tasmā”tiādi. Idāni “katha”nti pucchitvā samādhissa ānubhāvaṃ vitthārato vibhāveti. “Abhi…pe… [P 1.0082] mūle”ti idaṃ yamakapāṭihāriyassa supākaṭabhāvadassanatthaṃ, aññehi bodhimūlañātisamāgamādīsu katapāṭihāriyehi visesanatthañca vuttaṃ. Yamakapāṭihāriyakaraṇatthāya hi bhagavato citte uppanne tadanucchavikaṃ ṭhānaṃ icchitabbanti ratanamaṇḍapādi sakkassa devarañño āṇāya vissakammunā nimmitanti vadanti, bhagavatāva nimmitanti apare. “Yo koci evarūpaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ kātuṃ samattho atthi ce, āgacchatū”ti codanāsadisattā vuttaṃ “attādānaparidīpana”nti. Tattha attādānaṃ anuyogo, titthiyānaṃ tathā [M 1.0064] kātuṃ asamatthattā, “karissāmā”ti pubbe uṭṭhitattā titthiyaparimaddanaṃ.

He says ‘by comparison with higher qualities’ because ‘little’ and ‘much’ are stated in comparison with each other, like the near and far shores. Here, in ‘For virtue,’ the particle ‘hi’ has the sense of reason. Thereby he shows this: ‘Because virtue, although it is of great help to concentration by being its foundation, does not come up to even a fraction of it when compared with its special qualities such as power, and similarly concentration in comparison with wisdom.’ Therefore he says, ‘Therefore,’ and so on. Now, having asked ‘How?,’ he explains in detail the power of concentration. ‘Abhi…pe… at the root’ is said to show the very clear nature of the Twin Miracle and to distinguish it from other miracles performed at the foot of the Bodhi tree, at the assembly of relatives, and so on. For when the thought arose in the Blessed One’s mind to perform the Twin Miracle, a suitable place was desired. Some say that the Jewelled Pavilion and so on were created by Vissakamma by order of Sakka, king of the gods; others say they were created by the Blessed One himself. Because it is like a challenge—‘Let whoever is able to perform such a miracle come forward’—it is called ‘a display of self-assumption.’ Here, ‘self-assumption’ means a challenge. Because the sectarians were unable to do so, and because they had previously stood up saying, ‘We will do it,’ it was a crushing of the sectarians.

Uparimakāyatotiādi paṭisambhidāmagge (paṭi. ma. 1.116).

The passage beginning ‘From the upper body,’ and so on, is from the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. Ma. 1.116).

Tatthāyaṃ pāḷiseso –

Here is the remainder of the Pāli text:

“Heṭṭhimakāyato aggikkhandho pavattati, uparimakāyato udakadhārā pavattati. Puratthimakāyato aggi, pacchimakāyato udakaṃ. Pacchimakāyato aggi, puratthimakāyato udakaṃ. Dakkhiṇaakkhito aggi, vāmaakkhito udakaṃ. Vāmaakkhito aggi, dakkhiṇaakkhito udakaṃ. Dakkhiṇakaṇṇasotato aggi, vāmakaṇṇasotato udakaṃ. Vāmakaṇṇasotato aggi, dakkhiṇakaṇṇasotato udakaṃ. Dakkhiṇanāsikāsotato aggi, vāmanāsikāsotato udakaṃ. Vāmanāsikāsotato aggi, dakkhiṇanāsikāsotato udakaṃ. Dakkhiṇaaṃsakūṭato aggi, vāmaaṃsakūṭato udakaṃ. Vāmaaṃsakūṭato aggi, dakkhiṇaaṃsakūṭato udakaṃ. Dakkhiṇahatthato aggi, vāmahatthato udakaṃ. Vāmahatthato aggi, dakkhiṇahatthato udakaṃ. Dakkhiṇapassato aggi, vāmapassato udakaṃ. Vāmapassato aggi, dakkhiṇapassato udakaṃ. Dakkhiṇapādato aggi[V 1.0058], vāmapādato udakaṃ. Vāmapādato aggi, dakkhiṇapādato udakaṃ. Aṅgulaṅgulehi aggi, aṅgulantarikāhi udakaṃ[P 1.0083]. Aṅgulantarikāhi aggi, aṅgulaṅgulehi udakaṃ. Ekekalomato aggi, ekekalomato udakaṃ. Lomakūpato lomakūpato aggikkhandho pavattati, lomakūpato lomakūpato udakadhārā pavattatī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.116).

From the lower part of the body a mass of fire proceeds; from the upper part of the body a stream of water proceeds. From the front of the body fire, from the back of the body water. From the back of the body fire, from the front of the body water. From the right eye fire, from the left eye water. From the left eye fire, from the right eye water. From the right ear-hole fire, from the left ear-hole water. From the left ear-hole fire, from the right ear-hole water. From the right nostril fire, from the left nostril water. From the left nostril fire, from the right nostril water. From the right shoulder fire, from the left shoulder water. From the left shoulder fire, from the right shoulder water. From the right hand fire, from the left hand water. From the left hand fire, from the right hand water. From the right side fire, from the left side water. From the left side fire, from the right side water. From the right foot fire, from the left foot water. From the left foot fire, from the right foot water. From the fingers and toes fire, from the spaces between them water. From the spaces between them fire, from the fingers and toes water. From each body-hair fire, from each body-hair water. From every hair-pore a mass of fire proceeds; from every hair-pore a stream of water proceeds.

Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “ekekalomakūpato”ti āgataṃ.

In the commentary, however, it is given as: 'from each single hair-pore.'

“Channaṃ vaṇṇānanti ādinayappavatta”nti etthāpi nīlānaṃ pītakānaṃ lohitakānaṃ odātānaṃ mañjiṭṭhānaṃ pabhassarānanti ayaṃ pāḷiseso. “Suvaṇṇavaṇṇā rasmiyo”ti idaṃ tāsaṃ yebhuyyatāya vuttaṃ. Vitthāretabbanti etthāpi [M 1.0065] “satthā tiṭṭhati, nimmito caṅkamati vā nisīdati vā seyyaṃ vā kappetī”tiādinā catūsu iriyāpathesu ekekamūlakā satthuvasena cattāro, nimmitavasena cattāroti sabbeva aṭṭha vāre vitthāretabbaṃ.

In the passage beginning 'Of six colors,' here too the remaining Pāli text is: blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and radiant. The phrase 'golden-colored rays' is stated on account of their prevalence. 'To be elaborated': here too, by way of the passage beginning 'the Teacher stands, while the created image walks or sits or lies down,' it should be elaborated in all eight cases: four in the four postures with the Teacher as the basis, and four with the created image as the basis.

Madhupāyāsanti madhusittaṃ pāyāsaṃ. Attā mitto majjhatto verīti catūsu sīmasambhedavasena caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ mettākammaṭṭhānaṃ. “Caturaṅgasamannāgata”nti idaṃ pana “vīriyādhiṭṭhāna”nti etenāpi yojetabbaṃ. Tattha “kāmaṃ taco ca nhāru cā”tiādipāḷi (ma. ni. 2.184; saṃ. ni. 2.22; a. ni. 2.5; a. ni. 8.13; mahāni. 196) vasena caturaṅgasamannāgatatā veditabbā. “Kicchaṃ vatāyaṃ loko āpanno”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.57; saṃ. ni. 2.4) jarāmaraṇamukhena paccayākāre ñāṇaṃ otāretvā. Ānāpānacatutthajjhānanti etthāpi “sabbabuddhānaṃ āciṇṇa”nti padaṃ vibhattivipariṇāmaṃ katvā yojetabbaṃ. Tampi hi sabbabuddhānaṃ āciṇṇamevāti vadanti. Chattiṃsakoṭisatasahassamukhena mahāvajirañāṇagabbhaṃ gaṇhāpento vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā. Dvattiṃsadoṇagaṇhanappamāṇaṃ [P 1.0084] kuṇḍaṃ kolambo. Daribhāgo kandaro. Cakkavāḷapādesu mahāsamuddo cakkavāḷamahāsamuddo.

Honey-rice-pudding means rice pudding sprinkled with honey. The meditation subject of loving-kindness is endowed with four factors by way of breaking down the barriers regarding four persons: oneself, a friend, a neutral person, and a hostile person. This phrase 'endowed with four factors' should also be connected with 'the resolution of energy.' Therein, the fourfold endowment should be understood by way of the Pāli passage beginning, 'Willingly, let only skin, sinews, and bone remain…' Having directed knowledge to the structure of conditionality through the gateway of aging-and-death, by way of the passage beginning, 'Alas, this world has fallen into affliction…' In regard to 'the fourth jhāna based on mindfulness of breathing,' here too the phrase 'practiced by all Buddhas' should be connected by changing the case ending. For they say that this too is indeed practiced by all Buddhas. Having developed insight, causing it to grasp the womb of the great diamond knowledge through the thirty-six hundred thousand koṭi gateways. A `kuṇḍa` or `kolamba` is a vessel with a capacity of thirty-two `doṇa`s. A mountain cleft is a cave. The great ocean at the foot of the world-sphere is the world-sphere’s great ocean.

“Duve puthujjanā”tiādi puthujjane labbhamānavibhāgadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na mūlapariyāyavaṇṇanādīsu viya puthujjanavisesaniddhāraṇatthaṃ. Sabbopi hi puthujjano bhagavato upari guṇe vibhāvetuṃ na sakkoti, tiṭṭhatu puthujjano, sāvakapaccekabuddhānampi avisayā buddhaguṇā. Tathā hi vakkhati “sotāpannā”tiādi (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.8). Vācuggatakaraṇaṃ uggaho. Atthaparipucchanaṃ paripucchā. Aṭṭhakathāvasena atthassa savanaṃ savanaṃ. Byañjanatthānaṃ [V 1.0059] sunikkhepasudassanena dhammassa pariharaṇaṃ dhāraṇaṃ. Evaṃ sutadhātaparicitānaṃ manasānupekkhanaṃ paccavekkhaṇaṃ. Bahūnaṃ nānappakārānaṃ kilesānaṃ sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā ca avihatattā tā janenti, tāhi vā janitāti puthujjanā. Avighātameva vā jana-saddo vadati. Puthu satthārānaṃ mukhullokikāti ettha puthū janā satthupaṭiññā etesanti puthujjanāti vacanattho. Puthu…pe… avuṭṭhitāti ettha janetabbā, jāyanti vā etthāti janā, gatiyo. Puthū janā etesanti puthujjanā. Ito pare jāyanti etehīti janā, abhisaṅkhārādayo. Te etesaṃ puthū vijjantīti puthujjanā. Abhisaṅkharaṇādi attho eva vā jana-saddo daṭṭhabbo. Kāmarāgabhavarāgadiṭṭhiavijjā oghā. Rāgaggiādayo [M 1.0066] santāpā. Teyeva, sabbepi vā kilesā pariḷāhā. Puthu pañcasu kāmaguṇesu rattāti ettha [P 1.0085] jāyatīti jano, rāgo gedhoti evaṃ ādiko. Puthu jano etesanti puthujjanā, puthūsu vā janā jātā rattāti evaṃ rāgādiattho eva vā jana-saddo daṭṭhabbo. Palibuddhāti sambuddhā, upaddutā vā. “Puthūnaṃ gaṇanapathamatītāna”ntiādinā puthū janā puthujjanāti dasseti.

The passage beginning 'Two worldlings' is stated to show the distinction that can be made among worldlings, not to determine the specific characteristics of a worldling as in the commentary on the Mūlapariyāya Sutta and so on. For no worldling at all can fathom the qualities of the Blessed One. Let alone a worldling, the qualities of a Buddha are beyond the range even of the disciples and paccekabuddhas. For so it will be said: 'stream-enterers,' etc. Learning by heart is 'learning.' Questioning about the meaning is 'inquiry.' Hearing the meaning by way of the commentary is 'hearing.' Retaining the Dhamma by clearly depositing and discerning the phrasing and the meaning is 'retention.' Thus, for those familiar with the element of what has been heard, mental consideration is 'reviewing.' They are called 'worldlings' (`puthujjanā`) because, since the numerous and diverse defilements and identity view have not been struck down, they generate (`janenti`) them, or are generated (`janitā`) by them. Or the word `jana` just means 'generation.' Here, where it is said they 'look up to the face of many teachers,' the meaning of the word `puthujjana` is that 'many (`puthū`) are the people (`janā`) who claim to be their teachers.' Here, where it is said they have 'not risen up from the many...': `janā` means that which is to be generated or that in which one is born, i.e., destinies. They have many (`puthū`) destinies (`janā`), hence `puthujjanā`. Further, `janā` means that by which they are born hereafter, i.e., formations, etc. These exist for them in many (`puthū`) ways, hence `puthujjanā`. Or the word `jana` should be seen as having the meaning of 'forming,' etc. The floods are sensual lust, lust for existence, views, and ignorance. The fevers are the fire of lust, etc. Those same things, or all defilements, are the torments. Here, where it is said they are 'attached in many ways to the five cords of sensual pleasure': `jana` is that which is born—lust, greed, and so on. They have much (`puthu`) of such `jana`, hence `puthujjanā`. Or the word `jana` should be seen as having the meaning of lust, etc., in the sense that they are born (`jātā`) and attached (`rattā`) to many (`puthūsu`) things. 'Ensnared' (`palibuddhā`) means bound (`sambaddhā`) or oppressed (`upaddutā`). By the phrase 'having gone beyond the count of the many,' it shows that `puthujjanā` means the many folk.

Yehi guṇavisesehi nimittabhūtehi bhagavati tathāgata-saddo pavatto, taṃdassanatthaṃ “aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi bhagavā tathāgato”tiādimāha. Guṇanemittakāneva hi bhagavato sabbāni nāmāni. Yathāha –

To show by which special qualities, serving as marks, the word 'Tathāgata' is applied to the Blessed One, he said: 'For eight reasons the Blessed One is a Tathāgata,' and so on. For indeed, all the names of the Blessed One are based on his qualities as their mark. As it is said:

“Asaṅkhyeyyāni nāmāni, saguṇena mahesino;

Guṇena nāmamuddheyyaṃ, api nāmasahassato”ti. (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1313; udā. aṭṭha. 53; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 1.1.76);

Innumerable are the names of the Great Sage, possessed of qualities; By a quality a name may be designated, even from a thousand names.

Tathā āgatoti ettha ākāraniyamanavasena opammasampaṭipādanattho tathā-saddo. Sāmaññajotanāya visesāvaṭṭhānato paṭipadāgamanattho āgata-saddo, na ñāṇagamanattho “tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgato”tiādīsu (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.7; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.12; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.4.78; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.170; udā. aṭṭha. 18; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 1.1.37; theragā. aṭṭha. 1.3; itivu. aṭṭha. 38; mahāni. aṭṭha. 14) viya, nāpi kāyagamanādiattho “āgato kho mahāsamaṇo, māgadhānaṃ giribbaja”ntiādīsu (mahāva. 62) viya. Tattha yadākāraniyamanavasena opammasampaṭipādanattho tathā-saddo, taṃ karuṇāpadhānattā mahākaruṇāmukhena purimabuddhānaṃ āgamanapaṭipadaṃ udāharaṇavasena sāmaññato dassento yaṃtaṃsaddānaṃ ekantasambandhabhāvato “yathā sabbaloka…pe… āgatā”ti āha. Taṃ pana [V 1.0060] paṭipadaṃ mahāpadānasuttādīsu (dī. ni. 2.4) sambahulaniddesena supākaṭānaṃ āsannānañca vipassīādīnaṃ channaṃ sammāsambuddhānaṃ vasena nidassento “yathā vipassī bhagavā”tiādimāha. Tattha yena [P 1.0086] abhinīhārenāti manussattaliṅgasampattihetusatthāradassanapabbajjāabhiññādiguṇasampattiadhikārachandānaṃ vasena aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatena kāyappaṇidhānamahāpaṇidhānena[M 1.0067]. Sabbesañhi buddhānaṃ kāyappaṇidhānaṃ imināva abhinīhārena samijjhatīti. Evaṃ mahābhinīhāravasena “tathāgato”ti padassa atthaṃ dassetvā idāni pāramīpūraṇavasena dassetuṃ “yathā vipassī bhagavā…pe… kassapo bhagavā dānapāramiṃ pūretvā”tiādimāha.

Here, in the phrase 'Thus Come' (Tathā āgato), the word 'tathā' has the meaning of demonstrating a simile by way of determining the mode. The word 'āgata' has the meaning of having come along a path, by establishing a specific instance through a general indication; it does not have the meaning of having come to knowledge, as in 'he has come to the true nature,' nor the meaning of bodily arrival, as in 'the great ascetic has come to Giribbaja of the Magadhans.' Therein, when the word 'tathā' has the meaning of demonstrating a simile by way of determining the mode, showing in a general way, by way of example, the course of arrival of previous Buddhas through the gateway of great compassion (since compassion is predominant), and because of the invariable connection of the relative pronouns, he said: 'Just as all the world… have come.' Then, indicating that path by way of the six Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones who are recent and well-known from the numerous descriptions in the Mahāpadāna Sutta and others—Vipassī and so on—he said: 'Just as the Blessed One Vipassī…' Therein, 'by which aspiration' means by the great resolution of bodily dedication, which is endowed with eight factors: the human state, possession of the right physical characteristics, a cause, seeing a Teacher, the going forth, possession of qualities, meritorious service, and will. For the bodily dedication of all Buddhas succeeds only through this aspiration. Having thus shown the meaning of the word 'Tathāgata' by way of the great aspiration, now to show it by way of the fulfillment of the perfections, he said: 'Just as the Blessed One Vipassī… having fulfilled the perfection of giving… the Blessed One Kassapa…' and so on.

Ettha ca suttantikānaṃ mahābodhiyānapaṭipadāya kosallajananatthaṃ pāramīsu ayaṃ vitthārakathā – kā panetā pāramiyo? Kenaṭṭhena pāramiyo? Katividhā cetā? Ko tāsaṃ kamo? Kāni lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānāni? Ko paccayo? Ko saṃkileso? Kiṃ vodānaṃ? Ko paṭipakkho? Kā paṭipatti? Ko vibhāgo? Ko saṅgaho? Ko sampādanūpāyo? Kittakena kālena sampādanaṃ? Ko ānisaṃso? Kiṃ cetāsaṃ phalanti?

And here, for the purpose of generating skill in the practice of the great vehicle of awakening for the Suttantikas, is this detailed discourse on the perfections: What are these perfections? In what sense are they perfections? How many kinds are there? What is their sequence? What are their characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause? What is their condition? What is their defilement? What is their purification? What is their opposite? What is the practice? What is the analysis? What is the summary? What is the means of their accomplishment? In how much time are they accomplished? What is their benefit? What is their fruit?

Tatridaṃ vissajjanaṃ – kā panetā pāramiyoti. Taṇhāmānādīhi anupahatā karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitā dānādayo guṇā pāramiyo.

Herein is the explanation. What are these perfections? The perfections are those qualities, beginning with giving, that are unspoiled by craving, conceit, and so on, and are guided by compassion and skill in means.

Kenaṭṭhena pāramiyoti dānasīlādiguṇavisesayogena [P 1.0087] sattuttamatāya paramā mahāsattā bodhisattā, tesaṃ bhāvo, kammaṃ vā pāramī, dānādikiriyā. Atha vā paratīti paramo, dānādiguṇānaṃ pūrako pālako ca bodhisatto. Paramassa ayaṃ, paramassa vā bhāvo, kammaṃ vā pāramī, dānādikiriyāva. Atha vā paraṃ sattaṃ attani mavati bandhati guṇavisesayogena, paraṃ vā adhikataraṃ majjati sujjhati saṃkilesamalato, paraṃ vā seṭṭhaṃ nibbānaṃ visesena mayati gacchati, paraṃ vā lokaṃ pamāṇabhūtena ñāṇavisesena idhalokaṃ viya munāti paricchindati, paraṃ vā ativiya sīlādiguṇagaṇaṃ attano santāne minoti pakkhipati, paraṃ vā attabhūtato dhammakāyato aññaṃ, paṭipakkhaṃ vā tadanatthakaraṃ kilesacoragaṇaṃ mināti hiṃsatīti paramo, mahāsatto. “Paramassa aya”ntiādi vuttanayeneva yojetabbaṃ. Pāre vā nibbāne majjati sujjhati satte ca sodheti, tattha vā satte mavati bandhati yojeti, taṃ vā mayati gacchati gameti ca, munāti vā taṃ [M 1.0068] yāthāvato, tattha vā satte minoti pakkhipati, kilesāriṃ vā sattānaṃ [V 1.0061] tattha mināti hiṃsatīti pāramī, mahāpuriso. Tassa bhāvo, kammaṃ vā pāramitā, dānādikiriyāva. Iminā nayena pāramīnaṃ saddattho veditabbo.

In what sense is it a 'perfection' (pāramī)? Because of their connection with the special qualities of giving, virtue, and so on, the great beings, the bodhisattas, are supreme (paramā) through their excellence among beings. Their state or their action is a perfection (pāramī), that is, the practice of giving and so on. Alternatively, he is supreme (parama) because he excels (parati); the bodhisatta is the one who fulfills and protects the qualities of giving and so on. This belongs to the supreme one, or it is the state or action of the supreme one, which is a perfection (pāramī), namely, the practice of giving and so on. Or, he binds other beings to himself by his connection with special qualities; or, he is especially cleansed from the stain of defilements; or, he especially goes to the supreme Nibbāna; or, with his special knowledge as a standard, he knows and defines the other world just like this world; or, he places an exceedingly great collection of qualities like virtue in his own mental continuum; or, he harms and destroys what is other than his own being, the Dhamma-body—that is, the opposing band of thieves, the defilements, which cause his detriment.
