Thus he is 'parama,' a great being. The phrase 'this belongs to the supreme one,' etc., should be applied in the way stated. Or, on the further shore (pāre), which is Nibbāna, he is purified and he purifies beings; or, there he binds and yokes beings; or, he goes to it and causes others to go to it; or, he knows it as it really is; or, he places beings there; or, there he harms the enemy of beings, the defilements. Thus he is a 'pāramī,' a great person. His state or his action is a perfection (pāramitā), namely, the practice of giving and so on. In this way, the literal meaning of the perfections should be understood.

Katividhāti saṅkhepato dasavidhā, tā pana pāḷiyaṃ sarūpato āgatāyeva. Yathāha –

How many kinds are there? In brief, there are ten kinds. And these are indeed found in the Pāli canon in their own form. As it is said:

“Vicinanto tadā dakkhiṃ, paṭhamaṃ dānapārami”ntiādi (bu. vaṃ. 116).

“Then, while investigating, I saw first the perfection of giving,” and so on (Bu.va. 116).

Yathā cāha –

And as it is said:

“Kati [P 1.0088] nu kho bhante buddhakārakā dhammā? Dasa kho sāriputta buddhakārakā dhammā. Katame dasa? Dānaṃ kho sāriputta buddhakārako dhammo, sīlaṃ nekkhammaṃ paññā vīriyaṃ khanti saccamadhiṭṭhānaṃ mettā upekkhā buddhakārako dhammo, ime kho sāriputta dasa buddhakārakā dhammāti. Idamavoca bhagavā, idaṃ vatvāna sugato athāparaṃ etadavoca satthā –

“Venerable sir, how many qualities are there that make a Buddha?” “Sāriputta, there are ten qualities that make a Buddha. What ten? Giving, Sāriputta, is a quality that makes a Buddha; virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity are qualities that make a Buddha. These, Sāriputta, are the ten qualities that make a Buddha.” This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:

‘Dānaṃ sīlañca nekkhammaṃ, paññā vīriyena pañcamaṃ;

Khanti saccaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ, mettupekkhāti te dasā’ti”.

“Giving, virtue, and renunciation, wisdom with energy as the fifth; patience, truth, determination, loving-kindness and equanimity—these are the ten.”

Keci pana “chabbidhā”ti vadanti, taṃ etāsaṃ saṅgahavasena vuttaṃ. So pana saṅgaho parato āvibhavissati.

Some, however, say that they are “sixfold,” but that is said by way of including these ten; that inclusion will become clear later.

Ko tāsaṃ kamoti ettha kamo nāma desanākkamo, so ca paṭhamasamādānahetuko, samādānaṃ pavicayahetukaṃ, iti yathā ādimhi pavicitā samādinnā ca, tathā desitā. Tattha ca dānaṃ sīlassa bahūpakāraṃ sukarañcāti taṃ ādimhi vuttaṃ. Dānaṃ sīlapariggahitaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti mahānisaṃsanti dānānantaraṃ sīlaṃ vuttaṃ. Sīlaṃ nekkhammapariggahitaṃ, nekkhammaṃ paññāpariggahitaṃ, paññā vīriyapariggahitā, vīriyaṃ khantipariggahitaṃ, khanti saccapariggahitā, saccaṃ adhiṭṭhānapariggahitaṃ, adhiṭṭhānaṃ mettāpariggahitaṃ, mettā upekkhāpariggahitā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsāti mettānantaraṃ upekkhā vuttā. Upekkhā pana karuṇāpariggahitā, karuṇā ca upekkhāpariggahitāti veditabbā. Kathaṃ pana mahākāruṇikā bodhisattā sattesu upekkhakā hontīti? Upekkhitabbayuttesu kañci kālaṃ upekkhakā [M 1.0069] honti, na [V 1.0062] pana sabbattha, sabbadā cāti keci. Apare pana na sattesu upekkhakā, sattakatesu pana vippakāresu upekkhakā hontīti.

What is their order? Here, the order is the order of the teaching, and this is because of the order of undertaking them, while the undertaking is because of investigation. Thus, as they were investigated and undertaken in the beginning, so they were taught. Therein, giving was stated first because it is of great help to virtue and is easy to do. After giving, virtue was stated because giving, when supported by virtue, is of great fruit and great benefit. Virtue is supported by renunciation, renunciation by wisdom, wisdom by energy, energy by patience, patience by truthfulness, truthfulness by determination, and determination by loving-kindness; after loving-kindness, equanimity was stated because loving-kindness, when supported by equanimity, is of great fruit and great benefit. However, it should be understood that equanimity is supported by compassion, and compassion by equanimity. But how can the greatly compassionate bodhisattas be equanimous toward beings? Some say that they are equanimous at certain times toward those who should be regarded with equanimity, but not in all cases and at all times. Others, however, say that they are not equanimous toward beings, but toward the wrongdoings committed by beings.

Aparo [P 1.0089] nayo – pacurajanesupi pavattiyā sabbasattasādhāraṇattā, appaphalattā, sukarattā ca ādimhi dānaṃ vuttaṃ. Sīlenadāyakapaṭiggāhakasuddhito, parānuggahaṃ vatvā parapīḷānivattivacanato, kiriyadhammaṃ vatvā akiriyadhammavacanato, bhogasampattihetuṃ vatvā bhavasampattihetuvacanato ca dānassa anantaraṃ sīlaṃ vuttaṃ. Nekkhammena sīlasampattisiddhito, kāyavacīsucaritaṃ vatvā manosucaritavacanato, visuddhasīlassa sukheneva jhānasamijjhanato, kammāparādhappahānena payogasuddhiṃ vatvā kilesāparādhappahānena āsayasuddhivacanato, vītikkamappahānena cittassa pariyuṭṭhānappahānavacanato ca sīlassa anantaraṃ nekkhammaṃ vuttaṃ. Paññāya nekkhammassa siddhiparisuddhito, jhānābhāve paññābhāvavacanato. Samādhipadaṭṭhānā hi paññā, paññāpaccupaṭṭhāno ca samādhi. Samathanimittaṃ vatvā upekkhānimittavacanato, parahitajjhānena parahitakaraṇūpāyakosallavacanato ca nekkhammassa anantaraṃ paññā vuttā. Vīriyārambhena paññākiccasiddhito, sattasuññatādhammanijjhānakkhantiṃ vatvā sattahitāya ārambhassa acchariyatāvacanato, upekkhānimittaṃ vatvā paggahanimittavacanato, nisammakāritaṃ vatvā uṭṭhānavacanato ca. Nisammakārino hi uṭṭhānaṃ phalavisesamāvahatīti paññāya anantaraṃ vīriyaṃ vuttaṃ.

Another method: Giving was stated first because it occurs even among the masses, is common to all beings, is of lesser fruit, and is easy to do. After giving, virtue was stated because of the purity of the giver and recipient through virtue; because having spoken of helping others, it speaks of refraining from harming others; because having spoken of a doctrine of action, it speaks of a doctrine of non-action; and because having spoken of the cause for accomplishment in wealth, it speaks of the cause for accomplishment in existence. After virtue, renunciation was stated because the accomplishment of virtue is perfected by renunciation; because having spoken of good conduct of body and speech, it speaks of good conduct of mind; because for one of purified virtue, jhāna is easily accomplished; because having spoken of purity of application by abandoning offenses in action, it speaks of purity of disposition by abandoning offenses of defilement; and because it speaks of abandoning the obsessions of the mind by abandoning transgression. After renunciation, wisdom was stated because the fulfillment and purity of renunciation is achieved through wisdom; because it is said that in the absence of jhāna there is an absence of wisdom—for wisdom has concentration as its proximate cause, and concentration has wisdom as its manifestation; because having spoken of the sign of serenity, it speaks of the sign of equanimity; and because through meditation on the welfare of others, it speaks of skill in the means for acting for the welfare of others. After wisdom, energy was stated because the task of wisdom is accomplished by the undertaking of energy; because having spoken of patience with the contemplation of the doctrine of the emptiness of beings, it speaks of the wonder of the undertaking for the welfare of beings; because having spoken of the sign of equanimity, it speaks of the sign of exertion; and because having spoken of considered action, it speaks of striving—for to one who acts with consideration, striving brings a special fruit.

Vīriyena titikkhāsiddhito. Vīriyavā hi āraddhavīriyattā sattasaṅkhārehi upanītaṃ dukkhaṃ abhibhuyya viharati vīriyassa titikkhālaṅkārabhāvato. Vīriyavato hi titikkhā sobhati. Paggahanimittaṃ vatvā samathanimittavacanato, accārambhena uddhaccadosappahānavacanato. Dhammanijjhānakkhantiyā hi uddhaccadoso pahīyati. Vīriyavato sātaccakaraṇavacanato. Khantibahulo hi anuddhato sātaccakārī hoti. Appamādavato parahitakiriyārambhe [P 1.0090] paccupakārataṇhābhāvavacanato. Yāthāvato dhammanijjhāne hi sati taṇhā na hoti. Parahitārambhe paramepi parakatadukkhasahanabhāvavacanato ca vīriyassa anantaraṃ khanti vuttā[M 1.0070]. Saccena khantiyā cirādhiṭṭhānato, apakārino apakārakhantiṃ vatvā tadupakārakaraṇe avisaṃvādavacanato, khantiyā apavādavācāvikampanena bhūtavāditāya avijahanavacanato, sattasuññatādhammanijjhānakkhantiṃ vatvā tadupabrūhitañāṇasaccavacanato ca khantiyā anantaraṃ saccaṃ vuttaṃ. Adhiṭṭhānena saccasiddhito. Acalādhiṭṭhānassa hi virati sijjhati. Avisaṃvāditaṃ vatvā tattha acalabhāvavacanato. Saccasandho hi dānādīsu paṭiññānurūpaṃ niccalova [V 1.0063] pavattati. Ñāṇasaccaṃ vatvā sambhāresu pavattiniṭṭhāpanavacanato. Yathābhūtañāṇavā hi bodhisambhāresu adhitiṭṭhati, te ca niṭṭhāpeti paṭipakkhehi akampiyabhāvatoti saccassa anantaraṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ vuttaṃ. Mettāya parahitakaraṇasamādānādhiṭṭhānasiddhito, adhiṭṭhānaṃ vatvā hitūpasaṃhāravacanato. Bodhisambhāre hi adhitiṭṭhamāno mettāvihārī hoti. Acalādhiṭṭhānassa samādānāvikopanato, samādānasambhavato ca adhiṭṭhānassa anantaraṃ mettā vuttā. Upekkhāya mettāvisuddhito, sattesu hitūpasaṃhāraṃ vatvā tadaparādhesu udāsīnatāvacanato, mettābhāvanaṃ vatvā tannissandabhāvanāvacanato, “hitakāmasattepi upekkhako”ti acchariyaguṇabhāvavacanato ca mettāya anantaraṃ upekkhā vuttāti evametāsaṃ kamo veditabbo.

After energy, patience was stated because forbearance is accomplished by energy. For one with energy, having aroused it, dwells overcoming the suffering produced by beings and conditioned things, because forbearance is an adornment for energy. Indeed, forbearance shines in one who possesses energy. It was stated after energy because, having spoken of the sign of exertion, it speaks of the sign of serenity; because it speaks of abandoning the fault of restlessness through excessive effort—for by patience with contemplating the Dhamma, the fault of restlessness is abandoned; because it speaks of constant practice for one with energy—for one who is full of patience, being unagitated, is a constant doer; because for one who is heedful, it speaks of the absence of craving for a return favor when undertaking action for the welfare of others—for when there is contemplation of the Dhamma as it really is, there is no craving; and because it speaks of enduring suffering caused by others even in the supreme undertaking for the welfare of others. After patience, truthfulness was stated because through truthfulness, patience is long-lasting; because having spoken of patience toward a wrongdoer, it speaks of not being false when conferring a benefit on him; because through patience, by not being shaken by words of blame, it speaks of not abandoning truthful speech; and because having spoken of patience with contemplating the doctrine of the emptiness of beings, it speaks of the truth of the knowledge that is augmented by that. After truthfulness, determination was stated because truthfulness is accomplished by determination. For the abstinence of one with unshakable determination succeeds. It was stated after truthfulness because having spoken of truthfulness, it speaks of being unshakable in that—for one who is bound by truth acts unmovingly in giving, etc., in accordance with his promise; and because having spoken of the truth of knowledge, it speaks of engaging in and completing the accumulations—for one with knowledge of things as they are is determined upon the accumulations for enlightenment and brings them to completion, being unshakable by opponents. After determination, loving-kindness was stated because the determination to undertake action for the welfare of others is accomplished by loving-kindness; because having spoken of determination, it speaks of bringing about welfare—for one who is determined upon the accumulations for enlightenment dwells in loving-kindness; and because for one with unshakable determination, the undertaking is not violated, and because the undertaking is possible. After loving-kindness, equanimity was stated because loving-kindness is purified by equanimity; because having spoken of bringing about the welfare of beings, it speaks of indifference to their offenses; because having spoken of the development of loving-kindness, it speaks of the development of its outflow; and because it speaks of the wonderful quality: ‘He is equanimous even toward a being who wishes him well.’ In this way, the order of these should be understood.

Kāni lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānānīti? Ettha [P 1.0091] avisesena tāva sabbāpi pāramiyo parānuggahalakkhaṇā, paresaṃ upakārakaraṇarasā, avikampanarasā vā, hitesitāpaccupaṭṭhānā, buddhattapaccupaṭṭhānā vā, mahākaruṇāpadaṭṭhānā, karuṇūpāyakosallapadaṭṭhānā vā.

What are their characteristics, functions, manifestations, and proximate causes? Here, without distinction, all the perfections have the characteristic of assisting others; the function of benefiting others, or the function of being unshakeable; the manifestation of wishing for their welfare, or the manifestation of Buddhahood; the proximate cause of great compassion, or the proximate cause of compassion and skill in means.

Visesena pana yasmā karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitā attupakaraṇapariccāgacetanā dānapāramitā. Karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitaṃ kāyavacīsucaritaṃ atthato akattabbavirati, kattabbakaraṇacetanādayo ca sīlapāramitā. Karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahito ādīnavadassanapubbaṅgamo kāmabhavehi nikkhamanacittuppādo nekkhammapāramitā. Karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahito dhammānaṃ sāmaññavisesalakkhaṇāvabodho paññāpāramitā. Karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahito kāyacittehi parahitārambho vīriyapāramitā. Karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitaṃ sattasaṅkhārāparādhasahanaṃ adosappadhāno tadākārappavatto cittuppādo khantipāramitā[M 1.0071]. Karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitaṃ viraticetanādibhedaṃ avisaṃvādanaṃ saccapāramitā. Karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitaṃ acalasamādānādhiṭṭhānaṃ tadākārappavatto cittuppādo adhiṭṭhānapāramitā. Karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahito lokassa hitūpasaṃhāro atthato abyāpādo mettāpāramitā. Karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitā anunayapaṭighaviddhaṃsinī iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu sattasaṅkhāresu samappavatti upekkhāpāramitā.

Moreover, because the volition to relinquish one's own possessions, embraced by compassion and skill in means, is the perfection of giving. Good conduct of body and speech, embraced by compassion and skill in means—which in essence is abstinence from what should not be done and the volition to do what should be done, and so on—is the perfection of virtue. The arising of a thought of renunciation from sensual pleasures and states of existence, preceded by seeing the danger in them and embraced by compassion and skill in means, is the perfection of renunciation. The understanding of the general and specific characteristics of phenomena, embraced by compassion and skill in means, is the perfection of wisdom. The undertaking for the welfare of others with body and mind, embraced by compassion and skill in means, is the perfection of energy. The endurance of offenses from beings and things, a mental state proceeding in that way with non-aversion as its chief feature, embraced by compassion and skill in means, is the perfection of patience. Non-deception, of various kinds such as the volition of abstinence, embraced by compassion and skill in means, is the perfection of truthfulness. An unwavering undertaking and determination, a mental state proceeding in that way, embraced by compassion and skill in means, is the perfection of resolve. The furthering of the world's welfare, which in essence is non-ill will, embraced by compassion and skill in means, is the perfection of loving-kindness. An even-minded disposition towards agreeable and disagreeable beings and things, which destroys attraction and repulsion, embraced by compassion and skill in means, is the perfection of equanimity.

Tasmā pariccāgalakkhaṇaṃ dānaṃ, deyyadhamme lobhaviddhaṃsanarasaṃ, anāsattipaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, bhavavibhavasampattipaccupaṭṭhānaṃ vā, pariccajitabbavatthupadaṭṭhānaṃ. Sīlanalakkhaṇaṃ sīlaṃ, samādhānalakkhaṇaṃ, patiṭṭhānalakkhaṇañcāti vuttaṃ hoti. Dussīlyaviddhaṃsanarasaṃ, anavajjarasaṃ vā, soceyyapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, hirottappapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Kāmato bhavato ca nikkhamanalakkhaṇaṃ nekkhammaṃ, tadādīnavavibhāvanarasaṃ[V 1.0064], tato eva vimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, saṃvegapadaṭṭhānaṃ[P 1.0092]. Yathāsabhāvapaṭivedhalakkhaṇā paññā, akkhalitapaṭivedhalakkhaṇā vā kusalissāsakhittausupaṭivedho viya, visayobhāsanarasā padīpo viya, asammohapaccupaṭṭhānā araññagatasudesako viya, samādhipadaṭṭhānā, catusaccapadaṭṭhānā vā. Ussāhalakkhaṇaṃ vīriyaṃ, upatthambhanarasaṃ, asaṃsīdanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, vīriyārambhavatthu (a. ni. 8.80) padaṭṭhānaṃ, saṃvegapadaṭṭhānaṃ vā. Khamanalakkhaṇā khanti, iṭṭhāniṭṭhasahanarasā, adhivāsanapaccupaṭṭhānā, avirodhapaccupaṭṭhānā vā, yathābhūtadassanapadaṭṭhānā. Avisaṃvādanalakkhaṇaṃ saccaṃ, yāthāvavibhāvanarasaṃ [yathāsabhāvavibhāvanarasaṃ (cariyā. aṭṭha. pakiṇṇakakathāya)], sādhutāpaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, soraccapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Bodhisambhāresu adhiṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ, tesaṃ paṭipakkhābhibhavanarasaṃ, tattha acalatāpaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, bodhisambhārapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Hitākārappavattilakkhaṇā mettā, hitūpasaṃhārarasā, āghātavinayanarasā vā, sommabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, sattānaṃ manāpabhāvadassanapadaṭṭhānā. Majjhattākārappavattilakkhaṇā upekkhā, samabhāvadassanarasā, paṭighānunayavūpasamapaccupaṭṭhānā, kammassakatāpaccavekkhaṇapadaṭṭhānā. Ettha ca karuṇūpāyakosallapariggahitatā dānādīnaṃ pariccāgādilakkhaṇassa visesanabhāvena vattabbā, yato tāni pāramīsaṅkhyaṃ labhantīti.

Therefore, the characteristic of giving (dāna) is relinquishing; its function is to destroy greed for the objects to be given; its manifestation is non-attachment or the attainment of prosperity in future existences; its proximate cause is the object to be relinquished. The characteristic of virtue (sīla) is composing or being a foundation; its function is to eliminate misconduct or to produce blamelessness; its manifestation is purity; its proximate cause is moral shame and fear of wrongdoing. The characteristic of renunciation (nekkhamma) is departing from sensual pleasures and existence; its function is to reveal their dangers; its manifestation is detachment from them; its proximate cause is a sense of spiritual urgency. The characteristic of wisdom (paññā) is penetrating things according to their true nature or unerring penetration, like the penetration of an arrow shot by a skilled archer; its function is illuminating its object, like a lamp; its manifestation is non-delusion, like a good guide in a forest; its proximate cause is concentration or the Four Noble Truths. The characteristic of energy (vīriya) is exertion; its function is supporting; its manifestation is unshaken persistence; its proximate cause is a basis for initiating effort or a sense of spiritual urgency. The characteristic of patience (khanti) is endurance; its function is tolerating the desirable and undesirable; its manifestation is forbearance or non-opposition; its proximate cause is seeing things as they truly are. The characteristic of truthfulness (sacca) is non-deceptiveness; its function is revealing things as they are; its manifestation is probity; its proximate cause is docility. The characteristic of determination (adhiṭṭhāna) is resolve regarding the requisites of enlightenment; its function is to overcome their opposites; its manifestation is steadfastness in them; its proximate cause is the requisites of enlightenment. The characteristic of loving-kindness (mettā) is promoting welfare; its function is to provide benefit or to remove resentment; its manifestation is amiability; its proximate cause is seeing beings as lovable. The characteristic of equanimity (upekkhā) is promoting neutrality; its function is seeing things impartially; its manifestation is the subsiding of aversion and attraction; its proximate cause is reflecting on ownership of kamma. Here, compassion and skill in means should be understood as distinguishing factors for the characteristics of giving and the like—such as relinquishing—because they enable these qualities to be classified as perfections.

Ko [M 1.0072] paccayoti abhinīhāro paccayo. Yo hi ayaṃ “manussattaṃ liṅgasampattī”tiādi (bu. vaṃ. 2.59) aṭṭhadhammasamodhānasampādito “tiṇṇo tāreyyaṃ, mutto moceyyaṃ, buddho bodheyyaṃ, suddho sodheyyaṃ, danto dameyyaṃ, santo sameyyaṃ, assattho assāseyyaṃ, parinibbuto parinibbāpeyya”ntiādinā [P 1.0093] (cariyā. aṭṭha. pakiṇṇakakathāya) pavatto abhinīhāro, so avisesena sabbapāramīnaṃ paccayo. Tappavattiyā hi uddhaṃ pāramīnaṃ pavicayupaṭṭhānasamādānādhiṭṭhānanipphattiyo mahāpurisānaṃ sambhavanti.

What is the condition? The aspiration is the condition. Indeed, this aspiration, which arises from the accomplishment of the eight conditions—such as “human existence and the possession of the right gender”—and which is expressed in such terms as “Having crossed over, may I lead others across; being liberated, may I liberate others; being awakened, may I awaken others; being purified, may I purify others; being tamed, may I tame others; being calmed, may I calm others; being consoled, may I console others; having attained final Nibbāna, may I lead others to final Nibbāna,” etc., is without distinction the condition for all perfections. For it is from the time of its arising onwards that the investigation, establishment, undertaking, determination, and accomplishment of the perfections come to be for great beings.

Yathā ca abhinīhāro, evaṃ mahākaruṇā, upāyakosallañca. Tattha upāyakosallaṃ nāma dānādīnaṃ bodhisambhārabhāvassa nimittabhūtā paññā, yāhi karuṇūpāyakosallatāhi mahāpurisānaṃ attasukhanirapekkhatā, nirantaraṃ parahitakaraṇapasutatā, sudukkarehipi mahābodhisattacaritehi visādābhāvo, pasādasambuddhidassanasavanānussaraṇāvatthāsupi sattānaṃ hitasukhapaṭilābhahetubhāvo ca sampajjati. Tathā hi paññāya buddhabhāvasiddhi, karuṇāya buddhakammasiddhi. Paññāya sayaṃ tarati, karuṇāya pare tāreti. Paññāya paradukkhaṃ parijānāti, karuṇāya paradukkhapaṭikāraṃ ārabhati. Paññāya ca dukkhe nibbindati, karuṇāya dukkhaṃ sampaṭicchati. Tathā paññāya parinibbānābhimukho hoti, karuṇāya taṃ na pāpuṇāti. Tathā karuṇāya saṃsārābhimukho hoti[V 1.0065], paññāya tatra nābhiramati. Paññāya ca sabbattha virajjati, karuṇānugatattā na ca na sabbesaṃ anuggahāya pavatto, karuṇāya sabbepi anukampati, paññānugatattā na ca na sabbattha virattacitto. Paññāya ca ahaṃkāramamaṃkārābhāvo, karuṇāya ālasiyadīnatābhāvo. Tathā paññākaruṇāhi yathākkamaṃ attaparanāthatā, dhīravīrabhāvo, anattantapaaparantapatā, attahitaparahitanipphatti, nibbhayābhiṃsanakabhāvo, dhammādhipatilokādhipatitā, kataññupubbakāribhāvo, mohataṇhāvigamo, vijjācaraṇasiddhi, balavesārajjanipphattīti sabbassāpi pāramitāphalassa visesena upāyabhāvato paññākaruṇā pāramīnaṃ paccayo. Idañca dvayaṃ pāramīnaṃ viya paṇidhānassāpi paccayo.

Just as the aspiration is, so too are great compassion and skill in means. Here, skill in means is the wisdom that is the cause for giving and other qualities to become requisites of enlightenment. Through this compassion and skill in means, great beings, indifferent to their own happiness, are constantly devoted to the welfare of others. They remain undaunted even by the most difficult practices of the great bodhisattvas, and they become a cause for beings to attain welfare and happiness even in states of faith, clear understanding, seeing, hearing, and recollection. Indeed, through wisdom, the attainment of Buddhahood is accomplished; through compassion, the work of a Buddha is accomplished. By wisdom, one crosses over; by compassion, one helps others cross over. By wisdom, one fully understands the suffering of others; by compassion, one undertakes to remedy that suffering. By wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with suffering; by compassion, one accepts suffering. Thus, by wisdom, one inclines toward final liberation; by compassion, one does not attain it. By compassion, one inclines toward the cycle of existence; by wisdom, one does not delight in it. By wisdom, one becomes dispassionate toward all; yet, being guided by compassion, one is ever inclined to help all beings. By compassion, one has compassion for all; yet, being guided by wisdom, one's mind is not without dispassion. By wisdom, there is the absence of the conceit 'I am' and 'mine'; by compassion, there is the absence of laziness and dejection. Thus, through wisdom and compassion, respectively, one becomes one's own protector and the protector of others; becomes steadfast and heroic; is not afflicted by tormenting oneself or tormenting others; accomplishes one’s own welfare and that of others; becomes fearless and intrepid; attains mastery over the Dhamma and mastery over the world; becomes grateful and a benefactor; dispels delusion and craving; achieves knowledge and conduct; and brings about the perfection of strength and intrepidity. Because wisdom and compassion are especially the means for all the fruits of the perfections, they are the conditions for the perfections. And these two are a condition for the aspiration, just as they are for the perfections.

Tathā [M 1.0073][P 1.0094] ussāhaummaṅgaavatthānahitacariyā ca pāramīnaṃ paccayoti veditabbā, yā buddhabhāvassa uppattiṭṭhānatāya “buddhabhūmiyo”ti pavuccanti. Yathāha –

Thus, striving, ingenuity, steadfastness, and beneficial conduct are to be understood as the conditions for the perfections, which are called “Buddha-grounds” because they serve as the basis for the arising of Buddhahood. As it is said:

“Kati pana bhante buddhabhūmiyo? Catasso kho sāriputta buddhabhūmiyo. Katamā catasso? Ussāho ca hoti vīriyaṃ, umaṅgo ca hoti paññābhāvanā, avatthānañca hoti adhiṭṭhānaṃ, mettābhāvanā ca hoti hitacariyā. Imā kho sāriputta catasso buddhabhūmiyo”ti (su. ni. aṭṭha. 1.khaggavisāṇasuttavaṇṇanāyampi).

“Venerable sir, how many Buddha-grounds are there?” “There are four Buddha-grounds, Sāriputta. What are the four? Striving, which is energy; ingenuity, which is the development of wisdom; steadfastness, which is determination; and the development of loving-kindness, which is beneficial conduct. These, Sāriputta, are the four Buddha-grounds.”

Tathā nekkhammapavivekaalobhādosāmohanissaraṇappabhedā cha ajjhāsayā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Likewise, there are six kinds of inclinations: renunciation, seclusion, non-greed, non-aversion, non-delusion, and escape. As it is stated:

“Nekkhammajjhāsayā ca bodhisattā kāme dosadassāvino, paviveka…pe… saṅgaṇikāya, alobha…pe… lobhe, adosa…pe… dose, amoha…pe… mohe, nissaraṇajjhāsayā ca bodhisattā sabbabhavesu dosadassāvino”ti (visuddhi. aṭṭha. 1.49 vākyakhandhepi).

“Bodhisattvas, inclined to renunciation, see danger in sensual pleasures; inclined to seclusion… in company; inclined to non-greed… in greed; inclined to non-aversion… in aversion; inclined to non-delusion… in delusion; and inclined to escape, see danger in all forms of existence.”

Tasmā ete bodhisattānaṃ cha ajjhāsayā dānādīnaṃ paccayāti veditabbā. Na hi lobhādīsu ādīnavadassanena, alobhādiadhikabhāvena ca vinā dānādipāramiyo sambhavanti. Alobhādīnañhi adhikabhāvena pariccāgādininnacittatā alobhajjhāsayāditāti. Yathā cete, evaṃ dānajjhāsayatādayopi. Yathāha –

Therefore, these six inclinations of Bodhisattvas are to be understood as the conditions for giving and the other perfections. For without seeing the danger in greed and the like, and without an abundance of non-greed and the like, the perfections such as giving cannot arise. For it is through the abundance of non-greed and the like that there is a mind inclined toward relinquishment and so forth—this is the inclination towards non-greed and the like. Just as these are, so too are the inclinations toward giving and the rest. As it is said:

“Kati pana bhante bodhāya carantānaṃ bodhisattānaṃ ajjhāsayā? Dasa kho sāriputta [V 1.0066] bodhāya carantānaṃ bodhisattānaṃ ajjhāsayā. Katame dasa? Dānajjhāsayā sāriputta bodhisattā macchere dosadassāvino, sīla…pe… upekkhajjhāsayā sāriputta bodhisattā sukhadukkhesu dosadassāvino”ti.

“Venerable sir, how many inclinations do bodhisattvas have who are practicing for enlightenment?” “Sāriputta, there are ten inclinations of bodhisattvas who are practicing for enlightenment. What are the ten? The inclination to giving, Sāriputta, is for a bodhisattva to see danger in stinginess; the inclination to virtue… and so on up to… the inclination to equanimity, Sāriputta, is for a bodhisattva to see danger in pleasure and pain.”

Etesu [P 1.0095] hi maccheraasaṃvarakāmavicikicchākosajjaakkhantivisaṃvādaanadhiṭṭhānabyāpāda- sukhadukkhasaṅkhātesu ādīnavadassanapubbaṅgamā dānādininnacittatāsaṅkhātā dānajjhāsayatādayo dānādipāramīnaṃ nibbattiyā kāraṇanti[M 1.0074]. Tathā apariccāgapariccāgādīsu yathākkamaṃ ādīnavānisaṃsapaccavekkhaṇā dānādipāramīnaṃ paccayo.

Herein, seeing the danger in stinginess, lack of restraint, sensual desire, doubt, indolence, impatience, dishonesty, lack of determination, ill will, and what are called pleasure and pain, is the forerunner of the disposition for generosity and the like, which is called the mind's inclination towards generosity and so on. These are the causes for the arising of the perfections such as generosity. Likewise, reflection on the danger in non-relinquishment and the benefit in relinquishment, in due order, is the condition for the perfections such as generosity.

Tatthāyaṃ paccavekkhaṇāvidhi – khettavatthuhiraññasuvaṇṇagomahiṃsadāsidāsaputtadārādipariggahabyāsattacittānaṃ sattānaṃ khettādīnaṃ vatthukāmabhāvena bahupatthanīyabhāvato, rājacorādisādhāraṇabhāvato, vivādādhiṭṭhānato, sapattakaraṇato, nissārato, paṭilābhaparipālanesu paraviheṭhanahetuto, vināsanimittañca sokādianekavihitabyasanāvahato, tadāsattinidānañca maccheramalapariyuṭṭhitacittānaṃ apāyūpapattisambhavatoti evaṃ vividhavipulānatthāvahā ete atthā nāma, tesaṃ pariccāgoyeveko sotthibhāvoti pariccāge appamādo karaṇīyo.

Herein is the method of reflection: For beings whose minds are engrossed in possessions such as fields, lands, gold, silver, cattle, buffalo, male and female slaves, children, and spouses, these possessions—fields and the like—are desirable as objects of sensual pleasure, highly cherished, common to kings and thieves, grounds for disputes, causes of enmity, without substance, a cause of harming others in their acquisition and protection, and a condition for destruction, bringing about various misfortunes such as sorrow. Moreover, attachment to them is the basis, for those whose minds are enveloped by the stain of miserliness, for the possibility of rebirth in the lower realms. Thus, these things bring about many diverse and extensive dangers. Their abandonment is the only state of well-being. Therefore, one should be diligent in abandoning them.

Apica “yācako yācamāno attano guyhassa ācikkhanato mayhaṃ vissāsiko”ti ca “pahāya gamanīyaṃ attano santakaṃ gahetvā paralokaṃ yāhīti mayhaṃ upadesako”ti ca “āditte viya agāre maraṇagginā āditte loke tato mayhaṃ santakassa apavāhakasahāyo”ti ca “apavāhitassa cassa nijjhāyanikkhepaṭṭhānabhūto”ti ca “dānasaṅkhāte kalyāṇakammasmiṃ sahāyabhāvato, sabbasampattīnaṃ aggabhūtāya paramadullabhāya buddhabhūmiyā sampattihetubhāvato ca paramo kalyāṇamitto”ti ca paccavekkhitabbaṃ.

Furthermore, one should reflect: "The beggar, by asking, points out my hidden fault; thus he is my confidant." And: "He is my instructor, showing me how to take to the next world my possessions that must otherwise be left behind." And: "Like a house on fire, the world is ablaze with the fire of death, so he is a companion in carrying away my possessions from it." And: "He is the repository for what is given away, and the basis for contemplating that act." And: "Through companionship in the meritorious act known as giving, and because it is a cause for the attainment of Buddhahood—the foremost of all attainments and exceedingly difficult to obtain—he is a supreme spiritual friend." Thus, one should reflect.

Tathā “uḷāre kammani anenāhaṃ sambhāvito, tasmā sā sambhāvanā avitathā kātabbā”ti ca “ekantabheditāya jīvitassa ayācitenapi mayā dātabbaṃ, pageva yācitenā”ti ca “uḷārajjhāsayehi gavesitvāpi dātabbo, sayamevāgato mama puññenā”ti ca “yācakassa dānāpadesena mayhamevāyamanuggaho”ti [P 1.0096] ca “ahaṃ viya ayaṃ sabbopi loko mayā anuggahetabbo”ti ca “asati yācake kathaṃ mayhaṃ dānapāramī pūreyyā”ti ca “yācakānamevatthāya mayā sabbo pariggahetabbo”ti ca “ayācitvā mama santakaṃ yācakā sayameva kadā gaṇheyyu”nti ca “kathamahaṃ yācakānaṃ piyo cassaṃ manāpo”ti ca “kathaṃ vā te [V 1.0067] mayhaṃ piyā cassu manāpā”ti ca “kathaṃ vāhaṃ [M 1.0075] dadamāno, datvāpi ca attamano assaṃ pamudito pītisomanassajāto”ti ca “kathaṃ vā me yācakā bhaveyyuṃ, uḷāro ca dānajjhāsayo”ti ca “kathaṃ vāhamayācitoyeva yācakānaṃ hadayamaññāya dadeyya”nti ca “sati dhane yācake ca apariccāgo mahatī mayhaṃ vañcanā”ti ca “kathaṃ vāhaṃ attano aṅgāni jīvitaṃ vāpi yācakānaṃ pariccajeyya”nti ca paccavekkhitabbaṃ.

Moreover, one should reflect: "Through this noble act, I am esteemed; therefore, that esteem should be made genuine." And: "Since life is certain to end, I should give even without being asked, all the more so when asked." And: "A gift should be given even after searching for one with noble aspirations, yet this one has come on his own through my merit." And: "Through the act of giving to a beggar, it is actually I who receive a blessing." And: "This entire world should be helped by me, just as I would help myself." And: "Without a beggar, how could my perfection of giving be fulfilled?" And: "I should acquire everything for the sake of beggars." And: "When will beggars, without being asked, take what is mine by their own accord?" And: "How can I become dear and pleasing to beggars?" And: "How can they become dear and pleasing to me?" And: "How can I, while giving, and after giving, be content, delighted, and filled with joy and gladness?" And: "How can it be that beggars exist for me, and that my disposition for giving is noble?" And: "How can I, without being asked, understand the hearts of beggars and give to them?" And: "When wealth and a beggar exist, not giving is a great deception of myself." And: "How can I give even my limbs or life to beggars?" Thus, one should reflect.

Apica “attho nāmāyaṃ nirapekkhaṃ dāyakaṃ anugacchati yathā taṃ nirapekkhaṃ khepakaṃ kiṭako”ti atthe nirapekkhatāya cittaṃ uppādetabbaṃ. Yācamāno pana yadi piyapuggalo hoti, “piyo maṃ yācatī”ti somanassaṃ uppādetabbaṃ. Atha udāsīnapuggalo hoti, “ayaṃ maṃ yācamāno addhā iminā pariccāgena mitto hotī”ti somanassaṃ uppādetabbaṃ. Dadantopi hi yācakānaṃ piyo hotīti. Atha pana verīpuggalo yācati, “paccatthiko maṃ yācati, ayaṃ maṃ yācamāno addhā iminā pariccāgena verīpi piyo mitto hotī”ti visesato somanassaṃ uppādetabbaṃ. Evaṃ piyapuggale viya majjhattaverīpuggalesupi mettāpubbaṅgamaṃ karuṇaṃ upaṭṭhapetvāva dātabbaṃ.

Furthermore, one should generate a mind of detachment regarding the benefit, [reflecting]: "This thing called benefit follows the detached giver, just as a chip of wood follows the detached thrower." However, if the one who asks is a beloved person, one should generate joy, thinking, "A beloved one is asking me." If the person is neutral, one should generate joy, thinking, "This person asking me will surely become a friend through this act of giving." For indeed, one who gives becomes dear to those who ask. But if a hostile person asks, one should especially generate joy, thinking, "An adversary is asking me. Surely, through this act of giving, even this enemy will become a beloved friend." Thus, just as with a beloved person, one should give to neutral and hostile individuals only after establishing compassion preceded by loving-kindness.

Sace panassa cirakālaparibhāvitattā lobhassa deyyadhammavisayā lobhadhammā uppajjeyyuṃ, tena bodhisattapaṭiññena iti paṭisañcikkhitabbaṃ “nanu tayā sappurisa sambodhāya abhinīhāraṃ karontena sabbasattānaṃ upakāratthāya ayaṃ kāyo nissaṭṭho, tappariccāgamayañca puññaṃ, tattha nāma te bāhirepi vatthusmiṃ atisaṅgappavatti [P 1.0097] hatthisinānasadisī hoti, tasmā tayā na katthaci saṅgo uppādetabbo. Seyyathāpi nāma mahato bhesajjarukkhassa tiṭṭhato mūlaṃ mūlatthikā haranti, papaṭikaṃ, tacaṃ, khandhaṃ, viṭapaṃ, sāraṃ, sākhaṃ, palāsaṃ, pupphaṃ, phalaṃ phalatthikā haranti, na tassa rukkhassa ‘mayhaṃ santakaṃ ete harantī”ti vitakkasamudācāro hoti, evameva sabbalokahitāya ussukkamāpajjantena mayā mahādukkhe akataññuke niccāsucimhi kāye paresaṃ upakārāya viniyujjamāne aṇumattopi micchāvitakko na uppādetabbo, ko vā ettha viseso ajjhattikabāhiresu mahābhūtesu ekantabhedanavikiraṇaviddhaṃsanadhammesu, kevalaṃ pana sammohavijambhitametaṃ, yadidaṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti abhiniveso. Tasmā bāhiresu viya ajjhattikesupi karacaraṇanayanādīsu[M 1.0076], maṃsādīsu ca anapekkhena hutvā ‘taṃtadatthikā harantū’ti nissaṭṭhacittena bhavitabba”nti. Evaṃ paṭisañcikkhato cassa bodhāya pahitattassa kāyajīvitesu nirapekkhassa appakasireneva kāyavacīmanokammāni suvisuddhāni honti. So visuddhakāyavacīmanokammanto visuddhājīvo ñāyapaṭipattiyaṃ ṭhito, āyāpāyupāyakosallasamannāgamena [V 1.0068] bhiyyoso mattāya deyyadhammapariccāgena, abhayadānasaddhammadānehi ca sabbasatte anuggaṇhituṃ samattho hotīti. Ayaṃ tāva dānapāramiyaṃ paccavekkhaṇānayo.

If, due to long-cultivated greed, greedy states should arise in him regarding objects suitable for giving, then that one who has vowed to be a Bodhisatta should reflect thus: "Is it not so, good man, that when you made the aspiration for perfect Awakening, you relinquished this body for the benefit of all beings? And the merit consists in that very relinquishment. In that case, that your excessive attachment should arise even toward external objects is like an elephant’s hide. Therefore, you must not generate attachment anywhere. Just as, when a great medicinal tree is standing, those who need its root take the root, and others take the bark, trunk, branches, heartwood, twigs, leaves, flowers, or fruits, yet that tree has no thought, ‘They are taking what belongs to me,’ even so, as I strive for the welfare of the whole world, not the slightest wrong thought should arise when this body—fraught with great suffering, ungrateful, and ever impure—is employed for others’ benefit. What difference is there between the internal and external great elements, all subject to the nature of inevitable breaking up, scattering, and destruction? This is merely the flourishing of delusion—this insistence, ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ Therefore, being without longing for internal things like hands, feet, eyes, and flesh, just as for external things, one should have a mind of relinquishment, thinking, ‘Let those who have need of this or that take it.’" For one reflecting thus, whose mind is set on Awakening and who is without longing for body and life, his bodily, verbal, and mental actions become thoroughly purified with little trouble. Being pure in bodily, verbal, and mental actions, of pure livelihood, and established in the right practice, through being endowed with skill in the means of income and expenditure, he becomes capable of helping all beings to a greater degree by the relinquishment of gifts, and by the gift of fearlessness and the gift of the good Dhamma. This, then, is the method of reflection on the perfection of giving.

Sīlapāramiyaṃ pana evaṃ paccavekkhitabbaṃ – idañhi sīlaṃ nāma gaṅgodakādīhi visodhetuṃ asakkuṇeyyassa dosamalassa vikkhālanajalaṃ, haricandanādīhi vinetuṃ asakkuṇeyyarāgādipariḷāhavinayanaṃ, hāramakuṭakuṇḍalādīhi pacurajanālaṅkārehi asādhāraṇo sādhūnaṃ [P 1.0098] alaṅkāraviseso, sabbadisāvāyanato akittimo, sabbakālānurūpo ca surabhigandho, khattiyamahāsālādīhi devatāhi ca vandanīyādibhāvāvahanato paramo vasīkaraṇamanto, cātumahārājikādi devalokārohanasopānapanti, jhānābhiññānaṃ adhigamupāyo, nibbānamahānagarassa sampāpakamaggo, sāvakabodhipaccekabodhisammāsambodhīnaṃ patiṭṭhānabhūmi, yaṃ yaṃ vā panicchitaṃ patthitaṃ, tassa tassa samijjhanūpāyabhāvato cintāmaṇikapparukkhādike ca atiseti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā “ijjhati bhikkhave sīlavato cetopaṇidhi visuddhattā”ti (a. ni. 8.35). Aparampi vuttaṃ “ākaṅkheyya ce bhikkhave bhikkhu sabrahmacārīnaṃ piyo ca assaṃ manāpo ca garu ca bhāvanīyo cāti, sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.61), tathā “avippaṭisāratthāni kho ānanda kusalāni sīlānī”ti (a. ni. 10.1; 11.1), “pañcime gahapatayo ānisaṃsā sīlavato sīlasampadāyā”ti (dī. ni. 2.150; udā. 76; mahāva. 185) suttānañca vasena sīlassa guṇā paccavekkhitabbā, tathā aggikkhandhopamasuttādīnaṃ (a. ni. 7.72) vasena sīlavirahe ādīnavā.

Now, the perfection of virtue should be reflected upon as follows: This virtue is water that washes away the stains of defilements, which cannot be cleansed by the waters of the Ganges and other rivers. It is the allaying of the burning fever of lust and other afflictions, which cannot be subdued by yellow sandalwood and other remedies. It is the supreme adornment of the virtuous, unique among the ornaments of many people, unmatched by necklaces, crowns, earrings, and other common ornaments; a natural fragrance, wafting in all directions and suitable for all times. It is the highest means of mastery, revered by great warrior nobles and deities alike, bringing about the state of being worthy of veneration. It is the staircase leading to the heavenly realms of the Four Great Kings and beyond. It is the way to attain meditative absorptions and higher knowledge, the road leading to the great city of Nibbāna, and the foundation for the enlightenment of disciples, paccekabuddhas, and fully awakened Buddhas. It surpasses even the wish-fulfilling gem and the wish-fulfilling tree in its capacity to bring about the success of whatever one conceives of or desires. As the Blessed One has said: "Monks, the aspiration of the virtuous succeeds because of their purity" (A.N. 8.35). It is further stated: "If a monk wishes to be dear, agreeable, respected, and esteemed by his fellow practitioners of the holy life, he should fulfill the training in virtue" (M.N. 1.61). Likewise: "Ānanda, wholesome virtues are for the sake of non-regret" (A.N. 10.1; 11.1). "Householders, there are these five benefits for one accomplished in virtue" (D.N. 2.150; Ud. 76; Mahāvagga 185). The qualities of virtue should be contemplated in accordance with these suttas, and the dangers of lacking virtue should be considered as taught in the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta (A.N. 7.72) and others.

Pītisomanassanimittato, attānuvādaparānuvādadaṇḍaduggatibhayābhāvato, viññūhi pāsaṃsabhāvato, avippaṭisārahetuto, sotthiṭṭhānato[M 1.0077], abhijanasāpateyyādhipateyyāyurūpaṭṭhānabandhumittasampattīnaṃ [P 1.0099] atisayanato ca sīlaṃ paccavekkhitabbaṃ. Sīlavato hi attano sīlasampadāhetu mahantaṃ pītisomanassaṃ uppajjati “kataṃ vata mayā kusalaṃ, kataṃ kalyāṇaṃ, kataṃ bhīruttāṇa”nti. Tathā sīlavato attā na upavadati, na pare viññū, daṇḍaduggatibhayānaṃ sambhavoyeva natthi, “sīlavā purisapuggalo kalyāṇadhammo”ti viññūnaṃ pāsaṃso hoti. Tathā sīlavato yvāyaṃ “kataṃ vata mayā pāpaṃ, kataṃ luddaṃ, kataṃ kibbisa”nti dussīlassa vippaṭisāro uppajjati, so na hoti. Sīlañca nāmetaṃ appamādādhiṭṭhānato, bhogabyasanādiparihāramukhena mahato atthassa sādhanato, maṅgalabhāvato ca paramaṃ sotthiṭṭhānaṃ, nihīnajaccopi [V 1.0069] sīlavā khattiyamahāsālādīnaṃ pūjanīyo hotīti kulasampattiṃ atiseti sīlasampadā, “taṃ kiṃ maññasi mahārāja, idha te assa puriso dāso kammakaro”tiādi (dī. ni. 1.183) vacanañcettha sādhakaṃ. Corādīhi asādhāraṇato, paralokānugamanato, mahapphalabhāvato, samathādiguṇādhiṭṭhānato ca bāhiradhanaṃ atiseti sīlaṃ, paramassa cittissariyassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato khattiyādīnaṃ issariyaṃ atiseti sīlaṃ. Sīlanimittañhi taṃtaṃsattanikāyesu sattānaṃ issariyaṃ vassasatadīghappamāṇato jīvitato ekāhampi sīlavato jīvitassa visiṭṭhatāvacanato, sati ca jīvite sikkhānikkhepassa maraṇatāvacanato sīlaṃ jīvitato visiṭṭhataraṃ. Verīnampi manuññabhāvāvahanato, jarārogavipattīhi anabhibhavanīyato ca rūpasampattiṃ atiseti sīlaṃ. Pāsādahammiyādiṭṭhānavisese, rājayuvarājasenāpatiādiṭṭhānavisese ca atiseti sīlaṃ sukhavisesādhiṭṭhānabhāvato[P 1.0100]. Sabhāvasiniddhe santikāvacarepi bandhujane mittajane ca atiseti ekantahitasampādanato, paralokānugamanato ca. “Na taṃ mātā pitā kayirā”tiādi (dha. pa. 43) vacanañcettha sādhakaṃ. Tathā hatthiassarathādibhedehi, mantāgadasotthānappayogehi ca durārakkhaṃ attānaṃ ārakkhabhāvena sīlameva visiṭṭhataraṃ attādhīnato, aparādhīnato, mahāvisayato ca. Tenevāha “dhammo have rakkhati dhammacāri”ntiādi (jā. 1.9.102). Evamanekaguṇasamannāgataṃ sīlanti paccavekkhantassa aparipuṇṇā ceva sīlasampadā pāripūriṃ gacchati aparisuddhā ca pārisuddhiṃ.

One should reflect on virtue as a cause of joy and happiness, as freedom from self-reproach, blame by others, punishment, and fear of bad destinations, as praised by the wise, as a cause of non-regret, as a foundation of well-being, and as surpassing the attainments of lineage, wealth, sovereignty, longevity, beauty, standing, relatives, and friends. For a virtuous person, great joy and happiness arise due to their own virtue, thinking, "I have done what is wholesome, I have done what is good, I have done a refuge from fear." Moreover, the virtuous do not reproach themselves, nor are they blamed by the wise. There is simply no possibility of punishment or fear of bad destinations. The wise praise them, saying, "This virtuous person is endowed with good qualities." Furthermore, the regret that arises in the immoral—"I have done evil, I have done cruel deeds, I have done wicked deeds"—does not occur in the virtuous. Virtue is indeed the supreme foundation of well-being, rooted in heedfulness. It secures great benefits by avoiding the loss of wealth and other misfortunes, and it is a source of blessings. Even a low-born person who is virtuous is worthy of honor by great warrior nobles and the like; thus, the attainment of virtue surpasses the attainment of family. As the saying goes, "What do you think, great king? If here you had a man as a slave, a worker..." (Dīgha Nikāya 1.183), this statement is proof here. Virtue surpasses external wealth because it is not shared with thieves and the like, accompanies one to the next life, yields great fruits, and serves as the foundation for qualities like tranquility. Virtue surpasses the sovereignty of kings and the like because it is the foundation of supreme mastery over the mind. Indeed, virtue is the mark of sovereignty for beings in their respective groups of beings, because a single day of virtuous life is more excellent than a life lasting a hundred years; and because, when life is present, the abandoning of training is said to be death, virtue is more excellent than life. Moreover, virtue surpasses the attainment of beauty because it brings even enemies to a state of agreeableness and cannot be overcome by the misfortunes of aging and sickness. Virtue surpasses distinctions of palaces and mansions, as well as distinctions of kings, princes, and generals, because it is the foundation of special happiness. Virtue also surpasses relatives and friends, even those naturally affectionate and dwelling nearby, because it brings complete welfare and accompanies one to the next life. As the verse states, "Not even mother or father can do that..." (Dhammapada 43), this statement is proof here. Furthermore, virtue itself is more excellent as a protector for oneself, who is difficult to protect, than elephants, horses, chariots, or the use of spells, charms, and auspicious rites, because it is self-dependent, not dependent on others, and has a vast scope. Thus it is said, "Dhamma surely protects the one who practices Dhamma" (Jātaka 1.9.102). Reflecting on virtue endowed with such manifold qualities, incomplete virtue becomes complete, and impure virtue becomes purified.

Sace [M 1.0078] panassa dīgharattaṃ paricayena sīlapaṭipakkhā dhammā dosādayo antarantarā uppajjeyyuṃ, tena bodhisattapaṭiññena evaṃ paṭisañcikkhitabbaṃ “nanu tayā sambodhāya paṇidhānaṃ kataṃ, sīlavikalena ca na sakkā lokiyāpi sampattiyo pāpuṇituṃ, pageva lokuttarā, sabbasampattīnaṃ pana aggabhūtāya sammāsambodhiyā adhiṭṭhānabhūtena sīlena paramukkaṃsagatena bhavitabbaṃ. Tasmā ‘kikīva aṇḍa’ntiādinā (visuddhi. 1.19; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.7) vuttanayena sammā sīlaṃ parirakkhantena suṭṭhu tayā pesalena bhavitabbaṃ. Api ca tayā dhammadesanāya yānattaye sattānaṃ avatāraṇaparipācanāni kātabbāni, sīlavikalassa ca vacanaṃ na paccetabbaṃ hoti asappāyāhāravicārassa viya vejjassa tikicchanaṃ, tasmā kathāhaṃ saddheyyo hutvā sattānaṃ avatāraṇaparipācanāni kareyya”nti sabhāvaparisuddhasīlena bhavitabbaṃ. Kiñca “jhānādiguṇavisesayogena me sattānaṃ upakārakaraṇasamatthatā[P 1.0101], paññāpāramīādiparipūraṇañca, jhānādayo ca guṇā sīlapārisuddhiṃ vinā na sambhavantī”ti sammadeva sīlaṃ parisodhetabbaṃ.

If, however, qualities opposed to virtue—such as anger and the like—arise intermittently over a long period of time due to familiarity, then one who has made the resolution to become a bodhisattva should reflect thus: "Did you not make the aspiration for enlightenment? With impaired virtue, it is not possible to attain even worldly successes, let alone the supramundane. Moreover, for supreme perfect enlightenment, which is the foremost of all attainments, one must possess virtue that is the foundation and has reached the highest excellence. Therefore, as stated in the phrase ‘like a hen guarding its egg,’ you must rightly guard your virtue and be thoroughly gentle. Furthermore, through your teaching of the Dhamma, you must guide and mature beings in the three vehicles. But if your virtue is flawed, your words will not be accepted, just as a doctor’s treatment is not trusted if they indulge in unsuitable food. Thus, how could I, by being trustworthy, guide and mature beings?" One must maintain virtue that is naturally pure. And further: "Through the special qualities of jhāna and so on, I will be capable of benefiting beings and fulfilling the perfection of wisdom, etc. But jhāna and other qualities cannot arise without purity of virtue." Therefore, one must rightly purify virtue.

Tathā [V 1.0070] “sambādho gharāvāso rajopatho”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.191; ma. ni. 1.291; saṃ. ni. 2.154; ma. ni. 2.10) gharāvāse “aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā kāmā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.234; pāci. 417; mahāni. 3, 6;), “mātāpi puttena vivadatī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.168, 178) ca kāmesu “seyyathāpi puriso iṇaṃ ādāya kammante payojeyyā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.218) kāmacchandādīsu ādīnavadassanapubbaṅgamā vuttavipariyāyena “abbhokāso pabbajjā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.1.91; saṃ. ni. 1.154) pabbajjādīsu ānisaṃsapaṭisaṅkhāvasena nekkhammapāramiyaṃ paccavekkhaṇā veditabbā. Ayamettha saṅkhepattho, vitthāro pana dukkhakkhandha (ma. ni. 1.163) vīmaṃsasuttādi (ma. ni. 1.487) vasena dukkhakkhandhaāsivisopamasuttādivasena (cariyā. aṭṭha. pakiṇṇakakathāyaṃ) veditabbo.

Thus, the reviewing of the perfection of renunciation should be understood as being preceded by seeing the disadvantages: in household life, as in 'Living in a house is cramped, a path of dust,' and so on (Dīgha Nikāya 1.191; Majjhima Nikāya 1.291; Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.154; Majjhima Nikāya 2.10); in sensual pleasures, as in 'sensual pleasures are like a skeleton,' and so on (Majjhima Nikāya 1.234; Pācittiya 417; Mahāniddesa 3, 6), and 'a mother may quarrel with her son,' and so on (Majjhima Nikāya 1.168, 178); and in sensual desires and the like, as in 'just as a man might take a loan and invest it in work,' and so on (Dīgha Nikāya 1.218). Conversely, it should be understood by way of reflecting on the benefits of renunciation and the like, as in 'The life of homelessness is the open air,' and so on (Dīgha Nikāya 1.191; Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.154). This is the meaning in brief here; the detailed explanation, however, should be understood by way of the Dukkhakkhandha Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 1.163), the Vīmaṃsa Sutta and others (Majjhima Nikāya 1.487), and by way of the Dukkhakkhandha Sutta, the Āsīvisopama Sutta, and others (in the miscellaneous section of the Cariyāpiṭaka Aṭṭhakathā).

Tathā “paññāya vinā dānādayo dhammā na visujjhanti, yathāsakaṃ byāpārasamatthā ca na hontī”ti paññāguṇā manasi kātabbā. Yatheva hi jīvitena vinā sarīrayantaṃ na sobhati, na ca attano kiriyāsu paṭipattisamatthaṃ hoti, yathā ca cakkhādīni indriyāni viññāṇena vinā yathāsakaṃ visayesu kiccaṃ kātuṃ nappahonti, evaṃ saddhādīni indriyāni paññāya [M 1.0079] vinā sakiccapaṭipattiyaṃ asamatthānīti pariccāgādipaṭipattiyaṃ paññā padhānakāraṇaṃ. Ummīlitapaññācakkhukā hi mahāsattā attano aṅgapaccaṅgānipi datvā anattukkaṃsakā, aparavambhakā ca honti, bhesajjarukkhā viya vikapparahitā kālattayepi [P 1.0102] somanassajātā. Paññāvasena upāyakosallayogato pariccāgo parahitappavattiyā dānapāramibhāvaṃ upeti. Attatthañhi dānaṃ vuḍḍhisadisaṃ hoti.

Thus, the qualities of wisdom should be kept in mind: "Without wisdom, virtues such as generosity and the like are not purified, nor are they capable of their respective functions." For just as a body without life does not shine, nor is it capable of engaging in its own activities, and just as faculties like the eye cannot perform their functions in their respective objects without consciousness, so too the faculties like faith are incapable of engaging in their respective duties without wisdom. Therefore, wisdom is the principal cause in practices like giving and the like. Indeed, great beings with the eye of wisdom opened, even after giving away their own limbs, are not self-exalting and not disparagers of others. Like medicinal trees, they are free from discrimination and become joyful in all three times. Through wisdom and the application of skillful means, giving, by its inclination to benefit others, reaches the state of the perfection of generosity. For giving for one's own benefit is like interest.

Tathā paññāya abhāvena taṇhādisaṃkilesāviyogato sīlassa visuddhiyeva na sambhavati, kuto sabbaññuguṇādhiṭṭhānabhāvo. Paññavā eva ca gharāvāse kāmaguṇesu saṃsāre ca ādīnavaṃ, pabbajjāya jhānasamāpattiyaṃ nibbāne ca ānisaṃsaṃ suṭṭhu sallakkhento pabbajitvā jhānasamāpattiyo nibbattetvā nibbānaninno, pare ca tattha patiṭṭhapetīti.

Thus, in the absence of wisdom, due to non-separation from defilements such as craving, the purification of virtue is not possible; how then could there be a foundation for the qualities of an omniscient one? It is the wise one who, thoroughly considering the drawbacks in household life, sensual pleasures, and saṃsāra, as well as the advantages in renunciation, meditative attainments, and Nibbāna, goes forth. Having developed meditative attainments, one is inclined toward Nibbāna and establishes others there as well.

Vīriyañca paññārahitaṃ yadicchitamatthaṃ na sādheti durārambhabhāvato. Varameva hi anārambho durārambhato, paññāsahitena pana vīriyena na kiñci duradhigamaṃ upāyapaṭipattito. Tathā paññavā eva parāpakārādiadhivāsakajātiyo hoti, na duppañño. Paññāvirahitassa ca parehi upanītā apakārā khantiyā paṭipakkhameva anubrūhenti, paññavato pana te khantisampattiyā [V 1.0071] paribrūhanavasena assā thirabhāvāya saṃvattanti. Paññavā eva tīṇi saccāni tesaṃ kāraṇāni paṭipakkhe ca yathābhūtaṃ jānitvā paresaṃ avisaṃvādako hoti. Tathā paññābalena attānaṃ upatthambhetvā dhitisampadāya sabbapāramīsu acalasamādānādhiṭṭhāno hoti, paññavā eva ca piyamajjhattaverīvibhāgaṃ akatvā sabbattha hitūpasaṃhārakusalo hoti. Tathā paññāvasena lābhādilokadhammasannipāte nibbikāratāya majjhatto hoti. Evaṃ sabbāsaṃ pāramīnaṃ paññāva pārisuddhihetūti paññāguṇā paccavekkhitabbā.

Energy without wisdom fails to achieve its desired goal due to its poor initiation. Indeed, it is better not to begin at all than to begin poorly. But with energy accompanied by wisdom, nothing is hard to attain when approached with the right method. Likewise, only the wise is of the nature to endure harm from others and the like—not the unwise. For one without wisdom, the harms brought by others strengthen what is contrary to patience, but for the wise, those same harms, by way of developing the accomplishment of patience, conduce to its steadfastness. The wise, knowing the three truths, their causes, and their opposing factors as they truly are, is not deceptive to others. Moreover, supported by the power of wisdom, through the accomplishment of fortitude, one becomes established in an unshakable resolve and undertaking of all the perfections. The wise, without making distinctions between the dear, the neutral, and the hostile, becomes skilled in promoting welfare everywhere. Through wisdom, one remains equanimous and unaltered amid the arising of worldly conditions such as gain and the like. Thus, wisdom alone is the cause of purification for all the perfections—these qualities of wisdom should be contemplated.

Apica paññāya vinā na dassanasampatti, antarena ca diṭṭhisampadaṃ na sīlasampadā, sīladiṭṭhisampadārahitassa na samādhisampadā, asamāhitena ca na sakkā attahitamattampi sādhetuṃ, pageva ukkaṃsagataṃ parahitanti parahitāya paṭipannena “nanu tayā sakkaccaṃ paññāpārisuddhiyaṃ [P 1.0103] āyogo karaṇīyo”ti bodhisattena attā ovaditabbo. Paññānubhāvena hi mahāsatto [M 1.0080] caturadhiṭṭhānādhiṭṭhito catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi (dī. ni. 3.210, 313; a. ni. 10.32) lokaṃ anuggaṇhanto satte niyyānikamagge avatāreti, indriyāni ca nesaṃ paripāceti. Tathā paññābalena khandhāyatanādīsu pavicayabahulo pavattinivattiyo yāthāvato parijānanto dānādayo guṇe visesanibbedhabhāgiyabhāvaṃ nayanto bodhisattasikkhāya paripūrakārī hotīti evamādinā anekākāravokāre paññāguṇe vavatthapetvā paññāpāramī anubrūhetabbā.

Moreover, without wisdom there is no attainment of vision; without the attainment of right view there is no attainment of virtue; for one lacking in the attainment of virtue and right view there is no attainment of concentration. And one who is unconcentrated cannot achieve even one's own welfare, how much less the supreme welfare of others. Therefore, the Bodhisatta, being committed to the welfare of others, should admonish himself thus: "Should you not diligently strive for the purification of wisdom?" For by the power of wisdom, the Great Being, firmly established in the four resolves and employing the four bases of beneficence, benefits the world, leads beings onto the path of liberation, and matures their faculties. Similarly, by the strength of wisdom, being abundant in the analysis of the aggregates, sense bases, and so forth, comprehending arising and cessation as they truly are, and leading the qualities of generosity and the like to a state partaking of distinction and penetration, one fulfills the training of a Bodhisatta. Thus, having established the manifold virtues of wisdom in various ways, the perfection of wisdom should be developed.

Tathā dissamānapārānipi lokiyāni kammāni nihīnavīriyena pāpuṇituṃ asakkuṇeyyāni, agaṇitakhedena pana āraddhavīriyena duradhigamaṃ nāma natthi. Nihīnavīriyo hi “saṃsāramahoghato sabbasatte santāressāmī”ti ārabhitumeva na sakkuṇoti. Majjhimo ārabhitvā antarāvosānamāpajjati. Ukkaṭṭhavīriyo pana attasukhanirapekkho ārambhapāraṃ adhigacchatīti vīriyasampatti paccavekkhitabbā. Apica “yassa attanoyeva saṃsārapaṅkato samuddharaṇatthamārambho, tassāpi vīriyassa sithilabhāvena manorathānaṃ matthakappatti na sakkā sambhāvetuṃ, pageva sadevakassa lokassa samuddharaṇatthaṃ katābhinīhārenā”ti ca “rāgādīnaṃ dosagaṇānaṃ mattamahāgajānaṃ viya dunnivārayabhāvato, tannidānānañca kammasamādānānaṃ ukkhittāsikavadhakasadisabhāvato, tannimittānañca duggatīnaṃ sabbadā vivaṭamukhabhāvato, tattha niyojakānañca pāpamittānaṃ sadā sannihitabhāvato, tadovādakāritāya ca bālassa puthujjanabhāvassa sati sambhave yuttaṃ sayameva saṃsāradukkhato nissaritu”nti ca “micchāvitakkā vīriyānubhāvena dūrī bhavantī”ti ca “yadi pana sambodhi attādhīnena vīriyena [V 1.0072] sakkā samadhigantuṃ[P 1.0104], kimettha dukkara”nti ca evamādinā nayena vīriyassa guṇāpaccavekkhitabbā.

Similarly, even worldly tasks whose completion is in sight cannot be accomplished by one with feeble energy, but for one with aroused energy who does not count the fatigue, nothing is unattainable. Indeed, one with feeble energy cannot even begin to think, "I will ferry all beings across the great flood of saṃsāra." One with middling energy starts but gives up midway. But one with strong energy, indifferent to personal comfort, reaches the end of the undertaking—thus, the accomplishment of energy should be contemplated. Moreover, the qualities of energy should be contemplated in such ways as these: "Even for one whose undertaking is only to extricate oneself from the mire of saṃsāra, the pinnacle of one's wishes cannot be attained if one's energy is weak; how much more so for one who has resolved to deliver the world with its devas?" And: "Since the hosts of defilements, such as lust, are like rutting elephants, hard to restrain; and the courses of action rooted in them are like an executioner with a raised sword; and the woeful states resulting from them always have their mouths wide open; and evil friends, who instigate such actions, are ever-present; and since the state of a foolish worldling, prone to act on their advice, exists, it is fitting to escape the suffering of saṃsāra by one's own effort." And: "By the power of energy, wrong thoughts are kept at a distance." And: "If awakening can be attained by energy under one’s own control, what difficulty is there in that?"

Tathā “khanti nāmāyaṃ niravasesaguṇapaṭipakkhassa kodhassa vidhamanato guṇasampādane sādhūnamappaṭihatamāyudhaṃ, parābhibhavane samatthānaṃ alaṅkāro, samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ balasampadā, kodhaggivinayanī udakadhārā, kalyāṇassa kittisaddassa sañjātideso, pāpapuggalānaṃ vacīvisavūpasamakaro mantāgado, saṃvare ṭhitānaṃ paramā dhīrapakati, gambhīrāsayatāya sāgaro, dosamahāsāgarassa velā, apāyadvārassa pidhānakavāṭaṃ, devabrahmalokānaṃ [M 1.0081] ārohaṇasopānaṃ, sabbaguṇānaṃ adhivāsanabhūmi, uttamā kāyavacīmanovisuddhī”ti manasi kātabbaṃ. Api ca “ete sattā khantisampattiyā abhāvato idha ceva tapanti, paraloke ca tapanīyadhammānuyogato”ti ca “yadipi parāpakāranimittaṃ dukkhaṃ uppajjati, tassa pana dukkhassa khettabhūto attabhāvo, bījabhūtañca kammaṃ mayāva abhisaṅkhata”nti ca “tassa dukkhassa āṇaṇyakāraṇameta”nti ca “apakārake asati kathaṃ mayhaṃ khantisampadā sambhavatī”ti ca “yadipāyaṃ etarahi apakārako, ayaṃ nāma pubbe anena mayhaṃ upakāro kato”ti ca “apakāro eva vā khantinimittatāya upakāro”ti ca “sabbepime sattā mayhaṃ puttasadisā, puttakatāparādhesu ca ko kujjhissatī”ti ca “yena kodhabhūtāvesena ayaṃ mayhaṃ aparajjhati, so kodhabhūtāveso mayā vinetabbo”ti ca “yena apakārena idaṃ mayhaṃ dukkhaṃ uppannaṃ, tassa ahampi nimitta”nti ca “yehi dhammehi aparādho kato, yattha ca kato, sabbepi te tasmiṃyeva khaṇe niruddhā, kassidāni kena kodho kātabbo”ti ca “anattatāya sabbadhammānaṃ ko kassa aparajjhatī”ti ca paccavekkhantena khantisampadā brūhetabbā.

Thus, it should be borne in mind: ‘Patience is the unhindered weapon of the good in accomplishing virtues, by destroying anger, which is the opponent of all virtues without exception; it is the ornament of those capable of overcoming others; the strength of ascetics and brahmins; the stream of water that extinguishes the fire of anger; the birthplace of good repute; the mantra-medicine that neutralizes the verbal poison of evil persons; the supreme steadfast nature of those established in restraint; an ocean due to its profound disposition; the shore of the great ocean of hatred; the closing door-panel of the door to the lower realms; the stairway for ascending to the worlds of devas and brahmas; the dwelling place of all virtues; the highest purity of body, speech, and mind.’ Furthermore, the perfection of patience should be developed by reflecting: ‘These beings suffer both here and in the next life due to the absence of the perfection of patience and their engagement in practices that cause torment.’ And: ‘Even if suffering arises because of another's wrongdoing, this body is the field for that suffering, and the karma is the seed sown by me alone.’ And: ‘This is the cause for becoming free from debt regarding that suffering.’ And: ‘If there were no one who harmed me, how could my perfection of patience arise?’ And: ‘Even if this person harms me now, this very person has previously done me a favor.’ And: ‘Harm itself is a benefit because it is the condition for patience.’ And: ‘All these beings are like my own children; who would be angry with their children for their transgressions?’ And: ‘The possession by the demon of anger that causes this person to offend me must be subdued by me.’ And: ‘I too am a condition for the harm by which this suffering has arisen in me.’ And: ‘The mental states by which the offense was committed, and where it was committed, have all ceased in that very instant; so now, towards whom and by whom should anger be made?’ And: ‘Since all things are without self, who wrongs whom?’

Yadi [P 1.0105] panassa dīgharattaṃ paricayena parāpakāranimittako kodho cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭheyya, iti paṭisañcikkhitabbaṃ “khanti nāmesā parāpakārassa paṭipakkhapaṭipattīnaṃ paccupakārakāraṇa”nti ca “apakāro ca mayhaṃ dukkhuppādanena dukkhupanisāya saddhāya, sabbaloke anabhiratisaññāya ca paccayo”ti ca “indriyapakatiresā, yadidaṃ iṭṭhāniṭṭhavisayasamāyogo, tattha aniṭṭhavisayasamāyogo mayhaṃ na siyāti taṃ kutettha labbhā”ti ca “kodhavasiko satto kodhena ummatto vikkhittacitto, tattha kiṃ paccapakārenā”ti ca “sabbe pime sattā sammāsambuddhena orasaputtā viya paripālitā, tasmā na tattha mayā cittakopopi kātabbo”ti ca “aparādhake ca sati guṇe guṇavati mayā na kopo kātabbo”ti ca “asati guṇe visesena karuṇāyitabbo”ti ca “kopena ca mayhaṃ guṇayasā [V 1.0073] nihīyantī”ti ca “kujjhanena mayhaṃ dubbaṇṇadukkhaseyyādayo sapattakantā āgacchantī”ti ca “kodho ca nāmāyaṃ sabbāhitakārako [M 1.0082] sabbahitavināsako balavā paccatthiko”ti ca “sati ca khantiyā na koci paccatthiko”ti ca “aparādhakena aparādhanimittaṃ yaṃ āyatiṃ laddhabbaṃ dukkhaṃ, sati ca khantiyā mayhaṃ tadabhāvo”ti ca “cintanena kujjhantena ca mayā paccatthikoyeva anuvattito hotī”ti ca “kodhe ca mayā khantiyā abhibhūte tassa dāsabhūto paccatthiko sammadeva abhibhūto hotī”ti ca “kodhanimittaṃ khantiguṇapariccāgo mayhaṃ na yutto”ti ca “sati ca kodhe guṇavirodhini (guṇavirodhapaccanīdhamme cariyā. aṭṭha. pakiṇṇakakathāyaṃ) kiṃ me sīlādidhammā pāripūriṃ gaccheyyuṃ, asati ca tesu kathāhaṃ sattānaṃ upakārabahulo paṭiññānurūpaṃ uttamaṃ sampattiṃ pāpuṇissāmī”ti ca “khantiyā ca sati bahiddhā vikkhepābhāvato samāhitassa sabbe saṅkhārā aniccato dukkhato sabbe dhammā anattato nibbānañca asaṅkhatāmatasantapaṇītādibhāvato nijjhānaṃ khamanti [P 1.0106] ‘buddhadhammā ca acinteyyāparimeyyapabhāvā’ti”, tato ca “anulomiyaṃ khantiyaṃ ṭhito ‘kevalā ime ca attattaniyabhāvarahitā dhammamattā yathāsakaṃ paccayehi uppajjanti vayanti, na kutoci āgacchanti, na kuhiñci gacchanti, na ca katthaci patiṭṭhitā, na cettha koci kassaci byāpāro’ti ahaṃkāramamaṃkārānadhiṭṭhānatā nijjhānaṃ khamati, yena bodhisatto bodhiyā niyato anāvattidhammo hotī”ti evamādinā khantipāramiyaṃ paccavekkhaṇā veditabbā.

If, however, anger rooted in another’s wrongdoing persists in his mind for a long time due to familiarity, he should reflect thus: ‘Patience is indeed the counter-practice to wrongdoing, the cause of returning a favor.’ And: ‘Harm done to me is a condition for the arising of suffering, for faith which has suffering as its proximate cause, and for the perception of dissatisfaction with the whole world.’ And: ‘This is the nature of the faculties—the encounter with pleasant and unpleasant objects. That I should not encounter unpleasant objects—how could that possibly be obtained?’ And: ‘A being under the sway of anger is mad and distracted in mind. What use is retaliation here?’ And: ‘All these beings are nurtured by the Fully Enlightened One as if they were his own children. Therefore, I should not harbor even a trace of anger toward them.’ And: ‘If the offender has virtues, is virtuous, I should not be angry.’ And: ‘If he lacks virtues, he should be regarded with special compassion.’ And: ‘By anger, my own virtues and fame decline.’ And: ‘By becoming angry, I invite ugliness, suffering, and poor sleep—things dear to my enemies.’ And: ‘Anger is indeed the cause of all that is unbeneficial, the destroyer of all that is beneficial—a powerful adversary.’ And: ‘With patience, there is no adversary.’ And: ‘With patience, I am free from that future suffering which is to be obtained by the wrongdoer on account of the wrongdoing.’ And: ‘By thinking and being angry, I am only following the adversary’s lead.’ And: ‘But if anger is overcome by me through patience, then that adversary, who is a slave to it, is truly overcome.’ And: ‘To abandon the virtue of patience on account of anger is not fitting for me.’ And: ‘If anger, which opposes virtues, is present, how can my moral qualities and other virtues reach fulfillment? Without them, how can I, being of great benefit to beings, attain the highest fulfillment in accordance with my vow?’ And: ‘With patience, due to the absence of external distraction, for one who is composed, all conditioned formations are fit for contemplation as impermanent and as suffering, all things as non-self, and Nibbāna as unconditioned, deathless, peaceful, sublime, and so forth. And they are fit for contemplation because “the qualities of the Buddha are of inconceivable and immeasurable power.”’ Then: ‘Established in conformity-patience, the non-establishment of “I-making” and “mine-making” is fit for contemplation thus: “These are merely phenomena, devoid of self or what belongs to self, arising and ceasing according to their respective conditions. They come from nowhere, go nowhere, and are not established anywhere. And here there is no agent acting upon any other.” By this, the Bodhisatta becomes destined for enlightenment, of a non-returning nature.’ In these and other ways, the reflection on the perfection of patience should be understood.

Tathā “saccena vinā sīlādīnaṃ asambhavato, paṭiññānurūpaṃ paṭipattiyā abhāvato ca saccadhammātikkame ca sabbapāpadhammānaṃ samosaraṇato, asaccasandhassa appaccayikabhāvato, āyatiñca anādeyyavacanatāvahanato, sampannasaccassa ca sabbaguṇādhiṭṭhānabhāvato, saccādhiṭṭhānena sabbabodhisambhārānaṃ pārisuddhipāripūrisamanvāyato, sabhāvadhammāvisaṃvādanena sabbabodhisambhārakiccakaraṇato, bodhisattapaṭipattiyā ca parinipphattito”tiādinā saccapāramiyā sampattiyo paccavekkhitabbā.

Similarly, the accomplishments of the perfection of truth should be reflected upon in these and other ways: ‘Since virtues like morality cannot exist without truth; and since without it there is no practice in accordance with one’s pledge; and since all evil qualities converge upon the transgression of the truth; since one of false promise is untrustworthy; since in the future it leads to one’s words being unworthy of acceptance; since one accomplished in truth is the foundation of all virtues; since through the foundation of truth all the requisites of enlightenment are accompanied by purification and fulfillment; since by not contradicting the true nature of things one performs the functions of all the requisites of enlightenment; and since the practice of a Bodhisatta is brought to perfection by it.’

Tathā “dānādīsu daḷhasamādānaṃ, tampaṭipakkhasannipāte ca nesaṃ acalāvatthānaṃ, tattha ca thirabhāvaṃ vinā na dānādisambhārā sambodhinimittā sambhavantī”tiādinā adhiṭṭhāne guṇā paccavekkhitabbā.

Similarly, the qualities of resolution should be reflected upon in these and other ways: ‘There should be firm commitment to generosity and so on, and their unshakeable establishment when opposing forces gather; for without firmness therein, the requisites of generosity and so on do not arise as a condition for enlightenment.’

Tathā [M 1.0083] “attahitamatte avatiṭṭhantenāpi sattesu hitacittataṃ vinā na sakkā idhalokaparalokasampattiyo [V 1.0074] pāpuṇituṃ, pageva sabbasatte nibbānasampattiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpetukāmenā”ti ca “pacchā sabbasattānaṃ lokuttarasampattiṃ ākaṅkhantena idāni lokiyasampattiṃ ākaṅkhā yuttarūpā”ti ca “idāni āsayamattena paresaṃ hitasukhūpasaṃhāraṃ kātuṃ asakkonto kadā payogena taṃ sādhessāmī”ti ca “idāni mayā hitasukhūpasaṃhārena saṃvaddhitā pacchā dhammasaṃvibhāgasahāyā [P 1.0107] mayhaṃ bhavissantī”ti ca “etehi vinā na mayhaṃ bodhisambhārā sambhavanti, tasmā sabbabuddhaguṇavibhūtinipphattikāraṇattā mayhaṃ ete paramaṃ puññakkhettaṃ anuttaraṃ kusalāyatanaṃ uttamaṃ gāravaṭṭhāna”nti ca “savisesaṃ sattesu sabbesu hitajjhāsayatā paccupaṭṭhapetabbā, kiñca karuṇādhiṭṭhānatopi sabbasattesu mettā anubrūhetabbā. Vimariyādīkatena hi cetasā sattesu hitasukhūpasaṃhāraniratassa tesaṃ ahitadukkhāpanayanakāmatā balavatī uppajjati daḷhamūlā, karuṇā ca sabbesaṃ buddhakārakadhammānamādi caraṇaṃ patiṭṭhā mūlaṃ mukhaṃ pamukha”nti evamādinā mettāya guṇā paccavekkhitabbā.

Furthermore, one should reflect on the qualities of loving-kindness in this way: even while remaining solely intent on one’s own welfare, without a mind inclined toward the welfare of beings, one cannot attain prosperity in this life or the next—much less establish all beings in the attainment of Nibbāna. For one who later aspires to the supramundane attainment of all beings, it is fitting now to aspire for worldly prosperity. Even if one is currently unable to bring welfare and happiness to others merely through inclination, one should resolve, ‘When will I accomplish this through effort?’ One should also think, ‘Those whom I now nurture with welfare and happiness will later become my companions in sharing the Dhamma.’ Without these, my requisites for enlightenment cannot arise. Therefore, because they are the cause for the accomplishment of all the glorious qualities of the Buddhas, for me, these beings are the supreme field of merit, the unsurpassed source of goodness, and the highest object of reverence. A special disposition for their welfare should be established toward all beings. Moreover, from a basis of compassion, loving-kindness should be further cultivated toward all beings. For when the mind is made boundless and intent on bringing welfare and happiness to beings, a strong and deeply rooted desire arises to remove their harm and suffering. And compassion is the beginning, the conduct, the foundation, the root, the face, and the foremost of all the qualities that lead to Buddhahood.

Tathā “upekkhāya abhāve sattehi katā vippakārā cittassa vikāraṃ uppādeyyuṃ, sati ca cittavikāre dānādisambhārānaṃ sambhavoyeva natthī”ti ca “mettāsinehena sinehite citte upekkhāya vinā sambhārānaṃ pārisuddhi na hotī”ti ca “anupekkhako sambhāresu puññasambhāraṃ tabbipākañca sattahitatthaṃ pariṇāmetuṃ na sakkotī”ti ca “upekkhāya abhāve deyyapaṭiggāhakesu vibhāgaṃ akatvā pariccajituṃ na sakkotī”ti ca “upekkhārahitena jīvitaparikkhārānaṃ jīvitassa ca antarāyaṃ amanasikaritvā saṃvaravisodhanaṃ kātuṃ na sakkā”ti ca “upekkhāvasena aratiratisahasseva nekkhammabalasiddhito, upapattito ikkhanavaseneva sabbasambhārakiccanipphattito, accāraddhassa vīriyassa anupekkhane padhānakiccākaraṇato, upekkhatoyeva titikkhānijjhānasambhavato, upekkhāvasena sattasaṅkhārānaṃ avisaṃvādanato, lokadhammānaṃ ajjhupekkhanena samādinnadhammesu acalādhiṭṭhānasiddhito, parāpakārādīsu anābhogavaseneva mettāvihāranipphattitoti sabbabodhisambhārānaṃ samādānādhiṭṭhānapāripūrinipphattiyo [P 1.0108] upekkhānubhāvena sampajjantī”ti evaṃ ādinā nayena upekkhāpāramī [M 1.0084] paccavekkhitabbā. Evaṃ apariccāgapariccāgādīsu yathākkamaṃ ādīnavānisaṃsapaccavekkhaṇā dānādipāramīnaṃ paccayoti veditabbā.

Similarly, the perfection of equanimity should be reflected upon in this way: Without equanimity, harm done by beings might cause a disturbance in the mind, and with a disturbance of mind, there is no possibility for the requisites like generosity to arise. When the mind is imbued with the affection of loving-kindness, the purity of the requisites is not achieved without equanimity. One lacking equanimity is unable to dedicate the accumulation of merit and its result for the welfare of beings. Without equanimity, one cannot relinquish offerings without making distinctions between the gift and the recipient. One devoid of equanimity cannot accomplish the purification of restraint, being unable to disregard danger to life and its necessities. Through equanimity, dislike and delight are overcome, hence the accomplishment of the power of renunciation; by seeing from the perspective of rebirth, all the duties of the requisites are accomplished; because without equanimity towards excessive effort, the main task of striving is not accomplished; from equanimity itself, patience and meditative absorption arise; through equanimity, one is not at variance with beings and their formations; by observing worldly conditions with equanimity, steadfast resolve in the undertaken practices is accomplished; and by not attending to harm from others, the dwelling in loving-kindness is perfected. Thus, the undertaking, resolve, and complete fulfillment of all the requisites for enlightenment are accomplished by the power of equanimity. In this way, the reflection on the dangers and benefits of non-relinquishment, relinquishment, and so forth, in due order, should be understood as a condition for the perfections of generosity and the others.

Tathā saparikkhārā pañcadasa caraṇadhammā pañca ca abhiññāyo. Tattha caraṇadhammā nāma sīlasaṃvaro, indriyesu guttadvāratā, bhojane mattaññutā, jāgariyānuyogo, satta saddhammā, cattāri jhānāni ca. Tesu sīlādīnaṃ catunnaṃ terasapi dhutadhammā, appicchatādayo ca parikkhāro[V 1.0075]. Saddhammesu saddhāya buddhadhammasaṅghasīlacāgadevatūpasamānussati- lūkhapuggalaparivajjanasiniddhapuggalasevanapasādanīya- dhammapaccavekkhaṇatadadhimuttatā parikkhāro, hirottappānaṃ akusalādīnavapaccavekkhaṇaapāyādīnavapaccavekkhaṇakusaladhammupatthambhana- bhāvapaccavekkhaṇahirottappa rahitapuggalaparivajjanahirottappasampannapuggalasevanatadadhimuttatā, bāhusaccassa pubbayogaparipucchakabhāvasaddhammābhiyogaanavajjavijjāṭṭhānādi- paricayaparipakkindriyatākilesadūrībhāvaappassutaparivajjanabahussutasevanatadadhimuttatā, vīriyassa apāyabhayapaccavekkhaṇagamanavīthipaccavekkhaṇadhammamahattapaccavekkhaṇa- thinamiddhavinodanakusītapuggalaparivajjanaāraddhavīriyapuggala- sevanasammappadhānapaccavekkhaṇatadadhimuttatā, satiyā satisampajaññamuṭṭhassatipuggalaparivajjanaupaṭṭhitassatipuggalasevanatadadhimuttatā, paññāya paripucchakabhāvavatthuvisadakiriyāindriyasamattapaṭipādanaduppañña- puggalaparivajjanapaññavantapuggalasevanagambhīrañāṇacariyapacca- vekkhaṇatadadhimuttatā, catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ sīlādicatukkaṃ aṭṭhatiṃsāya ārammaṇesu [P 1.0109] pubbabhāgabhāvanā, āvajjanādivasībhāvakaraṇañca parikkhāro. Tattha sīlādīhi payogasuddhiyā sattānaṃ abhayadāne, āsayasuddhiyā āmisadāne, ubhayasuddhiyā ca dhammadāne samattho hotītiādinā caraṇādīnaṃ dānādisambhārānaṃ paccayabhāvo yathārahaṃ niddhāretabbo, ativitthārabhayena na niddhārayimha. Evaṃ sampatticakkādayopi dānādīnaṃ paccayoti veditabbā.

Similarly, there are the fifteen practices of conduct along with their requisites, and the five higher knowledges. Among these, the practices of conduct are: restraint in virtue, guarding the sense doors, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, the seven good qualities, and the four jhānas. Of these, for the four beginning with virtue, the thirteen ascetic practices and qualities like fewness of wishes are the requisites. For the good qualities, the requisites are as follows. For faith: recollection of the Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha, virtue, generosity, deities, and peace; avoiding coarse people and associating with the refined; reflecting on inspiring qualities and being resolved on them.
