For conscience and moral shame: reflecting on the dangers of unwholesome states, the perils of the lower realms, and the state of being supported by wholesome qualities; avoiding those devoid of conscience and moral shame, associating with those who possess them, and being resolved on these qualities. For much learning: prior application, questioning, dedication to the true Dhamma, familiarity with blameless fields of knowledge, maturity of faculties, being far from defilements, avoiding the unlearned, associating with the learned, and being resolved on this. For energy: reflecting on the fear of the lower realms, reflecting on the path of progress, reflecting on the greatness of the Dhamma, dispelling sloth and torpor, avoiding the lazy, associating with the energetic, reflecting on right effort, and being resolved on it. For mindfulness: mindfulness and clear comprehension, avoiding the unmindful, associating with the mindful, and being resolved on it. For wisdom: a questioning attitude, making the subject-matter clear, bringing the faculties to balance, avoiding the unwise, associating with the wise, reflecting on the profound conduct of knowledge, and being resolved on it. For the four jhānas, the requisites are the fourfold foundation beginning with virtue, the preliminary development on the thirty-eight objects, and the making of mastery in adverting and so on. Herein, through purity of practice by means of virtue and so on, one becomes capable of giving fearlessness to beings; through purity of intention, of giving material gifts; and through purity of both, of giving the gift of the Dhamma. In this way, the status of the practices of conduct and so on as conditions for the requisites of generosity and so on should be determined as appropriate. We have not elaborated for fear of excessive detail. Thus, the wheels of accomplishment and other factors should also be understood as conditions for generosity and the like.

Ko saṃkilesoti avisesena taṇhādīhi parāmaṭṭhabhāvo pāramīnaṃ saṃkileso, visesena deyyapaṭiggāhakavikappā dānapāramiyā saṃkileso, sattakālavikappā sīlapāramiyā, kāmabhavatadupasamesu abhiratianabhirativikappā nekkhammapāramiyā, “ahaṃ mamā”ti vikappā paññāpāramiyā, līnuddhaccavikappā vīriyapāramiyā, attaparavikappā khantipāramiyā, adiṭṭhādīsu diṭṭhādivikappā saccapāramiyā, bodhisambhāratabbipakkhesu dosaguṇavikappā [M 1.0085] adhiṭṭhānapāramiyā, hitāhitavikappā mettāpāramiyā, iṭṭhāniṭṭhavikappā upekkhāpāramiyā saṃkilesoti veditabbo.

What is defilement? Generally, the defilement of the perfections is their being grasped by craving and so on. Specifically, the defilements are as follows: for the perfection of giving, the distinction between the gift and the recipient; for the perfection of virtue, the distinction regarding beings and time; for the perfection of renunciation, the distinction between delight and non-delight in sensual pleasures, existence, and their appeasement; for the perfection of wisdom, the distinction of “I” and “mine”; for the perfection of energy, the distinction of sluggishness and agitation; for the perfection of patience, the distinction between self and others; for the perfection of truth, the distinction of seen and unseen, and so on; for the perfection of resolution, the distinction between faults and virtues regarding the requisites for enlightenment and their opposites; for the perfection of loving-kindness, the distinction between beneficial and unbeneficial; for the perfection of equanimity, the distinction between the liked and disliked. This should be understood as defilement.

Kiṃ vodānanti taṇhādīhi anupaghāto, yathāvuttavikappaviraho ca etāsaṃ vodānanti veditabbaṃ. Anupahatā hi taṇhāmānadiṭṭhikodhūpanāhamakkhapalāsaissāmacchariyamāyāsāṭheyyathambhasārambha- madapamādādīhi kilesehi deyyapaṭiggāhakavikappādirahitā ca dānādipāramiyo parisuddhā pabhassarā bhavantīti.

What is purification? It should be understood as non-affliction by craving and the like, and the absence of the aforementioned distinctions. For the perfections of giving and so forth, when unharmed by defilements such as craving, conceit, wrong view, anger, resentment, denigration, hypocrisy, envy, stinginess, deceit, dishonesty, obstinacy, rivalry, intoxication, and heedlessness, and when devoid of distinctions such as those between the gift and the recipient, they become pure and radiant.

Ko [V 1.0076] paṭipakkhoti avisesena sabbepi kilesā sabbepi akusalā dhammā etāsaṃ paṭipakkho, visesena pana pubbe vuttā maccherādayoti veditabbā. Apica deyyapaṭiggāhakadānaphalesu alobhādosāmohaguṇayogato lobhadosamohapaṭipakkhaṃ dānaṃ, kāyādidosavaṅkāpagamanato lobhādipaṭipakkhaṃ sīlaṃ[P 1.0110], kāmasukhaparūpaghātaattakilamathaparivajjanato dosattayapaṭipakkhaṃ nekkhammaṃ, lobhādīnaṃ andhīkaraṇato, ñāṇassa ca anandhīkaraṇato lobhādipaṭipakkhā paññā, alīnānuddhatañāyārambhavasena lobhādipaṭipakkhaṃ vīriyaṃ, iṭṭhāniṭṭhasuññatānaṃ khamanato lobhādipaṭipakkhā khanti, satipi paresaṃ upakāre apakāre ca yathābhūtappavattiyā lobhādipaṭipakkhaṃ saccaṃ, lokadhamme abhibhuyya yathāsamādinnesu sambhāresu acalanato lobhādipaṭipakkhaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ, nīvaraṇavivekato lobhādipaṭipakkhā mettā, iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu anunayapaṭighaviddhaṃsanato, samappavattito ca lobhādipaṭipakkhā upekkhāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

What is the opposite? Generally, all defilements and all unwholesome states are the opposite of these perfections. Specifically, the previously mentioned stinginess, etc., should be understood as the specific opposites. Moreover: generosity is the antidote to greed, hatred, and delusion by virtue of its association with the qualities of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion in respect to the gift, the recipient, and the fruit of giving. Virtue is the antidote to greed, etc., by abandoning the crookedness of body, etc. Renunciation is the antidote to the three faults by avoiding sensual pleasures, harming others, and self-mortification. Wisdom is the antidote to greed, etc., by blinding them and not blinding knowledge. Energy is the antidote to greed, etc., by undertaking in a way that is neither slack nor agitated. Patience is the antidote to greed, etc., by enduring the pleasant and the unpleasant. Truth, by acting according to reality even when there is benefit or harm from others, is the antidote to greed, etc. Determination is the antidote to greed, etc., by overcoming the worldly conditions and not wavering in the requisites undertaken. Loving-kindness is the antidote to greed, etc., by seclusion from the hindrances. Equanimity is the antidote to greed, etc., by destroying attraction and repulsion towards the desired and undesired, and by proceeding evenly. Thus it should be understood.

Kā paṭipattīti sukhūpakaraṇasarīrajīvitapariccāgena bhayāpanūdanena dhammopadesena ca bahudhā sattānaṃ anuggahakaraṇaṃ dāne paṭipatti. Tatthāyaṃ vitthāranayo – “imināhaṃ dānena sattānaṃ āyuvaṇṇasukhabalapaṭibhānādisampattiṃ ramaṇīyaṃ aggaphalasampattiṃ nipphādeyya”nti annadānaṃ deti, tathā sattānaṃ kammakilesapipāsavūpasamāya pānaṃ deti, tathā suvaṇṇavaṇṇatāya, hirottappālaṅkārassa ca nipphattiyā vatthāni deti, tathā iddhividhassa ceva nibbānasukhassa ca nipphattiyā yānaṃ deti, tathā sīlagandhanipphattiyā gandhaṃ, buddhaguṇasobhānipphattiyā mālāvilepanaṃ, bodhimaṇḍāsananipphattiyā āsanaṃ[M 1.0086], tathāgataseyyānipphattiyā seyyaṃ, saraṇabhāvanipphattiyā āvasathaṃ, pañcacakkhupaṭilābhāya padīpeyyaṃ deti. Byāmappabhānipphattiyā rūpadānaṃ, brahmassaranipphattiyā saddadānaṃ, sabbalokassa piyabhāvāya rasadānaṃ, buddhasukhumālabhāvāya phoṭṭhabbadānaṃ, ajarāmaraṇabhāvāya bhesajjadānaṃ, kilesadāsabyavimocanatthaṃ [P 1.0111] dāsānaṃ bhujissatādānaṃ, saddhammābhiratiyā anavajjakhiḍḍāratihetudānaṃ, sabbepi satte ariyāya jātiyā attano puttabhāvūpanayanāya puttadānaṃ, sakalassa lokassa patibhāvūpagamanāya dāradānaṃ, subhalakkhaṇasampattiyā suvaṇṇamaṇimuttāpavāḷādidānaṃ, anubyañjanasampattiyā nānāvidhavibhūsanadānaṃ, saddhammakosādhigamāya vittakosadānaṃ, dhammarājabhāvāya rajjadānaṃ, jhānādisampattiyā ārāmuyyānādivanadānaṃ, cakkaṅkitehi pādehi bodhimaṇḍūpasaṅkamanāya caraṇadānaṃ, caturoghanittharaṇāya sattānaṃ saddhammahatthadānatthaṃ hatthadānaṃ, saddhindriyādipaṭilābhāya kaṇṇanāsādidānaṃ, samantacakkhupaṭilābhāya cakkhudānaṃ, “dassanasavanānussaraṇapāricariyādīsu sabbakālaṃ sabbasattānaṃ hitasukhāvaho, sabbalokena ca upajīvitabbo me kāyo bhaveyyā”ti maṃsalohitādidānaṃ, “sabbalokuttamo bhaveyya”nti uttamaṅgadānaṃ deti.

What is the practice? The practice of giving is benefiting beings in many ways—through the relinquishing of comforts and requisites, one’s body and life; through the dispelling of fear; and through the teaching of the Dhamma. Here is the detailed explanation: "By this gift, may I bring beings the attainment of long life, beauty, happiness, strength, ready wit, and other excellent qualities, as well as the supreme attainment of bliss." Thus, one gives food. For the quenching of beings' thirst for kamma and defilements, one gives drink. For the attainment of a golden complexion and the adornment of moral shame and moral dread, one gives clothing. For the attainment of psychic powers and the bliss of Nibbāna, one gives vehicles. For the attainment of the fragrance of virtue, one gives perfumes. For the attainment of the splendor of the Buddha’s qualities, one gives garlands and ointments. For the attainment of the seat of enlightenment, one gives a seat. For the attainment of the Tathāgata’s resting place, one gives a bed. For the attainment of refuge, one gives shelter. For the attainment of the five eyes, one gives lamps. For the attainment of a fathom-wide aura, one gives forms. For the attainment of the Brahma-like voice, one gives sounds. For becoming dear to the whole world, one gives tastes. For the attainment of the Buddha’s refined nature, one gives tactile objects. For freedom from aging and death, one gives medicine. For liberation from the slavery of defilements, one gives freedom to slaves. For delight in the true Dhamma, one gives gifts that are the cause of blameless amusements and pleasure. For leading all beings to the noble birth and to become like one’s own children, one gives one's children. For becoming the master of the entire world, one gives a spouse. For the attainment of auspicious marks, one gives gold, gems, pearls, and corals. For the attainment of minor marks, one gives various ornaments. For the attainment of the treasure of the true Dhamma, one gives the treasure of wealth. For becoming a righteous king, one gives a kingdom. For the attainment of meditative achievements, one gives parks, groves, and forests. For approaching the seat of enlightenment with feet marked by wheels, one gives one's feet. For the purpose of giving the hand of the true Dhamma to beings for crossing the four floods, one gives one's hands. For the attainment of faculties like faith, one gives ears, noses, etc. For the attainment of all-seeing vision, one gives the eye. "May my body be of use to all beings at all times for seeing, hearing, recollecting, serving, and bringing them welfare and happiness. May the whole world sustain itself through me." Thus, one gives flesh, blood, etc. "May I become the highest in all the world." Thus, one gives the gift of the head.

Evaṃ [V 1.0077] dadanto ca na anesanāya deti, na paropaghātena, na bhayena, na lajjāya, na dakkhiṇeyyarosanena, na paṇīte sati lūkhaṃ, na attukkaṃsanena, na paravambhanena, na phalābhikaṅkhāya, na yācakajigucchāya, na acittīkārena deti, atha kho sakkaccaṃ deti, sahatthena deti, kālena deti, cittiṃ katvā deti, avibhāgena deti, tīsu kālesu somanassito deti. Tatoyeva datvā na pacchānutāpī hoti, na paṭiggāhakavasena mānāvamānaṃ karoti, paṭiggāhakānaṃ piyasamudācāro hoti vadaññū yācayogo saparivāradāyī. Tañca dānasampattiṃ sakalalokahitasukhāya pariṇāmeti, attano ca akuppāya vimuttiyā, aparikkhayassa chandassa, aparikkhayassa vīriyassa, aparikkhayassa samādhānassa, aparikkhayassa ñāṇassa, aparikkhayāya sammāsambodhiyā [P 1.0112] pariṇāmeti. Imañca dānapāramiṃ paṭipajjantena mahāsattena jīvite, bhogesu [M 1.0087] ca aniccasaññā paccupaṭṭhapetabbā, sattesu ca mahākaruṇā. Evañhi bhoge gahetabbasāraṃ gaṇhanto ādittasmā viya agārasmā sabbaṃ sāpateyyaṃ, attānañca bahi nīharanto na kiñci seseti, niravasesato nissajjatiyeva. Ayaṃ tāva dānapāramiyā paṭipattikkamo.

Giving in this way, one does not give by unrighteous means, nor to harm others, nor out of fear, nor out of shame, nor out of resentment toward those worthy of gifts, nor giving coarse things when fine ones are available, nor for self-praise, nor to disparage others, nor with expectation of reward, nor out of disgust for beggars, nor without respect. Instead, one gives attentively, gives with one's own hand, gives at the proper time, gives reverently, gives impartially, and gives joyfully at three times. Having given in this way, one does not later regret it, does not create honor or dishonor based on the recipient, is pleasant in speech toward the recipients, is generous, approachable by supplicants, and gives along with one's retinue. One dedicates this accomplishment of giving to the welfare and happiness of the whole world, and also to one's own unshakeable liberation, to inexhaustible aspiration, energy, concentration, wisdom, and perfect enlightenment. While practicing this perfection of giving, the great being should establish awareness of impermanence in life and wealth and cultivate great compassion for beings. Thus, taking the essence from possessions, like carrying all one's belongings out of a burning house, one brings everything out without leaving anything behind—relinquishing it all completely. This, then, is the mode of practice for the perfection of giving.

Sīlapāramiyā pana yasmā sabbaññusīlālaṅkārehi satte alaṅkaritukāmena attanoyeva tāva sīlaṃ visodhetabbaṃ, tasmā sattesu tathā dayāpannacittena bhavitabbaṃ, yathā supinantenapi na āghāto uppajjeyya. Parūpakāraniratatāya parasantako alagaddo viya na parāmasitabbo. Abrahmacariyatopi ārācārī, sattavidhamethuna saṃyogavirato, pageva paradāragamanato. Saccaṃ hitaṃ piyaṃ parimitameva ca kālena dhammiṃ kathaṃ bhāsitā hoti, anabhijjhālu abyāpanno aviparītadassano sammāsambuddhe niviṭṭhasaddho niviṭṭhapemo. Iti caturāpāyavaṭṭadukkhapathehi akusalakammapathehi, akusaladhammehi ca oramitvā saggamokkhapathesu kusalakammapathesu patiṭṭhitassa suddhāsayapayogatāya yathābhipatthitā sattānaṃ hitasukhūpasañhitā manorathā sīghaṃ abhinipphajjanti.

Regarding the perfection of virtue, since one who desires to adorn beings with the ornaments of virtue like the All-Knowing One must first purify their own virtue, one should cultivate a mind full of compassion toward beings, so that not even anger arises even in dreams. Being intent on helping others, one should not handle others as one would a snake belonging to someone else. One should be far removed from unchastity, refraining from the seven kinds of sexual union, let alone adultery. One speaks truthfully, beneficially, pleasingly, and moderately, and at the right time, speaks on the Dhamma. One is free from covetousness, free from ill will, and possesses right view, with unwavering faith and love fixed on the Perfectly Enlightened One. Thus, having desisted from the paths of suffering in the four woeful states, the paths of unwholesome actions, and unwholesome qualities, and being established in the paths of wholesome actions leading to heaven and liberation, due to pure intention and effort, the aspirations for the welfare and happiness of beings are swiftly fulfilled according to one's wishes.

Tattha hiṃsānivattiyā sabbasattānaṃ abhayadānaṃ deti, appakasireneva mettābhāvanaṃ sampādeti, ekādasa mettānisaṃse adhigacchati, appābādho hoti appātaṅko dīghāyuko sukhabahulo, lakkhaṇavisese pāpuṇāti, dosavāsanañca samucchindati. Tathā adinnādānanivattiyā corādiasādhāraṇe uḷāre bhoge adhigacchati, anāsaṅkanīyo piyo manāpo vissasanīyo, vibhavasampattīsu alaggacitto pariccāgasīlo[P 1.0113], lobhavāsanañca samucchindati. Abrahmacariyanivattiyā alobho hoti santakāyacitto, sattānaṃ piyo hoti manāpo [V 1.0078] aparisaṅkanīyo, kalyāṇo cassa kittisaddo abbhuggacchati, alaggacitto hoti mātugāmesu aluddhāsayo, nekkhammabahulo, lakkhaṇavisese adhigacchati, lobhavāsanañca samucchindati.

By abstaining from harming, one gives the gift of fearlessness to all beings, easily perfects the cultivation of loving-kindness, attains the eleven benefits of loving-kindness, becomes free from illness and disease, enjoys long life and abundant happiness, achieves distinctive marks, and eradicates the latent tendency to hatred. By abstaining from taking what is not given, one attains abundant wealth uncommon to thieves, becomes unsuspected, beloved, and pleasing, is reliable, develops a mind unattached to possessions, is generous by nature, and eradicates the latent tendency to greed. By abstaining from unchastity, one becomes ungreedy and has a tranquil body and mind, beloved and pleasing to beings, unsuspected, a good report of him rises up, remains unattached to women, free from greed, inclined to renunciation, achieves distinctive marks, and eradicates the latent tendency to greed.

Musāvādanivattiyā sattānaṃ pamāṇabhūto hoti paccayiko theto ādeyyavacano devatānaṃ piyo manāpo surabhigandhamukho ārakkhiyakāyavacīsamācāro[M 1.0088], lakkhaṇavisese ca adhigacchati, kilesavāsanañca samucchindati. Pesuññanivattiyā parūpakkamehi abhejjakāyo hoti abhejjaparivāro, saddhamme ca abhijjanakasaddho, daḷhamitto bhavantaraparicitānampi sattānaṃ ekantapiyo, asaṃkilesabahulo. Pharusavācānivattiyā sattānaṃ piyo hoti manāpo sukhasīlo madhuravacano sambhāvanīyo, aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgato cassa saro (ma. ni. 2.387) nibbattati. Samphappalāpanivattiyā ca sattānaṃ piyo hoti manāpo garubhāvanīyo ca ādeyyavacano ca parimitālāpo, mahesakkho ca hoti mahānubhāvo, ṭhānuppattikena paṭibhānena pañhānaṃ byākaraṇakusalo, buddhabhūmiyañca ekāya eva vācāya anekabhāsānaṃ sattānaṃ anekesaṃ pañhānaṃ byākaraṇasamattho hoti.

By abstaining from false speech, one becomes a standard for beings, reliable, trustworthy, with words to be heeded, dear and pleasing to the devas, with a mouth of fragrant scent, and guarded in bodily and verbal conduct. One also attains distinctive marks and eradicates the latent tendency to defilements. By abstaining from divisive speech, one's body becomes unbreakable by the attacks of others and one's retinue unbreakable; one possesses unbreakable faith in the true Dhamma, is a firm friend, exceedingly beloved even by beings familiar from previous existences, and is largely free from defilement. By abstaining from harsh speech, one becomes dear and pleasing to beings, of pleasant disposition, sweet-spoken, and worthy of respect, and a voice endowed with eight qualities arises. And by abstaining from idle chatter, one becomes dear and pleasing to beings, worthy of esteem, with words to be heeded, and speaks in moderation; one becomes of great influence and great power, skilled in answering questions with spontaneously arising insight, and on the Buddha-stage, with a single utterance, is capable of responding to the many questions of beings in various languages.

Anabhijjhālutāya icchitalābhī hoti, uḷāresu ca bhogesu ruciṃ paṭilabhati, khattiyamahāsālādīnaṃ sammato hoti, paccatthikehi anabhibhavanīyo, indriyavekallaṃ na pāpuṇāti, appaṭipuggalo ca hoti. Abyāpādena piyadassano hoti sattānaṃ sambhāvanīyo, parahitābhinanditāya ca satte appakasireneva pasādeti, alūkhasabhāvo ca hoti mettāvihārī, mahesakkho ca hoti mahānubhāvo. Micchādassanābhāvena kalyāṇe sahāye paṭilabhati, sīsacchedampi pāpuṇanto pāpakammaṃ na karoti, kammassakatādassanato akotūhalamaṅgaliko ca hoti, saddhamme cassa saddhā patiṭṭhitā hoti mūlajātā, saddahati ca tathāgatānaṃ bodhiṃ[P 1.0114], samayantaresu nābhiramati ukkāraṭṭhāne viya rājahaṃso, lakkhaṇattayaparijānanakusalo hoti, ante ca anāvaraṇañāṇalābhī, yāva bodhiṃ na pāpuṇāti, tāva tasmiṃ tasmiṃ sattanikāye ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭho ca hoti, uḷāruḷārasampattiyo pāpuṇāti.

By non-covetousness, one obtains what is desired and finds delight in splendid possessions. One is esteemed by great noble families and is unconquerable by enemies. One does not incur impairment of the faculties and is without an equal. By non-ill will, one becomes pleasant to behold and esteemed by beings. With delight in others' welfare, one easily gladdens beings. One is of a gentle nature, abiding in loving-kindness, and becomes of great might and great power. By absence of wrong view, one gains good companions. Even if one were to face decapitation, one does not commit evil. Seeing kamma as one's own, one is free from superstitious rites and omens, and one's faith in the True Dhamma becomes rooted and established. One believes in the enlightenment of the Tathāgatas, and does not delight in other systems, like a royal swan in a dung heap. One becomes skilled in discerning the three characteristics and ultimately gains unobstructed knowledge. Until one attains enlightenment, one is supreme among beings in each and every realm, and attains the most excellent attainments.

“Iti hidaṃ sīlaṃ nāma sabbasampattīnaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ, sabbabuddhaguṇānaṃ pabhavabhūmi, sabbabuddhakaradhammānamādi caraṇaṃ mukhaṃ pamukha”nti bahumānaṃ uppādetvā kāyavacīsaṃyame, indriyadamane, ājīvasampadāya, paccayaparibhoge ca satisampajaññabalena appamattena lābhasakkārasilokaṃ mittamukhapaccatthikaṃ viya sallakkhetvā “kikīva aṇḍa”ntiādinā (visuddhi. 1.19; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.7) vuttanayena [V 1.0079] sakkaccaṃ sīlaṃ sampādetabbaṃ[M 1.0089]. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.6) vuttanayena veditabbo. Tañca panetaṃ sīlaṃ na attano duggatiparikilesavimuttiyā, sugatiyampi, na rajjasampattiyā, nacakkavatti-nadeva-nasakka-namāra-nabrahmasampattiyā, nāpi attano tevijjatādihetu, na paccekabodhiyā, atha kho sabbaññubhāvena sabbasattānaṃ anuttarasīlālaṅkārasampādanatthamevāti pariṇāmetabbaṃ.

"Thus, this virtue is the foundation of all accomplishments, the ground from which all Buddha-qualities arise, the beginning, the practice, the face, and the foremost of all qualities that make one a Buddha." Having generated great respect, one should carefully perfect virtue with diligence, by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension, restraining body and speech, mastering the senses, maintaining purity of livelihood, and wisely using requisites, discerning gain, honor, and fame as if they were an enemy with the face of a friend, and regarding them as "a bird's egg" and so forth, as described in the Visuddhimagga (1.19) and the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary (1.7). This is the summary here; the detailed explanation should be understood according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga (1.6). Moreover, this virtue should not be dedicated for one’s own liberation from the defilements of miserable states or even for a happy destination, nor for sovereignty, nor for the attainments of a wheel-turning monarch, a deity, Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā, nor for the sake of attaining the threefold knowledge and so forth, nor for Paccekabodhi. Rather, it should be dedicated solely for the purpose of providing all beings with the adornment of unsurpassed virtue through the state of omniscience.

Tathā sakalasaṃkilesanivāsaṭṭhānatāya, puttadārādīhi mahāsambādhatāya, kasivaṇijjādinānāvidhakammantādhiṭṭhānabyākulatāya ca gharāvāsassa nekkhammasukhādīnaṃ anokāsataṃ, kāmānañca “satthadhārālaggamadhubindu viya ca avaleyhamānā parittassādā vipulānatthānubandhā”ti ca “vijjulatobhāsena gahetabbaṃ naccaṃ viya parittakālopalabbhā, ummattakālaṅkāro viya viparītasaññāya anubhavitabbā[P 1.0115], karīsāvacchādanasukhaṃ viya paṭikārabhūtā, udakatemitaṅguliyā ussāvakodakapānaṃ viya atittikarā, chātajjhattabhojanaṃ viya sābādhā, balisāmisaṃ viya byasanasannipātakāraṇā, aggisantāpo viya kālattayepi dukkhuppattihetubhūtā, makkaṭālepo viya bandhanimittā ghātakāvacchādanakimilayo viya anatthacchādanā, sapattagāmavāso viya bhayaṭṭhānabhūtā, paccatthikaposako viya kilesamārādīnaṃ āmisabhūtā, chaṇasampattiyo viya vipariṇāmadukkhā, koṭaraggi viya antodāhakā, purāṇakūpāvalambabīraṇamadhupiṇḍaṃ viya anekādīnavā, loṇūdakapānaṃ viya pipāsahetubhūtā, surāmerayaṃ viya nīcajanasevitā, appassādatāya aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā”tiādinā ca nayena ādīnavaṃ sallakkhetvā tabbipariyāyena nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ passantena nekkhammapavivekaupasamasukhādīsu ninnapoṇapabbhāracittena nekkhammapāramī pūretabbā.

Because household life is a dwelling place for all defilements, greatly crowded with children, wives, and the like, and agitated by various occupations such as farming and trade, leaving no opportunity for the bliss of renunciation and so forth; and because sensual pleasures, when licked, are like a drop of honey on a sword’s edge, of little taste but entailing great suffering; like a dance to be grasped by a flash of lightning, available for only a short time; like a madman’s adornment, to be experienced with distorted perception; like the pleasure of covering oneself with excrement, being merely a countermeasure; like drinking dew from a moistened finger, unsatisfying; like food eaten by one who is starving, causing affliction; like bait on a hook, a cause for the accumulation of misfortune; like the heat of a fire, a cause for the arising of suffering in all three times; like monkey lime, a cause of bondage; like worms concealed by a murderer's rags, hiding what is harmful; like dwelling in an enemy village, a place of fear; like nourishing one's adversary, being food for the defilements, Māra, and so forth; like festive occasions, suffering due to change; like a fire in a hollow tree, burning internally; like a lump of honey clinging to a rope in an old well, full of many dangers; like drinking saltwater, a cause for thirst; like strong drink, indulged in by lowly people; like a skeleton, offering little delight—having thus considered the drawbacks in this way, and seeing the benefits in renunciation as the contrary, with a mind inclining, sloping, and tending toward the bliss of renunciation, seclusion, and peace, and so forth, one should fulfill the perfection of renunciation.

Tathā yasmā paññā āloko viya andhakārena, mohena saha na vattati, tasmā mohakāraṇāni tāva bodhisattena parivajjitabbāni. Tatthimāni mohakāraṇāni – arati tandī vijambhitā ālasiyaṃ gaṇasaṅgaṇikārāmatā niddāsīlatā anicchayasīlatā ñāṇasmiṃ akutūhalatā micchādhimāno aparipucchakatā kāyassa na sammāparihāro asamāhitacittatā [M 1.0090] duppaññānaṃ puggalānaṃ sevanā paññavantānaṃ apayirupāsanā attaparibhavo micchāvikappo [P 1.0116] viparītābhiniveso kāyadaḷhībahulatā asaṃvegasīlatā pañca nīvaraṇāni. Saṅkhepato ye vā pana dhamme āsevato anuppannā paññā na uppajjati, uppannā parihāyati, iti imāni sammohakāraṇāni parivajjantena bāhusacce jhānādīsu ca yogo karaṇīyo.

Moreover, just as light does not coexist with darkness, so wisdom does not coexist with delusion; therefore, a bodhisatta must first abandon the causes of delusion. These causes of delusion are: discontent, torpor, yawning, sloth, fondness for company and socializing, habit of sleeping, habit of indecision, lack of curiosity in knowledge, wrong conceit, not asking questions, not properly attending to the body, an unconcentrated mind, associating with unwise individuals, not attending upon the wise, self-contempt, wrong thoughts, perverted adherence, much bodily rigidity, habit of not being stirred, and the five hindrances. In short, whatever qualities, when cultivated, prevent unarisen wisdom from arising or cause arisen wisdom to decline—these causes of delusion must be abandoned. One should cultivate extensive learning and apply oneself to jhāna and other such practices.

Tatthāyaṃ [V 1.0080] bāhusaccassa visayavibhāgo – pañca khandhā dvādasāyatanāni, aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo cattāri saccāni bāvīsatindriyāni dvādasapadiko paṭiccasamuppādo, tathā satipaṭṭhānādayo kusalādidhammappakārabhedā ca. Yāni ca loke anavajjāni vijjaṭṭhānāni, ye ca sattānaṃ hitasukhavidhānayogyā byākaraṇavisesā. Iti evaṃ pakāraṃ sakalameva sutavisayaṃ upāyakosallapubbaṅgamāya paññāya sativīriyupatthambhakāraṇāya sādhukaṃ uggahaṇasavanadhāraṇaparicayaparipucchāhi ogāhetvā tattha ca paresaṃ patiṭṭhapanena sutamayā paññā nibbattetabbā, tathā khandhādīnaṃ sabhāvadhammānaṃ ākāraparivitakkanamukhena te nijjhānaṃ khamāpentena cintāmayā, khandhādīnaṃyeva pana salakkhaṇasāmaññalakkhaṇapariggahavasena lokiyaṃ pariññaṃ nibbattentena pubbabhāgabhāvanāpaññā sampādetabbā. Evañhi “nāmarūpamattamidaṃ yathārahaṃ paccayehi uppajjati ceva nirujjhati ca, na ettha koci kattā vā kāretā vā, hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccaṃ, udayabbayapaṭipīḷanaṭṭhena dukkhaṃ, avasavattanaṭṭhena anattā”ti ajjhattikabāhire dhamme nibbisesaṃ parijānanto tattha āsaṅgaṃ pajahitvā, pare ca tattha taṃ jahāpetvā kevalaṃ karuṇāvaseneva yāva na buddhaguṇā hatthatalaṃ āgacchanti, tāva yānattaye satte avatāraṇaparipācanehi patiṭṭhāpento, jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattiyo ca vasībhāvaṃ pāpento paññāya ativiya matthakaṃ pāpuṇātīti.

Herein is the classification of the scope of extensive learning: the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, the eighteen elements, the four truths, the twenty-two faculties, the twelve-linked dependent origination, as well as the foundations of mindfulness and the various kinds of wholesome and other phenomena. And also the blameless fields of knowledge in the world, and the special declarations suitable for bringing about the welfare and happiness of beings. Thus, having thoroughly immersed oneself in the entire range of learning of this kind through careful study, listening, retention, familiarity, and questioning—with wisdom preceded by skillful means, and supported by mindfulness and energy—wisdom born of learning should be produced by establishing others therein. Moreover, by reflecting on the intrinsic nature of the aggregates and other phenomena through the mode of thorough investigation, making them amenable to contemplation, wisdom born of reflection should be produced. Furthermore, by discerning the specific and general characteristics of the aggregates themselves, one should accomplish mundane full understanding through the preliminary stage of meditative wisdom. For in this way, one thoroughly understands internal and external phenomena without distinction, realizing: "This is merely name-and-form; it arises and ceases according to conditions as is appropriate; there is no doer or instigator here. By the nature of having been and then not being, it is impermanent; by the nature of oppression through rise and fall, it is suffering; by the nature of uncontrollability, it is non-self." Having abandoned attachment in this regard, and also leading others to abandon it, solely out of compassion, until the qualities of a Buddha become as clear as the palm of one’s hand, one establishes beings in the three vehicles through guidance and maturation. And by mastering the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments, one reaches the very pinnacle of wisdom.

Tathā [P 1.0117] sammāsambodhiyā katābhinīhārena mahāsattena “ko nu ajja puññañāṇasambhāro upacito, kiñca mayā kataṃ parahita”nti divase divase paccavekkhantena sattahitatthaṃ ussāho karaṇīyo, sabbesampi sattānaṃ upakārāya attano kāyaṃ jīvitañca ossajjitabbaṃ, sabbepi sattā anodhiso mettāya karuṇāya ca pharitabbā, yā kāci [M 1.0091] sattānaṃ dukkhuppatti, sabbā sā attani pāṭikaṅkhitabbā, sabbesañca sattānaṃ puññaṃ abbhanumoditabbaṃ, buddhamahantatā abhiṇhaṃ paccavekkhitabbā, yañca kiñci kammaṃ karoti kāyena vācāya vā, taṃ sabbaṃ bodhininnacittapubbaṅgamaṃ kātabbaṃ. Iminā hi upāyena bodhisattānaṃ aparimeyyo puññabhāgo upacīyati. Apica sattānaṃ paribhogatthaṃ paripālanatthañca attano sarīraṃ jīvitañca pariccajitvā khuppipāsāsītuṇhavātātapādidukkhapaṭikāro pariyesitabbo. Yañca yathāvuttadukkhapaṭikārajaṃ sukhaṃ attanā paṭilabhati, tathā ramaṇīyesu ārāmuyyānapāsādatalādīsu, araññāyatanesu ca kāyacittasantāpābhāvena abhinibbutattā sukhaṃ vindati, yañca suṇāti buddhānubuddhapaccekabuddhabodhisattānaṃ diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārabhūtaṃ jhānasamāpattisukhaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ sattesu anodhiso upasaṃharati. Ayaṃ tāva asamāhitabhūmiyaṃ nayo.

Thus, a great being who has made the aspiration for perfect self-enlightenment should reflect daily: 'What accumulation of merit and knowledge have I made today? What have I done for the welfare of others?' and should make effort for the welfare of beings. One's own body and life should be relinquished for the benefit of all beings. All beings should be pervaded with boundless loving-kindness and compassion. Whatever suffering arises for beings, all of it should be taken upon oneself. The merit of all beings should be rejoiced in. The greatness of the Buddha should be frequently contemplated. And whatever action one does, whether by body or speech, all of that should be done with a mind inclined towards enlightenment, foremost. By this means, an immeasurable share of merit is accumulated by bodhisattvas. Moreover, having relinquished one’s own body and life for the use and protection of beings, remedies should be sought for sufferings such as hunger, thirst, cold, heat, wind, and sun. And whatever happiness one obtains through remedies for the aforementioned sufferings; likewise the happiness one finds in delightful parks, gardens, palaces, and so on, and in forest dwellings, being completely stilled due to the absence of bodily and mental agitation; and whatever happiness of meditative attainments one hears of—which is the blissful abiding in the present life for Buddhas, their enlightened disciples, Paccekabuddhas, and Bodhisattas—all of that should be dedicated unreservedly to all beings. This, for now, is the method in the sphere of the unconcentrated.

Samāhito [V 1.0081] pana attanā yathānubhūtaṃ visesādhigamanibbattaṃ pītipassaddhisukhaṃ sabbasattesu adhimuccati, tathā mahati saṃsāradukkhe, tannimittabhūte ca kilesābhisaṅkhāradukkhe nimuggaṃ sattanikāyaṃ disvā tatthapi chedanabhedanaphālanapisanaggisantāpādijanitā dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā nirantaraṃ cirakālaṃ vediyante nārake, aññamaññaṃ kujjhanasantāpanaviheṭhanahiṃsanaparādhīnatādīhi dukkhaṃ anubhavante tiracchāne, jotimālā’kulasarīre uddhabāhuviravante [P 1.0118] ukkāmukhe khuppipāsādīhi ḍayhamāne ca vantakheḷādiāhāre ca mahādukkhaṃ vedayamāne pete ca pariyeṭṭhimūlakaṃ mahantaṃ anayabyasanaṃ pāpuṇante hatthacchedādikāraṇayogena dubbaṇṇaduddasikadaliddatādibhāvena khuppipāsādiyogena balavantehi abhibhavanīyato, paresaṃ vahanato, parādhīnato ca nārake pete tiracchāne ca atisayante apāyadukkhanibbisesaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavante manusse ca tathā visayavisaparibhogavikkhittacittatāya rāgādipariyuṭṭhānena ḍayhamāne vāyuvegasamuṭṭhitajālāsamiddhasukkhakaṭṭhasannipāte aggikkhandhe viya anupasantapariḷāhavuttike anihataparādhīne kāmāvacaradeve ca mahatā vāyāmena vidūramākāsaṃ vigāhitasakuntā viya, balavantehi khittasarā viya ca “satipi cirappavattiyaṃ anaccantikatāya pātapariyosānā anatikkantajātijarāmaraṇā evā”ti rūpāvacarārūpāvacaradeve ca [M 1.0092] passantena mettāya karuṇāya ca anodhiso sattā pharitabbā. Evaṃ kāyena vācāya manasā ca bodhisambhāre nirantaraṃ upacinantena ussāho pavattetabbo.

But one who is concentrated projects upon all beings the joy, tranquility, and happiness born of a special attainment that one has personally experienced. Likewise, seeing the host of beings submerged in the great suffering of saṃsāra and in the suffering of defilements and volitional formations which is its cause, one observes the various realms. In hell, intense, harsh, and bitter pains born of cutting, breaking, splitting, grinding, and fierce burning are continuously experienced for a long time. Animals experience suffering through mutual anger, torment, harassment, harm, and dependence on others. Petas have bodies engulfed in garlands of flame, cry out with arms upraised, have mouths like torches, burn with hunger and thirst, and experience great misery with vomit and phlegm as their food. Humans encounter great misfortune and disaster rooted in their searching, experiencing suffering indistinguishable from that of the lower realms and even surpassing that of those in hell, the peta-realm, and the animal-realm, through such things as having their hands cut off, ugliness, poverty, hunger, thirst, being oppressed by the powerful, carrying burdens for others, and being dependent on others. The devas of the sense-sphere burn with the obsession of lust and other defilements because their minds are distracted by enjoying sense-objects which are like poison; they are like a mass of fire in a heap of dry wood, well-kindled and fanned by a gust of wind, their state being an unquenched burning, unceasingly dependent on others. And the devas of the form and formless spheres, like birds that have plunged far into the sky with great effort or like arrows shot by the powerful, have a long-lasting existence that is nevertheless not final, ends in a fall, and has not transcended birth, aging, and death. Seeing all this, one should pervade all beings boundlessly with loving-kindness and compassion. Thus, one should exert effort, continuously accumulating the requisites for enlightenment with body, speech, and mind.

Apica “acinteyyāparimitavipuloḷāravimalanirupamanirupakkilesaguṇanicayanidānabhūtassa buddhabhāvassa ussakkitvā sampahaṃsanayogyaṃ vīriyaṃ nāma acinteyyānubhāvameva. Yaṃ na pacurajanā sotumpi sakkuṇanti, pageva paṭipajjituṃ. Tathā hi tividhā abhinīhāracittuppatti, catasso buddhabhūmiyo, cattāri saṅgahavatthūni (dī. ni. 3.210, 313; a. ni. 4.32), karuṇokāsatā, buddhadhammesu nijjhānakkhanti, sabbadhammesu nirupalepo, sabbasattesu puttasaññā, saṃsāradukkhehi aparikhedo, sabbadeyyadhammapariccāgo, tena ca niratimānatā, adhisīlasikkhādiadhiṭṭhānaṃ, tattha [P 1.0119] ca acalatā, kusalakiriyāsu pītipāmojjaṃ, vivekaninnacittatā, jhānānuyogo, anavajjasutena atitti, yathāsutassa dhammassa paresaṃ hitajjhāsayena desanā, sattānaṃ ñāye nivesanaṃ, ārambhadaḷhatā, dhīravīrabhāvo, parāpavādaparāpakāresu vikārābhāvo, saccādhiṭṭhānaṃ, samāpattīsu vasībhāvo, abhiññāsu balappatti, lakkhaṇattayāvabodho, satipaṭṭhānādīsu abhiyogena lokuttaramaggasambhārasambharaṇaṃ, navalokuttarāvakkantī”ti evamādikā sabbā bodhisambhārapaṭipatti vīriyānubhāveneva samijjhatīti [V 1.0082] abhinīhārato yāva mahābodhi anossajjantena sakkaccaṃ nirantaraṃ vīriyaṃ sampādetabbaṃ. Sampajjamāne ca vīriye khantiādayo dānādayo ca sabbepi bodhisambhārā tadadhīnavuttitāya sampannā eva hontīti. Khantiādīsupi iminā nayena paṭipatti veditabbā.

Furthermore, the effort worthy of praise and exertion for the attainment of Buddhahood—which is inconceivable, immeasurable, vast, expansive, stainless, incomparable, free from defilements, and the foundation of an accumulation of virtues—is itself of inconceivable power. Few people are even capable of hearing about it, let alone practicing it. For there are the threefold initial aspirations, the four grounds of Buddhahood (DN 3.210, 313; AN 4.32), the four bases of beneficence, scope for compassion, patient reflection on the Buddha’s teachings, detachment from all phenomena, perceiving all beings as one’s own children, wearilessness amid the sufferings of saṃsāra, relinquishment of all things that can be given, absence of pride therein, the resolve to adhere to higher virtue and so forth—and steadfastness therein, joy and delight in wholesome deeds, a mind inclined towards seclusion, dedication to meditation, insatiability in listening to the blameless teachings, teaching the Dhamma as heard with the intention of welfare for others, establishing beings in the right way, firmness in undertaking, steadfast heroism, imperturbability in the face of others’ blame and harm, adherence to truth, mastery over meditative attainments, attainment of power in higher knowledges, comprehension of the three characteristics, and the accumulation of requisites for the supramundane path through diligent application of the foundations of mindfulness and so forth—along with the descent into the nine supramundane states. Thus, all such practices for the requisites of enlightenment succeed solely through the power of effort. From the initial aspiration up to the great enlightenment, one must diligently and unremittingly perfect effort without slackening. When effort is properly maintained, then patience and the other perfections, as well as all the requisites for enlightenment, become fulfilled by depending on its activity. The practice of patience and the rest should be understood in this same way.

Iti sattānaṃ sukhūpakaraṇapariccāgena bahudhā anuggahakaraṇaṃ dānena paṭipatti, sīlena tesaṃ jīvitasāpateyyadārarakkhaabhedapiyahitavacanāvihiṃsādikaraṇāni, nekkhammena nesaṃ āmisapaṭiggahaṇadhammadānādinā anekadhā hitacariyā, paññāya tesaṃ hitakaraṇūpāyakosallaṃ, vīriyena tattha ussāhārambhaasaṃhīrāni, khantiyā tadaparādhasahanaṃ, saccena tesaṃ [M 1.0093] avañcanatadupakārakiriyāsamādānāvisaṃvādanādi, adhiṭṭhānena tadupakārakaraṇe anatthasampātepi acalanaṃ, mettāya tesaṃ hitasukhānucintanaṃ, upekkhāya tesaṃ upakārāpakāresu vikārānāpattīti evaṃ aparimāṇe satte ārabbha anukampitasabbasattassa bodhisattassa puthujjanehi asādhāraṇo aparimāṇo puññañāṇasambhārūpacayo ettha paṭipattīti veditabbaṃ. Yo cetāsaṃ paccayo vutto, tassa ca sakkaccaṃ sampādanaṃ.

Thus, the practice is: with generosity, the manifold assistance to beings through the relinquishment of things conducive to their happiness; with virtue, actions such as protecting their lives, property, and spouses, not breaking pleasant and beneficial speech, and non-harming; with renunciation, beneficial conduct in various ways, such as through the acceptance of material offerings and the giving of the Dhamma; with wisdom, skill in devising means for their welfare; with energy, enthusiastic exertion and unwavering effort in that; with patience, the endurance of their transgressions; with truthfulness, non-deception, undertaking to help them, not betraying promises, and so forth; with resolve, remaining unshaken in benefiting them, even when faced with adverse circumstances; with loving-kindness, constantly thinking of their welfare and happiness; with equanimity, not falling into agitation concerning their help or harm. Thus, with regard to immeasurable beings, the accumulation of merit and knowledge of the Bodhisatta, who has compassion for all beings, is immeasurable and not shared by ordinary people; this is to be understood as practice here. And that which was said as the condition for these things, that should be accomplished respectfully.

Ko vibhāgoti dasa [P 1.0120] pāramiyo, dasa upapāramiyo, dasa paramatthapāramiyoti samattiṃsa pāramiyo. Tattha katābhinīhārassa bodhisattassa parahitakaraṇābhininnaāsayappayogassa kaṇhadhammavokiṇṇā sukkadhammā pāramiyo, tehi avokiṇṇā sukkā dhammā upapāramiyo, akaṇhā asukkā paramatthapāramiyoti keci. Samudāgamanakālesu pūriyamānā pāramiyo, bodhisattabhūmiyaṃ puṇṇā upapāramiyo, buddhabhūmiyaṃ sabbākāraparipuṇṇā paramatthapāramiyo. Bodhisattabhūmiyaṃ vā parahitakaraṇato pāramiyo, attahitakaraṇato upapāramiyo, buddhabhūmiyaṃ balavesārajjasamadhigamena ubhayahitaparipūraṇato paramatthapāramiyoti evaṃ ādimajjhapariyosānesu paṇidhānārambhapariniṭṭhānesu tesaṃ vibhāgoti apare. Dosupasamakaruṇāpakatikānaṃ bhavasukhavimuttisukhaparamasukhappattānaṃ puññūpacayabhedato tabbibhāgoti aññe.

What is the division? The ten perfections, the ten higher perfections, and the ten ultimate perfections make thirty perfections in total. Here, for a bodhisatta whose aspiration is established and whose intention and effort are directed toward benefiting others, the bright qualities mixed with dark qualities are the perfections; those bright qualities unmixed with dark qualities are the higher perfections; qualities that are neither dark nor bright are the ultimate perfections—so say some. As they are being fulfilled during the times of accumulation, they are the perfections; in the bodhisatta stage, they are full as the higher perfections; in the buddha stage, they are completely fulfilled in every way as the ultimate perfections. Alternatively, in the bodhisatta stage, because of benefiting others, they are the perfections; because of benefiting oneself, they are the higher perfections; in the buddha stage, because of completely fulfilling the benefit of both through the attainment of powers and self-confidence, they are the ultimate perfections. Thus, others say that this is their division in the beginning, middle, and end—in aspiration, commencement, and accomplishment. Still others say that for those who have subdued hatred and are naturally compassionate, and who have attained the happiness of existence, the happiness of liberation, and the ultimate happiness, that division is according to the difference in the accumulation of merit.

Lajjāsatimānāpassayānaṃ lokuttaradhammādhipatīnaṃ sīlasamādhipaññāgarukānaṃ tāritataritatārayitūnaṃ anubuddhapaccekabuddhasammāsambuddhānaṃ pāramī, upapāramī, paramatthapāramīti bodhittayappattito yathāvuttavibhāgoti keci. Cittapaṇidhito yāva vacīpaṇidhi, tāva pavattā sambhārā pāramiyo, vacīpaṇidhito yāva kāyapaṇidhi, tāva pavattā upapāramiyo, kāyapaṇidhito pabhuti paramatthapāramiyoti apare. Aññe pana “parapuññānumodanavasena pavattā sambhārā pāramiyo, paresaṃ kārāpanavasena pavattā upapāramiyo, sayaṃ karaṇavasena pavattā paramatthapāramiyo”ti [V 1.0083] vadanti. Tathā bhavasukhāvaho puññañāṇasambhāro pāramī, attano nibbānasukhāvaho upapāramī, paresaṃ tadubhayasukhāvaho paramatthapāramīti eke.

Some say that for the Hearer-Enlightened Ones, the Paccekabuddhas, and the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones—who rely on moral shame, mindfulness, and respect; who are masters of the supramundane states; who revere virtue, concentration, and wisdom; and who have been helped to cross, have crossed, and will help others cross—the division into perfection (pāramī), higher perfection (upapāramī), and ultimate perfection (paramatthapāramī) is based on the attainment of these three kinds of enlightenment. Others say that from the aspiration of the mind until the aspiration of speech, the accumulations that occur are the perfections (pāramī); from the aspiration of speech until the aspiration of the body, the accumulations that occur are the higher perfections (upapāramī); and from the aspiration of the body onward, the accumulations that occur are the ultimate perfections (paramatthapāramī). Still others say: 'The accumulations that occur by way of rejoicing in others' merit are the perfections (pāramī); those that occur by way of causing others to act are the higher perfections (upapāramī); and those that occur by way of one's own actions are the ultimate perfections (paramatthapāramī).' Similarly, some say: 'The accumulation of merit and knowledge that brings happiness in existence is the perfection (pāramī); that which brings the happiness of one's own Nibbāna is the higher perfection (upapāramī); and that which brings both kinds of happiness for others is the ultimate perfection (paramatthapāramī).'

Puttadāradhanādiupakaraṇapariccāgo [M 1.0094] pana dānapāramī, attano aṅgapariccāgo dānaupapāramī, attano jīvitapariccāgo [P 1.0121] dānaparamatthapāramī. Tathā puttadārādikassa tividhassapi hetu avītikkamanavasena tisso sīlapāramiyo, tesu eva tividhesu vatthūsu ālayaṃ upacchinditvā nikkhamanavasena tisso nekkhammapāramiyo, upakaraṇaṅgajīvitataṇhaṃ samūhanitvā sattānaṃ hitāhitavinicchayakaraṇavasena tisso paññāpāramiyo, yathāvuttabhedānaṃ pariccāgādīnaṃ vāyamanavasena tisso vīriyapāramiyo, upakaraṇaṅgajīvitantarāyakarānaṃ khamanavasena tisso khantipāramiyo, upakaraṇaṅgajīvitahetu saccāpariccāgavasena tisso saccapāramiyo, dānādipāramiyo akuppādhiṭṭhānavaseneva samijjhantīti upakaraṇādivināsepi acalādhiṭṭhānavasena tisso adhiṭṭhānapāramiyo, upakaraṇādiupaghātakesupi sattesu mettāya avijahanavasena tisso mettāpāramiyo, yathāvuttavatthuttayassa upakārāpakāresu sattasaṅkhāresu majjhattatāpaṭilābhavasena tisso upekkhāpāramiyoti evamādinā etāsaṃ vibhāgo veditabbo.

The relinquishment of external possessions such as children, spouse, and wealth is the perfection of giving (dānapāramī). The relinquishment of one’s own limbs is the higher perfection of giving (dānaupapāramī). The relinquishment of one’s own life is the ultimate perfection of giving (dānaparamatthapāramī). Similarly, the three perfections of virtue are fulfilled by not transgressing for the sake of these three: possessions, limbs, and life. The three perfections of renunciation are fulfilled by cutting off attachment to these same three things and going forth. The three perfections of wisdom are fulfilled by uprooting craving for possessions, limbs, and life, and by determining what is beneficial and harmful for beings. The three perfections of energy are fulfilled through exertion in the aforesaid kinds of relinquishment and other acts. The three perfections of patience are fulfilled by enduring those who cause harm to one's possessions, limbs, and life. The three perfections of truthfulness are fulfilled by not abandoning truth for the sake of possessions, limbs, or life. Since the perfections of giving and so forth are accomplished only through unshakable resolve, the three perfections of resolve are fulfilled by remaining resolute even when possessions and so forth are destroyed. The three perfections of loving-kindness are fulfilled by not abandoning loving-kindness even toward beings who harm one's possessions and so forth. The three perfections of equanimity are fulfilled by attaining a state of balance toward beings who help or harm with respect to the three aforesaid things. In this way, the classification of these perfections should be understood.

Ko saṅgahoti ettha pana yathā etā vibhāgato tiṃsavidhāpi dānapāramīādibhāvato dasavidhā, evaṃ dānasīlakhantivīriyajhānapaññāsabhāvena chabbidhā. Etāsu hi nekkhammapāramī sīlapāramiyā saṅgahitā tassā pabbajjābhāve, nīvaraṇavivekabhāve pana jhānapāramiyā, kusaladhammabhāve chahipi saṅgahitā. Saccapāramī sīlapāramiyā ekadesoyeva vacīsaccaviratisaccapakkhe, ñāṇasaccapakkhe pana paññāpāramiyā saṅgahitā. Mettāpāramī jhānapāramiyā eva, upekkhāpāramī jhānapaññāpāramīhi, adhiṭṭhānapāramī sabbāhipi saṅgahitāti.

How are they comprised? Here, though these are thirtyfold by way of division, they are tenfold by way of being the perfections of giving and so forth, and sixfold by way of the nature of giving, virtue, patience, energy, jhāna, and wisdom. For among these, the perfection of renunciation is comprised in the perfection of virtue when it is the state of going forth; but when it is the state of seclusion from the hindrances, it is comprised in the perfection of jhāna. When it is the state of a wholesome quality, it is comprised in all six. The perfection of truth is only a part of the perfection of virtue in the aspect of truthful speech and abstention from falsehood; but in the aspect of truth of knowledge, it is comprised in the perfection of wisdom. The perfection of loving-kindness is comprised in the perfection of jhāna itself, the perfection of equanimity in the perfections of jhāna and wisdom, and the perfection of resolve in all of them.

Etesañca dānādīnaṃ channaṃ guṇānaṃ aññamaññaṃ sambandhānaṃ pañcadasayugaḷādīni pañcadasayugaḷādisādhakāni honti – seyyathidaṃ? Dānasīlayugaḷena parahitāhitānaṃ karaṇākaraṇayugaḷasiddhi, dānakhantiyugaḷena [P 1.0122] alobhādosayugaḷasiddhi, dānavīriyayugaḷena cāgasutayugaḷasiddhi, dānajhānayugaḷena kāmadosappahānayugaḷasiddhi, dānapaññāyugaḷena ariyayānadhurayugaḷasiddhi, sīlakhantidvayena payogāsayasuddhidvayasiddhi, sīlavīriyadvayena bhāvanādvayasiddhi, sīlajhānadvayena dussīlyapariyuṭṭhānappahānadvayasiddhi, sīlapaññādvayena dānadvayasiddhi, khantivīriyayugaḷena khamātejadvayasiddhi, khantijhānayugaḷena [M 1.0095] virodhānurodhappahānayugaḷasiddhi[V 1.0084], khantipaññāyugaḷena suññatākhantipaṭivedhadukasiddhi, vīriyajhānadukena paggāhāvikkhepadukasiddhi, vīriyapaññādukena saraṇadukasiddhi, jhānapaññādukena yānadukasiddhi. Dānasīlakhantittikena lobhadosamohappahānattikasiddhi, dānasīlavīriyattikena bhogajīvitakāyasārādānattikasiddhi, dānasīlajhānattikena puññakiriyavatthuttikasiddhi, dānasīlapaññātikena āmisābhayadhammadānattikasiddhīti evaṃ itarehipi tikehi catukkādīhi ca yathāsambhavaṃ tikāni catukkādīni ca yojetabbāni.

And these six qualities, giving, etc., when connected with each other, accomplish fifteen pairs, etc.—namely: The pair of giving and virtue accomplishes the pair of doing and not doing good and harm to others. The pair of giving and patience accomplishes the pair of non-greed and non-aversion. The pair of giving and energy accomplishes the pair of renunciation and learning. The pair of giving and jhāna accomplishes the pair of abandoning sensual desire and ill will. The pair of giving and wisdom accomplishes the pair of the burden of the Noble Vehicle. The pair of virtue and patience accomplishes the pair of purity of application and intention. The pair of virtue and energy accomplishes the pair of development (of serenity and insight). The pair of virtue and jhāna accomplishes the pair of abandoning immorality and mental defilements. The pair of virtue and wisdom accomplishes the two kinds of giving. The pair of patience and energy accomplishes the pair of forbearance and vigor. The pair of patience and jhāna accomplishes the pair of abandoning opposition and compliance. The pair of patience and wisdom accomplishes the pair of acceptance of emptiness and penetration. The pair of energy and jhāna accomplishes the pair of exertion and non-distraction. The pair of energy and wisdom accomplishes the pair of mindfulness and recollection. The pair of jhāna and wisdom accomplishes the pair of vehicles. The triad of giving, virtue, and patience accomplishes the triad of abandoning greed, aversion, and delusion. The triad of giving, virtue, and energy accomplishes the triad of taking the essence of wealth, life, and body. The triad of giving, virtue, and jhāna accomplishes the triad of the bases for meritorious action. The triad of giving, virtue, and wisdom accomplishes the triad of the gift of material things, the gift of safety, and the gift of the Dhamma. In this way, the remaining triads and tetrads should be connected accordingly as is suitable.

Evaṃ chabbidhānampi pana imāsaṃ pāramīnaṃ catūhi adhiṭṭhānehi saṅgaho veditabbo. Sabbapāramīnaṃ samūhasaṅgahato hi cattāri adhiṭṭhānāni. Seyyathidaṃ – saccādhiṭṭhānaṃ, cāgādhiṭṭhānaṃ, upasamādhiṭṭhānaṃ, paññādhiṭṭhānanti. Tattha adhitiṭṭhati etena, ettha vā adhitiṭṭhati, adhiṭṭhānamattameva vā tanti adhiṭṭhānaṃ. Saccañca taṃ adhiṭṭhānañca, saccassa vā adhiṭṭhānaṃ, saccaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ etassāti vā saccādhiṭṭhānaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi. Tattha avisesato tāva lokuttaraguṇe katābhinīhārassa anukampitasabbasattassa mahāsattassa pariññānurūpaṃ sabbapāramipariggahato saccādhiṭṭhānaṃ, tesaṃ paṭipakkhapariccāgato cāgādhiṭṭhānaṃ, sabbapāramitāguṇehi upasamato upasamādhiṭṭhānaṃ[P 1.0123], tehiyeva parahitopāyakosallato paññādhiṭṭhānaṃ. Visesato pana “atthikajanaṃ avisaṃvādetvā dassāmī”ti paṭijānato, paṭiññaṃ avisaṃvādetvā dānato, dānaṃ avisaṃvādetvā anumodanato, macchariyādipaṭipakkhapariccāgato, deyyapaṭiggāhakadānadeyyadhammakkhayesu lobhadosamohabhayavūpasamato, yathārahaṃ yathākālaṃ yathāvidhānañca dānato, paññuttarato ca kusaladhammānaṃ caturadhiṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānaṃ dānaṃ. Tathā saṃvarasamādānassa avītikkamato, dussīlyapariccāgato, duccaritavūpasamato, paññuttarato ca caturadhiṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānaṃ sīlaṃ. Yathāpaṭiññaṃ khamanato, parāparādhavikappapariccāgato, kodhapariyuṭṭhānavūpasamato, paññuttarato ca caturadhiṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānā khanti. Paṭiññānurūpaṃ parahitakaraṇato, visādapariccāgato, akusaladhammānaṃ vūpasamato, paññuttarato ca caturadhiṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānaṃ vīriyaṃ. Paṭiññānurūpaṃ lokahitānucintanato, nīvaraṇapariccāgato, cittavūpasamato, paññuttarato ca caturadhiṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānaṃ jhānaṃ. Yathāpaṭiññaṃ parahitūpāyakosallato, anupāyakiriyāpariccāgato[M 1.0096], mohajapariḷāhavūpasamato, sabbaññutāpaṭilābhato ca caturadhiṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānā paññā.

Thus, the inclusion of these six kinds of perfections in the four determinations should be understood. For the collective inclusion of all perfections, there are four determinations. Namely: the determination of truth, the determination of relinquishment, the determination of peace, and the determination of wisdom. Herein, that by which one determines, or that in which one determines, or merely determination itself, is determination. And that which is truth and determination, or the determination of truth, or that of which truth is the determination, is the determination of truth. The same applies to the others. Generally, for the great being who has made an aspiration for supramundane qualities, out of compassion for all beings, the determination of truth is the acquisition of all perfections in accordance with his full understanding. The determination of relinquishment is the abandonment of their opposing factors. The determination of peace is the pacification by means of all the qualities of the perfections. The determination of wisdom is the skill in means for the welfare of others by means of those very qualities. Specifically, giving—from declaring, “I will give without deceiving those in need,” from giving without breaking that promise, from rejoicing without deceit in giving, from abandoning opposing factors like stinginess, from the pacification of greed, hatred, delusion, and fear concerning the gift, the recipient, the act of giving, and the destruction of the gift itself, from giving appropriately, at the right time, and in the right manner, and being supreme in wisdom—is the proximate cause of the four determinations for wholesome qualities. Similarly, virtue—from not transgressing the undertaking of restraint, from abandoning immorality, from the pacification of misconduct, and being supreme in wisdom—is the proximate cause of the four determinations. Patience—from enduring in accordance with one's promise, from abandoning thoughts of others' offenses, from the pacification of the agitation of anger, and being supreme in wisdom—is the proximate cause of the four determinations. Energy—from acting for the welfare of others in accordance with one's promise, from abandoning discouragement, from the pacification of unwholesome states, and being supreme in wisdom—is the proximate cause of the four determinations. Jhāna—from reflecting on the welfare of the world in accordance with one's promise, from abandoning hindrances, from the pacification of the mind, and being supreme in wisdom—is the proximate cause of the four determinations. Wisdom—from skill in means for the welfare of others in accordance with one's promise, from abandoning unskillful actions, from the pacification of the fever born of delusion, and from the attainment of omniscience—is the proximate cause of the four determinations.

Tattha ñeyyapaṭiññānuvidhānehi saccādhiṭṭhānaṃ, vatthukāmakilesakāmapariccāgehi cāgādhiṭṭhānaṃ, dosadukkhavūpasamehi upasamādhiṭṭhānaṃ, anubodhapaṭivedhehi paññādhiṭṭhānaṃ. Tividhasaccapariggahitaṃ [V 1.0085] dosattayavirodhi saccādhiṭṭhānaṃ, tividhacāgapariggahitaṃ dosattayavirodhi cāgādhiṭṭhānaṃ, tividhavūpasamapariggahitaṃ dosattayavirodhi upasamādhiṭṭhānaṃ, tividhañāṇapariggahitaṃ dosattayavirodhi paññādhiṭṭhānaṃ. Saccādhiṭṭhānapariggahitāni cāgūpasamapaññādhiṭṭhānāni avisaṃvādanato[P 1.0124], paṭiññānuvidhānato ca. Cāgādhiṭṭhānapariggahitāni saccūpasamapaññādhiṭṭhānāni paṭipakkhapariccāgato, sabbapariccāgaphalattā ca. Upasamādhiṭṭhānapariggahitāni saccacāgapaññādhiṭṭhānāni kilesapariḷāhūpasamato, kāmūpasamato, kāmapariḷāhūpasamato ca. Paññādhiṭṭhānapariggahitāni saccacāgūpasamādhiṭṭhānāni ñāṇapubbaṅgamato, ñāṇānuparivattanato cāti evaṃ sabbāpi pāramiyo saccappabhāvitā cāgaparibyañjitā upasamopabrūhitā paññāparisuddhā. Saccañhi etāsaṃ janakahetu, cāgo pariggāhakahetu, upasamo parivuḍḍhihetu, paññā pārisuddhihetu. Tathā ādimhi saccādhiṭṭhānaṃ saccapaṭiññattā, majjhe cāgādhiṭṭhānaṃ katapaṇidhānassa parahitāya attapariccāgato, ante upasamādhiṭṭhānaṃ sabbūpasamapariyosānattā, ādimajjhapariyosānesu paññādhiṭṭhānaṃ tasmiṃ sati sambhavato, asati abhāvato, yathāpaṭiññañca bhāvato.

Herein, the determination of truth is by means of acknowledging what is to be known and conforming to that acknowledgment. The determination of relinquishment is by means of relinquishing object-sensual-desire and defilement-sensual-desire. The determination of peace is by means of the pacification of ill will and suffering. The determination of wisdom is by means of comprehension and penetration. The determination of truth, encompassed by the threefold truth, opposes the threefold defilements. The determination of relinquishment, encompassed by the threefold relinquishment, opposes the threefold defilements. The determination of peace, encompassed by the threefold pacification, opposes the threefold defilements. The determination of wisdom, encompassed by the threefold knowledge, opposes the threefold defilements. The determinations of relinquishment, peace, and wisdom, when encompassed by the determination of truth, are unfailing due to non-deception and conformity to acknowledgment. The determinations of truth, peace, and wisdom, when encompassed by the determination of relinquishment, arise from abandoning opposing factors and because they are the fruit of complete relinquishment. The determinations of truth, relinquishment, and wisdom, when encompassed by the determination of peace, arise from the pacification of the fever of defilements, the pacification of sensual desire, and the pacification of the fever of sensual desire. The determinations of truth, relinquishment, and peace, when encompassed by the determination of wisdom, arise from wisdom as the forerunner and from revolving around wisdom. Thus, all the perfections are illuminated by truth, manifested by relinquishment, strengthened by peace, and purified by wisdom. For truth is their generative cause, relinquishment their sustaining cause, peace their cause of growth, and wisdom their cause of purification. Likewise, at the beginning, the determination of truth is due to the acknowledgment of truth. In the middle, the determination of relinquishment is due to the relinquishment of self for the welfare of others, by one who has made a vow. At the end, the determination of peace is due to its culmination in all pacification. And throughout the beginning, middle, and end, the determination of wisdom exists because it is possible when that is present and impossible when it is not, and because it develops according to what has been acknowledged.

Tattha mahāpurisā attahitaparahitakarehi garupiyabhāvakarehi saccacāgādhiṭṭhānehi gihibhūtā āmisadānena pare anuggaṇhanti. Tathā attahitaparahitakarehi garupiyabhāvakarehi upasamapaññādhiṭṭhānehi ca pabbajitabhūtā dhammadānena pare anuggaṇhanti.

Herein, great beings, having become householders, working for their own welfare and that of others, inspiring respect and affection, and by means of the determinations of truth and relinquishment, help others through material gifts. Similarly, great beings, having become renunciants, working for their own welfare and that of others, inspiring respect and affection, and by means of the determinations of peace and wisdom, help others through the gift of Dhamma.

Tattha antimabhave bodhisattassa caturadhiṭṭhānaparipūraṇaṃ. Paripuṇṇacaturadhiṭṭhānassa hi carimakabhavūpapattīti eke. Tatra hi gabbhokkantiṭhitiabhinikkhamanesu paññādhiṭṭhānasamudāgamena sato sampajāno saccādhiṭṭhānapāripūriyā sampatijāto uttarābhimukho sattapadavītihārena gantvā sabbā disā oloketvā saccānuparivattinā vacasā “aggohamasmi lokassa, jeṭṭho…pe… seṭṭhohamasmi lokassā”ti (dī. ni. 2.31; ma. ni. 3.207) tikkhattuṃ [M 1.0097][P 1.0125] sīhanādaṃ nadi, upasamādhiṭṭhānasamudāgamena jiṇṇāturamatapabbajitadassāvino catudhammapadesakovidassa yobbanārogyajīvitasampattimadānaṃ upasamo, cāgādhiṭṭhānasamudāgamena mahato ñātiparivaṭṭassa hatthagatassa ca cakkavattirajjassa anapekkhapariccāgoti.

Herein, for the Bodhisatta in his final existence, is the fulfillment of the four determinations. For some say that the last arising of becoming is for one who has fully perfected the four determinations. There, in the descent into the womb, abiding, and going forth from home, he was mindful and clearly comprehending through the emergence of the determination of wisdom. By the complete fulfillment of the determination of truth, just after birth, facing north, having gone seven strides, having surveyed all directions, and with words conforming to truth, he roared the lion's roar three times: “I am the chief in the world, the eldest... the best in the world.” Through the emergence of the determination of peace, for one who saw the aged, the sick, the dead, and the renunciant, and was skilled in the fourfold exposition of the Dhamma, there was the calming of the intoxication with youth, health, and the possession of life. And through the emergence of the determination of relinquishment, there was the unconcerned relinquishment of a great retinue of relatives and the sovereignty of a wheel-turning king which was in his hand.

Dutiye ṭhāne abhisambodhiyaṃ caturadhiṭṭhānaṃ paripuṇṇanti keci. Tattha hi yathāpaṭiññaṃ saccādhiṭṭhānasamudāgamena catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ abhisamayo, tato hi saccādhiṭṭhānaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ. Cāgādhiṭṭhānasamudāgamena [V 1.0086] sabbakilesopakkilesapariccāgo, tato hi cāgādhiṭṭhānaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ. Upasamādhiṭṭhānasamudāgamena paramūpasamasampatti, tato hi upasamādhiṭṭhānaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ. Paññādhiṭṭhānasamudāgamena anāvaraṇañāṇapaṭilābho, tato hi paññādhiṭṭhānaṃ paripuṇṇanti, taṃ asiddhaṃ abhisambodhiyāpi paramatthabhāvato.

In the second instance, some say the four determinations are fulfilled at the time of full enlightenment. There, through the emergence of the determination of truth, there is the realization of the four noble truths in accordance with his vow—thus, the determination of truth is fulfilled. Through the emergence of the determination of relinquishment, there is the complete abandonment of all defilements and corruptions—thus, the determination of relinquishment is fulfilled. Through the emergence of the determination of tranquility, there is the attainment of supreme tranquility—thus, the determination of tranquility is fulfilled. Through the emergence of the determination of wisdom, there is the acquisition of unobstructed knowledge—thus, the determination of wisdom is fulfilled. Yet, that is not established, because full enlightenment is also of the nature of ultimate reality.

Tatiye ṭhāne dhammacakkappavattane (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 13; paṭi. ma. 2.30) caturadhiṭṭhānaṃ paripuṇṇanti aññe. Tattha hi saccādhiṭṭhānasamudāgatassa dvādasahi ākārehi ariyasaccadesanāya saccādhiṭṭhānaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ, cāgādhiṭṭhānasamudāgatassa saddhammamahāyāgakaraṇena cāgādhiṭṭhānaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ. Upasamādhiṭṭhānasamudāgatassa sayaṃ upasantassa paresaṃ upasamanena upasamādhiṭṭhānaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ, paññādhiṭṭhānasamudāgatassa vineyyānaṃ āsayādiparijānanena paññādhiṭṭhānaṃ paripuṇṇanti, tadapi asiddhaṃ apariyositattā buddhakiccassa.

In the third instance, others say the four determinations are fulfilled at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma. There, for one in whom the determination of truth has arisen, the determination of truth is fulfilled by the teaching of the noble truths in twelve aspects. For one in whom the determination of relinquishment has arisen, the determination of relinquishment is fulfilled by performing the great sacrifice of the true Dhamma. For one in whom the determination of tranquility has arisen, the determination of tranquility is fulfilled by oneself being tranquil and bringing tranquility to others. For one in whom the determination of wisdom has arisen, the determination of wisdom is fulfilled by discerning the inclinations and dispositions of those to be trained. Yet, that too is not established, because the Buddha’s task is not yet concluded.

Catutthe ṭhāne parinibbāne caturadhiṭṭhānaparipuṇṇanti apare. Tatra hi parinibbutattā paramatthasaccasampattiyā saccādhiṭṭhānaparipūraṇaṃ, sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggena cāgādhiṭṭhānaparipūraṇaṃ, sabbasaṅkhārūpasamena [P 1.0126] upasamādhiṭṭhānaparipūraṇaṃ, paññāpayojanapariniṭṭhānena paññādhiṭṭhānaparipūraṇanti.

In the fourth instance, at final Nibbāna, others say the four determinations are fulfilled. There, because of being fully extinguished, the determination of truth is fulfilled by the attainment of ultimate truth. The determination of relinquishment is fulfilled by the relinquishment of all substrates of existence. The determination of tranquility is fulfilled by the stilling of all formations. The determination of wisdom is fulfilled by the complete fulfillment of the purpose of wisdom.

Tatra mahāpurisassa visesena mettākhette abhijātiyaṃ saccādhiṭṭhānasamudāgatassa saccādhiṭṭhānaparipūraṇamabhibyattaṃ, visesena karuṇākhette abhisambodhiyaṃ paññādhiṭṭhānasamudāgatassa paññādhiṭṭhānaparipūraṇamabhibyattaṃ, visesena muditākhette dhammacakkappavattane (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 13; paṭi. ma. 2.30) cāgādhiṭṭhānasamudāgatassa cāgādhiṭṭhānaparipūraṇamabhibyattaṃ, visesena upekkhākhette parinibbāne upasamādhiṭṭhānasamudāgatassa upasamādhiṭṭhānaparipūraṇamabhibyattanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here, in the case of a great being, the fulfillment of the determination of truth, for one in whom the determination of truth has arisen, is distinctly evident in the field of loving-kindness at birth. The fulfillment of the determination of wisdom, for one in whom the determination of wisdom has arisen, is distinctly evident in the field of compassion at full enlightenment. The fulfillment of the determination of relinquishment, for one in whom the determination of relinquishment has arisen, is distinctly evident in the field of sympathetic joy at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma. The fulfillment of the determination of tranquility, for one in whom the determination of tranquility has arisen, is distinctly evident in the field of equanimity at final Nibbāna. This should be understood.

Tatrapi [M 1.0098] saccādhiṭṭhānasamudāgatassa saṃvāsena sīlaṃ veditabbaṃ, cāgādhiṭṭhānasamudāgatassa saṃvohārena soceyyaṃ veditabbaṃ, upasamādhiṭṭhānasamudāgatassa āpadāsu thāmo veditabbo, paññādhiṭṭhānasamudāgatassa sākacchāya paññā veditabbā. Evaṃ sīlājīvacittadiṭṭhivisuddhiyo veditabbā.

Furthermore, through living with one in whom the determination of truth has arisen, virtue should be understood; through dealings with one in whom the determination of relinquishment has arisen, purity should be understood; in misfortunes, the steadfastness of one in whom the determination of tranquility has arisen should be understood; through discussion with one in whom the determination of wisdom has arisen, wisdom should be understood. Thus, the purifications of virtue, livelihood, mind, and view should be understood.

Tathā [V 1.0087] saccādhiṭṭhānasamudāgamena dosā agatiṃ na gacchati avisaṃvādanato, cāgādhiṭṭhānasamudāgamena lobhā agatiṃ na gacchati anabhisaṅgato, upasamādhiṭṭhānasamudāgamena bhayā agatiṃ na gacchati anaparādhato, paññādhiṭṭhānasamudāgamena mohā agatiṃ na gacchati yathābhūtāvabodhato.

Similarly, through the emergence of the determination of truth, one does not go on a wrong course from hatred, due to non-deception; through the emergence of the determination of relinquishment, one does not go on a wrong course from greed, due to non-attachment; through the emergence of the determination of tranquility, one does not go on a wrong course from fear, due to being without offense; through the emergence of the determination of wisdom, one does not go on a wrong course from delusion, due to the understanding of reality as it is.

Tathā paṭhamena aduṭṭho adhivāseti, dutiyena aluddho paṭisevati, tatiyena abhīto parivajjeti, catutthena asammūḷho vinodeti. Paṭhamena nekkhammasukhappatti, itarehi pavivekaupasamasambodhisukhappattiyo hontīti daṭṭhabbā. Tathā vivekajapītisukhasamādhijapītisukhaappītijakāyasukhasatipārisuddhijaupekkhāsukhappattiyo etehi catūhi yathākkamaṃ hontīti. Evamanekaguṇānubandhehi catūhi adhiṭṭhānehi sabbapāramisamūhasaṅgaho veditabbo. Yathā ca catūhi adhiṭṭhānehi sabbapāramisaṅgaho, evaṃ karuṇāpaññāhipīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sabbopi [P 1.0127] hi bodhisambhāro karuṇāpaññāhi saṅgahito. Karuṇāpaññāpariggahitā hi dānādiguṇā mahābodhisambhārā bhavanti buddhattasiddhipariyosānāti evametāsaṃ saṅgaho veditabbo.

Thus, by the first, he endures without aversion; by the second, he associates without greed; by the third, he avoids without fear; by the fourth, he dispels without delusion. By the first, there is the attainment of the bliss of renunciation; by the others, the attainments of the bliss of seclusion, tranquility, and awakening are to be seen. Similarly, the attainments of joy and bliss born of seclusion, joy and bliss born of concentration, bodily bliss devoid of joy, and the bliss of equanimity born from the purity of mindfulness arise in sequence from these four. Thus, the complete collection of all perfections should be understood through these four determinations, which are connected with many virtues. Just as all perfections are collected through these four determinations, so too should it be seen with compassion and wisdom. Indeed, all the requisites for enlightenment are comprised by compassion and wisdom. For qualities such as generosity, when embraced by compassion and wisdom, become great requisites for enlightenment, culminating in the attainment of Buddhahood. Thus, their collection should be understood in this way.

Ko sampādanūpāyoti sakalassāpi puññādisambhārassa sammāsambodhiṃ, uddissa anavasesasambharaṇaṃ avekallakāritāyogena, tattha ca sakkaccakāritā ādarabahumānayogena, sātaccakāritā nirantarapayogena, cirakālādiyogo ca antarā avosānāpajjanenāti caturaṅgayogo etāsaṃ sampādanūpāyo. Apica samāsato katābhinīhārassa attani sinehassa pariyādānaṃ, paresu ca sinehassa parivaḍḍhanaṃ etāsaṃ sampādanūpāyo. Sammāsambodhisamadhigamāya hi katamahāpaṇidhānassa mahāsattassa yāthāvato parijānanena sabbesu dhammesu anupalittassa attani sineho parikkhayaṃ pariyādānaṃ gacchati, mahākaruṇāsamāyogavasena pana piye putte viya sabbasatte sampassamānassa tesu mettāsineho parivaḍḍhati. Tato ca taṃtadāvatthānurūpamattaparasantānesu [M 1.0099] lobhadosamohavigamena vidūrīkatamacchariyādibodhisambhārapaṭipakkho mahāpuriso dānapiyavacanaatthacariyāsamānattatāsaṅkhātehi catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi (dī. ni. 3.210; a. ni. 4.32) caturadhiṭṭhānānugatehi accantaṃ janassa saṅgahakaraṇavasena upari yānattaye avatāraṇaṃ paripācanañca karoti. Mahāsattānañhi mahāpaññā mahākaruṇā ca dānena alaṅkatā; dānaṃ piyavacanena; piyavacanaṃ atthacariyāya; atthacariyā samānattatāya alaṅkatā saṅgahitā ca. Sabbabhūtattabhūtassa hi bodhisattassa sabbattha samānasukhadukkhatāya samānattatāsiddhi. Buddhabhūto pana teheva saṅgahavatthūhi caturadhiṭṭhānaparipūritābhibuddhehi janassa accantikasaṅgahakaraṇena abhivinayanaṃ karoti. Dānañhi [V 1.0088] sammāsambuddhānaṃ cāgādhiṭṭhānena paripūritābhibuddhaṃ[P 1.0128]; piyavacanaṃ saccādhiṭṭhānena; atthacariyā paññādhiṭṭhānena; samānattatā upasamādhiṭṭhānena paripūritābhibuddhā. Tathāgatānañhi sabbasāvakapaccekabuddhehi samānattatā parinibbāne. Tatra hi tesaṃ avisesato ekībhāvo. Tenevāha “natthi vimuttiyā nānatta”nti.

What is the means of fulfillment? It is the fourfold application: the gathering of all requisites such as merit, without remainder, directed toward perfect enlightenment, through the practice of acting without deficiency; and therein, acting with care, through the practice of respect and high regard; acting persistently, through uninterrupted application; and the practice over a long period by not abandoning it midway—this four-limbed application is the means of their fulfillment. Moreover, in brief, for one who has made the aspiration, the complete exhaustion of affection for oneself and the increase of affection for others is the means of their fulfillment. Indeed, for the great being who has made the great resolve for the attainment of perfect enlightenment, who through understanding things as they truly are is unsullied by all phenomena, affection for oneself goes to destruction and complete exhaustion. But through the application of great compassion, seeing all beings as if they were a beloved child, loving affection towards them increases. Then, the great person, having driven far away stinginess and other opponents to the requisites for enlightenment by the removal of greed, hatred, and delusion in his own and others' mental continuums in a way appropriate to each particular situation, employs the four bases of sympathy—namely, giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality—which are accompanied by the four determinations. By way of completely gathering people, he causes them to enter and mature in the three higher vehicles. Indeed, for great beings, great wisdom and great compassion are adorned with generosity; generosity is adorned with kind speech; kind speech is adorned with beneficial conduct; and beneficial conduct is adorned with and embraced by impartiality. For the Bodhisatta who has become one with all beings, the accomplishment of impartiality is achieved through having equal happiness and sorrow everywhere. But having become a Buddha, through these same bases of sympathy—fulfilled and fully awakened by the four determinations—he thoroughly trains people by means of ultimate gathering. Indeed, for the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones, generosity is fulfilled and fully awakened by the determination of relinquishment; kind speech by the determination of truth; beneficial conduct by the determination of wisdom; and impartiality by the determination of tranquility. Indeed, for the Tathāgatas, their impartiality with all disciples and Paccekabuddhas is at parinibbāna. For there, their oneness is without distinction. Therefore it is said: 'There is no diversity in liberation.'

Honti cettha –

Herein are these stanzas:

“Sacco cāgī upasanto, paññavā anukampako,

Sambhatasabbasambhāro, kaṃ nāmatthaṃ na sādhaye.

Truthful, generous, tranquil, wise, compassionate, having gathered all requisites, what aim would he not accomplish?

Mahākāruṇiko satthā, hitesī ca upekkhako,

Nirapekkho ca sabbattha, aho acchariyo jino.

The Teacher is greatly compassionate, a well-wisher and equanimous, and unattached in every way—oh, how wonderful the Conqueror!

Viratto sabbadhammesu, sattesu ca upekkhako,

Sadā sattahite yutto, aho acchariyo jino.

Dispassionate towards all phenomena, and equanimous towards beings, always engaged in the welfare of beings—oh, how wonderful the Conqueror!

Sabbadā sabbasattānaṃ, hitāya ca sukhāya ca,

Uyyutto akilāsū ca, aho acchariyo jino”ti. (cariyā. aṭṭha. 320 pakiṇṇakakathā);

Always for the welfare and happiness of all beings, diligent and untiring—oh, how wonderful the Conqueror!

Kittakena kālena sampādananti heṭṭhimena tāva paricchedena cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca, majjhimena aṭṭhāsaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca, uparimena soḷasāsaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca, ete ca [M 1.0100] bhedā yathākkamaṃ paññādhikasaddhādhikavīriyādhikavasena ñātabbā. Paññādhikānañhi saddhā mandā hoti, paññā tikkhā. Saddhādhikānaṃ paññā majjhimā hoti, vīriyādhikānaṃ paññā mandā. Paññānubhāvena ca sammāsambodhi abhigantabbāti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Avisesena pana vimuttiparipācanīyānaṃ dhammānaṃ tikkhamajjhimamudubhāvena tayopete bhedā yuttāti vadanti. Tividhā hi bodhisattā abhinīhārakkhaṇe [P 1.0129] bhavanti ugghaṭitaññūvipañcitaññūneyyabhedena. Tesu ugghaṭitaññū sammāsambuddhassa sammukhā catuppadikaṃ gāthaṃ suṇanto tatiyapade apariyositeyeva chaabhiññāhi saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pattuṃ samatthupanissayo hoti, dutiyo satthu sammukhā catuppadikaṃ gāthaṃ suṇanto apariyositeyeva catutthapade chahi abhiññāhi arahattaṃ pattuṃ samatthupanissayo hoti, itaro bhagavato sammukhā catuppadikaṃ gāthaṃ [V 1.0089] sutvā pariyositāya gāthāya chahi abhiññāhi arahattaṃ pattuṃ samatthupanissayo bhavati.
