Tayopete vinā kālabhedena katābhinīhāraladdhabyākaraṇā pāramiyo pūrentā yathākkamaṃ yathāvuttabhedena kālena sammāsambodhiṃ pāpuṇanti. Tesu tesu pana kālabhedesu aparipuṇṇesu te te mahāsattā divase divase vessantaradānasadisaṃ dānaṃ dentāpi tadanurūpe sīlādisabbapāramidhamme ācinantāpi antarā buddhā bhavissantīti akāraṇametaṃ. Kasmā? Ñāṇassa aparipaccanato. Paricchinnakālanipphāditaṃ viya hi sassaṃ paricchinnakāle parinipphāditā sammāsambodhi. Tadantarā pana sabbussāhena vāyamantenāpi na sakkā pāpuṇitunti pāramipāripūrī yathāvuttakālavisesaṃ vinā na sampajjatīti veditabbaṃ.

By how much time is it accomplished? By the lower reckoning, it is four incalculable periods and one hundred thousand eons. By the middle reckoning, it is eight incalculable periods and one hundred thousand eons. By the higher reckoning, it is sixteen incalculable periods and one hundred thousand eons. And these divisions should be understood in order as pertaining to those with wisdom predominant, faith predominant, and energy predominant. For those with wisdom predominant, faith is weak, but wisdom is sharp. For those with faith predominant, wisdom is moderate. For those with energy predominant, wisdom is weak. And it is said in the commentary that perfect enlightenment is to be attained through the power of wisdom. Generally, however, some say that these three divisions are appropriate due to the sharp, moderate, or mild nature of the qualities that ripen for liberation. For bodhisattas are of three kinds at the moment of making the aspiration—those of quick understanding, those of developed understanding, and those to be guided. Among them, one of quick understanding, upon hearing a four-line verse in the presence of a Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha, has the supporting condition to be capable of attaining arahantship with the six superknowledges and the analytical knowledges even before the third line is finished. The second, upon hearing a four-line verse in the presence of the Teacher, has the supporting condition to be capable of attaining arahantship with the six superknowledges even before the fourth line is finished. The other, upon hearing a four-line verse in the presence of the Blessed One, has the supporting condition to be capable of attaining arahantship with the six superknowledges after the verse is fully recited. These three, having made their aspiration and received the prediction without distinction of time, fulfill the perfections and attain perfect enlightenment in the time as stated, according to their respective division. But in those cases where the respective divisions of time are incomplete, even if those great beings give gifts like Vessantara’s gift every day, and accumulate all the corresponding qualities of the perfections such as virtue, it is impossible for them to become Buddhas in the meantime. Why? Because their knowledge has not matured. For just as a crop is produced only in its fixed season, perfect enlightenment is completed only in its predetermined time. But in the interim, even if one strives with all one’s effort, it cannot be attained. Thus, it should be understood that the fulfillment of the perfections does not occur without the specific period of time as stated.

Ko ānisaṃsoti ye te katābhinīhārānaṃ bodhisattānaṃ –

What is the benefit? For those Bodhisattas who have made their aspiration—

“Evaṃ sabbaṅgasampannā, bodhiyā niyatā narā;

Saṃsaraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ, kappakoṭisatehipi;

Avīcimhi nuppajjanti, tathā lokantaresu cā”ti. ādinā (abhi. aṭṭha. 1.nidānakathā; apa. aṭṭha. 1.dūrenidānakathā; jā. aṭṭha. 1.dūrenidānakathā; bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 27.dūrenidānakathā; cariyā. aṭṭha. pakiṇṇakakathā) –

"Thus, people endowed with all qualities, destined for enlightenment, wandering through the long course of saṃsāra, even for hundreds of crores of eons, are not reborn in Avīci, nor in the world-interstices." (Abhidhamma Aṭṭhakathā 1, Nidānakathā; Apadāna Aṭṭhakathā 1, Dūrenidānakathā; Jātaka Aṭṭhakathā 1, Dūrenidānakathā; Buddhavaṃsa Aṭṭhakathā 27, Dūrenidānakathā; Cariyāpiṭaka Aṭṭhakathā, Pakiṇṇakakathā)

Aṭṭhārasa abhabbaṭṭhānānupagamanappakārā ānisaṃsā saṃvaṇṇitā. Ye ca “sato [P 1.0130] sampajāno ānanda bodhisatto tusitākāyā cavitvā [M 1.0101] mātukucchiṃ okkamī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 3.199) soḷasa acchariyabbhutadhammappakārā, ye ca “sītaṃ byapagataṃ hoti, uṇhañca upasammatī”tiādinā (bu. vaṃ. 83), “jāyamāne kho sāriputta bodhisatte ayaṃ dasasahassilokadhātu saṅkampati sampakampati sampavedhatī”tiādinā ca dvattiṃsa pubbanimittappakārā, ye vā panaññepi “bodhisattānaṃ adhippāyasamijjhanaṃ kammādīsu vasībhāvo”ti evamādayo tattha tattha jātakabuddhavaṃsādīsu dassitappakārā ānisaṃsā, te sabbepi etāsaṃ ānisaṃsā, tathā yathānidassitabhedā alobhādosādiguṇayugaḷādayo cāti veditabbā.

The eighteen kinds of benefits consisting of not arriving at the states of incapability are described. And those sixteen kinds of marvelous and wonderful qualities, such as, "Mindful and clearly comprehending, Ānanda, the Bodhisatta, having passed away from the Tusita realm, descended into his mother’s womb," and so on (Majjhima Nikāya 3.199); and those thirty-two kinds of portents, such as, "The cold is dispelled, and the heat is pacified," and so on (Buddhavaṃsa 83), and "When the Bodhisatta is born, Sāriputta, this ten-thousandfold world system trembles, shakes, and quakes," and so on; and whatever other kinds of benefits are shown here and there in the Jātakas, Buddhavaṃsa, and so forth—such as "the fulfillment of the Bodhisattas’ aspirations, mastery over actions, etc.”—all these are the benefits of these perfections; and likewise, the pairs of virtues such as non-greed and non-hatred, with their divisions as indicated, should also be understood as such.

Kiṃ [V 1.0090] phalanti samāsato tāva sammāsambuddhabhāvo etāsaṃ phalaṃ, vitthārato pana dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇa- (dī. ni. 2.24 ādayo; 3.168 ādayo; ma. ni. 2.385) asītianubyañjanabyāmappabhādianekaguṇagaṇasamujjalarūpakāyasampattiadhiṭṭhānā dasabalacatuvesārajjachaasādhāraṇañāṇaaṭṭhārasāveṇikabuddhadhamma- (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.305; mūlaṭī. 2.suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā) -pabhutianekasatasahassaguṇasamudayopasobhinī dhammakāyasirī, yāvatā pana buddhaguṇā ye anekehipi kappehi sammāsambuddhenāpi vācāya pariyosāpetuṃ na sakkā, idaṃ etāsaṃ phalanti ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana buddhavaṃsacariyāpiṭakajātakamahāpadānasuttādīnaṃ vasena veditabbo.

What is their fruit, in brief? The state of a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha is their fruit. In detail, it includes the thirty-two marks of a great man (Dī. Ni. 2.24 ff.; 3.168 ff.; Ma. Ni. 2.385), the eighty minor characteristics, the radiant aura of a fathom, the perfection of the physical body resplendent with countless groups of virtues, the ten powers, the four kinds of fearlessness, the six kinds of unexcelled knowledge, the eighteen unshared qualities of a Buddha (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 3.305; Mūlaṭī. 2, Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā), and the glory of the Dhamma-body, adorned with the arising of countless hundreds of thousands of virtues. Moreover, the virtues of a Buddha are such that even over many eons a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha could not fully describe them with words. This is their fruit in summary. The detailed account, however, should be understood by way of the chronicles of the Buddhas, the Cariyāpiṭaka, the Jātakas, the Mahāpadāna Sutta, and other texts.

Yathāvuttāya paṭipadāya yathāvuttavibhāgānaṃ pāramīnaṃ pūritabhāvaṃ sandhāyāha “samatiṃsa pāramiyo pūretvā”ti. Satipi mahāpariccāgānaṃ dānapāramibhāve pariccāgavisesabhāvadassanatthañceva sudukkarabhāvadassanatthañca [P 1.0131] “pañca mahāpariccāge”ti visuṃ gahaṇaṃ, tatoyeva ca aṅgapariccāgato visuṃ nayanapariccāgaggahaṇaṃ, pariggahapariccāgabhāvasāmaññepi dhanarajjapariccāgato puttadārapariccāgaggahaṇañca kataṃ. Gatapaccāgatikavattasaṅkhātāya pubbabhāgapaṭipadāya saddhiṃ abhiññāsamāpattinipphādanaṃ pubbayogo. Dānādīsuyeva sātisayapaṭipattinipphādanaṃ pubbacariyā, yā cariyāpiṭakasaṅgahitā. Abhinīhāro pubbayogo, dānādipaṭipatti, kāyavivekavasena ekacariyā vā pubbacariyāti keci. Dānādīnañceva appicchatādīnañca saṃsāranibbānesu [M 1.0102] ādīnavānisaṃsādīnañca vibhāvanavasena sattānaṃ bodhittaye patiṭṭhāpanaparipācanavasena pavattā kathā dhammakkhānaṃ. Ñātīnaṃ atthacariyā ñātatthacariyā, sāpi karuṇāyanavaseneva. Ādi-saddena lokatthacariyādayo saṅgaṇhāti. Kammassakatāñāṇavasena, anavajjakammāyatanavijjāṭṭhānaparicayavasena, khandhāyatanādiparicayavasena, lakkhaṇattayatīraṇavasena ca ñāṇacāro buddhicariyā, sā pana atthato paññāpāramīyeva, ñāṇasambhāradassanatthaṃ visuṃ gahaṇaṃ. Koṭinti pariyanto, ukkaṃsoti attho. Cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhāvetvā brūhetvāti sambandho. Tattha bhāvetvāti uppādetvā. Brūhetvāti vaḍḍhetvā. Satipaṭṭhānādiggahaṇena āgamanapaṭipadaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā dasseti, vipassanāsahagatā eva vā satipaṭṭhānādayo daṭṭhabbā. Ettha ca “yena abhinīhārenā”tiādinā āgamanapaṭipadāya ādiṃ dasseti, “dānapāramī”tiādinā majjhaṃ, “cattāro satipaṭṭhāne”tiādinā pariyosānanti veditabbaṃ.

Referring to the fulfillment of the perfections according to the aforementioned path and its divisions, it is said, 'having fulfilled the thirty perfections.' Although great sacrifices are instances of the perfection of giving, 'the five great sacrifices' are mentioned separately to show their special nature as sacrifices and to demonstrate their extreme difficulty. For the same reason, the sacrifice of limbs is distinguished from the sacrifice of eyes; and although they share the general nature of relinquishing possessions, the sacrifice of children and wife is distinguished from the sacrifice of wealth and kingdom. The preliminary undertaking is the accomplishment of the higher knowledges and meditative attainments, together with the preliminary practice known as the duty of going and returning. The preliminary conduct is the accomplishment of an extraordinary practice in giving and so forth, which is included in the Cariyāpiṭaka. Some say that aspiration is the preliminary undertaking; the practice of giving and so forth, or solitary conduct by way of physical seclusion, is the preliminary conduct. The exposition of the Dhamma is the teaching that proceeds by way of explaining the dangers in saṃsāra and the benefits in nibbāna, and by way of establishing and maturing beings in the three kinds of enlightenment. The conduct for the welfare of relatives is the conduct for the welfare of relatives, which is rooted in compassion. By the word 'etc.' the conduct for the welfare of the world and so forth are included. The conduct of wisdom is the intellectual conduct, through the knowledge of kamma as one's own, familiarity with the bases of blameless kamma and fields of knowledge, familiarity with the aggregates and sense bases, and discernment of the three characteristics. In essence, this is the perfection of wisdom itself, but it is mentioned separately to show the accumulation of knowledge. 'Summit' means the end, the highest point. The connection is with 'having developed and cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness.' Here, 'having developed' means having generated, and 'having cultivated' means having increased. By mentioning the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, it shows the completion of the path of approach; or, the foundations of mindfulness and so forth should be understood as accompanied by insight. Herein, it should be understood that the beginning of the path of approach is shown by 'by which aspiration,' the middle by 'the perfection of giving,' and the end by 'the four foundations of mindfulness.'

Sampatijātoti hatthato muccitvā muhuttajāto, na mātukucchito nikkhantamatto. Nikkhantamattañhi [V 1.0091] mahāsattaṃ paṭhamaṃ brahmāno suvaṇṇajālena paṭiggaṇhiṃsu, tesaṃ hatthato cattāro mahārājāno ajinappaveṇiyā, tesaṃ hatthato manussā dukūlacumbaṭakena paṭiggaṇhiṃsu, manussānaṃ hatthato muñcitvā pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhitoti yathāha [P 1.0132] bhagavā mahāpadānadesanāyaṃ. Setamhi chatteti dibbasetacchatte. Anuhīramāneti dhāriyamāne. Ettha ca chattaggahaṇeneva khaggādīni pañca kakudhabhaṇḍānipi (jā. 2.19.72) vuttānevāti veditabbaṃ. Khaggatālavaṇṭamorahatthakavāḷabījanīuṇhīsapaṭṭāpi hi chattena saha tadā upaṭṭhitā ahesuṃ. Chattādīniyeva ca tadā paññāyiṃsu, na chattādigāhakā. Sabbā ca disāti dasapi disā. Nayidaṃ sabbadisāvilokanaṃ sattapadavītihāruttarakālaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Mahāsatto hi manussānaṃ hatthato muccitvā puratthimadisaṃ olokesi, tattha devamanussā gandhamālādīhi pūjayamānā “mahāpurisa idha tumhehi sadisopi natthi, kuto uttaritaro”ti āhaṃsu. Evaṃ catasso disā, catasso anudisā, heṭṭhā, uparīti sabbā disā anuviloketvā sabbattha attanā sadisaṃ adisvā “ayaṃ uttarā disā”ti tattha sattapadavītihārena [M 1.0103] agamāsi. Āsabhinti uttamaṃ. Aggoti sabbapaṭhamo. Jeṭṭho seṭṭhoti ca tasseva vevacanaṃ. Ayamantimā jāti, natthi dāni punabbhavoti imasmiṃ attabhāve pattabbaṃ arahattaṃ byākāsi.

‘Just born’ means born a moment after being released from the hands, not merely having emerged from the mother’s womb. For when the Great Being had just emerged, the Brahmās first received him with a golden net; from their hands the Four Great Kings received him with a cloth of antelope hide; from their hands humans received him with a pad of fine cloth. Having been released from the hands of humans, he stood firm on the ground, as the Blessed One declared in the discourse on the Mahāpadāna. ‘A white parasol’ refers to a divine white parasol. ‘Being held up’ means being carried. Here, by the mention of the parasol, the five royal emblems—the sword and so on—should be understood as also being mentioned. Indeed, the sword, the palm-leaf fan, the peacock-feather fan, the yak-tail whisk, the turban, and the fillet were also present along with the parasol at that time. Only the parasol and other emblems were visible then, not those who carried them. ‘All directions’ means all ten directions. This surveying of all directions should not be understood as happening after the seven steps. For the Great Being, released from the hands of humans, looked toward the eastern direction. There, gods and humans, honoring him with perfumes and garlands, said, ‘Great Being, here there is none equal to you, let alone superior.’ Thus, having surveyed the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, below, and above—all directions—and seeing no one equal to himself anywhere, he said, ‘This is the northern direction,’ and took seven steps in that direction. ‘Bull-like’ means supreme. ‘Foremost’ means the very first. ‘Eldest and best’ are synonyms for it. ‘This is my last birth; now there is no more rebirth’—with this, he proclaimed the arahantship to be attained in this very life.

“Anekesaṃ visesādhigamānaṃ pubbanimittabhāvenā”ti saṅkhittena vuttamatthaṃ “yañhī”tiādinā vitthārato dasseti. Tattha etthāti –

Having briefly stated the meaning with the phrase 'as the preliminary signs for the attainment of various superior qualities,' he explains it in detail beginning with 'for indeed.' Therein, 'in this' means—

“Anekasākhañca sahassamaṇḍalaṃ,

Chattaṃ marū dhārayumantalikkhe;

Suvaṇṇadaṇḍā vītipatanti cāmarā,

Na dissare cāmarachattagāhakā”ti. (su. ni. 693);

‘Many-branched and thousand-ribbed, the parasol the Maruts hold aloft in the sky; golden-handled, the chowries wave, yet no bearers of chowries or parasols are seen.’ (Sn 693)

Imissā gāthāya. Sabbaññutaññāṇameva sabbattha appaṭihatacāratāya anāvaraṇañāṇanti āha “sabbaññutānāvaraṇañāṇapaṭilābhassā”ti. “Tathā ayaṃ bhagavāpi gato…pe… pubbanimittabhāvenā”ti etena abhijātiyaṃ dhammatāvasena uppajjanavisesā [P 1.0133] sabbabodhisattānaṃ sādhāraṇāti dasseti. Pāramitānissandā hi teti.

Regarding this verse: He says that the knowledge of omniscience itself is unobstructed knowledge because of its unimpeded movement everywhere; hence the phrase 'for the attainment of the knowledge that is omniscient and unobstructed.' By the phrase 'Thus, this Blessed One also went… as preliminary signs,' it is shown that the special occurrences at his noble birth, which happen as a matter of natural law, are common to all Bodhisattas. For these are indeed the outflow of the perfections.

Vikkamīti agamāsi. Marūti devā. Samāti vilokanasamatāya samā sadisiyo. Mahāpuriso hi yathā ekaṃ disaṃ vilokesi, evaṃ sesā disāpi, na katthaci vilokane vibandho [V 1.0092] tassa ahosīti. Samāti vā viloketuṃ yuttāti attho. Na hi tadā bodhisattassa virūpabībhacchavisamarūpāni viloketuṃ ayuttāni disāsu upaṭṭhahantīti.

‘He strode’ means he went. ‘Maruts’ means gods. ‘Samā’ means equal, similar, in terms of the evenness of surveying. Indeed, just as the Great Being surveyed one direction, so too did he survey the remaining directions; there was no obstruction to his vision anywhere. Or ‘samā’ means suitable for looking upon. For at that time, no ugly, repulsive, or deformed sights, which would be unsuitable for the Bodhisatta to behold, presented themselves in any direction.

“Evaṃ tathāgato”ti kāyagamanaṭṭhena gata-saddena tathāgata-saddaṃ niddisitvā idāni ñāṇagamanaṭṭhena taṃ dassetuṃ “atha vā”tiādimāha. Tattha nekkhammenāti alobhappadhānena kusalacittuppādena. Kusalā hi dhammā idha nekkhammaṃ, na pabbajjādayo, “paṭhamajjhānenā”ti ca vadanti. Pahāyāti pajahitvā. Gato adhigato, paṭipanno uttarivisesanti attho. Pahāyāti vā pahānahetu, pahānalakkhaṇaṃ vā. Hetulakkhaṇattho hi ayaṃ pahāya-saddo. “Kāmacchandādippahānahetukaṃ gato”ti hettha vuttaṃ gamanaṃ avabodho, paṭipatti eva vā. Kāmacchandādippahānena ca taṃ lakkhīyati. Esa nayo “padāletvā”tiādīsupi. Abyāpādenāti mettāya. Ālokasaññāyāti vibhūtaṃ katvā manasikaraṇena upaṭṭhitaālokasañjānanena[M 1.0104]. Avikkhepenāti samādhinā. Dhammavavatthānenāti kusalādidhammānaṃ yāthāvavinicchayena, “sappaccayanāmarūpavavatthānenā”tipi vadanti.

‘Thus the Tathāgata’—having indicated the word ‘Tathāgata’ by the word ‘gata’ in the sense of bodily movement, he now says ‘or else,’ and so on, to show it in the sense of movement by knowledge. Herein, ‘by renunciation’ means by the arising of a wholesome consciousness with non-greed as its principal component. For here, wholesome states are renunciation, not the act of going forth and so on; and some say, ‘by the first jhāna.’ ‘Having abandoned’ means having relinquished. ‘Gone’ means attained, entered upon, or a superior attainment; this is the meaning. Or, ‘having abandoned’ means the cause of abandoning or the characteristic of abandoning, for this word ‘pahāya’ has the meaning of cause and characteristic. Here, the ‘going’ spoken of as ‘gone on account of abandoning sensual desire, etc.’ is understanding, or even the practice itself. And it is characterized by the abandoning of sensual desire and so on. This is the method also in ‘having shattered,’ and so on. ‘By non-ill will’ means by loving-kindness. ‘By the perception of light’ means by the perception of light established through attention that has made it manifest. ‘By non-distraction’ means by concentration. ‘By the discernment of phenomena’ means by the correct determination of states such as wholesome, and some say, ‘by the discernment of name-and-form with its conditions.’

Evaṃ kāmacchandādinīvaraṇappahānena “abhijjhaṃ loke pahāyā”tiādinā (vibha. 508) vuttāya paṭhamajjhānassa pubbabhāgapaṭipadāya bhagavato tathāgatabhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni saha upāyena aṭṭhahi samāpattīhi, aṭṭhārasahi ca mahāvipassanāhi taṃ dassetuṃ “ñāṇenā”tiādimāha. Nāmarūpapariggahakaṅkhāvitaraṇānañhi vibandhabhūtassa mohassa dūrīkaraṇena ñātapariññāyaṃ [P 1.0134] ṭhitassa aniccasaññādayo sijjhanti, tathā jhānasamāpattīsu abhiratinimittena pāmojjena, tattha anabhiratiyā vinoditāya jhānādi samadhigamoti samāpattivipassanānaṃ arativinodanaavijjāpadālanādi upāyo, uppaṭipāṭiniddeso pana nīvaraṇasabhāvāya avijjāya heṭṭhā nīvaraṇesupi saṅgahadassanatthanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Samāpattivihārappavesavibandhanena nīvaraṇāni kavāṭasadisānīti āha “nīvaraṇakavāṭaṃ ugghāṭetvā”ti. “Rattiṃ vitakketvā vicāretvā divā kammante payojetī”ti vuttaṭṭhāne viya vitakkavicārā dhūmāyanāti adhippetāti āha “vitakkavicāradhūma”nti. Kiñcāpi paṭhamajjhānūpacāreyeva ca dukkhaṃ, catutthajjhānūpacāreyeva sukhaṃ pahīyati, atisayappahānaṃ pana sandhāyāha “catutthajjhānena sukhadukkhaṃ pahāyā”ti.

Thus, having shown the Blessed One’s state of being a Tathāgata by the preliminary practice for the first jhāna—which is the abandoning of hindrances such as sensual desire, as stated in the phrase ‘having abandoned covetousness in the world,’ etc. (Vibh. 508)—he now says ‘with knowledge,’ etc., to demonstrate it through the eight attainments and the eighteen great insights, together with their means. For one established in understanding by knowing, through the removal of delusion which is a barrier to the full grasp of name-and-form and the overcoming of doubt, the perceptions of impermanence, etc., are accomplished. Similarly, in the jhāna-attainments, through joy which is a sign of delight, and by the dispelling of non-delight therein, jhāna, etc., are attained. Thus, the means for the attainments and insights are the dispelling of discontent, the tearing apart of ignorance, and so on. The out-of-sequence exposition, however, should be understood as for the purpose of showing the inclusion of ignorance, which has the nature of a hindrance, even among the hindrances below. Because they obstruct entry into the abiding in the attainments, the hindrances are like doors; hence he says, ‘having opened the door of the hindrances.’ Just as in the place where it is said, ‘Having applied initial thought and sustained thought at night, one engages in work by day,’ it is intended that initial and sustained thoughts are like smoke; hence he says, ‘the smoke of initial and sustained thought.’ Although suffering is abandoned even in the access concentration of the first jhāna, and pleasure in the access concentration of the fourth jhāna, he says, ‘having abandoned pleasure and pain with the fourth jhāna,’ with reference to the surpassing abandonment.

Aniccassa, aniccanti anupassanā aniccānupassanā, tebhūmakadhammānaṃ aniccataṃ gahetvā pavattāya vipassanāyetaṃ nāmaṃ. Niccasaññanti saṅkhatadhamme “niccā, sassatā”ti evaṃ pavattamicchāsaññaṃ[V 1.0093], saññāsīsena diṭṭhicittānampi gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Esa nayo ito paresupi. Nibbidānupassanāyāti saṅkhāresu nibbijjanākārena pavattāya anupassanāya. Nandinti sappītikataṇhaṃ. Tathā virāgānupassanāyāti virajjanākārena pavattāya anupassanāya. Nirodhānupassanāyāti saṅkhārānaṃ nirodhassa anupassanāya. “Te saṅkhārā nirujjhantiyeva, āyatiṃ samudayavasena na uppajjantī”ti evaṃ vā anupassanā nirodhānupassanā. Tenevāha “nirodhānupassanāya nirodheti, no samudetī”ti. Muñcitukamyatā hi ayaṃ balappattāti. Paṭinissajjanākārena [P 1.0135] pavattā anupassanā paṭinissaggānupassanā[M 1.0105]. Paṭisaṅkhā santiṭṭhanā hi ayaṃ. Ādānanti niccādivasena gahaṇaṃ. Santatisamūhakiccārammaṇānaṃ vasena ekattaggahaṇaṃ ghanasaññā. Āyūhanaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇaṃ. Avatthāvisesāpatti vipariṇāmo. Dhuvasaññanti thirabhāvaggahaṇaṃ. Nimittanti samūhādighanavasena, sakiccaparicchedatāya ca saṅkhārānaṃ saviggahaggahaṇaṃ. Paṇidhinti rāgādipaṇidhiṃ, sā panatthato taṇhānaṃ vasena saṅkhāresu ninnatā.

Contemplation of the impermanent as ‘impermanent’ is the contemplation of impermanence; this is the name for the insight that proceeds by grasping the impermanence of phenomena belonging to the three planes. The perception of permanence is the wrong perception that proceeds regarding conditioned phenomena as ‘permanent, eternal’; it should be understood that this includes, under the heading of perception, consciousness associated with wrong view. This is the method in the subsequent cases as well. By the contemplation of disenchantment means by the contemplation that proceeds in the manner of being disenchanted with formations. ‘Delight’ means craving accompanied by joy. Similarly, by the contemplation of dispassion means by the contemplation that proceeds in the manner of fading away. By the contemplation of cessation means by the contemplation of the cessation of formations. Or, the contemplation that, ‘These formations are indeed ceasing; they do not arise in the future by way of origination,’ is the contemplation of cessation. For that reason he says, ‘Through the contemplation of cessation, it ceases, it does not originate.’ For this is the desire for release that has attained strength. The contemplation that proceeds in the manner of relinquishment is the contemplation of relinquishment. For this is the settling down through reflective understanding. ‘Grasping’ means the grasping by way of permanence, etc. The perception of compactness is the grasping of unity by way of continuity, collection, function, and object. ‘Accumulation’ is volitional formation. The attainment of a different state is change. The perception of stability is the grasping of a state of firmness. ‘The sign’ is the grasping of formations as having a concrete form by way of compactness due to being a collection, etc., and by being defined by their own function. ‘Longing’ means the aspiration for lust, etc.; but in meaning, it is the inclination towards formations by way of craving.

Abhinivesanti attānudiṭṭhiṃ. Aniccadukkhādivasena sabbadhammatīraṇaṃ adhipaññādhammavipassanā. Sārādānābhinivesanti asāre sāraggahaṇavipallāsaṃ. “Issarakuttādivasena loko samuppanno”ti abhiniveso sammohābhiniveso. Keci pana “ahosiṃ nu kho ahamatītamaddhānantiādinā pavattasaṃsayāpatti sammohābhiniveso”ti vadanti. Saṅkhāresu leṇatāṇabhāvaggahaṇaṃ ālayābhiniveso. “Ālayaratā ālayasamuditā”ti vacanato ālayo taṇhā, sāyeva cakkhādīsu rūpādīsu ca abhinivisanavasena pavattiyā ālayābhinivesoti keci. “Evaṃvidhā saṅkhārā paṭinissajjīyantī”ti pavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ paṭisaṅkhānupassanā. Vaṭṭato vigatattā vivaṭṭaṃ nibbānaṃ, tattha ārammaṇakaraṇasaṅkhātena anupassanena pavattiyā vivaṭṭānupassanā gotrabhu. Saṃyogābhinivesanti saṃyujjanavasena saṅkhāresu abhinivisanaṃ. Diṭṭhekaṭṭheti diṭṭhiyā sahajātekaṭṭhe, pahānekaṭṭhe ca. “Oḷārike”ti uparimaggavajjhe kilese apekkhitvā [P 1.0136] vuttaṃ, aññathā dassanapahātabbāpi dutiyamaggavajjhehi oḷārikāti. Aṇusahagateti aṇubhūte, idaṃ heṭṭhimamaggavajjhe apekkhitvā vuttaṃ. Sabbakileseti avasiṭṭhasabbakilese. Na hi paṭhamādimaggehi pahīnā kilesā puna pahīyantīti.

Clinging is the view of self. The insight into phenomena of higher wisdom is the judging of all phenomena by way of impermanence, suffering, etc. Clinging to grasping the essence is the perversion of grasping essence in what is essenceless. The adherence that, “The world arose by way of a creator, etc.,” is clinging due to delusion. Some, however, say that clinging due to delusion is the occurrence of doubt that proceeds as, “Did I exist in the past?” and so on. Clinging to a resort is the grasping of formations as a shelter and refuge. From the statement, “Delighting in a resort, engrossed in a resort,” a resort is craving; some say that this very craving, when it proceeds by way of adhering to the eye, etc., and to forms, etc., is clinging to a resort. The knowledge that proceeds as, “Formations of this kind are to be relinquished,” is the contemplation of reflection. Nibbāna is the turning away because it has departed from the round. The contemplation of turning away, which proceeds by way of making that an object, is the change-of-lineage consciousness. Clinging to bondage is adhering to formations by way of being yoked. ‘Of one part with view’ means of one part by being co-nascent with view, and of one part by abandonment. ‘Gross’ is said with reference to the defilements to be abandoned by the higher paths; otherwise, even those to be abandoned by seeing are gross compared to those to be abandoned by the second path. ‘Accompanied by the subtle’ means being subtle; this is said with reference to the defilements to be abandoned by the lower paths. ‘All defilements’ means all the remaining defilements, for the defilements abandoned by the first path, etc., are not abandoned again.

Kakkhaḷattaṃ kaṭhinabhāvo. Paggharaṇaṃ dravabhāvo. Lokiyavāyunā bhastassa viya yena taṃtaṃkalāpassa uddhumāyanaṃ, thambhabhāvo vā, taṃ vitthambhanaṃ. Vijjamānepi kalāpantarabhūtānaṃ kalāpantarabhūtehi asamphuṭṭhabhāve, taṃtaṃbhūtavivittatā rūpapariyanto ākāsoti yesaṃ yo paricchedo, tehi so asamphuṭṭhova, aññathā bhūtānaṃ paricchedasabhāvo na siyā byāpībhāvāpattito[V 1.0094]. Abyāpitā hi asamphuṭṭhatāti. Yasmiṃ [M 1.0106] kalāpe bhūtānaṃ paricchedo, tehi asamphuṭṭhabhāvo asamphuṭṭhalakkhaṇaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā ākāsadhātuniddese “asamphuṭṭhaṃ catūhi mahābhūtehī”ti (dha. sa. 637).

Hardness is the state of being hard. Flowing is the state of being liquid. That by which there is the swelling of this or that material group, like a bellows with worldly wind, or the state of stiffness, that is distension. Even when there exists the state of non-contact of the elements of one group with the elements of another group, the separation of the various elements is the boundary of matter, which is space. That by which they are delimited, by that they are untouched. Otherwise, the nature of the elements as delimited would not exist, because they would fall into a state of pervasiveness. For non-pervasiveness is non-contact. The characteristic of being untouched is the state of being untouched by those elements which are delimited within a certain material group. Therefore, the Blessed One said in the exposition of the space element: “Untouched by the four great elements” (Dhs. 637).

Virodhipaccayasannipāte visadisuppatti ruppanaṃ. Cetanāpadhānattā saṅkhārakkhandhadhammānaṃ cetanāvasenetaṃ vuttaṃ “saṅkhārānaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇa”nti. Tathā hi suttantabhājanīye saṅkhārakkhandhavibhaṅge “cakkhusamphassajā cetanā”tiādinā (vibha. 92) cetanāva vibhattā, abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇā ca cetanā. Yathāha “tattha katamo puññābhisaṅkhāro? Kusalā cetanā kāmāvacarā”tiādi [P 1.0137] (vibha. 226). Pharaṇaṃ savipphārikatā. Assaddhiyeti assaddhiyahetu, nimittatthe bhummaṃ. Esa nayo “kosajje”tiādīsu. Vūpasamalakkhaṇanti kāyacittapariḷāhūpasamalakkhaṇaṃ. Līnuddhaccarahite adhicitte pavattamāne paggahaniggahasampahaṃsanesu abyāvaṭatāya ajjhupekkhanaṃ paṭisaṅkhānaṃ pakkhapātupacchedato.

In the presence of opposing conditions, dissimilar arising is 'disruption.' Because of the dominance of volition, the phenomena of the formations aggregate are spoken of in terms of volition: 'The characteristic of formations is active formation.' Indeed, in the analysis of the formations aggregate in the Suttanta exposition, volition itself is analyzed, beginning with 'Volition born of eye-contact,' and so on (Vibh. 92); and volition has the characteristic of active formation. As it is said: 'Here, what is the meritorious formation? Wholesome volition pertaining to the sensuous sphere,' and so on (Vibh. 226). 'Pervading' means being thoroughly diffused. 'In lack of faith' means because of lack of faith; the locative is used in the sense of cause. This is the method in cases like 'in sloth,' and so on. 'The characteristic of tranquility' is the characteristic of calming the fever of body and mind. When the higher mind is operating, free from sluggishness and restlessness, equanimity is reflection, arising from non-interference with exertion, restraint, and gladdening, and from the cutting off of bias.

Musāvādādīnaṃ visaṃvādanādikiccatāya lūkhānaṃ apariggāhakānaṃ paṭipakkhabhāvato pariggāhikā sammāvācā siniddhabhāvato sampayuttadhamme, sammāvācāpaccayasubhāsitānaṃ sotārañca puggalaṃ pariggaṇhātīti sā pariggahalakkhaṇā sammāvācā. Kāyikakiriyā kiñci kattabbaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Sayañca samuṭṭhahanaṃ ghaṭanaṃ hotīti sammākammantasaṅkhātā virati samuṭṭhānalakkhaṇā daṭṭhabbā, sampayuttadhammānaṃ vā ukkhipanaṃ samuṭṭhāpanaṃ kāyikakiriyāya bhārukkhipanaṃ viya. Jīvamānassa sattassa, sampayuttadhammānaṃ vā jīvitindriyavuttiyā, ājīvasseva vā suddhi vodānaṃ. Sasampayuttadhammassa cittassa saṃkilesapakkhe patituṃ adatvā sammadeva paggaṇhanaṃ paggaho.

Right speech is protective because it stands in opposition to false speech and so on, which are coarse and non-embracing due to their function of deceit and so on. Because of its gentle nature, it embraces the associated states, and it embraces the person who listens to well-spoken words conditioned by right speech; therefore, right speech has the characteristic of embracing. Bodily action initiates something to be done. And its own arising is an effort; thus, the abstinence called right action should be understood as having the characteristic of initiating. Alternatively, it is the uplifting of the associated states, just as bodily action lifts a burden. Purity and cleansing is the characteristic of livelihood for a living being, or of the functioning of the life faculty for the associated states. Not allowing the mind with its associated states to fall into the side of defilement, but rightly uplifting it, is exertion.

“Saṅkhārā”ti idha cetanā adhippetāti vuttaṃ “saṅkhārānaṃ cetanālakkhaṇa”nti. Namanaṃ ārammaṇābhimukhabhāvo. Āyatanaṃpavattanaṃ. Āyatanānaṃ vasena hi āyasaṅkhātānaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ pavatti. Taṇhāya hetulakkhaṇanti vaṭṭassa janakahetubhāvo, maggassa pana nibbānasampāpakattanti ayameva tesaṃ viseso.

Here 'formations' is intended to mean volition; thus it is said, 'the characteristic of formations is volition.' Bending is the state of being turned towards an object. The characteristic of a sense base is its functioning. For it is by way of the sense bases that the mind and mental factors, which are called 'income,' function. The characteristic of craving is being the generating cause of the round, while that of the path is leading to the attainment of Nibbāna—this is the distinction between them.

Tathalakkhaṇaṃ [M 1.0107] aviparītasabhāvo. Ekaraso aññamaññānativattanaṃ anūnādhikabhāvo. Yuganaddhā samathavipassanāva, “saddhāpaññā paggahāvikkhepā”tipi vadanti.

The characteristic of suchness is its invariable nature. It has a single essence, not transgressing one another, without deficiency or excess. They are yoked in pairs, namely, tranquility and insight; they also say, “faith and wisdom, exertion and non-distraction.”

Khiṇoti [V 1.0095] kileseti khayo, maggo. Anuppādapariyosānatāya anuppādo, phalaṃ. Passaddhi kilesavūpasamo.

It destroys defilements, therefore it is destruction, which is the path. Non-arising, because its conclusion is non-arising, is the fruit. Tranquility is the subsiding of defilements.

Chandassāti [P 1.0138] kattukamyatāchandassa. Mūlalakkhaṇaṃ patiṭṭhābhāvo. Samuṭṭhāpanalakkhaṇaṃ ārammaṇapaṭipādakatāya sampayuttadhammānaṃ uppattihetutā. Samodhānaṃ visayādisannipātena gahetabbākāro, yā “saṅgatī”ti vuccati. Samaṃ saha odahanti anena sampayuttadhammāti vā samodhānaṃ, phasso. Samosaranti sannipatanti etthāti samosaraṇaṃ. Vedanāya vinā appavattamānā sampayuttadhammā vedanānubhavananimittaṃ samosaṭā viya hontīti evaṃ vuttaṃ. Gopānasīnaṃ kūṭaṃ viya sampayuttānaṃ pāmokkhabhāvo pamukhalakkhaṇaṃ. Tato, tesaṃ vā sampayuttadhammānaṃ uttari padhānanti taduttari. Paññuttarā hi kusalā dhammā. Vimuttiyāti phalassa. Tañhi sīlādiguṇasārassa paramukkaṃsabhāvena sāraṃ. Ayañca lakkhaṇavibhāgo chadhātupañcajhānaṅgādivasena taṃtaṃsuttapadānusārena, porāṇaṭṭhakathāya āgatanayena ca katoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā hi vuttopi koci dhammo pariyāyantarappakāsanatthaṃ puna dassito, tato eva ca “chandamūlakā kusalā dhammā manasikārasamuṭṭhānā, phassasamodhānā, vedanāsamosaraṇā”ti, “paññuttarā kusalā dhammā”ti, “vimuttisāramidaṃ brahmacariya”nti, “nibbānogadhañhi āvuso brahmacariyaṃ nibbānapariyosāna”nti ca suttapadānaṃ vasena “chandassa mūlalakkhaṇa”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

‘Chanda’ means the desire to act. Its root characteristic is the state of being a foundation. The characteristic of causing to arise is being the cause for the production of associated states by presenting the object. “Samodhāna” refers to the mode of grasping through the convergence of the object, etc., which is called “connection.” Alternatively, “samodhāna” is contact because associated states are brought together (“samaṃ saha odahanti”) by it. “Samosaraṇa” is where things converge and gather. Without feeling, the associated states do not function; yet they are as if converged on the mark of experiencing feeling—thus it is said. Like the peak of a gabled roof, the foremost position of the associated states is the characteristic of leadership. Beyond that, or the further pre-eminence of those associated states, is what surpasses it. For wholesome states are led by wisdom. “Vimutti” refers to the fruit. It is the essence because it is the supreme excellence of the essence of virtues such as morality. This analysis of characteristics should be understood as made according to the six elements, five jhāna factors, etc., following the wording of the respective suttas and the method found in the ancient commentaries. Thus, any teaching repeated to clarify another aspect is shown again for that very reason. Hence, based on the sutta passages: “Wholesome states are rooted in desire, arise from attention, are connected by contact, and converge upon feeling,” “Wholesome states are led by wisdom,” “This holy life has liberation as its essence,” and “For, friends, the holy life is grounded in Nibbāna and culminates in Nibbāna,” it is said: “The root characteristic of desire,” etc.

Tathadhammā [P 1.0139] nāma cattāri ariyasaccāni aviparītasabhāvattā. Tathāni taṃsabhāvattā. Avitathāni amusāsabhāvattā. Anaññathāni aññākārarahitattā.

The Four Noble Truths are called 'tatha' (true) because their nature is invariable. They are 'tatha' because they possess that very nature. They are 'avitatha' (unmistaken) because their nature is not false. They are 'anaññatha' (unalterable) because they are devoid of any other mode.

Jātipaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭhoti jātipaccayā sambhūtaṃ hutvā sahitassa attano paccayānurūpassa uddhaṃ uddhaṃ āgatabhāvo, anupavattatthoti attho. Atha vā sambhūtaṭṭho ca samudāgataṭṭho ca sambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho, na jātito jarāmaraṇaṃ na hoti, na ca jātiṃ vinā aññato hotīti jātipaccayasambhūtaṭṭho. Itthañca jātito samudāgacchatīti [M 1.0108] jātipaccayasamudāgataṭṭho. Yā yā jāti yathā yathā paccayo hoti, tadanurūpaṃ pātubhāvoti attho. Avijjāya saṅkhārānaṃ paccayaṭṭhoti etthāpi na avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo na hoti, na ca avijjaṃ vinā saṅkhārā uppajjanti. Yā yā avijjā yesaṃ yesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ yathā yathā paccayo hoti, ayaṃ avijjāya saṅkhārānaṃ paccayaṭṭho, paccayabhāvoti attho.

The meaning of ‘born from the condition of birth and arisen from it’ is the state of having been born from the condition of birth and, being conjoined with it, having come about further and further in accordance with its own conditions; this is the meaning of 'continuing to arise.' Alternatively, the meaning of ‘born’ and the meaning of ‘arisen’ together constitute the meaning of ‘born and arisen.’ Aging and death do not occur without birth, nor do they arise from anything else apart from birth—this is the meaning of ‘born from the condition of birth.’ And thus, it arises from birth—this is the meaning of ‘arisen from the condition of birth.’ Whatever birth, in whatever way, becomes a condition, its manifestation is in accordance with that. This is the meaning. In the same way, regarding ‘the conditionality of formations by ignorance’: here also, it is not that ignorance is not a condition for formations, and formations do not arise without ignorance. Whatever ignorance, for whatever formations, in whatever way, becomes a condition, this is the conditionality of formations by ignorance, which is the state of being a condition. This is the meaning.

Bhagavā [V 1.0096] taṃ jānāti passatīti sambandho. Tenāti bhagavatā. Taṃ vibhajjamānanti yojetabbaṃ. Tanti rūpāyatanaṃ. Iṭṭhāniṭṭhādīti ādi-saddena majjhattaṃ saṅgaṇhāti, tathā atītānāgatapaccuppannaparittaajjhattabahiddhātadubhayādibhedaṃ. Labbhamānakapadavasenāti “rūpāyatanaṃ diṭṭhaṃ saddāyatanaṃ sutaṃ gandhāyatanaṃ rasāyatanaṃ phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ mutaṃ, sabbaṃ rūpaṃ manasā viññāta”nti (dha. sa. 966) vacanato diṭṭhapadañca viññātapadañca rūpārammaṇe labbhati. “Rūpārammaṇaṃ iṭṭhaṃ aniṭṭhaṃ majjhattaṃ parittaṃ atītaṃ anāgataṃ paccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ bahiddhā diṭṭhaṃ viññātaṃ rūpaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ rūpadhātu vaṇṇanibhā sanidassanaṃ sappaṭighaṃ nīlaṃ pītaka”nti evamādīhi anekehi nāmehi. “Terasahi vārehī”ti rūpakaṇḍe (dha. sa. 614 ādayo) āgate terasa niddesavāre sandhāyāha. Ekekasmiñca vāre catunnaṃ catunnaṃ vavatthāpananayānaṃ vasena “dvipaññāsāya [P 1.0140] nayehī”ti āha. Tathameva aviparītadassitāya, appaṭivattiyadesanatāya ca. Jānāmi abbhaññāsinti vattamānātītakālesu ñāṇappavattidassanena anāgatepi ñāṇappavatti vuttāyevāti daṭṭhabbā. Vidita-saddo anāmaṭṭhakālaviseso veditabbo, “diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ muta”ntiādīsu (dha. sa. 966) viya. Na upaṭṭhāsīti attattaniyavasena na upagacchi. Yathā rūpārammaṇādayo dhammā yaṃsabhāvā yaṃpakārā ca, tathā ne passati jānāti gacchatīti tathāgatoti evaṃ padasambhavo veditabbo. Keci pana “niruttinayena pisodarādipakkhepena vā dassī-saddassa lopaṃ, āgata-saddassa cāgamaṃ katvā tathāgato”ti vaṇṇenti.

The Blessed One knows and sees it: this is the connection. By 'tena' (by him) is meant the Blessed One. The phrase 'taṃ vibhajjamānaṃ' (that which is being analyzed) should be connected. 'Taṃ' (that) refers to the form base. By 'iṭṭhāniṭṭhādī' (pleasant, unpleasant, etc.), the word 'ādi' (etc.) includes the neutral, as well as distinctions such as past, future, present, limited, internal, external, both, and so on. By the phrase 'labbhamānakapadavasena' (through the mode of obtainable terms), from the statement: 'The form base is seen, the sound base is heard, the smell base is sensed, the taste base is tasted, the touch base is contacted, all forms are cognized by the mind' (Dhammasaṅgaṇi 966), the terms 'seen' and 'cognized' are obtainable in relation to form as object. By many such names as 'form as object—pleasant, unpleasant, neutral, limited, past, future, present, internal, external, seen, cognized—form, the form base, the form element, appearance, visible, resistant, blue, yellow,' and so on. By 'terasahi vārehi' (by thirteen instances), he refers to the thirteen instances of exposition that occur in the Form Section (Dhammasaṅgaṇi 614ff.). And in each instance, by the method of establishing fourfold categories, he says, 'by fifty-two methods.' Similarly, because of showing without perversion and because of teaching in a way that does not revert. By showing the occurrence of knowledge in the present and past tenses in 'jānāmi abbhaññāsiṃ' (I know, I have directly known), it is to be seen that the occurrence of knowledge in the future is also stated. The term 'vidita' (known) should be understood as unspecific regarding tense, like in 'seen, heard, contacted,' etc. (Dhammasaṅgaṇi 966). 'Na upaṭṭhāsi' (did not approach) means it did not approach in terms of self or belonging to self. Just as form objects and other phenomena are of such a nature and of such a kind, so he sees, knows, and goes to them—thus the origin of the word 'Tathāgata' should be understood. But some explain that through the method of etymology, 'Tathāgata' is formed either by applying the pisodarādi principle or by eliding the word dassī and adding the word āgata.

Niddosatāya anupavajjaṃ. Pakkhipitabbābhāvena anūnaṃ. Apanetabbābhāvena anadhikaṃ. Atthabyañjanādisampattiyā sabbākāraparipuṇṇaṃ. No aññathāti “tathevā”ti vuttamevatthaṃ byatirekena sampādeti. Tena yadatthaṃ [M 1.0109] bhāsitaṃ, ekantena tadatthanipphādanato yathā bhāsitaṃ bhagavatā, tathevāti aviparītadesanataṃ dasseti. “Gadattho”ti etena tathaṃ gadatīti tathāgatoti da-kārassa ta-kāro kato niruttinayenāti dasseti.

By being free from fault, it is blameless. By being without anything to be added, it is not deficient. By being without anything to be removed, it is not excessive. By the accomplishment of meaning, phrasing, and so on, it is perfect in every way. 'No aññathā' (not otherwise) thus establishes the meaning stated by 'tathevā' (just so) by way of exclusion. Therefore, because it unfailingly accomplishes the purpose for which it was spoken, just as it was spoken by the Blessed One, so it is—this shows the teaching is not perverted. By 'gadattho' (one whose words are true), it is shown that because he speaks what is true, he is the Tathāgata, the letter 'da' being changed to 'ta' according to the method of etymology.

Tathā gatamassāti tathāgato, gatanti ca kāyassa vācāya vā pavattīti attho. Tathāti ca vutte yaṃtaṃ-saddānaṃ abyabhicārisambandhitāya “yathā”ti ayamattho upaṭṭhitoyeva hoti. Kāyavacīkiriyānañca aññamaññānulomena vacanicchāyaṃ, kāyassa vācā, vācāya ca kāyo sambandhībhāvena upatiṭṭhatīti imamatthaṃ dassento āha “bhagavato hī”tiādi. Imasmiṃ pana atthe tathāvāditāya tathāgatoti ayampi attho siddho hoti. So pana pubbe pakārantarena dassitoti āha “evaṃ tathākāritāya tathāgato”ti.

'Tathā gatamassa' (thus gone for him) is Tathāgata; and 'gata' means the movement of the body or speech. And when 'tathā' (thus) is said, due to the inseparable connection of the words 'yaṃ' and 'taṃ' (that which, that), the meaning 'yathā' (as) is already established. And when there is an intention to speak in mutual conformity with bodily and verbal actions, the body stands in relation to speech, and speech to the body—showing this meaning, he says, 'For the Blessed One,' etc. In this meaning, 'Tathāgata' as 'one who speaks thus' is also established. But since this was previously shown in another way, he says, 'Thus, by acting accordingly, he is the Tathāgata.'

“Tiriyaṃ [V 1.0097] aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsū”ti etena yadeke “tiriyaṃ [P 1.0141] viya upari adho ca santi lokadhātuyo”ti vadanti, taṃ paṭisedheti. Desanāvilāsoyeva desanāvilāsamayo yathā “puññamayaṃ, dānamaya”ntiādīsu.

By 'tiriyaṃ aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu' (in the immeasurable world-systems extending horizontally), he refutes those who say, 'There are world-systems horizontally, as well as above and below.' 'Desanāvilāsa' (display of the teaching) is indeed 'desanāvilāsamayo' (consisting of the display of the teaching), just as in phrases like 'puññamayaṃ' (made of merit), 'dānamayaṃ' (made of generosity), and so on.

Upasagganipātānaṃ vācakasaddasannidhāne tadatthajotanabhāvena pavattanato gata-saddoyeva avagatatthaṃ atītatthañca vadatīti āha “gatoti avagato atīto”ti. Atha vā abhinīhārato paṭṭhāya yāva sambodhi, etthantare mahābodhiyānapaṭipattiyā hānaṭhānasaṃkilesanivattīnaṃ abhāvato yathā paṇidhānaṃ, tathā gato abhinīhārānurūpaṃ paṭipannoti tathāgato. Atha vā mahiddhikatāya, paṭisambhidānaṃ ukkaṃsādhigamena anāvaraṇatāya ca katthaci paṭighātābhāvato yathā ruci, tathā kāyavacīcittānaṃ gatāni gamanāni pavattiyo etassāti tathāgato. Yasmā ca loke vidhayuttagatapakāra-saddā samānatthā dissanti, tasmā yathā vidhā vipassīādayo bhagavanto, ayampi bhagavā tathā vidhoti tathāgato. Yathā yuttā ca te bhagavanto ayampi bhagavā tathā yuttoti tathāgato. Atha vā yasmā saccaṃ tacchaṃ tathanti ñāṇassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, tasmā tathena ñāṇena āgatoti tathāgatoti. Evampi tathāgata-saddassa attho veditabbo –

Since prefixes and particles function by illuminating meaning when in the presence of a content word, the word 'gata' (gone) itself conveys the meaning of 'understood' and 'past'—thus he says, 'gata means understood and past.' Alternatively, from the time of his aspiration until enlightenment, within that interval, due to the absence of decline, stagnation, and defilement in the practice of the great vehicle of enlightenment, he has gone in accordance with his aspiration, having practiced in conformity with his aspiration—thus, he is the Tathāgata. Alternatively, due to great power, the supreme attainment of the discriminations, and unobstructedness, and the absence of hindrance anywhere, the movements and activities of his body, speech, and mind go as he wishes—thus, he is the Tathāgata. And since in the world, words like 'vidha,' 'yutta,' and 'gatapakāra' are seen to have similar meanings, therefore, just as the Blessed Ones like Vipassī were 'tathā vidha' (of such a kind), so too is this Blessed One 'tathā vidha'—thus, he is the Tathāgata. And just as those Blessed Ones were 'tathā yutta' (thus endowed), so too is this Blessed One 'tathā yutta'—thus, he is the Tathāgata. Or, because 'saccaṃ' (truth), 'tacchaṃ' (reality), and 'tathaṃ' (thus) are terms for knowledge, therefore, he has come by that knowledge—thus, he is the Tathāgata. In this way too, the meaning of the word 'Tathāgata' should be understood:

“Pahāya [M 1.0110] kāmādimale yathā gatā,

Samādhiñāṇehi vipassiādayo;

Mahesino sakyamunī jutindharo,

Tathāgato tena tathāgato mato.

Having abandoned defilements such as sensual desire, just as Vipassī and other great seers went, endowed with concentration and wisdom; so too the great sage, the Sakyan sage, the radiant one, has gone thus, and is therefore known as the Tathāgata.

Tathañca dhātāyatanādilakkhaṇaṃ,

Sabhāvasāmaññavibhāgabhedato;

Sayambhuñāṇena jino samāgato,

Tathāgato vuccati sakyapuṅgavo.

And thus the characteristics of elements, sense bases, and so on, distinguished by their nature, commonality, and difference—the Victor, endowed with self-existent knowledge, has come to them; therefore, the Sakyan Bull is called the Tathāgata.

Tathāni [P 1.0142] saccāni samantacakkhunā,

Tathā idappaccayatā ca sabbaso;

Anaññaneyyena yato vibhāvitā,

Yāthāvato tena jino tathāgato.

And thus the truths, and thus specific conditionality in every way, have been fully revealed as they truly are by the All-Seeing One through non-derivative insight; therefore, the Victor is the Tathāgata.

Anekabhedāsupi [V 1.0098] lokadhātusu,

Jinassa rūpāyatanādigocare;

Vicittabhedaṃ tathameva dassanaṃ,

Tathāgato tena samantalocano.

Even in the many diverse world-realms, in the Victor's range of vision, which extends to forms and so on, there is indeed a seeing of diverse kinds; therefore, the Tathāgata is the All-Seeing One.

Yato ca dhammaṃ tathameva bhāsati,

Karoti vācāyanuloma mattano;

Guṇehi lokaṃ abhibhuyya iriyati,

Tathāgato tenapi lokanāyako.

Since he speaks the Dhamma just as it is, and acts in accordance with his own words, and moves about having overcome the world with his virtues; therefore, the Tathāgata is also a leader of the world.

Yathābhinīhāramato yathāruci,

Pavattavācātanucittabhāvato;

Yathāvidhā yena purā mahesino,

Tathāvidho tena jino tathāgato”ti. (itivu. aṭṭha. 38);

Because his speech, body, and mind proceed as he aspired and as he wishes, and because the great seers of old were of such a kind, therefore, the Victor is the Tathāgata of such a kind.

Saṅgahagāthā mukhamattameva. Kasmā? Appamādapadaṃ viya sakaladhammapaṭipattiyā sabbabuddhaguṇānaṃ saṅgāhakattā. Tenevāha “sabbākārenā”tiādi.

The summary verses are merely an introduction. Why? Because, like the 'path of heedfulness,' they encompass all the qualities of the Buddhas through the practice of the entire Dhamma. Therefore, he says, 'in every way,' and so on.

“Taṃ [M 1.0111] katamanti pucchatī”ti etena “katamañca taṃ bhikkhave”tiādivacanassa sāmaññato pucchābhāvo dassito avisesato hi tassa pucchāvisesabhāvañāpanatthaṃ mahāniddese āgatā sabbāva pucchā atthuddhāranayena dasseti “tattha pucchā nāmā”tiādinā. Tattha tatthāti “taṃ katamanti pucchatī”ti ettha yadetaṃ sāmaññato pucchāvacanaṃ, tasmiṃ.

By 'taṃ katamanti pucchati' (he asks 'What is that?'), the general nature of the question in the statement 'And what is that, monks?' and so on, is shown. For, in order to explain the particular nature of that question without distinction, all the questions that appear in the Mahāniddesa are shown by way of extracting the meaning, as in 'Here, what is called a question?' and so on. Therein, the word 'tattha' refers to that general expression of a question in 'taṃ katamanti pucchati' (he asks 'What is that?').

Lakkhaṇanti ñātuṃ icchito yo koci sabhāvo. “Aññāta”nti yena kenaci ñāṇena aññātabhāvamāha, “adiṭṭha”nti dassanabhūtena ñāṇena paccakkhaṃ viya adiṭṭhataṃ. “Atulita”nti [P 1.0143] “ettakameta”nti tulanabhūtena atūlitataṃ, “atīrita”nti tīraṇabhūtena akatañāṇakiriyāsamāpanataṃ, “avibhūta”nti ñāṇassa apākaṭabhāvaṃ, “avibhāvita”nti ñāṇena apākaṭīkatabhāvaṃ. Adiṭṭhaṃ jotīyati etāyāti adiṭṭhajotanā. Diṭṭhaṃ saṃsandīyati etāyāti diṭṭhasaṃsandanā, sākacchāvasena vinicchayakaraṇaṃ. Vimati chijjati etāyāti vimaticchedanā. Anumatiyā pucchā anumatipucchā. “Taṃ kiṃ maññatha bhikkhave”tiādi pucchāya [V 1.0099] hi “kā tumhākaṃ anumatī”ti anumati pucchitā hoti. Kathetukamyatāti kathetukamyatāya.

'Lakkhaṇa' (characteristic) is any nature that one wishes to know. 'Aññāta' (unknown) refers to the state of being unknown by any kind of knowledge. 'Adiṭṭha' (unseen) refers to the state of being unseen, as if not directly perceived by knowledge that functions as seeing. 'Atulita' (unmeasured) refers to the state of being unmeasured by knowledge that functions as weighing, as in 'this much.' 'Atīrita' (uninvestigated) refers to the act of knowing not being brought to completion by knowledge that functions as investigating. 'Avibhūta' (unmanifest) refers to the state of being unmanifest to knowledge. 'Avibhāvita' (unrevealed) refers to the state of not being made manifest by knowledge. 'Adiṭṭhajotanā' (illumination of the unseen) is that by which the unseen is illuminated. 'Diṭṭhasaṃsandanā' (examination of the seen) is that by which the seen is examined, which means making a determination by way of discussion. 'Vimaticchedanā' (cutting off doubt) is that by which doubt is cut off. 'Anumatipucchā' (question about agreement) is a question for agreement. For by the question, 'Taṃ kiṃ maññatha bhikkhave?' (What do you think, monks?) and so on, agreement is asked for, as in, 'Kā tumhākaṃ anumatī?' (What is your agreement?). 'Kathetukamyatā' (desire to speak) means because of the desire to speak.

8. Saraseneva patanasabhāvassa antarā eva atīva pātanaṃ atipāto, saṇikaṃ patituṃ adatvā sīghaṃ pātananti attho. Atikkamma vā satthādīhi abhibhavitvā pātanaṃ atipāto. Sattoti khandhasantāno. Tattha hi sattapaññatti. Jīvitindriyanti rūpārūpajīvitindriyaṃ. Rūpajīvitindriye hi vikopite itarampi taṃsambandhatāya vinassati. Kasmā panettha “pāṇassa atipāto, pāṇoti cettha vohārato satto”ti ca ekavacananiddeso kato, nanu niravasesānaṃ pāṇānaṃ atipātato virati idha adhippetā. Tathā hi vakkhati “sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampīti sabbe pāṇabhūte”tiādinā (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.cūḷasīlavaṇṇanā) bahuvacananiddesanti? Saccametaṃ, pāṇabhāvasāmaññavasena panettha ekavacananiddeso kato, sabbasaddasannidhānena tattha puthuttaṃ viññāyamānamevāti sāmaññaniddesaṃ akatvā bhedavacanicchāvasena bahuvacananiddeso katoti[M 1.0112]. Kiñca bhiyyosāmaññato saṃvarasamādānaṃ, tabbisesato saṃvarabhedoti imassa visesassa ñāpanatthaṃ ayaṃ vacanabhedo katoti veditabbo. Yāya cetanāya vattamānassa jīvitindriyassa nissayabhūtesu mahābhūtesu [P 1.0144] upakkamakaraṇahetu taṃ mahābhūtappaccayā uppajjanakamahābhūtā nuppajjissanti, sā tādisappayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā pāṇātipāto. Laddhupakkamāni hi bhūtāni itarabhūtāni viya na visadānīti samānajātiyānaṃ kāraṇaṃ na hontīti. “Kāyavacīdvārāna”nti etena manodvāre pavattāya vadhakacetanāya pāṇātipātabhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati.

8. “Atipāto” is an excessive falling, a very swift falling even before the natural falling of something whose nature is to fall; the meaning is causing a swift fall without allowing it to fall slowly. Alternatively, “atipāto” means causing a fall by overcoming and overpowering with weapons and so on. “Satta” (a being) is the continuum of aggregates, for it is there that the designation of a being occurs. “Jīvitindriya” (life faculty) means the life faculty of both material and immaterial forms. For when the material life faculty is disrupted, the other also perishes due to its connection with it. Why, then, is the singular form used here—“pāṇassa atipāto,” where “pāṇa” conventionally refers to a being—when abstinence from killing all beings without exception is intended? For it will be said elsewhere, “compassionate for the welfare of all living beings” (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1, Cūḷasīlavaṇṇanā), using the plural form. This is true. Here, the singular form is used to denote the general commonality of life, and because the presence of the word “sabba” (all) implies plurality there, the plural form is used based on the desire for a differentiated expression, without making a general designation. Moreover, it should be understood that this difference in wording is made to make known this distinction: that taking up restraint is general, while the breaking of restraint is specific. The volition by which, due to an assault on the great elements that support the present life faculty, the great elements that would arise dependent on those great elements will not arise—that volition, which originates such an action, is the taking of life. For when the elements have been assaulted, they are not clear like other elements and, therefore, do not become causes for those of the same kind. By “through the doors of body and speech,” it excludes a murderous volition arising at the mind-door from being the act of taking life.

Payogavatthumahantatādīhi mahāsāvajjatā tehi paccayehi uppajjamānāya cetanāya balavabhāvato veditabbā. Yathādhippetassa hi payogassa sahasā nipphādanavasena kiccasādhikāya bahukkhattuṃ pavattajavanehi laddhāsevanāya ca sanniṭṭhāpakacetanāya vasena payogassa mahantabhāvo. Satipi kadāci khuddake ceva mahante ca pāṇe payogassa samabhāve mahantaṃ hanantassa cetanā tibbatarā uppajjatīti vatthussa mahantabhāvo. Iti ubhayaṃ petaṃ cetanāya balavabhāveneva hoti. Tathā hi hantabbassa mahāguṇabhāvena tattha pavattaupakāracetanā viya khettavisesanibbattiyā apakāracetanāpi balavatī, tibbatarā ca uppajjatīti tassā mahāsāvajjatā daṭṭhabbā. Tasmā payogavatthuādipaccayānaṃ amahattepi mahāguṇatādipaccayehi cetanāya balavabhāvādivaseneva mahāsāvajjabhāvo veditabbo.

Great blameworthiness should be understood as due to the strength of the volition arising from such conditions as the greatness of the effort and the object. For the greatness of the effort is due to the decisive volition, which accomplishes the intended task quickly and has gained practice through many instances of swift impulses. Even when the effort applied to small and great beings is sometimes equal, the volition arising in one who kills a great being is more intense—thus, the greatness of the object. Thus, both of these are due to the strength of the volition. For, just as a helpful volition is strong on account of the great qualities of the recipient, so too a harmful volition is strong and arises more intensely due to the distinction of the field, on account of the great qualities of the one to be killed. Thus, its great blameworthiness should be seen. Therefore, even when conditions such as the effort and the object are not great, great blameworthiness should be understood as due to the strength of the volition, which is dependent on conditions such as the great qualities of the object.

Sambharīyanti [V 1.0100] etehīti sambhārā, aṅgāni. Tesu pāṇasaññitāvadhakacittāni pubbabhāgiyānipi honti. Upakkamo vadhakacetanāsamuṭṭhāpito. Pañcasambhāravatī pāṇātipātacetanāti sā pañcasambhāravinimuttā daṭṭhabbā. Vijjāmayo mantaparijappanapayogo āthabbaṇikādīnaṃ viya. Iddhimayo kammavipākajiddhimayo dāṭhākoṭakādīnaṃ viya. Ativiya papañcoti atimahāvitthāro.

They are called ‘sambhārā’ (requisites) because they are brought together; they are the constituents. Among these, the perception of a living being and the thought of killing are also preliminary stages. The assault is initiated by the volition to kill. The volition of taking life, which possesses the five requisites, should be understood as distinct from those five requisites. The application of spells and incantations, like that of the Atharvaṇa experts, is knowledge-based. The application based on psychic power, that is, psychic power born as the result of kamma, is like that of beings with venomous fangs. 'Excessive proliferation' means an extremely great elaboration.

Etthāha – khaṇe khaṇe nirujjhanasabhāvesu saṅkhāresu ko hanti, ko vā haññati, yadi cittacetasikasantāno, so arūpatāya na chedanabhedanādivasena [M 1.0113] vikopanasamattho, nāpi [P 1.0145] vikopanīyo, atha rūpasantāno, so acetanatāya kaṭṭhakaliṅgarūpamoti na tattha chedanādinā pāṇātipāto labbhati yathā matasarīre, payogopi pāṇātipātassa paharaṇappakārādi atītesu vā saṅkhāresu bhaveyya anāgatesu vā paccuppannesu vā, tattha na tāva atītānāgatesu sambhavati tesaṃ abhāvato, paccuppannesu ca saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇikattā saraseneva nirujjhanasabhāvatāya vināsābhimukhesu nippayojano payogo siyā, vināsassa ca kāraṇarahitattā na paharaṇappakārādipayogahetukaṃ maraṇaṃ, nirīhakatāya ca saṅkhārānaṃ kassa so payogo, khaṇikattā vadhādhippāyasamakālabhijjanakassa kiriyāpariyosānakālānavaṭṭhānato kassa vā pāṇātipātakammabaddhoti.

Here it is said: Among conditioned phenomena, which by nature cease moment by moment, who kills, and who is killed? If it is the continuum of mind and mental factors, being formless, it is incapable of being disrupted by cutting or breaking, nor can it be disrupted. If it is the continuum of material form, being insentient like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, there is no taking of life by cutting and so on, just as in a dead body. Furthermore, the application of taking life, such as striking, could pertain to past, future, or present formations. It cannot pertain to past or future formations, as they do not exist. As for present formations, due to their momentary nature and their inherent tendency to cease, they are already facing destruction, so any effort would be pointless. And since their destruction is without a cause, death is not caused by the application of striking and so on. Since formations are devoid of volition, whose application is it? And due to momentariness, since the one who has the intention to kill perishes at that same moment and does not endure until the time of the action's completion, to whom is the kamma of taking life bound?

Vuccate – yathāvuttavadhakacetanāsahito saṅkhārānaṃ puñjo sattasaṅkhāto hantā, tena pavattitavadhakapayoganimittaṃ apagatusmāviññāṇajīvitindriyo matavohārappavattinibandho yathāvuttavadhappayogākaraṇe uppajjanāraho rūpārūpadhammasamūho haññati, kevalo vā cittacetasikasantāno. Vadhappayogāvisayabhāvepi tassa pañcavokārabhave rūpasantānādhīnavuttitāya rūpasantāne parena payojitajīvitindriyupacchedakapayogavasena tannibbattivibandhakavisadisarūpuppattiyā vihate vicchedo hotīti na pāṇātipātassa asambhavo, nāpi ahetuko pāṇātipāto, na ca payogo nippayojano paccuppannesu saṅkhāresu katapayogavasena tadanantaraṃ uppajjanārahassa saṅkhārakalāpassa tathā anuppattito, khaṇikānaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇikamaraṇassa idha maraṇabhāvena anadhippetattā, santatimaraṇassa ca yathāvuttanayena sahetukabhāvato na ahetukaṃ maraṇaṃ, na ca katturahito pāṇātipātappayogo nirīhakesupi saṅkhāresu sannihitatāmattena upakārakesu attano anurūpaphaluppādananiyatesu [P 1.0146] kāraṇesu kattuvohārasiddhito yathā “padīpo pakāseti nisākaro candimā”ti ca, na ca kevalassa vadhādhippāyasahabhuno cittacetasikakalāpassa pāṇātipāto icchito santānavasena avaṭṭhitasseva paṭijānanato, santānavasena [V 1.0101] pavattamānānañca padīpādīnaṃ atthakiriyāsiddhi dissatīti attheva pāṇātipātena kammabaddho. Ayañca vicāro adinnādānādīsupi yathāsambhavaṃ vibhāvetabbo.

It is said: The aggregate of formations, designated as a being, when accompanied by the volition to kill as described, is the killer. By that (killer), the aggregate of material and immaterial phenomena—or merely a continuum of mind and mental factors—is killed. This (killed entity) is one from which consciousness and the life faculty have departed due to the sign of the effort to kill initiated by that (killer), and which thereby becomes the basis for the designation of a dead person, and which would have been liable to arise in the absence of such an effort to kill as described. Even if it is not the direct object of the effort to kill, due to its existence in the five-aggregate existence being dependent on the material continuum, when the material continuum is destroyed by another’s effort to cut off the life faculty, and with the arising of dissimilar material phenomena that obstruct its production, its cessation occurs. Thus, there is no impossibility of the destruction of life, nor is the destruction of life without cause. Nor is the effort without purpose, since, due to the effort made in the present formations, the aggregate of formations liable to arise immediately thereafter does not arise in that way. Because the momentary death of momentary formations is not intended here as death, and because the death of the continuum occurs with a cause as described, death is not without cause. Nor is the effort to kill devoid of a doer, since, even in inactive formations, the designation of a doer is established in causes that are helpful merely by being present and are determined to produce a result suitable for themselves, just as it is said, “the lamp illuminates,” and “the moon is the night-maker.” Nor is the destruction of life intended to be merely the aggregate of mind and mental factors co-arisen with the intention to kill, since only that which is established by way of a continuum is acknowledged. And since the accomplishment of the function of lamps and so forth is seen to occur by way of a continuum, one is indeed karmically bound by the destruction of life. This analysis should be similarly applied to taking what is not given and other offenses as is appropriate.

“Pahīnakālato [M 1.0114] paṭṭhāya viratovā”ti etena pahānahetukā idhādhippetā samucchedaviratīti dasseti. Kammakkhayañāṇena hi pāṇātipātadussīlyassa pahīnattā bhagavā accantameva tato paṭiviratoti vuccati samucchedavasena pahānaviratīnaṃ adhippetattā. Kiñcāpi pahānaviramaṇānaṃ purimapacchimakālatā natthi, maggadhammānaṃ pana sammādiṭṭhiādīnaṃ sammāvācādīnañca paccayapaccayuppannabhāve apekkhite sahajātānampi paccayapaccayuppannabhāvena gahaṇaṃ purimapacchimabhāveneva hotīti gahaṇappavattiākāravasena paccayabhūtesu sammādiṭṭhiādīsu pahāyakadhammesu pahānakiriyāya purimakālavohāro, paccayuppannāsu ca viratīsu viramaṇakiriyāya aparakālavohāro ca hotīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Pahānaṃ vā samucchedavasena, virati paṭippassaddhivasena yojetabbā. Atha vā pāṇo atipātīyati etenāti pāṇātipāto, pāṇaghātahetubhūto dhammasamūho. Ko paneso? Ahirikānottappadosamohavihiṃsādayo kilesā. Te hi bhagavā ariyamaggena pahāya samugghāṭetvā pāṇātipātadussīlyato accantameva paṭiviratoti vuccati kilesesu pahīnesu kilesanimittassa kammassa anuppajjanato. “Adinnādānaṃ pahāyā”tiādīsupi eseva nayo. Viratovāti avadhāraṇena tassā viratiyā kālādivasena apariyantataṃ dasseti. Yathā hi aññe samādinnaviratikāpi [P 1.0147] anavaṭṭhitacittatāya lābhajīvitādihetu samādānaṃ bhindanti, na evaṃ bhagavā. Bhagavā pana sabbaso pahīnapāṇātipātattā accantavirato evāti. Vītikkamissāmīti anavajjadhammehi vokiṇṇā antarantarā uppajjanakā dubbalākusalā. Yasmā pana kāyavacīpayogaṃ upalabhitvā “imassa kilesā uppannā”ti viññunā sakkā ñātuṃ, tasmā te iminā pariyāyena “cakkhusotaviññeyyā”ti vuttāti daṭṭhabbā. Kāyikāti pāṇātipātādinipphādake balavākusale sandhāyāha.

“From the time of abandoning, he abstains”—this indicates that the abstinence intended here is abstinence by eradication, which is rooted in abandoning. For, since the immorality of destroying life has been abandoned through the knowledge of the destruction of kamma, the Blessed One is said to be entirely abstinent from it, because abstinence through abandoning by way of eradication is intended. Although there is no prior or later time for abandoning and abstaining, when the relationship of cause and effect between the path factors—such as right view and so forth, and right speech and so forth—is considered, even their simultaneous arising is apprehended as cause and effect, which occurs as if they were prior and later. Thus, in terms of the mode of apprehension, the act of abandoning in relation to the abandoning states, such as right view, is designated as occurring at an earlier time, while the act of abstaining in relation to the abstinences that arise as their effects is designated as occurring at a later time. This is how the meaning should be understood here. Alternatively, abandoning should be connected with eradication, and abstinence with pacification. Or, `pāṇātipāta` (destruction of life) means the group of states that are the cause of killing living beings. What are these? Shamelessness, lack of fear of wrongdoing, hatred, delusion, cruelty, and other defilements. The Blessed One, having abandoned and uprooted these defilements through the noble path, is said to be entirely abstinent from the immorality of destroying life because, with the defilements abandoned, the kamma that is their sign does not arise. The same method applies to “having abandoned taking what is not given” and so on. In `virato vā`, the emphatic particle indicates that this abstinence is boundless in terms of time and other conditions. For while others who undertake precepts may break them due to wavering minds or for the sake of gain or livelihood, the Blessed One does not. The Blessed One, having completely abandoned the destruction of life, is entirely abstinent. The thought, “I will transgress,” refers to weak unwholesome states that arise intermittently, mixed with blameless states. But since these defilements can be known by the wise only after bodily or verbal action has occurred—by observing, “These defilements have arisen in this one”—they are therefore, by this method, described as “cognizable by eye and ear.” By “bodily” is meant the strong unwholesome states that produce the destruction of life and the like.

Gottavasena laddhavohāroti sambandho. Dīpetuṃ vaṭṭati brahmadattena bhāsitavaṇṇassa anusandhidassanavasena imissā desanāya āraddhattā. Tatthāyaṃ dīpanā – “pāṇātipātaṃ pahāya pāṇātipātā paṭivirato samaṇassa gotamassa sāvakasaṅgho nihitadaṇḍo nihitasattho”ti vitthāretabbaṃ. Nanu ca dhammassāpi vaṇṇo [M 1.0115] brahmadattena bhāsito? Saccaṃ bhāsito, so pana sammāsambuddhapabhavattā, ariyasaṅghādhārattā ca dhammassa dhammānubhāvasiddhattā ca tesaṃ tadubhayadīpaneneva dīpito hotīti visuṃ na uddhaṭo. Saddhammānubhāveneva hi bhagavā bhikkhusaṅgho [V 1.0102] ca pāṇātipātādippahānasamattho ahosi, desanā pana ādito paṭṭhāya evaṃ āgatāti.

The connection is that the designation is obtained by way of lineage. It is fitting to explain this, as this discourse was initiated to show the connection with the praise spoken by Brahmadatta. Herein lies the explanation: “Having abandoned the destruction of life, abstaining from the destruction of life, the community of disciples of the ascetic Gotama has laid down the rod and laid down the weapon”—this should be elaborated in detail. But was not the praise of the Dhamma also spoken by Brahmadatta? Indeed, it was spoken. However, because the Dhamma originates from the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One and is the support of the Noble Sangha, and because their qualities are established through the power of the Dhamma, its praise is illuminated by the explanation of both of these, and thus is not separately extracted. For it was by the power of the True Dhamma that the Blessed One and the community of monks were capable of abandoning the destruction of life and so forth. But the discourse has come down in this way from the very beginning.

Etthāyaṃ adhippāyo – “atthi bhikkhave aññe ca dhammā”tiādinā anaññasādhāraṇe buddhaguṇe ārabbha upari desanaṃ vaḍḍhetukāmo bhagavā ādito paṭṭhāya “tathāgatassa vaṇṇaṃ vadamāno vadeyyā”tiādinā buddhaguṇavaseneva desanaṃ ārabhi, na bhikkhusaṅghavasenāti. Esā hi bhagavato desanāya pakati, yaṃ ekaraseneva desanaṃ dassetuṃ labbhamānassāpi kassaci aggahaṇaṃ. Tathā hi rūpakaṇḍe dukādīsu tanniddesesu ca hadayavatthu na gahitaṃ. Itaravatthūhi asamānagatikattā desanābhedo hotīti. Yathā hi [P 1.0148] cakkhuviññāṇādīni ekantato cakkhādinissayāni, na evaṃ manoviññāṇaṃ ekantena hadayavatthunissayaṃ, nissitavasena ca vatthudukādidesanā pavattā “atthi rūpaṃ cakkhuviññāṇassa vatthu, atthi rūpaṃ na cakkhuviññāṇassa vatthū”tiādinā. Yampi ekantato hadayavatthunissayaṃ, tassa vasena “atthi rūpaṃ manoviññāṇassa vatthū”tiādinā dukādīsu vuccamānesupi na tadanurūpā ārammaṇadukādayo sambhavanti. Na hi “atthi rūpaṃ manoviññāṇassa ārammaṇaṃ, atthi rūpaṃ na manoviññāṇassa ārammaṇa”nti sakkā vattunti vatthārammaṇadukā bhinnagatikā siyunti na ekarasā desanā bhaveyyāti. Tathā nikkhepakaṇḍe cittuppādavibhāgena avuccamānattā avitakkaavicārapadavissajjane “vicāro cā”ti vattuṃ na sakkāti avitakkavicāramattapadavissajjane labbhamānopi vitakko na uddhaṭo, aññathā “vitakko cā”ti vattabbaṃ siyā.

Herein, the intention is this: The Blessed One, wishing to expand the discourse further concerning the Buddha’s unique qualities that are not shared with others, began with the phrase, “There are, monks, other qualities,” and commenced the discourse solely by way of the Buddha’s qualities, not by way of the Sangha of monks. For this is the nature of the Blessed One’s discourse: that even when it is possible to present the teaching in a single, consistent tone, something may not be included. For instance, in the section on form, the heart-basis is not included in the dyads and so forth, nor in their explanations. This is because the discourse would be divided, as it follows a different course from the other bases. For just as eye-consciousness and so on are entirely dependent on the eye-basis and so on, mental consciousness is not entirely dependent on the heart-basis. And the discourse on the basis-dyads and so forth proceeds by way of dependence, as in: “There is form that is the basis for eye-consciousness; there is form that is not the basis for eye-consciousness,” and so on. Even regarding that which is entirely dependent on the heart-basis, when it is spoken of in the dyads and so forth by way of that dependence, as in “There is form that is the basis for mental consciousness,” the corresponding object-dyads and so forth are not possible. For it cannot be said, “There is form that is the object of mental consciousness; there is form that is not the object of mental consciousness.” Thus, the basis-object dyads would have different courses, and the discourse would not have a single, consistent tone. Similarly, in the section on classification, because it is not discussed by way of the analysis of the arising of consciousness, in the explanation of the term “without initial thought and without sustained thought,” it is not possible to say “and sustained thought.” And in the explanation of the term “without initial thought, with only sustained thought,” initial thought is not included, even though it is available elsewhere; otherwise, one would have to say “and initial thought.”

Daṇḍanasaṅkhātassa daṇḍassa paraviheṭhanassa vivajjitabhāvadīpanatthaṃ daṇḍasatthānaṃ nikkhepavacananti āha “parūpaghātatthāyā”tiādi. Viheṭhanabhāvatoti vihiṃsanabhāvato. “Bhikkhusaṅghavasenāpi dīpetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttattā tampi ekadesena dīpento “yaṃ pana bhikkhū”tiādimāha.

To explain the avoidance of harming others, which is the meaning of the rod designated as punishment, it is said that the statement about laying down the rod and weapons is “for the purpose of not harming others,” and so forth. By “nature of harm” is meant the state of injuring. Since it is said, “It is fitting to explain even by way of the community of monks,” he explains that too in part by saying, “But whatever monk,” and so forth.

Lajjīti [M 1.0116] ettha vuttalajjāya ottappampi vuttamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi pāpajigucchanaṃ pāputtāsanarahitaṃ, pāpabhayaṃ vā alajjanaṃ atthīti. Dhammagarutāya vā buddhānaṃ, dhammassa ca attādhīnattā attādhipatibhūtā lajjāva vuttā, na pana lokādhipati ottappaṃ. “Dayaṃ mettacittataṃ āpanno”ti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu dayā-saddo “dayāpanno”tiādīsu karuṇāya pavattatīti? Saccametaṃ[P 1.0149], ayaṃ pana dayā-saddo anurakkhaṇamatthaṃ antonītaṃ katvā pavattamāno mettāya [V 1.0103] karuṇāya ca pavattatīti idha mettāya pavattamāno vutto. Midati siniyhatīti mettā, mettā etassa atthīti mettaṃ, mettaṃ cittaṃ etassāti mettacitto, tassa bhāvo mettacittatā, mettā icceva attho. “Sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampī”ti etena tassā viratiyā sattavasena apariyantataṃ dasseti. Pāṇabhūteti pāṇajāte. Anukampakoti karuṇāyanako. Yasmā pana mettā karuṇāya visesapaccayo hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “tāya eva dayāpannatāyā”ti. Evaṃ yehi dhammehi pāṇātipātā virati sampajjati, tehi lajjāmettākaruṇāhi samaṅgībhāvo dassito. Viharatīti evaṃbhūto hutvā ekasmiṃ iriyāpathe uppannaṃ dukkhaṃ aññena iriyāpathena vicchinditvā harati pavatteti, attabhāvaṃ vā yāpetīti attho. Tenevāha “iriyati yapeti yāpeti pāletī”ti.

Here, it should be understood that by the shame mentioned, fear of wrongdoing is also mentioned. For there is no disgust for evil without fear of its consequences, nor fear of evil without shame. Alternatively, due to the Buddhas’ reverence for the Dhamma, and because the Dhamma is self-dependent, shame is spoken of as self-governing, but not fear of wrongdoing as world-governing. Why is it said, “endowed with kindness and a mind of loving-kindness”? Doesn’t the word `dayā` occur in contexts like `dayāpanno` to denote compassion? Indeed, it is so. But here, the word `dayā`, taking the meaning of protection inwardly, occurs in relation to both loving-kindness and compassion; here it is said to occur in relation to loving-kindness. `Mettā` means ‘to be friendly, to be affectionate.’ `Mettaṃ` is that which possesses mettā. `Mettacitta` is one whose mind is filled with mettā. The state of such a one is `mettacittatā`; the meaning is simply mettā. “Sympathetic for the welfare of all living beings” shows that his abstinence is boundless in terms of beings. By `pāṇabhūta` is meant the class of living beings. By `anukampaka` is meant one who inclines towards compassion. Because loving-kindness is a specific condition for compassion, it is said, “by that very state of being endowed with kindness.” Thus, the qualities by which abstinence from the destruction of life is accomplished—shame, loving-kindness, and compassion—are shown to be fully possessed. By `viharati` (he dwells) is meant that, being thus, he removes or carries on the suffering arisen in one posture by adopting another posture, or he maintains his existence. Hence it is said, “he moves, supports, maintains, and protects.”

Ācārasīlamattakanti sādhujanācārasīlamattakaṃ, tena indriyasaṃvarādiguṇehipi lokiyaputhujjano tathāgatassa vaṇṇaṃ vattuṃ na sakkotīti dasseti. Tathā hi indriyasaṃvarapaccayaparibhogasīlāni idha sīlakathāyaṃ na vibhattāni.

By `ācārasīlamattaka` is meant merely the virtuous conduct of good people. By this it is shown that an ordinary worldling cannot describe the Tathāgata’s virtues such as sense-restraint. For here, in this discourse on virtue, the virtues of sense-restraint and of the proper use of requisites are not analyzed.

Parasaṃharaṇanti parassa santakaharaṇaṃ. Theno vuccati coro, tassa bhāvo theyyaṃ. Idhāpi khuddake parasantake appasāvajjaṃ, mahante mahāsāvajjaṃ. Kasmā? Payogamahantatāya, vatthuguṇānaṃ pana samabhāve sati kilesānaṃ upakkamānañca mudutāya appasāvajjaṃ, tibbatāya mahāsāvajjanti ayampi nayo yojetabbo.

By `parasaṃharaṇa` is meant taking what belongs to another. `Thena` is called a thief; the state of a thief is `theyya`. Here too, in the case of a small amount of another’s property, the fault is small; in the case of a large amount, the fault is large. Why? Because of the magnitude of the effort. But when the qualities of the object are equal, if the defilements and the undertakings are mild, the fault is small; if intense, the fault is large. This method should also be applied.

Sāhatthikādayoti ettha mantaparijappanena parasantakaharaṇaṃ vijjāmayo, vinā mantena kāyavacīpayogena parasantakassa ākaḍḍhanaṃ tādisaiddhānubhāvena iddhimayo payogo.
