By `sāhatthikādayo` (with one’s own hand and so forth), here, taking another’s property through the muttering of spells is the magical method (`vijjāmayo`); while, without spells, drawing another’s property near through the application of body and speech by means of such psychic power is the method of psychic power (`iddhimayo`).

Sesanti [M 1.0117] “pahāya paṭivirato”ti evamādikaṃ. Tañhi pubbe vuttanayaṃ. Kiñcāpi nayidha sikkhāpadavohārena virati vuttā, ito aññesu pana suttapadesesu vinayābhidhammesu ca pavattavohārena viratiyo cetanā ca adhisīlasikkhādīnaṃ adhiṭṭhānabhāvato, tesu aññatarakoṭṭhāsabhāvato [P 1.0150] ca sikkhāpadanti āha “paṭhamasikkhāpade”ti. Kāmañcettha “lajjī dayāpanno”ti na vuttaṃ, adhikāravasena pana atthato vā vuttamevāti veditabbaṃ. Yathā hi lajjādayo pāṇātipātappahānassa visesappaccayo, evaṃ adinnādānappahānassāpīti, tasmā sāpi pāḷi ānetvā vattabbā. Eseva nayo ito paresupi. Atha vā “sucibhūtenā”ti etena [V 1.0104] hirottappādīhi samannāgamo, ahirikādīnañca pahānaṃ vuttamevāti “lajjī”tiādi na vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The rest means 'having abandoned, he abstains,' and so on. That indeed is the method stated previously. Although here abstention is not stated in terms of a training precept, in other sutta passages, as well as in the Vinaya and Abhidhamma, abstentions and intentions are called 'training precepts' by common designation, because they are the basis for the higher trainings in virtue and so on, and because they are a constituent part of them; hence he says 'in the first training precept.' Although here 'one who is conscientious and compassionate' is not stated, it should be understood as already stated in effect by the force of the context. Just as conscience and compassion are special conditions for abandoning the destruction of life, so too are they for abandoning the taking of what is not given. Therefore, that passage too should be brought in and mentioned. The same method applies to the others that follow. Or alternatively, by 'with a pure being,' it is stated that one is endowed with conscience and shame and that the abandoning of shamelessness, etc., is already stated. Thus, it should be understood that 'conscientious,' etc., is not stated.

Aseṭṭhacariyanti aseṭṭhānaṃ hīnānaṃ, aseṭṭhaṃ vā lāmakaṃ nihīnaṃ vuttiṃ, methunanti attho. “Brahmaṃ seṭṭhaṃ ācāra”nti methunaviratimāha. “Ārācārī methunā”ti etena “idha brāhmaṇa ekacco…pe… na heva kho mātugāmena saddhiṃ dvayaṃdvayasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati, apica kho mātugāmassa ucchādanaparimaddananhāpanasambāhanaṃ sādiyati, so taṃ assādeti, taṃ nikāmeti, tena ca vittiṃ āpajjatī”tiādinā (a. ni. 7.50) vuttā sattavidhamethunasaṃyogāpi paṭivirati dassitāti daṭṭhabbā. Idhāpi asaddhammasevanādhippāyena kāyadvārappavattā maggenamaggapaṭipattisamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā abrahmacariyaṃ, micchācāre pana agamanīyaṭṭhānavītikkamacetanāti yojetabbaṃ. Tattha agamanīyaṭṭhānaṃ nāma purisānaṃ māturakkhitādayo dasa, dhanakkītādayo dasāti vīsati itthiyo. Itthīsu pana dasannaṃ dhanakkitādīnaṃ sārakkhasaparidaṇḍānañca vasena dvādasannaṃ aññe purisā. Guṇavirahite vippaṭipatti appasāvajjā, mahāguṇe mahāsāvajjā. Guṇarahitepi ca abhibhavitvā pavatti mahāsāvajjā, ubhinnaṃ samānacchandabhāvepi kilesānaṃ upakkamānañca mudutāya appasāvajjā, tibbatāya mahāsāvajjāti [P 1.0151] veditabbā. Tassa dve sambhārā sevetukāmatācittaṃ, maggenamaggapaṭipattīti. Micchācāre pana agamanīyaṭṭhānatā, sevanācittaṃ maggenamaggapaṭipatti, sādiyanañcāti cattāro. “Abhibhavitvā vītikkamane maggenamaggapaṭipattiadhivāsane satipi purimuppannasevanābhisandhipayogābhāvato [M 1.0118] abhibhuyyamānassa micchācāro na hotī”ti vadanti. Sevanācitte sati payogābhāvo na pamāṇaṃ itthiyā sevanāpayogassa yebhuyyena abhāvato, itthiyā puretaraṃ upaṭṭhāpitasevanācittāyapi micchācāro na siyāti āpajjati payogābhāvato. Tasmā purisassa vasena ukkaṃsato cattāro vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ, aññathā itthiyā purisakiccakaraṇakāle purisassapi sevanāpayogābhāvato micchācāro na siyāti eke. Idaṃ panettha sanniṭṭhānaṃ – attano ruciyā pavattitassa tayo, balakkārena pavattitassa tayo, anavasesaggahaṇena pana cattāroti. Eko payogo sāhatthikova.

Aseṭṭhacariya means the conduct of the base and inferior, or a base, vile, and inferior way of life, meaning sexual intercourse. 'The supreme Brahma-conduct' refers to abstinence from sexual intercourse. 'One who abstains from sexual intercourse'—by this, it should be understood that abstinence from the seven kinds of sexual connection mentioned in (AN 7.50) is also shown, such as: 'Here, a brahmin... does not engage in sexual intercourse with women, but consents to being anointed, massaged, bathed, or rubbed by women; he enjoys it, delights in it, and finds satisfaction in it.' Here, the intention that arises through the body-door with the aim of engaging in unrighteous conduct, which gives rise to the practice of the path in an improper manner, is called unchastity. In the case of wrong conduct, it should be connected with the intention to transgress in a place where one should not go. In this context, 'a place where one should not go' refers, for men, to twenty women: ten such as those protected by their mothers, and ten such as those purchased with wealth. For women, other men are twelve, based on ten such as those purchased with wealth and the addition of those who are protected and subject to penalty. Transgression with one lacking in virtues is a minor offense; with one possessing great virtues, it is a grave offense. Even with one lacking in virtues, if the act is done by overpowering her, it is a grave offense. Even if both parties have equal desire, the offense is minor if the defilements and the instigation are mild, but grave if they are intense. There are two conditions for this: the mind desiring to engage, and the practice of the path in an improper manner. In wrong conduct, there are four factors: the place where one should not go, the mind to engage, the practice of the path in an improper manner, and enjoying it. Some say: 'For one who is overpowered and transgressed against, there is no wrong conduct, because there is no prior intention to engage or application of effort, even when the practice of the path in an improper manner is sustained.' If there is a mind to engage but no application of effort, it is not a valid argument, since usually there is no application of effort from the woman’s side. It would follow that even for a woman who presents herself first with a mind to engage, there would be no wrong conduct on her part, due to the absence of application of effort. Thus, it should be understood that, from the man’s perspective, four factors are stated as the most significant. Otherwise, some say that when a woman performs the man’s role, there is no wrong conduct for the man due to the absence of application of effort on his part. Here, the conclusion in this regard is: three factors arise from one’s own desire, three from coercion, and four from complete inclusion. A single effort is direct and self-made.

9. Kammapathappattaṃ dassetuṃ “atthabhañjanako”ti vuttaṃ. Vacīpayogo kāyapayogo vāti musā-saddassa kiriyāpadhānataṃ dasseti. Visaṃvādanādhippāyo pubbabhāgakkhaṇe taṅkhaṇe ca. Vuttañhi “pubbevassa hoti ‘musā bhaṇissa’nti, bhaṇantassa hoti ‘musā bhaṇāmī’ti” (pārā. 205). Etañhi dvayaṃ aṅgabhūtaṃ, itaraṃ pana hotu vā mā vā, akāraṇametaṃ. Assāti visaṃvādakassa[V 1.0105]. Yathāvuttaṃ payogabhūtaṃ musā vadati viññāpeti, samuṭṭhāpeti vā etāyāti cetanā musāvādo.

9. To show that it has reached the path of action, it is called 'one who breaks the meaning.' 'The application of speech or the application of body' shows the predominance of action for the word 'falsehood.' The intention to deceive is present both in the preliminary moment and at that very moment. For it is said, 'Beforehand, he has the thought, “I will speak falsely,” and while speaking, he has the thought, “I am speaking falsely”' (Pārā. 205). Indeed, these two are constituent parts; as for the other factor, whether it is present or not, it is not a cause for this. 'His' refers to the deceiver. The volition by which one, through the aforesaid application, speaks falsehood, makes it known, or brings it about, is false speech.

Purimanaye lakkhaṇassa abyāpitatāya, musā-saddassa ca visaṃvaditabbatthavācakattasambhavato [P 1.0152] paripuṇṇaṃ katvā musāvādalakkhaṇaṃ dassetuṃ “musāti abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ vatthū”tiādinā dutiyanayo āraddho. Imasmiñca naye musā vadīyati vuccati etāyāti cetanā musāvādo. “Yamatthaṃ bhañjatī”ti vatthuvasena musāvādassa appasāvajjamahāsāvajjatamāha. Yassa atthaṃ bhañjati, tassa appaguṇatāya appasāvajjo, mahāguṇatāya mahāsāvajjoti adinnādāne viya guṇavasenāpi yojetabbaṃ. Kilesānaṃ mudutibbatāvasenāpi appasāvajjamahāsāvajjatā labbhatiyeva.

Because in the first method the characteristic was not comprehensive, and since the word 'false' can denote a matter to be misrepresented, the second method is introduced with 'false means an unreal, untrue matter,' and so on, to show the characteristic of false speech completely. In this method, the volition by which one speaks falsehood is called false speech. 'Whatever meaning it breaks' explains the minor or major blameworthiness of false speech based on the object. If the meaning it breaks is of little quality, the blame is minor; if of great quality, the blame is major—just as in taking what is not given, it should also be applied based on quality. The minor or major blameworthiness is indeed also determined by the mildness or intensity of the defilements.

Attano santakaṃ adātukāmatāya, pūraṇakathānayena ca visaṃvādanapurekkhārasseva musāvādo. Tattha pana cetanā balavatī na hotīti appasāvajjatā [M 1.0119] vuttā. Appatāya ūnassa atthassa pūraṇavasena pavattā kathā pūraṇakathā.

False speech occurs for one who has the intention to deceive, due to an unwillingness to give what is one's own and by the method of 'filling-in talk.' But in that case, because the intention is not strong, it is said to be of minor blame. 'Filling-in talk' is talk that proceeds by way of completing a deficient matter for a trifle.

Tajjoti tassāruppo, visaṃvādanānurūpoti attho. “Vāyāmo”ti vāyāmasīsena payogamāha. Visaṃvādanādhippāyena payoge katepi parena tasmiṃ atthe aviññāte visaṃvādanassa asijjhanato parassa tadatthavijānanaṃ eko sambhāro vutto. Keci pana “abhūtavacanaṃ visaṃvādanacittaṃ parassa tadatthavijānananti tayo sambhārā”ti vadanti. Kiriyāsamuṭṭhāpakacetanākkhaṇeyeva musāvādakakammunā bajjhati sanniṭṭhāpakacetanāya nibbattattā, sacepi dandhatāya vicāretvā paro tamatthaṃ jānātīti adhippāyo.

'Tajjo' means suitable for that; the meaning is 'in conformity with the deception.' 'Effort' refers to the application, with effort as its heading. Even when the application is made with the intention to deceive, since the deception does not succeed if that meaning is not understood by the other person, the other's understanding of that meaning is stated as one requisite. Some, however, say, 'An untrue statement, a mind set on deception, and the other's understanding of that meaning—these are the three requisites.' The intention is that one is bound by the kamma of false speech at the very moment of the volition that initiates the action, because it is produced by the concluding volition, even if the other person comes to understand that meaning after slowly investigating.

“Saccato thetato”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.19) viya theta-saddo thirapariyāyo, thirabhāvo ca saccavāditāya adhikatattā kathāvasena veditabboti āha “thirakathoti attho”ti. Nathirakathoti yathā haliddirāgādayo [P 1.0153] anavaṭṭhitasabhāvatāya na thirā, evaṃ na thirā kathā yassa so na thirakathoti haliddirāgādayo yathā kathāya upamā honti, evaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Esa nayo “pāsāṇalekhā viyā”tiādīsupi.

As in phrases like 'from truth, from firmness' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.19), the word 'theta' is a synonym for 'firm.' And because the state of firmness is additional to truthfulness, it should be understood in terms of speech; thus, he says, 'the meaning is “firm in speech.”' 'One not firm in speech' means: just as turmeric dye and so on are not firm due to their unstable nature, so too, one whose speech is not firm is 'one not firm in speech.' In this way, turmeric dye and so on are a simile for speech; it should be so connected. This method also applies in phrases like 'like a line on a rock,' and so on.

Saddhā ayati pavattati etthāti saddhāyo, saddhāyo eva saddhāyiko yathā “venayiko”ti [V 1.0106] (a. ni. 8.11; pārā. 8). Saddhāya vā ayitabbo saddhāyiko, saddheyyoti attho. Vattabbataṃ āpajjati visaṃvādanatoti adhippāyo.

'Saddhāyo' means 'faith proceeds in this one,' hence 'saddhāyo.' 'Saddhāyiko' is derived from 'saddhāyo,' just like 'venayiko' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.11; Pārājika 8). Alternatively, 'saddhāyiko' means 'one who should be approached with faith'; the meaning is 'trustworthy.' The intended meaning is that one becomes worthy of being spoken to because of not deceiving.

Suññabhāvanti pītivirahitatāya rittataṃ. Sā pisuṇavācāti yāyaṃ yathāvuttā saddasabhāvā vācā, sā piyasuññakaraṇato pisuṇavācāti niruttinayena atthamāha. Pisatīti vā pisuṇā, samagge satte avayavabhūte vagge bhinne karotīti attho.

'The state of being void' means emptiness due to being devoid of affection. 'That is divisive speech': this speech, which has the nature of sound as described, is called 'divisive speech' because it makes one void of what is dear; this is the meaning stated by way of etymology. Alternatively, 'pisuṇā' is so called because it grinds (pisati); the meaning is that it divides beings who are in concord, splitting a group that was a unified whole.

Pharusanti sinehābhāvena lūkhaṃ. Sayampi pharusāti domanassasamuṭṭhitattā sabhāvenapi kakkasā. Ettha ca pharusaṃ karotīti phalūpacārena, pharusayatīti vā vācāya pharusa-saddappavatti veditabbā. Sayampi pharusāti paresaṃ mammacchedavasena pavattiyā ekantaniṭṭhuratāya sabhāvena, kāraṇavohārena [M 1.0120] ca vācāya pharusa-saddappavatti daṭṭhabbā. Tatoyeva ca neva kaṇṇasukhā. Atthavipannatāya na hadayaṅgamā.

'Harsh' means rough due to the absence of affection. 'Harsh in itself' means that because it arises from displeasure, it is also coarse by nature. And here, the application of the word 'harsh' to speech should be understood figuratively from its effect, as 'it makes harsh,' or as 'it is harsh.' 'Harsh in itself' means that the application of the word 'harsh' to speech should be seen both by its nature—due to its proceeding by way of cutting the vital spots of others and its utter cruelty—and by causal convention. For that very reason, it is not pleasant to the ear. Due to the corruption of its meaning, it is not pleasing to the heart.

Yena samphaṃ palapatīti yena palāpasaṅkhātena niratthakavacanena sukhaṃ hitañca phalati vidarati vināsetīti “sampha”nti laddhanāmaṃ attano paresañca anupakārakaṃ yaṃ kiñci palapati.

'By which one prattles 'sampha'': this refers to prattling whatever is unhelpful to oneself and others. It is useless speech, designated as prattle, which has obtained the name 'sampha' because by it, happiness and welfare are split, torn apart, and destroyed.

Saṃkiliṭṭhacittassāti lobhena dosena vā vibādhitacittassa, upatāpitacittassa vā, dūsitacittassāti attho. Cetanā pisuṇavācā pisuṇaṃ vadanti etāyāti. Yassa yato bhedaṃ karoti, tesu abhinnesu appasāvajjaṃ, bhinnesu mahāsāvajjaṃ, tathā kilesānaṃ mudutibbatāvisesesu.

'Of one with a defiled mind' means of one whose mind is afflicted by greed or hatred, or whose mind is tormented, or whose mind is corrupted. The volition is divisive speech, because by it one speaks divisively. Regarding the one from whom one creates division: if they remain undivided, it is of minor blame; if they become divided, it is of major blame. The same applies with respect to the different degrees of mildness and intensity of the defilements.

Yassa pesuññaṃ [P 1.0154] upasaṃharati, so bhijjatu vā mā vā, tassa atthassa viññāpanameva pamāṇanti āha “tadatthavijānana”nti, kammapathappatti pana bhinne eva.

Regarding the one to whom one directs the slander: whether that person is divided from the other or not, the mere communication of that meaning is the standard—thus it is said, 'the understanding of that meaning.' The reaching of the path of action, however, occurs only when they are divided.

Anuppadātāti anubalappadātā, anuvattanavasena vā padātā. Kassa pana anuvattanaṃ padānañca? “Sahitāna”nti vuttattā “sandhānassā”ti viññāyati. Tenevāha “sandhānānuppadātā”ti. Yasmā pana anuvattanavasena sandhānassa padānaṃ ādhānaṃ, rakkhaṇaṃ vā daḷhīkaraṇaṃ hoti, tena vuttaṃ “daḷhīkammaṃ kattāti attho”ti. Āramanti etthāti ārāmo, ramitabbaṭṭhānaṃ[V 1.0107]. Yasmā pana ākārena vināpi ayamevattho labbhati, tasmā vuttaṃ “samaggarāmotipi pāḷi, ayamevettha attho”ti.

'Anuppadātā' means a giver of supporting strength, or a giver by way of conforming. But conforming to what, and giving of what? Since it is said 'of the united,' it is understood as 'of union.' Therefore, he says 'a supporter of union.' Moreover, because the giving to the union by way of conforming is a placing, a protecting, or a strengthening, it is said, 'the meaning is one who makes it firm.' 'They delight here' (āramanti), thus 'ārāma'; a place for delighting. And because this same meaning is obtained even without the long 'ā', it is said, 'samaggaramo is also a Pāḷi reading, and this is the very meaning here.'

Mammāni viya mammāni, yesu pharusavācāya chupitamattesu duṭṭhārūsu viya ghaṭṭitesu cittaṃ adhimattaṃ dukkhappattaṃ hoti. Kāni pana tāni? Jātiādīni akkosavatthūni. Tāni chijjanti, bhijjanti vā yena kāyavacīpayogena, so mammacchedako. Ekantena pharusacetanā pharusavācā pharusaṃ vadati etāyāti. Kathaṃ pana ekantapharusacetanā hoti? Duṭṭhacittatāya. Tassāti ekantapharusacetanāya eva pharusavācābhāvassa. Mammacchedako savanapharusatāyāti adhippāyo. Cittasaṇhatāya pharusavācā na hoti kammapatha’ppattattā, kammabhāvaṃ pana na sakkā vāretunti. Evaṃ anvayavasena cetanāpharusatāya pharusavācaṃ sādhetvā idāni tameva paṭipakkhanayena sādhetuṃ “vacanasaṇhatāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sā pharusavācā[M 1.0121]. Yanti yaṃ puggalaṃ. Etthāpi kammapathabhāvaṃ appattā appasāvajjā, itarā mahāsāvajjā, tathā kilesānaṃ mudutibbatābhāve. Keci pana “yaṃ uddissa pharusavācā payujjanti, tassa sammukhāva sīsaṃ etī”ti, eke “parammukhāpi pharusavācā hotiyevā”ti vadanti. Tatthāyamadhippāyo yutto siyā – sammukhā payoge agāravādīnaṃ balavabhāvato siyā cetanā [P 1.0155] balavatī, parassa ca tadatthajānanaṃ, na tathā asammukhāti. Yathā pana akkosite mate āḷahane katā khamanā upavādantarāyaṃ nivatteti, evaṃ “parammukhā payuttāpi pharusavācā hotiyevā”ti sakkā viññātunti. Kupitacittanti akkosādhippāyeneva kupitacittaṃ, na maraṇādhippāyena. Maraṇādhippāyena hi cittakope sati byāpādoyeva hotīti. Etthāti –

Like vital spots upon vital spots, when merely touched by harsh speech, as if festering sores were struck, the mind becomes exceedingly afflicted with suffering. And what are those? The bases for abuse, such as birth, etc. That bodily and verbal action by which they are cut or broken is a 'cutter of vital spots.' Harsh speech is entirely harsh intention; by means of it one speaks harshly. But how does one have entirely harsh intention? Through a malicious mind. That is, the state of being harsh speech arises from entirely harsh intention. The 'cutter of vital spots' refers to the harshness to the hearing. Due to the gentleness of mind, harsh speech does not become a full course of action (kammapatha), yet its karmic nature cannot be prevented. Thus, by way of direct correspondence, harsh speech is established through the harshness of intention. Now, to establish the same through the opposite method, it is said, 'through the gentleness of speech,' etc. That is harsh speech. 'Yanti' means 'which person.' Here too, if it does not reach the level of a full course of action, it is less blameworthy; otherwise, it is highly blameworthy, likewise, depending on the mildness or intensity of the defilements. Some say, 'Harsh speech is directed toward someone, and it culminates only in their presence.' Others say, 'Harsh speech occurs even in absence.' Here, this intended meaning is appropriate—in an application in person, due to the strength of disrespect and so on, the intention is stronger, and the other person's understanding of the meaning is also greater; it is not the same when not in person. Just as forgiveness offered at the funeral pyre of one who has died after being abused removes the obstacle of reproach, so too it can be understood that 'even harsh speech directed in absence still occurs.' 'With an angry mind'—this refers to a mind angry with the intent to abuse, not with the intent to kill. For if the mind is angry with intent to kill, it is simply ill will (byāpāda). Here—

“Nelaṅgo setapacchādo, ekāro vattatī ratho;

Anīghaṃ passa āyantaṃ, chinnasotaṃ abandhana”nti. (saṃ. ni. 4.347; udā. 65);

"The chariot, Nelaṅga, with a white covering and a single wheel, rolls on. See him coming, free from affliction, with the stream cut, unbound." (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.347; Udāna 65)

Imissā gāthāya. Sīlañhettha “nelaṅga”nti vuttaṃ. Tenevāha citto gahapati “nelaṅganti kho bhante sīlānametaṃ adhivacana”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.347). Sukumārāti apharusatāya mudukā. Purassāti ettha pura-saddo tannivāsīvācako daṭṭhabbo “gāmo āgato”tiādīsu viya. Tenevāha “nagaravāsīna”nti. Manaṃ appāyati vaḍḍhetīti manāpā. Tena vuttaṃ “cittavuḍḍhikarā”ti. Āsevanaṃ bhāvanaṃ bahulīkaraṇaṃ. Yaṃ gāhayituṃ pavattito, tena aggahite appasāvajjo [V 1.0108] gahite mahāsāvajjoti, idhāpi kilesānaṃ mudutibbatāvasenāpi appasāvajjamahāsāvajjatā labbhatiyeva.

Of this verse. Here, virtue is called 'nelaṅga.' Therefore, the householder Citta said, "Venerable sir, 'nelaṅga' is a designation for virtue" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.347). 'Sukumārā' means soft due to being uncoarse. Regarding 'Purassā,' here the word 'pura' should be understood as referring to those dwelling there, just as in phrases like 'the village has come.' Hence, it is said, 'for town-dwellers.' 'Manāpā' means that which pleases and increases the mind. Therefore, it is said, 'enhancing the mind.' Āsevana is practice, cultivation, frequent repetition. That which is set forth to be grasped: if not grasped, it is of little fault; if grasped, it is of great fault. Here too, depending on the mildness or intensity of the defilements, the state of having little or great fault is obtained.

“Kālavādī”tiādi samphappalāpā paṭiviratassa paṭipattidassanaṃ. Yathā hi “pāṇātipātā paṭivirato”tiādi pāṇātipātappahānapaṭipattidassanaṃ. “Pāṇātipātaṃ pahāya viharatī”ti hi vutte kathaṃ pāṇātipātappahānaṃ hotīti? Apekkhāsabbhāvato “pāṇātipātā paṭivirato hotī”ti vuttaṃ, sā pana virati kathanti [P 1.0156] āha “nihitadaṇḍo nihitasattho”ti, tañca daṇḍasatthanidhānaṃ kathanti vuttaṃ “lajjī”tiādi, evaṃ uttaruttaraṃ purimassa purimassa upāyasandassanaṃ, tathā adinnādānādīsu [M 1.0122] yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “kālavādītiādi samphappalāpā paṭiviratassa paṭipattidassana”nti. Atthasañhitāpi hi vācā ayuttakālappayogena atthāvahā na siyāti anatthaviññāpanavācaṃ anulometi, tasmā samphappalāpaṃ pajahantena akālavāditā parivajjetabbāti vuttaṃ “kālavādī”ti. Kālena vadantenāpi ubhayānatthasādhanato abhūtaṃ parivajjetabbanti āha “bhūtavādī”ti. Bhūtañca vadantena yaṃ idhalokaparalokahitasampādakaṃ, tadeva vattabbanti dassetuṃ “atthavādī”ti vuttaṃ. Atthaṃ vadantenāpi na lokiyadhammasannissitameva vattabbaṃ, atha kho lokuttaradhammasannissitaṃ pīti dassetuṃ “dhammavādī”ti vuttaṃ. Yathā ca attho lokuttaradhammasannissito hoti, taṃ dassanatthaṃ “vinayavādī”ti vuttaṃ. Pātimokkhasaṃvaro satisaṃvaro ñāṇasaṃvaro khantisaṃvaro vīriyasaṃvaroti hi pañcannaṃ saṃvarānaṃ, tadaṅgavinayo vikkhambhanavinayo samucchedavinayo paṭippassaddhivinayo nissaraṇavinayoti pañcannaṃ vinayānañca vasena vuccamāno attho nibbānādhigamahetubhāvato lokuttaradhammasannissito hotīti.

"Speaking at the right time," etc., is a demonstration of the practice of one who abstains from frivolous talk. Just as "abstaining from killing living beings," etc., demonstrates the practice of abandoning killing. For when it is said, "He dwells having abandoned killing living beings," in anticipation of the question, "How is the abandonment of killing accomplished?" it is said, "He abstains from killing living beings." But how is that abstinence accomplished? It is said, "having laid down the rod, having laid down the weapon." And how is that laying down of the rod and weapon accomplished? It is said, "being conscientious," etc. Thus, successively, the means for each preceding point is shown. Similarly, it should be applied to taking what is not given, etc., as appropriate. Therefore, it is said, "'Speaking at the right time,' etc., is a demonstration of the practice of one who abstains from frivolous talk." For even speech connected with meaning, if spoken at the wrong time, would not bring benefit; thus, it amounts to speech that conveys what is unbeneficial. Therefore, one abandoning frivolous talk should avoid speaking at the wrong time—hence, "speaking at the right time." Even when speaking at the right time, one should avoid falsehood because it accomplishes harm for both—hence, "speaking what is true." And when speaking what is true, one should speak only what is conducive to benefit in this world and the next—hence, "speaking what is meaningful." When speaking what is meaningful, one should not speak only of worldly matters, but also of matters connected with the supramundane—hence, "speaking the Dhamma." To show how the meaning is connected with the supramundane Dhamma, it is said, "speaking the discipline." For the meaning, when spoken of in terms of the five restraints—restraint by the Pātimokkha, restraint by mindfulness, restraint by knowledge, restraint by patience, and restraint by energy—and the five kinds of discipline—discipline by temporary suspension, discipline by suppression, discipline by eradication, discipline by tranquilization, and discipline by escape—is connected with the supramundane Dhamma because it serves as a cause for attaining Nibbāna.

Evaṃ guṇavisesayutto ca attho vuccamāno desanākosalle sati sobhati, kiccakaro ca hoti, nāññathāti dassetuṃ “nidhānavatiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā”ti vuttaṃ. Idāni taṃ desanākosallaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “kālenā”tiādimāha. Ajjhāsayaṭṭhuppattīnaṃ pucchāya ca vasena otiṇṇe desanāvisaye ekaṃsādibyākaraṇavibhāgaṃ sallakkhetvā ṭhapanāhetudāharaṇasaṃsandanāni taṃtaṃkālānurūpaṃ vibhāventiyā parimitaparicchinnarūpāya vipulataragambhīrudārapahūtatthavitthārasaṅgāhakāya [P 1.0157] desanāya pare yathājjhāsayaṃ paramatthasiddhiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpento “desanākusalo”ti vuccatīti evamettha atthayojanā veditabbā.

Thus, to show that when a meaning endowed with special qualities is expressed, it shines and becomes effective if there is skill in teaching, and not otherwise, it is said, "He has spoken words that are like a treasure." Now, to elaborate on that skill in teaching, it begins with "at the right time." When the subject of teaching has been entered upon by way of inclinations, arising circumstances, and questions, having considered the distinctions of definitive answers and the like, one who establishes others in the highest attainment according to their inclinations by means of a teaching that is of limited and defined form, yet which gathers vast, profound, noble, and abundant meanings and details, and which appropriately explains the setting aside of questions, reasons, examples, and connections in accordance with the particular time—such a one is called "skilled in teaching." This is how the meaning should be understood here.

10. Evaṃ paṭipāṭiyā satta mūlasikkhāpadāni vibhajitvā satipi abhijjhādippahānassa [V 1.0109] saṃvarasīlasikkhāsaṅgahe upariguṇasaṅgahato, lokiyaputhujjanāvisayato ca uttaradesanāya saṅgaṇhituṃ taṃ pariharitvā pacurajanapākaṭaṃ ācārasīlameva vibhajanto bhagavā “bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhā”tiādimāha. Tattha gāmoti samūho. Nanu ca rukkhādayo cittarahitatāya na jīvā, cittarahitatā ca paripphandābhāvato[M 1.0123], chinne viruhanato, visadisajātikabhāvato, catuyoniappariyāpannato ca veditabbā, vuḍḍhi pana pavāḷasilālavaṇānampi vijjatīti na tesaṃ jīvabhāve kāraṇaṃ, visayaggahaṇañca parikappanāmattaṃ supanaṃ viya ciñcādīnaṃ, tathā dohaḷādayo, tattha kasmā bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhā paṭivirati icchitāti? Samaṇasāruppato, sannissitasattānurakkhaṇato ca. Tenevāha “jīvasaññino hi moghapurisā manussā rukkhasmi”ntiādi (pāci. 89). Nīlatiṇarukkhādikassāti allatiṇassa ceva allarukkhādikassa ca. Ādi-saddena osadhigacchalatādayo veditabbā.

10. Thus, having analyzed the seven root training rules in sequence, the Blessed One—even though the abandonment of covetousness and so forth is included in the training in the virtue of restraint—avoided that topic in order to include it in a higher teaching on account of its inclusion of higher qualities and because it is beyond the scope of ordinary worldlings. Instead, analyzing just the virtue of conduct, which is manifest to many people, he began with the phrase, "from the destruction of seed-kinds and plant-kinds." Therein, 'gāma' means a collection. Now, are not trees and the like non-living because they lack consciousness? And their lack of consciousness is to be understood from their lack of movement, from their growing when cut, from their being of a dissimilar class of birth, and from their not being included among the four kinds of birth. Growth, however, is also found in coral, rock-salt, and salt, so that is not a reason for their being alive. The perception of them as objects is merely conceptual, like a dream, for plants like the Ciñcā, and similarly with longings and the like. So why is abstention from destroying seed-kinds and plant-kinds desired? Because it is fitting for an ascetic and because it protects the living beings who depend on them. For this reason, it is said, "Foolish people, humans have the perception of life in a tree" (Pāc. 89). "Of green grass and trees, etc." means of fresh grass and fresh trees, etc. By the word "etc." should be understood medicinal plants, shrubs, and vines.

Ekaṃ bhattaṃ ekabhattaṃ, taṃ assa atthīti ekabhattiko, ekasmiṃ divase ekavārameva bhuñjanako. Tayidaṃ rattibhojanopi siyāti tannivattanatthamāha “rattūparato”ti. Evampi aparaṇhabhojīpi siyā ekabhattikoti tadāsaṅkānivattanatthaṃ “virato vikālabhojanā”ti vuttaṃ. Aruṇuggamanato paṭṭhāya yāva [P 1.0158] majjhanhikā, ayaṃ buddhānaṃ āciṇṇasamāciṇṇo bhojanassa kālo nāma, tadañño vikālo. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana dutiyapadena rattibhojanassa paṭikkhittattā aparaṇho “vikālo”ti vutto.

One meal, a single meal—he who has that is a one-meal eater, one who eats only once a day. This could include eating at night, so to prevent that, it is stated: “abstaining from night-eating.” Even so, one might eat in the afternoon and still be a one-meal eater, so to dispel that doubt, it is said: “abstaining from untimely eating.” From the rising of the dawn until midday—this is the time for eating, habitually practiced by the Buddhas; any other time is untimely. However, in the commentary, because eating at night is prohibited by the second term, the afternoon is called “untimely.”

Saṅkhepato “sabbapāpassa akaraṇa”ntiādi (dī. ni. 2.90; dha. pa. 183; netti. 30, 50, 116, 124) nayappavattaṃ bhagavato sāsanaṃ accantachandarāgappavattito naccādīnaṃ dassanaṃ na anulometīti āha “sāsanassa ananulomattā”ti. Attanā payojiyamānaṃ, parehi payojāpiyamānañca naccaṃ naccabhāvasāmaññato pāḷiyaṃ ekeneva nacca-saddena gahitaṃ, tathā gītavādita-saddena cāti āha “naccananaccāpanādivasenā”ti. Ādi-saddena gāyanagāyāpanavādanavādāpanāni saṅgaṇhāti. Dassanena cettha savanampi saṅgahitaṃ virūpekasesanayena. Ālocanasabhāvatāya vā pañcannaṃ viññāṇānaṃ savanakiriyāyapi dassanasaṅkhepasabbhāvato “dassanā” icceva vuttaṃ. Avisūkabhūtassa gītassa savanaṃ kadāci vaṭṭatīti āha “visūkabhūtā dassanā”ti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ paramatthajotikāya khuddakapāṭhaṭṭhakathāya (khu. pā. aṭṭha. pacchimapañcasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) “dhammūpasaṃhitampi cettha gītaṃ vaṭṭati, gītūpasaṃhito dhammo na vaṭṭatī”ti.

In brief, the Blessed One’s teaching, as conveyed in the method of “abstaining from all evil” (Dī. Ni. 2.90; Dha. Pa. 183; Netti. 30, 50, 116, 124), does not endorse the viewing of dances and the like, which arise from excessive desire and passion. Hence, it is said, “because it is contrary to the teaching.” Dancing, whether performed by oneself or induced by others, is referred to in the Pāli texts by the single term “nacca” (dancing), and similarly by the terms “gīta” (singing) and “vādita” (instrumental music). Thus, it is stated, “by way of dancing, causing to dance, and so on.” The term “and so on” includes singing, causing to sing, playing instruments, and causing to play instruments. Here, hearing is also included under seeing, following the ekasesa method. Alternatively, due to the perceptual nature of the five consciousnesses, the act of hearing is also summarized under “seeing,” hence the term “dassanā” (seeing) is used. The hearing of song that is not frivolous is occasionally permissible, hence it is said, “frivolous seeing.” As stated in the Paramatthajotikā commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha (Khu. Pā. Aṭṭha., explanation of the last five training rules): “Here, song connected with the Dhamma is permissible, but the Dhamma connected with song is not permissible.”

Uccāti [V 1.0110][M 1.0124] uccasaddena samānatthaṃ ekaṃ saddantaraṃ, seti etthāti sayanaṃ. Uccāsayanaṃ mahāsayanañca samaṇasārupparahitaṃ adhippetanti āha “pamāṇātikkantaṃ, akappiyattharaṇa”nti[P 1.0159]. Āsandādiāsanañcettha sayanena saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yasmā pana ādhāre paṭikkhitte tadādhārakiriyā paṭikkhittāva hoti, tasmā “uccāsayanamahāsayanā” icceva vuttaṃ, atthato pana tadupabhogabhūta nisajjānipajjanehi virati dassitāti daṭṭhabbā. Uccāsayanasayanamahāsayanasayanāti vā etasmiṃ atthe ekasesanayena ayaṃ niddeso kato yathā “nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatana”nti (ma. ni. 3.126; saṃ. ni. 2.1; udā. 1). Āsanakiriyāpubbakattā sayanakiriyāya sayanaggahaṇeneva āsanaṃ gahitanti veditabbaṃ.

“Uccā” is another word synonymous with “ucca” (high); “sayanaṃ” (bed/couch) means that on which one lies down. High beds and luxurious beds are intended to be unsuitable for ascetics, hence it is said: “Beyond measure, an unallowable covering.” Here, seats such as chairs are to be understood as included under “sayanaṃ.” However, since when the support is rejected, the action supported is also rejected, therefore, only “high beds and luxurious beds” are mentioned. In meaning, however, abstaining from both sitting and lying down on such things is to be understood. Alternatively, in this context, this explanation is given concisely, using the ekasesa method, as in: “Name-and-form conditions the six sense bases” (Majjhima Nikāya 3.126; Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.1; Udāna 1). Because sitting precedes lying down, the seat is included by the single mention of “bed,” and this should be understood.

Aññehi gāhāpane upanikkhittasādiyane ca paṭiggahaṇattho labbhatīti āha “na uggaṇhāpeti, na upanikkhittaṃ sādīyatī”ti. Atha vā tividhaṃ paṭiggahaṇaṃ kāyena vācāya manasā. Tattha kāyena paṭiggahaṇaṃ uggaṇhanaṃ, vācāya paṭiggahaṇaṃ uggahāpanaṃ, manasā paṭiggahaṇaṃ sādiyananti tividhampi paṭiggahaṇaṃ sāmaññaniddesena, ekasesanayena vā gahetvā “paṭiggahaṇā”ti vuttanti āha “neva naṃ uggaṇhātī”tiādi. Esa nayo “āmakadhaññapaṭiggahaṇā”tiādīsupi. Nīvārādiupadhaññassa sāliyādimūladhaññantogadhattā vuttaṃ “sattavidhassā”ti. “Anujānāmi bhikkhave pañca vasāni bhesajjāni acchavasaṃ macchavasaṃ susukāvasaṃ sūkaravasaṃ gadrabhavasa”nti (mahāva. 262) vuttattā idaṃ odissa anuññātaṃ nāma, tassa pana “kāle paṭiggahita”nti (mahāva. 262) vuttattā paṭiggahaṇaṃ vaṭṭatīti āha “aññatra odissa anuññātā”ti.

The meaning of acceptance is obtained through causing others to take and through approving of what is placed nearby, hence it is said: “He does not cause to take, nor does he approve of what is placed nearby.” Alternatively, acceptance is threefold: by body, speech, or mind. Here, acceptance by body is taking, acceptance by speech is causing to take, and acceptance by mind is approving. Thus, all three types of acceptance are included by a general designation, or by the ekasesa method, and thus the term “acceptances” is used, as stated: “He does not take it himself,” etc. This is the method in cases like “acceptance of raw grain,” etc. The phrase “of seven kinds” is stated because inferior grains like nīvāra rice are included under staple grains such as rice. “I allow, monks, five kinds of fat as medicine: bear fat, fish fat, alligator fat, pig fat, donkey fat” (Mahāvagga 262). Therefore, this is specifically permitted. However, since it is said, “[if] received at the proper time” (Mahāvagga 262), acceptance is allowable—hence the statement, “except what is specifically permitted.”

Akkamatīti nippīḷeti. Pubbabhāge akkamatīti sambandho. Hadayanti nāḷiādimānabhājanānaṃ abbhantaraṃ. Tilādīnaṃ [P 1.0160] nāḷiādīhi minanakāle ussāpitasikhāyeva sikhā, tassā bhedo hāpanaṃ. Kecīti sārasamāsācariyā, uttaravihāravāsino ca.

“Akkamati” means “it crushes,” that is, “it oppresses.” “It crushes” is connected to the earlier part. “Hadaya” refers to the interior of measuring vessels such as tubes and the like. When measuring grains like sesame with tubes and the like, the raised tip is the crest, and its breaking is the removal. Some, meaning the teachers of the Sārasamāsa and the residents of the Uttara Vihāra.

Vadhoti muṭṭhippahārakasātāḷanādīhi hiṃsanaṃ, viheṭhananti attho. Viheṭhanatthopi hi vadhasaddo dissati “attānaṃ vadhitvā vadhitvā”tiādīsu (pāci. 880). Yathā hi appaṭiggahabhāvasāmaññe satipi pabbajitehi appaṭiggahitabbavatthuvisesabhāvasandassanatthaṃ itthikumāridāsidāsādayo vibhāgena vuttā[M 1.0125], evaṃ parassaharaṇabhāvato adinnādānabhāvasāmaññe satipi tulākūṭādayo adinnādānavisesabhāvadassanatthaṃ vibhāgena vuttā, na evaṃ pāṇātipātapariyāyassa vadhassa punaggahaṇe payojanaṃ atthi. “Tattha sayaṅkāro, idha paraṃkāro”ti ca [V 1.0111] na sakkā vattuṃ “kāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā chappayogā”ti ca vuttattā. Tasmā yathāvuttoyeva attho sundarataro. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “vadhoti māraṇa”nti vuttaṃ, tampi pothanameva sandhāyāti ca sakkā viññātuṃ māraṇa-saddassa vihiṃsanepi dissanato.

“Vadha” means harming with blows of the fist, slaps, and the like; it means torment (viheṭhana). The term “vadha” is also seen in the sense of torment (viheṭhana), as in phrases like “having tormented oneself again and again” (Pāc. 880). Just as, despite the general principle of non-acceptance (appaṭiggaha-bhāva), specific items like women, girls, male slaves, and female slaves are separately mentioned to clarify the specific nature of things not to be accepted by renunciants, so too, despite the general principle of taking what belongs to another (parassa-haraṇa-bhāva) as theft (adinnādāna-bhāva), specific cases like false scales and counterfeit coins are separately mentioned to illustrate particular forms of theft (adinnādāna). However, there is no need to repeat the definition of killing (pāṇātipāta) under the term “vadha.” Nor can it be said, “There it is self-inflicted, here it is inflicted by another,” because it has been stated that 'volition, which originates action through body and speech, has six applications.' Therefore, the meaning as previously explained is more fitting. In the commentary, however, it is said, “‘Vadha’ means killing (māraṇa),” but this too can be understood as referring to striking (pothana), since the term ‘killing’ (māraṇa) is also seen in the sense of harming (vihiṃsana).

Ettāvatāti “pāṇātipātaṃ pahāyā”tiādinā “chedana…pe… sahasākārā paṭivirato”ti etaparimāṇena pāṭhena. Antarābhedaṃ aggahetvā pāḷiyaṃ āgatanayena chabbīsatisikkhāpadasaṅgahaṃ yebhuyyena sikkhāpadānaṃ avibhattattā cūḷasīlaṃ nāma. Desanāvasena hi idha cūḷamajjhimādibhāvo adhippeto, na dhammavasena. Tathā hi idha saṅkhittena uddiṭṭhānaṃ sikkhāpadānaṃ avibhattānaṃ vibhajanavasena [P 1.0161] majjhimasīladesanā pavattā. Tenevāha “majjhimasīlaṃ vitthārento”ti.

“Up to this point” (ettāvatā) means by the passage beginning with “abstaining from the destruction of life” and ending with “refraining from violence” (sahasākārā paṭivirato)—this extent of the text. Because the collection of twenty-six training rules is presented in the Pāli text without internal divisions, and because the majority of the training rules are undifferentiated, it is called the “Minor Morality.” Here, the terms “minor,” “middle,” etc., refer to the manner of teaching, not to the nature of the Dhamma itself. For here, the exposition of the Middle Morality proceeds by way of dividing the undifferentiated training rules concisely enumerated here. Hence, it is said, “expounding the Middle Morality.”

Cūḷasīlavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the Minor Morality is concluded.

Majjhimasīlavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Middle Morality

11. Tattha yathāti opammatthe nipāto. Vāti vikappanatthe. Panāti vacanālaṅkāre. Eketi aññe. Bhontoti sādhūnaṃ piyasamudāhāro. Sādhavo hi pare “bhonto”ti vā, “devānaṃ piyā”ti vā “āyasmanto”ti vā samālapanti. Yaṃ kiñci pabbajjaṃ upagatā samaṇā. Jātimattena brāhmaṇā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ussāhaṃ katvā mama vaṇṇaṃ vadamānopi puthujjano “pāṇātipātaṃ pahāya pāṇātipātā paṭivirato”tiādinā parānuddesikanayena vā yathā paneke bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇabhāvaṃ paṭijānamānā, parehi ca tathāsambhāviyamānā tadanurūpapaṭipattiṃ ajānanato, asamatthato ca na abhisambhuṇanti, na evamayaṃ, ayaṃ pana samaṇo gotamo sabbathāpi samaṇasāruppapaṭipadaṃ pūresiyevāti evaṃ aññuddesikanayena vā sabbathāpi ācārasīlamattameva vadeyyuṃ, na taduttarinti.

11. Here, 'yathā' is a particle in the sense of comparison. 'Vā' is in the sense of an alternative. 'Pana' is a verbal embellishment. 'Eke' means others. 'Bhonto' is an affectionate address of the virtuous. Indeed, virtuous people address others as 'bhonto,' 'dear to the gods,' or 'venerable ones.' Recluses are those who have gone forth into any form of homelessness. Brahmins are so by birth alone. This is what is meant: An ordinary person, making an effort and speaking my praise, might speak either by way of indirect reference, saying: 'Just as some honorable recluses and brahmins, while claiming their status and being esteemed as such by others, do not accomplish the corresponding practice due to ignorance and incapability, this one is not like that; this recluse Gotama, on the contrary, fully accomplishes the conduct befitting a recluse in every respect.' Or they might speak by way of referring to another, saying: 'Having abandoned the destruction of life, he refrains from the destruction of life,' and so on. In any case, they would speak only of mere conduct and virtue, and nothing beyond that.

Bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhapade [M 1.0126] saddakkamena appadhānabhūtopi bījagāmabhūtagāmo niddisitabbatāya padhānabhāvaṃ paṭilabhati. Añño hi saddakkamo añño atthakkamoti āha “katamo so bījagāmabhūtagāmo”ti. Tasmiñhi vibhatte tabbisayatāya samārambhopi vibhattova hotīti[V 1.0112]. Tenevāha bhagavā “mūlabīja”ntiādi. Mūlameva bījaṃ mūlabījaṃ, mūlaṃ bījaṃ etassātipi mūlabījaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Phaḷubījanti pabbabījaṃ. Paccayantarasamavāye sadisaphaluppattiyā visesakāraṇabhāvato viruhaṇasamatthe sāraphale niruḷho bīja-saddo tadatthasaṃsiddhiyā mūlādīsupi kesuci pavattatīti mūlādito nivattanatthaṃ ekena bīja-saddena visesetvā vuttaṃ “bījabīja”nti. “Rūparūpaṃ[P 1.0162], dukkhadukkha”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.327) ca yathā. Kasmā panettha bījagāmabhūtagāmaṃ pucchitvā bījagāmo eva vibhattoti? Na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nanu avocumha “mūlameva bījaṃ mūlabījaṃ, mūlaṃ bījaṃ etassātipi mūlabījanti”. Tattha purimena bījagāmo niddiṭṭho, dutiyena bhūtagāmo, duvidhopesa sāmaññaniddesena, mūlabījañca mūlabījañca mūlabījanti ekasesanayena vā pāḷiyaṃ niddiṭṭhoti veditabbo. Tenevāha “sabbañheta”ntiādi.

In the term ‘injuring seed-life and plant-life,’ even though seed-life and plant-life are secondary in the sequence of terms, they attain prominence because they must be specifically identified. For the sequence of terms is one thing, and the sequence of meaning is another; hence the question, “What is this seed-life and plant-life?” When that is distinguished, the injuring related to it is also distinguished. Therefore the Blessed One said, “root-seed,” and so on. “Root-seed” means the root itself is the seed, or that the root is the seed belonging to it. The same method applies to the rest. “Joint-seed” means seed from nodes. Because the word ‘seed’ (bīja) is established in the essential fruit capable of sprouting, due to its being a specific cause for the production of similar fruit when other conditions are present, and because it sometimes applies to roots and so forth for the fulfillment of its meaning, the term ‘seed-seed’ is used to distinguish it from roots and the like. Just as in “form-form” and “suffering-suffering” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.327). But why, after asking about seed-life and plant-life here, is only seed-life explicitly defined? This should not be seen as such. Did we not say, “The root itself is the seed—root-seed; or the root is the seed belonging to it—thus, root-seed”? In that case, by the former, seed-life is defined, and by the latter, plant-life; this is a twofold general explanation, or alternatively, it should be understood that in the Pāli text, 'root-seed' is stated by way of the 'single remainder' method, where two instances are reduced to one. Therefore it is said, “All this,” and so on.

12. “Sannidhikatassā”ti etena “sannidhikāraparibhoga”nti ettha kāra-saddassa kammatthataṃ dasseti. Yathā vā “ācayaṃgamino”ti vattabbe anunāsikalopena “ācayagāmino”ti (dha. sa. 10) niddeso kato, evaṃ “sannidhikāraṃ paribhoga”nti vattabbe anunāsikalopena “sannidhikāraparibhoga”nti vuttaṃ, sannidhiṃ katvā paribhoganti attho.

12. By “sannidhikatassa” (of one who has made a store), it shows that in “sannidhikāraparibhoga” (using after having made a store), the word kāra has the meaning of action. Just as when “ācayaṃgamino” should be said, the elision of the nasal results in the designation “ācayagāmino” (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 10), so too when “sannidhikāraṃ paribhoga” should be said, the elision of the nasal results in “sannidhikāraparibhoga,” meaning “using after having made a store.”

Sammā kilese likhatīti sallekho, suttantanayena paṭipatti. Pariyāyati kappīyatīti pariyāyo, kappiyavācānusārena paṭipatti. Kilesehi āmasitabbato āmisaṃ, yaṃ kiñci upabhogārahaṃ vatthu. Tenevāha “āmisanti vuttāvasesa”nti. Nayadassanañhetaṃ sannidhivatthūnaṃ. Udakakaddameti udake ca kaddame ca. Acchathāti nisīdatha. Gīvāyāmakanti gīvaṃ āyamitvā, yathā ca bhutte atibhuttatāya gīvā āyamitabbāva hoti, evanti attho. Catubhāgamattanti kuḍubamattaṃ. “Kappiyakuṭiya”ntiādi vinayavasena vuttaṃ.

“Rightly scratches away defilements” is sallekha, the practice according to the Suttanta method. “It is fashioned comprehensively, thus it is a pariyāya,” the practice following the words of suitability. “Liable to be clung to by defilements” is āmisa, any object fit for enjoyment. Therefore it is said, “āmisa means the remaining things spoken of.” This is a way of showing regarding stored objects. “Water and mud” means in water and in mud. “Acchatha” means to sit. “Stretching out the neck” means stretching out the neck, just as when one has eaten excessively the neck has to be stretched out; such is the meaning. “A quarter part” means about a kuḍuba. “The allowable hut” and so on is said according to the Vinaya.

13. Ettakampīti [M 1.0127] vinicchayavicāraṇāvatthukittanampi[P 1.0163]. Payojanamattamevāti padatthayojanamattameva. Yassa pana padassa vitthārakathaṃ vinā na sakkā attho viññātuṃ, tattha vitthārakathāpi padatthasaṅgahameva gacchati. Kutūhalavasena pekkhitabbato pekkhā, naṭasatthavidhinā naṭānañca payogo. Naṭasamūhena pana janasamūhe karaṇavasena “naṭasamajja”nti vuttaṃ, sārasamāse “pekkhā maha”nti vuttaṃ. Ghanatāḷaṃ nāma daṇḍamayatāḷaṃ, silāsalākatāḷaṃ vā. Eketi sārasamāsācariyā, uttaravihāravāsino ca. Yathā cettha, evaṃ ito paresupi “eke”ti āgataṭṭhānesu. Caturassaambaṇakatāḷaṃ nāma rukkhasāradaṇḍādīsu yena kenaci caturassaambaṇakaṃ katvā [V 1.0113] catūsu passesu cammena onandhitvā katavāditaṃ. Abbhokkiraṇaṃ raṅgabalīkaraṇaṃ, yā “nandī”ti vuccati. Sobhanakaranti sobhanakaraṇaṃ, “sobhanagharaka”nti sārasamāse vuttaṃ. Caṇḍālānamidanti caṇḍālaṃ. Sāṇe udakena temetvā aññamaññaṃ ākoṭanakīḷā sāṇadhovanaṃ. Indajālenāti aṭṭhidhovanamantaṃ parijappitvā yathā pare aṭṭhīniyeva passanti, evaṃ tacādīnaṃ antaradhāpanamāyāya. Sakaṭabyūhādīti ādi-saddena cakkapadumakaḷīrabyūhādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

13. “Ettakampi” refers to the mentioning of the basis for investigation and deliberation. “Payojanamattamevāti” means merely the application of the word’s meaning. However, for words whose meaning cannot be understood without detailed explanation, that detailed explanation is also included in the collection of the word’s meaning. “Pekkhā” means viewing out of curiosity, and also the performance of actors according to the rules of their craft. Because of the performance by a group of actors in a crowd of people, it is called an “actor’s assembly” (naṭasamajja); in concise composition, it is called “pekkhā maha” (a great spectacle). “Ghanatāḷa” means a cymbal made of wood, or a castanet of stone slivers. “Eke” refers to the teachers of concise composition and also the residents of the Uttara Vihāra. As it is here, so too in other places where “eke” appears. “Caturassaambaṇakatāḷa” refers to a four-sided ambaṇaka drum made by stretching leather over a frame of wood or other materials, making it playable on all four sides. “Abbhokkiraṇa” means sprinkling and making offerings on the stage, which is called “nandī” (joy). “Sobhanakara” means beautifying, and in concise composition, it is called “sobhanagharaka” (a beautiful house). “Caṇḍālānamidaṃ” means the caṇḍāla performance. “Sāṇadhovana” refers to the game of wetting hemp with water and striking each other. “Indajāla” means by the net of Indra, that is, by muttering the bone-washing mantra so that others see only the bones, thus concealing the skin and other parts by illusion. “Sakaṭabyūhādī” (cart formations, etc.)—the word “etc.” includes formations like wheels, lotuses, and bamboo shoots.

14. Padānīti [P 1.0164] sārīnaṃ patiṭṭhānaṭṭhānāni. Dasapadaṃ nāma dvīhi pantīhi vīsatiyā padehi kīḷanajūtaṃ. Pāsakaṃ vuccati chasu passesu ekekaṃ yāva chakkaṃ dassetvā katakīḷanakaṃ, taṃ vaḍḍhetvā yathāladdhaṃ ekakādivasena sāriyo apanentā upanentā ca kīḷanti. Ghaṭena kīḷā ghaṭikāti eke. Bahūsu salākāsu visesarahitaṃ ekaṃ salākaṃ gahetvā tāsu pakkhipitvā puna tasseva uddharaṇaṃ salākahatthanti eke. Paṇṇena vaṃsākārena katā nāḷikā. Tenevāha “taṃ dhamantā”ti. “Pucchantassa mukhāgataṃ akkharaṃ gahetvā naṭṭhamutti lābhālābhādijānanakīḷā akkharikā”tipi vadanti. “Vāditānurūpaṃ naccanaṃ gāyanaṃ vā yathāvajjaṃ” tipi vadanti. “Evaṃ kate jayo bhavissati, aññathā parājayo”ti jayaparājaye purakkhatvā payogakaraṇavasena parihārapathādīnampi jūtapamādaṭṭhānabhāvo veditabbo. Paṅgacīrādīhipi vaṃsādīhi kātabbakiccasiddhiasiddhijayaparājayāvaho payogo vuttoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Yathāvajja”nti ca [M 1.0128] kāṇādīhi sadisatākāradassanehi jayaparājayavasena jūtakīḷitabhāvena vuttaṃ.

14. “Padāni” refers to the places where the pieces are set. “Dasapada” is a gambling game played with twenty squares in two rows. “Pāsaka” refers to a game played with a die, which is made to show from one up to six on its six sides; they play by increasing the throw and moving pieces forward and backward according to what is obtained, by ones and so on. Some say that “ghaṭikā” is a game played with a pot. Some say that “salākahattha” is taking one stick without distinction from many sticks, putting it among them, and then drawing that same one out again. “Nāḷikā” is a tube made from a leaf in the shape of bamboo. Therefore it is said, “blowing it.” Some also say that “akkharikā” is a game of knowing gain or loss, or lost items, by taking a letter that comes from the mouth of the one asking. Others also say that 'yathāvajjaṃ' is 'dancing or singing according to the music.' “If done thus, there will be victory; otherwise, defeat”—thus, by making effort with victory and defeat in mind, the state of being a basis for gambling and negligence in things like avoidance paths should be understood. It should be seen that a performance involving things like paṅgacīra, bamboo, etc., which brings about accomplishment or non-accomplishment, victory or defeat, is also mentioned. And “yathāvajja” is said to be a form of gambling based on victory or defeat, by showing mimicry of the blind and so on.

15. Vāḷarūpānīti āharimāni vāḷarūpāni. “Akappiyamañcova pallaṅko”ti sārasamāse. Vānavicittanti bhitticchadādivasena vānena vicitraṃ. Rukkhatūlalatātūlapoṭakītūlānaṃ vasena tiṇṇaṃ tūlānaṃ. Uddalomiyaṃ kecīti sārasamāsācariyā, uttaravihāravāsino ca. Tathā ekantalomiyaṃ. Koseyyakaṭṭissamayanti koseyyakassaṭamayaṃ. Suddhakoseyyanti [P 1.0165] ratanaparisibbanarahitaṃ. “Ṭhapetvā tūlika”nti etena ratanaparisibbanarahitāpi tūlikā na vaṭṭatīti dīpeti. “Ratanaparisibbitānī”ti iminā yāni ratanaparisibbitāni, tāni bhūmattharaṇavasena, yathānurūpaṃ mañcapīṭhādīsu ca upanetuṃ vaṭṭatīti dīpitaṃ hoti. Ajinacammehīti ajinamigacammehi. Tāni kira cammāni sukhumāni, tasmā dupaṭṭatipaṭṭāni katvā sibbanti. Tena vuttaṃ “ajinappaveṇī”ti. Vuttanayenāti vinaye vuttanayena.

15. “Vāḷarūpāni” means artificial animal figures. In the Sārasamāsa, “pallaṅka” means an unallowable couch. “Vānavicitta” means decorated with canopies, wall hangings, etc., by means of weaving. “Rukkhatūla,” “latātūla,” and “poṭakītūla” refer to three types of stuffing: from trees, creepers, and pods. Some, namely the teachers of the Sārasamāsa and the residents of the Uttara Vihāra, say “uddalomīyaṃ.” Likewise, “ekantalomīyaṃ.” “Koseyyakaṭṭissamaya” means made of silk mixed with kaṭṭissa cloth. “Suddhakoseyya” means pure silk, without gem-studded borders. By “except for a mattress,” it indicates that even a mattress without gem-studded borders is not allowed. By “adorned with gems,” it is indicated that those items adorned with gems are allowed to be used as floor coverings or appropriately on beds, seats, etc. “Ajinacammehi” means with the hides of ajina deer. It is said these hides are fine, so they are stitched together with doubled or tripled layers. Hence, it is called “ajinappaveṇī.” “Vuttanayena” means according to the method stated in the Vinaya.

16. Alaṅkārañjanameva na bhesajjaṃ maṇḍanānuyogassa adhippetattā. Mālā-saddo sāsane suddhapupphesupi [V 1.0114] niruḷhoti āha “baddhamālā vā”ti. Mattikakakkanti osadhehi abhisaṅkhataṃ yogamattikakakkaṃ. Caliteti kupite. Lohite sannisinneti duṭṭhalohite khīṇe.

16. “Alaṅkārañjana” is only for adornment, not medicine, since its intention is beautification. The word “mālā” in the Dispensation is conventionally used even for loose flowers, hence he said, “or a bound garland.” “Mattikakakka” is medicinal clay compounded with herbs. “Calita” means angered. “Lohite sannisinne” means when corrupted blood has subsided or diminished.

17. Duggatito saṃsārato ca niyyāti etenāti niyyānaṃ, saggamaggo mokkhamaggo ca. Taṃ niyyānaṃ arahati, niyyāne vā niyuttā, niyyānaṃ vā phalabhūtaṃ etissā atthīti niyyānikā, vacīduccaritasaṃkilesato niyyātīti vā ī-kārassa rassattaṃ, ya-kārassa ca ka-kāraṃ katvā niyyānikā, cetanāya saddhiṃ samphappalāpā veramaṇi. Tappaṭipakkhato aniyyānikā, tassā bhāvo aniyyānikattaṃ, tasmā aniyyānikattā. Tiracchānabhūtāti tirokaraṇabhūtā. Kammaṭṭhānabhāveti aniccatāpaṭisaṃyuttacatusaccakammaṭṭhānabhāve. Saha atthenāti sātthakaṃ, hitapaṭisaṃyuttanti attho. Visikhāti gharasanniveso, visikhāgahaṇena ca tannivāsino gahitā “gāmo āgato”tiādīsu viya. Tenevāha “sūrā samatthā”ti, “saddhā pasannā”ti ca. Kumbhaṭṭhānāpadesena [M 1.0129][P 1.0166] kumbhadāsiyo vuttāti āha “kumbhadāsīkathā vā”ti. Uppattiṭhitisambhārādivasena lokaṃ akkhāyatīti lokakkhāyikā.

17. It leads out from the bad destinations and from saṃsāra, thus it is deliverance (niyyāna)—the path to heaven and the path to liberation. It is worthy of deliverance, or it is yoked to deliverance, or deliverance is its fruit—thus it is niyyānikā. Or, it leads out from the defilement of wrong speech, hence the shortening of the vowel 'ī' and the change of 'ya' to 'ka,' making it 'niyyānikā'; it is abstinence from idle chatter together with intention. Its opposite is 'aniyyānikā,' and its state is 'aniyyānikattaṃ'; therefore, due to 'aniyyānikattaṃ.' 'Tiracchānabhūtā' means being an obstruction. 'Kammaṭṭhānabhāve' refers to the development of meditation subjects connected with impermanence and the four truths. 'Saha atthenāti' means meaningful (sātthakaṃ), that is, connected with benefit. 'Visikhā' refers to a street; and by the term 'visikhā,' its inhabitants are included, as in phrases like 'the village has come.' Hence it is said, 'the heroes are capable,' and 'the faithful are devoted.' By the pretext of 'kumbhaṭṭhāna,' female water-carriers are meant, hence it is said, 'or talk about female water-carriers.' It explains the world in terms of origin, duration, and constituents—thus it is called 'lokakkhāyikā.'

18. Sahitanti pubbāparāviruddhaṃ.

18. “Sahita” means non-contradictory from beginning to end.

19. Dūtassa kammaṃ dūteyyaṃ, tassa kathā dūteyyakathā.

19. The work of a messenger is dūteyya, and his talk is dūteyyakathā.

20. Tividhenāti sāmantajappanairiyāpathasannissitapaccayapaṭisevanabhedato tippakārena. Vimhāpayantīti “aho acchariyapuriso”ti attani paresaṃ vimhayaṃ uppādenti. Lapantīti attānaṃ, dāyakaṃ vā ukkhipitvā yathā so kiñci dadāti, evaṃ ukkācetvā kathenti. Nimittena caranti, nimittaṃ vā karontīti nemittikā nimittanti ca paresaṃ paccaya dānasaññuppādakaṃ kāyavacīkammaṃ vuccati. Nippiṃsantīti nippesā, nippesāyeva nippesikā, nippesoti ca saṭhapuriso viya lābhasakkāratthaṃ akkosakhuṃsanuppaṇḍanaparapiṭṭhimaṃsikatādi.

20. “Tividhena” means threefold: by flattering speech, by affected mannerisms, and by hinting through the use of requisites. “Vimhāpayanti” means they arouse astonishment in others, causing them to think, “Ah, what a marvelous person!” “Lapanti” means they praise themselves or, by extolling a donor, they speak in a flattering way so that he gives something. “Nimittena caranti, nimittaṃ vā karonti” means they conduct themselves by signs or make signs—thus they are called nemittikā; “nimitta” refers to bodily or verbal action that induces in others the perception of giving a gift. “Nippiṃsanti” means they engage in nippesā; “nippesā” itself is “nippesikā”; and “nippesoti” means, like a deceitful person, seeking gain and honor, engaging in abuse, disparagement, deceitful talk, and backbiting.

Majjhimasīlavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the middling morality is concluded.

Mahāsīlavaṇṇanā

The exposition of the great morality.

21. Aṅgāni [V 1.0115] ārabbha pavattattā aṅgasahacaritaṃ satthaṃ “aṅga”nti vuttaṃ. Nimittanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Keci pana “aṅganti aṅgavikāra”nti vadanti, paresaṃ aṅgavikāradassanenāpi lābhālābhādivijjāti. Paṇḍurājāti dakkhiṇāmadhurādhipati. “Mahantāna”nti etena appakaṃ nimittaṃ, mahantaṃ nimittaṃ uppātoti dasseti. Idaṃ nāma passatīti yo vasabhaṃ kuñjaraṃ pāsādaṃ pabbataṃ vā āruḷhaṃ supine attānaṃ passati, tassa idaṃ nāma phalaṃ hotīti. Supinakanti supinasatthaṃ. Aṅgasampattivipattidassanamattena [P 1.0167] ādisanaṃ vuttaṃ “aṅga”nti iminā, “lakkhaṇa”nti iminā pana mahānubhāvatānipphādakaaṅgalakkhaṇavisesadassanenāti ayametesaṃ visesoti. Ahateti nave. Ito paṭṭhāyāti devarakkhasamanussādibhedena vividhavatthabhāge ito vā etto vā sañchinne idaṃ nāma bhogādi hotīti. Dabbihomadīni [M 1.0130] homassupakaraṇādivisesehi phalavisesadassanavasena pavattāni. Aggihomaṃ vuttāvasesasādhanavasena pavattaṃ homaṃ. Aṅgalaṭṭhinti sarīraṃ. Abbhino satthaṃ abbheyyaṃ, māsurakkhena kato gantho māsurakkho. Bhūrivijjā sassabuddhikaraṇavijjāti sārasamāse. Sapakkhaka…pe… catuppadānanti piṅgalamakkhikādisapakkhaka gharagolikādiapakkhakadevamanussakoñcādidvipadakakaṇṭakajambukādicatuppadānaṃ.

21. Because it operates in relation to the limbs, the science concerned with the limbs is called 'aṅga.' The same principle applies to 'nimitta' here. But some say, 'aṅga means deformity of limbs,' implying that knowledge of gain, loss, and so on, is also derived from observing the deformity of limbs in others. Paṇḍurāja is the ruler of Southern Madhurā. By 'mahantānaṃ,' it shows that a small sign is a nimitta, and a great sign is an uppāta. 'Idaṃ nāma passati' means that if one sees oneself in a dream riding a bull, elephant, palace, or mountain, this is the result. 'Supinaka' means the science of dreams. The term 'aṅga' indicates prediction based merely on observation of the perfection or imperfection of limbs; however, the term 'lakkhaṇa' indicates prediction based on the observation of special bodily marks that bring about great power—this is the difference between them. 'Ahata' means new. 'Ito paṭṭhāyāti' means that, based on various categories such as gods, demons, and humans, if something is cut off from here or there, it results in such-and-such wealth, etc. 'Dabbihoma' and other rites are performed showing different results based on variations in sacrificial implements and the like. 'Aggihoma' is a fire sacrifice performed in order to gain the remaining benefits. 'Aṅgalaṭṭhi' means the body. 'Abbhino satthaṃ' is 'abbheyyaṃ,' a treatise on the sky; 'māsurakkha' is a text composed by Māsurakkha. 'Bhūrivijjā' is the knowledge that increases quickness of intellect, according to the Sārasamāsa. 'Sapakkhaka... catuppadānaṃ' refers to winged creatures such as the Piṅgala fly, wingless creatures such as house lizards, two-legged beings such as gods, humans, and herons, and four-legged beings such as thorny bushes and jackals.

23. “Asukadivase”ti “pakkhassa dutiye tatiye”tiādi tithivasena vuttaṃ. Asukanakkhattenāti rohiṇīādinakkhattayogavasena.

23. “On such-and-such a day” is stated in terms of the lunar date, such as 'the second or third of the fortnight.' 'Under such-and-such a constellation' refers to conjunction with constellations such as Rohiṇī.

24. Ukkānaṃ patananti ukkobhāsānaṃ patanaṃ. Vātasaṅghātesu hi vegena aññamaññaṃ saṅghaṭṭentesu dīpakobhāso viya obhāso uppajjitvā ākāsato patati, tatthāyaṃ ukkāpātavohāro. Avisuddhatā abbhamahikādīhi.

24. The falling of meteors (ukkānaṃ patanaṃ) means the falling of fiery lights. When wind currents violently collide with each other, a light resembling a lamp's glow arises and falls from the sky—this is called the phenomenon of a meteor fall. Impurity (avisuddhatā) refers to atmospheric phenomena like mist and fog.

25. Dhārānupavecchanaṃ vassanaṃ. Hatthena adhippetaviññāpanaṃ hatthamuddā, taṃ pana aṅgulisaṅkocanena [P 1.0168] gaṇanāyeva. Pārasika milakkhakādayo viya navantavasena gaṇanā acchiddakagaṇanā. Saṭuppādanādīti ādi-saddena vokalanabhāgahārādike saṅgaṇhāti. Cintāvasenāti vatthuṃ anusandhiñca sayameva cirena cintetvā karaṇavasena cintākavi veditabbo, kiñci sutvā sutena assutaṃ anusandhetvā karaṇavasena sutakavi, kañci atthaṃ upadhāretvā tassa [V 1.0116] saṅkhipanavitthāraṇādivasena atthakavi, yaṃ kiñci parena kataṃ kabbaṃ nāṭakaṃ vā disvā taṃ sadisameva aññaṃ attano ṭhānuppattikapaṭibhānena karaṇavasena paṭibhānakavi veditabbo.

25. The act of raining is dhārānupavecchanaṃ or vassanaṃ. Making one's intention known with the hand is called hatthamuddā, which is simply a method of counting by the bending of fingers. Like the Persians and barbarians, counting by marking lines is acchiddakagaṇanā, complete counting without omission. Saṭuppādanādīti—the word ādi includes things like dropping vowels and grammatical divisions. A cintākavi should be understood as one who composes through their own deliberation, after long reflection on the subject and its connections; a sutakavi as one who composes by hearing something and connecting what was heard to what was not; an atthakavi as one who, after reflecting on some meaning, composes by way of condensing or elaborating it; a paṭibhānakavi should be understood as one who, upon seeing a poem or drama made by another, creates something similar through their own spontaneously arising wit.

26. Pariggahabhāvena dārikāya gaṇhāpanaṃ āvāhanaṃ. Tathā dāpanaṃ vivāhanaṃ. Desantare diguṇatiguṇādigahaṇavasena bhaṇḍappayojanaṃ payogo. Tattha vā aññattha vā yathākālaparicchedaṃ vaḍḍhigahaṇavasena payojanaṃ uddhāro. “Bhaṇḍamūlarahitānaṃ vāṇijjaṃ katvā ettakenudayena saha mūlaṃ dethāti dhanadānaṃ payogo, tāvakālikadānaṃ uddhāro”ti ca vadanti. Tīhi kāraṇehīti ettha vātena, pāṇakehi vā gabbhe vinassante na purimakammunā okāso kato, tappaccayā kammaṃ vipaccati. Sayameva [M 1.0131] pana kammunā okāse kate na ekantena vāto pāṇakā vā apekkhitabbāti kammassa visuṃ kāraṇabhāvo vuttoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nibbāpanīyanti upasamakaraṃ. Paṭikammanti yathā te na khādanti, tathā paṭikaraṇaṃ. Parivattanatthanti āvudhādinā saha ukkhittahatthassa ukkhipanavasena parivattanatthaṃ. Icchitatthassa devatāya kaṇṇe kathanavasena jappanaṃ kaṇṇajappananti. Ādiccapāricariyāti [P 1.0169] karavīramālāhi pūjaṃ katvā sakaladivasaṃ ādiccābhimukhāvaṭṭhānena ādiccassa paricaraṇaṃ. “Siravhāyana”nti keci paṭhanti, tassatthomantaṃ parijappitvā sirasā icchitassa atthassa avhāyananti.

26. Taking a girl with the intention of marriage is called āvāhana. Similarly, giving her away is called vivāhana. Lending out goods in another country on the condition of receiving them back doubled, tripled, and so on, is called payoga. Lending there or elsewhere on the condition of receiving interest according to a fixed period is called uddhāra. Some say: 'Giving money to merchants who lack capital, saying, "Do business and return the principal together with this much profit," is called payoga, while a temporary loan is called uddhāra.' Herein, regarding 'by three causes': when a crop is destroyed by wind or by pests, an opportunity is not created by the previous kamma alone; the kamma ripens conditioned by that factor. However, when an opportunity is created by the kamma itself, wind or pests are not absolutely required. Thus, it should be understood that the distinct causal nature of kamma has been stated. Nibbāpanīya means calming. Paṭikamma means taking countermeasures so that they do not consume it. Parivattanatthaṃ means for the purpose of brandishing, as in brandishing a weapon by raising one's hand. Kaṇṇajappana is whispering a desired matter in the ear of a deity. Ādiccapāricariyā means attending to the sun by making offerings with garlands of oleander and standing facing it for the entire day. Some read it as 'siravhāyana,' the meaning of which is: invoking a desired outcome by murmuring a mantra over the head.

27. Samiddhikāleti āyācitassa atthassa siddhikāle. Santipaṭissavakammanti devatāyācanāya yā santi paṭikattabbā, tassā paṭiññāpaṭissavakammakaraṇaṃ, santiyā āyācanappayogoti attho. Tasminti paṭissavaphalabhūte yathābhipatthitakammasmiṃ, yaṃ “sace me idaṃ nāma samijjhissatī”ti vuttaṃ. Tassāti santipaṭissavassa, yo “paṇidhī”ti ca vutto. Yathāpaṭissavañhi upahāre kate paṇidhi āyācanā katā niyyātitā hotīti. Acchandikabhāvamattanti itthiyā akāmakabhāvamattaṃ. Liṅganti purisaliṅgaṃ. Balikammakaraṇaṃ upaddavapaṭibāhanatthañceva vaḍḍhiāvahanatthañca. Dosānanti pittādidosānaṃ. Ettha ca vamananti pacchaṭṭanaṃ adhippetaṃ. Uddhaṃvirecananti vamanaṃ “uddhaṃ dosānaṃ nīharaṇa”nti vuttattā. Tathā virecananti virecanameva. Adhovirecananti pana suddhivatthikasāvatthiādi vatthikiriyāpi adhippetā “adho dosānaṃ nīharaṇa”nti vuttattā. Sīsavirecanaṃ semhanīharaṇādi. Paṭalānīti akkhipaṭalāni. Salākavejjakammanti akkhivejjakammaṃ, idaṃ vuttāvasesasālākiyasaṅgahaṇatthaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbanti. Tappanādayopi hi sālākiyānevāti. Mūlāni [P 1.0170] padhānāni rogūpasame samatthāni bhesajjāni mūlabhesajjāni, mūlānaṃ vā byādhīnaṃ bhesajjāni mūlabhesajjāni. Mūlānubandhavasena hi duvidho byādhi. Mūlaroge ca tikicchite yebhuyyena itaraṃ vūpasamatīti. “Kāyatikicchanaṃ [V 1.0117] dassetī”ti idaṃ komārabhaccasallakattasālākiyādikaraṇavisesabhūtatantīnaṃ tattha tattha vuttattā pārisesavasena vuttaṃ, tasmā tadavasesāya tantiyāpi idha saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Sabbāni cetāni ājīvahetukāniyeva idhādhippetāni “micchājīvena jīvikaṃ kappentī”ti vuttattā[M 1.0132]. Yaṃ pana tattha tattha pāḷiyaṃ “iti vā”ti vuttaṃ, tattha itīti pakāratthe nipāto, vā-iti vikappanatthe. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti iminā pakārena, ito aññe na vāti. Tena yāni ito bāhirakapabbajitā sippāyatanavijjāṭṭhānādīni jīvikopāyabhūtāni ājīvapakatā upajīvanti, tesaṃ pariggaho katoti veditabbo.

27. Samiddhikāle means at the time of achieving the desired purpose. Santipaṭissavakamma means the act of making a vow concerning the appeasement to be performed in return for a request made to a deity; the meaning is the application of a request for appeasement. Tasmiṃ refers to that desired work which is the fruit of the vow, as stated: "If this thing will succeed for me." Tassā refers to that vow for appeasement, which is also called "aspiration." For when offerings are made according to the vow, the aspiration, the request that was made, is fulfilled. Acchandikabhāvamatta means merely the state of unwillingness in a woman. Liṅga means the male organ. The performance of bali-rites is done both to ward off dangers and to bring prosperity. Dosānaṃ refers to the humors like bile, etc. Here, vamana (vomiting) is intended as regurgitation. Uddhaṃvirecana (upward purging) means vomiting, because it is said 'expelling humors upwards.' Similarly, virecana means purging itself. Adhovirecana (downward purging) also refers to the application of enemas like suddhivatthika, sāvatthi, etc., because it is said 'expelling humors downwards.' Sīsavirecana (head purging) means expelling phlegm, etc. Paṭalāni refers to the membranes of the eye. Salākavejjakamma (surgery with a probe) means eye surgery; this should be understood as stated for the inclusion of the remaining ophthalmic procedures mentioned. For even tappanā, etc., are ophthalmic procedures. Mūlabhesajjāni (root remedies) are medicines that are primary and capable of pacifying diseases, or they are medicines for root diseases. For diseases are of two kinds based on their root connection, and when the root disease is treated, the other mostly subsides. The phrase 'shows treatment of the body' is stated by way of remainder, because the specific branches of treatment such as pediatrics, surgery, and ophthalmology are mentioned here and there. Therefore, the inclusion of the remaining branches of treatment should also be understood here. All these are intended here as means of livelihood, because it is said: 'they make a living by wrong livelihood.' However, where 'iti vā' is stated here and there in the Pāḷi, there 'iti' is a particle indicating manner, and 'vā' is for alternative. This means: 'in this manner, or not other than this.' Therefore, it should be understood that those arts, sciences, and fields of knowledge, etc., which are means of livelihood for external ascetics and by which they live, are included.

Mahāsīlavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Great Morality is concluded.

Pubbantakappikasassatavādavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of Speculating on the Past and Eternalism

28. Bhikkhusaṅghena vuttavaṇṇo nāma “yāvañcidaṃ tena bhagavatā”tiādinā vuttavaṇṇo. Etthāyaṃ sambandho – na bhikkhave ettakā eva buddhaguṇā, ye tumhākaṃ pākaṭā, apākaṭā pana “atthi bhikkhave aññe dhammā”ti vitthāro. Tattha “ime diṭṭhiṭṭhānā evaṃ gahitā”tiādinā sassatādidiṭṭhiṭṭhānānaṃ yathāgahitākārasuññatabhāvappakāsanato, “tañca pajānanaṃ na parāmasatī”ti sīlādīnañca aparāmāsaniyyānikabhāvadīpanena niccasārādivirahappakāsanato, yāsu vedanāsu avītarāgatāya bāhirakānaṃ etāni diṭṭhivipphanditāni sambhavanti, tesaṃ paccayabhūtānañca sammohādīnaṃ vedakakārakasabhāvābhāvadassanamukhena [P 1.0171] sabbadhammānaṃ attattaniyatāvirahadīpanato, anupādāparinibbānadīpanato ca ayaṃ desanā suññatāvibhāvanappadhānāti āha “suññatāpakāsanaṃ ārabhī”ti. Pariyattīti vinayādibhedabhinnā tanti. Desanāti tassā tantiyā manasāvavatthāpitāya vibhāvanā, yathādhammaṃ dhammābhilāpabhūtā vā paññāpanā, anulomādivasena vā kathananti pariyattidesanānaṃ viseso pubbeyeva vavatthāpitoti āha “desanāyaṃ pariyattiya”nti. Evaṃ ādīsūti ettha ādi-saddena saccasabhāvasamādhipaññāpakatipuññaāpattiñeyyādayo saṅgayhanti. Tathā hi ayaṃ dhamma-saddo “catunnaṃ bhikkhave dhammānaṃ ananubodhā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.186; a. ni. 4.1) sacce vattati, “kusalā dhammā akusalā dhammā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 1) sabhāve, “evaṃdhammā te bhagavanto ahesu”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.378) samādhimhi, “saccaṃ dhammo [V 1.0118] dhiti cāgo, sa ve pecca na socatī”tiādīsu (su. ni. 190) paññāya, “jātidhammānaṃ [M 1.0133] bhikkhave sattānaṃ evaṃ icchā uppajjatī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.373; paṭi. ma. 1.33) pakatiyaṃ, “dhammo suciṇṇo sukhamāvahātī”tiādīsu (su. ni. 184; theragā. 303; jā. 1.10.102) puññe, “cattāro [P 1.0172] pārājikā dhammā”tiādīsu (pārā. 233) āpattiyaṃ, “sabbe dhammā sabbākārena buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇamukhe āpāthaṃ āgacchantī”tiādīsu (mahāni. 156; cūḷani. 85; paṭi. ma. 3.6) ñeyye vattati (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.suttanikkhepavaṇṇanā; abhi. aṭṭha. 1.tikamātikāpadavaṇṇanā; bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. ratanacaṅkamanakaṇḍavaṇṇanā). Dhammā hontīti suññā dhammamattā hontīti attho.

28. The description spoken by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is the description that begins with 'as far as this by that Blessed One,' and so on. Here is the connection: 'Bhikkhus, the qualities of the Buddha are not only those that are evident to you, for there are other qualities as well'—thus the detailed explanation. Herein, from the statement 'these views are held thus,' the emptiness of the grasped forms of eternalist and other views is shown; and by the statement 'that understanding does not cling,' the non-clinging and liberating nature of virtues like morality and so on is shown, thereby revealing the absence of eternal essence and so on. Furthermore, in those feelings where outsiders have not abandoned craving, these writhings of views arise; and by seeing the absence of the nature of experiencer and agent in the conditions like delusion, which give rise to them, the absence of self and what belongs to self in all phenomena is shown; and by showing Nibbāna without clinging—this teaching is primarily for the elucidation of emptiness. Therefore, it is said, 'he began to reveal emptiness.' Pariyatti (scriptural learning) is the text divided into sections like Vinaya, etc. Desanā (teaching) is the analysis of that text established in the mind, or the exposition of phenomena according to the Dhamma, which becomes the expression of Dhamma, or the explanation in accordance with what is suitable, etc. The distinction between scriptural learning and teaching was established earlier, therefore it is said 'in the teaching and the scriptural learning.' Thus, in 'etc.' here, the word 'etc.' includes truth, nature, concentration, wisdom, natural disposition, merit, offenses, the knowable, and so on. For this term 'Dhamma' is used in such contexts as 'bhikkhus, without understanding these four things' (Dīgha Nikāya 2.186; Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.1) with reference to truth; 'wholesome phenomena, unwholesome phenomena' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 1) with reference to nature; 'such were the Blessed Ones in their Dhamma' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.378) with reference to concentration; 'truth, Dhamma, steadfastness, generosity—he does not grieve after death' (Sutta Nipāta 190) with reference to wisdom; 'bhikkhus, for beings subject to birth, such a wish arises' (Majjhima Nikāya 3.373; Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.33) with reference to natural disposition; 'the Dhamma, well-practiced, brings happiness' (Sutta Nipāta 184; Theragāthā 303; Jātaka 1.10.102) with reference to merit; 'the four offenses entailing expulsion' (Pārājika 233) with reference to offenses; 'all phenomena in every way enter the range of the knowledge of the Blessed One, the Buddha' (Mahāniddesa 156; Cūḷaniddesa 85; Paṭisambhidāmagga 3.6) with reference to the knowable (Majjhima Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 1, Suttanikkhepa-vaṇṇanā; Abhidhamma Aṭṭhakathā 1, Tikamātikāpada-vaṇṇanā; Buddhavaṃsa Aṭṭhakathā, Ratana-caṅkamana-kaṇḍa-vaṇṇanā). 'They become phenomena'—they are empty, mere phenomena—this is the meaning.

“Duddasā”ti eteneva tesaṃ dhammānaṃ dukkhogāhatā pakāsitā hoti. Sace pana koci attano pamāṇaṃ ajānanto ñāṇena te dhamme ogāhituṃ ussāhaṃ kareyya, tassa taṃ ñāṇaṃ appatiṭṭhameva makasatuṇḍasūci viya mahāsamuddeti āha “alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhā”ti. Alabbhaneyyā patiṭṭhā etthāti alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhāti padaviggaho veditabbo. Alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhānaṃ ogāhituṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya “ettakā ete īdisā cā”ti passituṃ na sakkāti vuttaṃ “gambhīrattā eva duddasā”ti. Ye pana daṭṭhumeva na sakkā, tesaṃ ogāhitvā anubujjhane kathā eva natthīti āha “duddasattā eva duranubodhā”ti. Sabbapariḷāhapaṭippassaddhimatthake samuppannattā, nibbutasabbapariḷāhasamāpattisamokiṇṇattā ca nibbutasabbapariḷāhā. Santārammaṇāni maggaphalanibbānāni anupasantasabhāvānaṃ kilesānaṃ saṅkhārānañca abhāvato. Atha vā samūhatavikkhepatāya niccasamāhitassa manasikārassa vasena tadārammaṇadhammānaṃ santabhāvo veditabbo kasiṇugghāṭimākāsatabbisayaviññāṇānaṃ anantabhāvo viya. Avirajjhitvā nimittapaṭivedho viya issāsānaṃ avirajjhitvā dhammānaṃ yathābhūtasabhāvabodho sāduraso mahāraso ca hotīti āha atittikaraṇaṭṭhenāti. Paṭivedhappattānaṃ, tesu ca buddhānaṃyeva sabbākārena visayabhāvūpagamanato na takkabuddhiyā gocarāti āha “uttamañāṇavisayattā”tiādi. “Nipuṇā”ti ñeyyesu tikkhavisadavuttiyā chekā. Yasmā pana so chekabhāvo ārammaṇe appaṭihatavuttitāya sukhumañeyyagahaṇasamatthatāya supākaṭo hoti, tena vuttaṃ “saṇhasukhumasabhāvattā”ti.

By this very term 'hard to see,' the difficulty of penetrating those states is revealed. But if someone, not knowing their own measure, were to strive to penetrate those states with knowledge, their knowledge would be ungrounded, like a needle as fine as a mosquito's proboscis in the great ocean—hence it is said, 'ungraspable as a foundation.' The word analysis should be understood as: 'ungraspable as a foundation' (alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhā) means 'a foundation is not obtainable here.' Because it is impossible to penetrate what is ungraspable as a foundation, it is said, 'They are hard to see due to their profundity,' meaning it is not possible to see 'they are such and such a number and kind.' And for those which cannot even be seen, there is no question of penetrating and realizing them—hence it is said, 'Because they are hard to see, they are hard to fully understand.' Since they arise at the peak of the complete stilling of all distress, and because they are interwoven with the attainment of the stilling of all distress, they are called 'extinguished of all distress.' The path, fruition, and Nibbāna have peaceful objects because of the absence of the defilements and formations, which are of an unpacified nature. Alternatively, the peaceful nature of those object-states should be understood as due to the constantly collected attention, free from agitation and distraction—like the boundless nature of consciousness whose object is the space opened up by the kasiṇa. Just as archers penetrate a target without missing the mark, so too, the understanding of the true nature of phenomena without missing is of sweet taste and great taste. Hence it is said, 'in the sense of causing non-satiety.' For those who have attained penetration, and because only for the Buddhas do they become objects in all aspects, they are not within the range of reasoning and intellect—hence it is said, 'because their domain is supreme knowledge,' etc. 'Subtle'—because they are skilled with sharp, clear functioning in knowable things. And since this skill is most evident due to its unobstructed functioning with the object and its ability to grasp the subtle knowable, it is said, 'because of their gentle and refined nature.'

Aparo nayo [M 1.0134][P 1.0173] – vinayapaṇṇattiādigambhīraneyyavibhāvanato gambhīrā. Kadāci asaṅkhyeyyamahākappe atikkamitvāpi dullabhadassanatāya duddasā.
