Dassanañcettha paññācakkhuvaseneva veditabbaṃ. Dhammanvayasaṅkhātassa anubodhassa kassacideva sambhavato duranubodhā[V 1.0119]. Santasabhāvato, veneyyānañca guṇasampadānaṃ pariyosānattā santā. Attano ca paccayehi padhānabhāvaṃ nītatāya paṇītā. Samadhigatasaccalakkhaṇatāya atakkehi, atakkena vā ñāṇena avacaritabbatāya atakkāvacarā. Nipuṇaṃ, nipuṇe vā atthe saccappaccayākārādivasena vibhāvanato nipuṇā. Loke aggapaṇḍitena sammāsambuddhena vedīyanti pakāsīyantīti paṇḍitavedanīyā. Anāvaraṇañāṇapaṭilābhato hi bhagavā “sabbavidū haṃ asmi, (dha. pa. 353; mahāva. 11; kathā. 405) dasabalasamannāgato bhikkhave tathāgato”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.21) attano sabbaññutādiguṇe pakāseti. Tenevāha “sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedetī”ti.

Another way: they are profound because they reveal the profound meanings of the Vinaya rules and other teachings. At times, they are difficult to see because they are rarely seen, even after countless great eons have passed. Here, seeing should be understood only by the eye of wisdom. They are difficult to comprehend because the comprehension called 'conformity to the Dhamma' arises only in some. They are peaceful due to their peaceful nature, and because they are the culmination of the virtuous accomplishments for those to be trained. They are exalted because they are brought to prominence by their own conditions. They are beyond the sphere of reasoning because their true characteristic is realized by those beyond speculation, and they are not to be traversed by knowledge based on reasoning. They are subtle because they make manifest subtle matters in terms of truth, condition, mode, and so on. They are to be known by the wise, for they are known and proclaimed by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, the foremost sage in the world. For the Blessed One, having attained unobstructed knowledge, declares his qualities of omniscience and so forth, saying, “I am the All-Knower” (Dh. 353; Mahāva. 11; Kathā. 405), and “Monks, the Tathāgata is endowed with the ten powers” (Saṃ. Ni. 2.21). Therefore, it is said, “Having directly known it for himself, he makes it known.”

Tattha kiñcāpi sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ phalanibbānāni viya sacchikātabbasabhāvaṃ na hoti, āsavakkhayañāṇe pana adhigate adhigatameva hotīti tassa paccakkhakaraṇaṃ sacchikiriyāti āha “abhivisiṭṭhena ñāṇena paccakkhaṃ katvā”ti. Abhivisiṭṭhena ñāṇenāti ca hetuatthe karaṇavacanaṃ, abhivisiṭṭhañāṇādhigamahetūti attho. Abhivisiṭṭhañāṇanti vā paccavekkhaṇañāṇe adhippete karaṇavacanampi yujjatiyeva. Pavedanañcettha aññāvisayānaṃ saccādīnaṃ desanākiccasādhanato, “ekomhi sammāsambuddho”tiādinā (mahāva. 11; kathā. 405) paṭijānanato ca veditabbaṃ. Vadamānāti [P 1.0174] ettha sattiattho māna-saddo, vattuṃ ussāhaṃ karontoti attho. Evaṃbhūtā ca vattukāmā nāma hontīti āha “vaṇṇaṃ vattukāmā”ti. Sāvasesaṃ vadantopi viparītaṃ vadanto viya “sammā vadatī”ti na vattabboti āha “ahāpetvā”ti, tena anavasesattho idha sammā-saddoti dasseti. “Vattuṃ sakkuṇeyyu”nti iminā “vadeyyu”nti sakatthadīpanabhāvamāha. Ettha ca kiñcāpi bhagavato dasabalādiñāṇānipi anaññasādhāraṇāni, sappadesavisayattā pana tesaṃ ñāṇānaṃ na tehi buddhaguṇā ahāpetvā gahitā nāma honti, nippadesavisayattā pana sabbaññutaññāṇassa [M 1.0135] tasmiṃ gahite sabbepi buddhaguṇā gahitā eva nāma hontīti imamatthaṃ dasseti “yehi…pe… vadeyyu”nti. Puthūni ārammaṇāni etassāti puthuārammaṇaṃ, sabbārammaṇattāti adhippāyo. Atha vā puthuārammaṇārammaṇatoti etasmiṃ atthe “puthuārammaṇato”ti vuttaṃ, ekassa ārammaṇa-saddassa lopaṃ katvā “oṭṭhamukho kāmāvacara”nti ādīsu viya, tenassa puthuñāṇakiccasādhakataṃ dasseti. Tathā hetaṃ tīsu kālesu appaṭihatañāṇaṃ, catuyoniparicchedakañāṇaṃ, pañcagatiparicchedakañāṇaṃ, chasu asādhāraṇañāṇesu sesāsādhāraṇañāṇāni, sattaariyapuggalavibhāvakañāṇaṃ, aṭṭhasupi parisāsu akampanañāṇaṃ, navasattāvāsaparijānanañāṇaṃ, dasabalañāṇanti evamādīnaṃ anekasatasahassabhedānaṃ ñāṇānaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ kiccaṃ sādhetīti. “Punappunaṃ uppattivasenā”ti etena [V 1.0120] sabbaññutaññāṇassa kamavuttitaṃ dasseti. Kamenāpi hi taṃ visayesu pavattati, na sakiṃyeva yathā bāhirakā vadanti “sakiṃyeva sabbaññū sabbaṃ jānāti, na kamenā”ti.

Here, although the knowledge of omniscience is not of a nature to be realized like the fruits of the path and Nibbāna, when the knowledge of the destruction of the taints is attained, it is indeed attained. Therefore, its direct experience is called realization, as stated: ‘Having directly experienced it with surpassing knowledge.’ The phrase ‘with surpassing knowledge’ is in the instrumental case to indicate the cause, meaning ‘due to the attainment of surpassing knowledge.’ Alternatively, if ‘surpassing knowledge’ is intended as the knowledge of reviewing, the instrumental case is still appropriate. The declaration here should be understood as serving the teaching function regarding truths and other matters beyond the scope of others' knowledge, as well as the proclamation, ‘I am the one Perfectly Self-Enlightened One,’ etc. (Mahāva. 11; Kathā. 405). In the word ‘vadamānā’, the suffix ‘-māna’ has the sense of ability; the meaning is ‘making an effort to speak.’ Such individuals are indeed those who wish to praise, as stated: ‘desiring to praise.’ One who speaks with reservation, just like one who speaks contrarily, should not be called ‘one who speaks rightly.’ Hence, it is said: ‘without omitting.’ By this, it is shown that the word ‘sammā’ here has the meaning of ‘without omission.’ The phrase ‘they would be able to speak’ explains that ‘they would speak’ indicates their own capability. Here, although the Blessed One’s knowledges, such as the ten powers, are indeed unique to him, because those knowledges pertain to specific domains, the Buddha’s qualities are not grasped completely when grasping them. But because the knowledge of omniscience pertains to all domains, when that is grasped, all the Buddha’s qualities are indeed grasped. This is the meaning conveyed by: ‘those who… would speak.’ ‘Having manifold objects’—because it has all objects as its domain, this is the intention. Alternatively, ‘puthuārammaṇato’ is said in the sense of ‘having manifold objects as objects' by omitting one instance of the word ‘object,’ as in phrases like ‘oṭṭhamukho kāmāvacaro,’ etc. Thus, it indicates the accomplishment of the function of manifold knowledge. For so it accomplishes the function of countless hundreds of thousands of types of knowledge accordingly, such as: unhindered knowledge in the three times, knowledge discerning the four origins, knowledge discerning the five destinations, the remaining uncommon knowledges from among the six uncommon knowledges, knowledge distinguishing the seven noble persons, unshaken knowledge in the eight assemblies, knowledge fully understanding the nine abodes of beings, and the knowledge of the ten powers. ‘By arising again and again’—this indicates the gradual functioning of the knowledge of omniscience. For it operates in its objects gradually, not just once, as outsiders say: ‘The omniscient one knows everything all at once, not gradually.’

Yadi evaṃ acinteyyāparimeyyabhedassa ñeyyassa paricchedavatā ekena ñāṇena niravasesato kathaṃ paṭivedhoti, ko [P 1.0175] vā evamāha “paricchedavantaṃ buddhañāṇa”nti. Anantañhi taṃ ñāṇaṃ ñeyyaṃ viya. Vuttañhetaṃ “yāvatakaṃ ñeyyaṃ tāvatakaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Yāvatakaṃ ñāṇaṃ, tāvatakaṃ ñeyya”nti (mahāni. 156; cūḷani. 85; paṭi. ma. 3.5). Evampi jātibhūmisabhāvādivasena disādesakālādivasena ca anekabhedabhinne ñeyye kamena gayhamāne anavasesapaṭivedho na sambhavati yevāti, nayidamevaṃ. Kasmā? Yaṃ kiñci bhagavatā ñātuṃ icchitaṃ sakalaṃ ekadeso vā. Tattha appaṭihatacāratāya paccakkhato ñāṇaṃ pavattati, vikkhepābhāvato ca bhagavā sabbakālaṃ samāhitova ñātuṃ, icchitassa paccakkhabhāvo na sakkā nivāretuṃ “ākaṅkhāpaṭibaddhaṃ buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇa”ntiādi (mahāni. 156; cūḷani. 85; paṭi. ma. 3.5) vacanato, na cettha dūrato cittapaṭaṃ passantānaṃ viya, “sabbe dhammā anattā”ti vipassantānaṃ viya ca anekadhammāvabodhakāle anirūpitarūpena bhagavato ñāṇaṃ pavattatīti gahetabbaṃ acinteyyānubhāvatāya buddhañāṇassa. Tenevāha “buddhavisayo acinteyyo”ti [M 1.0136] (a. ni. 4.77). Idaṃ panettha sanniṭṭhānaṃsabbākārena sabbadhammāvabodhanasamatthassa ākaṅkhāpaṭibaddhavuttino anāvaraṇañāṇassa paṭilābhena bhagavā santānena sabbadhammapaṭivedhasamattho ahosi sabbaneyyāvaraṇassa pahānato, tasmā sabbaññū, na sakiṃyeva sabbadhammāvabodhato[P 1.0176], yathā santānena sabbaindhanassa dahanasamatthatāya pāvako “sabbabhū”ti vuccatīti.

If so, how can that which is knowable, being of inconceivable and immeasurable kinds, be fully penetrated without remainder by a single, limited knowledge? But who says, "the Buddha's knowledge is limited?" For that knowledge is infinite, like the knowable itself. For it was said: "As far as the knowable extends, so far extends knowledge; as far as knowledge extends, so far extends the knowable." Even so, if the knowable, being divided into many kinds by way of birth, plane, nature, and so on, and by way of direction, region, time, and so on, were grasped sequentially, complete penetration without remainder would not be possible at all—but this is not so. Why? Whatever the Blessed One wishes to know, whether the whole or a part, his knowledge proceeds directly, unimpeded in its range. And because there is no distraction, the Blessed One is always concentrated for knowing. The direct manifestation of what he wishes cannot be prevented, since it is said: "The knowledge of the Blessed One, the Buddha, is bound to his aspiration." And here, it should not be taken that the Blessed One's knowledge proceeds in an uninvestigated manner when comprehending many phenomena, like those seeing a painted cloth from afar, or like those practicing insight on "all phenomena are not-self." This is because of the inconceivable power of the Buddha's knowledge. Therefore, it is said: "The sphere of a Buddha is inconceivable." The conclusion here is this: Through the attainment of unobstructed knowledge, capable of comprehending all phenomena in every aspect and functioning in accordance with his aspiration, the Blessed One, by the abandoning of all obstructions to the knowable, became capable of fully penetrating all phenomena through his continuity. Therefore, he is the All-Knowing One, not from comprehending all phenomena at once, but just as fire is called "all-consuming" because of its capacity to burn all fuel through its continuity.

Vavatthāpanavacananti sanniṭṭhāpanavacanaṃ, avadhāraṇavacananti attho. Aññe vāti ettha avadhāraṇena nivattitaṃ dasseti “na pāṇātipātā veramaṇiādayo”ti, ayañca eva-saddo aniyatadesatāya ca-saddo viya yattha vutto, tato aññatthāpi vacanicchāvasena upatiṭṭhatīti āha “gambhīrā vā”tiādi. Sabbapadehīti yāva “paṇḍitavedanīyā”ti idaṃ padaṃ, tāva sabbapadehi. Sāvakapāramiñāṇanti sāvakānaṃ dānādipāripūriyā nipphannaṃ vijjattayachaḷabhiññācatuppaṭisambhidādibhedaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Tatoti sāvakapāramiñāṇato. Tatthāti sāvakapāramiñāṇe. Tatopīti anantaraniddiṭṭhato paccekabuddhañāṇatopi, ko pana vādo sāvakapāramiñāṇatoti adhippāyo. Etthāyaṃ atthayojanā – kiñcāpi sāvakapāramiñāṇaṃ heṭṭhimasekkhañāṇaṃ puthujjanañāṇañca upādāya gambhīraṃ, paccekabuddhañāṇaṃ upādāya na tathā gambhīranti [V 1.0121] “gambhīramevā”ti na sakkā vattuṃ. Tathā paccekabuddhañāṇampi sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ upādāyāti tattha vavatthānaṃ na labbhati, sabbaññutaññāṇadhammā pana sāvakapāramiñāṇādīnaṃ viya kiñci upādāya agambhīrabhāvābhāvato gambhīrā vāti. Yathā cettha vavatthānaṃ dassitaṃ, evaṃ sāvakapāramiñāṇaṃ duddasaṃ, paccekabuddhañāṇaṃ pana tato duddasataranti tattha vavatthānaṃ natthītiādinā vavatthānasabbhāvo netabbo. Tenevāha “tathā duddasāva…pe… veditabba”nti.

A statement of establishing means a statement of conclusion; the meaning is a statement of determination. In 'and others,' by determination, it indicates what is excluded, such as 'abstinence from killing living beings' and so on. And this word 'eva' (indeed), due to its indeterminate location, is like the word 'ca' (and): wherever it is mentioned, it applies elsewhere too according to the speaker's intention. Hence, it is said, 'profound, or...' and so on. 'With all phrases' means up to the phrase 'to be known by the wise,' all those phrases are included. 'The knowledge of a disciple's perfection' refers to the knowledge attained by disciples through the fulfillment of perfections such as generosity, etc., which includes the threefold knowledge, the six higher knowledges, the four analytical knowledges, and so on. 'From that' means from the knowledge of a disciple's perfection. 'Therein' means in the knowledge of a disciple's perfection. 'Even beyond that' means beyond the immediately preceding mention of the knowledge of the Paccekabuddhas; what to speak of the knowledge of a disciple's perfection. Here, the meaning should be interpreted thus: Although the knowledge of a disciple's perfection is profound when considering the knowledge of lower trainees and ordinary people, it is not so profound when compared to the knowledge of the Paccekabuddhas. Therefore, one cannot say, 'It is indeed profound.' Similarly, regarding the knowledge of the Paccekabuddhas, when compared to omniscient knowledge, a determination is not obtained. However, the qualities of omniscient knowledge, unlike those of a disciple's perfection and others, are without any non-profoundness in relation to anything; hence, they are indeed profound. Just as the determination is shown here, so too, by the reasoning that 'the knowledge of a disciple's perfection is hard to see, while the knowledge of the Paccekabuddhas is even harder to see than that, so there is no determination there,' and so on, the existence of determination is to be understood. Therefore, it is said, 'Similarly, it is hard to see... should be understood,' and so on.

Kasmā panetaṃ evaṃ āraddhaṃti etthāyaṃ adhippāyo – bhavatu tāva niravasesabuddhaguṇavibhāvanūpāyabhāvato sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ ekampi puthunissayārammaṇañākiccasiddhiyā “atthi bhikkhave aññeva dhammā”tiādinā bahuvacanena uddiṭṭhaṃ, tassa pana vissajjanaṃ saccapaccayākārādivisesavasena anaññasādhāraṇena vibhajananayena anārabhitvā sanissayānaṃ [P 1.0177] diṭṭhīnaṃ vibhajanavasena kasmā āraddhanti. Tattha yathā saccapaccayākārādīnaṃ [M 1.0137] vibhajanaṃ anaññasādhāraṇaṃ, sabbaññutaññāṇasseva visayo, evaṃ niravasesena diṭṭhigatavibhajanampīti dassetuṃ “buddhānañhī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha ṭhānānīti kāraṇāni. Gajjitaṃ mahantaṃ hotīti desetabbassa atthassa anekavidhatāya, duviññeyyatāya ca nānānayehi pavattamānaṃ desanāgajjitaṃ mahantaṃ vipulaṃ, bahubhedañca hoti. Ñāṇaṃ anupavisatīti tato eva ca desanāñāṇaṃ desetabbadhamme vibhāgaso kurumānaṃ anupavisati, te anupavissa ṭhitaṃ viya hotīti attho.

But why is this begun thus? Here is the meaning: Granted that omniscience, although a single knowledge, is a means for demonstrating the Buddha's qualities without remainder, accomplishes its function with various supports and objects, and is pointed out in the plural with 'There are, monks, other phenomena,' etc.; why then is its explanation not begun with the unique analytical method, by way of the distinctions of truths, modes of conditionality, and so on, but is instead begun by way of analyzing views with their supports? To show that just as the analysis of truths, modes of conditionality, and so on, is unique and the domain of omniscience alone, so too is the analysis of views without remainder, the passage 'For the Buddhas, indeed...' etc., is begun. Therein, 'bases' (ṭhānāni) means causes (kāraṇāni). 'The roaring is great' means that due to the manifold nature of the meaning to be taught and its difficulty to understand, the roaring of the teaching, proceeding by various methods, is great, vast, and of many kinds. 'Knowledge penetrates' means that from that very reason, the teaching-knowledge, making divisions in the Dhamma to be taught, penetrates it. Having penetrated them, it is as if it stands established—this is the meaning.

Buddhañāṇassa mahantabhāvo paññāyatīti evaṃvidhassa nāma dhammassa desakaṃ paṭivedhakañcāti buddhānaṃ desanāñāṇassa paṭivedhañāṇassa ca uḷārabhāvo pākaṭo hoti. Ettha ca kiñcāpi “sabbaṃ vacīkammaṃ buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇapubbaṅgamaṃ ñāṇānuparivattī”ti (mahāni. 69; cūḷani. 85; paṭi. ma. 3.5; netti. 14) vacanato sabbāpi bhagavato desanā ñāṇarahitā natthi, sīhasamānavuttitāya ca sabbattha samānussāhappavatti desetabbadhammavasena pana desanā visesato ñāṇena anupaviṭṭhā gambhīratarā ca hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kathaṃ pana vinayapaṇṇattiṃ patvā desanā tilakkhaṇāhatā suññatāpaṭisaṃyuttā hotīti? Tatthāpi ca sannisinnaparisāya ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ pavattamānā desanā saṅkhārānaṃ aniccatādivibhāvanī, sabbadhammānaṃ attattaniyatābhāvappakāsanī ca hoti. Tenevāha “anekapariyāyena dhammiṃ kathaṃ katvā”tiādi.

'The greatness of the Buddha’s knowledge becomes apparent' means that as the expounder and penetrator of such a Dhamma, the sublime nature of the Buddhas’ teaching-knowledge and penetration-knowledge becomes manifest. Here, although it is said, “All verbal actions of the Blessed One are preceded by knowledge and follow knowledge,” none of the Blessed One’s teachings are devoid of knowledge. Moreover, due to his lion-like conduct, his exertion proceeds equally everywhere. However, it should be understood that depending on the Dhamma to be taught, the teaching is especially penetrated by knowledge and is more profound. But how, with regard to the Vinaya regulations, is the teaching imbued with the three characteristics and connected with emptiness? Even there, the teaching, proceeding in accordance with the disposition of the assembled audience, is a demonstrator of the impermanence and so forth of formations, and a proclaimer of the absence of a fixed self-nature in all phenomena. Therefore it is said, “Having given a Dhamma talk in many ways,” and so on.

Bhūmantaranti dhammānaṃ avatthāvisesañca ṭhānavisesañca. Tattha avatthāvisesosatiādidhammānaṃ [V 1.0122] satipaṭṭhānindriyabalabojjhaṅgamaggaṅgādibhedo. Ṭhānaviseso [P 1.0178] kāmāvacarādibhedo. Paccayākārapadassa attho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Samayantaranti diṭṭhivisesā, nānāvihitā diṭṭhiyoti attho, aññasamayaṃ vā. Evaṃ otiṇṇe vatthusminti evaṃ lahukagarukādivasena tadanurūpe otiṇṇe vatthusmiṃ sikkhāpadapaññāpanaṃ.

‘Bhūmantara’ means the distinction of states and the distinction of planes of phenomena. Therein, the distinction of states is the division of phenomena such as mindfulness into the foundations of mindfulness, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and factors of the path, and so on. The distinction of planes is the division into the sense-sphere realm and so forth. The meaning of the term ‘mode of conditionality’ has already been stated below. ‘Samayantara’ means distinctions of views—that is, various kinds of views—or another school. ‘When the matter is thus incurred’ means the laying down of a training rule when a corresponding matter is incurred in this way by way of being light, heavy, and so forth.

Yadipi kāyānupassanādivasena satipaṭṭhānādayo suttantapiṭakepi (dī. ni. 2.374; ma. ni. 1.107) vibhattā, suttantabhājanīyādivasena pana abhidhammeyeva te savisesaṃ vibhattāti āha “ime cattāro satipaṭṭhānā…pe… abhidhammapiṭakaṃ vibhajitvā”ti. Tattha “satta phassā”ti sattaviññāṇadhātusampayogavasena vuttaṃ. Tathā “satta vedanā”tiādīsupi. Lokuttarā dhammā nāmāti [M 1.0138] ettha iti-saddo ādiattho, pakārattho vā, tena vuttāvasesaṃ abhidhamme āgataṃ dhammānaṃ vibhajitabbākāraṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Catuvīsati samantapaṭṭhānāni etthāti catuvīsatisamantapaṭṭhānaṃ, abhidhammapiṭakaṃ. Ettha paccayanayaṃ aggahetvā dhammavaseneva samantapaṭṭhānassa catuvīsatividhatā vuttā. Yathāha –

Even though the foundations of mindfulness and so forth are analyzed in the Sutta Piṭaka by way of the contemplation of the body and so on (Dī. Ni. 2.374; Ma. Ni. 1.107), yet they are analyzed with special detail in the Abhidhamma by way of the Suttanta analysis and so on. Thus it is said: 'These four foundations of mindfulness... having analyzed the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.' Herein, 'seven contacts' is stated by way of association with the seven consciousness-elements. Likewise for 'seven feelings' and so on. In the phrase 'supramundane states, namely...' (`Lokuttarā dhammā nāmāti`), the word `iti` here has the meaning of 'and so on' or 'manner,' by which it includes the remaining ways of analyzing phenomena that are found in the Abhidhamma. The Abhidhamma Piṭaka is the 'twenty-four-comprehensive-foundation' because 'there are twenty-four comprehensive foundations herein.' Here, without taking the method of conditions, the twenty-fourfold nature of the comprehensive foundation is stated solely by way of phenomena. As it is said—

“Tikañca paṭṭhānavaraṃ dukuttamaṃ,

Dukatikañceva tikadukañca;

Tikatikañceva dukadukañca,

Cha anulomamhi nayā sugambhīrā. (paṭṭhā. 1.paccayaniddesa 41, 44, 48, 52);

“The excellent Triad and the supreme Dyad,

And the Dyad-triad and the Triad-dyad;

And the Triad-triad and the Dyad-dyad—

Six methods in the direct order, very profound.” (Paṭṭhāna 1, Paccayaniddesa 41, 44, 48, 52)

Tathā –

Likewise –

Tikañca…pe… cha paccanīyamhi nayā sugambhīrā;

Tikañca…pe… cha anulomapaccanīyamhi nayā sugambhīrā;

Tikañca…pe… paccanīyānulomamhi nayā sugambhīrā”ti. (paṭṭhā. 1.paccayaniddesa 44, 52);

“The Triad... and so on, six methods in the negative order, very profound; The Triad... and so on, six methods in the direct-negative order, very profound; The Triad... and so on, six methods in the negative-direct order, very profound.” (Paṭṭhāna 1, Paccayaniddesa 44, 52).

Evaṃ dhammavasena catuvīsatibhedesu tikapaṭṭhānādīsu ekekaṃ paccayanayena anulomādivasena catubbidhaṃ hotīti channavuti samantapaṭṭhānāni. Tattha pana dhammānulome tikapaṭṭhāne kusalattike paṭiccavāre paccayānulome [P 1.0179] hetumūlake hetupaccayavasena ekūnapaññāsa pucchānayā satta vissajjananayāti [V 1.0123] ādinā dassiyamānā anantabhedā nayāti āha “anantanaya”nti. Hoti cettha –

Thus, by way of phenomena, in the twenty-four divisions such as the Triad-foundations, each becomes fourfold by way of the method of conditions in the direct order and so on, making ninety-six comprehensive foundations. Therein, in the direct order of phenomena, in the Triad-foundation on the wholesome triad, in the section on dependence, in the direct order of conditions, in the root-cause section, by way of the root-condition, the modes shown—such as forty-nine modes of questions and seven modes of answers—are of infinite variety. Therefore, it is said, “infinite modes.” And here it is—

“Paṭṭhānaṃ nāma paccekaṃ dhammānaṃ anulomādimhi tikadukādīsu yā paccayamūlavisiṭṭhā catunayato sattadhā gatī”ti.

“‘Paṭṭhāna’ is the sevenfold course of individual phenomena, which, in the direct order and so on, in the triads, dyads, and so on, is distinguished by its causal root and proceeds by four methods.”

Navahākārehīti uppādādīhi navahi paccayākārehi. Tattha uppajjati etasmā phalanti uppādo, uppattiyā kāraṇabhāvo. Sati ca avijjāya saṅkhārā uppajjanti, na asati, tasmā avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ uppādo hutvā paccayo hoti. Tathā avijjāya sati saṅkhārā pavattanti dharanti, nivisanti ca, te avijjāya sati phalaṃ bhavādīsu khipanti, āyūhanti phaluppattiyā ghaṭanti, saṃyujjanti attano phalena, yasmiṃ santāne sayañca uppannā, taṃ palibundhanti, paccayantarasamavāye udayanti uppajjanti, hinoti ca saṅkhārānaṃ kāraṇabhāvaṃ gacchati, paṭicca avijjaṃ saṅkhārā ayanti pavattantīti evaṃ avijjāya saṅkhārānaṃ [M 1.0139] kāraṇabhāvūpagamanavisesā uppādādayo veditabbā. Tathā saṅkhārādīnaṃ viññāṇādīsu.

‘By nine modes’ means by the nine modes of conditionality such as arising and so on. Herein, ‘arising’ means that a result arises from this; it is the state of being a cause for arising. When ignorance exists, formations arise, not when it does not exist. Therefore, ignorance, being the arising of formations, is a condition. Likewise, when ignorance exists, formations proceed, endure, and become established; they cast the result into existences, etc.; strive for the arising of the result; are conjoined with their own result; bind the continuum in which they themselves have arisen; arise and come into being through the convergence of other conditions; and go to the state of being a cause for formations. Because formations proceed dependent on ignorance, in this way these specific modes by which ignorance becomes a cause for formations, such as arising and so on, should be understood. Similarly, for formations and so on in relation to consciousness and so on.

Uppādaṭṭhitītiādīsu ca tiṭṭhati etenāti ṭhiti, kāraṇaṃ. Uppādo eva ṭhiti uppādaṭṭhiti. Esa nayo sesesupi. Yasmā ayonisomanasikāro, “āsavasamudayā avijjāsamudayo”ti (ma. ni. 1.103) vacanato āsavā ca avijjāya paccayo, tasmā vuttaṃ “ubhopete dhammā paccayasamuppannā”ti. Paccayapariggahe paññāti saṅkhārānaṃ avijjāya ca uppādādike paccayākāre paricchinditvā gahaṇavasena pavattā paññā. Dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇanti dhammānaṃ paccayuppannānaṃ paccayabhāvato dhammaṭṭhitisaṅkhāte paṭiccasamuppāde ñāṇaṃ. Paccayadhammā hi paṭiccasamuppāde “dvādasa paṭiccasamuppādā”ti vacanato [P 1.0180] dvādasa paccayā. Ayañca nayo na paccuppanne eva, atha kho atītānāgatakālepi, na ca avijjāya eva saṅkhāresu, atha kho saṅkhārādīnampi viññāṇādīsu labbhatīti paripuṇṇaṃ katvā paccayākārassa vibhattabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “atītampi addhāna”ntiādi pāḷiṃ ārabhi. Paṭṭhāne (paṭṭhā. 1.paccayaniddesa 1) dassitā hetādipaccayā evettha uppādādipaccayākārehi gahitāti te yathāsambhavaṃ nīharitvā yojetabbā, ativitthārabhayena pana na yojayimha.

In the case of ‘arising-persistence’ and so on, ‘persistence’ means that by which it persists, the cause. Arising itself is persistence—thus, arising-persistence. This method applies to the rest as well. Because unwise attention and the taints are also conditions for ignorance, as stated in “with the arising of the taints comes the arising of ignorance” (MN 1.103), therefore it is said: “Both these phenomena are conditionally arisen.” ‘Wisdom in comprehending conditions’ is the wisdom that proceeds by way of delimiting and grasping the modes of conditionality, such as arising and so on, in formations and ignorance. ‘Knowledge of the stability of phenomena’ is the knowledge of dependent origination, designated as the stability of phenomena, regarding the conditional nature of phenomena that arise dependently. For the conditional phenomena in dependent origination are the twelve conditions, as stated in “the twelve factors of dependent origination.” This method applies not only to the present but also to past and future times, and not only to ignorance in relation to formations but also to formations and so on in relation to consciousness and so on. To fully demonstrate the analyzed nature of the modes of conditionality, the passage beginning with “the past period” was introduced. The root conditions and so on, shown in the Paṭṭhāna (Paṭṭhāna 1, Paccayaniddesa 1), are here included under the modes of conditionality such as arising and so on. These should be extracted and applied as appropriate, but due to fear of excessive elaboration, we have not applied them here.

Tassa tassa dhammassāti tassa tassa saṅkhārādipaccayuppannadhammassa. Tathā tathā paccayabhāvenāti uppādādihetādipaccayabhāvena. Atītapaccuppannānāgatavasena tayo addhā kālā etassāti [V 1.0124] tiyaddhaṃ. Hetuphalaphalahetuhetuphalavasena tayo sandhī etassāti tisandhiṃ. Saṅkhippanti ettha avijjādayo viññāṇādayo cāti saṅkhepo, kammaṃ vipāko ca. Saṅkhippanti etthāti vā saṅkhepo, avijjādayo viññāṇādayo ca. Koṭṭhāsapariyāyo vā saṅkhepa-saddo. Atīte kammasaṅkhepādivasena cattāro saṅkhepā etassāti catusaṅkhepaṃ. Sarūpato avuttāpi tasmiṃ tasmiṃ saṅkhepe ākirīyanti avijjāsaṅkhārādiggahaṇehi pakāsīyantīti ākārā, atīte hetuādīnaṃ vā pakārā ākārā, te saṅkhepe pañca pañca katvā vīsatiākārā etassāti vīsatākāraṃ.

‘Of that very phenomenon’ means of that very phenomenon arisen from conditions such as formations. ‘Thus, thus, by way of being a condition’ means by way of being a condition such as arising, root-condition, and so on. ‘Threefold time’ means that by way of past, present, and future, three periods belong to it. ‘Threefold connection’ means that by way of cause-result, result-cause, and cause-result, three connections belong to it. ‘Summary’ means that here ignorance and so on, and consciousness and so on, are summarized—kamma and its result. Or, ‘summary’ means that here ignorance and so on, and consciousness and so on, are summarized. Or, the word ‘summary’ is a term for sections or divisions. ‘Fourfold summary’ means that in the past, by way of the summary of kamma and so on, four summaries belong to it. The 'modes' are so called because, though not explicitly stated in their own form, they are scattered throughout each summary and revealed by the inclusion of ignorance, formations, and so on. Or, the modes are the types of causes and so on in the past. The 'twentyfold mode' is so called because in those summaries, arranged five by five, twenty modes belong to it.

Khattiyādibhedena anekabhedabhinnāpi sassatavādino jātisatasahassānussaraṇādino abhinivesahetuno vasena cattārova honti[M 1.0140], na tato uddhaṃ adhoti sassatavādādīnaṃ parimāṇaparicchedassa anaññavisayataṃ dassetuṃ “cattāro janā”tiādimāha. Tattha cattāro janāti cattāro janasamūhā. Idaṃ nissāyāti idaṃ idappaccayatāya sammā aggahaṇaṃ, tatthāpi ca hetuphalabhāvena sambandhānaṃ [P 1.0181] santatighanassa abheditattā paramatthato vijjamānampi bhedanibandhanaṃ nānattanayaṃ anupadhāretvā gahitaṃ ekattaggahaṇaṃ nissāya. Idaṃ gaṇhantīti idaṃ sassataggahaṇaṃ abhinivissa voharanti, iminā nayena ekaccasassatavādādayopettha yathāsambhavaṃ yojetvā vattabbā. Bhinditvāti “ātappamanvāyā”tiādinā vibhajitvā “tayidaṃ bhikkhave tathāgato pajānātī”tiādinā vimadditvā nijjaṭaṃ nigumbaṃ katvā diṭṭhijaṭāvijaṭanena diṭṭhigumbavivaraṇena ca.

Though divided into many kinds by distinctions such as Khattiyas and so forth, eternalists—due to their adherence based on recollecting hundreds of thousands of past lives and so on—are only four, not more or less. To show that the scope and limitation of eternalist views and so forth have no other range, it is said, 'four kinds of people,' and so on. Here, 'four kinds of people' means four groups of people. 'Depending on this' means depending on this wrong grasp of specific conditionality, and on the grasp of unity. This grasp of unity is taken without considering the method of diversity—which is the basis for division and truly exists in an ultimate sense—because the dense continuity of things related as cause and effect is unbroken. 'They grasp this' means they speak, having adhered to this eternalist grasp. By this method, the partial-eternalist views and so on should be connected and stated here as appropriate. 'Having split' means: having analyzed it with phrases like 'by means of ardour,' having crushed it with phrases like 'This, monks, the Tathāgata understands,' and having made it free from tangle and thicket by disentangling the tangle of views and opening up the thicket of views.

“Tasmā”tiādinā buddhaguṇe ārabbha desanāya samuṭṭhitattā sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ uddisitvā desanākusalo bhagavā samayantaraviggāhaṇavasena sabbaññutaññāṇameva vissajjetīti dasseti. “Santī”ti iminā tesaṃ diṭṭhigatikānaṃ vijjamānatāya avicchinnataṃ, tato ca nesaṃ micchāgāhato sithilakaraṇavivecanehi attano desanāya kiccakāritaṃ, avitathatañca dīpeti dhammarājā.

Beginning with 'Therefore,' it is shown that the Blessed One, skilled in teaching—since the discourse arose concerning the qualities of the Buddha—having indicated the knowledge of omniscience, resolves it by means of the knowledge of omniscience itself, by way of refuting other doctrines. By 'There are,' the King of Dhamma reveals the unbroken continuity of those who hold such views, due to their existence; and thereby, by loosening and analyzing their wrong grasp, he demonstrates the effectiveness and the truthfulness of his own teaching.

29. Atthīti “saṃvijjantī”ti iminā samānattho puthuvacanavisayo eko nipāto “atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.377; ma. ni. 1.110; ma. ni. 3.154; saṃ. ni. 4.127; khu. pā. 3.1) viya. Sassatādivasena pubbantaṃ kappentīti pubbantakappikā. Yasmā pana te taṃ pubbantaṃ purimasiddhehi taṇhādiṭṭhikappehi kappetvā, āsevanabalavatāya vicittavuttitāya ca vikappetvā aparabhāgasiddhehi abhinivesabhūtehi taṇhādiṭṭhiggāhehi gaṇhanti abhinivisanti parāmasanti, tasmā vuttaṃ “pubbantaṃ [V 1.0125] kappetvā vikappetvā gaṇhantī”ti. Taṇhupādānavasena vā kappanaggahaṇāni veditabbāni. Taṇhāpaccayā hi upādānaṃ. Koṭṭhāsesūti [P 1.0182] ettha koṭṭhāsādīsūti attho veditabbo. Padapūraṇasamīpaummaggādīsupi hi anta-saddo dissati. Tathā hi “iṅgha tvaṃ suttante vā gāthāyo vā abhidhammaṃ vā pariyāpuṇassu (pāci. 442), suttante okāsaṃ kārāpetvā”ti (pāci. 1221) ca ādīsu padapūraṇe anta-saddo vattati, gāmantaṃ osareyya, (pārā. 409; cūḷava. 343) gāmantasenāsana”ntiādīsu samīpe[M 1.0141], “kāmasukhallikānuyogo eko anto, atthīti kho kaccāna ayameko anto”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.15; 3.90) ummaggeti.

29. The particle 'atthi' is synonymous with 'saṃvijjantī' and, as a single particle, has a plural meaning, as in 'there are hairs on this body,' and so on. Those who speculate about the past in terms of eternalism and so forth are called 'pubbantakappikā' (speculators on the past). Because they, having speculated on that past with previously established speculations of craving and views, and having variously speculated due to the strength of habituation and the diversity of their ways, grasp, adhere to, and are attached to those grasps of craving and views that are subsequently established and are of the nature of adherence, it is therefore said, 'they speculate, variously speculate, and grasp at the past.' Alternatively, the speculating and grasping should be understood in terms of craving and clinging, for clinging is conditioned by craving. Here, 'koṭṭhāsesu' should be understood to mean 'in sections, and so on.' For the word 'anta' is also seen in such senses as a metrical filler, proximity, and an extreme. For example, the word 'anta' is used as a metrical filler in 'Come, you should learn the Suttas, or verses, or the Abhidhamma' and 'having had an opportunity made in the Suttas'; in the sense of proximity in 'he might descend to the vicinity of the village' and 'a dwelling in the vicinity of a village'; and in the sense of an extreme in 'the practice of indulgence in sensual pleasures is one extreme' and '“It exists,” Kaccāna, this is one extreme.'

Kappa-saddo mahākappasamantabhāvakilesakāmavitakkakālapaññattisadisabhāvādīsu vattatīti āha “sambahulesu atthesu vattatī”ti. Tathā hesa “cattārimāni bhikkhave kappassa asaṅkhyeyyānī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.156) mahākappe vattati, “kevalakappaṃ veḷuvanaṃ obhāsetvā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.94) samantabhāve, “saṅkappo kāmo, rāgo kāmo, saṅkapparāgo kāmo”tiādīsu (mahāni. 1; cūḷani. 8) kilesakāme, “takko vitakko saṅkappo”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 7) vitakke, “yena [P 1.0183] sudaṃ niccakappaṃ viharāmī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.387) kāle, “iccāyasmā kappo”tiādīsu (su. ni. 1090; cūḷani. 113) paññattiyaṃ, “satthukappena vata kira bho sāvakena saddhiṃ mantayamānā na jānimhā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.260) sadisabhāve vattatīti. Vuttampi cetanti mahāniddesaṃ (mahāni. 28) sandhāyāha. Taṇhādiṭṭhivasenāti diṭṭhiyā upanissayabhūtāya sahajātāya abhinandanabhūtāya ca taṇhāya, sassatādiākārena abhinivisantassa micchāgāhassa ca vasena. Pubbenivutthadhammavisayāya kappanāya adhippetattā atītakālavācako idha pubba-saddo, rūpādikhandhavinimuttassa kappanāvatthuno abhāvā anta-saddo ca bhāgavācakoti āha “atītaṃ khandhakoṭṭhāsa”nti. “Kappetvā”ti ca tasmiṃ pubbante taṇhāyanābhinivesānaṃ samatthanaṃ pariniṭṭhāpanamāha. Ṭhitāti tassā laddhiyā avijahanaṃ. Ārabbhāti ālambitvā. Visayo hi tassā diṭṭhiyā pubbanto. Visayabhāvato eva hi so tassā āgamanaṭṭhānaṃ, ārammaṇapaccayo cāti vuttaṃ “āgamma paṭiccā”ti.

The term 'kappa' is used in many senses, such as a great eon, all-pervasiveness, sensual defilement, thought, time, designation, and similarity. For example, in 'Monks, these four are incalculable eons,' it refers to a great eon. In 'having illuminated the entire Veḷuvana grove,' it denotes all-pervasiveness. In 'intention is desire, lust is desire, intention and lust are desire,' it pertains to sensual defilement. In 'reasoning, thought, intention,' it refers to thought. In 'where we dwell constantly,' it signifies time. In 'thus, Venerable Kappa,' it denotes a designation. And in 'indeed, we did not know while conversing with the disciple in the manner of the Teacher,' it indicates similarity. When it is said, 'This is also stated,' this is said with reference to the Mahāniddesa. 'By the power of craving and views' means by the power of craving—which is the supporting condition for the view, co-arisen with it, and of the nature of delight—and by the power of the wrong grasp which adheres in the mode of eternalism and so forth. Because the speculation is intended with regard to things experienced in the past, the word 'pubba' here designates past time. And because there is no object of speculation apart from the aggregates such as form, the word 'anta' designates a part; thus it is said, 'the past portion of the aggregates.' 'Having speculated' states the establishing and completion of craving and adherence regarding that past end. 'Established' means the non-abandonment of that doctrine. 'Based on' means having taken as an object. For the object of that view is the past. Precisely because it is the object, it is its ground of arising and its object-condition; thus it is said, 'dependent on, conditioned by.'

Adhivacanapadānīti paññattipadāni. Dāsādīsu sirivaḍḍhakādi-saddā viya vacanamattameva adhikāraṃ katvā pavattiyā adhivacanaṃ paññatti. Atha vā adhi-saddo uparibhāve, vuccatīti vacanaṃ, upari vacanaṃ adhivacanaṃ, upādābhūtarūpādīnaṃ upari paññāpiyamānā upādāpaññattīti attho[V 1.0126], tasmā paññattidīpakapadānīti attho daṭṭhabbo. Paññattimattañhetaṃ vuccati, yadidaṃ “attā, loko”ti ca, na rūpavedanādayo viya paramattho. Adhikavuttitāya vā adhivuttiyoti diṭṭhiyo vuccanti. Adhikañhi [P 1.0184] sabhāvadhammesu sassatādiṃ [M 1.0142] pakatiādidabbādiṃ jīvādiṃ kāyādiñca abhūtamatthaṃ ajjhāropetvā diṭṭhiyo pavattantīti.

'Terms of designation' means terms of concept. Just as words like 'Sirivaḍḍhaka' for slaves and so on, a designation is an 'adhivacana' because it proceeds by making a mere word authoritative. Alternatively, the prefix 'adhi-' has the sense of 'over,' and 'vacana' means 'word'; thus 'adhivacana' is a word placed over something, meaning a derivative concept (`upādāpaññatti`) that is conceptualized over and above derivative phenomena such as form. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as 'terms that indicate a concept.' For this—that is, 'self' and 'world'—is called a mere concept, not an ultimate reality like form, feeling, and so on. Or, views are called 'adhivutti' because of their excessive assertion. For views proceed by superimposing an unreal meaning—such as permanence, primordial nature, substance, a soul, a body, and so forth—onto phenomena that have an intrinsic nature.

30. Abhivadantīti “idameva saccaṃ, moghamañña”nti (ma. ni. 2.187, 203, 427; ma. ni. 3.27, 29) abhinivisitvā vadanti “ayaṃ dhammo, nāyaṃ dhammo”tiādinā vivadanti. Abhivadanakiriyāya ajjāpi avicchedabhāvadassanatthaṃ vattamānakālavacanaṃ. Diṭṭhi eva diṭṭhigataṃ “muttagataṃ, (ma. ni. 2.119; a. ni. 9.11) saṅkhāragata”ntiādīsu (mahāni. 41) viya. Gantabbābhāvato vā diṭṭhiyā gatamattaṃ, diṭṭhiyā gahaṇamattanti attho. Diṭṭhippakāro vā diṭṭhigataṃ. Lokiyā hi vidhayuttagatapakāra-sadde samānatthe icchanti. Ekekasmiñca “attā”ti, “loko”ti ca gahaṇavisesaṃ upādāya paññāpanaṃ hotīti āha “rūpādīsu aññataraṃ attā ca loko cāti gahetvā”ti. Amaraṃ niccaṃ dhuvanti sassatavevacanāni. Maraṇābhāvena vā amaraṃ, uppādābhāvena sabbathāpi atthitāya niccaṃ, thiraṭṭhena vikārābhāvena dhuvaṃ. “Yathāhā”tiādinā yathāvuttamatthaṃ niddesapaṭisambhidāpāḷīhi vibhāveti. Ayañca attho “rūpaṃ attato samanupassati, vedanaṃ, saññaṃ, saṅkhāre, viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassatī”ti imissā pañcavidhāya sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā vasena vutto. “Rūpavantaṃ attāna”ntiādikāya pana pañcadasavidhāya sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā vasena cattāro cattāro khandhe “attā”ti gahetvā tadaññaṃ “loko”ti paññapentīti ayampi attho labbhati. Tathā ekaṃ khandhaṃ [P 1.0185]”attā”ti gahetvā tadaññe attano upabhogabhūto lokoti, sasantatipatite vā khandhe “attā”ti gahetvā tadaññe “loko”ti paññapentīti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Etthāha – sassato vādo etesanti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu tesaṃ attā loko ca sassatoti adhippeto, na vādo ti? Saccametaṃ, sassatasahacaritatāya pana “vādo sassato”ti vuttaṃ yathā “kuntā pacarantī”ti. Sassato iti vādo etesanti vā iti-saddalopo daṭṭhabbo. Atha vā sassataṃ vadanti “idameva sacca”nti abhinivissa voharantīti sassatavādā, sassatadiṭṭhinoti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

30. 'They declare' means, having adhered to the view, 'This alone is true, all else is false,' they speak and dispute, saying, 'This is the Dhamma, that is not the Dhamma,' and so forth. The present tense is used to show that the act of declaring is still uninterrupted. A view is itself a 'view-adherence' (diṭṭhigata), like 'gone to the liberated' (muttagata) or 'gone to the conditioned' (saṅkhāragata). Or, because there is nowhere to go, it means the mere going to a view, the mere grasping of a view. Alternatively, 'view-adherence' signifies a kind of view. For worldly people hold that the words `vidha`, `yutta`, `gata`, and `pakāra` have the same meaning. And because a designation is made in each case depending on the specific way of grasping 'self' and 'world,' it is said: 'having taken one of form and so on as self and world.' 'Deathless' (amara), 'permanent' (nicca), and 'stable' (dhuva) are synonyms for 'eternal.' It is 'deathless' due to the absence of death; 'permanent' due to existing in every way, without arising; and 'stable' due to its firm nature, without alteration. By 'As was said,' etc., the aforesaid meaning is clarified with the Pāli texts of the Niddesa and Paṭisambhidāmagga. This meaning is stated in terms of the fivefold identity view: 'One regards form as self, feeling as self, perception as self, formations as self, consciousness as self.' Alternatively, in terms of the fifteenfold identity view, such as 'self possessing form,' etc., this meaning is also obtained: they take four aggregates as 'self' and designate what is other than that as 'world.' Similarly, the meaning should be understood in this way: they take one aggregate as 'self' and the others, which are for their own enjoyment, as 'world'; or they take the aggregates that fall within their own continuity as 'self' and designate others as 'world.' Here it is asked: Why is it said, 'theirs is an eternal doctrine'? Is it not their intention that the self and the world are eternal, not the doctrine? That is true. But it is said, 'the doctrine is eternal,' because of its association with the eternal, just as when it is said, 'the lances advance.' Or, the elision of the word 'iti' should be seen here, as in 'sassato iti vādo etesaṃ' (eternal is the doctrine of these). Or, they are 'eternalists' (sassatavādā) because they speak of the eternal, adhering to and proclaiming, 'This alone is true'; thus they are holders of eternalist views (sassatadiṭṭhino). This is how the meaning should be understood here.

31. Ātāpanaṃ [M 1.0143] kilesānaṃ vibādhanaṃ pahānaṃ. Padahanaṃ kosajjapakkhe patituṃ adatvā cittassa ussahanaṃ. Anuyogo yathā samādhi visesabhāgiyataṃ pāpuṇāti, evaṃ vīriyassa bahulīkaraṇaṃ. Idha upacārappanācittaparidamanavīriyānaṃ adhippetattā āha “tippabhedaṃ vīriya”nti[V 1.0127]. Nappamajjati etenāti appamādo, asammoso. Sammā upāyena manasi karoti kammaṭṭhānaṃ etenāti sammāmanasikāro ñāṇanti āha “vīriyañca satiñca ñāṇañcā”ti. Etthāti “ātappa…pe… manasikāraṃ anvāyā”ti imasmiṃ pāṭhe. Sīlavisuddhiyā saddhiṃ catunnaṃ rūpāvacarajjhānānaṃ adhigamanapaṭipadā vattabbā, sā pana visuddhimagge vitthārato vuttāti āha “saṅkhepattho”ti. “Tathārūpa”nti cuddasavidhehi cittadamanehi rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānassa damitataṃ vadati.

31. Ardor is the tormenting and abandoning of defilements. Exertion is the rousing of the mind, not allowing it to fall into the side of laziness. Application is the cultivation of energy in such a way that concentration attains a distinctive quality. Here, because energy for taming the mind in both access and absorption is intended, it is said, 'threefold energy.' 'Heedfulness' (appamāda) is not being negligent; it is non-confusion. 'Right attention' (sammāmanasikāra) is knowledge, whereby one rightly and skillfully attends to the meditation subject; thus it is said, 'energy, mindfulness, and knowledge.' Here, in this passage 'ardor... up to attention,' the path of practice for the attainment of the four form-sphere jhānas together with the purification of virtue should be stated. But since that is explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga, it is said, 'this is the meaning in brief.' 'Of such a kind' refers to the fact that the fourth form-sphere jhāna has been tamed by the fourteen methods of taming the mind.

Samādhānādiaṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatarūpāvacaracatutthajjhānassa yogino samādhivijambhanabhūtā lokiyābhiññā jhānānubhāvo. “Jhānādīna”nti idaṃ jhānalābhissa visesena jhānadhammā āpāthaṃ āgacchanti, taṃmukhena sesadhammāti imamatthaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Janakabhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati. Sati hi janakabhāve rūpādidhammānaṃ viya sukhādidhammānaṃ viya, ca paccayāyattavuttitāya uppādavantatā [P 1.0186] viññāyati, uppāde ca sati avassambhāvī nirodhoti anavakāsāva niccatā siyāti. Kūṭaṭṭha-saddo vā loke accantanicce niruḷho daṭṭhabbo. “Esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhito”ti etena yathā esikā vātappahārādīhi na calati, evaṃ na kenaci vikāraṃ āpajjatīti vikārābhāvamāha, “kūṭaṭṭho”ti iminā pana aniccatābhāvaṃ. Vikāropi vināsoyevāti āha, “ubhayenapi lokassa vināsābhāvaṃ dīpetī”ti. “Vijjamānamevā”ti etena kāraṇe phalassa atthibhāvadassanena abhibyattivādaṃ dīpeti. Nikkhamatīti ca abhibyattiṃ gacchatīti attho. Kathaṃ pana vijjamānoyeva pubbe anabhibyatto abhibyattiṃ gacchatīti? Yathā andhakārena paṭicchanno ghaṭo ālokena abhibyattiṃ gacchati.

For the yogi endowed with the fourth form-sphere jhāna, which includes the eight factors beginning with concentration, mundane higher knowledge is the power of jhāna, serving to dispel sloth regarding concentration. 'Through jhāna and so on' (jhānādīnaṃ): This is said with reference to the meaning that for one who has attained jhāna, the jhāna qualities especially come into view, and through that door, the remaining qualities. It denies the state of being a generator. For if there were a generator, then just as material things and pleasant experiences are understood to have arising due to their dependence on conditions, and when there is arising, cessation is inevitable, so there would be no possibility of permanence. Or the word 'kūṭaṭṭha' (unshakeable) should be understood as established in the world as utterly permanent. 'Like a pillar firmly fixed' (esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhito): By this, it is said that just as a pillar is not shaken by wind or other forces, so too it undergoes no alteration—thus indicating the absence of change. By 'kūṭaṭṭha,' however, the absence of impermanence is indicated. It is also said that change itself is destruction. Thus, it is explained, "by both, the absence of destruction of the world is shown." 'While existing' (vijjamānameva): By this, the doctrine of manifestation is shown by demonstrating the existence of the effect in the cause. And 'emerges' (nikkhamati) means it becomes manifest. But how can what already exists, though previously unmanifest, become manifest? Just as a pot hidden in darkness becomes manifest when light shines upon it.

Idamettha vicāretabbaṃ – kiṃ karonto āloko ghaṭaṃ pakāsetīti vuccati, yadi ghaṭavisayaṃ buddhiṃ karonto, buddhiyā anuppannāya uppattidīpanato abhibyattivādo hāyati. Atha ghaṭabuddhiyā āvaraṇabhūtaṃ andhakāraṃ vidhamanto, evampi abhibyattivādo hāyatiyeva. Sati hi ghaṭabuddhiyā andhakāro kathaṃ tassā āvaraṇaṃ hotīti, yathā ghaṭassa [M 1.0144] abhibyatti na yujjati, evaṃ attanopi. Tatthāpi hi yadi indriyavisayādisannipātena anuppannāya buddhiyā uppatti, uppattivacaneneva abhibyattivādo hāyati, tathā sassatavādo. Atha buddhippavattiyā āvaraṇabhūtassa andhakāraṭṭhāniyassa mohassa vidhamanena. Sati buddhiyā kathaṃ moho āvaraṇanti, kiñci bhedasambhavato. Na hi abhibyañjanakānaṃ candasūriyamaṇipadīpādīnaṃ bhedena abhibyañjitabbānaṃ ghaṭādīnaṃ bhedo hoti, hoti ca visayabhedena buddhibhedoti bhiyyopi abhibyatti na yujjatiyeva, na cettha vuttikappanā yuttā vuttiyā vuttimato ca anaññathānujānanatoti[V 1.0128]. Te [P 1.0187] ca sattā sandhāvantīti ye idha manussabhāvena avaṭṭhitā, teyeva devabhāvādiupagamanena ito aññattha gacchanti, aññathā katassa kammassa vināso, akatassa ca abbhāgamo āpajjeyyāti adhippāyo.

This should be considered here: By doing what is light said to reveal the pot? If it is by producing a cognition of the pot-object, then the doctrine of manifestation fails, because this shows the arising of a previously non-existent cognition. Or if it is by dispelling the darkness that is an obstruction to the cognition of the pot, even then the doctrine of manifestation fails. For if the cognition of the pot exists, how can darkness be an obstruction to it? Just as the manifestation of the pot is untenable, so too is that of the self. Here too, if there is an arising of a previously non-existent cognition due to the conjunction of sense faculty, object, etc., then by the very statement of 'arising,' the doctrine of manifestation fails, and so does the doctrine of eternalism. Or if it is by dispelling delusion, which is like darkness obstructing the process of cognition, then how can delusion be an obstruction when cognition exists? Because some distinction is possible. For there is no difference in the things to be manifested, like pots, due to a difference in the manifesting agents like the moon, sun, gems, or lamps; but there is a difference in cognition due to a difference in the object. Thus, manifestation is even more untenable. And here, the postulation of a function is not appropriate, because the function and the possessor of the function are not admitted to be otherwise. And 'those beings who transmigrate' (sandhāvantīti) means: those who are established here in the human state are the very ones who go elsewhere by attaining a divine state or the like. Otherwise, the destruction of karma that has been done and the arrival of karma that has not been done would result; this is the intention.

Aparāparanti aparasmā bhavā aparaṃ bhavaṃ. Evaṃ saṅkhyaṃ gacchantīti attano niccasabhāvattā na cutūpapattiyo, sabbabyāpitāya nāpi sandhāvanasaṃsaraṇāni, dhammānaṃyeva pana pavattivisesena evaṃ saṅkhyaṃ gacchanti, evaṃ voharīyantīti adhippāyo. Etena avaṭṭhitasabhāvassa attano, dhammino ca dhammamattaṃ uppajjati ceva vinassati cāti imaṃ vipariṇāmavādaṃ dasseti. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ parato vakkhāma. Attano vādaṃ bhindatīti sandhāvanādivacanasiddhāya aniccatāya pubbe paṭiññātaṃ sassatavādaṃ bhindati, viddhaṃsetīti attho. Sassatisamanti vā etassa sassataṃ thāvaraṃ niccakālanti attho daṭṭhabbo.

'Again and again' (aparāparaṃ) means from one existence to another. Thus, they are reckoned as such: not through death and rebirth, because of the self's permanent nature, nor through running and wandering, due to its all-pervasiveness. Rather, it is only due to the particular process of phenomena that they are reckoned and spoken of in this way—this is the meaning. By this, he shows the doctrine of transformation, which holds that for the self whose nature is fixed, and for the possessor of phenomena, mere phenomena arise and cease. What should be said on this matter, we will explain later. 'He refutes his own doctrine' (attano vādaṃ bhindati): by means of impermanence, which is established by the statement about running and so on, he refutes the eternalist doctrine previously affirmed; that is, he demolishes it. Or 'eternal' (sassatisamaṃ) here should be understood as meaning eternal, stable, and permanent in time.

Hetuṃ dassentoti yesaṃ “sassato”ti attānañca lokañca paññapeti ayaṃ diṭṭhigatiko, tesaṃ hetuṃ dassentoti attho. Na hi attano diṭṭhiyā paccakkhakatamatthaṃ attanoyeva sādheti, attano pana paccakkhakatena atthena attano appaccakkhabhūtampi atthaṃ sādheti. Attanā hi yathānicchitaṃ parehi viññāpeti, na anicchitaṃ. “Hetuṃ dassento”ti ettha idaṃ hetudassanaṃ – etesu anekesu jātisatasahassesu ekovāyaṃ me attā, loko ca anussaraṇasabbhāvato. Yo hi yamatthaṃ anubhavati, so eva taṃ anussarati, na añño. Na hi aññena anubhūtamatthaṃ añño anussarituṃ sakkoti yathā taṃ buddharakkhitena anubhūtaṃ dhammarakkhito. Yathā cetāsu, evaṃ ito purimatarāsupi jātīsūti. Kasmā sassato me attā ca loko [M 1.0145] ca. Yathā ca me, evaṃ aññesampi sattānaṃ sassato attā ca loko cāti? Sassatavasena diṭṭhigahanaṃ pakkhando [P 1.0188] diṭṭhigatiko parepi tattha patiṭṭhapeti, pāḷiyaṃ pana “anekavihitāni adhivuttipadāni abhivadanti. So evaṃ āhā”ti ca vacanato parānumānavasena idha hetudassanaṃ adhippetanti viññāyati. Kāraṇanti tividhaṃ kāraṇaṃ sampāpakaṃ nibbattakaṃ ñāpakanti. Tattha ariyamaggo nibbānassa sampāpakaṃ kāraṇaṃ, bījaṃ aṅkurassa nibbattakaṃ kāraṇaṃ, paccayuppannatādayo aniccatādīnaṃ ñāpakaṃ kāraṇaṃ, idhāpi ñāpakakāraṇameva adhippetaṃ. Ñāpako hi ñāpetabbatthavisayassa ñāṇassa hetubhāvato kāraṇanti. Tadāyattavuttitāya taṃ ñāṇaṃ tiṭṭhati tatthāti “ṭhāna”nti, vasati tattha pavattatīti “vatthū”ti ca vuccati. Tathā hi bhagavatā vatthu-saddena uddisitvāpi ṭhānasaddena niddiṭṭhanti.

'He shows the cause' (hetuṃ dassento): This means he shows the cause for those view-holders who proclaim the self and the world as 'eternal.' For one does not prove to oneself a matter already made evident by one's own view; rather, by means of a matter made evident to oneself, one establishes even a matter not directly evident to oneself. Indeed, one makes others understand according to what one desires, not what one does not desire. 'He shows the cause' (hetuṃ dassento): Here, this is the demonstration of the cause: 'In these countless hundreds of thousands of births, this self of mine is one and the same, and so is the world, due to the nature of recollection. For whoever experiences something, that very one remembers it, not another. Indeed, another cannot remember something experienced by someone else, just as Dhammarakkhita cannot remember what was experienced by Buddharakkhita. As in these cases, so also in births even earlier than these.' Why is my self and the world eternal? And as it is for me, so too for other beings, the self and the world are eternal. Having plunged into the thicket of views by way of eternity, the view-holder establishes others as well in that view. But in the Pāli, from 'they declare various speculative tenets,' and 'So he said,' it is understood that here the demonstration of the cause is intended by way of inference about others. Cause (kāraṇaṃ) means a threefold cause: the accomplishing, the producing, and the indicative. Among these, the noble path is the accomplishing cause of Nibbāna, the seed is the producing cause of the sprout, and conditionality, etc., is the indicative cause of impermanence, etc. Here, only the indicative cause is intended. For the indicator is a cause because it is the condition for the knowledge regarding the object to be indicated. Because that knowledge depends on it and exists there, it is called 'basis' (ṭhāna); and because it abides there and operates, it is called 'ground' (vatthu). Thus, the Blessed One, after designating with the word 'ground,' also indicated with the word 'basis.'

32-33. Dutiyatatiyavādānaṃ [V 1.0129] paṭhamavādato natthi viseso ṭhapetvā kālavisesanti āha “upari vādadvayepi eseva nayo”ti. Yadi evaṃ kasmā sassatavādo catudhā vibhatto, nanu adhiccasamuppannikavādo viya duvidheneva vibhajitabbo siyāti āha “mandapañño hi titthiyo”tiādi.

32-33. There is no difference between the second and third doctrines and the first doctrine, except for the difference in time. Hence he said, 'The same method applies in the two doctrines above' (upari vādadvayepi eseva nayo). If so, why is the eternalist doctrine divided into four ways? Surely, like the doctrine of spontaneous origination, it should be divided in just two ways? To this he said, 'For the sectarian is of weak wisdom' (mandapañño hi titthiyo), and so on.

34. Takkayatīti ūhayati, sassatādiākārena tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ārammaṇe cittaṃ abhiniropetīti attho. Takkoti ākoṭanalakkhaṇo vinicchayalakkhaṇo vā diṭṭhiṭṭhānabhūto vitakko. Vīmaṃsā nāma vicāraṇā, sā panettha atthato paññāpatirūpako lobhasahagatacittuppādo, micchābhiniveso vā ayonisomanasikāro, pubbabhāge vā diṭṭhivipphanditanti daṭṭhabbā. Tenevāha “tulanā ruccanā khamanā”ti. Pariyāhananaṃ vitakkassa ārammaṇaūhanaṃ evāti āha “tena tena pakārena takketvā”ti. Anuvicaritanti [P 1.0189] vīmaṃsāya anupavattitaṃ, vīmaṃsānugatena vā vicārena anumajjitaṃ. Paṭi paṭi bhātīti paṭibhānaṃ, yathāsamihitākāravisesavibhāvako cittuppādo. Paṭibhānato jātaṃ paṭibhānaṃ, sayaṃ attano paṭibhānaṃ sayaṃ paṭibhānaṃ. Tenevāha “attano paṭibhānamattasañjāta”nti. Matta-saddena visesādhigamādayo nivatteti.

34. 'He speculates' (takkayati) means he conjectures; that is, he applies the mind to this and that object in the manner of eternalism, etc. 'Speculation' (takko) is thought characterized by striking or by discernment, which is the basis of views. 'Investigation' (vīmaṃsā) means inquiry. Here, however, in essence, it should be understood as a mind-state accompanied by greed that appears like wisdom, or wrong adherence, or unwise attention, or, in its preliminary stage, a stirring of views. Hence it is said, 'weighing, approving, accepting' (tulanā ruccanā khamanā). 'Pariyāhananaṃ' is the conjecturing about an object by thought; hence it is said, 'having speculated in this and that way' (tena tena pakārena takketvā). 'Anuvicaritaṃ' means pursued by investigation, or polished by reflection accompanying investigation. 'Paṭibhānaṃ' is that which shines forth again and again, a mental state that reveals distinctive aspects according to what is intended. What arises from inspiration is 'paṭibhāna.' One's own inspiration is 'sayaṃ paṭibhānaṃ.' Hence it is said, 'born merely of one's own inspiration' (attano paṭibhānamattasañjātaṃ). The word 'matta' (merely) excludes special attainments and so on.

“Anāgatepi [M 1.0146] evaṃ bhavissatī”ti idaṃ na idhādhippetatakkīvaseneva vuttaṃ, lābhītakkino evampi sambhavatīti sambhavadassanavasena vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yaṃ kiñci attanā paṭiladdhaṃ rūpādi sukhādi ca idha labbhatīti lābho, na jhānādiviseso. “Evaṃ sati idaṃ hotī”ti aniccesu bhāvesu añño karoti, añño paṭisaṃvedetīti āpajjati, tathā ca sati katassa vināso, akatassa ca abbhāgamo siyā. Niccesu pana bhāvesu yo karoti, so paṭisaṃvedetīti na doso āpajjatīti takkikassa yuttigavesanākāraṃ dasseti.

'In the future, it will be like this'—this is not said here only with reference to the reasoner under discussion, but it should be understood as stated to show a possibility, since it is possible even for a reasoner who has some attainment to think in this way. Whatever form or pleasure one has personally obtained is called a 'gain' here—not special attainments like jhāna. 'When this exists, that arises'—in the case of impermanent phenomena, it would follow that one person acts and another experiences the result, which would lead to the destruction of what was done and the arising of what was not done. But in the case of permanent phenomena, the one who acts is the one who experiences the result—no fault arises in this. This shows the way a reasoner seeks for a logical argument.

Takkamattenevāti āgamādhigamādīnaṃ anussavādīnañca abhāvā suddhatakkeneva. Nanu ca visesalābhinopi sassatavādino attano visesādhigamahetu anekesu jātisatasahassesu dasasu saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭesu cattālīsāya saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭesu yathānubhūtaṃ attano santānaṃ tappaṭibaddhañca “attā, loko”ti ca anussaritvā tato purimapurimatarāsupi jātīsu tathābhūtassa atthitānuvitakkanamukhena sabbesampi sattānaṃ tathābhāvānuvitakkanavaseneva sassatābhinivesino jātā, evañca sati sabbopi sassatavādī anussutijātissaratakkikā viya attano upaladdhavatthunibandhanena takkanena pavattavādattā takkīpakkheyeva tiṭṭheyya, avassañca vuttappakāraṃ takkanamicchitabbaṃ[V 1.0130], aññathā visesalābhī sassatavādī ekaccasassatikapakkhaṃ, adhiccasamuppannikapakkhaṃ vā bhajeyyāti[P 1.0190]? Na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, yasmā visesalābhīnaṃ khandhasantānassa dīghadīghataradīghatamakālānussaraṇaṃ sassataggāhassa asādhāraṇakāraṇaṃ. Tathā hi “anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarāmi. Imināmahametaṃ jānāmī”ti anussaraṇameva padhānakāraṇabhāvena dassitaṃ. Yaṃ pana tassa “imināmahametaṃ jānāmī”ti pavattaṃ takkanaṃ, na taṃ idha padhānaṃ anussaraṇaṃ pati tassa appadhānabhūtattā. Yadi evaṃ anussavādīnampi padhānabhāvo āpajjatīti ce? Na, tesaṃ sacchikiriyāya abhāvena takkapadhānattā, padhānakāraṇena ca niddeso niruḷho sāsane loke ca yathā “cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, yavaṅkuro”ti ca.

“Merely by reasoning” means solely through pure reasoning, due to the absence of scripture, direct realization, hearsay, and so forth. But is it not so that even those eternalists who have special attainments become attached to eternalism by recalling their own continuity and what is connected to it—as “self” and “world”—as experienced over countless hundreds of thousands of births, through ten or forty world-cycles of contraction and expansion, and then, by way of reflecting on the existence of such a state in even earlier and earlier lives, and by way of reflecting on the similar state of all beings? And if this is so, would not every eternalist—like those who rely on hearsay, memory of past lives, or reasoning—stand in the category of reasoners, since their doctrine proceeds from reasoning based on grounds they have themselves discovered? And must not reasoning of the kind described be accepted? Otherwise, the eternalist with special attainments might adopt the position of the partial-eternalists or the spontaneous-originists. But this should not be seen thus. For those with special attainments, the recollection of the continuity of their aggregates over long, longer, and very long periods of time is the uncommon cause for grasping eternalism. Thus it is said: “I recall my manifold past lives... By this I know this,” where recollection itself is shown to be the primary cause. As for the reasoning that occurs to him, “By this I know this,” that is not primary here, because it is subordinate to recollection. If it is argued that, in that case, primacy would also apply to those who rely on hearsay and so on—no, because for them, in the absence of direct realization, reasoning is primary. And designation by the primary cause is established in the teaching and in the world, as in the case of “eye-consciousness” and “a barley sprout.”

Atha vā visesādhigamanibandhanarahitassa takkanassa visuṃ sassataggāhe kāraṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ visesādhigamo visuṃ sassataggāhakāraṇaṃ vattabbo[M 1.0147], so ca mandamajjhatikkhapaññāvasena tividhoti bhagavatā sabbatakkino takkībhāvasāmaññena ekajjhaṃ gahetvā catudhā vavatthāpito sassatavādo. Yadipi anussavādivasena takkikānaṃ viya mandapaññādīnampi hīnādivasena anekabhedasabbhāvato visesalābhīnampi bahudhā bhedo sambhavati, sabbe pana visesalābhino mandapaññādivasena tayo rāsī katvā tattha ukkaṭṭhavasena anekajātisatasahassadasasaṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭacattārīsasaṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭānussaraṇena ayaṃ vibhāgo vutto. Tīsupi rāsīsu ye hīnamajjhapaññā, te vuttaparicchedato ūnakameva anussaranti. Ye pana tattha ukkaṭṭhapaññā, te vuttaparicchedaṃ atikkamitvā nānussarantīti evaṃ panāyaṃ desanā. Tasmā aññatarabhedasaṅgahavaseneva [P 1.0191] bhagavatā cattāriṭṭhānāni vibhattānīti vavatthitā sassatavādīnaṃ catubbidhatā. Na hi idha sāvasesaṃ dhammaṃ deseti dhammarājā.

Or, to show that reasoning, which is not bound by special attainment, is a separate cause for the eternalist view, it is declared that special attainment is also a separate cause for the eternalist view. And that, due to the threefold division based on dull, middling, and sharp wisdom, the Blessed One has classified the eternalist doctrine into four types by gathering all reasoners together under the common designation of “reasoners.” Even though, through hearsay and other means, the distinctions among reasoners—like those with dull wisdom and others—may be of many kinds due to their inferior, middling, and superior natures, and even though those who attain distinctions may be of many kinds, all those who attain distinctions are grouped into three categories based on dull, middling, and sharp wisdom. Among these, this division is spoken of in terms of the highest, with the recollection of many hundreds of thousands of births, and of ten and forty world-cycles of contraction and expansion. Among these three groups, those with inferior or middling wisdom remember less than the stated limit, while those with the highest wisdom do not remember beyond the stated limit. Thus is this teaching. Therefore, the fourfold nature of the eternalists is established, as the Blessed One has divided the four grounds by including them under a certain division. For here, the King of Dhamma does not teach a doctrine with anything left out.

35. “Aññatarenā”ti etassa atthaṃ dassetuṃ “ekenā”ti vuttaṃ. Vā-saddassa pana aniyamatthataṃ dassetuṃ “dvīhi vā tīhi vā”ti vuttaṃ. Tena catūsu ṭhānesu yathārahaṃ ekaccaṃ ekaccassa paññāpane sahakārīkāraṇanti dasseti. Kiṃ panetāni vatthūni abhinivesassa hetu, udāhu patiṭṭhāpanassa. Kiñcettha yadi tāva abhinivesassa, kasmā anussaraṇatakkanāniyeva gahitāni, na saññāvipallāsādayo. Tathāhi viparītasaññā ayonisomanasikāraasappurisūpanissayaasaddhammassavanādīni micchādiṭṭhiyā pavattanaṭṭhānāni. Atha patiṭṭhāpanassa adhigamayuttiyo viya āgamopi vatthubhāvena vattabbo, ubhayatthāpi “natthi ito bahiddhā”ti vacanaṃ na yujjatīti? Na. Kasmā? Abhinivesapakkhe tāva ayaṃ diṭṭhigatiko [V 1.0131] asappurisūpanissayaasaddhammassavanehi ayoniso ummujjitvā vipallāsasañño rūpādidhammānaṃ khaṇe khaṇe bhijjanasabhāvassa anavabodhato dhammayuttiṃ atidhāvanto ekattanayaṃ micchā gahetvā yathāvuttānussaraṇatakkehi khandhesu “sassato attā ca loko cā”ti (dī. ni. 1.31) abhinivesaṃ janesi. Iti āsannakāraṇattā, padhānakāraṇattā, taggahaṇeneva ca itaresampi gahitattā anussaraṇatakkanāniyeva idha gahitāni. Patiṭṭhāpanapakkhe pana āgamopi yuttipakkheyeva ṭhito visesato bāhirakānaṃ takkagāhibhāvatoti anussaraṇatakkanāniyeva [M 1.0148] diṭṭhiyā vatthubhāvena gahitāni. Kiñca bhiyyo duvidhaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ paramatthadhammānaṃ sabhāvalakkhaṇaṃ sāmaññalakkhaṇañcāti. Tattha sabhāvalakkhaṇāvabodho paccakkhañāṇaṃ, sāmaññalakkhaṇāvabodho [P 1.0192] anumānañāṇaṃ, āgamo ca sutamayāya paññāya sādhanato anumānañāṇameva āvahati, sutānaṃ pana dhammānaṃ ākāraparivitakkanena nijjhānakkhantiyaṃ ṭhito cintāmayaṃ paññaṃ nibbattetvā anukkamena bhāvanāya paccakkhañāṇaṃ adhigacchatīti evaṃ āgamopi takkavisayaṃ nātikkamatīti taggahaṇena gahitovāti veditabbo. So aṭṭhakathāyaṃ anussutitakkaggahaṇena vibhāvitoti yuttaṃ evidaṃ “natthi ito bahiddhā”ti. “Anekavihitāni adhivuttipadāni abhivadanti, sassataṃ attānañca lokañca paññapentī”ti (dī. ni. 1.30) ca vacanato patiṭṭhāpanavatthūni idhādhippetānīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

35. To show the meaning of ‘by one or another,’ it is said ‘by one.’ To indicate the indefinite meaning of the word ‘or,’ it is said ‘by two or three.’ Thus, in the four grounds, it shows that each assists in establishing the other appropriately. But are these bases causes for insistence or for establishment? If they are for insistence, why are only recollection and reasoning taken, and not perceptual distortions, etc.? Indeed, distorted perception, unwise attention, association with bad people, listening to the false Dhamma, and so on are the grounds for the arising of wrong view. Or if they are for establishment, should scripture also be affirmed as a basis, like logical grounds for realization? In both cases, the statement “there is nothing beyond this” would not apply. Why not? On the side of insistence, this holder of views, emerging unwisely from association with bad people and listening to the false Dhamma, with distorted perception and unaware of the momentary disintegration of phenomena like form, etc., oversteps the logical consistency of phenomena, wrongly grasps the doctrine of unity, and through the aforementioned recollection and reasoning, generates insistence regarding the aggregates that: “The self and the world are eternal” (Dī. Ni. 1.31). Thus, because they are proximate causes, primary causes, and because the others are also included by their inclusion, only recollection and reasoning are taken here. On the side of establishment, scripture also stands on the side of reasoning. Particularly because outsiders are of the nature of grasping reasoning, recollection and reasoning are taken as the bases for wrong view. Furthermore, the characteristics of ultimate phenomena are twofold: the specific characteristic and the general characteristic. Therein, understanding the specific characteristic is direct knowledge, while understanding the general characteristic is inferential knowledge. Scripture, being based on wisdom derived from learning, brings inferential knowledge. By thoroughly examining the learned teachings in accordance with the manner and attaining acquiescence through reflection, one generates wisdom born of reflection and gradually attains direct knowledge through meditation. Thus, scripture does not transcend the domain of reasoning—this should be understood by its inclusion. That is clarified in the commentary through the inclusion of tradition and reasoning. Hence, the statement “there is nothing beyond this” is appropriate. From the passage, “They declare various assertions, proclaiming the self and the world as eternal” (Dī. Ni. 1.30), it should be seen that the bases for establishment are intended here.

36. Diṭṭhiyeva diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ paramavajjatāya anekavihitānaṃ anatthānaṃ hetubhāvato. Yathāha “micchādiṭṭhiparamāhaṃ bhikkhave vajjaṃ vadāmī”ti (a. ni. 1.310) “yathāhā”tiādinā paṭisambhidāpāḷiyā (paṭi. ma. 1.124) diṭṭhiyā ṭhānavibhāgaṃ dasseti. Tattha khandhāpi diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ ārammaṇaṭṭhena “rūpaṃ attato samanupassatī”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 3.81, 345) vacanato. Avijjāpi diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ upanissayādibhāvena pavattanato. Yathāha “assutavā bhikkhave puthujjano ariyānaṃ adassāvī ariyadhammassa akovido”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.2; paṭi. ma. 1.130). Phassopi diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ. Yathā cāha “tadapi phassapaccayā, (dī. ni. 1.118 ādayo) phussa phussa paṭisaṃvedentī”ti (dī. ni. 1.144) ca[P 1.0193]. Saññāpi diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ. Vuttañcetaṃ “saññānidānā hi papañcasaṅkhā, (su. ni. 880; mahāni. 109) pathavito saññatvā”ti (ma. ni. 1.2) ca ādi. Vitakkopi diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ “takkañca diṭṭhīsu pakappayitvā, saccaṃ musāti dvayadhammamāhū”ti (su. ni. 892) “takkī hoti vīmaṃsī”ti (dī. ni. 1.34) ca ādi. Ayonisomanasikāropi diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā “tassa evaṃ ayoniso manasi karoto channaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ aññatarā diṭṭhi uppajjati. ‘Atthi me attā’ti vā assa saccato thetato [V 1.0132] diṭṭhi uppajjatī”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.19). Samuṭṭhāti etenāti samuṭṭhānaṃ samuṭṭhānabhāvo samuṭṭhānaṭṭho. Pavattitāti parasantānesu uppāditā. Pariniṭṭhāpitāti abhinivesassa pariyosānaṃ [M 1.0149] matthakaṃ pāpitāti attho. “Ārammaṇavasenā”ti aṭṭhasu diṭṭhiṭṭhānesu khandhe sandhāyāha. Pavattanavasenāti avijjādayo. Āsevanavasenāti pāpamittaparatoghosādīnampi sevanaṃ labbhatiyeva. Atha vā evaṃgatikāti evaṃgamanā, evaṃniṭṭhāti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ime diṭṭhisaṅkhātā diṭṭhiṭṭhānā evaṃ paramatthato asantaṃ attānaṃ sassatabhāvañcassa ajjhāropetvā gahitā, parāmaṭṭhā ca bālalapanā yāva paṇḍitā na samanuyuñjanti, tāva gacchanti pavattanti. Paṇḍitehi samanuyuñjiyamānā pana anavaṭṭhitavatthukā avimaddakkhamā sūriyuggamane ussāvabindū [P 1.0194] viya khajjopanakā viya ca bhijjanti vinassanti cāti.

36. A view itself is a basis for views, because of being the highest fault and the cause of many kinds of harm. As it is said: 'Monks, I declare wrong view to be the highest fault' (A. Ni. 1.310). By the phrase 'as it is said,' etc., in the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. Ma. 1.124), the classification of the bases of views is shown. There, the aggregates are also a basis for views in the sense of being their object, as stated: 'One regards form as self,' and so on (Saṃ. Ni. 3.81, 345). Ignorance too is a basis for views because it serves as a support-condition for their occurrence. As it is said: 'An uninstructed worldling, monks, who has not seen the noble ones, is unskilled in the noble Dhamma,' and so on (Ma. Ni. 1.2; Paṭi. Ma. 1.130). Contact is also a basis for views. As it is said: 'That too is conditioned by contact' (Dī. Ni. 1.118, etc.), and 'experiencing again and again through contact' (Dī. Ni. 1.144). Perception too is a basis for views. This is stated: 'For perceptions are the source of conceptual proliferation' (Su. Ni. 880; Mahāni. 109), and 'having perceived earth as earth,' and so on (Ma. Ni. 1.2). Thought is also a basis for views. This is stated: 'Having fashioned views based on reasoning, they declare truth and falsehood as two things' (Su. Ni. 892), and 'he is a reasoner, an investigator,' and so on (Dī. Ni. 1.34). Unwise attention is also a basis for views. Therefore the Blessed One said: 'When one attends unwisely in this way, one of six views arises. The view, “I have a self,” arises in him as true and established,' and so on (Ma. Ni. 1.19). 'Origin' (samuṭṭhāna) means that from which it originates; the state of being an origin; the meaning of origin. 'Occurred' (pavattiṭā) means produced in the continuities of others. 'Brought to a conclusion' (pariniṭṭhāpitā) means brought to the culmination, the peak of adherence—this is the meaning. 'By way of object' refers to the aggregates among the eight bases of views. 'By way of occurrence' refers to ignorance and the rest. 'By way of cultivation' refers also to the cultivation of association with bad friends, reports from others, and the like. Alternatively, 'having such a destination' (evaṃgatikā) means having such a destination, that is, having such a conclusion. This is what is meant: These so-called bases of views, being grasped and misapprehended by superimposing on them an ultimately non-existent self and its eternal nature, are the prattle of fools; as long as they are not scrutinized by the wise, they proceed and continue. But when scrutinized by the wise, lacking a stable foundation and unable to withstand examination, they break up and perish like dewdrops at sunrise or like fireflies.

Tatthāyaṃ anuyuñjane saṅkhepakathā – yadi hi parena parikappito attā loko vā sassato siyā, tassa nibbikāratāya purimarūpāvijahanato kassaci visesādhānassa kātuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya ahitato nivattanatthaṃ, hite ca paṭipattiatthaṃ upadeso eva nippayojano siyā sassatavādino, kathaṃ vā so upadeso pavattīyati vikārābhāvato, evañca attano ajaṭākāsassa viya dānādikiriyā hiṃsādikiriyā ca na sambhavati. Tathā sukhassa dukkhassa anubhavananibandho eva sassatavādino na yujjati kammabaddhābhāvato, jātiādīnañca asambhavato kuto vimokkho, atha pana dhammamattaṃ tassa uppajjati ceva vinassati ca, yassa vasenāyaṃ kiriyādivohāroti vadeyya, evampi purimarūpāvijahanena avaṭṭhitassa attano dhammamattanti na sakkā sambhāvetuṃ, te vā panassa dhammā avatthābhūtā aññe vā siyuṃ anaññe vā. Yadi aññe, na tāhi tassa uppannāhipi koci viseso atthi. Yāhi karoti paṭisaṃvedeti cavati upapajjati cāti icchitaṃ, tasmā tadavattho eva yathāvuttadoso. Kiñca dhammakappanāpi niratthikā siyā, athānaññe uppādavināsavantīhi avatthāhi anaññassa attano tāsaṃ viya uppādavināsasabbhāvato kuto niccatāvakāso, tāsampi vā attano viya niccatāti bandhavimokkhānaṃ asambhavo evāti na yujjatiyeva sassatavādo. Na cettha koci vādī dhammānaṃ sassatabhāve parisuddhaṃ yuttiṃ vattuṃ samattho, yuttirahitañca vacanaṃ [P 1.0195] na paṇḍitānaṃ cittaṃ ārādhetīti. Tena vuttaṃ “yāva paṇḍitā na samanuyuñjanti, tāva gacchanti pavattantī”ti. Kammavasena abhimukho sampareti etthāti abhisamparāyo, paroloko.

Here is the concise discussion on inquiry: If the self or the world were eternal as conceived by another, due to its unchanging nature and the inability to abandon prior forms, no one could make any special effort to turn away from harm or to practice for welfare. Thus, instruction would be entirely useless for an eternalist; how could such instruction proceed, given the absence of change? Likewise, for such a self, like unmatted space, actions such as giving and harming would not be possible. Similarly, for an eternalist, a necessary connection with the experience of pleasure and pain is untenable because there would be no bondage to kamma, and since birth and so forth could not occur, how could there be liberation? But if one argues that a mere phenomenon arises and ceases for him, and that this is the basis for the convention of action and experience, even then, for a self that is stable by not abandoning its prior form, one cannot reasonably conceive of a 'mere phenomenon.' Moreover, those phenomena of his, being states, would they be different from him or not different? If they are different, then even when they arise, there is no special quality for him by which he does, feels, passes away, and is reborn, as is wished; therefore, that position has the same flaw as stated. Furthermore, even the postulation of phenomena would be meaningless. If, however, for a self not different from the states that arise and perish, there were, like them, the existence of arising and perishing, how could there be room for permanence? Or if those states were permanent like the self, then bondage and liberation would be impossible. Thus, the doctrine of eternalism is altogether untenable. Here, no proponent can present a perfectly sound argument for the eternity of phenomena, and a statement devoid of reason does not satisfy the minds of the wise. Therefore, it is said: 'As long as they are not scrutinized by the wise, they proceed and continue.' The future life (abhisamparāyo) is that to which one fares on account of kamma; it is the next world.

“Sabbaññutaññāṇañcā”ti [M 1.0150] idaṃ idha sabbaññutaññāṇassa vibhajiyamānattā vuttaṃ, tasmiṃ vā [V 1.0133] vutte tadadhiṭṭhānato āsavakkhayañāṇaṃ, tadavinābhāvato sabbampi vā bhagavato dasabalādiñāṇaṃ gahitameva hotīti katvā. Pajānantopīti pi-saddo sambhāvane, tena “tañcā”ti ettha vuttaṃ ca-saddatthamāha. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – taṃ diṭṭhigatato uttaritaraṃ sārabhūtaṃ sīlādiguṇavisesampi tathāgato nābhinivisati, ko pana vādo vaṭṭāmiseti. “Aha”nti diṭṭhivasena vā taṃ parāmasanākāramāha. Pajānāmīti ettha iti-saddo pakārattho, tena “mama”nti taṇhāvasena parāmasanākāraṃ dasseti. Dhammasabhāvaṃ atikkamitvā parato āmasanaṃ parāmāso. Na hi taṃ atthi, khandhesu yaṃ “aha”nti vā, “mama”nti vā gahetabbaṃ siyā. Yo pana parāmāso taṇhādayova, te ca bhagavato bodhimūleyeva pahīnāti āha “parāmāsakilesāna”ntiādi. Aparāmāsatoti vā nibbutivedanassa hetuvacanaṃ, “viditā”ti idaṃ padaṃ apekkhitvā kattari sāmivacanaṃ, aparāmasanahetu parāmāsarahitāya paṭipattiyā tathāgatena sayameva asaṅkhatadhātu adhigatāti evaṃ vā ettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

'And the knowledge of omniscience' is mentioned here because the knowledge of omniscience is being analyzed. Or, when that is stated, the knowledge of the destruction of the taints is implied by being its foundation, and by their inseparability, all the Blessed One's knowledge, such as the ten powers, is also included. The particle pi in pajānanto pi is used in the sense of possibility; thus he explains the meaning of the particle ca in tañca. This is what is meant: The Tathāgata does not cling even to the superior and essential qualities such as virtue, which are beyond views—what need be said of the bait of the round? He indicates the mode of misapprehension by way of view with 'I.' In pajānāmi, the particle iti indicates manner; thereby he shows the mode of misapprehension by way of craving with 'mine.'
