Misapprehension is touching upon something beyond the intrinsic nature of phenomena. For there is nothing in the aggregates that could be grasped as 'I' or 'mine.' That misapprehension is just craving and other defilements, and these were abandoned by the Blessed One at the root of enlightenment; hence the phrase 'of the defilements of misapprehension,' and so on. Alternatively, 'from non-misapprehension' is a statement of the cause for the feeling of Nibbāna. With reference to the word 'known' (viditā), this is a genitive in the sense of agent. Or, the meaning here should be seen thus: because of the cause of non-misapprehension, through the practice devoid of misapprehension, the unconditioned element has been attained by the Tathāgata himself.

“Yāsu vedanāsū”tiādinā bhagavato desanāvilāsaṃ dasseti. Tathā hi khandhāyatanādivasena anekavidhāsu catusaccadesanāsu sambhavantīsupi ayaṃ tathāgatānaṃ desanāsu paṭipatti, yaṃ diṭṭhigatikā micchāpaṭipattiyā diṭṭhigahanaṃ pakkhandāti dassanatthaṃ vedanāyeva pariññāya bhūmidassanatthaṃ [P 1.0196] uddhaṭā. Kammaṭṭhānanti catusaccakammaṭṭhānaṃ. Yathābhūtaṃ viditvāti vipassanāpaññāya vedanāya samudayādīni ārammaṇapaṭivedhavasena maggapaññāya asammohapaṭivedhavasena jānitvā, paṭivijjhitvāti attho. Paccayasamudayaṭṭhenāti “imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti, imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.404; saṃ. ni. 2.21; udā. 1) vuttalakkhaṇena avijjādīnaṃ paccayānaṃ uppādena ceva maggena asamugghātena ca. Nibbattilakkhaṇanti uppādalakkhaṇaṃ, jātinti attho. Pañcannaṃ lakkhaṇānanti ettha catunnaṃ paccayānampi uppādalakkhaṇameva gahetvā vuttanti gahetabbaṃ, yasmā paccayalakkhaṇampi labbhatiyeva, tathā ceva saṃvaṇṇitaṃ. Paccayanirodhaṭṭhenāti etthāpi vuttanayānusārena attho veditabbo. Yanti yasmā, yaṃ vā sukhaṃ somanassaṃ. Paṭiccāti ārammaṇapaccayādibhūtaṃ [M 1.0151] vedanaṃ labhitvā. Ayanti sukhasomanassānaṃ paccayabhāvo, sukhasomanassameva vā, “assādo”ti padaṃ pana apekkhitvā pulliṅganiddeso. Ayañhettha saṅkhepattho – purimuppannaṃ vedanaṃ ārabbha somanassuppattiyaṃ yo purimavedanāya assādetabbākāro somanassassādanākāro, ayaṃ assādoti. Kathaṃ pana vedanaṃ ārabbha sukhaṃ uppajjatīti? Cetasikasukhassa adhippetattā nāyaṃ doso. Visesanaṃ hettha somanassaggahaṇaṃ sukhaṃ somanassanti “rukkho siṃsapā”ti yathā.

With 'in which feelings,' and so on, he shows the grace of the Blessed One's teaching. Thus, although the teaching of the four truths can occur in many ways through aggregates, sense bases, and so on, this is the method of the Tathāgatas in their teachings: to show that those who follow wrong views plunge into the thicket of views through wrong practice, feeling itself is extracted to show the ground for full understanding. 'Meditation subject' refers to the meditation subject of the four truths. 'Having known as it really is' means knowing and penetrating the origin, etc., of feeling with insight wisdom by way of comprehending the object, and with path wisdom by way of penetrating non-delusion; that is the meaning of 'having penetrated.' 'By way of the arising of conditions' means by the arising of conditions such as ignorance, etc., in the manner stated: 'When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises' (MN 1.404; SN 2.21; Ud 1), and by their not being eradicated by the path. 'The characteristic of production' means the characteristic of arising, that is, birth. Regarding 'the five characteristics,' it should be understood that this is said by also taking the characteristic of arising of the four conditions, since the characteristic of a condition can also be obtained, and it is explained thus. 'By way of the cessation of conditions'—here too the meaning should be understood following the method stated above. Yanti means 'because of which,' or 'whatever pleasure and joy.' 'Dependent on' means having obtained feeling as an object-condition, etc. Ayanti refers to the conditionality of pleasure and joy, or to pleasure and joy themselves; but the masculine designation is made with reference to the word 'gratification.' Here, the meaning in brief is this: regarding the arising of joy dependent on a previously arisen feeling, the aspect of that previous feeling to be gratified—the aspect of savoring the joy—this is gratification. But how does pleasure arise dependent on feeling? Since mental pleasure is intended here, there is no fault. The qualification here is the inclusion of joy—'pleasure and joy'—just as 'a tree, a siṃsapa tree.'

“Aniccā”ti [V 1.0134] iminā saṅkhāradukkhatāvasena upekkhāvedanāya, sabbavedanāsuyeva vā ādīnavamāha, itarehi itaradukkhatāvasena yathākkamaṃ dukkhasukhavedanānaṃ, avisesena vā tīṇipi padāni sabbāsampi vedanānaṃ vasena yojetabbāni. Ayanti yo vedanāya hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena [P 1.0197] aniccabhāvo, udayabbayapaṭipīḷanaṭṭhena dukkhabhāvo, jarāya maraṇena cāti dvedhā vipariṇāmetabbabhāvo ca, ayaṃ vedanāya ādīnavo, yato vā ādīnaṃ paramakāruññaṃ vāti pavattatīti. Vedanāya nissaraṇanti ettha vedanāyāti nissakkavacanaṃ, yāva vedanāpaṭibaddhaṃ chandarāgaṃ na pajahati, tāvāyaṃ puriso vedanaṃ allīnoyeva hoti. Yadā pana taṃ chandarāgaṃ pajahati, tadāyaṃ puriso vedanāya nissaṭo visaṃyutto hotīti chandarāgappahānaṃ vedanāya nissaraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Ettha ca vedanāggahaṇena vedanāya sahajātanissayārammaṇabhūtā ca rūpārūpadhammā gahitā eva hontīti pañcannampi upādānakkhandhānaṃ gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vedanāsīsena pana desanā āgatā, tattha kāraṇaṃ vuttameva, lakkhaṇahāranayena vā ayamattho vibhāvetabbo. Tattha vedanāggahaṇena gahitā pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhasaccaṃ, vedanānaṃ samudayaggahaṇena gahitā avijjādayo samudayasaccaṃ, atthaṅgamanissaraṇapariyāyehi nirodhasaccaṃ, “yathābhūtaṃ viditvā”ti etena maggasaccanti evamettha cattāri saccāni veditabbāni. Kāmupādānamūlakattā sesupādānānaṃ, pahīne ca kāmupādāne upādānasesābhāvato “vigatachandarāgatāya anupādāno”ti vuttaṃ. Anupādāvimuttoti attano maggaphalappattiṃ bhagavā dasseti. “Vedanāna”ntiādinā hi yassā dhammadhātuyā suppaṭividdhattā imaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ sakāraṇaṃ sagatikaṃ pabhedato vibhajituṃ samattho ahosi[M 1.0152], tassa sabbaññutaññāṇassa saddhiṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadāya uppattibhūmiṃ dasseti dhammarājā.

By 'impermanent,' he speaks of the drawback of equanimous feeling by way of the suffering inherent in formations, or indeed of all feelings. By the other terms, he speaks of the drawback of painful and pleasant feelings respectively, by way of the other kinds of suffering. Or, without distinction, all three terms should be applied to all feelings. Here, the impermanent nature of feeling is its non-existence after having been; its suffering nature is its oppression by arising and passing away; and its liability to change in two ways, through aging and death—this is the drawback of feeling. Or, it is called a 'drawback' because supreme compassion proceeds from what is afflicted. In 'the escape from feeling,' the term 'from feeling' is a term for escape. As long as a person does not abandon the desire and lust bound up with feeling, they remain clinging to feeling. But when they abandon that desire and lust, they are freed and detached from feeling. Thus, the abandonment of desire and lust is called the escape from feeling. Here, by the taking up of 'feeling,' the material and immaterial phenomena that are co-nascent with, a support for, and an object of feeling are also included. Thus, the inclusion of all five aggregates of clinging should be understood. The teaching, however, is presented with feeling as the heading. The reason for this has already been stated, or this meaning should be analyzed by the method of extracting characteristics. In this context, the five aggregates of clinging, included by the taking up of 'feeling,' constitute the truth of suffering. Ignorance and so forth, included by the taking up of 'the origin of feelings,' constitute the truth of the origin. The truth of cessation is expressed through the terms 'passing away' and 'escape.' The truth of the path is indicated by the phrase 'having known as it really is.' Thus, the four truths should be understood here. Because sensual clinging is the root of the other clingings, and when sensual clinging is abandoned, the remaining clingings cease to exist, it is said, 'free from desire and lust, without clinging.' By 'freed through non-clinging,' the Blessed One here reveals his attainment of the path and fruit. By the phrase 'of feelings' and so on, the King of Dhamma shows the ground for the arising of his omniscience, together with the preliminary practice, on account of which, through having thoroughly penetrated a certain element of the Dhamma, he was able to analyze this view with its cause, its destination, and its divisions.

Paṭhamabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the first recitation section is completed.

Ekaccasassatavādavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of Partial Eternalism.

38. Sattesu saṅkhāresu ca ekaccaṃ sassataṃ etassāti ekaccasassato, ekaccasassatavādo. So etesaṃ atthīti ekaccasassatikā[P 1.0198]. Te pana yasmā ekaccasassato vādo diṭṭhi etesanti ekaccasassatavādā nāma honti, tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento āha “ekaccasassatavādā”ti. Iminā nayena ekaccaasassatikā dipadassapi attho veditabbo. Nanu [V 1.0135] ca “ekaccasassatikā”ti vutte tadaññassa ekaccassa asassatatāsanniṭṭhānaṃ siddhameva hotīti? Saccaṃ siddhameva hoti atthato, na pana saddato. Tasmā supākaṭaṃ katvā dassetuṃ “ekaccaasassatikā”ti vuttaṃ. Na hi idha sāvasesaṃ katvā dhammaṃ deseti dhammassāmī. Idhāti “ekaccasassatikā”ti imasmiṃ pade. Gahitāti vuttā, tathā ceva attho dassito. Idhāti vā imissā desanāya. Tathā hi purimakā tayo vādā sattavasena, catuttho saṅkhāravasena vibhatto. “Saṅkhārekaccasassatikā”ti idaṃ tehi sassatabhāvena gayhamānānaṃ dhammānaṃ yāthāvasabhāvadassanavasena vuttaṃ, na panekaccasassatikamatadassanavasena. Tassa hi sassatābhimataṃ asaṅkhatamevāti laddhi. Tenevāha “cittanti vā…pe… ṭhassatī”ti. Na hi yassa bhāvassa paccayehi abhisaṅkhatabhāvaṃ paṭijānāti, tasseva niccadhuvādibhāvo anummattakena sakkā paṭiññātuṃ. Etena “uppādavayadhuvatāyuttabhāvā siyā niccā, siyā aniccā siyā na vattabbā”tiādinā pavattassa sattabhaṅgavādassa ayuttatā vibhāvitā hoti.

38. Regarding beings and conditioned phenomena, some are eternal—this is what one who holds to partial eternalism maintains, the doctrine of partial eternalism. Those who hold that some of these are eternal are called 'partial eternalists.' Since their view and doctrine assert that some things are eternal, they are called 'partial eternalists.' Therefore, to clarify this meaning, it is said, 'partial eternalists.' In this way, the meaning of the two-part term 'partial non-eternalists' should also be understood. Now, when it is said 'partial eternalists,' does it not inherently establish that the other part is non-eternal? Indeed, in meaning it is established, but not explicitly in wording. Therefore, to make it perfectly clear, the term 'partial non-eternalists' is used. The Lord of the Dhamma does not teach the Dhamma here by leaving anything incomplete. Here—in the phrase 'partial eternalists'—the meaning is grasped and explained accordingly. Alternatively, 'here' refers to this teaching. For the first three doctrines are analyzed in terms of beings, while the fourth is analyzed in terms of conditioned phenomena. The phrase 'partial eternalism regarding conditioned phenomena' is stated to show the true nature of those phenomena that they consider eternal, not to present the view of partial eternalism itself. For their belief is that what they regard as eternal is unconditioned. Hence it is said, 'the mind... will remain.' Indeed, for one who acknowledges that a phenomenon is conditioned by causes, it is impossible for anyone who is not mad to claim that very phenomenon as permanent, stable, or eternal. In this way, the untenability of the sevenfold analysis—such as 'it may be permanent, impermanent, or indeterminate'—is made clear.

Tatthāyaṃ ayuttatāvibhāvanā – yadi “yena sabhāvena yo dhammo atthīti vuccati, teneva sabhāvena so dhammo natthī”tiādinā vucceyya, siyā anekantavādo. Atha aññena, siyā na anekantavādo. Na cettha desantarādisambandhabhāvo yutto vattuṃ tassa sabbalokasiddhattā, vivādābhāvato[M 1.0153]. Ye pana vadanti “yathā suvaṇṇaghaṭena makuṭe kate ghaṭabhāvo nassati, makuṭabhāvo [P 1.0199] uppajjati, suvaṇṇabhāvo tiṭṭhatiyeva, evaṃ sabbabhāvānaṃ koci dhammo nassati, koci dhammo uppajjati, sabhāvo pana tiṭṭhatī”ti. Te vattabbā “kiṃ taṃ suvaṇṇaṃ, yaṃ ghaṭe makuṭe ca avaṭṭhitaṃ, yadi rūpādi, so saddo viya anicco. Atha rūpādi samūho, samūho nāma sammutimattaṃ. Na tassa atthitā natthitā niccatā vā labbhatī”ti anekantavādo na siyā. Dhammānañca dhammino aññathānaññathāsu doso vuttoyeva sassatavādavicāraṇāyaṃ. Tasmā so tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Apica niccāniccanavattabbarūpo attā loko ca paramatthato vijjamānatāpaṭijānanato yathā niccādīnaṃ aññataraṃ rūpaṃ, yathā vā dīpādayo. Na hi dīpādīnaṃ udayabbayasabhāvānaṃ niccāniccanavattabbasabhāvatā sakkā viññātuṃ, jīvassa niccādīsu aññataraṃ rūpaṃ viyāti evaṃ sattabhaṅgassa viya sesabhaṅgānampi asambhavoyevāti sattabhaṅgavādassa ayuttatā veditabbā.

Herein is the demonstration of incorrectness: If it were said, 'By the very nature by which a phenomenon is said to exist, by that same nature it does not exist,' and so on, it would be a doctrine of uncertainty. But if by another nature, it would not be a doctrine of uncertainty. And here, it is not appropriate to speak of a connection with a different place and so on, because that is universally established and free from dispute. However, those who say, 'Just as when a golden pot is fashioned into a crown, the pot-form ceases, the crown-form arises, but the gold-nature remains the same—so too, for all phenomena, some states cease, some arise, but their intrinsic nature persists'—they should be told: 'What is that gold which remains unchanged in both pot and crown? If it is form, etc., then like sound, it is impermanent. If it is an aggregate of form, etc., an aggregate is merely a convention. Its existence, non-existence, or permanence cannot be established.' Thus, there would be no doctrine of uncertainty. Moreover, the fault of difference or non-difference between phenomena and their bearers has already been discussed in the examination of eternalism. Therefore, it should be understood here in the same way as previously explained. Furthermore, regarding the claim that the self and the world exist in an ultimate sense and have a nature that is inexpressible as permanent or impermanent: just as it is impossible to conceive of things like lamps, which have a nature of arising and passing away, as having a nature that is inexpressible as permanent or impermanent, and just as the soul cannot have a nature that is one of permanent, etc., so too is there an utter impossibility for the remaining alternatives of the seven-fold analysis. Thus, the incorrectness of the seven-fold doctrine should be understood.

Ettha ca “issaro nicco, aññe sattā aniccā”ti evaṃ pavattavādā sattekaccasassatikā seyyathāpi issaravādā. “Paramāṇavo niccā dhuvā, aṇukādayo aniccā”ti evaṃ pavattavādā saṅkhārekaccasassatikā seyyathāpi kāṇādā. Nanu “ekacce dhammā [V 1.0136] sassatā, ekacce asassatā”ti etasmiṃ vāde cakkhādīnaṃ asassatatāsanniṭṭhānaṃ yathāsabhāvāvabodho eva, tayidaṃ kathaṃ micchādassananti, ko vā evamāha “cakkhādīnaṃ asassatabhāvasanniṭṭhānaṃ micchādassana”nti? Asassatesuyeva pana kesañci dhammānaṃ sassatabhāvābhiniveso idha micchādassanaṃ. Tena pana ekavāre pavattamānena cakkhādīnaṃ asassatabhāvāvabodho [P 1.0200] vidūsito saṃsaṭṭhabhāvato visasaṃsaṭṭho viya sappimaṇḍo sakiccakaraṇāsamatthatāya sammādassanapakkhe ṭhapetabbataṃ nārahatīti. Asassatabhāvena nicchitāpi vā cakkhuādayo samāropitajīvasabhāvā eva diṭṭhigatikehi gayhantīti tadavabodhassa micchādassanabhāvo na sakkā nivāretuṃ. Tenevāha “cakkhuṃ itipi…pe… kāyo itipi ayaṃ me attā”tiādi. Evañca katvā asaṅkhatāya saṅkhatāya ca dhātuyā vasena yathākkamaṃ “ekacce dhammā sassatā, ekacce asassatā”ti evaṃ pavatto [M 1.0154] vibhajjavādopi ekaccasassatavādo āpajjatīti evaṃpakārā codanā anavakāsā hoti aviparītadhammasabhāvasampaṭipattibhāvato.

Herein, those who hold the view that 'the Lord is eternal, other beings are impermanent,' are partial eternalists regarding beings, like the proponents of the doctrine of a creator god. Those who hold the view that 'atoms are eternal and permanent, while molecules and so forth are impermanent,' are partial eternalists regarding formations, like the followers of Kaṇāda. Now, in the view that 'some phenomena are eternal, some are not,' the ascertainment of the impermanent nature of the eye and so forth is precisely a true understanding of their nature—so how can this be a wrong view? And who says that 'ascertaining the impermanent nature of the eye and so forth is a wrong view'? Here, however, the adherence to the eternal nature of certain phenomena that are in fact impermanent is what constitutes wrong view. And because of that, the understanding of the impermanent nature of the eye and so forth, occurring in the same instance, is corrupted by being mixed with it, just as a drop of ghee is corrupted when mixed with poison. Due to its inability to perform its proper function, it does not deserve to be placed on the side of right view. Or, even though the eye and other faculties have been determined to be impermanent, they are still grasped by those holding such views as having the nature of a soul superimposed upon them; thus, it cannot be denied that this understanding is a wrong view. Therefore, it is said: 'The eye... and so on... the body, this is my self,' and so forth. This being the case, the charge that even the analytical view—which holds that 'some phenomena are eternal, some are not,' based respectively on the unconditioned and conditioned elements—falls into partial eternalism, is groundless, because it is a correct understanding of the unperverted nature of phenomena.

Kāmañcettha purimavādepi asassatānaṃ dhammānaṃ “sassatā”ti gahaṇaṃ visesato micchādassanaṃ, sassatānaṃ pana “sassatā”ti gāho na micchādassanaṃ yathāsabhāvaggahaṇabhāvato. Asassatesuyeva pana “kecideva dhammā sassatā, keci asassatā”ti gahetabbadhammesu vibhāgappavattiyā imassa vādassa vādantaratā vuttā, na cettha “samudāyantogadhattā ekadesassa sappadesasassataggāho nippadesasassataggāhe samodhānaṃ gacchatī”ti sakkā vattuṃ vādī tabbisayavisesavasena vādadvayassa pavattattā. Aññe eva hi diṭṭhigatikā “sabbe dhammā sassatā”ti abhiniviṭṭhā, aññe “ekaccasassatā”ti. Saṅkhārānaṃ anavasesapariyādānaṃ, ekadesapariggaho ca vādadvayassa paribyattoyeva. Kiñca bhiyyo anekavidhasamussaye ekavidhasamussaye ca khandhapabandhe abhinivesabhāvato. Catubbidhopi hi sassatavādī jātivisesavasena nānāvidharūpakāyasannissaye eva arūpadhammapuñje sassatābhinivesī jāto abhiññāṇena anussavādīhi ca rūpakāyabhedaggahaṇato. Tathā ca vuttaṃ “tato cuto amutra udapādi”nti (dī. ni. 1.32) “cavanti upapajjantī”ti ca ādi. Visesalābhī [P 1.0201] ekaccasassatiko anupadhāritabhedasamussayeva dhammapabandhe sassatākāraggahaṇena abhinivisanaṃ janesi ekabhavapariyāpannakhandhasantānavisayattā tadabhinivesassa. Tathā ca tīsupi vādesu “taṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, tato paraṃ nānussaratī”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ, takkīnaṃ pana sassatekaccasassatavādīnaṃ sassatābhinivesaviseso rūpārūpadhammavisayatāya supākaṭoyevāti.

Granted, even in the former view, the grasping of impermanent phenomena as 'permanent' is specifically a wrong view, but the grasping of permanent phenomena as 'permanent' is not a wrong view, because it is a grasping of their true nature. However, this view is said to be a different doctrine because it proceeds by making a distinction among phenomena that are to be grasped—all of which are in fact impermanent—as 'some phenomena are permanent, some are impermanent.' Nor can it be said here that 'because a part is included in the whole, the grasping of a partial permanence merges with the grasping of a total permanence,' since the two doctrines arise for the proponent based on their distinct subject matters. Indeed, some adherents of fixed views are firmly convinced that 'all phenomena are permanent,' while others hold that 'some are permanent.' The complete inclusion of formations and the partial inclusion are very clear distinguishing features of these two doctrines. Furthermore, this is due to the adherence to the continuum of aggregates as either a manifold composite or a single composite. For the fourfold eternalist, based on distinctions of birth, has become one who adheres to permanence precisely in the mass of immaterial phenomena dependent on various kinds of material bodies, due to grasping the dissolution of the material body through direct knowledge, tradition, and so on. Thus it is said: 'Having passed away from there, he arose elsewhere' (Dī. Ni. 1.32) and 'they pass away and are reborn,' and so forth. The partial eternalist, having gained a special attainment, generated adherence by grasping the aspect of permanence in a continuum of phenomena that is a composite whose distinctions have not been discerned, because that adherence has as its object the continuity of aggregates comprised within a single existence. Similarly, in all three views, it is only said: 'He recollects his past abodes, but beyond that he does not recollect.' Yet, for the logicians, the difference in adherence to permanence between the eternalists and the partial eternalists is quite evident due to their focus on material and immaterial phenomena.

39. Dīghassa [V 1.0137] kālassa atikkamenāti vivaṭṭavivaṭṭaṭṭhāyīnaṃ apagamena. Anekatthattā dhātūnaṃ saṃ-saddena yutto vaṭṭa-saddo vināsavācīti āha “vinassatī”ti, saṅkhayavasena vattatīti attho. Vipattikaramahāmeghasamuppattito paṭṭhāya hi yāva aṇusahagatopi saṅkhāro na hoti, tāva loko saṃvaṭṭatīti vuccati. Lokoti cettha pathavīādibhājanaloko adhippeto. Uparibrahmalokesūti parittasubhādīsu [M 1.0155] rūpībrahmalokesu. Agginā hi kappavuṭṭhānaṃ idhādhippetaṃ bahulaṃ pavattanato. Tenevāha bhagavā “ābhassarasaṃvattanikā hontī”ti. Arūpesu vāti vā-saddena saṃvaṭṭamānalokadhātūhi aññalokadhātūsu vāti vikappanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Na hi “sabbe apāyasattā tadā rūpārūpabhavesu uppajjantī”ti sakkā viññātuṃ apāyesu dīghatamāyukānaṃ manussalokūpattiyā asambhavato. Satipi sabbasattānaṃ abhisaṅkhāramanasā nibbattabhāve bāhirapaccayehi vinā manasāva nibbattattā “manomayā”ti vuccanti rūpāvacarasattā. Yadi evaṃ kāmabhave opapātikasattānampi manomayabhāvo āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati adhicittabhūtena atisayamanasā nibbattasattesu manomayavohāratoti dassanto āha “jhānamanena nibbattattā manomayā”ti. Evaṃ arūpāvacarasattānampi manomayabhāvo āpajjatīti ce? Na, tattha [P 1.0202] bāhirapaccayehi nibbattetabbatāsaṅkāya eva abhāvato, “manasāva nibbattā”ti avadhāraṇāsambhavato. Niruḷho vāyaṃ loke manomayavohāro rūpāvacarasattesu. Tathā hi “annamayo pānamayo manomayo ānandamayo viññāṇamayo”ti pañcadhā attānaṃ vedavādino vadanti. Ucchedavādepi vakkhati “dibbo rūpī manomayo”ti (dī. ni. 1.86). Sobhanā pabhā etesu santīti subhā. “Ukkaṃsenā”ti ābhassaradeve sandhāyāha, parittābhā appamāṇābhā pana dve cattāro ca kappe tiṭṭhanti. Aṭṭhakappeti aṭṭha mahākappe.

39. After a long time has passed: by the disappearance of those who remain through the evolution and dissolution of world-systems. Since the root 'vaṭṭa' when combined with the prefix 'saṃ-' has multiple meanings, it signifies destruction; hence it is said, 'it perishes,' meaning it proceeds by way of annihilation. Indeed, from the arising of the great destructive rain cloud until not even the smallest conditioned phenomenon remains, the world is said to be in a state of dissolution. Here, 'world' refers to the container world, such as the earth and so on. In the higher Brahmā worlds: in the fine-material Brahmā worlds such as the Parittasubhā and others. For here, the destruction of the eon by fire is primarily intended, as it commonly occurs. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'They are subject to the dissolution that reaches the Ābhassara realm.' Or in the formless realms: the word 'or' (vā) should be understood as indicating an alternative, meaning in the formless realms of the world-systems undergoing dissolution, or in other world-systems. For it cannot be understood that 'all beings in the woeful states are then reborn in the fine-material or formless realms,' since rebirth in the human world is impossible for those with extremely long lifespans in the woeful states. Although all beings are produced by a mind that creates formations, the beings of the fine-material realm are called 'mind-made' because they are produced by mind alone, without external conditions. If so, would the state of being mind-made also apply to spontaneously born beings in the sense-sphere realm? It would not. Showing that the term 'mind-made' is used for beings produced by a superior mind that is the basis of higher consciousness, it is said: 'They are mind-made because they are produced by the jhāna-mind.' If so, would the state of being mind-made also apply to beings of the formless realm? No, because in that case, there is no suspicion of their being produced by external conditions, and thus the exclusive statement 'produced by mind alone' is not possible. This term 'mind-made' is well-established in the world for beings in the fine-material realm. Indeed, the proponents of the Vedas speak of the self as fivefold: 'made of food, made of drink, made of mind, made of bliss, made of consciousness.' In the context of the annihilationist view it will also be said, 'divine, possessing form, mind-made' (Dī. Ni. 1.86). They possess splendid radiance, hence they are called 'Subhā.' 'At most': this refers to the Ābhassara devas. The Parittābhā and Appamāṇābhā devas, however, remain for two and four aeons, respectively. Eight eons: eight great eons.

40. Saṇṭhātīti sampattikaramahāmeghasamuppattito paṭṭhāya pathavīsandhārakudakataṃsandhārakavāyumahāpathavīādīnaṃ samuppattivasena ṭhāti, “sambhavati” icceva vā attho anekatthattā dhātūnaṃ. Pakatiyāti sabhāvena, tassa “suñña”nti iminā sambandho. Tattha kāraṇamāha “nibbattasattānaṃ natthitāyā”ti, anuppannattāti attho, tena yathā ekaccāni vimānāni tattha nibbattasattānaṃ cutattā suññāni honti, na evamidanti dasseti. Brahmapārisajjabrahmapurohitamahābrahmāno brahmakāyikā, tesaṃ nivāso bhūmipi “brahmakāyikā”ti vuttā. Kammaṃ upanissayavasena paccayo etissāti kammapaccayā. Atha vā tattha nibbattasattānaṃ vipaccanakakammassa sahakārīpaccayabhāvato, kammassa paccayāti kammapaccayā[M 1.0156]. Utu samuṭṭhānaṃ etissāti utusamuṭṭhānā. “Kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhānā”ti vā pāṭho, kammasahāyo paccayo, kammassa vā sahāyabhūto paccayo kammapaccayo[P 1.0203], sova utu kammapaccayautu, so samuṭṭhānaṃ etissāti [V 1.0138] yojetabbaṃ. Etthāti “brahmavimāna”nti vuttāya brahmakāyikabhūmiyā. Kathaṃ paṇītāya dutiyajjhānabhūmiyaṃ ṭhitānaṃ hīnāya paṭhamajjhānabhūmiyā upapatti hotīti āha “atha sattāna”ntiādi. Otarantīti upapajjanavasena heṭṭhābhūmiṃ gacchanti.

40. It stands firm: starting from the arising of the great rain cloud that brings prosperity, it remains by way of the arising of the earth-supporting water, the water-supporting wind, the great earth, and so on. Or the meaning is "it arises," due to the multiple meanings of the roots. By nature: by its intrinsic quality; its connection is with "empty." There, the reason is stated: "due to the non-existence of beings who have arisen," meaning they have not arisen. Thus, it shows that just as some celestial mansions are empty because the beings born there have passed away, it is not so here. The Brahmā's attendants, Brahmā's ministers, and the Great Brahmās are the Brahmā hosts; their abode, the realm, is also called the "Brahmā host realm." Kamma is a condition as a decisive support for this, hence "kamma-conditioned." Alternatively, because it acts as a cooperative condition for the ripening kamma of beings born there, it is a condition for kamma, hence "kamma-conditioned." Season is the originating cause for this, hence "season-originated." Alternatively, the reading may be "kamma-conditioned-season-originated." Kamma is the assisting condition, or a condition that assists kamma is a kamma-condition; that very season is a kamma-conditioned-season, and that is the originating cause for this—this should be construed. Here: in the Brahmā host realm which is called the "Brahmā mansion." How can rebirth in the inferior first jhāna realm occur for those established in the superior second jhāna realm? It is explained thus: "Then, beings..." They descend: they go to the lower realm by way of rebirth.

Appāyuketi yaṃ uḷāraṃ puññakammaṃ kataṃ, tassa uppajjanārahavipākapabandhato appaparimāṇāyuke. Āyuppamāṇenevāti paramāyuppamāṇeneva. Kiṃ panetaṃ paramāyu nāma, kathaṃ vā taṃ paricchinnapamāṇanti? Vuccate – yo tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ bhavavisese purimasiddhabhavapatthanūpanissayavasena sarīrāvayavavaṇṇasaṇṭhānapamāṇādivisesā viya taṃtaṃgatinikāyādīsu yebhuyyena niyataparicchedo gabbhaseyyakakāmāvacaradevarūpāvacarasattānaṃ sukkasoṇitautubhojanādi utuādipaccayuppannapaccayūpatthambhito vipākapabandhassa ṭhitikālaniyamo, so yathāsakaṃ khaṇamattāvaṭṭhāyīnampi attano sahajātānaṃ rūpārūpadhammānaṃ ṭhapanākāravuttitāya pavattakāni rūpārūpajīvitindriyāni yasmā na kevalaṃ nesaṃ khaṇaṭhitiyā eva kāraṇabhāvena anupālakāni, atha kho yāva bhavaṅgupacchedā anupabandhassa avicchedahetubhāvenāpi, tasmā āyuhetukattā kāraṇūpacārena āyu, ukkaṃsaparicchedavasena paramāyūti ca vuccati. Taṃ pana devānaṃ nerayikānaṃ uttarakurukānañca niyataparicchedaṃ, uttarakurukānaṃ pana ekantaniyataparicchedameva, avasiṭṭhamanussapetatiracchānānaṃ pana ciraṭṭhitisaṃvattanikakammabahule kāle taṃkammasahitasantānajanitasukkasoṇitappaccayānaṃ taṃmūlakānañca candasūriyasamavisamaparivattanādijanitautuāhārādisamavisama paccayānaṃ vasena [P 1.0204] cirācirakālato aniyataparicchedaṃ, tassa ca yathā purimasiddhabhavapatthanāvasena taṃtaṃgatinikāyādīsu vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādivisesaniyamo siddho dassanānussavādīhi, tathā ādito gahaṇasiddhiyā. Evaṃ tāsu tāsu upapattīsu nibbattasattānaṃ yebhuyyena samappamāṇaṭṭhitikālaṃ dassanānussavehi labhitvā taṃ paramataṃ ajjhosāya pavattitabhavapatthanāvasena ādito paricchedaniyamo veditabbo. Yasmā pana kammaṃ tāsu [M 1.0157] tāsu upapattīsu yathā taṃtaṃupapattiniyatavaṇṇādinibbattane samatthaṃ, evaṃ niyatāyuparicchedāsu upapattīsu paricchedātikkamena vipākanibbattane samatthaṃ na hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “āyuppamāṇeneva cavantī”ti. Yasmā pana upatthambhakasahāyehi anupālakappaccayehi upādinnakakkhandhānaṃ pavattetabbākāro atthato paramāyu, tassa yathāvuttaparicchedānatikkamanato satipi kammāvasese ṭhānaṃ na sambhavati, tena vuttaṃ “attano puññabaleneva ṭhātuṃ na sakkotī”ti. Kappaṃ vāti asaṅkhyeyyakappaṃ vā tassa upaḍḍhaṃ vā upaḍḍhakappato ūnamadhikaṃ vāti vikappanattho vā-saddo.

"Short-lived" (appāyuke) means that the great meritorious deed that was done, due to the sequence of its ripening, which is capable of arising, results in a short lifespan. "By the measure of life itself" (āyuppamāṇeneva) means by the ultimate measure of life itself. But what is this ultimate lifespan, and how is its definite measure established? It is said: That which is the rule for the duration of the sequence of ripening for beings in a particular state of existence—a rule which, like the distinctive features of body parts, color, shape, and size, is generally fixed in the various classes of beings based on their past aspirations and conditions for becoming; for beings in the womb, celestial realms of the sense-sphere, or form realms, this rule is supported by conditions such as semen, blood, seasonal factors, and food—that rule is the material and immaterial life faculties, which cause co-nascent mental and physical phenomena to proceed. And since these faculties, though lasting only for a moment, are not only the cause for their momentary existence but also the cause for the uninterrupted continuity until the cutting off of the life-continuum, it is therefore called "life" (āyu) by metaphor, because it is the cause of life, and it is termed the "ultimate lifespan" (paramāyu) because of its supreme and definite measure. For gods, hell-beings, and those in Uttarakuru, the lifespan is of a fixed measure. For Uttarakuru beings, it is of an absolutely fixed measure. For the remaining humans, spirits, and animals, however, the lifespan is of indefinite measure, being long or short, depending on factors such as the abundance of kamma conducive to long life, and the regular or irregular conditions of sustenance and season, which are influenced by the revolutions of the moon and sun. Just as the distinctive features of color, shape, and size are established in various realms based on past aspirations, and are known through observation and tradition, so too is the lifespan's measure established from the beginning through such grasping. Thus, in various rebirths, the generally consistent duration of beings is known through observation and tradition, and based on this, the initial fixed measure should be understood as based on the aspiration that occurred previously. Because kamma is capable of producing rebirth with fixed features like color and form in those rebirths, but cannot produce a result that exceeds the fixed lifespan in those rebirths, it is said: "They pass away only when their lifespan is exhausted." Moreover, since the ultimate lifespan is, in essence, the manner in which the appropriated aggregates are made to proceed by supporting and sustaining conditions, and since this stated measure cannot be transgressed, there is no possibility of remaining even if residual kamma exists. Hence, it is said: "They cannot remain by the power of their merit alone." "An eon" (kappaṃ) or: this word "or" (vā) indicates an alternative, meaning an incalculable eon, or half of it, or more or less than half an eon.

41. Anabhiratīti [V 1.0139] ekavihārena anabhirati. Sā pana yasmā aññehi samāgamicchā hoti, tena vuttaṃ “aparassāpi sattassa āgamanapatthanā”ti. Piyavatthuvirahena piyavatthualābhena vā cittavighāto ukkaṇṭhitā, sā atthato domanassacittuppādo yevāti āha “paṭighasampayuttā”ti. Dīgharattaṃ jhānaratiyā ramamānassa vuttappakāraṃ anabhiratinimittaṃ uppannā “mama”nti ca “aha”nti ca gahaṇassa kāraṇabhūtā taṇhādiṭṭhiyo idha paritassanā. Tā pana cittassa purimāvatthāya calanaṃ kampananti [P 1.0205] āha “ubbijjanā phandanā”ti. Tenevāha “taṇhātassanāpi diṭṭhitassanāpi vaṭṭatī”ti. Yaṃ pana atthuddhāre “aho vata aññepi sattā itthattaṃ āgaccheyyunti ayaṃ taṇhātassanā nāmā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ diṭṭhitassanāya visuṃ udāharaṇaṃ dassentena taṇhātassanaṃyeva tato niddhāretvā vuttaṃ, na pana tattha diṭṭhitassanāya abhāvatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tāsatassanā cittutrāso. Bhayānakanti bheravārammaṇanimittaṃ balavabhayaṃ. Tena sarīrassa thaddhabhāvo chambhitattaṃ bhayaṃ saṃveganti ettha bhayanti bhaṅgānupassanāya ciṇṇante sabbasaṅkhārato bhāyanavasena uppannaṃ bhayañāṇaṃ. Saṃveganti sahottappañāṇaṃ, ottappameva vā. Santāsanti ādīnavanibbidānupassanāhi saṅkhārehi santassanañāṇaṃ. Saha byāyati pavattati, dosaṃ vā chādetīti sahabyo, sahāyo, tassa bhāvaṃ sahabyataṃ.

41. "Discontent" (anabhirati) refers to discontent with living alone. Since this discontent involves a desire to associate with others, it is said, "longing for the arrival of another being." The agitation of mind due to separation from beloved objects or not obtaining beloved objects is "yearning" (ukkaṇṭhitā); this, in essence, is the arising of a sorrowful mind, hence it is said, "connected with aversion" (paṭighasampayuttā). For one who has long delighted in meditative joy, when a sign of discontent of the type described has arisen, craving and views—which are the causes of grasping "mine" and "I"—are here "tormenting" (paritassanā). These, however, cause the mind to waver and tremble from its initial state; therefore, this is called "agitation" (ubbijjanā) and "trembling" (phandanā). Therefore, it is said, "both craving-tormenting and view-tormenting occur." However, in the explanation of meaning, it is stated, "Oh, if only other beings would come into this state of existence—this is called craving-tormenting." This is given as a separate example in order to show view-tormenting, but craving-tormenting alone is extracted and mentioned here; it should be understood that view-tormenting is not absent there. "Fear-tormenting" (tāsatassanā) is terror of the mind. "Terror" (bhayānaka) is intense fear with a frightening object as its cause. Because of this, stiffness of the body is 'being startled' (chambhitattaṃ). In the phrase 'fear and alarm' (bhayaṃ saṃvegaṃ), 'fear' here is the knowledge of fear arising for one practiced in the contemplation of dissolution, from seeing all formations as fearful. "Alarm" (saṃvega) is knowledge accompanied by moral dread, or simply moral dread itself. "Distress" (santāsa) is the knowledge of being distressed by formations through the contemplations of danger and disenchantment. "Sahabyo" means it goes along with, it proceeds together, or it conceals hatred; it means a companion. The state of being a companion is sahabyataṃ, companionship.

42. Abhibhavitvā ṭhito ime satteti adhippāyo. Yasmā pana so pāsaṃsabhāvena uttamabhāvena ca “te satte abhibhavitvā ṭhito”ti attānaṃ maññati, tasmā vuttaṃ “jeṭṭhakohamasmī”ti. Aññadatthu dasoti [M 1.0158] dassane antarāyābhāvavacanena, ñeyyavisesapariggāhikabhāvena ca anāvaraṇadassāvitaṃ paṭijānātīti āha “sabbaṃ passāmīti attho”ti. Bhūtabhabyānanti ahesunti bhūtā, bhavanti bhavissantīti bhabyā, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana vattamānakālavaseneva bhabya-saddassa attho dassito. Paṭhamacittakkhaṇeti paṭisandhicittakkhaṇe. Kiñcāpi so brahmā anavaṭṭhitadassanattā puthujjanassa purimatarajātiparicitampi kammassakataññāṇaṃ vissajjetvā vikubbaniddhivasena cittuppattimattapaṭibaddhena [P 1.0206] sattanimmānena vipallaṭṭho “ahaṃ issaro kattā nimmātā”tiādinā issarakuttadassanaṃ pakkhandamāno abhinivisanavaseneva patiṭṭhito, na patiṭṭhāpanavasena “tassa evaṃ hotī”ti vuttattā, patiṭṭhāpanakkameneva pana tassa so abhiniveso jātoti dassanatthaṃ “kāraṇato sādhetukāmo”ti, “paṭiññaṃ katvā”ti ca vuttaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā “taṃ kissa hetū”tiādi. Tattha manopaṇidhīti manasā eva patthanā, tathā cittappavattimattamevāti attho, itthabhāvanti idappakārataṃ. Yasmā pana itthanti brahmattabhāvo idhādhippeto, tasmā “brahmabhāvanti attho”ti vuttaṃ. Nanu ca devānaṃ upapattisamanantaraṃ “imissā nāma gatiyā cavitvā iminā nāma kammunā [V 1.0140] idhūpapannā”ti paccavekkhaṇā hotīti? Saccaṃ hoti, sā pana purimajātīsu kammassakataññāṇe sammadeva niviṭṭhajjhāsayānaṃ. Ime pana sattā purimāsupi jātīsu issarakuttadassanavasena vinibandhābhinivesā ahesunti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “iminā maya”ntiādi.

42. The meaning is: 'Having overcome these beings, he stands.' However, because he conceives of himself as praiseworthy and supreme, thinking, 'Having overcome these beings, I stand,' it is said, 'I am the eldest.' Furthermore, regarding 'daso', by its stating the absence of obstacles in vision and its nature of grasping the distinctions of the knowable, he professes unimpeded vision; thus he says, 'I see all,' meaning 'I perceive everything.' 'Bhūtabhabyāni' means 'those that have been' (bhūtā) and 'those that are to be' (bhabyā), from 'they are' or 'they will be.' In the commentary, however, the meaning of the term 'bhabya' is explained in relation to the present time. 'The first moment of consciousness' refers to the rebirth-linking moment of consciousness. Although that Brahmā, being a worldling with unstable perception, having rejected the knowledge of kamma as one's own which was familiar from past lives, becomes deluded by the creation of beings connected merely with the arising of a thought through his power of transformation, and leaps into the view of a creator god—'I am the lord, the maker, the creator'—he is established merely through adherence, not through proof. Since it is said, 'Thus it is for him,' it is to show that this adherence of his arose through a process of proof that it is said, 'wishing to establish by reason' and 'having made a declaration.' Therefore, the Blessed One says, 'For what reason?' and so on. Here, 'manopaṇidhi' means an aspiration by mind alone, that is, merely the process of thought. 'Itthabhāva' means 'this state.' Since 'ittha' here refers to the state of Brahmā, it is said, 'meaning the state of Brahmā.' Now, is it not true that immediately after their rebirth, devas reflect, 'Having passed away from such-and-such a state, I have been reborn here due to such-and-such kamma'? It is true, but that occurs for those whose inclination in past lives was properly established in the knowledge of kamma as one's own. These beings, however, it should be understood, were bound by adherence to the view of a creator god even in past lives. Thus, it is said, 'by this we,' and so on.

43. Īsatīti īso, abhibhūti attho. Mahā īso maheso, suppatiṭṭhamahesatāya pana parehi “maheso”ti akkhātabbatāya mahesakkho, atisayena mahesakkho mahesakkhataroti vacanattho daṭṭhabbo. Yasmā pana so mahesakkhabhāvo ādhipateyyaparivārasampattiyā viññāyati, tasmā “issariyaparivāravasena mahāyasataro”ti vuttaṃ.

43. One who rules (īsati) is a lord (īso), with the meaning of 'overcomer.' A great lord (mahā īso) is a Maheso. However, because of his well-established great lordship, and because he is to be called 'Maheso' by others, he is 'Mahesakkho' (of great power). The meaning of the word 'Mahesakkhataro' should be understood as 'more greatly powerful.' Since this state of great power is recognized through the accomplishment of sovereignty and retinue, it is said, 'more greatly glorious by way of a retinue of sovereignty.'

44. Idheva āgacchatīti imasmiṃ manussaloke eva paṭisandhivasena āgacchati. Yaṃ aññataro sattoti ettha yanti nipātamattaṃ, karaṇe vā paccattaniddeso, yena ṭhānenāti attho, kiriyāparāmasanaṃ vā. Itthattaṃ āgacchatīti ettha yadetaṃ itthattassa āgamanaṃ, etaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatīti [M 1.0159] attho. Esa nayo “pabbajati, cetosamādhiṃ phusati, pubbenivāsaṃ anussaratī”ti etesupi padesu. “Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ bhikkhave [P 1.0207] vijjati, yaṃ aññataro satto”ti imañhi padaṃ “pabbajatī”tiādīhi padehi paccekaṃ yojetabbanti.

44. 'Here indeed he comes' (idheva āgacchati) means he comes into this human world through rebirth-linking. In 'a certain being' (yaṃ aññataro satto), 'yaṃ' is merely a particle, or it is a specific reference in the instrumental case, meaning 'by which reason.' Or it is a reference to the action. In 'comes to this state' (itthattaṃ āgacchati), the meaning is that this coming to this state is a possibility. This is the method in phrases like 'he goes forth,' 'he attains mental concentration,' and 'he recollects past lives.' The phrase 'Indeed, monks, there is a possibility that a certain being' should be individually connected with phrases like 'he goes forth,' and so on.

45. Khiḍḍāya padussantīti khiḍḍāpadosino, khiḍḍāpadosino eva khiḍḍāpadosikā, khiḍḍāpadoso vā etesaṃ atthīti khiḍḍāpadosikā. Atikkantavelaṃ ativelaṃ, āhārūpabhogakālaṃ atikkamitvāti attho. Methunasampayogena uppajjanakasukhaṃ keḷihassasukhaṃ ratidhammo ratisabhāvo. Āhāranti ettha ko devānaṃ āhāro, kā āhāravelāti? Sabbesampi kāmāvacaradevānaṃ sudhā āhāro, sā heṭṭhimehi uparimānaṃ paṇītatamā hoti, taṃ yathāsakaṃ divasavasena divase divase bhuñjanti. Keci pana “biḷārapadappamāṇaṃ sudhāhāraṃ bhuñjanti, so jivhāya ṭhapitamatto yāva kesagganakhaggā kāyaṃ pharati, tesaṃyeva divasavasena sattadivase yāpanasamattho ca hotī”ti vadanti. “Nirantaraṃ khādantā pivantā”ti idaṃ parikappanavasena vuttaṃ. Kammajatejassa balavabhāvo uḷārapuññanibbattattā, uḷāragarusiniddhasudhāhārajīraṇato ca. Karajakāyassa mandabhāvo mudusukhumālabhāvato. Teneva hi bhagavā indasālaguhāyaṃ pakatipathaviyaṃ saṇṭhātuṃ asakkontaṃ sakkaṃ devarājānaṃ “oḷārikaṃ kāyaṃ adhiṭṭhehī”ti āha. Tesanti manussānaṃ. Vatthunti karajakāyaṃ. Kecīti abhayagirivāsino.

45. 'Corrupted by play' (khiḍḍāpadosino) are those who are corrupted by play; 'khiḍḍāpadosikā' is the same, or it means those who have corruption through play. 'Beyond the time' (ativelaṃ) means having exceeded the time for consuming food. The nature of delight (ratidhammo), the quality of pleasure (ratisabhāvo), is the pleasure of play and laughter, the pleasure arising from sexual union. Regarding 'food': what is the food of the devas, and what is their mealtime? For all devas of the sense-sphere, ambrosia is their food, which for the higher devas is more refined than that of the lower ones. They consume it day by day, according to their own respective days. Some, however, say: 'They consume a portion of ambrosia the size of a cat’s paw, which, as soon as it is placed on the tongue, pervades the body up to the tips of the hair and nails, and is sufficient to sustain them for seven of their own days.' 'Continuously eating and drinking' is said by way of assumption. The strength of their kamma-born energy is due to its being produced by great merit, and to the digestion of their abundant, heavy, and smooth ambrosia. The weakness of the physical body is due to its soft, subtle, and delicate nature. For this reason, the Blessed One, in the Indasāla Cave, told Sakka, king of the devas, who was unable to stand on the natural earth, to 'resolve upon a grosser body.' 'Theirs' refers to humans. 'The object' (vatthu) refers to the physical body. 'Some' refers to the Abhayagiri dwellers.

47. Manenāti [V 1.0141][P 1.0208] issāpakatattā paduṭṭhena manasā. Usūyāvasena manasova padoso manopadoso, so etesaṃ atthi vināsahetubhūtoti manopadosikāti evaṃ vā ettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Akuddho rakkhatīti kuddhassa so kodho itarasmiṃ akujjhante anupādāno ekavārameva uppattiyā anāsevano cāvetuṃ na sakkoti udakantaṃ patvā aggi viya nibbāyati, tasmā akuddho taṃ cavanato rakkhati, ubhosu pana kuddhesu bhiyyo bhiyyo aññamaññamhi parivaḍḍhanavasena tikhiṇasamudācāro nissayadahanaraso kodho uppajjamāno hadayavatthuṃ nidahanto accantasukhumālakarajakāyaṃ vināseti, tato sakalopi attabhāvo antaradhāyati. Tenāha “ubhosu panā”tiādi[M 1.0160]. Tathā cāha bhagavā “aññamaññaṃ paduṭṭhacittā kilantakāyā…pe… cavantī”ti. Dhammatāti dhammaniyāmo. So ca tesaṃ karajakāyassa mandatāya, tathāuppajjanakakodhassa ca balavatāya ṭhānaso cavanaṃ, tesaṃ rūpārūpadhammānaṃ sabhāvoti adhippāyo.

47. 'By mind' means by a mind corrupted due to envy. Or, the meaning here should be understood thus: corruption of mind (manopadoso) is by way of jealousy; that exists for them as a cause of destruction, hence they are 'mentally corruptible' (manopadosikā). 'The non-angry one protects' means that the anger of an angry person, finding no fuel in the other who is not angry, arising only once and not being cultivated, cannot cause them to fall; like a fire reaching water, it is extinguished. Therefore, the non-angry one protects the other from passing away. However, when both are angry, anger with its sharp conduct and its nature of burning its support arises, growing ever more intense between them, and burning the heart-base, it destroys the extremely subtle and delicate physical body. Then the entire individual existence vanishes. Thus it is said, 'But when both...' and so on. And so the Blessed One said: 'With minds corrupted toward each other, with bodies exhausted... they pass away.' 'By nature' (dhammatā) means the fixed order of phenomena. The meaning is: and that passing away from their state, due to the weakness of their physical bodies and the strength of such arising anger, is the inherent nature of their material and immaterial phenomena.

49. Cakkhādīnaṃ bhedaṃ passatīti virodhipaccayasannipāte vikārāpattidassanato, ante ca adassanūpagamanato vināsaṃ passati oḷārikattā rūpadhammabhedassa. Paccayaṃ datvāti anantarapaccayādivasena paccayo hutvā. “Balavatara”nti cittassa lahutaraṃ bhedaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tathā hi ekasmiṃ rūpe dharanteyeva soḷasa cittāni bhijjanti. Bhedaṃ na passatīti khaṇe khaṇe bhijjantampi cittaṃ parassa anantarapaccayabhāveneva bhijjatīti purimacittassa abhāvaṃ paṭicchādetvā viya pacchimacittassa uppattito bhāvapakkho balavataro pākaṭo ca hoti, na abhāvapakkhoti cittassa vināsaṃ na passati, ayañca attho alātacakkadassanena supākaṭo viññāyati. Yasmā [P 1.0209] pana takkīvādī nānattanayassa dūrataratāya ekattanayassapi micchāgahitattā “yadevidaṃ viññāṇaṃ sabbadāpi ekarūpena pavattati, ayameva attā nicco”tiādinā abhinivesaṃ janeti, tasmā vuttaṃ “so taṃ apassanto”tiādi.

49. “‘Sees the breaking of the eye, etc.’ means one sees destruction due to seeing the occurrence of alteration at the convergence of opposing conditions, and ultimately, due to its ceasing to be seen, because of the grossness of the breaking of material phenomena. ‘Having given a condition’ means having become a condition by way of a proximate condition, etc. ‘Stronger’ is said with reference to the quicker breaking of the mind. For while a single material phenomenon persists, sixteen mind-moments break up. ‘Does not see the breaking’ means that although the mind breaks from moment to moment, it breaks only by being a proximate condition for another. Because the arising of the subsequent mind conceals, as it were, the absence of the preceding mind, the aspect of existence is stronger and more manifest, not the aspect of non-existence—hence, one does not see the destruction of the mind. And this meaning is made very clear by the sight of a firebrand-circle. However, because a sophist, being very far from the method of diversity and having wrongly grasped the method of unity, generates the adherence that, ‘This very consciousness always proceeds in a uniform manner; this is the permanent self,’ etc., it is therefore said, ‘not seeing that,’ etc.

Antānantavādavaṇṇanā

An Exposition of the Doctrines of Finitude and Infinitude

53. Antānantikāti ettha amati gacchati ettha sabhāvo osānanti anto, mariyādā. Tappaṭisedhena ananto, anto ca ananto ca antānanto ca nevantānānanto ca antānantā sāmaññaniddesena, ekasesena vā “nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatana”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.176; saṃ. ni. 2.1; udā. 1) viya. Kassa pana antānantoti? Lokīyati saṃsāranissaraṇatthikehi diṭṭhigatikehi, lokīyanti vā ettha tehi puññāpuññaṃ tabbipāko [V 1.0142] cāti lokoti saṅkhyaṃ gatassa attano. Tenāha bhagavā “antānantaṃ lokassa paññapentī”ti. Ko pana eso attāti? Jhānavisayabhūtakasiṇanimittaṃ. Tattha hi ayaṃ diṭṭhigatiko lokasaññī. Tathā ca vuttaṃ “taṃ lokoti gahetvā”ti. Keci pana “jhānaṃ taṃsampayuttadhammā ca idha ‘attā[M 1.0161], loko’ti ca gahitā”ti vadanti. Antānantasahacaritavādo antānanto, yathā “kuntā pacarantī”ti antānantasannissayo vā yathā “mañcā ghosantī”ti. So etesaṃ atthīti antānantikā. Te pana yasmā yathāvuttanayena antānanto vādo diṭṭhi etesanti “antānantavādā”ti vuccanti. Tasmā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “antānantavādā”ti vatvā “antaṃ vā”tiādinā attho vibhatto.

53. Regarding ‘Antānantikā’: here, ‘anto’ (end) is where one goes to death, where nature comes to an end; it is a boundary. By its negation, there is ‘ananto’ (endless). ‘Anto’ (finite), ‘ananto’ (infinite), ‘antānanto’ (both finite and infinite), and ‘nevantānānanto’ (neither finite nor infinite) are collectively ‘antānantā’ by general designation, or by ellipsis, as in ‘from name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases,’ etc. But of what is it finite and infinite? Of the self, which has come to be designated as ‘world.’ It is called ‘world’ because it is viewed by those with wrong views who seek release from saṃsāra; or, it is where merit and demerit and their results are experienced by them. Therefore the Blessed One said, ‘They declare the world to be finite and infinite.’ But what is this self? It is the kasiṇa-sign that has become the object of jhāna. For in that, this holder of wrong views has the perception of ‘world.’ And so it was said: ‘having taken that as “world.”’ Some, however, say that here ‘jhāna and its associated states’ are taken as ‘self’ and ‘world.’ The view associated with the finite and infinite is ‘antānanto,’ like ‘the spears are advancing’; or it is a view dependent on the finite and infinite, like ‘the beds are shouting.’ Because they have this, they are ‘antānantikā.’ And since, according to the method stated, they have this view or doctrine of the finite and infinite, they are called ‘antānantavādā.’ Therefore, in the commentary, having said ‘antānantavādā,’ the meaning is analyzed with the words ‘the finite, or…,’ etc.

Etthāha – yuttaṃ tāva purimānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vādīnaṃ [P 1.0210] antattañca anantattañca antānantattañca ārabbha pavattavādattā antānantikattaṃ, pacchimassa pana tadubhayapaṭisedhanavasena pavattavādattā katha antānantikattanti? Tadubhayapaṭisedhanavasena pavattavādattā eva. Yasmā antānantapaṭisedhavādopi antānantavisayo eva taṃ ārabbha pavattattā. Etadatthaṃyeva hi sandhāya aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “ārabbha pavattavādā”ti vuttaṃ. Atha vā yathā tatiyavāde desabhedavasena ekasseva antavantatā anantatā ca sambhavati, evaṃ takkīvādepi kālabhedavasena ubhayasambhavato aññamaññapaṭisedhena ubhayaññeva vuccati. Kathaṃ? Antavantatāpaṭisedhena hi anantatā vuccati, anantatāpaṭisedhena ca antavantatā, antānantānañca na tatiyavādabhāvo kālabhedassa adhippetattā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yasmā ayaṃ lokasaññito attā adhigatavisesehi mahesīhi ananto kadāci sakkhidiṭṭhoti anusuyyati, tasmā nevantavā. Yasmā pana tehiyeva kadāci antavā sakkhidiṭṭhoti anusuyyati, tasmā na pana anantoti. Yathā ca anussutitakkīvasena, evaṃ jātissaratakkī ādīnañca vasena yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Ayañhi takkiko avaḍḍhitabhāvapubbakattā paṭibhāganimittānaṃ vaḍḍhitabhāvassa vaḍḍhitakālavasena appaccakkhakāritāya anussavādimatte ṭhatvā “nevantavā”ti paṭikkhipati. Avaḍḍhitakālavasena pana “na panānanto”ti, na pana antatānantatānaṃ accantamabhāvena yathā taṃ “nevasaññināsaññī”ti. Purimavādattayapaṭikkhepo ca attanā yathādhippetappakāravilakkhaṇatāya tesaṃ, avassañcetaṃ evaṃ viññātabbaṃ, aññathā vikkhepapakkhaṃyeva bhajeyya catutthavādo. Na hi antatāanantatātadubhayavinimutto [P 1.0211] attano pakāro atthi, takkīvādī ca yuttimaggako, kālabhedavasena ca tadubhayaṃ ekasmimpi na na yujjatīti.

Here it is said: It is fitting that the first three doctrines are called ‘doctrines of the finite and infinite’ because their views proceed with respect to finitude, infinitude, and both finitude and infinitude. But how can the last one be a ‘doctrine of the finite and infinite,’ since its view proceeds by way of negating both? Precisely because its view proceeds by way of negating both. For a doctrine that negates the finite and infinite still has the finite and infinite as its object, since it proceeds with respect to them. It is precisely with this meaning in mind that the commentary says, ‘views that proceed with respect to them.’ Alternatively, just as in the third doctrine, finitude and infinitude can exist for a single thing due to a difference in location, so too in the doctrine of the sophists, due to a difference in time, both can exist, and through mutual negation, both are asserted. How so? By negating finitude, infinitude is asserted; and by negating infinitude, finitude is asserted. And this is not the third doctrine because a difference in time is intended. This is what is meant: It is heard that this self, perceived as the world, is sometimes directly seen as infinite by great seers who have attained special qualities; therefore, it is not finite. And since it is heard that it is sometimes directly seen as finite by those same seers, it is therefore not infinite. And as this applies to the sophist who relies on tradition, so it should be applied, as may be appropriate, to the sophist who remembers past lives, and so on. For this sophist, because the counterpart sign has not been previously developed, and because its developed state is not directly perceived due to the time required for its development, stands merely on hearsay and the like and rejects, saying, ‘It is not finite.’ But due to the time when it is not developed, he says, ‘Nor is it infinite.’ This is not, however, due to a complete absence of finitude and infinitude, as in the case of ‘neither-perception-nor-non-perception.’ The rejection of the first three doctrines is because they are different from the mode he intends. This must certainly be understood thus; otherwise, the fourth doctrine would just fall into the category of equivocation. For there is no mode of the self that is separate from finitude, infinitude, and both. And the sophist follows the path of logic, and due to a difference in time, both are not illogical in a single thing.

Keci [V 1.0143][M 1.0162] pana yadi panāyaṃ attā antavā siyā, dūradese upapajjanānussaraṇādi kiccanipphatti na siyā. Atha ananto, idha ṭhitassa devalokanirayādīsu sukhadukkhānubhavanampi siyā. Sace pana antavā ca ananto ca, tadubhayadosasamāyogo. Tasmā “antavā, ananto”ti ca abyākaraṇīyo attāti evaṃ takkanavasena catutthavādappavattiṃ vaṇṇenti. Evampi yuttaṃ tāva pacchimavādīdvayassa antānantikattaṃ antānantānaṃ vasena ubhayavisayattā tesaṃ vādassa. Purimavādīdvayassa pana kathaṃ visuṃ antānantikattanti? Upacāravuttiyā. Samuditesu hi antānantavādīsu pavattamāno antānantika-saddo tattha niruḷhatāya paccekampi antānantikavādīsu pavattati, yathā arūpajjhānesu paccekaṃ aṭṭhavimokkhapariyāyo, yathā ca loke sattāsayoti. Atha vā abhinivesato purimakālappavattivasena ayaṃ tattha vohāro kato. Tesañhi diṭṭhigatikānaṃ tathārūpacetosamādhisamadhigamato pubbakālaṃ “antavā nu ayaṃ loko, ananto nū”ti ubhayākārāvalambino parivitakkassa vasena niruḷho antānantikabhāvo visesalābhena tattha uppannepi ekaṃsaggāhe purimasiddharuḷhiyā voharīyatīti.

Some, however, explain the arising of the fourth view by way of reasoning thus: If this self were finite, the accomplishment of such tasks as recollecting rebirths in distant places would not be possible. If it were infinite, one could experience pleasure and pain in the deva worlds, hells, etc., even while remaining here. If it were both finite and infinite, there would be a combination of the faults of both. Therefore, the self is undeclarable as ‘finite’ or ‘infinite.’ Even on this account, it is fitting to call the latter two views ‘doctrines of the finite and infinite,’ since their doctrine has a dual object by way of the finite and the infinite. But how can the former two views each be called a ‘doctrine of the finite and infinite’? By metaphorical usage. For the term ‘antānantika,’ which applies to the proponents of the finite and infinite collectively, also applies to them individually because of its established usage, just as the designation ‘the eight liberations’ applies to each of the formless jhānas, and as in the worldly expression ‘seven hundred.’ Alternatively, this is a conventional expression based on a previous state of adherence. For, in the period before those holders of wrong views attained such concentration of mind, the state of being an ‘antānantika’ was established through their reflection which entertained both alternatives: ‘Is this world finite? Or is it infinite?’ Even when, upon attaining a special state, they adopted a one-sided grasp, they are still designated according to the previously established convention.

54-60. Vuttanayenāti “takkayatīti takkī”tiādinā (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.34) saddato, “catubbidho takkī”tiādinā [P 1.0212] (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.34) atthato ca sassatavāde vuttavidhinā. Diṭṭhapubbānusārenāti dassanabhūtena viññāṇena upaladdhapubbassa antavantādino anussaraṇena. Evañca katvā anussutitakkīsuddhatakkīnampi idha saṅgaho siddho hoti. Atha vā diṭṭhaggahaṇeneva “naccagītavāditavisūkadassanā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 10, 194) viya sutādīnampi gahitatā veditabbā. “Antavā”tiādinā icchitassa attano sabbadā bhāvaparāmasanavaseneva imesaṃ vādānaṃ pavattanato sassatadiṭṭhisaṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tathā hi vakkhati “sesā sassatadiṭṭhiyo”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 97-98).

54-60. “By the stated method” means by the method stated in the section on eternalism: by way of the term, as in “one who speculates is a speculator,” and by way of the meaning, as in “the speculator is of four kinds.” “Based on what has been previously seen” refers to recalling what has been previously grasped by the consciousness that has experienced it, such as finitude and so on. By this, the inclusion here of those who speculate based on hearsay and those who are pure speculators is established. Alternatively, by the term “seen,” it should be understood that what is heard, and so on, is also included, as in the case of “seeing dancing, singing, music, and shows.” By “finite” and so on, the inclusion in eternalist views should be understood, because these doctrines proceed only from grasping at the constant existence of one's desired self. For it will be said: “The rest are eternalist views.”

Amarāvikkhepavādavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Doctrine of Evasive Equivocation

61. Na maratīti na ucchijjati. “Evampi me no”tiādinā vividho nānappakāro khepo parena paravādīnaṃ khipanaṃ vikkhepo. Amarāya diṭṭhiyā [M 1.0163] vācāya ca vikkhipantīti vā amarāvikkhepino. Amarāvikkhepino eva amarāvikkhepikā. Ito cito ca sandhāvati ekasmiṃ sabhāve anavaṭṭhānato. Amarā viya vikkhipantīti vā purimanayeneva saddattho daṭṭhabbo.

61. “Not dying” means not being annihilated. By “Even so, this is not for me,” and so on, is meant various and diverse evasion, a casting aside, the refutation of other disputants. Or, they are `amarāvikkhepino` because they evade with an immortal (`amarā`) view and speech. The `amarāvikkhepino` are themselves the `amarāvikkhepikā`. One runs about here and there, not being established in any single state. Or, the meaning of the word should be understood as “they evade like an eel” (`amarā`).

62. Vikkhepavādino [V 1.0144] uttarimanussadhamme, akusaladhammepi sabhāvabhedavaseneva ñātuṃ ñāṇabalaṃ natthīti kusalākusalapadānaṃ kusalākusalakammapathavaseneva attho. Paṭhamanayavaseneva apariyantavikkhepatāya amarāvikkhepaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “evantipi me noti aniyamitavikkhepo”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha aniyamitavikkhepoti sassatādīsu ekasmimpi pakāre aṭṭhatvā vikkhepakaraṇaṃ, paravādinā yasmiṃ kismiñci pucchite pakāre tassa paṭikkhepoti attho. Dutiyanayavasena amarāsadisāya amarāya vikkhepaṃ dassetuṃ “idaṃ kusalanti vā puṭṭho”tiādimāha. Atha vā “evantipi [P 1.0213] me no”tiādinā aniyamatova sassatekaccasassatucchedatakkīvādānaṃ paṭisedhanena taṃ taṃ vādaṃ paṭikkhipateva apariyantavikkhepavādattā amarāvikkhepino. Attanā pana anavaṭṭhitavādattā na kismiñci pakkhe avatiṭṭhatīti āha “sayaṃ pana…pe… byākarotī”ti. Idāni kusalādīnaṃ abyākaraṇena tameva anavaṭṭhānaṃ vibhāveti “idaṃ kusalanti vā puṭṭho”tiādinā. Tenevāha “ekasmimpi pakkhe na tiṭṭhatī”ti.

62. For the evasive reasoners, since they lack the power of knowledge to discern even unwholesome states by their intrinsic distinctions, let alone superhuman states, the terms ‘wholesome’ and ‘unwholesome’ have meaning only in terms of wholesome and unwholesome courses of action. According to the first method, to explain the evasive equivocation as endless evasion, it is said: “Even this is not for me”—this is undetermined evasion. Herein, “undetermined evasion” means to evade without being established in any one type of doctrine, such as eternalism. The meaning is that when questioned by an opponent on any point whatsoever, one rejects it. According to the second method, to show the evasion that resembles an eel, it is said: “When asked, ‘Is this wholesome?’” and so on. Alternatively, by “Even this is not for me,” and so on, the evasive equivocators, on account of their doctrine of endless evasion, reject each and every doctrine through an undetermined refutation of the doctrines of eternalism, partial eternalism, annihilationism, and speculation. Moreover, because they themselves hold no fixed doctrine, they do not take a stand on any side—thus it is said: “But he himself… does not declare.” Now, by not declaring what is wholesome and so on, he reveals that very lack of a fixed position, as in the passage: “When asked, ‘Is this wholesome?’” and so on. Therefore, it is said: “He does not take a stand on any single side.”

63. Kusalākusalaṃ yathābhūtaṃ appajānantopi yesamahaṃ samayena kusalameva “kusala”nti, akusalameva ca “akusala”nti byākareyyaṃ, tesu tathā byākaraṇahetu “aho vata re paṇḍito”ti sakkārasammānaṃ karontesu mama chando vā rāgo vā assāti evampettha attho sambhavati. Doso vā paṭigho vāti ettha vuttavipariyāyena yojetabbaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana attano paṇḍitabhāvavisayānaṃ rāgādīnaṃ vasena yojanā katā. “Chandarāgadvayaṃ upādāna”nti abhidhammanayena vuttaṃ. Abhidhamme hi taṇhādiṭṭhiyova “upādāna”nti āgatā, suttante pana dosopi “upādāna”nti vutto “kodhupādānavinibandhā vighātaṃ āpajjantī”tiādīsu. Tena vuttaṃ “ubhayampi vā daḷhaggahaṇavasena upādāna”nti[M 1.0164]. Daḷhaggahaṇaṃ amuñcanaṃ. Paṭighopi hi upanāhādivasena pavatto ārammaṇaṃ na muñcati. Vihananaṃ hiṃsanaṃ vibādhanaṃ. Rāgopi hi pariḷāhavasena sāraddhavuttitāya nissayaṃ vibādhatīti. Vināsetukāmatāya ārammaṇaṃ gaṇhātīti sambandho.

63. The meaning here can be understood thus: “Although I do not know what is wholesome and unwholesome as it really is, if I were to declare at some time what is wholesome as ‘wholesome’ and what is unwholesome as ‘unwholesome,’ then, on account of that declaration, among those who would pay me honor and respect, saying, ‘Ah, what a wise man!’, desire or lust might arise in me.” Regarding “hatred or aversion,” the opposite case should be applied here. In the commentary, however, the connection is made in terms of lust and similar states concerning one's own state of being wise. “The pair, desire and lust, is clinging”—this is stated according to the Abhidhamma method. For in the Abhidhamma, only craving and wrong view are designated as “clinging,” but in the Suttas, hatred is also called “clinging,” as in passages like, “Bound by the clinging of anger, they fall into distress.” Therefore, it is said, “Or both are clinging in the sense of firm grasping.” Firm grasping is not releasing. For aversion, too, proceeding by way of harboring grudges and so on, does not release its object. Vexation means harming, obstructing. Lust, too, due to its burning nature and agitated state, obstructs its support. The connection is that it (aversion) seizes its object with the desire to destroy.

64. Paṇḍiccenāti paññāya. Yena hi dhammena yutto “paṇḍito”ti [P 1.0214] vuccati, so dhammo paṇḍiccaṃ, tena sutacintāmayaṃ paññaṃ dasseti, na pākatikakammanibbattaṃ sābhāvikapaññaṃ. Kata-saddassa kiriyāsāmaññavācakattā “katavijjo”tiādīsu viya kata-saddo ñāṇānuyuttataṃ vadatīti āha “viññātaparappavādā”ti. Sattadhā bhinnassa vālaggassa aṃsukoṭivedhako “vālavedhī”ti adhippeto.

64. “By `paṇḍicca`” means by wisdom. For by whatever quality one is endowed with and called “wise,” that quality is `paṇḍicca`. By this, it indicates wisdom born of learning and reflection, not the natural wisdom produced by ordinary kamma. Since the word `kata` is a general indicator of action, as in phrases like `katavijjo` (“one who has accomplished knowledge”), the word `kata` indicates application to knowledge. Hence, it is said, “one who understands the doctrines of others.” “Hair-splitter” is intended to mean one who can pierce the tip of a hair split sevenfold.

65-6. Ettha [V 1.0145] ca kiñcāpi purimānampi tiṇṇaṃ kusalādidhammasabhāvānavabodhato attheva mandabhāvo, tesaṃ pana attano kusalādidhammānavabodhassa avabodhaviseso atthi, tadabhāvā pacchimoyeva mandamomūhabhāvena vutto. Nanu ca pacchimassāpi “atthi paroloko’ti iti ce me assa, ‘atthi paroloko’ti iti te naṃ byākareyyaṃ, evantipi me no”tiādi (dī. ni. 1.65) vacanato attano dhammānavabodhassa avabodho atthiyevāti? Kiñcāpi atthi, na tassa purimānaṃ viya apariññātadhammabyākaraṇanibandhanamusāvādādibhayaparijigucchanakāro atthi, atha kho mahāmūḷhoyeva. Atha vā “evantipi me no”tiādinā pucchāya vikkhepakaraṇatthaṃ “atthi paroloko’ti iti ce maṃ pucchasī”ti pucchāṭhapanameva tena dassīyati, na attano dhammānavabodhoti ayameva visesena “mando ceva momūho cā”ti vutto. Teneva hi tathāvādinaṃ sañjayaṃ belaṭṭhaputtaṃ ārabbha “ayaṃ vā imesaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sabbamando sabbamūḷho”ti (dī. ni. 1.181) vuttaṃ. Tattha “atthi paroloko”ti sassatadassanavasena [P 1.0215] sammādiṭṭhivasena vā pucchā. “Natthi paroloko”ti natthikadassanavasena sammādassanavasena vā pucchā. “Atthi ca natthi ca paroloko”ti ucchedadassanavasena sammādiṭṭhivasena eva vā pucchā. “Neva atthi na natthi paroloko”ti vuttappakārattayapaṭikkhepe sati pakārantarassa asambhavato atthitānatthitāhi navattabbākāro parolokoti [M 1.0165] vikkhepaññeva purekkhārena sammādiṭṭhivasena vā pucchā. Sesacatukkattayepi vuttanayānusārena attho veditabbo. Puññasaṅkhārattiko viya hi kāyasaṅkhārattikena purimacatukkasaṅgahito eva attho. Sesacatukkattayena attaparāmāsapuññādi phalatācodanānayena saṅgahitoti.

65-6. Here, although for the first three there is also dullness due to not understanding the nature of wholesome states and so on, they have a specific understanding: the understanding of their own lack of comprehension of wholesome states and so on. Because he lacks this, the last one is said to be dull and utterly deluded. But does not the last one also have an understanding of his own lack of comprehension of the Dhamma, according to the statement, “If it were for me ‘there is another world,’ I would declare to you ‘there is another world,’ but even this is not for me,” and so on? Although he has, he does not have, like the first three, the fear of lying and disgust which is the reason for not declaring a not-fully-understood Dhamma; rather, he is simply greatly deluded. Or alternatively, with “even this is not for me,” and so on, he only shows the setting up of a question—“If you ask me, ‘is there another world?’” —for the purpose of evading the question, not his own lack of understanding of the Dhamma. For this very reason he is specifically called “dull and utterly deluded.” It is indeed with reference to Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta, who spoke in such a way, that it was said, “This one among these ascetics and brahmins is the most dull and the most deluded.” Here, the question “Is there another world?” is a question from the perspective of the eternalist view or of right view. “Is there no other world?” is a question from the perspective of the nihilist view or of right view. “Is there both another world and no other world?” is a question from the perspective of the annihilationist view or even of right view. “Is there neither another world nor no other world?”—since this rejects the three previously stated positions, and another alternative is not possible, it is a question about the other world having a nature that cannot be spoken of in terms of existence or non-existence, posed either from the perspective of right view or with evasion as the primary motive. The meaning of the remaining three tetrads should be understood in accordance with the stated method. For the meaning is included in the first tetrad, just as the triad of meritorious formations is included by the triad of bodily formations. The remaining three tetrads are included by the method of questioning the results of self-grasping, merit, and so on.

Amarāvikkhepiko sassatādīnaṃ attano aruccanatāya sabbattha “evantipi me no”tiādinā vikkhepaññeva karoti. Tattha “evantipi me no”tiādi tattha tattha pucchitākārapaṭisedhanavasena vikkhipanākāradassanaṃ. Nanu ca vikkhepavādino vikkhepapakkhassa anujānanaṃ vikkhepapakkhe avaṭṭhānaṃ yuttarūpanti? Na, tatthāpi tassa sammūḷhattā, paṭikkhepavaseneva ca vikkhepavādassa pavattanato. Tathā hi sañcayo belaṭṭhaputto raññā ajātasattunā sandiṭṭhikaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ puṭṭho paralokattikādīnaṃ paṭisedhanamukhena vikkhepaṃ byākāsi.

The eel-wriggler, due to his own dislike of eternalism and other views, simply creates evasion everywhere with "It is not thus for me," and so on. Here, "It is not thus for me," and the like show the manner of evasion by way of denying the form of the question in each case. Now, is it not proper that the exponent of evasion, by approving the side of evasion, should be established on the side of evasion? No, because even there he is bewildered, and the doctrine of evasion proceeds solely by way of denial. For instance, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta, when asked by King Ajātasattu about the visible fruit of recluseship, explained evasion through the denial of the triad concerning the other world and so on.

Etthāha – nanu cāyaṃ sabbopi amarāvikkhepiko kusalādayo dhamme, paralokattikādīni ca yathābhūtaṃ anavabujjhamāno tattha tattha pañhaṃ puṭṭho pucchāya vikkhepanamattaṃ āpajjati, tassa kathaṃ [V 1.0146] diṭṭhigatikabhāvo. Na hi avattukāmassa viya pucchitamatthamajānantassa vikkhepakaraṇamattena diṭṭhigatikatā [P 1.0216] yuttāti? Vuccate – na heva kho pucchāya vikkhepakaraṇamattena tassa diṭṭhigatikatā, atha kho micchābhinivesavasena. Sassatābhinivesena micchābhiniviṭṭhoyeva hi puggalo mandabuddhitāya kusalādidhamme paralokattikādīni ca yāthāvato appaṭipajjamāno attanā aviññātassa atthassa paraṃ viññāpetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya musāvādādibhayena ca vikkhepaṃ āpajjatīti. Tathā hi vakkhati “yāsaṃ satteva ucchedadiṭṭhiyo, sesā sassatadiṭṭhiyo”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.97-98) atha vā puññapāpānaṃ tabbipākānañca anavabodhena asaddahanena ca tabbisayāya pucchāya vikkhepakaraṇaṃyeva sundaranti khantiṃ ruciṃ uppādetvā abhinivisantassa uppannā visuṃyevesā ekā diṭṭhi sattabhaṅgadiṭṭhi viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā ca vuttaṃ “pariyantarahitā diṭṭhigatikassa diṭṭhi ceva vācā cā”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.61). Kathaṃ panassā sassatadiṭṭhisaṅgaho? Ucchedavasena anabhinivesato. Natthi koci dhammānaṃ yathābhūtavedī vivādabahulattā [M 1.0166] lokassa, “evameva”nti pana saddantarena “dhammanijjhānanā anādikālikā loke”ti gāhavasena sassatalesopettha labbhatiyeva.

Here it is said: 'But does not this eel-wriggler, not understanding wholesome and other states, the triad concerning the other world, and so forth, as they truly are, when questioned here and there, resort to mere evasion? How then does he become a holder of views? For it is not fitting that one who is like someone unwilling to speak or who does not know the meaning of what is asked should, by the mere act of evasion, become a holder of views.' It is replied: 'It is not merely by the act of evasion when questioned that one becomes a holder of views, but rather by wrong adherence. Indeed, a person who is wrongly entrenched through adherence to eternalism, due to dull understanding, does not properly engage with wholesome and other states, the triad concerning the other world, and so forth. Being unable to explain to others what they themselves do not understand, and fearing false speech and the like, they resort to evasion.' Thus it will be said: 'Seven of which are annihilationist views; the rest are eternalist views.' Alternatively, due to not comprehending merit and demerit and their results, and lacking faith in them, one may develop a liking and preference for mere evasion when questioned on such matters. This should be seen as a distinct view arising in them, like the sevenfold fracturing view. And thus it is stated: 'For one who holds views, there is no end to views and speech.' But how is this included among eternalist views? By not adhering to annihilationism. There is no one who truly knows phenomena as they are, because the world is full of disputes. Yet, by merely saying, 'It is just so,' and grasping at the notion that 'the contemplation of phenomena is beginningless in the world,' a trace of eternalism can indeed be found here.

Adhiccasamuppannavādavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Doctrine of Accidental Origination

67. Adhicca yadicchakaṃ yaṃ kiñci kāraṇaṃ, kassaci vuddhipubbaṃ vā vinā samuppannoti attalokasaññitānaṃ khandhānaṃ adhiccuppattiākārārammaṇaṃ dassanaṃ tadākārasannissayena pavattito, tadākārasahacaritatāya ca “adhiccasamuppanna”nti vuccati yathā “mañcā ghosanti, kuntā pacarantī”ti ca [P 1.0217] imamatthaṃ dassento āha “adhiccasamuppanno attā ca loko cāti dassanaṃ adhiccasamuppanna”nti.

67. The view that takes as its object the mode of accidental origination of the aggregates perceived as self and world—a view holding that they arise by chance, spontaneously, without any cause or prior development—proceeds by relying on that very mode. Due to its being accompanied by that mode, it is called 'accidentally arisen,' just as it is said, 'The couches creak, the spears move.' To illustrate this meaning, it is said: "The view that the self and the world arise by chance is called 'accidentally arisen.'"

68-73. Desanāsīsanti desanāya jeṭṭhakabhāvena gahaṇaṃ, tena saññaṃyeva dhuraṃ katvā bhagavatā ayaṃ desanā katā, na pana tattha aññesaṃ arūpadhammānaṃ atthibhāvatoti dasseti. Tenevāha “acittuppādā”tiādi. Bhagavā hi yathā lokuttaradhammaṃ desento samādhiṃ paññaṃ vā dhuraṃ karoti, evaṃ lokiyadhammaṃ desento cittaṃ saññaṃ vā dhuraṃ karoti. Tattha “yasmiṃ samaye lokuttaraṃ jhānaṃ bhāveti (dha. sa. 277) pañcaṅgiko sammāsamādhi [dī. ni. 3.355 (kha)] pañcañāṇiko sammāsamādhi, [dī. ni. 3.355 (ja); vibha. 2.804] paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā hontī”ti (ma. ni. 1.271) tathā “yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ [V 1.0147] kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, (dha. sa. 1) kiṃcitto tvaṃ bhikkhu (pārā. 146, 180) manopubbaṅgamā dhammā, (dha. pa. 1, 2; netti. 90; peṭako. 83) santi bhikkhave sattā nānattakāyā nānattasaññino, (dī. ni. 3.332, 342, 357; a. ni. 9.24; cūḷani. 83) na nevasaññānāsaññāyatana”ntiādīni suttāni (dī. ni. 3.358) etassa atthassa sādhakāni daṭṭhabbāni. Titthāyataneti aññatitthiyasamaye. Titthiyā hi upapattivisese vimuttisaññino, saññāvirāgāvirāgesu ādīnavānisaṃsadassino vā hutvā asaññasamāpattiṃ nibbattetvā akkhaṇabhūmiyaṃ uppajjanti, na sāsanikā. Vāyokasiṇe parikammaṃ katvāti vāyokasiṇe paṭhamādīni tīṇi jhānāni nibbattetvā tatiyajjhāne ciṇṇavasī hutvā [M 1.0167] tato vuṭṭhāya catutthajjhānādhigamāya [P 1.0218] parikammaṃ katvā. Tenevāha “catutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā”ti.

68-73. 'Teaching foremost' means taking it as the principal part of the teaching. Therefore, the Blessed One made this teaching with perception as the leading factor, but not to indicate the existence of other formless phenomena there. Hence, he said, "Without the arising of mind," etc. For when the Blessed One teaches the supramundane Dhamma, he makes concentration or wisdom the foremost factor, but when teaching the mundane Dhamma, he makes mind or perception the foremost. In this regard, passages such as, "At the time when one develops the supramundane jhāna," "The five-factored right concentration," "The five-knowledge right concentration," "And through wisdom seeing this, his taints are destroyed," as well as, "At the time when wholesome sense-sphere consciousness arises," "What is your mind, monk?" "Mind precedes all mental states," "There are, monks, beings with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions," and "Neither perception nor non-perception"—these suttas should be seen as supporting this meaning. 'Sectarian basis' refers to the doctrines of other sectarians. For sectarians, perceiving liberation in particular rebirths, or having seen the danger and advantage in the fading away of perception and the non-fading away of perception, cultivate the perceptionless attainment and are reborn in an inopportune realm; they are not the Buddha's disciples. 'Having performed the preliminary work with the air kasiṇa' means having produced the first three jhānas based on the air kasiṇa, having become proficient in the third jhāna, and then emerging from it to perform the preliminary work for attaining the fourth jhāna. Hence, it is said, "Having produced the fourth jhāna."

Kasmā panettha vāyokasiṇeyeva parikammaṃ vuttanti?
