Vuccate – yatheva hi rūpapaṭibhāgabhūtesu kasiṇavisesesu rūpavibhāvanena rūpavirāgabhāvanāsaṅkhāto arūpasamāpattiviseso sacchikarīyati, evaṃ aparibyattaviggahatāya arūpapaṭibhāgabhūte kasiṇavisese arūpavibhāvanena arūpavirāgabhāvanāsaṅkhāto rūpasamāpattiviseso adhigamīyatīti ettha “saññā rogo saññā gaṇḍo”tiādinā (ma. ni. 3.24) “dhi cittaṃ, dhibbate taṃ citta”ntiādinā ca nayena arūpappavattiyā ādīnavadassanena, tadabhāve ca santapaṇītabhāvasanniṭṭhānena rūpasamāpattiyā abhisaṅkharaṇaṃ, rūpavirāgabhāvanā pana saddhiṃ upacārena arūpasamāpattiyo, tatthāpi visesena paṭhamāruppajjhānaṃ. Yadi evaṃ “paricchinnākāsakasiṇepī”ti vattabbaṃ. Tassāpi hi arūpapaṭibhāgatā labbhatīti? Icchitamevetaṃ kesañci avacanaṃ panettha pubbācariyehi aggahitabhāvena. Yathā hi rūpavirāgabhāvanā virajjanīyadhammabhāvamattena parinipphannā, virajjanīyadhammapaṭibhāgabhūte ca visayavisese pātubhavati, evaṃ arūpavirāgabhāvanāpīti vuccamāne na koci virodho, titthiyeheva pana tassā samāpattiyā paṭipajjitabbatāya, tesañca visayapathesupanibandhanasseva tassa jhānassa paṭipattito diṭṭhivantehi pubbācariyehi catuttheyeva bhūtakasiṇe arūpavirāgabhāvanāparikammaṃ [P 1.0219] vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kiñca vaṇṇakasiṇesu viya purimabhūtakasiṇattayepi vaṇṇapaṭicchāyāva paṇṇatti ārammaṇaṃ jhānassa lokavohārānurodheneva pavattito. Evañca katvā visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.57) pathavīkasiṇassa ādāsacandamaṇḍalūpamāvacanañca samatthitaṃ hoti, catutthaṃ pana bhūtakasiṇaṃ bhūtappaṭicchāyameva jhānassa [V 1.0148] gocarabhāvaṃ gacchatīti tasseva arūpapaṭibhāgatā yuttāti vāyokasiṇeyeva parikammaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

But why is the preparatory work mentioned here only for the air kasiṇa? It is said: just as in the case of the various kasiṇas that are counterparts of form, a particular formless attainment, known as the development of dispassion towards form, is realized through the analysis of form, so too, in the case of a kasiṇa that is a counterpart of the formless due to its indistinct configuration, a particular form attainment, known as the development of dispassion towards the formless, is achieved through the analysis of the formless. Here, the preparation for the form attainment is accomplished by seeing the danger in the arising of the formless, in accordance with such statements as, 'Perception is a disease, perception is a boil' (MN 3.24) and, 'Fie on consciousness! Fie on that consciousness!', and by concluding that in its absence there is peace and excellence. The development of dispassion towards form, however, together with access concentration, constitutes the formless attainments, especially the first formless jhāna. If this is so, then it should be said, 'Even in the case of the limited space kasiṇa.' For that too can be considered a counterpart of the formless. This is indeed desired by some, but its non-mention here is due to its not having been taken up by the ancient teachers. Just as the development of dispassion towards form is perfected simply by its nature as a state that should be dispassionately regarded, and it arises in a particular objective field that is a counterpart to such a state, so too, when the development of dispassion towards the formless is spoken of, there is no contradiction. However, since that attainment is to be practiced by the sectarians, and since for them the practice of that jhāna is bound to their path of objects, it should be understood that the ancient teachers, who possessed right view, mentioned the preparatory work for the development of dispassion towards the formless only in the fourth elemental kasiṇa. Moreover, just as in the case of the color kasiṇas, in the first three elemental kasiṇas too, the object of the jhāna is a concept which is a mere reflection of color, operating only in accordance with worldly convention. This being the case, the statement in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. 1.57) comparing the earth kasiṇa to a mirror or the moon’s disk is also supported. But the fourth elemental kasiṇa, being a mere reflection of the element, becomes the object of the jhāna, and thus its status as a counterpart of the formless is appropriate. Therefore, it should be understood that the preparatory work is mentioned only for the air kasiṇa.

Idhevāti pañcavokārabhaveyeva. Tatthāti asaññabhave. Yadi rūpakkhandhamattameva asaññabhave pātubhavati, kathamarūpasannissayena vinā tattha rūpaṃ pavattati, kathaṃ pana rūpasannissayena vinā arūpadhātuyaṃ arūpaṃ pavattati, idampi tena samānajātiyameva. Kasmā? Idheva adassanato. Yadi evaṃ kabaḷīkārāhārena vinā rūpadhātuyaṃ rūpena na pavattitabbaṃ, kiṃ kāraṇaṃ[M 1.0168]? Idheva adassanato. Api ca yathā yassa cittasantānassa nibbattikāraṇaṃ rūpe avigatataṇhaṃ, tassa saha rūpena sambhavato rūpaṃ nissāya pavatti, yassa pana nibbattikāraṇaṃ rūpe vigatataṇhaṃ, tassa vinā rūpena rūpanirapekkhatāya kāraṇassa, evaṃ yassa rūpappabandhassa nibbattikāraṇaṃ vigatataṇhaṃ arūpe, tassa vinā arūpena pavatti hotīti asaññabhave rūpakkhandhamattameva nibbattati. Kathaṃ pana tattha kevalo rūpappabandho paccuppannapaccayarahito cirakālaṃ pavattatīti paccetabbaṃ, kittakaṃ vā kālaṃ pavattatīti codanaṃ manasi katvā āha “yathā nāma jiyāvegukkhitto saro”tiādi, tena na kevalamāgamoyeva ayamettha yuttīti dasseti. Tattakameva kālanti ukkaṃsato pañca mahākappasatānipi tiṭṭhanti asaññasattā. Jhānavegeti asaññasamāpattiparikkhate kammavege. Antaradhāyatīti [P 1.0220] paccayanirodhena nirujjhati nappavattati.

'Here' means in the five-aggregate existence. 'There' means in the realm of non-perception. If only the aggregate of form manifests in the realm of non-perception, how does form persist there without reliance on the formless? And how does the formless persist in the formless realm without reliance on form? This too is of the same nature. Why? Because it is not seen here. If so, form should not persist in the form realm without the nutriment of edible food. What is the reason? Because it is not seen here. Moreover, just as for one whose mental continuum has as its cause of rebirth a craving for form that has not been abandoned, for him there is an arising together with form and a persistence dependent on form; but for one whose cause of rebirth is a craving for form that has been abandoned, for him there is persistence without form, because the cause is independent of form. So too, for one whose form-continuum has as its cause of rebirth a craving for the formless that has been abandoned, for him there is persistence without the formless. Thus, in the realm of non-perception, only the aggregate of form arises. But how is it to be understood that there, the mere form-continuum continues for a long time without presently arisen conditions? Or for how long does it continue? Having considered this objection, he says, 'Just as an arrow shot by the force of a bowstring,' etc. By this, he shows that not only is this a matter of scripture, but there is also reasoning for it here. For that very length of time—at most, for five hundred great eons—the non-percipient beings remain. 'By the force of absorption' means by the force of kamma conditioned by the attainment of non-perception. 'It disappears' means it ceases due to the cessation of conditions and does not continue.

Idhāti kāmabhave. Kathaṃ pana anekakappasatasamatikkamena ciraniruddhato viññāṇato idha viññāṇaṃ samuppajjati. Na hi niruddhe cakkhumhi cakkhuviññāṇamuppajjamānaṃ diṭṭhanti? Nayidamekantato daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ciraniruddhampi hi cittaṃ samānajātikassa antarānuppajjanato anantarapaccayamattaṃ hotiyeva, na bījaṃ, bījaṃ pana kammaṃ. Tasmā kammato bījabhūtato ārammaṇādīhi paccayehi asaññabhavato cutānaṃ kāmadhātuyā upapattiviññāṇaṃ hotiyeva. Tenāha “idha paṭisandhisaññā uppajjatī”ti. Ettha ca yathā nāma utuniyāmena pupphaggahaṇe niyatakālānaṃ rukkhānaṃ vekhe dinne vekhabalena na yathā niyāmatā hoti pupphaggahaṇassa, evameva pañcavokārabhave avippayogena vattamānesu rūpārūpadhammesu rūpārūpavirāgabhāvanāvekhe dinne tassa samāpattivekhabalassa anurūpato arūpabhave asaññābhave ca yathākkamaṃ rūparahitā arūparahitā ca khandhānaṃ pavatti hotīti veditabbaṃ. Nanu ettha jātisatasahassadasasaṃvaṭṭādīnaṃ matthake, abbhantarato vā pavattāya asaññūpavattiyā vasena lābhīadhiccasamuppannikavādo lābhīsassatavādo viya anekabhedo sambhavatīti? Saccaṃ sambhavati, anantarattā pana āpannāya [V 1.0149] asaññūpapattiyā vasena lābhīadhiccasamuppannikavādo nayadassanavasena ekova dassitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā sassatadiṭṭhisaṅgahato adhiccasamuppannikavādassa sassatavāde āgato sabbo desanānayo yathāsambhavaṃ adhiccasamuppannikavādepi [M 1.0169] gahetabboti [P 1.0221] imassa visesassa dassanatthaṃ bhagavatā lābhīadhiccasamuppannikavādo avibhajitvā desito. Avassañca sassatadiṭṭhisaṅgaho adhiccasamuppannikavādassa icchitabbo saṃkilesapakkhe sattānaṃ ajjhāsayassa duvidhattā. Tathā hi vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “sassatucchedadiṭṭhi cā”ti. Tathā ca vakkhati “yāsaṃ satteva ucchedadiṭṭhiyo, sesā sassatadiṭṭhiyo”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.97-98).

'Here' means in the realm of sensual existence. But how does consciousness arise here from a consciousness that has ceased long ago, having passed through many hundreds of eons? For when the eye has ceased, it is not seen that eye-consciousness arises. This should not be seen as absolute. For even a consciousness that has long ceased can still be a proximate condition, provided that no intermediate consciousness of the same kind has arisen; it is not, however, a seed. The seed, rather, is kamma. Therefore, for beings who have passed away from the realm of non-perception, rebirth-consciousness in the sensual realm arises from kamma as the seed, along with other conditions such as the object. Hence it is said, 'Here, rebirth-perception arises.' In this context, just as for trees that flower at a fixed time according to the seasonal rule, when a special stimulus is applied, their flowering does not occur according to that rule but by the force of that stimulus; so too, when material and immaterial phenomena are present without separation in the five-aggregate existence, when the stimulus of cultivating dispassion towards material and immaterial states is applied, there occurs a process of aggregates devoid of form or devoid of the formless, respectively, in the immaterial realm and the realm of non-perception, in accordance with the power of the stimulus of that attainment. Now, in this regard, at the culmination of vast eons, or internally within them, does not the doctrine of accidental origination held by an attainer, like the doctrine of eternalism held by an attainer, become manifold due to the occurrence of non-percipient existence? Indeed, it does. But because of the immediacy of the attained non-percipient existence, the doctrine of accidental origination held by an attainer is presented as a single view for the sake of showing the method. Alternatively, the Blessed One taught the doctrine of accidental origination held by an attainer without division in order to show this distinction: since the doctrine of accidental origination is included in the eternalist view, the entire teaching method that applies to the eternalist view should, as far as possible, be understood as applicable also to the doctrine of accidental origination. And certainly, the inclusion of the doctrine of accidental origination in the eternalist view is to be desired, because the inclinations of beings in the sphere of defilement are twofold. Thus, it is said in the commentary: '...and the eternalist and annihilationist views.' And it will be said: 'Of these, seven are annihilationist views; the rest are eternalist views' (DN-a 1.97-98).

Nanu ca adhiccasamuppannikavādassa sassatadiṭṭhisaṅgaho na yutto. “Ahañhi pubbe nāhosi”ntiādivasena pavattanato, apubbasattapātubhāvaggāhattā, attano lokassa ca sadābhāvagāhinī ca sassatadiṭṭhi “atthitveva sassatisama”nti pavattanato? No na yutto anāgate koṭiadassanato. Yadipi hi ayaṃ vādo “somhi etarahi ahutvā santatāya pariṇato”ti (dī. ni. 1.68) attano lokassa ca atītakoṭiparāmasanavasena pavatto, tathāpi vattamānakālato paṭṭhāya na tesaṃ katthaci anāgate pariyantaṃ passati, visesena ca paccuppannānāgatakālesu pariyantādassanapabhāvito sassatavādo. Yathāha “sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassatī”ti. Yadi evaṃ imassa vādassa, sassatavādādīnañca pubbantakappikesu saṅgaho na yutto anāgatakālaparāmasanavasena pavattattāti? Na, samudāgamassa atītakoṭṭhāsikattā. Tathā hi nesaṃ samuppatti atītaṃsapubbenivāsañāṇehi, tappaṭirūpakānussavādippabhāvitatakkanehi ca saṅgahitāti, tathā ceva saṃvaṇṇitaṃ. Atha vā sabbattha appaṭihatañāṇena vādivarena dhammassāminā niravasesato agatiñca gatiñca yathābhūtaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā paveditā etā diṭṭhiyo, tasmā yāvatikā diṭṭhiyo bhagavatā desitā, yathā ca desitā, tathā tathāva [P 1.0222] sanniṭṭhānato sampaṭicchitabbā, na ettha yuttivicāraṇā kātabbā buddhavisayattā. Acinteyyo hi buddhavisayoti.

But is it not inappropriate to include the doctrine of accidental origination in the category of the eternalist view? Because it proceeds with statements like, 'I did not exist before,' and grasps the appearance of a being that was not before, while the eternalist view asserts 'it exists eternally the same,' maintaining that oneself and the world have always existed? No, it is not inappropriate, because it sees no limit in the future. For even though this doctrine proceeds by referring to the past limit concerning oneself and the world with statements like, 'I am now, having not been before, transformed by continuity' (Dī. Ni. 1.68), still, from the present moment onward, it does not perceive any end for them anywhere in the future. And the eternalist doctrine is particularly influenced by the inability to see a limit in the present and future, as it says: 'It will remain the same eternally.' If so, is it not inappropriate to include this doctrine, along with eternalism and others, among the past-oriented speculations, since it proceeds by referring to the future? No, because their origination belongs to the past portion. For their arising is comprised of knowledge of past lives and reasoning influenced by traditions and the like which resemble it; and thus it has been described. Alternatively, these views were taught by the Lord of the Dhamma, the foremost of speakers, with his unobstructed knowledge, having directly known and realized for himself without omission both the wrong course and the right course as they truly are. Therefore, whatever views the Blessed One has taught, and just as they were taught, so they should be accepted as definitively established. Here, logical scrutiny should not be undertaken, because it pertains to the domain of a Buddha. For the domain of a Buddha is inconceivable.

Dutiyabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the second recitation division is finished.

Aparantakappikavādavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Doctrines Speculating on the Future

74. “Aparante [V 1.0150][M 1.0170] ñāṇaṃ, aparantānudiṭṭhino”tiādīsu viya apara-saddo idha anāgatakālavācakoti āha “anāgatakoṭṭhāsasaṅkhāta”nti. Aparantaṃ kappetvātiādīsu “pubbantaṃ kappetvā”tiādīsu vuttanayena attho veditabbo. Visesamattameva vakkhāma.

74. Just as in phrases such as 'knowledge of the future' and 'one who has views regarding the future,' the word 'apara' here signifies future time; hence it is said, 'reckoned as the portion of the future.' As for 'speculating on the future' and so on, the meaning should be understood in the manner described for 'speculating on the past' and so on. We will state only the differences.

Saññīvādavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Doctrine of a Percipient Self

75. Uddhamāghātanāti pavatto vādo uddhamāghātano, so etesaṃ atthīti uddhamāghātanikā. Yasmā pana te diṭṭhigatikā “uddhaṃ maraṇā attā nibbikāro”ti vadanti, tasmā “uddhamāghātanā attānaṃ vadantīti uddhamāghātanikā”ti vuttaṃ. Saññīvādo etesaṃ atthīti saññīvādā “buddhaṃ assa atthīti buddho”ti yathā. Atha vā saññīti pavatto vādo saññī sahacaraṇanayena, saññī vādo etesanti saññīvādā.

75. `Uddhamāghātana` means a doctrine that extends upwards; those who hold it are `uddhamāghātanikā`. Because these adherents of the view say, 'Upwards from death, the self is immutable,' therefore it is said, 'They declare the self to be `uddhamāghātana`, hence they are `uddhamāghātanikā`.' They hold the doctrine of a percipient self (`saññīvāda`), hence they are `saññīvādā`, just as one might say, 'Because he possesses enlightenment, he is a Buddha.' Alternatively, the doctrine that proceeds is called `saññī` by way of association; their doctrine is `saññī`, hence they are `saññīvādā`.

76-77. Rūpī attāti ettha nanu rūpavinimuttena attanā bhavitabbaṃ saññāya viya rūpassapi attaniyattā. Na hi “saññī attā”ti ettha saññā attā. Teneva hi “tattha pavattasaññañcassa saññāti gahetvā”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ sati kasmā kasiṇarūpaṃ “attā”ti gahetvā vuttanti? Na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ “rūpaṃ assa atthīti rūpī”ti, atha kho “ruppanasīlo rūpī”ti. Ruppanañcettha rūpasarikkhatāya kasiṇarūpassa vaḍḍhitāvaḍḍhitakālavasena visesāpatti, sā ca “natthī”ti na sakkā vattuṃ parittavipulatādivisesasabbhāvato. Yadi evaṃ imassa vādassa sassatadiṭṭhisaṅgaho na yujjatīti? No na yujjati kāyabhedato uddhaṃ attano nibbikāratāya tena adhippetattā. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “arogo [P 1.0223] paraṃ maraṇā”ti. Atha vā “rūpaṃ assa atthīti rūpī”ti vuccamānepi na doso. Kappanāsiddhenapi hi bhedena abhedassāpi niddesadassanato, yathā “silāputtakassa sarīra”nti. Ruppanaṃ vā rūpasabhāvo rūpaṃ, taṃ etassa atthīti rūpī, attā “rūpino dhammā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. dukamātikā 11) viya. Evañca katvā rūpasabhāvattā attano “rūpī attā”ti vacanaṃ ñāyāgatamevāti “kasiṇarūpaṃ ‘attā’ti gahetvā”ti vuttaṃ. Niyatavāditāya kammaphalapaṭikkhepato natthi ājīvakesu jhānasamāpattilābhoti [M 1.0171] āha “ājīvakādayo viya takkamatteneva vā rūpī attā”ti. Tathā hi kaṇhābhijātiādīsu chaḷābhijātīsu aññataraṃ attānaṃ ekacce ājīvakā paṭijānanti. Natthi etassa rogo bhaṅgoti arogoti aroga-saddassa niccapariyāyatā [V 1.0151] veditabbā, rogarahitatāsīsena vā nibbikāratāya niccataṃ paṭijānāti diṭṭhigatikoti āha “arogoti nicco”ti.

76-77. Regarding 'the self is corporeal': should not the self be separate from form, since form, like perception, is possessed by the self? For in the statement 'the self is percipient,' perception is not the self. For this reason it was said, 'taking the perception occurring there as perception.' This being so, why was it stated by taking the kasiṇa-form as 'self'? This should not be seen as 'it is corporeal because it has form,' but rather as 'it is corporeal because it has the nature of being afflicted.' Here, 'being afflicted' refers to the attainment of a special state by the kasiṇa-form, which resembles material form, through its periods of increase and decrease. And it cannot be said that this does not exist, because of the presence of distinctions such as being limited or extensive. If so, is not the inclusion of this view in the eternalist view inappropriate? No, it is not inappropriate, because it is intended by that person that the self is immutable upwards from the breaking up of the body. Thus it is said, 'unafflicted after death.' Alternatively, even when it is said, 'it is corporeal because it has form,' there is no fault. For the designation of what is undivided is seen even by a distinction established by imagination, as in 'the body of a stone doll.' Or, affliction (`ruppana`) is the nature of form (`rūpa`); it has this, hence it is corporeal (`rūpī`), the self, just as in 'corporeal phenomena' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Dukamātikā 11). And so, because the self has the nature of form, the statement 'the self is corporeal' is indeed logical; hence it was said, 'taking the kasiṇa-form as "self."' Because of their fatalism, which rejects kamma and its fruit, the Ājīvakas do not attain meditative absorptions. Thus it is said, 'like the Ājīvakas and others, the self is corporeal merely through reasoning.' For some Ājīvakas profess one of the six classes of birth, such as the dark-born, to be the self. 'There is no disease or breaking up for it, hence it is unafflicted (`aroga`)'; the word 'unafflicted' should be understood as a synonym for 'permanent'. Or, under the heading of 'freedom from disease,' the adherent of the view professes permanence through immutability; hence it is said, 'unafflicted means permanent.'

Kasiṇugghāṭimākāsapaṭhamāruppaviññāṇanatthibhāvaākiñcaññāyatanāni arūpasamāpattinimittaṃ nimbapaṇṇe tittakaraso viya sarīraparimāṇo arūpī attā tattha tiṭṭhatīti nigaṇṭhāti āha “nigaṇṭhādayo viyā”ti. Missakagāhavasenāti rūpārūpasamāpattīnaṃ nimittāni ekajjhaṃ katvā “eko attā”ti, tattha pavattasaññañcassa “saññā”ti gahaṇavasena. Ayañhi diṭṭhigatiko rūpārūpasamāpattilābhitāya tannimittaṃ rūpabhāvena arūpabhāvena ca attā upatiṭṭhati, tasmā “rūpī ca arūpī cā”ti abhinivesaṃ janesi ajjhattavādino viya, takkamatteneva vā rūpārūpadhammānaṃ missakaggahaṇavasena “rūpī arūpī ca attā hotī”ti.

The signs of the formless attainments are: space from the removal of the kasiṇa, the consciousness of the first formless attainment, non-existence, and the base of nothingness. 'Just as the bitter taste is in the neem leaf, so an immaterial self the size of the body abides there'—thus say the Nigaṇṭhas; hence it is said, 'like the Nigaṇṭhas and others.' 'By way of mixed grasping' means: by way of combining the signs of the material and immaterial attainments and grasping 'there is one self,' and by grasping the perception that arises there as 'perception.' For to this adherent of a view, because he has attained the material and immaterial attainments, the self appears through those signs in a material form and in an immaterial form. Therefore, he generated the adherence, 'The self is both material and immaterial,' like one who speculates about the self; or merely by reasoning, through the mixed grasping of material and immaterial phenomena, he thinks, 'the self is both material and immaterial.'

Takkagāhenevāti saṅkhārāvasesasukhumabhāvappattadhammā [P 1.0224] viya accantasukhumabhāvappattiyā sakiccasādhanāsamatthatāya thambhakuṭṭahatthapādādisaṅghāto viya neva rūpī, rūpasabhāvānativattanato na arūpīti evaṃ pavattatakkagāhena. Atha vā antānantikacatukkavāde viya aññamaññapaṭikkhepavasena attho veditabbo. Kevalaṃ pana tattha desakālabhedavasena tatiyacatutthavādā dassitā, idha kālavatthubhedavasenāti ayameva visesoti. Kālabhedavasena cettha tatiyavādassa pavatti rūpārūpanimittānaṃ saha anupaṭṭhānato. Catutthavādassa pana vatthubhedavasena pavatti rūpārūpadhammānaṃ samūhato “eko attā”ti takkanavasenāti tattha vuttanayānusārena veditabbaṃ.

'By the grasp of reasoning alone' means: by a grasp of reasoning that proceeds thus: like phenomena that have attained a state of subtle residual formations, due to having reached an extremely subtle state and being incapable of accomplishing its own function, it is like a collection of posts, walls, hands, feet, and so on—it is neither material, nor is it immaterial, because it does not transcend the nature of form. Alternatively, as in the fourfold doctrine on the finite and infinite, the meaning should be understood by way of mutual exclusion. However, there the third and fourth doctrines are shown based on distinctions of space and time, while here it is based on distinctions of time and object—this alone is the difference. And here, the third doctrine proceeds based on a distinction of time, due to the non-simultaneous appearance of the signs of the material and the immaterial. The fourth doctrine, however, proceeds based on a distinction of object, due to reasoning from the collection of material and immaterial phenomena that 'there is one self.' This should be understood according to the method explained there.

Dutiyacatukke yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ “amati gacchati ettha bhāvo osāna”ntiādinā antānantikavāde vuttanayena veditabbaṃ.

In the second tetrad, whatever is to be said should be understood in the manner explained in the doctrine of the finite and infinite, beginning with 'Here, existence goes to cessation; this is the end,' and so on.

Yadipi aṭṭhasamāpattilābhino diṭṭhigatikassa vasena samāpattibhedena saññābhedasambhavato “nānattasaññī attā”ti ayampi vādo samāpannakavasena [M 1.0172] labbhati. Tathāpi samāpattiyaṃ ekarūpeneva saññāya upaṭṭhānato samāpannakavasena “ekattasaññī”ti āha. Tenevettha samāpannakaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Ekasamāpattilābhino eva vā vasena attho veditabbo. Samāpattibhedena saññābhedasambhavepi bahiddhā puthuttārammaṇe saññānānattena oḷārikena nānattasaññitaṃ dassetuṃ “asamāpannakavasena nānattasaññī”ti vuttaṃ. “Parittakasiṇavasena parittasaññī”ti iminā satipi saññāvinimutte dhamme “saññāyeva attā”ti vadatīti dassitaṃ [V 1.0152] hoti. Kasiṇaggahaṇañcettha saññāya visayadassanaṃ, evaṃ vipulakasiṇavasenāti etthāpi attho veditabbo. Evañca katvā antānantikavāde[P 1.0225], idha ca antānantikacatukke paṭhamadutiyavādehi imesaṃ dvinnaṃ vādānaṃ viseso siddho hoti, aññathā vuttappakāresu vādesu pubbantāparantakappanabhedena satipi kehici visese kehici natthi yevāti. Atha vā “aṅguṭṭhappamāṇo attā, yavappamāṇo, aṇumatto vā attā”ti ādidassanavasena paritto saññī cāti parittasaññī, kapilakaṇādādayo viya attano sabbagatabhāvapaṭijānanavasena appamāṇo saññī cāti appamāṇasaññīti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

Even though for an adherent of views who has attained the eight meditative absorptions, a diversity of perceptions can arise from the diversity of attainments, this view, ‘the self has diverse perceptions,’ is also held by way of one who has attained such states. Nevertheless, because in a meditative attainment perception arises in a single form, it is said, ‘one has a unified perception,’ by way of one who has attained such a state. Therefore, the term ‘one who has attained’ is used here. Or, the meaning should be understood as pertaining only to one who attains a single absorption. Even though a diversity of perceptions can arise from the diversity of attainments, to show the state of having diverse perceptions by means of the gross diversity of perception concerning external, manifold objects, it is said, ‘one has diverse perceptions,’ by way of one who has not attained such a state. By the statement, ‘one has limited perception by way of a limited kasiṇa,’ it is shown that even when there is a state free from perception, one says, ‘perception itself is the self.’ Here, the mention of the kasiṇa indicates the object of perception, and thus the meaning should also be understood as ‘by way of an extensive kasiṇa.’ By doing so, in the doctrine of finiteness and infinitude, and here in the tetrad of finiteness and infinitude, the distinction of these two doctrines from the first and second doctrines is established. Otherwise, in the doctrines as previously described, even with the division of past and future speculation, some distinctions exist for some, while for others, there are none. Alternatively, the meaning here should be seen in this way: based on views such as, ‘the self is the size of a thumb, the size of a barley grain, or atomic,’ one has limited perception, thus ‘one has limited perception’; and, like Kapila and Kaṇāda, based on the claim of the self’s all-pervading nature, one has immeasurable perception, thus ‘one has immeasurable perception.’

Dibbacakkhuparibhaṇḍatāya yathākammūpagañāṇassa dibbacakkhupabhāvajanitena yathākammūpagañāṇena dissamānāpi sattānaṃ sukhādisamaṅgitā dibbacakkhunāva diṭṭhā hotīti āha “dibbena cakkhunā”tiādi. Nanu ca “ekantasukhī attā”tiādivādānaṃ aparantadiṭṭhibhāvato “nibbattamānaṃ disvā”ti vacanaṃ anupannanti? Nānupapannaṃ, anāgatassa ekantasukhibhāvādikassa pakappanaṃ paccuppannāya nibbattiyā dassanena adhippetanti. Tenevāha “nibbattamānaṃ disvā ‘ekantasukhī’ti gaṇhātī”ti. Ettha ca tassaṃ tassaṃ bhūmiyaṃ bahulaṃ sukhādisahitadhammappavattidassanena tesaṃ “ekantasukhī”ti gāho daṭṭhabbo. Atha vā hatthidassakaandhā viya diṭṭhigatikā yaṃ yadeva passanti, taṃ tadeva abhinivissa voharantīti na ettha yutti maggitabbā.

Because the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their kamma is an accessory of the divine eye, even though the state of beings being endowed with happiness and so forth is seen by this knowledge—which is itself generated by the power of the divine eye—it is said to be seen by the divine eye itself. Thus it is stated, ‘with the divine eye,’ and so on. But is not the statement ‘seeing them being reborn’ inappropriate, since views like ‘the self is entirely happy’ are views concerning the future? It is not inappropriate. The speculation about a future state of complete happiness and so on is intended through the seeing of present becoming. Hence, it is said: ‘Seeing them being reborn, one grasps them as entirely happy.’ Here, their being grasped as ‘entirely happy’ should be understood as due to seeing the frequent occurrence of states associated with happiness and so on in those various realms. Alternatively, just like blind men describing an elephant, those whose destination is views cling to and declare whatever they perceive; thus, no logical consistency should be sought here.

Asaññī nevasaññīnāsaññīvādavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Doctrine of the Non-Percipient and Neither-Percipient-Nor-Non-Percipient.

78-83. Asaññīvāde asaññabhave nibbattasattavasena paṭhamavādo, “saññaṃ attato samanupassatī”ti ettha vuttanayena saññaṃyeva “attā”ti gahetvā tassa kiñcanabhāvena ṭhitāya aññāya [P 1.0226] saññāya abhāvato “asaññī”ti [M 1.0173] pavatto dutiyavādo, tathā saññāya saha rūpadhamme, sabbe eva vā rūpārūpadhamme “attā”ti gahetvā pavatto tatiyavādo, takkagāhavaseneva catutthavādo pavatto. Tassa pubbe vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Dutiyacatukkepi kasiṇarūpassa asañjānanasabhāvatāya asaññīti katvā antānantikavāde vuttanayeneva cattāropi veditabbā. Tathā nevasaññīnāsaññīvādepi nevasaññīnāsaññībhave nibbattasattasseva cutipaṭisandhīsu, sabbattha vā paṭusaññākiccaṃ kātuṃ asamatthāya sukhumāya saññāya atthibhāvapaṭijānanavasena paṭhamavādo, asaññīvāde vuttanayena sukhumāya saññāya vasena, sañjānanasabhāvatāpaṭijānena ca dutiyavādādayo pavattāti evaṃ ekena pakārena satipi [V 1.0153] kāraṇapariyesanassa sambhave diṭṭhigatikavādānaṃ anādaraṇīyabhāvadassanatthaṃ “tattha na ekantena kāraṇaṃ pariyesitabba”nti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Etesañca saññīasaññīnevasaññīnāsaññīvādānaṃ “arogo paraṃ maraṇā”ti vacanato sassatadiṭṭhisaṅgaho pākaṭoyeva.

78-83. In the doctrine of the non-percipient, the first argument is based on beings reborn in the non-percipient realm. The second argument arises by taking perception itself as 'self,' in the way stated, ‘one regards perception as self,’ and because there is no other perception existing as 'something' (kiñcana), the term 'non-percipient' is applied. Similarly, the third argument arises by taking perception along with material phenomena, or all material and immaterial phenomena, as the 'self'. The fourth argument arises from mere speculative clinging. Its meaning should be understood as previously explained. In the second tetrad, due to the kasiṇa-form's nature of not perceiving, it is treated as non-percipient, and all four arguments should be understood in the same way as in the doctrine of the finite and infinite. Likewise, in the doctrine of neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, the first argument arises by way of acknowledging the existence of subtle perception in beings reborn in the neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient realm—whether at death and rebirth or everywhere—because it is unable to perform the function of gross perception. The second and subsequent arguments proceed by way of subtle perception, according to the method explained in the doctrine of the non-percipient, and by acknowledging the nature of perceiving. Thus, even when there is a possibility of investigating causes in one way, to demonstrate that the doctrines of those with view-inclinations should not be taken seriously, it is said, 'Here, one should not investigate the cause absolutely.' Moreover, from the statement 'after death, one is without affliction,' it is evident that these doctrines of the percipient, non-percipient, and neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient are included under the classification of eternalist views.

Ucchedavādavaṇṇanā

Exposition of Annihilationism.

84. Asato vināsāsambhavato atthibhāvanibandhano ucchedoti vuttaṃ “sato”ti. Yathā hetuphalabhāvena pavattamānānaṃ sabhāvadhammānaṃ satipi ekasantānapariyāpannānaṃ bhinnasantatipatitehi visese hetuphalānaṃ paramatthato bhinnasabhāvattā bhinnasantānapatitānaṃ viya accantabhedasanniṭṭhānena nānattanayassa micchāgahaṇaṃ ucchedābhinivesassa kāraṇaṃ, evaṃ hetuphalabhūtānaṃ dhammānaṃ vijjamānepi sabhāvabhede ekasantatipariyāpannatāya ekattanayena accantamabhedaggahaṇampi kāraṇaṃ evāti dassetuṃ “sattassā”ti vuttaṃ pāḷiyaṃ. Santānavasena hi vattamānesu khandhesu ghanavinibbhogābhāvena sattagāho, sattassa ca atthibhāvagāhanibandhano ucchedagāho yāvāyaṃ attā na ucchijjati, tāvāyaṃ vijjatiyevāti gahaṇato, nirudayavināso vā idha ucchedoti adhippetoti āha “upaccheda”nti. Visesena [P 1.0227] nāso vināso, abhāvo. So pana maṃsacakkhupaññācakkhūnaṃ dassanapathātikkamoyeva hotīti āha “adassana”nti. Adassane hi nāsa-saddo loke niruḷhoti. Bhāvavigamanti sabhāvāpagamaṃ. Yo hi nirudayavināsavasena ucchijjati, na so attano sabhāvena tiṭṭhatīti. Lābhīti dibbacakkhuñāṇalābhī. Cutimattamevāti [M 1.0174] sekkhaputhujjanānampi cutimattameva. Na upapātanti pubbayogābhāvena, parikammākaraṇena vā upapātaṃ daṭṭhuṃ na sakkoti. “Alābhī ca ko paralokaṃ na jānātī”ti natthikavādavasena, mahāmūḷhabhāveneva vā “ito añño paraloko atthī”ti anavabodhamāha. Ettakoyeva visayo, yo yaṃ indriyagocaroti. Attano dhītuyā hatthagaṇhanakarājādi viya kāmasukhagiddhatāya vā. “Na puna viruhantī”ti patitapaṇṇānaṃ vaṇṭena appaṭisandhikabhāvamāha. Evameva sattāti yathā paṇḍupalāso bandhanā pavutto na paṭisandhiyati, evaṃ sabbe sattā appaṭisandhikamaraṇameva nigacchantīti. Jalapubbūḷakūpamā hi sattāti tassa laddhi. Tathāti vuttappakārena. Lābhinopi cutito uddhaṃ adassaneneva imā diṭṭhiyo uppajjantīti āha “vikappetvā vā”ti.

84. Because the destruction of the non-existent is impossible, annihilation is said to be tied to the existent, as in 'of the existent.' Just as the mistaken grasping of the diversity view—with its conviction of absolute difference, whereby phenomena occurring as cause and effect, though included in a single continuum, are seen as utterly different in nature in ultimate reality, as if they belonged to different continuities—is the cause of clinging to annihilationism; so too, to show that the grasping of absolute non-difference by way of unity, due to their inclusion in a single continuum, is also a cause, even though phenomena that are cause and effect have distinct natures, the term 'of a being' is used in the Pāli. For when the aggregates are proceeding by way of continuity, the grasping of a 'being' arises from the absence of analysis of the compact. And the clinging to annihilationism, tied to the grasping of the existence of a being, is due to the notion that 'as long as this self is not annihilated, it exists.' Or, it is intended that 'destruction without re-arising' is annihilation here, hence it is said 'upaccheda' (cutting off). Specifically, 'destruction' (vināso) means destruction (nāso), non-existence. However, this is merely the transcending of the range of vision for the physical eye and the eye of wisdom—hence the term 'non-seeing' (adassana). For in the world, the word 'destruction' (nāsa) is commonly used when something is no longer seen. 'Disappearance of existence' means the departure of intrinsic nature. For whatever is annihilated by way of destruction without re-arising does not persist in its own nature. 'A possessor' refers to one who has attained the divine eye and knowledge. 'Only death' means that even for trainees and ordinary people, there is only death. 'No rebirth' means that due to the absence of prior practice or preparatory work, one cannot see rebirth. 'And who, not being a possessor, does not know the other world'—this refers to either nihilism or extreme delusion, meaning the non-comprehension that 'there is another world beyond this one.' 'This much is the scope, what falls within the range of the faculties.' Or it is due to greed for sensual pleasure, like a king who takes his own daughter's hand. 'They do not grow again'—this refers to the state of not re-connecting, like fallen leaves from their stem. 'In the same way, beings' means that just as a withered leaf, released from its bond, does not re-connect, so all beings meet only with a death that has no re-connection. For their belief is that beings are like bubbles on water. 'In that way'—as described. Even for one who possesses the divine eye, these views arise simply from not seeing beyond death—hence the phrase 'or by speculating.'

Etthāha – yathā amarāvikkhepikavādā ekantaalābhīvaseneva dassitā, yathā ca uddhamāghātanikasaññīvādacatukko [V 1.0154] ekantalābhīvaseneva, na evamayaṃ. Ayaṃ pana sassatekaccasassatavādādayo viya lābhīalābhīvasena pavatto. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “tattha dve janā”tiādi. Yadi evaṃ kasmā sassatavādādidesanāhi idha aññathā desanā pavattāti? Vuccate – desanāvilāsappattito. Desanāvilāsappattā hi buddhā bhagavanto, te veneyyajjhāsayānurūpaṃ [P 1.0228] vividhenākārena dhammaṃ desenti, aññathā idhāpi ca evaṃ bhagavā deseyya “idha bhikkhave ekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā ātappamanvāya…pe… yathāsamāhite citte sattānaṃ cutūpapātañāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmeti, so dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena arahato cuticittaṃ passati, puthūnaṃ vā parasattānaṃ, na heva kho taduddhaṃ upapattiṃ, so evamāha ‘yathā kho bho ayaṃ attā’” tiādinā visesalābhino, takkino ca visuṃ katvā, tasmā desanāvilāsena veneyyajjhāsayānurūpaṃ sassatavādādidesanāhi aññathāyaṃ desanā pavattāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here it is said: Just as the doctrines of the eel-wrigglers are shown entirely by way of non-attainment, and just as the tetrad of doctrines of those conscious after death is shown entirely by way of attainment, this is not so. This doctrine, however, like the doctrines of eternalism and partial-eternalism, proceeds by way of both attainment and non-attainment. For so it is said: 'Therein, two persons,' and so on. If so, why does this teaching proceed differently from the teachings on eternalism and so forth? It is said: Due to mastery in teaching. For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, having attained mastery in teaching, expound the Dhamma in various ways according to the dispositions of those to be trained. Otherwise, the Blessed One might have taught even here in this way: 'Here, bhikkhus, some ascetic or brahmin, by means of ardour... when his mind is thus concentrated, directs and inclines his mind to the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees the passing-away-consciousness of an arahant, or of many other beings, but he does not see their rebirth. He says thus: "Sirs, this self..."' and so on, thereby distinguishing those who have special attainments from the reasoners. Therefore, it should be understood that this teaching proceeds differently from the teachings on eternalism and so forth due to mastery in teaching, in accordance with the dispositions of those to be trained.

Atha vā ekaccasassatavādādīsu viya na idha takkīvādito visesalābhīvādo bhinnākāro, atha kho samānabhedatāya samānākāroyevāti imassa visesassa pakāsanatthaṃ bhagavatā ayamucchedavādo purimavādehi visiṭṭhākāro desito. Sambhavati hi takkinopi [M 1.0175] anussavādivasena adhigamavato viya idha abhiniveso. Atha vā na imā diṭṭhiyo bhagavatā anāgate evaṃ bhāvīvasena desitā, nāpi parikappavasena, atha kho yathā yathā diṭṭhigatikehi “idameva saccaṃ, moghamañña”nti paññattā, tathā tathā yathābhuccaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇena paricchinditvā pakāsitā. Yehi gambhīrādippakārā aputhujjanagocarā buddhadhammā pakāsanti, yesañca parikittanena tathāgatā sammadeva thomitā honti. Ucchedavādīhi ca diṭṭhigatikehi yathā uttaruttarabhavadassīhi aparabhavadassīnaṃ tesaṃ vādapaṭisedhavasena sakasakavādā patiṭṭhāpitā, tathāyaṃ desanā pavattāti purimadesanāhi imissā desanāya pavattibhedo na codetabbo. Evañca katvā arūpabhavabhedavasena viya kāmarūpabhavabhedavasenāpi ucchedavādo vibhajitvā daṭṭhabbo. Atha vā paccekaṃ kāmarūpabhavabhedavasena viya arūpabhavavasenāpi na vibhajitvā vattabbo, evañca sati bhagavatā [P 1.0229] vuttasattakato bahutarabhedo, appatarabhedo vā ucchedavādo āpajjatīti evaṃ pakārāpi codanā anavakāsāvāti.

Alternatively, unlike in the case of the doctrines of partial-eternalism and so forth, here the doctrine of one with special attainment is not different in form from the doctrine of a reasoner; rather, it is of the same form due to having the same divisions. To make this distinction clear, this doctrine of annihilationism was taught by the Blessed One in a form distinct from the previous doctrines. For it is possible even for a reasoner to have adherence here, like one who has an attainment by way of oral tradition and so on. Alternatively, these views were not taught by the Blessed One as things that will be so in the future, nor by way of speculation. Rather, in whatever way they were formulated by the holders of views who declare, 'This alone is true, anything else is false,' in that same way they were revealed in accordance with reality, having been precisely determined by the knowledge of omniscience. By these teachings, the profound and other kinds of Buddha-dhammas, which are not the domain of worldlings, are made manifest, and by the recounting of which the Tathāgatas are rightly praised. And just as the annihilationist view-holders who see successive future existences established their own doctrines by way of refuting the doctrines of those who do not see a future existence, so this teaching proceeds. Therefore, the difference in the way this teaching proceeds from the previous teachings should not be questioned. And this being so, the doctrine of annihilationism should be understood as being divided by way of the distinction of the sense-sphere and form-sphere existences, as well as by way of the distinction of the formless-sphere existence. Alternatively, it should not be spoken of as divided by way of the formless-sphere existence, just as it is not divided by way of each of the sense-sphere and form-sphere existences. And if this is so, then any such objection—that the doctrine of annihilationism would have more or fewer divisions than the sevenfold classification taught by the Blessed One—is without basis.

Etthāha – yuttaṃ tāva purimesu tīsu vādesu “kāyassa bhedā”ti vuttaṃ pañcavokārabhavapariyāpannaṃ attabhāvaṃ ārabbha pavattattā tesaṃ vādānaṃ, catuvokārabhavapariyāpannaṃ pana attabhāvaṃ nissāya pavattesu catutthādīsu catūsu vādesu kasmā “kāyassa bhedā”ti vuttaṃ[V 1.0155]. Na hi arūpīnaṃ kāyo vijjatīti? Saccametaṃ, rūpattabhāve pavattavohāreneva pana diṭṭhigatiko arūpattabhāvepi kāyavohāraṃ āropetvā āha “kāyassa bhedā”ti. Yathā ca diṭṭhigatikā diṭṭhiyo paññāpenti, tathā ca bhagavā dassetīti, arūpakāyabhāvato vā phassādidhammasamūhabhūte arūpattabhāve kāyaniddeso daṭṭhabbo. Ettha ca kāmadevattabhāvādiniravasesavibhavapatiṭṭhāpakānaṃ dutiyavādādīnaṃ yutto aparantakappikabhāvo anāgataddhavisayattā tesaṃ vādānaṃ, na pana diṭṭhigatikapaccakkhabhūtamanussattabhāvasamucchedapatiṭṭhāpakassa paṭhamavādassa paccuppannavisayattā. Dutiyavādādīnañhi purimapurimavādasaṅgahitasseva attano taduttaruttaribhavopapannassa samucchedato yujjati aparantakappikatā, tathā ca “no ca kho [M 1.0176] bho ayaṃ attā ettāvatā sammā samucchinno hotī”tiādi vuttaṃ, yaṃ pana tattha vuttaṃ “atthi kho bho añño attā”ti, taṃ manussakāyavisesāpekkhāya vuttaṃ, na sabbathā aññabhāvatoti? No na yutto, idhalokapariyāpannattepi ca paṭhamavādavisayassa anāgatakālasseva tassa adhippetattā paṭhamavādinopi aparantakappikatāya na koci virodhoti.

Here it is said: It is fitting that in the first three doctrines the phrase 'with the breakup of the body' is stated, since those doctrines proceed in reference to an individual existence included in the five-constituent becoming. But in the subsequent four doctrines, which proceed based on an individual existence included in the four-constituent becoming, why is it said, 'with the breakup of the body'? For beings in the formless realm have no body. This is true. However, the holder of the view, by the very convention current for a material existence, superimposes the convention of 'body' even on a non-material existence and says, 'with the breakup of the body.' And just as the holders of views formulate their views, so the Blessed One teaches them. Or, the designation 'body' in the case of a non-material existence should be understood as referring to the collection of phenomena such as contact, etc., since it is a non-material body. And here, for the second doctrine and the others, which establish the complete annihilation of the state of a sense-sphere deity and so on, it is fitting that they are speculators on the future, since the domain of those doctrines is the future. But this is not so for the first doctrine, which establishes the annihilation of the human existence that is directly perceived by the holder of the view, since its domain is the present. For the second doctrine and the others, their being speculators on the future is fitting because it is the annihilation of oneself reborn in successively higher existences—included in the preceding doctrines—that is at issue; and so it is said, 'But, sirs, this self is not completely annihilated to that extent,' and so on. As for what is said there, 'There is, sirs, another self,' that is said with reference to a distinction from the human body, not to its being another in every way. Is this not fitting? No, it is not unfitting. For even though the domain of the first doctrine is included in this world, since what is intended by it is precisely a future time, there is no contradiction in the proponent of the first doctrine also being a speculator on the future.

Diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādavaṇṇanā

An Explanation of the Doctrines of Nibbāna in This Very Life

93. Diṭṭhadhammoti [P 1.0230] dassanabhūtena ñāṇena upaladdhadhammo. Tattha yo anindriyavisayo, sopi supākaṭabhāvena indriyavisayo viya hotīti āha “diṭṭhadhammoti paccakkhadhammo vuccatī”ti. Teneva ca “tattha tattha paṭiladdhattabhāvassetaṃ adhivacana”nti vuttaṃ.

93. 'Diṭṭhadhamma' means a phenomenon apprehended by knowledge that is seeing. Therein, even that which is not an object of the sense faculties, due to its very clear manifestation, becomes as if it were an object of the sense faculties. Hence, it is said, 'Diṭṭhadhamma is called a directly perceived phenomenon.' And for that very reason, it is stated, 'This is a designation for the individual existence attained here and there.'

95. Antonijjhāyanalakkhaṇoti ñātibhogarogasīladiṭṭhibyasanehi phuṭṭhassa cetaso anto abbhantaraṃ nijjhāyanaṃ socanaṃ antonijjhāyanaṃ, taṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etassāti antonijjhāyanalakkhaṇo. Tannissitalālappanalakkhaṇoti taṃ sokaṃ samuṭṭhānahetuṃ nissitaṃ tannissitaṃ, bhusaṃ vilāpanaṃ lālappanaṃ, tannissitañca lālappanañca tannissitalālappanaṃ, taṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etassāti tannissitalālappanalakkhaṇo. Ñātibyasanādinā phuṭṭhassa paridevenāpi asakkuṇantassa antogatasokasamuṭṭhito bhuso āyāso upāyāso. So pana yasmā cetaso appasannākāro hoti, tasmā “visādalakkhaṇo”ti vutto.

95. Having the characteristic of inward brooding: 'inward brooding' is the internal brooding and sorrow of a mind afflicted by misfortunes concerning relatives, possessions, illness, virtue, or views; that is its characteristic, thus it has the characteristic of inward brooding. Having the characteristic of lamentation dependent on that: 'dependent on that' means dependent on that sorrow as its originating cause; 'lamentation' (lālappana) is intense wailing; that which is lamentation dependent on that has that as its characteristic, thus it has the characteristic of lamentation dependent on that. For one afflicted by misfortunes concerning relatives and so on, who is unable even to lament, intense trouble and despair (upāyāso) arise from sorrow that has gone inward. And since that is a state of mental disquietude, it is called 'characterized by dejection'.

96. Vitakkanaṃ vitakkitaṃ, taṃ pana abhiniropanasabhāvo vitakkoyevāti āha “abhi…pe… vitakko”ti. Esa nayo vicāritanti etthāpi. Khobhakarasabhāvattā vitakkavicārānaṃ [V 1.0156] taṃsahitaṃ jhānaṃ saubbilanaṃ viya hotīti vuttaṃ “sakaṇḍakaṃ viya khāyatī”ti.

96. Thinking (vitakkanaṃ) is what is thought (vitakkitaṃ). But that is vitakka itself, which has the nature of application; thus it is said, 'application... is vitakka.' This same method applies here also to 'what is examined' (vicāritaṃ). Because vitakka and vicāra have a nature that causes agitation, the jhāna accompanied by them is like a disturbance, and so it is said that it 'seems like something with thorns.'

97. Yāya ubbilāpanapītiyā uppannāya cittaṃ “ubbilāvita”nti vuccati, sā pīti ubbilāvitattaṃ yasmā pana cittassa ubbilabhāvo tassā pītiyā sati hoti, nāsati, tasmā sā “ubbilabhāvakāraṇa”nti vuttā.

97. That uplifting joy, on account of which the mind is said to be 'elated' when it has arisen—that joy is the state of elation. And since the mind's state of elation exists when that joy is present and not when it is absent, it is therefore called 'the cause of the state of elation'.

98. Ābhogoti [M 1.0177] vā cittassa ābhuggabhāvo, ārammaṇe oṇatabhāvoti attho. Sukhena hi cittaṃ ārammaṇe abhinataṃ hoti, na dukkhena viya apanataṃ, nāpi adukkhamasukhena [P 1.0231] viya anabhinataṃ anapanatañca. Tattha “khuppipāsādiabhibhūtassa viya manuññabhojanādīsu kāmehi viveciyamānassupādārammaṇapatthanā visesato abhivaḍḍhati, uḷārassa pana kāmarasassa yāvadatthaṃ tittassa manuññarasabhojanaṃ bhuttāvino viya suhitassa bhottukāmatā kāmesu pātabyatā na hoti, visayassāgiddhatāya visayehi dummociyehipi jalūkā viya sayameva muñcatī”ti ca ayoniso ummujjitvā kāmaguṇasantappitatāya saṃsāradukkhavūpasamaṃ byākāsi paṭhamavādī. Kāmādīnaṃ ādīnavadassitāya, paṭhamādijjhānasukhassa santabhāvadassitāya ca paṭhamādijjhānasukhatittiyā saṃsāradukkhupacchedaṃ byākaṃsu dutiyādivādino, idhāpi ucchedavāde vuttappakāro vicāro yathāsambhavaṃ ānetvā vattabbo. Ayaṃ panettha viseso – ekasmiñhi attabhāve pañca vādā labbhanti. Teneva hi pāḷiyaṃ “añño attā”ti aññaggahaṇaṃ na kataṃ. Kathaṃ panettha accantanibbānapaññāpakassa attano diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādassa sassatadiṭṭhiyā saṅgaho, na pana ucchedadiṭṭhiyāti? Taṃtaṃsukhavisesasamaṅgitāpaṭiladdhena bandhavimokkhena suddhassa attano sakarūpe avaṭṭhānadīpanato.

98. Ābhoga means the mind's state of being inclined, that is, the state of leaning towards an object. For the mind is naturally drawn toward an object with pleasure, not repelled as with pain, nor is it neither inclined nor disinclined as with neither-pain-nor-pleasure. Here, the first proponent, having emerged improperly and being filled with satisfaction from sensual qualities, explained the cessation of suffering in saṃsāra, saying: 'Just as for one oppressed by hunger and thirst, when separated from sensual pleasures, the desire for objects of clinging especially increases. But for one who is satisfied to the full with the supreme taste of sensual pleasures, like one who has eaten delightful and tasty food to satisfaction, there is no desire to eat or drink sensual pleasures, being contented; due to non-greed for objects, one naturally releases oneself even from objects that are hard to be detached from, like a leech.' The second and other proponents, having shown the danger in sensual pleasures and so on, and the peaceful nature of the bliss of the first jhāna and so on, declared the cessation of suffering in saṃsāra through satisfaction with the bliss of the first jhāna and so on. Here too, the same kind of investigation as stated in the annihilationist view should be brought in and explained as appropriate. But this is the difference here: in one individual existence, five views can be obtained. Therefore, in the Pāli, the term 'another' (añña) is not used for 'self'. How then, in this case, is the view of Nibbāna in this very life of one who proclaims absolute Nibbāna for the self included under the eternalist view, and not with the annihilationist view? Because it shows the liberation from bondage attained through being endowed with various kinds of bliss, and the manifestation of the pure self's abiding in its own true form.

Sesāti sesā pañcapaññāsa diṭṭhiyo. Tāsu antānantikavādādīnaṃ sassatadiṭṭhibhāvo tattha tattha pakāsitoyeva.

The rest: these are the remaining fifty-five views. Among them, the eternalist nature of the views of the antānantikas and so forth has been explained in various places.

101-3. Kiṃ pana kāraṇaṃ pubbantāparantā eva diṭṭhābhinivesassa visayabhāvena dassitā, na pana tadubhayamekajjhanti? Asambhavato. Na hi pubbantāparantesu viya tadubhayavinimutte majjhante diṭṭhikappanā sambhavati ittarakālattā, atha pana paccuppannabhavo tadubhayavemajjhaṃ, evaṃ sati diṭṭhikappanakkhamo tassa [P 1.0232] ubhayasabhāvo pubbantāparantesuyeva antogadhoti kathamadassitaṃ. Atha vā pubbantāparantavantatāya “pubbantāparanto”ti majjhanto vuccati[V 1.0157], so ca “pubbantāparantakappikā vā pubbantāparantānudiṭṭhino”ti vadantena pubbantāparantehi visuṃ katvā vuttoyevāti daṭṭhabbo. Aṭṭhakathāyampi “sabbepi te aparantakappike pubbantāparantakappike”ti etena sāmaññaniddesena, ekasesena vā saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ, aññathā [M 1.0178] saṅkaḍḍhitvā vuttavacanassa anatthakatā āpajjeyyāti. Ke pana te pubbantāparantakappikā? Ye antānantikā hutvā diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādāti evaṃ pakārā veditabbā.

101-3. But what is the reason that only the past and future extremes are shown as the domain of adherence to views, and not both together? Because it is impossible. For unlike the past and future extremes, no dogmatic conception can arise in the middle, which is free from both, due to its being a fleeting time. Rather, if present existence is the middle ground between those two, in such a case, its dual nature, which is capable of dogmatic conceptions, is already included within the past and future extremes. Why then is it not shown? Alternatively, because the middle is bounded by the past and future, it is called 'past and future extreme'. And when it is said, 'those who are conceivers of the past and future extremes or adherents of the past and future extremes,' it should be understood that the middle is mentioned separately from the past and future extremes. In the commentary as well, it should be understood that 'All of them are conceivers of the future extreme or conceivers of the past and future extremes' – by this general designation, or by ekasesa (ellipsis), all are included; otherwise, the statement, having been forcibly interpreted, would become meaningless. But who are these conceivers of the past and future extremes? They should be understood as those who, being antānantikas, are diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādins, and those of such kinds.

Ettha ca “sabbe te imeheva dvāsaṭṭhiyā vatthūhi, etesaṃ vā aññatarena, natthi ito bahiddhā”ti vacanato, pubbantakappikādittayavinimuttassa ca kassaci diṭṭhigatikassa abhāvato yāni tāni sāmaññaphalādi (dī. ni. 1.166) suttantaresu vuttappakārāni akiriyāhetukanatthikavādādīni, yāni ca issarapajāpatipurisakālasabhāvaniyatiyadicchāvādādippabhedāni diṭṭhigatāni (visuddhi. ṭī. 2.563; vibha. anuṭī. 189 passitabbaṃ) bahiddhāpi dissamānāni, tesaṃ ettheva saṅgaho, antogadhatā ca veditabbā. Kathaṃ? Akiriyavādo tāva “vañjho kūṭaṭṭho”tiādinā kiriyābhāvadīpanato sassatavāde antogadho, tathā “sattime kāyā”tiādi [P 1.0233] (dī. ni. 1.174) nayappavatto pakudhavādo, “natthi hetu natthi paccayo sattānaṃ saṃkilesāyā”tiādi (dī. ni. 1.168) vacanato ahetukavādo adhiccasamuppannikavāde antogadho. “Natthi paro loko”tiādi (dī. ni. 1.171) vacanato natthikavādo ucchedavāde antogadho. Tathā hi tattha “kāyassa bhedā ucchijjatī”tiādi (dī. ni. 1.86) vuttaṃ. Paṭhamena ādi-saddena nigaṇṭhavādādayo saṅgahitā.

Here, by the statement 'all these are included within these sixty-two grounds, or by any one of them, there is nothing beyond this' (Dī. Ni. 1.166), and since there is no dogmatist whatsoever apart from the three kinds of conceivers of the past extreme and so forth, whatever views are mentioned in other suttas like the Sāmaññaphala Sutta and so forth, such as the doctrines of non-action, causelessness, nihilism, and so forth, and whatever views appear externally—like those divided into the doctrines of a creator, primordial being, time, nature, fate, or chance (see Visuddhi. Ṭī. 2.563; Vibha. Anuṭī. 189)—their inclusion here and their being encompassed within should be understood. How so? For instance, the doctrine of non-action, by describing the absence of action through phrases like 'barren, steadfast' and so forth, is included under eternalism. Similarly, the doctrine of Pakudha Kaccāyana, which proceeds according to the method of 'these seven bodies' and so forth (Dī. Ni. 1.174), and the doctrine of no-cause, by the statement 'there is no cause, no condition for the defilement of beings' and so forth (Dī. Ni. 1.168), are included under the doctrine of uncaused origination. The doctrine of nihilism, by the statement 'there is no other world' and so forth (Dī. Ni. 1.171), is included under annihilationism. For there it is stated, 'with the breakup of the body, one is annihilated' and so forth (Dī. Ni. 1.86). By the first word 'and so forth' (ādi-saddena), the doctrines of the Nigaṇṭhas and others are included.

Yadipi pāḷiyaṃ nāṭaputtavāda (dī. ni. 1.178) bhāvena cātuyāmasaṃvaro āgato, tathāpi sattavatātikkamena vikkhepavāditāya nāṭaputtavādopi sañcayavādo viya amarāvikkhepavādesu antogadho. “Taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīraṃ, aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīra”nti (dī. ni. 1.377; ma. ni. 2.122; saṃ. ni. 2.35) evaṃ pakārā vādā “rūpī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā”tiādivādesu saṅgahaṃ gacchanti, “hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā, “atthi sattā opapātikā”ti evaṃ pakārā sassatavāde. “Na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā, natthi sattā opapātikā”ti evaṃ pakārā ucchedavādena saṅgahitā. “Hoti ca na hoti ca tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā, atthi ca natthi ca sattā opapātikā”ti evaṃ pakārā ekaccasassatavāde antogadhā. “Neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā, nevatthi na natthi [V 1.0158] sattā opapātikā”ti ca [P 1.0234] evaṃ pakārā amarāvikkhepavāde [M 1.0179] antogadhā. Issarapajāpatipurisakālavādā ekaccasassatavāde antogadhā, tathā kaṇādavādo. Sabhāvaniyatiyadicchāvādā adhiccasamuppannikavādena saṅgahitā. Iminā nayena suttantaresu, bahiddhā ca dissamānānaṃ diṭṭhigatānaṃ imāsu dvāsaṭṭhiyā diṭṭhīsu antogadhatā veditabbā.

Even though the fourfold restraint is mentioned in the Pāli texts (Dī. Ni. 1.178) as Nātaputta’s doctrine, still, due to its equivocal speech by way of transgressing the vow concerning beings, Nātaputta’s doctrine, like the doctrine of accumulation, is included among the doctrines of endless equivocation. Statements such as, “The soul is the same as the body,” or “The soul is one thing, the body another” (Dī. Ni. 1.377; Ma. Ni. 2.122; Saṃ. Ni. 2.35), are included in views like “The self is material, healthy after death,” and so forth. Views such as “The Tathāgata exists after death,” or “There are spontaneously born beings,” are included in eternalist doctrines. Views such as “The Tathāgata does not exist after death,” or “There are no spontaneously born beings,” are included in annihilationist doctrines. Views such as “The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,” or “There both are and are not spontaneously born beings,” are included in partial eternalism. Views such as “The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death,” or “There neither are nor are not spontaneously born beings,” are included in the doctrines of endless equivocation. The doctrines of creation by a supreme being, by Prajāpati, by a primal person, or by time, are included in partial eternalism, as is the doctrine of Kaṇāda. The doctrines of inherent nature, necessity, or chance are included in the doctrine of fortuitous origination. In this way, the inclusion of views found in other suttas and externally within these sixty-two views should be understood.

Ajjhāsayanti diṭṭhijjhāsayaṃ. Sassatucchedadiṭṭhivasena hi sattānaṃ saṃkilesapakkhe duvidho ajjhāsayo, tañca bhagavā aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ aparimāṇe eva ñeyyavisese uppajjanavasena anekabhedabhinnānampi “cattāro janā sassatavādā”tiādinā dvāsaṭṭhiyā pabhedehi saṅgaṇhanavasena sabbaññutaññāṇena paricchinditvā dassento pamāṇabhūtāya tulāya dhārayamāno viya hotīti āha “tulāya tulayanto viyā”ti. Tathā hi vakkhati “anto jālīkatā”tiādi (dī. ni. 1.146). “Sinerupādato vālukaṃ uddharanto viyā”ti etena sabbaññutaññāṇato aññassa imissā desanāya asakkuṇeyyataṃ dasseti.

Inclination (ajjhāsaya) means the inclination of views. Indeed, beings have a twofold inclination towards the side of defilement through views of eternalism and annihilationism. The Blessed One, having comprehended this through omniscient knowledge, demonstrates it by encompassing the immeasurable distinctions of knowable things arising in immeasurable world-systems among immeasurable beings—even though they are divided into many types—through classifications such as “four people who are eternalists,” and so on, in sixty-two divisions. He is like one holding them with a standard balance, thus it is said, “as if weighing with a balance.” For so he will say: “They are enmeshed within,” and so on (Dī. Ni. 1.146). “Like one extracting a grain of sand from the foot of Mount Sineru”—this shows the incapability of anyone other than one with omniscient knowledge to deliver such a teaching.

Anusandhānaṃ anusandhi, pucchāya kato anusandhi pucchānusandhi. Atha vā anusandhayatīti anusandhi, pucchā anusandhi etassāti pucchānusandhi. Pucchāya anusandhiyatīti vā pucchānusandhi. Ajjhāsayānusandhimhipi eseva nayo. Yathānusandhīti ettha pana anusandhīyatīti anusandhi, yā yā anusandhi yathānusandhi, anusandhianurūpaṃ vā yathānusandhīti saddattho veditabbo, so “yena pana dhammena ādimhi desanā uṭṭhitā, tassa dhammassa anurūpadhammavasena vā paṭipakkhavasena vā yesu suttesu upari desanā āgacchati, tesaṃ [P 1.0235] vasena yathānusandhi veditabbo. Seyyathidaṃ? Ākaṅkheyyasutte (ma. ni. 1.64-69) heṭṭhā sīlena desanā uṭṭhitā, upari cha abhiññā āgatā…pe… kakacūpame (ma. ni. 1.222) heṭṭhā akkhantiyā uṭṭhitā, upari kakacūpamā āgatā”tiādinā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.100-104) vutto.

Anusandhāna is connection (anusandhi); a connection made by a question is a question-connection. Alternatively, that which connects is a connection; a question is its connection, thus it is a question-connection. Or, it is a question-connection because it is connected by a question. The same principle applies to the connection of intention. As for “according to the connection” (yathānusandhi), here “connection” (anusandhi) means that which is connected. Whatever connection there is, that is “according to the connection,” or the meaning of the term should be understood as “in accordance with the connection.” This is stated in the commentary (DN-a 1.100-104) in such words as: “By whatever teaching the discourse initially arose, the subsequent teachings in the suttas that follow—whether in accordance with that teaching or in opposition to it—should be understood as ‘according to the connection.’ For example, in the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta (MN 1.64-69), the discourse begins with virtue, and later the six higher knowledges appear… In the Kakacūpama Sutta (MN 1.222), the discourse begins with impatience, and later the simile of the saw appears.”

Iti kirāti bhagavato yathādesitāya attasuññatāya attano aruccanabhāvadīpanaṃ. Bhoti dhammālapanaṃ. Anattakatānīti attanā na katāni, anattakehi vā khandhehi katāni. Kamattānaṃ phusissantīti asati attani [M 1.0180] khandhānañca khaṇikattā kammāni kaṃ attānaṃ attano phalena phusissanti, ko kammaphalaṃ paṭisaṃvedetīti attho. Avidvāti sutādivirahena ariyadhammassa akovidatāya na vidvā. Avijjāgatoti avijjāya upagato, ariyadhamme avinītatāya appahīnāvijjoti attho. Taṇhādhipateyyena cetasāti “yadi ahaṃ nāma koci natthi[V 1.0159], mayā katassa kammassa ko phalaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti, sati pana tasmiṃ siyā phalūpabhogo”ti taṇhādhipatito āgato taṇhādhipateyyo, tena. Attavādupādānasahagata cetasā. Atidhāvitabbanti khaṇikattepi saṅkhārānaṃ yasmiṃ santāne kammaṃ kataṃ, tattheva phaluppattito dhammapuñjamattasseva ca siddhe kammaphalasambandhe ekattanayaṃ micchā gahetvā ekena kārakavedakabhūtena bhavitabbaṃ, aññathā “kammaphalānaṃ sambandho na siyā”ti attattaniyasuññatāpakāsanaṃ satthusāsanaṃ atikkamitabbaṃ maññeyyāti attho.

“Thus, it is said” indicates a demonstration of one’s own displeasure with the emptiness of self as taught by the Blessed One. “Bho” is a term of address concerning the Dhamma. “Not made by self” means not made by a self, or made by the non-self aggregates. “What self will they touch?” means: since there is no self and the aggregates are momentary, what self will actions touch with their own fruit? Who experiences the fruit of action? This is the meaning. “Unwise” means one who is not wise due to the absence of learning and so forth, and due to being unskilled in the noble Dhamma. “Gone to ignorance” means overcome by ignorance; it means that ignorance has not been abandoned due to being untamed in the noble Dhamma. “With a mind dominated by craving” means: with a mind dominated by craving, which arises from the dominance of craving, thinking, “If there is no one called ‘I,’ who experiences the fruit of an action done by me? But if there were such a one, there could be enjoyment of the fruit.” It is a mind accompanied by clinging to the doctrine of self. “It should be overstepped” means: although formations are momentary, since the fruit arises in the very same continuity in which the action was done, and since the connection between action and fruit is established for a mere mass of phenomena, one wrongly grasps the principle of oneness, thinking there must be a single agent and experiencer. Otherwise, thinking, “There would be no connection between actions and their fruits,” one might think that the Teacher’s teaching, which clarifies the emptiness of self and what belongs to self, should be transgressed. This is the meaning.

“Upari cha abhiññā āgatā”ti anurūpadhammavasena yathānusandhiṃ dasseti, itarehi paṭipakkhavasena. Kilesenāti “lobho cittassa upakkileso”tiādinā kilesavasena. Imasmimpīti pi-saddena yathā vuttasuttādīsu paṭipakkhavasena yathānusandhi, evaṃ imasmimpi [P 1.0236] sutteti dasseti. Tathā hi niccasārādipaññāpakānaṃ diṭṭhigatānaṃ vasena uṭṭhitā ayaṃ desanā niccasārādisuññatāpakāsanena niṭṭhāpitāti.

“Above, the six higher knowledges came” shows the connection by way of corresponding phenomena, while the others show it by way of opposition. “By defilement” means by way of defilement, as in “greed is a defilement of the mind,” and so on. In “in this one also,” the word “pi” (also) shows that just as in the aforementioned suttas and so on the connection is by way of opposition, so it is in this sutta. For this teaching, which arose in connection with views that declare permanence, essence, and so on, was concluded by clarifying the emptiness of permanence, essence, and so on.

Paritassitavipphanditavāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on Agitation and Wavering

105-117. Mariyādavibhāgadassanatthanti sassatādidiṭṭhidassanassa sammādassanena saṅkarābhāvavibhāvanatthaṃ. Tadapi vedayitanti sambandho. Ajānataṃ apassatanti “sassato attā ca loko cā”ti “idaṃ diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ evaṃgahikaṃ evaṃparāmaṭṭhaṃ evaṃgahitaṃ hoti evaṃabhisamparāya”nti yathābhūtaṃ ajānantānaṃ apassantānaṃ. Tathā yasmiṃ vedayite avītataṇhatāya evaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ upādiyanti, taṃ vedayitaṃ samudayādito yathābhūtaṃ ajānantānaṃ apassantānaṃ, etena anāvaraṇañāṇasamantacakkhūhi yathā tathāgatānaṃ yathābhūtamettha ñāṇadassanaṃ, na evaṃ diṭṭhigatikānaṃ, atha kho taṇhādiṭṭhiparāmāsoyevāti dasseti. Teneva cāyaṃ desanā mariyādavibhāgadassanatthā jātā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “yathābhūtaṃ dhammānaṃ [M 1.0181] sabhāvaṃ ajānantānaṃ apassantāna”nti avisesena vuttaṃ. Na hi saṅkhatadhammasabhāvaṃ ajānanamattena micchā abhinivisantīti. Sāmaññajotanā visese avatiṭṭhatīti ayaṃ visesayojanā katā. Vedayitanti “sassato attā ca loko cā”ti diṭṭhipaññāpanavasena pavattaṃ diṭṭhiyā anubhūtaṃ anubhavanaṃ. Taṇhāgatānanti taṇhāya gatānaṃ upagatānaṃ, pavattānaṃ vā. Tañca kho panetanti ca yathāvuttaṃ vedayitaṃ paccāmasati. Tañhi vaṭṭāmisabhūtaṃ diṭṭhitaṇhāsallānuviddhatāya saubbilattā cañcalaṃ, na maggaphalasukhaṃ viya ekarūpena avatiṭṭhatīti. Tenevāha “paritassitenā”tiādi.

105-117. “For the purpose of showing the division of boundaries” means for the purpose of clarifying the absence of confusion between the view of eternalism, etc., and right view. The connection is: “that also is a feeling.” “For those not knowing, not seeing” means for those not knowing, not seeing as it truly is that “the self and the world are eternal,” and that “this is a basis for views, thus held, thus misapprehended, thus grasped, and thus for a future state.” Likewise, for those who, due to unabandoned craving, cling to such a view regarding some feeling, not knowing, not seeing that feeling, its origin, etc., as it truly is. By this it is shown that just as the knowledge and vision of the Tathāgatas regarding this is as it truly is, with unobstructed knowledge and the all-seeing eye, it is not so for those holding such views, but rather it is just the misapprehension of craving and views. For this very reason, this teaching arose for the purpose of showing the division of boundaries. In the commentary, however, it is said without specification: “not knowing, not seeing the inherent nature of phenomena as it truly is.” For it is not merely by not knowing the nature of conditioned phenomena that they wrongly adhere. A general explanation stands on a specific instance; thus this specific application is made. “Feeling” means the experience, experienced by the view, that proceeds by way of propounding the view “the self and the world are eternal.” “Those gone to craving” means those who have gone to, approached, or are engaged in craving. “And that very thing” refers back to the aforementioned feeling. For that, being bait in the round of existence, pierced by the dart of view and craving, and being fragile, is unstable; it does not remain in a single form like the happiness of the path and fruition. Therefore, he said, “by the agitated,” etc.

Atha [V 1.0160] vā evaṃ visesakāraṇato dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhigatāni vibhajitvā idāni avisesakāraṇato tāni dassetuṃ “tatra bhikkhave”tiādikā desanā āraddhā. Sabbesañhi diṭṭhigatikānaṃ vedanā avijjā taṇhā ca avisiṭṭhakāranti. Tattha tadapīti “sassataṃ attānañca lokañca paññapenti”ti ettha yadetaṃ [P 1.0237] “sassato attā ca loko cā”ti paññāpanaṃ, tadapi. Sukhādibhedaṃ tividhavedayitaṃ yathākkamaṃ dukkhasallāniccato, avisesena samudayatthaṅgamassādādīnavanissaraṇato vā yathābhūtaṃ ajānantānaṃ apassantānaṃ, tato eva ca sukhādipatthanāsambhavato taṇhāya upagatattā taṇhāgatānaṃ taṇhāparitassitena diṭṭhivipphanditameva diṭṭhicalanameva, “asati attani ko vedanaṃ anubhavatī”ti kāyavacīdvāresu diṭṭhiyā copanappattimattameva vā, na pana diṭṭhiyā paññāpetabbo sassato koci dhammo atthīti attho. Ekaccasassatavādādīsupi eseva nayo.

Alternatively, having thus divided the sixty-two views according to specific causes, the teaching beginning with “There, monks…” was started in order to now show them according to non-specific causes. For, for all who hold views, feeling, ignorance, and craving are the non-specific causes. Therein, “that also” refers to this proclamation, “the self and the world are eternal,” in the phrase “they proclaim the self and the world as eternal.” For those not knowing, not seeing as it truly is the threefold feeling divided into pleasure, etc., in accordance with the dart of suffering and impermanence respectively, or without distinction, according to arising, passing away, gratification, danger, and escape; and because of that, from the possibility of longing for pleasure, etc., for those who have gone to craving because they are overcome by craving, it is merely a throbbing of views agitated by craving, a stirring of views. Or it is merely the attainment of prompting by the view at the doors of body and speech, thinking, “If there is no self, who experiences feeling?” But there is no eternal phenomenon whatsoever to be proclaimed by a view; this is the meaning. The same principle applies also to the partial-eternalists and others.

Phassapaccayavāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on Contact as a Condition

118. Yena taṇhāparitassitena etāni diṭṭhigatāni pavattanti, tassa vedayitaṃ paccayo, vedayitassāpi phasso paccayoti desanā diṭṭhiyā paccayaparamparaniddhāraṇanti āha “paramparapaccayadassanattha”nti, tena yathā paññāpanadhammo diṭṭhi, tappaccayadhammā ca yathāsakaṃ paccayavaseneva uppajjanti, na paccayehi vinā, evaṃ paññāpetabbā dhammāpi rūpavedanādayo, na ettha koci attā vā loko vā sassatoti ayamattho dassitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

118. The teaching that feeling is the condition for that by which, agitated by craving, these views proceed, and that contact is the condition for feeling, is the determination of the sequence of conditions for views. He said, “for the purpose of showing the succession of conditions.” By this it should be seen that the following meaning is shown: just as a view is a proclaiming phenomenon, and the phenomena conditioned by it arise only by the power of their respective conditions, not without conditions, so too the phenomena to be proclaimed are form, feeling, and so on. Herein there is no eternal self or world whatsoever.

Netaṃṭhānaṃvijjativāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on 'This Is Not a Possible Case'

131. Tassa [M 1.0182] paccayassāti phassapaccayassa diṭṭhivedayiteti diṭṭhiyā paccayabhūte vedayite, phassapadhānehi attano paccayehi nipphādetabbeti attho. Vināpi cakkhādivatthūhi, sampayuttadhammehi ca kehici vedanā uppajjati, na pana kadāci phassena vināti phasso vedanāya balavakāraṇanti āha “balavabhāvadassanattha”nti. Sannihitopi hi visayo sace phusanākārarahito hoti cittuppādo, na tassa ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo hotīti phassova sampayuttadhammānaṃ visesapaccayo. Tathā hi bhagavatā cittuppādaṃ vibhajantena phassoyeva paṭhamaṃ uddhaṭo, vedanāya pana adhiṭṭhānameva.

131. “Of that condition” refers to the condition of contact. This means that feeling, which is a condition for view, must be produced by its own conditions, with contact as the primary factor. Even without physical bases such as the eye, etc., and some associated mental factors, feeling can arise, but never without contact. Thus, contact is the strong cause of feeling, as stated, “to show its powerful nature.” For even if an object is present, if the arising of consciousness is devoid of the mode of contacting, that object does not serve as a condition by way of object-condition. Hence, contact is the special condition for associated phenomena. Indeed, when the Blessed One analyzed the arising of consciousness, contact was the first to be identified, while for feeling, it is merely the foundation.

Diṭṭhigatikādhiṭṭhānavaṭṭakathāvaṇṇanā

An Explanation of the Discourse on the Round of Views, Destinations, and Bases.

144. Heṭṭhā [V 1.0161] tīsupi vāresu adhikatattā, upari ca “paṭisaṃvedentī”ti vakkhamānattā vedayitamettha padhānanti āha “sabbadiṭṭhivedayitāni sampiṇḍetī”ti. Sampiṇḍetīti ca “yepi te”ti tattha tattha āgatassa pi-saddassa atthaṃ dasseti. Vedayitassa phasse pakkhipanaṃ phassapaccayatādassanameva “chahi ajjhattikāyatanehi [P 1.0238] chaḷārammaṇapaṭisaṃvedanaṃ ekantato chaphassahetukamevā”ti. Sañjāyanti etthāti adhikaraṇattho sañjāti-saddoti āha “sañjātiṭṭhāne”ti. Evaṃ samosaraṇasaddopi daṭṭhabbo. Āyatati ettha phalaṃ tadāyattavuttitāya, āyabhūtaṃ vā attano phalaṃ tanoti pavattetīti āyatanaṃ, kāraṇaṃ. Rukkhagacchasamūhe araññavohāro araññameva araññāyatananti āha “paṇṇattimatte”ti. Atthattayepīti pi-saddena avuttatthasampiṇḍanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, tena ākāranivāsādhiṭṭhānatthe saṅgaṇhāti. Hiraññāyatanaṃ suvaṇṇāyatanaṃ, vāsudevāyatanaṃ kammāyatananti ādīsu ākaranivāsādhiṭṭhānesu āyatanasaddo. Cakkhādīsu ca phassādayo ākiṇṇā, tāni ca nesaṃ nivāso, adhiṭṭhānañca nissayapaccayabhāvatoti. Tiṇṇampi visayindriyaviññāṇānaṃ saṅgatibhāvena gahetabbo phassoti “saṅgatī”ti vutto. Tathā hi so “sannipātapaccupaṭṭhāno”ti vuccati. Iminā nayenāti vijjamānesupi aññesu sampayuttadhammesu yathā “cakkhuñca…pe… phasso”ti [M 1.0183] (ma. ni. 1.204; ma. ni. 3.421, 425, 426; saṃ. ni. 2.43-45; saṃ. ni. 4.60; kathā. 465) etasmiṃ sutte vedanāya padhānakāraṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ phassasīsena desanā katā, evamidhāpi brahmajāle “phassapaccayā vedanā”tiādinā phassaṃ ādiṃ katvā aparantapaṭiccasamuppādadīpanena paccayaparamparaṃ dassetuṃ “phassāyatanehi phussa phussā”ti phassamukhena vuttaṃ.

144. In the three sections below, because it is the topic, and above, because it will be said “they experience,” feeling is primary here; hence it is said, “he consolidates all feelings connected with views.” The term “consolidates” also shows the meaning of the particle 'pi' which occurs here and there in the phrase 'yepi te.' The inclusion of feeling within contact is simply the demonstration of contact as its condition, as in “the experiencing of six objects through the six internal sense bases is entirely caused by the six contacts.” The word 'sañjāti' has a locative sense, “they are born herein”; hence it is said, “at the place of arising.” Similarly, the word 'samosaraṇa' (convergence) should also be understood. The fruit extends (āyatati) here because its occurrence depends on that; or, being a source of income (āya-bhūtaṃ), it extends (tanoti) or causes to proceed (pavattetīti) its own fruit: thus āyatana (sphere), a cause. Just as a collection of trees and plants is designated 'wilderness' (arañña), so 'wilderness' itself is a 'sphere of wilderness' (araññāyatana); hence he says this is 'in a mere designation' (paṇṇattimatte). Even in the three meanings, the particle 'pi' should be understood as consolidating unstated meanings, thereby encompassing the senses of source, dwelling, and basis. In examples such as “the sphere of gold” (hiraññāyatana), “the sphere of gold” (suvaṇṇāyatana), “the sphere of Vāsudeva” (vāsudevāyatana), and “the sphere of action” (kammāyatana), the word 'āyatana' is used in the sense of source, dwelling, and basis. And in the case of the eye, etc., contact and other factors are pervasive, and these sense bases are their dwelling and basis due to their nature as a support condition. Contact should be understood as the coming together of the three—object, faculty, and consciousness—hence it is called “coming together” (saṅgati). For thus it is said to have “conjunction as its manifestation.” By this method, even though other associated phenomena exist, just as in the Sutta (M.I, 204; M.III, 421, 425, 426; S.II, 43–45; S.IV, 60; Kathāvatthu 465) beginning “the eye… contact,” the teaching was given with contact as the head to show its nature as the principal cause for feeling; so too here in the Brahmajāla, to show the sequence of conditions by explaining dependent origination concerning the future, it is said through the medium of contact, “having been touched again and again by the spheres of contact,” beginning with “feeling conditioned by contact,” etc.

Phasso arūpadhammopi samāno ekadesena ārammaṇe anallīyamānopi phusanākārena pavattati phusanto viya hotīti āha “phassova taṃ taṃ ārammaṇaṃ phusatī”ti, yena so “phusanalakkhaṇo, saṅghaṭṭanaraso”ti ca [P 1.0239] vuccati. “Phassāyatanehi phussa phussā”ti aphusanakiccānipi āyatanāni “mañcā ghosantī”tiādīsu viya nissitavohārena phusanakiccāni katvā dassitānīti āha “phasse upanikkhipitvā”ti, phassagatikāni katvā phassūpacāraṃ āropetvāti attho. Upacāro hi nāma vohāramattaṃ, na tena atthasiddhi hotīti āha “tasmā”tiādi.
