Contact, although it is a formless phenomenon and does not adhere to the object with a part, proceeds in the manner of touching, as if it touches; hence it is said, “Contact itself touches that very object,” whereby it is also called “having touching as its characteristic, having impacting as its function.” In the phrase “having been touched again and again by the spheres of contact,” the sense bases, which do not have the function of touching, are shown as having the function of touching by means of a dependent designation, just as in the saying “the beds are shouting,” etc.; hence it is said, “having placed them upon contact,” meaning having made them have contact as their destination, having superimposed the figurative usage of contact. For a figurative usage is merely a convention, and a real state is not established by it; hence it is said, “therefore,” etc.

Attano [V 1.0162] paccayabhūtānaṃ channaṃ phassānaṃ vasena cakkhusamphassajā yāva manosamphassajāti saṅkhepato chabbidhā vedanā, vitthārato pana aṭṭhasatapariyāyena aṭṭhasatabhedā. Rūpataṇhādibhedāyāti rūpataṇhā yāva dhammataṇhāti saṅkhepato chappabhedāya, vitthārato aṭṭhasatabhedāya. Upanissayakoṭiyāti upanissayasīsena. Kasmā panettha upanissayapaccayova uddhaṭo, nanu sukhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā ca taṇhāya ārammaṇamattaārammaṇādhipatiārammaṇūpanissayapakatūpanissayavasena catudhā paccayo, dukkhā ca ārammaṇamattapakatūpanissayavasena dvidhāti? Saccametaṃ, upanissaye eva pana taṃ sabbaṃ antogadhaṃ. Yuttaṃ tāva ārammaṇūpanissayassa upanissayasāmaññato upanissayena saṅgaho, ārammaṇamattaārammaṇādhipatīnaṃ pana kathanti? Tesampi ārammaṇasāmaññato ārammaṇūpanissayena saṅgahova kato, na pakatūpanissayenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Etadatthamevettha “upanissayakoṭiyā”ti vuttaṃ, na “upanissayenā”ti.

By way of the six contacts which are its conditions, feeling—born of eye-contact up to that born of mind-contact—is briefly sixfold; but in detail, it has 108 divisions by way of 108 modes. For craving, divided as craving for forms, etc., up to craving for mental phenomena, it is briefly of six kinds, and in detail of 108 kinds. “By way of the aspect of decisive support” (upanissayakoṭiyā) means “by the heading of decisive support” (upanissayasīsena). Why is only the decisive support condition extracted here? Is it not true that pleasant feeling and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling are a condition for craving in four ways—as simple object, object predominance, object decisive support, and natural decisive support—while painful feeling is a condition in two ways—as simple object and natural decisive support? This is true, but all that is included within decisive support itself. It is fitting, first, that object decisive support is included by decisive support due to the generality of decisive support. But how about simple object and object predominance? It should be understood that these too are included by object decisive support due to the generality of object, not by natural decisive support. For this very reason it is stated here as “by way of the aspect of decisive support,” not “by decisive support.”

Catubbidhassāti kāmupādānaṃ yāva attavādupādānanti catubbidhassa. Nanu ca taṇhāva kāmupādānanti? Saccametaṃ. Tattha dubbalā [P 1.0240] taṇhā taṇhāva, balavatī [M 1.0184] taṇhā kāmupādānaṃ. Atha vā appattavisayapatthanā taṇhā tamasi corānaṃ karapasāraṇaṃ viya. Sampattavisayaggahaṇaṃ upādānaṃ, corānaṃ karappattadhanaggahaṇaṃ viya. Appicchatāpaṭipakkhā taṇhā, santosapaṭipakkhā upādānaṃ. Pariyesanadukkhamūlaṃ taṇhā, ārakkhadukkhamūlaṃ upādānanti ayametesaṃ viseso. Upādānassāti asahajātassa upādānassa upanissayakoṭiyā, itarassa sahajātakoṭiyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tattha anantarassa anantarasamanantaraanantarūpanissayanatthivigatāsevanapaccayehi, anānantarassa upanissayena, ārammaṇabhūtā pana ārammaṇādhipatiārammaṇūpanissayehi, ārammaṇamatteneva vāti taṃ sabbaṃ upanissayeneva gahetvā “upanissayakoṭiyā”ti vuttaṃ. Yasmā ca taṇhāya rūpādīni assādetvā kāmesu pātabyataṃ āpajjati, tasmā taṇhā kāmupādānassa upanissayo. Tathā rūpādibhedeva sammūḷho “natthi dinna”ntiādinā (dī. ni. 1.171; ma. ni. 1.445; ma. ni. 2.94, 95, 225; ma. ni. 3.91, 116, 136; saṃ. ni. 3.210; dha. sa. 1221; vibha. 938) micchādassanaṃ, saṃsārato muccitukāmo asuddhimagge suddhimaggaparāmasanaṃ, khandhesu attattaniyagāhabhūtaṃ sakkāyadassanaṃ gaṇhāti, tasmā itaresampi taṇhā upanissayoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sahajātassa pana sahajātaaññamaññanissayasampayuttaatthiavigatahetuvasena taṇhā paccayo hoti. Taṃ sabbaṃ sandhāya “sahajātakoṭiyā”ti vuttaṃ.

“Of the fourfold” is meant of the fourfold clinging, from clinging to sensual pleasures up to clinging to the doctrine of self. But is not craving itself clinging to sensual pleasures? This is true. Here, weak craving is just craving, while strong craving is clinging to sensual pleasures. Alternatively, craving is the longing for an unattained object, like thieves stretching out their hands in the dark. Clinging is the grasping of an attained object, like thieves seizing wealth that has come into their hands. Craving is the opposite of having few wishes; clinging is the opposite of contentment. Craving is the root of the suffering of seeking; clinging is the root of the suffering of guarding—this is the distinction between them. “For clinging” it should be understood that for non-conascent clinging it is by way of the aspect of decisive support, and for the other (conascent clinging) it is by way of the aspect of conascence. Therein, for the immediately proximate, it is by way of the conditions of contiguity, immediate contiguity, immediate decisive support, absence, disappearance, and repetition; for the non-immediately proximate, it is by decisive support. But for that which has become an object, it is by object, object-predominance, object-decisive-support, or by simple object. All that, having been included by “decisive support,” is spoken of as “by way of the aspect of decisive support.” And because, through craving, one savors forms, etc., and falls into a state of being prone to sensual pleasures, craving is the decisive support for clinging to sensual pleasures. Similarly, being deluded by the diversity of forms, etc., one grasps wrong view such as “there is no fruit of giving,” etc.; desiring to be freed from saṃsāra, one misapprehends an impure path as a pure path; and one grasps the personality-view which is the grasping of self and what belongs to self in the aggregates. Therefore, craving should be understood as a decisive support for the other types as well. But for conascent clinging, craving is a condition by way of conascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, non-disappearance, and root. Referring to all that, it is said “by way of the aspect of conascence.”

Tathāti [V 1.0163] upanissayakoṭiyā ceva sahajātakoṭiyā cāti attho. Bhavassāti kammabhavassa ceva upapattibhavassa ca. Tattha cetanādisaṅkhā taṃ sabbaṃ bhavagāmikammaṃ kammabhavo, kāmabhavādiko navavidho upapattibhavo, tesaṃ upapattibhavassa catubbidhampi upādānaṃ upapattibhavakāraṇakammabhavakāraṇabhāvato[P 1.0241], tassa ca sahāyabhāvūpagamanato pakatūpanissayavasena paccayo hoti. Kammārammaṇakaraṇakāle pana kammasahajātakāmupādānaṃ upapattibhavassa ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo hoti. Kammabhavassa pana sahajātassa sahajātaṃ upādānaṃ sahajātaaññamaññanissayasampayuttaatthiavigatavasena ceva hetumaggavasena ca anekadhā paccayo hoti, asahajātassa anantarasamanantaraanantarūpanissayanatthivigatāsevanavasena, itarassa pakatūpanissayavasena, sammasanādikālesu ārammaṇavasena ca paccayo hoti. Tattha anantarādike [M 1.0185] upanissayapaccaye, sahajātādike sahajātapaccaye pakkhipitvā vuttaṃ “upanissayakoṭiyā ceva sahajātakoṭiyā cā”ti.

By 'thus' is meant by way of the aspect of decisive support and by way of the aspect of co-nascence. By 'of existence' is meant of kamma-existence and of rebirth-existence. Therein, kamma-existence is all that kamma leading to existence, designated as volition and so forth; rebirth-existence is the ninefold existence beginning with sensual existence. For rebirth-existence, the fourfold clinging is a condition by way of natural decisive support, due to its being a cause of the kamma-existence that is a cause for rebirth-existence, and due to its approaching the state of an aid to it. But at the time of making kamma its object, kamma-co-nascent clinging to sensual pleasures is a condition for rebirth-existence by way of object condition. But for co-nascent kamma-existence, co-nascent clinging is a condition in many ways: by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, non-disappearance, and also by way of root and path. For non-co-nascent kamma-existence, it is a condition by way of contiguity, immediate contiguity, immediate decisive support, absence, disappearance, and repetition; for the other, it is a condition by way of natural decisive support; and at times of reflection and so forth, it is a condition by way of object. Herein, having included contiguity and so forth under the decisive support condition, and co-nascence and so forth under the co-nascence condition, it is said: 'by way of the aspect of decisive support and by way of the aspect of co-nascence.'

Bhavo jātiyāti ettha bhavoti kammabhavo adhippeto. So hi jātiyā paccayo, na upapattibhavo. Upapattibhavo hi paṭhamābhinibbattā khandhā jātiyeva. Tena vuttaṃ “jātīti panettha savikārā pañcakkhandhā daṭṭhabbā”ti. Savikārāti ca nibbattivikārena savikārā, te ca atthato upapattibhavoyeva. Na hi tadeva tassa kāraṇaṃ bhavituṃ yuttanti. Kammabhavo ca upapattibhavassa kammapaccayena ceva upanissayapaccayena ca paccayo hotīti āha “bhavo jātiyā upanissayakoṭiyā paccayo”ti.

Here, in 'existence is a condition for birth,' by 'existence' is meant kamma-existence. For that is the condition for birth, not rebirth-existence. For rebirth-existence is simply the aggregates that first arise, which is birth itself. Therefore it is said: 'Here, birth should be understood as the five aggregates subject to change.' And 'subject to change' means subject to change by the modification of arising; and in essence, those are indeed rebirth-existence. For it is not reasonable for that same thing to be its own cause. And kamma-existence is a condition for rebirth-existence by way of kamma condition and also by way of decisive support condition; hence it is said, 'existence is a condition for birth by way of the aspect of decisive support.'

Yasmā ca sati jātiyā jarāmaraṇaṃ, jarāmaraṇādinā phuṭṭhassa bālassa sokādayo ca sambhavanti, nāsati, tasmā “jāti…pe… paccayo hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Sahajātūpanissayasīsena paccayavicāraṇāya dassitattā, aṅgavicāraṇāya ca anāmaṭṭhattā āha “ayamettha saṅkhepo”ti. Mahāvisayattā paṭiccasamuppādavicāraṇāya sā niravasesā kuto laddhabbāti āha “vitthārato”tiādi. Ekadesena cettha kathitassa paṭiccasamuppādassa tathā kathane saddhiṃ udāharaṇena kāraṇaṃ dassento “bhagavā hī”tiādimāha. Tattha koṭi na paññāyatīti asukassa nāma sammāsambuddhassa, cakkavattino vā kāle avijjā uppannā, na tato pubbeti avijjāya ādimariyādā appaṭihatassa mama sabbaññutaññāṇassāpi na paññāyati avijjamānattāyevāti attho. Ayaṃ paccayo idappaccayo, tasmā idappaccayā, imasmā kāraṇā [P 1.0242] āsavapaccayāti attho. Bhavataṇhāyāti bhavasaṃyojanabhūtāya taṇhāya. Bhavadiṭṭhiyāti [V 1.0164] sassatadiṭṭhiyā. “Ito ettha etto idhā”ti apariyantaṃ aparāparuppattiṃ dasseti.

Because when there is birth, aging-and-death occurs, and for the fool afflicted by aging-and-death and so forth, sorrow and the like arise, but not when there is no birth; therefore it is said, 'birth... is a condition.' Since the examination of conditions is shown under the heading of co-nascent decisive support, and the examination of the factors is not touched upon, it is said, 'Here, this is the summary.' Due to the vast scope of the examination of dependent origination, how could it be obtained in its entirety? Therefore, it is said, 'in detail,' and so on. Showing the reason, with an example, for this partial explanation of dependent origination, it is said, 'For the Blessed One,' and so on. Here, 'the beginning is not discerned' means: that ignorance arose at the time of a certain Perfectly Enlightened One or wheel-turning monarch, and not before that—such a starting point of ignorance is not discerned even by my unobstructed omniscient knowledge, simply because it does not exist. 'This condition is a this-condition'; therefore, 'from this conditionality' means 'from this cause, it is conditioned by the taints.' 'Craving for existence' means craving that has become a fetter of existence. 'View of existence' means the eternalist view. 'Ito ettha etto idhā' indicates endless successive arising.

Vivaṭṭakathādivaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Unrolling, and so forth.

145. “Vedanānaṃ samudaya”ntiādipāḷi vedanākammaṭṭhānanti daṭṭhabbā. Tanti “phassasamudayā phassanirodhā”ti vuttaphassaṭṭhānaṃ. Āhāroti kabaḷīkāro āhāro veditabbo. So hi “kabaḷīkāro āhāro imassa [M 1.0186] kāyassa āhārapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.paccayaniddesa 429) vacanato kammasamuṭṭhānānampi upatthambhakapaccayo hotiyeva. Yadipi sotāpannādayo yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti, ukkaṃsagativijānanavasena pana desanā arahattanikūṭena niṭṭhāpitā. Ettha ca “yato kho bhikkhave bhikkhu…pe… yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”ti etena dhammassa niyyānikabhāvena saddhiṃ saṅghassa suppaṭipattiṃ dasseti. Teneva hi aṭṭhakathāyamettha “ko evaṃ jānātīti? Khīṇāsavo jānāti, yāva āraddhavipassako jānātī”ti paripuṇṇaṃ katvā bhikkhusaṅgho dassito, tena yaṃ vuttaṃ “bhikkhusaṅghavasenapi dīpetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti, (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.8) taṃ yathārutavaseneva dīpitaṃ hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

145. The Pāli text beginning with 'the arising of feelings' should be understood as the meditation subject of feelings. 'The text' refers to the section on contact, spoken of as: 'from the arising of contact, from the cessation of contact.' 'Food' should be understood as edible food. For it is said: 'Edible food is a condition for this body by way of the food condition' (Paṭṭhāna 1, Paccayaniddesa 429), and thus it also serves as a supporting condition even for kamma-originated phenomena. Although stream-enterers and others understand things as they truly are, the teaching is presented by way of understanding the highest destination, culminating with the peak of Arahantship. Here, the phrase 'when, monks, a monk... understands as it really is' demonstrates the liberating nature of the Dhamma along with the excellent practice of the Saṅgha. For this reason, in the commentary here, the community of monks is shown in its completeness by stating: 'Who knows thus? One whose taints are destroyed knows, down to one who has undertaken insight meditation.' Thus, what was said—'it is fitting to illuminate even by way of the Saṅgha' (Dīgha Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 1.8)—should be understood as having been illuminated according to the traditional text.

146. Anto jālassāti antojālaṃ, antojāle katāti antojālīkatā. Apāyūpapattivasena adho osīdanaṃ, sampattibhavavasena uddhaṃ uggamanaṃ. Tathā parittabhūmimahaggatabhūmivasena, olīnatā’tidhāvanavasena, pubbantānudiṭṭhiaparantānudiṭṭhivasena ca yathākkamaṃ adho osīdanaṃ uddhaṃ uggamanaṃ yojetabbaṃ. “Dasasahassilokadhātū”ti [P 1.0243] jātikhettaṃ sandhāyāha.

146. 'Within the net' (`anto jālassa`) means `antojālaṃ`; 'made to be within the net' (`antojāle katā`) means `antojālīkatā`. Sinking downwards is by way of arising in the woeful states; rising upwards is by way of fortunate existences. Likewise, sinking downwards and rising upwards should be connected respectively with: limited realms and exalted realms; sluggishness and agitation; and views concerning the past and views concerning the future. 'Ten-thousand world-system' is said in reference to the birth-field.

147. Apaṇṇattikabhāvanti dharamānakapaṇṇattiyā apaṇṇattikabhāvaṃ. Atītabhāvena pana tathā paṇṇatti yāva sāsanantaradhānā, tato uddhampi aññabuddhuppādesu vattati eva. Tathā hi vakkhati “vohāramattameva bhavissatī”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.147). Kāyoti attabhāvo, yo rūpārūpadhammasamūho. Evaṃ hissa ambarukkhasadisatā, tadavayavānañca rūpakkhandhacakkhādīnaṃ ambapakkasadisatā yujjatīti. Ettha ca vaṇṭacchede vaṇṭūpanibandhānaṃ ambapakkānaṃ ambarukkhato vicchedo viya bhavanettichede tadupanibandhānaṃ rūpakkhandhādīnaṃ santānato vicchedoti ettāvatā opammaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

147. 'The state of being without designation' (`apaṇṇattikabhāva`) means the state of being without a current designation. By way of the past, however, such a designation persists until the disappearance of the Dispensation, and even after that it continues to exist during the arising of other Buddhas. For it will be said: 'It will be merely a matter of convention.' 'Body' (`kāya`) means individual existence, which is the collection of material and immaterial phenomena. Thus, its likeness to a mango tree is fitting, as is the likeness of its components—such as the form aggregate, the eye, and so forth—to ripe mango fruits. Here, the simile should be understood to this extent: just as when the stalk is cut, the ripe mangoes attached to the stalk are severed from the mango tree, so too when the guide to existence is cut, the form aggregate and so forth which are attached to it are severed from the continuum.

148. Dhammapariyāyeti [V 1.0165] pāḷiyaṃ. Idhatthoti diṭṭhadhammahitaṃ. Paratthoti samparāyahitaṃ. Saṅgāmaṃ vijināti etenāti saṅgāmavijayo. Atthasampattiyā atthajālaṃ. Byañjanasampattiyā, sīlādianavajjadhammaniddesato ca dhammajālaṃ. Seṭṭhaṭṭhena brahmabhūtānaṃ maggaphalanibbānānaṃ vibhattattā brahmajālaṃ. Diṭṭhivivecanamukhena suññatāpakāsanena sammādiṭṭhiyā vibhāvitattā diṭṭhijālaṃ. Titthiyavādanimmaddanūpāyattā anuttaro saṅgāmavijayoti evampettha yojanā veditabbā.

148. 'Discourse on the Dhamma' (`dhammapariyāya`) is the reading in the Pāḷi. 'Benefit here' (`idhattha`) means welfare in this visible life. 'Benefit hereafter' (`parattha`) means welfare in the life to come. 'One conquers the battle with this' (`saṅgāmaṃ vijināti etena`), therefore it is 'victory in battle' (`saṅgāmavijayo`). It is the 'net of meaning' (`atthajālaṃ`) due to the accomplishment of meaning. It is the 'net of Dhamma' (`dhammajālaṃ`) due to the accomplishment of expression and the exposition of blameless qualities like virtue, etc. It is the 'Brahma-net' (`brahmajālaṃ`) because the path, fruition, and Nibbāna, which are supreme (`brahmabhūtānaṃ`), are analyzed. It is the 'net of views' (`diṭṭhijālaṃ`) because right view is clarified through the portal of discriminating views by way of revealing emptiness. It is the 'unsurpassed victory in battle' (`anuttaro saṅgāmavijayo`) because it is a means for crushing the doctrines of the sectarians. Thus the application here should be understood.

149. Attamanāti [M 1.0187] pītiyā gahitacittā. Tenevāha “buddhagatāyā”tiādi. Yathā pana anattamanā attano anatthacaratāya paramanā verimanā nāma honti. Yathāha “diso disa”nti (dha. pa. 42; udā. 33) gāthā, na evaṃ attamanā. Ime pana attano atthacaratāya [P 1.0244] sakamanā hontīti āha “attamanāti sakamanā”ti. Atha vā attamanāti samattamanā, imāya desanāya paripuṇṇamanasaṅkappāti attho. Abhinandatīti taṇhāyatīti atthoti āha “taṇhāyampi āgato”ti. Anekatthattā dhātūnaṃ abhinandantīti upagacchanti sevantīti atthoti āha “upagamanepi āgato”ti. Tathā abhinandantīti sampaṭicchantīti atthoti āha “sampaṭicchanepi āgato”ti. “Abhinanditvā”ti iminā padena vuttoyeva attho “anumoditvā”ti iminā pakāsīyatīti abhinandanasaddo idha anumodanasaddatthoti āha “anumodanepi āgato”ti. “Katamañca taṃ bhikkhave”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.7) tattha tattha pavattāya kathetukamyatāpucchāya vissajjanavasena pavattattā idaṃ suttaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ hoti. Yasmā pana pucchāvissajjanavasena pavattampi sagāthakaṃ suttaṃ geyyaṃ nāma hoti, niggāthakattameva pana aṅganti gāthārahitaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “niggāthakattā hi idaṃ veyyākaraṇanti vutta”nti.

149. 'Attamanā' means those whose minds are seized by joy. Hence it is said, 'with joy related to the Buddha,' and so on. Just as those who are displeased (anattamanā) are called 'verimanā' because they act against their own welfare, as stated in the verse, 'Diso disa' (Dhp. 42; Ud. 33), it is not so for those who are pleased (attamanā). These, however, are called 'sakamanā' because they act for their own welfare—hence it is said, 'attamanā means sakamanā.' Alternatively, 'attamanā' means 'samattamanā' (fulfilled in mind), the meaning being that their mental resolve is completely fulfilled by this teaching. 'Abhinandati' means 'to crave'—hence it is said, 'it also occurs in the sense of craving.' Because verbal roots have various meanings, 'abhinandanti' also means 'they approach and associate with'—hence it is said, 'it also occurs in the sense of approaching.' Similarly, 'abhinandanti' means 'to accept'—hence it is said, 'it also occurs in the sense of accepting.' The meaning expressed by the word 'abhinanditvā' is the same as that clarified by 'anumoditvā'—hence the word 'abhinandana' here has the meaning of 'anumodana,' and it is said, 'it also occurs in the sense of rejoicing.' Since this proceeds as an answer to a question posed in various contexts out of a desire to explain, as in 'And what, monks...' (DN 1.7) and so on, this discourse is an exposition (veyyākaraṇa). However, because a discourse that proceeds through questions and answers and contains verses is called 'geyya,' while an exposition is without verses, this being its characteristic feature, it is said, 'Since it lacks verses, this is called an exposition.'

Aparesupīti ettha pisaddena pāramiparicayampi saṅgaṇhāti. Vuttañhi buddhavaṃse –

Regarding 'aparesupi,' the particle 'pi' here also includes the accumulation of perfections. For it was said in the Buddhavamsa:

“Ime dhamme sammasato, sabhāvasarasalakkhaṇe;

Dhammatejena vasudhā, dasasahassī pakampathā”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.166);

'While rightly understanding these phenomena, with their own-being, specific essence, and characteristics, by the power of the Dhamma, the ten-thousandfold world-system trembled.'

Vīriyabalenāti mahābhinikkhamane cakkavattisiripariccāgahetubhūtavīriyappabhāvena, bodhimaṇḍūpasaṅkamane “kāmaṃ taco ca nhāru ca, aṭṭhi ca avasissatū”tiādinā (ma. ni. 2.184; saṃ. ni. 2.22; mahāni. 196) vuttacaturaṅgasamannāgatavīriyānubhāvena. Acchariyavegābhihatāti vimhayāvahakiriyānubhāvaghaṭṭitā[P 1.0245]. Paṃsukūladhovane keci “puññatejenā”ti vadanti[V 1.0166], acchariyavegābhihatāti yuttaṃ viya dissati, vessantarajātake pāramiparipūraṇapuññatejena anekakkhattuṃ kampitattā “akālakampanenā”ti vuttaṃ. Sādhukāradānavasena akampittha [M 1.0188] yathā taṃ dhammacakkappavattane (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 13; paṭi. ma. 2.30). Saṅgītikālādīsupi sādhukāradānavasena akampitthāti veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ tāvettha aṭṭhakathāya līnatthavaṇṇanā.

By the power of energy: by the influence of the energy that was the cause for the great renunciation, the relinquishing of the glory of a wheel-turning monarch; and, when approaching the seat of enlightenment, by the influence of the energy endowed with four factors as stated in the phrase, 'Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain...' (Majjhima Nikāya 2.184; Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.22; Mahāniddesa 196). Struck by a marvelous force: agitated by the influence of an astonishing action. Regarding the washing of the rag-robes, some say it was 'by the power of merit,' but 'struck by a marvelous force' seems more appropriate; in the Vessantara Jātaka, it is said to be an 'untimely quake' because the earth shook many times due to the power of merit from the fulfillment of perfections. It shook in response to giving approval, as happened at the turning of the Dhamma wheel (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.1081; Mahāvagga 13; Paṭisambhidāmagga 2.30). It should also be understood that during the times of the councils and such, the earth shook in response to giving approval. This, indeed, is the explanation of the hidden meaning in the commentary here.

Pakaraṇanayavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Method of the Treatise

Ayaṃ pana pakaraṇanayena pāḷiyā atthavaṇṇanā – sā panāyaṃ atthavaṇṇanā yasmā desanāya samuṭṭhānappayojanabhājanesu piṇḍatthesu ca niddhāritesu sukarā hoti suviññeyyā ca, tasmā suttadesanāya samuṭṭhānādīni paṭhamaṃ niddhārayissāma. Tattha samuṭṭhānaṃ tāva vuttaṃ “vaṇṇāvaṇṇabhaṇana”nti. Apica nindāpasaṃsāsu vineyyāghātānandādibhāvānāpatti, tattha ca ādīnavadassanaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ. Tathā nindāpasaṃsāsu paṭipajjanakkamassa, pasaṃsāvisayassa khuddakādivasena anekavidhassa sīlassa, sabbaññutaññāṇassa sassatādidiṭṭhiṭṭhānesu tatuttari ca appaṭihatacāratāya, tathāgatassa ca katthaci apariyāpannatāya anavabodho samuṭṭhānaṃ.

This, however, is the exposition of the meaning of the Pāli text according to the method of the treatise. Since this exposition of the meaning becomes easy and well-understood when the origins, purposes, recipients of the teaching, and summary meanings have been determined, we shall therefore first determine the origins and so on of the sutta's teaching. Herein, the origin is stated as 'the speaking of praise and blame.' Moreover, the non-occurrence of states such as hatred and joy in trainees in response to censure and praise, and therein, seeing the danger, is an origin. Likewise, the non-understanding of the order of practice regarding censure and praise; of virtue, the object of praise, which is of many kinds, such as minor and so on; of the knowledge of omniscience, due to its unobstructed range in the grounds of eternalism and other views and beyond; and of the Tathāgata's being unincluded in certain cases—these are the origins.

Vuttavipariyāyena payojanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Vineyyāghātānandādibhāvāpatti ādikañhi imaṃ desanaṃ payojetīti. Tathā kuhanalapanādinānāvidhamicchājīvaviddhaṃsanaṃ, dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhijālaviniveṭhanaṃ, diṭṭhisīsena paccayākāravibhāvanaṃ, chaphassāyatanavasena catusaccakammaṭṭhānaniddeso, sabbadiṭṭhigatānaṃ anavasesapariyādānaṃ, attano anupādāparinibbānadīpanañca payojanāni.

The purpose should be understood as the opposite of what has been stated. For the arising of states such as hatred and joy in trainees is what occasions this teaching. Likewise, the destruction of various wrong livelihoods such as deception and chatter; the disentanglement from the net of sixty-two views; the analysis of dependent origination with right view as the principal factor; the exposition of the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths by way of the six sense bases; the complete eradication of all wrong views; and the declaration of one’s own final Nibbāna without clinging—these are the purposes.

Vaṇṇāvaṇṇanimittaṃ anurodhavirodhavantacittā kuhanādivividhamicchājīvaniratā sassatādidiṭṭhipaṅkaṃ nimuggā, sīlakkhandhādīsu aparipūrakāritāya anavabuddhaguṇavisesañāṇā vineyyā imissā dhammadesanāya bhājanaṃ.

Those whose minds possess attachment and aversion based on the signs of praise and blame, who are devoted to various wrong livelihoods such as deception, who are sunk in the mire of eternalist and other views, and who, due to non-fulfillment in the aggregates of virtue and so on, have not understood the knowledge of special qualities—such trainees are the recipients of this Dhamma teaching.

Piṇḍatthā [P 1.0246] pana āghātādīnaṃ akaraṇīyatāvacanena paṭiññānurūpaṃ samaṇasaññāya niyojanaṃ, khantisoraccānuṭṭhānaṃ, brahmavihārabhāvanānuyogo, saddhāpaññāsamāyogo, satisampajaññādhiṭṭhānaṃ, paṭisaṅkhānabhāvanābalasiddhi, pariyuṭṭhānānusayappahānaṃ, ubhayahitapaṭipatti, lokadhammehi anupalepo ca dassitā honti. Tathā pāṇātipātādīhi paṭivirativacanena sīlavisuddhi [V 1.0167] dassitā, tāya ca hirottappasampatti, mettākaruṇāsamaṅgitā[M 1.0189], vītikkamappahānaṃ, tadaṅgapahānaṃ, duccaritasaṃkilesappahānaṃ, viratittayasiddhi, piyamanāpagarubhāvanīyatānipphatti, lābhasakkārasilokasamudāgamo, samathavipassanānaṃ adhiṭṭhānabhāvo, akusalamūlatanukaraṇaṃ, kusalamūlaropanaṃ, ubhayānatthadūrīkaraṇaṃ, parisāsu visāradatā, appamādavihāro,parehi duppadhaṃsiyatā, avippaṭisārādisamaṅgitā ca dassitā honti.

Moreover, the summary meanings shown are: by the statement of the non-doing of hatred and the like, the commitment to the perception of an ascetic in accordance with one's vow; the practice of patience and gentleness; engagement in the cultivation of the divine abodes; the combination of faith and wisdom; the establishment of mindfulness and clear comprehension; the accomplishment of strength through reflective cultivation; the abandonment of obsessional and underlying defilements; the practice beneficial to both oneself and others; and being unsullied by worldly conditions. Likewise, by the statement of refraining from killing living beings and so on, the purification of virtue is shown. Through this are also shown: the attainment of moral shame and fear of wrongdoing; the possession of loving-kindness and compassion; the abandonment of transgression; abandonment by substitution; the abandonment of misconduct and defilement; the accomplishment of the threefold abstinence; the attainment of being dear, agreeable, respected, and venerable; the arising of gain, honor, and fame; the state of being a foundation for serenity and insight; the attenuation of unwholesome roots; the planting of wholesome roots; the removal of what is disadvantageous to both; confidence in assemblies; dwelling in heedfulness; being difficult to overcome by others; and the possession of non-remorse and the like.

“Gambhīrā”tiādivacanehi gambhīradhammavibhāvanaṃ, alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhatā, kappānaṃ asaṅkhyeyyenāpi dullabhapātubhāvatā, sukhumenapi ñāṇena paccakkhato paṭivijjhituṃ asakkuṇeyyatā, dhammanvayasaṅkhātena anumānañāṇenāpi duradhigamanīyatā, passaddhasabbadarathatā, santadhammavibhāvanaṃ, sobhanapariyosānatā, atittikarabhāvo, padhānabhāvappatti, yathābhūtañāṇagocaratā, sukhumasabhāvatā, mahāpaññāvibhāvanā ca dassitā honti. Diṭṭhidīpakapadehi samāsato sassatucchedadiṭṭhiyo pakāsitāti olīnatātidhāvanavibhāvanaṃ, upāyavinibaddhaniddeso, micchābhinivesakittanaṃ, kummaggapaṭipattiyā pakāsanā, vipariyesaggāhapaññāpanaṃ, parāmāsapariggaho, pubbantāparantānudiṭṭhipatiṭṭhāpanaṃ, bhavavibhavadiṭṭhivibhāgo, taṇhāvijjāpavatti, antavānantavādiṭṭhiniddeso, antadvayāvatāraṇaṃ, āsavoghayogakilesaganthasaṃyojanūpādānavisesavibhajjanañca dassitāni honti. Tathā “vedanānaṃ samudaya”ntiādivacanehi catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ anubodhapaṭivedhasiddhi, vikkhambhanasamucchedappahānaṃ[P 1.0247], taṇhāvijjāvigamo, saddhammaṭṭhitinimittapariggaho, āgamādhigamasampatti, ubhayahitapaṭipatti, tividhapaññāpariggaho, satisampajaññānuṭṭhānaṃ, saddhāpaññāsamāyogo, sammāvīriyasamathānuyojanaṃ, samathavipassanānipphatti ca dassitā honti.

“The profound” and similar terms indicate the profound analysis of the Dhamma, its unattainability by ordinary means, the rarity of its appearance even over countless eons, the inability to directly comprehend it even with subtle knowledge, the difficulty of grasping it even through inferential knowledge characterized by logical consistency, the pacification of all disturbances, the serene analysis of the Dhamma, the beauty of its culmination, its insatiable nature, the attainment of the state of foremostness, the domain of knowledge as it actually is, the subtlety of its nature, and the manifestation of great wisdom. In the expressions that illuminate views, the eternalist and annihilationist views are briefly revealed, showing the analysis of sluggishness and excessive haste, the precise instruction bound by means, the declaration of wrong adherence, the exposition of wrong paths, the making known of inverted perceptions, the grasp of misapprehension, the establishing of views about the past and future, the distinction between views of being and non-being, the arising of craving and ignorance, the designation of views regarding finitude and infinitude, the descent into the two extremes, and the detailed classification of cankers, floods, yokes, defilements, ties, fetters, and clingings. Likewise, in the phrase “the origin of feelings” and similar statements, the accomplishment of understanding and penetration of the Four Noble Truths, abandoning by way of suppression and eradication, the cessation of craving and ignorance, the comprehension of the sign of the true Dhamma's stability, the achievement of learning and direct knowledge, practice beneficial to both, the acquisition of the three kinds of wisdom, the practice of mindfulness and clear comprehension, the union of faith and wisdom, the pursuit of right effort and tranquility, and the attainment of serenity and insight are all indicated.

“Ajānataṃ apassata”nti avijjāsiddhi, “taṇhāgatānaṃ paritassitavipphanditanti taṇhāsiddhi, tadubhayena ca nīvaraṇasaṃyojanadvayasiddhi, anamataggasaṃsāravaṭṭānucchedo, pubbantāharaṇaaparantapaṭisandhānāni, atītapaccuppannakālavasena hetuvibhāgo, avijjātaṇhānaṃ aññamaññānativattanaṭṭhena aññamaññūpakāritā, paññāvimutticetovimuttīnaṃ paṭipakkhaniddeso ca dassitā honti. “Tadapi phassapaccayā”ti sassatādipaññāpanassa paccayādhīnavuttitākathanena [M 1.0190] dhammānaṃ niccatāpaṭisedho, aniccatāpatiṭṭhāpanaṃ, paramatthato kārakādipaṭikkhepo, evaṃdhammatādiniddeso, suññatāpakāsanaṃ, samattaniyāmapaccayalakkhaṇavibhāvanañca dassitāni honti.

“Not knowing, not seeing” establishes ignorance; “those overcome by craving tremble and thrash about” establishes craving; and through both, the establishment of the twofold hindrance and fetter, the uninterrupted round of beginningless wandering in saṃsāra, the linking of the past to the future, the division of causes according to past and present time, the mutual support of ignorance and craving through their not transcending each other, and the pointing out of wisdom-deliverance and mind-deliverance as their opposites are shown. “That too is conditioned by contact” refutes the imputation of eternalism and similar views by stating the dependent mode of operation, denies the permanence of phenomena, establishes impermanence, rejects a doer in the ultimate sense, indicates suchness, reveals emptiness, and illustrates the characteristics of completeness, necessity, and the nature of conditionality—all these are shown.

“Ucchinnabhavanettiko”tiādinā [V 1.0168] bhagavato pahānasampatti, vijjādhimutti, vasībhāvo, sikkhattayanipphatti, nibbānadhātudvayavibhāgo, caturadhiṭṭhānaparipūraṇaṃ, bhavayoniādīsu apariyāpannatā ca dassitā honti. Sakalena pana suttapadena iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu bhagavato tādibhāvo, tattha ca paresaṃ patiṭṭhāpanaṃ, kusaladhammānaṃ ādibhūtadhammadvayassa niddeso, sikkhattayūpadeso, attantapādipuggalacatukkasiddhi, kaṇhākaṇhavipākādikammacatukkavibhāgo, caturappamaññāvisayaniddeso, samudayādipañcakassa yathābhūtāvabodho, chasāraṇīyadhammavibhāvanā[P 1.0248], dasanāthakaradhammapatiṭṭhāpanti evamādayo niddhāretabbā.

“The one who has cut off the guide to becoming”—through such statements, the Blessed One's accomplishment in abandoning, his release through knowledge, his mastery, the perfection of the threefold training, the distinction between the two Nibbāna elements, the complete fulfillment of the four determinations, and his non-inclusion in the womb of existence and other states are shown. Moreover, through the entire sutta, the Blessed One's equanimity toward the desirable and undesirable is revealed, along with his establishment of others in that state. The indication of the two fundamental wholesome qualities, the instruction in the threefold training, the attainment of the four types of individuals beginning with the self-mortifier, the analysis of the fourfold kamma with its dark and bright results, the indication of the sphere of the four immeasurables, the true understanding of the five aggregates and their origination, the elucidation of the six qualities conducive to cordiality, and the establishment of the ten grounds for protection—these and other points should be ascertained.

Soḷasahāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Sixteen Modes

Desanāhāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Mode of Teaching

Tattha “attā, loko”ti ca diṭṭhiyā adhiṭṭhānabhāvena, vedanāphassāyatanādimukhena ca gahitesu pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu taṇhāvajjā pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhasaccaṃ. Taṇhā samudayasaccaṃ. Sā pana paritassanāggahaṇena “taṇhāgatāna”nti, “vedanāpaccayā taṇhā”ti ca sarūpeneva samudayaggahaṇena, bhavanettiggahaṇena ca pāḷiyaṃ gahitāva. Ayaṃ tāva suttantanayo. Abhidhammanayena pana āghātānandādivacanehi, ātappādipadehi, cittappadosavacanena, sabbadiṭṭhidīpakapadehi, kusalākusalaggahaṇena, bhavaggahaṇena, sokādiggahaṇena, tattha tattha samudayaggahaṇena cāti saṅkhepato sabbalokiyakusalākusaladhammavibhāvanapadehi gahitā kammakilesā samudayasaccaṃ. Ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ. Tassa tattha tattha vedanānaṃ atthaṅgamanissaraṇapariyāyehi, paccattaṃ nibbutivacanena, anupādāvimuttivacanena ca pāḷiyaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Nirodhapajānanā paṭipadā maggasaccaṃ. Tassāpi tattha tattha vedanānaṃ samudayādiyathābhūtavedanāpadesena, channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ samudayādiyathābhūtapajānanapariyāyena, bhavanettiyā ucchedapariyāyena ca gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tattha samudayena assādo, dukkhena ādīnavo, magganirodhehi [M 1.0191] nissaraṇanti evaṃ catusaccavasena, yāni pāḷiyaṃ (netti. 9) sarūpeneva āgatāni assādādīnavanissaraṇāni, tesañca vasena idha assādādayo veditabbā. Vineyyānantādibhāvāpattiādikaṃ yathāvuttavibhāgaṃ payojanameva phalaṃ. Āghātādīnaṃ akaraṇīyatā, āghātādiphalassa ca anaññasantānabhāvitā, nindāpasaṃsāsu yathāsabhāvapaṭijānananibbeṭhanāti evaṃ taṃtaṃpayojanādhigamahetu upāyo. Āghātādīnaṃ [P 1.0249] karaṇapaṭisedhanādiapadesena dhammarājassa āṇatti veditabbāti ayaṃ desanāhāro.

Here, the five aggregates subject to clinging are taken up as the basis for the view of "self, world," and by way of feeling, contact, sense bases, etc. These five aggregates subject to clinging, excluding craving, constitute the truth of suffering. Craving is the truth of origin. This craving is grasped in the texts by grasping agitation, by expressions like "those gone to craving (taṇhāgatāna)," "craving conditioned by feeling," by grasping origin in its own form, and by grasping the guide to becoming. This is the Suttanta method. In the Abhidhamma method, however, kamma and defilements are the truth of origin, grasped concisely by terms explaining all worldly wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, such as expressions of resentment and delight, terms like ardour, expressions of mental corruption, terms illuminating all views, the grasping of wholesome and unwholesome states, the grasping of becoming, the grasping of sorrow, etc., and by grasping origin in various places. The non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation. Its grasping in the texts is to be understood through phrases about the passing away and escape from feelings, the expression of personal extinguishment, and the expression of liberation without clinging. The practice which is the understanding of cessation is the truth of the path. Its grasping is also to be understood through statements about the true knowledge of the origin, etc., of feelings, by way of the true knowledge of the origin, etc., of the six sense bases, and by way of the cutting off of the guide to becoming. Here, by way of the four truths, gratification is seen in the origin, danger in suffering, and escape in the path and cessation. These gratification, danger, and escape, which appear in the texts (Netti. 9) in their own form, should be understood accordingly. The purpose itself is the fruit, which, according to the aforementioned division, is the attainment of the final state and so on by those to be disciplined. The means for achieving that specific purpose is the non-doability of resentment, etc., the non-occurrence of the fruit of resentment, etc., in another's continuum, and the explanation of blame and praise by recognizing their true nature. The command of the King of Dhamma, given by way of prohibiting the doing of resentment, etc., should be understood. This is the Mode of Teaching.

Vicayahāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Mode of Investigation

Kappanābhāvepi [V 1.0169] vohāravasena, anuvādavasena ca “mama”nti vuttaṃ, niyamābhāvato vikappanatthaṃ vāggahaṇaṃ kataṃ, guṇasamaṅgitāya, abhimukhīkaraṇāya ca “bhikkhave”ti āmantanaṃ. Aññabhāvato, paṭiviruddhabhāvato ca “pare”ti vuttaṃ, vaṇṇapaṭipakkhato, avaṇṇanīyato ca “avaṇṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Byattivasena, vitthāravasena ca “bhāseyyu”nti vuttaṃ, dhāraṇabhāvato, adhammapaṭipakkhato ca “dhammassā”ti vuttaṃ, diṭṭhisīlehi saṃhatabhāvato, kilesānaṃ saṅghātakaraṇato ca “saṅghassā”ti vuttaṃ. Vuttapaṭiniddesato, vacanupanyāsanato ca “tatrā”ti vuttaṃ, sammukhabhāvato, puthubhāvato ca “tumhehī”ti vuttaṃ. Cittassa hananato, ārammaṇābhighātato ca “āghāto”ti vuttaṃ, ārammaṇe saṅkocavuttiyā, atuṭṭhākāratāya ca “appaccayo”ti vuttaṃ, ārammaṇacintanato, nissayato ca “cetaso”ti vuttaṃ, atthāsādhanato, anu anu “anatthasādhanato” ca “anabhiraddhī”ti vuttaṃ, kāraṇānarahattā, satthusāsane ṭhitehi kātuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā ca “na karaṇīyā”ti vuttanti. Iminā nayena sabbapadesu vinicchayo kātabbo. Iti anupadavicayato vicayo hāro ativitthārabhayena, sakkā ca aṭṭhakathaṃ tassā līnatthavaṇṇanañca anugantvā ayamattho viññunā vibhāvetunti na vitthārayimha.

Even in the absence of a fixed designation, the term "mine" is used conventionally and by way of reference. Due to the lack of a fixed rule, the word 'or' is employed for the purpose of differentiation. The address "bhikkhus" is used for being endowed with qualities and for addressing them directly. The term "others" is used due to being of another nature and of an opposite nature. The term "blame" is used because it is the opposite of praise and not worthy of praise. The term "would speak" is used because of being clear and detailed. The term "of the Dhamma" is used due to its sustaining nature and being the opposite of non-Dhamma. The term "of the Saṅgha" is used because of being united in view and virtue, and because it causes the destruction of defilements. The term "therein" is used by way of re-explaining what has been said and by way of introducing the statement. The term "by you" is used due to being face-to-face and being numerous. The term "resentment" is used because it harms the mind and strikes its object. The term "displeasure" is used due to the mind shrinking from the object and a state of dissatisfaction. The term "of the mind" is used because of thinking of the object and dependence. The term "discontent" is used because it accomplishes no good and repeatedly accomplishes non-benefit. The term "should not be done" is said because it is unfit to be done and because those established in the Teacher’s instruction are unable to do it. In this way, the analysis should be applied to all passages. Thus, the mode of investigation by word-by-word analysis is not elaborated by us due to fear of excessive elaboration, though it is possible for a discerning person to elucidate this meaning by following the commentary and its explanation of hidden meanings.

Yuttihāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Mode of Reasoning

Sabbena [M 1.0192] sabbaṃ āghātādīnaṃ akaraṇaṃ tādibhāvāya saṃvattatīti yujjati iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu samappavattisabbhāvato. Yasmiṃ santāne āghātādayo uppannā, tannimittako antarāyo tasseva sampattivibandhāya saṃvattatīti [P 1.0250] yujjati. Kasmā? Santānantaresu asaṅkamanato. Cittaṃ abhibhavitvā uppannā āghātādayo subhāsitādisallakkhaṇepi asamatthatāya saṃvattantīti yujjati sakodhalobhānaṃ andhatamasabbhāvato. Pāṇātipātādidussīlyato veramaṇi sabbasattānaṃ pāmojjapāsaṃsabhāvāya saṃvattatīti yujjati. Sīlasampattiyā hi mahato kittisaddassa abbhuggamo hotīti. Gambhīratādivisesayuttena guṇena tathāgatassa vaṇṇanā ekadesabhūtāpi sakalasabbaññuguṇaggahaṇāya saṃvattatīti yujjati anaññasādhāraṇattā. Tajjāayonisomanasikāraparikkhatāni adhigamatakkanāni sassatavādādiabhinivesāya saṃvattantīti yujjati kappanājālassa asamugghāṭitattā. Vedanādīnavānavabodhena vedanāya taṇhā pavaḍḍhatīti yujjati assādānupassanāsabbhāvato. Sati ca vedayitarāge tattha attattaniyagāho, sassatādigāho ca vipariphandatīti yujjati kāraṇassa sannihitattā. Taṇhāpaccayā hi upādānaṃ sassatādivāde paññapentānaṃ[V 1.0170], tadanucchavikaṃ vā vedanaṃ vedayantānaṃ phasso hetūti yujjati visayindriyaviññāṇasaṅgatiyā vinā tadabhāvato. Chaphassāyatananimittavaṭṭassa anupacchedoti yujjati tattha avijjātaṇhānaṃ appahīnattā. Channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ samudayādipajānanā sabbadiṭṭhigatikasaññaṃ aticca tiṭṭhatīti yujjati catusaccapaṭivedhabhāvato. Imāheva dvāsaṭṭhiyā diṭṭhīhi sabbadiṭṭhigatānaṃ antojālīkatabhāvoti yujjati akiriyavādādīnaṃ issaravādādīnañca tadantogadhattā. Tathā ceva saṃvaṇṇitaṃ. Ucchinnabhavanettiko tathāgatassa kāyoti yujjati, yasmā bhagavā abhinīhārasampattiyā catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu patiṭṭhitacitto [P 1.0251] sattabojjhaṅgeyeva yathābhūtaṃ bhāvesi. Kāyassa bhedā parinibbutaṃ na dakkhantīti yujjati anupādisesanibbānappattiyaṃ rūpādīsu kassacipi anavasesatoti ayaṃ yuttihāro.

The complete non-performance of all forms of hatred and the like leads to such a state—this is fitting, due to the nature of even-mindedness towards the pleasant and unpleasant. In whichever mental continuum hatred and the like arise, the obstacle caused by them leads to the obstruction of that very one’s success—this is fitting. Why? Because they do not transfer between different mental continuums. Hatred and the like, having overpowered the mind, arise and lead to incapacity even in discerning well-spoken words, etc.—this is fitting, due to the nature of blindness and darkness in those with anger and greed. Abstaining from unwholesome conduct such as killing living beings leads to joy and praise for all beings—this is fitting. For through the attainment of virtue, a great sound of fame indeed arises. Even a partial description of the Tathāgata, endowed with profound and special qualities, leads to grasping all the qualities of omniscience—this is fitting, due to their unparalleled nature. The inferences of understanding, corrupted by inappropriate attention arising from that, lead to adherence to eternalism and the like—this is fitting, because the net of conceptual proliferation has not been uprooted. Through not understanding the danger in feelings, craving for feelings grows—this is fitting, due to the nature of contemplating gratification. And when there is desire for what is felt, the grasping of self and what belongs to self, as well as adherence to eternalism and the like, is agitated therein—this is fitting, because the cause is present. For craving conditions clinging; it is fitting that contact is the cause for those who proclaim eternalist doctrines or those who experience corresponding feelings, because without the conjunction of object, faculty, and consciousness, that does not occur. The cycle of the sign of the six sense bases is not cut off—this is fitting, because ignorance and craving have not been abandoned there. Understanding the origin and cessation of the six sense bases surpasses all perceptions of speculative views—this is fitting, due to the penetration of the four truths. These very sixty-two views encompass all speculative views, being netted within them—this is fitting, because doctrines of non-action, divine creation, and the like are included within them. Thus it has been well explained. The Tathāgata’s body is one whose guide to becoming is cut off—this is fitting, because the Blessed One, having fulfilled his aspiration, established his mind in the four foundations of mindfulness and developed the seven factors of enlightenment as they really are. After the breakup of the body, they do not see the one who has attained final Nibbāna—this is fitting, because in the attainment of remainderless Nibbāna, nothing whatsoever remains of form and the like. This is the Mode of Reasoning.

Padaṭṭhānahāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Mode of Proximate Causes

Avaṇṇārahaavaṇṇānurūpasampattānādeyyavacanatādivipattīnaṃ [M 1.0193] padaṭṭhānaṃ. Vaṇṇārahavaṇṇānurūsampattasaddheyyavacanatādisampattīnaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ. Tathā āghātādayo nirayādidukkhassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Āghātādīnaṃ akaraṇaṃ saggasampattiādisabbasampattīnaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ. Pāṇātipātādīhi paṭivirati ariyassa sīlakkhandhassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Ariyo sīlakkhandho ariyassa samādhikkhandhassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Ariyo samādhikkhandho ariyassa paññākkhandhassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Gambhīratādivisesayuttaṃ bhagavato paṭivedhappakārañāṇaṃ desanāñāṇassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Desanāñāṇaṃ vineyyānaṃ sakalavaṭṭadukkhanissaraṇassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Sabbāpi diṭṭhi diṭṭhupādānti sā yathārahaṃ navavidhassāpi bhavassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Bhavo jātiyā, jāti jarāmaraṇassa, sokādīnañca padaṭṭhānaṃ. Vedanānaṃ samudayādiyathābhūtavedanaṃ catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ anubodhapaṭivedho. Tattha anubodho paṭivedhassa padaṭṭhānaṃ, paṭivedho catubbidhassa sāmaññaphalassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. “Ajānataṃ apassata”nti avijjāgahaṇaṃ, tattha avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ padaṭṭhānti yāva vedanā taṇhāya padaṭṭhānti netabbaṃ. “Taṇhāgatānaṃ paritassitavipphandita”nti ettha taṇhā upādānassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. “Tadapi phassapaccayā”ti ettha sassatādipaññāpanaṃ paresaṃ micchābhinivesassa padaṭṭhānaṃ, micchābhiniveso saddhammassavanasappurisūpassayayonisomanasikāradhammānudhammapaṭipattīhi vimukhatāya, asaddhammassavanādīnañca padaṭṭhānaṃ, “aññatra phassā”tiādīsu phasso vedanāya padaṭṭhānaṃ, cha phassāyatanāni phassassa, sakalavaṭṭadukkhassa ca padaṭṭhānaṃ, channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ [P 1.0252] samudayādiyathābhūtappajānanaṃ nibbidāya padaṭṭhānaṃ, nibbidā virāgassāti yāva anupādāparinibbānaṃ netabbaṃ. Bhagavato bhavanettisamucchedo sabbaññutāya padaṭṭhānaṃ. Tathā anupādāparinibbānassāti ayaṃ padaṭṭhānahāro.

The proximate cause for failures such as speech unworthy of praise, attainments unsuitable for praise, and lack of credible speech. The proximate cause for successes such as speech worthy of praise, attainments suitable for praise, and credible speech. Similarly, ill will and the like are the proximate cause for suffering in hell and other realms. The non-doing of ill will and the like is the proximate cause for heavenly attainments and all successes. Abstaining from the destruction of life and other transgressions is the proximate cause for the noble aggregate of virtue. The noble aggregate of virtue is the proximate cause for the noble aggregate of concentration. The noble aggregate of concentration is the proximate cause for the noble aggregate of wisdom. The Blessed One’s knowledge of the manner of penetration, endowed with profundity and other distinctions, is the proximate cause for his knowledge of teaching. The knowledge of teaching is the proximate cause for the liberation of those to be trained from all suffering in the round of existence. All views, as clinging to views, are, as appropriate, the proximate cause for the ninefold becoming. Becoming is the proximate cause for birth, and birth is the proximate cause for aging and death, as well as sorrow and the like. The true understanding of the arising and passing away of feelings is the comprehension and penetration of the four noble truths. Therein, comprehension is the proximate cause for penetration, and penetration is the proximate cause for the fourfold fruit of recluseship. “For those who do not know, who do not see”—this is the taking up of ignorance. Therein, ignorance is the proximate cause for formations, and so on up to feeling being the proximate cause for craving—this should be extended. “For those overcome by craving, trembling and agitated”—here, craving is the proximate cause for clinging. “That too is conditioned by contact”—here, the assertion of eternalism and the like by others is the proximate cause for wrong adherence. Wrong adherence is the proximate cause for aversion to listening to the true Dhamma, not associating with virtuous people, unwise attention, and not practicing in accordance with the Dhamma—as well as for listening to false teachings and the like. “Apart from contact” and similar statements—here, contact is the proximate cause for feeling. The six sense bases are the proximate cause for contact and for all suffering in the round of existence. The true understanding of the arising and passing away of the six sense bases is the proximate cause for disenchantment. Disenchantment is the proximate cause for dispassion—and so on up to final Nibbāna without clinging—this should be extended. The Blessed One’s destruction of the guide to existence is the proximate cause for his omniscience. Similarly, for final Nibbāna without clinging—this is the mode of proximate causes.

Lakkhaṇahāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Mode of Characteristics

Āghātādiggahaṇena [V 1.0171] kodhupanāhamakkhapalāsaissāmacchariyasārambhaparavambhanādīnaṃ saṅgaho paṭighacittuppādapariyāpannatāya ekalakkhaṇattā. Ānandādiggahaṇena abhijjhāvisamalobhamānātimānamadappamādādīnaṃ saṅgaho lobhacittuppādapariyāpannatāya samānalakkhaṇattā. Tathā [M 1.0194] āghātaggahaṇena avasiṭṭhaganthanīvaraṇānaṃ saṅgaho kāyaganthanīvaraṇalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattā. Ānandaggahaṇena phassādīnaṃ saṅgaho saṅkhārakkhandhalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattā. Sīlaggahaṇena adhicittaadhipaññāsikkhānampi saṅgaho sikkhālakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattā. Idha pana sīlasseva indriyasaṃvarādikassa daṭṭhabbaṃ. Diṭṭhiggahaṇena avasiṭṭhaupādānānampi saṅgaho upādānalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattā. “Vedanāna”nti ettha vedanāggahaṇena avasiṭṭhaupādānakkhandhānampi saṅgaho khandhalakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattā. Tathā vedanāya dhammāyatanadhammadhātupariyāpannattā sammasanūpagānaṃ sabbesaṃ āyatanānaṃ dhātūnañca saṅgaho āyatanalakkhaṇena, dhātulakkhaṇena ca ekalakkhaṇattā. “Ajānataṃ apassata”nti ettha avijjāggahaṇena hetuāsavoghayoganīvaraṇādisaṅgaho hetādilakkhaṇena ekalakkhaṇattā avijjāya, tathā “taṇhāgatānaṃ paritassitavipphandita”nti ettha taṇhāggahaṇenāpi. “Tadapi phassapaccayā”ti ettha phassaggahaṇena saññāsaṅkhāraviññāṇānaṃ saṅgaho vipallāsahetubhāvena, khandhalakkhaṇena ca ekalakkhaṇattā. Chaphassāyatanaggahaṇena khandhindriyadhātādīnaṃ saṅgaho phassuppattinimittatāya, sammasanasabhāvena ca ekalakkhaṇattā. Bhavanettiggahaṇena avijjādīnampi [P 1.0253] saṃkilesadhammānaṃ saṅgaho vaṭṭahetubhāvena ekalakkhaṇattāti ayaṃ lakkhaṇahāro.

The inclusion of anger, resentment, denigration, envy, miserliness, rivalry, and disparagement through the term 'ill will' is due to their shared characteristic of being comprised within the arising of a mind of aversion. The inclusion of covetousness, unrighteous greed, conceit, excessive pride, intoxication, heedlessness, and so on through the term 'delight' is due to their shared characteristic of being comprised within the arising of a mind of greed. Similarly, the inclusion of the remaining fetters and hindrances through the term 'ill will' is due to their shared characteristic of being a bodily fetter and hindrance. The inclusion of contact and other factors through the term 'delight' is due to their shared characteristic of being the formations aggregate. The inclusion of the trainings in higher mind and higher wisdom through the term 'virtue' is due to their shared characteristic of being a training. Here, however, the restraint of the senses and the like should be seen as pertaining to virtue alone. The inclusion of the remaining clingings through the term 'view' is due to their shared characteristic of being a clinging. In the phrase 'of feelings,' the inclusion of the remaining aggregates of clinging through the term 'feeling' is due to their shared characteristic of being an aggregate. Likewise, because feeling is comprised within the sense-sphere of phenomena and the element of phenomena, the inclusion of all sense-spheres and elements that are fit for contemplation is due to their shared characteristic of being a sense-sphere and an element. In the phrase 'of those who do not know, who do not see,' the inclusion of roots, influxes, floods, yokes, hindrances, and so on through the term 'ignorance' is due to their shared characteristic of being roots and the like, pertaining to ignorance. Similarly, in the phrase 'of those who are afflicted and agitated with craving,' the inclusion is also through the term 'craving.' In the phrase 'that too is conditioned by contact,' the inclusion of perception, formations, and consciousness through the term 'contact' is due to their shared characteristic of being a cause of perversion and being an aggregate. Through the term 'the six sense-spheres of contact', the inclusion of aggregates, faculties, elements, and so on is due to their shared characteristic of being the basis for the arising of contact and their nature of being fit for contemplation. The inclusion of ignorance and other defiling factors through the term 'craving for existence' is due to their shared characteristic of being causes of the round of existence. This is the mode of characteristics.

Catubyūhahāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Fourfold Arrangement

Nindāpasaṃsāhi sammākampitacetasā micchājīvato anoratā sassatādimicchābhinivesino sīlādidhammakkhandhesu appatiṭṭhitatāya sammāsambuddhaguṇarasassādavimukhā veneyyā imissā desanāya nidānaṃ. Te yathāvuttadosavinimuttā kathaṃ nu kho sammāpaṭipattiyā ubhayahitaparā bhaveyyunti ayamettha bhagavato adhippāyo. Padanibbacanaṃ nirutti. Taṃ “eva”ntiādinidānapadānaṃ, “mama”ntiādipāḷipadānañca aṭṭhakathāvasena suviññeyyattā ativitthārabhayena na vitthārayimha. Padapadatthaniddesanikkhepasuttadesanāsandhivasena chabbidhā sandhi. Tattha padassa padantarena sambandho padasandhi. Tathā padatthassa padatthantarena sambandho padatthasandhi[M 1.0195]. Nānānusandhikassa suttassa taṃtaṃanusandhīhi sambandho, ekānusandhikassa ca pubbāparasambandho niddesasandhi[V 1.0172], yā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pucchānusandhiajjhāsayānusandhiyathānusandhivasena tividhā vibhattā, tā panetā tissopi sandhiyo aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vicāritā eva. Suttasandhi ca paṭhamaṃ nikkhepavasena amhehi pubbe dassitāyeva. Ekissā desanāya desanāntarena saddhiṃ saṃsandanaṃ desanāsandhi, sā evaṃ veditabbā – “mamaṃ vā bhikkhave…pe… na cetaso anabhiraddhi karaṇīyā”ti ayaṃ desanā “ubhatodaṇḍakena cepi bhikkhave kakacena corā ocarakā aṅgamaṅgāni okkanteyyuṃ, tatrapi yo mano padūseyya, na me so tena sāsanakaro”ti (ma. ni. 1.232) imāya [P 1.0254] desanāya saddhiṃ saṃsandati. “Tumhaṃ yevassa tena antarāyo”ti “kammassakā māṇava sattā…pe… dāyādā bhavissantī”ti (a. ni. 10.216) imāya desanāya saṃsandati. “Api tumhe…pe… ājāneyyāthā”ti “kuddho atthaṃ…pe… sahate nara”nti (a. ni. 7.64; mahāni. 5, 156, 195) imāya desanāya saṃsandati.

Those whose minds are swayed by blame and praise, who are unrestrained in wrong livelihood, and who hold wrong views such as eternalism—being unestablished in the aggregates of virtue and other qualities—are averse to the taste of the qualities of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Such teachable beings are the basis for this discourse. The Blessed One’s intention here is this: “How might they, freed from the faults as described, become devoted to the welfare of both through right practice?” The analysis of words is the explanation of terms. That includes the derivation of words like 'eva' and others, as well as the explanation of Pāli words like 'mama.' Due to their clarity through the commentary and to avoid excessive elaboration, we have not expanded on them. Connection is sixfold: word-connection (padasandhi), meaning-connection (padatthasandhi), explanation-connection (niddesasandhi), summary-connection (nikkhepasandhi), sutta-connection (suttasandhi), and discourse-connection (desanāsandhi). Among these: Word-connection (padasandhi) is the relation between one word and another word. Meaning-connection (padatthasandhi) is the relation between one meaning and another meaning. Explanation-connection (niddesasandhi) is the relation in a discourse with multiple connections through its various links, or in a single-connected discourse, the relation between what precedes and follows. In the commentary, these connections are analyzed as threefold: question-based connection (pucchānusandhi), intention-based connection (ajjhāsayānusandhi), and sequential connection (yathānusandhi). These three connections have been examined in the commentary. Sutta-connection (suttasandhi) was previously shown by us first through the method of summary (nikkhepa). Discourse-connection (desanāsandhi) is the connection of one discourse with another. It should be understood thus: The teaching, “Monks, whether others praise me… there should be no displeasure of mind,” connects with the teaching, “Monks, even if bandits were to sever your limbs one by one with a two-handled saw, even then, should you corrupt your mind, you would not be following my instruction” (MN 1.232). The teaching, “That would be an obstacle for you,” connects with the teaching, “Beings are owners of their deeds, young man… they will be heirs to their deeds” (AN 10.216). The teaching, “If you would know…” connects with the teaching, “An angry person does not understand the meaning… a person endures” (AN 7.64; Mahāni. 5, 156, 195).

“Mamaṃ vā bhikkhave pare vaṇṇaṃ…pe… na cetaso ubbillāvitattaṃ karaṇīya”nti “dhammāpi vo bhikkhave pahātabbā, pageva adhammā (ma. ni. 1.240). Kullūpamaṃ vo bhikkhave dhammaṃ desessāmi, nittharaṇatthāya, no gahaṇatthāyā”ti (ma. ni. 1.240) imāya desanāya saṃsandati. “Tatra ce tumhehi…pe… ubbilāvitā, tumhaṃ yevassa tena antarāyo”ti “luddhoatthaṃ…pe… sahate nara”nti (itivu. 88; mahāni. 5.156, 195; cūḷani. 128) “kāmandhā jālasañchannā, taṇhāchadanachāditā”ti (udā. 64; netti. 27, 90; peṭako. 14) imāhi desanāhi saṃsandati.

The teaching, “Monks, whether others praise me… there should be no elation of mind,” connects with the teachings, “Monks, even the Dhamma should be abandoned, how much more so what is not-Dhamma,” and “Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma like a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping” (MN 1.240). The teaching, “If you… become elated, that itself would be an obstruction for you,” connects with the teachings, “A greedy person does not understand the meaning… a person endures” (Itivu. 88; Mahāni. 5.156, 195; Cūḷani. 128) and “Blinded by desire, covered by the net, shrouded in craving” (Udā. 64; Netti. 27, 90; Peṭako. 14).

“Appamattakaṃ…pe… sīlamattaka”nti “paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ kho brāhmaṇa yañño purimehi yaññehi appaṭṭhataro ca appasamārambhataro ca mahapphalataro ca mahānisaṃsataro cā”tiādikāya [P 1.0255] (dī. ni. 1.353) desanāya saṃsandati, paṭhamajjhānassa sīlato mahapphalamahānisaṃsatarabhāvavacanena jhānato sīlassa appabhāvadīpanato.

The teaching, “Even a little… even just virtue,” connects with the teaching, “Having attained the first jhāna, he dwells therein. This, O brahmin, is a sacrifice less elaborate and less laborious than the former sacrifices, yet more fruitful and more beneficial” (DN 1.353). This connection is made by the statement of the first jhāna’s greater fruit and benefit compared to virtue, thereby indicating virtue’s lesser significance in relation to jhāna.

“Pāṇātipātaṃ [M 1.0196] pahāyā”tiādi “samaṇo khalu bho gotamo sīlavā…pe… kusalasīlena samannāgato”tiādikāhi (dī. ni. 1.304) desanāhi saṃsandati.

The teaching, “Having abandoned the taking of life,” and so on, connects with teachings such as, “Indeed, the ascetic Gotama is virtuous… endowed with skillful virtue,” and so on (DN 1.304).

“Aññeva dhammā gambhīrā”tiādi “adhigato kho myāyaṃ dhammo gambhīro”tiādi (dī. ni. 2.67; ma. ni. 1.281; 2.337; saṃ. ni. 1.172; mahāva. 7, 8) pāḷiyā [V 1.0173] saṃsandati. Gambhīratādivisesayuttadhammapaṭivedhena hi ñāṇassa gambhīrādibhāvo viññāyatīti.

The teaching, “The teachings are profound,” and so on, connects with the Pāli text, “This teaching I have attained is profound,” and so on (DN 2.67; MN 1.281; 2.337; SN 1.172; Mahāva. 7, 8). For it is through the realization of the teachings endowed with profundity and other distinctions that the profundity and other qualities of knowledge are discerned.

“Santi bhikkhave eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā”tiādi “santi bhikkhave eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā pubbantakappikā…pe… abhivadanti, sassato attā ca loko ca, idameva saccaṃ, moghamaññanti ittheke abhivadanti, asassato, sassato ca asassato ca, neva sassato ca nāsassato ca, antavā, anantavā, antavā ca anantavā ca, nevantavā nānantavā ca attā ca loko ca idameva saccaṃ, moghamaññanti ittheke abhivadantī”tiādikāhi (ma. ni. 3.27) desanāhi saṃsandati.

The teaching, “Monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins,” and so on, connects with teachings such as, “Monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins who are speculators about the past… who declare: ‘The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.’ Some declare: ‘The self and the world are not eternal… both eternal and not eternal… neither eternal nor not eternal… finite… infinite… both finite and infinite… neither finite nor infinite; the self and the world are thus; this alone is true, all else is false’” (MN 3.27).

“Santi bhikkhave eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā aparantakappikā”tiādi “santi bhikkhave eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā aparantakappikā…pe… abhivadanti, saññī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā. Ittheke abhivadanti asaññī, nevasaññīnāsaññī ca attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā. Ittheke abhivadanti sato vā pana sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapenti, diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ vā paneke abhivadantī”tiādikāhi (ma. ni. 3.21) desanāhi saṃsandati. “Vedanānaṃ…pe… tathāgato”ti “tayidaṃ [P 1.0256] saṅkhataṃ oḷārikaṃ, atthi kho pana saṅkhārānaṃ nirodho, atthetanti iti viditvā tassa nissaraṇadassāvī tathāgato tadupātivatto”tiādikāhi (ma. ni. 3.28) desanāhi saṃsandati.

The teaching, “Bhikkhus, there are some ascetics and brahmins who are speculators about the future,” and so on, connects with teachings such as, “Bhikkhus, there are some ascetics and brahmins who are speculators about the future… they declare that the self is percipient and healthy after death. Some among them declare that the self is non-percipient, or neither percipient nor non-percipient, and healthy after death. Some among them propound the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existent being, while others declare Nibbāna in this very life” (MN 3.21). The teaching, “Regarding feelings… the Tathāgata,” connects with teachings such as, “This is conditioned and coarse, but there is the cessation of formations. Having known, ‘There is this,’ the Tathāgata, seeing the escape from it, has transcended it” (MN 3.28).

“Tadapi tesaṃ…pe… vipphanditamevā”ti idaṃ “tesaṃ bhavataṃ aññatreva chandāya aññatra ruciyā aññatra anussavā aññatra ākāraparivitakkā aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā paccattaṃyeva ñāṇaṃ bhavissati parisuddhaṃ pariyodātanti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Paccattaṃ kho pana bhikkhave ñāṇe asati parisuddhe pariyodāte yadapi te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā tattha ñāṇabhāgamattameva [M 1.0197] pariyodāpenti, tadapi tesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ upādānamakkhāyatī”tiādikāhi (ma. ni. 3.29) desanāhi saṃsandati.

The teaching, “That too is their… floundering,” connects with the teachings beginning, “For those venerable ones, apart from inclination, apart from liking, apart from oral tradition, apart from considering reasons, apart from reflection on and approval of a view, that ‘personal knowledge will be theirs, purified and clarified’—this is not possible. But, bhikkhus, when personal knowledge, purified and clarified, does not exist, even if those venerable ascetics and brahmins purify just a mere portion of knowledge there, that too, for those venerable ascetics and brahmins, is reckoned as clinging,” and so on (MN 3.29).

“Tadapi phassapaccayā”ti idañca “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā, vedanāpaccayā taṇhā, taṇhāpaccayā upādāna”nti, (saṃ. ni. 2.44) “chandamūlakā ime āvuso dhammā manasikārasamuṭṭhānā [V 1.0174] phassasamodhānā vedanāsamosaraṇā”ti (a. ni. 8.83) ca ādikāhi desanāhi saṃsandati.

The teaching, “That too is conditioned by contact,” connects with teachings such as: “Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; conditioned by contact, feeling arises; conditioned by feeling, craving arises; conditioned by craving, clinging arises” (SN 2.44). And: “Friend, these phenomena are rooted in desire, originate from attention, have their confluence in contact, and converge on feeling” (AN 8.83).

“Yato kho bhikkhave bhikkhu channaṃ phassāyatanāna”ntiādi “yato kho ānanda bhikkhu neva vedanaṃ attānaṃ samanupassati, na saññaṃ, na saṅkhāre, na viññāṇaṃ attānaṃ samanupassati, so evaṃ asamanupassanto na kiñci loke upādiyati, anupādiyaṃ na paritassati, aparitassaṃ paccattaṃyeva parinibbāyatī”tiādikāhi desanāhi saṃsandati.

The teaching, “When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu [does not regard] the six sense bases…” and so on, connects with teachings such as, “When, Ānanda, a bhikkhu does not regard feeling as self, nor perception, nor volitional formations, nor consciousness as self, then, thus not regarding, he clings to nothing in the world. Not clinging, he is not agitated, and being unagitated, he personally attains Parinibbāna.”

“Sabbe te imeheva dvāsaṭṭhiyā vatthūhi antojālīkatā”tiādi “ye [P 1.0257] hi keci bhikkhave…pe… abhivadanti, sabbe te imāneva pañca kāyāni abhivadanti etesaṃ vā aññatara”ntiādikāhi (ma. ni. 3.26) desanāhi saṃsandati. “Kāyassa bhedā…pe… devamanussā”ti –

The teaching, “All these are encompassed within these sixty-two grounds,” and so on, connects with teachings such as, “Indeed, bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins… propound, all of them propound just these five aggregates or one among them” (MN 3.26). The teaching, “Upon the breakup of the body… gods and humans arise,” is followed by:

“Accī yathā vātavegena khittā, (upasivāti bhagavā)

Atthaṃ paleti na upeti saṅkhaṃ;

Evaṃ munī nāmakāyā vimutto,

Atthaṃ paleti na upeti saṅkha”nti. (su. ni. 1080; cūḷani. 43);

“As a flame scattered by the force of the wind, (Upasīva,” said the Blessed One), “goes to its setting and cannot be reckoned; so too a sage, freed from the name-group, goes to his setting and cannot be reckoned” (Sn 1080; Cūḷaniddesa 43);

Ādikāhi desanāhi saṃsandatīti ayaṃ cātubyūho hāro.

It connects with teachings such as these. This is the fourfold arrangement method.

Āvattahāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Method of Implication.

Āghātādīnaṃ akaraṇīyatāvacanena khantisoraccānuṭṭhānaṃ. Tattha khantiyā saddhāpaññāparāpakāradukkhasahagatānaṃ saṅgaho, soraccena sīlassa. Saddhādiggahaṇena ca saddhindriyādisakalabodhipakkhiyadhammā āvattanti. Sīlaggahaṇena avippaṭisārādayo sabbepi sīlānisaṃsadhammā āvattanti. Pāṇātipātādīhi paṭivirativacanena appamādavihāro, tena [M 1.0198] sakalaṃ sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ āvattati. Gambhīratādivisesayuttadhammaggahaṇena mahābodhipakittanaṃ. Anāvaraṇañāṇapadaṭṭhānañhi āsavakkhayañāṇaṃ, āsavakkhayañāṇapadaṭṭhānañca anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ mahābodhi, tena dasabalādayo sabbe buddhaguṇā āvattanti. Sassatādidiṭṭhiggahaṇena taṇhāvijjāya [V 1.0175] saṅgaho, tāhi anamataggasaṃsāravaṭṭaṃ āvattati. Vedanānaṃ samudayādiyathābhūtavedanena bhagavato pariññāttayavisuddhi, tāya paññāpāramimukhena sabbapāramiyo āvattanti. “Ajānataṃ apassata”nti avijjāggahaṇena ayonisomanasikārapariggaho, tena ca ayonisomanasikāramūlakā dhammā āvattanti. “Taṇhāgatānaṃ paritassitavipphandita”nti taṇhāggahaṇena nava taṇhāmūlakā dhammā āvattanti, “tadapi phassapaccayā”tiādi sassatādipaññāpanassa [P 1.0258] paccayādhīnavuttidassanaṃ, tena aniccatādilakkhaṇattayaṃ āvattati. Channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānanena vimuttisampadāniddeso, tena sattapi visuddhiyo āvattanti. “Ucchinnabhavanettiko tathāgatassa kāyo”ti taṇhāpahānaṃ, tena bhagavato sakalasaṃkilesappahānaṃ āvattatīti ayaṃ āvatto hāro.

By the statement that things like ill will should not be done, the practice of patience and gentleness is implied. Herein, by patience is included faith, wisdom, and endurance of suffering caused by others; by gentleness is included morality. And by the inclusion of faith and so forth, all the factors conducive to enlightenment, such as the faculty of faith, are implied. By the inclusion of morality, all the benefits of morality, such as freedom from remorse, are implied. By the statement of abstaining from killing living beings and so forth, abiding in heedfulness is implied; by that, the entire holy life of the Dispensation is implied. By the inclusion of states endowed with profundity and other distinctions, the proclamation of the Great Enlightenment is implied. For the knowledge of the destruction of the taints is the proximate cause of unobstructed knowledge, and unobstructed knowledge—the Great Enlightenment—is the proximate cause of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. By that, all the Buddha's qualities, such as the ten powers, are implied. By the inclusion of eternalist and other views, craving and ignorance are included; by these, the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra is implied. By the true understanding of the arising, etc., of feelings, the Blessed One's threefold purity of full understanding is implied; by that, all the perfections are implied through the gateway of the perfection of wisdom. By the inclusion of ignorance in “for those who do not know, who do not see,” unwise attention is encompassed; and by that, all states rooted in unwise attention are implied. By the inclusion of craving in “the agitated floundering of those who have come to craving,” the nine states rooted in craving are implied. The statement “that too is conditioned by contact,” etc., shows that the propounding of eternalism and other views is dependent on conditions; by that, the three characteristics of impermanence, etc., are implied. By truly understanding the six sense bases, the declaration of the accomplishment of liberation is implied; by that, the seven purifications are implied. The phrase “the Tathāgata’s aggregate-body has severed the conduit of becoming” implies the abandonment of craving; by that, the Blessed One’s complete abandonment of all defilements is implied. This is the method of implication.

Vibhattihāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Method of Analysis.

Āghātānandādayo akusalā dhammā, tesaṃ ayonisomanasikārādi padaṭṭhānaṃ. Yehi pana dhammehi āghātānandādīnaṃ akaraṇaṃ appavatti, te abyāpādādayo kusalā dhammā, tesaṃ yonisomanasikārādi padaṭṭhānaṃ. Tesu āghātādayo kāmāvacarāva, abyāpādādayo catubhūmakā. Tathā pāṇātipātādīhi paṭivirati kusalā vā abyākatā vā, tassā hirottappādayo dhammā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Tattha kusalā siyā kāmāvacarā, siyā lokuttarā, abyākatā lokuttarāva. “Atthi bhikkhave aññeva dhammā gambhīrā”ti vuttadhammā siyā kusalā, siyā abyākatā, tattha kusalānaṃ vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Abyākatānaṃ maggadhammā, vipassanā, āvajjanā vā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Tesu kusalā lokuttarā, abyākatā siyā kāmāvacarā, siyā lokuttarā, sabbāpi diṭṭhiyo akusalāva kāmāvacarāva, tāsaṃ avisesena micchābhinivese ayonisomanasikāro padaṭṭhānaṃ. Visesato pana santatighanavinibbhogābhāvato ekattanayassa micchāgāho [M 1.0199] atītajātianussaraṇatakkasahito sassatadiṭṭhiyā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Hetuphalabhāvena sambandhabhāvassa aggahaṇato nānattanayassa micchāgāho tajjāsamannāhārasahito ucchedadiṭṭhiyā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Evaṃ sesadiṭṭhīnampi yathāsambhavaṃ vattabbaṃ. “Vedanāna”nti ettha vedanā siyā kusalā, siyā abyākatā, siyā kāmāvacarā, siyā rūpāvacarā, siyā arūpāvacarā, phasso tāsaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ. Vedanānaṃ samudayādiyathābhūtavedanaṃ maggañāṇaṃ, anupādāvimutti phalaṃ[P 1.0259], tesaṃ “aññeva dhammā gambhīrā”ti ettha vuttanayena dhammādivibhāgo netabbo. “Ajānataṃ apassata”ntiādīsu avijjā taṇhā akusalā kāmāvacarā, tāsu avijjāya āsavā, ayonisomanasikāro eva vā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Taṇhāya saṃyojaniyesu dhammesu assādadassanaṃ [V 1.0176] padaṭṭhānaṃ. “Tadapi phassapaccayā”ti ettha phassassa vedanāya viya dhammādivibhāgo veditabbo. Iminā nayena phassāyatanādīnampi yathārahaṃ dhammādivibhāgo netabboti ayaṃ vibhattihāro.

Ill will, delight, and so forth are unwholesome states; their proximate cause is unwise attention and so forth. But the states by which ill will, delight, and so forth do not arise or occur are the wholesome states of non-ill-will and so forth; their proximate cause is wise attention and so forth. Among these, ill will and the like pertain only to the sense-sphere, while non-ill-will and the like pertain to the four planes. Similarly, abstaining from killing living beings and so on is either wholesome or indeterminate; its proximate cause is moral shame, moral dread, and so forth. Here, the wholesome may be of the sense-sphere or supramundane, while the indeterminate is only supramundane. The states mentioned in "There are, monks, other states that are profound" may be wholesome or indeterminate. Among these, the proximate cause of the wholesome is insight leading to emergence. For the indeterminate, the proximate causes are path factors, insight, or attention. Among these, the wholesome is supramundane, while the indeterminate may be of the sense-sphere or supramundane. All views are unwholesome and pertain only to the sense-sphere. Their general proximate cause, with regard to wrong adherence, is unwise attention. Specifically, the wrong grasp of unity—due to the absence of analyzing continuity and compactness—combined with recollection of past births and reasoning, is the proximate cause of eternalism. The wrong grasp of diversity—due to the failure to recognize the connection in terms of cause and effect—combined with associated attention, is the proximate cause of annihilationism. Thus, the remaining views should also be explained as appropriate. Regarding "feelings," here feelings may be wholesome, indeterminate, of the sense-sphere, the form-sphere, or the formless-sphere. Contact is their proximate cause. Path-knowledge is the knowing of the origin and so forth of feelings as they truly are, and liberation through non-clinging is the fruit; the classification of these into states and so forth should be understood according to the method explained in the statement, "There are other states that are profound." In the passage, "For those who do not know, who do not see," ignorance and craving are unwholesome and pertain to the sense-sphere. Among these, the proximate cause of ignorance is the influxes, or simply unwise attention. The proximate cause of craving is seeing gratification in things that fetter. In the statement, "That too is conditioned by contact," the classification of contact should be understood in the same way as that of feeling. In this manner, the classification of the sense bases and so forth should also be appropriately determined. This is the analysis section.

Parivattahāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Parivatta-Hāra

Āghātādīnaṃ akaraṇaṃ khantisoraccāni anubrūhetvā paṭisaṅkhānabhāvanābalasiddhiyā ubhayahitapaṭipattiṃ āvahati. Āghātādayo pana pavattiyamānā dubbaṇṇataṃ dukkhaseyyaṃ bhogahāniṃ akittiṃ parehi durupasaṅkamanatañca nipphādentā nirayādīsu mahādukkhaṃ āvahanti. Pāṇātipātādīhi paṭivirati avippaṭisārādikalyāṇaṃ paramparaṃ āvahati. Pāṇātipātādi pana vippaṭisārādiakalyāṇaṃ paramparaṃ, gambhīratādivisesayuttaṃ ñāṇaṃ vineyyānaṃ yathārahaṃ vijjābhiññādiguṇavisesaṃ āvahati sabbañeyyaṃ yathāsabhāvāvabodhato. Tathā gambhīratādivisesarahitaṃ pana ñāṇaṃ ñeyyesu sāvaraṇato yathāvuttaguṇavisesaṃ nāvahati. Sabbāpi cetā diṭṭhiyo yathārahaṃ sassatucchedabhāvato antadvayabhūtā sakkāyatīraṃ nātivattanti aniyyānikasabhāvattā. Niyyānikasabhāvattā pana sammādiṭṭhi saparikkhārā majjhimapaṭipadābhūtā atikkamma sakkāyatīraṃ pāraṃ āgacchati. Vedanānaṃ samudayādiyathābhūtavedanaṃ anupādāvimuttiṃ āvahati maggabhāvato. Vedanānaṃ samudayādiasampaṭivedho saṃsāracārakāvarodhaṃ āvahati saṅkhārānaṃ paccayabhāvato. Vedayitasabhāvapaṭicchādako sammoho tadabhinandanaṃ āvahati[M 1.0200]. Yathābhūtāvabodho pana tattha nibbedaṃ virāgañca āvahati. Micchābhinivese ayonisomanasikārasahitā taṇhā [P 1.0260] anekavihitaṃ diṭṭhijālaṃ pasāreti. Yathāvuttataṇhāsamucchedo paṭhamamaggo taṃ diṭṭhijālaṃ saṅkoceti. Sassatavādādipaññāpanassa phasso paccayo hoti asati phasse tadabhāvato.
