Diṭṭhibandhanabandhānaṃ phassāyatanādīnaṃ anirodhena phassādianirodho saṃsāradukkhassa anivattiyeva, yāthāvato phassāyatanādipariññā sabbadiṭṭhidassanāni ativattati, phassāyatanādiapariññā taṃdiṭṭhigahanaṃ nātivattati, bhavanettisamucchedo āyatiṃ attabhāvassa anibbattiyā saṃvattati, asamucchinnāya bhavanettiyā anāgate bhavappabandho parivattatiyevāti ayaṃ parivatto hāro.

Refraining from ill will and other harmful actions, cultivating patience and gentleness, and developing the power of reflective meditation bring about the practice beneficial to both oneself and others. Ill will and similar states, when active, lead to ugliness, painful sleep, loss of wealth, disrepute, and difficulty in approaching others, ultimately bringing great suffering in hell and other realms. Abstaining from killing living beings and other harmful actions brings successive benefits such as freedom from remorse and other virtues. Engaging in killing and similar actions, however, brings successive harms such as remorse and other unwholesome states. Deep knowledge endowed with profundity and other distinctions, suited to the inclinations of those to be trained, brings special qualities such as higher knowledge and insight, leading to the full understanding of all knowable phenomena as they truly are. Knowledge lacking depth and special qualities does not bring such distinctions in understanding, remaining obstructed in regard to what is to be known. All these views, depending on their nature, are rooted in the extremes of eternalism or annihilationism and do not transcend the shore of personal existence due to their unliberating nature. Right view, equipped with its factors and following the middle path, transcends the shore of personal existence and reaches the far shore due to its liberating nature. Understanding the arising and passing away of feelings as they truly are leads to liberation through non-clinging, as it constitutes the path. Failing to comprehend the arising and passing away of feelings perpetuates wandering in the cycle of existence due to the conditioned nature of formations. Delusion, which conceals the true nature of what is felt, leads to delight in it. But clear comprehension of it as it truly is brings disenchantment and dispassion. Wrong adherence, accompanied by unwise attention, spreads the net of views in many ways. The cutting off of craving, as described, through the first path, contracts that net of views. Contact is the condition for the proclamation of eternalism and other doctrines; in the absence of contact, such doctrines do not arise. Without the cessation of the sense bases such as contact, the cessation of contact and other factors does not occur, and thus the suffering of saṃsāra continues unceasingly. Full understanding of the sense bases such as contact transcends all views and perceptions. Without such understanding, one does not transcend the thicket of views. The cutting off of the craving that is the guide to becoming leads to the non-arising of future states of existence. If the craving that is the guide to becoming is not cut off, the continuum of existence continues to revolve in the future. This is the revolving section.

Vevacanahāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on Synonyms

“Mama mayhaṃ me”ti pariyāyavacanaṃ. “Bhikkhave samaṇā tapassino”ti pariyāyavacanaṃ. “Pare [V 1.0177] aññe paṭiviruddhā”ti pariyāyavacanaṃ. “Avaṇṇaṃ akittiṃ ninda”nti pariyāyavacanaṃ. “Bhāseyyuṃ bhaṇeyyuṃ kareyyu”nti pariyāyavacanaṃ. “Dhammassa vinayassa satthusāsanassā”ti pariyāyavacanaṃ. “Saṅghassa samūhassa gaṇassā”ti pariyāyavacanaṃ. “Tatra tattha tesū”ti pariyāyavacanaṃ. “Tumhehi vo bhavantehī”ti pariyāyavacanaṃ. “Āghāto doso byāpādo”ti pariyāyavacanaṃ. “Appaccayo domanassaṃ cetasikadukkha”nti pariyāyavacanaṃ. “Cetaso anabhiraddhi cittassa byāpatti manopadoso”ti pariyāyavacanaṃ. “Na karaṇīyā na uppādetabbā na pavattetabbā”ti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Iti iminā nayena sabbapadesu vevacanaṃ vattabbanti ayaṃ vevacano hāro.

"Mine, belonging to me, me" are synonyms. "Monks, recluses, ascetics" are synonyms. "Others, different, opposed" are synonyms. "Disgrace, dishonor, blame" are synonyms. "They might say, speak, or do" are synonyms. "Of the Dhamma, the Discipline, the Teacher’s instruction" are synonyms. "Of the Saṅgha, the assembly, the group" are synonyms. "There, there, among them" are synonyms. "By you, to you, by you venerable ones" are synonyms. "Aversion, hatred, ill-will" are synonyms. "Displeasure, sadness, mental pain" are synonyms. "Discontent of mind, corruption of mind, mental hatred" are synonyms. "It should not be done, it should not be produced, it should not be started" are synonyms. In this way, in all instances, synonyms should be expressed—this is the section on synonyms.

Paññattihāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on Designations

Āghāto vatthuvasena dasavidhena ekūnavīsatividhena vā paññatto. Appaccayo upavicāravasena chadhā paññatto. Ānandopītiādivasena navadhā paññatto. Pīti sāmaññato khuddikādivasena pañcadhā paññattā. Somanassaṃ upavicāravasena chadhā paññattaṃ. Sīlaṃ vārittacārittādivasena anekadhā paññattaṃ. Gambhīratādivisesayuttaṃ ñāṇaṃ cittuppādavasena catudhā, dvādasavidhena vā, visayabhedato anekadhā ca paññattaṃ. Diṭṭhisassatādivasena [M 1.0201][P 1.0261] dvāsaṭṭhiyā bhedehi, tadantogadhavibhāgena anekadhā ca paññattā. Vedanā chadhā aṭṭhasatadhā anekadhā ca paññattā. Tassā samudayo pañcadhā paññatto, tathā atthaṅgamo. Assādo duvidhena paññatto. Ādīnavo tividhena paññatto. Nissaraṇaṃ ekadhā catudhā ca paññattaṃ…pe… anupādāvimutti duvidhena paññattā.

Ill will is designated in ten ways based on its object, or in nineteen ways. Displeasure is designated in six ways based on investigation. Joy is designated in nine ways, such as joy and rapture. Rapture is generally designated in five ways, such as minor rapture and so on. Happiness is designated in six ways based on investigation. Virtue is designated in many ways, such as through abstinence and performance. Knowledge connected with profundity and other distinctions is designated in four ways based on thought-moments, or in twelve ways, and in many ways according to the diversity of its objects. Views are designated in sixty-two divisions, such as eternalism, and in many ways according to analysis of their inner contents. Feeling is designated in six ways, one hundred and eight ways, and many other ways. Its origin is designated in five ways, and so is its passing away. Gratification is designated in two ways. Danger is designated in three ways. Escape is designated in one way and four ways… up to… liberation without clinging is designated in two ways.

“Ajānataṃ apassata”nti vuttā avijjā visayabhedena catudhā aṭṭhadhā ca paññattā. “Taṇhāgatāna”ntiādinā vuttā taṇhā chadhā aṭṭhasatadhā anekadhā ca paññattā. Phasso nissayavasena chadhā paññatto. Upādānaṃ catudhā paññattaṃ. Bhavo dvidhā anekadhā ca paññatto. Jāti vevacanavasena chadhā paññattā. Tathā jarā sattadhā paññattā. Maraṇaṃ aṭṭhadhā navadhā ca paññattaṃ. Soko pañcadhā paññatto. Paridevo chadhā paññatto. Dukkhaṃ catudhā paññattaṃ, tathā domanassaṃ. Upāyāso catudhā paññatto. “Samudayo hotī”ti pabhavapaññatti, “yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”ti dukkhassa pariññāpaññatti, samudayassa pahānapaññatti, nirodhassa sacchikiriyāpaññatti, maggassa bhāvanāpaññatti.

“Not knowing, not seeing,” thus ignorance is designated in four ways and eight ways according to the diversity of objects. “For those overcome by craving,” and so on, thus craving is designated in six ways, in one hundred and eight ways, and in many ways. Contact is designated in six ways based on dependence. Clinging is designated in four ways. Becoming is designated in two ways and in many ways. Birth is designated in six ways by way of synonyms. Similarly, aging is designated in seven ways. Death is designated in eight ways and nine ways. Sorrow is designated in five ways. Lamentation is designated in six ways. Suffering is designated in four ways, and similarly, grief. Despair is designated in four ways. “Origination occurs,” this is the designation of origin. “One understands as it really is,” this is the designation of the full understanding of suffering, the designation of abandoning the origin, the designation of realizing cessation, and the designation of developing the path.

“Antojālīkatā”tiādi [V 1.0178] sabbadiṭṭhīnaṃ saṅgahapaññatti. “Ucchinnabhavanettiko”tiādi duvidhena parinibbānapaññatti. Evaṃ āghātādīnaṃ akusalakusalādidhammānaṃ yathāpabhavapaññattiādivasena, tathā “āghāto”ti byāpādassa vevacanapaññatti, “appaccayo”ti domanassassa vevacanapaññattītiādinā nayena paññattibhedo vibhajitabboti ayaṃ paññattihāro.

“Internal entanglement,” and so forth, is a designation encompassing all views. “One who has cut off the guide to becoming,” and so forth, is a designation of Nibbāna in two ways. Thus, for resentment and other unwholesome and wholesome states, designations are given according to their origin, and so forth; similarly, “resentment” is a synonymous designation for ill-will, “displeasure” is a synonymous designation for grief, and so forth. In this way, the distinctions of designations should be analyzed. This is the section on designations.

Otaraṇahāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Mode of Entry

Āghātaggahaṇena saṅkhārakkhandhasaṅgaho, tathā anabhiraddhigahaṇena. Appaccayaggahaṇena vedanākkhandhasaṅgahoti idaṃ khandhamukhena otaraṇaṃ. Tathā āghātādiggahaṇena dhammāyatanaṃ dhammadhātu dukkhasaccaṃ samudayasaccaṃ vā gahitanti idaṃ āyatanamukhena dhātumukhena saccamukhena ca otaraṇaṃ. Tathā āghātādīnaṃ [P 1.0262] sahajātā avijjā hetusahajātaaññamaññanissayasampayuttaatthiavigatapaccayehi paccayo hoti, asahajātā pana anantarasamanantaraanantarūpanissayanatthivigatāsevanapaccayehi paccayo hoti, anantarā upanissayavaseneva paccayo hoti[M 1.0202]. Taṇhāupādānādīnaṃ, phassādīnampi tesaṃ sahajātānaṃ asahajātānañca yathārahaṃ paccayabhāvo vattabbo. Koci panettha adhipativasena, koci kammavasena, koci āhāravasena, koci indriyavasena, koci jhānavasena, koci maggavasenapi paccayo hotīti. Ayampi viseso veditabboti idaṃ paṭiccasamuppādamukhena otaraṇaṃ. Ānandādīnampi imināva nayena khandhādimukhena otaraṇaṃ vibhāvetabbaṃ.

By the grasping of resentment, the aggregate of formations is included, and likewise by the grasping of dissatisfaction. By the grasping of displeasure, the aggregate of feeling is included—this is the mode of entry through the aggregates. Similarly, by grasping resentment and the like, the mind-base, the mind element, the truth of suffering, or the truth of origin is taken—this is the mode of entry through the bases, elements, and truths. Further, for resentment and the like, ignorance that arises together with them becomes a condition by way of the causal condition, co-nascence condition, mutual condition, dependence condition, association condition, presence condition, and non-disappearance condition; but for those not arising together, it becomes a condition by way of the immediately contiguous condition, contiguous condition, decisive support condition, absence condition, disappearance condition, and repetition condition; the immediately subsequent states become a condition only by way of decisive support. For craving, clinging, and the like, and also for contact and others, the conditionality of those arising together and not arising together should be stated appropriately. Here, some become conditions by way of dominance, some by way of kamma, some by way of nutriment, some by way of faculties, some by way of jhāna, and some even by way of the path. This distinction should also be understood—this is the mode of entry through dependent origination. For Ānanda and others as well, the mode of entry through aggregates and so forth should be explained by this same method.

Tathā sīlaṃ pāṇātipātādīhi viraticetanā, abyāpādādicetasikadhammā ca, pāṇātipātādayo cetanāva, tesaṃ tadupakārakadhammānañca lajjādayādīnaṃ saṅkhārakkhandhadhammāyatanādisaṅgaho, purimanayeneva khandhādimukhena ca otaraṇaṃ vibhāvetabbaṃ. Esa nayo ñāṇadiṭṭhivedanāavijjātaṇhādiggahaṇesu. Nissaraṇaanupādāvimuttigahaṇesu asaṅkhatadhātuvasenapi dhātumukhena otaraṇaṃ vibhāvetabbaṃ. Tathā “vedanānaṃ…pe… anupādāvimutto”ti etena bhagavato sīlādayo pañca dhammakkhandhā, satipaṭṭhānādayo ca bodhipakkhiyadhammā pakāsitā hontīti taṃ mukhenapi otaraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. “Tadapi phassapaccayā”ti diṭṭhipaññāpanassa paccayādhīnavuttitādīpanena aniccatāmukhena otaraṇaṃ, tathā evaṃdhammatāya paṭiccasamuppādamukhena otaraṇaṃ, aniccassa dukkhānattabhāvato appaṇihitamukhena suññatāmukhena ca otaraṇaṃ. Sesapadesupi eseva nayoti ayaṃ otaraṇo hāro.

Thus, virtue is the volition of abstention from killing living beings, etc., and mental factors such as non-ill-will, etc. Actions like killing living beings, etc., are themselves volitions, and the inclusion of their supporting phenomena such as moral shame and so forth in the aggregate of formations, mind-base, etc. The mode of entry through the aggregates and so forth should be explained in the same way as before. This method applies to the grasping of knowledge, views, feelings, ignorance, craving, and so forth. For the grasping of deliverance and liberation without clinging, the mode of entry should also be explained through the element aspect, even by way of the unconditioned element. Likewise, in the passage, “For feelings... liberated through non-clinging,” the Blessed One’s five Dhamma-aggregates beginning with virtue, etc., and the wings to awakening such as the foundations of mindfulness are revealed; thus, the mode of entry should also be understood through this approach. “That too is conditioned by contact”—for the designation of the view, the mode of entry by way of impermanence is shown by indicating dependence on conditions. Similarly, by the nature of things, the mode of entry is shown through dependent origination. Because the impermanent is suffering and non-self, the mode of entry is shown by way of the desireless and by way of emptiness. In the remaining passages, this same method applies. This is the mode of entry.

Sodhanahāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Mode of Purification

“Mamaṃ [V 1.0179] vā…pe… bhāseyyu”nti ārambho. “Dhammassa…pe… saṅghassa…pe… bhāseyyu”nti padasuddhi, no ārambhasuddhi. “Tatra tumhehi…pe… karaṇīyā”ti padasuddhi ceva ārambhasuddhi ca. Dutiyanayādīsupi eseva nayo[P 1.0263]. Tathā “appamattakaṃ kho paneta”ntiādi ārambho. “Katama”ntiādi pucchā. “Pāṇātipātaṃ pahāyā”tiādi padasuddhi, no ārambhasuddhi, no ca pucchāsuddhi. “Idaṃ kho”tiādi pucchāsuddhi ceva padasuddhi ca ārambhasuddhi ca.

“‘They might speak about me…’ is the beginning. “‘They might speak about the Dhamma…about the Saṅgha…’” is purity of the words, not purity of the beginning. “‘There you should…do what is to be done,’” is purity of the words and purity of the beginning. The same method applies in the second method and so on. Similarly, “‘But this is a minor matter…’” and so on is the beginning. “‘What…?’” and so on is the question. “‘Having abandoned the taking of life…’” and so on is purity of the words, not purity of the beginning, nor purity of the question. “‘This indeed…’” and so on is purity of the question, purity of the words, and purity of the beginning.

Tathā “atthi bhikkhave”tiādi ārambho. “Katame ca te”tiādi pucchā. “Santi bhikkhave”tiādi ārambho. “Ki”ntiādi ārambha pucchā. “Yathāsamāhite”tiādi [M 1.0203] padasuddhi, no ārambhasuddhi no ca pucchāsuddhi. “Ime kho te”tiādi padasuddhi ceva pucchāsuddhi ca ārambhasuddhi ca. Iminā nayena sabbattha ārambhādayo veditabbāti. Ayaṃ sodhano hāro.

Thus, “Monks, there is,” and so on is the beginning. “And what are these?” and so on is the question. “Monks, there are,” and so on is the beginning. “What?” and so on is the beginning and the question. “As one is concentrated” and so on is the purity of words, but not the purity of the beginning, nor the purity of the question. “These, indeed, are those” and so on is the purity of words, and the purity of the question, and the purity of the beginning. In this way, the beginning and so on should be understood in all cases. This is the mode of purification.

Adhiṭṭhānahāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Mode of Determination

“Avaṇṇa”nti sāmaññato adhiṭṭhānaṃ taṃ, avikappetvā visesavacanaṃ “mamaṃ vā dhammassa vā saṅghassa vā”ti. Sukkapakkhepi eseva nayo.

“Disparagement” is a general determination; without distinguishing it, the specific expression is: “of me, or of the Dhamma, or of the Saṅgha.” The same method applies to the wholesome side.

Tathā “sīla”nti sāmaññato adhiṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ avikappetvā visesavacanaṃ “pāṇātipātā paṭivirato”tiādi.

Thus, “virtue” is a general determination; without distinguishing it, the specific expression is: “abstaining from killing living beings,” and so forth.

“Aññeva dhammā”tiādi sāmaññato adhiṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ avikappetvā visesavacanaṃ “tayidaṃ bhikkhave tathāgato pajānātī”tiādi.

“Other phenomena” and so on is a general determination; without distinguishing it, the specific expression is: “This, monks, the Tathāgata understands,” and so forth.

Tathā “pubbantakappikā”tiādi sāmaññato adhiṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ avikappetvā visesavacanaṃ “sassatavādā”tiādi. Iminā nayena sabbattha sāmaññaviseso niddhāretabboti ayaṃ adhiṭṭhāno hāro.

Similarly, “those who speculate about the past” and so on is a general determination; without distinguishing it, the specific expression is “eternalists” and so on. In this way, everywhere the general and the specific should be determined; this is the mode of determination.

Parikkhārahāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Mode of Requisites

Āghātādīnaṃ [V 1.0180] “anatthaṃ me acarī”tiādīni (dha. sa. 1237; vibha. 909) ca ekūnavīsati āghātavatthūni hetu. Ānandādīnaṃ ārammaṇe abhisineho hetu. Sīlassa hiriottappaṃ appicchatādayo ca hetu. “Gambhīrā”tiādinā vuttadhammassa sabbāpi pāramiyo hetu, visesena paññāpāramī. Diṭṭhīnaṃ asappurisūpassayo, asaddhammassavanaṃ, micchābhinivesena ayonisomanasikāro ca avisesena [P 1.0264] hetu, visesena pana sassatavādādīnaṃ atītajātianussaraṇādi hetu. Vedanānaṃ avijjātaṇhākammāni phasso ca hetu. Anupādāvimuttiyā ariyamaggo hetu. Paññāpanassa ayonisomanasikāro hetu. Taṇhāya saṃyojaniyesu assādānupassanā hetu. Phassassa chaḷāyatanāni, chaḷāyatanassa nāmarūpaṃ hetu. Bhavanettisamucchedassa visuddhibhāvanā hetūti ayaṃ parikkhāro hāro.

For resentment and so on, “they have done me harm” and so on (Dhs § 1237; Vibh § 909) and the nineteen bases of resentment are the cause. For joy and so on, attachment to the object is the cause. For virtue, moral shame and fear of wrongdoing, contentment, and so on are causes. For the Dhamma described as “profound” and so on, all the perfections are causes, especially the perfection of wisdom. For views, association with unworthy persons, listening to untrue Dhamma, and improper attention due to wrong adherence are generally the causes; specifically, for eternalist views and so on, recollection of past lives and so on is the cause. For feelings, ignorance, craving, kamma, and contact are causes. For liberation without clinging, the Noble Path is the cause. For designation, improper attention is the cause. For craving, seeing gratification in what is subject to the fetters is the cause. For contact, the six sense bases are the cause; for the six sense bases, name-and-form is the cause. For the eradication of the guide to renewed existence, the development of purification is the cause—this is the mode of requisites.

Samāropanahāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Mode of Application

Āghātādīnaṃ [M 1.0204] akaraṇīyatāvacanena khantisampadā dassitā hoti. “Appamattakaṃ kho paneta”ntiādinā soraccasampadā, “atthi bhikkhave”tiādinā ñāṇasampadā, “aparāmasato cassa paccattaññeva nibbuti viditā”ti, “vedanānaṃ…pe… yathābhūtaṃ viditvā anupādāvimutto”ti etehi samādhisampadāya saddhiṃ vijjāvimuttivasībhāvasampadā dassitā hoti. Tattha khantisampadā paṭisaṅkhānabalasiddhito soraccasampadāya padaṭṭhānaṃ. Soraccasampadā pana atthato sīlameva, tathā pāṇātipātādīhi paṭivirativacanaṃ sīlassa pariyāyavibhāgadassanatthaṃ. Tattha sīlaṃ samādhissa padaṭṭhānaṃ, samādhi paññāya padaṭṭhānaṃ. Tesu sīlena vītikkamappahānaṃ duccaritasaṃkilesappahānañca sijjhati, samādhinā pariyuṭṭhānappahānaṃ, vikkhambhanappahānaṃ, taṇhāsaṃkilesappahānañca sijjhati. Paññāya diṭṭhisaṃkilesappahānaṃ, samucchedappahānaṃ, anusayappahānañca sijjhatīti sīlādīhi tīhi dhammakkhandhehi samathavipassanābhāvanāpāripūrī, pahānattayasiddhi cāti ayaṃ samāropano hāro.

By the statement that one should not harbor anger and so forth, the perfection of patience is shown. By the phrase, 'This is but a trifle,' and so on, the perfection of gentleness is shown. By the phrase, 'There is, monks,' and so on, the perfection of knowledge is shown. By the statements, 'For one who does not grasp, Nibbāna is known personally,' and 'having understood feelings... as they truly are, one is liberated through non-clinging,' the perfection of mastery in knowledge and liberation is shown, together with the perfection of concentration. Therein, the perfection of patience, being accomplished through the power of reflection, is the foundation for the perfection of gentleness. The perfection of gentleness, in essence, is virtue itself. Similarly, the statement about refraining from killing living beings and so forth is for the purpose of showing the classification of virtue through its various expressions. Therein, virtue is the foundation for concentration, and concentration is the foundation for wisdom. Among these, through virtue, the abandoning of transgression and the abandoning of the defilement of misconduct are accomplished. Through concentration, the abandoning of obsession, the abandoning by suppression, and the abandoning of the defilement of craving are accomplished. Through wisdom, the abandoning of the defilement of views, the abandoning by eradication, and the abandoning of latent tendencies are accomplished. Thus, through these three aggregates of the Dhamma—virtue and so forth—the complete fulfillment of the development of serenity and insight and the achievement of the threefold abandoning are accomplished. This is the method of application.

Soḷasahāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Sixteen Methods is completed.

Pañcavidhanayavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Fivefold Method

Nandiyāvaṭṭanayavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Nandiyāvaṭṭana Method

Āghātādīnaṃ [V 1.0181] akaraṇavacanena taṇhāvijjāsaṅkoco dassito hoti. Sati hi attattaniyavatthūsu sinehe sammose ca “anatthaṃ me acarī”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1237, vibha. 909) āghāto jāyatīti, tathā “pāṇātipātā paṭivirato”tiādivacanehi[P 1.0265], “paccattaññeva nibbuti viditā, anupādāvimutto, channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ…pe… yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”tiādīhi vacanehi ca taṇhāvijjānaṃ accantappahānaṃ dassitaṃ hoti. Tāsaṃ pana pubbantakappikādipadehi “ajānataṃ apassata”ntiādipadehi ca sarūpato dassitānaṃ taṇhāvijjānaṃ rūpadhammā arūpadhammā ca adhiṭṭhānaṃ. Yathākkamaṃ samatho ca vipassanā ca paṭipakkho. Tesaṃ cetovimutti paññāvimutti ca phalaṃ. Tattha [M 1.0205] taṇhā, taṇhāvijjā vā samudayasaccaṃ, tadadhiṭṭhānabhūtā rūpārūpadhammā dukkhasaccaṃ, tesaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, nirodhapajānanā samathavipassanā maggasaccanti evaṃ catusaccayojanā veditabbā. Taṇhāggahaṇena cettha māyāsāṭheyyamānātimānamadappamādapāpicchatāpāpamittatāahirikānottappādivasena sabbo akusalapakkho netabbo. Tathā avijjāggahaṇena viparītamanasikārakodhupanāhamakkhapalāsaissāmacchariyasārambhadovacassatā- bhavadiṭṭhivibhavadiṭṭhādivasena akusalapakkho netabbo. Vuttavipariyāyena amāyāasāṭheyyādiaviparītamanasikārādivasena, tathā samathapakkhiyānaṃ saddhindriyādīnaṃ, vipassanāpakkhiyānañca aniccasaññādīnaṃ vasena kusalapakkho netabboti. Ayaṃ nandiyāvaṭṭassa nayassa bhūmi.

By the statement that one should not harbor hatred and so forth, the curtailment of craving and ignorance is shown. For when there is attachment and confusion regarding things pertaining to oneself and what is one's own, hatred arises with thoughts like, 'They have done me harm,' and so on (Dhammasaṅgaṇi 1237, Vibhaṅga 909). Similarly, through statements like, 'One abstains from killing living beings,' and 'Nibbāna is known personally; one is liberated without clinging; one understands the six sense bases… as they actually are,' the complete abandonment of craving and ignorance is shown. Furthermore, for craving and ignorance—which are shown in their own nature by terms like 'those who speculate about the past' and 'not knowing, not seeing'—material and immaterial phenomena are the basis. In sequence, serenity and insight are their antidotes. The result for them is liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. Herein, craving—or craving and ignorance—is the truth of the origin. The material and immaterial phenomena that are their basis constitute the truth of suffering. Their non-arising is the truth of cessation. The understanding of cessation, which is serenity and insight, is the truth of the path. Thus, the connection to the Four Noble Truths should be understood. By the term 'craving' here, the entire unwholesome side should be understood—such as deceit, craftiness, pride, conceit, intoxication, negligence, evil wishes, bad friendship, shamelessness, and lack of moral dread. Similarly, by the term 'ignorance,' the unwholesome side should be understood—such as improper attention, anger, animosity, disparagement, insolence, envy, stinginess, contentiousness, obstinacy, the view of existence, and the view of non-existence. Conversely, the wholesome side should be understood through their opposites—such as honesty, absence of craftiness, proper attention, and so on—as well as through the factors belonging to serenity, like the faculty of faith, and the factors belonging to insight, like the perception of impermanence. This is the basis of the Nandiyāvaṭṭana method.

Tipukkhalanayavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Threefold Method

Āghātādīnaṃ akaraṇavacanena adosasiddhi, tathā pāṇātipātapharusavācāhi paṭivirativacanena. Ānandādīnaṃ akaraṇavacanena alobhasiddhi, tathā abrahmacariyato paṭivirativacanena. Adinnādānādīhi pana paṭivirativacanena ubhayasiddhi. “Tayidaṃ bhikkhave tathāgato pajānātī”tiādinā amohasiddhi. Iti tīhi akusalamūlehi gahitehi tappaṭipakkhato, āghātādiakaraṇavacanena ca tīṇi kusalamūlāni siddhāniyeva honti. Tattha tīhi akusalamūlehi [P 1.0266] tividhaduccaritasaṃkilesamalavisamākusalasaññāvitakkāsaddhammādivasena sabbo akusalapakkho vitthāretabbo. Tathā tīhi kusalamūlehi tividhasucaritavodānasamakusalasaññāvitakkapaññāsaddhammasamādhi- vimokkhamukhavimokkhādivasena [V 1.0182] sabbo kusalapakkho vibhāvetabbo. Etthāpi ca saccayojanā veditabbā. Kathaṃ? Lobho sabbāni vā kusalākusalamūlāni samudayasaccaṃ, tehi pana nibbattā tesaṃ adhiṭṭhānagocarabhūtā upādānakkhandhā dukkhasaccantiādinā nayena saccayojanā veditabbāti ayaṃ tipukkhalassa nayassa bhūmi.

By the statement that one should not harbor ill will and so forth, the establishment of non-aversion is achieved, and similarly by the statement of refraining from killing living beings and from harsh speech. By the statement that one should not indulge in delight and so forth, the establishment of non-greed is achieved, and similarly by the statement of refraining from unchastity. By the statement of refraining from taking what is not given and so forth, however, both are established. Through the passage beginning, 'This, monks, the Tathāgata understands,' the establishment of non-delusion is achieved. Thus, when the three unwholesome roots are grasped, the three wholesome roots are thereby established through their opposites and through the statement that one should not harbor ill will and so forth. Here, the entire unwholesome side should be elaborated in terms of the three unwholesome roots, as threefold misconduct, defilements, impurity, unwholesome perceptions, unwholesome thoughts, false doctrines, and so on. Similarly, the entire wholesome side should be explained in terms of the three wholesome roots, as threefold good conduct, purity, wholesome perceptions, wholesome thoughts, wisdom, the true Dhamma, concentration, liberation, the doors to liberation, and so on. Here too, the connection to the truths should be understood. How? Greed, or all the wholesome and unwholesome roots, is the truth of the origin; the aggregates of clinging, which are produced by them and serve as their basis and object, are the truth of suffering. In this way, the connection to the truths should be understood. This is the basis of the Tipukkhala method.

Sīhavikkīḷitanayavavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Lion's Play Method

Āghātānandanādīnaṃ akaraṇavacanena satisiddhi. Satiyā hi sāvajjānavajje, tattha ca ādīnavānisaṃse sallakkhetvā sāvajjaṃ pahāya anavajjaṃ [M 1.0206] samādāya vattatīti. Tathā micchājīvā paṭivirativacanena vīriyasiddhi. Vīriyena hi kāmabyāpādavihiṃsāvitakke vinodeti, vīriyasādhanañca ājīvapārisuddhisīlanti. Pāṇātipātādīhi paṭivirativacanena satisiddhi. Satiyā hi sāvajjānavajje, tattha ca ādīnavānisaṃse sallakkhetvā sāvajjaṃ pahāya anavajjaṃ samādāya vattati. Tathā hi sā “visayābhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā”ti ca vuccati. “Tayidaṃ bhikkhave tathāgato pajānātī”tiādinā samādhipaññāsiddhi. Paññāya hi yathābhūtāvabodho, samāhito ca yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti. Tathā “nicco dhuvo”tiādinā anicce “nicca”nti vipallāso, “arogo paraṃ maraṇā, ekantasukhī attā diṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto”ti ca evamādīhi asukhe “sukha”nti vipallāso, “pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito”tiādinā asubhe “subha”nti vipallāso, sabbeheva ca diṭṭhidīpakapadehi anattani “attā”ti vipallāsoti evamettha cattāro vipallāsā siddhā honti, tesaṃ paṭipakkhato cattāri satipaṭṭhānāni siddhāneva honti. Tattha catūhi indriyehi cattāro puggalā niddisitabbā.

The establishment of mindfulness is achieved by the statement that one should not harbor ill will, indulge in delight, and so forth. For it is through mindfulness that one discerns what is blameworthy and what is blameless, and having reflected on the dangers and benefits therein, one abandons the blameworthy and undertakes the blameless, thus conducting oneself accordingly. Similarly, the establishment of energy is achieved by the statement of abstaining from wrong livelihood. For it is through energy that one dispels thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, and harm; and the virtue of purity of livelihood is an accomplishment of energy. The establishment of mindfulness is also achieved by the statement of abstaining from killing living beings and so forth. For through mindfulness, one discerns what is blameworthy and what is blameless, and having reflected on the dangers and benefits therein, one abandons the blameworthy and undertakes the blameless, thus conducting oneself. For it is also said that mindfulness has the characteristic of 'confronting an object.' Through the passage beginning, 'This, monks, the Tathāgata understands,' the establishment of concentration and wisdom is achieved. For through wisdom there is understanding of things as they truly are, and one who is concentrated understands things as they truly are. Similarly, through passages like 'permanent, stable,' the distortion of perceiving the impermanent as permanent arises. Through statements like 'free from illness after death, the self is perfectly happy, having attained Nibbāna in this very life,' the distortion of perceiving the unsatisfactory as happiness arises. Through passages like 'endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure,' the distortion of perceiving the foul as beautiful arises. And through all the passages that illuminate views, the distortion of perceiving what is not-self as self arises. Thus, in this way the four distortions are established, and through their opposites, the four foundations of mindfulness are likewise established. Herein, four types of individuals should be indicated by the four faculties.

Kathaṃ? Duvidho hi taṇhācarito mudindriyo ca tikkhindriyo cāti, tathā diṭṭhicarito. Tesu paṭhamo asubhe “subha”nti vipallattadiṭṭhi satibalena yathābhūtaṃ kāyasabhāvaṃ sallakkhetvā sammattaniyāmaṃ okkamati. Dutiyo asukhe “sukha”nti vipallattadiṭṭhi “uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāsetī”tiādinā [P 1.0267] (ma. ni. 1.26; a. ni. 4.14; 6.58) vuttena vīriyasaṃvarasaṅkhātena vīriyabalena taṃ vipallāsaṃ vidhamati. Tatiyo anicce “nicca”nti ayāthāvagāhī samathabalena samāhitabhāvato saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇikabhāvaṃ yathābhūtaṃ paṭivijjhati. Catuttho santatisamūhakiccārammaṇaghanavicittattā phassādidhammapuñjamatte anattani “attā”ti [V 1.0183] micchābhinivesī catukoṭikasuññatāmanasikārena taṃ micchābhinivesaṃ viddhaṃseti. Catūhi cettha vipallāsehi caturāsavoghayogakāyaganthaagatitaṇhuppādupādānasattaviññāṇaṭṭhitiapariññādivasena sabbo akusalapakkho netabbo. Tathā catūhi satipaṭṭhānehi catubbidhajhānavihārādhiṭṭhānasukhabhāgiyadhammaappamaññāsammappadhānaiddhipādādivasena sabbo vodānapakkho netabboti ayaṃ sīhavikkīḷitassa nayassa bhūmi. Idhāpi subhasaññāsukhasaññāhi, catūhipi vā vipallāsehi samudayasaccaṃ[M 1.0207], tesaṃ adhiṭṭhānārammaṇabhūtā pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhasaccantiādinā saccayojanā veditabbā.

How? For the craving-natured person is of two kinds: one with dull faculties and one with sharp faculties; likewise the view-natured person. Among them, the first, whose view is perverted to see 'beauty' in the unattractive, discerns the true nature of the body with the power of mindfulness and enters the fixed course of rightness. The second, whose view is perverted to see 'pleasure' in what is suffering, shatters that perversion with the power of energy, which is termed restraint by energy, spoken of as 'one does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensuality' (MN 1.26; AN 4.14; 6.58), and so on. The third, who wrongly grasps 'permanence' in the impermanent, penetrates the momentary nature of formations as they truly are with the power of tranquility, due to having a concentrated mind. The fourth, who wrongly adheres to 'self' in what is merely a collection of phenomena such as contact—due to its continuity, collection, function, object, density, and variety—destroys that wrong adherence through the contemplation of the four-limbed emptiness. Here, through these four perversions, the entire unwholesome side should be understood in terms of the four taints, floods, yokes, bodily knots, wrong courses, the arising of craving, clinging, beings, stations of consciousness, non-full-comprehension, and so on. Similarly, through the four establishments of mindfulness, the entire side of purification should be understood in terms of the four kinds of jhānic dwellings, determination, qualities partaking of happiness, the immeasurables, right strivings, bases of psychic power, and so on. This is the ground for the method of the lion's sport. Here too, the truth of the origin should be understood through the perceptions of beauty and pleasure, or through all four perversions; and the five aggregates of clinging, which are the basis and object for them, are the truth of suffering, and so on. Thus the connection to the truths should be understood.

Disālocanaaṅkusanayadvayavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Two Methods of Directional Survey and the Goad.

Iti tiṇṇaṃ atthanayānaṃ siddhiyā vohāranayadvayampi siddhameva hoti. Tathā hi atthanayadisābhūtadhammānaṃ samālocanaṃ disālocanaṃ, tesaṃ samānayanaṃ aṅkusoti niyuttā pañca nayā.

Thus, with the accomplishment of the three methods of meaning, the two methods of expression are also accomplished. For the thorough survey of phenomena that are the directions for the methods of meaning is the Directional Survey (disālocana), and their bringing together is the Goad (aṅkusa); thus, the five methods are designated.

Pañcavidhanayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Fivefold Method is concluded.

Sāsanapaṭṭhānavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Foundation of the Teaching.

Idaṃ suttaṃ soḷasavidhe suttantapaṭṭhāne saṃkilesavāsanāsekkhabhāgiyaṃ, saṃkilesanibbedhāsekkhabhāgiyameva vā. Aṭṭhavīsatividhe pana suttantapaṭṭhāne lokiyalokuttaraṃ sattadhammādhiṭṭhānaṃ ñāṇañeyyadassanabhāvanaṃ sakavacanaparavacanaṃ vissajjanīyāvissajjanīyaṃ kusalākusalaṃ anuññātapaṭikkhittañcāti veditabbaṃ.

This discourse, in the sixteenfold classification of discourses, pertains either to the defilements and latent tendencies of one in higher training, or it pertains to the breakthrough of defilements of one in higher training. In the twenty-eightfold classification of discourses, it should be understood as worldly and supramundane; founded on the seven qualities; knowledge, the knowable, vision, and development; one's own words and the words of others; what requires explanation and what does not; wholesome and unwholesome; and what is permitted and prohibited.

Pakaraṇanayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Method of Treatises is concluded.

Brahmajālasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Brahmajāla Sutta is concluded.

2. Sāmaññaphalasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Sāmaññaphala Sutta.

Rājāmaccakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Account of the King and his Minister.

150. Rājagaheti [V 1.0184][M 1.0208][P 1.0268] ettha duggajanapadaṭṭhānavisesasampadādiyogato padhānabhāvena rājūhi gahitanti rājagahanti āha “mandhātu…pe… vuccatī”ti. Tattha mahāgovindena mahāsattena pariggahitaṃ reṇuādīhi rājūhi pariggahitameva hotīti mahāgovindaggahaṇaṃ. Mahāgovindoti mahānubhāvo eko purātano rājāti keci. Pariggahitattāti rājadhānībhāvena pariggahitattā. Pakāreti nagaramāpanena raññā kāritasabbagehattā rājagahaṃ, gijjhakūṭādīhi parikkhittattā pabbatarājehi parikkhittagehasadisantipi rājagahaṃ, sampannabhavanatāya rājamānaṃ gehanti pi rājagahaṃ, saṃvihitārakkhatāya anatthāvahabhāvena upagatānaṃ paṭirājūnaṃ gahaṃ gehabhūtantipi rājagahaṃ, rājūhi disvā sammā patiṭṭhāpitattā tesaṃ gahaṃ gehabhūtantipi rājagahaṃ, ārāmarāmaṇeyyakādīhi rājate, nivāsasukhatādinā sattehi mamattavasena gayhati, pariggayhatīti vā rājagahanti edise pakāre so padeso ṭhānavisesabhāvena uḷārasattaparibhogoti āha “taṃ paneta”ntiādi. Tesanti yakkhānaṃ. Vasanavananti āpānabhūmibhūtaṃ upavanaṃ.

150. Herein, Rājagaha is so called because it was primarily seized by kings due to its excellent qualities, such as being a special place in a region difficult of access; it is said, "Mandhātu… and so on… is called." There, because it was occupied by the great being Mahāgovinda, it was effectively occupied by kings such as Reṇu—hence the mention of Mahāgovinda. Some say, "Mahāgovinda" refers to a powerful ancient king. "Because of being occupied" means because of being occupied as a royal capital. It is Rājagaha because it is a house for all, made by a king with city planning; because it is surrounded by mountains like Vulture Peak, it is like a house surrounded by kingly mountains, thus it is also Rājagaha; because of its splendid buildings, it is a shining house (rājamānaṃ gehaṃ), thus it is also Rājagaha; because it is well-guarded, it is a house, a prison, for hostile kings who have come bringing misfortune, thus it is also Rājagaha; because kings, having seen it, properly established it, it is their house, thus it is also Rājagaha; and because it shines (rājate) with delightful parks and so on, or because beings grasp it (gayhati) with a sense of 'mine' due to the comfort of dwelling there, or because it is embraced (pariggayhati). In such ways, that region is a special place for the enjoyment of great beings, hence it is said, "But that…" and so on. "Of them" means of the yakkhas. "Vasanavana" means a pleasure grove that is a place of resort.

Avisesenāti “pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharati” (ma. ni. 1.69; 3.75; vibha. 508), “paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, (dī. ni. 1.226; saṃ. ni. 2.152; a. ni. 4.123; pārā. 11) “mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati”, (dī. ni. 1.556; 3.308; ma. ni. 1.77, 459, 509; 2.309, 315, 451, 471; 3.230; vibha. 642) “sabbanimittānaṃ [P 1.0269] amanasikārā animittaṃ cetosamādhiṃ samāpajjitvā viharatī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.459) viya saddantarasannidhānasiddhena visesaparāmasanena vinā. Iriyāya kāyikakiriyāya pavattanūpāyabhāvato [V 1.0185] pathoti iriyāpatho. Ṭhānādīnañhi gatinivatti ādiavatthāhi vinā na kañci kāyikakiriyaṃ pavattetuṃ sakkā. Viharati pavattati etena, viharaṇañcāti vihāro, dibbabhāvāvaho vihāro dibbavihāro, mahaggatajjhānāni. Nettiyaṃ pana “catasso āruppasamāpattiyo āneñjā vihārā”ti vuttaṃ[M 1.0209]. Taṃ tāsaṃ mettājhānādīnaṃ brahmavihāratā viya bhāvanāvisesabhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana dibbabhāvāvahasāmaññato tāpi “dibbavihārā” tveva vuttā. Hitūpasaṃhārādivasena pavattiyā brahmabhūtā seṭṭhabhūtā vihārāti brahmavihārā, mettājhānādikā. Anaññasādhāraṇattā ariyānaṃ vihārāti ariyavihārā, catassopi phalasamāpattiyo. Samaṅgīparidīpananti samaṅgibhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Iriyāpathasamāyogaparidīpanaṃ itaravihārasamāyogaparidīpanassa visesavacanassa abhāvato, iriyāpathasamāyogaparidīpanassa ca atthasiddhattā. Viharatīti ettha vi-saddo vicchedatthajotano, haratīti neti, pavattetīti attho. Tattha kassa kena vicchindanaṃ, kathaṃ kassa pavattananti antolīnaṃ codanaṃ sandhāyāha “so hī”tiādi.

Without specification means without the specific qualification achieved by the proximity of other words, as in: "He dwells, restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha" (MN 1.69; 3.75; Vibh 508); "having attained the first jhāna, he dwells" (DN 1.226; SN 2.152; AN 4.123; Pār 11); "with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, he dwells pervading one direction" (DN 1.556; 3.308; MN 1.77, 459, 509; 2.309, 315, 451, 471; 3.230; Vibh 642); "having entered the signless concentration of mind by not attending to any signs, he dwells" (MN 1.459), and so on. A posture (iriyāpatha) is a 'path' because it is the means (upāya) for the proceeding (pavattana) of bodily action (iriyā). For without the initial states of the cessation of movement, such as standing, no bodily action can be made to proceed. One dwells (viharati), one proceeds (pavattati) by means of it, and it is a dwelling (viharaṇa); therefore it is a vihāra. A dwelling that brings about a divine state is a divine dwelling (dibbavihāra); these are the sublime jhānas. In the Netti, however, it is said, "The four formless attainments are the imperturbable dwellings." That is said in reference to their being a special kind of development, just as the loving-kindness jhānas and so on have the quality of being divine abodes (brahmavihāra). But in the commentaries, because of the general characteristic of bringing about a divine state, they too are called "divine dwellings." Because they proceed by way of bringing benefit and so on, they are sublime (brahmabhūtā) and supreme (seṭṭhabhūtā) dwellings; therefore they are divine abodes (brahmavihārā), such as the loving-kindness jhānas. Because they are not shared by others, they are the noble ones' dwellings (ariyavihārā); these are the four fruition attainments. "Elucidation of being endowed" means the clarification of the state of being endowed. This refers to the clarification of the connection with posture, because there is no specific statement clarifying the connection with other dwellings, and because the clarification of the connection with posture is established by the meaning. Herein, in the word viharati, the prefix vi- indicates the meaning of separation; harati means 'carries,' that is, 'causes to proceed.' In this context, to address the implicit question, "Whose separation from what? How is whose proceeding carried on?" it is said, "For he..." and so on.

Gocaragāmadassanatthaṃ “rājagahe”ti vatvā buddhānaṃ anurūpanivāsanaṭṭhānadassanatthaṃ “ambavane”ti vuttanti āha “idamassā”tiādi. Etanti etaṃ “rājagahe”ti bhummavacanaṃ samīpatthe “gaṅgāya gāvo caranti, kūpe gaggakula”nti ca yathā. Kumārena [P 1.0270] bhatoti kumārabhato, so eva komārabhacco yathā bhisaggameva bhesajjaṃ. Dosābhisannanti vātapittādivasena ussannadosaṃ. Virecetvāti dosapakopato vivecetvā.

Having stated "in Rājagaha" to show the alms-resort village, it is said "in the mango grove" to show the place of residence suitable for Buddhas—thus, it is said, "this was his..." and so on. This word "in Rājagaha" is a locative of proximity, as in "cows graze by the Ganges" and "the Gagga family is at the well." "Nourished by the prince" (kumārena bhato) is kumārabhato; he is Komārabhacca, just as medicine (bhesajja) is from a physician (bhisagga). "Afflicted by humors" means with excessive humors, such as wind, bile, and so on. "Having purged" means having separated from the agitation of the humors.

Aḍḍhateḷasahīti aḍḍhena terasahi aḍḍhaterasahi bhikkhusatehi. Tāni pana paññāsāya ūnāni terasabhikkhusatāni hontīti āha “aḍḍhasatenā”tiādi.

Aḍḍhateḷasahi means with twelve and a half hundreds of monks. These are thirteen hundred monks less fifty, hence it is said, "by half a hundred less," etc.

Rājatīti dibbati, sobhatīti attho. Rañjetīti rameti. Raññoti pitu bimbisārarañño. Sāsanaṭṭhena hiṃsanaṭṭhena sattu.

"Rājati" means 'shines' or 'is splendid.' "Rañjeti" means 'gladdens.' "Rañño" refers to his father, King Bimbisāra. An enemy (sattu) is so called in the sense of 'instructing' (sāsana) and in the sense of 'injuring' (hiṃsana).

Bhāriyeti garuke aññesaṃ asakkuṇeyye vā. Suvaṇṇasatthakenāti suvaṇṇamayena satthakena. Ayomayañhi rañño sarīraṃ upanetuṃ ayuttanti vadati. Suvaṇṇasatthakenāti vā suvaṇṇaparikkhatena satthakena bāhuṃ phālāpetvāti sirāvedhavasena bāhuṃ phalāpetvā udakena sambhinditvā pāyesi kevalassa lohitassa gabbhinitthiyā dujjīrabhāvato. Dhurāti dhurabhūtā, gaṇassa[V 1.0186], dhorayhāti attho. Dhuraṃ nīharāmīti gaṇadhuraṃ gaṇabandhiyaṃ nibbattemi. “Pubbe kho”tiādi khandhakapāḷi eva.

"Bhāriye" means heavy or difficult for others to bear. "Suvaṇṇasatthakena" means with a golden knife. For it is said that an iron knife is unsuitable for approaching the king's body. Or, "suvaṇṇasatthakena" means with a gold-decorated knife; having split the arm by opening a vein, and having mixed it with water, he gave it to drink, because the blood alone would be difficult for a pregnant woman to digest. "Dhurā" means bearing the burden, meaning the responsibility of the group. "Dhuraṃ nīharāmi" means I will fulfill the group's burden, I will accomplish the group's bond. The passage beginning "Pubbe kho" is indeed from the Khandhaka text.

Potthaniyanti [M 1.0210] churikaṃ, yaṃ “nakhara”ntipi [pothanikanti churikaṃ, yaṃ kharantipi (sārattha. ṭī. 3.339) pothanikanti churikaṃ, kharantipi (vi. vi. ṭī. 2.cūḷavaggavaṇṇanā 339)] vuccati. Divā divassāti divassapi divā, majjhanhikavelāyanti attho.

"Potthanī" means a knife, which is also called a "nakhara." "Divā divassa" means by day, even of the day, meaning at midday.

Tassā sarīraṃ lehitvā yāpeti attūpakkamena maraṇaṃ na yuttanti. Na hi ariyasāvakā attānaṃ vinipātentīti. Maggaphalasukhenāti maggaphalasukhāvahena sotāpattimaggaphalasukhūpasañhitena caṅkamena yāpeti. Cetiyaṅgaṇeti gandhapupphādīhi pūjanaṭṭhānabhūte cetiyaṅgaṇe[P 1.0271]. Nisajjanatthāyāti bhikkhusaṅghanisīdanatthāya. Cātumahārājikadevaloke…pe… yakkho hutvā nibbatti tattha bahulaṃ nibbattapubbatāya ciraparicitanikantivasena.

He sustains himself by licking her body, thinking self-inflicted death is not proper. For noble disciples do not destroy themselves. "Maggaphalasukhena" means he sustains himself by means of walking meditation that is conducive to the joy of the path and fruit, and is imbued with the joy of the path and fruit of stream-entry. "Cetiyaṅgaṇe" means in the courtyard of the shrine, a place for offering worship with perfumes and flowers. "Nisajjanatthāya" means for the purpose of seating the assembly of monks. In the Cātumahārājika heaven... having become a yakkha, he was reborn there because he had been reborn there frequently before, due to long familiarity and attachment.

Khobhetvāti puttasinehassa balavabhāvato, sahajātapītivegassa ca savipphāratāya taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpadhammehi pharaṇavasena sakalasarīraṃ āloḷetvā. Tenāha “aṭṭhimiñjaṃ āhacca aṭṭhāsī”ti. Pituguṇanti pitu attani sinehaguṇaṃ. Muñcāpetvāti ettha iti-saddo pakārattho, tena “abhimārakapurisapesanādippakārenā”ti vutte eva pakāre paccāmasati. Vitthārakathānayoti ajātasattupasādanādivasena vitthārato vattabbāya kathāya nayamattaṃ. Kasmā panettha vitthāranayā kathā na vuttāti āha “āgatattā pana sabbaṃ na vutta”nti.

"Khobhetvā" means having agitated the entire body by pervading it with the material phenomena arising therefrom, due to the strength of affection for his son and the intensity of the force of innate joy. Hence it is said, "piercing the marrow, he remained." "Pituguṇa" means the quality of the father's affection for himself. Regarding "Muñcāpetvā," here the word "iti" has the meaning of manner; therefore, it refers to the very manner spoken of, such as "by sending a killer man, etc." "Vitthārakathānayo" means simply the approach to a discourse that should be spoken in detail, such as the pacifying of Ajātasattu, etc. Why then is the discourse not given here in detail? He says, "However, not all is stated, due to its having been given elsewhere."

Kosalaraññoti mahākosalarañño. Paṇḍitādhivacananti paṇḍitavevacanaṃ. Vidantīti jānanti. Vedena ñāṇena karaṇabhūtena īhati pavattatīti vedehi.

"Kosalarañño" means of the great Kosala king. "Paṇḍitādhivacana" means a synonym for the wise. "Vidanti" means they know. It proceeds with knowledge as an instrument—thus, "vedehi."

Etthāti etasmiṃ divase. Anasanena vāti vā-saddo aniyamattho, tena ekaccamanoduccaritadussīlyādīni saṅgaṇhāti. Tathā hi gopālakūposatho abhijjhāsahagatacittassa vasena vutto, nigaṇṭhuposatho mosavajjādivasena. Yathāha “so tena abhijjhāsahagatena cetasā divasaṃ atināmetī”ti (a. ni. 1.71), “iti yasmiṃ samaye sacce samādapetabbā, musāvāde tasmiṃ samaye samādapentī”ti (a. ni. 1.71) ca ādi. Etthāti uposathasadde. Atthuddhāroti vattabbaatthānaṃ uddhāraṇaṃ.

Here, "ettha" means on this day. Regarding "anasanena vā," the word "vā" has the meaning of indefiniteness; thus, it encompasses some mental misconduct, bad conduct, and so forth. For instance, the cowherd's observance is described in terms of a mind accompanied by covetousness, while the Nigaṇṭha's observance involves false speech, etc. As it is said: "He spends the day with a mind accompanied by covetousness," and "At the time when one should be exhorted to truth, they exhort to false speech," and so on. Here, "ettha" refers to the word "uposatha." "Atthuddhāro" means the extraction of the meanings to be stated.

Nanu [V 1.0187][M 1.0211] ca atthamattaṃ pati [P 1.0272] saddā abhinivisantīti na ekena saddena aneke atthā abhidhīyantīti? Saccametaṃ saddavisese apekkhite, tesaṃ pana atthānaṃ uposathasaddavacanīyatā sāmaññaṃ upādāya vuccamāno ayaṃ vicāro uposathasaddassa atthuddhāroti vutto. Heṭṭhā “evaṃ me suta”ntiādīsu āgate atthuddhārepi eseva nayo. Kāmañca pātimokkhuddesādivisayopi uposathasaddo sāmaññarūpo eva visesasaddassa avācakabhāvato, tādisaṃ pana sāmaññaṃ anādiyitvā ayamattho vuttoti veditabbaṃ. Sīlasuddhivasena upetehi samaggehi vasīyati anuṭṭhīyatīti uposatho, pātimokkhuddeso. Samādānavasena adhiṭṭhānavasena vā upecca ariyavāsādiatthaṃ vasitabbato uposatho, sīlaṃ. Anasanādivasena upecca vasitabbato anuvasitabbato uposatho. Upavāsoti samādānaṃ. Uposathakulabhūtatāya navamahatthinikāyapariyāpanne hatthināge kiñci kiriyaṃ anapekkhitvā rūḷhivasena samaññāmattaṃ uposathoti āha “uposatho nāgarājātiādīsu paññattī”ti. Divase pana uposathasaddappavatti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttā eva. Suddhassa ve sadā phaggūti ettha pana suddhassāti sabbaso kilesamalābhāvena suddhassa. Veti nipātamattaṃ. Veti vā byattanti attho. Sadā phaggūti niccakālampi phagguṇanakkhattameva. Yassa hi phagguṇamāse uttaraphagguṇadivase titthanhānaṃ karontassa saṃvaccharikapāpapavāhanaṃ hotīti laddhi, taṃ tato vivecetuṃ idaṃ bhagavatā vuttaṃ. Suddhassuposatho sadāti yathāvuttasuddhiyā suddhassa uposathaṅgāni vatasamādānāni ca asamādiyatopi niccaṃ uposatho, uposathavāso evāti attho. Pañcadasannaṃ tithīnaṃ pūraṇavasena pannaraso.

Is it not the case that words adhere to a specific meaning, and that many meanings are not expressed by a single word? This is true when specific words are considered. However, this discussion, which is stated by taking the generality of the word 'uposatha' to denote those meanings, is called an 'extraction of the meaning of the word uposatha'. Earlier, in passages like 'Thus have I heard,' the same method applies to extracting meanings. Moreover, even in contexts like the recitation of the Pātimokkha, the term 'uposatha' is general in nature due to its not expressing a specific meaning. However, one should understand that this meaning is stated without taking such generality into account. By means of purity of virtue, it is dwelt in and observed by those in harmony—this is the uposatha, the Pātimokkha recitation. By undertaking, by resolve, or by approaching with the intention of dwelling in the noble abodes, etc., it is to be dwelt in—this is the uposatha, the virtue. By abstaining from food, etc., it is to be dwelt in or observed—this is the uposatha. Upavāsa means undertaking. And regarding the elephant king, included in the nine great elephant groups, who is of the Uposatha lineage, it is said that 'Uposatha is the king of elephants,' etc., as a mere designation by common usage, without considering any particular action. As for the occurrence of the term 'uposatha' in relation to the day, this has already been explained in the commentary. 'For the pure one, it is always the auspicious time'—here, 'for the pure one' means one who is entirely pure due to the absence of the stains of defilements. 'Ve' is merely a particle. Or 've' means 'manifest,' this is the meaning. 'Always the auspicious time' means that it is always the Phagguṇa constellation. For those who believe that on the day of Uttaraphalgunī in the month of Phagguna, performing a bathing ritual removes the sins of the year, the Blessed One spoke this to distinguish it from that. 'For the pure one, the uposatha is always'—for one possessing the purity as described, even if one does not undertake the uposatha factors and vows, it is always the uposatha; it is indeed the uposatha dwelling, this is the meaning. 'Fifteenth'—the fifteenth, by way of the completion of fifteen lunar days.

Bahuso[P 1.0273], atisayato vā kumudāni ettha santīti kumudavatī, tissaṃ kumudavatiyā. Catunnaṃ māsānaṃ pāripūribhūtāti cātumāsī. Sā eva pāḷiyaṃ cātumāsinīti vuttāti āha “idha pana cātumāsinīti vuccatī”ti. Tadā kattikamāsassa puṇṇatāya māsapuṇṇatā. Vassānassa utuno puṇṇatāya utupuṇṇatā. Kattikamāsalakkhitassa saṃvaccharassa puṇṇatāya saṃvaccharapuṇṇatā. “Mā” iti cando vuccati tassa gatiyā divasassa minitabbato. Ettha puṇṇoti etissā rattiyā sabbakalāpāripūriyā puṇṇo. Tadā hi cando sabbaso paripuṇṇo hutvā dissati. Ettha ca “tadahuposathe [M 1.0212] pannarase”ti padāni divasavasena vuttāni, “komudiyā”tiādīni rattivasena.

Because there are many lotuses here, or an abundance of them, it is called Kumudavatī; this refers to that Kumudavatī. Because it is the complete fulfillment of four months, it is called Cātumāsī. Because that same night is called Cātumāsinī in the Pāli, he says, "Here, however, it is called Cātumāsinī." At that time, because of the full moon of the month of Kattika, there is the fullness of the month. Because of the fullness of the rainy season, there is the fullness of the season. Because of the fullness of the year marked by the month of Kattika, there is the fullness of the year. "Mā" is said to be the moon, because the days are measured by its movement. Here, "puṇṇa" means it is full with the complete fullness of all phases of that night. At that time, indeed, the moon appears entirely full. Here, the words "on that uposatha, the fifteenth" are spoken with reference to the day, while the terms "Komudiyā" and so on are spoken with reference to the night.

Rājāmaccaparivutoti rājakulasamudāgatehi amaccehi parivuto. Atha vā anuyuttakarājūhi [V 1.0188] ceva amaccehi ca parivuto. Caturupakkilesāti abbhā mahikā dhūmarajo rāhūti imehi catūhi upakkilesehi. Sanniṭṭhānaṃ kataṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ.

"Surrounded by the king’s ministers" means surrounded by ministers who have arisen from the royal family. Alternatively, it means surrounded by both the appointed kings and the ministers. "The four impurities" refers to these four: clouds, mist, smoke and dust, and Rāhu. This has been established in the commentary.

Pītivacananti pītisamuṭṭhānaṃ vacanaṃ. Yañhi vacanaṃ paṭiggāhakanirapekkhaṃ kevalaṃ uḷārāya pītiyā vasena sarasato sahasāva mukhato niccharati, taṃ idha “udāna”nti adhippetaṃ. Tenāha “yaṃ pītivacanaṃ hadayaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkotī”tiādi.

"Words of joy" means speech originating from joy. For that speech which, independent of a receiver, bursts forth spontaneously and suddenly from the mouth due solely to the power of intense joy, is here intended by the term "udāna." Hence it is said, "that joyful utterance which the heart is unable to hold," and so on.

Dosehi itā gatā apagatāti dosinā ta-kārassa na-kāraṃ katvā yathā “kilese jito vijitāvīti jino”ti. Anīya-saddo kattuatthe veditabboti āha “manaṃ ramayatī”ti “ramaṇīyā”ti yathā “niyyānikā dhammā”ti. Juṇhavasena rattiyā surūpatāti āha “vuttadosavimuttāyā”tiādi. Tattha [P 1.0274] abbhādayo vuttadosā, tabbigameneva cassā dassanīyatā, tena, utusampattiyā ca pāsādikatā veditabbā. Lakkhaṇaṃ bhavituṃ yuttāti etissā rattiyā yutto divaso māso utu saṃvaccharoti evaṃ divasamāsautusaṃvaccharānaṃ sallakkhaṇaṃ bhavituṃ yuttā lakkhaññā, lakkhaṇīyāti attho.

She is called `dosinā` (the night) because faults have gone, departed, and gone away from her; this is formed by changing the letter 't' to 'n', just as one is called a `jina` because he has conquered the defilements. The word `ramaṇīyā` should be understood in the sense of an agent, as in 'it delights the mind,' just as in 'the teachings that lead out.' The beauty of the night due to the moonlight is described by the phrase 'free from the stated faults,' and so on. Here, clouds and so forth are the stated faults; by their very absence her loveliness is to be understood, and by the excellence of the season, her charm. She is `lakkhaññā` because she is fit to be a characteristic; that is, the day, month, season, and year associated with this night are suitable. Thus, she is `lakkhaññā` because she is fit to be a characteristic for discerning days, months, seasons, and years; the meaning is 'to be characterized.'

“Yaṃ no payirupāsato cittaṃ pasīdeyyā”ti vuttattā “samaṇaṃ vā brāhmaṇaṃ vā”ti ettha paramatthasamaṇo ca paramatthabrāhmaṇo ca adhippeto, na pabbajjāmattasamaṇo, na jātimattabrāhmaṇo cāti āha “samitapāpatāya samaṇaṃ. Bāhitapāpatāya brāhmaṇa”nti. Bahuvacane vattabbe ekavacanaṃ, ekavacane vā vattabbe bahuvacanaṃ vacanabyatayo. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana ekavacanavaseneva byatayo dassito. Attani, garuṭṭhāniye ca ekasmimpi bahuvacanappayogo nirūḷhoti. Sabbenapīti “ramaṇīyā vatā”tiādinā sabbena vacanena. Obhāsanimittakammanti obhāsabhūtanimittakammaṃ paribyattaṃ nimittakaraṇanti attho. Devadatto cāti. Ca-saddo attūpanayane, tena yathā rājā ajātasattu attano pitu ariyasāvakassa satthuupaṭṭhākassa ghātanena mahāparādho[M 1.0213], evaṃ bhagavato mahāanatthakarassa devadattassa avassayabhāvena pīti imamatthaṃ upaneti. Tassa piṭṭhichāyāyāti tassa jīvakassa piṭṭhiapassayena, taṃ pamukhaṃ katvā taṃ apassāyāti attho. Vikkhepapacchedanatthanti bhāviniyā attano kathāya uppajjanakavikkhepanassa pacchindanatthaṃ, anuppattiatthanti adhippāyo. Tenāha “tassaṃ hī”tiādi.

Because it was said, 'By attending on whom our minds might become bright,' here the ascetic in the ultimate sense and the brahmin in the ultimate sense are intended, not an ascetic merely by having gone forth, nor a brahmin merely by birth. Thus it is said: 'An ascetic, due to having stilled evil; a brahmin, due to having banished evil.' When the plural should be said, the singular is used, or when the singular should be said, the plural is used—this is a deviation of grammatical number. In the commentary, however, the deviation is shown by way of the singular. For oneself and for one in a respected position, the use of the plural for a single person is established. 'By all this' means by the entire statement beginning with, 'How delightful indeed!' 'The work of making a manifest sign' means the work of a sign that has become manifest; the meaning is the making of a clear sign. 'And Devadatta': the particle 'ca' is for introducing a comparison. Thus, just as King Ajātasattu was a great offender for killing his father, a noble disciple and attendant of the Teacher, so too this introduces the meaning regarding the inevitability of Devadatta, the great harm-doer to the Blessed One. 'In the shade of his back' means by leaning on Jīvaka's back, making him foremost, relying on him. 'For the purpose of cutting off distraction' means for the purpose of cutting off the distraction that would arise from his own future speech; the intended meaning is its non-arising. Therefore, it is said: 'For in that...' and so on.

151. “So kirā”tiādi porāṇaṭṭhakathāya āgatanayo. Eseva nayo parato makkhalipadanibbacanepi[V 1.0189]. Upasaṅkamantīti upagatā. Tadeva pabbajjaṃ aggahesīti tadeva naggarūpaṃ pabbajjaṃ katvā gaṇhi.

151. 'So, it is said,' and so forth is the method that has come down in the ancient commentary. This same method also applies later in the explanation of the word 'Makkhali.' 'Approaching' means having approached. 'He took up that very going forth' means he undertook the going forth in that very naked form.

Pabbajitasamūhasaṅkhāto [P 1.0275] saṅghoti pabbajitasamūhatāmattena saṅgho, na niyyānikadiṭṭhisuvisuddhasīlasāmaññavasena saṃhatattāti adhippāyo. Assa atthīti assa satthupaṭiññassa parivārabhūto atthi. Svevāti pabbajitasamūhasaṅkhātova. Keci pana “pabbajitasamūhavasena saṅghī, gahaṭṭhasamūhavasena gaṇī”ti vadanti, taṃ tesaṃ matimattaṃ gaṇe eva loke saṅgha-saddassa nirūḷhattā. Ācārasikkhāpanavasenāti acelaka vatacariyādiācārasikkhāpanavasena. Pākaṭoti saṅghīādibhāvena pakāsito. “Appiccho”ti vatvā tattha labbhamānaṃ appicchattaṃ dassetuṃ “appicchatāya vatthampi na nivāsetī”ti vuttaṃ. Na hi tasmiṃ sāsanike viya santaguṇanigūhaṇalakkhaṇā appicchatā labbhatīti. Yasoti kittisaddo. “Taranti etena saṃsārogha”nti evaṃ sammatattā titthaṃ vuccati laddhīti āha “titthakaroti laddhikaro”ti. Sādhusammatoti “sādhū”ti sammato, na sādhūhi sammatoti āha “ayaṃ sādhū”tiādi. “Imāni me vatasamādānāni ettakaṃ kālaṃ suciṇānī”ti pabbajitato paṭṭhāya atikkantā bahū rattiyo jānātīti rattaññū. Tā panassa rattiyo cirakālabhūtāti katvā ciraṃ pabbajitassa assāti cirapabbajito. Tattha cirapabbajitatāgahaṇena buddhisīlataṃ dasseti, rattaññutāgahaṇena tattha sampajānataṃ. Addhānanti dīghakālaṃ. Kittako pana soti āha “dve tayo rājaparivaṭṭe”ti, dvinnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ rājūnaṃ rajjaṃ anusāsanapaṭipāṭiyoti attho. “Addhagato”ti vatvā kataṃ vayogahaṇaṃ osānavayāpekkhanti āha “pacchimavayaṃ anuppatto”ti. Ubhayanti “addhagato, vayoanuppatto”ti padadvayaṃ.

The term 'Sangha' refers to the assembly of those who have gone forth, meaning it is a Sangha simply by being a gathering of those who have renounced, not by virtue of being united by views that lead to liberation and thoroughly purified virtue; this is the intended meaning. 'He has' means that he who claims to be a teacher has a following. 'The very same' means the very same assembly of those who have gone forth. Some, however, say, 'One is called a `saṅghī` due to an assembly of renouncers, and a `gaṇī` due to an assembly of householders,' but this is merely their opinion, for in the world, the term 'Sangha' is firmly established in reference to a community of renunciants. 'By training in conduct' refers to training in conduct such as the practices of naked ascetics and so on. 'Renowned' means made known by his status as a `saṅghī` or similar. Having stated 'of few wishes,' to show the quality of having few wishes found there, it is said, 'Out of having few wishes, he does not even wear a cloth.' For in him, the quality of having few wishes, which is characterized by concealing one's good qualities as in a follower of the Buddha's teaching, is not found. 'Fame' is the word for renown. 'They cross the flood of saṃsāra by this,' thus a doctrine is called a ford (`tittha`); hence it is said, 'a ford-maker' (`titthakaro`) means 'a doctrine-maker.' 'Esteemed as good' means esteemed as 'good,' not 'esteemed by the good'; hence it is said, 'This one is good,' and so forth. 'These vows I have undertaken, I have observed them well for so long'—knowing that many nights have passed since his renunciation, he is called a 'knower of nights' (`rattaññū`). And since those nights of his were of long duration, he is called 'long-renounced' (`cirapabbajito`). Here, by taking 'long-renounced' it indicates wisdom and virtue, while by taking 'knower of nights' it shows his clear comprehension in that regard. 'A long journey' means a long time. How long? It is said, 'two or three successions of kings,' meaning the sequence of the reigns of two or three kings. Having said 'far-gone on the journey,' the taking of 'age' refers to the final age, hence it is said, 'he has reached the last stage of life.' 'Both' refers to the two phrases: 'far-gone on the journey' and 'attained old age.'

Pubbe [M 1.0214][P 1.0276] pitarā saddhiṃ satthu santikaṃ gantvā desanāya sutapubbataṃ sandhāyāha “jhānābhiññādi…pe… sotukāmo”ti. Dassanenāti na dassanamattaṃ, disvā pana tena saddhiṃ ālāpasallāpaṃ katvā tato akiriyavādaṃ sutvā tesaṃ anattamano ahosi. Guṇakathāyāti abhūtaguṇakathāya. Tenāha “suṭṭhutaraṃ anattamano hutvā”ti. Yadi anattamano, kasmā tuṇhī ahosīti āha “anattamano samānopī”tiādi.

Referring to his prior experience of having gone to the Teacher’s presence with his father and heard the discourse, it is said, 'desiring to hear about jhāna, higher knowledge, and so forth.' 'By seeing' does not mean merely seeing; rather, after seeing him and engaging in conversation, and then hearing the doctrine of non-action from them, he became displeased. 'By the talk of virtues' means by the talk of non-existent virtues. Therefore, it is said, 'having become extremely displeased.' If he was displeased, why did he remain silent? It is said: 'although being displeased,' and so forth.

152. Gosālāyāti evaṃ nāmake gāme. Vassānakāle gunnaṃ tiṭṭhanasālāti eke.

152. 'In Gosālā' means in a village of that name. Some say it was a hall for cattle to stay in during the rainy season.

153. Paṭikiṭṭhataranti [V 1.0190] nihīnataraṃ. Tantāvutānīti tante pasāretvā vītāni. “Sīte sīto”tiādinā chahākārehi tassa nihīnassa nihīnatarataṃ dasseti.

153. 'More wretched' means more base. 'Woven with threads' means woven after spreading out the threads. By the six ways beginning with 'cold in the cold,' it shows the greater baseness of that base one.

154. Vaccaṃ katvāpīti pi-saddena bhojanaṃ bhuñjitvāpi kenaci asucinā makkhito pīti imamatthaṃ sampiṇḍeti. Vālikathūpaṃ katvāti vattavasena vālikāya thūpaṃ katvā.

154. 'Even after defecating': the particle 'pi' also includes this meaning: 'and even after eating food, and being smeared with some impurity.' 'Having made a sand stupa' means having made a stupa of sand according to custom.

156. Palibuddhanakilesoti saṃsāre palibuddhanakicco rāgādikileso khettavatthuputtadārādivisayo.

156. 'The defilement that is an obstruction' refers to the defilements such as lust, which have the function of creating an obstruction in saṃsāra, and which have as their domain fields, property, sons, wives, and so forth.

Komārabhaccajīvakakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of Jīvaka Komārabhacca

157. Na yathādhippāyaṃ vattatīti katvā vuttaṃ “anattho vata me”ti. Jīvakassa tuṇhībhāvo mama adhippāyassa maddanasadiso, tasmā taṃ pucchitvā kathāpanena mama adhippāyo pūretabboti ayamettha rañño ajjhāsayoti dassento “hatthimhi nu kho panā”tiādimāha. Kiṃ tuṇhīti kiṃ kāraṇā tuṇhī, kiṃ taṃ kāraṇaṃ, yena tuvaṃ tuṇhīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenāha “kena kāraṇena tuṇhī”ti.

157. Thinking, 'It is not proceeding according to my intention,' it was said, 'Alas, my purpose is lost!' Jīvaka’s silence is like the crushing of my intention; therefore, my intention should be fulfilled by questioning him and making him speak. Showing that this was the king's inclination here, he said, 'But what about on the elephant...?' and so forth. 'Why are you silent?' means 'For what reason are you silent? What is that reason for which you are silent?'—this is what is said. Therefore, he said, 'For what reason are you silent?'

Kāmaṃ sabbāpi tathāgatassa paṭipatti anaññasādhāraṇā acchariyaabbhutarūpā ca, tathāpi gabbhokkanti- [P 1.0277] abhijātiabhinikkhamanaabhisambodhidhammacakkappavattana- yamakapāṭihāriyadevorohaṇāni sadevake loke ativiya [M 1.0215] supākaṭāni, na sakkā kenaci paṭibāhitunti tāniyevettha uddhaṭāni. Itthambhūtākhyānattheti itthaṃ evaṃ pakāro bhūto jātoti evaṃ kathanatthe. Upayogavacananti. “Abbhuggato”ti ettha abhīti upasaggo itthambhūtākhyānatthajotako, tena yogato “taṃ kho pana bhagavanta”nti idaṃ sāmiatthe upayogavacanaṃ, tenāha “tassa kho pana bhagavatoti attho”ti. Kalyāṇaguṇasamannāgatoti kalyāṇehi guṇehi yutto, taṃ nissito tabbisayatāyāti adhippāyo. Seṭṭhoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Kittetabbato kitti, sā eva saddanīyato saddoti āha “kittisaddoti kittiyevā”ti. Abhitthavanavasena pavatto saddo thutighoso. Anaññasādhāraṇaguṇe ārabbha pavattattā sadevakaṃ lokaṃ ajjhottharitvā abhibhavitvā uggato.

Indeed, while all of the Tathāgata’s conduct is unique, marvelous, and wonderful, nevertheless, his descent into the womb, noble birth, renunciation, supreme enlightenment, turning of the Dhamma wheel, the twin miracle, and the descent from the world of gods are especially well-known in the world with its gods. Since no one can deny them, these alone are highlighted here. ‘Itthambhūtākhyānatthe’ means in the sense of narrating that such a type has been born. ‘Upayogavacana’ refers to the use of the accusative case. In the phrase ‘abbhuggato,’ the prefix ‘abhi-’ highlights the sense of narrating such a state; through connection with that, the phrase ‘taṃ kho pana bhagavantaṃ’ is an accusative used in the sense of the genitive. Therefore, he says, ‘the meaning is: of that Blessed One.’ ‘Kalyāṇaguṇasamannāgato’ means endowed with excellent qualities, implying that he is possessed of them and they are his domain. ‘Seṭṭho’ follows the same method. Fame (kitti) comes from that which is to be praised; it is called ‘sadda’ (sound) because it is what is to be heard; hence he said: ‘the sound of fame (kittisadda) is just fame.’ A sound occurring by way of intense praise is a roar of acclaim. Because it occurs regarding unique qualities, it has risen up, pervading and overcoming the world with its gods.

So bhagavāti yo so samatiṃ sapāramiyo pūretvā sabbakilese bhañjitvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ [V 1.0191] abhisambuddho devānaṃ atidevo sakkānaṃ atisakko brahmānaṃ atibrahmā lokanātho bhāgyavantatādīhi kāraṇehi sadevake loke “bhagavā”ti sabbattha patthaṭakittisaddo, so bhagavā. “Bhagavā”ti ca idaṃ satthu nāmakittanaṃ. Tenāha āyasmā dhammasenāpati “bhagavāti netaṃ nāmaṃ mātarā kata”ntiādi (mahāni. 84). Parato pana bhagavāti guṇakittanaṃ.

‘The Blessed One’ refers to him who, having fulfilled the thirty perfections, destroyed all defilements, and awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, is the God beyond gods, the Sakka beyond Sakkas, the Brahmā beyond Brahmās, and the Protector of the World. For reasons such as being fortunate, his sound of fame as ‘the Blessed One’ is spread everywhere in the world with its gods; he is the Blessed One. And ‘Bhagavā’ is an utterance of the Teacher’s name. Therefore, the Venerable Captain of the Dhamma said: ‘The name “Bhagavā” was not given by his mother,’ and so forth (Mahāni. 84). But further on, ‘Bhagavā’ is a praise of his virtues.

Yathā kammaṭṭhānikena “araha”ntiādīsu navaṭṭhānesu paccekaṃ iti-saddaṃ yojetvā buddhaguṇā anussarīyanti, evaṃ buddhaguṇasaṅkittakenāpīti dassento “itipi arahaṃ, itipi sammāsambuddho…pe… itipi bhagavā”ti āha. “Itipetaṃ [P 1.0278] abhūtaṃ, itipetaṃ ataccha”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.5) viya idha iti-saddo āsannapaccakkhakaraṇattho, pi-saddo sampiṇḍanattho, tena ca tesaṃ guṇānaṃ bahubhāvo dīpito. Tāni ca saṅkittentena viññunā cittassa sammukhībhūtāneva katvā saṅkittetabbānīti dassento “iminā ca iminā ca kāraṇenāti vuttaṃ hotī”ti āha. Evañhi nirūpetvā kittente yassa saṅkitteti, tassa bhagavati ativiya abhippasādo hoti. Ārakattāti suvidūrattā. Arīnanti kilesārīnaṃ. Arānanti saṃsāracakkassa arānaṃ. Hatattāti vihatattā. Paccayādīnanti cīvarādipaccayānañceva [M 1.0216] pūjāvisesānañca. Tatoti visuddhimaggato. Yathā ca visuddhimaggato, evaṃ taṃsaṃvaṇṇanatopi nesaṃ vitthāro gahetabbo.

Just as a meditator recollects the Buddha’s virtues by applying the word ‘iti’ (thus) individually in nine places such as ‘arahaṃ,’ so too the one who praises the Buddha’s virtues shows this by saying: ‘Thus indeed is the Arahant, thus indeed is the Perfectly Enlightened One… thus indeed is the Blessed One.’ Here, the word ‘iti’ has the sense of making something immediately present, as in ‘iti petaṃ abhūtaṃ, iti petaṃ atacchaṃ’ (thus this is false, thus this is untrue), and so forth (Dī. Ni. 1.5). The word ‘pi’ has the sense of aggregation, and through it, the abundance of those virtues is indicated. One who praises these should do so by making them clearly present to the mind. To show this, he says: ‘It means: for this reason and for that reason.’ For when one praises having investigated in this way, the one to whom he praises develops great confidence in the Blessed One. ‘Ārakattā’ means because of being very far. ‘Arīnaṃ’ means of the enemies, the defilements. ‘Arānaṃ’ means of the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra. ‘Hatattā’ means because of being destroyed. ‘Paccayādīnaṃ’ means of the requisites such as robes and of special offerings. ‘Tato’ means from the Visuddhimagga. And as they are in the Visuddhimagga, so also their details should be taken from its commentary.

Yasmā jīvako bahuso satthusantike buddhaguṇe sutvā ṭhito, diṭṭhasaccatāya ca satthusāsane vigatakathaṃkatho vesārajjappatto, tasmā āha “jīvako panā”tiādi. Pañcavaṇṇāyāti khuddikādivasena pañcappakārāya. Nirantaraṃ phuṭaṃ ahosi katādhikārabhāvato. Kammantarāyavasena hissa rañño guṇasarīraṃ khatupahataṃ ahosi.

Because Jīvaka had often stood near the Teacher hearing the Buddha’s virtues and, having seen the truth, was free from doubt in the Teacher’s dispensation and had attained confidence, therefore he said: ‘But Jīvaka,’ and so forth. ‘Pañcavaṇṇāyā’ means of five kinds of rapture, such as the minor rapture, etc. It was continuously pervading because of his state of having performed meritorious services. For, due to the obstruction of his evil action, the king’s body of virtue was wounded and damaged.

158. “Uttama”nti vatvā na kevalaṃ seṭṭhabhāvo evettha kāraṇaṃ, atha kho appasaddatāpi kāraṇanti dassetuṃ “assayānarathayānānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Hatthiyānesu nibbisevanameva gaṇhanto hatthiniyova kappāpesi. Rañño āsaṅkānivattanatthaṃ āsannacārībhāvena tattha itthiyova nisajjāpitā. Rañño paresaṃ durupasaṅkamanabhāvadassanatthaṃ [P 1.0279] tā purisavesaṃ gāhāpetvā āvudhahatthā kāritā. Paṭivedesīti ñāpesi. Tadevāti gamanaṃ, agamanameva vā.

158. Having said ‘the highest,’ he meant that not only is the state of being the best the reason here, but also the quality of quietness is a reason; to show this, he said ‘elephant-vehicles, chariots,’ and so forth. Among elephant-vehicles, choosing the quiet ones, he had only female elephants prepared. To remove the king’s suspicion, women were made to sit there as they were his close attendants. To show the difficulty for others to approach the king, he made them take on the appearance of men and hold weapons. ‘Paṭivedesī’ means he informed him. ‘Tadeva’ means that very going, or indeed, the not going.

159. Mahañcāti karaṇatthe paccattavacananti āha “mahatācā”ti. Mahaccāti mahatiyā[V 1.0192], liṅgavipallāsavasena vuttaṃ, mahantenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenāha “rājānubhāvenā”ti “dvinnaṃ mahāraṭṭhānaṃ issariyasirī”ti aṅgamagadharaṭṭhānaṃ ādhipaccamāha. Āsattakhaggānīti aṃse olambanavasena sannaddhaasīni. Kulabhogaissariyādivasena mahatī mattā etesanti mahāmattā, mahānubhāvā rājapurisā. Vijjādharataruṇā viyāti vijjādharakumārā viya. Raṭṭhiyaputtāti bhojaputtā. Hatthighaṭāti hatthisamūhā. Aññamaññasaṅghaṭṭanāti avicchedavasena gamanena aññamaññasambandhā.

159.The word mahañca is an instrumental singular used in the sense of an instrument; hence it says, 'and by the great' (mahatā ca). Mahaccā means mahatiyā; this is stated with a change of gender, meaning mahantena. Therefore it says, 'by the king's power.' 'The sovereignty and glory of the two great kingdoms' refers to the dominion over the kingdoms of Aṅga and Magadha. 'Swords fastened' means swords fastened by being hung from the shoulder. 'Great ministers' are those whose measure is great in terms of lineage, wealth, lordship, and so on—royal officials of great power. 'Like young sorcerers' means like young sorcerer princes. 'Territorial princes' means sons of the Bhoja clan. 'Herds of elephants' means groups of elephants. 'Mutual collision' means mutually connected by moving without a break.

Cittutrāso sayaṃ bhāyanaṭṭhena bhayaṃ yathā tathā bhāyatīti katvā. Ñāṇaṃ bhāyitabbe eva vatthusmiṃ bhayato upaṭṭhite “bhāyitabbamida”nti bhayato tīraṇato bhayaṃ. Tenevāha “bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇaṃ pana bhāyati nabhāyatīti? Na bhāyati. Tañhi atītā saṅkhārā niruddhā, paccuppannā nirujjhanti, anāgatā nirujjhissantīti tīraṇamattameva hotī”ti (visuddhi. 2.751). Ārammaṇaṃ [M 1.0217] bhāyati etasmāti bhayaṃ. Otappaṃ pāpato bhāyati etenāti bhayaṃ. Bhayānakanti bhāyanākāro. Bhayanti ñāṇabhayaṃ. Saṃveganti sahottappañāṇaṃ santāsanti sabbaso ubbijjanaṃ. Bhāyitabbaṭṭhena bhayaṃ bhīmabhāvena bheravanti bhayabheravaṃ, bhītabbavatthu. Tenāha “āgacchatī”ti.

Mental terror is fear in the sense that it fears by itself; that is, it fears just as fear does. Knowledge is fear because it discerns 'this is to be feared' when fear has arisen in an object that should be feared. Therefore it is said: 'Does the knowledge of the appearance of fear fear or not? It does not fear. For it is merely the discernment: “Past formations have ceased, present ones are ceasing, and future ones will cease”' (Vism XXI.34). The object is fear because one fears on account of it. Moral dread is fear because one fears evil by means of it. 'Terrifying' means the mode of fearing. 'Fear' means the fear that is knowledge. 'Spiritual urgency' means knowledge together with moral dread. 'Terror' means complete agitation. 'Fear and terror' means fear in the sense of what is to be feared, and terror in the sense of what is dreadful—an object to be feared. Therefore it says, 'it is coming.'

Bhīruṃ [P 1.0280] pasaṃsantīti pāpato bhāyanato uttasanato bhīruṃ pasaṃsanti paṇḍitā. Na hi tattha sūranti tasmiṃ pāpakaraṇe sūraṃ pagabbhadhaṃsinaṃ na hi pasaṃsanti. Tenāha “bhayā hi santo na karonti pāpa”nti. Tattha bhayāti pāputrāsato, ottappahetūti attho. Sarīracalananti bhayavasenasarīrasaṃkampo. Eketi uttaravihāravāsino. “Rājagahe”tiādi tesaṃ adhippāyavivaraṇaṃ. Kāmaṃ vayatulyo “vayasso”ti vuccati, rūḷhireso, yo koci pana sahāyo vayasso, tasmā vayassābhilāpoti sahāyābhilāpo. Na vippalambhesīti na visaṃvādesi. Vinasseyyāti cittavighātena vihaññeyya.

They praise the timid: the wise praise the timid because they are afraid of and terrified by evil. For they do not praise the brave in that: they do not praise one who is brave, audacious, and destructive in the doing of evil. Hence it is said: 'For the good do no evil out of fear.' Here, 'out of fear' means out of dread of evil, that is, because of moral dread. 'Bodily movement' means trembling of the body due to fear. 'Some' (eke) refers to the dwellers of the Uttaravihāra. 'At Rājagaha,' etc., is an explanation of their intention. Though one of equal age is called a 'friend' (vayassa), this is a conventional term; any companion is a 'friend.'
