Therefore, 'addressing as a friend' means addressing a companion. 'You did not deceive' means you did not betray. 'Would perish' means would be afflicted with mental distress.

Sāmaññaphalapucchāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Question on the Fruits of Recluseship

160. Bhagavato tejoti buddhānubhāvo. Rañño sarīraṃ phari yathā taṃ soṇadaṇḍassa brāhmaṇassa bhagavato santikaṃ gacchantassa antovanasaṇḍagatassa. Eketi uttaravihāravāsino.

160.'The Blessed One's radiance' means the Buddha's power. It suffused the king's body just as it did that of the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa when he was going to the Blessed One and had entered the thicket of the inner woods. 'Some' (eke) refers to the dwellers of the Uttaravihāra.

161. Yena, tenāti ca bhummatthe karaṇavacananti āha “yattha bhagavā, tattha gato”ti. Tadā [V 1.0193] tasmiṃ bhikkhusaṅghe tuṇhībhāvassa anavasesato byāpibhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “tuṇhībhūtaṃ tuṇhībhūta”nti vuttanti āha “yato yato…pe… mevāti attho”ti. Hatthassa kukatattā asaṃyamo asampajaññakiriyā hatthakukkuccanti veditabbo. Vā-saddo avuttavikappattho, tena tadañño asaṃyamabhāvo vibhāvitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tattha pana cakkhuasaṃyamo sabbapaṭhamo, dunnivāro cāti tadabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ [P 1.0281] “sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍita”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Kāyikavācasikena upasamena laddhena itaropi anumānato laddho eva hotīti āha “mānasikena cā”ti. Upasamanti saṃyamaṃ, ācārasampattinti attho. Pañcaparivaṭṭeti pañcapurisaparivaṭṭe. Pañcahākārehīti “iṭṭhāniṭṭhe [M 1.0218] tādī”ti (mahāni. 38, 192) evaṃ ādinā āgatehi, pañcavidhaariyiddhisiddhehi ca pañcahi pakārehi. Tādilakkhaṇeti tādibhāve.

161. The words yena and tena, which are instrumental expressions, are used here in a locative sense; hence it says, 'where the Blessed One was, there he went.' To show the all-pervasive nature of the silence in the Saṅgha of bhikkhus at that time, without remainder, it is said, 'silent, silent.' Hence it is explained: 'from wherever... etc. ... this is the meaning.' 'Misconduct with the hands' should be understood as lack of restraint and unmindful action due to misdeed of the hands. The word vā ('or') has the sense of an unstated alternative; by this, it should be seen that another kind of lack of restraint is indicated. Here, however, lack of restraint of the eye is primary and hard to prevent. To show its absence, it is said, 'adorned with all ornaments,' etc. Since the other is obtained by inference from the obtained bodily and verbal tranquility, it says, 'and with the mental.' 'Tranquility' means restraint, that is, accomplishment in conduct. 'In five circles' means in circles of five persons. 'In five ways' means by the five modes that come in such passages as 'such a one in regard to the pleasant and unpleasant' (Mahānid. 38, 192), and by the five kinds of accomplishment in the noble supernormal powers. 'The characteristic of such a one' means the state of being such a one.

162. Na me pañhavissajjane bhāro atthīti satthu sabbattha appaṭihatañāṇacāratādassanaṃ. Yadākaṅkhasīti na vadanti, kathaṃ pana vadantīti āha “sutvā vedissāmā”ti padesañāṇe ṭhitattā. Buddhā pana sabbaññupavāraṇaṃ pavārentīti sambandho. “Yakkhanarindadevasamaṇabrāhmaṇaparibbājakāna”nti idaṃ “pucchāvuso yadākaṅkhasī”tiādīni (saṃ. ni. 1.237, 246; su. ni. āḷavakasutte) suttapadāni pucchantānaṃ yesaṃ puggalānaṃ vasena āgatāni, taṃ dassanatthaṃ. “Pucchāvuso yadākaṅkhasī”ti idaṃ āḷavakassa yakkhassa okāsakaraṇaṃ, sesāni narindādīnaṃ. Manasicchasīti manasā icchasi. Pucchavho, yaṃ kiñci manasicchathāti bāvarissa saṃsayaṃ manasā pucchavho. Tumhākaṃ pana sabbesaṃ yaṃ kiñci sabbasaṃsayaṃ manasā, aññathā ca, yathā icchatha, tathā pucchavhoti adhippāyo.

162. 'There is no burden for me in answering questions': this shows the Teacher's unobstructed sphere of knowledge in all respects. They do not say, 'Ask what you wish.' How then do they speak? It says, 'Having heard, we will know,' because they stand on partial knowledge. The Buddhas, however, make the invitation of the omniscient one; this is the connection. The phrase 'of yakkhas, kings, devas, ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers' is stated to show the persons who ask, in connection with whom the sutta passages beginning 'Friend, ask what you wish' (SN 1.237, 246; Sn, Āḷavakasutta) occur. 'Friend, ask what you wish' is the granting of an opportunity to the yakkha Āḷavaka; the others pertain to kings and so on. 'If you wish in mind' means 'you wish with the mind.' 'Ask whatever you wish in mind' means: ask about Bāvari's doubt with your mind. The meaning is: 'But all of you, ask whatever doubt you have, with your mind or otherwise, as you wish.'

Sādhurūpāti sādhusabhāvā. Dhammoti paveṇīdhammo. Vuddhanti sīlādīhi buddhippattaṃ, garunti attho. Esa bhāroti esa saṃsayūpacchedanasaṅkhāto bhāro, āgato bhāro avassaṃ āvahitabboti adhippāyo. Ñatvā sayanti parūpadesena vinā sayameva ñatvā.

'Of good form' means of good nature. 'Dhamma' means the traditional custom. 'Venerable' means one who has attained growth in virtue and so on; the meaning is 'respected.' 'This is the burden' means this burden designated as the cutting off of doubt; the meaning is that a burden that has come must certainly be borne. 'Knowing, they lie down' means knowing by themselves without the instruction of others.

Suciratenāti evaṃ nāmakena brāhmaṇena. Tagghāti [P 1.0282] ekaṃsena. Yathāpi kusalo tathāti yathā sabbadhammakusalo sabbavidū jānāti katheti, tathā ahamakkhissaṃ. Rājā ca kho taṃ yadi kāhati vā na vāti yo taṃ idha pucchituṃ pesesi, so rājānaṃ tayā pucchitaṃ karotu vā mā vā, ahaṃ pana te akkhissaṃ akkhissāmi, ācikkhissāmīti attho.

'By Suciratena' refers to a brahmin of that name. 'Indeed' (taggha) means certainly. 'Just as a skilled one, so': just as one who is skilled in all things, all-knowing, knows and speaks, so will I explain. 'And whether the king will act on it or not': He who sent you here to ask—that king—let him act on what you have asked, or not; but I for my part will explain to you. 'I will explain' means I will declare, I will tell; this is the meaning.

163. Sippanaṭṭhena sikkhitabbatāya ca sippameva sippāyatanaṃ jīvikāya kāraṇabhāvato[V 1.0194]. Seyyathidanti nipāto, tassa te katameti attho. Puthu sippāyatanānīti hi sādhāraṇato sippāni uddisitvā upari taṃtaṃsippūpajīvino niddiṭṭhā puggalādhiṭṭhānakathāya papañcaṃ pariharituṃ. Aññathā yathādhippetāni tāva sippāyatanāni dassetvā puna taṃtaṃsippūpajīvīsu dassiyamānesu papañco siyāti. Tenāha “hatthārohā”tiādi.

163. A craft is a 'field of craft' because it is a craft, because it must be learned, and because it is a cause of livelihood. Seyyathidaṃ is a particle; its meaning is 'namely, which?' The phrase 'various fields of craft' indicates the crafts in general, and then those who live by those specific crafts are pointed out in order to avoid proliferation in a discourse based on persons. Otherwise, if the intended fields of craft were shown first and then those living by those specific crafts were shown, there would be proliferation. Hence it says, 'elephant-riders,' etc.

Hatthiṃ [M 1.0219] ārohanti, ārohāpayanti cāti hatthārohā. Yehi payogehi puriso hatthino ārohanayoggo hoti, hatthissa taṃ payogaṃ vidhāyataṃ sabbesaṃ petesaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Tenāha “sabbepī”tiādi. Tattha hatthācariyā nāma ye hatthino hatthārohakānañca sikkhapakā. Hatthivejjā nāma hatthibhisakkā. Hatthimeṇḍā nāma hatthīnaṃ pādarakkhakā. Ādi-saddena hatthīnaṃ yavasadāyakādike saṅgaṇhāti. Assārohā rathikāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Rathe niyuttā rathikā. Ratharakkhā nāma rathassa āṇirakkhakā. Dhanuṃ gaṇhanti, gaṇhāpenti cāti dhanuggahā, issāsā [P 1.0283] dhanusippassa sikkhāpakā ca. Tenāha “dhanuācariyā issāsā”ti. Celena celapaṭākāya yuddhe akanti gacchantīti celakāti āha “ye yuddhe jayadhajaṃ gahetvā purato gacchantī”ti. Yathā tathā ṭhite senike byūhakaraṇavasena tato calayanti uccālentīti calakā. Sakuṇagghiādayo viya maṃsapiṇḍaṃ parasenāsamūhaṃ sāhasikamahāyodhatāya chetvā chetvā dayanti uppatitvā uppatitvā gacchantīti piṇḍadāyakā. Dutiyavikappe piṇḍe dayanti janasammadde uppatantā viya gacchantīti piṇḍadāyakāti attho veditabbo. Uggatuggatāti thāmajavaparakkamādivasena ativiya uggatā uggāti attho. Pakkhandantīti attano vīrasūrabhāvena asajjamānā parasenaṃ anupavisantīti attho. Thāmajavabalaparakkamādisampattiyā mahānāgā viya mahānāgā. Ekantasūrāti ekākisūrā attano sūrabhāveneva ekākino hutvā yujjhanakā. Sajālikāti savammikā. Saraparittāṇacammanti cammaparisibbitaṃ kheṭakaṃ, cammamayaṃ vā phalakaṃ. Gharadāsayodhāti antojātayodhā.

'Elephant-riders' are those who mount elephants and cause others to mount them. This includes all those who provide the means by which a man becomes fit to mount an elephant and who arrange those means for the elephant. Hence it says, 'all indeed,' etc. Here, 'elephant masters' are those who train elephants and elephant-riders. 'Elephant doctors' are elephant physicians. 'Elephant grooms' are protectors of the elephants' feet. By the word 'etc.,' it includes those who give fodder to elephants and so on. The same method applies here to 'horse-riders' and 'charioteers.' 'Charioteers' are those employed in a chariot. 'Chariot guards' are protectors of the chariot's linchpin. 'Bowmen' are those who take up a bow and cause others to take one up; archers are also teachers of the art of the bow. Hence it says, 'bow masters and archers.' 'Banner-bearers' are those who go into battle with a cloth banner; it says: 'those who go in front in battle holding a victory banner.' 'Movers' are those who move and stir up soldiers standing here and there by forming battle arrays. 'Lump-givers' are those who, like vultures, having cut up the enemy host—a lump of flesh—with their audacity and great warrior status, fly up and go. In the second alternative, the meaning of 'lump-givers' should be understood as those who fly through the lumps of people, going as if leaping up in a throng. 'Fierce, very fierce' means exceedingly fierce by reason of strength, speed, exertion, etc.; this is the meaning of 'fierce.' 'Charging forward' means they enter the enemy army, not hesitating because of their own heroic and brave nature. 'Great nāgas' are like great elephants, due to their endowment with strength, speed, power, exertion, etc. 'Exclusively brave' means singly brave, those who fight alone just because of their own bravery. 'With nets' means with armor. 'Leather for protection from arrows' means a shield covered with leather, or a board made of leather. 'Warriors who are household slaves' means warriors born within the household.

Āḷāraṃ vuccati mahānasaṃ, tattha niyuttāti āḷārikā, bhattakārā. Pūvikāti pūvasampādakā, ye pūvameva nānappakārato sampādetvā vikkiṇantā jīvanti. Kesanakhalikhanādivasena manussānaṃ alaṅkāravidhiṃ kappenti saṃvidahantīti kappakā. Nhāpakāti cuṇṇavilepanādīhi [P 1.0284] malaharaṇavaṇṇasampādanavidhinā nhāpentīti nhāpakā. Navantādividhinā pavatto gaṇanagantho antarā chiddābhāvena acchiddakoti vuccati, taṃ gaṇanaṃ upanissāya jīvantā acchiddakapāṭhakā. Hatthena adhippāyaviññāpanaṃ hatthamuddā [M 1.0220] hattha-saddo cettha tadekadesesu aṅgulīsu daṭṭhabbo. “Na bhuñjamāno sabbaṃ hatthaṃ mukhe pakkhipissāmī”tiādīsu viya, tasmā aṅgulisaṅkocanādinā [V 1.0195] gaṇanā hatthamuddāya gaṇanā. Cittakārādīnīti. Ādi-saddena bhamakārakoṭṭakalekhaka vilīvakārādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Diṭṭheva dhammeti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve. Sandiṭṭhikamevāti asamparāyikatāya sāmaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, sayaṃ anubhavitabbaṃ attapaccakkhaṃ diṭṭhadhammikanti attho. Sukhitanti sukhappattaṃ. Uparīti devaloke. So hi manussalokato uparimo. Kammassa katattā nibbattanato tassa phalaṃ tassa aggisikhā viya hoti, tañca uddhaṃ devaloketi āha “uddhaṃ aggaṃ assā atthīti uddhaggikā”ti. Saggaṃ arahatīti attano phalabhūtaṃ saggaṃ arahati, tattha sā nibbattanārahoti attho. Sukhavipākāti iṭṭhavipākavipaccanīkā. Suṭṭhu aggeti ativiya uttame uḷāre. Dakkhanti vaḍḍhanti etāyāti dakkhiṇā, pariccāgamayaṃ puññanti āha “dakkhiṇaṃ dāna”nti.

Āḷāra is called a great kitchen; those employed there are called āḷārikā, that is, cooks. Pūvikā are those who prepare cakes, who live by preparing and selling various kinds of cakes. Kappakā are those who arrange and prepare methods of adornment for people, such as cutting hair and nails. Nhāpakā are those who bathe others by removing dirt and enhancing their complexion with powders, ointments, and so on. The method of counting that proceeds by nava and so on is called 'acchiddaka' because it is uninterrupted, being without gaps. Those who live by relying on this counting are called 'acchiddakapāṭhakā'. Hatthamuddā is the conveying of intention by hand; here, the word 'hand' should be understood as referring to its parts, such as the fingers. Just as in phrases such as, 'While eating, I will not put the whole hand into my mouth,' so too, counting by contracting the fingers and so on is called 'counting by hand gestures'. Cittakārā and so on: by the word 'ādi' one should understand the inclusion of bhamakāra, koṭṭaka, lekhaka, vilīvakārā, and others. Diṭṭheva dhamma means in this very existence. Sandiṭṭhika means to be seen by oneself, not pertaining to the next life, to be experienced personally, directly visible in this life. Sukhita means one who has attained happiness. Uparī means in the heavenly world, for it is above the human world. Because the result arises from the doing of kamma, its fruit is like the tip of a flame, and that leads upward to the heavenly world; hence it is called 'uddhaggikā,' meaning 'having an upward tip.' Saggaṃ arahati means it is worthy of heaven, which is its fruit; the meaning is that it is worthy of rebirth there. Sukhavipākā means having a desirable result. Suṭṭhu agga means exceedingly excellent, sublime. Dakkhanti means they prosper; dakkhiṇā is that by which they prosper. It is merit consisting of relinquishment; thus it is said, 'dakkhiṇaṃ dānaṃ,' a gift.

Maggo [P 1.0285] sāmaññaṃ samitapāpasamaṇabhāvoti katvā. Yasmā ayaṃ rājā pabbajitānaṃ dāsakassakādīnaṃ lokato abhivādanādilābho sandiṭṭhikaṃ sāmaññaphalanti cintetvā “atthi nu kho koci samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā īdisamatthaṃ jānanto”ti vīmaṃsanto pūraṇādike pucchitvā tesaṃ kathāya anārādhitacitto bhagavantampi tamatthaṃ pucchi, tasmā vuttaṃ “upari āgataṃ pana dāsakassakopamaṃ sandhāya pucchatī”ti.

The path is the state of a samaṇa, the state of a recluse who has calmed evil. Because this king, considering the visible fruit of the ascetic life to be the homage and gains received from the world by those gone forth who were formerly servants, farmers, and so on, thought, 'Is there any recluse or brahmin who knows such an attainment?' and, inquiring from Pūraṇa and others, was not pleased with their answers, he asked the Blessed One about that matter. Therefore, it is said, 'He asks with reference to the simile of the servant and the farmer which comes later.'

Kaṇhapakkhanti yathāpucchite atthe labbhamānaṃ diṭṭhigatūpasañhitaṃ saṃkilesapakkhaṃ. Sukkapakkhanti tabbidhuraṃ uparisuttāgataṃ vodānapakkhaṃ. Samaṇakolāhalanti samaṇakotūhalaṃ taṃtaṃsamaṇavādānaṃ aññamaññavirodhaṃ. Samaṇabhaṇḍananti teneva virodhena “evaṃvādīnaṃ tesaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ ayaṃ doso, evaṃvādīnaṃ ayaṃ doso”ti evaṃ taṃtaṃvādassa paribhāsanaṃ. Rañño bhāraṃ karonto attano desanākosallenāti adhippāyo.

Kaṇhapakka (the dark side) refers to the side of defilement associated with views, which is obtained in the matter as questioned. Sukkapakkha (the bright side) refers to the opposite of that, the side of purification, which comes later in the Sutta. Samaṇakolāhala (the clamor of ascetics) means the excitement about ascetics, the mutual contradiction of the various ascetic doctrines. Samaṇabhaṇḍana (the bickering of ascetics) means the disparagement of those various doctrines due to that very contradiction, saying, 'This is the fault of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views, this is their fault.' The meaning is that he is taking on the king's burden by his own skill in teaching.

164. Paṇḍitapatirūpakānanti āmaṃ viya pakkānaṃ paṇḍitābhāsānaṃ.

164. Paṇḍitapatirūpakāna (of those who resemble the wise) means of those who appear wise, like unripe fruits resembling ripe ones.

Pūraṇakassapavādavaṇṇanā

An Explanation of Pūraṇa Kassapa's Doctrine

165. Ekaṃ [M 1.0221] idāhanti ekāhaṃ. Idha-saddo cettha nipātamattaṃ, ekāhaṃ samayaṃ ticceva attho. Saritabbayuttanti anussaraṇānucchavikaṃ.

165. Ekaṃ idāha means 'one day.' Here, the word 'idha' is merely a particle; the meaning is simply 'on one day, at one time.' Saritabbayutta means suitable for recollection.

166. Sahatthā karontassāti sahattheneva karontassa. Nissaggiyathāvarādayopi idha sahatthakaraṇeneva [V 1.0196] saṅgahitā. Hatthādīnīti hatthapādakaṇṇanāsādīni. Pacanaṃ dahanaṃ vibādhananti āha “daṇḍena uppīḷentassā”ti. Papañcasūdaniyaṃ “tajjentassa vā”ti attho vutto, idha pana tajjanaṃ paribhāsanaṃ daṇḍeneva saṅgahetvā “daṇḍena uppīḷentassa” icceva vuttaṃ. Sokaṃ sayaṃ [P 1.0286] karontassāti parassa sokakāraṇaṃ sayaṃ karontassa, sokaṃ vā uppādentassa. Parehīti attano vacanakarehi. Sayampi phandatoti parassa vibādhanapayogena sayampi phandato. “Atipātāpayato”ti padaṃ suddhakattuatthe hetukattuatthe ca vattatīti āha “hanantassāpi hanāpentassāpī”ti. Kāraṇavasenāti kārāpanavasena.

166. Sahatthā karontassa means doing solely with one’s own hand. Even things requiring relinquishment, immovable property, and so on are included here under the act of doing with one’s own hand. Hatthādīni means hands, feet, ears, nose, and so on. Pacanaṃ dahanaṃ vibādhana means tormenting, burning, and harassing; he says, 'by oppressing with a stick.' In the Papañcasūdanī, the meaning is given as 'or by threatening,' but here, threatening and abuse are included under 'with a stick,' and thus it is said, 'by oppressing with a stick.' Sokaṃ sayaṃ karontassa (causing sorrow oneself) means causing another’s sorrow oneself, or producing sorrow. Parehi (by others) means by those who carry out one’s word. Sayampi phandato (even he himself trembles) means that by the action of tormenting another, he himself also trembles. The phrase 'atipātāpayato' applies both in the sense of doing oneself and causing another to do; as he says, 'of one who is killing and of one who is causing to kill.' Kāraṇavasena (by way of instigation) means through causing another to act.

Gharassa bhitti anto bahi ca sandhitā hutvā ṭhitā gharasandhi. Kiñcipi asesetvā niravaseso lopo nillopo. Ekāgāre niyutto vilopo ekāgāriko. Parito sabbaso panthe hananaṃ paripantho. Pāpaṃ na karīyati pubbe asaññato uppādetuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā, tasmā natthi pāpaṃ. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ sattā pāpe paṭipajjantīti āha “sattā pana pāpaṃ karomāti evaṃ saññino hontī”ti. Evaṃ kirassa hoti – imesañhi sattānaṃ hiṃsādikiriyā na attānaṃ phusati tassa niccatāya nibbikārattā sarīraṃ pana acetanaṃ kaṭṭhakaliṅgarūpamaṃ, tasmiṃ vikopitepi na kiñci pāpanti. Khuranemināti nisitakhuramayaneminā.

Gharasandhi is the joint of a house, where the wall of a house is joined inside and outside. Nillopa means complete destruction, leaving nothing behind. Ekāgāriko is a plunderer appointed to a single house. Paripantho is killing on the path all around. Pāpaṃ na karīyati (evil is not done) because one is unable to produce it from a prior lack of perception; therefore, there is no evil. If so, how do beings engage in evil? He says, 'Beings, however, have the perception, "We are doing evil."' Thus it is for him: For these beings, acts of violence and so on do not affect the self, because of its permanence and immutability; the body, however, is insentient, like a log of wood. Even when it is harmed, there is no evil. Khuraneminā (with a razor-wheel) means with a wheel having a sharp razor rim.

Gaṅgāya dakkhiṇā disā appatirūpadeso, uttarā disā patirūpadesoti adhippāyena“dakkhiṇañca”tiādi vuttanti āha “dakkhiṇatīre manussā kakkhaḷā”tiādi. Mahāyāganti mahāvijitayaññasadisaṃ mahāyāgaṃ. Uposathakammena vāti uposathakammena ca. Dama-saddo hi indriyasaṃvarassa uposathasīlassa ca vācako idhādhippeto. Keci pana “uposathakammenāti idaṃ indriyadamanassa visesanaṃ, tasmā ‘uposathakammabhūtena indriyadamanenā”ti atthaṃ vadanti[P 1.0287]. Sīlasaṃyamenāti kāyikavācasikasaṃvarena[M 1.0222]. Saccavajjenāti saccavācāya, tassā visuṃ vacanaṃ loke garutarapuññasammatabhāvato. Yathā hi pāpadhammesu musāvādo garu, evaṃ puññadhammesu saccavācā. Tenāha bhagavā “ekaṃ dhammaṃ atītassā”tiādi. Pavattīti yo “karotī”ti vuccati, tassa santāne phaluppattipaccayabhāvena uppatti. Sabbathāti “karoto”tiādinā vuttena sabbappakārena. Kiriyameva paṭikkhipati, na raññā puṭṭhaṃ sandiṭṭhikaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ byākarotīti adhippāyo. Idaṃ avadhāraṇaṃ vipākapaṭikkhepanivattanatthaṃ. Yo hi kammaṃ paṭikkhipati, tena atthato vipākopi paṭikkhitto eva nāma hoti. Tathā hi vakkhati “kammaṃ paṭibāhantenāpī”tiādi (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.170-172).

The southern bank of the Ganges is an unsuitable place, while the northern bank is a suitable place—this is the intended meaning; hence, it is said, 'the southern side,' etc., and it is explained, 'the people on the southern bank are harsh,' etc. Mahāyāga means a grand sacrifice comparable to the great victory sacrifice (Mahāvijitayañña). Uposathakammena vā means 'and by the Uposatha observance.' Here, the term 'dama' (restraint) is intended as a designation for both sense-restraint and the Uposatha precept. Some, however, say that 'by the Uposatha observance' is a qualifier of sense-restraint; thus, they explain the meaning as 'by sense-restraint which has become the Uposatha observance.' Sīlasaṃyamena (by moral discipline and self-control) refers to bodily and verbal restraint. Saccavajjena (by truthfulness) means by truthful speech; its separate mention is because in the world it is regarded as a weighty meritorious act. Just as false speech is grave among evil qualities, so too is truthful speech among meritorious qualities. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'One who transgresses in a single thing,' etc. Pavatti (occurrence) is the arising in the continuum of one who is said to be 'acting,' as a condition for the arising of a result. Sabbathā (in every way) means in every manner stated by 'of the one who acts,' etc. The meaning is that he denies only the action itself and does not explain the visible fruit of the ascetic life about which he was asked by the king. This emphasis is for the purpose of precluding the denial of the result. For one who denies action, in effect, denies its result as well. As will be said, 'Even by rejecting action,' etc.

Paṭirājūhi [V 1.0197] anabhibhavanīyabhāvena visesato jitanti vijitaṃ, āṇāpavattideso. “Mā mayhaṃ vijite vasathā”ti apasādanā pabbajitassa viheṭhanā pabbājanāti katvā vuttaṃ “apasādetabbanti viheṭhetabba”nti. Uggaṇhanaṃ tena vuttassa atthassa “evameta”nti upadhāraṇaṃ sallakkhaṇaṃ, nikujjanaṃ tassa addhaniyabhāvāpādanavasena cittena sandhāraṇaṃ. Tadubhayaṃ paṭikkhipanto āha “anuggaṇhanto anikujjanto”ti. Tenāha “sāravasena aggaṇhanto”tiādi.

Vijita is that which is especially conquered by not being overpowered by rival kings, the domain where commands prevail. Apasādanā (rejection) is the harassment and banishment of one gone forth, as in 'Do not dwell in my conquered territory.' Thus, it is said, 'one should reject, one should harass.' Uggaṇhana (grasping) is acknowledging the meaning stated by him, 'Thus it is,' recognition, noting; nikujjana (overturning) is mentally fixing it by way of reducing its trustworthiness. Rejecting both, he says, 'anuggaṇhanto anikujjanto' (not grasping, not overturning). Therefore, it is said, 'not grasping by way of essence,' and so on.

Makkhaligosālavādavaṇṇanā

The Description of Makkhali Gosāla's Doctrine

168. Ubhayenāti hetupaccayapaṭisedhanavacanena. Saṃkilesapaccayanti saṃkilissanassa malīnabhāvassa kāraṇaṃ. Visuddhipaccayanti saṅkikilesato visuddhiyā vodānassa kāraṇaṃ. Attakāroti [P 1.0288] tena tena sattena attanā kātabbakammaṃ attanā nipphādetabbapayogo. Parakāranti parassa vāhasā ijjhanakapayojanaṃ. Tenāha “yenā”tiādi. Mahāsattanti antimabhavikaṃ mahābodhisattaṃ, paccekabodhisattassapi ettheva saṅgaho veditabbo. Manussasobhagyatanti manussesu subhagabhāvaṃ. Evanti vuttappakārena. Kammavādassa kiriyavādassa paṭikkhipanena “atthi bhikkhave kammaṃ kaṇhaṃ kaṇhavipāka”ntiādi (a. ni. 4.232) nayappavatte jinacakke pahāraṃ deti nāma. Natthi purisakāreti yathāvuttaattakāraparakārābhāvato eva sattānaṃ paccattapurisakāro nāma koci natthīti attho. Tenāha “yenā”tiādi. Natthi balanti sattānaṃ diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikanibbānasampattiāvahaṃ balaṃ nāma kiñci natthi. Tenāha [M 1.0223] “yamhī”tiādi. Nidassanamattañcetaṃ, saṃkilesikampi cāyaṃ balaṃ paṭikkhipateva. Yadi vīriyādīni purisakāravevacanāni, kasmā visuṃ gahaṇanti āha “idaṃ no vīriyenā”tiādi. Saddatthato pana tassā tassā kiriyāya ussannaṭṭhena balaṃ. Sūravīrabhāvāvahaṭṭhena vīriyaṃ. Tadeva daḷhabhāvato, porisadhuraṃ vahantena pavattetabbato ca purisathāmo. Paraṃ paraṃ ṭhānaṃ akkamanappavattiyā purisaparakkamoti vuttoti veditabbaṃ.

168. 'Ubhayena' means by the statement denying both cause and condition. 'Saṃkilesapaccaya' refers to the cause of defilement, the reason for the state of being tainted. 'Visuddhipaccaya' means the cause of purification, the reason for the state of being cleansed from defilement. 'Attakāra' refers to the action to be done by oneself, the effort to be accomplished by oneself. 'Parakāra' means the purpose accomplished by the force of another. Hence it is said, 'by which,' etc. 'Mahāsatta' refers to the great Bodhisatta in the final existence; the Paccekabodhisatta should also be understood as included here. 'Manussasobhagyatā' means the state of good fortune among humans. 'Evaṃ' means in the manner stated. By rejecting the doctrine of action and the doctrine of activity, he delivers a blow to the wheel of the Jina, which proceeds according to the method stated in 'Monks, there is dark kamma with dark result' (AN 4.232), etc. 'Natthi purisakāra' means that since there is no self-effort or other-effort as previously stated, there is no individual effort of beings whatsoever. Hence it is said, 'by which,' etc. 'Natthi bala' means that beings have no power whatsoever to bring about worldly or otherworldly attainments, including Nibbāna. Hence it is said, 'in which,' etc. This is merely an illustration, and this also rejects defiling power. If energy, etc., are synonyms for personal effort, why are they mentioned separately? It is said, 'this is not by energy,' etc. In terms of meaning, 'bala' refers to the intensity of a particular action. 'Vīriya' refers to the state of being heroic and courageous. The same, due to firmness, and because it must be initiated and sustained by one who bears the burden of manliness, is called 'purisathāma'. 'Purisaparakkama' is said to mean the progress of advancing from one state to the next. This should be understood.

Sattayogato rūpādīsu sattavisattatāya sattā. Pāṇanato assasanapassasanavasena pavattiyā pāṇā. Te pana so ekindriyādivasena vibhajitvā vadatīti āha “ekindriyo”tiādi. Aṇḍakosādīsu bhavanato “bhūtā”ti vuccantīti āha “aṇḍakosa…pe… vadatī”ti[P 1.0289]. Jīvanato pāṇaṃ dhārentā viya vaḍḍhanato jīvā. Tenāha “sāliyavā”tiādi. Natthi etesaṃ saṃkilesavisuddhīsu vasoti avasā. Natthi nesaṃ balaṃ vīriyaṃ [V 1.0198] cāti abalā avīriyā. Niyatāti acchejjasuttāvutābhejjamaṇino viya niyatappavattitāya gatijātibandhāpavaggavasena niyāmo. Tattha tattha gamananti channaṃ abhijātīnaṃ tāsu tāsu gatīsu upagamanaṃ samavāyena samāgamo. Sabhāvoyevāti yathā kaṇṭakassa tikhiṇatā, kapitthaphalānaṃ parimaṇḍalatā, migapakkhīnaṃ vicittākāratā, evaṃ sabbassāpi lokassa hetupaccayena vinā tathā tathā pariṇāmo ayaṃ sabhāvo eva akittimoyeva. Tenāha “yena hī”tiādi. Chaḷābhijātiyo parato vitthārīyanti. “Sukhañca dukkhañca paṭisaṃvedentī”ti vadanto adukkhamasukhabhūmiṃ sabbena sabbaṃ na jānātīti ulliṅganto “aññā adukkhamasukhabhūmi natthīti dassetī”ti āha.

'Sattā' (beings) are so called from their sevenfold connection, due to their sevenfold attachment to forms and so on. 'Pāṇā' (living beings) are so called from breathing, because of the continuous process of inhalation and exhalation. He then classifies them by faculties and so on, saying, ''ekindriyo' (one-facultied being),' etc. From being born in eggs, etc., they are called 'bhūtā' (beings), hence it is said, ''aṇḍakosa...pe...vadati' (egg-born, etc.).' From living, as if sustaining life, and from growth, they are called 'jīvā' (living beings); hence it is said, ''sāliyavā' (rice-born),' etc. They have no power over defilement or purification; hence, 'avasā' (powerless). They lack strength and energy; hence, 'abalā avīriyā' (weak and without vigor). 'Niyatā' (determined) means their course is fixed, like unbreakable threads or an unbreakable gem, due to their predetermined movement, the process being governed by destiny, birth, bondage, and deliverance. 'Tattha tattha gamana' (going here and there) refers to the coming together of the six classes of beings in their respective destinies through association. 'Sabhāvo eva' (it is their nature itself) means, just as thorns are sharp, wood-apples are round, and animals and birds have varied forms, so too is the entire world—its transformations are simply its nature, without any cause, uncreated. Hence it is said, 'for by which,' etc. The six classes of beings are explained in detail elsewhere. By saying, 'They experience pleasure and pain,' he indicates his own complete ignorance of the state of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, and thus shows that 'no other state of neither-pain-nor-pleasure exists.'

Pamukhayonīnanti manussatiracchānādīsu khattiyabrāhmaṇādisīhabyagghādivasena padhānayonīnaṃ. Saṭṭhisatānīti chasahassāni. “Pañca ca kammuno satānī”ti padassa atthadassanaṃ “pañcakammasatāni cā”ti. “Eseva nayo”ti iminā “kevalaṃ takkamattakena niratthakaṃ diṭṭhiṃ dīpetī”ti imamevatthaṃ atidisati. Ettha ca “takkamattakenā”ti iminā yasmā takkikā niraṅkusatāya parikappanassa yaṃ kiñci attano parikappitaṃ sārato [M 1.0224] maññamānā tatheva abhinivissa takkadiṭṭhigāhaṃ gaṇhanti, tasmā na tesaṃ diṭṭhivatthusmiṃ viññūhi vicāraṇā kātabbāti dasseti. Kecīti uttaravihāravāsino. Te hi “pañca kammānīti cakkhusotaghānajivhākāyā imāni pañcindriyāni ‘pañca kammānī’ti paññāpentī”ti vadanti. Kammanti laddhīti oḷārikabhāvato paripuṇṇakammanti laddhi. Manokammaṃ [P 1.0290] anoḷārikattā upaḍḍhakammanti laddhīti yojanā. Dvaṭṭhipaṭipadāti “dvāsaṭṭhi paṭipadā”ti vattabbe sabhāvaniruttiṃ ajānanto “dvaṭṭhipaṭipadā”ti vadati. Ekasmiṃ kappeti ekasmiṃ mahākappe, tatthāpi ca vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyīsaññite ekasmiṃ asaṅkhyeyyekappe.

'Pamukhayonīnaṃ' (of chief lineages) refers to the chief lineages among humans and animals, such as the khattiyas, brahmins, lions, tigers, and so on. 'Saṭṭhisatāni' (sixty hundreds) means six thousand. The phrase 'Pañca ca kammuno satāni' (five hundred of kamma) explains the meaning of 'five hundred actions' as 'five hundred kammas.' By ''Eseva nayo' (this is the method),' he refers to the meaning that 'it reveals a view that is merely speculative and meaningless.' In this context, by ''takkamattakena' (merely by speculation),' it is shown that since logicians, unrestrained in their conceiving, consider whatever they conceive to be essential and thus cling to it, grasping speculative views, therefore the wise should not engage in examining their views. 'Keci' (some) refers to some residents of Uttara Vihāra. They say, 'The five faculties—eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—are called 'pañca kammāni' (the five actions).' The doctrine is that action is a full kamma due to its gross nature, and that mental action is a half-kamma due to its subtlety; this is the explanation. 'Dvaṭṭhipaṭipadā' (sixty-two practices) is said because, not knowing the proper grammar, one says 'dvaṭṭhipaṭipadā' instead of 'dvāsaṭṭhi paṭipadā' (sixty-two practices). 'Ekasmiṃ kappe' (in one eon) means in one great eon, and even within that, in one immeasurable eon called the stage of evolution-and-stasis (vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī).

Urabbhe hanantīti orabbhikā. Evaṃ sūkarikādayo veditabbā. Luddāti aññepi ye keci māgavikanesādā. Te pāpakammapasutatāya “kaṇhābhijātīti vadati. Bhikkhū”ti buddhasāsane bhikkhū. Te kira “sachandarāgā paribhuñjantī”ti adhippāyena “catūsu paccayesu kaṇṭake pakkhipitvā khādantī”ti vadati. Kasmāti ce? Yasmā “te paṇītapaṇīte paccaye paṭisevantī”ti tassa micchāgāho, tasmā ñāyaladdhepi paccaye bhuñjamānā ājīvakasamayassa vilomagāhitāya paccayesu kaṇṭake pakkhipitvā khādanti nāmāti vadatīti apare. Eke pabbajitā, ye savisesaṃ attakilamathānuyogaṃ anuyuttā. Tathā hi te kaṇṭake vattantā viya hontīti “kaṇṭakavuttikā”ti vuttā. Ṭhatvā bhuñjananahānapaṭikkhepādivatasamāyogena paṇḍaratarā[V 1.0199]. “Acelakasāvakā”ti ājīvakasāvake vadati. Te kira ājīvakaladdhiyā visuddhacittatāya nigaṇṭhehipi paṇḍaratarā. Nandādayo hi tathārūpaṃ ājīvakapaṭipattiṃ ukkaṃsaṃ pāpetvā ṭhitā. Tasmā nigaṇṭhehi ājīvakasāvakehi ca paṇḍaratarā paramasukkābhijātīti ayaṃ tassa laddhi.

'Orabbhikā' (sheep-butchers) are those who kill sheep. Similarly, swine-butchers and others should be understood. 'Luddā' (hunters) refers to others, such as deer-hunters, fowlers, and the like. Due to their addiction to evil deeds, he calls them 'kaṇhābhijāti' (of dark birth). 'Bhikkhū' (monks) refers to monks in the Buddha’s dispensation. He says that they, with the intention that 'they consume with desire and lust,' 'eat food after throwing thorns into the four requisites.' Why? Because it is his wrong grasp that 'they indulge in the most refined requisites'; therefore, others say that even when consuming rightfully obtained requisites, due to their opposition to the ascetic practice of the Ājīvakas, they are said to 'eat food after throwing thorns into the requisites.' Some ascetics are those who are devoted to self-mortification in its extreme form. Indeed, they are called 'kaṇṭakavuttikā' (thorn-practitioners) because they seem to live as if among thorns. By adhering to practices like refusing to eat while standing, refusing to bathe, and similar austerities, they are excessively white. He refers to the followers of the Ājīvakas as 'acelakasāvakā' (disciples of the naked ascetics). It is said that due to the purity of mind attained through the Ājīvaka doctrine, they are even whiter than the Nigaṇṭhas (Jains). For Nanda and others, having elevated such Ājīvaka practices, stood firm. Thus, his doctrine is that they are whiter than the Nigaṇṭhas and the Ājīvaka disciples, called 'paramasukkābhijāti' (of the purest white birth).

Purisabhūmiyoti padhānapuggalena niddeso. Itthīnampi tā bhūmiyo icchanteva. “Bhikkhu ca pannako”tiādi tesaṃ pāḷiyeva. Tattha pannakoti bhikkhāya vicaraṇako, tesaṃ vā paṭipattiyā paṭipannako. Jinoti jiṇṇo jarāvasena hīnadhātuko, attano [P 1.0291] vā paṭipattiyā paṭipakkhaṃ jinitvā ṭhito. So kira tathābhūto dhammampi kassaci na kathesi. Tenāha “na kiñci āhā”ti. Oṭṭhavadanādivippakāre katepi khamanavasena na kiñci vadatītipi vadanti. Alābhinti “so na kumbhimukhā paṭiggaṇhātī”tiādinā [M 1.0225] (dī. ni. 1.394) nayena vuttaalābhahetusamāyogena alābhiṃ, tatoyeva jighacchādubbalaparetatāya sayanaparāyanaṃ “samaṇaṃ pannabhūmī”ti vadati.

'Purisabhūmi' (the stage of a man) is a designation by way of the principal individual. Those stages are also intended for women. 'Bhikkhu ca pannako' (a monk and a fallen one), etc., is their own Pāli text. Therein, 'pannaka' (a fallen one) means one who wanders for alms, or one who is committed to their practice. 'Jina' (conqueror) means aged, with weakened faculties due to old age, or one who, through his own practice, has conquered the opposition and stands firm. It is said that such a one did not teach the Dhamma to anyone. Therefore, it is said, 'he said nothing.' Even when various forms of contemptuous expressions are made, they also say that he speaks nothing because of forbearance. 'Alābhi' (without gain) means being without gain due to the association of causes for lack of gain, in the manner stated by way of 'he did not receive from the mouth of a pot,' etc. (Dī. Ni. 1.394); because of that, being overcome by hunger and weakness and devoted to lying down, he is called 'a recluse in the stage of the fallen.'

Ājīvavuttisatānīti sattānaṃ ājīvabhūtāni jīvikāvuttisatāni. Pasuggahaṇena eḷakajāti gahitā, migaggahaṇena rurugavayādisabbamigajāti. Bahū devāti cātumahārājikādibrahmakāyikādivasena, tesaṃ antarabhedavasena bahū devā. Tattha cātumahārājikānaṃ ekaccabhedo mahāsamayasuttavasena (dī. ni. 2.331) dīpetabbo. Manussāpi anantāti dīpadesakulavaṃsājīvādivibhāgavasena manussāpi anantabhedā. Pisācā eva pesācā. Te aparapetādayo mahantamahantā. Chaddantadahamandākiniyo kuvāḷiyamucalindanāmena vadati.

'Ājīvavuttisatāni' (hundreds of livelihoods) refers to the hundreds of ways of living that are the livelihood of beings. By the term 'cattle', the species of goats is included; by the term 'wild animals', all species like ruru deer, gayal, etc., are included. 'Bahū devā' (many devas) refers to many devas from the Four Great Kings up to the Brahmā realms, etc., according to their internal divisions. Therein, a certain division of the Four Great Kings should be explained by way of the Mahāsamaya Sutta (Dī. Ni. 2.331). 'Manussāpi anantā' (humans too are endless) means humans too are of endless variety according to divisions of island, country, clan, lineage, livelihood, etc. Pisācas are the same as pesācas. They, the Aparapetas and others, are very great. He speaks of the Chaddanta, Daha, and Mandākinī by the names Kuvāḷiya and Mucalinda.

Pavuṭāti pabbagaṇṭhikā. Paṇḍitopi [P 1.0292] …pe… uddhaṃ na gacchati, kasmā? Sattānaṃ saṃsaraṇakālassa niyatabhāvato. Aparipakkaṃ saṃsaraṇanimittaṃ sīlādinā paripāceti nāma sīghaṃyeva visuddhippattiyā. Paripakkaṃ kammaṃ phussa phussa patvā patvā kālena paripakkabhāvānāpādanena byantiṃ karoti nāma.

'Pavuṭa' means a mountain ridge. 'Even the wise... does not go beyond'—why? Because the period of beings' wandering in saṃsāra is fixed. An unripened cause for wandering is ripened by virtue and so on, for the sake of quickly attaining purity. A ripened kamma, having been experienced again and again, is brought to an end over time by not producing a further state of ripening.

Suttaguḷeti suttavaṭṭiyaṃ. “Nibbeṭhiyamānameva paletī”ti upamāya sattānaṃ saṃsāro anukkamena khīyateva, na tassa vaḍḍhatīti dasseti paricchinnarūpattā.

'Suttaguḷa' (a ball of thread) means a coil of thread. By the simile, 'While being unwound, it runs out,' it is shown that the wandering of beings in saṃsāra gradually comes to an end and does not increase, because its nature is limited.

Ajitakesakambalavādavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Doctrine of Ajita Kesakambala

171. Dinnanti [V 1.0200] deyyadhammasīsena dānaṃ vuttanti āha “dinnassa phalābhāvaṃ vadatī”ti, dinnaṃ pana annādivatthuṃ kathaṃ paṭikkhipati. Eseva nayo yiṭṭhaṃ hutanti etthāpi. Mahāyāgoti sabbasādhāraṇaṃ mahādānaṃ. Pāhunakasakkāroti pāhunabhāvena kātabbasakkāro. Phalanti ānisaṃsaphalaṃ, nissandaphalañca. Vipākoti sadisaphalaṃ. Paraloke ṭhitassa ayaṃ loko natthīti paraloke ṭhitassa kammunā laddhabbo ayaṃ loko na hoti. Idhaloke ṭhitassāpi paraloko natthīti idhaloke ṭhitassa kammunā laddhabbo paraloko na hoti. Tattha kāraṇamāha “sabbe [M 1.0226] tattha tattheva ucchijjantī”ti. Ime sattā yattha yattha bhave, yoniādīsu ca ṭhitā tattha tattheva ucchijjanti nirudayavināsavasena vinassanti. Phalābhāvavasenāti mātāpitūsu sammāpaṭipattimicchāpaṭipattīnaṃ phalassa abhāvavasena “natthi mātā, natthi pitā”ti vadati, na mātāpitūnaṃ, nāpi tesu idāni kayiramānasakkārāsakkārānaṃ abhāvavasena tesaṃ lokapaccakkhattā. Pubbuḷakassa viya imesaṃ sattānaṃ uppādo nāma kevalo, na cavitvā āgamanapubbakoti dassanatthaṃ “natthi sattā opapātikā”ti vuttanti āha “cavitvā upapajjanakasattā nāma natthīti vadatī”ti. Samaṇena nāma yāthāvato [P 1.0293] jānantena kassaci kiñci akathetvā saññatena bhavitabbaṃ, aññathā āhopurisikā nāma siyā. Kiñhi paro parassa karissati? Tathā ca attano sampādanassa kassaci avassayo eva na siyā tattha tattheva ucchijjanatoti āha “ye imañca…pe… pavedentī”ti.

171. 'Given' (dinnaṃ) is said to be a gift (dānaṃ) under the heading of a thing to be given, for he says, 'he declares the non-existence of the fruit of what is given.' But how does he reject a given thing, such as food? The same method applies here also to 'sacrificed' (yiṭṭhaṃ) and 'offered' (hutaṃ). 'A great sacrifice' (mahāyāgo) means a great gift common to all. 'Hospitality' (pāhunakasakkāro) means the honor to be shown to one as a guest. 'Fruit' (phalaṃ) refers to the fruit of benefit (ānisaṃsaphalaṃ) and the fruit of outflow (nissandaphalaṃ). 'Result' (vipāko) means a corresponding fruit. 'For one established in the other world, this world does not exist' means that this world is not to be obtained by the kamma of one established in the other world. 'For one established in this world, the other world does not exist' means that the other world is not to be obtained by the kamma of one established in this world. He states the reason for that: 'All perish right there.' These beings, wherever they are established in any existence, womb, and so on, perish right there; they are destroyed by way of a destruction without re-arising. 'Due to the absence of fruit' means that he says, 'There is no mother, there is no father,' due to the absence of fruit from proper and improper conduct towards one's mother and father, not due to the non-existence of mother and father, nor due to the absence of honor and dishonor currently being done to them, since they are directly perceptible to the world. To show that the arising of these beings is merely so, like that of a bubble, and is not preceded by passing away and coming again, it is said, 'There are no spontaneously arisen beings,' about which he says, 'he says there are no beings who pass away and are reborn.' A recluse, knowing things as they are, should be restrained, not saying anything to anyone; otherwise, it would be mere boastfulness. For what can one person do for another? And so, there would be no reliance on anyone for one's own accomplishment, since they perish right there. Therefore, he says, 'Those who declare this... and so on.'

Catūsu mahābhūtesu niyuttoti cātumahābhūtiko. Yathā pana mattikāya nibbattaṃ bhājanaṃ mattikāmayaṃ, evaṃ ayaṃ catūhi mahābhūtehi nibbattoti āha “catumahābhūtamayo”ti. Ajjhattikapathavīdhātūti sattasantānagatā pathavīdhātu. Bāhirapathavīdhātunti bahiddhā mahāpathaviṃ. Upagacchatīti bāhirapathavikāyato tadekadesabhūtā pathavī āgantvā ajjhattikabhāvappattiyā sattabhāvena saṇṭhitā idāni ghaṭādigatapathavī viya tameva bāhirapathavikāyaṃ upeti upagacchati sabbaso tena nibbisesataṃ ekībhāvameva gacchati. Āpādīsupi eseva nayoti ettha pajjunnena mahāsamuddato gahitaāpo viya vassodakabhāvena punapi mahāsamuddameva, sūriyarasmito gahitaṃ indaggisaṅkhātatejo viya puna sūriyarasmiṃ, mahāvāyukhandhato niggatamahāvāto viya tameva vāyukhandhaṃ upeti upagacchatīti diṭṭhigatikassa adhippāyo. Manacchaṭṭhāni indriyāni ākāsaṃ pakkhandanti tesaṃ visayābhāvāti vadanti. Visayigahaṇena hi visayāpi gahitā eva hontīti. Guṇāguṇapadānīti guṇadosakoṭṭhāsā. Sarīrameva padānīti adhippetaṃ sarīrena taṃtaṃkiriyāya [V 1.0201] pajjitabbato. Dabbanti muyhantīti dattū, mūḷhapuggalā. Tehi dattūhi [P 1.0294] bālamanussehi. “Paraloko atthī”ti mati yesaṃ, te atthikā, tesaṃ vādoti atthikavādo, taṃ atthikavādaṃ.

Because it is bound to the four great elements, it is called 'composed of the four great elements' (cātumahābhūtiko). Just as a pot made from clay is called 'made of clay' (mattikāmayaṃ), so too this is produced from the four great elements; thus it is said to be 'made of the four great elements' (catumahābhūtamayo). 'The internal earth element' is the earth element that has entered the continuity of a being. 'The external earth element' is the great earth outside. 'It returns' means this: the earth element, which came from the external earth-body and became a part of it, and which, having attained an internal state, was established as a being, now returns to that very external earth-body, goes up to it, just like the earth element that has gone into a pot; it completely attains a state of non-difference, a state of oneness, with it. The same method applies to water and the other elements. Here, the intention of the holder of the speculative view is that just as water taken from the great ocean by a cloud returns to the great ocean as rainwater, and just as fire, called the fire of Indra, taken from the sun's rays returns to the sun's rays, and just as a great wind that has issued from the great mass of wind returns to that very mass of wind. 'The sense faculties, with the mind as the sixth, leap into space' means they say they do so because of the absence of their objects. For by the grasping of the subject, the objects are also grasped. 'Bases of good and bad' (guṇāguṇapadāni) means the divisions of virtue and fault. 'The body itself is the basis' is the intention, because this or that action is to be undertaken by the body. `Dattū` (fools) are so called because they are deluded (`muyhanti`); they are deluded individuals. By those fools, by those foolish humans. Those whose view is 'the other world exists' are the believers (atthikā); their doctrine is the belief in existence (atthikavādo)—that doctrine of the believers.

Kammaṃ [M 1.0227] paṭibāhati akiriyavādibhāvato. Vipākaṃ paṭibāhati sabbena sabbaṃ āyatiṃ upapattiyā paṭikkhipanato. Ubhayaṃ paṭibāhati sabbaso hetupaṭibāhaneneva phalassapi paṭikkhittattā. Ubhayanti hi kammaṃ vipākañcāti ubhayaṃ. So hi “ahetū appaccayā sattā saṃkilissanti, visujjhanti cā”ti (dī. ni. 1.168; ma. ni. 2.100, 227; saṃ. ni. 3.212) vadanto kammassa viya vipākassāpi saṃkilesavisuddhīnaṃ paccayattābhāvavacanato tadubhayaṃ paṭibāhati nāma. Vipāko paṭibāhito hoti asati kamme vipākābhāvato. Kammaṃ paṭibāhitaṃ hoti asati vipāke kammassa niratthakabhāvāpattito. Atthatoti sarūpena. Ubhayappaṭibāhakāti visuṃ visuṃ taṃtaṃdiṭṭhidīpakabhāvena pāḷiyaṃ āgatāpi paccekaṃ tividhadiṭṭhikā eva ubhayapaṭibāhakattā. Ubhayappaṭibāhakāti hi hetuvacanaṃ. “Ahetukavādā cevā”tiādi paṭiññāvacanaṃ. Yo hi vipākapaṭibāhanena natthikadiṭṭhiko ucchedavādī, so atthato kammapaṭibāhanena akiriyadiṭṭhiko, ubhayapaṭibāhanena ahetukadiṭṭhiko ca hoti. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo.

Action is denied on account of the doctrine of inaction. Result is denied by completely rejecting future rebirth. Both are denied by entirely rejecting the cause, since the fruit is also rejected. Indeed, 'both' refers to action and result. For he who says, 'Beings are defiled and purified without cause or condition,' thereby denies both by stating that there is no conditionality for defilement and purification, which are the result, just as there is none for action. Result is denied because without action, there is no result. Action is denied because without result, action becomes meaningless. `Atthato` means 'in essence.' 'Deniers of both': although they appear separately in the Pāli text as illuminators of their respective views, each is in fact of a threefold view, because they deny both. For 'because they deny both' is the statement of the reason, while 'And proponents of no-cause...' and so on is the declaration. For one who, by denying the result, is a nihilist and an annihilationist, is in essence, by denying action, a proponent of inaction, and by denying both, a proponent of no-cause. The same principle applies to the other two.

Sajjhāyantīti taṃ diṭṭhidīpakaṃ ganthaṃ uggahetvā paṭhanti. Vīmaṃsantīti tassa atthaṃ vicārenti. “Tesa”ntiādi vīmaṃsanākāradassanaṃ. Tasmiṃ ārammaṇeti yathāparikappitakammaphalābhāvādike “karoto na karīyati pāpa”nti ādinayappavattāya laddhiyā ārammaṇe. Micchāsati santiṭṭhatīti “karoto na karīyati pāpa”ntiādivasena anussavūpaladdhe atthe tadākāraparivitakkanehi saviggahe viya sarūpato cittassa paccupaṭṭhite cirakālaparicayena evametanti nijjhānakkhamabhāvūpagamanena nijjhānakkhantiyā [P 1.0295] tathāgahite punappunaṃ tatheva āsevantassa bahulīkarontassa micchāvitakkena samādiyamānā micchāvāyāmūpatthambhitā ataṃsabhāvaṃ “taṃsabhāva”nti gaṇhantī micchāsatīti laddhanāmā taṃladdhisahagatā taṇhā santiṭṭhati. Cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hotīti yathāsakaṃ vitakkādipaccayalābhena tasmiṃ ārammaṇe avaṭṭhitatāya anekaggataṃ pahāya ekaggaṃ appitaṃ viya hoti. Cittasīsena micchāsamādhi eva vutto. Sopi hi paccayavisesehi laddhabhāvanābalo īdise ṭhāne samādhānapatirūpakiccakaroyeva, vāḷavijjhanādīsu viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Javanāni javantīti anekakkhattuṃ tenākārena pubbabhāgiyesu javanavāresu pavattesu [M 1.0228] sabbapacchime javanavāre satta javanāni [V 1.0202] javanti. Paṭhame javane satekicchā honti. Tathā dutiyādīsūti dhammasabhāvadassanamattametaṃ, na pana tasmiṃ khaṇe tesaṃ tikicchā kenaci sakkā kātuṃ.

'They recite' means they take up and recite that scripture which illuminates views. 'They investigate' means they examine its meaning. 'Of those' and so on illustrates the manner of investigation. 'In that object' refers to the object, such as the non-existence of karmic results as conceived, in the doctrine that proceeds according to the principle 'for the doer, no evil is done,' and so forth. 'Wrong mindfulness becomes established' means that craving associated with that doctrine, which has gained the name 'wrong mindfulness' by grasping the nature of non-truth as 'truth,' becomes established in the object. This occurs when, in the meaning learned from tradition (such as 'for the doer, no evil is done'), the mind is present by its nature as if taking a firm hold with thoughts of that form, and through prolonged familiarity, by accepting it as true with conviction, repeatedly cultivating and reinforcing it, being taken up by wrong thought and supported by wrong effort. 'The mind becomes one-pointed' means that, due to the attainment of its own conditions of thought and the like, the mind, being established on that object, abandons distraction and becomes one-pointed, as if fixed. Wrong concentration itself is spoken of as the head of the mind. Indeed, even that, when strengthened by the power of development through specific conditions, performs a function resembling concentration in such a situation, just as in piercing a horse-hair and the like—this should be understood. 'Impulsions proceed' means that when preliminary volitional processes occur repeatedly in that manner, in the last volitional process, seven impulsions proceed. In the first impulsion, they are remediable. Similarly, in the second and so on—this is merely a description of the nature of phenomena; however, at that moment, no one can apply a remedy to them.

Tatthāti tesu tīsu micchādassanesu. Koci ekaṃ dassanaṃ okkamatīti yassa ekasmiṃyeva abhiniveso āsevanā ca pavattā, so ekameva dassanaṃ okkamati. Yassa pana dvīsu tīsupi vā abhiniveso āsevanā ca pavattā, so dve tīṇipi okkamati, etena yā pubbe ubhayapaṭibāhakatāmukhena dīpitā atthasiddhā sabbadiṭṭhikatā, sā pubbabhāgiyā. Yā pana micchattaniyāmokkantibhūtā, sā yathāsakaṃ paccayasamudāgamasiddhito bhinnārammaṇānaṃ viya visesādhigamānaṃ ekajjhaṃ anuppattiyā asaṅkiṇṇā evāti dasseti. “Ekasmiṃ okkantepī”tiādinā tissannampi diṭṭhīnaṃ samānabalataṃ samānaphalatañca dasseti. Tasmā tissopi cetā ekassa uppannā abbokiṇṇā eva, ekāya vipāke dinne [P 1.0296] itarā anubalappadāyikāyo honti. “Vaṭṭakhāṇu nāmesā”ti idaṃ vacanaṃ neyyatthaṃ, na nītatthaṃ. Tathā hi papañcasūdaniyaṃ “kiṃ panesa ekasmiṃyeva attabhāve niyato hoti, udāhu aññasmiṃ pīti? Ekasmiṃyeva niyato, āsevanavasena pana bhavantarepi taṃ taṃ diṭṭhiṃ roceti yevā”ti (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 3.129) vuttaṃ. Akusalañhi nāmetaṃ abalaṃ dubbalaṃ, na kusalaṃ viya sabalaṃ mahābalaṃ. Tasmā “ekasmiṃyeva attabhāve niyato”ti vuttaṃ. Aññathā sammattaniyāmo viya micchattaniyāmopi accantiko siyā, na ca accantiko. Yadi evaṃ vaṭṭakhāṇujotanā kathanti āha “āsevanavasena panā”tiādi. Tasmā yathā “sakiṃ nimuggopi nimuggo eva bālo”ti vuttaṃ, evaṃ vaṭṭakhāṇujotanā. Yādise hi paccaye paṭicca ayaṃ taṃ taṃ dassanaṃ okkanto puna kadāci tappaṭipakkhe paccaye paṭicca tato sīsukkhipanamassa na hotīti na vattabbaṃ, tasmā “yebhuyyena hi evarūpassa bhavato vuṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthī”ti vuttaṃ.

'Therein' refers to those three wrong views. 'Someone enters into one view' means: for whom there is adherence to and practice of only one, that one enters into that one view alone. But for whom there is adherence to and practice of two or even three, that one enters into two or three. By this, it is shown that the state of all views being established in essence, which was previously explained by way of denying both, is the preliminary stage. But the stage that is the descent into the certainty of wrongness, due to its arising from its respective conditions, is unmixed, like the distinct attainments of those with different objects, because of their non-convergence into one. 'Even when entering into one,' etc., shows that all three views are equal in strength and equal in result. Therefore, even if these three arise for one person, they remain unmixed. When the result of one is given, the others are contributors of supporting strength. 'This is called a stake in the round of rebirths': This statement is interpretable, not of definitive meaning. For in the Papañcasūdanī, it is said: 'But is this fixed in only one existence, or in another as well? It is fixed in only one, but due to habitual practice, in another existence, one inclines toward that view.' For this unwholesome state is weak and feeble, not like a wholesome state, which is strong and powerful. Thus, it is said, 'fixed in only one existence.' Otherwise, like the certainty of rightness, the certainty of wrongness would also be absolute—but it is not absolute. If this is so, why is it illustrated by 'a stake in the round of rebirths'? It is said, 'but due to habitual practice,' etc. Therefore, just as it is said, 'Even if a fool sinks once, he is still sunk,' so too is the illustration of the stake in the round of rebirths. For when this person, having entered a particular view due to certain conditions, encounters opposing conditions, it should not be said that they will never lift their head from it. Thus, it is said, 'For such a one, for the most part, there is no rising up.'

Tasmāti yasmā evaṃ saṃsārakhāṇubhāvassapi paccayo apaṇṇakajāto, tasmā. Bhūtikāmoti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthānaṃ vasena attano guṇehi vaḍḍhikāmo.

'Therefore': because the cause of even the state of being a stake in the round of rebirths is of this unerring kind, therefore. 'Desiring welfare' means desiring growth through one's own virtues in terms of benefits in this life, benefits in the next life, and the ultimate benefit.

Pakudhakaccāyanavādavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Doctrine of Pakudha Kaccāyana

174. Akatāti [M 1.0229] samena visamena vā kenaci hetunā na katā na vihitā. Katavidho karaṇavidhi natthi etesanti akatavidhānā[P 1.0297]. Padadvayenāpi loke kenaci hetupaccayena nesaṃ anibbattanabhāvaṃ dasseti. Iddhiyāpi na nimmitāti kassaci iddhimato cetovasippattassa devassa[V 1.0203], issarādino vā iddhiyāpi na nimmitā. Animmāpitā kassaci animmāpitā. Vuttatthamevāti brahmajālavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.30) vuttatthameva. Vañjhāti vañjhapasuvañjhatālādayo viya aphalā, kassaci ajanakāti attho, etena pathavikāyādīnaṃ rūpādijanakabhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati. Rūpasaddādayo hi pathavikāyādīhi appaṭibaddhavuttikāti tassa laddhi. Pabbatakūṭaṃ viya ṭhitāti kūṭaṭṭhā, yathā pabbatakūṭaṃ kenaci anibbattitaṃ, kassaci ca anibbattakaṃ, evamete pīti adhippāyo. Yamidaṃ “bījato aṅkurādi jāyatī”ti vuccati, taṃ vijjamānameva tato nikkhamati, na avijjamānaṃ, aññathā aññatopi aññassa upaladdhi siyāti adhippāyo. Ṭhitattāti nibbikārābhāvena ṭhitattā. Na calantīti vikāraṃ nāpajjanti. Vikārābhāvato hi tesaṃ sattannaṃ kāyānaṃ esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhitatā. Aniñjanañca attano pakatiyā avaṭṭhānameva. Tenāha “na vipariṇamantī”ti. Avipariṇāmadhammattā eva hi te aññamaññaṃ na byābādhenti. Sati hi vikāraṃ āpādetabbatāya byābādhakatāpi siyā, tathā anuggahetabbatāya anuggāhakatāti tadabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ pāḷiyaṃ nālantiādi vuttaṃ. Pathavī eva kāyekadesattā pathavikāyo. Jīvasattamānaṃ kāyānaṃ niccatāya nibbikārabhāvato na [P 1.0298] hantabbatā, na ghātetabbatā cāti neva koci hantā vā ghātetā vā, tenevāha “sattannaṃ tveva kāyāna”ntiādi. Yadi koci hantā natthi, kathaṃ satthappahāroti āha “yathā muggarāsi ādīsū”tiādi. Kevalaṃ saññāmattameva hoti. Hananaghātanādi pana paramatthato nattheva kāyānaṃ avikopanīyabhāvatoti adhippāyo.

174. "Unmade" (akatā) means not made or created by any cause, whether equal or unequal. "Without a mode of making" (akatavidhānā) means that for them there is no process or mode of making. By these two words, it is shown that they do not arise in the world due to any cause or condition. "Not created even by psychic power" (iddhiyāpi na nimmitā) means they are not created even by the psychic power of any deity who has attained mastery over the mind, or by a lord or similar being. "Not fashioned" (animmāpitā) means not fashioned by anyone. It is the same meaning as stated in the Brahmajāla Commentary (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.30). "Barren" (vañjhā) means fruitless, like sterile cattle or a barren palm tree, meaning they do not generate anything for anyone. By this, he denies that the earth-body, and so on, can generate form, and so on. For his doctrine is that forms, sounds, and so on, do not depend on the earth-body, and so on, for their existence. "Standing like a mountain peak" (pabbatakūṭaṃ viya ṭhitā) means they are peak-like (kūṭaṭṭhā); just as a mountain peak is not produced by anyone nor produces anything for anyone, so too are these—this is the intended meaning. When it is said, "From a seed, a sprout arises," that which already exists emerges from it, not what does not exist. Otherwise, one might perceive something from another source—this is the intended meaning. "Due to their stability" (ṭhitattā) means due to their being stable because of the absence of transformation. "They do not move" (na calanti) means they do not undergo change. For because they are free from alteration, these seven bodies have the quality of standing firm like a pillar. "Non-wavering" (aniñjana) is simply their natural state of stability. Hence, it is said, "They do not transform." For because they are of an immutable nature, they do not harm one another. If there were the possibility of being made to undergo change, there could also be the state of harming; likewise, if there were the possibility of being supported, there could be the state of supporting. To show the absence of this, 'they are not able' (nālaṃ), and so on, is said in the Pāḷi. The earth itself, being a part of the body, is the earth-body. Because these seven bodies, including the life-body, are eternal and unchanging, they cannot be killed or destroyed. Thus, there is no killer or destroyer, as stated: "Of these seven bodies..." and so on. If there is no killer, how can there be a blow from a weapon? The text explains, "Just as in the case of a heap of rushes..." and so on. It is merely a matter of perception. But in ultimate truth, there is no killing, destruction, and so on, because the bodies are indestructible—this is the intended meaning.

Nigaṇṭhanāṭaputtavādavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Doctrine of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta

177. Cattāro yāmā bhāgā catuyāmā, catuyāmā eva cātuyāmā, bhāgattho hi idha yāma-saddo yathā “rattiyā paṭhamo yāmo”ti[M 1.0230]. So panettha bhāgo saṃvaralakkhaṇoti āha “cātuyāmasaṃvutoti catukoṭṭhāsena saṃvarena saṃvuto”ti. Paṭikkhittasabbasītodakoti paṭikkhittasabbasītodakaparibhogo. Sabbena pāpavāraṇena yuttoti sabbappakārena saṃvaralakkhaṇena samannāgato. Dhutapāpoti sabbena nijjaralakkhaṇena pāpavāraṇena vidhutapāpo. Phuṭṭhoti aṭṭhannampi kammānaṃ khepanena mokkhappattiyā kammakkhayalakkhaṇena sabbena pāpavāraṇena phuṭṭho taṃ patvā ṭhito. Koṭippattacittoti mokkhādhigameneva uttamamariyādappattacitto. Yatattoti kāyādīsu indriyesu saṃyametabbassa abhāvato saṃyatacitto. Suppatiṭṭhitacittoti nissesato suṭṭhu patiṭṭhitacitto. Sāsanānulomaṃ nāma pāpavāraṇena yuttatā. Tenāha “dhutapāpo”tiādi. Asuddhaladdhitāyāti “atthi jīvo, so ca siyā nicco, siyā anicco”ti evamādiasuddhaladdhitāya[V 1.0204]. Sabbāti kammapakativibhāgādivisayā sabbā nijjhānakkhantiyo. Diṭṭhiye vāti micchādiṭṭhiyo eva jātā.

177. The four watches are the four parts; the four parts are indeed the four watches. For here the word 'yāma' means 'part,' as in 'the first watch of the night.' Here, however, that part refers to the characteristic of restraint. Thus it is said: 'restrained by the fourfold restraint' means 'restrained by restraint in four aspects.' 'Rejecting all cold water' means 'abstaining from the use of all cold water.' 'Endowed with all barriers against evil' means 'possessed of the characteristic of restraint in every way.' 'Shaken off evil' means: one who has shaken off evil by means of the all-encompassing barrier against evil, which has the characteristic of wearing away kamma. 'Touched' means: having attained that state and stood firm, he is touched by the all-encompassing barrier against evil, which is characterized by the destruction of kamma, for the attainment of liberation through the exhaustion of all eight kinds of kamma. 'A mind that has reached the peak' means 'a mind that has attained the highest limit simply by the realization of liberation.' 'Self-controlled' means 'the mind is restrained due to the absence of anything that needs to be restrained in the faculties such as the body.' 'Well-established mind' means 'a mind thoroughly well-established without remainder.' 'In accordance with the teaching' means 'being endowed with barriers against evil.' Hence it is said: 'shaken off evil,' and so forth. 'Due to an impure doctrine' refers to 'an impure doctrine such as, "There is a soul, and it may be eternal or non-eternal," and so forth.' 'All' refers to 'all forms of acceptance through reflection concerning the divisions of kamma and its nature, and so forth.' 'Or views' means 'wrong views that have arisen.'

Sañcayabelaṭṭhaputtavādavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of Sañcaya Belaṭṭhaputta's Doctrine

179-181. Amarāvikkhepe [P 1.0299] vuttanayo evāti brahmajāle amarāvikkhepavādasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.61-63) vuttanayo eva vikkhepabyākaraṇabhāvato, tatheva cettha vikkhepavādassa āgatattā.

179-181. The method concerning the Amarāvikkhepa is just as stated. That is, the method stated in the commentary on the Amarāvikkhepa doctrine in the Brahmajāla Sutta (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.61-63) is the same here, due to its being an evasive exposition, and because the doctrine of evasion has similarly appeared here.

Paṭhamasandiṭṭhikasāmaññaphalavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the First Visible Fruit of Recluseship

183. Yathā te rucceyyāti idāni mayā pucchiyamāno attho yathā tava citte roceyya. Gharadāsiyā kucchismiṃ jāto antojāto. Dhanena kīto dhanakkīto. Bandhaggāhagahito karamarānīto. Sāmanti sayameva. Dāsabyanti dāsabhāvaṃ. Koci dāsopi samāno alaso kammaṃ akaronto “kammakāro”ti na vuccatīti āha “analaso kammakaraṇasīloyevā”ti. Paṭhamamevāti āsannataraṭṭhānūpasaṅkamanato pageva puretarameva. Pacchāti sāmikassa nipajjāya pacchā. Sayanato avuṭṭhiteti rattiyā vibhāyanavelāya seyyato avuṭṭhite. Paccūsakālato paṭṭhāyāti atītāya [M 1.0231] rattiyā paccūsakālato paṭṭhāya. Yāva sāmino rattiṃ niddokkamananti aparāya padosavelāyaṃ yāva niddokkamanaṃ. Kiṃ kāranti kiṃ karaṇīyaṃ, kiṃkārabhāvato pucchitvā kātabbaveyyāvaccanti attho.

183. 'As it pleases you' means: 'As the matter now being asked by me pleases your mind.' 'Born in the womb of a household slave' means 'born within.' 'Bought with wealth' means 'bought with money.' 'Seized by capture' means 'brought as a prisoner of war.' 'Sāmaṃ' means 'by himself.' 'Slavery' means 'the state of being a slave.' Some slave, being idle and not doing work, is not called a 'worker'; hence it is said: 'not lazy, but habitually performing work.' 'First' means 'even earlier, because of approaching a nearer place.' 'After' means 'after the master has lain down.' 'Not rising from bed' means 'not having risen from his bed at the time the night is dawning.' 'From the early morning' means 'starting from the early morning of the night that has passed.' 'Until the master goes to sleep for the night' means 'until he goes to sleep in the late evening.' 'What should be done?' means 'what is to be done?'; the meaning is, being one who asks what to do, he then performs the required service.

Devo viyāti ādhipaccaparivārādisampattisamannāgato padhānadevo viya. So vatassāhanti so vata assaṃ ahaṃ. So rājā viya ahampi bhaveyyaṃ, kathaṃ puññāni kareyyaṃ, yadi puññāni uḷārāni kareyyanti yojanā. “So vatassa’ssa”nti pāṭhe so rājā assa ahaṃ assaṃ vata, yadi puññāni kareyyanti yojanā. Tenāha “ayamevattho”ti. Assanti uttamapurisappayoge ahaṃ-saddo appayuttopi payutto eva hoti. Yāvajīvaṃ na sakkhissāmi dātunti yāvajīvaṃ dānatthāya ussāhaṃ karontopi yaṃ rājā ekaṃ divasaṃ deti[P 1.0300], tato satabhāgampi dātuṃ na sakkhissāmi. Tasmā pabbajissāmīti pabbajjāyaṃ ussāhaṃ katvāti yojanā.

'Like a god' means 'like a principal god endowed with attainments such as sovereignty and retinue.' 'So vatassāhaṃ' means 'so indeed may I be.' The connection is: 'May I too be like that king; how should I make merit? If I were to make abundant merit?' In the reading 'so vatassa'ssa,' the connection is: 'May I indeed be that king, if I were to make merit.' Therefore, it is said: 'This is indeed the meaning.' Regarding 'assaṃ,' in the first-person usage, even if the word 'ahaṃ' (I) is not employed, it is nevertheless implied. 'For my whole life, I will not be able to give' means: 'Even if I strive to give for my whole life, I will not be able to give even a hundredth part of what the king gives in a single day.' Therefore, the connection is: 'I will go forth,' having made an effort towards ordination.

Kāyena [V 1.0205] saṃvutoti kāyena saṃvaritabbaṃ kāyadvārena pavattanakaṃ pāpadhammaṃ saṃvaritvā vihareyyāti ayamettha atthoti āha “kāyena pihito hutvā”tiādi. Ghāsacchādanena paramatāyāti ghāsacchādanapariyesane sallekhavasena paramatāya, ukkaṭṭhabhāve saṇṭhito ghāsacchādanameva vā paramaṃ parā koṭi etassa, na tato paraṃ kiñci āmisajātaṃ pariyesati paccāsisati cāti ghāsacchādanaparamo, tabbhāvo ghāsacchādanaparamatā, tassā ghāsacchādanaparamatāya. Vivekaṭṭhakāyānanti gaṇasaṅgaṇikato pavivitte ṭhitakāyānaṃ. Nekkhammābhiratānanti jhānābhiratānaṃ. Tāya eva jhānābhiratiyā paramaṃ uttamaṃ vodānaṃ visuddhiṃ pattatāya paramavodānappattānaṃ. Kilesūpadhiabhisaṅkhārūpadhīnaṃ accantavigamena nirupadhīnaṃ. Visaṅkhāragatānanti adhigatanibbānānaṃ. Ettha ca paṭhamo viveko itarehi dvīhi vivekehi sahāpi pattabbo vināpi, tathā dutiyo. Tatiyo pana itarehi dvīhi saheva pattabbo, na vināti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Gaṇe janasamāgame sannipatanaṃ gaṇasaṅgaṇikā, taṃ pahāya eko viharati carati puggalavasena asahāyattā. Citte kilesānaṃ sannipatanaṃ cittakilesasaṅgaṇikā, taṃ pahāya eko viharati kilesavasena asahāyattā. Maggassa [M 1.0232] ekacittakkhaṇikattā, gotrabhuādīnañca ārammaṇamattattā na tesaṃ vasena sātisayā nibbutisukhasamphusanā, phalasamāpattinirodhasamāpattivasena sātisayāti āha “phalasamāpattiṃ vā nirodhasamāpattiṃ vā pavisitvā”ti. Phalapariyosāno hi nirodhoti.

'Restrained in body' means: 'One should restrain unwholesome actions that arise through the bodily door, which are to be restrained by the body, and dwell thus.' This is the meaning here. Thus it is said: 'being guarded in body,' and so forth. 'Supreme in almsfood and robes' means: 'supreme in the sense of austerity in seeking almsfood and robes, being established in the highest state.' Or, 'almsfood and robes alone are the ultimate limit for him; he does not seek or expect any material gain beyond that.' Thus, he is 'supreme in almsfood and robes,' and that state is 'supremacy in almsfood and robes,' and by that supremacy in almsfood and robes. 'Those whose bodies delight in seclusion' means 'those whose bodies abide apart from crowds and social gatherings.' 'Those who rejoice in renunciation' means 'those who delight in jhāna.' Through that very delight in jhāna, having attained the highest, supreme purity, they are 'supreme in purity.' 'Free from acquisitions' means 'utterly free from the acquisitions of defilements and formations.' 'Those who have reached the unconditioned' means 'those who have attained Nibbāna.' Here, the first kind of seclusion can be attained with or without the other two kinds, and likewise the second. But the third kind can only be attained together with the other two, not without them—this should be understood. 'Crowds and social gatherings' refers to the assembling of people in a group. Abandoning that, one dwells and moves about alone, being without companionship in terms of individuals. 'Defilements crowding the mind' refers to the gathering of defilements in the mind. Abandoning that, one dwells alone, being without companionship in terms of defilements. Because the path is of a single mind-moment, and because the change-of-lineage and other states are merely objects, there is no surpassing contact with the bliss of Nibbāna through them. But through fruition attainment or cessation attainment, there is a surpassing contact. Thus it is said: 'having entered fruition attainment or cessation attainment.' For cessation has its conclusion in fruition.

184. Abhiharitvāti abhimukhībhāvena netvā. “Ahaṃ cīvarādīhi payojanaṃ sādhessāmī”ti vacanaseso. Sappāyanti [P 1.0301] sabbagelaññapaharaṇavasena upakārāvahaṃ. Bhāvinā anatthato paripālanavasena gopanā rakkhāgutti. Paccuppannassa nisedhavasena āvaraṇagutti.

184. 'Abhiharitvā' means 'having brought it forward, having led it near.' The remainder of the statement is: 'I will accomplish my purpose with robes and other requisites.' 'Sappāya' means 'beneficial,' being helpful by way of removing all sickness. Protection, guarding, and security are by way of safeguarding from future harm; guarding by obstruction is by way of preventing present harm.

Dutiyasandiṭṭhikasāmaññaphalavaṇṇanā

The Second Explanation of the Visible Fruits of Asceticism

186. Kasatīti kasiṃ karoti. Gahapatikoti ettha ka-saddo appatthoti āha “ekagehamatte jeṭṭhako”ti, tena anekakulajeṭṭhakabhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati. Karaṃ karotīti karaṃ sampādeti. Vaḍḍhetīti uparūpari sampādanena vaḍḍheti. Evaṃ appampi pahāya pabbajituṃ dukkaranti ayamattho laṭukikopamasuttena (ma. ni. 2.151, 152) dīpetabbo. Tenāha “seyyathāpi, udāyi, puriso daliddo assako anāḷhiyo, tassassa ekaṃ agārakaṃ oluggaviluggaṃ kākātidāyiṃ naparamarūpa”nti vitthāro. Yadi appampi bhogaṃ pahāya pabbajituṃ dukkaraṃ, kasmā dāsavāre bhogaggahaṇaṃ na katanti āha “dāsavāre panā”tiādi. Yathā [V 1.0206] ca dāsassa bhogāpi abhogā parāyattabhāvato, evaṃ ñātayo pīti dāsavāre ñātiparivaṭṭaggahaṇampi na katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

186. "Kasati" means he cultivates. "Gahapatiko" here, the syllable 'ka' is of little meaning, so it is said: 'the eldest in a single household,' thereby rejecting the state of being the eldest of many families. "Karaṃ karoti" means he accomplishes the task. "Vaḍḍheti" means he increases it by repeated accomplishment. Thus, that it is difficult to go forth even after abandoning little—this meaning should be illustrated by the Quail Simile (MN 2.151, 152). Therefore, it is said: 'Suppose, Udāyi, a man is poor, destitute, without means, and he has only one dilapidated house, exposed to crows and other birds, with nothing more.' If it is difficult to go forth even after abandoning little wealth, why was the acceptance of wealth not mentioned in the case of the slave? It is said: 'But in the case of the slave...' And just as a slave's possessions are as if non-possessions due to their dependent state, so too with relatives—thus, it should be understood that in the slave's case, the acceptance of a group of relatives was also not mentioned.

Paṇītatarasāmaññaphalavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the More Excellent Fruits of Asceticism

189. Evarūpāhīti yathāvuttadāsakassakūpamāsadisāhi upamāhi sāmaññaphalaṃ dīpetuṃ pahoti bhagavā sakalampi rattindivaṃ tato bhiyyopi anantapaṭibhānatāya vicittanayadesanabhāvato. Tathāpīti satipi desanāya uttaruttarādhikanānānayavicittabhāve.

189. "Evarūpāhi" means that the Blessed One is capable of illuminating the fruits of asceticism through similes such as those of the slave and the farmer, throughout the entire day and night, and even more so, due to his boundless eloquence and the diverse nature of his teachings. "Tathāpi" means even though the teaching possesses diverse and subtle methods that are increasingly higher.

Ekatthametaṃ padaṃ sādhusaddasseva ka-kārena vaḍḍhitvā vuttattā, teneva sādhuka-saddassa atthaṃ vadantena atthuddhāravasena sādhu-saddo udāhaṭo. Āyācaneti abhimukhayācane, abhipatthanāyanti attho[P 1.0302]. Sampaṭicchaneti paṭiggaṇhane[M 1.0233]. Sampahaṃsaneti saṃvijjamānaguṇavasena haṃsane tosane, udaggatākaraṇeti attho. Dhammarucīti puññakāmo. Paññāṇavāti paññavā. Addubbhoti adūsako, anupaghātakoti attho. Idhāpīti imasmiṃ sāmaññaphalepi. Ayaṃ sādhu-saddo. Daḷhīkammeti sakkacca kiriyāyaṃ. Āṇattiyanti āṇāpane. “Suṇohi sādhukaṃ manasi karohī”ti hi vutte sādhuka-saddena savanamanasikārānaṃ sakkaccakiriyā viya tadāṇāpanampi jotitaṃ hoti, āyācanatthatā viya cassa āṇāpanatthatā veditabbā. Sundarepīti sundaratthepi. Idāni yathāvuttena sādhuka-saddassa atthattayena pakāsitaṃ visesaṃ dassetuṃ “daḷhīkammatthena hī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

This word is of one meaning, having been spoken after being expanded by the syllable 'ka' of the word 'sādhu' itself. Therefore, by one who speaks the meaning of the word 'sādhuka,' the word 'sādhu' is cited by way of extracting the meaning. 'Āyācana' means a request made face-to-face; it is the meaning of 'abhipatthana' (petition). 'Sampaṭicchana' means acceptance, receiving. 'Sampahaṃsana' means delighting and gladdening by means of existing virtues; it is the meaning of causing elation. 'Dhammarucī' means one who delights in the Dhamma, one who desires merit. 'Paññāṇavā' means one endowed with wisdom, wise. 'Addubbho' means non-malicious, non-injurious—this is the meaning. 'Idhāpi' means even in this fruit of asceticism. This is the word 'sādhu.' 'Daḷhīkamma' means diligent action, acting with respect. 'Āṇattiya' means command, ordering. For when it is said: 'Listen carefully, pay attention,' the word 'sādhuka' illuminates the diligent performance of listening and attention, just as that command does. Its meaning should be understood as that of a command, just as it has the meaning of a request. 'Sundarepi' means even in the sense of beauty. Now, in order to show the distinction made clear by the threefold meaning of the word 'sādhuka' as previously stated, the passage beginning with 'by the meaning of steadfastness' was spoken.

Manasi karohīti ettha manasikāro na ārammaṇapaṭipādanalakkhaṇo, atha kho vīthipaṭipādanajavanapaṭipādanamanasikārapubbakaṃ citte ṭhapanalakkhaṇoti dassento “āvajjā”tiādimāha. Sotindriyavikkhepavāraṇaṃ savane niyojanavasena kiriyantarapaṭisedhanabhāvato, sotaṃ odahāti attho. Manindriyavikkhepavāraṇaṃ aññacintāpaṭisedhanato. Byañjanavipallāsaggāhavāraṇaṃ “sādhuka”nti visesetvā vuttattā. Pacchimassa atthavipallāsaggāhavāraṇepi eseva nayo. Dhāraṇūpaparikkhādīsūti ādi-saddena tulanatīraṇādike, diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividhe ca saṅgaṇhāti. Sabyañjanoti ettha yathādhippetamatthaṃ byañjayatīti byañjanaṃ, sabhāvanirutti. Saha byañjanenāti sabyañjano, byañjanasampannoti attho. Sātthoti araṇīyato upagantabbato anudhātabbato attho, catupārisuddhisīlādiko[P 1.0303]. Tena saha atthenāti sāttho, atthasampannoti attho. Dhammagambhīrotiādīsu dhammo nāma tanti. Desanā [V 1.0207] nāma tassā manasā vavatthāpitāya tantiyā desanā. Attho nāma tantiyā attho. Paṭivedho nāma tantiyā, tantiatthassa ca yathābhūtāvabodho. Yasmā cete dhammadesanā atthappaṭivedhā sasādīhi viya mahāsamuddo mandabuddhīhi dukkhogāhā, alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhā ca, tasmā gambhīrā. Tena vuttaṃ “yasmā ayaṃ dhammo…pe… sādhukaṃ manasi karohī”ti. Ettha ca paṭivedhassa dukkarabhāvato dhammatthānaṃ, desanāñāṇassa dukkarabhāvato desanāya dukkhogāhatā, paṭivedhassa pana uppādetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya, ñāṇuppattiyā ca dukkarabhāvato dukkhogāhatā veditabbā. Desanaṃ nāma [M 1.0234] uddisanaṃ, tassa niddisanaṃ bhāsananti idhādhippetanti āha “vitthārato bhāsissāmī”ti. Paribyattaṃ kathanañhi bhāsanaṃ, tenāha “desessāmīti…pe… vitthāradīpana”nti.

Here, 'apply the mind' (manasi karohi) means that mental advertence is not characterized by the presentation of an object, but rather by the characteristic of establishing the mind, preceded by mental advertence that brings about the cognitive process and the impulsion. Thus, it is shown by saying 'advertence,' etc. The prevention of distraction of the ear faculty is the meaning of 'inclining the ear,' by engaging in listening and preventing other activities. The prevention of distraction of the mind faculty is by preventing other thoughts. The prevention of misapprehending the wording is due to its being stated with the specification 'carefully.' The same method applies to the prevention of misapprehending the meaning in the latter case. In 'retention, examination, etc.,' the word 'etc.' includes comparison, scrutiny, and so on, and also encompasses clear comprehension regarding views. 'With the wording' (sabyañjano) here means that which reveals the intended meaning is 'wording' (byañjana), which is natural language. 'Together with the wording' means 'possessed of wording,' this is the meaning. 'With meaning' (sāttho) means that which is worthy of being sought, approached, and followed—such as the fourfold purity of virtue, etc. 'Together with the meaning' means 'possessed of meaning,' this is the meaning. In 'profound in Dhamma,' etc., 'Dhamma' refers to the text. 'Teaching' refers to the exposition of that text mentally ascertained. 'Meaning' refers to the meaning of that text. 'Penetration' refers to the true understanding of the text and the meaning of the text. Because these teachings of the Dhamma and the penetration of meaning are difficult to fathom for those of weak intellect, like the great ocean with its creatures, and are unattainable in their foundation, therefore they are profound. Hence it is said: 'Because this Dhamma... (etc.)... apply the mind carefully.' Here, the difficulty in fathoming the Dhamma and its meaning is due to the difficulty of penetration; the difficulty in fathoming the teaching is due to the difficulty of the knowledge of teaching. Furthermore, this difficulty in fathoming should be understood as due to the inability to produce penetration and the difficulty in the arising of knowledge. 'Teaching' here refers to recitation; its detailed explanation is exposition—this is intended here by saying: 'I will explain in detail.' For detailed statement is indeed exposition, hence it is said: 'I will teach... (etc.)... detailed clarification.'

Yathāvuttamatthaṃ suttapadena samatthetuṃ “tenāhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sāḷikāyiva nigghosoti sāḷikāya ālāpo viya madhuro kaṇṇasukho pemanīyo. Paṭibhānanti saddo. Udīrayīti uccārīyati, vuccati vā.

To support the meaning as stated by the words of the Sutta, the passage beginning with 'Therefore he said' was spoken. 'Like the sound of a myna bird' means sweet, pleasing to the ear, and lovely, like the myna's call. 'Paṭibhāna' means sound. 'Udīrayi' means it is uttered, or said.

Evaṃ vutte ussāhajātoti evaṃ “suṇohi sādhukaṃ manasi karohi bhāsissāmī”ti vutte “na kira bhagavā saṅkhepeneva desessati, vitthārenapi bhāsissatī”ti sañjātussāho haṭṭhatuṭṭho hutvā.

When this was said, 'born of enthusiasm' means that when it was said: 'Listen carefully, pay attention, I will speak,' he, thinking: 'Surely the Blessed One will teach not only concisely, but also in detail,' became inspired, joyful, and elated.

190. “Idhā”ti iminā vuccamānaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ tathāgatassa uppattiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ adhippetanti āha “desāpadese nipāto”ti. “Svāya”nti sāmaññato idhasaddamattaṃ gaṇhāti, na yathāvisesitabbaṃ idha-saddaṃ. Tathā hi vakkhati “katthaci padapūraṇamattamevā”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.190). Lokaṃ upādāya vuccati loka-saddena samānādhikaraṇabhāvena vuttattā[P 1.0304].
