Sesapadadvaye pana padantarasannidhānamattena taṃ taṃ upādāya vuttatā daṭṭhabbā. Idha tathāgato loketi hi jātikhettaṃ, tatthāpi ayaṃ cakkavāḷo “loko”ti adhippeto. Samaṇoti sotāpanno. Dutiyo samaṇoti sakadāgāmī. Vuttañhetaṃ “katamo ca bhikkhave samaṇo? Idha bhikkhave bhikkhu tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā sotāpanno hotī”tiādi (a. ni. 4.241). “Katamo ca bhikkhave dutiyo samaṇo? Idha bhikkhave bhikkhu tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā rāgadosamohānaṃ tanuttā”tiādi (a. ni. 4.241). Okāsanti kañci padesaṃ. Idheva tiṭṭhamānassāti imissā eva indasālaguhāyaṃ tiṭṭhamānassa.

190. 'Here' (idha) means that the location spoken of by this word is intended as the place of the Tathāgata's arising. Thus, it is said: 'It is a particle referring to places.' 'That very' (svāyaṃ) takes the word 'here' in a general sense, not as a specifically qualified 'here.' For it will be said: 'Sometimes it is merely for filling out the sentence' (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.190). It is spoken of with reference to the world (lokaṃ), because it is stated by the word 'world' (loka-saddena) in the same grammatical case. But in the case of the remaining two words, it should be understood that they are spoken of with reference to each of them by means of the mere proximity of other words. For here, 'the Tathāgata in the world' refers to the birth-field; specifically, this world-system is intended by 'world' (loko). 'An ascetic' (samaṇo) refers to a stream-enterer. The 'second ascetic' (dutiyo samaṇo) refers to a once-returner. For it has been said: 'And what, bhikkhus, is an ascetic? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, with the destruction of three fetters, becomes a stream-enterer...' (AN 4.241). 'And what, bhikkhus, is the second ascetic? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, with the destruction of three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion...' (AN 4.241). 'A place' (okāsaṃ) means some region. 'Standing right here' (idheva tiṭṭhamānassa) means standing right in this very Indasāla Cave.

Padapūraṇamattameva [V 1.0208] okāsāpadisanassāpi asambhavato atthantarassa abodhanato. Arahanti ādayo saddā vitthāritāti yojanā. Atthato vitthāraṇaṃ saddamukheneva hotīti saddaggahaṇaṃ. Yasmā. “Aparehipi aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi bhagavā tathāgato”tiādinā udānaṭṭhakathādīsu, (udā. aṭṭha. 18; itivu. aṭṭha. 38) arahanti ādayo visuddhimaggaṭīkāyaṃ aparehi pakārehi vitthāritā[M 1.0235], tasmātesu vuttānayenapi so (visuddhi. ṭī. 1.129, 130) attho veditabbo. Tathāgatassa sattanikāyantogadhatāya “idha pana sattaloko adhippeto”ti vatvā tatthāyaṃ yasmiṃ sattanikāye yasmiñca okāse uppajjati, taṃ dassetuṃ “sattaloke uppajjamānopi cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Tathāgato na devaloke uppajjatī”tiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ parato āgamissati. Sārappattāti kulabhogissariyādivasena sārabhūtā. Brāhmaṇagahapatikāti brahmāyupokkharasātiādibrāhmaṇā [P 1.0305] ceva anāthapiṇḍikādigahapatikā ca.

It is merely for filling out the sentence, as there is no possibility even of indicating a place, and because no other meaning is understood. The connection is that the words 'arahant' and so on are explained in detail. The detailed explanation in terms of meaning occurs through the words themselves, hence the mention of 'words.' Because 'the Blessed One is a Tathāgata by eight other reasons,' and so on, as explained in the Udāna Commentary and elsewhere (Udāna Aṭṭhakathā 18; Itivuttaka Aṭṭhakathā 38), and the words 'arahant' and so on are elaborated upon in the Visuddhimagga Sub-commentary by other means, therefore that meaning should also be understood in accordance with the method stated there (Visuddhimagga Ṭīkā 1.129, 130). Because the Tathāgata is included within the seven groups of beings, it is said: 'Here, however, the world of beings is intended.' To show in which group of beings and in which sphere he arises, the passage beginning with 'even when arising in the world of beings' was spoken. What should be said regarding 'the Tathāgata does not arise in the deva-world,' etc., will come later. 'Having attained the essence' means being essential in terms of family, wealth, lordship, and so on. 'Brahmins and householders' refers to brahmins such as Brahmāyu and Pokkharasāti, and householders such as Anāthapiṇḍika and others.

“Sujātāyā”tiādinā vuttesu catūsu vikappesu paṭhamo vikappo buddhabhāvāya āsannatarapaṭipattidassanavasena vutto. Āsannatarāya hi paṭipattiyā ṭhito “uppajjatīti” vuccati uppādassa ekantikattā, pageva paṭipattiyā matthake ṭhito. Dutiyo buddhabhāvāvahapabbajjato paṭṭhāya āsannapaṭipattidassanavasena, tatiyo buddhakaradhamma pāripūrito paṭṭhāya buddhabhāvāya paṭipattidassanavasena. Na hi mahāsattānaṃ uppatibhavūpapattito paṭṭhāya bodhisambhārasambharaṇaṃ nāma atthi. Catuttho buddhakaradhammasamārambhato paṭṭhāya. Bodhiyā niyatabhāvappattito pabhuti hi viññūhi “buddho uppajjatī”ti vattuṃ sakkā uppādassa ekantikattā. Yathā pana sandanti nadiyoti sandanakiriyāya avicchedamupādāya vattamānappayogo, evaṃ uppādatthāya paṭipajjanakiriyāya avicchedamupādāya catūsu vikappesu “uppajjati nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Sabbapaṭhamaṃ uppannabhāvanti catūsu vikappesu sabbapaṭhamaṃ vuttaṃ tathāgatassa uppannatāsaṅkhātaṃ atthibhāvaṃ. Tenāha “uppanno hotīti ayañhettha attho”ti.

In the four alternatives mentioned, beginning with 'Sujātā,' the first alternative is stated to show the practice that is nearer to Buddhahood. For one established in a very near practice is said to 'arise' because of the certainty of arising; how much more so for one at the peak of practice. The second alternative shows the near practice starting from the going forth that leads to Buddhahood. The third shows the practice for Buddhahood starting from the fulfillment of the qualities that make one a Buddha. For there is no accumulation of the requisites of enlightenment for great beings starting from their arising and rebirth. The fourth alternative starts from the undertaking of the qualities that make one a Buddha. From the time of attaining the state of certainty regarding enlightenment, the wise can say, 'A Buddha arises,' due to the certainty of arising. Just as the present tense is used in 'the rivers flow' on account of the uninterrupted action of flowing, so too, 'he arises' is said in the four alternatives on account of the uninterrupted action of practicing for the sake of arising. The phrase 'first arisen' refers to the state of being, designated as the Tathāgata's arising, which is mentioned first among the four alternatives. Therefore, it is said, 'This is the meaning here: he has arisen.'

So bhagavāti yo “tathāgato araha”ntiādinā kittitaguṇo, so bhagavā. “Imaṃ loka”nti nayidaṃ mahājanassa sammukhamattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, atha kho anavasesaṃ pariyādāyāti dassetuṃ “sadevaka”ntiādi vuttaṃ, tenāha “idāni vattabbaṃ nidassetī”ti. Pajātattāti yathāsakaṃ kammakilesehi nibbattattā. Pañcakāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ pārisesañāyena itaresaṃ padantarehi saṅgahitattā. Sadevakanti ca avayavena viggaho samudāyo samāsattho. Chaṭṭhakāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ paccāsattiñāyena. Tattha hi so jāto, taṃnivāsī ca. Brahmakāyikādibrahmaggahaṇanti etthāpi eseva [P 1.0306] nayo. Paccatthika [M 1.0236] …pe… samaṇabrāhmaṇaggahaṇanti nidassanamattametaṃ apaccatthikānaṃ, asamitābāhitapāpānañca samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sassamaṇabrāhmaṇīvacanena gahitattā. Kāmaṃ “sadevaka”ntiādi [V 1.0209] visesanānaṃ vasena sattavisayo lokasaddoti viññāyati tulyayogavisayattā tesaṃ, “salomako sapakkhako”tiādīsu pana atulyayogepi ayaṃ samāso labbhatīti byabhicāradassanato pajāgahaṇanti āha “pajāvacanena sattalokaggahaṇa”nti.

'That Blessed One'—the one extolled with qualities such as 'Tathāgata, Arahant'—is the Blessed One. 'This world' is not said merely with reference to what is visible to the multitude, but to indicate the entirety without remainder; hence phrases like 'with its devas' are used. Therefore, it is said, 'Now it indicates what is to be said.' 'Born' means produced by their respective kamma and defilements. The inclusion of the five sense-sphere devas is by way of the remainder, as the others are included by the intervening terms. 'With its devas' is a compound whose meaning is a collection, analyzed by its parts. The inclusion of the sixth sense-sphere deva is by way of proximity, for he was born there and is its inhabitant. The inclusion of the Brahmā realms like the Brahmakāyika follows the same method. 'With its adversaries' ... 'with its ascetics and brahmins'—this is merely illustrative, for those who are not adversaries and those ascetics and brahmins who have not pacified and expelled evil are included by the term 'with its ascetics and brahmins.' Indeed, through qualifiers like 'with its devas,' the term 'world' is understood as the realm of beings, due to the equal applicability of the terms. But in phrases like 'with its hairs and feathers,' this compound is found even where the applicability is unequal. To show this deviation, it is said, 'By the word "pajā" the world of beings is included.'

Arūpino sattā attano āneñjavihārena viharantā dibbantīti devāti imaṃ nibbacanaṃ labhantīti āha “sadevakaggahaṇena arūpāvacaraloko gahito”ti. Tenāha “ākāsānañcāyatanūpagānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyata”nti (a. ni. 3.117). Samārakaggahaṇena chakāmāvacaradevaloko gahito tassa savisesaṃ mārassa vase vattanato. Rūpī brahmaloko gahito arūpībrahmalokassa visuṃ gahitattā. Catuparisavasenāti khattiyādicatuparisavasena, itarā pana catasso parisā samārakādiggahaṇena gahitā evāti. Avasesasabbasattaloko nāgagaruḷādibhedo.

Formless beings, dwelling in their own immovable abiding, are divine, and thus they attain the designation 'devas.' Therefore, it is said, 'The formless realm is included by the mention of the world with its devas.' Therefore it is said, 'The fellowship of the devas who have attained the base of infinite space' (AN 3.117). The six sense-sphere heavenly worlds are included by the mention of Māra, because they are specifically under Māra's control. The Brahmā world with form is included, as the formless Brahmā world is included separately. 'By way of the four assemblies' means by way of the four assemblies beginning with khattiyas. But the other four assemblies are included by the mention of Māra, etc. The remaining world of all beings is differentiated into kinds such as nāgas and garuḷas.

Ettāvatā ca bhāgaso lokaṃ gahetvā yojanaṃ dassetvā idāni tena tena visesena abhāgaso lokaṃ gahetvā yojanaṃ dassetuṃ “api cetthā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ukkaṭṭhaparicchedatoti ukkaṃsagativijānanena. Pañcasu hi gatīsu devagatipariyāpannāva seṭṭhā, tatthāpi arūpino dūrasamussāritakilesadukkhatāya, santapaṇītaāneñjavihārasamaṅgitāya, atidīghāyukatāyāti evamādīhi visesehi ativiya ukkaṭṭhā. “Brahmā mahānubhāvo”tiādi dasasahassiyaṃ mahābrahmuno vasena vadati. “Ukkaṭṭhaparicchedato”ti [P 1.0307] hi vuttaṃ. Anuttaranti seṭṭhaṃ nava lokuttaraṃ. Bhāvānukkamoti bhāvavasena paresaṃ ajjhāsayavasena “sadevaka”ntiādīnaṃ padānaṃ anukkamo.

Having thus taken the world by division and shown the connection, now, to take the world without division and show the connection with various distinctions, the phrase 'and even here,' etc., is stated. Herein, 'by the distinction of excellence' means by knowing the highest destination. For among the five destinations, that which is included in the divine destination is indeed the best. Therein, the formless beings are especially excellent due to the remoteness of their defilements and suffering, their being endowed with peaceful, refined, and immovable abiding, and their extremely long lifespan, among other distinctions. 'Brahmā is of great power,' etc., is said with reference to Mahā Brahmā in the ten-thousandfold world. For it is said, 'by the distinction of excellence.' 'Unsurpassed' means the best, the nine supramundane states. 'Sequence of meaning' means the sequence of terms like 'with the devas' according to the state and the intention of others.

Tīhākārehīti devamārabrahmasahitatāsaṅkhātehi tīhi pakārehi. Tīsu padesūti “sadevaka”ntiādīsu tīsu padesu. Tena tenākārenāti sadevakattādinā tena tena pakārena. Tedhātukameva pariyādinnanti porāṇā panāhūti yojanā.

'By three modes' means by the three ways designated as being accompanied by devas, Māra, and Brahmā. 'In three terms' means in the three terms such as 'with its devas,' etc. 'By that particular mode' means by that particular way, such as being with devas, etc. The ancients, however, explain: 'It is entirely encompassed by the three realms.'

Abhiññāti [M 1.0237] ya-kāralopenāyaṃ niddeso, abhijānitvāti ayamettha atthoti āha “abhiññāya adhikena ñāṇena ñatvā”ti. Anumānādipaṭikkhepoti anumānaupamānaatthāpattiādipaṭikkhepo ekappamāṇattā. Sabbattha appaṭihatañāṇacāratāya hi sabbapaccakkhā buddhā bhagavanto.

The word `abhiññā` is an instruction involving the elision of the letter 'ya'; the meaning here is 'having known thoroughly.' Therefore, it is said, 'having known by higher knowledge, by superior knowledge.' The rejection of inference and so on means the rejection of inference, analogy, implication, etc., because for a Buddha there is only one standard of knowledge. Indeed, the Blessed Buddhas have knowledge that operates unimpeded everywhere, and thus they have direct knowledge of everything.

Anuttaraṃ [V 1.0210] vivekasukhanti phalasamāpattisukhaṃ, tena ṭhitimissāpi [vīthimissāpi (sārattha. ṭī. 1.verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanāyaṃ) dhitimissāpi (ka)] kadāci bhagavato dhammadesanā hotīti hitvāpīti pi-saddaggahaṇaṃ. Bhagavā hi dhammaṃ desento yasmiṃ khaṇe parisā sādhukāraṃ vā deti, yathāsutaṃ vā dhammaṃ paccavekkhati, taṃ khaṇaṃ pubbabhāgena paricchinditvā phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati, yathāparicchedañca samāpattito vuṭṭhāya ṭhitaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya dhammaṃ deseti. Ugghaṭitaññussa vasena appaṃ vā vipañcitaññussa, neyyassa vā vasena bahuṃ vā desento. Dhammassa kalyāṇatā niyyānikatāya, niyyānikatā ca sabbaso anavajjabhāvenevāti āha “anavajjameva katvā”ti. Desakāyattena āṇādividhinā abhisajjanaṃ pabodhanaṃ desanāti sā pariyattidhammavasena veditabbāti āha “desanāya tāva catuppadikāyapi gāthāyā”tiādi. Nidānanigamanānipi satthuno desanāya anuvidhānato tadantogadhāni evāti āha “nidānamādi, idaṃ evocāti pariyosāna”nti.

The supreme bliss of seclusion is the bliss of fruition-attainment. Therefore, sometimes the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma even while mixed with that state—or even while mixed with the cognitive process—hence the inclusion of the word 'pi' (even) in 'hitvāpi.' For when the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma, at the moment when the assembly either applauds or reflects on the Dhamma as they have heard it, he delimits that moment by its prior part, enters fruition-attainment, and having emerged from that attainment according to the delimitation, he teaches the Dhamma starting from where he left off. He teaches either little for one of quick understanding, or much for one of developed understanding, or for one who is to be guided. The Dhamma's excellence is due to its leading to liberation, and its leading to liberation is due to its being entirely blameless; therefore, it is said, 'making it entirely blameless.' Teaching—which is admonishing and awakening, dependent on the teacher and proceeding by way of command, etc.—should be understood in terms of the scriptural Dhamma. Therefore, it is said, 'even in a four-line stanza of teaching,' etc. The introduction and conclusion, too, being in accordance with the Teacher's instruction, are indeed included within it. Therefore, it is said, 'the introduction is the beginning, and 'this was said' is the conclusion.'

Sāsitabbapuggalagatena yathāparādhādisāsitabbabhāvena [P 1.0308] anusāsanaṃ tadaṅgavinayādivasena vinayanaṃ sāsananti taṃ paṭipattidhammavasena veditabbanti āha “sīlasamādhivipassanā”tiādi. Kusalānaṃ dhammānanti anavajjadhammānaṃ sīlassa, samathavipassanānañca sīladiṭṭhīnaṃ ādibhāvo taṃ mūlakattā uttarimanussadhammānaṃ. Ariyamaggassa antadvayavigamena majjhimapaṭipadābhāvo viya, sammāpaṭipattiyā ārabbhanipphattīnaṃ vemajjhattāpi majjhabhāvoti vuttaṃ. “Atthi bhikkhave…pe… majjhaṃ nāmā”ti. Phalaṃ pariyosānaṃ nāma saupādisesatāvasena, nibbānaṃ pariyosānaṃ nāma anupādisesatāvasena. Idāni tesaṃ dvinnampi sāsanassa pariyosānataṃ āgamena dassetuṃ “etadatthamida”ntiādi āha. Idha desanāya ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ adhippetaṃ “sabyañjana”ntiādi vacanato. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ atthe katāvadhisaddappabandho gāthāvasena, suttavasena ca vavatthito pariyattidhammo, yo [M 1.0238] idha “desanā”ti vutto, tassa pana attho visesato sīlādi evāti āha “bhagavā hi dhammaṃ desento…pe… dassetī”ti. Tattha sīlaṃ dassetvāti sīlaggahaṇena sasambhāraṃ sīlaṃ gahitaṃ, tathā maggaggahaṇena sasambhāro maggoti tadubhayavasena anavasesato pariyatti atthaṃ pariyādiyati. Tenāti sīlādidassanena. Atthavasena hi idha desanāya ādikalyāṇādibhāvo adhippeto. Kathikasaṇṭhitīti kathikassa saṇṭhānaṃ kathanavasena samavaṭṭhānaṃ.

Instruction (sāsana) is the act of instructing a person according to their faults, etc., and their instructability, and it is the act of disciplining by means of the discipline that is a component of training, etc.; this should be understood in terms of the practice-Dhamma. Therefore, it is said, 'virtue, concentration, insight,' etc. 'Of wholesome qualities' refers to blameless qualities, and the primary nature of virtue, serenity, and insight, as well as virtuous views, because they are the root of supramundane qualities. Just as the Noble Path is the middle way by avoiding the two extremes, so too, it is said to be the middle state due to the impartiality of right practice in its beginning and accomplishment. 'There is, bhikkhus... a middle.' Culmination in fruition refers to the state with residue, while culmination in Nibbāna refers to the state without residue. Now, to show the culmination of both of these as the culmination of the teaching by means of scripture, he says, 'This is for this purpose,' etc. Here, the beginning, middle, and end of the teaching are intended, as indicated by the phrase 'with its phrasing,' etc. In each context, the range of words is determined by verses and discourses, and the scriptural Dhamma is established. This, which is here called 'teaching,' has its meaning specifically as virtue, etc. Therefore, it is said, 'The Blessed One, while teaching the Dhamma... shows.' There, 'showing virtue' means virtue is grasped along with its constituents by the inclusion of virtue. Similarly, the path is grasped along with its constituents by the inclusion of the path. In this way, by means of both of these, the scripture fully encompasses the meaning without remainder. Therefore, by showing virtue, etc., the excellence at the beginning, middle, and end of the teaching is intended here in terms of meaning. 'The Kathika's stability' means the Kathika's established state, his firm standing by way of speaking.

Na so sātthaṃ deseti niyyānatthavirahato tassā desanāya. Ekabyañjanādiyuttā vāti sithilādibhedesu byañjanesu ekappakāremeva, dvipakāremeva vā byañjanena yuttā vā damiḷabhāsā viya[V 1.0211]. Vivaṭakaraṇatāya oṭṭhe aphusāpetvā uccāretabbato sabbaniroṭṭhabyañjanā vā kirātabhāsā [P 1.0309] viya. Sabbasseva [sabbattheva (sārattha. ṭī. 1.verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanāyaṃ 1)] vissajjanīyayuttatāya sabbavissaṭṭhabyañjanā vā savarabhāsā [yavanabhāsā (sārattha. ṭī. 1.verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanāyaṃ)] viya. Sabbasseva [sabbattheva (sārattha. ṭī. 1.verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanāyaṃ)] sānusāratāya sabbaniggahitabyañjanā vā pārasikādimilakkhubhāsā viya. Sabbāpesā byañjanekadesavasena pavattiyā aparipuṇṇabyañjanāti katvā “abyañjanā”ti vuttā.

He does not teach the Dhamma with a beneficial aim, because his teaching is devoid of the aim of liberation. Or, it is connected with a single consonant, etc., meaning that among the lax and other types of consonants, it is connected with only one kind of consonant, or perhaps two, like the Tamil language. Due to the nature of requiring wide articulation, it must be pronounced without touching the lips, like the Kirāta language, which has all non-labial consonants. Or, because all of it has visarga, it has all released consonants, like the Savara language. Or, because all of it is nasalized, it has all nasal consonants, like the Persian and other barbarian languages. All these are called 'without consonants' because they function by means of a portion of consonants, and are therefore incomplete in consonants. Thus they are called 'abyañjanā' (lacking consonants).

Ṭhānakaraṇāni sithilāni katvā uccāretabbaṃ akkharaṃ pañcasu vaggesu paṭhamatatiyanti evamādi sithilaṃ. Tāni asithilāni katvā uccāretabbaṃ akkharaṃ vaggesu dutiyacatutthanti evamādi dhanitaṃ. Dvimattakālaṃ dīghaṃ. Ekamattakālaṃ rassaṃ tadeva lahukaṃ. Lahukameva saṃyogaparaṃ, dīghañca garukaṃ. Ṭhānakaraṇāni niggahetvā uccāretabbaṃ niggahitaṃ. Parena sambandhaṃ katvā uccāretabbaṃ sambandhaṃ. Tathā nasambandhaṃ vavatthitaṃ. Ṭhānakaraṇāni nissaṭṭhāni katvā uccāretabbaṃ vimuttaṃ. Dasadhāti evaṃ sithilādivasena byañjanabuddhiyā akkharuppādakacittassa sabbākārena pabhedo. Sabbāni hi akkharāni cittasamuṭṭhānāni yathādhippetatthaṃ byañjanato byañjanāni cāti.

A letter that should be pronounced by loosening the articulatory organs, such as the first and third in the five groups, is called 'lax.' A letter that should be pronounced by making those same organs tense, such as the second and fourth in the groups, is called 'aspirated.' A sound lasting two measures is 'long.' A sound lasting one measure is 'short,' and that is also 'light.' A light syllable followed by a conjunct consonant, and a long syllable, are 'heavy.' The 'restrained' sound (niggahita) is produced by contracting the articulatory organs. What is connected with what follows is called 'connected.' Similarly, what is not connected is 'separate.' The 'released' sound is produced by disengaging the articulatory organs. Thus, in ten ways—through laxness and so on—the differentiation of the mind that produces letters occurs in all respects by means of the understanding of consonants. Indeed, all letters arise from the mind, and because they express the intended meaning, they are called 'consonants.'

Amakkhetvāti amilecchetvā, avināsetvā, ahāpetvāti vā attho. Bhagavā yamatthaṃ ñāpetuṃ ekaṃ gāthaṃ, ekaṃ vākyaṃ vā deseti, tamatthaṃ tāya desanāya parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanāya eva desetīti āha “paripuṇṇabyañjanameva katvā dhammaṃ desetī”ti. Idha kevalasaddo anavasesavācako, na avomissakādivācakoti āha “sakalādhivacana”nti. Paripuṇṇanti sabbaso puṇṇaṃ, taṃ pana kenaci ūnaṃ, adhikaṃ vā na hotīti [M 1.0239] “anūnādhikavacana”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha yadatthaṃ [P 1.0310] desito, tassa sādhakattā anūnatā veditabbā, tabbidhurassa pana asādhakattā anadhikatā. Sakalanti sabbabhāgavantaṃ. Paripuṇṇanti sabbaso paripuṇṇameva, tenāha “ekadesanāpi aparipuṇṇā natthī”ti. Aparisuddhā desanā hoti taṇhāya saṃkiliṭṭhattā. Lokāmisaṃ cīvarādayo paccayā tattha agadhitacittatāya lokāmisanirapekkho. Hitapharaṇenāti hitūpasaṃhārena. Mettābhāvanāya karaṇabhūtāya muduhadayo. Ullumpanasabhāvasaṇṭhitenāti sakalasaṃkilesato, vaṭṭadukkhato ca uddharaṇākārāvaṭṭhitena cittena, kāruṇādhippāyenāti attho.

`Amakkhetvāti` means without corrupting, without destroying, or without abandoning. The Blessed One, in order to make known a meaning, teaches a single verse or a single sentence, and he teaches that meaning with that very teaching, which has well-rounded words and phrases; thus it is said, 'He teaches the Dhamma having made the expression complete.' Here, the word `kevala` signifies entirety without omission, not indicating partiality or mixture; hence it is called `sakalādhivacana` (a term for totality). `Paripuṇṇa` means entirely full, such that it is neither deficient nor excessive in any way; thus it is called `anūnādhikavacana` (a term for neither deficient nor excessive). Therein, non-deficiency should be understood from its accomplishment of the intended meaning, and non-excess from its not accomplishing anything other than that. `Sakala` means possessing all parts. `Paripuṇṇa` means entirely complete; therefore it is said, 'Not even a single teaching is incomplete.' An impure teaching is one that is defiled by craving. Worldly gain means requisites such as robes; being without a greedy mind for them, one is independent of worldly gain. `Hitapharaṇena` means by bestowing benefit. By the cultivation of loving-kindness, which is the cause, one's heart is tender. `Ullumpanasabhāvasaṇṭhitena` means with a mind established in the nature of uplifting—that is, in the manner of rescuing from all defilements and from the suffering of the round of existence—with a compassionate intention; this is the meaning.

“Ito paṭṭhāya dassāmeva, evañca dassāmī”ti samādātabbaṭṭhena vataṃ. Paṇḍitapaññattatāya [V 1.0212] seṭṭhaṭṭhena brahmaṃ brahmānaṃ vā cariyanti brahmacariyaṃ dānaṃ. Macchariyalobhādiniggaṇhanena suciṇṇassa. Iddhīti deviddhi. Jutīti pabhā, ānubhāvo vā. Balavīriyūpapattīti evaṃ mahatā balena ca vīriyena ca samannāgamo. Puññanti puññaphalaṃ. Veyyāvaccaṃ brahmacariyaṃ seṭṭhā cariyāti katvā. Esa nayo sesepi.

'From now on, I will surely give, and I will give in this way'—this is a vow in the sense of what is to be undertaken. Because it is prescribed by the wise, it is excellent (`brahmaṃ`) conduct (`cariyaṃ`) in the sense of being the best; or it is the conduct of Brahmas (`brahmānaṃ`). Thus, giving is `brahmacariya`. Of that which is well-practiced through the suppression of stinginess, greed, and so on. `Iddhi` means divine power. `Juti` means radiance or power. `Balavīriyūpapatti` means endowment with such great strength and energy. `Puñña` means the fruit of merit. Service (`veyyāvacca`) is a holy life (`brahmacariya`) because it is considered the best conduct. This is the method for the remaining terms as well.

Tasmāti yasmā sikkhattayasaṅgahaṃ sakalaṃ sāsanaṃ idha “brahmacariya”nti adhippetaṃ tasmā. “Brahmacariya”nti iminā samānādhikaraṇāni sabbapadāni yojetvā atthaṃ dassento “so dhammaṃ deseti…pe… pakāsetīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo”ti āha.

`Tasmā` (Therefore): Because the entire teaching, which comprises the threefold training, is intended here by the term `brahmacariya`, therefore... Showing the meaning by connecting all the words in apposition with this term `brahmacariya`, he said: 'He teaches the Dhamma... clarifies it'—thus the meaning here should be understood.

191. Vuttappakārasampadanti yathāvuttaṃ ādikalyāṇatādiguṇasampadaṃ, dūrasamussāritamānasseva sāsane sammāpaṭipatti sambhavati, na mānajātikassāti āha “nihatamānattā”ti. Ussannattāti bahulabhāvato. Bhogārogyādivatthukā madā suppaheyyā honti nimittassa anavatthānato, na tathā kulavijjāmadā, tasmā khattiyabrāhmaṇakulānaṃ pabbajitānampi [P 1.0311] jātivijjā nissāya mānajappanaṃ duppajahanti āha “yebhuyyena hi…pe… mānaṃ karontī”ti. Vijātitāyāti nihīnajātitāya. Patiṭṭhātuṃ na sakkontīti suvisuddhaṃ katvā sīlaṃ rakkhituṃ na sakkonti. Sīlavasena hi sāsane patiṭṭhā, patiṭṭhātunti vā saccapaṭivedhena lokuttarāya patiṭṭhāya patiṭṭhātuṃ. Sā hi nippariyāyato sāsane patiṭṭhā nāma, yebhuyyena ca upanissayasampannā sujātā eva honti, na dujjātā.

191. `Vuttappakārasampadaṃ` means the accomplishment of qualities as stated, such as being good in the beginning. Right practice in the teaching is possible only for one whose conceit has been cast far away, not for one who is conceited; thus it is said, `nihatamānattā` (because of having struck down conceit). `Ussannattā` means because of abundance. Intoxications based on things like wealth and health are easy to abandon because their basis is unstable, but not so the intoxications of clan and knowledge. Therefore, even for those gone forth from khattiya and brahmin families, the muttering of conceit based on birth and knowledge is hard to abandon; thus it is said, 'For the most part... they are conceited.' `Vijātitāya` means because of being of low birth. `Patiṭṭhātuṃ na sakkonti` means they are not able to make their virtue perfectly pure and protect it. For establishment in the teaching is through virtue. Or, `patiṭṭhātuṃ` means to be established in the supramundane establishment through the penetration of the truths. For that, in the absolute sense, is called establishment in the teaching. And for the most part, those endowed with supporting conditions are of good birth, not of low birth.

Parisuddhanti [M 1.0240] rāgādīnaṃ accantameva pahānadīpanato nirupakkilesatāya sabbaso parisuddhaṃ. Saddhaṃ paṭilabhatīti pothujjanikasaddhāvasena saddahati. Viññūjātikānañhi dhammasampattiggahaṇapubbikā saddhā siddhi dhammappamāṇadhammappasannabhāvato. “Sammāsambuddho vata so bhagavā, yo evaṃ svākkhātadhammo”ti saddhaṃ paṭilabhati. Jāyampatikāti gharaṇīpatikā. Kāmaṃ “jāyampatikā”ti vutte gharasāmikagharasāminīvasena dvinnaṃyeva gahaṇaṃ viññāyati. Yassa pana purisassa anekā pajāpatiyo, tattha kiṃ vattabbaṃ, ekāyāpi saṃvāso sambādhoti dassanatthaṃ “dve”ti vuttaṃ. Rāgādinā sakiñcanaṭṭhena, khettavatthu ādinā sapalibodhaṭṭhena rāgarajādīnaṃ āgamanapathatāpi uṭṭhānaṭṭhānatā evāti dvepi vaṇṇanā ekatthā, byañjanameva nānaṃ. Alagganaṭṭhenāti assajjanaṭṭhena appaṭibaddhabhāvena. Evaṃ akusalakusalappavattīnaṃ ṭhānabhāvena gharāvāsapabbajjānaṃ sambādhabbhokāsataṃ dassetvā idāni kusalappavattiyā eva aṭṭhānaṭṭhānabhāvena tesaṃ taṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

`Parisuddhaṃ` means completely pure, because it shows the utter abandonment of lust and so on, and is thus entirely without defilement. `Saddhaṃ paṭilabhati` means he has faith in the manner of an ordinary person's faith. For those of a discerning nature, faith is established, preceded by grasping the excellence of the Dhamma, because of taking the Dhamma as the standard and having confidence in the Dhamma. He acquires faith, thinking: 'Indeed, that Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One, whose Dhamma is so well-expounded.' `Jāyampatikā` means mistress and master of the house. Although when `jāyampatikā` is said, the taking of just two—the master and mistress of the house—is understood, what is to be said in the case of a man who has many wives? To show that cohabitation even with one is constricting, 'two' is stated. Because of lust and so on, one is 'with impediment' (`sakiñcana`); because of fields, property, and so on, one is 'with obstruction' (`sapalibodha`). Since these are the path for the arrival of the dust of lust and so on, they are also the basis for its arising. Thus, both explanations have the same meaning; only the expression differs. `Alagganaṭṭhena` means in the sense of not being attached, in the state of not being bound. Having thus shown the constricted and open nature of the household life and the going forth, respectively, by their being the basis for the occurrence of unwholesome and wholesome states, now, to show their nature as the improper and proper ground, respectively, for the occurrence of wholesome states alone, the passage beginning `apicā` (furthermore) is stated.

Saṅkhepakathāti [V 1.0213] visuṃ visuṃ paduddhāraṃ akatvā samāsato atthavaṇṇanā. Ekampi divasanti ekadivasamattampi. Akhaṇḍaṃ katvāti dukkaṭamattassapi anāpajjanena akhaṇḍitaṃ katvā. Kilesamalena amalīnanti taṇhāsaṃkilesādinā asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ katvā. Pariyodātaṭṭhena nimmalabhāvena saṅkhaṃ viya likhitaṃ dhotanti saṅkhalikhitanti [P 1.0312] āha “dhotasaṅkhasappaṭibhāga”nti. “Ajjhāvasatā”ti padappayogena “agāra”nti bhummatthe upayogavacananti āha “agāramajjhe”ti. Kasāyena rattāni vatthāni kāsāyānīti āha “kasāyarasapītatāyā”ti. Paridahitvāti nivāsetvā ceva pārupitvā ca. Agāravāso agāraṃ uttarapadalopena, tassa vaḍḍhiāvahaṃ agārassa hitaṃ.

`Saṅkhepakathā` is an explanation of the meaning in brief, without analyzing each word separately. `Ekampi divasaṃ` means for even a single day. `Akhaṇḍaṃ katvā` means having made it unbroken by not committing even an offense of wrong-doing. `Amalīnaṃ kilesamalena` means having made it unstained by the stain of defilements, such as craving. Because of its purity and stainlessness, like a conch that is scraped and washed, it is 'conch-polished' (`saṅkhalikhita`); thus he said `dhotasaṅkhasappaṭibhāgaṃ` (resembling a washed conch). By the use of the word `ajjhāvasatā` (by one dwelling), the word `agāra` is a locative expression; thus he said `agāramajjhe` (in the middle of the house). Robes dyed with an astringent dye are `kāsāyāni`; thus he said `kasāyarasapītatāya` (because of being imbued with the color of the astringent dye). `Paridahitvā` means having both worn it as a lower garment and draped it as an upper garment. `Agāravāso` becomes `agāraṃ` by elision of the latter part of the word; that which brings it increase is beneficial for the house.

192. Bhogakkhandhoti bhogasamudāyo. Ābandhanaṭṭhenāti “putto nattā”tiādinā pemavasena saparicchedaṃ bandhanaṭṭhena. “Amhākamete”ti ñāyantīti ñātī. Pitāmahapituputtādivasena parivattanaṭṭhena parivaṭṭo.

192. `Bhogakkhandho` means an accumulation of possessions. `Ābandhanaṭṭhena` means in the sense of a bond; that is, in the sense of binding with delimitation through affection, as in 'son, grandson,' and so on. They are known as 'ours' (`amhākaṃ ete`), thus they are relatives (`ñātī`). `Parivaṭṭo` means a circle, in the sense of revolving through grandfather, father, son, and so on.

193. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutoti pātimokkhasaṃvarena pihitakāyavacīdvāro, tathābhūto ca yasmā tena saṃvarena upeto nāma hoti[M 1.0241], tasmā vuttaṃ “pātimokkhasaṃvarena samannāgato”ti. “Ācāragocarasampanno”tiādi tasseva pātimokkhasaṃvarasamannāgamassa paccayadassanaṃ. Appamattakesūti asañcicca āpannaanukhuddakesu ceva sahasā uppannaakusalacittuppādesu ca. Bhayadassāvīti bhayadassanasīlo. Sammā ādiyitvāti sakkaccaṃ yāvajīvaṃ avītikkamavasena ādiyitvā. Taṃ taṃ sikkhāpadanti taṃ taṃ sikkhākoṭṭhāsaṃ. Etthāti etasmiṃ “pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto”ti pāṭhe. Saṅkhepoti saṅkhepavaṇṇanā. Vitthāro visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.14) vutto, tasmā so tattha, taṃsaṃvaṇṇanāya (visuddhi. ṭī. 1.14) ca vuttanayena veditabbo.

193. `Pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto` means one whose doors of body and speech are closed by the restraint of the Pātimokkha. And because one who is like that is called 'endowed' with that restraint, it is said, 'endowed with the restraint of the Pātimokkha.' The phrase `ācāragocarasampanno` (accomplished in conduct and resort) and so on shows a condition for that very endowment with the restraint of the Pātimokkha. `Appamattakesu` means in regard to minor and trifling offenses committed unintentionally, and in regard to unwholesome states of mind that have arisen suddenly. `Bhayadassāvī` means one who is in the habit of seeing danger. `Sammā ādiyitvā` means having undertaken them properly, for as long as life lasts, in such a way that they are not transgressed. `Taṃ taṃ sikkhāpadaṃ` means each particular portion of the training. `Ettha` means in this text, `pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto`. `Saṅkhepo` means a brief explanation. The detailed explanation is given in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. I, 14); therefore, it should be understood there according to the method stated in its commentary (Vism-ṭ I, 14).

Ācāragocaraggahaṇenevāti “ācāragocarasampanno”ti vacaneneva. Tenāha “kusale kāyakammavacīkamme gahitepī”ti. Adhikavacanaṃ aññamatthaṃ bodhetīti katvā tassa ājīvapārisuddhisīlassa uppattidvāradassanatthaṃ…pe… kusalenāti vuttaṃ, sabbaso anesanappahānena anavajjenāti attho. Yasmā “katame [P 1.0313] ca thapati kusalā sīlā kusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ kusalaṃ vacīkamma”nti (ma. ni. 2.265) sīlassa kusalakāyavacībhāvaṃ dassetvā “ājīvaparisuddhampi kho ahaṃ thapati sīlasmiṃ vadāmī”ti (ma. ni. 2.265) evaṃ pavattāya muṇḍikasuttadesanāya “kāyakammavacīkammena samannāgato kusalena, parisuddhājīvo”ti [V 1.0214] ayaṃ desanā ekasaṅgahā aññadatthu saṃsandati sametīti dassento āha “muṇḍikasuttavasena vā evaṃ vutta”nti. Sīlasmiṃ vadāmīti “sīla”nti vadāmi, “sīlasmiṃ antogadhaṃ pariyāpanna”nti vadāmīti vā attho. Pariyādānatthanti pariggahatthaṃ.

By the grasping of 'conduct and resort' alone—that is, by the statement 'accomplished in conduct and resort.' Therefore, it is said, 'even when wholesome bodily and verbal actions are included.' The additional words indicate another meaning, for the purpose of showing the door of origin for the virtue of purity of livelihood…and so on. 'By the wholesome' is said, meaning entirely by the abandoning of wrong livelihood, and as blameless. Because in the Muṇḍika Sutta, after showing that virtue consists of wholesome bodily and verbal action by saying, 'And what, householder, are wholesome virtues, wholesome bodily action, and wholesome verbal action?' (M. ii, 265), it is then said, 'I, householder, also declare purity of livelihood to be within virtue' (M. ii, 265). Thus, showing that this teaching—'endowed with wholesome bodily and verbal action, with pure livelihood'—corresponds and agrees with that other teaching as a single collection, he says, 'or it is thus stated in accordance with the Muṇḍika Sutta.' 'I declare in virtue' means 'I declare it as “virtue,”' or 'I declare it as included and comprised within virtue.' 'For the purpose of full comprehension' means for the purpose of grasping.

Tividhena sīlenāti cūḷasīlaṃ majjhimasīlaṃ mahāsīlanti evaṃ tividhena sīlena. Manacchaṭṭhesu indriyesu, na kāyapañcamesu. Yathālābhayathābalayathāsāruppappakāravasena tividhena santosena.

'By virtue in three ways' means the minor virtue, the intermediate virtue, and the great virtue—thus by virtue in three ways. In the faculties with mind as the sixth, not in those with the body as the fifth. By contentment in three ways means according to what is gained, according to one’s strength, and according to what is appropriate.

Cūḷamajjhimamahāsīlavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Minor, Intermediate, and Great Virtue

194-211. “Sīlasmi”nti idaṃ niddhāraṇe bhummanti āha “ekaṃ sīlaṃ hotīti attho”ti. Ayameva atthoti paccattavacanattho eva. Brahmajāleti brahmajālavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.7).

194-211. 'In virtue' (sīlasmiṃ)—this is the locative of determination, he says, meaning, 'it is one virtue.' This very meaning is precisely the meaning of the singular expression. 'In the Brahmajāla' refers to the commentary on the Brahmajāla (Dī. Ni. aṭṭha. 1.7).

212. Attānuvādaparānuvādadaṇḍabhayādīni [M 1.0242] asaṃvaramūlakāni. Sīlassāsaṃvaratoti sīlassa asaṃvaraṇato, sīlasaṃvarābhāvatoti attho. Bhaveyyāti uppajjeyya. Yathāvidhānavihitenāti yathāvidhānasampāditena. Avippaṭisārādinimittaṃ [P 1.0314] uppannacetasikasukhasamuṭṭhānehi paṇītarūpehi phuṭṭhasarīrassa uḷāraṃ kāyikaṃ sukhaṃ bhavatīti āha “avippaṭisāra…pe… paṭisaṃvedetī”ti.

212. Fear of self-reproach, fear of others' reproach, fear of punishment, and so on, are rooted in non-restraint. 'Because of the non-restraint of virtue' means because of the non-guarding of virtue, signifying the absence of restraint in virtue. 'Would be' means would arise. 'As performed according to the method' means as accomplished according to the method. Because non-remorse and so on is the cause, for one whose body is pervaded by sublime matter originating from arisen mental happiness, abundant physical pleasure arises. Thus it is said: 'Without remorse... he experiences.'

Indriyasaṃvarakathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Discourse on Restraint of the Senses

213. Viseso kammatthāpekkhatāya sāmaññassa na tehi paricattoti āha “cakkhu-saddo katthaci buddhacakkhumhi vattatī”ti. Vijjamānameva hi abhidheyye visesatthaṃ visesantaranivattanavasena visesasaddo vibhāveti, na avijjamānaṃ. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Aññehi asādhāraṇaṃ buddhānaṃyeva cakkhudassananti buddhacakkhu, āsayānusayañāṇaṃ, indriyaparopariyattañāṇañca. Samantato sabbaso dassanaṭṭhena samantacakkhu, sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ. Ariyamaggattayapaññāti heṭṭhime ariyamaggattaye paññā. Idhāti “cakkhunā rūpa”nti imasmiṃ pāṭhe. Ayaṃ cakkhu-saddo pasāda…pe… vattati nissayavohāre nissitassa vattabbato yathā. “Mañcā ukkuṭṭhiṃ karontī”ti. Asammissanti kilesadukkhena avomissaṃ. Tenāha “parisuddha”nti[V 1.0215]. Sati hi suvisuddhe indriyasaṃvare, padhānabhūtapāpadhammavigamena adhicittānuyogo hatthagato evaṃ hotīti āha “adhicittasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedetī”ti.

213. The specific meaning of a general term is not abandoned by them due to consideration of the meditation subject; hence it is said: 'The term “eye” is sometimes used with reference to the Buddha-eye.' For a specific word clarifies a specific meaning that already exists in what is denoted, by way of excluding other specific meanings, not a non-existent one. The same principle applies to the remaining terms. The Buddha-eye, which is unique to the Buddhas alone, is the eye-seeing that is uncommon to others: the knowledge of dispositions and latent tendencies, and the knowledge regarding the maturity or immaturity of the faculties of others. The all-seeing eye, because of seeing all around, in every respect, is the knowledge of omniscience. The wisdom of the three noble paths refers to the wisdom in the lower three noble paths. 'Here' means in this text, 'with the eye, a form.' This term 'eye' refers to the sensitive organ... and so on. It is used in conventional speech based on dependence, where the dependent is spoken of by that on which it depends, as in: 'The beds are shouting.' 'Unmixed' means not mixed with the suffering of defilements; hence it is said, 'purified.' For when restraint of the senses is thoroughly purified through the removal of evil states, which is the principal task, then the application to the higher mind becomes easily accessible. Thus it is said: 'He experiences the happiness of the higher mind.'

Satisampajaññakathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Discourse on Mindfulness and Clear Comprehension

214. Samantato, pakaṭṭhaṃ vā savisesaṃ jānātīti sampajāno, sampajānassa bhāvo sampajaññaṃ, tathāpavattañāṇaṃ. Tassa vibhajanaṃ sampajaññabhājanīyaṃ, tasmiṃ sampajaññabhājanīyamhi. Abhikkamanaṃ abhikkantanti āha “abhikkantaṃ vuccati gamana”nti. Tathā paṭikkamanaṃ [P 1.0315] paṭikkantanti āha “paṭikkantaṃ nivattana”nti. Nivattananti ca nivattimattaṃ. Nivattitvā pana gamanaṃ gamanameva. Abhiharantoti gamanavasena kāyaṃ upanento. Ṭhānanisajjāsayanesu yo gamanavidhuro kāyassa purato abhihāro, so abhikkamo, pacchato apaharaṇaṃ paṭikkamoti dassento “ṭhānepī”tiādimāha. Āsanassāti [M 1.0243] pīṭhakādiāsanassa. Purimaaṅgābhimukhoti aṭanikādipurimāvayavābhimukho. Saṃsarantoti saṃsappanto. Paccāsaṃsarantoti paṭiāsappanto. “Eseva nayo”ti iminā nipannasseva abhimukhasaṃsappanapaṭiāsappanāni nidasseti.

214. One who knows all around, or excellently and in detail, is 'one who clearly knows' (sampajāno). The state of one who clearly knows is 'clear comprehension' (sampajañña), which is the knowledge that proceeds in such a way. Its analysis is the 'section on clear comprehension' (sampajaññabhājanīya), and in that section on clear comprehension. 'Going forward' (abhikkamana) is 'advancing' (abhikkanta), hence it is said, 'advancing is called going.' Similarly, 'going back' (paṭikkamana) is 'retreating' (paṭikkanta), hence it is said, 'retreating is turning back.' And 'turning back' is just the act of turning back. But after turning back, going is still going. 'Bringing forward' (abhiharanto) means bringing the body forward by way of movement. Showing that in standing, sitting, or lying down, the forward movement of the body, which is devoid of locomotion, is 'advancing' (abhikkama), and the backward withdrawal is 'retreating' (paṭikkama), he said, 'even in standing,' etc. 'Of the seat' (āsanassa) refers to a stool or similar seat. 'Facing the front limbs' (purimaaṅgābhimukho) means facing the front parts of the body such as the knees. 'Moving along' (saṃsaranto) means creeping. 'Moving back' (paccāsaṃsaranto) means creeping back. By 'this is the method' (eseva nayo), he indicates the forward creeping and backward creeping of one who is lying down.

Sammā pajānanaṃ sampajānaṃ, tena attanā kātabbakiccassa karaṇasīlo sampajānakārīti āha “sampajaññena sabbakiccakārī”ti. Sampajānasaddassa sampajaññapariyāyatā pubbe vuttā eva. Sampajaññaṃ karotevāti abhikkantādīsu asammohaṃ uppādeti eva. Sampajaññassa vā kāro etassa atthīti sampajānakārī. Dhammato vaḍḍhisaṅkhātena saha atthena vattatīti sātthakaṃ, abhikkantādi. Sātthakassa sampajānanaṃ sātthakasampajaññaṃ. Sappāyassa attano hitassa sampajānanaṃ sappāyasampajaññaṃ. Abhikkamādīsu bhikkhācāragocare, aññatthāpi ca pavattesu avijahite kammaṭṭhānasaṅkhāte gocare sampajaññaṃ gocarasampajaññaṃ. Abhikkamādīsu asammuyhanameva sampajaññaṃ asammohasampajaññaṃ. Pariggahetvāti tūletvā tīretvā paṭisaṅkhāyāti, attho. Saṅghadassaneneva uposathapavāraṇādiatthaṃ gamanaṃ saṅgahitaṃ. Asubhadassanādīti ādi-saddena kasiṇaparikammādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo[P 1.0316]. Saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vivarituṃ “cetiyaṃ vā bodhiṃ vā disvāpi hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Arahattaṃ pāpuṇātīti ukkaṭṭhaniddeso eso. Samathavipassanuppādanampi hi bhikkhuno vaḍḍhiyeva. Kecīti abhayagirivāsino.

Rightly knowing is 'clear knowing' (sampajāna). One who is by nature a doer of a duty to be done by oneself with that is called 'one who acts with clear comprehension' (sampajānakārī), hence it is said, 'one who performs all duties with clear comprehension.' The fact that the word 'sampajāna' is a synonym for 'sampajañña' has indeed been stated previously. He indeed makes clear comprehension, that is, he indeed produces non-confusion in actions like going forward, etc. Alternatively, 'one who acts with clear comprehension' (sampajānakārī) means one who possesses the making of clear comprehension. It is 'meaningful' (sātthaka) because it proceeds with a benefit which is designated as growth in the Dhamma, as in going forward, etc. The clear comprehension of what is meaningful is 'meaningful clear comprehension' (sātthakasampajañña). The clear comprehension of what is suitable (sappāya), of one's own benefit, is 'suitable clear comprehension' (sappāyasampajañña). Clear comprehension in the sphere of a monk's conduct, such as going forward, etc., and in the field of alms-seeking, and in other activities where the meditation subject, which is designated as the domain (gocara), is not abandoned, is 'domain clear comprehension' (gocarasampajañña). Clear comprehension that is simply non-bewilderment in actions like going forward, etc., is 'non-bewilderment clear comprehension' (asammohasampajañña). 'Having grasped' (pariggahetvā) means having weighed, judged, and reflected upon—this is the meaning. Going for the purpose of the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā is included by the very seeing of the Saṅgha. 'Seeing the unattractive,' etc.—by the word 'etc.,' the inclusion of the preliminary work on kasiṇas, etc., should be understood. To explain the meaning stated briefly, 'for even having seen a shrine or a Bodhi tree,' etc., was stated. 'He attains Arahantship'—this is a statement of the highest. For a monk, the arising of serenity and insight is indeed growth. 'Some' refers to the dwellers at Abhayagiri.

Tasmiṃ panāti sātthakasampajaññavasena pariggahitaatthe. “Atthoti dhammato vaḍḍhī”ti yaṃ sātthakanti [V 1.0216] adhippetaṃ, taṃ sappāyaṃ evāti siyā kassaci āsaṅkāti tannivattanatthaṃ “cetiyadassanaṃ tāvā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Cittakammarūpakāni viyāti cittakammakatā paṭimāyo viya, yantapayogena vā vicittakammā paṭimāyo viya. Asamapekkhanaṃ gehassita aññāṇupekkhāvasena ārammaṇassa ayoniso gahaṇaṃ. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. “Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā uppajjati upekkhā bālassa mūḷhassa puthujjanassā”tiādi (ma. ni. 3.308). Hatthiādisammaddena jīvitantarāyo. Visabhāgarūpadassanādinā brahmacariyantarāyo.

'But in that' (tasmiṃ pana) refers to a meaning grasped by way of 'meaningful clear comprehension' (sātthakasampajañña). Lest someone should doubt that 'benefit' (attha), which is 'growth in the Dhamma,' and which is intended as 'meaningful,' is always 'suitable' (sappāya), the passage beginning 'seeing a shrine, for instance,' etc., was introduced to dispel that doubt. 'Like painted and crafted forms' (cittakammarūpakāni viya) means like images made by painting, or like intricately crafted images made by mechanical devices. 'Non-consideration' (asamapekkhana) is the unwise grasping of an object due to the household-based indifference of ignorance. In reference to which it was said: 'When a fool, a deluded ordinary person, sees a form with the eye, indifference arises,' etc. (Majjhima Nikāya 3.308). Danger to life from being crushed by elephants and the like. Danger to the holy life from seeing disagreeable forms and the like.

Pabbajitadivasato [M 1.0244] paṭṭhāya bhikkhūnaṃ anuvattanakathā āciṇṇā, ananuvattanakathā pana tassā dutiyā nāma hotīti āha “dve kathā nāma na kathitapubbā”ti. Evanti “sace panā”tiādikaṃ sabbampi vuttākāraṃ paccāmasati, na “purisassa mātugāmāsubha”ntiādikaṃ vuccamānaṃ.

From the day of ordination onwards, talk of conforming behavior among bhikkhus is customary, while talk of non-conforming behavior is, in fact, its second name—hence it is said, 'two kinds of talk never spoken before.' 'Thus' (evaṃ) refers back to everything previously stated, such as 'but if,' etc., and not to what is about to be said, such as 'the unattractiveness of a woman to a man,' etc.

Yogakammassa pavattiṭṭhānatāya bhāvanāya ārammaṇaṃ “kammaṭṭhāna”nti vuccatīti āha “kammaṭṭhānasaṅkhātaṃ gocara”nti. Uggahetvāti yathā uggahanimittaṃ uppajjati, evaṃ uggahakosallassa sampādanavasena uggahetvā[P 1.0317].

Because it is the foundation for the engagement in yogic practice, the object of meditation is called a 'meditation subject' (kammaṭṭhāna)—hence it is said, 'the domain designated as a meditation subject.' 'Having grasped' (uggahetvā) means having grasped it skillfully in the manner of producing the learning sign (uggahanimitta).

Haratīti kammaṭṭhānaṃ pavatteti, yāva piṇḍapātapaṭikkamā anuyuñjatīti attho. Na paccāharatīti āhārūpayogato yāva divāṭhānupasaṅkamanā kammaṭṭhānaṃ na paṭineti. Sarīraparikammanti mukhadhovanādisarīrapaṭijagganaṃ. Dve tayo pallaṅketi dve tayo nisajjāvāre dve tīṇi uṇhāsanāni. Tenāha “usumaṃ gāhāpento”ti. Kammaṭṭhānasīsenevāti kammaṭṭhānamukheneva kammaṭṭhānaṃ avijahanto eva, tena “pattopi acetano”tiādinā (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.214) vakkhamānaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ, yathāparihariyamānaṃ vā avijahitvāti dasseti. Tathevāti tikkhattumeva. Paribhogacetiyato sārīrikacetiyaṃ garutaranti katvā “cetiyaṃ vanditvā”ti pubbakālakiriyāya vasena vuttaṃ. Tathā hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “cetiyaṃ bādhayamānā bodhisākhā haritabbā”ti vuttā. Buddhaguṇānussaraṇavaseneva bodhiyaṃ paṇipātakaraṇanti āha “buddhassa bhagavato sammukhā viya nipaccakāraṃ dassetvā”ti. Gāmasamīpeti gāmassa upacāraṭṭhāne. Janasaṅgahatthanti “mayi akathente etesaṃ ko kathessatī”ti dhammānuggahena janasaṅgahatthaṃ. Tasmāti yasmā “dhammakathā nāma kathetabbā evā”ti aṭṭhakathācariyā vadanti, yasmā ca dhammakathā kammaṭṭhānavinimuttā nāma natthi, tasmā. Kammaṭṭhānasīsenevāti attanā parihariyamānaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ avijahanto [V 1.0217] tadanuguṇaṃyeva dhammakathaṃ kathetvā. Anumodanaṃ vatvāti etthāpi “kammaṭṭhānasīsenevā”ti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ.

'Maintains' (harati) means one applies the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), that is, one applies oneself until returning from the alms round. 'Does not bring it back' (na paccāharati) means one does not withdraw the meditation subject from the partaking of food until approaching the daytime resting place. 'Bodily care' (sarīraparikamma) refers to washing the face and other bodily maintenance. 'Two or three pallaṅkas' (dve tayo pallaṅke) means two or three sitting sessions, two or three warm seats. Hence it is said, 'causing warmth to be taken.' 'With the meditation subject foremost' (kammaṭṭhānasīseneva) means keeping the meditation subject at the forefront, without abandoning it; thus, it shows that the meditation subject, as will be mentioned later in the phrase 'even the bowl is inanimate,' etc. (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.214), is maintained and not abandoned. 'Similarly' (tatheva) means three times. Considering the bodily relic shrine (sārīrikacetiya) more venerable than the shrine of use (paribhogacetiya), it is said, 'having paid homage to the shrine,' using the form of a prior action. Indeed, the commentary states, 'if a Bodhi tree branch obstructs the shrine, it should be removed.' Making obeisance to the Bodhi tree is itself an act of recollecting the Buddha’s qualities. Thus, it is said, 'showing reverence as if in the presence of the Blessed One.' 'Near the village' (gāmasamīpe) means in the area adjacent to the village. 'For the sake of gathering people' (janasaṅgahatthaṃ) means, 'if I do not speak, who will speak to them?'—thus gathering people through the support of the Dhamma. 'Therefore' (tasmā)—since the commentary teachers say, 'a Dhamma talk should certainly be given,' and since there is no Dhamma talk entirely separate from the meditation subject, therefore— 'With the meditation subject foremost' (kammaṭṭhānasīseneva) means giving a Dhamma talk in accordance with the meditation subject, while maintaining the meditation subject oneself without abandoning it. Having given the anumodana—here too, 'with the meditation subject foremost' should be brought in and connected.

Sampattaparicchedenevāti “paricito aparicito”tiādi vibhāgaṃ akatvā sampattakoṭiyā eva, samāgamamattenevāti attho. Bhayeti paracakkādibhaye.

'By the limit of attainment' (sampattaparicchedeneva) means, without making distinctions such as 'familiar' and 'unfamiliar,' but simply by the limit of attainment itself, that is, by the mere fact of meeting. 'Fear' (bhaye) refers to fear from dangers such as foreign armies, etc.

“Kammajatejo”ti [M 1.0245][P 1.0318] gahaṇiṃ sandhāyāha. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ vīthiṃ nārohati khudāparissamena kilantakāyattā samādhānābhāvato. Avasesaṭṭhāneti yāguyā aggahitaṭṭhāne. Poṅkhānupoṅkhanti kammaṭṭhānupaṭṭhānassa avicchedadassanametaṃ, yathā poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ pavattāya sarapaṭipātiyā anavicchedo, evametassapīti.

'Fire born of kamma' (kammajatejo) refers to the digestive faculty. The meditation subject does not enter the cognitive process because the body is exhausted from hunger and fatigue, and concentration is absent. 'In the remaining places' (avasesaṭṭhāne) are the places where rice gruel was not taken. 'In successive order' (poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ) is a demonstration of the uninterrupted attention to the meditation subject; just as the uninterrupted flow of a series of arrows proceeds in succession, so too this.

Nikkhittadhuro bhāvanānuyoge. Vattapaṭipattiyā apūraṇena sabbavattāni bhinditvā. “Kāmesu avītarāgo hoti, kāye avītarāgo, rūpe avītarāgo, yāvadatthaṃ udarāvadehakaṃ bhuñjitvā seyyasukhaṃ passasukhaṃ middhasukhaṃ anuyutto viharati, aññataraṃ devanikāyaṃ paṇidhāya brahmacariyaṃ caratī”ti (dī. ni. 3.320; ma. ni. 1.186) evaṃ vuttapañcavidhacetokhilavinibandhacitto. Caritvāti pavattitvā.

One who has laid down the burden (nikkhittadhuro) in the application to meditation. By not fulfilling the duties of practice, having broken all observances. His mind is bound by the five kinds of mental barrenness as stated: 'He is not devoid of passion for sensual pleasures, not devoid of passion for the body, not devoid of passion for forms; having eaten to the point of stuffing his belly, he is addicted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, the pleasure of drowsiness; he lives the holy life aspiring to a certain group of deities' (Dī. Ni. 3.320; Ma. Ni. 1.186). 'Having lived thus' (caritvā) means having behaved.

Gatapaccāgatikavattavasenāti bhāvanāsahitaṃyeva bhikkhāya gatapaccāgataṃ gamanapaccāgamanaṃ etassa atthīti gatapaccāgatikaṃ, tadeva vattaṃ, tassa vasena. Attakāmāti attano hitasukhaṃ icchantā, dhammacchandavantoti attho. Dhammo hi hitaṃ tannimittakañca sukhanti. Atha vā viññūnaṃ nibbisesattā, attabhāvapariyāpannattā ca attā nāma dhammo, taṃ kāmenti icchantīti attakāmā.

'By means of the practice of going and returning' (gatapaccāgatikavattavasena): this refers to one who possesses the characteristic of going and returning (gatapaccāgatika), meaning that going and returning for alms which is associated with meditation is characteristic of him; by means of that very practice. 'Those who desire their own good' (attakāmā) means those who desire their own well-being and happiness, meaning those who possess zeal for the Dhamma. For the Dhamma is well-being, and happiness arises on account of it. Or, because for the wise there is no distinction, and because it is included within one's own being, the Dhamma is called 'self'; they desire that, meaning they seek it—thus, 'those who desire their own good' (attakāmā).

Usabhaṃ nāma vīsati yaṭṭhiyo. Tāya saññāyāti tāya pāsāṇasaññāya, ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgatāti jānantāti adhippāyo. Soyeva nayoti “ayaṃ bhikkhū”tiādiko yo ṭhāne vutto, so eva nisajjāyapi nayo. Pacchato āgacchantānaṃ chinnabhattabhāvabhayenapi yonisomanasikāraṃ paribrūheti. Maddantāti [P 1.0319] dhaññakaraṇaṭṭhāne sālisīsāni maddantā.

An 'usabha' is twenty rods. 'By that perception' (tāya saññāya) means by that perception of a stone, knowing that so much space has been reached—this is the meaning. 'That very method' (so yeva nayo)—the method stated in the case of 'this bhikkhu,' etc., which was mentioned in relation to standing, is also the method for sitting. He develops wise attention also out of fear that the meal will be cut off for those coming behind. 'Threshing' (maddantā) means crushing heads of rice at the threshing place.

Mahāpadhānaṃ pūjessāmīti amhākaṃ atthāya lokanāthena chavassāni kataṃ dukkaracariyamevāhaṃ yathāsatti pūjessāmīti. Paṭipattipūjā hi satthupūjā, na āmisapūjāti. “Ṭhānacaṅkamamevā”ti [V 1.0218] adhiṭṭhātabbairiyāpathavasena vuttaṃ, na bhojanādikālesu avassaṃ kattabbanisajjāya paṭikkhepavasena.

'I will honor the Great Striving'—meaning, 'For our sake, the Lord of the World practiced the difficult asceticism for six years; I will honor it to the best of my ability.' For honor through practice is indeed honor to the Teacher, not material honor. 'Only standing and walking'—this is said with reference to the determined postures, not as a rejection of the necessary sitting at mealtimes, etc.

Vīthiṃ otaritvā ito cito ca anoloketvā paṭhamameva vīthiyo sallakkhetabbāti āha “vīthiyo sallakkhetvā”ti. Yaṃ sandhāya vuccati [M 1.0246] “pāsādikena abhikkantenā”ti, taṃ dassetuṃ “tattha cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Āhāre paṭikkūlasaññaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā”tiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ parato āgamissati. Aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatanti “yāvadeva imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.23; a. ni. 6.58; mahāni. 206) vuttehi aṭṭhahi aṅgehi samannāgataṃ katvā. “Neva davāyā”tiādi paṭikkhepadassanaṃ.

Having entered the street, without looking here and there, one should first observe the streets—thus it is said, 'having observed the streets.' To show what is meant by 'with pleasing forward movement,' 'and there,' etc., is stated. What should be said regarding 'establishing the perception of loathsomeness in food,' etc., will come later. Endowed with eight factors—meaning, having made it endowed with the eight factors stated in 'just for the maintenance of this body,' etc. (MN 1.23; AN 6.58; Mahāni. 206). 'Not for sport,' etc., shows the rejection.

Paccekabodhiṃ sacchikaroti, yadi upanissayasampanno hotīti sambandho. Evaṃ sabbattha ito paresupi. Tattha paccekabodhiyā upanissayasampadā kappānaṃ dve asaṅkhyeyyāni, satasahassañca tajjāpuññañāṇasambharaṇaṃ. Sāvakabodhiyā aggasāvakānaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ, kappasatasahassañca, mahāsāvakānaṃ (theragā. aṭṭha. 2.1288) satasahassameva tajjāpuññañāṇasambharaṇaṃ. Itaresaṃ atītāsu jātīsu vivaṭṭasannissayavasena nibbattitaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ kusalaṃ. Bāhiyo dārucīriyoti bāhiyavisaye sañjātasaṃvaḍḍhatāya bāhiyo, dārucīrapariharaṇena dārucīriyoti ca samaññāto. So hi āyasmā “tasmātiha [P 1.0320] te, bāhiya, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ ‘diṭṭhe diṭṭhamattaṃ bhavissati, sute, mute, viññāte viññātamattaṃ bhavissatī’ti, evañhi te bāhiya sikkhitabbaṃ. Yato kho te bāhiya diṭṭhe diṭṭhamattaṃ bhavissati, sute, mute, viññāte viññātamattaṃ bhavissati, tato tvaṃ, bāhiya, na tena. Yato tvaṃ, bāhiya, na tena, tato tvaṃ, bāhiya, na tattha. Yato tvaṃ, bāhiya, na tattha, tato tvaṃ, bāhiya, nevidha na huraṃ na ubhayamantarena. Esevanto dukkhassā”ti (udā. 10) ettakāya desanāya arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. Evaṃ sāriputtattherādīnaṃ mahāpaññatādidīpanāni suttapadāni vitthārato veditabbāni.

He realizes individual enlightenment if he is endowed with the supporting conditions—this is the connection. The same applies everywhere hereafter as well. Here, the fulfillment of supporting conditions for individual enlightenment requires the accumulation of merit and knowledge conducive to it for two incalculable eons and a hundred thousand eons. For the enlightenment of a disciple, the foremost disciples require an incalculable eon and a hundred thousand eons, while the great disciples (as in Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā 2.1288) require only a hundred thousand eons for the accumulation of merit and knowledge conducive to it. For others, it is the wholesome states conducive to penetration, developed in past lives through conditions that lead away from the round of rebirth. Bāhiya Dārucīriya—so named because he was born and raised in the Bāhiya region, and because he wore a bark garment. This venerable one attained arahantship upon hearing this brief teaching: "Therefore, Bāhiya, you should train thus: ‘In the seen, there will be merely the seen; in the heard, merely the heard; in the sensed, merely the sensed; in the cognized, merely the cognized.’ That is how you should train, Bāhiya. When, Bāhiya, in the seen there is merely the seen, in the heard merely the heard, in the sensed merely the sensed, in the cognized merely the cognized, then you, Bāhiya, will not be ‘with that.’ When you, Bāhiya, are not ‘with that,’ then you, Bāhiya, will not be ‘in that.’ When you, Bāhiya, are not ‘in that,’ then you, Bāhiya, will be neither here nor beyond nor in between. This itself is the end of suffering." (Udāna 10) Similarly, the sutta passages illustrating the great wisdom of the Elder Sāriputta and others should be understood in detail.

Tanti asammuyhanaṃ evanti idāni vuccamānamākāreneva veditabbaṃ. “Attā abhikkamatī”ti iminā andhaputhujjanassa diṭṭhigāhavasena abhikkame sammuyhanaṃ dasseti, “ahaṃ abhikkamāmī”ti pana iminā mānagāhavasena. Tadubhayaṃ pana taṇhāya vinā na hotīti taṇhagāhavasenapi sammuyhanaṃ dassitameva hoti. “Tathā asammuyhanto”ti vatvā taṃ asammuyhanaṃ yena ghanavinibbhogena hoti, taṃ dassento “abhikkamāmī”tiādimāha. Tattha [M 1.0247] yasmā [V 1.0219] vāyodhātuyā anugatā tejodhātu uddharaṇassa paccayo. Uddharaṇagatikā hi tejodhātūti. Uddharaṇe vāyodhātuyā tassā anugatabhāvo, tasmā imāsaṃ dvinnamettha sāmatthiyato adhimattatā, itarāsañca omattatāti dassento “ekekapāduddharaṇe…pe… balavatiyoti āha. Yasmā pana tejodhātuyā anugatā vāyodhātu atiharaṇavītiharaṇānaṃ paccayo. Tiriyagatikāya hi vāyodhātuyā atiharaṇavītiharaṇesu sātisayo byāpāroti. Tejodhātuyā tassā anugatabhāvo, tasmā imāsaṃ dvinnamettha sāmatthiyato adhimattatā, itarāsañca omattatāti dassento [P 1.0321] “tathā atiharaṇavītiharaṇesū”ti āha. Satipi anugamakaanugantabbatāvisese tejodhātuvāyodhātubhāvamattaṃ sandhāya tathā-saddaggahaṇaṃ,. Tattha akkantaṭṭhānato pādassa ukkhipanaṃ uddharaṇaṃ. Ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ atikkamitvā purato haraṇaṃ atiharaṇaṃ, khāṇuādipariharaṇatthaṃ, patiṭṭhitapādaghaṭṭanapariharaṇatthaṃ vā passena haraṇaṃ vītiharaṇaṃ. Yāva patiṭṭhitapādo, tāva āharaṇaṃ atiharaṇaṃ, tato paraṃ haraṇaṃ vītiharaṇanti ayaṃ vā etesaṃ viseso.

Non-delusion is simply this—this should now be understood in the manner being explained. 'The self moves forward'—this shows delusion in the act of moving forward through a blind ordinary person's clinging to views. 'But I move forward'—this shows delusion through clinging to conceit. Both of these, however, do not occur without craving—thus, delusion is also shown through clinging to craving. Having stated, 'Thus, without delusion,' he then explains that non-delusion which arises through the analysis of solidity, saying, 'I move forward,' and so on. Here, because the fire element, accompanied by the wind element, is the condition for lifting. For the fire element has an upward-moving nature. In lifting, it is accompanied by the wind element—thus, to show the predominance of these two in terms of capability here and the lesser role of the others, he says, 'In lifting each foot... when it is strong.' But because the wind element, accompanied by the fire element, is the condition for moving forward and moving aside. For the wind element moves horizontally—its primary function is in moving forward and moving aside. It is accompanied by the fire element—thus, to show the predominance of these two in terms of capability here and the lesser role of the others, he says, 'Similarly, in moving forward and moving aside.' Even though there is a distinction between the accompanier and the accompanied, the word 'thus' is used merely with reference to the nature of the fire and wind elements. Here, raising the foot from the place it was placed is called 'lifting.' Carrying it forward beyond the standing position is 'moving forward.' Carrying it sideways, either to avoid obstacles like stumps or to avoid striking the foot already placed, is 'moving aside.' Alternatively, the distinction is this: carrying it forward up to the point where the foot is placed is 'moving forward,' and carrying it beyond that is 'moving aside.'

Yasmā pathavīdhātuyā anugatā āpodhātu vossajjanassa paccayo. Garutarasabhāvā hi āpodhātūti. Vossajjane pathavīdhātuyā tassā anugatabhāvo, tasmā tāsaṃ dvinnamettha sāmatthiyato adhimattatā, itarāsañca omattatāti dassento āha “vossajjane…pe… balavatiyo”ti. Yasmā pana āpodhātuyā anugatā pathavīdhātu sannikkhepanassa paccayo, patiṭṭhābhāve viya patiṭṭhāpanepi tassā sātisayakiccattā āpodhātuyā tassā anugatabhāvo, tathā ghaṭṭanakiriyāya pathavīdhātuyā vasena sannirujjhanassa sijjhanato tatthāpi pathavīdhātuyā āpodhātuanugatabhāvo, tasmā vuttaṃ “tathā sannikkhepanasannirujjhanesū”ti.

Because the water element, accompanied by the earth element, is a condition for letting go. For the water element has a heavier nature. In letting go, it is accompanied by the earth element—thus, to show the predominance of these two in terms of capability here and the lesser role of the others, he says, 'In letting go... they are strong.' Moreover, because the earth element, accompanied by the water element, is a condition for placing down; and because it has a superior function in establishing, just as in the state of being established, it is accompanied by the water element. Similarly, because in the action of contact the arresting is accomplished by means of the earth element, there too the earth element is accompanied by the water element. Therefore, it is said: 'Likewise, in placing down and arresting.'

Tatthāti tasmiṃ abhikkamane, tesu vā vuttesu uddaraṇādīsu koṭṭhāsesu. Uddharaṇeti uddharaṇakkhaṇe. Rūpārūpadhammāti uddharaṇākārena pavattā rūpadhammā, taṃsamuṭṭhāpakā arūpadhammā ca. Atiharaṇaṃ [M 1.0248] na pāpuṇanti khaṇamattāvaṭṭhānato. Tattha tatthevāti yattha yattha uppannā, tattha tattheva. Na hi dhammānaṃ desantarasaṅkamanaṃ atthi. “Pabbaṃ pabba”tiādi uddharaṇādikoṭṭhāse sandhāya sabhāgasantativasena vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Atiittaro hi rūpadhammānampi [P 1.0322] pavattikkhaṇo, gamanassādīnaṃ, devaputtānaṃ heṭṭhupariyena paṭimukhaṃ dhāvantānaṃ sirasi pāde ca bandhakhuradhārā samāgamatopi sīghataro. Yathā tilānaṃ bhajjiyamānānaṃ paṭapaṭāyanena bhedo lakkhīyati, evaṃ saṅkhatadhammānaṃ uppādenāti dassanatthaṃ “paṭapaṭāyantā”ti vuttaṃ. Uppannā hi ekantato bhijjantīti. “Saddhiṃ rūpenā”ti idaṃ tassa tassa cittassa nirodhena saddhiṃ nirujjhanakarūpadhammānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ, yaṃ tato sattarasamacittassa uppādakkhaṇe uppannaṃ. Aññathā yadi [V 1.0220] rūpārūpadhammā samānakkhaṇā siyuṃ, “rūpaṃ garupariṇāmaṃ dandhanirodha”ntiādivacanehi virodho siyā, tathā “nāhaṃ bhikkhave aññaṃ ekadhammampi samanupassāmi, yaṃ evaṃ lahuparivattaṃ, yathayidaṃ citta”nti (a. ni. 1.48) evaṃ ādipāḷiyā. Cittacetasikā hi sārammaṇasabhāvā yathābalaṃ attano ārammaṇapaccayabhūtamatthaṃ vibhāvento eva uppajjantīti tesaṃ taṃsabhāvanipphattianantaraṃ nirodho. Rūpadhammā pana anārammaṇā pakāsetabbā, evaṃ tesaṃ pakāsetabbabhāvanipphatti soḷasahi cittehi hotīti taṅkhaṇāyukatā tesaṃ icchitā, lahuviññāṇavisayasaṅgatimattappaccayatāya tiṇṇaṃ khandhānaṃ, visayasaṅgatimattatāya ca viññāṇassa lahuparivattitā, dandhamahābhūtappaccayatāya rūpadhammānaṃ dandhaparivattitā. Nānādhātuyā yathābhūtañāṇaṃ kho pana tathāgatasseva, tena ca purejātapaccayo rūpadhammova vutto, pacchājātapaccayo ca tathevāti rūpārūpadhammānaṃ samānakkhaṇatā na yujjateva. Tasmā vuttanayenevettha attho veditabbo.

‘Therein’ means in that act of moving forward, or in those mentioned sections on lifting and so on. ‘Lifting’ refers to the moment of lifting. ‘Material and immaterial phenomena’ are the material phenomena occurring in the manner of lifting, and the immaterial phenomena that give rise to them. They do not reach the state of being carried further, because they last only for a moment. ‘There and there’ means wherever they arise, right there. For phenomena do not travel to another place. ‘Bit by bit,’ etc., should be understood as referring to the sections on lifting and so on, spoken in terms of a continuous series of similar phenomena. The moment of occurrence of even material phenomena is extremely brief, faster than the meeting of the sharp edges of hooves on the head and feet of celestial beings running toward each other from below and above. Just as the breaking of sesame seeds being roasted is perceived by their crackling sound, so too, the phrase ‘crackling’ is used to show the breaking of conditioned phenomena upon their arising. For what has arisen is unfailingly destroyed. ‘Together with form’ is said with reference to those material phenomena that cease together with the cessation of each respective consciousness—those that arose at the arising moment of the seventeenth consciousness prior. Otherwise, if material and immaterial phenomena were of the same duration, it would contradict statements like ‘form is slow in transformation, slow to cease,’ etc., as well as scriptural passages such as: ‘Monks, I do not see any other single phenomenon that changes as swiftly as this mind.’ (AN 1.48) For consciousness and mental factors, having the nature of taking an object, arise while analyzing, according to their capacity, the object that is their condition, and they cease immediately after the fulfillment of that nature. Material phenomena, however, are without an object and must be made manifest. Thus, their duration for that many moments is accepted because the fulfillment of their nature of being made manifest occurs over sixteen mind-moments. The swift changeability of the three aggregates is due to their being conditioned merely by connection with the object of a swift consciousness, and the swift changeability of consciousness is due to its being merely a connection with an object. The slowness of material phenomena is due to their being conditioned by the slow great elements. However, the knowledge of the various elements as they really are belongs only to the Tathāgata. And by him, the pre-arisen condition has been stated to be material phenomena, and the post-arisen condition likewise. Therefore, the simultaneity of material and immaterial phenomena is indeed untenable. Thus, the meaning here should be understood in the manner stated.

Aññaṃ [P 1.0323] uppajjate cittaṃ, aññaṃ cittaṃ nirujjhatīti yaṃ purimuppannaṃ cittaṃ, taṃ aññaṃ, taṃ pana nirujjhantaṃ aparassa anantarādipaccayabhāveneva nirujjhatīti tathāladdhapaccayaṃ aññaṃ uppajjate cittaṃ. Yadi evaṃ tesaṃ antaro labbheyyāti? Noti āha “avīci manuppabandho”ti, yathā vīci antaro na labbhati, “tadeveta”nti avisesavidū maññanti, evaṃ anu anu pabandho cittasantāno rūpasantāno ca nadīsotova nadiyaṃ udakappavāho viya vattati.

One mind arises, another mind ceases. The mind that arose previously is one thing, and that very mind, as it ceases, does so precisely by being the immediately preceding condition, and so on, for another. Thus, another mind arises, having obtained its condition in that way. If that is so, could an interval be found between them? No, he said, for 'the mental continuity is without interval.' Just as no interval is found between waves, the undiscriminating think 'it is the very same.' Thus, moment by moment, the continuum of mind and the continuum of form proceed like the current of a river, like the flow of water in a river.

Abhimukhaṃ [M 1.0249] lokitaṃ ālokitanti āha “purato pekkhana”nti. Yasmā yaṃdisābhimukho gacchati, tiṭṭhati, nisīdati vā tadabhimukhaṃ pekkhanaṃ ālokitaṃ, tasmā tadanugatavidisālokanaṃ vilokitanti āha “vilokitaṃ nāma anudisāpekkhana”nti. Sammajjanaparibhaṇḍādikaraṇe olokitassa, ullokaharaṇādīsu ullokitassa, pacchato āgacchantaparissayassa parivajjanādīsu apalokitassa siyā sambhavoti āha “iminā vā mukhena sabbānipi tāni gahitānevā”ti.

He said: 'Looking directly ahead is called “looking ahead,” meaning looking forward.' Since looking in the direction one faces when going, standing, or sitting is called 'looking ahead,' therefore, looking in a direction that follows on from that is called 'looking around,' meaning looking in secondary directions. He said that in sweeping, cleaning vessels, and similar tasks, looking down is possible; in raising or lifting up, looking up is possible; in avoiding dangers coming from behind, looking back is possible. 'Thus, all those are indeed included by this expression.'

Kāyasakkhinti kāyena sacchikatavantaṃ, paccakkhakārinanti attho. So hi āyasmā vipassanākāle “yamevāhaṃ indriyesu aguttadvārataṃ nissāya sāsane anabhiratiādivippakāraṃ patto, tameva suṭṭhu niggahessāmī”ti ussāhajāto balavahirottappo, tattha ca katādhikārattā indriyasaṃvare ukkaṃsapāramippatto, teneva naṃ satthā “etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ indriyesu guttadvārānaṃ, yadidaṃ nando”ti (a. ni. 1.235) etadagge ṭhapesi.

'Body-witness' means one who has realized with the body, meaning one who has directly witnessed. For that venerable one, at the time of insight meditation, arose with strong effort and powerful moral shame and fear of wrongdoing, thinking, 'Whatever corruption I have attained due to lack of guarding the sense doors, such as dissatisfaction with the teaching, I will thoroughly restrain.' Due to his having developed skill in that area, he reached the highest perfection in sense restraint. Therefore, the Teacher placed him foremost, saying, 'Monks, among my monk disciples who are restrained in their senses, this is the foremost, namely, Nanda.' (AN 1.235)

Sātthakatā [V 1.0221] ca sappāyatā ca veditabbā ālokitavilokitassāti ānetvā sambandho. Tasmāti kammaṭṭhānāvijahanasseva gocarasampajaññabhāvatoti vuttamevatthaṃ hetubhāvena paccāmasati. Attano [P 1.0324] kammaṭṭhānavaseneva ālokanavilokanaṃ kātabbaṃ, khandhādikammaṭṭhānā añño upāyo na gavesitabboti adhippāyo. Ālokitādisamaññāpi yasmā dhammamattasseva pavattiviseso, tasmā tassa yāthāvato pajānanaṃ asammohasampajaññanti dassetuṃ “abbhantare”tiādi vuttaṃ. Cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāravasenāti kiriyamayacittasamuṭṭhānāya vāyodhātuyā calanākārappavattivasena. Adho sīdatīti adho gacchati. Uddhaṃ laṅghetīti laṅghaṃ viya upari gacchati.

The benefit and suitability of looking ahead and looking around should be understood; thus, the connection is established by bringing it in. Therefore, it recalls the meaning already stated, by way of cause, that only through not abandoning the meditation subject does one have clear comprehension of the domain. The meaning is that one should look ahead and around only in accordance with one's meditation subject; no other means should be sought, apart from meditation subjects such as the aggregates. Since the terms like 'looking ahead' merely denote a particular mode of occurrence of mere phenomena, therefore, to show that the accurate understanding of it is clear comprehension as non-delusion, the phrase 'internally,' etc., is stated. 'Through the manifestation of the wind element by mental activity' means through the mode of movement caused by the wind element arising from functional consciousness. 'Sinks downward' means it goes downward. 'Leaps upward' means it goes upward like a leap.

Aṅgakiccaṃ sādhayamānanti padhānabhūtaaṅgakiccaṃ nipphādentaṃ hutvāti attho. “Paṭhamajavanepi…pe… na hotī”ti idaṃ pañcadvāravīthiyaṃ “itthī puriso”ti rajjanādīnaṃ abhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tattha hi āvajjana voṭṭhabbapanānaṃ ayoniso āvajjanavoṭṭhabbanavasena iṭṭhe itthirūpādimhi lobhamattaṃ, aniṭṭhe [M 1.0250] ca paṭighamattaṃ uppajjati, manodvāre pana “itthī puriso”ti rajjanādi hoti. Tassa pañcadvārajavanaṃ mūlaṃ, yathāvuttaṃ vā sabbaṃ bhavaṅgādi. Evaṃ manodvārajavanassa mūlavasena mūlapariññā vuttā. Āgantukatāvakālikatā pana pañcadvārajavanasseva apubbabhāvavasena, ittarabhāvavasena ca vuttā. “Heṭṭhupariyavasena bhijjitvā patitesū”ti heṭṭhimassa uparimassa ca aparāparaṃ bhaṅgappattimāha.

Performing the function of the limbs means accomplishing the primary function of the limbs—this is the meaning. 'In the first javana...it does not occur'—this is said with reference to the absence of lust and other defilements in the five-door sensory process regarding perceptions like 'a woman, a man.' For here, through unwise adverting and determining, mere lust arises toward desirable objects like a woman's form, and mere aversion toward undesirable objects. In the mind-door process, however, lust and so on arise regarding 'a woman, a man.' The five-door javana is the root of that, or, as has been said, everything from bhavaṅga onwards. Thus, the full understanding of the root is explained by way of the root of the mind-door javana. The adventitious and temporary nature, however, is stated with respect to the five-door javana due to its unprecedented nature and its briefness. 'Breaking apart and falling away in terms of lower and upper'—this describes the successive attainment of dissolution of the lower and upper.

Tanti javanaṃ, tassa ayuttanti sambandho. Āgantuko abbhāgato.

'That' refers to javana; the connection is with the phrase 'is improper for it.' An adventitious one is a newcomer.

Udayabbayaparicchinno tāvatako kālo etesanti tāvakālikāni.

Their time is just so much, being bounded by arising and passing away; thus, they are temporary.

Etaṃ asammohasampajaññaṃ. Samavāyeti sāmaggiyaṃ[P 1.0325]. Tatthāti pañcakkhandhavasena ālokanavilokane paññāyamāne tabbinimutto ko eko āloketi, ko viloketi.

This is clear comprehension as non-delusion. 'Samavāya' means harmony. Here, when looking ahead and looking around are understood in terms of the five aggregates, who is the one freed from them that looks ahead, who is the one that looks around?

“Upanissayapaccayo”ti idaṃ suttantanayena pariyāyato vuttaṃ. Sahajātapaccayoti nidassanamattametaṃ aññamaññasampayuttaatthiavigatādipaccayānampi labbhanato.

'Decisive support condition'—this is stated indirectly by way of the Suttanta method. 'Co-nascence condition'—this is merely an example, since it can also be obtained from other conditions such as mutuality, association, presence, non-departure, and so on.

Kāle samañchituṃ yuttakāle samañchantassa. Tathā pasārentassāti etthāpi. Maṇisappo nāma ekā sappajātīti vadanti. Laḷananti kampanaṃ, līḷākaraṇaṃ vā.

At the proper time to coil up, for one who coils up at the proper time. Likewise, also for one who stretches out. They say that the 'jewel snake' is a kind of snake. 'Laḷana' means trembling or playful action.

Uṇhapakatiko [V 1.0222] pariḷāhabahulakāyo. Sīlavidūsanena ahitāvahattā micchājīvavasena uppannaṃ asappāyaṃ. “Cīvarampi acetana”ntiādinā cīvarassa viya kāyopi acetanoti kāyassa attasuññatāvibhāvanena “abbhantare”tiādinā vuttamevatthaṃ paridīpento itarītarasantosassa kāraṇaṃ dasseti, tenāha “tasmā”tiādi.

The body is naturally hot and prone to much burning. Unsuitability arises through wrong livelihood, due to its bringing harm by the violation of virtue. Elucidating the meaning already stated by 'internally,' etc., by showing the emptiness of self in the body—just as with the robe, through 'even the robe is inanimate,' etc.—he shows the reason for contentment with whatever comes. Therefore, he says, 'therefore,' etc.

Catupañcagaṇṭhikāhatoti āhatacatupañcagaṇṭhiko, catupañcagaṇṭhikāhi vā āhato tathā.
