'Struck by four or five knots' means one struck by four or five knots, or struck in such a way by four or five knots.

Aṭṭhavidhopi [M 1.0251] atthoti aṭṭhavidhopi payojanaviseso mahāsivattheravādavasena “imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.23, 422; ma. ni. 2.387; a. ni. 2.341; 8.9; dha. sa. 1355; vibha. 518; mahāni. 206) nayena vutto daṭṭhabbo. Imasmiṃ pakkhe “neva davāyātiādinā (ma. ni. 1.23, 422; ma. ni. 2.387; a. ni. 8.9; dha. sa. 1355; vibha. 518; mahāni. 206) nayenā”ti pana paṭikkhepaṅgadassanamukhena desanāya āgatattā vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Even the eightfold benefit—the eightfold special purpose—should be understood as stated according to the doctrine of the great Elder Sīva, in the manner of the passage beginning 'for the maintenance of this body' (MN 1.23, 422; MN 2.387; AN 2.341; 8.9; DhS 1355; Vibh 518; Mahāni 206). But in this respect, it should be understood that it is stated since the teaching comes in the manner of showing a prohibitive aspect by way of phrases beginning 'not for pleasure,' etc. (MN 1.23, 422; MN 2.387; AN 8.9; DhS 1355; Vibh 518; Mahāni 206).

Pathavisandhārakajalassa taṃsandhārakavāyunā viya paribhuttassa āhārassa vāyodhātuyāva āsaye avaṭṭhānanti āha “vāyodhātuvaseneva tiṭṭhatī”ti. Atiharatīti yāva mukhā abhiharati. Vītiharatīti tato kucchiyaṃ vīmissaṃ karonto [P 1.0326] harati. Atiharatīti vā mukhadvāraṃ atikkāmento harati. Vītiharatīti kucchigataṃ passato harati, parivattetīti aparāparaṃ cāreti. Ettha ca āhārassa dhāraṇaparivattanasañcuṇṇanavisosanāni pathavīdhātusahitā eva vāyodhātu karoti, na kevalāti tāni pathavīdhātuyāpi kiccabhāvena vuttāni. Allattañca anupāletīti yathā vāyodhātu ādīhi aññehi visosanaṃ na hoti, tathā allattañca anupāleti. Tejodhātūti gahaṇīsaṅkhātā tejodhātu. Sā hi antopaviṭṭhaṃ āhāraṃ paripāceti. Añjaso hotīti āhārassa pavesanādīnaṃ maggo hoti. Ābhujatīti pariyesanavasena, ajjhoharaṇajiṇṇājiṇṇatādipaṭisaṃvedanavasena ca āvajjeti, vijānātīti attho. Taṃtaṃvijānanassa paccayabhūtoyeva hi payogo “sammāpayogo”ti vutto. Yena hi payogena pariyesanādi nipphajjati, so tabbisayavijānanampi nipphādeti nāma tadavinābhāvato. Atha vā sammāpayogaṃ sammāpaṭipatti manvāya āgamma ābhujati samannāharati. Ābhogapubbako hi sabbopi viññāṇabyāpāroti tathā vuttaṃ.

Just as the earth supports water and the wind supports that, so too the consumed food remains in the stomach by means of the wind element—hence he said, 'it stands by the power of the wind element.' 'Atiharati' means it brings it as far as the mouth. 'Vītiharati' means it then carries it into the stomach, mixing it. Or 'Atiharati' means it carries it past the mouth-door. 'Vītiharati' means it carries it, seeing it as being in the stomach. 'Parivatteti' means it circulates it again and again. Here, the wind element, together with the earth element, performs the functions of holding, circulating, grinding, and drying the food—not alone; thus, these are also said to be functions of the earth element. 'And maintains moisture' means it maintains moisture so that drying by the wind element and others does not occur. 'The fire element' means the fire element known as the digestive fire. For it cooks the food that has entered inside. 'Añjaso hoti' means it becomes the path for the food's entry and so on. 'Ābhujati' means it attends by way of searching and by way of experiencing swallowing, digestion, indigestion, and so on; the meaning is 'it knows.' For the application that is the very condition for knowing this or that is called 'right application.' For by that application through which searching and so on is accomplished, it also produces the knowing pertaining to that object, since they are inseparable. Or alternatively, it applies itself and directs its attention, having approached and relied upon right application as right practice. For all cognitive activity is preceded by attention—thus it is said.

Gamanatoti bhikkhācāravasena gocaragāmaṃ uddissa gamanato. Pariyesanatoti gocaragāme bhikkhatthaṃ [V 1.0223] āhiṇḍanato. Paribhogatoti āhārassa paribhuñjanato. Āsayatoti pittādiāsayato. Āsayati ettha ekajjhaṃ pavattamānopi kammaphalavavatthito hutvā mariyādavasena aññamaññaṃ asaṅkarato sayati tiṭṭhati pavattatīti āsayo[M 1.0252], āmāsayassa upari tiṭṭhanako pittādiko. Mariyādattho hi ayamākāro. Nidhānanti yathābhutto āhāro [P 1.0327] nicito hutvā tiṭṭhati etthāti nidhānaṃ, āmāsayo. Tato nidhānato. Aparipakkatoti gahaṇīsaṅkhātena kammajatejena avipakkato. Paripakkatoti yathābhuttassa āhārasa vipakkabhāvato. Phalatoti nipphattito. Nissandatoti ito cito ca nissandanato. Sammakkhanatoti sabbaso makkhanato. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāya (visuddhi. ṭī. 1.294) gahetabbo.

'Going' means from going towards the alms-village by means of the practice of alms-seeking. 'Searching' means from wandering in the alms-village for alms. 'Consuming' means from the consuming of food. 'Receptacle' means from the receptacle of bile, etc. Here, 'āsaya' (receptacle) means that even though occurring together, it lies, stands, and proceeds, distinguished by boundaries as not mixing with one another, being established by the results of kamma; it refers to the bile, etc., that stands above the stomach. This aspect is indeed for the purpose of boundaries. 'Storehouse' means where the food, as it has been taken, is accumulated and remains—this is the storehouse (nidhāna), the stomach. From that storehouse. 'Unripened' means not matured by the digestive heat produced by kamma, known as gahaṇī. 'Ripened' means from the state of the food as it has been taken being digested. 'Fruit' means from the production. 'Emanation' means from the emanation here and there. 'Smearing' means from the complete smearing. This here is the summary; the detailed explanation should be taken from the commentary on the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga Ṭīkā 1.294).

Sarīrato sedā muccantīti vegasaṃdhāraṇena uppannapariḷāhato sarīrato sedā muccanti. Aññe ca rogā kaṇṇasūlabhagandarādayo. Aṭṭhāneti manussāmanussapariggahite ayuttaṭṭhāne khettadevāyatanādike. Kuddhā hi amanussā, manussāpi vā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpenti. Nissaṭṭhattā neva attano, kassaci anissajjitattā, jigucchanīyattā ca na parassa. Udakatumbatoti veḷunāḷiādiudakabhājanato. Tanti chaḍḍitaudakaṃ.

Sweat is released from the body: that is, sweat is released from the body due to the heat that arises from suppressing urges. And other diseases arise, such as earaches, fistulas, and so forth. In an improper place: that is, in an unsuitable place frequented by humans and non-humans, such as fields, shrines, and the like. For angry non-humans, or even humans, can bring about the destruction of life. Because it is discharged, it belongs neither to oneself, nor is it given to anyone; and because it is repulsive, it is not for others. From a water-gourd: that is, from a water vessel made of bamboo stalk or similar materials. That is discarded water.

Addhānairiyāpathā ciratarappavattikā dīghakālikā iriyāpathā. Majjhimā bhikkhācaraṇādivasena pavattā. Cuṇṇiyairiyāpathā vihāre, aññatthāpi ito cito ca parivattanādivasena pavattāti vadanti. “Gateti gamane”ti pubbe abhikkamapaṭikkamaggahaṇena gamanenapi purato pacchato ca kāyassa abhiharaṇaṃ vuttanti idha gamanameva gahitanti keci.

Long-duration postures are those postures that continue for a very long time. Medium postures are those that occur by way of activities such as going for alms. Fragmentary postures, they say, are those that occur in the monastery or elsewhere by way of turning this way and that, and so forth. “Gati means going”: previously, by taking ‘going forward’ and ‘going backward’, the movement of the body forward and backward was described as ‘going’; here, some say, only ‘going’ is meant.

Yasmā mahāsivattheravāde anantare anantare iriyāpathe pavattarūpārūpadhammānaṃ tattha tattheva nirodhadassanavasena sampajānakāritā gahitāti taṃ sampajaññavipassanācāravasena veditabbaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “tayidaṃ mahāsivattherena vuttaṃ asammohadhuraṃ mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutte adhippeta”nti. Imasmiṃ pana sāmaññaphale sabbampi [P 1.0328] catubbidhaṃ sampajaññaṃ labbhati yāvadeva sāmaññaphalavisesadassanaparattā imissā desanāya. “Satisampayuttassevā”ti idaṃ yathā sampajaññassa kiccato padhānatā gahitā, evaṃ satiyā pīti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na satiyā sabbhāvamattadassanatthaṃ. Na hi kadāci satirahitā ñāṇappavatti atthi. “Etassa hi padassa ayaṃ vitthāro”ti iminā satiyā ñāṇena samadhurataṃyeva vibhāveti. Etāni [M 1.0253] padānīti “abhikkante paṭikkante sampajānakārī hotī”tiādīni [V 1.0224] padāni. Vibhattānevāti visuṃ katvā vibhattāniyeva, imināpi sampajaññassa viya satiyāpettha padhānatameva vibhāveti.

Because in the Mahāsivattheravāda, clear comprehension is taken as being active through seeing the cessation of material and immaterial phenomena arising in successive postures, then and there; therefore, it should be understood as conduct involving clear comprehension and insight. Hence it was said, “This was stated by the Mahāsivatthera as the burden of non-delusion, intended in the Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness.” But in this fruit of recluseship, all four kinds of clear comprehension are obtained, insofar as this teaching is for the purpose of showing the distinction of the fruit of recluseship. The phrase “only of one associated with mindfulness” is stated to show the pre-eminence of mindfulness by way of function, just as that of clear comprehension is taken as pre-eminent, and not to show merely the existence of mindfulness. For there is never any occurrence of knowledge devoid of mindfulness. “This is the detailed explanation of this term”: with this, it highlights that mindfulness and knowledge are of equal weight. “These terms”: that is, terms such as “one acts with clear comprehension when going forward, when going backward.” “Are distinctly analyzed”: meaning they are indeed analyzed by making them separate; even with this, it highlights that mindfulness, like clear comprehension, is pre-eminent here.

Majjhimabhāṇakā pana bhaṇanti – eko bhikkhu gacchanto aññaṃ cintento aññaṃ vitakkento gacchati, eko kammaṭṭhānaṃ avissajjetvāva gacchati. Tathā eko tiṭṭhanto…pe… nisīdanto…pe… sayanto aññaṃ cintento aññaṃ vitakkento sayati, eko kammaṭṭhānaṃ avissajjetvāva sayati, ettakena pana na pākaṭaṃ hotīti caṅkamanena dīpenti. Yo hi bhikkhu caṅkamaṃ otaritvā ca caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ ṭhito pariggaṇhāti “pācīnacaṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ pavattā rūpārūpadhammā pacchimacaṅkamanakoṭiṃ appatvā ettheva niruddhā, pacchimacaṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ pavattāpi pācīnacaṅkamanakoṭiṃ appatvā ettheva niruddhā, caṅkamanamajjhe pavattā ubho koṭiyo appatvā ettheva niruddhā, caṅkamane pavattā rūpārūpadhammā ṭhānaṃ appatvā ettheva niruddhā, ṭhāne pavattā nisajjaṃ appatvā ettheva niruddhā, nisajjāya pavattā sayanaṃ appatvā ettheva niruddhā”ti evaṃ pariggaṇhanto pariggaṇhantoyeva bhavaṅgaṃ otarati. Uṭṭhahanto kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvāva uṭṭhahati, ayaṃ bhikkhu gatādīsu sampajānakārī nāma hotīti[P 1.0329]. Evampi na sotte kammaṭṭhānaṃ avibhūtaṃ hoti, tasmā bhikkhu yāva sakkoti, tāva caṅkamitvā ṭhatvā nisīditvā sayamāno evaṃ pariggahetvā sayati “kāyo acetano, mañco acetano, kāyo na jānāti ‘ahaṃ mañce sayito’ti, mañco na jānāti ‘mayi kāyo sayito’ti, acetano kāyo acetane mañce sayito”ti evaṃ pariggaṇhanto eva cittaṃ bhavaṅge otāreti. Pabujjhanto kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvāva pabujjhati, ayaṃ sotte sampajānakārī nāma hoti. Kāyādīkiriyānibbattanena tammayattā, āvajjanakiriyā samuṭṭhitattā ca javanaṃ sabbampi vā chadvārappavattaṃ kiriyamayapavattaṃ nāma. Tasmiṃ sati jāgaritaṃ nāma hotīti pariggaṇhanto jāgarite sampajānakārī nāma. Api ca rattindivaṃ cha koṭṭhāse katvā pañca koṭṭhāse jaggantopi jāgarite sampajānakārī nāma hoti. Vimuttāyatanasīsena dhammaṃ desentopi battiṃsatiracchānakathaṃ pahāya dasakathāvatthunissitasappāyakathaṃ kathentopi bhāsite sampajānakārī nāma. Aṭṭhatiṃsāya ārammaṇesu cittaruciyaṃ manasikāraṃ pavattentopi dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannopi [M 1.0254] tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī nāma. Dutiyañhi jhānaṃ vacīsaṅkhāravirahato visesato tuṇhībhāvo nāmāti. Evanti vuttappakārena, sattasupi ṭhānesu catudhāti attho.

The Middle Reciters, however, say: One monk walks while thinking one thing and pondering another, while another walks without abandoning his meditation subject. Similarly, one stands… sits… lies down while thinking one thing and pondering another, while another lies down without abandoning his meditation subject. But by this much it is not made clear, so they explain it by way of walking meditation. For a monk who, having entered the walking path and standing at the end of it, comprehends thus: “The material and immaterial phenomena that arise at the eastern end of the walking path cease right there without reaching the western end. Those that arise at the western end also cease right there without reaching the eastern end. Those that arise in the middle cease right there without reaching either end. The material and immaterial phenomena that arise while walking cease right there without reaching the standing posture. Those that arise while standing cease right there without reaching the sitting posture. Those that arise while sitting cease right there without reaching the lying down posture.” While comprehending thus, he sinks into the life-continuum. When rising, he rises only after taking up his meditation subject. Such a monk is called one who acts with clear comprehension in going, and so forth. Even so, the meditation subject is not indistinct while sleeping. Therefore, a monk, for as long as he is able, having walked, stood, and sat, should lie down after comprehending thus: “The body is without consciousness; the bed is without consciousness. The body does not know, ‘I am lying on the bed,’ nor does the bed know, ‘The body is lying on me.’ A body without consciousness lies on a bed without consciousness.” While comprehending thus, he lets his mind sink into the life-continuum. When waking, he wakes only after taking up his meditation subject. Such a one is called one who acts with clear comprehension in sleep. Because it is constituted by the performance of bodily and other actions, and because it arises from the act of adverting, all impulsion (javana), or that which occurs through the six doors, is called a process composed of action. When this is present, it is called wakefulness. One who comprehends thus is called one who acts with clear comprehension in wakefulness. Moreover, one who stays awake for five out of the six portions of the day and night is also called one who acts with clear comprehension in wakefulness. One who teaches the Dhamma with the principle of the bases of liberation, abandoning the thirty-two kinds of worldly talk and speaking only on suitable topics based on the ten subjects of discussion, is called one who acts with clear comprehension in speech. One who directs attention to one of the thirty-eight objects according to the mind’s preference, or one who has attained the second jhāna, is called one who acts with clear comprehension in silence. For the second jhāna is especially called silence because it is free from verbal formations. Thus, in the manner stated, the meaning is fourfold in all seven instances.

Santosakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Discourse on Contentment

215. Yassa [V 1.0225] santosassa attani atthitāya bhikkhu “santuṭṭho”ti vuccati, taṃ dassento “itarītarapaccayasantosena samannāgato”ti āha. Cīvarādi yattha katthaci paccaye [P 1.0330] santussanena samaṅgībhūtoti attho. Atha vā itaraṃ vuccati hīnaṃ paṇītato aññattā, tathā paṇītaṃ itaraṃ hīnato aññattā. Apekkhāsiddhā hi itaratāti. Iti yena dhammena hīnena vā paṇītena vā cīvarādipaccayena santussati, so tathā pavatto alobho itarītarapaccayasantoso, tena samannāgato. Yathālābhaṃ attano lābhānurūpaṃ santoso yathālābhasantoso. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo. Labbhatīti vā lābho, yo yo lābho yathālābhaṃ, tena santoso yathālābhasantoso. Balanti kāyabalaṃ. Sāruppanti pakatidubbalādīnaṃ anucchavikatā.

215. A bhikkhu is called 'content' because of the existence of contentment within him. Showing this, the text states: 'He is endowed with contentment with any kind of requisite' (itarītarapaccayasantosena samannāgato). The meaning is that he is endowed with satisfaction in whatever requisite there may be, such as robes and so forth. Alternatively, the inferior is called 'itara' because it is other than the excellent; similarly, the excellent is called 'itara' because it is other than the inferior. For otherness is established by relation. Thus, when he is content with any requisite, such as a robe, whether it be inferior or excellent, that non-greed which has so arisen is 'contentment with any kind of requisite,' and with that he is endowed. 'Contentment with what is obtained' (yathālābhasantoso) is contentment in accordance with one's gain. The same method applies to the remaining two. Or, 'gain' (lābho) is what is received; whatever gain, as it is received, contentment with that is 'contentment with what is obtained' (yathālābhasantoso). 'Strength' (bala) is bodily strength. 'Suitability' (sāruppa) refers to what is appropriate, avoiding what is unsuitable for those who are naturally weak and so on.

Yathāladdhato aññassa apatthanā nāma siyā appicchatāyapi pavattiākāroti tato vinivattitameva santosassa sarūpaṃ dassento “labhantopi na gaṇhātī”ti āha. Taṃ parivattetvāti pakatidubbalādīnaṃ garucīvaraṃ na phāsubhāvāvahaṃ, sarīrakhedāvahañca hotīti payojanavasena, na atricchatādivasena taṃ parivattetvā. Lahukacīvaraparibhogo na santosavirodhīti āha “lahukena yāpentopi santuṭṭhova hotī”ti. Mahagghaṃ cīvaraṃ bahūni vā cīvarāni labhitvāpi tāni vissajjetvā tadaññassa gahaṇaṃ yathāsāruppanaye ṭhitattā na santosavirodhīti āha “tesaṃ…pe… dhārentopi santuṭṭhova hotī”ti. Evaṃ sesapaccayepi yathābalayathāsāruppaniddesesu api-saddaggahaṇe adhippāyo veditabbo.

Because not desiring something other than what one has obtained can also be a characteristic of having few wishes (appicchatā), to show the nature of contentment as distinct from that, the text states: 'Even when obtaining, he does not take it.' 'Having exchanged it' (taṃ parivattetvā) means that for those who are naturally weak and so on, a heavy robe is not conducive to comfort and causes bodily fatigue; thus, one exchanges it for practical reasons, not out of excessive desire (atricchatā) and so forth. The use of a light robe is not contrary to contentment, as it is said: 'Even maintaining oneself with a light robe, one is content.' Even having obtained an expensive robe or many robes, giving them away and taking another, being established in the principle of suitability (yathāsāruppa), is not contrary to contentment, as it is said: 'Even wearing them... one is content.' Similarly, regarding the remaining requisites, the intention behind the inclusion of the word 'api' (even) in the explanations of 'according to one's strength' (yathābala) and 'according to suitability' (yathāsāruppa) should be understood.

Muttaharītakanti gomuttaparibhāvitaṃ, pūtibhāvena vā chaḍḍitaṃ harītakaṃ. Buddhādīhi vaṇṇitanti “pūtimuttabhesajjaṃ nissāya pabbajjā”tiādinā (mahāva. 73, 128) sammāsambuddhādīhi [M 1.0255] pasatthaṃ. Appicchatāsantuṭṭhīsu [P 1.0331] bhikkhū niyojento paramasantuṭṭhova hoti paramena ukkaṃsagatena santosena samannāgatattā.

'Muttaharītaka' is harītaka (myrobalan) treated with cow's urine, or harītaka discarded due to its putrid nature. 'Praised by the Buddha and others' (Buddhādīhi vaṇṇitaṃ) refers to what is commended by the Perfectly Enlightened One and others, as stated in 'The going forth is dependent on medicine of putrid urine' and so on (Mahāvagga 73, 128). By encouraging bhikkhus in fewness of wishes (appicchatā) and contentment (santuṭṭhi), one becomes supremely content, being endowed with contentment that has reached the highest excellence.

Kāyaṃ pariharanti posentīti kāyaparihārikā. Tathā kucchiparihārikā veditabbā. Kucchiparihārikatā ca ajjhoharaṇena sarīrassa ṭhitiyā upakārakatāvasena icchitāti bahiddhāva kāyassa upakārakatāvasena kāyaparihārikatā daṭṭhabbā.

They maintain and nourish the body (kāyaṃ pariharanti posenti); thus, they are 'body-requisites' (kāyaparihārikā). Similarly, 'belly-requisites' (kucchiparihārikā) should be understood. 'Belly-maintenance' (kucchiparihārikatā) is intended to assist in the body's sustenance through ingestion. Likewise, 'body-maintenance' (kāyaparihārikatā) should be seen as assisting the body externally.

Parikkhāramattāti parikkhāraggahaṇaṃ. Tatraṭṭhakapaccattharaṇanti attanā anadhiṭṭhahitvā tattheva tiṭṭhanakapaccattharaṇaṃ[V 1.0226]. Paccattharaṇādīnañcettha navamādibhāvo yathāvuttapaṭipāṭiyā daṭṭhabbo, na tesaṃ tathā patiniyatabhāvato. Kasmā? Tathā nadhāraṇato. Dupposabhāvena mahāgajā viyāti mahāgajā. Yadi itarepi appicchatādisabhāvā, kiṃ tesampi vasena ayaṃ desanā icchitāti? Noti āha “bhagavā panā”tiādi. Kāyaparihāro payojanaṃ etenāti kāyaparihārikaṃ. Tenāha “kāyaṃ pariharaṇamattakenā”ti.

'The mere measure of a requisite' (parikkhāramattaṃ) means the taking of a requisite. 'A covering that remains there' (tatraṭṭhakapaccattharaṇaṃ) is a covering that remains in its place, not having been personally appropriated. Here, the seat covering and so forth being the ninth and subsequent items should be understood according to the sequence as stated, not because they are fixed in that order. Why? Because they are not regarded in that way. Because they are difficult to support, they are like great elephants; hence, 'great elephants' (mahāgajā). If others, too, have a nature of few wishes and so on, is this teaching intended for them as well? To this, it is said, 'No,' with the words, 'But the Blessed One...' and so on. A 'body-requisite' (kāyaparihārikaṃ) is so called because its purpose (payojanaṃ) is the maintenance of the body (kāyaparihāro). Therefore, it is said: 'with just enough to maintain the body.'

Catūsu disāsu sukhavihāratāya sukhavihāraṭṭhānabhūtā catasso disā etassāti catuddiso catuddiso eva cātuddiso. Tāsu eva katthaci satte vā saṅkhāre vā bhayena na paṭihanati, sayaṃ vā tena na paṭihaññatīti appaṭigho. Santussamāno itarītarenāti uccāvacena paccayena sakena, santena, samameva ca tussanako. Paricca sayanti, kāyacittāni parisayanti abhibhavantīti parissayā, sīhabyagghādayo, kāmacchandādayo ca, te parissaye adhivāsanakhantiyā vinayādīhi ca sahitā khantā, abhibhavitā ca. Thaddhabhāvakarabhayābhāvena achambhī. Eko careti ekākī hutvā carituṃ sakkuṇeyya. Khaggavisāṇakappoti tāya eva ekavihāritāya khaggamigasiṅgasamo.

‘Catuddiso’ means that the four directions are a place for pleasant dwelling for the sake of pleasant dwelling in the four directions; ‘cātuddiso’ is simply ‘catuddiso’. In these, one does not strike any being or formation out of fear, nor is one struck by them—thus ‘unobstructed’ (appaṭigho). ‘Santussamāno itarītarena’ means being content with any kind of requisite, whether high or low, one's own, peaceful, and being equally satisfied. ‘Paricca sayanti’ means that they overwhelm (parisayanti) the body and mind; these are ‘dangers’ (parissayā), such as lions, tigers, and so forth, and sensual desire and so forth. These dangers are endured with the patience of endurance and are overcome by means of removal and so forth. ‘Achambhī’ means fearless due to the absence of fear that causes rigidity. ‘Eko care’ means one should be able to wander alone, being solitary. ‘Khaggavisāṇakappo’ means like a rhinoceros horn, on account of that very solitary dwelling.

Asañjātavātābhighātehi [P 1.0332] siyā sakuṇo apakkhakoti “pakkhī sakuṇo”ti visesetvā vutto.

It is stated, specifying ‘pakkhī sakuṇo’ (a winged bird), because a bird might be without wings due to the non-arising of wind-blasts.

Nīvaraṇappahānakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Abandoning of the Hindrances

216. Vattabbataṃ āpajjatīti “asukassa bhikkhuno araññe tiracchānagatānaṃ viya, vanacarakānaṃ viya ca nivāsamattameva, na pana araññavāsānucchavikā [M 1.0256] kāci sammāpaṭipattī”ti apavādavasena vattabbataṃ, āraññakehi vā tiracchānagatehi, vanacaravisabhāgajanehi vā saddhiṃ vippaṭipattivasena vattabbataṃ āpajjati. Kāḷakasadisattā kāḷakaṃ, thullavajjaṃ. Tilakasadisattā tilakaṃ, aṇumattavajjaṃ.

216. ‘Vattabbataṃ āpajjati’ means ‘one becomes subject to being spoken against.’ This implies that ‘for such and such a monk, his dwelling in the wilderness is merely a dwelling place, like that of animals or forest dwellers; there is no proper practice befitting a wilderness dweller.’ Thus, one becomes subject to being spoken against by way of criticism, or by way of wrong practice in association with wilderness dwellers, animals, or people dissimilar to forest dwellers. ‘Kāḷakasadisattā’ means ‘like a black mark,’ a gross offense. ‘Tilakasadisattā’ means ‘like a sesame seed,’ a minor offense.

Vivittanti janavivittaṃ. Tenāha “suñña”nti. Taṃ pana janasaddaghosābhāveneva veditabbaṃ saddakaṇṭakattā jhānassāti āha “appasaddaṃ appanigghosanti attho”ti. Etadevāti nissaddataṃyeva. Vihāro pākāraparicchinno sakalo āvāso. Aḍḍhayogoti dīghapāsādo, “garuḷasaṇṭhānapāsādo”tipi vadanti. Pāsādoti caturassapāsādo. Hammiyaṃ muṇḍacchadanapāsādo[V 1.0227]. Aṭṭo paṭirājūnaṃ paṭibāhanayoggo catupañcabhūmako patissayaviseso. Māḷo ekakūṭasaṅgahito anekakoṇavanto patissayaviseso. Aparo nayo vihāro nāma dīghamukhapāsādo. Aḍḍhayogo ekapassacchadanakasenāsanaṃ. Tassa kira ekapasse bhitti uccatarā hoti, itarapasse nīcā, tena taṃ ekapassachadanakaṃ hoti. Pāsādo nāma āyatacaturassapāsādo. Hammiyaṃ muṇḍacchadanakaṃ candikaṅgaṇayuttaṃ. Guhā nāma kevalā pabbataguhā. Leṇaṃ dvārabaddhaṃ pabbhāraṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Maṇḍapoti sākhāmaṇḍapo.

‘Secluded’ (vivittaṃ) means secluded from people. Hence, it is called ‘empty’ (suññaṃ). This should be understood as the absence of the noise of people, because sound is a thorn to meditation. Therefore, it is said, ‘quiet, free from noise’—this is the meaning. Indeed, this very thing is stillness. A vihāra is an entire residence enclosed by walls. An aḍḍhayoga is a long mansion; some also call it a ‘garuḷa-shaped mansion.’ A pāsāda is a four-sided mansion. A hammiya is a mansion with a flat roof. An aṭṭa is a special kind of shelter with four or five stories, suitable for repelling enemy kings. A māḷa is a special kind of shelter with one peak and multiple corners. Another interpretation is that a vihāra is a long-faced mansion. An aḍḍhayoga is a dwelling with a roof on one side. It is said that on one side the wall is higher, while the other side is lower, thus it is a single-sided roofed structure. A pāsāda is a long, four-sided mansion. A hammiya is a flat-roofed structure with a moonlit courtyard. A guhā refers solely to a mountain cave. A leṇa is a rock shelter with a door. The rest is as previously described. A maṇḍapa is a pavilion made of branches.

Vihārasenāsananti patissayabhūtaṃ senāsanaṃ. Mañcapīṭhasenāsananti mañcapīṭhañceva mañcapīṭhasambandhasenāsanañca. Cimilikādi santharitabbato santhatasenāsanaṃ. Abhisaṅkharaṇābhāvato [P 1.0333] sayanassa nisajjāya ca kevalaṃ okāsabhūtaṃ senāsanaṃ. “Vivittaṃ senāsana”nti iminā senāsanaggahaṇena saṅgahitameva sāmaññajotanābhāvato.

A dwelling place (vihārasenāsanaṃ) means a lodging that serves as a shelter. A bed or seat lodging (mañcapīṭhasenāsanaṃ) means both the bed or seat itself and a lodging associated with a bed or seat. A spread lodging (santhatasenāsanaṃ) is a lodging that is to be spread with rugs and the like. A mere space lodging is a lodging that, due to the absence of preparation, serves only as a place for lying down or sitting. The term ‘secluded lodging’ (vivittaṃ senāsanaṃ) is already encompassed by this general use of the word ‘lodging’ (senāsanaṃ), as there is no indication of a general meaning.

Yadi evaṃ kasmā “arañña”ntiādi vuttanti āha “ima panā”tiādi. “Bhikkhunīnaṃ vasena āgata”nti idaṃ vinaye tathā āgatataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, abhidhammepi pana “araññanti nikkhamitvā bahi indakhīlā, sabbametaṃ arañña”nti (vibha. 529) āgatameva. Tattha hi yaṃ na gāmapadesantogadhaṃ, taṃ “arañña”nti nippariyāyavasena tathā vuttaṃ. Dhutaṅganiddese (visuddhi. 1.31) yaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ yuttaṃ,tasmā tattha vuttanayena gahetabbanti adhippāyo. Rukkhamūlanti rukkhasamīpaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ “yāvatā [M 1.0257] majjhanhike kāle samantā chāyā pharati, nivāte paṇṇāni nipatanti, ettāvatā rukkhamūla”nti. Sela-saddo avisesato pabbatapariyāyoti katvā vuttaṃ “pabbatanti sela”nti, na silāmayameva, paṃsumayādiko tividhopi pabbato evāti. Vivaranti dvinnaṃ pabbatānaṃ mitho āsannatare ṭhitānaṃ ovarakādisadisaṃ vivaraṃ, ekasmiṃyeva vā pabbate. Umaṅgasadisanti suduṅgāsadisaṃ. Manussānaṃ anupacāraṭṭhānanti pakatisañcāravasena manussehi na sañcaritabbaṭṭhānaṃ. Ādi-saddena “vanapatthanti [P 1.0334] vanasaṇṭhānametaṃ senāsanānaṃ adhivacanaṃ, vanapatthanti bhīsanakānametaṃ, vanapatthanti salomahaṃsānametaṃ, vanapatthanti pariyantānametaṃ, vanapatthanti na manussūpacārānametaṃ, vanapatthanti durabhisambhavānametaṃ senāsanānaṃ adhivacana”nti (vibha. 531) imaṃ pāḷisesaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Acchannanti kenaci chadanena antamaso rukkhasākhāyapi na chāditaṃ. Nikkaḍḍhitvāti nīharitvā. Pabbhāraleṇasadiseti pabbhārasadise leṇasadise ca.

If so, why is it said, ‘the wilderness’ (araññaṃ), etc.? It is said, ‘but this,’ etc. This phrase ‘it came to be by way of the bhikkhunīs’ (bhikkhunīnaṃ vasena āgataṃ) refers to its occurrence in the Vinaya in that manner. However, in the Abhidhamma too, it is stated: ‘The wilderness (araññaṃ) is going out beyond the city-post; all this is wilderness’ (Vibh. 529). There, whatever is not included within the village area is called ‘wilderness’ in an unqualified sense. What is said in the Dhutaṅganiddesa (Visuddhi. 1.31) is appropriate; therefore, the intention is that it should be understood according to the method stated there. The root of a tree (rukkhamūlaṃ) means near a tree. For it is said: ‘As far as the shadow spreads all around at midday, and as far as leaves fall in a windless place—that is the root of a tree.’ The word ‘sela,’ taking it as a general synonym for mountain, it is said, ‘mountain means sela,’ not just rocky, but also of earth and the like—mountains are of three types. A vivara is a space resembling a small chamber between two mountains situated very near each other, or within a single mountain. ‘Umaṅgasadisaṃ’ means resembling a tunnel. A place not frequented by people (manussānaṃ anupacāraṭṭhānaṃ) means a place that is not to be frequented by people through ordinary travel. The word ‘etc.’ (ādi-saddena) includes the remaining passage: ‘A forest thicket (vanapatthaṃ) is a term for these forest dwellings; a forest thicket is for the fearful; a forest thicket is for those with hair standing on end; a forest thicket is for those on the periphery; a forest thicket is a term for dwellings not frequented by people; a forest thicket is a term for dwellings hard to approach’ (Vibh. 531). Uncovered (acchannaṃ) means not covered by any covering whatsoever, not even by a tree branch. ‘Nikkaḍḍhitvā’ means having taken out. ‘Pabbhāraleṇasadise’ means resembling a cliff and resembling a cave.

Piṇḍapātapariyesanaṃ piṇḍapāto uttarapadalopenāti āha “piṇḍapātapariyesanato paṭikkanto”ti[V 1.0228]. Pallaṅkanti ettha parisaddo “samantato”ti etassa atthe, tasmā vāmoruñca dakkhiṇoruñca samaṃ ṭhapetvā ubho pāde aññamaññaṃ sambandhitvā nisajjā pallaṅkanti āha “samantato ūrubaddhāsana”nti. Ūrūnaṃ bandhanavasena nisajjā pallaṅkaṃ. Ābhujitvāti ca yathā pallaṅkavasena nisajjā hoti, evaṃ ubho pāde ābhugge bhañjite katvā, taṃ pana ubhinnaṃ pādānaṃ tathā sambandhatākaraṇanti āha “bandhitvā”ti.

The word ‘piṇḍapāto’ is used for ‘piṇḍapātapariyesanaṃ’ (seeking almsfood) through the elision of the final word; thus it is said, ‘returned from seeking almsfood’ (piṇḍapātapariyesanato paṭikkanto). Regarding ‘pallaṅkaṃ’ (cross-legged), here the prefix ‘pari-’ has the meaning of ‘all around.’ Therefore, the sitting posture with the left and right thighs placed evenly and both feet connected to each other is called ‘pallaṅka’; thus it is said, ‘a seat bound around the thighs.’ The sitting posture is called pallaṅka by way of the binding of the thighs. And ‘having bent’ (ābhujitvā) means having made both feet bent and folded so that the sitting is in the cross-legged manner. That action of connecting both feet in that way is why it is said ‘having bound’ (bandhitvā).

Heṭṭhimakāyassa ca anujukaṃ ṭhapanaṃ nisajjāvacaneneva bodhitanti “ujuṃ kāya”nti ettha kāya-saddo uparimakāyavisayoti āha “uparimaṃ sarīraṃ ujuṃ ṭhapetvā”ti. Taṃ pana ujukaṭhapanaṃ sarūpato, payojanato ca dassetuṃ “aṭṭhārasā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Na paṇamantīti na onamanti. Na paripatatīti na vigacchati vīthiṃ na laṅgheti. Tato eva pubbenāparaṃ visesappattiyā kammaṭṭhānaṃ vuḍḍhiṃ phātiṃ vepullaṃ upagacchati. Parimukhanti ettha parisaddo abhi-saddena samānatthoti [P 1.0335] āha “kammaṭṭhānābhimukha”nti, bahiddhā puthuttārammaṇato nivāretvā kammaṭṭhānaṃyeva purakkhatvāti attho. Samīpattho vā parisaddoti dassento “mukhasamīpe vā katvā”ti āha. Ettha ca yathā “vivittaṃ senāsanaṃ bhajatī”tiādinā [M 1.0258] bhāvanānurūpaṃ senāsanaṃ dassitaṃ, evaṃ “nisīdatī”ti iminā alīnānuddhaccapakkhiyo santo iriyāpatho dassito. “Pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā”ti iminā nisajjāya daḷhabhāvo, “parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā”ti iminā ārammaṇapariggahūpāyo. Parīti pariggahaṭṭho “pariṇāyikā”tiādīsu viya. Mukhanti niyyānaṭṭho “suññatavimokkhamukha”ntiādīsu viya. Paṭipakkhato niggamanaṭṭho hi niyyānaṭṭho, tasmā pariggahitaniyyānanti sabbathā gahitāsammosaṃ paricattasammosaṃ satiṃ katvā, paramaṃ satinepakkaṃ upaṭṭhapetvāti attho.

The placing straight of the lower body is indicated by the word for sitting; hence, in 'straighten the body' (ujuṃ kāyaṃ), the term 'body' refers to the upper body, as stated: 'having placed the upper body straight.' This placing straight, both in its form and purpose, is explained with the phrase 'eighteen,' etc. 'They do not bend' (na paṇamanti) means they do not stoop. 'It does not fall around' (na paripatatī) means it does not deviate, it does not transgress the path. From this very thing, through the attainment of distinction from one to the next, the meditation subject attains growth, increase, and abundance. In 'parimukhaṃ,' the prefix 'pari-' is synonymous with the particle 'abhi-,' as stated: 'facing the meditation subject.' It means having set aside external, diverse objects and having placed the meditation subject itself in front. Alternatively, to show that 'pari-' has the meaning of proximity, it is stated: 'or having placed it near the mouth.' Here, just as a suitable dwelling for meditation is described with phrases like 'he resorts to a secluded lodging' (vivittaṃ senāsanaṃ bhajati), so too a posture that is on the side of non-sluggishness and non-restlessness is indicated by 'sits.' 'Having folded the legs crosswise' (pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā) demonstrates firmness in sitting, while 'having established mindfulness in front' (parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā) shows the method of grasping the object. 'Pari-' conveys the sense of encompassing, as in terms like 'pariṇāyikā' (guide). 'Mukha' conveys the sense of outlet, as in phrases like 'the outlet to liberation through emptiness' (suññatavimokkhamukhaṃ). For the meaning of outlet is 'going forth from what is opposed.' Thus, it means having established mindfulness with its outlet grasped, having made it completely grasped and with confusion abandoned, having established supreme mindfulness and clear comprehension.

217. Abhijjhāyati gijjhati abhikaṅkhati etāyāti abhijjhā, lobho. Lujjanaṭṭhenāti bhijjanaṭṭhena, khaṇe khaṇe bhijjanaṭṭhenāti attho. Vikkhambhanavasenāti ettha vikkhambhanaṃ anuppādanaṃ appavattanaṃ, na paṭipakkhānaṃ suppahīnatā. “Pahīnattā”ti ca pahīnasadisataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ jhānassa anadhigatattā. Tathāpi nayidaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ viya sabhāvato vigatābhijjhaṃ, atha kho bhāvanāvasena, tenāha “na cakkhuviññāṇasadisenā”ti. Eseva nayoti yathā imassa cittassa bhāvanāya paribhāvitattā vigatābhijjhatā, evaṃ abyāpannaṃ vigatathinamiddhaṃ anuddhataṃ nibbicikicchañcāti attho. Purimapakatinti parisuddhapaṇḍarasabhāvaṃ. “Yā [P 1.0336] cittassa akalyatāti”ādinā (dha. sa. 1162; vibha. 546) thinassa, “yā kāyassa akalyatā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1163; vibha. 546) ca middhassa abhidhamme niddiṭṭhattā [V 1.0229] vuttaṃ “thinaṃ cittagelaññaṃ, middhaṃ cetasikagelañña”nti. Satipi aññamaññaṃ avippayoge cittakāyalahutādīnaṃ viya cittacetasikānaṃ yathākammaṃ taṃ taṃ visesassa yā tesaṃ akalyatādīnaṃ visesappaccayatā, ayametesaṃ sabhāvoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ālokasaññīti ettha atisayatthavisiṭṭhaatthi atthāvabodhako ayamīkāroti dassento āha “rattimpi…pe… samannāgato”ti. Idaṃ ubhayanti satisampajaññamāha. Atikkamitvā vikkhambhanavasena pajahitvā. “Kathamida”nti pavattiyā kathaṅkathā, vicikicchā. Sā etassa atthīti kathaṅkathī, na kathaṅkathīti akathaṃkathī, nibbicikiccho. Lakkhaṇādibhedatoti ettha ādi-saddena paccayapahānapahāyakādīnampi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tepi hi bhedato vattabbāti.

217. One covets, is greedy, longs for with this—this is covetousness (abhijjhā), which is greed (lobha). By the meaning of 'breaking' means by the meaning of breaking up, that is, breaking up moment by moment. By way of suppression (vikkhambhana)—here, suppression means non-arising, non-occurrence, but not the complete abandonment of opposing states. 'Because it is abandoned' is said in reference to a state similar to abandonment, as jhāna has not been attained. Nevertheless, this is not like eye-consciousness, which is naturally free from covetousness; rather, it is through the power of cultivation. Hence it is said, 'not like eye-consciousness.' This is the same method: just as this mind, through being cultivated by cultivation, becomes free from covetousness, so too it becomes free from ill will, free from sloth and torpor, not restless, and free from doubt. 'Former nature' refers to the state of being pure and bright. Because sloth is specified in the Abhidhamma by 'the unhealthiness of the mind,' etc. (Dhs. 1162; Vibh. 546), and torpor by 'the unhealthiness of the body,' etc. (Dhs. 1163; Vibh. 546), it is said: 'Sloth is the sickness of the mind, torpor is the sickness of mental factors.' Although they are mutually non-disassociated, just as with lightness of mind, lightness of body, and so on, it should be understood that for mind and mental factors, according to their respective functions, the specific conditionality for their unhealthiness and so on, for this or that distinction, is their nature. 'One perceiving light'—here, showing that the ī-kāra indicates the meaning of 'atthi' (there is) distinguished by an excellent meaning, it is said, 'at night… endowed with.' 'This both' refers to mindfulness and clear comprehension. 'Having overcome' means having abandoned by way of suppression. 'How is this?'—this in its occurrence is 'how-is-it-ness' (kathaṅkathā), which is doubt (vicikicchā). One who has this is doubtful (kathaṅkathī); one who does not have it is not doubtful (akathaṃkathī), free from doubt. 'By the distinction of characteristic, etc.'—here, by the word 'etc.' the inclusion of conditions, abandonment, the abandoner, and so on should also be understood. For these too should be spoken of in terms of their distinctions.

218. Tesanti [M 1.0259] iṇavasena gahitadhanānaṃ. Pariyantoti dātabbaseso. So balavapāmojjaṃ labhati “iṇapalibodhato muttomhī”ti. Somanassaṃ adhigacchati “jīvikānimittaṃ atthī”ti.

218. 'Of them' refers to those who have taken wealth by way of debt. 'The remainder' is the balance left to be paid. He gains strong joy, thinking, 'I am freed from the encumbrance of debt.' He attains gladness, thinking, 'There is a basis for my livelihood.'

219. Visabhāgavedanuppattiyāti dukkhavedanuppattiyā. Dukkhavedanā hi sukhavedanāya kusalavipākasantānassa virodhitāya visabhāgā. Catuiriyāpathaṃ chindantoti [P 1.0337] catubbidhampi iriyāpathappavattiṃ pacchindanto. Byādhiko hi yathā ṭhānagamanesu asamattho, evaṃ nisajjādīsupi asamattho hoti. Ābādhetīti pīḷeti. Vātādīnaṃ vikāro visamāvatthā byādhīti āha “taṃsamuṭṭhānena dukkhena dukkhito”ti. Dukkhavedanāya pana byādhibhāve mūlabyādhinā ābādhiko ādito bādhatīti katvā. Anubandhabyādhinā dukkhito aparāparaṃ sañjātadukkhoti katvā. Gilānoti dhātusaṅkhayena parikkhīṇasarīro. Appamattakaṃ vā balaṃ balamattā. Tadubhayanti pāmojjaṃ, somanassañca. Tattha labhetha pāmojjaṃ “rogato muttomhī”ti. Adhigaccheyya somanassaṃ “atthi me kāye bala”nti.

219. 'The arising of a dissimilar feeling' means the arising of a painful feeling. For painful feeling is dissimilar to pleasant feeling because it opposes the continuity of wholesome-resultant consciousness. 'Cutting off the four postures' means obstructing the occurrence of all four kinds of postures. For a sick person is unable to maintain standing or walking, just as they are unable to maintain sitting or other postures. 'Afflicts' means oppresses. The disorder of the humors (wind, etc.), an unbalanced state, is illness; hence it is said: 'afflicted by the suffering arising from that.' Regarding the painful feeling as the state of being ill, it is because the one who is ill is afflicted from the beginning by the root illness, and because one is afflicted by the subsequent illness, with suffering arising again and again. 'Sick' refers to one whose body is wasted away by the exhaustion of the elements, or who has little strength, a mere measure of strength. 'That both' refers to joy and gladness. There, one might gain joy thinking, 'I am freed from illness,' and attain gladness thinking, 'There is strength in my body.'

220. Sesanti “tassa hi ‘bandhanā muttomhī’ti āvajjayato tadubhayaṃ hoti. Tena vutta”nti evamādi. Vuttanayenevāti paṭhamadutiyapadesu vuttanayeneva. Sabbapadesūti avasiṭṭhapadesu tatiyādīsu koṭṭhāsesu.

220. 'The rest' means: 'For when one reflects, “I am freed from bondage,” both occur. Thus it is said,' and so on. 'In the same way as explained' refers to the method explained in the first and second sections. 'In all sections' refers to the remaining sections, the third and subsequent parts.

221-222. Na attani adhīnoti na attāyatto. Parādhīnoti parāyatto. Aparādhīnatāya bhujo viya attano kicce esitabboti bhujisso. Savasoti āha “attano santako”ti. Anudakatāya kaṃ pānīyaṃ tārenti etthāti kantāroti āha “nirudakaṃ dīghamagga”nti.

221-222. 'Not dependent on oneself' means not self-controlled. 'Dependent on others' means controlled by others. Because, not being dependent on others, one should seek one's own affairs like a free man, one is called a 'bhujisso' (a free man). 'One's own,' he said, means 'belonging to oneself.' Because of the lack of water, they cross this place with drinking water; therefore, it is called a 'wilderness,' as in 'a long road without water.'

223. Tatrāti [V 1.0230] tasmiṃ dassane. Ayanti idāni vuccamānā sadisatā. Yena iṇādīnaṃ upamābhāvo, kāmacchandādīnañca upameyyabhāvo hoti, so nesaṃ upamopameyyasambandho [P 1.0338] sadisatāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yo yamhi kāmacchandena rajjatīti yo puggalo yamhi kāmarāgassa vatthubhūte puggale kāmacchandavasena ratto hoti. Taṃ vatthuṃ gaṇhātīti taṃ taṇhāvatthuṃ “mameta”nti gaṇhāti.

223. 'There' means in that vision. 'This' refers to the similarity now being explained. It should be understood that the similarity is their relationship as simile and object of comparison, whereby debt and so on are the similes, and sensual desire and so on are the objects of comparison. 'Whoever is attached by sensual desire' means the person who, through sensual desire, is attached to an object that is the basis for sensual lust. 'Seizes that object' means grasping that object of craving, thinking, 'This is mine.'

Upaddavethāti [M 1.0260] upaddavaṃ karotha.

'You should harass' means you should create a disturbance.

Nakkhattassāti mahassa. Muttoti bandhanato mutto.

'Of the festival' means of the great one. 'Freed' means freed from bondage.

Vinaye apakataññunāti vinayakkame akusalena. So hi kappiyākappiyaṃ yāthāvato na jānāti. Tenāha “kismiñcidevā”tiādi.

'Unskilled in the discipline' means being unskilled in the procedure of the discipline. For he does not truly know what is allowable and what is unallowable. Therefore, it is said, 'in any way whatsoever,' etc.

Gacchatipīti thokaṃ thokaṃ gacchatipi. Gacchanto pana tāya eva ussaṅkitaparisaṅkitatāya tattha tattha tiṭṭhatipi. Īdise kantāre gato “ko jānāti kiṃ bhavissatī”ti nivattatipi, tasmā gataṭṭhānato agataṭṭhānameva bahutaraṃ hoti. Saddhāya gaṇhituṃ saddheyyaṃ vatthuṃ “idameva”nti saddahituṃ na sakkoti. Atthi natthīti “atthi nu kho, natthi nu kho”ti. Araññaṃ paviṭṭhassa ādimhi eva sappanaṃ āsappanaṃ. Pari parito, uparūpari vā sappanaṃ parisappanaṃ. Ubhayenapi tattheva paribbhamanaṃ vadati. Tenāha “apariyogāhana”nti. Chambhitattanti araññasaññāya uppannaṃ chambhitabhāvaṃ, utrāsanti attho.

He goes, that is, he goes little by little. While going, due to that very apprehension and suspicion, he stops here and there. Having gone into such a wilderness, he thinks, 'Who knows what will happen?' and turns back. Thus, the distance untraveled is far greater than the distance traveled. Unable to grasp with faith a credible object, he cannot truly believe, thinking, 'This is it.' 'Is there or is there not?' means 'Is there perhaps? Is there not perhaps?' For one who has entered the forest, at the very beginning there is creeping and struggling. 'Creeping about' is creeping all around, or over and over. By both these terms, it speaks of wandering about right there. Hence it is said, 'not plunging in.' The state of being terrified is the state of terror arising from the perception of the forest; the meaning is fright.

224. Tatrāyaṃ sadisatāti etthāpi vuttanayānusārena sadisatā veditabbā. Yadaggena hi kāmacchandādayo iṇādisadisā, tadaggena tesaṃ pahānaṃ āṇaṇyādisadisaṃ abhāvoti katvā. Cha dhammeti asubhanimittassa uggaho, asubhabhāvanānuyogo, indriyesu guttadvāratā, bhojane mattaññutā, kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyakathāti ime cha dhamme. Bhāvetvāti brūhetvā. Mahāsatipaṭṭhāne (dī. ni. 2.372-374) vaṇṇayissāma tatthassa anuppannānuppādanauppannapahānādivibhāvanavasena savisesaṃ pāḷiyā āgatattā. Esa nayo [P 1.0339] byāpādādippahānakabhāvepi. Paravatthumhīti ārammaṇabhūte parasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ.

224. Here, the term 'similarity' should be understood in the same way as previously explained. For just as sensual desire and other defilements are like debts, their abandonment is like being free from debt, on account of their non-existence. The six qualities are: grasping the sign of the unattractive, applying oneself to the development of unattractiveness, guarding the sense doors, moderation in eating, good friendship, and suitable talk. 'Having developed' means having cultivated. We will elaborate on this in the Great Frames of Reference (Dīgha Nikāya 2.372–374) there, since in that place it comes in detail in the Pali, with the distinction of the non-arising of the unarisen, the abandoning of the arisen, and so on. This same method applies to the case of the abandonment of ill will and the like. 'In another's object' means in another object that is the object of perception.

Anatthakaroti attano parassa ca anatthāvaho. Cha dhammeti mettānimittassa uggaho, mettābhāvanānuyogo[V 1.0231], kammassakatā, paṭisaṅkhānabahulatā, kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyakathāti ime cha dhamme. Tatthevāti mahāsatipaṭṭhāneyeva (dī. ni. 2.372-374). Cārittasīlaṃ uddissa paññattasikkhāpadaṃ ācārapaṇṇatti.

‘Causing harm’ means bringing harm to oneself and others. These six qualities are: taking up the sign of loving-kindness, dedication to the development of loving-kindness, ownership of actions, frequent reflection, good friendship, and suitable talk. Just there, namely, in the Great Frames of Reference (Dī. Ni. 2.372-374). A training rule enacted with regard to morality of practice is a code of conduct.

Bandhanāgāraṃ [M 1.0261] pavesitattā aladdhanakkhattānubhavo puriso “nakkhattadivase bandhanāgāraṃ pavesito puriso”ti vutto, nakkhattadivase eva vā tadananubhavanatthaṃ tathā kato. Mahāanatthakaranti diṭṭhadhammikādiatthahāpanamukhena mahato anatthassa kārakaṃ. Cha dhammeti atibhojane nanimittaggāho, iriyāpathasamparivattanatā, ālokasaññāmanasikāro, abbhokāsavāso, kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyakathāti ime cha dhamme.

Because he was imprisoned and unable to experience the festival, the man was called 'the one imprisoned on a festival day,' or alternatively, he was treated in that way on the festival day precisely to prevent him from experiencing it. 'The great harm-doer' means causing great harm by way of losing benefits related to the present life and so on. The six qualities are: not grasping the sign in overeating, changing postures, attention to the perception of light, dwelling in the open air, good friendship, and suitable talk.

Uddhaccakukkucce mahāanatthakaranti parāyattatāpādanato vuttanayena mahato anatthassa kārakanti. Attho cha dhammeti bahussutatā, paripucchakatā, vinaye pakataññutā, vuḍḍhasevitā, kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyakathāti ime cha dhamme.

Restlessness and remorse cause great harm, as they lead to dependence, thus being the cause of great misfortune as previously stated. The meaning is these six qualities: extensive learning, inquiry, expertise in the Vinaya, associating with elders, good friendship, and suitable talk.

Balavāti paccatthikavidhamanasamatthena balena balavā. Sajjāvudhoti sannaddhadhanuādiāvudho. Sūravīrasevakajanavasena saparivāro. Tanti yathāvuttaṃ purisaṃ. Balavantatāya, sajjāvudhatāya, saparivāratāya ca corā dūratova disvā palāyeyyuṃ. Anatthakārikāti sammāpaṭipattiyā vibandhakaraṇato vuttanayena anatthakārikā. Cha dhammeti bahussutatā, paripucchakatā, vinaye pakataññutā, adhimokkhabahulatā, kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyakathāti [P 1.0340] ime cha dhamme. Yathā bāhusaccādīni uddhaccakukkuccassa pahānāya saṃvattanti, evaṃ vicikicchāya pīti idhāpi bahussutatādayo gahitā. Kalyāṇamittatā sappāyakathā viya pañcannaṃ, tasmā tassa tassa anucchavikasevanatā veditabbā. Sammāpaṭipattiyā appaṭipattinimittatāmukhena vicikicchā micchāpaṭipattimeva paribrūhetīti tassā pahānaṃ duccaritavidhūnanūpāyoti āha “duccaritakantāraṃ nittharitvā”tiādi.

“Strong” (balavā) means strong with strength capable of overcoming enemies. “Armed” (sajjāvudho) means equipped with bows and other weapons. “With a retinue” (saparivāro) means accompanied by a retinue of brave and heroic men. Such a man, as described, due to his strength, being armed, and having a retinue, would make thieves flee at the mere sight of him from afar. “Harmful” (anatthakārikā) means harmful in the way explained, because it creates obstacles to right practice. “The six qualities” (cha dhamme) are these six qualities: being well-learned, being inquisitive, proficiency in the Vinaya, frequent resoluteness, good friendship, and suitable conversation. Just as extensive learning and other qualities lead to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse, so too, in the case of doubt, extensive learning and the rest are taken. Good friendship and suitable conversation are common to the remedies for the five hindrances; therefore, for each respective hindrance, the cultivation appropriate to it should be understood. Doubt, through the aspect of being the cause of non-practice of right practice, only strengthens wrong practice itself. Therefore, its abandonment is the means to dispel misconduct, as stated: “Having crossed the wilderness of misconduct,” and so on.

225. Pāmojjaṃ nāma taruṇapīti, sā kathañcipi tuṭṭhāvatthāti āha “pāmojjaṃ jāyatīti tuṭṭhākāro jāyatī”ti. Tuṭṭhassāti okkantikabhāvappattāya pītiyā vasena tuṭṭhassa. Attano savipphārikatāya, attasamuṭṭhānapaṇītarūpuppattiyā ca sakalasarīraṃ khobhayamānā pharaṇalakkhaṇā pīti jāyati. Pītisahitaṃ pīti uttarapadalopena, kiṃ pana taṃ[M 1.0262]? Mano. Pīti mano etassāti pītimano, tassa pītimanassa. Tayidaṃ atthamattameva dassento “pītisampayuttacittassā”ti [V 1.0232] āha. Kāyoti idha arūpakalāpo adhippeto, na vedanādikkhandhattayamevāti āha “nāmakāyo passambhatī”ti, passaddhidvayassa pītivasenettha passambhanaṃ adhippetaṃ. Vigatadarathoti pahīnauddhaccādikilesadaratho. Vuttappakārāya pubbabhāgabhāvanāya vasena cetasikasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedentoyeva taṃsamuṭṭhānapaṇītarūpaphuṭṭhasarīratāya kāyikampi sukhaṃ vedetīti āha “kāyikampi cetasikampi sukhaṃ vedayatī”ti. Imināti “sukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedetī”ti evaṃ vuttena. Saṃkilesapakkhato nikkhantattā, paṭhamajjhānapakkhikattā ca nekkhammasukhena. Sukhitassāti sukhino.

225. “Joy” (pāmojjaṃ) is initial delight; it is a state of satisfaction in any way, thus it is said: “Joy arises” means “a state of satisfaction arises.” “Of one who is satisfied” (tuṭṭhassa) means of one who is satisfied by way of joy having attained the state of pervading. Joy arises with the characteristic of pervasion, shaking the entire body due to its self-radiating nature and the production of refined material form originating from itself. “With joy” (pītisahitaṃ) is by way of the elision of the subsequent word. What is that? Mind. “Joyful mind” (pītimano) means “joy is his mind”; “of the joyful mind” (tassa pītimanassa) means of that joyful mind. To indicate only this meaning, it is said: “of a mind associated with joy.” “Body” (kāyo) here refers to the mental body, not merely the three aggregates of feeling and so on, thus it is said: “the mental body becomes tranquil.” Here, tranquility refers to the dual tranquility influenced by joy. “Free from distress” (vigatadaratho) means one has abandoned the distress of restlessness and other defilements. Through the preliminary practice described, experiencing mental happiness, and due to the body being pervaded by refined material form originating from it, one also experiences bodily happiness, thus it is said: “one experiences both bodily and mental happiness.” “By this” (iminā) means by what is thus stated: “one experiences happiness.” Because it has transcended the side of defilement and belongs to the side of the first jhāna, it is called “the happiness of renunciation.” “Of the happy one” (sukhitassa) means of one who is happy.

Paṭhamajjhānakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the First Jhāna

226. “Cittaṃ [P 1.0341] samādhiyatī”ti etena upacāravasenapi appanāvasenapi cittassa samādhānaṃ kathitaṃ. Evaṃ sante “so vivicceva kāmehī”tiādikā desanā kimatthiyāti āha “so vivicceva kāmehi…pe… vutta”nti. Tattha uparivisesadassanatthanti paṭhamajjhānādiuparivattabbavisesadassanatthaṃ. Na hi upacārasamādhisamadhigamena vinā paṭhamajjhānādiviseso samadhigantuṃ sakkā. Pāmojjuppādādīhi kāraṇaparamparā dutiyajjhānādisamadhigamepi icchitabbāva paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi viya dutiyamaggādisamadhigameti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tassa samādhinoti “sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyatī”ti evaṃ sādhāraṇavasena vutto yo appanālakkhaṇo, tassa samādhino. Pabhedadassanatthanti dutiyajjhānādivibhāgassa ceva abhiññādivibhāgassa ca pabhedadassanatthaṃ. Karo vuccati pupphasambhavaṃ gabbhāsaye karīyatīti katvā, karato jāto kāyo karajakāyo, tadupasanissayo catusantatirūpasamudāyo. Kāmaṃ nāmakāyopi vivekajena pītisukhena tathāladdhupakāro, “abhisandetī”tiādivacanato pana rūpakāyo idhādhippetoti āha “imaṃ karajakāya”nti. Abhisandetīti abhisandanaṃ karoti. Taṃ pana jhānamayena pītisukhena karajakāyassa tintabhāvāpādanaṃ, sabbatthakameva lūkhabhāvāpanayananti āha “temetī”tiādi, tayidaṃ abhisandanaṃ atthato yathāvuttapītisukhasamuṭṭhānehi paṇītarūpehi kāyassa parippharaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Parisandetī”tiādīsupi eseva nayo. Sabbaṃ etassa atthīti sabbavā, tassa sabbāvato. Avayavāvayavisambandhe avayavini sāmivacananti [M 1.0263] avayavīvisayo sabba-saddo, tasmā vuttaṃ “sabbakoṭṭhāsavato”ti. Aphuṭaṃ [P 1.0342] nāma na hoti yattha yattha kammajarūpaṃ, tattha tattha cittajarūpassa abhibyāpanato. Tenāha “upādinnakasantatī”tiādi.

226. “The mind is concentrated”—by this, the concentration of the mind is stated both in terms of access and absorption. This being so, what is the purpose of the teaching beginning “He, secluded from sensual pleasures…”? It is said: “He, secluded from sensual pleasures… is spoken of.” There, it is for the purpose of showing the higher distinctions—namely, the distinctions to be stated above, such as the first jhāna and beyond. For without attaining access concentration, one cannot attain the distinctions of the first jhāna and so on. The sequence of causes beginning with the arising of joy should be desired even for the attainment of the second jhāna and so on, just as the purification of knowledge and vision of the path should be understood for the attainment of the second path and so on. “His concentration”—this refers to that concentration characterized by absorption, which is stated in a general way as, “The mind of the happy one is concentrated.” For the purpose of showing distinctions—this means for showing the divisions of the second jhāna and so on, and also the divisions of higher knowledge and so on. “Kara” is so called because it is made in the womb, being born of the flower (of karma). The body born from the maker is the “karaja-body,” which is supported by the aggregate of material form of the four continuities. Although the mental body is also benefited by the joy and happiness born of seclusion, yet from phrases like “it suffuses” and so on, the physical body is intended here, thus it is said: “this karaja-body.” “It suffuses” (abhisandeti) means it performs suffusion. This means making the karaja-body moist with jhāna-born joy and happiness, and removing coarseness everywhere, thus it is said: “it moistens” and so on. This suffusion should be understood in meaning as the pervasion of the body by refined material forms originating from the aforementioned joy and happiness. The same principle applies to “it pervades” and so on. “All of this is his” (sabbaṃ etassa atthīti) means he is “all-possessed” (sabbavā); “of him who is all-possessed” (tassa sabbāvato). In the relationship between parts and the whole, the word “sabba” (all) refers to the whole, thus it is said: “possessed of all parts.” “Unpervaded” (aphutaṃ) means there is no place where kamma-born material form exists that citta-born material form does not pervade. Therefore, it is said: “the continuity of what is clung to…” and so on.

227. Chekoti [V 1.0233] kusalo. Taṃ panassa kosallaṃ nhāniyacuṇṇānaṃ sannane piṇḍīkaraṇe ca samatthatāvasena veditabbanti āha “paṭibalo”tiādi. Kaṃsa-saddo “mahatiyā kaṃsapātiyā”tiādīsu suvaṇṇe āgato.

227. “Skilled” (cheko) means expert. That skill of his should be understood as his ability to prepare and form bathing powders into balls, thus it is said: “capable” and so on. The word “kaṃsa” appears in phrases like “with a large golden bowl” and so on, referring to gold.

“Kaṃso upahato yathā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 134) kittimalohe, katthaci paṇṇattimatte “upakaṃso nāma rājāpi mahākaṃsassa atrajo”tiādi, [jā. aṭṭha. 4.10 ghaṭapaṇḍitajātakavaṇṇanāyaṃ (atthato samānaṃ)] idha pana yattha katthaci loheti āha “yena kenaci lohena katabhājane”ti. Snehānugatāti udakasinehena anupavisanavasena gatā upagatā. Snehaparetāti udakasinehena parito gatā samantato phuṭṭhā, tato eva santarabāhirā phuṭṭhā sinehena, etena sabbaso udakena temitabhāvamāha. “Na ca paggharaṇī”ti etena tintassapi tassa ghanathaddhabhāvaṃ vadati. Tenāha “na ca binduṃ bindu”ntiādi.

In phrases like “Just as a beaten gong” and so on (Dhp. 134), “kaṃsa” refers to a manufactured metal (alloy). Sometimes it is merely a designation, as in “Upakaṃsa, a king, was the son of Mahākaṃsa,” and so on [Jātaka Aṭṭhakathā 4.10, in the commentary on the Ghaṭapaṇḍita Jātaka (similar in meaning)]. But here, it refers to any kind of metal, thus it is said “in a vessel made of any kind of metal.” “Accompanied by moisture” (snehānugatā) means having entered by way of penetrating with the moisture of water, having gone close. “Surrounded by moisture” (snehaparetā) means completely gone around by the moisture of water, pervaded all around, and thus pervaded internally and externally by moisture. By this, it states the state of being entirely moistened by water. “Nor does it drip” (na ca paggharaṇī) indicates that even though moist, it retains its dense, solid nature. Therefore, it is said: “not even drop by drop,” and so on.

Dutiyajjhānakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Second Jhāna

229. Tāhi tāhi udakasirāhi ubbhijjatīti ubbhidaṃ, ubbhidaṃ udakaṃ etassāti ubbhidodako. Ubbhinnaudakoti nadītīre khatakūpako viya ubbhijjanakaudako. Uggacchanakaudakoti dhārāvasena uṭṭhahanaudako. Kasmā panettha ubbhidodakova rahado gahito, na itaroti āha “heṭṭhā uggacchanaudakañhī”tiādi. Dhārānipātapubbuḷakehīti [P 1.0343] dhārānipātehi udakapubbuḷakehi ca, “pheṇapaṭalehi cā”ti vattabbaṃ. Sannisinnamevāti aparikkhobhatāya niccalameva, suppasannamevāti adhippāyo. Sesanti “abhisandetī”tiādikaṃ.

229. It is called “ubbhidaṃ” because it springs up (ubbhijjati) through those water veins. “Ubbhidodako” means ‘having springing water,’ as in ‘water springs up from it’ (ubbhidaṃ udakaṃ etassa). “Ubbhinnaudako” refers to water that springs up, like a well dug on a riverbank, having water that springs up. “Uggacchanakaudako” means water that rises in a stream. Why is only “ubbhidodako” taken here as a lake, and not the others? It is said, “because below it is rising water,” and so on. “By falling streams and bubbles” (dhārānipātapubbuḷakehi) means by falling streams and water bubbles; it should also be said, “and by layers of foam.” “Settled” (sannisinnameva) means perfectly still due to being undisturbed; the meaning is ‘very clear.’ The rest is “it suffuses,” and so on.

Tatiyajjhānakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Third Jhāna

231. Uppalānīti uppalagacchāni. Setarattanīlesūti uppalesu, setuppalarattuppalanīluppalesūti attho. Yaṃ kiñci uppalaṃ uppalameva sāmaññagahaṇato[M 1.0264]. Satapattanti ettha sata-saddo bahupariyāyo “satagghī”tiādīsu viya, tena anekasatapattassapi saṅgaho siddho hoti. Loke pana “rattaṃ padumaṃ, setaṃ puṇḍarīka”ntipi vuccati. Yāva aggā, yāva ca mūlā udakena abhisandanādisambhavadassanatthaṃ udakānuggataggahaṇaṃ. Idha uppalādīni viya karajakāyo, udakaṃ viya tatiyajjhānasukhaṃ.

231. “Uppalāni” means lotus clumps. “In the white, red, and blue” (setarattanīlesu) refers to lotuses, meaning white lotuses, red lotuses, and blue lotuses. Whatever lotus there is, it is simply called “uppala” due to the general term. In “satapatta” (hundred-petaled), the word “sata” (hundred) has many meanings, as in “satagghī” (worth a hundred) and similar terms. Thus, even lotuses with many hundreds of petals are included. In the world, however, it is also said, “the red is the paduma, the white is the puṇḍarīka.” The taking of [the lotus] as not having emerged from the water (udakānuggataggahaṇaṃ) is to show the possibility of pervasion by water from the tip to the root. Here, the karaja-body is like the lotuses, and the bliss of the third jhāna is like the water.

Catutthajjhānakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Fourth Jhāna

233. Yasmā [V 1.0234] “parisuddhena cetasā”ti catutthajjhānacittamāha, tañca rāgādiupakkilesāpagamanato nirupakkilesaṃ nimmalaṃ, tasmā āha “nirupakkilesaṭṭhena parisuddha”nti. Yasmā pana pārisuddhiyā eva paccayavisesena pavattiviseso pariyodātatā suvaṇṇassa nighaṃsanena pabhassaratā viya, tasmā āha “pabhassaraṭṭhena pariyodātanti veditabba”nti. Idanti odātavacanaṃ. Utupharaṇatthanti uṇhautuno pharaṇadassanatthaṃ. Utupharaṇaṃ na hoti savisesanti adhippāyo, tenāha “taṅkhaṇa…pe… balavaṃ hotī”ti. Vatthaṃ viya karajakāyoti yogino karajakāyo vatthaṃ viya daṭṭhabbo utupharaṇasadisena catutthajjhānasukhena pharitabbattā. Purisassa sarīraṃ viya catutthajjhānaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ utupharaṇaṭṭhāniyassa sukhassa nissayabhāvato, tenāha “tasmā”tiādi. Ettha ca “parisuddhena cetasā”ti ceto gahaṇena jhānasukhaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ, tenāha “utupharaṇaṃ viya catutthajjhānasukha”nti. Nanu ca catutthajjhāne sukhameva natthīti? Saccaṃ natthi sātalakkhaṇasantasabhāvattā panettha [P 1.0344] upekkhā “sukha”nti adhippetā. Tena vuttaṃ sammohavinodaniyaṃ “upekkhā pana santattā, sukhamicceva bhāsitā”ti. (Vibha. aṭṭha. 232; visuddhi. 2.644; paṭi. ma. 105, mahāni. aṭṭha. 27)

233. Because “with a purified mind” refers to the fourth jhāna consciousness, and since that consciousness is free from defilements like lust, being stainless and undefiled due to the removal of defilements, therefore it is said, “purified in the sense of being undefiled.” Moreover, because the distinctiveness of its occurrence, namely thorough purity, arises from the special condition of purity—like the radiance of gold when polished—therefore it is said, “it should be understood as thoroughly purified in the sense of being radiant.” This is the meaning of “white” (odāta). “For the purpose of temperature diffusion” (utupharaṇatthaṃ) means for showing the diffusion of heat. The intention is that the diffusion of temperature is not specific, hence it is said, “At that moment… it becomes strong.” The karaja-body is like a cloth: the yogi’s karaja-body should be regarded as like a cloth, because it is to be pervaded by the bliss of the fourth jhāna, which is similar to the diffusion of temperature. The fourth jhāna should be regarded as like a man’s body, as it serves as the basis for the bliss that occupies the place of temperature diffusion. Hence it is said, “therefore,” and so on. Here, by the taking of “mind” in “with a purified mind,” it should be understood that the bliss of jhāna is spoken of. Therefore it is said, “the bliss of the fourth jhāna is like the diffusion of temperature.” But is it not so that in the fourth jhāna there is no bliss? Indeed, there is no [feeling] with the characteristic of pleasure; however, because of its peaceful nature, equanimity is here intended as “bliss.” Thus it is stated in the Sammohavinodanī: “Equanimity, being peaceful, is spoken of precisely as bliss.” (Vibh-a. 232; Vism. 2.644; Paṭis-m. 105, Mahā-nidd-a. 27)

Na arūpajjhānalābhīti na veditabbo avinābhāvato, tenāha “na hī”tiādi. Tattha cuddasahākārehīti kasiṇānulomato, kasiṇapaṭilomato, kasiṇānulomapaṭilomato, jhānānulomato, jhānapaṭilomato, jhānānulomapaṭilomato, jhānukkantikato, kasiṇukkantikato, jhānakasiṇukkantikato, aṅgasaṅkantito, ārammaṇasaṅkantito, aṅgārammaṇasaṅkantito, aṅgavavatthānato[M 1.0265], ārammaṇavavatthānatoti imehi cuddasahākārehi. Satipi jhānesu āvajjanādivasībhāve ayaṃ vasībhāvo abhiññānibbattane ekantena icchitabboti dassento āha “na hi…pe… hotī”ti. Svāyaṃ nayo arūpasamāpattīhi vinā na ijjhatīti tāyapettha avinābhāvo veditabbo. Yadi evaṃ kasmā pāḷiyaṃ na āruppajjhānāni āgatānīti? Visesato ca rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānapādakattā sabbābhiññānaṃ tadantogadhā katvā tāya desitā, na arūpāvacarajjhānānaṃ idha anupayogato, tenāha “arūpajjhānāni āharitvā kathetabbānī”ti.

It should not be understood that one is not an attainer of the formless jhānas, because of their inseparability; hence it is said, 'For indeed...' and so on. Here, 'by fourteen modes' refers to these fourteen modes: in the forward order with the kasiṇas, in the reverse order with the kasiṇas, in the forward and reverse order with the kasiṇas, in the forward order with the jhānas, in the reverse order with the jhānas, in the forward and reverse order with the jhānas, by skipping jhānas, by skipping kasiṇas, by skipping both jhānas and kasiṇas, by shifting the factors, by shifting the objects, by shifting both factors and objects, by determining the factors, and by determining the objects. Even when there is mastery in the jhānas regarding adverting and so forth, to show that this mastery is absolutely desirable for producing the higher knowledges, it is said, 'For indeed... it is.' This method does not succeed without the formless attainments; thus their inseparability should be understood here. If so, why have the formless jhānas not come up in the Pāli text? Because all the higher knowledges are specifically based on the fourth jhāna of the form realm, they are taught as being included within that; it is not because the formless-realm jhānas are inapplicable here. Therefore, it is said, 'The formless jhānas should be brought up and discussed.'

Vipassanāñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Insight Knowledge

234. Sesanti [V 1.0235] “evaṃ samāhite citte”tiādīsu vattabbaṃ. Ñeyyaṃ jānātīti ñāṇaṃ, taṃ pana ñeyyaṃ paccakkhaṃ katvā passatīti dassanaṃ, ñāṇameva dassananti ñāṇadassanaṃ. Tayidaṃ ñāṇadassanapadaṃ sāsane aññattha ñāṇavisese nirūḷhaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ atthuddhāravasena dassento “ñāṇadassananti maggañāṇampi vuccatī”tiādimāha. Yasmā vipassanāñāṇaṃ tebhūmakasaṅkhāre aniccādito jānāti, bhaṅgānupassanato paṭṭhāya paccakkhato ca te passati tasmā āha “idha pana…pe… ñāṇadassananti vutta”nti.

234. The remaining points are to be stated in passages such as 'with a mind thus concentrated.' It knows what should be known, thus it is knowledge (ñāṇa). That knowledge, having made the knowable directly evident, sees it—thus it is vision (dassana). Knowledge itself is vision—thus it is knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana). This term 'knowledge and vision' is established elsewhere in the Teaching with reference to specific kinds of knowledge. Showing all this by way of extracting the meaning, he says, '“Knowledge and vision” is also said to be path knowledge,' and so on. Because insight knowledge knows the formations of the three planes as impermanent, etc., and from the contemplation of dissolution onward, it also sees them directly, therefore he says, 'But here... “knowledge and vision” is said.'

Abhinīharatīti [P 1.0345] vuttanayena aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgate tasmiṃ citte vipassanākkamena jāte vipassanābhimukhaṃ peseti, tenāha “vipassanā…pe… karotī”ti. Tadabhimukhabhāvo eva hissa tanninnatādikaratā. Vuttoyeva brahmajāle. Odanakummāsehi upacīyatīti odanakummāsūpacayo. Aniccadhammoti pabhaṅgutāya addhuvasabhāvo. Duggandhavighātatthāyāti sarīre duggandhassa vigamāya. Ucchādanadhammoti ucchādetabbatāsabhāvo. Ucchādanena hi sarīre sedagūthapittasemhādidhātukkhobhagarubhāvaduggandhānaṃ apagamo hoti. Mahāsambāhanaṃ mallādīnaṃ bāhuvaḍḍhanādiatthaṃ hotīti “khuddakasambāhanenā”ti vuttaṃ. Parimaddanadhammoti parimadditabbatāsabhāvo. Bhijjati ceva vikirati cāti aniccatāvasena bhijjati ca bhinnañca kiñci payojanaṃ asādhentaṃ vippakiṇṇañca hoti. Rūpīti attano paccayabhūtena utuāhāralakkhaṇena rūpavāti ayamettha attho icchitoti āha “chahi padehi samudayo kathito”ti. Saṃsagge hi ayamīkāro. Saṇṭhānasampādanampi tathārūparūpuppādaneneva hotīti ucchādanaparimaddanapadehipi [M 1.0266] samudayo kathitoti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ navahi yathārahaṃ kāye samudayavayadhammānupassitā dassitā. Nissitañca chaṭṭhavatthunissitattā vipassanāñāṇassa. Paṭibaddhañca tena vinā appavattanato, kāyasaññitānaṃ rūpadhammānaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇato ca.

'He directs it' means that, in the manner stated, when it has arisen in the sequence of insight in that mind endowed with the eight factors, he directs it toward insight. Hence it is said, 'He practices insight...'. That state of being turned towards it is itself what makes it tend towards that. This is as stated in the Brahmajāla Sutta. 'Accumulation of rice and gruel' means the accumulation by means of rice and gruel. 'Having an impermanent nature' means having an unstable essence due to its destructibility. 'For the purpose of eliminating foul odors' means for the removal of foul odors from the body. 'Having the nature of being anointed' means having the nature of being fit for anointing. For, through anointing, the removal of bodily disturbances—such as sweat, excrement, bile, and phlegm—along with heaviness and foul odors, occurs. A great massage is for the purpose of increasing the arms, etc., of wrestlers and so on; therefore, 'by a small massage' is said. 'Having the nature of being massaged' means having the nature of being fit for massaging. 'It breaks and scatters'—due to impermanence, it breaks, and, being broken, it becomes scattered, not accomplishing any purpose. 'Having form' means possessing form characterized by its conditioning causes, temperature and nutriment. This is the intended meaning here, thus he says, 'The arising is explained by six terms'. For, this 'ī' vowel is in the sense of connection. The accomplishment of shape also occurs merely through the production of such-and-such form; thus, it is said that arising is explained even by the terms 'anointing' and 'massaging.' In this way, the contemplation of the phenomena of arising and passing away in the body is shown appropriately by nine terms. 'Dependent' because insight knowledge is dependent on the sixth base. 'Connected' because it does not proceed without that, and because it takes as its object the material phenomena designated as 'body'.

235. Suṭṭhu bhāti obhāsatīti subho, pabhāsampattiyāpi maṇino bhaddatāti āha “subhoti sundaro”ti. Kuruvindajāti ādijātivisesopi maṇino ākaraparisuddhimūlako evāti āha “parisuddhākarasamuṭṭhito”ti dosanīharaṇavasena parikammanipphattīti āha “suṭṭhu kataparikammo apanītapāsāṇasakkharo”ti. Chaviyā saṇhabhāvenassa acchatā, na saṅghātassāti āha “acchoti tanucchavī”ti, tenāha [P 1.0346] “vippasanno”ti. Dhovanavedhanādīhīti catūsu pāsāṇesu dhovanena ceva kāḷakādiapaharaṇatthāya suttena āvunanatthāya ca vijjhanena. Tāpasaṇhakaraṇādīnaṃ [V 1.0236] saṅgaho ādi-saddena. Vaṇṇasampattinti suttassa vaṇṇasampattiṃ. Maṇi viya karajakāyo paccavekkhitabbato. Āvutasuttaṃ viya vipassanāñāṇaṃ anupavisitvā ṭhitattā. Cakkhumā puriso viya vipassanālābhī bhikkhu sammadeva dassanato. Tadārammaṇānanti rūpadhammārammaṇānaṃ. Phassapañcamakacittacetasikaggahaṇena gahitadhammāpi vipassanācittuppādapariyāpannā evāti veditabbaṃ. Evañhi tesaṃ vipassanāñāṇagatikattā “āvutasuttaṃ viya vipassanāñāṇa”nti vacanaṃ avirodhitaṃ hoti. Kiṃ panete ñāṇassa āvi bhavanti, udāhu puggalassāti? Ñāṇassa. Tassa pana āvibhāvattā puggalassa āvibhūtā nāma honti. Ñāṇassāti ca paccavekkhaṇāñāṇassa.

235. 'It shines well, it radiates,' thus it is `subho` (bright); because of the gem's excellence through the attainment of radiance, he says, '`subho` means beautiful.' Even a specific type of gem, such as the Kuruvinda variety, has the purity of its mine as its root; hence, he says, 'arisen from a purified mine.' Because of the accomplishment of the preparatory work by way of removing faults, he says, 'thoroughly worked, with stones and gravel removed.' Its transparency is due to the fineness of its surface, not of its mass; therefore he says, '`accho` means having a fine surface.' For that reason, he says, 'perfectly clear.' 'By washing, piercing, and so forth' means: on the four sides, by washing to remove black spots and the like, and by piercing for the purpose of threading with a string. The inclusion of heating, polishing, and so on is by the word 'etc.' 'The excellence of color' means the excellence of the string's color. The perishable body is to be reviewed like a gem. Insight knowledge is like a threaded string because it has penetrated and remains. The bhikkhu who has attained insight is like a man with good sight because he sees correctly. 'Of those with that as object' means of those with material phenomena as object. It should be understood that even the states grasped by the inclusion of consciousness and mental factors, with contact as the fifth, are comprised within the arising of insight consciousness. For in this way, because they fall within the scope of insight knowledge, the statement 'insight knowledge is like a threaded string' is not contradicted. But do these phenomena become manifest to the knowledge, or to the person? To the knowledge. But because they become manifest to it, they are said to be manifest to the person. And 'to the knowledge' means to the knowledge of reviewing.

Maggañāṇassa anantaraṃ, tasmā lokiyābhiññānaṃ parato chaṭṭhābhiññāya purato vattabbaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ. Evaṃ santepīti yadipāyaṃ ñāṇānupubbī, evaṃ santepi. Etassa antarāvāro natthīti pañcasu lokiyābhiññāsu kathitāsu ākaṅkheyyasuttādīsu (ma. ni. 1.65) viya chaṭṭhābhiññā kathetabbāti etassa anabhiññālakkhaṇassa vipassanāñāṇassa tāsaṃ antarāvāro na hoti. Tasmā tattha avasarābhāvato idheva rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānānantarameva [M 1.0267] dassitaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ. Yasmā cāti ca-saddo samuccayattho, tena na kevalaṃ tadeva, atha kho idampi kāraṇaṃ vipassanāñāṇassa idheva dassaneti imamatthaṃ dīpeti. Dibbena cakkhunā bheravampi rūpaṃ passatoti ettha “iddhividhañāṇena bheravaṃ rūpaṃ nimminitvā cakkhunā passato”tipi vattabbaṃ, evampi abhiññālābhino apariññātavatthukassa bhayaṃ santāso uppajjati. Uccāvālikavāsi mahānāgattherassa viya. Pāṭiyekkaṃ sandiṭṭhikaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā –

Insight knowledge should be stated immediately preceding path knowledge, and therefore after the mundane higher knowledges and before the sixth higher knowledge. 'Even so' means: even if this is the sequence of knowledges, even so. 'There is no interval for this' means: when the five mundane higher knowledges have been discussed, the sixth higher knowledge is to be discussed, as in the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta and other texts; for this insight knowledge, which does not have the characteristic of a higher knowledge, there is no place in between them. Therefore, since there is no opportunity there, insight knowledge is shown here, immediately after the fourth jhāna of the form realm. 'And because'—the word 'ca' (and) has a conjunctive meaning, by which he indicates this meaning: not only that reason, but this too is a reason for showing insight knowledge here. Regarding 'With the divine eye, one sees even terrifying forms,' here it should also be said: 'having created a terrifying form through the knowledge of psychic power and seeing it with the eye.' Even so, for one who has attained the higher knowledges but whose object is not fully understood, fear and terror arise, as in the case of the Elder Mahānāga, the resident of Uccāvālika. The individual, directly visible fruit of the ascetic life. Therefore, the Blessed One said—

“Yato [P 1.0347] yato sammasati, khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ;

Labhatī pītipāmojjaṃ, amataṃ taṃ vijānata”ntiādi. (dha. pa. 374);

'Whenever one comprehends the arising and passing away of the aggregates, one obtains joy and delight; that is the deathless for those who know.' And so on. (Dhammapada 374)

Manomayiddhiñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Knowledge of Mind-Made Psychic Power

236-7. Manena nibbattitanti abhiññāmanena nibbattitaṃ. Hatthapādādi aṅgehi ca kapparajaṇṇuādi paccaṅgehi ca. Saṇṭhānavasenāti kamaladalādisadisasaṇṭhānamattavasena, na rūpābhighātārahabhūtappasādiindriyavasena. Sabbākārehīti vaṇṇasaṇṭhānaavayavavisesādisabbākārehi. Tena iddhimatā. Sadisabhāvadassanatthamevāti saṇṭhānatopi vaṇṇatopi avayavavisesatopi sadisabhāvadassanatthameva. Sajātiyaṃ ṭhito, na nāgiddhiyā aññajātirūpo.

236-7. “Produced by mind” means produced by the mind of supernormal knowledge. With limbs such as hands and feet, and secondary limbs such as elbows and knees. “In terms of shape” means only in terms of resemblance to shapes like lotus petals, not in terms of the sensitive material qualities capable of impingement by visible objects. “In all aspects” means in all aspects such as color, shape, and distinctive features. By that possessor of psychic power. “Only for the purpose of showing similarity” means solely to demonstrate similarity in shape, color, and distinctive features. He remains in his own kind, not as a form of another kind through the psychic power of a nāga.

Iddhividhañāṇādikakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Knowledge of the Various Kinds of Psychic Power, and So On.

239. Suparikammakatamattikādayo [V 1.0237] viya iddhividhañāṇaṃ vikubbanakiriyāya nissayabhāvato.

239. Just as well-prepared clay and other materials are a basis for the act of transformation, so too is the knowledge of the kinds of psychic power a basis for the performance of transformations, due to its nature as a support.

241. Sukhanti akicchena, akasirenāti attho.

241. ‘Easily’ means without difficulty, without toil—this is the meaning.

243. Mando uttānaseyyakadārakopi “daharo”ti vuccatīti tato visesanatthaṃ “yuvā”ti vuttaṃ.
