Yuvāpi koci anicchanako amaṇḍanajātiko hotīti tato visesanatthaṃ “maṇḍanakajātiko”tiādi vuttaṃ, tenāha “yuvāpīti”ādi. Kāḷatilappamāṇā bindavo kāḷatilakāni kāḷā vā kammāsā, tilappamāṇā bindavo tilakāni. Vaṅgaṃ nāma viyaṅgaṃ. Yobbanapīḷakādayo mukhadūsipīḷakā. Mukhagato [M 1.0268] doso mukhadoso, lakkhaṇavacanañcetaṃ mukhe adosassāpi pākaṭabhāvassa adhippetattā. Yathā vā mukhe doso, evaṃ mukhe adosopi mukhadoso saralopena. Mukhadoso ca mukhadoso ca mukhadosoti ekasesanayenapettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Evañhi “paresaṃ soḷasavidhaṃ cittaṃ pākaṭaṃ hotī”ti vacanaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti.

243. Even a dull child lying on its back is also called ‘dahara’ (young), therefore ‘yuvā’ (youthful) is said to specify further. Even a youth may be unwilling and not naturally fond of adornment, therefore to specify further, ‘fond of adornment’ and so on is said. Hence, it is said, ‘Even a youth,’ and so on. Spots the size of black sesame seeds are black marks, or black variegated spots; sesame-sized spots are freckles. ‘Vaṅga’ means a blemish. Pimples of youth and so on are facial blemishes. A defect occurring on the face is a facial defect—and this is a characteristic expression because it implies the obvious presence of even the absence of defect on the face. Or, just as a defect on the face is a facial defect, so too is the absence of defect on the face a facial defect, by the elision of the vowel. And ‘mukhadoso ca mukhadoso ca mukhadoso’ is the way the meaning should be understood here, according to the rule of ekasesa (leaving only one). In this way, the statement ‘the sixteen kinds of thoughts of others become apparent’ is justified.

245. Pubbenivāsañāṇūpamāyanti [P 1.0348] pubbenivāsañāṇassa dassitaupamāyaṃ. Taṃ divasaṃ katakiriyā nāma pākatikasattassapi yebhuyyena pākaṭā hotīti dassanatthaṃ taṃdivasa-ggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Taṃdivasagatagāmattaya-ggahaṇeneva mahābhinīhārehi aññesampi pubbenivāsañāṇalābhīnaṃ tīsu bhavesu katakiriyā yebhuyyena pākaṭā hotīti dīpitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

245. ‘Like an illustration of the knowledge of former abodes’—this is the simile shown for the knowledge of former abodes. The mention of ‘that day’ is to show that even for an ordinary being, actions done on that day are generally evident. It should be understood that by mentioning ‘the three villages visited that day,’ it is shown that for others who attain the knowledge of former abodes through great aspiration, actions done in the three existences are generally evident.

247. Aparāparaṃ sañcaranteti taṃtaṃkiccavasena ito cito ca sañcarante. Yathāvuttapāsādoviya bhikkhuno karajakāyo daṭṭhabbo tattha patiṭṭhitassa daṭṭhabbadassanasiddhito. Cakkhumato hi dibbacakkhusamadhigamo. Yathāha “maṃsacakkhussa uppādo, maggo dibbassa cakkhuno”ti (itivu. 61). Cakkhumā puriso viya ayameva dibbacakkhuṃ patvā ṭhito bhikkhu daṭṭhabbassa dassanato. Gehaṃ pavisantā viya etaṃ attabhāvagehaṃ okkamantā, upapajjantāti attho. Gehā nikkhamantā viya etasmā attabhāvagehato pakkantā, cavantāti attho. Evaṃ vā ettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Aparāparaṃ sañcaraṇakasattāti pana punappunaṃ saṃsāre paribbhamantā sattā. “Tattha tattha nibbattasattā”ti pana iminā tasmiṃ bhave jātasaṃvaddhe satte vadati. Nanu cāyaṃ dibbacakkhuñāṇakathā, ettha kasmā “tīsu bhavesū”ti catuvokārabhavassāpi saṅgaho katoti āha [V 1.0238] “idañcā”tiādi. Tattha idanti “tīsu bhavesu nibbattasattāna”nti idaṃ vacanaṃ. Desanāsukhatthamevāti kevalaṃ desanāsukhatthaṃ, na catuvokārabhave nibbattasattānaṃ dibbacakkhuno āvibhāvasabbhāvato. Na hi “ṭhapetvā arūpabhava”nti vā “dvīsu [P 1.0349] bhavesū”ti vā vuccamāne desanā sukhāvabodhā ca hotīti.

247. ‘Wandering from one state to another’ means moving here and there according to their respective functions. The monk’s body born of kamma should be understood as being like the aforementioned palace, because for one established therein, the seeing of what is to be seen is accomplished. For one endowed with the eye, indeed, there is the attainment of the divine eye. As it is said: ‘The arising of the fleshly eye is the path to the divine eye’ (Itivuttaka 61). Like a man with the eye, this very monk, having attained the divine eye, stands for the purpose of seeing what is to be seen. Just as those entering a house, they enter this house of individuality, meaning they are reborn. Just as those leaving a house, they depart from this house of individuality, meaning they pass away. Or the meaning here should be understood in this way. ‘Beings wandering repeatedly’ means beings roaming again and again in the cycle of existence. ‘Beings born here and there’ refers to beings born and grown in that existence. Now, this is a discussion about the knowledge of the divine eye. Why then is the four-constituent existence also included here with the phrase ‘in the three existences’? To this, it is said: ‘This and so on.’ Here, ‘this’ refers to the statement ‘of beings born in the three existences.’ It is solely for the sake of ease in teaching, not because there is any manifestation for the divine eye of beings born in the four-constituent existence. For if it were said ‘excluding the formless existence’ or ‘in two existences,’ the teaching would not be easy to understand.

Āsavakkhayañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints.

248. Vipassanāpādakanti [M 1.0269] vipassanāya padaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ. Vipassanā ca tividhā vipassakapuggalabhedena. Mahābodhisattānañhi paccekabodhisattānañca vipassanā cintāmayañāṇasaṃvaddhitā sayambhuñāṇabhūtā, itaresaṃ sutamayañāṇasaṃvaddhitā paropadesasambhūtā nāma. Sā “ṭhapetvā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ avasesarūpārūpajjhānānaṃ aññatarato vuṭṭhāyā”tiādinā anekadhā, arūpamukhavasena catudhātuvavatthāne vuttānaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ dhātupariggahamukhānañca aññataramukhavasena anekadhā ca visuddhimagge nānānayato vibhāvitā. Mahābodhisattānaṃ pana catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassamukhena pabhedagamanato nānānayaṃ sabbaññutañāṇasannissayassa ariyamaggañāṇassa adhiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ pubbabhāgañāṇagabbhaṃ gaṇhāpentaṃ pariṇataṃ gacchantaṃ paramagambhīraṃ saṇhasukhumataraṃ anaññasādhāraṇaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ hoti, yaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu “mahāvajirañāṇa”nti vuccati. Yassa ca pavattivibhāgena catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassappabhedassa pādakabhāvena samāpajjiyamānā catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassasaṅkhyā devasikaṃ satthu vaḷañjanakasamāpattiyo vuccanti, svāyaṃ buddhānaṃ vipassanācāro paramatthamañjusāyaṃ visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ (visuddhi. ṭī. 1.216) uddesato dassito. Atthikehi tato gahetabbo, idha pana sāvakānaṃ vipassanā adhippetā.

248. ‘The foundation of insight’ means the basis for insight. Insight is of three kinds, distinguished by the type of person practicing it. For the great bodhisattvas and the solitary bodhisattas, insight is cultivated through wisdom based on reflection, being self-realized knowledge. For others, it is cultivated through wisdom based on learning, originating from the instruction of others. This insight is explained in various ways, such as ‘emerging from any of the remaining form and formless jhānas except the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,’ and in various ways in the determination of the four elements by way of the formless entrance, and by way of any of those modes of apprehending the elements, as expounded in the Visuddhimagga through multiple approaches. For the great bodhisattas, however, insight unfolds through twenty-four trillion modes, serving as the precursor and womb of knowledge that leads to the noble path-knowledge, the foundation of omniscience. This insight is profound, exceedingly subtle, and unique, maturing into what the commentaries call ‘the great diamond knowledge.’ By the division of its occurrence, the twenty-four trillion variations serve as the basis for the daily attainments for the Teacher’s use, which are entered into. This is the Buddha’s practice of insight, described in outline in the Paramatthamañjūsā, the commentary on the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhi-ṭīkā 1.216). Those who seek it should take it from there. Here, however, the insight intended is that of the disciples.

Āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāyāti āsavānaṃ khepanato samucchindanato āsavakkhayo, ariyamaggo, tattha ñāṇaṃ āsavānaṃ khayañāṇaṃ, tadatthaṃ tenāha “āsavānaṃ khayañāṇanibbattanatthāyā”ti. Āsavā ettha khīyantīti āsavānaṃ khayo nibbānaṃ. Khepeti pāpadhammeti khayo, maggo. So pana pāpakkhayo āsavakkhayena vinā natthīti “khaye ñāṇa”nti ettha khayaggahaṇena [P 1.0350] āsavakkhayo vuttoti āha “khaye ñāṇa”ntiādi. Samitapāpo samaṇoti katvā āsavānaṃ khīṇattā samaṇo nāma hotīti āha “āsavānaṃ khayā samaṇo hotīti ettha phala”nti. Āsavavaḍḍhiyā saṅkhāre vaḍḍhento visaṅkhārato suvidūravidūroti “ārā so āsavakkhayā”ti ettha āsavakkhayapadaṃ visaṅkhārādhivacananti āha [V 1.0239] “āsavakkhayāti ettha nibbānaṃ vutta”nti. Bhaṅgoti [M 1.0270] āsavānaṃ khaṇanirodho “āsavānaṃ khayo”ti vuttoti yojanā.

‘For the knowledge of the destruction of the taints’: Because it eradicates and cuts off the taints, the ‘destruction of the taints’ is the noble path. The knowledge therein is the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. For that purpose, it is said: ‘for the sake of producing the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.’ Alternatively, ‘Herein the taints are destroyed’; thus, the destruction of the taints is Nibbāna. Or, ‘It eradicates evil states’; thus, ‘destruction’ is the path. But since that destruction of evil does not exist without the destruction of the taints, in the phrase ‘knowledge in destruction,’ by the term ‘destruction,’ the destruction of the taints is meant. Thus it is said: ‘knowledge in destruction,’ and so on. Based on the saying, ‘A recluse is one who has pacified evil,’ because the taints are destroyed, one is called a recluse. Thus it is said: ‘Through the destruction of the taints, one becomes a recluse’; here, the fruit is stated. One who increases formations by increasing the taints is very, very far from the unconditioned; therefore, in the phrase ‘He is far from the destruction of the taints,’ the term ‘destruction of the taints’ is a synonym for the unconditioned. Thus it is said: ‘The destruction of the taints—here, Nibbāna is meant.’ ‘Breaking’ means the momentary cessation of the taints; this is called ‘the destruction of the taints.’ This is the application.

“Idaṃ dukkha”nti dukkhassa ariyasaccassa tadā bhikkhuno paccakkhato gahitabhāvadassanaṃ. “Ettakaṃ dukkha”nti tassa paricchijjaggahitabhāvadassanaṃ. “Na ito bhiyyo”ti tassa anavasesetvā gahitabhāvadassanaṃ. Tenāha “sabbampi dukkhasacca”ntiādi. Sarasalakkhaṇapaṭivedhenāti sabhāvasaṅkhātassa lakkhaṇassa asammohato paṭivijjhanena, asammohapaṭivedhoti ca. Yathā tasmiṃ ñāṇe pavatte pacchā dukkhasaccassa sarūpādiparicchede sammoho na hoti, tathā pavatti, tenāha “yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”ti. Dukkhaṃ samudeti etasmāti dukkhasamudayo, taṇhāti āha “tassa cā”tiādi. Yaṃ ṭhānaṃ patvāti yaṃ nibbānaṃ maggassa ārammaṇapaccayaṭṭhena kāraṇabhūtaṃ āgamma, “patvā”ti ca tadubhayavato puggalassa patti tadubhayassa patti viyāti katvā vuttaṃ. Patvāti vā pāpuṇanahetu. Appavattīti appavattinimittaṃ, te vā nappavattanti etthāti appavatti, nibbānaṃ. Tassāti dukkhanirodhassa. Sampāpakanti sacchikaraṇavasena sammadeva pāpakaṃ.

‘This is suffering’—this shows the monk’s direct grasping of the noble truth of suffering at that time. ‘This much is suffering’—this shows the state of being grasped by delimitation. ‘No more than this’—this shows the state of being grasped without remainder. Therefore, it is said, ‘all of the truth of suffering,’ and so on. By penetration of the essential characteristic—by penetrating without confusion the characteristic designated as intrinsic nature; this is penetration without delusion. Just as when that knowledge arises, afterwards there is no delusion in distinguishing the truth of suffering by its intrinsic nature and so on, thus it occurs. Therefore, it is said, ‘he understands it as it truly is.’ Suffering arises from this—this is the origin of suffering, craving. Thus it is said, ‘and of its,’ and so on. ‘Having reached that state’ means having reached Nibbāna, which is the cause in the sense of being the object-condition for the path; ‘having reached’ is stated because the attainment of the person possessing both (path and fruition) is like the attainment of both. Or, ‘having reached’ means the cause of attaining. ‘Non-occurrence’ means the condition for non-occurrence; or, that wherein they do not occur is non-occurrence, Nibbāna. ‘Of that’ means of the cessation of suffering. ‘Leading to accomplishment’ means that which brings to accomplishment rightly by way of direct realization.

Kilesavasenāti āsavasaṅkhātakilesavasena. Yasmā āsavānaṃ dukkhasaccapariyāyo tappariyāpannattā, sesasaccānañca taṃsamudayādipariyāyo atthi, tasmā vuttaṃ “pariyāyato”ti. Dassento saccānīti yojanā. Āsavānaṃyeva cettha gahaṇaṃ “āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāyā”ti āraddhattā. Tathā hi “kāmāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccatī”tiādinā [P 1.0351] (dī. ni. 1.248; ma. ni. 1.433; ma. ni. 3.19) āsavavimuttisīseneva sabbakilesavimutti vuttā. “Idaṃ dukkhanti yathābhūtaṃ pajanātī”tiādinā missakamaggo idha kathitoti “saha vipassanāya koṭippattaṃ maggaṃ kathesī”ti vuttaṃ. “Jānato passato”ti iminā pariññāsacchikiriyābhāvanābhisamayā vuttā. “Vimuccatī”ti iminā pahānābhisamayo vuttoti āha “iminā maggakkhaṇaṃ dassetī”ti. “Jānato passato”ti vā hetuniddesoyaṃ. Jānanahetu dassanahetu kāmāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccatīti yojanā. Dhammānañhi samānakālikānampi paccayappaccayuppannatā sahajātakoṭiyā labbhatīti. Bhavāsavaggahaṇena cettha bhavarāgassa viya bhavadiṭṭhiyāpi samavarodhoti diṭṭhāsavassāpi [M 1.0271] saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Khīṇā jātītiādīhi padehi. Tassāti paccavekkhaṇāñāṇassa. Bhūminti pavattiṭṭhānaṃ.

By ‘by way of the power of defilements’ is meant by way of the defilements designated as taints. Because the taints are an aspect of the truth of suffering, being included therein, and the other truths also have their aspects of origination and so on, therefore it is said ‘by way of aspect.’ The connection is: ‘showing the truths.’ Here, only the taints are taken because the discourse was begun with ‘for the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.’ For thus, by phrases such as ‘the mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire,’ the liberation from all defilements is spoken of with liberation from the taints as the principal part. Since the mixed path is discussed here by phrases such as ‘he understands “this is suffering” as it really is,’ it is said, ‘he taught the path that has reached its culmination along with insight.’ By ‘for one who knows and sees’ are stated the direct comprehensions of full understanding, realization, and development. By ‘is liberated’ is stated the direct comprehension of abandonment; thus he says, ‘by this, he shows the moment of the path.’ Alternatively, ‘for one who knows and sees’ is an indication of the cause. The connection is that the mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire due to the cause of knowing and the cause of seeing. For even in the case of simultaneously occurring phenomena, their nature as condition and conditioned is obtained in the category of co-nascence. Here, by the taking of the taint of existence, the inclusion of the taint of views should be understood, since the view of existence is included just like the craving for existence. By the words ‘birth is destroyed,’ and so on. ‘Of that’ means of the reviewing knowledge. ‘Ground’ means the place of occurrence.

Yenādhippāyena “katamā panassā”tiādinā codanā katā, taṃ vivaranto “na tāvassā”tiādimāha[V 1.0240]. Tattha na tāvassa atītā jāti khīṇā maggabhāvanāyāti adhippāyo. Tattha kāraṇamāha “pubbeva khīṇattā”ti. Na anāgatā assa jāti khīṇāti yojanā. Na anāgatāti ca anāgatabhāvasāmaññaṃ gahetvā lesena codeti, tenāha “anāgate vāyāmābhāvato”ti. Anāgataviseso panettha adhippeto, tassa ca khepane vāyāmopi labbhateva, tenāha “yā pana maggassā”tiādi. Ekacatupañcavokārabhavesūti bhavattayaggahaṇaṃ vuttanayena anavasesato jātiyā khīṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Tanti yathāvuttaṃ jātiṃ. Soti khīṇāsavo bhikkhu.

Clarifying the intention with which the objection ‘But what of his...?’ and so on was made, he says, ‘It is not that...’ and so on. Here, the meaning is: it is not that his past birth is destroyed by the development of the path. Regarding this, he states the reason: ‘Because it was already destroyed.’ The connection is: his future birth is not destroyed. And by ‘not future,’ he raises a subtle objection by taking the general sense of the future state; hence he says, ‘due to the absence of effort regarding the future.’ However, a specific future is intended here, and in its elimination, effort is indeed found. Therefore, he says, ‘But that which of the path...’ and so on. By ‘in the one-, four-, and five-constituent existences’ is meant the taking of the three states of existence, in the manner stated, in order to show the state of birth being destroyed without remainder. ‘That’ means birth as explained. ‘He’ means the monk whose taints are destroyed.

Brahmacariyavāso nāma ukkaṭṭhaniddesena maggabrahmacariyassa nibbattanaṃ evāti āha “parivuttha”nti. Sammādiṭṭhiyā catūsu saccesu pariññādikiccasādhanavasena pavattamānāya sammāsaṅkappādīnampi dukkhasacce pariññābhisamayānuguṇā pavatti, itarasaccesu ca [P 1.0352] nesaṃ pahānābhisamayādipavatti pākaṭā eva, tena vuttaṃ “catūsu saccesu catūhi maggehi pariññāpahānasacchikiriyābhāvanāvasenā”ti. Dukkhanirodhamaggesu pariññāsacchikiriyābhāvanā yāvadeva samudayappahānatthāyāti āha “tena tena maggena pahātabbakilesā pahīnā”ti. Itthattāyāti ime pakārā itthaṃ, tabbhāvo itthattaṃ, tadatthanti vuttaṃ hoti. Te pana pakārā ariyamaggabyāpārabhūtā pariññādayo idhādhippetāti āha “evaṃ soḷasakiccabhāvāyā”ti. Te hi maggaṃ paccavekkhato maggānubhāvena pākaṭā hutvā upaṭṭhahanti, pariññādīsu ca pahānameva padhānaṃ tadatthattā itaresanti āha “kilesakkhayabhāvāya vā”ti. Pahīnakilesapaccavekkhaṇavasena vā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Dutiyavikappe itthattāyāti nissakke sampadānavacananti āha “itthabhāvato”ti. Aparanti anāgataṃ. Ime pana carimakattabhāvasaṅkhātā pañcakkhandhā pariññātā tiṭṭhanti, etena tesaṃ appatiṭṭhataṃ dasseti. Apariññāmūlikā hi patiṭṭhā. Yathāha “kabaḷīkāre ce bhikkhave āhāre atthi rāgo atthi nandī atthi [M 1.0272] taṇhā, patiṭṭhitaṃ tattha viññāṇaṃ virūḷha”ntiādi. (Saṃ. ni. 2.64; kathā. 296; mahāni. 7) tenevāha “chinnamūlakā rukkhā viyā”tiādi.

The living of the holy life is precisely the production of the path of the holy life, by way of the supreme designation; thus he says, ‘has been lived.’ As right view proceeds by way of accomplishing the functions of full understanding and so on regarding the four truths, the proceeding of right intention and the others is in accordance with the direct comprehension of full understanding regarding the truth of suffering, and their proceeding in relation to the direct comprehension of abandonment and so on regarding the other truths is indeed evident. Therefore, it is said, ‘by way of full understanding, abandonment, realization, and development by means of the four paths in relation to the four truths.’ The full understanding, realization, and development regarding the path to the cessation of suffering are solely for the purpose of abandoning the origin; thus he says, ‘the defilements to be abandoned by this or that path are abandoned.’ For ‘itthattāya’ means: these modes are ‘thus’ (itthaṃ); the state of that is ‘thusness’ (itthattaṃ); for the sake of that. These modes, however, which are the functions of the noble path—full understanding and so on—are intended here; thus he says, ‘thus, for the state of the sixteen functions.’ For when one reviews the path, these become evident and present themselves through the power of the path. And among full understanding and the others, abandonment is primary because the others are for its sake; thus he says, ‘or for the state of the destruction of defilements.’ Or it is said thus by way of reviewing the abandoned defilements. In the second alternative, ‘itthattāya’ is a dative of purpose; thus he says, ‘from the state of being thus.’ ‘Further’ means future. These five aggregates, however, designated as the final existence, remain fully understood; by this, he shows their non-establishment. For establishment is rooted in non-full-understanding. As it is said: ‘Monks, if there is lust, delight, or craving for physical nutriment, consciousness is established there and grows,’ and so on. Therefore, he says, ‘like trees with their roots cut,’ and so on.

249. Pabbatamatthaketi pabbatasikhare. Tañhi yebhuyyena saṅkhittaṃ saṅkucitaṃ hotīti pāḷiyaṃ “pabbatasaṅkhepe”ti vuttaṃ. Pabbatapariyāpanno vā padeso pabbatasaṅkhepo[P 1.0353]. Anāviloti akālusiyo, sā cassa anāvilatā kaddamābhāvena hotīti āha “nikkaddamo”ti. Sippiyoti suttiyo. Sambukāti saṅkhalikā. Ṭhitāsupi nisinnāsupi gāvīsu. Vijjamānāsūti labbhamānāsu, itarā ṭhitāpi nisinnāpi “carantī”ti vuccanti sahacaraṇanayena. Tiṭṭhantameva, na pana kadācipi carantaṃ. Dvayanti sippisambukaṃ, macchagumbanti idaṃ ubhayaṃ. Tiṭṭhantanti vuttaṃ carantaṃ [V 1.0241] pīti adhippāyo. “Itarañca dvaya”nti ca yathāvuttameva sippisambukādidvayaṃ vadati. Tañhi caratīti. Kiṃ vā imāya sahacariyāya, yathālābhaggahaṇaṃ panettha daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sakkharakathalassa hi vasena tiṭṭhantanti. Sippisambukassa macchagumbassa ca vasena tiṭṭhantampi carantaṃ pīti yojanā kātabbā.

249. ‘On a mountain top’ means on a mountain peak. Because that is for the most part compact, in the Pāli it is said ‘in a mountain cleft.’ Or, a region included within the mountain is a ‘mountain cleft.’ ‘Undisturbed’ means not turbid; and its undisturbed nature is due to the absence of mud, thus he says ‘free from mud.’ ‘Oyster shells’ means mussels. ‘Snails’ means conch shells. Among cows, whether standing or sitting, ‘existing’ means available; other cows, though standing or sitting, are called ‘grazing’ by way of association with the herd. ‘Standing’ refers to that which is only standing, never moving. ‘The pair’ means oyster shells and snails; ‘a school of fish’ means both of these, that is, both standing and moving. The meaning is that ‘standing’ is said even of that which is moving. And by ‘the other pair’ he refers to the aforementioned pair of oyster shells, snails, and so on, for that moves. Or what is the point of this association? Here, it should be seen as a taking of what is available. For ‘standing’ is said with reference to gravel and pebbles. With reference to oyster shells, snails, and schools of fish, the connection should be made that they are both standing and moving.

Tesaṃ dasannaṃ ñāṇānaṃ. Tatthāti tasmiṃ ārammaṇavibhāge, tesu vā ñāṇesu. Bhūmibhedato, kālabhedato, santānabhedato cāti sattavidhārammaṇaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ. “Rūpāyatanamattamevā”ti idaṃ tassa ñāṇassa abhinimmiyamāne manomaye kāye rūpāyatanamevārabbha pavattanato vuttaṃ, na tattha gandhāyataṃ ādīnaṃ abhāvato. Na hi rūpakalāpo gandhāyataṃ ādirahito atthi. Parinipphannameva nimmitarūpaṃ, tenāha “parittapaccuppannabahiddhārammaṇa”nti. Āsavakkhayañāṇaṃ nibbānārammaṇameva samānaṃ parittattikavasena appamāṇārammaṇaṃ, ajjhattattikavasena bahiddhārammaṇaṃ, atītattikavasena navattabbārammaṇañca hotīti āha “appamāṇabahiddhānavattabbārammaṇa”nti. Kūṭo [P 1.0354] viya kūṭāgārassa bhagavato desanāya arahattaṃ uttamaṅgabhūtanti āha “arahattanikūṭenā”ti. Desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesīti titthakaramataharavibhāviniṃ nānāvidhakuhanalapanādimicchājīvaviddhaṃsiniṃ tividhasīlālaṅkataṃ paramasallekhapaṭipattidīpaniṃ jhānābhiññādiuttarimanussadhammavibhūsitaṃ cuddasavidhamahāsāmaññaphalapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ anaññasādhāraṇaṃ desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

Of those ten knowledges. By 'tatthā' is meant in that division of objects, or in those knowledges. Insight knowledge has seven types of objects: by way of division of plane, by way of division of time, and by way of division of continuity. By 'only the form base' it is said that this knowledge arises by taking as its object only the form base in the mind-made body being created, not because the smell base and so on are absent there. For no material group exists without the smell base and so on. The created form is fully perfected; therefore, he says, 'a limited, present, external object.' The knowledge of the destruction of the taints, though having Nibbāna as its object, becomes an immeasurable object by way of the limited triad, an external object by way of the internal triad, and an object not to be spoken of by way of the past triad; thus he says, 'an immeasurable, external, and not-to-be-spoken-of object.' Just as the pinnacle of a gabled house, so too arahantship is the supreme part of the Blessed One's teaching; thus he says, 'with the pinnacle of arahantship.' By 'he completed the teaching' is meant he completed the teaching which clarifies and refutes the doctrines of heretical teachers, which destroys various deceptive practices and wrong livelihoods such as cunning talk, which is adorned with the threefold virtue, which illuminates the supreme practice of effacement, which is embellished with jhānas, superknowledges, and other supramundane qualities, which is adorned with the fourteenfold great fruits of recluseship, and which is unparalleled.

Ajātasattuupāsakattapaṭivedanākathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Account of Ajātasattu's Acknowledgment as a Lay Follower.

250. Ādimajjhapariyosānanti [M 1.0273] ādiñca majjhañca pariyosānañca. Sakkaccaṃ sagāravaṃ. Āraddhaṃ dhammasaṅgāhakehi.

250. “Beginning, middle, and end” means the beginning, the middle, and the end. Carefully and with respect. Begun by the compilers of the Dhamma.

Abhikkantā vigatāti atthoti āha “khaye dissatī”ti. Tathā hi “nikkhanto paṭhamo yāmo”ti upari vuttaṃ. Abhikkantataroti ativiya kantataro manoramo, tādiso ca sundaro bhaddako nāma hotīti āha “sundare dissatī”ti. Koti devanāgayakkhagandhabbādīsu ko katamo. Meti mama. Pādānīti pāde. Iddhiyāti imāya evarūpāya deviddhiyā. Yasasāti iminā edisena parivārena, parijanena ca. Jalanti vijjotamāno. Abhikkantenāti ativiya kantena kamanīyena abhirūpena. Vaṇṇenāti chavivaṇṇena sarīravaṇṇanibhāya[V 1.0242]. Sabbā obhāsayaṃ disāti dasapi disā pabhāsento cando viya, sūriyo viya ca ekobhāsaṃ ekālokaṃ karontoti gāthāya attho. Abhirūpeti uḷārarūpe sampannarūpe.

“Passed, departed” (abhikkantā vigatā) is the meaning; thus it is said, “it is seen in destruction” (khaye dissati). For it is stated above, “The first watch has passed” (nikkhanto paṭhamo yāmo). “More excellent” (abhikkantataro) means exceedingly lovely and charming; and such a one is called beautiful and auspicious, thus it is said, “it is seen in beauty” (sundare dissati). “Who” (ko) means: who, which one (ko katamo) among gods, nāgas, yakkhas, gandhabbas, and so on. “Mine” (me) means my. “Feet” (pādāni) means the feet. “By psychic power” (iddhiyā) means by this kind of divine psychic power. “By glory” (yasasā) means by this kind of retinue and attendants. “Shining” (jalanti) means shining brightly. “By excellence” (abhikkantena) means by being exceedingly lovely, desirable, and beautiful. “By complexion” (vaṇṇena) means by the skin’s hue, by the radiance of the body. “Illuminating all directions” (sabbā obhāsayaṃ disā) means illuminating all ten directions like the moon or the sun, making a single radiance, a single light—this is the meaning of the verse. “In a beautiful form” (abhirūpe) means in a magnificent form, in an accomplished form.

“Coro coro, sappo sappo”tiādīsu bhaye āmeḍitaṃ, “vijjha vijjha, pahara paharā”tiādīsu kodhe, “sādhu sādhūtiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.327; saṃ. ni. 2.127; 3.35; 5.1005) pasaṃsāyaṃ, “gaccha gaccha, lunāhi lunāhī”tiādīsu turite, “āgaccha āgacchā”tiādīsu kotūhale, “buddho buddhoti cintento”tiādīsu (bu. vaṃ. 44) acchare[P 1.0355], “abhikkamathāyasmanto abhikkamathāyasmanto”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.20; a. ni. 9.11) hāse, “kahaṃ ekaputtaka kahaṃ ekaputtakā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.63) soke, “aho sukhaṃ aho sukha”ntiādīsu (udā. 20; dī. ni. 3.305; cūḷava. 332) pasāde. Ca-saddo avuttasamuccayattho, tena garahāasammānādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tattha “pāpo pāpo”tiādīsu garahāyaṃ, “abhirūpaka abhirūpakā”tiādīsu asammāne daṭṭhabbaṃ.

In phrases like “thief, thief,” “snake, snake,” and so on, repetition indicates fear; in phrases like “shoot, shoot,” “strike, strike,” and so on, it indicates anger; in phrases like “good, good,” and so on, it indicates praise; in phrases like “go, go,” “cut, cut,” and so on, it indicates urgency; in phrases like “come, come,” and so on, it indicates curiosity; in phrases like “the Buddha, the Buddha,” thinking thus, and so on, it indicates wonder; in phrases like “come forward, venerable ones, come forward, venerable ones,” and so on, it indicates amusement; in phrases like “where is my only son, where is my only son,” and so on, it indicates sorrow; in phrases like “ah, happiness, ah, happiness,” and so on, it indicates serenity. The particle “ca” serves to include what has not been said; thus, the inclusion of blame, disrespect, and so on should be understood. There, in phrases like “evil, evil,” and so on, it indicates blame; in phrases like “handsome one, handsome one,” and so on, it indicates disrespect.

Nayidaṃ āmeḍitavasena dvikkhattuṃ vuttaṃ, atha kho atthadvayavasenāti dassento “atha vā”tiādimāha “abhikkanta”nti vacanaṃ apekkhitvā napuṃsakaliṅgavasena vuttaṃ. Taṃ pana bhagavato vacanaṃ dhammassa desanāti katvā [M 1.0274] tathā vuttaṃ. Atthamattadassanaṃ vā etaṃ, tasmā atthavasenettha liṅgavibhattipariṇāmo veditabbo. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Dosanāsanatoti rāgādikilesavidhamanato. Guṇādhigamanatoti sīlādiguṇānaṃ sampādanato. Ye guṇe desanā adhigameti, tesu padhānabhūtā dassetabbāti te padhānabhūte tāva dassetuṃ “saddhājananato paññājananato”ti vuttaṃ. Saddhāpamukhā hi lokiyā guṇā paññāpamukhā lokuttarā. Sīlādiatthasampattiyā sātthato. Sabhāvaniruttisampattiyā sabyañjanato. Suviññeyyasaddapayogatāya uttānapadato. Saṇhasukhumabhāvena dubbiññeyyatthatāya gambhīratthato. Siniddhamudumadhurasaddapayogatāya kaṇṇasukhato. Vipulavisuddhapemanīyatthatāya hadayaṅgamato. Mānātimānavidhamanena anattukkaṃsanato. Thambhasārambhanimmaddanena aparavambhanato. Hitādhippāyappavattiyā, paresaṃ rāgapariḷāhādivūpagamanena [P 1.0356] ca karuṇāsītalato. Kilesandhakāravidhamanena paññāvadātato. Karavīkarutamañjutāya āpātharamaṇīyato. Pubbāparāviruddhasuvisuddhatāya vimaddakkhamato. Āpātharamaṇīyatāya eva suyyamānasukhato. Vimaddakkhamatāya, hitajjhāsayappavattitāya ca vīmaṃsiyamānahitato. Evamādīhīti ādi-saddena saṃsāracakkanivattanato saddhammacakkappavattanato, micchāvādaviddhaṃsanato sammāvādapatiṭṭhāpanato, akusalamūlasamuddharaṇato [V 1.0243] kusalamūlasaṃropanato, apāyadvārapidhānato saggamaggadvāravivaraṇato, pariyuṭṭhānavūpasamanato anusayasamugghāṭanatoti evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

This was not stated twice for emphasis, but to show two meanings; hence the phrase “or else” and so on is given. The word “excellent” is used in the neuter gender in reference to the speech. That speech of the Blessed One is the teaching of the Dhamma, and it is spoken of as such. Or this is merely showing the meaning; therefore, the change of gender and case ending here should be understood according to the meaning. The same principle applies to the second term. “By dispelling faults” means by destroying defilements such as lust. “By attaining virtues” means by accomplishing qualities such as virtue. Among the qualities that the teaching leads to, the principal ones should be shown; to show those principal ones, it is said, “by generating faith, by generating wisdom.” For worldly qualities have faith as their chief, while supramundane qualities have wisdom as their chief. It is 'with meaning' (sāttha) because it accomplishes the substance of virtue and so on. It is 'with phrasing' (sabyañjana) because it possesses excellence of expression. It has 'clear wording' (uttānapada) because it uses easily intelligible words. It has 'profound meaning' (gambhīrattha) because its meaning is difficult to comprehend due to its subtlety. It is 'pleasant to the ear' (kaṇṇasukha) because it uses smooth, gentle, and sweet words. It is 'heart-touching' (hadayaṅgama) because its meaning is vast, pure, and lovely. It is 'not self-praising' (anattukkaṃsana) because it destroys conceit and arrogance. It is 'not disparaging of others' (aparavambhana) because it crushes stubbornness and contention. It is 'cool with compassion' (karuṇāsītala) because it proceeds from a beneficial intention and calms the fever of lust and so on in others. It is 'bright with wisdom' (paññāvadāta) because it dispels the darkness of defilements. It is 'charming on first hearing' (āpātharamaṇīya), like the sweet call of the Karavīka bird. It is 'able to withstand scrutiny' (vimaddakkhama) because it is perfectly pure and without contradiction between earlier and later parts. It is 'pleasant to hear' (suyyamānasukha) because it is charming on first hearing. It is 'beneficial when examined' (vīmaṃsiyamānahita) because it can withstand scrutiny and proceeds from a beneficial disposition. By “and so on,” the inclusion of the following should be understood: turning back the wheel of saṃsāra, setting in motion the wheel of the true Dhamma, demolishing wrong views, establishing right views, uprooting unwholesome roots, planting wholesome roots, closing the doors to the lower realms, opening the doors to the heavenly path and the path to Nibbāna, calming obsessive defilements, and eradicating latent tendencies.

Adhomukhaṭṭhapitanti kenaci adhomukhaṃ ṭhapitaṃ. Heṭṭhāmukhajātanti sabhāveneva heṭṭhāmukhaṃ jātaṃ. Ugghāṭeyyāti vivaṭaṃ kareyya. Hatthe gahetvā “puratthābhimukho, uttarābhimukho vā gacchā”tiādīni avatvā hatthe gahetvā nissandehaṃ katvā. “Esa maggo, evaṃ gacchā”ti dasseyya. Kāḷapakkhacātuddasīti kāḷapakkhe cātuddasī. Nikkujjitaṃ ādheyyassa anādhārabhūtaṃ bhājanaṃ ādhārabhāvāpādanavasena ukkujjeyya. Aññāṇassa abhimukhattā heṭṭhāmukhajātatāya saddhammavimukhaṃ adhomukhaṭṭhapitatāya asaddhamme patitanti evaṃ padadvayaṃ yathārahaṃ yojetabbaṃ, na yathāsaṅkhyaṃ. Kāmaṃ kāmacchandādayo paṭicchādakā nīvaraṇabhāvato, micchādiṭṭhi pana savisesaṃ paṭicchādikā satte micchābhinivesanavasenāti āha [M 1.0275] “micchādiṭṭhigahanapaṭicchanna”nti. Tenāha bhagavā “micchādiṭṭhiparamāhaṃ [P 1.0357] bhikkhave vajjaṃ vadāmī”ti. Sabbo apāyagāmimaggo kummaggo kucchito maggoti katvā. Sammādiṭṭhiādīnaṃ ujupaṭipakkhatāya micchādiṭṭhiādayo aṭṭha micchattadhammā micchāmaggā. Teneva hi tadubhayapaṭipakkhataṃ sandhāya “saggamokkhamaggaṃ āvikarontenā”ti vuttaṃ. Sappiādisannissayo padīpo na tathā ujjalo, yathā telasannissayoti telapajjota-ggahaṇaṃ. Etehi pariyāyehīti etehi nikkujjitukkujjanapaṭicchannavivaraṇādiupamopamitabbappakārehi, etehi vā yathāvuttehi nānāvidhakuhanalapanādimicchājīvavividhamanādivibhāvanapariyāyehi. Tenāha “anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito”ti.

“Placed upside down” means placed upside down by someone. “Naturally facing downward” means it is naturally facing downward from birth. “Should open” means should make it open. Taking them by the hand, without saying, “Face east or north and go,” and so on, but taking them by the hand and making it without doubt, one should show, “This is the path, go thus.” “The fourteenth of the dark fortnight” means the fourteenth day in the dark fortnight. “An overturned vessel” means one should turn upright a vessel that is not a support for what is placed in it, by way of bringing it to a state of being a support. Due to facing ignorance and being naturally downward-facing, one is turned away from the true Dhamma; due to being placed upside down, one has fallen into the false Dhamma. Thus, these two phrases should be connected as is appropriate, not in numerical order. Indeed, sensual desire and so on are concealers because of their nature as hindrances, but wrong view in particular conceals beings by way of wrong adherence; thus, it is said, “concealed by the thicket of wrong view.” Hence, the Blessed One said, “Monks, I say that wrong view is the ultimate fault.” All paths leading to the planes of misery are wrong paths, being bad paths. Because they are the direct opposite of right view and so on, the eight states of wrongness beginning with wrong view are wrong paths. For this very reason, with reference to the opposition of both, it is said, “by one who reveals the path to heaven and liberation.” A lamp dependent on ghee and so on is not as bright as one dependent on oil—hence the taking of an oil lamp. “By these methods” means by these illustrative methods of similes and things to be compared, such as overturning, righting, concealing, revealing, and so on, or by these various methods of explaining the dispelling of various wrong livelihoods such as deceit, talkativeness, and so on, as has been stated. Therefore, it is said, “the Dhamma has been illuminated in many ways.”

Pasannakāranti pasannehi kātabbaṃ sakkāraṃ. Saraṇanti paṭisaraṇaṃ, tenāha “parāyaṇa”nti. Parāyaṇabhāvo ca anatthanisedhanena, atthasampaṭipādanena ca hotīti āha “aghassa tātā, hitassa ca vidhātā”ti. Aghassāti dukkhatoti vadanti, pāpatoti pana attho yutto, nissakke cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Ettha ca nāyaṃ gamu-saddo nī-saddādayo viya dvikammako, tasmā yathā “ajaṃ gāmaṃ netī”ti vuccati, evaṃ “bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī”ti vattuṃ na sakkā, “saraṇanti gacchāmī”ti pana vattabbaṃ. Iti-saddo cettha luttaniddiṭṭho. Tassa cāyamattho. Gamanañca tadadhippāyena bhajanaṃ jānanaṃ vāti dassento “iminā adhippāyenā”tiādimāha. Tattha “bhajāmī”tiādīsu purimassa purimassa pacchimaṃ pacchimaṃ atthavacanaṃ, bhajanaṃ vā saraṇādhippāyena upasaṅkamanaṃ, sevanaṃ santikāvacaratā, payirupāsanaṃ vattapaṭivattakaraṇena upaṭṭhānanti [V 1.0244] evaṃ sabbathāpi anaññasaraṇataṃyeva dīpeti. “Gacchāmī”ti [P 1.0358] padassa bujjhāmīti ayamattho kathaṃ labbhatīti āha “yesañhī”tiādi.

“Pasannakāra” means the respect that should be shown by those who are confident. “Saraṇa” is a refuge; therefore, it is said to be a “parāyaṇa” (final resort). The state of being a final resort comes about through the prevention of harm and the provision of benefit; thus, it is said, “the protector from evil, and the provider of welfare.” “Aghassa” (of evil) is said to mean “from suffering,” but the meaning “from evil” is more fitting, and this is a genitive in the sense of separation. Here, the root “gam” (to go) is not ditransitive like the root “nī” (to lead), and so on. Therefore, just as one says, “ajaṃ gāmaṃ neti” (he leads the goat to the village), one cannot say, “bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi.” Instead, one should say, “saraṇanti gacchāmi” (I go to it as refuge). Here, the word “iti” is indicated as elided. And this is its meaning: showing that “going” means resorting to or knowing with that intention, he says, “with this intention,” and so on. Therein, in phrases like “I resort,” and so on, each subsequent term is an explanation of the meaning of each preceding one. Or, “resorting” is approaching with the intention of refuge; “serving” is being in close proximity; “attending” is service by performing one’s duties and counter-duties. Thus, in every way, it indicates having no other refuge. How is the meaning “I understand” obtained for the word “gacchāmi” (I go)? He says, “For those who…” and so on.

“Adhigatamagge sacchikatanirodhe”ti padadvayenāpi phalaṭṭhā eva dassitā, na maggaṭṭhāti te dassento “yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne cā”tiādimāha. Nanu ca kalyāṇaputhujjanopi “yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjatī”ti vuccatīti? Kiñcāpi vuccati, nippariyāyena pana maggaṭṭhā eva tathā vattabbā, na itaro niyāmokkamanābhāvato. Tathā hi te eva vuttā “apāyesu apatamāne dhāretī”ti. Sammattaniyāmokkamanena hi apāyavinimuttasambhavo[M 1.0276]. Akkhāyatīti ettha iti-saddo ādiattho, pakārattho vā, tena “yāvatā bhikkhave dhammā saṅkhatā vā asaṅkhatā vā, virāgo tesaṃ aggaṃ akkhāyatī”ti (itivu. 90; a. ni. 4.34) suttapadaṃ saṅgaṇhāti, “vitthāro”ti vā iminā. Ettha ca ariyamaggo niyyānikatāya, nibbānaṃ tassa tadatthasiddhihetutāyāti ubhayameva nippariyāyena “dhammo”ti vutto. Nibbānañhi ārammaṇapaccayabhūtaṃ labhitvā ariyamaggassa tadatthasiddhi. Tathāpi yasmā ariyaphalānaṃ “tāya saddhāya avūpasantāyā”tiādi vacanato maggena samucchinnānaṃ kilesānaṃ paṭipassaddhippahānakiccatāya, niyyānānuguṇatāya, niyyānapariyosānatāya ca, pariyattidhammassa pana “niyyānadhammassa samadhigamanahetutāyā”ti iminā pariyāyena vuttanayena dhammabhāvo labbhati eva. Svāyamattho pāṭhārūḷho evāti dassento “na kevala”ntiādimāha.

“By the two phrases ‘one who has attained the path and realized cessation,’ those standing in the fruit are shown, not those standing in the path.” Pointing this out, he says, “and for one practicing as instructed,” and so on. But is not even a virtuous ordinary person said to be “practicing as instructed”? Although it is said so, in the strict sense, only those standing in the path should be spoken of in that way, not the other, due to the absence of entry into the fixed course of rightness. For they are indeed described thus: “It supports one who is not falling into the planes of misery.” For through entry into the fixed course of rightness, liberation from the planes of misery becomes possible. “It is declared”—here the word “iti” has the meaning of “and so forth” or “in this way.” Thus, it includes the sutta passage: “Monks, of all things conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared the highest” (Itivuttaka 90; Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.34), or by this, it means “in detail.” Here, both the Noble Path, because it leads out, and Nibbāna, because it is the cause for the accomplishment of that purpose for the path, are called “the Dhamma” in the strict sense. For the Noble Path accomplishes its purpose by obtaining Nibbāna, which has become its object-condition. Nevertheless, because for the noble fruits, its nature as Dhamma is indeed obtained by the method stated in this way: “because of the function of tranquillizing-abandonment of the defilements cut off by the path, because of its conduciveness to liberation, and because of its culmination in liberation,” according to such statements as “with that faith not yet stilled,” and for the scriptural Dhamma, “because it is the cause for attaining the liberating Dhamma.” To show that this meaning is established in the text itself, he says, “not only,” and so on.

“Kāmarāgo bhavarāgo”ti evamādi bhedo sabbopi rāgo virajjati etenāti rāgavirāgoti maggo kathito. Ejāsaṅkhātāya [P 1.0359] taṇhāya, antonijjhānalakkhaṇassa sokassa ca taduppattiyaṃ sabbaso parikkhīṇattā anejaṃ asokanti phalaṃ kathitaṃ. Appaṭikūlanti avirodhadīpanato kenaci aviruddhaṃ, iṭṭhaṃ paṇītanti vā attho. Paguṇarūpena pavattitattā, pakaṭṭhaguṇavibhāvanato vā paguṇaṃ. Yathāha “vihiṃsasaññī paguṇaṃ na bhāsiṃ, dhammaṃ paṇītaṃ manujesu brahme”ti. (Ma. ni. 1.283; ma. ni. 2.339; mahāva. 9) sabbadhammakkhandhā kathitāti yojanā.

“Lust for sensual pleasures, lust for existence”—all divisions of lust such as these fade away through this; hence, the path is called ‘the fading away of lust.’ Because of the complete exhaustion of craving, known as ‘agitation,’ and of sorrow, which is characterized by inner burning and arises from that craving, the fruit is called ‘free from agitation and sorrow.’ ‘Not disagreeable’ means not opposed by anyone, because it reveals non-opposition; or its meaning is ‘desirable and sublime.’ It is ‘proficient’ because it proceeds in a proficient manner, or because it makes manifest excellent qualities. As it is said: “With a perception of harming, I did not speak what is proficient; I spoke the Dhamma, sublime among humans, O Brahmā.” (Majjhima Nikāya 1.283; 2.339; Mahāvagga 9). The connection is that all aggregates of the Dhamma have been spoken of.

Diṭṭhisīlasaṅghātenāti “yāyaṃ diṭṭhi ariyā niyyānikā niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāya, tathārūpāya diṭṭhiyā diṭṭhisāmaññagato viharatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.324; ma. ni. 4.92; 3.54) evaṃ vuttāya diṭṭhiyā, “yāni tāni sīlāni akhaṇḍāni acchiddāni asabalāni akammāsāni bhujissāni viññuppasatthāni aparāmaṭṭhāni samādhisaṃvattanikāni[V 1.0245], tathārūpehi sīlehi sīlasāmaññagato viharatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.323; ma. ni. 1.492; 3.54; a. ni. 6.11; pari. 274) evaṃ vuttānaṃ sīlānañca saṃhatabhāvena, diṭṭhisīlasāmaññenāti attho. Saṃhatoti ghaṭito, sametoti attho. Ariyapuggalā hi yattha katthaci dūre ṭhitāpi attano guṇasāmaggiyā saṃhatā eva[M 1.0277]. Aṭṭha ca puggaladhammadasā teti te purisayugavasena cattāropi puggalavasena aṭṭheva ariyadhammassa paccakkhadassāvitāya dhammadasā. Tīṇi vatthūni “saraṇa”nti gamanena, tikkhattuṃ gamanena ca tīṇi saraṇagamanāni. Paṭivedesīti attano hadayagataṃ vācāya pavedesi.

“By the combination of view and virtue” means by the combined state of the view spoken of thus: “That view which is noble, leading out, which leads one who acts upon it to the complete destruction of suffering—with such a view one abides in commonality of view,” and of the virtues spoken of thus: “Those virtues which are unbroken, un-torn, unblemished, un-mottled, liberating, praised by the wise, not clung to, and conducive to concentration—with such virtues one abides in commonality of virtue”; the meaning is by the commonality of view and virtue. “Combined” means joined, united. For noble individuals, even when situated far away, are indeed united by the harmony of their qualities. And the eight individuals who are seers of the Dhamma—that is, those who, whether as four pairs of persons or as eight individuals, are seers of the Dhamma because they see the noble Dhamma directly. By going to the three objects “as refuge,” and by going three times, there are three acts of going for refuge. “He declared” means he made known with speech what was in his heart.

Saraṇagamanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Talk on Going for Refuge

Saraṇagamanassa visayappabhedaphalasaṃkilesabhedānaṃ [P 1.0360] viya kattu ca vibhāvanā tattha kosallāya hotīti “saraṇagamanesu kosallatthaṃ saraṇaṃ…pe… veditabbo”ti vuttaṃ tena vinā saraṇagamanasseva asambhavato. Kasmā panettha vodānaṃ na gahitaṃ, nanu vodānavibhāvanāpi tattha kosallāvahāti? Saccametaṃ, taṃ pana saṃkilesaggahaṇeneva atthato dīpitaṃ hotīti na gahitaṃ. Yāni hi nesaṃ saṃkilesakāraṇāni aññāṇādīni, tesaṃ sabbena sabbaṃ anuppannānaṃ anuppādanena, uppannānañca pahānena vodānaṃ hotīti. Hiṃsatthassa sara-saddassa vasenetaṃ padaṃ daṭṭhabbanti “hiṃsatīti saraṇa”nti vatvā taṃ pana hiṃsanaṃ kesaṃ kathaṃ kassa vāti codanaṃ sodhento “saraṇagatāna”ntiādimāha. Tattha bhayanti vaṭṭabhayaṃ. Santāsanti cittutrāsaṃ teneva cetasikadukkhassa gahitattā. Dukkhanti kāyikadukkhaṃ. Duggatiparikilesanti duggatipariyāpannaṃ sabbampi dukkhaṃ, tayidaṃ sabbaṃ parato phalakathāyaṃ āvibhavissati. Etanti “saraṇa”nti padaṃ.

The analysis of the agent, as well as the distinctions of scope, fruit, and defilement of going for refuge, is for the sake of skill therein. Therefore, it is said, “For the sake of skill in going for refuge, the refuge… should be known,” because without this, going for refuge itself would be impossible. Why, then, is cleansing not included here? Is not the analysis of cleansing also conducive to skill in this matter? This is true, but it is implicitly indicated by the inclusion of defilements, and thus it is not mentioned separately. For cleansing occurs through the complete non-arising of the causes of their defilements—ignorance and so on—that have not yet arisen, and through the abandoning of those that have arisen. This word should be understood in terms of the root ‘sara,’ which has the meaning of harming. Having stated, “It harms, thus it is ‘saraṇa,’” he resolves the objection, “Whom does it harm? How? And for whom?” by stating, “for those who have gone for refuge,” and so on. Herein, ‘bhaya’ means the fear of the round of existence. ‘Santāsa’ means mental dread, and by this, mental suffering is included. ‘Dukkha’ refers to bodily suffering. ‘Duggatiparikilesa’ encompasses all suffering connected with bad destinations; all this will become clear later in the discussion of the fruit. ‘This’ refers to the word ‘saraṇa.’”

Evaṃ avisesato saraṇa-saddassa atthaṃ dassetvā idāni visesato dassetuṃ “atha vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Hite pavattanenāti “sampannasīlā bhikkhave viharathā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.64, 69) atthe niyojanena. Ahitā ca nivattanenāti. “Pāṇātipātassa kho pāpako vipāko, pāpakaṃ abhisamparāya”ntiādinā ādīnavadassanādimukhena anatthato nivattanena. Bhayaṃ hiṃsatīti hitāhitesu appavattipavattihetukaṃ byasanaṃ appavattikaraṇena vināseti. Bhavakantārā uttāraṇena maggasaṅkhāto dhammo, itaro assāsadānena sattānaṃ [P 1.0361] bhayaṃ hiṃsatīti yojanā. Kārānanti dānavasena pūjāvasena ca upanītānaṃ sakkārānaṃ. Vipulaphalapaṭilābhakaraṇena sattānaṃ bhayaṃ hiṃsatīti yojanā, anuttaradakkhiṇeyyabhāvatoti [M 1.0278] adhippāyo. Imināpi pariyāyenāti imināpi vibhajitvā vuttena kāraṇena.

Having thus explained the meaning of the term ‘refuge’ in general, now to explain it in particular, the phrase “or else” and so on is stated. ‘By promoting what is beneficial’ means by enjoining one to the goal with statements like, “Dwell, monks, endowed with virtue.” ‘And by turning away from what is unbeneficial’ means by turning away from what is disadvantageous by means of showing the drawbacks, such as, “The killing of living beings has a bad result, a bad future life.” ‘It harms fear’ means it destroys, by preventing its occurrence, the misfortune caused by non-engagement in what is beneficial and engagement in what is harmful. The Dhamma, designated as the path, harms the fear of beings by leading them across the wilderness of existence; the other [the Saṅgha] does so by giving them assurance. This is the connection. It harms the fear of beings by causing them to attain the abundant fruit of the honors brought to them through giving and reverence. This is the connection. The implication is that this is due to their being an unsurpassed field for offerings. ‘By this method too’ means by this reason, stated through analysis.

“Sammāsambuddho [V 1.0246] bhagavā, svākkhāto dhammo, suppaṭipanno saṅgho”ti evaṃ pavatto tattha ratanattaye pasādo tappasādo, tadeva ratanattayaṃ garu etassāti taggaru tabbhāvo taggarutā, tappasādo ca taggarutā ca tappasādataggarutā, tāhi tappasādataggarutāhi. Vidhūtadiṭṭhivicikicchāsammohaassaddhiyāditāya vihatakileso. Tadeva ratanattayaṃ parāyaṇaṃ parāgati tāṇaṃ leṇanti evaṃ pavattiyā tapparāyaṇatākārappavatto cittuppādo saraṇagamanaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchati etenāti. Taṃsamaṅgīti tena yathāvuttacittuppādena samannāgato. Evaṃ upetīti bhajati sevati payirupāsati, evaṃ vā jānāti bujjhatīti evamattho veditabbo. Ettha ca pasāda-ggahaṇena lokiyasaraṇagamanamāha. Tañhi pasādappadhānaṃ. Garutāgahaṇena lokuttaraṃ. Ariyā hi ratanattayaṃ guṇābhiññatāya pāsāṇacchattaṃ viya garuṃ katvā passanti. Tasmā tappasādena vikkhambhanavasena vigatakileso, taggarutāya samucchedavasenāti yojetabbaṃ agāravakaraṇahetūnaṃ samucchindanato. Tapparāyaṇatā panettha taggatikatāti tāya catubbidhampi vakkhamānaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ gahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Avisesena [P 1.0362] vā pasādagarutā jotitāti pasādaggahaṇena aveccappasādassa itarassa ca gahaṇaṃ, tathā garutāgahaṇenāti ubhayenāpi ubhayaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ yojetabbaṃ.

Faith in the Triple Gem that occurs thus—“The Blessed One is a Fully Enlightened One, the Dhamma is well-expounded, the Saṅgha is of good conduct”—is ‘that faith.’ One for whom that very Triple Gem is weighty is a ‘taggaru’; the state of being such is ‘taggarutā’ (reverence for it). That faith and that reverence together are ‘faith-and-reverence.’ Through that faith-and-reverence, one’s defilements are destroyed, having dispelled wrong view, doubt, delusion, lack of faith, and so on. The arising of mind that proceeds with the characteristic of being devoted to it, occurring thus: ‘That very Triple Gem is the final resort, the supreme goal, the protection, the shelter,’ is ‘going for refuge,’ because one goes for refuge by means of it. ‘Endowed with that’ means possessed of that aforementioned arising of mind. ‘Thus one approaches’ means one resorts to, serves, and attends upon it; or ‘thus one knows, understands’—this is the meaning to be understood. Here, by the inclusion of ‘faith,’ the mundane going for refuge is indicated, for it is primarily based on faith. By the inclusion of ‘reverence,’ the supramundane is indicated. For the noble ones, through direct knowledge of its qualities, regard the Triple Gem as weighty, like a stone umbrella. Therefore, it should be understood that through that faith, one is free from defilements by way of suppression, and through that reverence, by way of eradication, because the causes of irreverence are cut off. Herein, ‘having it as the final resort’ means being dedicated to it; by this, it should be understood that all four types of going for refuge, which will be explained, are included. Alternatively, faith and reverence are illuminated without distinction; thus, by the inclusion of faith, both unwavering faith and the other (mundane faith) are included, and likewise by the inclusion of reverence. Thus, by both, both kinds of going for refuge should be connected.

Maggakkhaṇe ijjhatīti yojanā. “Nibbānārammaṇaṃ hutvā”ti etena atthato catusaccādhigamo eva lokuttarasaraṇagamananti dasseti. Tattha hi nibbānadhammo sacchikiriyābhisamayavasena, maggadhammo bhāvanābhisamayavasena paṭivijjhiyamānoyeva saraṇagamanatthaṃ sādheti. Buddhaguṇā pana sāvakagocarabhūtā pariññābhisamayavasena, tathā ariyasaṅghaguṇā, tenāha “kiccato sakalepi ratanattaye ijjhatī”ti. Ijjhantañca saheva ijjhati, na lokiyaṃ viya patipāṭiyā asammohapaṭivedhena paṭividdhattāti adhippāyo. Ye pana vadanti “na saraṇagamanaṃ nibbānārammaṇaṃ hutvā pavattati. Maggassa adhigatattā pana adhigatameva hoti ekaccānaṃ tevijjādīnaṃ lokiyavijjādayo viyā”ti, tesaṃ lokiyameva saraṇagamanaṃ siyā, na lokuttaraṃ, tañca ayuttaṃ duvidhassāpi icchitabbattā.

It succeeds at the moment of the path—this is the connection. By the phrase, “having Nibbāna as its object,” it shows that in substance the attainment of the Four Truths is itself the supramundane going for refuge. For in this case, only the Dhamma of Nibbāna, being penetrated by way of the comprehension of realization, and the Dhamma of the path, being penetrated by way of the comprehension of development, accomplish the purpose of going for refuge. The qualities of the Buddha, however, being the domain of disciples, are penetrated by way of the comprehension of full understanding, and likewise the qualities of the noble Saṅgha. Therefore, it is said, “In terms of function, it succeeds in the entire Triple Gem.” And when it succeeds, it does so simultaneously, not sequentially as in the mundane case, because it is penetrated with non-deluded penetration—this is the meaning. But as for those who say, “Going for refuge does not occur with Nibbāna as its object. Rather, because the path is attained, it is simply attained, like the mundane knowledges and so on of some who possess the threefold knowledge”—for them, going for refuge would be only mundane, not supramundane. And that is inappropriate, because both kinds are to be desired.

Tanti [M 1.0279] lokiyaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ. Saddhāpaṭilābho “sammāsambuddho bhagavā”tiādinā. Saddhāmūlikāti yathāvuttasaddhāpubbaṅgamā sammādiṭṭhiti buddhasubuddhataṃ, dhammasudhammataṃ, saṅghasuppaṭipattiñca lokiyāvabodhavaseneva sammā ñāyena dassanato. “Saddhāmūlikā sammādiṭṭhī”ti etena saddhūpanissayā yathāvuttalakkhaṇā paññā lokiyasaraṇagamananti dasseti, tenāha “diṭṭhijukammanti vuccatī”ti. Diṭṭhi eva attano paccayehi uju karīyatīti katvā diṭṭhi vā uju karīyati etenāti diṭṭhijukammaṃ, tathā pavatto cittuppādo. Evañca katvā “tapparāyaṇatākārappavatto [V 1.0247] cittuppādo”ti idaṃ vacanaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti. Saddhāpubbaṅgamasammādiṭṭhiggahaṇaṃ pana cittuppādassa [P 1.0363] tappadhānatāyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Saddhāpaṭilābho”ti iminā mātādīhi ussāhitadārakādīnaṃ viya ñāṇavippayuttaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ dasseti, “sammādiṭṭhī”ti iminā ñāṇasampayuttaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ. Tayidaṃ lokiyaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ. Attā sanniyyātīyati appīyati pariccajīyati etenāti attasanniyyātanaṃ, yathāvuttaṃ diṭṭhijukammaṃ. Taṃ ratanattayaṃ parāyaṇaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ etassāti tapparāyaṇo, puggalo, cittuppādo vā. Tassa bhāvo tapparāyaṇatā, yathāvuttaṃ diṭṭhijukammameva. “Saraṇa”nti adhippāyena sissabhāvaṃ antevāsikabhāvaṃ upagacchati etenāti sissabhāvūpagamanaṃ. Saraṇagamanādhippāyeneva paṇipatati etenāti paṇipāto. Sabbattha yathāvuttadiṭṭhijukammavaseneva attho veditabbo.

That is the mundane going for refuge. The acquisition of faith is expressed by such phrases as, “The Blessed One is a Fully Enlightened One.” ‘Rooted in faith’ refers to right view preceded by faith as described, which is the seeing, by right method and through mundane understanding, of the Buddha's perfect enlightenment, the Dhamma's perfect excellence, and the Saṅgha's good practice. By the phrase “right view rooted in faith,” it shows that wisdom, which has faith as its support and possesses the aforementioned characteristics, is the mundane going for refuge. Hence, it is called “the straightening of view.” Because view is made straight by its own conditions, or because view is made straight by this, it is ‘the straightening of view,’ which is an arising of mind that proceeds thus. And in this way, the statement “the arising of mind that proceeds with the characteristic of having that as its final resort” is supported. The inclusion of right view preceded by faith should be understood as due to its predominance in the arising of mind. By “the acquisition of faith,” it indicates a going for refuge dissociated from knowledge, like that of children urged by their mothers. By “right view,” it indicates a going for refuge associated with knowledge. This is the mundane going for refuge. The self is surrendered, offered, and abandoned by this; thus it is ‘self-surrender,’ which is the straightening of view as described. One for whom that Triple Gem is the final resort and refuge is ‘one who has it as final resort,’ whether a person or an arising of mind. The state of being such is ‘having it as final resort,’ which is precisely the straightening of view as described. With the intention of ‘refuge,’ one undertakes the state of a disciple, the state of a pupil, by this; thus it is ‘undertaking discipleship.’ One prostrates by this with the very intention of going for refuge; thus it is ‘prostration.’ In all cases, the meaning should be understood in terms of the straightening of view as described.

Attapariccajananti saṃsāradukkhanittharaṇatthaṃ attano attabhāvassa pariccajanaṃ. Eseva nayo sesesupi. Buddhādīnaṃ yevāti avadhāraṇaṃ attasanniyyātanādīsupi tattha tattha vattabbaṃ. Evañhi tadaññanivattanaṃ kataṃ hoti.

"Self-relinquishment" means the relinquishment of one's own existence for the purpose of crossing over the suffering of saṃsāra. The same method applies in the remaining cases as well. The specification "only of the Buddhas, etc." should be stated in self-surrender and other such instances, wherever relevant. Thus, the exclusion of others is accomplished.

Evaṃ attasanniyyātanādīni ekena pakārena dassetvā idāni aparehipi pakārehi dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi āraddhaṃ, tena pariyāyantarehipi attasanniyyātanādi katameva hoti atthassa abhinnattāti dasseti. Āḷavakādīnanti ādi-saddena sātāgirahemavatādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Nanu cete āḷavakādayo maggeneva āgatasaraṇagamanā, kathaṃ tesaṃ tapparāyaṇatāsaraṇagamanaṃ vuttanti? Maggenāgatasaraṇagamanehipi. “So ahaṃ vicarissāmi…pe… sudhammataṃ” (saṃ. ni. 1.246; su. ni. 194) “te mayaṃ vicarissāma[M 1.0280], gāmā gāmaṃ nagā nagaṃ…pe… sudhammata”nti, (su. ni. 182) tehi [P 1.0364] tapparāyaṇatākārassa paveditattā tathā vuttaṃ.

Having shown self-surrender and other such things in one way, now, to explain them through other methods, the text begins with 'moreover,' indicating that self-surrender and similar practices are indeed accomplished, even when expressed through different modes, due to the non-divergence of meaning. Regarding 'Āḷavakādīnaṃ' (of Āḷavaka and others), by the word 'ādi' (and others), the inclusion of Sātāgira, Hemavata, and others should be understood. But did not these beings, such as Āḷavaka, come to the going for refuge through the path itself? How then is their going for refuge as reliance on him stated? Even though they came to the going for refuge through the path, it is stated thus because they themselves proclaimed their reliance on him in this manner: 'So I will wander... up to the good Dhamma' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.246; Sutta Nipāta 194), and 'We will wander, from village to village, from mountain to mountain... up to the good Dhamma' (Sutta Nipāta 182).

So panesa ñāti…pe… vasenāti ettha ñātivasena, bhayavasena, ācariyavasena, dakkhiṇeyyavasenāti paccekaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Tattha ñātivasenāti ñātibhāvavasena. Evaṃ sesesupi. Dakkhiṇeyyapaṇipātenāti dakkhiṇeyyatāhetukena paṇipātena. Itarehīti ñātibhāvādivasappavattehi tīhi paṇipātehi. “Itarehī”tiādinā saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “tasmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Vandatīti paṇipātassa lakkhaṇavacanaṃ. Evarūpanti diṭṭhadhammikaṃ sandhāya vadati. Samparāyikañhi niyyānikaṃ vā anusāsaniṃ paccāsisanto dakkhiṇeyyapaṇipātameva karotīti adhippāyo.

Here, 'this relative... and so on... by means of'—here, 'by means of kinship,' 'by means of fear,' 'by means of being a teacher,' 'by means of being worthy of offerings'—each should be connected separately. In this context, 'by means of kinship' means by reason of the state of kinship. The same applies to the rest. 'With reverence for one worthy of offerings' means with reverence caused by worthiness of offerings. 'By the others' means by the three reverences arising from kinship, etc. To explain in detail the meaning stated briefly with the phrase 'By the others,' etc., the phrase 'therefore,' etc., is stated. 'Pays homage' is a word describing the characteristic of reverence. 'Of such a kind'—this is said with reference to what is immediately visible. For in regard to the future, one who expects a teaching leading to liberation pays reverence only to one worthy of offerings—this is the meaning.

Saraṇagamanappabhedoti [V 1.0248] saraṇagamanavibhāgo.

The classification of going for refuge is the analysis of going for refuge.

Ariyamaggo eva lokuttaraṃ saraṇagamananti “cattāri sāmaññaphalāni vipākaphala”nti vuttaṃ. Sabbadukkhakkhayoti sakalassa vaṭṭadukkhassa anuppādanirodho. Etanti “cattāri ariyasaccāni, sammappaññāya passatī”ti evaṃ vuttaṃ ariyasaccassa dassanaṃ.

The noble path is indeed the supramundane going for refuge, as it is said, 'The four fruits of recluseship are the fruits of result.' The cessation of all suffering means the non-arising and cessation of all suffering of the round of existence. This is as stated, 'One sees the four Noble Truths with right wisdom'—thus, the seeing of the Noble Truths is described.

Niccādito anupagamanādivasenāti “nicca”nti aggahaṇādivasena. Aṭṭhānanti hetupaṭikkhepo. Anavakāsoti paccayapaṭikkhepo. Ubhayenāpi kāraṇameva paṭikkhipati. Yanti yena kāraṇena. Diṭṭhisampannoti maggadiṭṭhiyā samannāgato sotāpanno. Kañci saṅkhāranti catubhūmakesu saṅkhatasaṅkhāresu ekasaṅkhārampi. Niccato upagaccheyyāti “nicco”ti gaṇheyya. “Sukhato upagaccheyyā”ti. “Ekantasukhī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā”ti (dī. ni. 1.76) evaṃ attadiṭṭhivasena sukhato gāhaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ[P 1.0365]. Diṭṭhivippayuttacittena pana ariyasāvako pariḷāhavūpasamanatthaṃ mattahatthiparittāsito viya cokkhabrāhmaṇo ukkārabhūmiṃ kañci saṅkhāraṃ sukhato upagacchati. Attavāre kasiṇādipaññattisaṅgahatthaṃ “saṅkhāra”nti avatvā “kañci dhamma”nti vuttaṃ. Imesupi vāresu catubhūmakavaseneva paricchedo veditabbo, tebhūmakavaseneva vā. Yaṃ yañhi puthujjano gāhavasena gaṇhāti, tato tato ariyasāvako gāhaṃ viniveṭheti.

'By way of non-approach to the permanent, etc.' means by way of not grasping as 'permanent,' etc. 'Impossible' refers to the rejection of a cause. 'No opportunity' refers to the rejection of a condition. In both cases, it rejects the cause itself. 'By which' means by which cause. 'Endowed with right view' means a stream-enterer endowed with the vision of the path. 'Any conditioned thing' refers to even a single conditioned formation among the conditioned formations in the four planes of existence. 'Would approach as permanent' means he would grasp it as 'permanent.' 'Would approach as pleasurable.' This is said with reference to grasping as pleasurable through the self-view, thinking, 'The self is entirely happy, free from illness after death' (Dīgha Nikāya 1.76). However, with a mind free from wrong view, a noble disciple, for the sake of calming torment, might approach some formation as pleasurable—like the Brahmin Cokkha, frightened by a rogue elephant, who sought refuge in a dung heap. In the section on self, instead of saying 'formations,' to include kasiṇa concepts, it is said 'any phenomenon.' In these sections as well, the distinction should be understood either in terms of the four planes of existence or the three planes of existence. For whatever the ordinary person grasps with clinging, the noble disciple disentangles himself from that very clinging.

“Mātara”ntiādīsu [M 1.0281] janikā mātā, janako pitā, manussabhūto khīṇāsavo arahāti adhippeto. Kiṃ pana ariyasāvako aññaṃ jīvitā voropeyyāti? Etampi aṭṭhānaṃ, puthujjanabhāvassa pana mahāsāvajjabhāvadassanatthaṃ, ariyasāvakassa ca phaladassanatthaṃ evaṃ vuttaṃ. Duṭṭhacittoti vadhakacittena paduṭṭhacitto. Lohitaṃ uppādeyyāti jīvamānakasarīre khuddakamakkhikāya pivanamattampi lohitaṃ uppādeyya. Saṅghaṃ bhindeyyāti samānasaṃvāsakaṃ samānasīmāyaṃ ṭhitaṃ saṅghaṃ. “Kammena, uddesena, voharanto, anussāvanena, salākaggāhenā”ti (pari. 458) evaṃ vuttehi pañcahi kāraṇehi bhindeyya. Aññaṃ satthāranti aññaṃ titthakaraṃ “ayaṃ me satthā”ti evaṃ gaṇheyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatīti attho. Na te gamissanti apāyabhūminti te buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gatā taṃnimittaṃ apāyaṃ na gamissanti, devakāyaṃ pana paripūressantīti attho.

In the phrase 'mother,' etc., the mother is the one who gives birth; the father is the one who begets; and a human arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, is intended. But would a noble disciple deprive another of life? This too is impossible. However, it is stated thus to show the grave blameworthiness of the state of an ordinary person and to illustrate the fruit for a noble disciple. 'With a corrupt mind' means with a mind corrupted by the intent to kill. 'Cause blood to flow' means causing even the slightest amount of blood to flow from a living body, even so much as a tiny fly might drink. 'Split the Saṅgha' means dividing a Saṅgha that shares the same residence and stands within the same boundary, through five means: by action, by recitation, by declaration, by announcement, or by ballot—as stated (in the Parivāra, 458). 'Follow another teacher' means accepting another sectarian teacher, thinking, 'This is my teacher.' Such a thing is not possible—this is the meaning. 'They will not go to the realms of suffering'—those who have gone to the Buddha for refuge will not, because of that, go to the realms of suffering. Instead, they will fill the divine realm—this is the meaning.

Dasahi ṭhānehīti dasahi kāraṇehi. Adhigaṇhantīti abhibhavanti. Velāmasuttādivasenāpīti ettha karīsassa catutthabhāgappamāṇānaṃ caturāsītisahassasaṅkhyānaṃ suvaṇṇapātirūpiyapātikaṃsapātīnaṃ [V 1.0249] yathākkamaṃ rūpiyasuvaṇṇahiraññapūrānaṃ, sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitānaṃ caturāsītiyā [P 1.0366] hatthisahassānaṃ, caturāsītiyā assasahassānaṃ, caturāsītiyā rathasahassānaṃ, caturāsītiyā dhenusahassānaṃ, caturāsītiyā kaññāsahassānaṃ, caturāsītiyā pallaṅkasahassānaṃ, caturāsītiyā vatthakoṭisahassānaṃ, aparimāṇassa ca khajjabhojjādibhedassa āhārassa pariccajanavasena sattamāsādhikāni sattasaṃvaccharāni nirantaraṃ pavattavelāmamahādānato ekassa sotāpannassa dinnadānaṃ mahapphalataraṃ, tato sataṃ sotāpannānaṃ dinnadānato ekassa sakadāgāmino, tato ekassa anāgāmino, tato ekassa arahato, tato ekassa paccekabuddhassa, tato sammāsambuddhassa, tato buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa dinnadānaṃ mahapphalataraṃ, tato cātuddisasaṅghaṃ uddissa vihārakaraṇaṃ, tato saraṇagamanaṃ mahapphalataranti imamatthaṃ pakāsentassa velāmasuttassa (a. ni. 9.20) vasena. Vuttañhetaṃ “yaṃ gahapati velāmo brāhmaṇo dānaṃ adāsi mahādānaṃ, yo cekaṃ diṭṭhisampannaṃ bhojeyya, idaṃ tato mahapphalatara”ntiādi [M 1.0282] (a. ni. 9.20). Velāmasuttādīti ādisaddena aggappasādasuttādīnaṃ (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90) saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

"By ten reasons" means by ten causes. "Overpower" means to dominate. "As in the Velāma Sutta and so forth"—here, from the great gift of Velāma, which was continuously given for seven years and seven months by relinquishing eighty-four thousand vessels of gold, silver, and bronze, each measuring a quarter-karīsa and filled respectively with silver, gold, and bullion; eighty-four thousand elephants, eighty-four thousand horses, eighty-four thousand chariots, eighty-four thousand cows, eighty-four thousand maidens, eighty-four thousand couches, all adorned with every ornament; eighty-four thousand crores of cloths; and immeasurable quantities of various foods such as hard and soft food—the gift given to a single stream-enterer is of greater fruit. Still more fruitful than a gift given to a hundred stream-enterers is a gift given to a single once-returner; still more fruitful than that, a gift given to a single non-returner; still more fruitful than that, a gift given to a single arahant; still more fruitful than that, a gift given to a single Paccekabuddha; still more fruitful than that, a gift given to a Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha; still more fruitful than that, a gift given to the Sangha headed by the Buddha; still more fruitful than that, building a monastery dedicated to the Sangha of the four directions; still more fruitful than that, taking refuge—this meaning is explained in the Velāma Sutta (Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.20). For it is said: "Householder, the great gift given by the brahmin Velāma—if one were to feed a single person accomplished in right view, this would be of far greater fruit than that," and so on (Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.20). "Velāma Sutta and so forth"—by the word "and so forth," the Aggappasāda Sutta (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.34; Itivuttaka 90) and so forth should be understood as included.

Aññāṇaṃ vatthuttayassa guṇānaṃ ajānanaṃ, tattha sammoho. “Buddho nu kho, na nu kho”tiādinā vicikicchā saṃsayo. Micchāñāṇaṃ tassa guṇānaṃ aguṇabhāvaparikappanena viparītaggāho. Ādi-saddena anādarāgāravādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Na mahājutikanti na ujjalaṃ, aparisuddhaṃ apariyodātanti attho. Na mahāvipphāranti anuḷāraṃ. Sāvajjoti taṇhādiṭṭhādivasena sadoso, lokiyasaraṇagamanaṃ sikkhāsamādānaṃ viya aggahitakālaparicchedaṃ jīvitapariyantameva hoti, tasmā tassa khandhabhedena bhedoti āha “anavajjo kālakiriyāyā”ti. Soti anavajjo saraṇagamanabhedo. Satipi anavajjatte iṭṭhaphalopi na [P 1.0367] hotīti āha “aphalo”ti. Kasmā? Avipākattā. Na hi taṃ akusalanti.

Ignorance is not knowing the qualities of the Triple Gem; delusion is confusion therein. 'Doubt' is uncertainty, such as thinking, 'Is it the Buddha or not?' and so forth. 'Wrong knowledge' is a distorted grasping, imagining those qualities to be without merit. By the word 'and so forth,' disrespect, irreverence, and so on are included. 'Not greatly luminous' means not bright, impure, and unpurified—this is the meaning. 'Not greatly radiant' means not magnificent. 'Faulty' means flawed due to craving, wrong view, and so forth. Worldly going for refuge, like the undertaking of training rules without a fixed time limit, lasts only until the end of life; therefore, its breaking occurs with the breaking of the aggregates. Thus it is said to be 'faultless at the time of death.' That refers to the faultless breaking of the going for refuge. Even though it is faultless, it does not have the desired fruit; thus it is said, 'fruitless.' Why? Because it is without result. For it is not unwholesome.

Ko upāsakoti sarūpapucchā, kiṃlakkhaṇo upāsakoti vuttaṃ hoti. Kasmāti hetupucchā, tena kena pavattinimittena upāsaka-saddo tasmiṃ puggale nirūḷhoti dasseti, tenāha “kasmā upāsakoti vuccatī”ti. Saddassa abhidheyye pavattinimittaṃ tadatthassa tabbhāvakāraṇaṃ. Kimassa sīlanti kīdisaṃ assa upāsakassa sīlaṃ, kittakena sīlenāyaṃ sīlasampanno nāma hotīti attho. Ko ājīvoti ko assa sammāājīvo, so pana micchājīvassa parivajjanena hotīti sopi vibhajīyati. Kā vipattīti kā assa sīlassa, ājīvassa [V 1.0250] vā vipatti. Anantarassa hi vidhi vā paṭisedho vā. Sampattīti etthāpi eseva nayo.

'Who is a lay follower?' This is a question about his nature, meaning what are the characteristics of a lay follower. 'Why?' This is a question about cause, meaning by what instigating cause is the term 'lay follower' established for that person. Therefore, it is said, 'Why is one called a lay follower?' The instigating cause of a word's application to its referent is the cause of that meaning's being so. 'What is his morality?' What kind of morality does this lay follower have? By how much morality is one called accomplished in morality? This is the meaning. 'What is his livelihood?' What is his right livelihood? This, however, occurs by avoiding wrong livelihood; this too is analyzed. 'What is failure?' What failure can befall his morality or livelihood? For of what immediately follows, there is either a prescription or a prohibition. 'What is attainment?' Here too, the same method applies.

Yo kocīti khattiyādīsu yo koci, tena saraṇagamanaṃ evaṃ kāraṇaṃ, na jāti ādivisesoti dasseti.

'Whoever it may be' means whoever it may be among Khattiyas and so forth. By this, it is shown that the going for refuge itself is the reason, not distinctions such as birth and so forth.

Upāsanatoti teneva saraṇagamanena, tattha ca sakkaccakiriyāya ādara gāravabahumānādiyogena payirupāsanato.

'By attending upon' means by that very going for refuge, and by attending upon it with diligent performance, by applying respect, reverence, high esteem, and so forth.

Veramaṇiyoti [M 1.0283] veraṃ vuccati pāṇātipātādidussīlyaṃ, tassa maṇanato hananato vināsanato veramaṇiyo, pañca viratiyo viratipadhānattā tassa sīlassa, tenevāha “paṭivirato hotī”ti.

'Abstinence' (veramaṇī) is so called because 'enmity' (vera) is said to be immoral conduct such as killing living beings and so forth, and because it measures, strikes down, and destroys that enmity. The five abstinences are so called because that morality has restraint as its primary factor. Therefore, it is said: 'He abstains.'

Micchāvaṇijjāti na sammāvaṇijjā ayuttavaṇijjā asāruppavaṇijjā. Pahāyāti akaraṇeneva pajahitvā. Dhammenāti dhammato anapetena, tena aññampi adhammikaṃ jīvikaṃ paṭikkhipati. Samenāti avisamena, tena kāyavisaṃ ādiduccaritaṃ vajjetvā kāyasamādinā sucaritena jīvikaṃ dasseti. Satthavaṇijjāti āvudhabhaṇḍaṃ katvā [P 1.0368] vā kāretvā vā yathākataṃ vā paṭilabhitvā tassa vikkayo. Sattavaṇijjāti manussavikkayo. Maṃsavaṇijjāti sūnakārādayo viya migasūkarādike posetvā maṃsaṃ sampādetvā vikkayo. Majjavaṇijjāti yaṃ kiñci majjaṃ yojetvā tassa vikkayo. Visavaṇijjāti visaṃ yojetvā vā visaṃ gahetvā vā tassa vikkayo. Tattha satthavaṇijjā paroparodhanimittatāya akaraṇīyā vuttā sattavaṇijjā abhujissabhāvakaraṇato, maṃsavaṇijjā vadhahetuto, majjavaṇijjā pamādaṭṭhānato.

'Wrong trade' means not right trade, improper trade, unsuitable trade. 'Having abandoned' means to abandon by not doing it. 'Righteously' means by means of what is righteous, without deviating from the Dhamma; thereby, one also rejects any other unrighteous means of living. 'Justly' means without injustice; thereby, avoiding bodily crookedness and so forth, one shows a livelihood by means of bodily rectitude and good conduct. 'Trade in weapons' means making or having weapons made, or acquiring weapons already made, and selling them. 'Trade in beings' means selling human beings. 'Trade in meat' means raising animals such as deer and pigs, like butchers and so forth, producing meat, and selling it. 'Trade in intoxicants' means preparing any intoxicant and selling it. 'Trade in poisons' means preparing or obtaining poison and selling it. Here, trade in weapons is said to be something not to be done because it is a cause for harming others; trade in beings, because it causes a state of non-freedom; trade in meat, because it is a cause for killing; trade in intoxicants, because it is a basis for heedlessness.

Tassevāti pañcaveramaṇilakkhaṇassa sīlassa ceva pañcamicchāvaṇijjālakkhaṇassa ājīvassa ca. Vipattīti bhedo, pakopo ca. Yāyāti yāya paṭipattiyā. Caṇḍāloti upāsakacaṇḍālo. Malanti upāsakamalaṃ. Paṭikiṭṭhoti upāsakanihīno. Buddhādīsu kammakammaphalesu ca saddhāvipariyāyo assaddhiyaṃ micchādhimokkho, yathāvuttena assaddhiyena samannāgato assaddho. Yathāvuttasīlavipattiājīvavipattivasena dussīlo. “Iminā diṭṭhādinā idaṃ nāma maṅgalaṃ hotī”ti evaṃ bālajanaparikappitakotūhalasaṅkhātena diṭṭhasutamutamaṅgalena samannāgato kotūhalamaṅgaliko. Maṅgalaṃ paccetīti diṭṭhamaṅgalādibhedaṃ maṅgalameva pattiyāyati. No kammanti [V 1.0251] kammassakataṃ no pattiyāyati. Ito ca bahiddhāti ito sabbaññubuddhasāsanato bahiddhā bāhirakasamaye. Dakkhiṇeyyaṃ pariyesatīti duppaṭipannaṃ dakkhiṇārahasaññī gavesati. Pubbakāraṃ karotīti dānamānaṃ ādikaṃ kusalakiriyaṃ paṭhamataraṃ karoti. Ettha ca dakkhiṇeyyapariyesanapubbakāre ekaṃ katvā pañca dhammā veditabbā.

'Of that very one' refers to the morality characterized by the five abstinences and the livelihood characterized by the five wrong trades. 'Failure' means breach and corruption. 'By which' means by which practice. 'Outcaste' refers to a lay follower who is an outcaste. 'Stain' means the stain of a lay follower. 'Despicable' means a low lay follower. The perversion of faith in the Buddha and so forth, and in kamma and its results, is faithlessness—wrong resolve. One endowed with such faithlessness is faithless. One is immoral due to the failure of virtue and livelihood as described. 'By this seen thing and so forth, this is indeed auspicious'—thus, one endowed with the auspicious signs of what is seen, heard, and thought, which are called 'curiosity' and are devised by foolish people, is one who relies on curious omens. 'He relies on omens' means he relies only on omens of the type of what is seen and so forth. 'Not on kamma' means he does not rely on the ownership of kamma. 'Outside of this' means outside the dispensation of the Omniscient Buddha, in external doctrines. 'He seeks those worthy of offerings' means he searches for those of wrong practice, considering them worthy of offerings. 'He performs a prior act' means he first engages in acts of merit like giving, honor, and so forth. Here, taking the seeking of those worthy of offerings and the performing of a prior act as one, five qualities should be understood.

Vipattiyaṃ vuttavipariyāyena sampatti veditabbā. Ayaṃ pana viseso – catunnampi parisānaṃ ratijananaṭṭhena upāsakova ratanaṃ upāsakaratanaṃ. Guṇasobhākittisaddasugandhatāya [M 1.0284][P 1.0369] upāsakova padumaṃ upāsakapadumaṃ. Tathā upāsakapuṇḍarīkaṃ.

Success should be understood as the opposite of what has been said concerning failure. Here, however, is the distinction: the lay follower is a jewel—the lay follower-jewel—because he generates delight in all four assemblies. The lay follower is a lotus—the lay follower-lotus—because of the splendor of his virtues, his fame, his reputation, and his sweet fragrance. Similarly, the lay follower is the white lotus.

Ādimhītiādiatthe. Koṭiyanti pariyantakoṭiyaṃ. Vihāraggenāti ovarakakoṭṭhāsena, “imasmiṃ gabbhe vasantānamidaṃ nāma panasaphalaṃ pāpuṇātī”tiādinā taṃ taṃvasanaṭṭhānakoṭṭhāsenāti attho. Ajjatagganti vā ajjadagganti vā ajja icceva attho.

'In the beginning' means in the sense of the beginning. 'At the limit' means at the final limit. 'At the head of the monastery' means by the portion of the private chamber; the meaning is by the respective dwelling portions, as in, 'those dwelling in this chamber will receive such-and-such jackfruit,' and so forth. 'Ajjatagge' or 'ajjadagge' simply means 'today.'

“Pāṇehi upeta”nti iminā tassa saraṇagamanassa āpāṇakoṭikataṃ dassento “yāva me jīvitaṃ pavattatī”tiādīni vatvā puna jīvitenāpi taṃ vatthuttayaṃ paṭipūjento “saraṇagamanaṃ rakkhāmī”ti uppannaṃ tassa rañño adhippāyaṃ vibhāvento “ahañhī”tiādimāha.
