Pāṇehi upetanti hi yāva me pāṇā dharanti, tāva saraṇaṃ upetaṃ, upento ca na vācāmattena, na ekavāraṃ cittuppādamattena, atha kho pāṇānaṃ pariccajanavasena yāvajīvaṃ upetanti evamettha attho veditabbo.

By this phrase, 'endowed with life,' showing that his going for refuge extends to the limit of his life, having said, 'as long as my life lasts,' and so forth, and then honoring that Triple Gem even with his life, he reveals the intention of that king, which had arisen, that 'I will protect the going for refuge.' Thus, he says, 'For I,' and so forth. 'Endowed with life' means that for as long as my life endures, refuge is undertaken; and in undertaking it, it is not merely by words, not merely by a single moment of thought, but it is undertaken lifelong by way of sacrificing one's life. This is how the meaning should be understood here.

Accayanaṃ sādhumariyādaṃ madditvā vītikkamanaṃ accayoti āha “aparādho”ti. Acceti atikkamati etenāti vā accayo, vītikkamassa pavattanako akusaladhammo. So eva aparajjhati etenāti aparādho. So hi aparajjhantaṃ purisaṃ abhibhavitvā pavattati, tenāha “atikkamma abhibhavitvā pavatto”ti. Caratīti ācarati karoti. Dhammenevāti dhammato anapetena payogena. Paṭiggaṇhātūti adhivāsanavasena sampaṭicchatūti atthoti āha “khamatū”ti.

'Transgression' (accaya) is overstepping, having crushed the good custom; therefore, it is called 'offense' (aparādho). Or, 'accaya' is that by which one oversteps or transgresses; it is the unwholesome state that causes transgression to occur. That very thing is an 'offense' because one offends by it. For it arises having overpowered the person who offends; therefore, it is said, 'It arises having transgressed and overpowered.' 'Carati' means to act or to do. 'Dhammena eva' means by means of an application not deviating from the Dhamma. 'Paṭiggaṇhātu' means 'may he consent by way of forbearance.' Thus, it is said, 'May he forgive.'

251. Sadevakena lokena “saraṇa”nti araṇīyato ariyo, tathāgatoti āha “ariyassa vinaye buddhassa bhagavato sāsane”ti. Puggalādhiṭṭhānaṃ karontoti kāmaṃ “vuddhi hesā”ti [V 1.0252] dhammādhiṭṭhānavasena vākyaṃ āraddhaṃ, tathāpi desanaṃ [P 1.0370] pana puggalādhiṭṭhānaṃ karonto saṃvaraṃ āpajjatīti āhāti yojanā.

251. By the world with its gods, the noble one is called 'refuge' because he is one to be gone to. Thus, it is said concerning the Tathāgata: 'in the discipline of the noble one, in the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One.' Although the statement was begun with the Dhamma as its basis, thinking, 'This is progress,' nevertheless, in teaching, if one makes a person the basis, one incurs partiality—this is the explanation.

253. Imasmiṃyeva attabhāve nippajjanakānaṃ attano kusalamūlānaṃ khaṇanena khato, tesaṃyeva upahananena upahato. Ubhayenāpi tassa kammāparādhameva vadati. Patiṭṭhāti sammattaniyāmokkamanaṃ etāyāti [M 1.0285] patiṭṭhā, tassa upanissayasampadā. Sā kiriyāparādhena bhinnā vināsitā etenāti bhinnapatiṭṭho, tenāha “tathā”tiādi. Dhammesu cakkhunti catusaccadhammesu tesaṃ dassanaṭṭhena cakkhu. Aññesu ṭhānesūti aññesu suttapadesu. Muccissatīti saṭṭhi vassasahassāni paccitvā lohakumbhī narakato muccissati.

253. In this very existence, one is wounded by the digging up of one's own wholesome roots that arise, and injured by the striking of those same roots. In both ways, it speaks only of the fault of one's actions. 'Establishment' (patiṭṭhā) is that by which one enters the fixed course of rightness; it is the perfection of supporting conditions. That establishment is broken and ruined by the fault of action—thus, he is called 'one with a broken establishment.' Therefore, it is said: 'Thus...' and so on. 'An eye in the Dhamma' means an eye for the Four Noble Truths, in the sense of seeing them. 'In other cases' refers to other passages in the Suttas. 'He will be freed' means that after being tormented for sixty thousand years, he will be liberated from the Lohakumbhī hell.

Yadi anantare attabhāve narake paccati, imaṃ pana suttaṃ sutvā rañño ko ānisaṃso laddhoti āha “mahānisaṃso”tiādi. So pana ānisaṃso niddālābhasīsena vutto tadā kāyikacetasikadukkhāpagamo, tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ mahāsakkārakiriyā, sātisayo pothujjanikasaddhāpaṭilābhoti evaṃpakāro diṭṭhadhammiko, samparāyiko pana aparāparesupi bhavesu aparimāṇo yevāti veditabbo.

If, in the immediately following existence, one is tormented in hell, what benefit did the king gain by hearing this sutta? It is said, 'Great benefit,' and so on. That benefit, however, is stated under the heading of 'the gain of sleep': the removal of physical and mental suffering at that time, the performance of great honor to the Three Jewels, and the surpassing acquisition of faith by an ordinary person. This kind of benefit is visible in this very life, while the benefit pertaining to the future is to be understood as truly immeasurable in subsequent existences.

Etthāha – yadi rañño kammantarāyābhāve tasmiṃyeva āsane dhammacakkhu uppajjissati, kathaṃ anāgate paccekabuddho hutvā parinibbāyissati. Atha [P 1.0371] paccekabuddho hutvā parinibbāyissati, kathaṃ tadā dhammacakkhuṃ uppajjissati, nanu ime sāvakabodhipaccekabodhiupanissayā bhinnanissayāti? Nāyaṃ virodho ito parato evassa paccekabodhisambhārānaṃ sambharaṇīyato. Sāvakabodhiyā bujjhanakasattāpi hi asati tassā samavāye kālantare paccekabodhiyā bujjhissanti katābhinīhārasambhavato. Apare pana bhaṇanti “paccekabodhiyā yevāyaṃ katābhinīhāro. Katābhinīhārāpi hi tattha niyatiṃ appattā tassa ñāṇassa paripākaṃ anupagatattā satthu sammukhībhāve sāvakabodhiṃ pāpuṇissantīti bhagavā ‘sacāyaṃ bhikkhave rājā’tiādimāha. Mahābodhisattānameva ca ānantariyaparimutti, na itarabodhisattānaṃ. Tathā hi paccekabodhiyaṃ niyato samāno devadatto cirakālasambhūtena lokanāthe āghātena garutarāni ānantariyāni pasavi, tasmā kammantarāyenāyaṃ idāni asamavetadassanābhisamayo rājā paccekabodhiniyāmena anāgate paccekabuddho hutvā parinibbāyissatī”ti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here it is said: If, in the absence of a karmic obstruction, the Dhamma-eye would have arisen for the king on that very seat, how will he, in the future, become a Paccekabuddha and attain Parinibbāna? And if he is to become a Paccekabuddha and attain Parinibbāna, how could the Dhamma-eye have arisen for him then? Are not the supporting conditions for a disciple's awakening and a Paccekabuddha's awakening different conditions? There is no contradiction here, because from this point on he had to accumulate the requisites for Paccekabuddha-awakening. For even beings who would awaken with a disciple's awakening, in the absence of the right conditions for it, will in another time awaken with a Paccekabuddha's awakening, due to the possibility of having made an aspiration. Others, however, say: 'This one had made an aspiration for Paccekabuddha-awakening itself. For even those who have made such an aspiration, not having reached certainty in that path, because their knowledge has not yet reached maturity, may attain a disciple's awakening in the presence of a Teacher.' Thus the Blessed One said, 'If, monks, this king…' and so on. Moreover, only Great Bodhisattas are exempt from the consequences of an immediately effective karma, not other Bodhisattas. For example, Devadatta, though fixed in the path of a Paccekabuddha, produced very grave immediately effective karmas through a long-held grudge against the Lord of the World. Therefore, due to a karmic obstruction, this king, not having attained the realization of the vision now, will in the future, by the fixed course of a Paccekabuddha, become a Paccekabuddha and attain Parinibbāna.' This should be understood.

Sāmaññaphalasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

The Elucidation of Hidden Meanings in the Commentary on the Sāmaññaphala Sutta.

3. Ambaṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Ambaṭṭha Sutta.

Addhānagamanavaṇṇanā

Commentary on Journeying.

254. Apubbapadavaṇṇanāti [V 1.0253][M 1.0286][P 1.0372] atthasaṃvaṇṇanāvasena heṭṭhā aggahitatāya apubbassa padassa vaṇṇanā atthavibhajanā. “Hitvā punappunāgatamattha”nti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.ganthārambhakathā) hi vuttaṃ. Janapadinoti janapadavanto, janapadassa vā issarā rājakumārā gottavasena kosalā nāma. Yadi eko janapado, kathaṃ bahuvacananti āha “rūḷhisaddenā”ti. Akkharacintakā hi īdisesu ṭhānesu yutte viya īdisaliṅgavacanāni icchanti, ayamettha rūḷhi yathā aññatthapi “kurūsu viharati, aṅgesu viharatī”ti ca. Tabbisesanepi janapada-sadde jāti-sadde ekavacanameva. Porāṇā panāti pana-saddo visesatthajotano, tena puthuatthavisayatāya evañcetaṃ puthuvacananti vakkhamānavisesaṃ joteti. Bahuppabhedo hi so padeso tiyojanasataparimāṇatāya. Naṅgalānipi chaḍḍetvāti kammappahānavasena naṅgalānipi pahāya, nidassanamattañcetaṃ. Na kevalaṃ kassakā eva, atha kho aññepi manussā attano attano kiccaṃ pahāya tattha sannipatiṃsu. “So padeso”ti padesasāmaññato vuttaṃ, vacanavipallāsena vā, te padesāti attho. Kosalāti vuccati kusalā eva kosalāti katvā.

254. 'The explanation of an unprecedented word' is an analysis of meaning, an explanation of a word not previously grasped, by way of a detailed explanation of its meaning. For it is said: 'Having abandoned the meaning that has come again and again.' 'Janapadino' means those possessing a country, or the princes who are lords of the country, known by their clan name as Kosalans. If it is one country, why the plural? To this, it is said: 'By conventional usage.' For grammarians, in such cases, accept such genders and numbers as proper. This is the convention here, just as elsewhere it is said, 'He dwells among the Kurus,' and 'He dwells among the Angas.' Even when it is a qualifier, the word 'janapada' and the word 'jāti' are in the singular. 'But the ancients'—here the word 'pana' indicates a specific point. It indicates the specific point to be explained next, namely that this plural form is used because the subject matter has diverse aspects. For that region was of many kinds, being three hundred yojanas in extent. 'Even abandoning their plows' means having abandoned their plows in the sense of giving up their work; and this is just an example. Not only the farmers, but other people too, abandoning their own duties, gathered there. 'That region'—this is said in a general sense, or it is a change of number; the meaning is 'those regions.' 'Kosalans' is said, taking it as 'they are indeed skilled (kusalā).'

Cārikanti caraṇaṃ, caraṇaṃ vā cāro, so eva cārikā. Tayidaṃ maggagamanaṃ idhādhippetaṃ, na cuṇṇikagamanamattanti āha “addhānagamanaṃ gacchanto”ti. Taṃ vibhāgena dassetuṃ “cārikā ca nāmesā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha dūrepīti nātidūrepi. Sahasā gamananti [P 1.0373] sīghagamanaṃ. Mahākassapapaccuggamanādiṃ ekadesena vatvā vanavāsītissasāmaṇerassa vatthuṃ vitthāretvā janapadacārikaṃ kathetuṃ “bhagavā hī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Ākāsagāmīhi eva saddhiṃ gantukāmo “chaḷabhiññānaṃ ārocehī”ti āha.

'Wandering' (cārikā) means walking (caraṇaṃ). Or, walking is a journey (cāro), and that itself is wandering (cārikā). Here, journeying on a path is intended, not merely walking a short distance. Thus it is said, 'traveling a long journey.' To explain this in detail, it is stated, 'This is called wandering...' and so on. Therein, 'even from afar' means even from not too far. 'Going suddenly' means going quickly. After stating in brief Mahākassapa's going to meet him and so on, the story of the novice Tissa, the forest-dweller, is elaborated. Then, to speak about the journey through the country, it begins, 'For the Blessed One...' and so on. Wishing to go only with those who could travel through the sky, he said, 'Inform those with the six supernormal powers.'

Saṅghakammavasena [V 1.0254][M 1.0287] sijjhamānāpi upasampadā satthu āṇāvaseneva sijjhanato “buddhadāyajjaṃ te dassāmī”ti vuttanti vadanti. Apare pana aparipuṇṇavīsativassasseva tassa upasampadaṃ anujānanto “dassāmī”ti avocāti vadanti. Upasampādetvāti dhammasenāpatinā upajjhāyena upasampādetvā.

They say that although ordination is accomplished by means of an act of the Sangha, because it is accomplished only by the Teacher's command, it was said, 'I will give you the Buddha's heritage.' Others, however, say that, permitting ordination for him even though he had not completed twenty years, he said, 'I will give it.' 'Having ordained' means having had him ordained with the Commander of the Dhamma as preceptor.

Navayojanasatikampi ṭhānaṃ majjhimadesapariyāpannameva, tato paraṃ nādhippetaṃ turitacārikāvasena agamanato. Samantāti gatagataṭṭhānassa catūsu passesu samantato. Aññenapi kāraṇenāti bhikkhūnaṃ samathavipassanātaruṇabhāvato aññenapi majjhimamaṇḍale veneyyānaṃ ñāṇaparipākādikāraṇena majjhimamaṇḍalaṃ osarati. “Sattahi vā”tiādi “ekamāsaṃ vā”tiādinā vuttānukkamena yojetabbaṃ.

A distance of even nine hundred yojanas is still included within the Middle Country; beyond that is not intended, as it cannot be reached by a swift journey. 'All around' means on all four sides of whatever place has been reached. 'By another reason' means that besides the monks' immaturity in tranquility and insight, he enters the Middle Country for another reason, such as the ripening of knowledge of those to be trained there. 'Seven or...' and so on should be connected with the sequence stated in 'one month or...' and so on.

Sarīraphāsukatthāyāti ekasmiṃyeva ṭhāne nibaddhavāsavasena ussannadhātukassa sarīrassa vicaraṇena phāsukatthāya. Aṭṭhuppattikālābhikaṅkhanatthāyāti aggikkhandhopamasutta (a. ni. 7.72) maghadevajātakādi (jā. 1.1.9) desanānaṃ viya dhammadesanāya aṭṭhuppattikālaṃ ākaṅkhamānena. Surāpānasikkhāpadapaññāpane (pāci. 328) viya sikkhāpadapaññāpanatthāya. Bodhaneyyasatte aṅgulimālādike (ma. ni. 2.347) bodhanatthāya. Kañci, katipaye vā puggale uddissa cārikā nibaddhacārikā. Tadaññā anibaddhacārikā.

'For the sake of bodily comfort' means for the comfort of a body whose elements have become excessive due to fixed residence in a single place, by wandering. 'For the sake of desiring an occasion for a teaching to arise' means by one desiring an occasion for the arising of a Dhamma teaching, like the teachings of the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta (A.N. 7.72), the Maghadeva Jātaka (Jā. 1.1.9), and so on. 'For the sake of laying down a training rule,' as in the laying down of the training rule on drinking intoxicants (Pāc. 51). 'For the sake of awakening beings to be awakened,' like Aṅgulimāla and others (M.N. 86). A journey undertaken for the sake of a certain person or a few individuals is a fixed journey. Other than that is an unfixed journey.

Dasasahassi lokadhātuyāti [P 1.0374] jātikhettabhūte dasasahassacakkavāḷe. Tattha hi satte paripakkindriye passituṃ buddhañāṇaṃ abhinīharitvā ṭhito bhagavā ñāṇajālaṃ pattharatīti vuccati. Sabbaññutaññāṇajālassa anto paviṭṭhoti tassa ñāṇassa gocarabhāvaṃ upagato. Bhagavā kira mahākaruṇāsamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā tato vuṭṭhāya “ye sattā bhabbā paripākañāṇā ajja mayā vinetabbā, te mayhaṃ ñāṇassa upaṭṭhahantū”ti cittaṃ adhiṭṭhāya samannāharati. Tassa saha samannāhārā eko vā dve vā bahū vā tadā vinayūpagā veneyyā ñāṇassa āpāthamāgacchanti ayamettha buddhānubhāvo. Evampi āpāthamāgatānaṃ pana nesaṃ upanissayaṃ pubbacariyaṃ pubbahetuṃ sampati vattamānañca paṭipattiṃ [M 1.0288] oloketi, tenāha “atha bhagavā”tiādi. Vādapaṭivādaṃ katvāti “evaṃ nu te ambaṭṭhā”tiādinā mayā vuttavacanassa “ye ca kho te bho gotama muṇḍakā samaṇakā”tiādinā paṭivacanaṃ katvā tikkhattuṃ ibbhavādanipātanavasena nānappakāraṃ asambhivākyaṃ sādhusabhāvāya vācāya vattuṃ ayuttavacanaṃ vakkhati. Nibbisevananti vigatatudanaṃ, mānadabbavasena apagataparipphandananti attho.

'In the ten-thousandfold world system' means in the ten-thousandfold universe, which has become the birth-field. For it is said that there the Blessed One, having directed his Buddha-knowledge to see beings with mature faculties, stands and spreads the net of knowledge. 'He has entered within the net of all-knowing knowledge' means he has come into the range of that knowledge. Indeed, the Blessed One, having entered the attainment of great compassion and emerged from it, adverts, resolving his mind: 'May those beings who are capable, whose knowledge is mature, and who are to be trained by me today, present themselves to my knowledge.' As soon as he adverts, one, two, or many teachable persons fit for training come into the range of his knowledge—this here is the Buddha's power. But even for those who have thus come into range, he examines their supporting conditions, past conduct, previous causes, and their present practice. Therefore, it is said: 'Then the Blessed One...' 'Having engaged in speech and counter-speech' means that to the words spoken by me, beginning with, 'Is it so, Ambaṭṭha?', he, having made a reply beginning with, 'But those, Venerable Gotama, who are shaven-headed ascetics...', will, by way of uttering the speech of menials three times, speak various incoherent words, speech unsuitable to be uttered with well-mannered speech. 'Without resentment' means without piercing; that is, devoid of agitation by way of the substance of conceit.

Avasaritabbanti [V 1.0255] upagantabbaṃ. Icchānaṅgaleti idaṃ tadā bhagavato gocaragāmanidassanaṃ samīpatthe bhummanti katvā. “Icchānaṅgalavanasaṇḍe”ti nivāsanaṭṭhānadassanaṃ adhikaraṇe bhummanti. Tadubhayaṃ vivaranto “icchānaṅgalaṃ upanissāyā”tiādimāha. Dhammarājassa bhagavato sabbaso adhammaniggaṇhanaparā paṭipatti, sā ca sīlasamādhipaññāvasenāti taṃ dassetuṃ “sīlakhandhāvāra”ntiādi [P 1.0375] vuttaṃ. Yathābhirucitenāti dibbavihārādīsu yena yena attano abhirucitena vihārena.

“Avasaritabbaṃ” means “it should be approached” or “it should be frequented.” “Icchānaṅgale” here indicates the Blessed One’s pointing out a village for alms, taking it as a locative in the sense of proximity. “In the woodland of Icchānaṅgala” shows the dwelling place, taking it as a locative in the sense of location. Explaining both, he said, “depending on Icchānaṅgala,” and so forth. The practice of the Blessed One, the King of Dhamma, is entirely devoted to suppressing what is not the Dhamma, and that is by way of virtue, concentration, and wisdom; to indicate this, “the encampment of the aggregate of virtue,” and so forth, is stated. “As one pleases” means by whatever dwelling one finds agreeable, such as divine abodes, and so forth.

Pokkharasātivatthuvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of Pokkharasāti.

255. Manteti irubbedādimantasatthe. Pokkhare kamale sayamāno nisīdīti pokkharasātī. Sāti vuccati samasaṇṭhānaṃ, pokkhare saṇṭhānāvayave jātoti “pokkharasātī”tipi vuccati. Setapokkharasadisoti setapadumavaṇṇo. Suvaṭṭitāti vaṭṭabhāvassa yuttaṭṭhāne suṭṭhu vaṭṭulā. Kāḷavaṅgatilakādīnaṃ abhāvena suparisuddhā.

255. “Manteti” refers to the mantra-treatises beginning with the Ṛgveda. “Pokkharasātī” is so called because 'he lies or sits on a lotus (pokkhare).' “Sāti” is said to mean “well-proportioned form”; and because he was born with limbs in the shape of a lotus, he is also called “Pokkharasātī.” “Similar to a white lotus” means “having the color of a white lotus.” “Well-rounded” means “perfectly circular in a place suitable for roundness.” “Extremely pure” means due to the absence of dark moles, spots, and the like.

Imassa brāhmaṇassa kīdiso pubbayogo, yena naṃ bhagavā anuggaṇhituṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ upagatoti āha “ayaṃ panā”tiādi. Padumagabbhe nibbatti tenāyaṃ saṃsedajo jāto. Na pupphatīti na vikasati. Rajatabimbakanti rūpiyamayaṃ rūpakaṃ.

To explain what past connection of this brahmin led the Blessed One to approach that place to favor him, it is said, “Now this,” and so forth. “Born in a lotus calyx” means he was born from moisture. “Does not bloom” means “it does not open.” “Rajatabimbakaṃ” means “a silver image.”

Ajjhāvasatīti ettha adhi-saddo issariyatthadīpano, āsaddo mariyādatthoti dassento “abhibhavitvā”tiādimāha. Tehi yuttattā hi ukkaṭṭhanti upayogavacanaṃ, tenāha “upasaggavasenā”tiādi. Yāya mariyādāyāti yāya avatthāya. Nagarassa vatthunti “ayaṃ khaṇo, sumuhuttaṃ mā atikkamī”ti rattivibhāyanaṃ anurakkhantā rattiyaṃ ukkā [M 1.0289] ṭhapetvā ukkāsu jalamānāsu nagarassa vatthuṃ aggahesuṃ, tasmā ukkāsu ṭhitāti ukkaṭṭhā, ukkāsu vijjotayantīsu ṭhitā patiṭṭhitāti mūlavibhujādipakkhepena saddasiddhi veditabbā, niruttinayena vā ukkāsu ṭhitāsu ṭhitā āsīti ukkaṭṭhā. Apare pana bhaṇanti “bhūmibhāgasampattiyā, upakaraṇasampattiyā, manussasampattiyā ca taṃ nagaraṃ ukkaṭṭhaguṇayogato ukkaṭṭhāti nāmaṃ labhī”ti[P 1.0376]. Tassāti “ukkaṭṭha”nti upayogavasena vuttapadassa. Anupayogattāti visesanabhāvena anupayuttattā. Sesapadesūti “sattussada”ntiādipadesu. Yathāvidhi hi anupayogo purimasmiṃ. Tatthāti “upasaggavasenā”tiādinā vuttavidhāne. “Saddasatthato pariyesitabba”nti etena saddalakkhaṇānugato [V 1.0256] vāyaṃ saddappayogoti dasseti. Upaanuadhiāitievaṃpubbake vasanakiriyāṭhāne upayogavacanameva pāpuṇātīti saddavidū icchanti.

Regarding 'ajjhāvasati' (he dwells): here, the prefix 'adhi-' indicates the sense of lordship, while the prefix 'ā-' indicates the sense of boundary; showing this, the text says 'having mastered,' and so forth. Indeed, because of its connection with them, 'ukkaṭṭha' is a word of application; hence, it is said, 'by means of the prefix,' and so forth. 'By which boundary' means 'by which condition.' Regarding 'the site of the city': those who guarded the division of the night, saying, 'This is the moment, do not let the auspicious moment pass,' placed torches at night. While the torches were burning, they took the site of the city. Therefore, 'standing (ṭhitā) by the torches (ukkāsu)' is Ukkaṭṭhā. Alternatively, the word-formation should be understood by the analysis of roots and so on as: 'established, standing while the torches were blazing.' Or, by the method of etymology, 'it was standing while the torches were standing' is Ukkaṭṭhā. Others, however, say: 'That city acquired the name "Ukkaṭṭhā" from its connection with exalted qualities, by virtue of the excellence of its land, the excellence of its resources, and the excellence of its people.' 'Of that' refers to the word 'ukkaṭṭha' as stated in the sense of application. 'Because it is not applied' means 'because it is not used as a qualifier.' 'In the remaining phrases' refers to phrases like 'sattussada' (crowded), and so forth. For in the former case, the non-application is according to the method. 'There' refers to the method stated beginning with 'by means of the prefix,' and so forth. By the phrase 'one should investigate according to the science of language,' it is shown that this usage of the word follows the characteristics of language. Those skilled in grammar hold that in the context of the action of dwelling preceded by prefixes such as upa-, anu-, adhi-, ā-, and so on, it only takes on the sense of application.

Ussadatā nāmettha bahulatāti, taṃ bahulataṃ dassetuṃ “bahujana”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Gahetvā posetabbaṃ posāvaniyaṃ. Āvijjhitvāti parikkhipitvā.

Here, “ussadatā” means “abundance”; to show that abundance, “bahujana” (many people) and so forth is stated. “Posāvaniyaṃ” means “it should be taken and nurtured.” “Āvijjhitvā” means “having encompassed.”

Raññā viya bhuñjitabbanti vā rājabhoggaṃ. Rañño dāyabhūtanti kulaparamparāya yogyabhāvena rājato laddhadāyabhūtaṃ. Tenāha “dāyajjanti attho”ti. Rājanīhārena paribhuñjitabbato uddhaṃ paribhogalābhassa seṭṭhadeyyatā nāma natthīti āha “chattaṃ ussāpetvā rājasaṅkhepena bhuñjitabba”nti. “Sabbaṃ chejjabhejja”nti sarīradaṇḍadhanadaṇḍādi bhedaṃ sabbaṃ daṇḍamāha. Nadītitthapabbatādīsūti nadītitthapabbatapādagāmadvāraaṭavimukhādīsu. “Rājadāya”nti imināva rañño dinnabhāve siddhe “raññā pasenadinā kosalena dinna”nti vacanaṃ kimatthiyanti āha “dāyakarājadīpanattha”ntiādi[P 1.0377]. Nissaṭṭhapariccattanti muttacāgavasena pariccattaṃ katvā. Evañhi taṃ seṭṭhadeyyaṃ uttamadeyyaṃ jātaṃ.

“A royal possession” means “it should be enjoyed like a king.” “The king’s inheritance” means “an inheritance received from the king by virtue of its suitability through family lineage.” Hence, he said, “It means an inheritance.” Since there is no superior form of gift of enjoyment beyond that to be enjoyed in the manner of a king, he said, “One should enjoy it with the royal umbrella raised, in the summary manner of a king.” “Everything subject to being cut or broken” refers to all kinds of punishment, such as bodily punishment, financial punishment, and so forth. “At river fords, mountains, etc.” means “at river fords, mountains, the foot of mountains, village gates, forest entrances, and so forth.” “The king’s gift”: Since the fact that it was given by the king is already established by this, what is the purpose of the statement “given by King Pasenadi of Kosala”? He said, “To indicate the king who is the giver,” and so forth. “Completely released and relinquished” means “having relinquished it by way of a free letting go.” Thus, it becomes the foremost gift, the supreme gift.

Upalabhīti savanavasena upalabhīti imamatthaṃ dassento “sotadvāra…pe… aññāsī”ti āha. Avadhāraṇaphalattā sabbampi vākyaṃ antogadhāvadhāraṇanti āha “padapūraṇamatte nipāto”ti. “Avadhāraṇatthe”ti pana iminā iṭṭhatovadhāraṇatthaṃ kho-saddaggahaṇanti dasseti[M 1.0290]. “Assosī”ti padaṃ kho-sadde gahite tena phullitamaṇḍitaṃ viya hontaṃ pūritaṃ nāma hoti, tena ca purimapacchimapadāni siliṭṭhāni honti, na tasmiṃ aggahiteti āha “padapūraṇena byañjanasiliṭṭhatāmattamevā”ti. Matta-saddo visesanivattiattho, tenassa anatthantaradīpanatā dassitā hoti, eva-saddena pana byañjanasiliṭṭhatāya ekantikatā.

“Upalabhī” (he perceived): To show that this means “he perceived by way of hearing,” it is said, “through the ear-door… he understood.” Because the entire sentence has emphasis as its result, the whole statement contains an implicit emphasis; thus, it is said, “the particle is merely a word-filler.” But with the phrase “in the sense of determination,” he indicates that the word ‘kho’ is taken for the sake of desired emphasis. The word “assosi” (he heard), when the word ‘kho’ is taken, becomes as if blossomed and adorned by it, and thus the preceding and following words are smoothly connected; this does not happen if ‘kho’ is not taken. Therefore, it is said, “only the smoothness of the expression by filling the word.” The word ‘matta’ (only) has the meaning of excluding a specification, thus showing that it does not indicate a different meaning. And by the word ‘eva’ (indeed), the smoothness of the expression is made absolute.

Samitapāpattāti accantaṃ anavasesato savāsanaṃ samitapāpattā. Evañhi bāhirakavirāgasekkhāsekkhapāpasamanato bhagavato pāpasamanaṃ visesitaṃ hoti, tenāha vuttañhetantiādi. Anekatthattā nipātānaṃ idha anussavattho adhippetoti āha “khalūti anussavatthe nipāto”ti. Ālapanamattanti piyālāpavacanamattaṃ. Piyasamudāhāro hete “bho”ti vā “āvuso”ti vā “devānaṃ piyā”ti vā. Gottavasenāti ettha gaṃ tāyatīti gottaṃ. Gotamoti hi pavattamānaṃ vacanaṃ, buddhiñca tāyati ekaṃsikavisayatāya rakkhatīti gottaṃ. Yathā hi buddhi ārammaṇabhūtena [P 1.0378] atthena vinā na vattati, evaṃ abhidhānaṃ abhidheyyabhūtena, tasmā [V 1.0257] so gottasaṅkhāto attho tāni tāyati rakkhatīti vuccati. Ko pana soti? Aññakulaparamparāsādhāraṇaṃ tassa kulassa ādipurisasamudāgataṃ taṃkulapariyāpannasādhāraṇaṃ sāmaññarūpanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ettha ca “samaṇo”ti iminā sarikkhakajanehi bhagavato bahumatabhāvo dassito samitapāpatākittanato. “Gotamo”ti iminā lokiyajanehi uḷārakulasambhūtatādīpanato.

Having stilled evil (Samitapāpattā) means having stilled evil completely and entirely, without remainder, along with its latent tendencies. Thus, the Blessed One’s stilling of evil is distinguished from the stilling of evil by outsiders devoid of passion, trainees, and those beyond training; therefore, it is said, beginning with, 'For this was said.' Because particles have multiple meanings, here the intended meaning is that of report; therefore, it is said, 'khalu is a particle in the sense of report.' Merely a term of address (Ālapanamattaṃ) means merely a term of affectionate address. For these are affectionate forms of address: 'bho,' 'āvuso,' or 'devānaṃ piyā.' By way of clan (Gottavasenā): here, 'gotta' is 'it protects the line' (gaṃ tāyatīti gottaṃ). For 'Gotama' is a current term, and 'gotta' also protects understanding by guarding it in its exclusive domain. For just as understanding does not operate without a meaning that has become its object, so a designation does not operate without what is designated. Therefore that meaning, called 'gotta,' is said to protect and guard them. But what is that? It should be seen as the general form, common to the succession of the family, originating from the first ancestor of that family, shared by and included in that family. And here, by 'recluse,' the Blessed One’s state of being highly esteemed by similar people is shown by the proclamation of his having stilled evil; by 'Gotama,' his birth in a noble family is indicated to worldly people.

Uccākulaparidīpanaṃ uditoditavipulakhattiyakulavibhāvanato. Sabbakhattiyānañhi ādibhūtamahāsammatamahārājato paṭṭhāya asambhinnaṃ uḷāratamaṃ sakyarājakulaṃ. Kenaci pārijuññenāti ñātipārijuññabhogapārijuññādinā kenaci pārijuññena pārihāniyā. Anabhibhūto anajjhotthato. Tathā hi tassa kulassa na kiñci pārijuññaṃ lokanāthassa abhijātiyaṃ, atha kho vaḍḍhiyeva. Abhinikkhamane ca tatopi samiddhatamabhāvo loke pākaṭo paññāto. Iti “sakyakulā pabbajito”ti idaṃ vacanaṃ bhagavato saddhāpabbajitabhāvadīpanaṃ vuttaṃ mahantaṃ ñātiparivaṭṭaṃ, mahantañca bhogakkhandhaṃ pahāya pabbajitabhāvasiddhito. Sundaranti bhaddakaṃ. Bhaddakatā ca passantassa hitasukhāvahabhāvena veditabbāti āha [M 1.0291] atthāvahaṃ sukhāvahanti. Tattha atthāvahanti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthasaṃhitahitāvahaṃ. Sukhāvahanti yathāvuttatividhasukhāvahaṃ. Tathārūpānanti tādisānaṃ. Yādisehi pana guṇehi bhagavā samannāgato, tehi catuppamāṇikassa lokassa sabbathāpi accantāya saddhāya pasādanīyo tesaṃ yathābhūtasabhāvattāti dassento yathārūpotiādimāha. Tattha yathābhūtaṃ…pe… [P 1.0379] arahatanti iminā dhammappamāṇānaṃ, lūkhappamāṇānañca sattānaṃ bhagavato pasādāvahataṃ dasseti. Taṃ dassaneneva ca itaresampi atthato pasādāvahatā dassitā hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ tadavinābhāvato. Dassanamattampi sādhu hotīti ettha kosiyasakuṇavatthuṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.144; khu. pā. aṭṭha. 10) kathetabbaṃ.

The illumination of the highest lineage is due to the flourishing and extensive development of the warrior clan. For the Sakyan royal lineage, beginning with the primordial great elected king Mahāsammata, is unbroken and most illustrious among all warrior clans. 'By any loss' means by any decline, such as loss of relatives, loss of wealth, and so forth. Unconquered, unassailed. Indeed, there was no loss whatsoever for that lineage in the noble birth of the Lord of the World; rather, there was only increase. And at his renunciation, a state of prosperity even greater than that became manifest and known in the world. Thus, the phrase 'gone forth from the Sakyan clan' is stated to indicate the Blessed One’s state of having gone forth out of faith, by virtue of the fact that he went forth having abandoned a vast retinue of relatives and an immense mass of wealth. 'Beautiful' means excellent. And its excellence should be understood by the observer as bringing benefit and happiness; hence, it is said, 'bringing benefit, bringing happiness.' Here, 'bringing benefit' refers to bringing benefit conducive to the good in this life, the next life, and the ultimate good. 'Bringing happiness' refers to bringing the threefold happiness as previously described. 'Of such qualities' means of such a kind. To demonstrate that the Blessed One is endowed with such qualities by which he is entirely worthy of the unwavering faith and confidence of the world of beings with its four standards, due to the true nature of those qualities, he said, 'as he truly is,' and so forth. Here, with 'as he truly is… the Arahant,' he shows how the Blessed One inspires faith in beings who measure by the Dhamma and those who measure by coarse standards. And by merely seeing him, the fact that he inspires faith in others is also shown in essence, because it is inseparable from that. 'Merely seeing him is beneficial': Here, the story of the Kosiyan bird (Majjhima Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 1.144; Khuddaka Pāṭha Aṭṭhakathā 10) should be recounted.

Ambaṭṭhamāṇavakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse to the Young Brahmin Ambaṭṭha.

256. Mante parivattetīti vede sajjhāyati, pariyāpuṇātīti attho. Mante dhāretīti yathāadhīte mante asammuṭṭhe katvā hadaye ṭhapeti oṭṭhapahatakaraṇavasena, na atthavibhāvanavasena.

256. 'He recites the mantras' means he studies the Vedas, that is, he learns them thoroughly. 'He retains the mantras' means he keeps the mantras as they were learned, unforgotten, in his heart by means of oral recitation, not by way of understanding their meaning.

Sanighaṇḍukeṭubhānanti ettha vacanīyavācakabhāvena atthaṃ saddañca nikhaḍati bhindati vibhajja dassetīti nikhaṇḍu, sā eva idha kha-kārassa gha-kāraṃ katvā “nighaṇḍū”ti vutto. Kiṭayati [V 1.0258] gameti ñāpeti kiriyādivibhāgaṃ, taṃ vā anavasesapariyādānato gamento pūretīti keṭubhaṃ. Vevacanappakāsakanti pariyāyasaddadīpakaṃ, ekekassa atthassa anekapariyāyavacanavibhāvakanti attho. Nidassanamattañcetaṃ anekesampi atthānaṃ ekasaddavacanīyatāvibhāvanavasenapi tassa ganthassa pavattattā. Vacībhedādilakkhaṇā kiriyā kappīyati etenāti kiriyākappo, so pana vaṇṇapadasambandhapadatthādivibhāgato bahuvikappoti āha “kiriyākappavikappo”ti. Idañca mūlakiriyākappaganthaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. So hi satasahassaparimāṇo nayacariyādipakaraṇaṃ. Ṭhānakaraṇādivibhāgato[P 1.0380], nibbacanavibhāgato ca akkharā pabhedīyanti etehīti akkharappabhedā, sikkhāniruttiyo. Etesanti vedānaṃ.

In the term 'Sanighaṇḍukeṭubhāna,' here, because it discerns, breaks down, and explains both meaning and sound by means of the relationship of the expressed and the expressing, it is called 'nikhaṇḍu'; and here, by changing the 'kha' sound to 'gha,' it is referred to as 'nighaṇḍu.' It signifies, makes known, and explains the divisions of actions, etc., or it fulfills by completely covering and signifying—hence, 'keṭubha.' As a revealer of synonyms, it illuminates synonymous terms, meaning it clarifies the many synonymous expressions for each meaning. This is merely an example, since that text proceeds also by way of showing how many meanings can be expressed by a single word. Action characterized by variations in speech is classified by this—hence, 'kiriyākappa'; however, due to its many variations—such as classifications of phonemes, words, their connections, and meanings—it is called 'kiriyākappavikappo.' This is said in reference to the root text on grammatical rules, which consists of a hundred thousand measures and includes treatises on conduct, etc. Letters are distinguished by divisions such as place of articulation, manner of articulation, etc., and by phonetic analysis—hence, 'akkharappabhedā,' which are phonetics and etymology. These belong to the Vedas.

Te [M 1.0292] eva vede padaso kāyatīti padako. Taṃ taṃ saddaṃ tadatthañca byākaroti byācikkhati etenāti byākaraṇaṃ, saddasatthaṃ. Āyatiṃ hitaṃ tena loko na yatati na īhatīti lokāyataṃ. Tañhi ganthaṃ nissāya sattā puññakiriyāya cittampi na uppādenti.

He is called a 'padako' because he recites those very Vedas word by word. It is called 'byākaraṇa' because it explains and elucidates each word and its meaning—this is grammar. The world does not strive or exert itself for future welfare through that—this is 'lokāyata.' Indeed, relying on that text, beings do not even generate a mind for meritorious deeds.

Vayatīti vayo, ādimajjhapariyosānesu katthaci aparikilamanto avitthāyanto te ganthe sandhāreti pūretīti attho. Dve paṭisedhā pakatiṃ gamentīti dassento “avayo na hotī”ti vatvā tattha avayaṃ dassetuṃ “avayo nāma…pe… na sakkotī”ti vuttaṃ. “Anuññāto”ti padassa kammasādhanavasena, “paṭiññāto”ti pana padassa kattusādhanavasena attho veditabboti dassento “ācariyenā”tiādimāha. Ācariyaparamparābhataṃ ācariyakaṃ. Garūti bhāriyaṃ attānaṃ tato mocetvā gamanaṃ dukkaraṃ hoti. Anatthopi uppajjati nindābyārosaupārambhādi.

'It decays,' thus 'vayo' (decay). The meaning of 'avayo' (without decay) is that he sustains and fulfills those texts without wearing out or being destroyed at any point—beginning, middle, or end. To show that two negations imply the original state, after the statement 'he is not without decay,' to then illustrate what decay is, it is said: 'Decay means… he cannot.' To show that the word 'anuññāto' should be understood in the sense of the passive construction, and the word 'paṭiññāto' in the sense of the active construction, it is said: 'by the teacher,' etc. What is brought in the lineage of teachers is called 'ācariyakaṃ' (the teacher's tradition). 'Garu' means weighty; it is difficult to go after freeing oneself from that. Harm also arises—blame, denunciation, disparagement, and the like.

257. “Abbhuggato”ti ettha abhisaddayogena itthambhūtākhyānatthavaseneva upayogavacanaṃ.

257. Here, in the word 'Abbhuggato,' the usage is in the sense of describing a particular state, due to its connection with the prefix 'abhi'.

258. Lakkhaṇānīti lakkhaṇadīpanāni mantapadāni. Antaradhāyantīti na kevalaṃ lakkhaṇamantāniyeva, atha kho aññānipi brāhmaṇānaṃ ñāṇabalābhāvena anukkamena antaradhāyanti. Tathā hi vadanti “ekasataṃ addhariyaṃ sākhā sahassavattako sāmā”tiādi. Paṇidhi [P 1.0381] …pe… mahatoti ettha paṇidhimahato samādānamahatoti ādinā paccekaṃ mahanta-saddo yojetabbo. Paṇidhimahantatādi cassa buddhavaṃsacariyāpiṭakavaṇṇanādivasena veditabbo. Niṭṭhāti nipphattiyo. Bhavabhedeti bhavavisese. Ito ca etto ca byāpetvā ṭhitatā visaṭabhāvo.

258. 'Lakkhaṇāni' (the marks) means the mantra words that reveal the marks. 'They disappear'—not only the mantras of the marks, but also other things of the brahmins gradually vanish due to the lack of the power of their knowledge. For they say, 'One hundred Addhariya branches, the Sāma with a thousand recitations,' and so on. 'Aspiration... great'—here, the word 'great' should be connected separately to 'great aspiration,' 'great undertaking,' and so on. The greatness of his aspiration, etc., should be understood by way of the commentaries on the Buddhavamsa, the Cariyapitaka, and so on. 'Niṭṭhā' (completion) means fulfilments. 'In a type of existence' (Bhavabhede) means in a particular existence. 'The state of pervading here and there' means the state of being spread out.

Jātisāmaññatoti lakkhaṇajātiyā lakkhaṇabhāvamattena samānabhāvato. Yathā hi buddhānaṃ lakkhaṇāni [V 1.0259] suvisadāni, suparibyattāni, paripuṇṇāni ca honti, na evaṃ cakkavattīnaṃ, tenāha “na teheva buddho hotī”ti. Abhirūpatā, dīghāyukatā, appātaṅkatā, brāhmaṇādīnaṃ piyamanāpatāti imehi catūhi acchariyasabhāvehi. Dānaṃ, piyavacanaṃ, atthacariyā, samānattatāti [M 1.0293] imehi catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi. Rañjanatoti pītijananato. Cakkaṃ cakkaratanaṃ vatteti pavattetīti cakkavattī. Sampatticakkehi sayaṃ vattati, tehi ca paraṃ sattanikāyaṃ vatteti pavattetīti cakkavattī. Parahitāvaho iriyāpathacakkānaṃ vatto vattanaṃ etassa, etthāti vā cakkavattī. Appaṭihataṃ vā āṇāsaṅkhātaṃ cakkaṃ vattetīti cakkavattī. Khattiyamaṇḍalādisaññitaṃ cakkaṃ samūhaṃ attano vase vattetīti cakkavattī cakkavattivattasaṅkhātaṃ dhammaṃ carati, cakkavattivattasaṅkhāto dhammo etasmiṃ atthīti vā dhammiko. Dhammato anapetattā dhammo rañjanaṭṭhena rājāti dhammarājā. “Rājā hoti cakkavattī”ti vuttattā “cāturanto”ti padaṃ catudīpissarataṃ vibhāvetīti āha “catusamuddaantāyā”tiādi. Tattha “catuddīpavibhūsitāyā”ti avatvā “catubbidhā”ti vidhaggahaṇaṃ taṃtaṃparittadīpānampi saṅgahatthanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kopādīti [P 1.0382] ādi-saddena kāmamohamānamadādike saṅgaṇhāti. Vijitāvīti vijitavā. Kenaci akampiyaṭṭhena janapade thāvariyappatto, daḷhabhattibhāvato vā, janapado thāvariyaṃ patto etthāti janapadatthāvariyappatto.

‘By commonality of birth’ means due to the state of being equal merely by being of the class of marks, by the nature of the marks. For just as the marks of the Buddhas are very clear, very distinct, and complete, not so for the wheel-turning monarchs—hence it is said, ‘He is not a Buddha because of those marks.’ By these four marvelous qualities: handsomeness, long life, freedom from illness, and being dear and beloved to brahmins and others. By these four bases of beneficence: generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality. ‘Delighting’ means generating joy. He turns the wheel, the wheel-treasure—thus he is a wheel-turning monarch. He himself proceeds by the wheels of prosperity, and by them he causes the multitude of beings to proceed—thus he is a wheel-turning monarch. Or, a wheel-turner is one for whom the turning of the wheels of the postures brings the welfare of others, or in whom this exists—thus, a wheel-turning monarch. Or, he turns the unopposed wheel known as command—thus he is a wheel-turning monarch. Or, he turns the wheel, the assembly designated as the circle of khattiyas and others, under his control—thus he is a wheel-turning monarch. He practices the Dhamma known as the wheel-turning monarch’s duty, or the Dhamma known as the wheel-turning monarch’s duty exists in him—thus he is righteous. Because he is not devoid of Dhamma, and because he is a king who delights by means of Dhamma, he is a righteous king. Since it is said, ‘He becomes a wheel-turning monarch,’ the phrase ‘possessor of the four quarters’ explains sovereignty over the four continents—hence it is said, ‘bounded by the four oceans,’ and so on. There, instead of saying ‘adorned with the four continents,’ the use of the term ‘fourfold’ should be seen as intending to include even the various minor continents. ‘Anger, etc.’—by the word ‘etc.,’ desire, delusion, pride, intoxication, and the like are included. ‘Victorious’ means one who has conquered. ‘Having attained steadfastness in the country’—unshakable in the country by anyone, or because of firm allegiance, the country has attained steadfastness in him—thus, ‘having attained steadfastness in the country.’

Cittīkatabhāvādināpi (khu. pā. aṭṭha. 3; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.33; su. ni. aṭṭha. 1.226; mahāni. aṭṭha. 50) cakkassa ratanaṭṭho veditabbo. Esa nayo sesesupi. Ratinimittatāya vā cittīkatādibhāvassa ratijananaṭṭhena ekasaṅgahatāya visuṃ aggahaṇaṃ. Imehi pana ratanehi rājā cakkavattī yaṃ yamatthaṃ paccanubhoti, taṃ taṃ dassetuṃ “imesu panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ajitaṃ jināti mahesakkhatāsaṃvattaniyakammanissandabhāvato. Vijite yathāsukhaṃ anuvicarati hatthiratanaṃ assaratanañca abhiruhitvā tesaṃ ānubhāvena antopātarāseyeva samuddapariyantaṃ pathaviṃ anusaṃyāyitvā rājadhānimeva paccāgamanato. Pariṇāyakaratanena vijitamanurakkhati tena tattha tattha kātabbakiccassa saṃvidhānato. Avasesehīti maṇiratanaitthiratanagahapatiratanehi. Tattha maṇiratanena yojanappamāṇe padese andhakāraṃ vidhamitvā ālokadassanādinā sukhamanubhavati, itthiratanena atikkantamānusakarūpasampattidassanādivasena, gahapatiratanena icchiticchitamaṇikanakarajatādidhanapaṭilābhavasena.

The quality of a treasure should be understood from the wheel’s being prized, and so on. This is the method for the rest as well. Or, since the state of being prized, etc., is a cause of delight, it is not mentioned separately, being included under the single meaning of ‘generating delight’. To show what purpose the wheel-turning monarch experiences with these treasures, it is said, ‘among these,’ and so on. He conquers the unconquered because it is the result of karma conducive to great power. In his conquered territory, he roams at will, having mounted the elephant-treasure and the horse-treasure. By their power, within the time of a morning meal, he travels the earth up to the ocean’s edge and returns to the capital itself. He protects his conquered territory with the counselor-treasure, by its arrangement of the duties to be performed in various places. By the remaining treasures are meant the gem-treasure, the woman-treasure, and the householder-treasure. Among these, with the gem-treasure, he dispels darkness over an area of a yojana and enjoys happiness by seeing light, and so on. With the woman-treasure, he experiences delight by seeing her attainment of beauty surpassing that of humans. With the householder-treasure, he obtains desired wealth such as gems, gold, and silver.

Ussāhasattiyogo [M 1.0294] tena kenaci appaṭihatāṇācakkabhāvasiddhito pacchimenāti pariṇāyakaratanena. Tañhi sabbarājakiccesu kusalaṃ avirajjhanayogaṃ, tenāha “mantasattiyogo”ti[V 1.0260]. Hatthiassaratanānaṃ mahānubhāvatāya kosasampattiyāpi pabhāvasampattisiddhito [P 1.0383] “hatthi…pe… yogo”ti vuttaṃ. (Koso hi nāma sati ussāhasampattiyaṃ duggaṃ tejaṃ kusumoraṃ parakkamaṃ pabbatomukhaṃ amosapaharaṇaṃ) tividhasattiyogaphalaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ hotīti sambandho. Sesehīti sesehi pañcahi ratanehi.

The connection with the power of exertion is through the last, that is, the counselor-treasure, because through it the state of an unopposed wheel of command is achieved by him. For it is skilled in all royal duties, its method unfailing; therefore, it is called ‘the connection with the power of counsel.’ Due to the great power of the elephant and horse treasures, and also through the attainment of wealth, the attainment of splendor is achieved—hence it is said ‘the connection with elephants…and so on.’ (For wealth, indeed, when accompanied by the attainment of exertion, is a fortress, splendor, a flower-garland, effort, a mountain-face, an unfailing weapon.) The complete fruit of the connection with the threefold power is thereby achieved—this is the connection. ‘With the rest’ means with the remaining five treasures.

Adosakusalamūlajanitakammānubhāvenāti adosasaṅkhātena kusalamūlena sahajātādipaccayavasena uppāditakammassa ānubhāvena sampajjanti sommatararatanajātikattā. Majjhimāni maṇiitthigahapatiratanāni. Alobha…pe… kammānubhāvena sampajjanti uḷārassa dhanassa, uḷāradhanapaṭilābhakāraṇassa ca pariccāgasampadāhetukattā. Pacchimanti pariṇāyakaratanaṃ. Tañhi amoha…pe… kammānubhāvena sampajjati mahāpaññeneva cakkavattirājakiccassa pariṇetabbattā. Upadeso nāma savisesaṃ sattannaṃ ratanānaṃ vicāraṇavasena pavatto kathābandho.

By the power of actions born from the wholesome root of non-ill-will—that is, by the influence of actions produced through the condition of being co-nascent, etc., with the wholesome root designated as non-ill-will—they arise, being of a class of most agreeable treasures. The middle ones are the gem-treasure, the woman-treasure, and the householder-treasure. By the power of actions born from non-greed… they arise, being caused by the perfection of generosity, which is the cause for the attainment of great wealth. The last is the counselor-treasure. Indeed, it arises by the power of actions born from non-delusion… because the affairs of a wheel-turning monarch must be guided by one of great wisdom. ‘Instruction’ is the name for a composition that proceeds by way of a detailed investigation of the seven treasures.

Saraṇato paṭipakkhavidhamanato sūrā, tenāha “abhīrukajātikā”ti. Asure vijinitvā ṭhitattā vīro, sakko devānaṃ indo. Tassa aṅgaṃ devaputto senaṅgabhāvatoti vuttaṃ “vīraṅgarūpāti devaputtasadisakāyā”ti. “Eke”ti sārasamāsācariyamāha. Sabhāvoti sabhāvabhūto attho. Vīrakāraṇanti vīrabhāvakāraṇaṃ. Vīriyamayasarīrā viyāti saviggahavīriyasadisā, saviggahaṃ ce vīriyaṃ siyā taṃsadisāti attho. Nanu rañño cakkavattissa paṭisenā nāma natthi, ya’massa puttā pamaddeyyuṃ, atha kasmā parasenappamaddanāti vuttanti codanaṃ sandhāyāha sacetiādi, tena parasenā hotu vā mā vā te pana evaṃ mahānubhāvāti dasseti. Dhammenāti katupacitena attano puññadhammena. Tena [P 1.0384] hi sañcoditā pathaviyaṃ sabbarājāno paccuggantvā “svāgataṃ te mahārājā”ti ādiṃ vatvā attano rajjaṃ rañño cakkavattissa niyyātenti, tena vuttaṃ “so imaṃ…pe… ajjhāvasatī”ti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ [M 1.0295] pana tassa yathāvuttassa dhammassa cirataraṃ vipaccituṃ paccayabhūtaṃ cakkavattivattasamudāgataṃ payogasampattisaṅkhātaṃ dhammaṃ dassetuṃ “pāṇo na hantabbotiādinā pañcasīladhammenā”ti vuttaṃ. Evañhi “adaṇḍena asatthenā”ti idaṃ vacanaṃ suṭṭhutaraṃ samatthitaṃ hotīti. Yasmā rāgādayo pāpadhammā uppajjamānā sattasantānaṃ chādetvā pariyonandhitvā tiṭṭhanti kusalappavattiṃ nivārenti, tasmā te “chadanā, chadā”ti ca vuttā. Vivaṭetvāti vigametvā. Pūjārahatā vuttā “arahatīti araha”nti. Tassā pūjārahatāya. Yasmā sammāsambuddho, tasmā arahanti. Buddhattahetubhūtā vivaṭṭacchadatā vuttā savāsanasabbakilesappahānapubbakattā buddhabhāvassa.

Because they go forth and destroy the opposition, they are ‘heroes’ (sūra); hence it is said, ‘of fearless nature’. Because he stands victorious over the asuras, he is a ‘hero’ (vīra)—Sakka, the lord of devas. A divine youth is his ‘limb’ (aṅga), due to being a component of his army; this is what is meant by ‘with a heroic form, like the body of a divine youth’. ‘Some’ refers to the teachers of the essence-compendium. ‘Natural’ (sabhāva) means the inherent meaning. ‘The cause of heroism’ (vīrakāraṇa) is the reason for being heroic. ‘Like bodies made of energy’ (vīriyamayasarīrā) means similar to embodied energy; if energy were embodied, they would be like that—this is the meaning. Now, a wheel-turning monarch has no opposing army that his sons might crush, so why is it said that he crushes foreign armies? Addressing this objection, it says ‘if’ (sace), and so on, showing that whether foreign armies exist or not, they are of such great power. ‘By righteousness’ (dhammena) means by his own Dhamma of merit that he has performed and accumulated. Urged on by this, all the kings on earth come forth to meet him, saying, ‘Welcome, great king,’ and so on, and they hand over their kingdoms to the wheel-turning monarch. Therefore, it is said, ‘he dwells... having conquered this earth’. In the commentary, however, to show the Dhamma called ‘the accomplishment of application’, which arises from the wheel-turning monarch’s duties and is a condition for that aforementioned Dhamma of merit to ripen for a longer time, it is said, ‘by the Dhamma of the five precepts, beginning with “a living being is not to be killed”.’ In this way, the statement ‘without rod, without sword’ becomes very well supported. Because defilements such as greed, when they arise, cover and envelop the mental continuum of beings and prevent the occurrence of the wholesome, they are called ‘coverings’ (chadanā, chadā). ‘Having uncovered’ (vivaṭetvā) means having removed. Worthiness of offerings is stated. Because of that worthiness of offerings, ‘he is worthy (arahati), thus an Arahant (arahaṃ)’. Because he is a Perfectly Enlightened One, he is an Arahant. The state of having the covering removed is said to be the cause of Buddhahood, because the state of being a Buddha is preceded by the abandonment of all defilements together with their latent tendencies.

Arahaṃ [V 1.0261] vaṭṭābhāvenāti phalena hetuanumānadassanaṃ. Sammāsambuddho chadanābhāvenāti hetunā phalānumānadassanaṃ. Hetudvayaṃ vuttaṃ “vivaṭṭo vicchado cā”ti. Dutiyena vesārajjenāti “khīṇāsavassa te paṭijānato”tiādinā vuttena vesārajjena. Purimasiddhīti purimassa padassa atthasiddhīti attho. Paṭhamenāti “sammāsambuddhassa [P 1.0385] te paṭijānato”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.150; a. ni. 4.8) vuttena vesārajjena. Dutiyasiddhīti dutiyassa padassa atthasiddhi, buddhatthasiddhīti attho. Tatiyacatutthehīti “ye kho pana te antarāyikā dhammā”tiādinā, (ma. ni. 1.150; a. ni. 4.8) “yassa kho pana te atthāyā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.150; a. ni. 4.8) ca vuttehi tatiyacatutthehi vesārajjehi. Tatiyasiddhīti vivaṭṭacchadanatāsiddhi yāthāvato antarāyikaniyyānikadhammāpadesena hi satthu vivaṭṭacchadanabhāvo loke pākaṭo ahosi. Purimaṃ dhammacakkhunti purimapadaṃ bhagavato dhammacakkhuṃ sādheti kilesārīnaṃ, saṃsāracakkassa ca arānaṃ hatabhāvadīpanato. Dutiyaṃ padaṃ buddhacakkhuṃ sādheti sammāsambuddhasseva taṃsabbhāvato. Tatiyaṃ padaṃ samantacakkhuṃ sādheti savāsanasabbakilesappahānadīpanato. “Sammāsambuddho”ti hi vatvā “vivaṭṭacchado”ti vacanaṃ buddhabhāvāvahameva sabbakilesappahānaṃ vibhāveti. “Sūrabhāva”nti lakkhaṇavibhāvane visadañāṇataṃ.

The Arahant is free from the round of rebirth — thus, the inference of the cause is shown by the fruit. The Perfectly Self-Enlightened One is free from coverings — thus, the inference of the fruit is shown by the cause. The two causes are stated as 'uncovered' (vivaṭṭa) and 'free from coverings' (vicchada). By the second kind of confidence (vesārajja) — that is, by the confidence stated in 'for the one who claims to have destroyed the taints,' etc. The accomplishment of the first (purimasiddhi) means the accomplishment of the meaning of the first word. By the first (paṭhamena) — that is, by the confidence stated in 'for the one who claims to be perfectly self-enlightened,' etc. The accomplishment of the second (dutiyasiddhi) means the accomplishment of the meaning of the second word, the establishment of Buddhahood. By the third and fourth (tatiyacatutthehi) — that is, by the third and fourth kinds of confidence stated in 'those obstructive states,' etc., and 'for the sake of that purpose,' etc. The accomplishment of the third (tatiyasiddhi) is the establishment of being uncovered and free from coverings. For by the teaching of obstructive and liberating states, the Teacher’s state of being uncovered and free from coverings became evident in the world. The first word establishes the Dhamma-eye (dhammacakkhu) of the Blessed One by revealing the destruction of the enemies—the defilements—and of the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra. The second word establishes the Buddha-eye (buddhacakkhu), because that is the very nature of a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. The third word establishes the all-seeing eye (samantacakkhu) by revealing the abandonment of all defilements along with their latent tendencies. For by saying 'Perfectly Self-Enlightened One' and then stating 'free from coverings,' the abandonment of all defilements is clearly shown as leading to Buddhahood. 'Heroism' (sūrabhāva)—in the clarification of characteristics, it is the clarity of knowledge.

259. Evaṃ [M 1.0296] bhoti ettha evanti vacanasampaṭicchane nipāto. Vacanasampaṭicchanañcettha “tathā mayaṃ taṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ vedissāma, tvaṃ mantānaṃ paṭiggahetā”ti ca evaṃ pavattassa pokkharasātino vacanassa sampaṭiggahoti āha. “Sopi tāyā”tiādi. Tattha tāyāti tāya yathāvuttāya samuttejanāya. Ayānabhūminti [P 1.0386] yānassa abhūmiṃ. Divāpadhānikāti divāpadhānānuyuñjanakā.

259. 'Thus, sir' (evaṃ bhoti)—here, 'thus' (evaṃ) is a particle used to indicate acceptance of speech. And here, the acceptance of speech is said to be an acceptance of Pokkharasāti’s statement, which went thus: 'Thus, we shall know you, Venerable Gotama, as one who receives the mantras.' 'And he too, by that' (sopi tāyā) and so on. Here, 'by that' (tāya) means by that aforementioned encouragement (samuttejanāya). 'Not a ground for vehicles' (ayānabhūmi) means a place not suitable for vehicles. 'Engaged in daytime exertion' (divāpadhānikā) means those who are engaged in exertion during the day.

260. Yadipi pubbe ambaṭṭhakulaṃ appaññātaṃ, tadā pana paññāyatīti āha “tadā kirā”tiādi. Aturitoti avegāyanto.

260. Though the Ambaṭṭha clan was previously obscure, at that time it became known—thus it is said: 'At that time, indeed' (tadā kira), and so on. 'Without haste' (aturito) means not rushing.

261. Yathā khamanīyādīni pucchantoti yathā bhagavā “kacci vo māṇavā khamanīyaṃ, kacci yāpanīya”ntiādinā khamanīyādīni pucchanto tehi māṇavehi saddhiṃ paṭhamaṃ pavattamodo ahosi pubbabhāsitāya tadanukaraṇena evaṃ tepi māṇavā bhagavatā saddhiṃ samappavattamodā ahesunti yojanā. Taṃ pana samappavattamodataṃ upamāya dassetuṃ “sītodakaṃ viyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sammoditanti saṃsanditaṃ. Ekībhāvanti sammodanakiriyāya samānataṃ[V 1.0262]. Khamanīyanti “idaṃ catucakkaṃ navadvāraṃ sarīrayantaṃ dukkhabahulatāya sabhāvato dussahaṃ kacci khamituṃ sakkuṇeyya”nti pucchanti, yāpanīyanti āhārādipaccayapaṭibaddhavuttikaṃ cirappabandhasaṅkhātāya yāpanāya kacci yāpetuṃ sakkuṇeyyaṃ. Sīsarogādiābādhābhāvena kacci appābādhaṃ, dukkhajīvikābhāvena kacci appātaṅkaṃ, taṃtaṃkiccakaraṇe uṭṭhānasukhatāya kacci lahuṭṭhānaṃ, tadanurūpabalayogato kacci balaṃ, sukhavihārasabbhāvena kacci phāsuvihāro atthīti sabbattha kacci-saddaṃ yojetvā attho veditabbo. Balappattā pīti pītiyeva. Taruṇapīti pāmojjaṃ. Sammodanaṃ janeti karotīti sammodanikaṃ tadeva sammodanīyaṃ. Sammoditabbato sammodanīyanti idaṃ pana atthaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ “sammodituṃ yuttabhāvato”ti. Saritabbabhāvato anussaritabbabhāvato “saraṇīya”nti vattabbe “sāraṇīya”nti dīghaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. “Suyyamānasukhato”ti āpāthamadhuratamāha, “anussariyamānasukhato”ti vimaddaramaṇīyataṃ. “Byañjanaparisuddhatāyā”ti sabhāvaniruttibhāvena [P 1.0387] tassā kathāya vacanacāturiyamāha, “atthaparisuddhatāyā”ti atthassa nirupakkilesataṃ. Anekehi pariyāyehīti anekehi kāraṇehi.

261. Just as the Blessed One, by asking about well-being and so on, saying 'I hope you young men are well, I hope you are getting by,' and so on, had a pleasant conversation with those young men, a conversation that first arose from his speaking and their imitation of it, so too those young men engaged in mutual pleasant conversation with the Blessed One. This is the explanation. To illustrate this mutual pleasant conversation, it is said, 'like cool water,' and so on. Here, 'exchanged in pleasant conversation' (sammoditaṃ) means mingled. 'Oneness' (ekībhāvaṃ) means sameness in the act of pleasant conversation. 'Are you well?' (khamanīyaṃ) refers to asking whether this body-vehicle, with its four wheels and nine doors, naturally full of suffering and difficult to endure, can be endured. 'Are you getting by?' (yāpanīyaṃ) refers to whether one can sustain oneself with the necessities of life, such as food, which is bound up with continued existence, reckoned as long-term maintenance. 'Free from affliction' (appābādhaṃ) means being free from ailments like headaches. 'Free from distress' (appātaṅkaṃ) means being free from the suffering of a difficult livelihood. 'Quick to rise' (lahuṭṭhānaṃ) means being quick to rise for one's duties due to the comfort of exertion. 'Strong' (balaṃ) means having strength in accordance with one's capacity. 'Dwelling at ease' (phāsuvihāro) means dwelling comfortably due to the nature of a happy life. In all these cases, the word 'kacci' (I hope) should be connected to understand the meaning. Strong joy (balappattā pīti) is simply joy (pīti). Tender joy (taruṇapīti) is delight (pāmojja). That which generates pleasant conversation (sammodanaṃ janeti) is 'conversational' (sammodanikaṃ), which is the same as 'fit for pleasant conversation' (sammodanīyaṃ). To explain the meaning 'fit for pleasant conversation,' it is said, 'due to being suitable for pleasant conversation' (sammodituṃ yuttabhāvato). Where 'saraṇīyaṃ' should be said, meaning 'worthy of remembrance' (saritabbabhāvato, anussaritabbabhāvato), it is instead lengthened to 'sāraṇīyaṃ'. 'Due to the pleasure of hearing it' (suyyamānasukhato) refers to its sweetness at first hearing. 'Due to the pleasure of recollecting it' (anussariyamānasukhato) refers to its charm on reflection. 'By purity of expression' (byañjanaparisuddhatāyā) refers to the verbal skill of that talk, due to its natural eloquence. 'By purity of meaning' (atthaparisuddhatāyā) refers to the undefiled nature of the meaning. 'In many ways' (anekehi pariyāyehi) means for many reasons.

Apasādessāmīti [M 1.0297] maṅkuṃ karissāmi. Kaṇṭhe olambetvāti ubhosu khandhesu sāṭakaṃ āsajjetvā kaṇṭhe olambitvā. Dussakaṇṇaṃ gahetvāti nivatthasāṭakassa dasākoṭiṃ ekena hatthena gahetvā. Caṅkamaṃ abhiruhitvāti caṅkamituṃ ārabhitvā. Dhātusamatāti rasādidhātūnaṃ samāvatthatā, arogatāti attho. Anācārabhāvasāraṇīyanti anācārabhāvena saraṇīyaṃ. “Anācāro vatāya”nti saritabbakaṃ.

'I will make him ashamed' (apasādessāmi) means 'I will make him confused' (maṅkuṃ karissāmi). 'Having hung it around the neck' (kaṇṭhe olambetvā) means having placed the robe over both shoulders and let it hang around the neck. 'Having taken the cloth by the corner' (dussakaṇṇaṃ gahetvā) means taking the corner of the worn robe with one hand. 'Having ascended the walking path' (caṅkamaṃ abhiruhitvā) means having begun to walk back and forth. 'Balance of the elements' (dhātusamata) means the state of equilibrium of the elements such as bodily humors; the meaning is health (arogatā). 'To be remembered as improper conduct' (anācārabhāvasāraṇīyaṃ) means it should be recalled as improper conduct. It is to be remembered as, 'Indeed, this is improper conduct' (anācāro vatāyaṃ).

262. “Bhavaggaṃ gahetukāmo viyā”tiādi asakkuṇeyyattā dukkaraṃ kiccaṃ ārabhatīti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Asakkuṇeyyañhetaṃ sadevakenāpi lokena, yadidaṃ bhagavato apasādanaṃ, tenāha “aṭṭhāne vāyamatī”ti. Ayaṃ bālo “mayi kiñci akathente mayā saddhiṃ kathetumpi na visahatī”ti mānameva paggaṇhissati, kathente pana kathāpasaṅgenassa jātigotte vibhāvite mānaniggaho bhavissatīti bhagavā “evaṃ nu te”tiādimāha. Tena vuttaṃ “atha kho bhagavā”tiādi. Ācārasamācārasikkhāpanena ācariyā, tesaṃ pana ācariyānaṃ pakaṭṭhā ācariyāti pācariyā yathā papitāmahoti, tenāha “ācariyehi ca tesaṃ pācariyehi cā”ti.

262. 'As if desiring to grasp the highest state of existence' (bhavaggaṃ gahetukāmo viya), and so on, is said to show that he undertakes a difficult task because it is unachievable. For it is indeed unachievable even for the world with its devas to disparage the Blessed One; hence it is said, 'He strives in vain' (aṭṭhāne vāyamati). This fool, thinking, 'Since he does not speak to me, he does not even dare to speak with me,' will only increase his pride. But if the Buddha speaks, then through the course of the conversation, when Ambaṭṭha's birth and clan are revealed, his pride will be subdued. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'Is that so?' (evaṃ nu te), and so on. Hence it is said, 'Then the Blessed One' (atha kho bhagavā), and so on. They are teachers (ācariyā) by training in conduct and proper behavior; and the pre-eminent teachers among those teachers are called 'foremost teachers' (pācariyā), just as there are grandfathers and great-grandfathers (papitāmaha). Therefore, it is said, 'by the teachers and by their foremost teachers' (ācariyehi ca tesaṃ pācariyehi ca).

Paṭhamaibbhavādavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on the Wealthy

263. Tīsu iriyāpathesūti ṭhānagamananisajjāsu. Kathāpaḷāsanti [P 1.0388] kathāvasena yugaggāhaṃ. Sayānena [V 1.0263] ācariyena saddhiṃ sayānassa kathā nāma ācāro na hoti, taṃ itarehi sadisaṃ katvā kathanaṃ idha kathāpaḷāso.

263. 'In the three postures' means in standing, walking, and sitting. 'Contentious speech' (kathāpaḷāsa) means engaging in a dispute by way of conversation. For one who is lying down, to converse with a teacher who is also lying down is not proper conduct; here, that talking, by treating it as similar to the other postures, is called contentious speech.

Tassa pana yaṃ anācārabhāvavibhāvanaṃ satthārā ambaṭṭhena saddhiṃ kathentena kataṃ, taṃ saṅgītianāruḷhaṃ paramparābhatanti upari pāḷiyā sambandhabhāvena dassento “tato kirā”tiādimāha. Muṇḍakā samaṇakāti ca garahāyaṃ ka-saddo, tenāha “hīḷento”ti. Ibhassa payogo ibho uttarapadalopena, taṃ ibhaṃ arahantīti ibbhā. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yathā ibho hatthivāhanabhūto parassa vasena vattati, na attano, evaṃ etepi brāhmaṇānaṃ sussusakā suddā parassa vasena [M 1.0298] vattanti, na attano, tasmā ibhasadisapayogatāya ibbhāti. Te pana kuṭumbikatāya gharavāsino gharassāmikā hontīti āha “gahapatikā”ti. Kaṇhāti kaṇhajātikā. Dijā eva hi suddhajātikā, na itareti tassa adhippāyo, tenāha “kāḷakā”ti. Mukhato nikkhantāti brāhmaṇānaṃ pubbapurisā brahmuno mukhato nikkhantā, ayaṃ tesaṃ paṭhamuppattīti adhippāyo. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. “Samaṇā piṭṭhipādato”ti idaṃ panassa “mukhato nikkhantā”tiādivacanatopi ativiya asamavekkhitavacanaṃ catuvaṇṇapariyāpannasseva samaṇabhāvasambhavato. Aniyametvāti avisesetvā, anuddesikabhāvenāti attho.

Now, regarding the exposition of improper conduct made by the Teacher while conversing with Ambaṭṭha, it is not included in the Saṅgīti but is handed down by tradition. Therefore, showing its connection to the preceding Pāli text, he begins with "tato kirā" and so on. The term 'muṇḍakā samaṇakā' contains the particle 'ka' for disparagement, hence it is said 'hīḷento' (scorning). The word 'ibbhā' is derived from 'ibha'; those who are fit for an 'ibha' are 'ibbhā'. What is meant by this? Just as an ibha, being an elephant used for riding, serves under another's control and not its own, so too do these suddā, being subservient to the brahmins, act under another's authority and not their own. Therefore, due to their resemblance to an 'ibha' in function, they are called 'ibbhā'. Moreover, because they are householders, dwellers in homes, and masters of homes, they are called 'gahapatikā'. 'Kaṇhā' means of dark birth. For only the twice-born (dijā) are of pure birth, not others—this is the intended meaning, hence the term 'kāḷakā'. "Born from the mouth" means the brahmins' ancestors emerged from Brahmā’s mouth; this is their first origin. The same applies to the remaining classes. "Monks [born] from the feet"—this statement, along with "born from the mouth" and so on, is an extremely ill-considered utterance, for the state of being a monk is possible only for those included in the four classes. 'Aniyametvā' means without specifying, implying an unspecified status.

Mānussayavasena kathetīti mānussayaṃ avassāya attānaṃ ukkaṃsento, pare ca vambhento “muṇḍakā”ti ādiṃ katheti. Jānāpemīti jātigottassa pamāṇaṃ [P 1.0389] yāthāvato vibhāvanena pamāṇaṃ jānāpemīti. Attho etassa atthīti atthikaṃ daṇḍikañāyena.

"Speaking in human terms" means exalting oneself, relying on human conceit, and disparaging others, saying things like "shavelings" and so forth. "I make known" means I make known the true measure of birth and lineage by way of detailed explanation. "There is meaning in this" means it is meaningful, in the manner of the 'daṇḍika' principle.

“Yāyeva kho panatthāyā”ti itthiliṅgavasena vuttanti vadanti, taṃ parato “purisaliṅgavasenevā”ti vakkhamānattā yuttaṃ. Yāya atthāyāti vā pulliṅgavaseneva tadatthe sampadānavacanaṃ, yassa atthassa atthāyāti attho. Assāti ambaṭṭhassa dassetvāti sambandho. Aññesanti aññesaṃ sādhurūpānaṃ. Santikaṃ āgatānanti guruṭṭhāniyānaṃ santikaṃ upagatānaṃ. Vattanti tehi caritabbaācāraṃ. Asikkhitoti ācāraṃ asikkhito. Tato eva appassuto. Bāhusaccañhi nāma yāvadeva upasamatthaṃ icchitabbaṃ, tadabhāvato ambaṭṭho appassuto asikkhito “avusito”ti viññāyati, tenāha “etassa hī”tiādi.

Some say that 'Yāyeva kho panatthāyā' is spoken in the feminine gender, but since it will be explained later as being in the masculine gender, that is appropriate. Or, 'yāya atthāya' is a dative expression in the masculine gender for that meaning; the meaning is 'for the sake of which purpose.' 'Assāti' shows the connection to Ambaṭṭha. 'Others' refers to others who are of good form. 'Those who have come near' means those who have approached the presence of venerable ones. 'They behave' means the conduct to be followed by them. 'Untrained' means not trained in conduct. From that very fact, he is of little learning. For extensive learning is to be desired only up to the point of tranquility; due to its absence, Ambaṭṭha is of little learning, untrained, and is known as 'not having lived the holy life.' Hence it is said, 'For this reason,' etc.

264. Kodhavasacittatāya asakamano. Mānanimmadanatthanti mānassa nimmadanatthaṃ. Uggiletvāti [V 1.0264] sinehapānena kilinnaṃ ubbamanaṃ katvā. Gottena gottanti tena vuttena purātanagottena idāni taṃ taṃ anavajjasaññitaṃ gottaṃ sāvajjato uṭṭhāpetvā uddharitvā. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Tattha gottaṃ ādipurisavasena, kulāpadoso, tadanvaye uppannaabhiññātapurisavasena veditabbo yathā “ādicco, maghadevo”ti. Gottamūlassa gārayhatāya amānavatthubhāvapavedanato “mānaddhajaṃ mūle chetvā”ti vuttaṃ. Ghaṭṭentoti [P 1.0390] omasanto.

264. Due to being under the sway of anger, his mind is not his own. "For the sake of dispelling pride" means for the purpose of destroying pride. "Having vomited" means having induced vomiting, making it wet with a drink of fat. "Lineage by lineage" means, by means of that ancient lineage mentioned, now raising up and bringing forth that very lineage, which was considered blameless, from a state of blame. The same method applies to the remaining phrases. There, lineage is to be understood in terms of the first man, the fault of the family, and in terms of the well-known men born in that lineage, such as "Ādicco, Maghadevo." Because the root of lineage is blameworthy, revealing it to be an object unworthy of pride, it is said, "having cut the banner of pride at the root." "Striking" means insulting.

Yasmiṃ [M 1.0299] mānussayakodhussayā aññamaññūpatthaddhā, so “caṇḍo”ti vuccatīti āha “caṇḍāti mānanissitakodhayuttā”ti. Kharāti cittena, vācāya ca kakkhaḷā. Lahukāti taruṇā. Bhassāti “sāhasikā”ti keci vadanti, “sārambhakā”ti apare. Samānāti hontā, bhavamānāti atthoti āha “santāti purimapadasseva vevacana”nti. Na sakkarontīti sakkāraṃ na karonti. Apacitikammanti paṇipātakamma nānulomanti attano jātiyā na anucchavikanti attho.

He in whom human conceit and an abundance of anger are mutually supported is called "fierce." Hence it is said, "fierce means connected with anger rooted in pride." "Harsh" means rough in mind and speech. "Light" means young. "Bhassa" —some say it means "rash," others say "aggressive." "Samāna" means "being," "becoming"—this is the meaning. Hence it is said, "'santa' is just a synonym of the previous word." "They do not honor" means they do not show respect. 'An act of reverence' ('apacitikamma') means an act of bowing down. Not conforming to it means it is not suitable for one's own birth—this is the meaning.

Dutiyaibbhavādavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Servants

265. Kāmaṃ sakyarājakule yo sabbesaṃ buddhataro samattho ca, so eva abhisekaṃ labhati, ekacco pana abhisitto samāno “idaṃ rajjaṃ nāma bahukiccaṃ bahubyāpāra”nti tato nibbijja rajjaṃ vayasā anantarassa niyyāteti, kadāci sopi aññassāti tādise sandhāyāha “sakyāti abhisittarājāno”ti. Kulavaṃsaṃ jānantīti kaṇhāyanato paṭṭhāya paramparāgataṃ anussavavasena jānanti. Kulābhimānino hi yebhuyyena paresaṃ uccāvacaṃ kulaṃ tathā tathā udāharanti, attano ca kulavaṃsaṃ jānanti, evaṃ ambaṭṭhopi. Tathā hi so parato bhagavatā pucchito vajirapāṇibhayena yāthāvato kathesi.

265. Indeed, in the Sakyan royal clan, whoever is the most senior and capable receives the consecration. But one who has been consecrated, thinking, "Kingship involves many duties and responsibilities," may become weary of it and hand over the kingdom to the one next in age. Sometimes, even he may pass it on to another. Bearing this in mind, he said, "The Sakyans are consecrated kings." They know their lineage—from Kanhayana onwards, they know their ancestral tradition through oral transmission. For those who take pride in their lineage often speak of the high and low birth of others in various ways, and they know their own lineage. So too did Ambaṭṭha. For when questioned later by the Blessed One, out of fear of Vajirapāṇi, he spoke the truth.

Tatiyaibbhavādavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Third Discourse on the Servants

266. Khettaleḍḍūnanti khette kasanavasena naṅgalena uṭṭhāpitaleḍḍūnaṃ. “Laṭukikā” icceva paññātā khuddakasakuṇikā laṭukikopamavaṇṇanāyaṃ “cātakasakuṇikā”ti (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 3.150) vuttā. Kodhavasena laggitunti upanayhituṃ, āghātaṃ bandhitunti [P 1.0391] attho. “Amhe haṃsakoñcamorasame karotī”ti iminā “na taṃ koci haṃso vā”tiādivacanaṃ saṅgītiṃ anāruḷhaṃ tadā bhagavatā vuttamevāti dasseti. “Evaṃ nu te”tiādivacanaṃ, “avusitavāyevā”tiādivacanañca [V 1.0265] mānavasena samaṇena gotamena vuttanti maññatīti adhippāyenāha “nimmāno dāni jātoti maññamāno”ti.

266. 'Of clods in the field' means of clods raised in the field by a plow through plowing. The small bird known as 'laṭukikā' (quail) is called 'cātaka bird' in the description using the quail as a simile. 'To be attached through anger' means to bear a grudge, that is, to bind with hatred. By the statement, 'He makes us the same as swans, herons, and peacocks,' it is shown that the saying, 'You are not a swan, etc.,' though not included in the Saṅgīti, was indeed spoken by the Blessed One at that time. He says, 'thinking, "Now he has become conceited,"' with the intention that he (Ambaṭṭha) thinks that the statements 'Is this how you...' and 'You have not lived...' were spoken by the ascetic Gotama out of conceit.

Dāsiputtavādavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Son of a Slave Woman

267. Nimmādetīti [M 1.0300] a-kārassa ā-kāraṃ katvā niddesoti āha “nimmadetī”ti. Kāmaṃ gottaṃ nāmetaṃ pitito laddhabbaṃ, na mātito na hi brāhmaṇānaṃ sagottāya āvāhavivāho icchito, gottanāmaṃ pana yasmā jātisiddhaṃ, na kittimaṃ, jāti ca ubhayasambandhinī, tasmā “mātāpettikanti mātāpitūnaṃ santaka”nti vuttaṃ. Nāmagottanti gottanāmaṃ, na kittimanāmaṃ, na guṇanāmaṃ vā. Tattha “kaṇhāyano”ti niruḷhā yā nāmapaṇṇatti, taṃ sandhāyāha “paṇṇattivasena nāmanti. Taṃ pana kaṇhaisito paṭṭhāya tasmiṃ kulaparamparāvasena āgataṃ, na etasmiṃyeva niruḷhaṃ, tena vuttaṃ “paveṇīvasena gotta”nti. Gotta-padassa pana attho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Anussaratoti ettha na kevalaṃ anussaraṇaṃ adhippetaṃ, atha kho kulasuddhivīmaṃsanavasenāti āha “kulakoṭiṃ sodhentassā”ti. Ayyaputtāti ayyikaputtāti āha “sāmino puttā”ti. Disā okkākarañño antojātā dāsīti āha “gharadāsiyā putto”ti. Ettha ca yasmā ambaṭṭho jātiṃ nissāya mānatthaddho, na cassa yāthāvato jātiyā avibhāvitāya mānaniggaho hoti, mānaniggahe ca kate aparabhāge ratanattaye pasīdissati[P 1.0392], na “dāsī”ti vācā pharusavācā nāma hoti cittassa saṇhabhāvato. Abhayasuttañcettha (ma. ni. 2.83; a. ni. 4.184) nidassanaṃ. Keci ca sattā agginā viya lohādayo kakkhaḷāya vācāya mudubhāvaṃ gacchanti, tasmā bhagavā ambaṭṭhaṃ nibbisevanaṃ kātukāmo “ayyaputtā sakyā bhavanti, dāsiputto tvamasi sakyāna”nti avoca.

267. 'Nimmādeti' is a designation made by changing the 'a' sound to an 'ā' sound; hence it is said 'nimmadetī'. Indeed, the lineage name (gotta) should be received from the father, not from the mother, for Brahmins do not desire marriage with those of the same lineage. However, since the lineage name is established by birth and not fabricated, and since birth is connected to both parents, it is said, 'mātāpettikaṃ' (belonging to mother and father), meaning 'mātāpitūnaṃ santakaṃ' (belonging to mother and father). 'Nāmagotta' refers to the lineage name (gotta-nāma), not a fabricated name or a name based on qualities. Here, 'Kaṇhāyano' is a conventional name established by usage; hence it is said, 'paṇṇattivasena nāmaṃ' (a name by convention). But this name has come down through that family lineage starting from the sage Kaṇha, not merely established in this very person; hence it is said, 'paveṇīvasena gottaṃ' (lineage by tradition). The meaning of the word 'gotta' has already been explained above. 'Anussarati' (recollects) here does not merely mean recollecting, but rather examining the purity of the lineage; hence it is said, 'kulakoṭiṃ sodhentassa' (of one who purifies the lineage). 'Ayyaputtā' (sons of the noble) means 'ayyikaputtā' (sons of the noble women); hence it is said, 'sāmino puttā' (sons of the master). The phrase 'Disā okkākarañño antojātā dāsī' (a slave woman born within the household of King Okkāka) means 'gharadāsiyā putto' (the son of a household slave). Here, because Ambaṭṭha was arrogant due to his birth, and since his actual birth had not been clearly revealed, his pride could not be subdued. Only when his pride was subdued would he later develop faith in the Triple Gem. Moreover, the word 'dāsī' (slave woman) is not considered harsh speech because of the gentleness of (the Buddha's) mind. The Abhayasutta (MN 2.83; AN 4.184) serves as an example here. Some beings, like metals softened by fire, become gentle through harsh speech. Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to thoroughly humble Ambaṭṭha, said, 'The Sakyans are sons of the noble, but you are the son of a slave of the Sakyans.'

Ṭhapentīti paññapenti, tenāha “okkāko”tiādi. Pabhā niccharati dantānaṃ ativiya pabhassarabhāvato.

'Ṭhapenti' means 'they make known' (paññapenti); hence it is said 'Okkāka' and so on. Light radiates from the teeth because of their exceedingly bright nature.

Paṭhamakappikānanti paṭhamakappassa ādikāle nibbattānaṃ. Kira-saddo anussavatthe, tena yo vuccamānāya rājaparamparāya kesañci matibhedo, taṃ ulliṅgeti. Mahāsammatassāti “ayaṃ no rājā”ti mahājanena sammannitvā ṭhapitattā “mahāsammato”ti evaṃ sammatassa. Yaṃ sandhāya vadanti –

'Paṭhamakappikānaṃ' means of those who arose in the beginning of the first aeon (paṭhamakappa). The word 'kira' indicates hearsay; by it, it hints at a difference of opinion among some regarding the royal lineage being discussed. 'Mahāsammatassa' refers to one who, having been agreed upon and installed by the great mass of people with the words 'This is our king,' was thus named 'Mahāsammato'. With reference to him, they say:

“Ādiccakulasambhūto[V 1.0266][M 1.0301], suvisuddhaguṇākaro;

Mahānubhāvo rājāsi, mahāsammatanāmako.

Born of the solar lineage, a repository of exceedingly pure virtues; he was a king of great power, known by the name Mahāsammata.

Yo cakkhubhūto lokassa, guṇaraṃsisamujjalo;

Tamonudo virocittha, dutiyo viya bhāṇumā.

He who was the Eye of the world, radiant with a blaze of virtues; a dispeller of darkness, he shone forth, like a second sun.

Ṭhapitā yena mariyādā, loke lokahitesinā;

Vavatthitā sakkuṇanti, na vilaṅghayituṃ janā.

The boundary established in the world by him, who sought the welfare of the world; people, being well-established, are not able to transgress it.

Yasassinaṃ tejassinaṃ, lokasīmānurakkhakaṃ;

Ādibhūtaṃ mahāvīraṃ, kathayanti ‘manū’ti ya”nti.

Him who is glorious, powerful, the guardian of the world's boundaries, primordial, the great hero—they call him 'Manu'.

Tassa ca puttapaputtaparamparaṃ sandhāya –

And concerning his continuous lineage of sons and grandsons—

“Tassa putto mahātejo, rojo nāma mahīpati;

Tassa putto vararojo, pavaro rājamaṇḍale.

His son was of great splendor, the lord of the earth named Roja; his son was the excellent Roja, the foremost in the royal circle.

Tassāsi [P 1.0393] kalyāṇaguṇo, kalyāṇo nāma atrajo;

Rājā tassāsi tanayo, varakalyāṇanāmako.

His son, of virtuous qualities, was named Kalyāṇa; his son, the king, was named Varakalyāṇa.

Tassa putto mahāvīro, mandhātā kāmabhoginaṃ;

Aggabhūto mahindena, aḍḍharajjena pūjito.

His son was the great hero, Mandhātā, foremost among enjoyers of sensual pleasures; he was honored by Mahinda with half a kingdom.

Tassa sūnu mahātejo, varamandhātunāmako;

‘Uposatho’ti nāmena, tassa putto mahāyaso.

His son, of great splendor, was named Varamandhātu; his son, of great fame, was named Uposatha.

Varo nāma mahātejo, tassa putto mahāvaro;

Tassāsi upavaroti, putto rājā mahābalo.

His son, of great splendor, was named Varo; his son was Mahāvaro. His son, the king of great strength, was named Upavaro.

Tassa [V 1.0267] putto maghadevo, devatulyo mahīpati;

Caturāsītisahassāni, tassa puttaparamparā.

His son was Maghadeva, a godlike lord of the earth; eighty-four thousand was his line of descendants.

Tesaṃ pacchimako rājā, ‘okkāko’ iti vissuto;

Mahāyaso mahātejo, akhuddo rājamaṇḍale”ti.

The last of those kings, well-known as 'Okkāka', was of great fame, great power, not insignificant in the royal circle.

Ādi tesaṃ pacchatoti tesaṃ maghadeva paramparabhūtānaṃ kaḷārajanakapariyosānānaṃ anekasatasahassānaṃ rājūnaṃ aparabhāge okkāko nāma [M 1.0302] rājā ahosi, tassa paramparābhūtānaṃ anekasatasahassānaṃ rājūnaṃ aparabhāge aparo okkāko nāma rājā ahosi, tassa paramparabhūtānaṃ anekasatasahassānaṃ rājūnaṃ aparabhāge punāparo okkāko nāma rājā ahosi, taṃ sandhāyāha “tayo okkākavaṃsā ahesuṃ. Tesu tatiyaokkākassā”tiādi.

'Ādi tesaṃ pacchato' means that after those many hundreds of thousands of kings who were in the lineage of Maghadeva and ended with Kaḷārajanaka, there was a king named Okkāka.
