After the many hundreds of thousands of kings who were in his lineage, there was another king named Okkāka. After the many hundreds of thousands of kings who were in his lineage, there was yet another king named Okkāka. Referring to this, it is said, 'There were three Okkāka lineages. Among them, of the third Okkāka,' and so on.

Sahasā varaṃ adāsinti puttadassanena somanassappatto sahasā avīmaṃsitvā tuṭṭhiyā vasena varaṃ adāsiṃ, “yaṃ icchasi, taṃ gaṇhā”ti. Rajjaṃ pariṇāmetuṃ icchatīti sā jantukumārassa mātā mama taṃ varadānaṃ antaraṃ katvā imaṃ rajjaṃ pariṇāmetuṃ icchatīti.

'I granted a boon rashly' (sahasā varaṃ adāsiṃ) means: overjoyed at seeing my son, I granted a boon impetuously, without deliberation, due to delight, saying, 'Take whatever you desire.' 'She wishes to transfer the kingdom' (rajjaṃ pariṇāmetuṃ icchati) means: the mother of Prince Jantu, taking my granting of that boon as an opportunity, wishes to transfer this kingdom to him.

Nappasaheyyāti [P 1.0394] na pariyatto bhaveyya.

'Nappasaheyya' means 'he would not be sufficient' or 'he would not be able'.

Nikkhammāti gharāvāsato, kāmehi ca nikkhamitvā. Heṭṭhā cāti ca-saddena “asītihatthe”ti idaṃ anukaḍḍhati. Tehīti migasūkarehi, maṇḍūkamūsikehi ca. Teti sīhabyagghādayo, sappabiḷārā ca.

'Nikkhammā' (having departed) means having departed from the household life and from sensual pleasures. 'Heṭṭhā ca' (and below) means that the word 'ca' (and) draws in 'asītihatthe' (eighty cubits). 'Tehi' (by them) refers to deer and boars, and frogs and mice. 'Te' (they) refers to lions, tigers, and so on, and also snakes and cats.

Avasesāhi attano attano kaniṭṭhāhi.

'Avasesāhi' (with the remaining ones) means with their own respective younger sisters.

Vaḍḍhamānānanti anādare sāmivacanaṃ. Kuṭṭharogo nāma sāsamasūrīrogā viya yebhuyyena saṅkamanasabhāvoti vuttaṃ “ayaṃ rogo saṅkamatīti cintetvā”ti.

'Vaḍḍhamānānaṃ' (of those growing) is a genitive case used in the sense of disregard. The disease called 'kuṭṭharoga' (leprosy) is mostly of a contagious nature, like the diseases of mustard seed and smallpox; hence it is said, 'thinking, "This disease is contagious."'

Migasūkarādīnanti ādi-saddena vanacarasoṇādike saṅgaṇhāti.

'Migasūkarādīnaṃ' (of deer, boars, and so on) means that the word 'ādi' (and so on) includes wild dogs and the like.

Tasmiṃ nisinneti sambandho. Khattiyamāyārocanena attano khattiyabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā.

'Tasmiṃ nisinne' (while he was seated there) is the connection. This means: having made his own Kshatriya status known through the announcement by the Kshatriya maiden.

Nagaraṃ [V 1.0268] māpehīti sāhāraṃ nagaraṃ māpehīti adhippāyo.

'Nagaraṃ māpehi' (build a city) means the intention is 'build a city together with its surrounding area' (sāhāraṃ nagaraṃ māpehi).

Kesaggahaṇanti kesaveṇibandhanaṃ. Dussaggahaṇanti vatthassa nivāsanākāro.

'Kesaggahaṇaṃ' (the taking of the hair) refers to the binding of the hair-braid. 'Dussaggahaṇaṃ' (the taking of the cloth) refers to the manner of wearing the cloth.

268. Attano upārambhamocanatthāyāti ācariyena ambaṭṭhena ca attano attano upari pāpetabbaupavādassa apanayanatthaṃ. Asmiṃ vacaneti “cattārome bho gotama vaṇṇā”tiādinā attanā vutte, bhotā ca gotamena vutte “jātivāde”ti imasmiṃ yathādhikate vacane. Tattha pana yasmā vede vuttavidhināva tena paṭimantetabbaṃ hoti[M 1.0303], tasmā vuttaṃ “vedattayavacane”ti, “etasmiṃ vā dāsiputtavacane”ti ca.

268. 'Attano upārambhamocanatthāya' (for the purpose of freeing oneself from blame) means for the removal of the reproach that was to be brought upon each of themselves by the teacher and Ambaṭṭha. 'Asmiṃ vacane' (in this statement) refers to this statement as it arose, such as when it was said by himself, 'These four, Master Gotama, are the classes,' and when it was said by the venerable Gotama, 'in a discussion of birth' (jātivāde). Here, since one should respond according to the method stated in the Vedas, therefore it is said, 'in the discourse of the three Vedas' (vedattayavacane), and 'or in this statement about being a slave’s son' (etasmiṃ vā dāsiputtavacane).

270. Dhammo nāma kāraṇaṃ “dhammapaṭisambhidā”tiādīsu (vibha. 718) viya, saha dhammenāti sahadhammo, sahadhammo [P 1.0395] eva sahadhammikoti āha “sahetuko”ti.

270. 'Dhamma' means cause, as in passages such as 'the analytical knowledge of dhamma' (dhammapaṭisambhidā) (Vb 718). 'Saha dhammena' (with dhamma) is 'sahadhammo' (accompanied by dhamma); 'sahadhammo' itself is 'sahadhammiko' (one who is accompanied by dhamma); hence it is said 'sahetuko' (with a cause).

271. Tasmā tadā paṭiññātattā. Tāsetvā pañhaṃ vissajjāpessāmīti āgato yathā taṃ saccakasamāgame. “Bhagavā ceva passati ambaṭṭho cā”ti ettha itaresaṃ adassane kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “yadi hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Āvāhetvāti mantabalena ānetvā. Tassāti ambaṭṭhassa. Vādasaṅghaṭṭeti vācāsaṅghaṭṭe.

271. Therefore, because it was acknowledged at that time. Having threatened him, he came intending, 'I will make him answer the question,' as was the case in the encounter with Saccaka. Here, to explain the reason for others not seeing in the phrase 'Both the Blessed One sees and Ambaṭṭha sees,' the words 'if indeed' and so on were stated. 'Āvāhetvā' (having summoned) means having brought over by the power of a mantra. 'Tassa' (his) refers to Ambaṭṭha. 'Vādasaṅghaṭṭe' (in the clash of debate) means in the clash of speech (vācāsaṅghaṭṭe).

272. Tāṇanti gavesamānoti, “ayameva samaṇo gotamo ito bhayato mama tāyako”ti bhagavantaṃyeva “tāṇa”nti pariyesanto upagacchanto. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Tāyatīti yathāupaṭṭhitabhayato pāleti, tenāha “rakkhatī”ti, etena tāṇa-saddassa kattusādhanatamāha. Yathupaṭṭhitena bhayena upadduto nilīyati etthāti leṇaṃ, upalayanaṃ, etena leṇa-saddassa adhikaraṇasādhanatamāha. “Saratī”ti etena saraṇa-saddassa kattusādhanatamāha.

272. 'Seeking refuge (tāṇaṃ)' means, thinking, 'This ascetic Gotama alone is my protector from this danger,' one approaches the Blessed One while seeking him as a refuge. The same method applies to the remaining two terms. 'Tāyati' (protects) means it protects from impending danger; hence it is said 'rakkhati' (safeguards), thereby explaining the agentive derivation of the word 'tāṇa'. 'Leṇaṃ' (shelter) is a place where one hides when oppressed by impending danger, a place of refuge (upalayanaṃ); thereby explaining the locative derivation of the word 'leṇa'. By 'saratī' (remembers), it explains the agentive derivation of the word 'saraṇa'.

Ambaṭṭhavaṃsakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse of the Ambaṭṭha Lineage.

274. Gaṅgāya dakkhiṇatoti gaṅgāya nadiyā dakkhiṇadisāya. Āvudhaṃ na parivattatīti saraṃ vāsattiādiṃ vā parassa upari khipitukāmassa hatthaṃ na parivattati, hatthe pana aparivattente kuto āvudhaparivattananti āha “āvudhaṃ na parivattatī”ti. So kira “kathaṃ nāmāhaṃ disāya dāsiyā kucchimhi nibbatto”ti taṃ hīnaṃ jātiṃ jigucchanto “handāhaṃ yathā tathā [V 1.0269] imaṃ jātiṃ sodhessāmī”ti niggato, tenāha “idāni me manorathaṃ pūressāmī”tiādi. Vijjābalena rājānaṃ tāsetvā tassa dhītuyā laddhakālato paṭṭhāya myāyaṃ jātisodhitā [M 1.0304] bhavissatīti tassa adhippāyo. Ambaṭṭhaṃ nāma vijjanti sattānaṃ sarīre abbhaṅgaṃ ṭhapetīti ambaṭṭhāti evaṃ [P 1.0396] laddhanāmaṃ vijjaṃ, mantanti attho. Yato ambaṭṭhā etasmiṃ atthīti ambaṭṭhoti kaṇho isi paññāyittha, taṃbaṃsajātatāya ayaṃ māṇavo “ambaṭṭho”ti voharīyati.

274. 'To the south of the Ganges' means in the southern direction of the river Ganges. 'The weapon does not turn' means that when one desires to hurl an arrow, a hatchet, or the like upon another, the hand does not turn; and when the hand does not turn, from where would the weapon turn? Thus it is said, 'the weapon does not turn.' It is said that he, disgusted by that low birth, thinking, 'How indeed was I born in the womb of a slave girl?' went forth, resolving, 'Come now, I shall purify this birth by some means or other.' Hence it is said, 'Now I shall fulfill my heart's desire,' and so on. His intention was that by the power of his knowledge, having terrified the king, from the time he obtained the king’s daughter, his birth would be purified. 'Ambaṭṭha' is the name of a knowledge so-called because it places non-breaking on the bodies of beings; its meaning is 'a spell'. Because this Ambaṭṭha knowledge was in him, the sage Kaṇha became known as 'Ambaṭṭha'. Due to being born in his lineage, this young man is called 'Ambaṭṭha'.

Seṭṭhamante vedamanteti adhippāyo. Mantānubhāvena rañño bāhukkhambhamattaṃ jātaṃ tena panassa bāhukkhambhena rājā, “ko jānāti, kiṃ bhavissatī”ti bhīto ussaṅkī utrāso ahosi, tenāha “bhayena vedhamāno aṭṭhāsī”ti. Sotthi bhaddanteti ādivacanaṃ avocuṃ. “Ayaṃ mahānubhāvo isī”ti maññamānā.

The intention is that 'the best mantra' means 'the Veda-mantra'. By the power of the mantra, the king's arm became the size of a pillar. Because of that pillar-like arm, the king, thinking, 'Who knows what will happen?' became frightened, anxious, and terrified. Hence it is said, 'He stood trembling with fear.' Thinking, 'This sage is of great power,' they spoke words beginning with, 'Well-being, venerable sir!'.

Undriyissatīti vippakiriyissati, tenāha “bhijjissatī”ti. Mante parivattiteti bāhukkhambhakamantassa paṭippassambhakavijjāsaṅkhāte mante “saro otaratū”ti parivattite. Evarūpānañhi mantānaṃ ekaṃseneva paṭippassambhakavijjā hontiyeva yathā taṃ kusumārakavijjānaṃ. Attano dhītu apavādamocanatthaṃ tassa bhujissakaraṇaṃ. Tassānurūpe issariye ṭhapanatthaṃ uḷāre ca naṃ ṭhāne ṭhapesi.

'It will burst' means it will be scattered; therefore, it is said, 'it will break.' 'When the mantra was changed' means when the mantra for the pillar-arm, known as the counteracting knowledge, was changed to 'may the arrow descend.' Indeed, such mantras invariably possess counteracting knowledge, just as for the Kusumaraka arts. To free his daughter from reproach, he made him a freedman. And to establish him in a lordship befitting him, he placed him in an eminent position.

Khattiyaseṭṭhabhāvavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Supremacy of the Khattiya Caste.

275. Samassāsanatthamāha karuṇāyanto, na kulīnabhāvadassanatthaṃ, tenāha “atha kho bhagavā”tiādi. Brāhmaṇesūti brāhmaṇānaṃ samīpe, tato brāhmaṇehi laddhabbaṃ āsanādiṃ sandhāya “brāhmaṇānaṃ antare”ti vuttaṃ. Kevalaṃ [P 1.0397] saddhāya kātabbaṃ saddhaṃ, paralokagate sandhāya na tato kiñci apatthentena kātabbanti attho, tenāha “matake uddissa katabhatte”ti. Maṅgalādibhatteti ādi-saddena ussavadevatārādhanādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Yaññabhatteti pāpasaññamādivasena katabhatte. Pāhunakānanti atithīnaṃ. Khattiyabhāvaṃ appatto ubhato sujātatābhāvato, tenāha “aparisuddhoti attho”ti.

275. He spoke for the purpose of consolation, out of compassion, not for the purpose of showing his noble lineage; therefore it is said, 'Then the Blessed One,' and so on. 'Among the brahmins' means in the vicinity of the brahmins; with regard to the seat and other things to be obtained from the brahmins, it is said, 'among the brahmins.' A funeral meal (saddha) is to be done solely out of faith; the meaning is that it is to be done with reference to one gone to the next world, without expecting anything in return; therefore it is said, 'on food made in dedication to the deceased.' In 'on food for auspicious occasions, etc.,' the term 'etc.' includes festivals, worship of deities, and the like. 'On sacrificial food' means on food prepared on account of a vow to a deity, and so on. 'For guests' means for visitors. Not having attained the status of a khattiya because of not being well-born on both sides; therefore the meaning is 'impure'.

276. Itthiṃ karitvāti ettha karaṇaṃ kiriyāsāmaññavisayanti āha “itthiṃ pariyesitvā”ti. Brāhmaṇakaññaṃ itthiṃ khattiyakumārassa bhariyābhūtaṃ [M 1.0305] gahetvāpi khattiyāva seṭṭhā, hīnā brāhmaṇāti yojanā. Purisena vā purisaṃ karitvāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Pakaraṇeti rāgādivasena [V 1.0270] paduṭṭhe pakkhalite kāraṇe, tenāha “dose”ti. Bhassati niratthakabhāvena khipīyatīti bhassaṃ, chārikā.

276. 'Having made a woman': here, 'making' refers to a general activity; hence it is said, 'having sought a woman.' Even having taken a brahmin maiden as a wife for a khattiya prince, the khattiyas are superior and the brahmins are inferior—this is the connection. 'Or having made a man with a man' also follows the same method. 'By reason' means by a cause that is corrupted and has stumbled on account of lust, etc.; hence it is said, 'by fault.' 'Bhassaṃ' is so-called because it is discarded and cast away as worthless; it is ash.

277. Janitasminti kammakilesehi nibbatte. Jane etasminti vā janetasmiṃ, manussesūti attho, tenāha “gottapaṭisārino”ti. Saṃsanditvāti ghaṭetvā, aviruddhaṃ katvāti attho.

277. 'In this that is born' means produced by action and defilements. Or, 'in this people,' meaning 'among humans'; hence it is said, 'those who rely on lineage.' 'Having compared' means having connected, the meaning is having made it non-conflicting.

Paṭhamabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the first recitation section is completed.

Vijjācaraṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on Knowledge and Conduct.

278. Idaṃ vaṭṭatīti idaṃ ajjhenādi kattuṃ labbhati. Jātivādavinibaddhāti jātisannissitavāde vinibaddhā. Brāhmaṇasseva ajjhenajjhāpanayajanayājanādayoti [P 1.0398] evaṃ ye attukkaṃsanaparavambhanavasena pavattā, tato eva te mānavādapaṭibaddhā ca honti. Ye pana āvāhavivāhavinibaddhā, te eva sambandhattayavasena “arahasi vā maṃ tvaṃ, na vā maṃ tvaṃ arahasī”ti evaṃ pavattanakā.

278. 'This is proper' means this studying, and so on, is permitted to be done. 'Bound by talk of caste' means bound in speech that is based on caste. 'Only a brahmin has the right to study, teach, sacrifice, and officiate at sacrifices,' and so on—thus, those who proceed by way of self-praise and disparagement of others are also bound by talk of conceit. But those who are bound by giving and taking in marriage are the ones who proceed in terms of the threefold connection, saying, 'You are worthy of me, or you are not worthy of me.'

Yatthāti yassaṃ vijjācaraṇasampattiyaṃ. Laggissāmāti olaggā antogadhā bhavissāmāti cintayimha. Paramatthato avijjācaraṇāniyeva “vijjācaraṇānī”ti gahetvā ṭhito paramatthato vijjācaraṇesu vibhajiyamānesu so tato dūrato apanīto nāma hotīti āha “dūrameva avakkhipī”ti. Samudāgamato pabhutītiādisamuṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya.

'Where' means in that accomplishment of knowledge and conduct. 'We shall cling' means we thought, 'we shall be attached, we shall be included within.' One who stands holding what are in the ultimate sense actually non-knowledge and non-conduct as 'knowledge and conduct', when knowledge and conduct are being analyzed in the ultimate sense, is indeed removed far from that; hence it is said, 'he is cast far away.' 'From the arising' means starting from the initial origin.

279. Tividhaṃ sīlanti khuddakādibhedaṃ tividhaṃ sīlaṃ. Sīlavasenevāti sīlapariyāyeneva. Kiñci kiñcīti ahiṃsanādiyamaniyamalakkhaṇaṃ kiñci kiñci sīlaṃ atthi. Tattha tattheva laggeyyāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃyeva brāhmaṇasamayasiddhe sīlamatte “caraṇa”nti laggeyya. Aṭṭhapi samāpattiyo caraṇanti niyyātitā honti rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānaniddeseneva arūpajjhānānampi niddiṭṭhabhāvāpattito niyyātitā nidassitā.

279. The threefold virtue means the threefold virtue distinguished as minor, and so on. 'By the power of virtue' means precisely by the way of virtue. 'Whatever little' refers to some virtue characterized by non-harming and other restraints and observances. 'Should cling to that very thing' means one should cling solely to that mere virtue established in the brahminical doctrine, calling it 'conduct.' The eight attainments are also designated as conduct; because the formless jhānas are also indicated by the description of the fourth jhāna of the form realm, they are designated and shown.

Catuapāyamukhakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Four Gateways to Downfall.

280. Asampāpuṇantoti [V 1.0271][M 1.0306] ārabhitvā sampattuṃ asakkonto. Avisahamānoti ārabhitumeva asakkonto. Khārinti parikkhāraṃ. Taṃ pana vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “araṇī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha araṇīti aggidhamanakaṃ araṇīdvayaṃ. Sujāti dabbi. Ādi-saddena tidaṇḍatighaṭikādiṃ [P 1.0399] saṅgaṇhāti khāribharitanti khārīhi puṇṇaṃ. Nanu upasampannassa bhikkhuno sāsanikopi yo koci anupasampanno atthato paricārakova, kiṃ aṅgaṃ pana bāhirakapabbajiteti tattha visesaṃ dassetuṃ “kāmañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Vuttanayenāti “kappiyakaraṇa…pe… vattakaraṇavasenā”ti evaṃ vuttena nayena. Paricārako hoti upasampannabhāvassa visiṭṭhabhāvato. “Navakoṭisahassānī”tiādinā (visuddhi. 1.20; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 37) vuttappabhedānaṃ anekasahassānaṃ saṃvaravinayānaṃ samādiyitvā vattanena uparibhūtā aggabhūtā sampadāti hi “upasampadā”ti vuccatīti. Guṇādhikopīti guṇehi ukkaṭṭhopi. Ayaṃ panāti vuttalakkhaṇo tāpaso.

280. "Unable to reach" means one who, having started, is incapable of attaining. "Unable to endure" means one is incapable of even beginning. "Burden" refers to requisites. But to show this dividedly, "fire-sticks" and so on are said. Here, "fire-sticks" means the pair of fire-kindling sticks. A "sujā" is a ladle. The term "etc." includes items like the three-pronged staff and the tripod. "Filled with bushels" means filled full with bushels. Now, for a fully ordained monk, any unordained person within the Dispensation is essentially a servant in purpose; what more then an external renunciant? To show this distinction, "as one wishes" and so on are stated. "In the manner explained" means in the way described, such as "making allowable… by the means of performing duties." He is a servant because of the distinguished nature of the state of full ordination. For it is called "full ordination" because it is a superior, foremost attainment through undertaking and practicing the many thousands of restraints and disciplines of the various kinds mentioned in such passages as "ninety thousand crores" and so on (Vism I.20; Paṭis-a 37). "Superior in virtues" means one who is pre-eminent in qualities. "But this" refers to the ascetic of the aforementioned characteristics.

Tāpasā nāma kammavādikiriyāvādino, na sāsanassa paṭāṇībhūtā, yato nesaṃ pabbajituṃ āgatānaṃ titthiyaparivāsena vināva pabbajjā anuññātāti katvā “kasmā panā”ti codanaṃ samuṭṭhapeti codako. Ācariyo “yasmā”tiādinā codanaṃ pariharati. “Osakkissatī”ti saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vivarituṃ “imasmiñhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Khuradhārūpamanti khuradhārānaṃ matthakeneva akkamitvā gamanūpamaṃ. Aññeti aññe bhikkhū. Aggisālanti aggihuttasālaṃ. Nānādārūhīti palāsadaṇḍādinānāvidhasamidhādārūhi.

Ascetics are those who advocate action and the efficacy of action, not being opposed to the Dispensation; for this reason, ordination is permitted for those who have come to go forth from their fold without the probationary period for sectarians. Thus, the objector raises the objection, "But why?" The teacher refutes the objection with "because" and so on. To elaborate on the meaning briefly stated as "will decline," it is said, "for in this case" and so on. "Like a razor's edge" is a simile for walking as if treading only on the very edge of a razor. "Others" means other monks. "Fire-hall" refers to the fire-offering hall. "With various kinds of firewood" means with various kinds of sacrificial firewood, such as palāsa sticks and so on.

Idanti “catudvāraṃ āgāraṃ katvā”tiādinā vuttaṃ. Assāti assa catutthassa puggalassa. Paṭipattimukhanti kohaññapaṭipattiyā mukhamattaṃ. So hi nānāvidhena kohaññena lokaṃ vimhāpento tattha acchati, tenāha “iminā hi mukhena so evaṃ paṭipajjatī”ti.

"This" is what is stated in the phrase "having made a house with four doors," etc. "Of this one" means of this fourth individual. "The entrance to the practice" refers to merely the entrance to the practice of hypocrisy. For he stays there astonishing the world with various forms of hypocrisy, hence it is said, "by this entrance he practices thus."

Khalādīsu [P 1.0400] manussānaṃ santike upatiṭṭhitvā vīhimuggatilamāsādīni bhikkhācariyāniyāmena saṅkaḍḍhitvā uñchanaṃ uñchā, sā eva cariyā vutti etesanti uñchācariyā. Aggipakkena jīvantīti aggipakkikā, na aggipakkikā anaggipakkikā[M 1.0307]. Uñchācariyā hi khalesu gantvā khalaggaṃ nāma manussehi diyyamānaṃ dhaññaṃ gaṇhanti, taṃ ime na gaṇhantīti anaggipakkikā nāma jātā. Asāmapākāti asayaṃpācakā. Asmamuṭṭhinā muṭṭhipāsāṇena [V 1.0272] vattantīti asmamuṭṭhikā. Dantena uppāṭitaṃ vakkalaṃ rukkhattaco dantavakkalaṃ, tena vattantīti dantavakkalikā. Pavattaṃ rukkhādito pātitaṃ phalaṃ bhuñjantīti pavattaphalabhojino. Jiṇṇapakkatāya paṇḍubhūtaṃ palāsaṃ, taṃsadisañca paṇḍupalāsaṃ, tena vattantīti paṇḍupalāsikā, sayaṃpatitapupphaphalapattabhojino.

At threshing floors and other such places, standing near people and collecting rice, beans, sesame, lentils, and so on, by the rule of alms-gathering, is called gleaning. Those whose practice and livelihood this is are called gleaners. Those who live on what is cooked by fire are called fire-eaters; those who are not fire-eaters are non-fire-eaters. For gleaners go to the threshing floors and accept the grain called 'the top of the heap' given by people, but these ascetics do not accept it; hence they are called non-fire-eaters. 'Those who do not cook' means those who do not cook for themselves. Those who live by a stone held in the fist, that is, a hand-stone, are called stone-fist ascetics. Bark torn off a tree with the teeth is tooth-bark; those who live by this are called tooth-bark ascetics. Those who eat fruit that has fallen from a tree are called fallen-fruit-eaters. A leaf that has become yellow from being old and ripe, and what is similar, is a yellow leaf; those who live on this are called yellow-leaf ascetics, that is, eaters of flowers, fruits, and leaves that have fallen by themselves.

Idāni te aṭṭhavidhepi sarūpato dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Saṅkaḍḍhitvāti bhikkhācariyāvasena laddhadhaññaṃ ekajjhaṃ katvā.

Now, to show these eight types in their own form, it is said, "therein," and so on. "Having collected" means having gathered into one place the grain obtained by way of alms-gathering.

Pariyeṭṭhi nāma dukkhāti paresaṃ gehato gehaṃ gantvā pariyeṭṭhi nāma dīnavuttibhāvena dukkhā. Pāsāṇassa pariggaho dukkho pabbajitassāti vā danteheva uppāṭetvā khādanti.

"Seeking is suffering" means that the search, going from others' house to house, is suffering because it is a wretched livelihood. "The taking up of a stone is suffering for one who has gone forth," or, they tear off with their teeth and eat.

Imāhi catūhiyevāti “khārividhaṃ ādāyā”tiādinā vuttāhi catūhi eva tāpasapabbajjāhīti.

"By these four alone" means by the four ascetic renunciations mentioned, beginning with "taking up the carrying-pole."

282. Apāye vināse niyutto āpāyiko. Tabbhāvaṃ paripūretuṃ asakkonto tena aparipuṇṇo aparipūramāno[P 1.0401], karaṇe cetaṃ paccattavacanaṃ, tenāha “āpāyikenāpi aparipūramānenā”ti.

282. One devoted to the lower realms, to destruction, is called an `āpāyika`. Being unable to fulfill that state, one is thereby unfulfilled, not bringing it to completion. This is a reflexive term in the instrumental case; hence it is said, "even by one bound for the lower realms who is not bringing it to completion."

Pubbakaisibhāvānuyogavaṇṇanā

An Explanation of the Practice of Former Seers

283. Dīyatīti datti, dattiyeva dattikanti āha “dinnaka”nti. Yadi brāhmaṇassa sammukhībhāvo rañño na dātabbo, kasmāssa upasaṅkamanaṃ na paṭikkhittanti āha “yasmā panā”tiādi. Khettavijjāyāti nītisatthe. Payātanti saddhaṃ, sassatikaṃ vā, tenāha “abhiharitvā dinna”nti. Kasmā bhagavā “rañño pasenadissa kosalassa dattikaṃ bhuñjatī”tiādinā brāhmaṇassa mammavacanaṃ avocāti tattha kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “idaṃ pana kāraṇa”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

283. "Because it is given" (`dīyati`), it is a gift (`datti`); a gift itself is a `dattika`. Hence it is said, `dinnaka` (what is given). If the presence of a brahmin is not to be granted to the king, why was his approach not prohibited? To this it is said, "but because," etc. "In the science of the field" means in the science of governance. "Payāta" means with faith, or with one's possessions; hence it is said, "having brought it forward, it is given." Why did the Blessed One speak words that cut to the quick, saying, "he enjoys the gift of King Pasenadi of Kosala," etc.? To explain the reason, it is said, "but this is the reason," etc.

284. Rathūpatthareti [M 1.0308] rathassa upari attharitapadese. Pākaṭamantananti pakāsabhūtaṃ mantanaṃ. Tañhi suddādīhi ñāyatīti na rahassamantanaṃ. Bhaṇatīti api nu bhaṇati.

284. "On the chariot's seat" means in the place spread out upon the chariot. "Open counsel" means counsel that has become public. Since it is known by the Śudras and others, it is not secret counsel. "He speaks" means "Does he indeed speak?"

285. Pavattāroti [V 1.0273] pāvacanabhāvena vattāro, yasmā te tesaṃ mantānaṃ pavattakā, tasmā āha “pavattayitāro”ti. Sudde bahi katvā raho bhāsitabbaṭṭhena mantā eva, taṃtaṃatthapaṭipattihetutāya padanti mantapadaṃ, anupanītāsādhāraṇatāya vā rahassabhāvena vattabbaṃ hitakiriyāya adhigamupāyaṃ. Sajjhāyitanti gāyanavasena sajjhāyitaṃ, taṃ pana udattānudattādīnaṃ sarānaṃ sampādanavaseneva icchitanti āha “sarasampattivasenā”ti. Aññesaṃ vuttanti pāvacanabhāvena aññesaṃ vuttaṃ. Samupabyūḷhanti saṅgahetvā uparūpari saññūḷhaṃ. Rāsikatanti iruvedayajuvedasāmavedādivasena[P 1.0402], tatthāpi paccekaṃ mantabrahmādivasena, ajjhāyānuvākādivasena ca rāsikataṃ.

285. "Originators" refers to those who speak by way of proclamation; because they are the originators of those mantras, they are called "pavattayitāro." They are mantras because they are to be spoken in secret, having excluded the Śudras. A `mantapada` is a `pada` (basis) because it is a cause for the attainment of various goals. Or, it is a means for attaining beneficial action, to be spoken in secret because it is not common to the uninitiated. "Recited" means recited by way of chanting, and this is desired specifically by way of achieving the perfection of tones, such as high and low accents; hence it is said, "by way of the perfection of tone." "Spoken to others" means spoken to others by way of proclamation. "Well-arranged" means collected and piled up one upon another. "Made into a collection" means made into a collection, as in the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, etc., and also collected within each of those by way of Mantra and Brāhmaṇa portions, and by way of chapters and sections.

Tesanti mantānaṃ kattūnaṃ. Dibbena cakkhunā oloketvāti dibbacakkhuparibhaṇḍena yathākammūpagañāṇena sattānaṃ kammassakatādiṃ paccakkhato dassanaṭṭhena dibbacakkhusadisena pubbenivāsañāṇena atītakappe brāhmaṇānaṃ mantajjhenavidhiñca oloketvā. Pāvacanena saha saṃsanditvāti kassapasammāsambuddhassa yaṃ vacanaṃ vaṭṭasannissitaṃ, tena saha aviruddhaṃ katvā. Na hi tesaṃ vivaṭṭasannissito attho paccakkho hoti. Aparāpare panāti aṭṭhakādīhi aparā pare pacchimā okkākarājakālādīsu uppannā. Pakkhipitvāti aṭṭhakādīhi ganthitamantapadesu kilesasannissitapadānaṃ tattha tattha pade pakkhipanaṃ katvā. Viruddhe akaṃsūti brāhmaṇadhammikasuttādīsu āgatanayena saṃkilesikatthadīpanato paccanīkabhūte akaṃsu. Idhāti “tyāhaṃ mante adhīyāmī”ti etasmiṃ ṭhāne. Paṭiññaṃ aggahetvāti “taṃ kiṃ maññasī”ti evaṃ paṭiññaṃ aggahetvāva.

"Of them" refers to the creators of the mantras. "Having observed with the divine eye" means having observed with the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their karma, which is the equipment for the divine eye, and with the knowledge of previous existences, which is like the divine eye in directly seeing beings' ownership of karma, and having observed the method of the brahmins' mantra recitation in past eons. "Harmonizing with the teaching" means making it not contradict the teaching of Kassapa the Perfectly Enlightened One, that is, the teaching that is dependent on the round of rebirths. For the meaning pertaining to the cessation of the round is not directly apparent to them. "Later ones" refers to those subsequent to Aṭṭhaka and others, the later, subsequent ones who arose in the time of King Okkāka and others. "Having inserted" means having inserted words connected with defilements here and there into the mantra passages composed by Aṭṭhaka and others. "They made them contradictory" means they made them contrary by showing a meaning connected with defilements, in the way that has come down in the Brāhmaṇadhammika Sutta and others. "Here" refers to this place: "Thus I study the mantras." "Without getting an admission" means without getting an admission by saying, "What do you think of this?"

286. Nirāmagandhāti kilesāsucivasena vissagandharahitā. Anitthigandhāti itthīnaṃ gandhamattassapi avisahanena itthigandharahitā. Ettha ca “nirāmagandhā”ti [M 1.0309] etena tesaṃ porāṇānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ vikkhambhitakilesataṃ dasseti, “anitthigandhā brahmacārino”ti etena ekavihāritaṃ, “rajojalladharā”ti etena maṇḍanavibhūsanānuyogābhāvaṃ, “araññāyatane pabbatapādesu vasiṃsū”ti etena manussūpacāraṃ [P 1.0403] pahāya vivittavāsaṃ, “vanamūlaphalāhārā vasiṃsū”ti etena sālimaṃsodanādipaṇītāhārapaṭikkhepaṃ, “yadā”tiādinā yānavāhanapaṭikkhepaṃ, “sabbadisāsū”tiādinā rakkhāvaraṇapaṭikkhepaṃ, evañca vadanto micchāpaṭipadāpakkhikaṃ sācariyassa ambaṭṭhassa vuttiṃ upādāya sammāpaṭipadāpakkhikāpi tesaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ vutti ariyavinaye sammāpaṭipattiṃ upādāya micchāpaṭipadāyeva. Kutassa sallekhapaṭipattiyuttatāti. “Evaṃ sute”tiādinā bhagavā ambaṭṭhaṃ santajjento niggaṇhātīti dasseti.

286. "Free from the raw-smell" means devoid of the stench of defilements, because of the impurity of defilements. "Free from the scent of women" means devoid of the scent of women, as they could not bear even the mere scent of women. Herein, by "free from the raw-smell," he shows the suppression of defilements of those ancient brahmins. By "free from the scent of women, celibate," he shows their solitary living. By "covered with dust and dirt," he shows their lack of engagement in adornment and embellishment. By "they dwelt in forest resorts at the foot of mountains," he shows their secluded life, having abandoned human company. By "they lived on wild roots and fruits," he shows their rejection of refined food such as rice with meat. By the words beginning "when," he shows their rejection of vehicles and conveyances. By the words beginning "in all directions," he shows their rejection of protection and barriers. Thus, speaking in this way, with reference to the conduct of Ambaṭṭha with his teacher, which is on the side of wrong practice, he shows that even the conduct of those brahmins, which is on the side of right practice, is itself wrong practice when compared to the right practice in the Noble Discipline. How could it be connected with the practice of effacement? By the words beginning "When this was heard," it is shown that the Blessed One, rebuking Ambaṭṭha, censures him.

Veṭhakehīti [V 1.0274] veṭhakapaṭṭakāhi. Samantānagaranti nagarassa samantato. Katasudhākammaṃ pākārassa adhobhāge ṭhānaṃ vuccatīti adhippāyo.

"With wrappings" means with wrapping-strips. "All around the city" means all around the city. "Work done with plaster" means the place at the lower part of the wall; this is the meaning.

Dvelakkhaṇadassanavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of Seeing the Two Characteristics

287. Na sakkotisaṅkucite iriyāpathe anavasesato tesaṃ dubbibhāvanato. Gavesīti ñāṇena pariyesanamakāsi. Samānayīti ñāṇena saṅkalento sammā ānayi samāhari. “Kaṅkhatī”ti padassa ākaṅkhatīti ayamatthoti āha “aho vata passeyyanti patthanaṃ uppādetī”ti. Kicchatīti kilamati. “Kaṅkhatī”ti padassa pubbe āsisanatthataṃ vatvā idānissa saṃsayatthatameva vikappantaravasena dassento “kaṅkhāya vā dubbalā vimati vuttā”ti āha. Tīhi dhammehīti tippakārehi saṃsayadhammehi. Kālusiyabhāvoti appasannatāya hetubhūto āvilabhāvo.

287. "He is not able": in a contracted posture, because of the difficulty of discerning them completely. "He sought" means he made a search with knowledge. "He brought together" means, reflecting with knowledge, he properly brought together, he collected. Regarding the word 'kaṅkhati' (he doubts), the meaning is 'he longs for'; thus, it is said, "he generates the wish, ‘Oh, that I might see!’" "He toils" means he becomes weary. Having previously stated that the word 'kaṅkhati' has the meaning of wishing, now, showing its meaning as uncertainty by way of an alternative, he said, "or by ‘doubt,’ a weak uncertainty is meant." "By three qualities" means by three kinds of qualities pertaining to doubt. "The state of being sullied" refers to the turbid state which is the cause of a lack of confidence.

Yasmā bhagavato kosohitaṃ sabbabuddhānaṃ āveṇikaṃ aññehi asādhāraṇaṃ vatthaguyhaṃ suvisuddhakañcanamaṇḍalasannikāsaṃ, attano saṇṭhānasannivesasundaratāya [P 1.0404] ājāneyyagandhahatthino varaṅgaparamacārubhāvaṃ, vikasamānatapaniyāravindasamujjalakesarāvattavilāsaṃ, sañjhāpabhānurañjitajalavanantarābhilakkhitasampuṇṇacandamaṇḍalasobhañca attano siriyā abhibhuyya virājati, yaṃ bāhirabbhantaramalehi anupakkiliṭṭhatāya, cirakālaṃ suparicitabrahmacariyādhikāratāya, susaṇṭhitasaṇṭhānasampattiyā ca[M 1.0310], kopīnampi santaṃ akopīnameva, tasmā vuttaṃ “bhagavato hī”tiādi. Pahūtabhāvanti puthulabhāvaṃ. Ettheva hi tassa saṃsayo, tanumudusukumāratādīsu panassa guṇesu vicāraṇā eva nāhosi.

Because the Blessed One’s private part is concealed in a sheath—a feature unique to all Buddhas and not shared by others, resembling a disc of perfectly pure gold; and because, due to the beauty of its form and placement, it shines, surpassing with its own splendor the supreme loveliness of the generative organ of a thoroughbred elephant in rut, the charm of the whorl of radiant filaments of a blossoming golden lotus, and the beauty of the full moon's disc seen amidst a forest by the water, colored by the evening light; and because it is unstained by external or internal defilements, due to the authority of the holy life well-practiced for a long time, and due to the perfection of its well-established form, though being a shameful part, it is not shameful—therefore, it is said, "the Blessed One’s," etc. "Abundant nature" means broadness. Here indeed was his doubt; regarding its qualities such as fineness, softness, and delicacy, there was no investigation at all.

288. Hirikaraṇokāsanti hiriyitabbaṭṭhānaṃ. Chāyanti paṭibimbaṃ. Kathaṃ kīdisanti āha “iddhiyā”tiādi. Chāyārūpakamattanti bhagavato paṭibimbarūpaṃ. Tañca kho buddhasantānato vinimuttattā rūpakamattaṃ bhagavato sarīravaṇṇasaṇṭhānāvayavaṃ iddhimayaṃ bimbakamattaṃ. Taṃ pana rūpakamattaṃ dassento bhagavā yathā attano buddharūpaṃ na dissati, tathā katvā dasseti. Ninnetvāti nīharitvā. Kallosīti pucchāvissajjane kusalo cheko asi. Tathākaraṇenāti kathinasūciṃ viya karaṇena. Etthāti pahūtajivhāya. Mudubhāvo pakāsito amuduno ghanasukhumabhāvāpādanatthaṃ asakkuṇeyyattā dīghabhāvo, tanubhāvo cāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

288. "A place for shame" means a ground for feeling shame. "Shadow" means reflection. "How? What kind?"—he explains with "by psychic power," etc. "Merely a form-image" refers to the Blessed One’s reflected image. And that, being separate from the Buddha’s continuum, is merely a form-image, a psychic creation resembling the Blessed One’s body in color, shape, and limbs. Showing this mere form-image, the Blessed One displayed it in such a way that his own Buddha-form was not visible. "Drawing out" means extracting. "You are skilled" means you are skilled and clever in questioning and answering. "By such action" means by an action like that of a stiff needle. Here, with the extensive tongue, its softness is revealed; its length and thinness are to be understood, because it is impossible for something not soft to be made both thick and fine.

291. “Atthacarakenā”ti [V 1.0275] iminā byatirekamukhena anatthacarakataṃyeva vibhāveti. Na aññatrāti na aññasmiṃ sugatiyanti attho. Upanetvā [P 1.0405] upanetvāti taṃ taṃ dosaṃ upanetvā upanetvā, tenāha “suṭṭhudāsādibhāvaṃ āropetvā”ti. Pātesīti pavaṭṭanavasena pātesi.

291. "'By one who pursues benefit'—by this, through the method of contrast, he explains the very state of pursuing what is not beneficial. "Not elsewhere" means not in any other good destination. "Repeatedly bringing up" means repeatedly bringing up each and every fault; therefore, he said, "after thoroughly imposing the state of being a bad slave," etc. "Caused to fall" means caused to fall by way of setting in motion.

Pokkharasātibuddhūpasaṅkamanavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of Pokkharasāti's Visit to the Buddha

293-6. Āgamā nūti āgato nu. Khoti nipātamattaṃ. Idhāti ettha, tumhākaṃ santikanti attho. Adhivāsetūti sādiyatu, taṃ pana sādiyanaṃ manasā sampaṭiggaho hotīti āha “sampaṭicchatū”ti.

293-6. "Āgamā nu" means "has he come?" "Kho" is merely a particle. "Idha" means "here," that is, "in your presence." "Adhivāsetu" means "may he consent"; but that consent is a mental acceptance, hence he says, "may he receive."

297. Yāvadatthanti yāva attho, tāva bhojanena tadā katanti attho. Oṇittanti āmisāpanayanena sucikataṃ, tenāha “hatthe ca pattañca dhovitvā”ti.

297. "As much as needed" means that as much was done with the food then as was required. "Cleansed" means made clean by the removal of food remnants; hence, he said, "having washed his hand and bowl."

298. Anupubbiṃ kathanti anupubbaṃ kathetabbakathaṃ, tenāha “anupaṭipāṭikatha”nti. Kā pana sā? Dānādikathāti āha “dānānantaraṃ sīla”ntiādi. Tena dānakathā tāva pacurajanesupi pavattiyā sabbasādhāraṇattā, sukarattā, sīle patiṭṭhānassa upāyabhāvato ca ādito [M 1.0311] kathetabbā. Pariccāgasīlo hi puggalo pariggahitavatthūsu nissaṅgabhāvato sukheneva sīlāni samādiyati, tattha ca suppatiṭṭhito hoti. Sīlena dāyakapaṭiggāhakasuddhito parānuggahaṃ vatvā parapīḷānivattivacanato, kiriyadhammaṃ vatvā akiriyadhammavacanato, bhogasampattihetuṃ vatvā bhavasampattihetuvacanato ca dānakathānantaraṃ sīlakathā kathetabbā, tañce dānasīlaṃ vaṭṭanissitaṃ, ayaṃ bhavasampatti tassa phalanti dassanatthaṃ imehi ca dānasīlamayehi paṇītapaṇītatarādibhedabhinnehi puññakiriyavatthūhi etā cātumahārājikādīsu paṇītapaṇītatarādibhedabhinnā [P 1.0406] aparimeyyā dibbabhogasampattiyo laddhabbāti dassanatthaṃ tadanantaraṃ saggakathā. Svāyaṃ saggo rāgādīhi upakkiliṭṭho, sabbathānupakkiliṭṭho ariyamaggoti dassanatthaṃ saggānantaraṃ maggo kathetabbo. Maggañca kathentena tadadhigamupāyasandassanatthaṃ saggapariyāpannāpi, pageva itare sabbepi kāmā nāma bahvādīnavā aniccā addhuvā vipariṇāmadhammāti kāmānaṃ ādīnavo, hīnā gammā pothujjanikā anariyā anatthasañhitāti tesaṃ okāro lāmakabhāvo, sabbepi bhavā kilesānaṃ vatthubhūtāti tattha saṃkileso, sabbasaṃkilesavippamuttaṃ nibbānanti nekkhamme ānisaṃso ca kathetabboti ayamattho bodhitoti veditabbo. Maggoti cettha iti-saddena ādiatthadīpanato “kāmānaṃ ādīnavo”ti evamādīnaṃ saṅgahoti [V 1.0276] evamayaṃ atthavaṇṇanā katāti veditabbā. “Tassa uppattiākāradassanattha”nti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu maggañāṇaṃ asaṅkhatadhammārammaṇaṃ, na saṅkhatadhammārammaṇanti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “tañhī”tiādi. Tattha paṭivijjhantanti asammohapaṭivedhavasena paṭivijjhantaṃ, tenāha “kiccavasenā”ti.

298. ‘Gradual talk’ means a talk that should be given gradually; hence, it is called a ‘sequential discourse.’ What is that? It is the talk on generosity and so forth, as stated: ‘After generosity, virtue,’ etc. Therefore, the talk on generosity should be given first because it is prevalent even among many people, because it is easy to practice, and because it serves as a foundation for virtue. A person inclined to generosity, being free from attachment to possessions, easily undertakes the precepts and becomes well-established in them. After discussing generosity, the talk on virtue should follow, explaining the purification of donors and recipients, speaking of compassion for others, speaking of abstaining from harming others, speaking of wholesome actions and speaking of refraining from unwholesome actions, speaking of the cause of prosperity in this life and speaking of the cause of prosperity in future existences. If this generosity and virtue are rooted in the round of existence, one should then explain that this prosperity is their fruit. Furthermore, by showing how immeasurable divine enjoyments, differing in higher and lower forms, can be attained in the realms of the Four Great Kings and beyond through these acts of generosity and virtue, which are different kinds of meritorious actions, the talk on heaven should follow. This heaven is defiled by lust and so forth, whereas the Noble Path is entirely undefiled – to show this, after the talk on heaven, the path should be explained. When teaching the path, to show the means to attain it, it should be taught that even the pleasures included in heavenly realms—let alone other sensual pleasures—are full of many dangers, impermanent, unstable, and subject to change. This is the drawback of sensual pleasures. They are low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and not connected to what is beneficial—this is their baseness and inferiority. All states of existence are the basis for defilements—this is their defilement. Complete liberation from all defilements is Nibbāna—this is the benefit of renunciation. This is the meaning that should be understood as having been explained. Here, regarding ‘the path,’ because the particle ‘iti’ indicates ‘and so forth,’ it encompasses points such as ‘the drawbacks of sensual pleasures.’ Thus, this explanation of the meaning should be understood as having been made. ‘Why is it said, “to show the manner of its arising”?’ In reference to the objection, ‘Does not the knowledge of the path have the unconditioned as its object, not the conditioned?’, it is said, ‘For it…’ and so on. Here, ‘penetrates’ means penetrating by way of non-deluded realization; hence, it is said, ‘by way of function.’

Pokkharasātiupāsakattapaṭivedanākathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of Pokkharasāti's Declaration of Lay Discipleship.

299. Ettha ca “diṭṭhadhammo”tiādi pāḷiyaṃ dassanaṃ nāma ñāṇadassanato aññampi atthi, tannivattanatthaṃ “pattadhammo”ti vuttaṃ. Patti ca ñāṇasampattito aññampi vijjatīti tato visesadassanatthaṃ “viditadhammo”ti vuttaṃ. Sā panesā viditadhammatā ekadesatopi hotīti nippadesato viditabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “pariyogāḷhadhammo”ti [P 1.0407] vuttaṃ. Tenassa saccābhisambodhaṃyeva dīpeti. Maggañāṇañhi ekābhisamayavasena pariññādikiccaṃ sādhentaṃ nippadesena [M 1.0312] catusaccadhammaṃ samantato ogāḷhaṃ nāma hoti, tenāha “diṭṭho ariyasaccadhammo etenāti diṭṭhadhammo”ti. Tiṇṇā vicikicchāti sappaṭibhayakantārasadisā soḷasavatthukā, aṭṭhavatthukā ca tiṇṇā vitiṇṇā vicikicchā. Vigatā kathaṅkathāti pavattiādīsu. “Evaṃ nu kho, na nu kho”ti evaṃ pavattikā vigatā samucchinnā kathaṅkathā. Vesārajjappattoti sārajjakarānaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ pahīnattā, tappaṭipakkhesu ca sīlādiguṇesu suppatiṭṭhitattā vesārajjaṃ visāradabhāvaṃ veyyattiyaṃ patto adhigato. Sāyaṃ vesārajjappatti suppatiṭṭhitabhāvoti katvā āha “satthusāsane”ti. Attanā paccakkhato diṭṭhattā adhigatattā na paraṃ pacceti, na tassa paro paccetabbo atthīti aparappaccayo. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ avuttaṃ, taṃ parato āgamissati. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

299. Here, in the phrase ‘diṭṭhadhammo’ (one who has seen the Dhamma) and so on in the Pāli, ‘seeing’ can mean something other than knowledge and vision; to preclude this, the term ‘pattadhammo’ (one who has attained the Dhamma) is used. And since attainment can exist apart from the attainment of knowledge, to show the distinction from that, the term ‘viditadhammo’ (one who has understood the Dhamma) is used. But since this understanding of the Dhamma can be partial, to indicate an understanding that is complete and without remainder, the term ‘pariyogāḷhadhammo’ (one who has thoroughly penetrated the Dhamma) is used. This reveals his full comprehension of the truths. For the knowledge of the path, by accomplishing the tasks of full understanding and so on through a single breakthrough, is said to have thoroughly penetrated the Dhamma of the Four Truths in its entirety and without remainder. Hence it is said: ‘The Dhamma of the Noble Truths has been seen by him—thus, he is “one who has seen the Dhamma.”’ ‘Crossed over doubt’ (tiṇṇā vicikicchā) means that the sixteen-fold and eight-fold doubts, which are like a terrifying wilderness, have been crossed over and surmounted. ‘Free from uncertainty’ (vigatā kathaṅkathā) means that in matters of origination and so on, the uncertainty of ‘Is it so? Is it not so?’ has been removed and eradicated. ‘Attained confidence’ (vesārajjappatto) means that because the evil qualities that cause timidity have been abandoned, and because he is well-established in their counteracting qualities like virtue, etc., he has attained fearlessness, self-confidence, and proficiency. This attainment of confidence is due to his well-established state; hence it is said: ‘in the Teacher’s dispensation.’ Having directly seen and realized it for himself, he does not rely on another, nor is there another for him to rely on—thus, he is ‘independent’ (aparappaccayo). Whatever remains to be said here but has not been stated will be addressed later. The rest is readily comprehensible.

Ambaṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Ambaṭṭha Sutta.

4. Soṇadaṇḍasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta.

300. Sundarabhāvena [V 1.0277][M 1.0313][P 1.0408] sātisayāni aṅgāni etesaṃ atthīti aṅgā, rājakumārāti āha “aṅgā nāma aṅgapāsādikatāyā”tiādi. Idhāpi adhippetā, na ambaṭṭhasutte eva. Āgantuṃ na dassantīti āgamane ādīnavaṃ dassetvā paṭikkhipanavasena āgantuṃ na dassanti, nānujānissantīti adhippāyo. Nīlāsokakaṇikārakoviḷārakundarājarukkhehi sammissatāya taṃ campakavanaṃ “nīlādipañcavaṇṇakusumapaṭimaṇḍita”nti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na campakarukkhānaṃyeva nīlādipañcakusumatāyāti vadanti. “Bhagavā kusumagandhasugandhe campakavane viharatī”ti iminā na māpanakāle eva tasmiṃ nagare campakarukkhā ussannā, atha kho aparabhāge pīti dasseti. Māpanakāle hi campakānaṃ ussannatāya sā nagarī “campā”ti nāmaṃ labhi. Issarattāti adhipatibhāvato. Senā etassa atthīti seniko, seniko eva seniyo, atthitā cettha bahubhāvavisiṭṭhāti vuttaṃ “mahatiyā senāya samannāgatattā”ti.

300. ‘Because they have limbs that are exceedingly beautiful, they are called “Aṅga”; they are princes,’ thus it is said, ‘Aṅga are so called because of their excellent limbs,’ and so on. Here too, this is implied, not only in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. ‘They do not allow coming’ means they refuse by showing the disadvantages of coming, thus not permitting it—this is the intended meaning. The Campaka grove, mingled with blue Asoka, Kanikara, Koviḷāra, and Kundarāja trees, should be seen as ‘adorned with flowers of five colors, such as blue.’ It is said that this is not because the Campaka trees themselves have flowers of five colors, including blue. ‘The Blessed One dwells in the Campaka grove, fragrant with the scent of flowers’—this indicates that Campaka trees were abundant in that city not only at the time of its founding, but also later. For at the time of its founding, the abundance of Campaka trees in that city led it to obtain the name ‘Campā.’ ‘By lordship’ (issarattā) means by supremacy. ‘He has an army’ (senā etassa atthi) means he is a senika; senika is indeed seniya. The state of having here is characterized by abundance, as stated: ‘because he is endowed with a great army.’

301-2. Saṃhatāti sannipatitā, “saṅghino”ti vattabbe “saṅghī”ti puthutthe ekavacanaṃ brāhmaṇagahapatikānaṃ adhippetattā, tenāha “etesa”nti. Rājarājaññādīnaṃ bhaṇḍadharā purisā khatā, nesaṃ [P 1.0409] tāyanato khattā. So hi yehi yattha pesito, tattha tesaṃ dosaṃ pariharanto yuttapattavasena pucchitamatthaṃ katheti, tenāha “pucchitapañhe byākaraṇasamattho”ti. Kulāpadesādinā mahatī mattā etassāti mahāmatto.

‘Assembled’ (saṃhatā) means gathered together (sannipatitā). Though ‘saṅghino’ (plural) should be said, ‘saṅghī’ (singular) is used in a collective sense, as brahmins and householders are intended; hence it is said ‘of these’ (etesaṃ). ‘Khattā’ are men who bear the goods of kings, princes, and so on. The term is derived from ‘protecting’ (tāyanato) them. For wherever he is sent by whomever, he explains the matter that has been asked in a fitting and appropriate manner, avoiding their faults; hence it is said he is ‘capable of answering questions when asked.’ ‘Mahāmatto’ means one whose measure (mattā) is great (mahatī) because of designation by family, and so on.

Soṇadaṇḍaguṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Soṇadaṇḍa's Qualities.

303. Visiṭṭhaṃ rajjaṃ virajjaṃ, virajjameva verajjaṃ yathā “vekataṃ vesaya”nti, nānāvidhaṃ verajjaṃ nānāverajjaṃ, tattha jātātiādinā sabbaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Uttamabrāhmaṇoti [V 1.0278] abhijanasampattiyā vittasampattiyā vijjāsampattiyā uggatataro, uḷāro vā brāhmaṇo. Asannipātoti lābhamaccharena nippīḷitatāya asannipāto viya bhavissati.

303. An excellent kingdom (visiṭṭhaṃ rajjaṃ) is a spotless kingdom (virajjaṃ); spotless itself (virajjam eva) becomes verajjaṃ, just as ‘vekataṃ’ becomes ‘vesayaṃ.’ A diverse kingdom (nānāvidhaṃ verajjaṃ) is nānāverajjaṃ. Everything from ‘born there’ onwards should be understood in the manner already stated. ‘The foremost brahmin’ (uttamabrāhmaṇo) means a brahmin who is superior or distinguished on account of his accomplishment in lineage, accomplishment in wealth, and accomplishment in knowledge. ‘Without gathering’ (asannipāto) means, due to being oppressed by stinginess regarding gain, it will be as if there is no gathering.

“Aṅgeti [M 1.0314] gameti ñāpetīti aṅgaṃ, hetūti āha “imināpi kāraṇenā”ti. “Ubhato sujāto”ti ettake vutte yehi kehici dvīhi bhāgehi sujātatā viññāyeyya. Sujāta-saddo ca “sujāto cārudassano”tiādīsu (theragā. 818) ārohasampattipariyāyoti jātivaseneva sujātataṃ vibhāvetuṃ “mātito ca pitito cā”ti vuttaṃ. Anorasaputtavasenāpi loke mātupitusamaññā dissati, idha panassa orasaputtavaseneva icchitāti dassetuṃ “saṃsuddhagahaṇiko”ti vuttaṃ. Gabbhaṃ gaṇhāti dhāretīti gahaṇī, gabbhāsayasaññito mātukucchippadeso. Yathābhuttassa [P 1.0410] āhārassa vipācanavasena gaṇhanato achaḍḍanato gahaṇī, kammajatejodhātu.

It is called 'aṅga' because it indicates, causes to go, and informs; the reason is stated as 'by this cause.' When only 'well-born on both sides' is said, well-bornness might be understood through any two factors. And since the word 'sujāta' in instances such as 'well-born and lovely to behold' (Theragāthā 818) is a synonym for accomplishment in stature, in order to distinguish well-bornness specifically by birth, 'from the mother and the father' is stated. In the world, the designation 'mother and father' is seen even in the case of non-biological sons; here, however, to show that only biological offspring is intended, 'of pure conception' is stated. 'Gahaṇī' is what takes and holds – the region of the mother's womb, synonymous with the uterus. Or, because of taking and not rejecting what has been consumed through the digestion of food, it is called 'gahaṇī'; it is the element of heat born of kamma.

Pitā ca mātā ca pitaro, pitūnaṃ pitaro pitāmahā, tesaṃ yugo dvando pitāmahayugo, tasmā, yāva sattamā pitāmahayugā pitāmahadvandāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Evañhi pitāmahaggahaṇeneva mātāmahopi gahitoti. So aṭṭhakathāyaṃ visuṃ na uddhaṭo. Yuga-saddo cettha ekasesanayena daṭṭhabbo “yugo ca yugo ca yugā”ti. Evañhi tattha tattha dvandaṃ gahitameva hoti, tenāha “tato uddhaṃ sabbepi pubbapurisā pitāmahaggahaṇeneva gahitā”ti. Purisaggahaṇañcettha ukkaṭṭhaniddesavasena katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evañhi “mātito”ti pāḷivacanaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti. Akkhittoti appattakhepo. Anavakkhittoti saddhathālipākādīsu na avakkhitto na chaḍḍito. Jātivādenāti hetumhi karaṇavacananti dassetuṃ “kena kāraṇenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ettha ca “ubhato…pe… pitāmahayugā”ti etena brāhmaṇassa yonidosābhāvo dassito saṃsuddhagahaṇikabhāvakittanato, “akkhitto”ti iminā kiriyāparādhābhāvo. Kiriyāparādhena hi sattā khepaṃ pāpuṇanti. “Anupakkuṭṭho”ti iminā ayuttasaṃsaggābhāvo. Ayuttasaṃsaggampi hi paṭicca sattā akkosaṃ labhanti.

Father and mother are parents; the fathers of the fathers are grandfathers; their pair, the grandfather-pair, thus, up to the seventh grandfather-pair, the pairs of grandfathers—thus the meaning here should be understood. For indeed, by the mention of grandfathers, maternal grandfathers are also included. Thus, it is not separately stated in the commentary. The word 'yuga' here should be understood in the sense of an ekasesa, as in 'a pair and a pair, pairs.' Thus, in each case, the pair is indeed taken, hence it is said, 'From there onwards, all ancestors are included by the mention of grandfathers.' The mention of 'purisa' here should be seen as an indication of excellence. Thus, the Pali expression 'from the mother’s side' is justified. 'Akkhitto' means not subject to rejection. 'Anavakkhitto' means not cast aside or abandoned in matters such as meals offered in faith. 'Jātivādena' is said to show the reason in the instrumental case, as in 'by what reason?' Here, by the phrase 'on both sides... up to the grandfather-pairs,' the absence of birth-defects in the brahmin is shown, praising the state of having a pure lineage. By 'akkhitto,' the absence of actional transgression is indicated. For beings incur rejection due to actional transgression. By 'anupakkuṭṭho,' the absence of improper association is shown. For beings receive abuse due to improper association.

Issaroti ādhipateyyasaṃvattaniyakammabalena īsanasīlo, sā panassa issaratā vibhavasampattipaccayā pākaṭā jātāti aḍḍhatāpariyāyabhāveneva vadanto “aḍḍhoti issaro”ti āha. Mahantaṃ dhanaṃ assa bhūmigatañceva vehāsaṭṭhañcāti mahaddhano. Tassāti tassa tassa[M 1.0315][P 1.0411]. Vadanti “anvayato, byatirekato ca anupasaṅkamanakāraṇaṃ kittemā”ti.

He is called 'issara' (lord) because he is inclined to rule through the power of kamma leading to lordship, and his lordship becomes evident due to the attainment of prosperity—thus, speaking in terms of wealth, he said, 'aḍḍho (wealthy) is the lord.' He possesses great wealth, both underground and in the sky—thus, he is 'mahaddhana' (greatly wealthy). 'Tassāti' means 'of that one, of that one.' They say, 'The reason for not approaching is proclaimed by way of positive and negative correlation.'

Adhikarūpoti [V 1.0279] visiṭṭharūpo uttamasarīro. Dassanaṃ arahatīti dassanīyo, tenāha “dassanayoggo”ti. Pasādaṃ āvahatīti pāsādiko, tenāha “cittappasādajananato”ti. Vaṇṇassāti vaṇṇadhātuyā. Sarīranti sannivesavisiṭṭhaṃ karacaraṇagīvāsīsādiavayavasamudāyaṃ, so ca saṇṭhānamukhena gayhatīti “paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāyāti…pe… sampattiyā cā”ti vuttaṃ. Sabbavaṇṇesu suvaṇṇavaṇṇova uttamoti vuttaṃ “seṭṭhena suvaṇṇavaṇṇena samannāgato”ti. Tathā hi buddhā, cakkavattino ca suvaṇṇavaṇṇāva honti. Brahmavacchasīti uttamasarīrābho, suvaṇṇābho icceva attho. Imameva hi atthaṃ sandhāya “mahābrahmuno sarīrasadiseneva sarīrena samannāgato”ti vuttaṃ, na brahmujugattataṃ. Akhuddāvakāso dassanāyāti ārohapariṇāhasampattiyā, avayavapāripūriyā ca dassanāya okāso na khuddako, tenāha “sabbānevā”tiādi.

"Adhikarūpo" (of superior form) means of distinguished form, of supreme body. Worthy of being seen, thus he is "dassanīyo" (worthy of sight); hence it is said "fit to be seen." It inspires confidence, thus he is "pāsādiko" (inspiring confidence); hence it is said "because it generates clarity of mind." "Vaṇṇassa" (of complexion) means of the element of complexion. The body refers to the distinguished arrangement—the collection of limbs such as hands, feet, neck, and head—and it is grasped through the aspect of proportion. Thus, it is said, "due to the supreme beauty of complexion... and attainment." Among all complexions, the golden complexion is supreme, as stated: "endowed with the finest golden complexion." Indeed, both Buddhas and universal monarchs possess a golden complexion. "Brahmavacchasī" (with Brahma-like radiance) means of supreme bodily radiance, indeed of golden radiance—this is the meaning. This very meaning is intended when it is said, "endowed with a body resembling that of the great Brahma," not referring to identity with Brahma. "Akhuddāvakāso dassanāya" (not of small space for seeing) means that due to the perfection of height and breadth, and the completeness of limbs, the space for seeing is not small; hence it is said, "all..." and so on.

Yamaniyamalakkhaṇaṃ sīlamassa atthīti sīlavā. Taṃ panassa rattaññutāya vuddhaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ atthīti vuddhasīlī. Tena ca sabbadā sammāyogato vuddhasīlena samannāgato. Sabbametaṃ pañcasīlamattameva sandhāya vadanti tato paraṃ sīlassa tattha abhāvato, tesañca ajānanato.

He possesses the characteristic of self-restraint and discipline, thus he is 'sīlavā' (virtuous). Moreover, his virtue is mature, increased and developed through long experience, thus he is 'vuddhasīlī' (one of mature virtue). And he is always endowed with this mature virtue through proper application. All this refers only to the five precepts, because beyond that there is no other virtue there, and because of their ignorance.

Ṭhānakaraṇasampattiyā, sikkhāsampattiyā ca katthacipi anūnatāya parimaṇḍalapadāni byañjanāni akkharāni etissāti parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanā. Atha vā pajjati attho [P 1.0412] etenāti padaṃ, nāmādi. Yathādhippetamatthaṃ byañjetīti byañjanaṃ, vākyaṃ. Tesaṃ paripuṇṇatāya parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanā. Atthañāpane sādhanatāya vācāva karaṇanti vākkaraṇaṃ, udāhāraghoso. Guṇaparipuṇṇabhāvena tassa brāhmaṇassa, tena vā bhāsitabbaatthassa. Pūre puṇṇabhāve. Pūreti ca purimasmiṃ atthe ādhāre bhummaṃ, dutiyasmiṃ visaye. “Sukhumālattanenā”ti iminā tassā vācāya mudusaṇhabhāvamāha. Apalibuddhāya pittasemhādīhi. Sandiṭṭhaṃ sabbaṃ dassetvā viya ekadesaṃ kathanaṃ. Vilambitaṃ saṇikaṃ cirāyitvā kathanaṃ. “Sandiddhavilambitādī”ti vā pāṭho. Tattha sandiddhaṃ sandehajanakaṃ. Ādi-saddena dukkhalitānukaḍḍhitādiṃ [M 1.0316] saṅgaṇhāti. “Ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā”ti iminā tassā vācāya atthapāripūriṃ vadanti.

Due to the perfection of the places and means of articulation, and the perfection of training, its words, syllables, and letters are nowhere deficient, but fully rounded—hence, “fully rounded words and syllables.” Alternatively, “pada” (word) is that by which meaning is attained—names and so on. “Byañjana” (expression) is that which expresses the intended meaning—a sentence. Their completeness makes them “fully rounded words and syllables.” “Vākkaraṇa” (speech) is the means of accomplishing the understanding of meaning—utterance, the sound of speech. Due to the perfection of qualities in that brahmin, or of the meaning to be spoken by him, it is complete. “Pūre” (full) signifies fullness. And “pūreti” fills the base (bhumma) in the former meaning, and the domain in the latter. By “softness and gentleness” he describes the soft and gentle nature of that speech, unhindered by bile, phlegm, etc. “Clearly seen” is like speaking only a part, as if showing everything. “Slowly spoken” is speaking slowly, after a long delay. Alternatively, the reading may be “sandiddha-vilambitādi” (doubtful, slow, etc.). There, “sandiddha” means causing doubt. The term “ādi” includes “dukkhalita” (faulty speech), “anukaḍḍhita” (drawn out), etc. By “making the beginning, middle, and end clear” they speak of the completeness of meaning in that speech.

“Jiṇṇo”tiādīni padāni suviññeyyāni, heṭṭhā vuttatthāni ca. Dutiyanaye pana jiṇṇoti nāyaṃ jiṇṇatā vayomattena, atha kho kulaparivaṭṭena purāṇatāti āha “jiṇṇoti porāṇo”tiādi, tena tassa brāhmaṇassa kulavasena uditoditabhāvamāha. Jātivuddhiyā “vayoanuppatto”ti vakkhamānattā, guṇavuddhiyā tato sātisayattā ca “vuddhoti sīlācārādiguṇavuddhiyā yutto”ti āha. Tathā jātimahallakatāya [P 1.0413] vakkhamānattā “mahallako”ti [V 1.0280] padena vibhavamahattatā yojitā. Maggapaṭipannoti brāhmaṇānaṃ paṭipattivīthiṃ upagato taṃ avokkamma caraṇato. Antimavayanti pacchimavayaṃ.

The words “old” and so forth are easily understood, and their meanings have been previously stated. In the second sense, however, “old” does not refer to aging in terms of years, but rather to antiquity through lineage; hence, it is said, “‘old’ means ancient,” and so on. Thus, it indicates the brahmin’s esteemed status through his lineage. Because “advanced in age” will be stated in terms of growth by birth, and because of the excellence of qualities surpassing that, it is said, “‘mature’ means endowed with maturity in virtue and conduct, and so forth.” Similarly, because “prominence of ancient lineage” will be stated, the word “elder” is connected to greatness of wealth and power. “Walking the path” means having entered the path of practice of the brahmins, by not deviating from that conduct. “Final age” means the last period of life.

Buddhaguṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Discourse on the Buddha's Qualities

304. Tādisehi mahānubhāvehi saddhiṃ yugaggāhavasenapi dahanaṃ na mādisānaṃ anucchavikaṃ, kuto pana ukkaṃsananti idaṃ brāhmaṇassa na yuttarūpanti dassento āha “na kho pana metaṃ yutta”ntiādi. Sadisāti ekadesena sadisā. Na hi buddhānaṃ guṇehi sabbathā sadisā kecipi guṇā aññesu labbhanti. Itareti attano guṇehi asadisaguṇe. Idanti idaṃ atthajātaṃ. Gopadakanti gāviyā pade ṭhitaudakaṃ.

304. Even to grasp at equality with such great powers is not fitting for the likes of us, let alone to exalt oneself. Showing that this is not appropriate for the brahmin, he said, “This is not fitting for me,” and so on. “Similar” means similar in part. For indeed, no virtues found in others are in every way similar to the virtues of the Buddhas. “The other” refers to those whose virtues are dissimilar to his own. “This” means this aggregate of meanings. “Cow’s footprint” means water standing in a cow's footprint.

Saṭṭhikulasatasahassanti saṭṭhisahassādhikaṃ kulasatasahassaṃ kulapariyāyenāti suddhodanamahārājassa kulānukkamena āgataṃ. Tesupīti tesupi catūsu nidhīsu. Gahitagahitanti gahitaṃ gahitaṃ ṭhānaṃ pūratiyeva dhanena paṭipākatikameva hoti. Aparimāṇoyevāti “ettako eso”ti kenaci paricchindituṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya aparicchinno eva.

“Sixty thousand clans” means one hundred and sixty thousand clans, counted by lineage, as descended in unbroken succession from King Suddhodana. “Even in them” refers to those four treasures. “Gathered and gathered” means each place that was taken is filled with wealth; it is restored to its original state. “Immeasurable indeed” means it is immeasurable because it is impossible for anyone to define it as ‘this much’.

Tatthāti mañcake. Sīhaseyyaṃ kappesīti yathā rāhu asurindo āyāmato, vitthārato ubbedhato ca bhagavato rūpakāyassa paricchedaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti, tathā rūpaṃ iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharonto sīhaseyyaṃ kappesi.

“There” means on the couch. “He arranged a lion's posture” means that just as Rāhu, the lord of the asuras, could not grasp the extent of the Blessed One's physical form in length, breadth, or height, so too, by forming a psychic formation of such a form, he arranged a lion's posture.

Kilesehi [M 1.0317] ārakattā parisuddhaṭṭhena ariyanti āha “ariyaṃ uttamaṃ parisuddha”nti. Anavajjaṭṭhena kusalaṃ, na sukhavipākaṭṭhena. Katthaci [P 1.0414] caturāsītipāṇasahassāni, katthaci aparimāṇāpi devamanussā yasmā catuvīsatiyā ṭhānesu asaṅkhyeyyā aparimeyyā devamanussā maggaphalāmataṃ piviṃsu, koṭisatasahassādiparimāṇenapi bahū eva, tasmā anuttarācārasikkhāpanavasena bhagavā bahūnaṃ ācariyo. Teti kāmarāgato aññe bhagavato pahīnakilese. Keḷanāti keḷāyanā dhanāyanā.

Because he is far from defilements, he is called “noble” in the sense of being pure. Thus, he says, “noble, supreme, and pure.” “Wholesome” in the sense of being blameless, not in the sense of resulting in happiness. In some places, eighty-four thousand beings; in others, countless devas and humans—since in twenty-four places, innumerable and immeasurable devas and humans drank the nectar of the path and fruit, and there were very many even by the measure of a hundred thousand koṭis, therefore, the Blessed One is the teacher of many by means of instructing in unsurpassed conduct. “They” refers to defilements eradicated by the Blessed One, other than sensual lust. “Play” means amusement and the pursuit of wealth.

Apāpapurekkhāroti apāpe pure karoti, na vā pāpaṃ purato karotītipi apāpapurekkhāroti imamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “apāpe navalokuttaradhamme”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha apāpeti pāpapaṭipakkhe, pāparahite ca. Brahmani seṭṭhe buddhe bhagavati bhavā tassa dhammadesanāvasena ariyāya [V 1.0281] jātiyā jātattā, brahmuno vā bhagavato hitā garukaraṇādinā, yathānusiṭṭhapaṭipattiyā ca, brahmaṃ vā seṭṭhaṃ ariyamaggaṃ jānātīti brahmaññā, ariyasāvakasaṅkhātā pajā, tenāha “sāriputtā”tiādi. Pakatibrāhmaṇajātivasenāpi “brahmaññāya pajāyā”ti padassa attho veditabboti dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

“Having no evil as a precursor” means one who puts non-evil before them, or one who does not place evil in front. To explain this meaning, it is said, “in non-evil, in the nine supramundane Dhammas,” etc. Herein, “apāpe” refers to the opposite of evil and that which is free from evil. “Brahmaññā” (knower of Brahma) refers to those who originate from the supreme Brahma, the Buddha, the Blessed One, because they are born into the noble birth through his teaching of the Dhamma; or because of their devotion to the Blessed One through reverence and so on, and their practice in accordance with his instructions; or, “knower of Brahma” because they know the supreme noble path, thus referring to the community of noble disciples. Therefore, it is said, “Sāriputta,” etc. To indicate that the meaning of the phrase “to the community of knowers of Brahma” can also be understood in terms of those born as brahmins by birth, it is said, “moreover,” etc.

Tiroraṭṭhā tirojanapadāti ettha rajjaṃ raṭṭhaṃ, rājanti rājāno etenāti, tadekadesabhūtā padesā pana janapado,janā pajjanti ettha sukhajīvikaṃ pāpuṇantīti. Pucchāya vā dosaṃ sallakkhetvāti sambandho. Asamatthatanti attano asamatthataṃ. Bhagavā vissajjeti tesaṃ upanissayasampattiṃ, ñāṇaparipākaṃ, cittācārañca ñatvāti adhippāyo.

“Those from beyond the country, from beyond the regions”—here, “kingdom” is “country”; “kings” are so called because they rule (rājanti) by this. However, the parts that constitute a portion of that are regions, because people settle (pajjanti) there and attain a comfortable livelihood. The connection is through “having discerned a fault in the question.” “Unable” means one's own inability. The Blessed One replies, knowing their accomplishment of supporting conditions, the maturity of their wisdom, and the conduct of their minds—this is the intended meaning.

“Ehi [P 1.0415] svāgatavādī”ti iminā sukhasambhāsapubbakaṃ piyavāditaṃ dasseti, “sakhilo”ti iminā saṇhavācataṃ, “sammodako”ti iminā paṭisandhārakusalataṃ, “abhākuṭiko”ti iminā sabbattheva vippasannamukhataṃ, “uttānamukho”ti iminā sukhālāpataṃ, “pubbabhāsī”ti iminā dhammānuggahassa okāsakaraṇato hitajjhāsayataṃ bhagavato vibhāveti.

By “Come, welcome,” he shows pleasant speech preceded by friendly conversation. By “affable,” he shows gentle speech. By “sociable,” he shows skill in friendly greetings. By “without a frown,” he shows a face that is always bright. By “open-faced,” he shows ease of conversation. By “speaking first,” he reveals the Blessed One's benevolent intention by creating an opportunity for assistance through the Dhamma.

Yattha kirāti kira-saddo arucisūcanattho, tena bhagavatā adhivutthapadese na devatānubhāvena manussānaṃ anupaddavatā, atha kho buddhānubhāvenāti dasseti. Tenāha “apicā”tiādi.

Where “kira” is used, the particle “kira” indicates disapproval. Thereby, he shows that in the place dwelt in by the Blessed One, the freedom of humans from affliction was not due to the power of deities, but rather to the power of the Buddha. Hence it is said, “moreover,” and so on.

Anusāsitabboti [M 1.0318] vineyyajanasamūho gayhatīti nibbattitaṃ ariyasaṅghameva dassetuṃ “sayaṃ vā”tiādi vuttaṃ, anantarassa vidhi paṭisedho vāti katvā. “Tādisovā”ti iminā “sayaṃ vā”tiādinā vuttavikappo eva paccāmaṭṭhoti. “Purimapadasseva vā”ti vikappantaraggahaṇaṃ. Bahūnaṃ titthakarānanti pūraṇādīnaṃ anekesaṃ titthakarānaṃ, niddhāraṇe cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Kāraṇenāti appicchasantuṭṭhatādisamāropanalakkhaṇena kāraṇena. Āgantukā navakāti abhinavā āgantukā abbhāgatā. Pariyāpuṇāmīti paricchindituṃ jānāmi sakkomi, tenāha “jānāmī”ti. “Kappampi ce aññamabhāsamāno”ti abhūtaparikappanavacanametaṃ tathā bhāsamānassa abhāvato.

By “to be instructed,” the group of persons to be trained is taken. To show that this refers to the noble Sangha that has come into being, the phrase “oneself or...” is stated, after determining whether the immediately following is an injunction or a prohibition. By “such a one,” the alternative stated by “oneself or...” and so on, is referred back to. “Or of the first phrase” indicates the taking of another alternative. “Of many founders of sects” refers to numerous sectarians like Pūraṇa and others; this is a genitive of specification. “By reason” means by a reason characterized by the attribution of having few wishes, contentment, and so on. “Newcomers, novices” refers to newly arrived guests. “I am able to comprehend” means “I am able to know and distinguish”; therefore it is said, “I know.” “Even if he were to speak otherwise for an aeon” is a statement of an unreal supposition, since there is no one who speaks in such a way.

305. Alaṃ-saddo [P 1.0416] arahattopi hoti “alameva nibbinditu”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.124) viyāti [V 1.0282] āha “alamevāti yuttamevā”ti. Puṭena netvā asitabbato paribhuñjitabbato puṭosaṃ vuccati pātheyyaṃ. Puṭaṃsena purisena.

305. The word “alaṃ” can also signify worthiness, as in “it is enough for disenchantment” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.124) and so on. Thus, he says, “‘alaṃ’ means ‘indeed fitting.’” Provisions are called `puṭosaṃ` because they are to be carried in a bundle and are to be eaten and consumed. “Puṭaṃsena” means by a man with a bundle.

Soṇadaṇḍaparivitakkavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of Soṇadaṇḍa's Reflections

307. Ubhatopakkhikāti micchādiṭṭhisammādiṭṭhīnaṃ vasena ubhayapakkhikā. Kerāṭikāti saṭhā.

307. “Ubhatopakkhikā” (belonging to both factions) means 'of both sides' by way of wrong view and right view. “Kerāṭikā” (deceitful) means 'cunning'.

Brāhmaṇapaññattivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Concept of a Brahmin

309. Vighātanti cittadukkhaṃ.

309. “Vighāta” means mental suffering.

311-3. Sujanti homadabbiṃ paggaṇhantesūti juhanatthaṃ gaṇhanakesu, irubbijjesūti attho. Paṭhamo vāti tattha sannipatitesu yajanakiriyāyaṃ sabbapadhāno vā. Dutiyo vāti tadanantaro vā. “Suja”nti karaṇe etaṃ upayogavacananti āha “sujāyā”ti. Aggihuttapamukhatāya yaññassa yaññe diyyamānaṃ sujāmukhena dīyatīti āha “sujāya diyyamāna”nti. Porāṇāti aṭṭhakathācariyā. Visesatoti vijjācaraṇavisesato, na brāhmaṇehi icchitavijjācaraṇamattato. Uttamabrāhmaṇassāti anuttaradakkhiṇeyyatāya ukkaṭṭhabrāhmaṇassa. Brāhmaṇasamayanti brāhmaṇasiddhantaṃ. Mā bhindi mā vināsesi.

311-3. “Sujanti homadabbiṃ paggaṇhantesūti” means ‘among those taking the sacrificial ladle for the purpose of offering’; this is the meaning of ‘among those learned in the Rigveda.’ “Paṭhamo vāti” means ‘or the foremost in the sacrificial act among those assembled there.’ “Dutiyo vāti” means ‘or the one immediately following.’ “‘Suja’nti” is a word used in the instrumental case; hence it is said “‘sujāyā’ti.” Because the sacrifice has the fire offering as its chief part, what is given in the sacrifice is given through the mouth of the ladle; hence it is said “‘sujāya diyyamāna’nti” (being given by the ladle). “Porāṇāti” refers to the ancient commentators. “Visesatoti” means ‘especially by knowledge and conduct, not merely by the knowledge and conduct desired by brahmins.’ “Uttamabrāhmaṇassāti” (of the supreme brahmin) means ‘of the excellent brahmin, because of being the unsurpassed recipient of offerings.’ “Brāhmaṇasamayanti” means ‘the established doctrine of brahmins.’ ‘Mā bhindi mā vināsesi’ means ‘Do not break it; do not destroy it.’

316. Samasamoti [M 1.0319] samoyeva hutvā samo. Hīnopamavasenapi samatā vuccatīti taṃ nivattento “ṭhapetvā ekadesasamatta”ntiādimāha. Kulakoṭiparidīpananti kulaādiparidīpanaṃ athāpi [P 1.0417] siyāti athāpi tumhākaṃ evaṃ parivitakko siyā. Brāhmaṇabhāvaṃ sādheti vaṇṇo. Mantajātīsupi eseva nayo. Sīlameva sādhessati brāhmaṇabhāvaṃ. Kasmāti ce? Āha “tasmiñhissā”tiādi. Sammohamattaṃ vaṇṇādayoti vaṇṇamantajātiyo hi brāhmaṇabhāvassa aṅganti sammohamattametaṃ asamavekkhitābhimānabhāvato.

316. “Samasamo” means ‘having become equal, one is equal.’ Because equality is spoken of even by way of an inferior comparison, rejecting that, he said, ‘setting aside partial equality,’ and so on. “Kulakoṭiparidīpananti” means ‘the illumination of family and so forth.’ ‘Athāpi siyā’ means ‘or it might be that such a reflection might arise for you.’ ‘Color establishes brahminhood.’ ‘The same method applies even to lineage based on mantras.’ ‘Virtue alone will establish brahminhood.’ ‘Why is that?’ he said, ‘for in that case,’ and so on. “Vaṇṇādayo” (color and so forth) are merely delusion; for the idea that color, mantras, and lineage are factors of brahminhood is merely delusion, because it is a state of unexamined conceit.

Sīlapaññākathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Virtue and Wisdom

317. Kathito brāhmaṇena pañhoti “sīlavā ca hotī”tiādinā dvinnameva aṅgānaṃ vasena [V 1.0283] yathāpucchito pañho yāthāvato vissajjito etthāti etasmiṃ yathāvissajjite atthe. Tassāti soṇadaṇḍassa. Sīlaparisuddhāti sīlasampattiyā sabbaso suddhā anupakkiliṭṭhā. Kuto dussīle paññā asamāhitattā tassa. Jaḷe eḷamūge kuto sīlanti jaḷe eḷamūge duppaññe kuto sīlaṃ sīlavibhāgassa, sīlaparisodhanūpāyassa ca ajānanato. Pakaṭṭhaṃ ukkaṭṭhaṃ ñāṇaṃ paññāṇanti, pākatikaṃ ñāṇaṃ nivattetuṃ “paññāṇa”nti vuttanti tayidaṃ pakārehi jānanato paññāvāti āha “paññāṇanti paññā yevā”ti.

317. Herein, in this matter that was answered, the question asked by the brahmin, beginning with ‘he is virtuous,’ was answered truthfully as it was asked, with respect to only these two factors. ‘His’ refers to Soṇadaṇḍa. ‘Pure in virtue’ means completely pure and unblemished due to the accomplishment of virtue. ‘How can one without virtue have wisdom, since he is not concentrated?’ ‘In a dull and mute person, how can there be virtue?’ means ‘in a dull, mute, and unwise person, how can there be virtue, since he does not know the analysis of virtue and the means of purifying virtue?’ ‘Paññāṇa’ is distinguished and superior knowledge; to exclude ordinary knowledge, it is said ‘paññāṇa.’ Because it is wisdom from knowing in various ways, he said, ‘paññāṇa is indeed wisdom.’

Sīlenadhotāti samādhipadaṭṭhānena sīlena sakalasaṃkilesamalavisuddhiyā dhotā visuddhā, tenāha “kathaṃ panā”tiādi. Tattha dhovatīti sujjhati. Mahāsaṭṭhivassatthero viyāti saṭṭhivassamahāthero viya. Vedanāpariggahamattampīti ettha vedanāpariggaho nāma yathāuppannaṃ vedanaṃ sabhāvarasato upadhāretvā “ayaṃ vedanā phassaṃ paṭicca, so phasso anicco dukkho vipariṇāmadhammo”ti lakkhaṇattayaṃ āropetvā pavattitavipassanā. Evaṃ vipassantena [P 1.0418] “sukhena sakkā sā vedanā adhivāsetuṃ “vedanā eva vediyatī”ti. Vedanaṃ vikkhambhetvāti yathāuppannaṃ dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ ananuvattitvā vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā vīthiṃ paṭipannāya vipassanāya taṃ vinodetvā. Saṃsumārapatitenāti kumbhīlena viya bhūmiyaṃ [M 1.0320] urena nipajjanena. Paññāya sīlaṃ dhovitvāti akhaṇḍādibhāvāpādanena sīlaṃ ādimajjhapariyosānesu paññāya suvisodhitaṃ katvā.

'Washed by virtue' means 'purified and cleansed by virtue, which is the foundation of concentration, through the purification from all defilements and stains'; hence it is said, 'but how,' and so on. There, 'washes' means 'becomes pure'. 'Like the elder Mahāsaṭṭhivassa' means 'like the great elder of sixty years'. 'Even the mere grasp of feelings'—here, the grasp of feelings means observing the feeling as it has arisen according to its characteristic and function: 'this feeling arises dependent on contact; that contact is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change,' and thus developing insight. By one who sees thus, 'it is possible to endure that feeling with ease,' thinking, 'it is just feeling that is felt'. 'Having suppressed the feeling' means 'not yielding to the painful feeling as it has arisen, but initiating insight and, by insight that has entered the path, dispelling it'. 'Like a crocodile fallen' means 'like a crocodile lying on the ground with its chest down'. 'Having washed virtue with wisdom' means 'having thoroughly purified virtue at the beginning, middle, and end with wisdom by bringing about its unbroken state and so on'.

318. “Kasmā āhā”ti uparidesanāya kāraṇaṃ pucchati. Lajjā nāma “sīlassa jātiyā ca guṇadosapakāsanena samaṇena gotamena pucchitapañhaṃ vissajjesī”ti parisāya paññātatā. Ettakaparamāti ettakaukkaṃsakoṭikā pañca sīlāni, vedattayavibhāvanaṃ paññañca lakkhaṇādito niddhāretvā jānanaṃ natthi, kevalaṃ tattha vacīparamā mayanti dassetīti āha “sīlapaññāṇanti vacanameva paramaṃ amhāka”nti. “Ayaṃ pana viseso”ti idaṃ niyyātanāpekkhaṃ sīlaniddese, tenāha “sīlamicceva niyyātita”nti. Sāmaññaphale pana “sāmaññaphala” micceva niyyātitaṃ, paññāniddese pana jhānapaññaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ katvā vipassanāpaññāvaseneva paññāniyyātanaṃ kataṃ, tenāha “paṭhamajjhānādīnī”ti.

318. 'Why did he say?'—he asks about the reason for the subsequent teaching. 'Shame' means 'it was known in the assembly that the ascetic Gotama answered the question asked by revealing the virtues and faults of virtue and birth'. 'Ettakaparamā' (this much is the highest) means 'having this much as the highest limit: there is no knowing of the five precepts, of the analysis of the three Vedas, and of wisdom by discerning it from its characteristics and so on; it shows that 'we are supreme only in speech there'; thus he said, 'for us, the statement 'virtue and wisdom' is the highest'. 'Ayaṃ pana viseso' (but this distinction) refers to the exposition of virtue, which is given expecting deliverance; therefore, he said, 'it is declared as virtue itself'. But in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, it is declared as 'the fruit of asceticism itself'. In the exposition of wisdom, however, having made jhāna-wisdom the basis, the declaration of wisdom is made solely by way of insight-wisdom; hence he said, 'the first jhāna and so on'.

Soṇadaṇḍaupāsakattapaṭivedanākathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Account of Soṇadaṇḍa's Declaration as a Lay Follower

321-2. Nattāti puttaputto. Agāravaṃ nāma natthi, na cāyaṃ bhagavati agāravena “ahañceva [V 1.0284] kho panā”tiādimāha, atha kho attalābhaparihānibhayena. Ayañhi yathā tathā attano mahājanassa sambhāvanaṃ uppādetvā kohaññena [P 1.0419] pare vimhāpetvā lābhuppādaṃ nijigisanto vicarati, tasmā tathā avoca, tenāha “iminā kirā”tiādi.

321-2. 'Nattā' means a son's son. There is no reverence, but it is not that he spoke to the Blessed One with disrespect, saying, 'I indeed,' etc., but rather out of fear for his own loss of gain. For this one, in whatever way, generates esteem for himself among the people, then bewilders others with deceit, and wanders about desiring to secure gain. Therefore, he spoke thus; hence it is said, 'By this, indeed,' etc.

Taṅkhaṇānurūpāyāti yādisī tadā tassa ajjhāsayappavatti, tadanurūpāyāti attho. Tassa tadā tādisassa vivaṭṭasannissitassa ñāṇassa paripākassa abhāvato kevalaṃ abbhudayanissito eva attho dassitoti āha “diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikamatthaṃ sandassetvā”ti, paccakkhato vibhāvetvāti attho. Kusale dhammeti tebhūmake kusale dhamme, “catubhūmake”tipi vattuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva, tenevāha “āyatiṃ nibbānatthāya vāsanābhāgiyā vā”ti. Tatthāti kusaladhamme yathā samādapite. Nanti brāhmaṇaṃ samuttejetvāti sammadeva uparūpari nisānetvā puññakiriyāya tikkhavisadabhāvaṃ āpādetvā. Taṃ pana atthato tattha ussāhajananaṃ hotīti āha “saussāhaṃ katvā”ti[M 1.0321]. Evaṃ puññakiriyāya saussāhatā, evarūpaṃ guṇasamaṅgitā ca niyamato diṭṭhadhammikā atthasampādanīti evaṃ saussāhatāya, aññehi ca tasmiṃ vijjamānaguṇehi sampahaṃsetvā sammadeva haṭṭhatuṭṭhabhāvaṃ āpādetvā.
