'Suitable for that moment' means that it was in accordance with the proceeding of his inclination at that time. Because at that time, for such a one, due to the immaturity of his knowledge which was dependent on liberation, only a meaning related to worldly progress was shown. Hence it is said, 'revealing the visible and future benefit,' meaning making it directly evident. Regarding 'wholesome qualities,' it refers to wholesome states in the three realms. It could also be said 'in the four realms,' and thus it is stated, 'or for the sake of future Nibbāna, or as a share of latent tendencies.' There, in the wholesome qualities as they are encouraged. 'Nanti' means rousing the brahmin, properly inspiring him step by step, making him keen and clear in meritorious action. But in meaning, it generates enthusiasm there; hence it is said, 'making him energetic.' Thus, being energetic in meritorious action, and being endowed with such virtues, certainly accomplishes visible benefits. In this way, by inspiring energy and praising other existing virtues in him, properly bringing about a state of joy and delight.

Yadi bhagavā dhammaratanavassaṃ vassi, atha kasmā so visesaṃ nādhigacchatīti āha “brāhmaṇo panā”tiādi. Yadi evaṃ kasmā bhagavā tassa tathā dhammaratanavassaṃ vassīti āha “kevalamassā”tiādi. Na hi bhagavato niratthakā desanā hotīti.

If the Blessed One showered the rain of the Dhamma-jewel, then why did he not attain distinction? He said, 'But the brahmin...' and so on. If so, why did the Blessed One shower the rain of the Dhamma-jewel upon him in that way? He said, 'Only for him...' and so on. Indeed, the Blessed One's teaching is not without purpose.

Soṇadaṇḍasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

Clarification of the Hidden Meaning in the Explanation of the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta

5. Kūṭadantasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Kūṭadanta Sutta

323. Purimasuttadvayeti [M 1.0322][V 1.0285][P 1.0420] ambaṭṭhasoṇadaṇḍasuttadvaye. Vuttanayamevāti yaṃ tattha āgatasadisaṃ idhāgataṃ taṃ atthavaṇṇanato vuttanayameva, tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbanti attho. “Taruṇo ambarukkho ambalaṭṭhikā”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.2) brahmajālasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanti āha “ambalaṭṭhikā brahmajāle vuttasadisāvā”ti.

323. 'In the previous two discourses' means in the Ambaṭṭha and Soṇadaṇḍa Suttas. 'The method is the same as stated before' means that whatever has come here that is similar to what came there is explained according to the method already stated, and should be understood by the method stated there; that is the meaning. 'A young mango tree, a mango sapling' was mentioned in the Brahmajāla Sutta commentary (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.2), hence it is said, 'The mango sapling is similar to what was stated in the Brahmajāla.'

Yaññāvāṭaṃ sampādetvā mahāyaññaṃ uddissa saviññāṇakāni, aviññāṇakāni ca yaññūpakaraṇāni upaṭṭhapitānīti vuttaṃ pāḷiyaṃ “mahāyañño upakkhaṭo”ti, taṃ upakkharaṇaṃ tesaṃ tathāsajjananti āha “upakkhaṭoti sajjito”ti. Vacchatarasatānīti yuvabhāvappattāni balavavacchasatāni, te pana vacchā eva honti, na dammā balibaddā cāti āha “vacchasatānī”ti. Eteti usabhādayo urabbhapariyosānā. Anekesanti anekajātikānaṃ. Saṅkhyāvasena anekatā sattasataggahaṇeneva paricchinnā. Migapakkhīnanti mahiṃsarurupasadakuruṅgagokaṇṇamigānañceva morakapiñjaratittirakapotādipakkhīnañca.

Having prepared the sacrificial site, aiming at a great sacrifice, sacrificial implements, both animate and inanimate, were set up. This is stated in the Pāli as, 'The great sacrifice is prepared.' The preparation refers to their proper arrangement, hence it is said, 'Prepared means arranged.' 'Hundreds of young calves' refers to hundreds of strong young calves that have reached youth. These are indeed calves, not tamed oxen or sacrificial bulls, hence it is said, 'Hundreds of calves.' 'These' include bulls and so on, ending with rams. 'Many' refers to those of various kinds. Their being many in number is defined by the mention of seven hundred. 'Wild animals and birds' include wild animals such as the buffalo, ruru deer, spotted deer, kuruṅga antelope, and gokaṇṇa deer, as well as birds such as peacocks, francolin partridges, partridges, and pigeons.

328. Yaññasaṅkhātassa puññassa yo saṃkileso, tassa nivāraṇato [P 1.0421] nisedhanato vidhā vuccanti vippaṭisāravinodanā. Tato eva tā taṃ puññābhisandaṃ avicchinditvā ṭhapentīti “ṭhapanā”ti vuttā. Tāsaṃ pana yaññassa ādimajjhapariyosānavasena tīsu kālesu pavattiyā yañño tiṭṭhapanoti āha “tiṭṭhapananti attho”ti. Parikkharonti abhisaṅkharontīti parikkhārā, parivārāti vuttaṃ. “Soḷasaparikkhāranti soḷasaparivāra”nti.

328. The ways that prevent and negate the defilement of the merit known as 'sacrifice' are called 'dispellers of regret.' Because they establish that stream of merit without interruption, they are called 'establishers.' And since they occur at the three times—the beginning, middle, and end of the sacrifice—the sacrifice is an 'establishment'; therefore, he says, 'the meaning is establishment.' 'Accessories' refer to what completes or elaborates, meaning attendants. 'Sixteen accessories' means 'sixteen attendants.'

Mahāvijitarājayaññakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discourse on King Mahāvijita's Sacrifice

336. Pubbacaritanti attano purimajātisambhūtaṃ bodhisambhārabhūtaṃ puññacariyaṃ. Tathā hissa [V 1.0286] anugāminova nidhissa thāvaro nidhi nidassito. Aḍḍhatā nāma vibhavasampannatā, sā taṃ taṃ upādāyupādāya vuccatīti āha “yo koci attano santakena vibhavena aḍḍho hotī”ti[M 1.0323]. Tathā mahaddhanatāpīti taṃ ukkaṃsagataṃ dassetuṃ “mahatā aparimāṇasaṅkhyena dhanena samannāgato”ti vuttaṃ. Bhuñjitabbato paribhuñjitabbato visesato kāmā bhogo nāmāti āha “pañcakāmaguṇavasenā”ti. Piṇḍapiṇḍavasenāti bhājanālaṅkārādivibhāgaṃ ahutvā kevalaṃ khaṇḍakhaṇḍavasena.

336. 'Previous conduct' refers to the virtuous conduct, the accumulation of merit as a requisite for enlightenment, which arose in his past lives. Thus, a stable treasure is shown, like a treasure that follows him. 'Wealth' (aḍḍhatā) means being endowed with possessions; it is called that in dependence on this and that acquisition, hence it is said, 'whoever is wealthy with their own possessions.' Similarly, to show that which has reached the highest degree – great riches – it is stated, 'endowed with great, immeasurable wealth.' 'Enjoyment' (bhoga) means specifically the objects suitable for enjoyment, suitable for experiencing, therefore it is said, 'by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure.' 'Piece by piece' means without division into vessels, ornaments, and so on, but simply in the manner of fragments.

Māsakādīti ādi-saddena thālakādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Bhājanādīti ādi-saddena vatthaseyyāvasathādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimuttāveḷuriyavajirapavāḷāni “sattaratanānī”ti vadanti. Sālivīhiādi pubbaṇṇaṃ purakkhataṃsassaphalanti katvā. Tabbipariyāyato muggamāsādi aparaṇṇaṃ. Devasikaṃ…pe… vasenāti divase divase paribhuñjitabbadātabbavaḍḍhetabbādividhinā parivattanakadhanadhaññavasena.

By 'coins and so forth,' the word 'so forth' includes bowls and so forth. By 'vessels and so forth,' the word 'so forth' encompasses items such as clothing, bedding, and dwellings. Gold, silver, gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, diamonds, and coral are called the 'seven treasures.' Rice, paddy, and so forth are the primary crop, being the foremost fruit of the harvest. Conversely, mung beans, black gram, and so forth are the secondary crop. 'Daily'... in terms of... means in terms of wealth and grain that should be enjoyed, given, or increased day by day, by way of revolving it.

Koṭṭhaṃ vuccati dhaññassa āṭhapanaṭṭhānaṃ, koṭṭhabhūtaṃ agāraṃ koṭṭhāgāraṃ tenāha “dhaññena…pe… gāro cā”ti. Evaṃ [P 1.0422] sāragabbhaṃ “koso”ti, dhaññassa āṭhapanaṭṭhānañca “koṭṭhāgāra”nti dassetvā idāni tato aññathā taṃ dassetuṃ “atha vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yathā asino tikkhabhāvaparihārato paricchado “koso”ti vuccati, evaṃ rañño tikkhabhāvapariharaṇattā caturaṅginī senā “koso”ti āha “catubbidho koso hatthī assā rathā pattī”ti. “Vatthakoṭṭhāgāraggahaṇeneva sabbassāpi bhaṇḍaṭṭhapanaṭṭhānassa gahitattā tividhaṃ koṭṭhāgāranti vuttaṃ. “Idaṃ evaṃ bahu”ntiādi rājā tamatthaṃ jānantova bhaṇḍāgārikena kathāpetvā parisāya nissaddabhāvāpādanatthañca āha evaṃ me pakatikkhobho na bhavissatīti.

A 'koṭṭha' is a place for storing grain; a building that serves as a 'koṭṭha' is called a 'koṭṭhāgāra,' hence it is said, 'with grain... and a house.' Having thus shown that the inner essence is a 'kosa,' and the place for storing grain is a 'koṭṭhāgāra,' now, to show it otherwise, 'or else,' etc., was said. Therein, just as a sheath is called a 'kosa' because it protects from the sharpness of a sword, so too the king’s fourfold army—elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—is called a 'kosa' because it protects the king's keenness. By the inclusion of 'storehouses for cloth,' all places for storing goods are included; hence 'the threefold storehouse' is said. 'This is indeed abundant,' etc.—the king, although knowing this matter, had the treasurer announce it to the assembly to bring about silence, thinking, 'Thus, there will be no disturbance of my normal condition.'

337-8. Brāhmaṇo cintesi janapadassa anupaddavatthañceva yaññassa ca cirānupavattanatthañca, tenāha “ayaṃ rājā”tiādi.

337-338. The brahmin reflected on the kingdom being free from harm and on the long continuation of sacrifices, hence he said, 'This king...' and so on.

Sattānaṃ hitassa sukhassa ca vidūsanato ahitassa dukkhassa ca āvahanato corā eva kaṇṭakā, tehi corakaṇṭakehi. Yathā gāmavāsīnaṃ ghātā gāmaghātā, evaṃ panthikānaṃ duhanā vibādhanā panthaduhanā. Adhammakārīti dhammato apetassa ayuttassa karaṇasīlo, attano vijite janapadādīnaṃ tato anatthato tāyanena khattiyo [M 1.0324] yo khattadhammo, tassa vā akaraṇasīloti attho. Dassavo eva khīlasadisattā dassukhīlaṃ. Yathā hi khette khīlaṃ kasanādīnaṃ sukhappavattiṃ[V 1.0287], mūlasantānena sassassa buddhiñca vibandhati, evaṃ dassavo rajje rājāṇāya sukhappavattiṃ, mūlaviruḷhiyā janapadānaṃ [P 1.0423] paribuddhiñca vibandhanti. Tena vuttaṃ “dassavo eva khīlasadisattā dassukhīla”nti. Vadha-saddo hiṃsanatthopi hotīti vuttaṃ “māraṇena vā koṭṭanena vā”ti. Addubandhanādināti ādi-saddena rajjubandhanasaṅkhalikabandhanādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Jāniyāti dhanajāniyā, tenāha “sataṃ gaṇhathā”tiādi. Pañcasikhamuṇḍakaraṇanti kākapakkhakaraṇaṃ. Gomayasiñcananti sīse chakaṇodakāvasecanaṃ. Kudaṇḍakabandhananti gaddulabandhanaṃ. Evamādīnīti ādi-saddena khuramuṇḍaṃ karitvā bhasmapuṭapothanādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Ūhanissāmīti uddharissāmi, apanessāmīti attho. Ussahantīti pubbe tattha kataparicayatāya ussāhaṃ kātuṃ sakkonti. Anuppadetūti anu anu padetu, tenāha “dinne appahonte”tiādi. Sakkhikaraṇapaṇṇāropanāni vaḍḍhiyā saha vā vinā vā puna gahetukāmassa, idha pana taṃ natthīti āha “sakkhiṃ akatvā”tiādi, tenāha “mūlacchejjavasenā”ti. Pakārato bhaṇḍāni ābharati sambharati paricayati etenāti pābhataṃ, bhaṇḍamūlaṃ.

Because they corrupt the welfare and happiness of beings and bring what is not welfare and suffering, thieves are indeed thorns; by those thief-thorns. Just as killers of villagers are village-killers, so too oppressors and harassers of travelers are road-oppressors. 'One who acts unrighteously' means one who is accustomed to doing what is improper, being devoid of righteousness; or it means a warrior who is accustomed to not performing the warrior's duty, which is to protect the people of the country and so forth in his own domain from harm. Bandits, because of their likeness to a stake, are a 'bandit-stake.' For just as a stake in a field obstructs the smooth progress of plowing and so on and hinders the growth of the crop by its root-system, so too do bandits in a kingdom obstruct the smooth operation of the king's command and hinder the full growth of the country by its root-growth. Therefore it is said: 'Bandits, because of their likeness to a stake, are a bandit-stake.' The word 'vadha' also has the meaning of harming—thus it is said: 'by killing or by tormenting.' By 'binding with fetters and so on'—the word 'and so on' includes binding with ropes, chains, and the like. 'By loss' means by loss of wealth; thus it is said: 'seize a hundred,' and so on. 'Making one bald with five tufts' means making one's hair like a crow's wing. 'Sprinkling with cow dung' means pouring water mixed with cow dung on the head. 'Binding with a crooked stick' means binding with a neck-stock. 'And so on'—by the word 'and so on,' it includes shaving the head with a razor and smearing with a bag of ashes. 'I will uproot' means I will remove, I will banish. 'They are able' means, being previously accustomed to that, they are able to make the effort. 'Let him provide in addition' means let him provide again and again; thus it is said: 'when what is given is not sufficient,' and so on. The acts of making a witness and drawing up a document, whether with interest or without, are for one who wishes to take back again—here, however, that is not the case; thus it is said: 'without making a witness,' and so on; therefore it is said: 'by way of cutting off at the root.' That by which one brings, gathers, and accumulates goods in various ways is 'pābhataṃ' (a gift); the capital of goods.

Divase divase dātabbabhattaṃ devasikabhattaṃ. “Anumāsaṃ, anuposatha”ntiādinā dātabbaṃ vetanaṃ māsikādiparibbayaṃ. Tassa tassa kulānurūpena kammānurūpena sūrabhāvānurūpenāti paccekaṃ anurūpa-saddo yojetabbo. Senāpaccādi ṭhānantaraṃ. Sakakammapasutattā[P 1.0424], anupaddavattā ca dhanadhaññānaṃ rāsiko rāsikārabhūto. Khemena ṭhitāti anupaddavena pavattā, tenāha “abhayā”ti, kutocipi bhayarahitāti attho.

Food to be given day by day is daily food. Wages to be given 'monthly, on each Uposatha day,' and so on, are monthly expenses and the like. The word 'suitable' (anurūpa) should be connected individually to each of these: 'suitable to the family,' 'suitable to the work,' 'suitable to the nature of bravery.' The position of army commander and so forth is a rank. Because they are diligent in their own work and free from trouble, their wealth and grain are like a heap, a great accumulation. 'Established in security' means proceeding without trouble; therefore, it is said, 'fearless,' meaning free from fear from anywhere.

Catuparikkhāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Four Requisites.

339. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kicce anuyanti anuvattantīti anuyantā, anuyantā eva ānuyantā yathā “anubhāvo eva ānubhāvo”ti. Assāti rañño. Teti ānuyantakhattiyādayo. Attamanā na bhavissanti “amhe ettha bahi karotī”ti. Nibandhavipulāgamo gāmo nigamo, vivaḍḍhitamahāāyo [M 1.0325] mahāgāmoti attho. Janapada-saddo heṭṭhā vuttattho eva. Channaṃ pakatīnaṃ vasena rañño hitasukhābhibuddhi, tadekadesā ca ānuyantādayoti vuttaṃ “yaṃ tumhākaṃ anujānanaṃ mama bhaveyya dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā”ti.

339. Those who follow and comply in each and every duty are called 'followers' (anuyantā); 'followers' are indeed 'attendants' (ānuyantā), just as 'influence' (anubhāvo) is indeed 'power' (ānubhāvo). 'His' means 'of the king.' 'They' refers to the attendant khattiyas and others. They will not be pleased in mind, thinking, 'He excludes us from this.' A village (gāmo) with constant and abundant income is a town (nigamo); the meaning is a great village (mahāgāmo) with greatly increased and large income. The term 'janapada' has the same meaning as stated previously. The king's welfare, happiness, and growth depend on the six constituents of state, and the attendants and others are a part of them; thus it is said: 'Whatever permission you grant would be for my long-term welfare and happiness.'

Amā saha bhavanti kiccesūti amaccā, rajjakiccavosāsanakā. Te pana rañño piyā, sahapavattanakā ca hontīti āha “piyasahāyakā”ti. Rañño parisati bhavāti pārisajjā[V 1.0288], te pana keti āha “sesā āṇattikarā”ti, yathāvuttaānuyantakhattiyādī hi avasesā rañño āṇākarāti attho. Satipi deyyadhamme ānubhāvasampattiyā, parivārasampattiyā ca abhāve tādisaṃ dātuṃ na sakkā, vuḍḍhakāle [P 1.0425] ca tādisānampi rājūnaṃ tadubhayaṃ hāyatevāti āha “mahallakakāle…pe… na sakkā”ti. Anumatiyāti anujānanena, pakkhāti sapakkhā yaññassa aṅgabhūtā. Parikkharontīti parikkhārā, sambhārā. Ime tassa yaññassa aṅgabhūtā parivārā viya hontīti āha “parivārā bhavantī”ti.

Those who are present together in duties are ministers (amaccā), because they bring royal duties to completion. They are dear to the king and act in harmony with him, hence he said, 'dear companions' (piyasahāyakā). Those who belong to the king’s assembly are courtiers (pārisajjā), and who are they? He said, 'the remaining ones carry out orders' (sesā āṇattikarā). That is, the remaining ones, such as the attendant khattiyas mentioned previously, are the king’s order-bearers. Even if there is a bestowable object, because of a lack of the power of influence or a retinue, such a gift cannot be given, and in old age, even for such kings, both decline, hence he said: 'In old age… it is not possible.' 'Anumatiyā' means with approval, with permission. 'Pakkhā' refers to the partisans, those that are an integral part of the sacrifice. Because they prepare, they are called requisites (parikkhārā), the equipment (sambhārā). These become like the retinue of that sacrifice, hence he said: 'They become the retinue.'

Aṭṭhaparikkhāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Eight Requisites.

340. Yasasāti ānubhāvena, tenāha “āṇāṭhapanasamatthatāyā”ti. Saddahatīti “dātā dānassa phalaṃ paccanubhotī”ti pattiyāyati. Dāne sūroti dānasūro deyyadhamme īsakampi saṅgaṃ akatvā muttacāgo. Svāyamattho kammassakataññāṇassa tikkhavisadabhāvena veditabbo, tenāha “na saddhāmattakenevā”tiādi. Yassa hi kammassakatā paccakkhato viya upaṭṭhāti, so evaṃ vutto. Yaṃ dānaṃ detīti yaṃ deyyadhammaṃ parassa deti. Tassa pati hutvāti tabbisayaṃ lobhaṃ suṭṭhu abhibhavanto tassa adhipati hutvā deti anadhibhavanīyattā. “Na dāso, na sahāyo”ti vatvā tadubhayaṃ anvayato, byatirekato ca dassetuṃ “yo hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Dāso hutvā deti taṇhāya dānassa dāsabyataṃ upagatattā. Sahāyo hutvā deti tassa piyabhāvānissajjanato. Sāmī hutvā deti tattha taṇhādāsabyato attānaṃ [M 1.0326] mocetvā abhibhuyya pavattanato. Sāmiparibhogasadisā hetassāyaṃ pavattatīti.

340. 'Yasasā' means through influence, hence it is said: 'through the ability to establish commands.' 'Saddahatī' means one believes, being convinced that 'the donor experiences the result of the gift.' 'Dāne sūro' means a hero in giving, one who, without the slightest attachment to the gift, is freely generous. This meaning should be understood by the sharp clarity of the knowledge that kamma is one's own; hence it is said: 'not merely by faith,' etc. For one for whom kamma as one's own appears as if directly perceived, this is said. 'Yaṃ dānaṃ deti' means whatever gift one gives to another. 'Tassa pati hutvā' means becoming the master of that, thoroughly overcoming greed in that sphere, and gives, having become its lord, because he is not to be overpowered by greed. Having stated, 'not a slave, not a friend,' the text then explains both by inclusion and exclusion: 'For one who…' etc. Giving as a slave means having become enslaved by craving in giving. Giving as a friend means giving without relinquishing affection for it. Giving as a master means freeing oneself from enslavement to craving there and giving by prevailing over it. This occurs similarly to the enjoyment of a master.

Samitapāpā [P 1.0426] samaṇā, bāhitapāpā brāhmaṇā ukkaṭṭhaniddesena, pabbajjāmattasamaṇā jātimattabrāhmaṇā pana kapaṇādiggahaṇenevettha gahitāti adhippāyo. Duggatāti dukkarajīvikaṃ upagatā kasiravuttikā, tenāha “daliddamanussā”ti. Addhikāti addhānamaggagāmino. Vaṇibbakāti dāyakānaṃ guṇakittanavasena, kammaphalakittanamukhena ca yācanakā seyyathāpi naggacariyādayo, tenāha “iṭṭhaṃ dinna”ntiādi. “Pasatamatta”nti vīhitaṇḍulādivasena vuttaṃ, “sarāvamatta”nti yāgubhattādivasena. Opānaṃ vuccati ogāhetvā pātabbato naditaḷākādīnaṃ sabbasādhāraṇatitthaṃ opānaṃ viya bhūtoti opānabhūto, tenāha “udapānabhūto”tiādi. Sutameva sutajātanti jāta-saddassa anatthantaravācakatamāha yathā “kosajāta”nti.

Ascetics (samaṇā) are those who have pacified evil, brahmins (brāhmaṇā) are those who have expelled evil—this is by way of the highest designation. But the meaning is that those who are merely ordained as ascetics or born as brahmins are included here by taking examples like the destitute. 'Poor' (duggatā) means those who have undertaken a difficult livelihood, a life of hardship—hence it is said, 'destitute people.' 'Wayfarers' (addhikā) are those who travel long roads. 'Beggars' (vaṇibbakā) are those who beg by praising the virtues of donors or through proclaiming the fruits of deeds, such as naked ascetics and the like—hence it is said, 'given what is desired,' etc. 'A handful' (pasatamatta) is said with reference to things like winnowed rice, while 'a bowlful' (sarāvamatta) is said with reference to rice porridge or cooked rice. A 'watering place' (opāna) is so called because it is a common bathing and drinking spot for rivers, ponds, and so on. Being like an opāna, it is 'opānabhūto,' hence it is said, 'like a well,' etc. 'It is well heard' (sutameva) means 'born of hearing' (sutajāta)—the word 'born' (jāta) is used to describe something not different from the origin, just as in 'born of a sheath' (kosajāta).

Atītādiatthacintanasamatthatā nāmassa rañño anumānavasena, itikattabbatāvasena ca veditabbā[V 1.0289], na buddhānaṃ viya tattha paccakkhadassitāyāti dassetuṃ “atīte”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aḍḍhatādayo tāva yaññassa parikkhārā hontu tehi vinā tassa asijjhanato, sujātatā surūpatā pana kathanti āha “etehi kirā”tiādi. Ettha ca keci “yathā aḍḍhatādayo yaññassa ekaṃsato aṅgāni, na evamabhijātatā, abhirūpatā cāti dassetuṃ kirasaddaggahaṇa”nti vadanti “ayaṃ dujjāto”tiādi vacanassa anekantikataṃ maññamānā, tayidaṃ asāraṃ, sabbasādhāraṇavasena hesa yaññārambho tattha siyā kesañci tathāparivitakkoti tassāpi avakāsābhāvādassanatthaṃ tathā vuttattā. Kira-saddo pana tadā brāhmaṇena cintitākārasūcanattho daṭṭhabbo. Evamādīnīti ādi-saddena “ayaṃ virūpo daliddo [P 1.0427] appesakkho assaddho appassuto anatthaññū na medhāvī”ti etesaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

The ability to consider past and other matters is to be understood as belonging to the king by way of inference and customary behavior, not like the direct seeing of the Buddhas. Therefore, 'in the past,' and so on, are stated to show this. First, let wealth and so forth be the requisites of the sacrifice, since without them it cannot be accomplished. But regarding noble birth and beauty, what is the point? he asks, 'with these, indeed,' and so on. Here, some say that just as wealth and so forth are definitely limbs of the sacrifice, noble birth and beauty are not, and to indicate this, the word 'indeed' (kira) is taken. Thinking that the statement 'this one is of low birth,' and so on, is not absolute, this is untenable. Since the commencement of the sacrifice is generally common, some might entertain such thoughts. To show that there is no room for even that, it is thus stated. The word 'kira,' however, should be seen as indicating the manner of the brahmin's reflection at that time. 'And so on'—by the word 'and so on,' the inclusion of 'this one is ugly, poor, of little power, faithless, unlearned, ignorant, and unwise' should be understood.

Catuparikkhārādivaṇṇanā

The Description of the Four Requisites and So Forth.

341. “Sujaṃ paggaṇhantāna”nti purohitassa sayameva kaṭacchuggahaṇajotanena evaṃ sahatthā, sakkaccañca dāne yuttatā icchitabbāti dasseti[M 1.0327]. Evaṃ dujjātassāti etthāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo.

341. ‘Sujaṃ paggaṇhantāna’ (while taking up the ladle) means that the chaplain himself, by the indication of taking up the ladle, thus with his own hand, shows that diligence and proper attention should be applied to giving. Similarly, for ‘dujjātassa’ (for one of bad birth), here too the meaning should be understood in the same way as explained below.

342. Tiṇṇaṃ ṭhānānanti dānassa ādimajjhapariyosānabhūtāsu tīsu bhūmīsu, avatthāsūti attho. Calantīti kampanti purimākārena na tiṭṭhanti. Karaṇattheti tatiyāvibhattiatthe. Kattari hetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ karaṇīyasaddāpekkhāya. “Paccānutāpo na kattabbo”ti vatvā tassa akaraṇūpāyaṃ dassetuṃ “pubbacetanā pana acalā patiṭṭhapetabbā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha acalāti daḷhā kenaci asaṃhīrā. Patiṭṭhapetabbāti supatiṭṭhitā kātabbā. Evaṃ karaṇena hi yathā taṃ dānaṃ sampati yathādhippāyaṃ nippajjati, evaṃ āyatimpi vipulaphalatāyāti āha “evañhi dānaṃ mahapphalaṃ hotīti dassetī”ti, vippaṭisārena anupakkiliṭṭhabhāvato. Muñcacetanāti pariccāgacetanā. Tassā niccalabhāvo nāma muttacāgatā pubbābhisaṅkhāravasena uḷārabhāvo, samanussaraṇacetanāya pana niccalabhāvo “aho mayā dānaṃ dinnaṃ sādhu suṭṭhū”ti tassa sakkaccaṃ paccavekkhaṇāvasena veditabbo. Tathā akarontassāti muñcacetanaṃ, tattha paccāsamanussaraṇacetanañca vuttanayena niccalaṃ akarontassa vippaṭisāraṃ uppādentassa. Khettavisese pariccāgassa katattā laddhesupi uḷāresu [P 1.0428] bhogesu cittaṃ nāpi namati. Yathā kathanti āha “mahāroruvaṃ upapannassa seṭṭhigahapatino viyā”ti.

342. ‘Tiṇṇaṃ ṭhānānaṃ’ (of the three stages) means the three stages of giving: the beginning, middle, and end, meaning the three phases or states. ‘Calantī’ (they waver) means they tremble, they do not remain in their former state. ‘Karaṇatthe’ (in the sense of the instrumental case) refers to the meaning of the instrumental case. Here, this is a genitive term dependent on the word ‘karaṇīya’ (to be done). Having stated, ‘Regret should not be made,’ the method to prevent it is explained: ‘But the initial intention should be firmly established.’ Here, ‘acalā’ (unwavering) means firm, unshaken by anything. ‘Patiṭṭhapetabbā’ (should be established) means it should be well-established. Thus, by acting in this way, the gift is fulfilled as intended and yields abundant fruit in the future. Hence, it is said, ‘In this way, a gift becomes of great fruit,’ showing its being unpolluted by regret. ‘Muñcacetanā’ (the intention of relinquishment) means the intention of giving up. Its steadfastness, ‘niccalabhāvo’, is called a noble state through previous volitional formations characterized by generosity. The steadfastness of recollection is understood as carefully reflecting, ‘Ah, the gift I gave was well and rightly given.’ Similarly, for one who does not act thus—who does not establish the intention of relinquishment and subsequent recollection firmly—regret arises. Even when great wealth is obtained due to relinquishment in exceptional fields, the mind does not incline toward it. As it is said, ‘Like the merchant householder who was reborn in the Mahāroruva hell.’

So [V 1.0290] kira tagarasikhiṃ paccekabuddhaṃ attano gehadvāre piṇḍāya ṭhitaṃ disvā “imassa samaṇassa piṇḍapātaṃ dehī”ti bhariyaṃ āṇāpetvā rājupaṭṭhānatthaṃ pakkāmi. Seṭṭhibhariyā sappaññajātikā, sā cintesi “mayā ettakena kālena ‘imassa dethā’ti vacanamattaṃ pissa na sutapubbaṃ, ayañca maññe ahosi paccekasambuddho, yathā tathā adatvā paṇītaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ dassāmī”ti upagantvā paccekasambuddhaṃ pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā pattaṃ ādāya antonivesane paññattāsane nisīdāpetvā parisuddhehi sālitaṇḍulehi bhattaṃ sampādetvā tadanurūpaṃ khādanīyaṃ, byañjanaṃ, sūpeyyañca abhisaṅkharitvā bahi gandhehi alaṅkaritvā paccekasambuddhassa hatthesu patiṭṭhapetvā vandi. Paccekabuddho “aññesampi paccekabuddhānaṃ saṅgahaṃ [M 1.0328] karissāmī”ti aparibhuñjitvāva anumodanaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Sopi kho seṭṭhi rājupaṭṭhānaṃ katvā āgacchanto paccekabuddhaṃ disvā ahaṃ “tumhākaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ dethā”ti vatvā pakkanto, api vo laddho piṇḍapātoti. Āma seṭṭhi laddhoti. “Passāmā”ti gīvaṃ ukkhipitvā olokesi. Athassa piṇḍapātagandho uṭṭhahitvā nāsapuṭaṃ pūresi. So “mahā vata me dhanabyayo jāto”ti cittaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkonto pacchā vippaṭisārī ahosi. Vippaṭisārassa pana uppannākāro “varameta”ntiādinā (saṃ. ni. 1.131) pāḷiyaṃ āgatoyeva. Bhātu panāyaṃ ekaṃ puttakaṃ [P 1.0429] sāpateyyakāraṇā jīvitā voropesi, tena mahāroruvaṃ upapanno. Piṇḍapātadānena panesa sattakkhattuṃ suggatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapanno, sattakkhattumeva ca seṭṭhikule nibbatto, na cāssa uḷāresu bhogesu cittaṃ nami, tena vuttaṃ “nāpi uḷāresu bhogesu cittaṃ namatī”ti.

It seems that when he saw the Paccekabuddha Tagarasikhi standing at his door for alms, he ordered his wife, ‘Give alms to this ascetic,’ and then left to attend on the king. The merchant’s wife was wise by nature. She thought, ‘In all this time, I have never before heard him utter even the words, “Give to this one.” This must indeed be a Paccekabuddha. I will not give just any alms, but will offer the finest alms food.’ Approaching the Paccekabuddha, she paid homage with the fivefold prostration, took his bowl, seated him on a prepared seat inside the house, and prepared a meal of the purest rice. She also prepared suitable snacks, curries, and soups, adorned the food with fragrant substances, placed it in the Paccekabuddha’s hands, and paid homage again. The Paccekabuddha, thinking, ‘I will share this with other Paccekabuddhas,’ did not consume it but gave his appreciation and departed. Meanwhile, the merchant, having attended on the king, was returning when he saw the Paccekabuddha and asked, ‘I left after saying, “Give alms to you.” Did you receive the alms food?’ ‘Yes, merchant, I received it,’ he replied. ‘Let me see,’ said the merchant, craning his neck to look. Then the fragrance of the alms food rose and filled his nostrils. Unable to restrain his thoughts, he lamented, ‘Ah, what a great expenditure of wealth has occurred for me!’ and later felt regret. The arising of regret in him is described in the Pāli canon with the phrase, ‘Better than this…’ and so forth (Saṃ. Ni. 1.131). Moreover, this man had once killed his brother’s only son out of greed for inheritance, and because of that, he was reborn in the Great Roruva hell. But due to his offering of alms food, he was reborn seven times in a good destination, the heavenly world. Seven times he was also reborn in a merchant’s family, yet his mind never inclined toward great wealth—hence it is said, ‘Nor does his mind incline toward great wealth.’

343. Ākaroti attano anurūpatāya samariyādaṃ saparicchedaṃ phalaṃ nibbattetīti ākāro, kāraṇanti āha “dasahi ākārehīti dasahi kāraṇehī”ti. Paṭiggāhakato vāti balavataro hutvā uppajjamāno paṭiggāhakatova uppajjati, itaro pana deyyadhammato, parivārajanatopi uppajjeyyeva. Uppajjituṃ yuttanti uppajjanārahaṃ. Tesaṃyeva pāṇātipātīnaṃ. Yajanaṃ nāmettha dānaṃ adhippetaṃ, na aggijuhananti āha “yajataṃ bhavanti detu bhava”nti. Vissajjatūti muttacāgavasena vissajjatu. Abbhantaranti ajjhattaṃ, sakasantāneti attho.

343. ‘Ākāra’ (mode) is so called because it produces a result that is in accordance with itself, bounded, and defined; it is a cause. Thus it is said, ‘by ten modes’ means ‘by ten causes.’ ‘Or from the recipient’ means that when it arises with greater strength, it arises from the recipient; but otherwise, it arises from the gift itself, or even from the retinue. ‘Fit to arise’ means worthy of arising. This refers to those very ones who kill living beings. Here, ‘yajanaṃ’ (sacrifice) is intended to mean giving, not a fire-offering; thus it is said, ‘Let them sacrifice’ means ‘Let them give.’ ‘Let him release’ means let him release by way of open-handed generosity. ‘Internal’ means within, that is, in one’s own continuum.

344. Heṭṭhā soḷasa parikkhārā vuttā yaññassa te vatthuṃ katvā, idha pana sandassanādivasena anumodanāya āraddhattā vuttaṃ “soḷasahi ākārehī”ti. Dassetvā attano desanānubhāvena paccakkhato viya phalaṃ dassetvā, anekavāraṃ pana kathanato ca āmeḍitavacanaṃ. Tamatthanti yathāvuttaṃ dānaphalavasena kammaphalasambandhaṃ. Samādapetvāti sutamattameva akatvā [V 1.0291] yathā rājā tamatthaṃ sammadeva ādiyati [P 1.0430] citte karonto suggahitaṃ katvā gaṇhāti, tathā sakkaccaṃ ādāpetvā. Āmeḍitakāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva.

344. Previously, the sixteen requisites of a sacrifice were stated as its basis, but here, because it is initiated for appreciation by way of showing and so forth, it is said, ‘by sixteen modes.’ ‘Having shown’ means having shown the result as if directly through the power of one’s teaching; and because of speaking many times, it is reiterated speech. ‘That purpose’ refers to the connection with the fruit of kamma in terms of the fruit of giving, as stated. ‘Having urged’ means not merely having it heard, but just as a king rightly takes up that purpose, placing it in his mind and grasping it well, he accepts it; in that way, having caused him to accept it carefully. The reason for reiteration is as stated previously.

“Vippaṭisāravinodanenā”ti [M 1.0329] idaṃ nidassanamattaṃ lobhadosamohaissāmacchariyamānādayopi hi dānacittassa upakkilesā, tesaṃ vinodanenapi taṃ samuttejitaṃ nāma hoti tikkhavisadabhāvappattito. Āsannatarabhāvato vā vippaṭisārassa tabbinodanameva gahitaṃ, pavattitepi hi dāne tassa sambhavato. Yāthāvato vijjamānehi guṇehi tuṭṭhapahaṭṭhabhāvāpādanaṃ sampahaṃsananti āha “sundaraṃ te…pe… thutiṃ katvā kathesī”ti. Dhammatoti saccato. Saccañhi dhammato anapetattā dhammaṃ, upasamacariyābhāvato samaṃ, yuttabhāvena kāraṇanti ca vuccatīti.

‘By dispelling regret’—this is merely an illustration. For greed, hatred, delusion, envy, stinginess, pride, and so forth are also defilements of the mind of giving. By dispelling these too, that giving is said to be stimulated, because it attains a state of sharpness and clarity. Alternatively, because regret is more imminent, its removal alone is mentioned, for it can arise even after the giving has been set in motion. ‘Making delighted’ means producing a state of satisfaction and joy with existing virtues as they really are—thus it is said, ‘It is beautiful for you… having praised, he spoke.’ ‘According to Dhamma’ means according to truth. For truth is called ‘Dhamma’ because it is not separate from nature, ‘peaceful’ because it is a state of peaceful conduct, and ‘cause’ because of its fittingness.

345. Tasmiṃ yaññe rukkhatiṇacchedopi nāma nāhosi, kuto pāṇavadhoti pāṇavadhābhāvasseva daḷhīkaraṇatthaṃ sabbaso viparītagāhāvidūsitañcassa dassetuṃ pāḷiyaṃ “neva gāvo haññiṃsū”ti ādiṃ vatvāpi “na rukkhā chijjiṃsū”tiādi vuttaṃ, tenāha “kiṃ pana gāvo”tiādi. Barihisatthāyāti paricchedanatthāya. Vanamālāsaṅkhepenāti vanapupphehi ganthitamālāniyāmena. Bhūmiyaṃ vā pattharantīti vedibhūmiṃ parikkhipantā tattha pantharanti. Antogehadāsādayoti antojātadhanakkītakaramarānītasayaṃdāsā. Pubbamevāti bhatikaraṇato pageva. Gahetvā karontīti divase divase gahetvā karonti. Tajjitāti [P 1.0431] gajjitā. Piyasamudācārenevāti iṭṭhavacaneneva. Phāṇitena cevāti ettha ca-saddo avuttasamuccayattho, tena paṇītapaṇītānaṃ nānappakārānaṃ khādanīyabhojanīyādīnañceva vatthamālāgandhavilepanayānaseyyādīnañca saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo, tenāha “paṇītehi sappitelādisammissehevā”tiādi.

345. At that sacrifice, there was not even the cutting of trees or grass to speak of, so how could there be the killing of living beings? To firmly establish the absence of killing living beings and to show that his sacrifice was completely uncorrupted by wrong practice, the Pāli text, after stating, ‘No cows were slain,’ and so on, also states, ‘No trees were cut,’ etc. Hence it is said, ‘What then of cows?’ and so on. ‘Barihisatthāya’ (for the purpose of cutting the sacrificial grass) means for the purpose of cutting. ‘Vanamālāsaṅkhepena’ (by way of a collection of forest garlands) means by way of garlands woven from forest flowers. ‘Or they spread on the ground’ means they spread them there, enclosing the altar ground. ‘Antogehadāsādayo’ (slaves within the house and so forth) refers to slaves born in the household, bought with wealth, brought as prisoners of war, or who became slaves voluntarily. ‘Pubbameva’ (even before) means even before making them wage-earners. ‘Gahetvā karonti’ (taking and doing) means they take and do it day by day. ‘Tajjitā’ (threatened) means roared at. ‘Piyasamudācāreneva’ (only with pleasing conduct) means only with pleasing speech. ‘Phāṇitena ceva’ (and with treacle)—here the word ‘and’ has the sense of including what is unstated; thereby, the inclusion of various excellent edibles and foods, as well as clothes, garlands, perfumes, ointments, vehicles, beds, etc., should be understood. Hence it is said, ‘mixed with fine ghee, oil, etc.’

346. Saṃ nāma dhanaṃ, tassa patīti sapati, dhanavā. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikahitāvahattā tassa hitanti sāpateyyaṃ, tadeva dhanaṃ. Tenāha “pahūtaṃ sāpateyyaṃ ādāyāti bahuṃ dhanaṃ gahetvā”ti. Gāmabhāgenāti saṅkittanavasena gāme vā gahetabbabhāgena.

346. ‘Saṃ’ is a name for wealth; its master is ‘sapati’, meaning wealthy. Because it brings benefit both in this life and in the life to come, it is called ‘sāpateyyaṃ’ (property), which is wealth itself. Hence it is said, ‘taking abundant property’ means ‘taking much wealth.’

347. “Yāguṃ pivitvā”ti yāgusīsena pātarāsabhojanamāha. Puratthimena yaññavāṭassāti rañño dānasālāya nātidūre puratthimadisābhāgeti [M 1.0330] attho, yato tattha pātarāsaṃ bhuñjitvā akilantarūpāyeva sāyanhe sālaṃ pāpuṇanti “dakkhiṇena yaññavāṭassā”ti ādīsupi eseva nayo.

347. ‘Having drunk gruel’ refers to the morning meal with gruel as its main part. ‘To the east of the sacrificial enclosure’ means in the eastern direction, not too far from the king’s alms-hall, from where, having eaten their morning meal, they could reach the hall in the evening without becoming fatigued. The same method applies to ‘to the south of the sacrificial enclosure’ and similar phrases.

348. Parihārenāti [V 1.0292] bhagavantaṃ garuṃ katvā agāravaparihārena.

348. ‘Parihārena’ (with attendance) means: by revering the Blessed One and avoiding disrespect.

Niccadānaanukulayaññavaṇṇanā

A Description of Constant Giving and Traditional Sacrifice.

349. Uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāyāti dāne uṭṭhānavīriyaṃ sakkaccaṃ katvā. Appasambhārataroti ativiya parittasambhāro. Samārabhīyati yañño etehīti samārambhā, sambhārasambharaṇavasena pavattasattapīḷā. Appaṭṭhataroti pana ativiya appakiccoti attho. Vipākasaññitaṃ atisayena mahantaṃ sadisaphalaṃ etassāti [P 1.0432] mahapphalataro. Udayasaññitaṃ atisayena mahantaṃ nissandādiphalaṃ etassāti mahānisaṃsataro. Dhuvadānānīti dhuvāni thirāni acchinnāni katvā dātabbadānāni. Anukulayaññānīti anukulaṃ kulānukkamaṃ upādāya dātabbadānāni, tenāha “amhāka”ntiādi. Nibaddhadānānīti nibandhetvā niyametvā paveṇīvasena pavattitadānāni.

349. "Uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāyāti" means exerting energetic effort in giving, having done it respectfully. "Appasambhārataroti" means having exceedingly minimal preparation. "Samārabhīyati yañño etehīti samārambhā" means the undertaking of a sacrifice, which is the suffering of beings caused by gathering and assembling materials. "Appaṭṭhataroti pana" means having exceedingly little to do. "Vipākasaññitaṃ atisayena mahantaṃ sadisaphalaṃ etassāti mahapphalataro" signifies that it has an exceedingly great, corresponding result, thus it is of greater fruit. "Udayasaññitaṃ atisayena mahantaṃ nissandādiphalaṃ etassāti mahānisaṃsataro" means it has an exceedingly great benefit, such as an outflowing result, thus it is of greater advantage. "Dhuvadānānīti" refers to gifts that should be given consistently, firmly, and without interruption. "Anukulayaññānīti" means gifts that should be given in accordance with family traditions; hence it is said, "of ours," etc. "Nibaddhadānānīti" refers to gifts given systematically, regulated, and established as a continuous tradition.

Hatthidantena pavattitā dantamayasalākā, yattha dāyakānaṃ nāmaṃ aṅkanti. Raññoti setavāhanarañño.

"Hatthidantena" refers to an ivory ticket, on which the names of donors are inscribed. "Raññoti" refers to King Setavāhana.

Ādīnīti ādi-saddena “seno viya maṃsapesiṃ kasmā okkhanditvā gaṇhāsī”ti evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Pubbacetanāmuñcacetanāaparacetanāsampattiyā dāyakassa vasena tīṇi aṅgāni, vītarāgatāvītadosatāvītamohatāpaṭipattiyā dakkhiṇeyyassa vasena tīṇīti evaṃ chaḷaṅgasamannāgatāya dakkhiṇāya. Aparāparaṃ uppajjanakacetanāvasena mahānadī viya, mahogho viya ca ito cito ca abhisanditvā okkhanditvā pavattiyā puññameva puññābhisando.

"Ādīnīti" includes the collection of examples beginning with, "Why do you seize me like a hawk swooping down on a lump of meat?". The three factors pertaining to the giver are the accomplishment of the initial intention, the intention at the time of giving, and the subsequent intention. The three factors pertaining to the recipient are the practice characterized by freedom from greed, freedom from hatred, and freedom from delusion. Thus, an offering is endowed with six factors. Like a great river, like a mighty torrent, due to the intention that arises again and again, merit overflows and surges from here and there, and this is indeed a flood of merit.

350. Kiccapariyosānaṃ natthi divase divase dāyakassa byāpārāpajjanato, tenāha “ekenā”tiādi. Kiccapariyosānaṃ atthi yathāraddhassa āvāsassa katipayenāpi kālena parisamāpetabbato, tenāha [M 1.0331] “paṇṇasāla”ntiādi. Suttantapariyāyenāti suttantapāḷinayena. (Ma. ni. 1.12, 13; a. ni. 2.58) nava ānisaṃsāti sītapaṭighātādayo paṭisallānārāmapariyosānā nava udayā. Appamattatāya cete vuttā.

350. "Kiccapariyosānaṃ natthi" means there is no end to the work because of the donor's daily engagement, hence it is said, "by one," etc. "Kiccapariyosānaṃ atthi" means there is an end to the work, since a dwelling that has been started can be completed in just a few days, hence it is said, "a leaf-hut," etc. "Suttantapariyāyenāti" means according to the method of the Suttanta texts. (Majjhima Nikāya 1.12, 13; Aṅguttara Nikāya 2.58) The nine benefits are nine advantages beginning with warding off the cold and ending with the delight of seclusion. These are stated for the sake of heedfulness.

Yasmā āvāsaṃ dentena nāma sabbampi paccayajātaṃ dinnameva hoti. Dve tayo gāme piṇḍāya caritvā kiñci [P 1.0433] aladdhā āgatassapi chāyūdakasampannaṃ ārāmaṃ pavisitvā nhāyitvā patissaye muhuttaṃ nipajjitvā vuṭṭhāya nisinnassa kāye balaṃ āharitvā pakkhittaṃ viya hoti[V 1.0293]. Bahi vicarantassa ca kāye vaṇṇadhātu vātātapehi kilamati, patissayaṃ pavisitvā dvāraṃ pidhāya muhuttaṃ nipannassa visabhāgasantati vūpasammati, sabhāgasantati patiṭṭhāti, vaṇṇadhātu āharitvā pakkhittā viya hoti. Bahi vicarantassa ca pāde kaṇṭako vijjhati, khāṇu paharati, sarīsapādiparissayā ceva corabhayañca uppajjati, patissayaṃ pavisitvā dvāraṃ pidhāya nipannassa sabbe te parissayā na honti, sajjhāyantassa dhammapītisukhaṃ, kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karontassa upasamasukhañca uppajjati bahiddhā vikkhepābhāvato. Bahi vicarantassa ca kāye sedā muccanti, akkhīni phandanti, senāsanaṃ pavisanakkhaṇe mañcapīṭhādīni na paññāyanti, muhuttaṃ nisinnassa pana akkhīnaṃ pasādo āharitvā pakkhitto viya hoti, dvāravātapānamañcapīṭhādīni paññāyanti. Etasmiñca āvāse vasantaṃ disvā manussā catūhi paccayehi sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhahanti. Tena vuttaṃ “āvāsaṃ dentena nāma sabbampi paccayajātaṃ dinnameva hotī”ti, tasmā ete yathāvuttā sabbepi ānisaṃsā veditabbā. Tena vuttaṃ “appamattatāya cete vuttā”ti.

Because by giving a dwelling, all kinds of requisites are indeed given. Having wandered through two or three villages for alms and obtained nothing, upon returning and entering a monastery endowed with shade and water, bathing, and lying down for a moment in a shelter, when one rises and sits, it is as if strength has been brought and placed in the body. For one wandering outside, the complexion is afflicted by wind and heat; but upon entering a shelter, closing the door, and lying down for a moment, the discordant continuity subsides, the harmonious continuity is established, and it is as if the complexion has been brought and restored. For one wandering outside, a thorn may pierce the foot, a stump may strike, dangers from snakes and other creatures arise, and fear of thieves occurs; but upon entering a shelter, closing the door, and lying down, all those dangers cease. For one reciting, the joy and happiness of the Dhamma arise; for one attending to a meditation subject, the happiness of tranquility arises due to the absence of external distractions. For one wandering outside, sweat pours from the body, the eyes flicker, and upon entering the lodging, the bed, seat, and so on are not discerned; but after sitting for a moment, it is as if the clarity of the eyes has been brought and restored, and the doors, windows, beds, and seats become discernible. Seeing one dwelling in such a place, people respectfully attend with the four requisites. Therefore, it is said: "By giving a dwelling, all kinds of requisites are indeed given." Thus, all these benefits should be understood as stated. Therefore, it is said: "And these are stated for the sake of heedfulness."

Sītanti ajjhattaṃ dhātukkhobhavasena vā bahiddhā utuvipariṇāmavasena vā uppajjanakasītaṃ. Uṇhanti aggisantāpaṃ, tassa vanaḍāhādīsu (vanadāhādīsu vā sārattha. ṭī. cūḷavagga 3.295) sambhavo veditabbo. Paṭihantīti paṭibāhati, yathā tadubhayavasena kāyacittānaṃ bādhanaṃ na hoti, evaṃ karoti. Sītuṇhabbhāhate [P 1.0434] hi sarīre vikkhittacitto bhikkhu yoniso padahituṃ na sakkoti. Vāḷamigānīti sīhabyagghādicaṇḍamige. Guttasenāsanañhi āraññakampi pavisitvā dvāraṃ pidhāya nisinnassa te parissayā na hontīti. Sarīsapeti ye keci sarante gacchante dīghajātike sappādike. Makaseti nidassanamattametaṃ, ḍaṃsādīnampi etesveva [M 1.0332] (etaneva sārattha. ṭī. cūḷavagga 3.295) saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Sisireti sisirakālavasena, sattāhavaddalikādivasena ca uppanne sisirasamphasse. Vuṭṭhiyoti yadā tadā uppannā vassavuṭṭhiyo paṭihanatīti yojanā.

"Cold" means the cold that arises either internally due to a disturbance of the elements or externally due to a change of season. "Heat" means the heat of fire, the occurrence of which should be understood in forest fires and the like. "It wards off" means it prevents; it acts in such a way that there is no affliction of body and mind on account of either. For when the body is afflicted by cold and heat, a monk with a distracted mind is not able to strive wisely. "Wild beasts" means fierce animals like lions and tigers. For one who has entered even a forest dwelling and sits with the door closed, these dangers do not arise. "Creeping things" means any long-bodied creatures that go by crawling, such as snakes. "Mosquitoes" is merely an indication; gadflies and the like should also be understood as included here. "In winter" refers to the touch of cold that arises during the winter season and during periods of cloudy weather lasting a week or so. "Rain": the connection is that it wards off the downpours of rain that arise from time to time.

Vātātapo ghoroti rukkhagacchādīnaṃ ummūlabhañjanādivasena pavattiyā ghoro sarajaarajādibhedo vāto ceva gimhapariḷāhasamayesu uppattiyā ghoro sūriyātapo ca. Paṭihaññatīti paṭibāhīyati. Leṇatthanti nānārammaṇato cittaṃ nivattetvā paṭisallānārāmatthaṃ. Sukhatthanti vuttaparissayābhāvena phāsuvihāratthaṃ. Jhāyitunti aṭṭhatiṃsāya ārammaṇesu yattha katthaci cittaṃ upanibandhitvā upanijjhāyituṃ. Vipassitunti aniccādito saṅkhāre sammasituṃ.

"The wind and sun are harsh" refers to the harsh wind that occurs by way of uprooting and breaking trees and so on, differentiated as with or without dust, as well as the harsh sunlight that arises during the hot season. "They are warded off" means they are kept away. "For the sake of a refuge" means for the purpose of the delight of seclusion, having withdrawn the mind from various objects. "For the sake of happiness" means for the purpose of dwelling in comfort, due to the absence of the aforementioned dangers. "To meditate" means to contemplate, having focused the mind on any of the thirty-eight objects. "To gain insight" means to comprehend conditioned formations as impermanent and so forth.

Vihāreti [V 1.0294] patissaye. Kārayeti kārāpeyya. Rammeti manorame nivāsasukhe. Vāsayettha bahussuteti kāretvā pana ettha vihāresu bahussute sīlavante kalyāṇadhamme nivāseyya, te nivāsento pana tesaṃ bahussutānaṃ yathā paccayehi kilamatho na hoti, evaṃ annañca pānañca vatthasenāsanāni ca dadeyya ujubhūtesu ajjhāsayasampannesu kammakammaphalānaṃ, ratanattayaguṇānañca saddahanena vippasannena cetasā.

"Vihāre" means in a shelter. "Kāraye" means one should have it built. "Ramme" means in a delightful and comfortable dwelling. "Vāsayettha bahussute" means having had them built, one should have the learned, virtuous, and good-natured ones dwell here in these dwellings. While having them dwell there, so that those learned ones do not suffer from a lack of requisites, one should give food, drink, clothing, and lodgings to those who are upright, endowed with right intention, and with a mind made serene through faith in action, the fruits of action, and the qualities of the Triple Gem.

Idāni gahaṭṭhapabbajitānaṃ aññamaññūpakāritaṃ dassetuṃ [P 1.0435] “te tassā”ti gāthamāha. Tattha teti bahussutā. Tassāti upāsakassa. Dhammaṃ desentīti sakalavaṭṭadukkhapanūdanaṃ saddhammaṃ desenti. Yaṃ so dhammaṃ idhaññāyāti so upāsako yaṃ saddhammaṃ imasmiṃ sāsane sammāpaṭipajjanena jānitvā aggamaggādhigamena anāsavo hutvā parinibbāti ekādasaggivūpasamena sīti bhavati.

Now, to show the mutual benefit between householders and monastics, the verse beginning "te tassa" is spoken. Herein, "te" refers to the learned ones. "Tassa" refers to the lay follower. "They teach the Dhamma" means they expound the true Dhamma, which removes all the suffering of the cycle of rebirth. "That Dhamma which he understands here" means that lay follower, having understood the true Dhamma in this dispensation through right practice, attains the supreme path, becomes without taints, and attains final Nibbāna with the stilling of the eleven fires, becoming cool.

Sītapaṭighātādayo vipassanāvasānā terasa, annādilābho, dhammassavanaṃ, dhammāvabodho, parinibbānanti evaṃ sattarasa.

The thirteen benefits beginning with the warding off of cold and ending with insight, plus the gain of food and so on, hearing the Dhamma, understanding the Dhamma, and final Nibbāna—thus there are seventeen.

351. Attano santakāti attaniyā. Duppariccajanaṃ lobhaṃ niggaṇhituṃ asakkontassa. Saṅghassa vā gaṇassa vā santiketi yojanā. Tatthāti [M 1.0333] yathāgahite saraṇe. Natthi punappunaṃ kattabbatā viññūjātikassāti adhippāyo. “Jīvitapariccāgamayaṃ puñña”nti “sace tvaṃ na yathāgahitaṃ saraṇaṃ bhindissati, evāhaṃ taṃ māremī”ti yadipi koci tiṇhena satthena jīvitā voropeyya, tathāpi “nevāhaṃ buddhaṃ na buddhoti, dhammaṃ na dhammoti, saṅghaṃ na saṅghoti vadāmī”ti daḷhataraṃ katvā gahitasaraṇassa vasena vuttaṃ.

351. “Belonging to oneself” means one's own possessions. This applies to one who is unable to restrain greed, which is difficult to relinquish. The construction is “in the presence of the Sangha or a group.” “Therein” means in the refuge as it was taken. The meaning is that for one of a wise nature, there is no need for repeated action. “Merit consisting of sacrificing one’s life” refers to the case where, even if someone were to threaten, “If you do not break the refuge you have taken, I will kill you,” and were to sever one's life with a sharp weapon, one would still resolve very firmly, “I will not say, ‘The Buddha is not the Buddha,’ ‘the Dhamma is not the Dhamma,’ ‘the Sangha is not the Sangha.’” This is said in connection with one who has taken refuge very firmly.

352. Saraṇaṃ upagatena kāyavācācittehi sakkaccaṃ vatthuttayapūjā kātabbā, tattha ca saṃkileso parihanitabbo, sikkhāpadāni pana samādānamattaṃ, sampattavatthuto viramaṇamattañcāti saraṇagamanato sīlassa appaṭṭhataratā, appasamārambhataratā ca veditabbā. Sabbesaṃ sattānaṃ jīvitadānādinā daṇḍanidhānato, sakalalokiyalokuttaraguṇādhiṭṭhānato cassa mahapphalamahānisaṃsataratā daṭṭhabbā.

352. Having gone for refuge, one should reverently perform offerings to the Triple Gem with body, speech, and mind. Therein, defilements should be abandoned. The training precepts, however, are a mere undertaking and a mere abstaining from an occasion that has arisen. Therefore, it should be understood that virtue is less established and less arduous than going for refuge. Its greater fruit and greater benefit should be seen from its being the laying down of the rod towards all beings through the giving of life and so on, and from its being the foundation for all worldly and supramundane qualities.

Vakkhamānanayena [P 1.0436] ca verahetutāya veraṃ vuccati pāṇātipātādipāpadhammo, taṃ maṇati “mayi idha ṭhitāya kathaṃ āgacchasī”ti tajjentī viya nīharatīti veramaṇī, tato vā pāpadhammato [V 1.0295] viramati etāyāti “viramaṇī”ti vattabbe niruttinayena ikārassa ekāraṃ katvā “veramaṇī”ti vuttā. Asamādinnasīlassa sampattato yathāupaṭṭhitavītikkamitabbavatthuto virati sampattavirati. Samādānavasena uppannā virati samādānavirati. Setu vuccati ariyamaggo, tappariyāpannā hutvā pāpadhammānaṃ samucchedavasena ghātanavirati setughātavirati. Idāni tisso viratiyo sarūpato dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pariharatīti avītikkamavasena parivajjeti. Na hanāmīti ettha iti-saddo ādiattho, tena “adinnaṃ nādiyāmī”ti evaṃ ādīnaṃ saṅgaho, vā-saddena vā, tenāha “sikkhāpadāni gaṇhantassā”ti.

By the method to be explained, and because it is the cause of enmity, the evil quality beginning with the destruction of life is called 'enmity' (vera). It (veramaṇī) drives away that enmity as if rebuking it, saying, 'How do you come here while I am standing here?'—thus it is 'veramaṇī' (restraint). Alternatively, because one refrains from that evil quality by means of it, it should be called 'viramaṇī' (refraining), but by the rule of etymology, the 'i' is changed to 'e,' and thus it is called 'veramaṇī.' For one who has not undertaken the precepts, the refraining that occurs upon encountering an object to be transgressed is called 'restraint on occasion' (sampattavirati). Restraint arising by way of undertaking is called 'restraint by undertaking' (samādānavirati). The Noble Path is called a causeway (setu). The restraint that, being included in that path, destroys evil qualities by way of complete eradication is called 'causeway-destruction restraint' (setughātavirati). Now, to show the three kinds of restraint in their own nature, 'herein' (tatthā), etc., is said. 'He avoids' means he avoids by way of non-transgression. In 'I will not kill,' the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'and so forth,' hence it includes phrases like 'I will not take what is not given.' Or, by the word 'vā,' he says, 'for one who takes up the training rules.'

Maggasampayuttāti sammādiṭṭhiyādimaggasampayuttā. Idāni tāsaṃ viratīnaṃ ārammaṇato vibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Purimā dveti sampattasamādānaviratiyo. Pacchimāti setughātavirati. Sabbānipi bhinnāni honti ekajjhaṃ samādinnattā. Tadeva bhijjati visuṃ visuṃ samādinnattā[M 1.0334]. Gahaṭṭhavasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Bhedo nāma natthi paṭipakkhasamucchindanena akuppasabhāvattā, tenāha “bhavantarepī”ti. Yonisiddhanti manussatiracchānānaṃ uddhaṃ tiriyameva dīghatā viya jātisiddhanti attho. Bodhisatte kucchigate bodhisattamātusīlaṃ viya dhammatāya sabhāveneva siddhaṃ dhammatāsiddhaṃ, maggadhammatāya vā ariyamaggānubhāvena siddhaṃ dhammatāsiddhaṃ. Diṭṭhiujukaraṇaṃ [P 1.0437] nāma bhāriyaṃ dukkhaṃ, tasmā saraṇagamanaṃ sikkhāpadasamādānato mahaṭṭhatarameva, na appaṭṭhataranti adhippāyo. Yathā tathā vā gaṇhantassāpīti ādaragāravaṃ akatvā samādiyantassāpi. Sādhukaṃ gaṇhantassāpīti sakkaccaṃ sīlāni samādiyantassāpi, na diguṇaṃ, tiguṇaṃ vā ussāho karaṇīyo.

'Path-associated' means associated with the path factors beginning with right view. Now, to show the distinctions of those abstinences according to their objects, 'herein' and so forth is said. The first two are restraint on occasion and restraint by undertaking. The latter is causeway-destruction restraint. All precepts are broken when they are undertaken together; only that one is broken when they are undertaken separately. This is said with reference to a householder. There is no breaking of this restraint, as it is of an unshakable nature due to the eradication of opposing factors. Therefore, it is said, 'even in another existence.' 'Established by origin' (yonisiddha) means 'established by birth' (jātisiddha), just as length is established vertically for humans and horizontally for animals. Like the virtue of the Bodhisatta’s mother when the Bodhisatta is in her womb, it is established by its own nature—established by the nature of things (dhammatāsiddha). Or, established by the nature of the path, it is established by the power of the noble path (dhammatāsiddha). Straightening of view is a difficult and weighty matter. Therefore, going for refuge is indeed more significant than undertaking the training precepts—not less significant—this is the meaning. 'However one takes it' means even for one who undertakes it without respect and reverence. 'Taking it well' means even for one who undertakes the precepts carefully; no double or triple effort need be made.

Abhayadānatāya sīlassa dānabhāvo, anavasesaṃ vā sattanikāyaṃ dayati tena rakkhatīti dānaṃ, sīlaṃ. “Aggānī”ti ñātattā aggaññāni. Cirarattatāya ñātattā rattaññāni. “Ariyānaṃ sādhūnaṃ vaṃsānī”ti ñātattā vaṃsaññāni. “Porāṇānī”tiādīsu purimānaṃ etāni porāṇāni. Sabbaso kenacipi pakārena sādhūhi na kiṇṇāni na khittāni na chaḍḍitānīti asaṅkiṇṇāni. Ayañca nayo nesaṃ yathā atīte, evaṃ etarahi, anāgate cāti āha “asaṅkiṇṇapubbāni na saṅkiyanti na saṅkiyissantī”ti. Tato eva appapikuṭṭhāni na paṭikkhittāni. Na hi kadācipi viññū samaṇabrāhmaṇā hiṃsādipāpadhammaṃ anujānanti. Aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ abhayaṃ detīti sabbesu bhūtesu nihitadaṇḍattā sakalassapi sattanikāyassa bhayābhāvaṃ deti. Na hi ariyasāvakato kassaci bhayaṃ hoti. Averanti verābhāvaṃ. Abyāpajjhanti niddukkhataṃ.

By the gift of safety, virtue has the quality of a gift; or, because it is compassionate to the entire community of beings without exception and thereby protects them, it is a gift, it is virtue. Because they are known as 'foremost' (aggāni), they are 'foremost-known' (aggaññāni). Because they are known for a long time, they are 'long-known' (rattaññāni). Because they are known as 'lineages of the noble and virtuous,' they are 'lineage-known' (vaṃsaññāni). In 'ancient' (porāṇāni) and so on, these are ancient because they belong to those of the past. They are in no way corrupted, rejected, or abandoned by the virtuous—thus, they are uncorrupted (asaṅkiṇṇāni). And this principle applies to them as in the past, so also now, and in the future—thus it is said, 'never before corrupted, they are not corrupted, nor will they be corrupted.' Therefore, they are not despised or rejected. For wise ascetics and brahmins never approve of evil qualities such as violence. Because it gives safety to immeasurable beings—thus, because the rod is laid down towards all beings, it gives the absence of fear to the entire community of beings. Indeed, from a noble disciple, no fear arises for anyone. 'Without enmity' (avera) means the absence of enmity. 'Without ill-will' (abyāpajjha) means the absence of suffering.

Nanu [V 1.0296] ca pañcasīlaṃ sabbakālikaṃ, na ca ekantato vimuttāyatanaṃ, saraṇagamanaṃ pana buddhuppādahetukaṃ, ekantavimuttāyatanañca, tattha kathaṃ saraṇāgamanato pañcasīlassa mahapphalatāti āha “kiñcāpī”tiādi. Jeṭṭhakanti uttamaṃ. “Saraṇagamaneyeva patiṭṭhāyā”ti [P 1.0438] iminā tassa sīlassa saraṇagamanena abhisaṅkhatatamāha.

Is it not so that the five precepts are for all time, and not exclusively a basis for liberation, whereas going for refuge is conditioned by the arising of a Buddha and is exclusively a basis for liberation? In that case, how can the five precepts have a greater fruit than going for refuge? To this, it is said, 'Although,' and so on. 'Foremost' (jeṭṭhaka) means supreme. By the phrase 'being established in the going for refuge itself,' he shows that this virtue is most excellently conditioned by the going for refuge.

353. Īdisamevāti evaṃ saṃkilesaṃ paṭipakkhameva hutvā. Heṭṭhā vuttehi guṇehīti ettha heṭṭhā vuttaguṇā nāma saraṇagamanaṃ, sīlasampadā, indriyesu guttadvāratāti evaṃ ādayo. Paṭhamajjhānaṃ nibbattento na kilamatīti [M 1.0335] yojanā. Tānīti paṭhamajjhānādīni. “Paṭhamajjhāna”nti ukkaṭṭhaniddeso ayanti āha “ekaṃ kappa”nti, ekaṃ mahākappanti attho. Hīnaṃ pana paṭhamajjhānaṃ, majjhimañca asaṅkhyeyyakappassa tatiyaṃ bhāgaṃ, upaḍḍhakappañca āyuṃ deti. “Dutiyaṃ aṭṭhakappe”ti ādīsupi iminā nayena attho veditabbo, mahākappavaseneva ca gahetabbaṃ. Yasmā vā paṇītāniyevettha jhānāni adhippetāni mahapphalatarabhāvadassanaparattā desanāya, tasmā “paṭhamajjhānaṃ ekaṃ kappa”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tadevāti catutthajjhānameva. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ āruppatāti āha “ākāsānañcāyatanādī”tiādi.

353. 'Just like this' means thus being the very opponent of defilement. 'By the qualities previously stated'—here, the qualities previously stated are going for refuge, perfection of virtue, guarding the doors of the senses, and so forth. The connection is: 'he does not become weary while producing the first jhāna.' 'Those' means the first jhāna and so on. 'The first jhāna'—this is a description of the highest level; thus it is said, 'one eon,' meaning one great eon. The inferior first jhāna, however, grants a lifespan of a third of an incalculable eon, and the middling one grants half an eon. In 'the second, eight eons,' and so on, the meaning should be understood in this way, and it should be taken in terms of great eons. Or, because it is the refined jhānas that are intended here, since the teaching is concerned with showing their state of greater fruitfulness, it is therefore said, 'the first jhāna for one eon,' and so on. 'That very one' means the fourth jhāna itself. If so, how are the formless attainments explained? To this, it is said, 'the base of infinite space,' and so on.

Sammadeva niccasaññādipaṭipakkhavidhamanavasena pavattamānā pubbabhāgiye eva bodhipakkhiyadhamme sammānentī vipassanā vipassakassa anappakaṃ pītisomanassaṃ samāvahatīti āha “vipassanā…pe… abhāvā”ti. Tenāha bhagavā –

Insight, proceeding by way of rightly dispelling opposing factors such as the perception of permanence, and establishing the factors of enlightenment in the preliminary stage itself, brings no small joy and gladness to the insight meditator. Thus it is said: 'Insight... due to the absence...'. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Yato yato sammasati, khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ;

Labhatī pītipāmojjaṃ, amataṃ taṃ vijānata”nti. (dha. pa. 374);

'Whenever one comprehends the rise and fall of the aggregates, one obtains joy and gladness; that is the Deathless for those who know.'

Yasmā ayaṃ desanā iminā anukkamena imāni ñāṇāni nibbattentassa [P 1.0439] vasena pavattitā, tasmā “vipassanāñāṇe patiṭṭhāya nibbattento”ti heṭṭhimaṃ heṭṭhimaṃ uparimassa uparimassa patiṭṭhābhūtaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Samānarūpanimmānaṃ nāma manomayiddhiyā aññehi asādhāraṇakiccanti āha “attano…pe… mahapphalā”ti. Vikubbanadassanasamatthatāyāti hatthiassādivividharūpakaraṇaṃ vikubbanaṃ, tassa dassanasamatthabhāvena. Icchiticchitaṭṭhānaṃ nāma purimajātīsu icchiticchito khandhappadeso. Samāpentoti pariyosāpento.

Because this teaching proceeds by way of generating these knowledges in this sequence, it is therefore said, 'generating based on insight knowledge,' establishing each lower stage as the foundation for the higher one. The term 'creation of a similar form' (samānarūpanimmāna) refers to a function unique to the mind-made power, not shared by others, hence it is said, 'for oneself... of great fruit.' The ability to display transformations (vikubbanadassanasamatthatā) refers to the power of creating various forms such as elephants and horses, which is transformation (vikubbana), by means of the ability to display them. The term 'desired place' refers to a region of the aggregates that was desired in previous lives. 'Brings to completion' (samāpento) means bringing to a conclusion (pariyosāpento).

Kūṭadantaupāsakattapaṭivedanākathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of Kūṭadanta's Declaration as a Lay Follower.

354-8. Sabbe [V 1.0297] te pāṇayoti “satta ca usabhasatānī”tiādinā vutte sabbe pāṇino. Ākulabhāvoti bhagavato santike dhammassa sutattā pāṇīsu anuddayaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā ṭhitassa “kathañhi nāma mayā tāva bahū pāṇino māraṇatthāya bandhāpitā”ti citte paribyākulabhāvo [M 1.0336] udapādi. Sutvāti “bandhanato mocitā”ti sutvā. Kāmacchandavigamena kallacittatā arogacittatā, byāpādavigamena mettāvasena muducittatā akathinacittatā, uddhaccakukkuccappahānena vikkhepavigamanato vinīvaraṇacittatā tehi na pihitacittatā, thinamiddhavigamena udaggacittatā saṃpaggaṇhanavasena alīnacittatā, vicikicchāvigamena sammāpaṭipattiyā adhimuttatāya pasannacittatā ca hotīti āha “kallacittantiādi anupubbikathānubhāvena vikkhambhitanīvaraṇataṃ sandhāya vutta”nti. Yaṃ panettha atthato avibhattaṃ, taṃ suviññeyyameva.

354-8. All those beings refers to all living beings mentioned, beginning with, 'seven hundred bulls.' A state of agitation means that after hearing the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One, as he stood there having established compassion for living beings, a state of mental agitation arose in him: 'How is it that I had so many living beings bound for slaughter?' Having heard means having heard, 'They were released from bondage.' Through the removal of sensual desire, the mind becomes workable, a mind free from disease. Through the removal of ill will, by way of loving-kindness, the mind becomes soft, not hardened. Through the abandoning of restlessness and remorse, with the removal of distraction, the mind is without hindrances, a mind not veiled by them. Through the removal of sloth and torpor, the mind is uplifted, by way of exertion, a mind not sluggish. And through the removal of doubt, by being resolved on the right practice, the mind becomes confident. Thus it is said: 'a workable mind, etc.' is stated in reference to the suppression of the hindrances by the power of the gradual discourse. Whatever herein is not analyzed in terms of meaning, that is very easy to understand.

Kūṭadantasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

The Elucidation of the Subtle Meaning in the Commentary on the Kūṭadanta Sutta.

6. Mahālisuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Mahāli Sutta.

Brāhmaṇadūtavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of the Brahmin Emissary.

359. Punappunaṃ [V 1.0298][M 1.0337][P 1.0440] visālībhāvūpagamanatoti pubbe kira puttadhītuvasena dve dve hutvā soḷasakkhattuṃ jātānaṃ licchavīrājakumārānaṃ saparivārānaṃ anukkameneva vaḍḍhantānaṃ nivāsanaṭṭhānārāmuyyānapokkharaṇīādīnaṃ patiṭṭhānassa appahonakatāya nagaraṃ tikkhattuṃ gāvutantarena gāvutantarena parikkhipiṃsu, tenassa punappunaṃ visālībhāvaṃ gatattā “vesālī” tveva nāmaṃ jātaṃ, tena vuttaṃ “punappunaṃ visālībhāvūpagamanato vesālīti laddhanāmake nagare”ti. Sayaṃjātanti sayameva jātaṃ aropimaṃ. Mahantabhāvenevāti rukkhagacchānaṃ, ṭhitokāsassa ca mahantabhāvena, tenāha “himavantena saddhiṃ ekābaddhaṃ hutvā”ti. Kūṭāgārasālāsaṅkhepenāti haṃsavaṭṭakacchannena kūṭāgārasālāniyāmena. Kosalesu jātā, bhavā vā, taṃ vā raṭṭhaṃ nivāso etesanti kosalakā. Evaṃ māgadhakā veditabbā. Yassa akaraṇe puggalo mahājāniyo hoti, taṃ karaṇaṃ arahatīti karaṇīyaṃ tena karaṇīyena, tenāha “avassaṃ kattabbakammenā”ti. Taṃ kiccanti vuccati sati samavāye kātabbato.

359. Because it repeatedly became vast: it is said that formerly, because the Licchavi princes—born sixteen times in pairs of sons and daughters—grew successively along with their retinues, the city was enclosed three times at intervals of a gāvuta, as there was not enough space to establish residences, parks, gardens, ponds, and so on. Thus, because it repeatedly became vast, its name became 'Vesālī.' Therefore it is said: 'in the city named Vesālī because it repeatedly became vast.' Self-arisen means arisen by itself, not planted. Because of its great size means because of the great size of its trees and shrubs, and of the place where it stood. Therefore it is said: 'having become a single continuous stretch with the Himālaya.' By the description 'peaked halls' is meant by the rule for peaked halls covered with curved tiles. Those born in Kosala, or originating there, or for whom that country is their residence, are Kosalans. Similarly, the Māgadhans are to be understood. That which one ought to do, because by not doing it a person incurs a great loss, is what should be done. By that which should be done: hence it is said, 'by a task that must be done.' That is called a 'duty' because it is to be done when the conditions are present.

360. Yā buddhānaṃ uppajjanārahā nānattasaññā, tāsaṃ [P 1.0441] vasena nānārammaṇācārato. Sambhavantasseva paṭisedho. Paṭikkammāti nivattitvā tathā cittaṃ anuppādetvā. Sallīnoti jhānasamāpattiyā ekattārammaṇaṃ allīno.

360. Because of engagement with diverse objects on account of those perceptions of diversity that are fit to arise for Buddhas. It is a negation of it even while it is arising. Turning back means, having withdrawn, not generating a mind like that. Sunk into means immersed in the single object of jhāna attainment.

Oṭṭhaddhalicchavīvatthuvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of Oṭṭhaddha the Licchavi.

361. Addhoṭṭhatāyāti tassa kira uttaroṭṭhaṃ appakatāya tiriyaṃ phāletvā apanītaddhaṃ viya khāyati cattāro dante, dve ca dāṭhā na chādeti, tena naṃ “oṭṭhaddho”ti voharanti. Ayaṃ [V 1.0299] kira upāsako saddho pasanno dāyako dānapati buddhamāmako dhammamāmako saṅghamāmako, tenāha purebhattantiādi.

361. Oṭṭhaddhatāyāti: It is said that his upper lip was naturally such that it appeared as if it had been split sideways and half removed, so that it did not cover four teeth and two canine teeth. Therefore, they called him 'Oṭṭhaddha.' This lay follower, it is said, was faithful, confident, a generous donor, a master of giving, a kinsman of the Buddha, a kinsman of the Dhamma, and a kinsman of the Sangha. Hence it is said: 'before the meal,' and so on.

362. Sāsane [M 1.0338] yuttapayuttoti bhāvanaṃ anuyutto. Sabbattha sīhasamānavuttinopi bhagavato parisāya mahante sati tadajjhāsayānurūpaṃ pavattiyamānāya dhammadesanāya viseso hotīti āha “mahantena ussāhena dhammaṃ desessatī”ti.

362. Sāsane yuttapayuttoti: This means he was devoted to mental cultivation. Although the Blessed One's conduct is like that of a lion in all circumstances, when his assembly is large, there is a special quality in the Dhamma teaching that proceeds in accordance with their dispositions. Thus he said: 'He will teach the Dhamma with great enthusiasm.'

“Vissāsiko”ti vatvā tamassa vissāsikabhāvaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “ayañhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Therassa khīṇā savassasato ālasiyabhāvo “appahīno”ti na vattabbo, vāsanālesaṃ pana upādāyāha “īsakaṃ appahīno viya hotī”ti. Na hi sāvakānaṃ savāsanā kilesā pahīyanti.

Vissāsiko: Having said this, in order to explain his trustworthiness, the passage beginning 'For this one...' was stated. In the case of the elder whose taints are destroyed, it cannot be said that his laziness is 'unabandoned.' However, with reference to a trace of his latent dispositions, it is said: 'it seems as if it is slightly unabandoned.' For the defilements of disciples are not abandoned together with their latent dispositions.

363. Vineyyajanānurodhena buddhānaṃ pāṭihāriyavijambhanaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ “atha kho bhagavā”tiādi, tenevāha “saṃsūcitanikkhamano”ti. Gandhakuṭito nikkhamanavelāyañhi chabbaṇṇā buddharasmiyo āveḷāveḷāyamalāyamalā hutvā savisesā pabhassarā vinicchariṃsu.

363. It is said that the Buddhas' display of miracles occurs in conformity with the people to be trained, as stated in the passage beginning, 'Then the Blessed One…'; therefore it is said: 'he whose departure was indicated.' For at the moment of his departure from the Fragrant Chamber, the six-colored Buddha-rays issued forth, exceptionally radiant, swirling and intertwining.

364. Tato paranti “hiyyo”ti vuttadivasato anantaraṃ paraṃ purimataraṃ atisayena purimattā. Iti imesu dvīsu vavatthito yathākkamaṃ purimapurimatarabhāvo. Evaṃ santepi yadettha “purimatara”nti vuttaṃ, tato pabhuti yaṃ [P 1.0442] yaṃ oraṃ, taṃ taṃ purimaṃ, yaṃ yaṃ paraṃ, taṃ taṃ purimataraṃ, orapārabhāvassa viya purimapurimatarabhāvassa ca apekkhāsiddhito, tenāha “tato paṭṭhāyā”tiādi. Mūladivasato paṭṭhāyātiādidivasato paṭṭhāya. Agganti paṭhamaṃ. Taṃ panettha parā atītā koṭi hotīti āha “parakoṭiṃ katvā”ti. Yaṃ-saddayogena cāyaṃ “viharāmī”ti vattamānappayogo, attho pana atītakālavaseneva veditabbo, tenāha “vihāsinti vuttaṃ hotī”ti. Paṭhamavikappe “viharāmī”ti padassa “yadagge”ti iminā ujukaṃ sambandho dassito, dutiyavikappe pana “tīṇi vassānī”ti imināpi.

364. Tato paraṃ: This means further back than the day called 'yesterday,' that is, even earlier, because of being exceedingly prior. Thus, in these two, the states of 'earlier' and 'even earlier' are established sequentially. Even so, with regard to what is here called 'even earlier,' from that point on, whatever is on this side is 'earlier,' and whatever is on the further side is 'even earlier,' because the state of being earlier and even earlier is established by relation, just like the state of being on this side and the further side. Therefore it is said: 'starting from that,' and so on. 'Starting from the root day' means starting from the first day. Aggaṃ means the first. Here, this is the remote past limit, so it is said: 'having made it the remote limit.' Although 'viharāmi' (I dwell) is a present tense usage due to its connection with the relative pronoun 'yaṃ,' its meaning should be understood as being in the past tense. Therefore it is said: 'it means "vihāsiṃ" (I dwelt).' In the first alternative interpretation, a direct connection of the word 'viharāmi' with 'yadagge' (since when) is shown; in the second alternative, however, it is also connected with 'tīṇi vassāni' (three years).

Piyajātikānīti iṭṭhasabhāvāni. Sātajātikānīti madhurasabhāvāni. Madhuraṃ viyāti hi “madhura”nti vuccati manoramaṃ yaṃ kiñci. Kāmūpasañhitānīti ārammaṇaṃ karontena kāmena upasaṃhitāni, kāmanīyānīti attho, tenāha “kāmassādayuttānī”ti, kāmassādassa yuttāni yogyānīti attho. Sarīrasaṇṭhāneti sarīrabimbe, ādhāre cetaṃ bhummaṃ. Tasmā saddenāti [M 1.0339] taṃ nissāya [V 1.0300] tato uppannena saddenāti attho. Madhurenāti iṭṭhena. Ettāvatāti dibbasotañāṇassa parikammākathanamattena. “Attanā ñātampi na katheti, kimassa sāsane adhiṭṭhānenā”ti kujjhanto āghātaṃ bandhitvā saha kujjhaneneva jhānābhiññāhi parihāyi. Cintesīti “kasmā nu kho mayhaṃ taṃ parikammaṃ na kathesī”ti parivitakkento ayoniso ummujjanavasena cintesi. Anukkamenāti pāthikasutte āgatanayena [P 1.0443] taṃ taṃ ayuttameva cintento, bhāsanto, karonto ca anukkamena. Bhagavati baddhāghātatāya sāsane patiṭṭhaṃ alabhanto gihibhāvaṃ patvā.

Piyajātikāni means of an agreeable nature. Sātajātikāni means of a sweet nature. For whatever is delightful is called 'madhura' (sweet), as in 'madhuraṃ viya' (like something sweet). Kāmūpasañhitāni means connected with sensual desire, which takes them as its object; the meaning is 'desirable.' Hence it is said, 'connected with the taste of sensual pleasure,' which means suitable for the taste of sensual pleasure. Sarīrasaṇṭhāne means in the bodily image; this is a locative of location. Tasmā saddena means by the sound that arose from that, depending on that. Madhurena means agreeable. Ettāvatā means merely by the talk about the preliminary practice for the knowledge of the divine ear. Becoming angry and conceiving hatred, thinking, 'He does not speak of what he himself knows! What is the point of his resolve in this dispensation?,' he fell away from his jhānas and supernormal knowledges along with his anger. Cintesi: he reflected by way of unmethodical emergence, pondering, 'Why indeed did he not tell me that preliminary practice?' Anukkamena: in due course, in the way that has come down in the Pāṭhika Sutta, thinking, speaking, and doing what was improper. Because he had conceived hatred toward the Blessed One, he did not gain a footing in the dispensation and reverted to the lay life.

Ekaṃsabhāvitasamādhivaṇṇanā

Exposition on Concentration Developed in One Aspect

366-371. Ekaṃsāyāti tadattheyeva catutthī, tasmā ekaṃsatthanti attho. Aṃsa-saddo cettha koṭṭhāsapariyāyo, so ca adhikārato dibbarūpadassanadibbasaddassavanavasena veditabboti āha “ekakoṭṭhāsāyā”tiādi. Anudisāyāti puratthimadakkhiṇādibhedāya catubbidhāya anudisāya. Ubhayakoṭṭhāsāyāti dibbarūpadassanatthāya, dibbasaddassavanatthāya ca. Bhāvitoti yathā dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ, dibbasotañāṇañca samadhigataṃ hoti, evaṃ bhāvito. Tayidaṃ visuṃ visuṃ parikammakaraṇena ijjhantīsu vattabbaṃ natthi, ekajjhaṃ ijjhantīsupi kameneva kiccasiddhi ekajjhaṃ kiccasiddhiyā asambhavato. Pāḷiyampi ekassa ubhayasamatthatāsandassanatthameva “dibbānañca rūpānaṃ dassanāya, dibbānañca saddānaṃ savanāyā”ti vuttaṃ, na ekajjhaṃ kiccasiddhisambhavato. “Ekaṃsabhāvito samādhihetū”ti iminā sunakkhatto dibbacakkhuñāṇāya eva parikammassa katattā vijjamānampi dibbasaddaṃ nāssossīti dasseti. Apaṇṇakanti avirajjhanakaṃ, anavajjanti vā attho.

366-371. Ekaṃsāya: This is the dative case meaning 'for the sake of that'; therefore, the meaning is 'for the sake of one aspect.' Here the word aṃsa is a synonym for 'portion,' and this should be understood in context as referring to the seeing of divine forms and the hearing of divine sounds. Thus it is said: 'for one portion,' and so on. Anudisāya refers to the fourfold subordinate directions distinguished as east, south, etc. Ubhayakoṭṭhāsāya means for the sake of both portions: for the sake of seeing divine forms and for the sake of hearing divine sounds. Bhāvito means developed in such a way that the knowledge of the divine eye and the knowledge of the divine ear are attained. Regarding this, it goes without saying that they succeed when the preliminary practice is done for each separately. Even when they succeed together, the accomplishment of the task is sequential, since simultaneous accomplishment of the task is impossible. Even in the Pāḷi text, it is said, 'for the seeing of divine forms and for the hearing of divine sounds,' only to show one person's capability in both respects, not because simultaneous accomplishment of the task is possible. By the phrase 'concentration is a cause when developed in one aspect,' it is shown that because Sunakkhatta had done the preliminary practice only for the knowledge of the divine eye, he did not hear the divine sound even though it was present. Apaṇṇakaṃ means 'unfailing' or 'faultless'.

372. “Samādhi eva” bhāvetabbaṭṭhena samādhibhāvanā. “Dibbasotañāṇaṃ seṭṭha”nti maññamānenāpi mahālinā dibbacakkhuñāṇampi tena saha gahetvā “etāsaṃ nūna bhante”tiādinā pucchitanti “ubhayaṃsabhāvitānaṃ samādhīnanti attho”ti vuttaṃ. Bāhirā [P 1.0444] etā samādhibhāvanā aniyyānikattā. Tā hi ito bāhirakānampi ijjhanti. Na ajjhattikā bhagavato sāmukkaṃsikabhāvena [M 1.0340] appaveditattā. Yadatthanti yesaṃ atthāya. Teti te ariyaphaladhamme. Te hi sacchikātabbāti.

372. Samādhibhāvanā (development of concentration) is so called because concentration itself is what is to be developed. Even though Mahāli thought, 'The knowledge of the divine ear is supreme,' he also included the knowledge of the divine eye and asked, 'Of these, venerable sir…,' etc. Thus it is said that the meaning is 'of concentrations developed in both aspects.' These developments of concentration are external because they are not emancipating. For they are successfully cultivated even by those outside this dispensation. They are not internal because they were not taught by the Blessed One as his own special teaching. Yadatthanti means 'for the sake of which things.' Teti means those things, the noble fruits. For they are to be realized.

Catuariyaphalavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Four Noble Fruits

373. Tasmāti [V 1.0301] vaṭṭadukkhe saṃyojanato. “Maggasotaṃ āpanno”ti phalaṭṭhassa vasena vuttaṃ. Maggaṭṭho hi maggasotaṃ āpajjati. Tenevāha “sotāpanne”ti, “sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipanne”ti (ma. ni. 3.379) ca. Apatanadhammoti anuppajjana- (ma. ni. 3.379) sabhāvo. Dhammaniyāmenāti maggadhammaniyāmena. Heṭṭhimantato sattamabhavato upari anuppajjanadhammatāya vā niyato. Paraṃ ayanaṃ parāgati.
