373. Therefore: because it is a fetter to the suffering of the round. ‘Having entered the stream of the path’ is said with reference to one who has attained the fruit. For it is one who is on the path who enters the stream of the path. Hence it is said, ‘a stream-enterer,’ and ‘one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry.’ ‘Of a nature not to fall away’ means having the nature of non-arising. ‘By the fixed order of the Dhamma’ means by the fixed order of the path-Dhamma. Or: he is fixed by his nature of not arising again above the seventh existence from the lowest. The further going is the supreme destiny.

Tanuttaṃ nāma pavattiyā mandatā, viraḷatā cāti āha “tanuttā”tiādi. Heṭṭhābhāgiyānanti heṭṭhābhāgassa kāmabhavassapaccayabhāvena hitānaṃ. Opapātikoti upapātiko upapatane sādhukārīti katvā. Vimuccatīti vimutti, cittameva vimutti cetovimuttīti āha “sabbakilesa…pe… adhivacana”nti. Cittasīsena cettha samādhi gahito “cittaṃ [P 1.0445] paññañca bhāvaya”nti. Ādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.23; peṭako. 22; mi. pa. 2.9) viya. Paññāvimuttīti etthāpi eseva nayo, tenāha “paññāva paññāvimuttī”ti. Sāmanti attanāva, aparappaccayenāti attho. Abhiññāti ya-kāralopena niddesoti āha “abhijānitvā”ti.

The term ‘attenuation’ means the weakness and sparseness of occurrence; thus it is said ‘attenuation,’ etc. ‘Pertaining to the lower part’ means those things that are connected by being conditions for the lower part, the realm of sensual existence. ‘Spontaneously arisen’: because he is one who arises spontaneously, one who fares well in arising. ‘Is liberated’ is liberation; liberation of the mind itself is liberation by mind; thus it is said: ‘a designation for freedom from all defilements… etc.’ Here, concentration is taken as the principal meaning of ‘mind,’ as in such passages as: ‘Develop mind and wisdom.’ The same method applies here to ‘liberation by wisdom’; hence it is said, ‘wisdom itself is liberation by wisdom.’ ‘By oneself’ means by one’s own self, that is, not through reliance on another. ‘Through direct knowledge’: this is a statement with the elision of the letter ‘y’; thus it is said, ‘having directly known.’

Ariyaaṭṭhaṅgikamaggavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Noble Eightfold Path

374-5. Ariyasāvako nibbānaṃ, ariyaphalañca paṭipajjati etāyāti paṭipadā, sā ca tassa pubbabhāgo evāti idha “pubbabhāgapaṭipadāyā”ti ariyamaggamāha. “Aṭṭha aṅgāni assā”ti aññapadatthasamāsaṃ akatvā aṭṭhaṅgāni assa santīti aṭṭhaṅgikoti padasiddhi daṭṭhabbā.

374-5. A noble disciple practices by means of this for Nibbāna and the noble fruit; thus it is the path of practice. And since that is its preliminary part, here ‘the preliminary path of practice’ refers to the noble path. The derivation of the word aṭṭhaṅgika should be understood as ‘possessing eight factors,’ without forming it as a relative compound.

Sammā aviparītaṃ yāthāvato catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ paccakkhato dassanasabhāvā sammā dassanalakkhaṇā. Sammadeva nibbānārammaṇe cittassa abhiniropanasabhāvo sammā abhiniropanalakkhaṇo. Caturaṅgasamannāgatā vācā janaṃ saṅgaṇhātīti tabbipakkhaviratisabhāvā sammāvācā bhedakaramicchāvācāpahānena [M 1.0341] jane sampayutte ca pariggaṇhanakiccavatī hotīti sammā pariggahaṇalakkhaṇā. Yathā cīvarakammādiko kammanto ekaṃ kātabbaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, taṃ taṃ kiriyānipphādako vā cetanāsaṅkhāto kammanto hatthapādacalanādikaṃ kiriyaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, evaṃ sāvajjakattabbakiriyāsamuṭṭhāpakamicchākammantappahānena [P 1.0446] sammākammanto niravajjasamuṭṭhāpanakiccavā [V 1.0302] hoti, sampayutte ca samuṭṭhāpento eva pavattatīti sammā samuṭṭhāpanalakkhaṇo sammākammanto. Kāyavācānaṃ, khandhasantānassa ca saṃkilesabhūtamicchājīvappahānena sammā vodāpanalakkhaṇo sammāājīvo. Kosajjapakkhato patituṃ adatvā sampayuttadhammānaṃ paggaṇhanasabhāvoti sammā paggāhalakkhaṇo sammāvāyāmo. Sammadeva upaṭṭhānasabhāvāti sammā upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇā sammāsati. Vikkhepaviddhaṃsanena sammadeva cittassa samādahanasabhāvoti sammā samādhānalakkhaṇo sammāsamādhi.

Right view has the characteristic of right seeing, being of the nature of seeing directly, correctly, and without distortion the four noble truths as they really are. Right intention has the characteristic of right application, being of the nature of rightly applying the mind to Nibbāna as its object. Right speech, which as speech endowed with four factors gathers people together, has the characteristic of right embracing; being of the nature of abstinence from its opposite, it has the function of embracing and uniting people by abandoning divisive wrong speech. Just as work, such as making a robe, originates a task to be done, or as the action called ‘intention’ that accomplishes a particular activity originates the activity of moving hands and feet, so too right action, by abandoning wrong action that originates blameworthy deeds, has the function of originating blameless deeds, and it proceeds by originating associated states; thus right action has the characteristic of right origination. Right livelihood has the characteristic of right purification by abandoning wrong livelihood, which defiles the body, speech, and the continuity of the aggregates. Right effort has the characteristic of right exertion, being of the nature of uplifting associated states and not allowing them to fall into the side of laziness. Right mindfulness has the characteristic of right establishment, being of the nature of right establishment. Right concentration has the characteristic of right composure, being of the nature of rightly composing the mind by destroying distraction.

Attano paccanīkakilesā diṭṭhekaṭṭhā avijjādayo. Passatīti pakāseti kiccapaṭivedhena paṭivijjhati, tenāha “tappaṭicchādaka…pe… asammohato”ti. Teneva hi sammādiṭṭhisaṅkhātena aṅgena tattha paccavekkhaṇā pavattatīti tathevāti attano paccanīkakilesehi saddhinti attho.

One's own opposing defilements—such as ignorance—are on the same footing as the view. ‘It sees’ means it illuminates, it penetrates by penetrating its function; hence it is said, ‘dispelling what conceals it… through non-delusion.’ For it is by that very factor called right view that reflection proceeds there. ‘In just that way’ means together with one’s own opposing defilements.

Kiccatoti pubbabhāgehi dukkhādiñāṇehi kātabbassa kiccassa idha sātisayaṃ nipphattito imasseva vā ñāṇassa dukkhādippakāsanakiccato. Cattāri nāmāni labhati catūsu saccesu kātabbakiccanipphattito. Tīṇi nāmāni labhati kāmasaṅkappādippahānakiccanipphattito. Sikkhāpadavibhaṅge (vibha. 703) “viraticetanā, sabbe sampayuttadhammā ca sikkhāpadānī”ti vuccantīti tattha padhānānaṃ viraticetanānaṃ vasena “viratiyopi [P 1.0447] honti cetanāyopī”ti āha. Musāvādādīhi viramaṇakāle vā viratiyo, subhāsitādivācābhāsanādikāle ca cetanāyo yojetabbā. Maggakkhaṇe viratiyova cetanānaṃ amaggaṅgattā ekassa ñāṇassa dukkhādiñāṇatā viya, ekāya viratiyā musāvādādiviratibhāvo viya ca ekāya cetanāya sammāvācādikiccattayasādhanasabhāvābhāvā sammāvācādibhāvāsiddhito, taṃsiddhiyañca aṅgattayattāsiddhito ca. Sammappadhānasatipaṭṭhānavasenāti [M 1.0342] catusammappadhānacatusatipaṭṭhānabhāvavasena.

‘Because of its function’: because the function to be performed by the preliminary knowledges of suffering, etc., is here accomplished pre-eminently, or because of this very knowledge’s function of illuminating suffering, etc. It obtains four names from accomplishing the functions to be performed in regard to the four truths. It obtains three names from accomplishing the function of abandoning sensual thought and the like. In the Analysis of the Training Rules, it is said: ‘The volition of abstinence and all associated states are training rules.’ Thus, with reference to the predominance of the volitions of abstinence, it is said: ‘They are both abstinences and volitions.’ Or, at the time of abstaining from false speech, etc., they are abstinences; and at the time of speaking well-spoken words, etc., they are volitions that should be applied. At the moment of the path, only the abstinences are path factors, since the positive volitions are not path factors. For unlike one knowledge having the nature of knowing suffering, etc., and one abstinence having the nature of abstaining from false speech, etc., a single volition does not have the nature of accomplishing the threefold function of right speech, etc. Therefore, the state of right speech, etc., is not established by it, and with that not established, the state of being a threefold factor is not established. ‘By way of the right efforts and the foundations of mindfulness’ means by way of being the four right efforts and the four foundations of mindfulness.

Pubbabhāgepi maggakkhaṇepi sammāsamādhiyevāti. Yadipi samādhiupakārakānaṃ abhiniropanānumajjanasampiyāyanabrūhanasantasukhānaṃ vitakkādīnaṃ vasena catūhi jhānehi sammāsamādhi vibhatto, tathāpi vāyāmo viya anuppannākusalānuppādanādicatuvāyāmakiccaṃ, sati viya ca asubhāsukhāniccānattesu kāyādīsu subhādisaññāpahānacatusatikiccaṃ eko samādhi catukkajjhānasamādhikiccaṃ na sādhetīti pubbabhāgepi paṭhamajjhānasamādhi paṭhamajjhānasamādhi eva maggakkhaṇepi, tathā pubbabhāgepi catutthajjhānasamādhi catutthajjhānasamādhi eva maggakkhaṇepīti attho.

Even in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the path, it is right concentration itself. Although right concentration is distinguished by means of the four jhānas according to the aspects of initial application of thought and other factors—such as fixing the mind, inclining it, delighting in it, fostering it, serenity, and happiness—which aid concentration, still, just as effort does not accomplish the fourfold task of preventing unarisen unwholesome states and so on, and just as mindfulness does not accomplish the fourfold task of abandoning perceptions of beauty and so on regarding the unattractive, suffering, impermanent, and non-self aspects of the body and so on, one concentration does not accomplish the task of the fourfold jhāna concentration. Thus, in the preliminary stage, the first jhāna concentration is simply the first jhāna concentration, and at the moment of the path, it is likewise. Similarly, in the preliminary stage, the fourth jhāna concentration is simply the fourth jhāna concentration, and at the moment of the path, it is likewise. This is the meaning.

Tasmāti [V 1.0303] paññāpajjotattā avijjandhakāraṃ vidhamitvā paññāsatthattā kilesacore ghātento. Bahukārattāti yvāyaṃ anādimati saṃsāre iminā kadācipi asamugghāṭitapubbo kilesagaṇo tassa samugghāṭako ariyamaggo[P 1.0448]. Tattha cāyaṃ sammādiṭṭhi pariññābhisamayādivasena pavattiyā pubbaṅgamā hotīti bahukārā, tasmā bahukārattā.

‘Therefore’: because wisdom is a lamp, it dispels the darkness of ignorance; because wisdom is a sword, it destroys the thieves of defilements. ‘Because it is highly beneficial’: this noble path is the uprooter of the mass of defilements that has never before been uprooted in this beginningless cycle of existence. And here, this right view, by way of its arising through full understanding, realization, and so on, is the forerunner. Thus, it is highly beneficial. Therefore, ‘because it is highly beneficial’.

Tassāti sammādiṭṭhiyā. “Bahukāro”ti vatvā taṃ bahukārataṃ upamāya vibhāvetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Ayaṃ” tambakaṃsādimayattā kūṭo. Ayaṃ samasāratāya mahāsāratāya cheko. Evanti yathā heraññikassa cakkhunā disvā kahāpaṇavibhāgajānane karaṇantaraṃ bahukāraṃ yadidaṃ hattho, evaṃ yogāvacarassa paññāya oloketvā dhammavibhāgajānane dhammantaraṃ bahukāraṃ yadidaṃ vitakko vitakketvā tadavabodhato, tasmā sammāsaṅkappo sammādiṭṭhiyā bahukāroti adhippāyo. Dutiyaupamāyaṃ evanti yathā tacchako parena parivattetvā parivattetvā dinnaṃ dabbasambhāraṃ vāsiyā tacchetvā gehakaraṇakamme upaneti, evaṃ yogāvacaro vitakkena lakkhaṇādito vitakketvā dinnadhamme yāthāvato paricchinditvā pariññābhisamayādikamme upanetīti yojanā. Vacībhedassa upakārako vitakko sāvajjānavajjavacībhedanivattanapavattanakarāya sammāvācāyapi upakārako evāti “svāya”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

‘Of it’ refers to right view. Having said ‘of great help,’ its helpfulness is illustrated by the simile beginning with ‘just as.’ ‘This one’ refers to the counterfeit coin, being made of base metals like copper and bronze. ‘This one’ is the genuine coin, being of great value due to its even substance. ‘Thus’—just as for a money-changer, after examining with his eye and discerning the kinds of coins, another instrument, the hand, is of great help for that task, so too for a meditator, after examining with wisdom and discerning divisions of the Dhamma, another mental state, thought, is of great help for understanding it, because one understands after having thought. Therefore, the meaning is that right thought is of great help to right view. In the second simile, ‘thus’—just as a carpenter, turning over and over the given timber and shaping it with an adze, applies it to the work of building a house, so too a meditator, by repeatedly examining the characteristics, etc., of given dhammas with thought, precisely defines them and applies them to the tasks of full understanding, realization, etc. Thought is helpful for distinctions in speech, and it is certainly also helpful for right speech, which causes the turning away from blameworthy speech and the undertaking of blameless speech. Hence, it is said, ‘that one is…’ and so on.

Vacībhedassa [M 1.0343] niyāmikā vācā kāyikakiriyāniyāmakassa kammantassa upakārikā. Tadubhayānantaranti duccaritadvayapahāyakassa sucaritadvayapāripūrihetubhūtassa sammāvācāsammākammantadvayassa anantaraṃ. Idaṃ vīriyanti catubbidhaṃ sammappadhānavīriyaṃ. Indriyasamatādayo samādhissa upakāradhammā. Tabbipariyāyato apakāradhammā [P 1.0449] veditabbā. Gatiyoti nipphattiyo, kiccādisabhāve vā. Samannesitvāti upadhāretvā.

Speech that regulates the distinctions in speech is helpful to the action that regulates bodily activity. ‘Immediately after both of them’ means immediately after the pair of right speech and right action, which is the cause for abandoning the two kinds of misconduct and for fulfilling the two kinds of good conduct. ‘This energy’ is the fourfold right effort. Balance of the faculties and so on are states that are helpful to concentration. Their opposites should be understood as states that are harmful. ‘Courses’ means accomplishments, or the nature of functions and so on. ‘Having investigated’ means having considered.

Dvepabbajitavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of the Two Who Went Forth

376-7. “Kasmā āraddha”nti anusandhikāraṇaṃ pucchitvā taṃ vibhāvetuṃ “ayaṃ kirā”tiādi vuttaṃ, tena ajjhāsayānusandhivasena upari desanā pavattāti dasseti. Tenāti tathāladdhikattā. Assāti licchavīrañño. Desanāyāti saṇhasukhumāyaṃ suññatapaṭisaṃyuttāyaṃ yathādesitadesanāyaṃ. Nādhimuccatīti na saddahati na pasīdati. Tantidhammaṃ nāma kathentoti yesaṃ atthāya dhammo kathīyati, tasmiṃ tesaṃ asatipi maggapaṭivedhe kevalaṃ sāsane tantidhammaṃ katvā kathento. Evarūpassāti sammāsambuddhattā aviparītadhammadesanatāya evaṃpākaṭadhammakāyassa satthu. Yuttaṃ [V 1.0304] nu kho etaṃ assāti assa paṭhamajjhānādisamadhigamena samāhitacittassa kulaputtassa etaṃ “taṃ jīva”ntiādinā ucchedādigāhagahaṇaṃ api nu yuttanti pucchati. Laddhiyā pana jhānādhigamamattena na tāva vivecitattā “tehi yutta”nti vuttaṃ taṃ vādaṃ paṭikkhipitvāti jhānalābhinopi taṃ gahaṇaṃ “ayuttamevā”ti taṃ ucchedavādaṃ sassatavādaṃ vā paṭikkhipitvā. Attamanā ahesunti yasmā khīṇāsavo vigatasammoho tiṇṇavicikiccho, “tasmā tassa tathā vattuṃ na yutta”nti uppannanicchayatāya taṃ mama vacanaṃ sutvā attamanā ahesunti attho. Sopi licchavī rājā te viya sañjātanicchayattā attamano ahosi. Yaṃ panettha atthato avibhattaṃ, taṃ suviññeyyameva.

376-7. Having asked the reason for the connection, 'Why was it begun?', to clarify it, the passage 'this, it is said,' and so forth was spoken, thereby showing that the teaching above proceeds by way of the connection of intention. 'By that' means because of having such a view. 'Of him' means of the Licchavi king. 'In the teaching' means in the gentle, subtle teaching connected with emptiness, the teaching as it was taught. 'He is not convinced' means he does not have faith, he does not have confidence. 'Teaching what is called the traditional Dhamma' means that even if there is no penetration of the path for those for whose benefit the Dhamma is taught, he teaches merely by making the Dhamma a tradition in the Dispensation. 'Of such a one' means of the Teacher, who, being a Perfectly Enlightened One, whose teaching of the Dhamma is not contrary, whose Dhamma-body is thus manifest. 'Is this fitting for him?' asks whether it is fitting for that clansman whose mind is concentrated through the attainment of the first jhāna and so forth to grasp annihilationism and so forth with 'that is the soul' and so on. However, because the view is not yet discriminated by the mere attainment of jhāna, the stated view 'it is fitting for them' is rejected. Even for one who has attained jhāna, such grasping is 'indeed unfitting,' thus rejecting that annihilationist or eternalist view. 'They were pleased' means: having heard my words, they were pleased because the conviction arose in them that 'since he is one whose taints are destroyed, whose delusion is dispelled, who has crossed beyond doubt, therefore it is not fitting for him to speak thus.' That Licchavi king, too, was pleased because his conviction arose in the same way as theirs. Whatever is not explicitly explained here in meaning is nevertheless quite easy to understand.

Mahālisuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

The Clarification of Hidden Meanings in the Explanation of the Mahāli Sutta

7. Jāliyasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Jāliya Sutta

Dvepabbajitavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of the Two Who Went Forth

378. “Ghositena [V 1.0305][M 1.0344][P 1.0450] seṭṭhinā kate ārāme”ti vatvā tattha koyaṃ ghositaseṭṭhi nāma, kathañcānena ārāmo kārito, kathaṃ vā tattha bhagavā vihāsīti taṃ sabbaṃ samudāgamato paṭṭhāya saṅkhepatova dassetuṃ “pubbe kirā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatoti allakapparaṭṭhato. Tadāti tesaṃ taṃ gāmaṃ paviṭṭhadivase. Balavapāyāsanti garutaraṃ bahupāyāsaṃ. Asannihiteti gehato bahi gate. Bhussatīti ravati. Ghosakadevaputtotveva nāmaṃ ahosi saraghosasampattiyā. Veyyattiyenāti paññāveyyattiyena. Ghositaseṭṭhi nāma jāto tāya eva cassa sarasampattiyā ghositanāmatā.

378. Having stated, 'in the monastery built by the merchant Ghosita,' to explain concisely from its origin who this merchant Ghosita was by name, how the monastery was built by him, and how the Blessed One dwelt there, the passage 'formerly, it is said,' and so forth was spoken. Tato means from the country of Allakappa. Tadā means on the day of their entry into that village. Balavapāyāsaṃ means very serious, abundant distress. Asannihite means having gone out from the house. Bhussati means he cries out. His name was indeed Ghosaka, the young deva, due to the excellence of his melodious voice. Veyyattiyena means by proficiency of wisdom. He was born as the merchant named Ghosita, and his name came from that same excellence of voice.

Sarīrasantappanatthanti himavante phalamūlāhāratāya kilantasarīrā loṇambilasevanena tassa santappanatthaṃ pīnanatthaṃ. Tasitāti pipāsitā. Kilantāti parissantakāyā. Te kira taṃ vaṭarukkhaṃ patvā tassa sobhāsampattiṃ disvā mahānubhāvā maññe ettha adhivatthā devatā, “sādhu vatāyaṃ devatā amhākaṃ addhānaparissamaṃ vinodeyyā”ti cintesuṃ, tena vuttaṃ “tattha adhivatthā…pe… nisīdiṃsū”ti. Soti anāthapiṇḍiko gahapati. Bhatakānanti bhatiyā veyyāvaccaṃ karontānaṃ dāsapesakammakarānaṃ. Pakatibhattavetananti pakatiyā dātabbabhattavetanaṃ, tadā uposathikattā [P 1.0451] kammaṃ akarontānampi kammakaraṇadivasena dātabbabhattavetanamevāti attho. Kañcīti kañcipi bhatakaṃ.

`Sarīrasantappanatthaṃ` means for the purpose of satisfying the body: for those whose bodies are weary from eating fruits and roots in the Himalayas, it is for the purpose of satisfying and nourishing it by consuming salt and sour foods. `Tasitā` means thirsty. `Kilantā` means exhausted in body. It is said that they, having reached that banyan tree and seeing its splendid beauty, thought, 'Surely, a deity of great power dwells here. It would be good if this deity could relieve our travel fatigue.' Therefore, it is said, 'There, the deity dwelling... sat down.' `So` means the householder Anāthapiṇḍika. `Bhatakānaṃ` means of those who perform service for wages, such as slaves, servants, and laborers. `Pakatibhattavetanaṃ` means the regular food and wages to be given; even though they did not work on that Uposatha day, the food and wages were to be given as on a working day—this is the meaning. `Kañci` means even a single worker.

Upecca parassa vācāya ārambhanaṃ bādhanaṃ upārambho, dosadassanavasena ghaṭṭananti attho, tenāha “upārambhādhippāyena vādaṃ āropetukāmā hutvā”ti. Vadanti nindanavasena kathenti etenāti hi vādo, doso. Taṃ āropetukāmā, patiṭṭhāpetukāmā hutvāti attho. “Taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīra”nti, idha yaṃ vatthuṃ jīvasaññitaṃ, tadeva sarīrasaññitanti “rūpaṃ attato samanupassatī”ti [V 1.0306] vādaṃ gahetvā vadanti. Rūpañca attānañca [M 1.0345] advayaṃ katvā samanupassanavasena “satto”ti vā bāhirakaparikappitaṃ attānaṃ sandhāya vadanti. Bhijjatīti nirudayavināsavasena vinassati. Tena jīvasarīrānaṃ anaññattānujānanato, sarīrassa ca bhedadassanato. Na hettha yathā bhedavatā sarīrato anaññattā adiṭṭhopi jīvassa bhedo vutto, evaṃ adiṭṭhabhedato anaññattā sarīrassāpi abhedoti sakkā viññātuṃ tassa bhedassa paccakkhasiddhattā, bhūtupādāyarūpavinimuttassa ca sarīrassa abhāvatoti āha “ucchedavādo hotī”ti.

`Upārambho` means approaching another's speech, assailing, or obstructing; that is, attacking by pointing out faults. Therefore, it is said, 'desiring to impose a dispute with the intention of accusing.' `Vādo` is so called because they declare (`vadanti`) or speak in a blaming manner by means of it; it is a fault. Desiring to impose it, desiring to establish it—this is the meaning. 'That life-principle, that body': here, that which is designated as the life-principle, that very thing is designated as the body. They speak having taken up the view 'one regards form as self.' Regarding form and self as non-dual, they speak with reference to the 'being,' or with reference to a self conceived of by outsiders. `Bhijjati` means it perishes through cessation and destruction. This is because of the acceptance of the non-otherness of the life-principle and the body, and because the breaking of the body is seen. Here, it cannot be understood that just as the breaking of the life-principle, though unseen, is spoken of due to its non-otherness from the body which breaks, so too, due to its non-otherness from that which has unseen breaking, the body is also unbreakable. This is because its breaking is directly evident, and because a body devoid of the primary elements and derived matter does not exist. Therefore, it is said, 'it is the annihilationist view.'

“Aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīra”nti aññadeva vatthuṃ jīvasaññitaṃ, aññaṃ vatthuṃ sarīrasaññitanti “rūpavantaṃ attānaṃ samanupassatī”tiādinayappavattaṃ [P 1.0452] vādaṃ gahetvā vadanti. Rūpe bhedassa diṭṭhattā, attani ca tadabhāvato attā niccoti āpannamevāti āha “tumhākaṃ…pe… āpajjatī”ti.

'The life-principle is one thing, the body is another' means one thing is designated as the life-principle, and another thing is designated as the body. They declare this, having taken up the view that proceeds from the method of 'one regards the self as possessing form,' and so forth. Since the breaking of form is seen, and since that is absent in the self, it follows that the self is eternal. Therefore, it is said: 'For you... it follows.'

379-380. Tayidaṃ nesaṃ vañjhāsutassa dīgharassatāparikappanasadisanti katvā ṭhapanīyoyaṃ pañhoti tattha rājanimīlanaṃ katvā satthā upari nesaṃ “tena hāvuso suṇāthā”tiādinā dhammadesanaṃ ārabhīti āha “atha bhagavā”tiādi. Tassā yevāti majjhimāya paṭipadāya.

379-380. This question of theirs is like speculating about the longness or shortness of a barren woman's son; having considered this, the question should be set aside. There, the Teacher, ignoring it, began the Dhamma discourse transcending their question with, 'Therefore, friends, listen,' and so on. Thus it is said, 'Then the Blessed One,' and so forth. `Tassā yeva` means of that very middle path.

Saddhāpabbajitassāti saddhāya pabbajitassa “evamahaṃ ito vaṭṭadukkhato nissarissāmī”ti evaṃ pabbajjaṃ upagatassa tadanurūpañca sīlaṃ pūretvā paṭhamajjhānena samāhitacittassa. Etaṃ vattunti etaṃ kilesavaṭṭaparibuddhidīpanaṃ “taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīra”ntiādikaṃ diṭṭhisaṃkilesanissitaṃ vacanaṃ vattunti attho. Nibbicikiccho na hotīti dhammesu tiṇṇavicikiccho na hoti, tattha tattha āsappanaparisappanavasena pavattatīti attho.

`Saddhāpabbajitassa` means of one who has gone forth out of faith; that is, of one who has undertaken the going forth with the thought, 'Thus I will escape from this suffering of the round of existence,' and having fulfilled the corresponding virtuous conduct, whose mind is concentrated by the first jhāna. `Etaṃ vattuṃ` means to speak this statement, which illuminates the round of defilements, such as 'That is the life-principle, that is the body,' a statement based on the defilement of view—this is the meaning. `Nibbicikiccho na hoti` means he has not crossed over doubt concerning the teachings; that is, he proceeds by wavering and wandering here and there.

Etamevaṃ jānāmīti yena so bhikkhu paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, etaṃ sasampayuttadhammaṃ cittanti evaṃ jānāmi. No ca evaṃ vadāmīti yathā diṭṭhigatikā taṃ dhammajātaṃ sanissayaṃ abhedato gaṇhantā “taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīra”nti vā tadubhayaṃ bhedato gaṇhantā “aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīra”nti vā attano micchāgāhaṃ pavedenti, ahaṃ pana na evaṃ vadāmi tassa dhammassa supariññātattā, tenāha “atha kho”tiādi[P 1.0453]. Bāhirakā yebhuyyena kasiṇajjhānāni [M 1.0346] eva nibbattentīti āha “kasiṇaparikammaṃ bhāvantessā”ti. Yasmā bhāvanānubhāvena jhānādhigamo, bhāvanā ca pathavīkasiṇādisañjānanamukhena hotīti saññāsīsena [V 1.0307] niddisīyati, tasmā āha “saññābalena uppanna”nti. Tenāha – “pathavīkasiṇameko sañjānātī”tiādi. “Na kallaṃ tasseta”nti idaṃ yasmā bhagavatā tattha tattha “atha ca panāhaṃ na vadāmī”ti vuttaṃ, tasmā na vattabbaṃ kiretaṃ kevalinā uttamapurisenāti adhippāyenāha, tena vuttaṃ “maññamānā vadantī”ti. Sesaṃ sabbattha suviññeyyameva.

'I know it thus' means: I know thus that mind with its associated states by which that bhikkhu dwells having attained the first jhāna. 'But I do not speak thus' means: unlike those holding certain views who, grasping that collection of phenomena with its support as indivisible, declare 'That is the life-principle, that is the body,' or, grasping them both as divisible, declare 'The life-principle is one thing, the body is another,' thus proclaiming their own wrong grasp, I, however, do not speak thus, because that phenomenon is well understood by me. Therefore, it is said, 'But then,' and so forth. Outsiders for the most part produce only kasiṇa-jhānas; therefore, it is said, 'for one developing the kasiṇa preliminary practice.' Because the attainment of jhāna comes about through the power of development, and development occurs by way of perceiving the earth-kasiṇa and so forth, it is indicated under the heading of perception. Therefore, it is said, 'arisen through the strength of perception.' Hence it is said, 'One perceives the earth-kasiṇa,' and so forth. Regarding 'It is not fitting for this': since the Blessed One has said here and there, 'And yet I do not say so,' this is said with the intention that this should not be spoken by a perfected one, a supreme person. For that reason it was said, 'thinking, they speak.' The rest is easily understood everywhere.

Jāliyasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

The Clarification of Hidden Meanings in the Explanation of the Jāliya Sutta.

8. Mahāsīhanādasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta

Acelakassapavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of Acela Kassapa

381. Yasmiṃ [V 1.0308][M 1.0347][P 1.0454] raṭṭhe taṃ nagaraṃ, tassa raṭṭhassapi yasmiṃ nagare tadā bhagavā vihāsi, tassa nagarassapi etadeva nāmaṃ, tasmā uruññāyanti uruññājanapade uruññāsaṅkhāte nagareti attho. Ramaṇīyoti manoharabhūmibhāgatāya chāyūdakasampattiyā, janavivittatāya ca manoramo. Nāmanti gottanāmaṃ. Tapanaṃ santapanaṃ kāyassa khedanaṃ tapo, so etassa atthīti tapassī, taṃ tapassiṃ. Yasmā tathābhūto tapaṃ nissito, tapo vā taṃ nissito, tasmā āha “tapanissitaka”nti. Lūkhaṃ vā pharusaṃ sādhusammatācāravirahato napasādanīyaṃ ājīvati vattatīti lūkhājīvī, taṃ lūkhājīviṃ. Muttācārādīti ādi-saddena parato pāḷiyaṃ (dī. ni. 1.397) āgatā hatthāpalekhanādayo saṅgahitā. Uppaṇḍetīti uhasanavasena paribhāsati. Upavadatīti avaññāpubbakaṃ apavadati, tenāha “hīḷeti vambhetī”ti. Dhammassa ca anudhammaṃti ettha dhammo nāma hetu “hetumhi ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā”tiādīsu (vibha. 720) viyāti āha “kāraṇassa anukāraṇa”nti. Kāraṇanti cettha tathāpavattassa saddassa attho adhippeto tassa pavattihetubhāvato. Atthappayutto hi saddappayogo. Anukāraṇanti ca so eva parehi tathā vuccamāno. Parehīti [P 1.0455] “ye te”ti vuttasattehi parehi. Vuttakāraṇenāti yathā tehi vuttaṃ, tathā ce tumhehi na vuttaṃ, evaṃ sati tehi vuttakāraṇena sakāraṇo hutvā tumhākaṃ vādo vā tato paraṃ tassa anuvādo koci appamattakopi viññūhi garahitabbaṃ ṭhānaṃ kāraṇaṃ nāgaccheyya, kimevaṃ nāgacchatīti yojanā. “Idaṃ vuttaṃ hotī”tiādinā tamevatthaṃ saṅkhepato dasseti.

381. In whichever country that city is, and in whichever city of that country the Blessed One then resided, that city too has this very name. Therefore, `Uruññāyaṃ` means in the Uruññā country, in the city called Uruññā. `Ramaṇīya` means delightful due to its charming landscape, abundance of shade and water, and seclusion from people, thus pleasing to the mind. `Nāma` refers to the clan name. `Tapana`, tormenting, is the affliction of the body; this is `tapa`, austerity. One who possesses this is a `tapassī`, an ascetic; to that ascetic. Since such a person relies on austerity, or austerity relies on him, it is said, `tapanissitaka`, 'dependent on austerity.' One who lives (`ājīvati`) or conducts oneself (`vattati`) in a harsh (`lūkha`) or rough (`pharusa`) way, which is not pleasing due to the absence of conduct approved by the good, is a `lūkhājīvī`, a practitioner of harsh living; to that practitioner of harsh living. `Muttācārādi` means: by the word `ādi` (etc.), the practices of unrestrained conduct, such as licking the hands, etc., which are mentioned later in the Pāli text (Dīgha Nikāya 1.397), are included. `Uppaṇḍeti` means one derides or mocks. `Upavadati` means one disparages with contempt; hence it is said, 'one scorns or reviles.' Regarding `dhammassa ca anudhammaṃ`: here, `dhamma` means cause, as in passages like 'knowledge in the cause is the analytical knowledge of principles' (Vibhaṅga 720). Thus, it is said, 'the imitation of the cause.' And here, by `kāraṇa` (cause), the meaning of the word so used is intended, because it is the cause of its usage. For the use of a word is connected with a meaning. And `anukāraṇa` is that very thing being spoken of in a similar way by others. `Parehi` means by others, that is, by the beings mentioned as 'those who.' `Vuttakāraṇena` means: if you have not spoken in the same way as they have, this being so, your statement, or any subsequent restatement of it, should not, on account of the reason stated by them, arrive at any ground for blame by the wise, not even the slightest. How could it be otherwise? This is the connection. By 'This is what is meant,' and so on, he briefly shows this very meaning.

382. Idāni yaṃ vibhajjavādaṃ sandhāya bhagavatā “na me te vuttavādino”ti saṅkhepato vatvā taṃ vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “idhāhaṃ kassapā”tiādi vuttaṃ, taṃ vibhāgena dassento “idhekacco”tiādimāha[V 1.0309]. Bhagavā [M 1.0348] hi niratthakaṃ anupasamasaṃvattanikaṃ kāyakilamathaṃ “attakilamathānuyogo dukkho anariyo anatthasaṃhito”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 3.1081; mahāva. 13; paṭi. ma. 2.30) garahati. Sātthakaṃ pana upasamasaṃvattanikaṃ “āraññiko hoti, paṃsukūliko hotī”tiādinā vaṇṇeti. Appapuññatāyāti apuññatāya. Tīṇi duccaritāni pūretvāti micchādiṭṭhibhāvato kammaphalaṃ paṭikkhipanto “natthi dinna”ntiādinā (dī. ni. 1.171; ma. ni. 1.445; 2.94, 95, 225; 3.91, 115; saṃ. ni. 3.210; dha. sa. 1221; vibha. 938) micchādiṭṭhiṃ purakkhatvā tathā tathā tīṇi duccaritāni pūretvā. Anesanavasenāti kohaññe ṭhatvā asantaguṇasambhāvanicchāya micchājīvavasena. Ime dveti “appapuñño puññavā”ti ca vutte duccaritakārino dve puggale sandhāya.

382. Now, with reference to the analytical doctrine, the Blessed One briefly stated, 'They are not expressing my view.' In order to show this in detail, he then said, 'Here, Kassapa,' etc. The commentator, presenting this in detail, now says, 'Here, a certain person,' etc. For the Blessed One condemns bodily mortification that is meaningless and does not lead to peace, saying, 'The pursuit of self-mortification is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial,' etc. (Saṃ. Ni. 3.1081; Mahāva. 13; Paṭi. Ma. 2.30). However, he praises that which is meaningful and conducive to peace, saying, 'He is a forest-dweller, a rag-robe wearer,' etc. 'Appapuññatāya' means 'due to lack of merit.' 'Having fulfilled the threefold misconduct' means, due to holding wrong view, rejecting the results of actions by saying, 'There is no giving,' etc. (Dī. Ni. 1.171; Ma. Ni. 1.445; 2.94, 95, 225; 3.91, 115; Saṃ. Ni. 3.210; Dha. Sa. 1221; Vibha. 938), and having prioritized wrong view, he thus fulfills the threefold misconduct. 'By way of improper seeking' means, being established in deceitfulness, with the desire to be esteemed for qualities one does not possess, through wrong livelihood. 'These two' refers to the two persons who engage in misconduct, mentioned when it is said, 'the one of little merit and the one of merit.'

“Ime [P 1.0456] dve sandhāyā”ti ettha pana dutiyanaye “appapuñño, puññavā”ti ca vutte sucaritakārinoti ādinā yojetabbaṃ. Kammakiriyavādino hi ime dve puggalā. Iti paṭhamadutiyanayesu vuttanayeneva tatiyacatutthanayesu yojanā veditabbā.

'These two are referred to': Here, in the second interpretation, when 'one of little merit, one of merit' is stated, it should be connected with 'one who performs good conduct,' etc. For these two individuals are proponents of the efficacy of action. Thus, the connection in the third and fourth interpretations should be understood in the same way as has been explained for the first and second interpretations.

Bāhirakācārayutto titthiyācārayutto, na vimuttācāro. Attānaṃ sukhetvāti adhammikena sukhena attānaṃ sukhetvā, tenāha “duccaritāni pūretvā”ti. “Na dāni mayā sadiso atthī”tiādinā tissannaṃ maññanānaṃ vasena duccaritapūraṇamāha. Micchādiṭṭhivasenāti “natthi kāmesu doso”ti evaṃ pavattamicchādiṭṭhivasena. Paribbājikāyāti pabbajjaṃ upagatāya tāpasadārikāya. Daharāyāti taruṇāya. Mudukāyāti sukhumālāya. Lomasāyāti tanutambalomatāya appalomāya. Kāmesūti vatthukāmesu. Pātabyatanti paribhuñjitabbaṃ, pātabyatanti vā paribhuñjanakataṃ. Āpajjantoti upagacchanto. Paribhogattho hi ayaṃ pā-saddo, kattusādhano ca tabba-saddo, yathāruci paribhuñjantoti attho. Kilesakāmopi hi assādiyamāno vatthukāmantogadhoyeva.

Associated with external conduct, associated with sectarian conduct, not with liberated conduct. 'Having pleased oneself' means having pleased oneself with unrighteous pleasure; hence it is said, 'having fulfilled misconduct.' Through the threefold conceit, 'Now there is none like me,' etc., he speaks of fulfilling misconduct. 'Through wrong view' means through the wrong view that arises as 'there is no fault in sensual pleasures.' 'With a female wanderer' means with a female ascetic who has undertaken the wandering life, a female recluse. 'Young' means youthful. 'Tender' means delicate. 'Lomasā' (hairy) means with fine, reddish body hair, having little hair. 'In sensual pleasures' means in the objects of sensual desire. 'Pātabya' (to be partaken of) means 'to be enjoyed,' or 'that which is made to be enjoyed.' 'Āpajjanto' (indulging) means 'approaching.' For this 'pā-' prefix is in the sense of enjoyment, and the '-tabba' suffix indicates the agent; the meaning is 'enjoying as one pleases.' Indeed, even the defilement of desire, being savored, is entirely included within the objects of sensual pleasure.

Idanti yathāvuttaṃ atthappabhedaṃ vibhajjanaṃ. Titthiyavasena āgataṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ tathā vibhattattā. Sāsanepīti imasmiṃ sāsanepi.

'This' means the classification, the division of meaning, as has been stated. It is presented in accordance with the sectarians because it is classified as such in the commentary. 'Even in the Dispensation' means 'even in this Dispensation.'

Arahattaṃ [M 1.0349] vā attani asantaṃ “atthī”ti vippaṭijānitvā. Sāmantajappanaṃ, paccayapaṭisevanaṃ, iriyāpathanissitanti imāni tīṇi vā kuhanavatthūni. Tādiso [P 1.0457] vāti dhutaṅga- (mi. pa. 4.2; visuddhi. 1.22) [V 1.0310] samādānavasena lūkhājīvī eva. Dullabhasukho bhavissāmi duggatīsu upapattiyāti adhippāyo.

Or having falsely claimed that arahantship, which is non-existent in oneself, 'exists.' Or, the three grounds for deceit: flattery, the use of requisites, and dependence on bodily postures. 'Such a one' means one who indeed lives a coarse life by way of undertaking ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) (Mi. Pa. 4.2; Visuddhi. 1.22). The intention is: 'By being reborn in miserable states, I will be one for whom happiness is difficult to obtain.'

383. Asukaṭṭhānatoti asukabhavato. Āgatāti nibbattanavasena idhāgatā. Idāni gantabbaṭṭhānanti āyatiṃ nibbattanaṭṭhānaṃ. Puna upapattinti āyatiṃ anantarabhavato tatiyaṃ upapattiṃ, puna upapattīti punappunaṃ nibbatti. Kena kāraṇenāti yathābhūtaṃ ajānanto hi icchādosavasena yaṃ kiñci garaheyya, ahaṃ pana yathābhūtaṃ jānanto sabbaṃ taṃ kena kāraṇena garahissāmi, taṃ kāraṇaṃ natthīti adhippāyo, tenāha “garahitabbamevā”tiādi. Tamatthanti garahitabbasseva garahaṇaṃ, pasaṃsitabbassa ca pasaṃsanaṃ.

383. 'From some state' means 'from some existence.' 'Have come' means 'have come here by way of being born.' 'Now the place to go' means 'the future place of rebirth.' 'Again rebirth' means the third rebirth after the immediately following future existence; 'again rebirth' means repeated birth. 'For what reason?': The intention is: 'Not knowing things as they really are, one might blame anything out of desire and hatred. But I, knowing things as they really are, for what reason would I blame all that? There is no such reason.' Hence it is said, 'only what is blameworthy should be blamed,' etc. 'That purpose' means blaming only what is blameworthy and praising what is praiseworthy.

Na koci “na sādhū”ti vadati diṭṭhadhammikassa, samparāyikassa ca atthassa sādhanavaseneva pavattiyā bhaddakattā. Pañcavidhaṃ veranti pāṇātipātādipañcavidhaṃ veraṃ. Tañhi pañcavidhassa sīlassa paṭisattubhāvato, sattānaṃ verahetutāya ca “vera”nti vuccati. Tato eva taṃ na koci “sādhū”ti vadati, tathā diṭṭhadhammikādiatthānaṃ asādhanato, sattānaṃ sādhubhāvassa ca dūsanato. Na nirundhitabbanti rūpaggahaṇe na nivāretabbaṃ. Dassanīyadassanattho hi cakkhupaṭilābhoti tesaṃ adhippāyo. Yadaggena tesaṃ pañcadvāre asaṃvaro sādhu[P 1.0458], tadaggena tattha saṃvaro na sādhūti āha “puna yaṃ te ekaccanti pañcadvāre saṃvara”nti.

No one says 'it is not good,' because it is excellent in that it proceeds by way of accomplishing benefit in this very life and in the life to come. 'Five kinds of enmity' means the five kinds of enmity beginning with the destruction of life. For it is called 'enmity' because it is the adversary of the fivefold virtue and because it is a cause of enmity for beings. Therefore, no one says 'it is good,' because it does not accomplish benefits in this very life, etc., and because it corrupts the good state of beings. 'Should not be obstructed' means it should not be prevented in the grasping of forms. For their intention is that the purpose of obtaining the eye is to see what is beautiful. To the extent that non-restraint at the five doors is good for them, to that same extent restraint there is not good—thus he said: 'but again, what some say... restraint at the five doors.'

Atha vā yaṃ te ekaccaṃ vadanti “sādhū”ti te “eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā”ti vuttā titthiyā yaṃ attakilamathānuyogādiṃ “sādhū”ti vadanti, mayaṃ taṃ na “sādhū”ti vadāma. Yaṃ te ekaccaṃ vadanti “na sādhū”ti yaṃ pana te anavajjapaccayaparibhogaṃ, sunivatthasupārupanādisammāpaṭipattiñca “na sādhū”ti vadanti, taṃ mayaṃ “sādhū”ti vadāmāti evaṃ pettha attho veditabbo.

Alternatively, what some—those sectarians called 'some ascetics and brahmins'—say is 'good,' namely, self-mortification and such, we do not say is 'good.' But what some say is 'not good,' namely, the blameless use of the requisites and proper conduct, such as being well-clothed and well-covered, that we say is 'good.' Thus, the meaning here should be understood.

Evaṃ [M 1.0350] yaṃ paravādamūlakaṃ catukkaṃ dassitaṃ, tadeva puna sakavādamūlakaṃ katvā dassitanti pakāsento “eva”ntiādimāha. Yañhi kiñci kenaci samānaṃ, tenapi taṃ samānameva, tathā asamānaṃ pīti. Samānāsamānatanti samānāsamānatāmattaṃ. Anavasesato hi pahātabbānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānaṃ sakavāde dissati, na paravāde. Tathā paripuṇṇameva ca upasampādetabbadhammānaṃ upasampādanaṃ sakavāde, na paravāde. Tena vuttaṃ “tyāha”ntiādi.

Thus, clarifying that the fourfold set rooted in the doctrines of others, which has been shown, is now shown again having been made rooted in one's own doctrine, he says 'Thus,' and so on. For whatever is similar for someone is indeed similar for them, and likewise what is dissimilar. 'Similarity and dissimilarity' means merely the state of being similar and dissimilar. For in one's own doctrine, the complete abandonment of things that should be abandoned is seen, not in the doctrine of others. Likewise, the full attainment of things that should be attained is in one's own doctrine, not in the doctrine of others. Therefore, it is said, 'Thus I…,' and so on.

Samanuyuñjāpanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Instigating Inquiry

385. Laddhiṃ [V 1.0311] pucchantoti “kiṃ samaṇo gotamo saṃkilesadhamme anavasesaṃ pahāya vattati, udāhu pare gaṇācariyā. Ettha tāva attano laddhiṃ vadā”ti laddhiṃ pucchanto. Kāraṇaṃ pucchantoti “samaṇo gotamo saṃkilesadhamme anavasesaṃ pahāya vattatī”ti vutte “kena kāraṇena evamatthaṃ gāhayā”ti kāraṇaṃ pucchanto. Ubhayaṃ pucchantoti “idaṃ nāmettha kāraṇa”nti kāraṇaṃ vatvā paṭiññāte atthe sādhiyamāne anvayato, byatirekato ca kāraṇaṃ samatthetuṃ sadisāsadisabhedaṃ upamodāharaṇadvayaṃ pucchanto, ubhayaṃ pucchanto kāraṇassa ca tilakkhaṇasampattiyā yathāpaṭiññāte atthe sādhite [P 1.0459] sammadeva anupacchā bhāsanto nigamento samanubhāsati nāma. Upasaṃharitvāti upanetvā. “Kiṃ te”tiādi upasaṃharaṇākāradassanaṃ. Dutiyapadeti “saṅghena vā saṅgha”nti imasmiṃ pade.

385. 'Asking about one's view' means asking: 'Does the ascetic Gotama live having completely abandoned defiling qualities, or do other teachers of sects? Here, first, state your own view.' 'Asking for the reason' means, when it is said, 'The ascetic Gotama lives having completely abandoned defiling qualities,' asking: 'For what reason do you maintain this?' 'Asking both' means: having stated the reason as, 'This here is the reason,' and while the admitted point is being established, asking for a pair of examples with similes, divided into similar and dissimilar, in order to support the reason through positive and negative concomitance. When the point has been established as admitted by means of the reason possessing its three characteristics, one who then speaks rightly and without concealment is said to be 'following up with a conclusion.' 'Having brought it forward' means having introduced it. 'What is it to you?' etc., shows the manner of bringing it forward. 'In the second phrase' refers to this phrase: 'by the Sangha or the Sangha.'

Tamatthanti taṃ pahātabbadhammānaṃ anavasesaṃ pahāya vattanasaṅkhātañca samādātabbadhammānaṃ anavasesaṃ samādāya vattanasaṅkhātañca atthaṃ. Yojetvāti akusalādipadehi yojetvā. Akosallasambhūtaṭṭhena akusalā ceva tatoyeva akusalāti ca saṅkhaṃ gatāti saṅkhātā tattha purimapadena ekantākusale vadati, dutiyapadena taṃsahagate, taṃpakkhiye ca, tenāha “koṭṭhāsaṃ vā katvā ṭhapitā”ti, akusalapakkhiyabhāvena vavatthāpitāti attho. Avajjaṭṭho dosaṭṭho gārayhapariyāyattāti āha “sāvajjāti sadosā”ti. Ariyā nāma niddosā, ime pana katthacipi niddosā na hontīti niddosaṭṭhena ariyā bhavituṃ nālaṃ asamatthā.

“That meaning” refers to the meaning designated as living, having completely abandoned what should be abandoned, and the meaning designated as living, having fully adopted what should be adopted. “Having applied” means having connected with terms such as “unwholesome.” Because of their nature of arising from unskillfulness, they are unwholesome, and are thus reckoned as unwholesome. Here, the first term speaks of what is entirely unwholesome, the second term of what is associated with it and belonging to its faction. Therefore, it is said, “or having made a portion and set it aside,” meaning they are distinguished by being on the side of the unwholesome. The meaning of 'blameworthy' is 'faulty,' as it is a synonym for 'censurable.' Therefore, it is said, 'blameworthy means with faults.' The noble ones are indeed faultless, but these are not faultless in any way; thus, they are incapable of being noble in the sense of being faultless.

386-392. Yanti [M 1.0351] kāraṇe etaṃ paccattavacananti āha “yena viññū”ti. Yaṃ vā panāti “yaṃ pana kiñcī”ti asambhāvanavacanametanti āha “yaṃ vā taṃ vā appamattaka”nti. Gaṇācariyā pūraṇādayo. Satthuppabhavattā saṅghassa saṅghasampattiyāpi satthusampatti vibhāvīyatīti āha “saṅghapasaṃsāyapi satthuyeva pasaṃsāsiddhito”ti. Sā pana pasaṃsā pasādahetukāti pasādamukhena taṃ dassetuṃ “pasīdamānāpi hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha pi-saddena yathā anvayato pasaṃsā samuccīyati, evaṃ satthuvippaṭipattiyā sāvakesu, sāvakavippaṭipattiyā ca satthari appasādo samuccīyatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sarīrasampattinti rūpasampattiṃ, rūpakāyapāripūrinti attho. Bhavanti vattāro rūpappamāṇā[P 1.0460], ghosadhammappamāṇā ca. Puna bhavanti vattāroti dhammappamāṇavaseneva yojetabbaṃ. Yā saṅghassa pasaṃsāti ānetvā sambandho.

386-392. Regarding 'Yanti kāraṇe,' this is a statement in the agentive sense, so he says 'yena viññū.' Regarding 'Yaṃ vā pana,' this is an expression of improbability, so he says 'yaṃ vā taṃ vā appamattaka,' meaning 'whatever little there may be.' Gaṇācariyā are teachers of sects, such as Pūraṇa and others. Because the Sangha has the Teacher as its origin, the Teacher's attainment is also revealed through the Sangha's attainment, so he says, 'because even through praise of the Sangha, the Teacher's praise alone is established.' That praise, however, is a cause for confidence. To show this through the aspect of confidence, it is said, 'pasīdamānāpi hī,' etc. There, the particle 'pi' should be seen as indicating that just as praise accumulates according to connection, so too does lack of confidence accumulate in the disciples due to the Teacher's misconduct, and in the Teacher due to the disciples' misconduct. 'Physical excellence' means excellence of form, that is, the perfection of the physical body. There are speakers who are measured by their appearance, and by their voice and Dhamma. Again, 'there are speakers' should be connected only in terms of the measure of the Dhamma. Bringing in 'the Sangha's praise' establishes the connection.

Tattha [V 1.0312] yā buddhānaṃ, buddhasāvakānaṃyeva ca pāsaṃsatā, aññesañca tadabhāvo jotito, taṃ viratippahānasaṃvaruddesavasena nīharitvā dassetuṃ “ayamadhippāyo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha setughātavirati nāma ariyamaggavirati. Vipassanāmattavasenāti “anicca”nti vā “dukkha”nti vā vividhaṃ dassanamattavasena, na pana nāmarūpavavatthānapaccayapariggaṇhanapubbakaṃ lakkhaṇattayaṃ āropetvā saṅkhārānaṃ sammasanavasena. Itarānīti samucchedapaṭippassaddhinissaraṇappahānāni. “Sesa”nti pañcasīlato añño sabbo sīlasaṃvaro, “khamo hotī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.24; 3.159; a. ni. 4.114) vutto suparisuddho khantisaṃvaro, “paññāyete pidhiyyare”ti (su. ni. 1041; cūḷani. 60) evaṃ vutto kilesānaṃ samucchedako maggañāṇasaṅkhāto ñāṇasaṃvaro, manacchaṭṭhānaṃ indriyānaṃ pidahanavasena pavatto parisuddho indriyasaṃvaro, “anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāyā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.402; ma. ni. 1.135; saṃ. ni. 5.8; vibha. 205) vutto sammappadhānasaṅkhāto vīriyasaṃvaroti imaṃ saṃvarapañcakaṃ sandhāyāha. Pañca kho panime pātimokkhuddesātiādi sāsane sīlassa bahubhāvaṃ dassetvā tadekadese eva paresaṃ avaṭṭhānadassanatthaṃ [P 1.0461] yathāvuttasīlasaṃvarasseva puna gahaṇaṃ.

Here, the praiseworthiness of the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas, and the absence of that in others, is illuminated. To show this, having extracted it by way of the headings of abstinence, abandonment, and restraint, it is said, “This is the intention,” and so on. Here, “abstinence from breaking the bridge” means the abstinence of the Noble Path. “Through mere insight” means through merely various perceptions such as “impermanent” or “suffering,” but not through the contemplation of formations by attributing the three characteristics after having determined name-and-form and grasped their conditions. “The others” are abandonment through eradication, tranquillization, and escape. “The rest” means all other restraints of virtue beyond the five precepts, such as the supremely purified restraint of patience as stated in “he is capable of endurance,” and so on. The restraint of wisdom, described as “these are barred by wisdom,” refers to the knowledge of the path that eradicates defilements. The pure restraint of the senses arises through the barring of the six sense faculties. The restraint of effort, described as “for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states,” and so on, refers to the four right exertions. This fivefold restraint is referred to here. “These five are the recitation of the Pātimokkha,” and so on, is stated to show the abundance of virtue in the Dispensation, while also reiterating the aforementioned restraint of virtue to clarify that it abides in just one part for others.

Ariyaaṭṭhaṅgikamaggavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Noble Eightfold Path

393. Sīhanādanti [M 1.0352] seṭṭhanādaṃ, abhītanādaṃ kenaci appaṭivattiyanādanti attho. “Ayaṃ yathāvutto mama vādo aviparīto, tassa aviparītabhāvo imaṃ maggaṃ paṭipajjitvā aparappaccayato jānitabbo”ti evaṃ aviparītabhāvāvabodhanatthaṃ. “Atthi kassapā”tiādīsu yaṃ maggaṃ paṭipanno samaṇo gotamo vadanto yuttapattakāle, tathabhāvato bhūtaṃ, ekaṃsato hitāvihabhāvena atthaṃ, dhammato anapetattā dhammaṃ, vinayayogato paresaṃ vinayanato ca vinayaṃ vadatīti sāmaṃyeva attapaccakkhatova jānissati, so mayā sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedito sakalavaṭṭadukkhanissaraṇabhūto atthi kassapa maggo, tassa ca adhigamūpāyabhūtā pubbabhāgapaṭipadāti ayamettha yojanā. Tena “samaṇo gotamo ime dhamme”tiādinayappavatto vādo kenaci asaṃkampiyo yathābhūtasīhanādoti dasseti.

393. ‘Lion’s roar’ means the supreme roar, the fearless roar, the roar that cannot be turned back by anyone. “This statement of mine, as declared, is not contrary; its quality of being not contrary is to be known by practicing this path, without reliance on another.” Thus, it is for the purpose of making known its quality of being not contrary. In passages such as “There is, Kassapa,” this is the connection: The path exists, Kassapa, which one will know for oneself through direct experience—the path which the ascetic Gotama, having entered upon it, speaks of at the proper time; which is true because it is so; which has meaning because it is solely beneficial; which is Dhamma because it does not deviate from the Dhamma; and which is Vinaya because of its connection to discipline and because it disciplines others. That path, which I myself have made known after realizing it through direct knowledge, is the escape from all the suffering of the round, and there is the preliminary practice which is the means for its attainment. Thus, he shows that the statement proceeding in the manner of “The ascetic Gotama teaches these Dhammas,” etc., is a true lion’s roar, unshakable by anyone.

“Evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya passatī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.134) viya maggañca paṭipadañca ekato katvā dassento. “Ayamevā”ti vacanaṃ maggassa puthubhāvapaṭikkhepanatthaṃ, sabbaariyasādhāraṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ, sāsane pākaṭabhāvadassanatthañca. Tenāha “ekāyano [V 1.0313] ayaṃ bhikkhave maggo”ti, (dī. ni. 2.373; ma. ni. 1.106; saṃ. ni. 5.367, 384, 409)“eseva maggo natthañño dassanassa visuddhiyā”ti (dha. pa. 274),

“Thus, one sees this as it truly is with right wisdom,” and so on, showing the path and the practice together. The statement “This alone” is to reject the multiplicity of paths, to show its being common to all noble ones, and to show its being manifest in the Dispensation. Therefore, it is said: “This, monks, is the one way,” “This is the path; there is no other for purity of vision.”

“Ekāyanaṃ jātikhayantadassī,

Maggaṃ pajānāti hitānukampī;

Etena maggena tariṃsu pubbe,

Tarissanti ye ca taranti ogha”nti. (saṃ. ni. 5.384, 409; mahāni. 191; cūḷani. 107, 121; netti. 170);

“The seer of the end of birth, compassionate for their welfare, knows the single path; by this path they crossed in former times, and those who cross, and who will cross the flood.”

Sabbesu [P 1.0462] suttapadesesu abhidhammapadesesu ca ekovāyaṃ maggo pākaṭo paññāto āgato cāti.

In all the passages of the Suttas and the passages of the Abhidhamma, this one path alone is manifest, known, and has come down.

Tapopakkamakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Discourse on Ascetic Striving

394. Tapoyeva upakkamitabbato ārabhitabbato tapopakkamoti āha “tapārambhā”ti. Ārambhanañcettha karaṇamevāti āha “tapokammānīti [M 1.0353] attho”ti. Samaṇakammasaṅkhātāti samaṇehi kattabbakammasaññitā. Niccoloti nissaṭṭhacelo sabbena sabbaṃ paṭikkhittacelo. Naggiyavatasamādānena naggo. “Ṭhitakova uccāraṃ karotī”tiādi nidassanamattaṃ, vamitvā mukhavikkhālanādiācārassapi tena vissaṭṭhattā. Jivhāya hatthaṃ apalikhati apalihati udakena adhovanato. Dutiyavikappepi eseva nayo. “Ehi bhaddante”ti vutte upagamanasaṅkhāto vidhi ehibhaddanto, taṃ caratīti ehibhaddantiko, tappaṭikkhepena na ehibhaddantiko. Na karoti samaṇena nāma parassa vacanakarena na bhavitabbanti adhippāyena. Puretaranti taṃ ṭhānaṃ attano upagamanato puretaraṃ. Taṃ kira so “bhikkhunā nāma yādicchakī eva bhikkhā gahetabbā”ti adhippāyena na gaṇhāti. Uddissakataṃ “mama nimittabhāvena bahū khuddakā pāṇā saṅghātaṃ āpāditā”ti na gaṇhāti. Nimantanaṃ na sādiyati “evaṃ tesaṃ vacanaṃ kataṃ bhavissatī”ti. Kumbhīādīsupi so sattasaññīti āha “kumbhīkaḷopiyo”tiādi.

394. It is called ‘tapopakkama’ because it is to be approached as austerity and to be commenced as austerity; hence it is said, ‘tapārambhā’. Here, commencement is indeed action; hence it is said, ‘the meaning is “actions of austerity”’. ‘Designated as the duty of an ascetic’ means it is known as the duty to be performed by ascetics. ‘Niccolo’ means one who has discarded robes, one who has completely rejected robes in every way. By undertaking the vow of nakedness, he is naked. “He defecates while standing,” and so on, is merely an illustration, as even the practice of rinsing the mouth after vomiting is abandoned by him. He licks his hand with his tongue, since he does not wash it with water. The same principle applies in the second alternative. When told, “Come, venerable sir,” the procedure designated as ‘coming’ is ‘ehibhaddanto’; he who practices this is ‘ehibhaddantiko’; by rejecting it, he is not an ‘ehibhaddantiko’. He does not do it, with the intention that an ascetic should not be one who acts on another’s word. ‘Puretaraṃ’ means that which is at a place prior to his own arrival. It is said that he does not accept it, thinking, “A monk should accept only such alms as are spontaneously offered.” He does not accept what is specially prepared, thinking, “On my account, many small creatures have been brought to destruction.” He does not consent to an invitation, thinking, “In that way, their word will have been done.” Even in pots and the like, he perceives beings; hence it is said, ‘kumbhīkaḷopiyo’ and so on.

Kabaḷantarāyoti kabaḷassa antarāyo hotīti. Gāmasabhāgādivasena saṅgamma kittenti etissāti saṅkitti, tathā saṃhaṭataṇḍulādisañcayo. Manussāti veyyāvaccakaramanussā.

‘Kabaḷantarāyo’ means there is an obstacle to a morsel. ‘Saṅkitti’ is that which is proclaimed by gathering in village assemblies and the like; similarly, it is an accumulation of collected rice and so on. ‘Manussā’ means humans who perform services.

Surāpānamevāti [V 1.0314] majjalakkhaṇappattāya surāya pānameva surāggahaṇena cettha merayampi saṅgahitaṃ. Ekāgārameva [P 1.0463] uñchatīti ekāgāriko. Ekālopeneva vattatīti ekālopiko. Dīyati etāyāti datti, dvattiālopamattagāhi khuddakaṃ bhikkhādānabhājanaṃ, tenāha “khuddakapātī”ti. Abhuñjanavasena eko aho etassa atthīti ekāhiko, āhāro. Taṃ ekāhikaṃ, so pana atthato ekadivasalaṅghakoti āha “ekadivasantarika”nti. “Dvīhika”ntiādīsupi eseva nayo. Ekāhaṃ abhuñjitvā ekāhaṃ bhuñjanaṃ ekāhavāro, taṃ ekāhikameva atthato. Dvīhaṃ abhuñjitvā dvīhaṃ bhuñjanaṃ dvīhavāro. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo. Ukkaṭṭho pana pariyāyabhattabhojaniko dvīhaṃ abhuñjitvā ekāhameva bhuñjati. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo.

‘Surāpānameva’ means only the drinking of intoxicants that have reached the characteristic of intoxication; and here, by the term ‘surā,’ fermented liquor is also included. ‘Ekāgāriko’ is one who gleans from a single house. ‘Ekālopiko’ is one who subsists on a single mouthful. ‘Datti’ is that by which something is given; it is a small alms-receiving vessel that holds a measure of two or three mouthfuls, hence it is called ‘khuddakapātī’ (a small bowl). ‘Ekāhiko’ means having one day of not eating, with reference to food. That is ‘ekāhikaṃ,’ but in meaning, it is one who skips a day; hence it is said, ‘ekadivasantarika’ (with a one-day interval). The same principle applies to ‘dvīhika’ and so on. A one-day turn is not eating for one day and then eating, which in meaning is ‘ekāhikaṃ’. A two-day turn is not eating for two days and then eating. The same principle applies to the remaining two. But the strict practitioner of eating by turns, not eating for two days, eats on only one day. The same principle applies to the remaining two.

395. Kuṇḍakanti tanutaraṃ taṇḍulasakalaṃ.

395. ‘Kuṇḍaka’ means a very small rice fragment.

396. Saṇehi [M 1.0354] saṇavākehi nibbattavatthāni sāṇāni. Missasāṇāni masāṇāni, na bhaṅgāni. Erakatiṇādīnīti ādi-saddena akkamakacikadalīvākādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Erakādīhi katāni hi chavāni lāmakāni dussānīti vattabbataṃ labhanti.

396. Cloths produced from hemp plants and hemp fibers are called ‘sāṇāni’. Mixed hemp cloths are ‘masāṇāni’, not ‘bhaṅgāni’. In ‘eraka grass, etc.,’ the word ‘etc.’ includes materials like akkama, kacikadalī bark, and vāka bark. Indeed, garments made from eraka and the like obtain the designation of being wretched and inferior cloths.

Micchāvāyāmavaseneva ukkuṭikavatānuyogoti āha “ukkuṭikavīriyaṃ anuyutto”ti. Thaṇḍilanti vā samā pakatibhūmi vuccati “patthaṇḍile pāturahosī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 4.10) viya, tasmā thaṇḍilaseyyanti anantarahitāya pakatibhūmiyaṃ seyyanti vuttaṃ hoti. Laddhaṃ āsananti nisīdituṃ yathāladdhaṃ āsanaṃ. Akopetvāti aññattha anupagantvā, tenāha “tattheva nisīdanasīlo”ti. So hi taṃ achaḍḍento apariccajanto akopento nāma hoti. Vikaṭanti gūthaṃ vuccati āsayavasena virūpaṃ jātanti katvā.

The practice of the crouching vow is due to wrong effort; hence it is said, ‘devoted to the exertion of crouching’. ‘Thaṇḍila’ refers to level, natural ground, as in “appeared on the level ground” (MN 4.10) and so on; therefore, ‘lying on a thaṇḍila’ means lying on the bare natural ground without anything intervening. ‘Obtained seat’ means whatever seat has been obtained for sitting. ‘Akopetvā’ (without disturbing) means not going elsewhere; hence it is said, ‘one who is in the habit of sitting in that very place’. For one who does not discard it and does not abandon it is called one who is ‘not disturbing’ it. ‘Vikaṭa’ means excrement; it is so called because it has become repulsive due to its place of origin.

Ettha ca “acelako hotī”tiādīni vatapadāni yāva “na [P 1.0464] thusodakaṃ pivatī”ti etāni ekavārāni. “Ekāgāriko vā”tiādīni nānāvārāni, nānākālikāni vā. Tathā “sākabhakkho vā”tiādīni, “sāṇānipi dhāretī”tiādīni ca. Tathā hettha vā-saddaggahaṇaṃ, pi-saddaggahaṇañca kataṃ. Pi-saddopi vikappattho eva daṭṭhabbo. Purimesu pana na kataṃ. Evañca katvā “acelako hotī”ti vatvā “sāṇānipi dhāretī”tiādi vacanassa, “rajojalladharo hotī”ti vatvā “udakorohanānuyogaṃ anuyutto”ti vacanassa ca avirodho siddho hoti. Atha vā kimettha avirodhacintāya. Ummattakapacchisadiso hi titthiyavādo. Atha [V 1.0315] vā “acelako hotī”ti ārabhitvā tappasaṅgena sabbampi attakilamathānuyogaṃ dassentena “sāṇānipi dhāretī”tiādi vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here, the vow-phrases such as “he is a naked ascetic” up to “he does not drink sour gruel” are a single set. The phrases like “or he is one who gleans from a single house” and so on are various sets, or pertain to different times. Similarly, the phrases like “or he is a vegetable-eater” and “he also wears hemp robes” and so on. Thus, here the word ‘vā’ (or) and the word ‘pi’ (also) are included. The word ‘pi’ should also be understood as having the meaning of an alternative. In the former phrases, however, this was not done. This being so, the non-contradiction is established between saying “he is a naked ascetic” and then stating “he also wears hemp robes,” and between saying “he is a bearer of dust and dirt” and then stating “he is devoted to the practice of descending into water.” Alternatively, what is the point of considering non-contradiction here? For the doctrine of the sectarians is like a madman’s basket. Or else, it should be understood that, beginning with “he is a naked ascetic,” in connection with that, “he also wears hemp robes” and so on was said to show the entire practice of self-mortification.

Tapopakkamaniratthakathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Futility of Ascetic Practices

397. Sīlasampadādīhi vināti sīlasampadā, samādhisampadā, paññāsampadāti imāhi lokuttarāhi sampadāhi vinā na kadāci sāmaññaṃ vā brahmaññaṃ vā sambhavati, yasmā ca tadevaṃ, tasmā tesaṃ tapopakkamānaṃ niratthakataṃ dassentoti yojanā. “Dosaveravirahita”nti idaṃ dosassa [M 1.0355] mettāya ujupaṭipakkhatāya vuttaṃ. Dosa-ggahaṇena vā sabbepi jhānapaṭipakkhā saṃkilesadhammā gahitā, vera-ggahaṇena paccatthikabhūtā sattā. Yadaggena hi dosarahitaṃ, tadaggena verarahitanti.

397. ‘Without the accomplishment of virtue, etc.’ means: without the accomplishment of virtue, the accomplishment of concentration, and the accomplishment of wisdom—these supramundane accomplishments—neither recluseship nor brahminhood ever arises. And since this is so, the connection is therefore made thus: ‘to show the fruitlessness of their ascetic practices’. ‘Free from ill will and enmity’: this is said because loving-kindness is the direct opposite of ill will. By the term ‘ill will,’ all defiling states opposed to jhāna are included; by the term ‘enmity,’ beings who are hostile are included. For to the extent that one is without ill will, to that extent one is without enmity.

398. Pākaṭabhāvena kāyati gametīti pakati, lokasiddhavādo, tenāha “pakati kho esāti pakatikathā esā”ti. Mattāyāti mattā-saddo “mattā sukhapariccāgā”tiādīsu [P 1.0465] (dha. pa. 290) viya appatthaṃ antonītaṃ katvā pamāṇavācakoti āha “iminā pamāṇena evaṃ parittakenā”ti. Tena pana pamāṇena pahātabbo pakaraṇappatto paṭipattikkamoti āha “paṭipattikkamenā”ti. Sabbatthāti sabbavāresu.

398. ‘Pakati’ is so called from the etymology that it proclaims or leads to a manifest state; it is a worldly convention. Hence it is said, “Indeed, this is nature; this is a talk of nature.” The word ‘mattā,’ as in “a measure of the relinquishing of pleasure” (Dhp. 290) and the like, denotes measure while implicitly containing the meaning of ‘a little’; hence it is said, “by this measure, by such a small amount.” But by that measure, the progressive course of practice relevant to the context is to be abandoned; hence it is said, ‘paṭipattikkamena’. ‘Sabbatthā’ means in all instances.

399. Aññathā vadathāti yadi acelakabhāvādinā sāmaññaṃ vā brahmaññaṃ vā abhavissa, suvijānova samaṇo suvijāno brāhmaṇo. Yasmā pana tumhe ito aññathāva sāmaññaṃ brahmaññañca vadatha, tasmā dujjānova samaṇo dujjāno brāhmaṇo, tenāha “idaṃ sandhāyāhā”ti. Taṃ pakativādaṃ paṭikkhipitvāti pubbe yaṃ pākatikaṃ sāmaññaṃ brahmaññañca hadaye ṭhapetvā tena “dukkara”ntiādi vuttaṃ, tameva sandhāya bhagavatāpi “pakati kho esā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Idha pana taṃ pakativādaṃ pākatikasamaṇabrāhmaṇavisayaṃ kathaṃ paṭikkhipitvā paṭisaṃharitvā sabhāvatova paramatthatova samaṇassa brāhmaṇassa ca dujjānabhāvaṃ āvikaronto pakāsento. Tatrāpīti samaṇabrāhmaṇavādepi vuttanayeneva.

399. ‘If you speak otherwise’ means: if recluseship or brahminhood existed through nakedness and so on, a recluse would be easy to know, a brahmin would be easy to know. But since you speak of recluseship and brahminhood otherwise than this, therefore a recluse is hard to know, a brahmin is hard to know. Hence it is said, “This was said with reference to this.” ‘Having rejected that doctrine of nature’ means: previously, having kept in mind that natural recluseship and brahminhood, it was said by him, “difficult,” etc. With reference to that very thing, the Blessed One also said, “This is indeed nature,” etc. But here, having rejected and withdrawn that doctrine of nature—the discourse concerning natural recluses and brahmins—he reveals and makes manifest that a recluse and a brahmin are hard to know, both in their intrinsic nature and in the ultimate sense. ‘Even there’ means: even in the discourse on recluses and brahmins, it is by the method already stated.

Sīlasamādhipaññāsampadāvaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Accomplishment of Virtue, Concentration, and Wisdom

400-1. Paṇḍitoti hetusampattisiddhena paṇḍiccena samannāgato, kathaṃ uggahesi paripakkañāṇattā [V 1.0316] ghaṭe padīpena viya abbhantare samujjalantena paññāveyyattiyena tattha tattha bhagavatā desitamatthaṃ pariggaṇhanto tampi desanaṃ upadhāresi. Tassa cāti yo acelako hoti yāva udakorohanānuyogaṃ anuyutto viharati, tassa ca. Tā sampattiyo pucchāmi, yāhi samaṇo ca hotīti adhippāyo. Sīlasampadāyāti iti-saddo ādiattho, tena “cittasampadāya paññāsampadāyā”ti padadvayaṃ [M 1.0356] saṅgaṇhāti asekkhasīlādikhandhattayasaṅgahitañhi arahattaṃ, tenāha “arahattaphalameva sandhāya vutta”ntiādi. Tattha idanti idaṃ vacanaṃ.

400–401. “Paṇḍita” means one endowed with wisdom, perfected by the attainment of causes. How does he grasp it? Through mature knowledge, like a lamp illuminating a pot from within, through the clarity of wisdom, he comprehends the meaning taught by the Blessed One in various places and attends to that teaching as well. “Tassa ca” refers to one who is a naked ascetic, engaged even in the practice of immersion in water. The intention is: “I ask about those accomplishments by which one becomes a recluse.” The word “sīlasampadāya” (by the accomplishment of virtue)—the word “iti” here has the meaning of “etcetera,” thereby including the two terms “cittasampadāya” (accomplishment of mind) and “paññāsampadāya” (accomplishment of wisdom), for arahantship is indeed comprised of the three aggregates beginning with consummate virtue. Therefore, it is said, “the fruit of arahantship itself is what is meant,” and so forth. Here, “this” refers to this statement.

Sīhanādakathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Lion's Roar Discourse

402. Anaññasādhāraṇatāya[P 1.0466], anaññasādhāraṇatthavisayatāya ca anuttaraṃ buddhasīhanādaṃ nadanto. Ativiya accantavisuddhatāya paramavisuddhaṃ. Paramanti ukkaṭṭhaṃ, tenāha “uttama”nti. Sīlameva lokiyasīlattā. Yathā anaññasādhāraṇaṃ bhagavato lokuttarasīlaṃ savāsanaṃ paṭipakkhaviddhaṃsanato, evaṃ lokiyasīlampi tassa anucchavikabhāvena sambhūtattā, samena samanti samasamanti ayamettha atthoti āha “mama sīlasamena sīlena mayā sama”nti. “Yadidaṃ adhisīla”nti lokiyaṃ, lokuttarañcāti duvidhampi buddhasīlaṃ ekajjhaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Tenāha “sīlepī”ti. Iti imanti evaṃ imaṃ sīlavisayaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ pavattattā paṭhamaṃ.

402. By its being unique and by its having a unique scope of meaning, he roars the unsurpassed lion’s roar of the Buddha. Due to its exceedingly and utterly pure nature, it is supremely pure. “Paramam” means excellent; therefore, it is said “supreme.” It is virtue itself, because it is worldly virtue. Just as the Blessed One’s supramundane virtue is unique, destroying opponents together with their latent tendencies, so too is his mundane virtue, because it has arisen in a manner befitting him. The meaning here of “samena sama” (equal with equal) is: “equal with me through virtue equal to my virtue.” “That which is higher virtue” is spoken having brought together the two kinds of Buddha’s virtue, both mundane and supramundane. Therefore, it is said, “even in virtue.” Thus, this is the scope of virtue. Because it arose first, it is first.

Tapatīti santappati, vidhamatīti attho. Jigucchatīti hīḷeti lāmakato ṭhapeti. Niddosattā ariyā ārakā kilesehīti. Maggaphalasampayuttā vīriyasaṅkhātā tapojigucchāti ānetvā sambandho. Paramā nāma sabbukkaṭṭhabhāvato. Yathā yuvino bhāvo yobbanaṃ, evaṃ jigucchino bhāvo jegucchaṃ. Kilesānaṃ samucchindanapaṭippassambhanāni samucchedapaṭipassaddhivimuttiyo. Nissaraṇavimutti nibbānaṃ. Atha vā sammāvācādīnaṃ adhisīlaggahaṇena, sammāvāyāmassa adhijegucchaggahaṇena, sammādiṭṭhiyā adhipaññāggahaṇena gahitattā aggahitaggahaṇena sammāsaṅkappasatisamādhayo maggaphalapariyāpannā samucchedapaṭipassaddhivimuttiyo daṭṭhabbā. Nissaraṇavimutti pana nibbānameva.

It burns, meaning it torments; the meaning is it dispels. It feels disgust, meaning it scorns and considers it base. Because they are faultless, the noble ones are distant from defilements. The connection is to be made by taking asceticism and disgust to be effort associated with the path and fruition. “Supreme” means the state of being the most excellent. Just as the state of the young is youth, so the state of one who feels disgust is ‘jegucchaṃ’. The eradication and tranquilization of defilements are the liberations of eradication and tranquilization. The liberation of escape is Nibbāna. Or, because right speech, etc., are grasped through higher virtue, right effort is grasped through higher disgust, and right view is grasped through higher wisdom, right intention, mindfulness, and concentration, being included within the path and fruition, should be seen as the liberations of eradication and tranquilization, by the grasping of what is not yet grasped. The liberation of escape, however, is simply Nibbāna.

403. Yaṃ kiñci janavivittaṃ ṭhānaṃ idha “suññāgāra”nti adhippetaṃ. Tattha nadantena vinā nādo natthīti āha “ekatova nisīditvā”ti. Aṭṭhasu parisāsūti khattiyaparisā, brāhmaṇaparisā, gahapatiparisā, samaṇaparisā, cātumahārājikaparisā, tāvatiṃsaparisā, māraparisā, brahmaparisāti [P 1.0467] imāsu aṭṭhasu parisāsu.

403. Any secluded place here is considered an “empty dwelling.” There, because there is no sound apart from the one roaring, it is said, “sitting alone.” The eight assemblies are: the assembly of nobles, the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, the assembly of recluses, the assembly of the Four Great Kings, the assembly of the Thirty-Three Gods, the assembly of Māra, and the assembly of Brahmā.

Vesārajjānīti [V 1.0317][M 1.0357] visāradabhāvā ñāṇappahānasampadānimittaṃ kutoci asantassanabhāvā nibbhayabhāvāti attho. Āsabhaṃ ṭhānanti seṭṭhaṃ ṭhānaṃ, uttamaṃ ṭhānanti attho. Āsabhā vā pubbabuddhā, tesaṃ ṭhānanti attho.

“Confidences” means the state of being confident, the sign of the accomplishment of knowledge and abandonment, the state of not trembling from any quarter, and the state of fearlessness. “The supreme position” means the excellent position, the highest position. Or, “āsabhā” are the former Buddhas, the meaning is their position.

Apica usabhassa idanti āsabhaṃ, āsabhaṃ viyāti āsabhaṃ. Yathā hi nisabhasaṅkhāto usabho attano usabhabalena catūhi pādehi pathaviṃ uppīḷetvā acalaṭṭhānena tiṭṭhati, evaṃ tathāgatopi dasahi tathāgatabalehi samannāgato catūhi vesārajjapādehi aṭṭhaparisāpathaviṃ uppīḷetvā sadevake loke kenaci paccatthikena akampiyo acalena ṭhānena tiṭṭhati. Evaṃ tiṭṭhamānova taṃ āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti upagacchati na paccakkhāti attani āropeti. Tena vuttaṃ “āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānātī”ti.

Moreover, 'āsabha' means 'belonging to a bull' (usabha), or 'like a bull'. Just as a bull, known as 'nisabha', stands in an unshakeable position, pressing down the earth with its four legs by its bull-strength, so too the Tathāgata, endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, stands in an unshakeable position, unshaken by any opponent in the world with its devas, pressing down the earth of the eight assemblies with his fourfold confidences. Thus standing, he acknowledges that supreme position, approaches it, does not reject it, and attributes it to himself. Therefore, it is said, “He acknowledges the supreme position.”

Sīhanādaṃ nadatīti yathā migarājā parissayānaṃ sahanato, vanamahiṃsamattavāraṇādīnaṃ hananato ca “sīho”ti vuccati, evaṃ tathāgato lokadhammānaṃ sahanato, parappavādānaṃ hananato ca “sīho”ti vuccati. Evaṃ vuttassa sīhassa nādaṃ sīhanādaṃ. Tattha yathā sīho sīhabalena samannāgato sabbattha visārado vigatalomahaṃso sīhanādaṃ nadati, evaṃ tathāgatasīhopi dasahi tathāgatabalehi samannāgato aṭṭhasu parisāsu visārado vigatalomahaṃso “iti rūpa”ntiādinā (saṃ. ni. 3.78; a. ni. 8.2) nayena nānāvilāsasampannaṃ sīhanādaṃ nadati.

“He roars the lion’s roar.” Just as the king of beasts is called a “lion” because of enduring perils and destroying wild buffaloes, intoxicated elephants, and other creatures, so too the Tathāgata is called a “lion” because of enduring worldly conditions and destroying the doctrines of others. The roar of such a lion is called the lion’s roar. There, just as a lion, endowed with a lion’s strength, confident everywhere, and without hair standing on end, roars the lion’s roar, so too the Tathāgata, the lion, endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, confident and without hair standing on end in the eight assemblies, roars the lion’s roar endowed with various modes of expression in the manner of “Such is form,” and so on (SN 22.59; AN 8.2).

Pañhaṃ abhisaṅkharitvāti ñātuṃ icchitamatthaṃ attano ñāṇabalānurūpaṃ abhiracitvā taṅkhaṇaṃyevāti pucchitakkhaṇeyeva [P 1.0468] ṭhānuppattikapaṭibhānena vissajjeti. Cittaṃ paritosetiyeva ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ vissajjanato. Sotabbañcassa maññanti aṭṭhakkhaṇavajjitena navamena khaṇena labbhamānattā. “Yaṃ no satthā bhāsati, taṃ no sossāmā”ti ādaragāravajātā mahantena ussāhena sotabbaṃ sampaṭicchitabbaṃ maññanti. Suppasannā pasādābhibuddhiyā vigatupakkilesatāya kallacittā muducittā honti. Pasannakāranti pasannehi kātabbasakkāraṃ, dhammāmisapūjanti attho. Tattha āmisapūjaṃ dassento “paṇītānī”tiādimāha. Dhammapūjā pana “tathattāyā”ti iminā dassitā. Tathābhāvāyāti yathattāya yassa vaṭṭadukkhanissaraṇatthāya [M 1.0358] dhammo desito, tathābhāvāya, tenāha “dhammānudhammapaṭipattipūraṇatthāyā”ti. Sā ca dhammānudhammapaṭipatti yāya anupubbiyā paṭipajjitabbā, paṭipajjantānañca sati ajjhattikaṅgasamavāye ekaṃsikā tassā pāripūrīti taṃ anupubbiṃ dassetuṃ “keci saraṇesū”tiādi vuttaṃ.

“Having prepared a question”—that is, having composed a meaning he desired to know, suitable to his own power of knowledge—he answers it immediately at the moment of asking, with spontaneous wisdom arising from the occasion. He satisfies the mind by giving an answer in accordance with the intention. And they think it is worth listening to because it is obtained in the ninth moment, which is free from the eight wrong moments. Thinking, “What the Teacher says, we will listen to,” they consider it worth listening to and worth accepting with great respect and enthusiasm. They become very confident; their minds, purified by the growth of faith and the removal of defilements, become pliable and soft. “An act of honoring by the faithful” means the honor to be done by the faithful; the meaning is the offering of the Dhamma and material gifts. Here, showing the offering of material gifts, he says, “the finest,” and so forth. But the offering of the Dhamma is shown by this phrase, “for the sake of suchness.” “For the sake of suchness” means for the sake of reality, for the sake of that reality for which the Dhamma was taught, for the purpose of escaping the suffering of the cycle. Therefore, he says, “for the fulfillment of practice in accordance with the Dhamma.” That practice in accordance with the Dhamma, by which gradual progression it should be practiced, and for those who practice, if there is a concurrence of internal factors, its fulfillment is certain. To show that gradual progression, it is said, “some go for refuge,” and so forth.

Imasmiṃ [V 1.0318] panokāse ṭhatvāti “paṭipannā ca ārādhentī”ti etasmiṃ sīhanādakiccapāripūridīpane pāḷipadese ṭhatvā. Samodhānetabbāti saṅkalitabbā. Eko sīhanādo asādhāraṇo aññehi appaṭivattiyo seṭṭhanādo abhītanādoti katvā. Esa nayo sesesupi. Purimānaṃ dasannantiādito paṭṭhāya yāva “vimuttiyā mayhaṃ sadiso natthī”ti etesaṃ purimānaṃ dasannaṃ sīhanādānaṃ, niddhāraṇe cettha sāmivacanaṃ, tenāha “ekekassā”ti. “Parisāsu ca nadatī”ti ādayo parivārā “ekaccaṃ tapassiṃ niraye nibbattaṃ passāmī”ti sīhanādaṃ nadanto bhagavā parisāyaṃ nadati visārado nadati yāva “paṭipannā ārādhentī”ti atthayojanāya sambhavato[P 1.0469]. Tathā sesesupi navasu.

Standing in this context, that is, standing in this Pali passage that illuminates the fulfillment of the lion's roar's function, 'those who practice, attain.' It is to be synthesized, that is, reckoned together. One lion's roar is unique, unmatched by others, the supreme roar, the fearless roar; thus, it is understood. This is the method for the rest as well. From 'among the former ten,' beginning with that phrase and going up to 'there is none equal to me in liberation,' concerning these former ten lion's roars, in this determination, the genitive case is used, therefore he said, 'for each one.' 'And roars in assemblies' and so on—the associated passages—'I see a certain ascetic reborn in hell,' the Blessed One, roaring the lion's roar, roars in the assembly, roars confidently, up to 'those who practice, attain'—this is the manner of connecting the meaning. Similarly, for the remaining nine.

“Eva”ntiādi yathāvuttānaṃ tesaṃ saṅkaletvā dassanaṃ. Te dasāti te “parisāsu ca nadatī”ti ādayo sīhanādā. Purimānaṃ dasannanti yathāvuttānaṃ purimānaṃ dasannaṃ. Parivāravasenāti paccekaṃ parivāravasena yojiyamānā sataṃ sīhanādā. Purimā ca dasāti tathā ayojiyamānā purimā ca dasāti evaṃ dasādhikaṃ sīhanādasataṃ hoti. Evaṃ vādīnaṃ vādanti evaṃ pavattavādānaṃ titthiyānaṃ vādaṃ. Paṭisedhetvāti tathābhāvābhāvadassanena paṭikkhipitvā. Yaṃ bhagavā udumbarikasutte “idha nigrodha tapassī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 3.33) upakkilesavibhāgaṃ, pārisuddhivibhāgañca dassento saparisassa nigrodhassa paribbājakassa purato sīhanādaṃ nadi, taṃ dassetuṃ “idāni parisati naditapubbaṃ sīhanādaṃ dassento”tiādi vuttaṃ.

“‘Thus,’ and so on, is the demonstration of those stated by collecting them. ‘Those ten’ are the lion’s roars beginning with ‘and he roars in assemblies.’ ‘The former ten’ are the former ten as previously stated. ‘By way of retinue’ means that when connected individually by way of a retinue, there are a hundred lion’s roars. And the former ten, when not so connected, are ten; thus, there are one hundred and ten lion’s roars. ‘The argument of those who argue thus’ means the argument of the sectarians who hold such prevailing views. ‘Having refuted’ means having rejected by showing the absence of such a state of affairs.
