To illustrate what the Blessed One declared in the Udumbarika Sutta, beginning with ‘Here, Nigrodha the ascetic,’ showing both the division of defilements and the division of purification, he roared a lion’s roar in the presence of Nigrodha the wanderer and his assembly. To show this, it is said, ‘Now, showing the lion’s roar previously roared in an assembly...’ and so on.

Titthiyaparivāsakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse concerning the Probation for Sectarians

404. Idanti “rājagahe gijjhakūṭe pabbate viharantaṃ maṃ…pe… pañhaṃ pucchī”ti idaṃ vacanaṃ. Kāmaṃ yadā nigrodho pañhaṃ pucchi, bhagavā cassa vissajjesi, na tadā [M 1.0359] gijjhakūṭe pabbate viharati, rājagahasamīpe pana viharatīti katvā “rājagahe gijjhakūṭe pabbate viharantaṃ ma”nti vuttaṃ, gijjhakūṭe viharaṇañcassa tadā avicchinnanti, tenāha “yaṃ taṃ bhagavā”tiādi. Yogeti naye, dukkhanissaraṇūpāyeti attho.

404. ‘This’ refers to the statement, ‘When I was dwelling on Vulture’s Peak Mountain in Rājagaha... he asked me a question.’ Although when Nigrodha asked the question and the Blessed One answered him, he was not dwelling on Vulture’s Peak Mountain at that time, but was staying near Rājagaha, it is said, ‘When I was dwelling on Vulture’s Peak Mountain in Rājagaha,’ because his dwelling on Vulture’s Peak was uninterrupted at that time. Hence it is said, ‘That which the Blessed One...’ and so on. ‘Yoga’ means the method, the means of escape from suffering—this is the meaning.

405. Yaṃ parivāsaṃ sāmaṇerabhūmiyaṃ ṭhito parivasatīti yojanā. Yasmā sāmaṇerabhūmiyaṃ ṭhitena parivasitabbaṃ, na gihibhūtena, tasmā aparivasitvāyeva pabbajjaṃ labhati. Ākaṅkhati pabbajjaṃ, ākaṅkhati upasampadanti ettha pana pabbajjā-ggahaṇaṃ vacanasiliṭṭhatāvaseneva “dirattatirattaṃ [P 1.0470][V 1.0319] sahaseyya”nti (pāci. 50) ettha dirattaggahaṇaṃ viya. Gāmappavesanādīnīti ādi-saddena vesiyāvidhavāthullakumāripaṇḍakabhikkhunigocaratā, sabrahmacārīnaṃ uccāvacesu kiṃkaraṇīyesu dakkhānalasāditā, uddesaparipucchādīsu tibbachandatā, yassa titthāyatanato idhāgato, tassa avaṇṇe, ratanattayassa ca vaṇṇe anattamanatā, tadubhayaṃ yathākkamaṃ vaṇṇe ca avaṇṇe ca attamanatāti imesaṃ saṅgaho veditabbo, tenāha “aṭṭha vattāni pūrentenā”ti. Ghaṃsitvā koṭṭetvāti ajjhāsayassa vīmaṃsanavasena suvaṇṇaṃ viya ghaṃsitvā koṭṭetvā.

405. The interpretation is: ‘one who is in the state of a novice undergoes that probation.’ Because probation must be undertaken while in the state of a novice, not as a householder, he therefore obtains the going forth without having undergone probation. In the phrase, ‘If one desires the going forth, if one desires higher ordination,’ the mention of ‘the going forth’ is merely for stylistic elegance, like the mention of ‘two nights’ in ‘he may lie down together for two or three nights’ (Pācittiya 50). By ‘entering the village, etc.,’ the word ‘etc.’ should be understood to include: resorting to prostitutes, widows, mature unmarried women, eunuchs, and nuns; being skillful or lazy in various duties for fellow monastics; having strong desire in recitation and questioning; dissatisfaction with dispraise of the sect from which one came and with praise of the Triple Gem; and conversely, satisfaction with praise of the former and dispraise of the latter. Therefore it is said, ‘by one who fulfills the eight duties.’ ‘Having rubbed and hammered’ means having rubbed and hammered like gold, by way of investigating one’s disposition.

Gaṇamajjhe nisīditvāti upasampadākammassa gaṇappahonakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ majjhe saṅghatthero viya tassa anuggahatthaṃ nisīditvā. Vūpakaṭṭhoti vivitto. Tādisassa sīlavisodhane appamādo avuttasiddhoti āha “kammaṭṭhāne satiṃ avijahanto”ti. Pesitacittoti nibbānaṃ pati pesitacitto taṃninno tappoṇo tappabbhāro. Jātikulaputtāpi ācārasampannā eva arahattādhigamāya pabbajjāpekkhā hontīti tepi tehi ekasaṅgahe karonto āha “kulaputtāti ācārakulaputtā”ti, tenāha “sammadevāti hetunāva kāraṇenevā”ti. “Otiṇṇomhi jātiyā”tiādinā nayena hi saṃvegapubbikaṃ yathānusiṭṭhaṃ pabbajjaṃ sandhāya idha “sammadevā”ti vuttaṃ. Hetunāti ñāyena. Pāpuṇitvāti patvā adhigantvā. Sampādetvāti asekkhā sīlasamādhipaññā nipphādetvā, paripūretvā vāti attho.

‘Sitting in the midst of the assembly’ means sitting for his support among the monks sufficient for the ordination ceremony, like the senior monk of the Sangha. ‘Secluded’ means withdrawn. For such a one, diligence in purifying virtue is implicitly established; thus it is said: ‘not neglecting mindfulness in the meditation subject.’ ‘With a mind directed’ means a mind directed towards Nibbāna, inclined toward it, tending towards it, gravitating towards it. Even sons of good families who are well-behaved seek the going forth for the attainment of arahantship—thus, including them in a single group, he says: ‘sons of good families’ means ‘sons of families with good conduct.’ Therefore, he says: ‘“rightly indeed” means “by reason, by cause.”’ With reference to the going forth according to the teaching, preceded by a sense of urgency, in the manner of ‘I am immersed in birth,’ and so on, it is here said ‘rightly indeed.’ ‘By reason’ means by the proper method. ‘Having reached’ means having attained, having realized. ‘Having accomplished’ means having brought to perfection the virtue, concentration, and wisdom of one beyond training, or having fulfilled them—this is the meaning.

Niṭṭhāpetunti [M 1.0360][P 1.0471] nigamanavasena pariyosāpetuṃ. “Brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ…pe… vihāsī”ti iminā eva hi arahattanikūṭena desanā pariyosāpitā. Taṃ pana nigamento “aññataro kho panā…pe… ahosī”ti vuttaṃ dhammasaṅgāhakehi. Yaṃ panettha atthato na vibhattaṃ, taṃ suviññeyyameva.

‘To conclude’ means to bring to an end by way of a summary. The teaching was indeed concluded by this very peak of arahantship: ‘The culmination of the holy life... he dwelled.’ However, in summarizing, it was said by the compilers of the Dhamma: ‘Now a certain one... became one of the arahants.’ Whatever herein is not distinguished in terms of meaning is indeed easily understood.

Mahāsīhanādasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta.

9. Poṭṭhapādasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta

Poṭṭhapādaparibbājakavatthuvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Story of the Wanderer Poṭṭhapāda

406. Sāvatthiyanti [V 1.0320][M 1.0361][P 1.0472] samīpatthe bhummanti āha “sāvatthiṃ upanissāyā”ti. Jetassa kumārassa vaneti jetena nāma rājakumārena ropite upavane. Nivāsaphāsutādinā pabbajitā āramanti etthāti ārāmo, vihāro. Phoṭo pādesu jātoti poṭṭhapādo. Vatthacchāyāchādanapabbajūpagatattā channaparibbājako. Brāhmaṇamahāsāloti mahāvibhavatāya mahāsāratāpatto brāhmaṇo. Samayanti sāmaññaniddeso, taṃ taṃ samayanti attho. Pavadantīti pakārato vadanti, attanā attanā uggahitaniyāmena yathā tathā samayaṃ vadantīti attho. “Pabhutayo”ti iminā todeyyajāṇusoṇīsoṇadaṇḍādike saṅgaṇhāti, paribbājakādayoti ādi-saddena channaparibbājakādike. Tindukācīramettha atthīti tindukācīro, ārāmo. Tathā ekā sālā etthāti ekasālako, tasmiṃ tindukācīre ekasālake.

406. ‘In Sāvatthī’ is a locative in the sense of proximity; hence it is said: ‘dwelling near Sāvatthī.’ ‘In the grove of Prince Jeta’ means in the park planted by the royal prince named Jeta. An ‘ārāma’ (monastery) is so called because renunciants (pabbajitā) delight (āramanti) in it due to the comfort of dwelling and so on; it is a vihāra (dwelling place). ‘Poṭṭhapāda’ means one with boils (phoṭo) born on his feet (pādesu). A ‘covered wanderer’ (channaparibbājako) is so called because of having undertaken the wandering life with a covering of cloth for shade. A ‘great brahmin householder’ is a brahmin who has attained great substance through great wealth. ‘Doctrine’ (samaya) is a general designation, meaning this or that particular doctrine. ‘They declare’ (pavadanti) means they speak in various ways; that is, they each declare their doctrine in whatever way accords with the principle they have individually grasped. By ‘and others’ (pabhutayo) it includes Todeyya, Jāṇussoṇi, Soṇadaṇḍa, and others. By ‘wanderers and so on,’ the word ‘and so on’ (ādi) includes the covered wanderers and others. ‘Tindukācīra’ is a park where there are tinduka trees. Similarly, ‘ekasālaka’ is a place where there is a single hall; thus, ‘in that Tindukācīra, in the single-halled place.’

Anekākārānavasesañeyyatthavibhāvanato, aparāparuppattito ca bhagavato ñāṇaṃ tattha patthaṭaṃ viya hotīti vuttaṃ “sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ pattharitvā”ti, yato tassa ñāṇajālatā vuccati, veneyyānaṃ tadantogadhatā heṭṭhā vuttāyeva. Veneyyasattapariggaṇhanatthaṃ samannāhāre kate paṭhamaṃ nesaṃ veneyyabhāveneva upaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, atha saraṇagamanādivasena kiccanipphatti vīmaṃsīyatīti āha “kiṃ nu kho bhavissatīti upaparikkhanto”ti[P 1.0473]. Nirodhanti saññānirodhaṃ. Nirodhā vuṭṭhānanti tato nirodhato vuṭṭhānaṃ saññuppattiṃ. Sabbabuddhānaṃ ñāṇena saṃsanditvāti yathā te nirodhaṃ, nirodhato vuṭṭhānañca byākariṃsu, byākarissanti ca, tathā byākaraṇavasena saṃsanditvā. Hatthisāriputtoti hatthisārino putto. “Yugandharapabbataṃ parikkhipitvā”ti idaṃ parikappavacanaṃ “tādisaṃ atthi ce, taṃ viyā”ti. Meghavaṇṇanti rattameghavaṇṇaṃ, sañjhāppabhānurañjitameghasaṅkāsanti attho. Paccagghanti abhinavaṃ ādito tathāladdhavohārena[M 1.0362], anaññaparibhogatāya[V 1.0321], tathā vā satthu adhiṭṭhānena so patto sabbakālaṃ “paccagghaṃ” tveva vuccati, silādivuttaratanalakkhaṇūpapattiyā vā so patto “paccaggha”nti vuccati.

Because the Blessed One’s knowledge illuminates the objects of knowledge in their manifold aspects without remainder, and because it arises in succession, it is as if spread out; hence it is said, ‘having spread out the net of omniscience.’ For this reason his knowledge is called a net, and the inclusion of those to be trained within it has already been stated above. When attention is directed toward gathering in beings to be trained, their trainability first becomes apparent, and then the accomplishment of their task—such as going for refuge—is investigated. Hence it is said, ‘examining what might come to be.’ ‘Cessation’ means the cessation of perception. ‘Emergence from cessation’ means emergence from that cessation, that is, the arising of perception. ‘In harmony with the knowledge of all Buddhas’ means that just as they declared and will declare cessation and emergence from cessation, so too he declared it, thus being in harmony by way of declaration. ‘Hatthisāriputta’ means the son of Hatthisāri. ‘Encircling Mount Yugandhara’ is a hypothetical statement, meaning: ‘if such a thing exists, it is like that.’ ‘Cloud-colored’ means the color of a red cloud, resembling a cloud tinged with the glow of twilight. The term `paccaggha` means new. Because it was designated as such from the start when it was obtained, because it was not used by another, or because of the Master’s determination, that bowl is always called `paccaggha`. Or, because it possesses the characteristics of a superior gem such as sapphire, that bowl is called `paccaggha`.

407. Attano rucivasena saddhammaṭṭhitijjhāsayavasena, na parena ussāhitoti adhippāyo. “Atippagabhāvameva disvā”ti idaṃ bhūtakathanaṃ na tāva bhikkhācāravelā sampattāti dassanatthaṃ. Bhagavā hi tadā kālasseva vihārato nikkhanto “vāsanābhāgiyāya dhammadesanāya poṭṭhapādaṃ anuggaṇhissāmī”ti. Yannūnāhanti aññattha saṃsayaparidīpano, idha pana saṃsayaparidīpano viya. Kasmāti āha “buddhāna”ntiādi. Saṃsayo nāma natthi bodhimūle eva samugghāṭitattā. Parivitakkapubbabhāgoti adhippetakiccassa pubbabhāgaparivitakko eva. Buddhānaṃ labbhatīti “karissāma, na karissāmā”tiādiko esa cittacāro buddhānaṃ labbhati sambhavati vicāraṇavasena pavattanato, na pana saṃsayavasena. Tenāhāti yena buddhānampi labbhati, tenevāha bhagavā “yannūnāha”nti. Parikappane vāyaṃ nipāto. “Upasaṅkameyya”nti [P 1.0474] kiriyāpadena vuccamāno eva hi attho “yannūnā”ti nipātapadena jotīyati. Ahaṃ yannūna upasaṅkameyyanti yojanā. Yadi panāti idampi tena samānatthanti āha “yadi panāhanti attho”ti.

407. The meaning is: not urged on by another, but by his own inclination and by his disposition to establish the good Dhamma. ‘Having seen that it was very early’ is a statement of fact to show that the time for the alms round had not yet arrived. For the Blessed One had left the monastery early in the morning, thinking: ‘I will favor Poṭṭhapāda with a Dhamma talk connected with his dispositions.’ The particle yannūna elsewhere indicates the dispelling of doubt, but here it is as if it dispels doubt. Why? It is said: ‘For the Buddhas…,’ etc. For them, there is no such thing as doubt, as it was eradicated at the very root of enlightenment. The preliminary part of reflection means simply the preliminary reflection on the intended action. It is available to Buddhas means that this mental process—‘Shall I do it or not?’ and so on—is found in Buddhas; it is possible, as it proceeds by way of investigation, not by way of doubt. Therefore it is said: because it is found even in Buddhas, the Blessed One said, ‘What if I…?’ (yannūnāha). This particle is used in the sense of consideration. The meaning expressed by the verb ‘I should approach’ (upasaṅkameyyaṃ) is illuminated by the particle yannūna. The construction is: ‘What if I were to approach?’ ‘But if’ (yadi pana) also has the same meaning as that, thus it is said: ‘the meaning is “but if I…”’

408. Yathā unnatappāyo saddo unnādo, evaṃ vipulabhāvena uparūpari pavattopi unnādoti tadubhayaṃ ekajjhaṃ katvā pāḷiyaṃ “unnādiniyā”ti vatvā puna vibhāgena dassetuṃ “uccāsaddamahāsaddāyā”ti vuttanti tamatthaṃ vivaranto “uccaṃ nadamānāyā”tiādimāha. Assāti parisāya. Uddhaṃgamanavasenāti unnatabahulatāya uggantvā uggantvā pavattanavasena. Disāsu patthaṭavasenāti vipulabhāvena bhūtaparamparāya sabbadisāsu pattharaṇavasena. Idāni paribbājakaparisāya uccāsaddamahāsaddatāya kāraṇaṃ, tassa ca pavattiākāraṃ dassento “tesañhī”tiādimāha. Kāmassādo nāma kāmaguṇassādo. Kāmabhavādigato assādo bhavassādo.

408. Just as a sound that is mostly elevated (unnata) is an uproar (unnādo), so too a sound that occurs again and again with great volume is an uproar. Combining both these meanings, the Pāli text says unnādiniyā (uproarious). Then, to explain this by analysis, it says uccāsaddamahāsaddāya (with loud sounds, great sounds). Elaborating on this meaning, the commentary says: ‘making a loud sound,’ etc. Of it means of the assembly. By way of going upwards means by way of occurring again and again with much elevation. By way of spreading in the directions means by way of spreading in all directions with great volume in a continuous succession. Now, showing the reason for the loud sounds and great sounds of the wanderers’ assembly and the manner of its occurrence, the commentary says: ‘For them…,’ etc. Gratification in sensual pleasures means gratification in the strands of sensual pleasure. Gratification that pertains to the sensual realm of existence and so on is gratification in existence.

409. Saṇṭhapesīti [M 1.0363] saṃyamanavasena sammadeva ṭhapesi, saṇṭhapanañcettha tiracchānakathāya aññamaññasmiṃ agāravassa jahāpanavasena ācārassa sikkhāpanaṃ, yathāvuttadosassa nigūhanañca hotīti āha “sikkhāpesī”tiādi. Appasaddanti nissaddaṃ, uccāsaddamahāsaddābhāvanti adhippāyo. Nappamajjantīti na agāravaṃ karonti.

409. He established them (saṇṭhapesi) means he settled them properly by way of restraint. And here, this establishing consists in training them in proper conduct by having them abandon disrespect for one another concerning lowly talk, and in suppressing the fault already mentioned. Hence it says: ‘He trained them,’ etc. With few sounds means silent; the intention is the absence of loud sounds and great sounds. They are not heedless means they do not show disrespect.

410. No [V 1.0322] āgate ānandoti bhagavati āgate no amhākaṃ ānando pīti hoti. Piyasamudācārāti piyālāpā. “Paccuggamanaṃ akāsī”ti vatvā na kevalamayameva, atha kho aññepi pabbajitā yebhuyyena bhagavato apacitiṃ karontevāti dassetuṃ “bhagavantañhī”tiādiṃ vatvā, tattha kāraṇamāha “uccākulīnatāyā”ti, tena sāsane appasannāpi kulagāravena bhagavati apacitiṃ karonte vāti dasseti. Etasmiṃ [P 1.0475] antare kā nāma kathāti etasmiṃ yathāvuttaparicchedabbhantare kathā kā nāma. Vippakatā āraddhā hutvā apariyositā. “Kā kathā vippakatā”ti vadanto atthato tassā pariyosāpanaṃ paṭijānāti nāma. “Kā kathā”ti ca avisesacodanāti yassā tassā sabbassāpi kathāya pariyosāpanaṃ paṭiññātañca hoti, tañca paresaṃ asabbaññūnaṃ avisayanti āha “pariyantaṃ netvā demīti sabbaññupavāraṇaṃ pavāresī”ti.

410. No joy for us when he arrives means: when the Blessed One arrives, no joy or delight arises for us. Pleasant conversation means endearing talk. Having said, ‘He went out to meet him,’ to show that it was not only this one, but that other renunciants too for the most part pay respect to the Blessed One, it says, ‘For to the Blessed One…,’ etc. There it gives the reason: ‘because of his high birth.’ This shows that even those not confident in the teaching pay respect to the Blessed One out of reverence for his clan. What was the talk in the meantime? means: within the aforementioned interval, what was the talk? Unfinished means begun but not concluded. By saying, ‘What talk was left unfinished?’ he in effect promises to bring it to a conclusion. And ‘What talk?’ is an unspecified prompting, so the conclusion of any and every talk is promised. And since this is not within the domain of other, non-omniscient ones, it says: ‘Having brought it to an end, I will give it,’ thus making the invitation of an omniscient one.

Abhisaññānirodhakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Discussion on the Cessation of Higher Perception.

411. Sukāraṇanti sundaraṃ atthāvahaṃ hitāvahaṃ kāraṇaṃ. Nānātitthesu nānāladdhīsu niyuttāti nānātitthikā, te eva nānātitthiyā ka-kārassa ya-kāraṃ katvā. Kutūhalamettha atthīti kotūhalā, sā eva sālāti kotūhalasālā, tenāha “kotūhaluppattiṭṭhānato”ti. Saññānirodheti saññāsīsenāyaṃ desanā, tasmā saññāsahagatā sabbepi dhammā saṅgayhanti, tattha pana cittaṃ padhānanti āha “cittanirodhe”ti. Accantanirodhassa pana tehi anadhippetattā, avisayattā ca “khaṇikanirodhe”ti āha. Kāmaṃ sopi tesaṃ avisayova, atthato pana nirodhakathā vuccamānā tattheva tiṭṭhatīti tathā vuttaṃ. Kittighosoti “aho buddhānubhāvo bhavantarapaṭicchannaṃ kāraṇaṃ evaṃ hatthāmalakaṃ viya paccakkhato dasseti, sāvake ca edise [M 1.0364] saṃvarasamādāne patiṭṭhāpetī”ti thutighoso yāva bhavaggā pattharati. Paṭibhāgakiriyanti paḷāsavasena paṭibhāgabhūtaṃ payogaṃ karonto. Bhavantarasamayanti tatra tatra vuṭṭhanasamayaṃ abhūtaparikappitaṃ kiñci uppādiyaṃ vatthuṃ attano samayaṃ katvā. Kiñcideva sikkhāpadanti “elamūgena bhavitabbaṃ[P 1.0476], ettakaṃ, velaṃ ekasmiṃyeva ṭhāne nisīditabba”nti evamādikaṃ kiñcideva kāraṇaṃ sikkhākoṭṭhāsaṃ katvā paññapenti. Nirodhakathanti nirodhasamāpattikathaṃ.

411. A good cause means a beautiful, meaningful, and beneficial cause. Those of various sects refers to those devoted to various sects and holding diverse views; the term nānātitthiyā is derived by replacing the 'ka' with a 'ya.' A hall of curiosity: because there is curiosity here, it is called a curiosity hall; hence it is said: 'from the place of the arising of curiosity.' In the cessation of perception: this teaching is headed by perception. Therefore, all phenomena associated with perception are included, but because the mind is primary, it is spoken of as 'in the cessation of mind.' However, because the ultimate cessation is beyond their scope and not intended by them, it is spoken of as 'in momentary cessation.' Indeed, even that is beyond their reach; but in fact, since a discussion on cessation is being given, it settles on that point, and so it was said. The sound of fame means the sound of praise spreading up to the highest state of existence, proclaiming, “Ah, the Buddha’s power reveals a cause hidden in another existence as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the hand, and establishes disciples in such restraint and commitment!” Performing a counterpart action means performing an action that is a counterpart by way of resemblance. The doctrine of another existence refers to making some fabricated event, arising at various times of emergence from a state, their own doctrine. Some training rule means they prescribe some training rule, such as 'one should be like a mute goat, or sit in one place for a certain time,' thus designating some cause as a training division. The discussion on cessation means the discussion on the attainment of cessation.

Tesūti kotūhalasālāyaṃ sannipatitesu titthiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇesu. Ekacceti eke. Purimoti “ahetū appaccayā”ti evaṃvādī. Yvāyaṃ idha uppajjatīti yojanā. Samāpattinti asaññabhāvāvahaṃ samāpattiṃ. Nirodheti saññānirodhe. Hetuṃ apassantoti yena hetunā asaññabhave [V 1.0323] saññāya nirodho sabbaso anuppādo, yena ca tato cutassa idha pañcavokārabhave tassā uppādo, taṃ avisayatāya apassanto.

Among them, that is, among the sectarians, ascetics, and brahmins gathered in the Hall of Curiosity. Some, that is, certain ones. The former, that is, one who holds the view, “Without cause, without condition.” The connection is: “This which arises here.” Attainment means the attainment that brings about the state of non-perception. In the cessation means in the cessation of perception. Not seeing the cause means not seeing, because it is beyond their scope, the cause by which perception entirely ceases and does not arise in the non-percipient state of existence, and by which it arises in this five-constituent existence for one who has passed away from there.

Nanti paṭhamavādiṃ. Nisedhetvāti “na kho nāmetaṃ bho evaṃ bhavissatī”ti evaṃ paṭikkhipitvā. Asaññikabhāvanti muñchāpattiyā kiriyamayasaññāvasena vigatasaññibhāvaṃ. Vakkhati hi “visaññī hutvā”ti. Vikkhambhanavasena kilesānaṃ santāpanena attantapo. Ghoratapoti dukkaratāya bhīmatapo. Parimāritindriyoti nibbisevanabhāvāpādanena sabbaso milāpitacakkhādindriyo. Bhaggoti bhañjitakusalajjhāsayo. Evamāhāti “evaṃ saññā hi bho purisassa attā”tiādiākārena saññānirodhamāha. Iminā nayena ito paresu dvīsu ṭhānesu yathārahaṃ yojanā veditabbā.

Him means the first speaker. Having denied means having rejected by saying, “No, sir, it will not be so.” The state of being without perception means the state of having lost perception by way of functional perception due to falling into a swoon. For it will be said, “having become non-percipient.” A self-tormentor is one who torments himself by burning away defilements through suppression. A practitioner of severe austerities means one whose austerities are terrifying because of their difficulty. One with faculties withered means one whose faculties, such as the eye, are completely withered by bringing about a state of non-indulgence. Broken means one whose inclination for wholesome states is shattered. Thus he speaks means he speaks of the cessation of perception in such terms as, “Thus, sir, perception is the self of a person,” and so on. In this manner, the application should be understood as appropriate in the two remaining instances.

Āthabbaṇapayoganti āthabbaṇavedavihitaṃ āthabbaṇikānaṃ visaññibhāvāpādanapayogaṃ. Āthabbaṇaṃ payojetvāti [P 1.0477] āthabbaṇavede āgataaggijuhanapubbakaṃ mantajappanaṃ payojetvā sīsacchinnatādidassanena saññānirodhamāha. Tassāti yassa sīsacchinnatādi dassitaṃ, tassa.

The use of the Atharvaṇa refers to a practice prescribed in the Atharvaṇa Veda, a practice employed by Atharvaṇa experts to induce a non-percipient state. Having employed the Atharvaṇa means having employed the recitation of mantras preceded by fire offerings as found in the Atharvaṇa Veda, and then declaring the cessation of perception by showing a severed head and so on. His refers to the one to whom the severed head and so on was shown.

Yakkhadāsīnanti [M 1.0365] devadāsīnaṃ, yā “devatābhatiyotipi” vuccanti. Madaniddanti surāmadanimittakaṃ supanaṃ devatūpahāranti naccanagāyanādinā devatānaṃ pūjaṃ. Surāpātinti pātipuṇṇaṃ suraṃ. Divāti atidivā ussūre.

'Female servants of the yakkhas' means female servants of the deities, who are also called 'supported by the deities.' 'Madaniddaṃ' means sleep caused by intoxication from liquor. 'Devatūpahāraṃ' means worship of deities through dancing, singing, and so on. 'Surāpātiṃ' means a bowl full of liquor. 'By day' means in broad daylight, at sunrise.

Elamūgakathā viyāti imesaṃ paṇḍitamānīnaṃ kathā andhabālakathāsadisī. Cattāro nirodheti aññamaññavidhure cattāro nirodhe ete paññapenti. Na ca aññamaññaviruddhanānāsabhāvena tena bhavitabbaṃ, atha kho ekasabhāvena, tenāha “iminā cā”tiādi. Aññenevāti imehi vuttākārato aññākāreneva bhavitabbaṃ. “Ayaṃ nirodho, ayaṃ nirodho”ti āmeḍitavacanaṃ satthā attano desanāvilāsena anekākāravokāraṃ nirodhaṃ vibhāvessatīti dassanatthaṃ kataṃ aho nūnāti ettha ahoti acchariye, nūnāti anussaraṇe nipāto. Tasmā aho nūna bhagavā anaññasādhāraṇadesanattā nirodhampi aho acchariyaṃ katvā katheyya maññeti adhippāyo. “Aho nūna sugato”ti etthāpi eseva nayo. Acchariyavibhāvanato eva cettha dvikkhattuṃ vacanaṃ, acchariyatthopi cettha aho-saddo. So yasmā anussaraṇamukheneva tena gahito, tasmā vuttaṃ “aho nūnāti anussaraṇatthe”ti. Kālapuggalādivibhāgena bahubhedattā imesaṃ nirodhadhammānanti bahuvacanaṃ, kusala-saddayogena sāmivacanaṃ bhummatthe daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ciṇṇavasitāyāti nirodhasamāpattiyaṃ [V 1.0324] vasībhāvassa ciṇṇattā. Sabhāvaṃ jānātīti nirodhassa sabhāvaṃ yāthāvato jānāti.

Like the talk of a deaf-mute, the talk of these conceited fools is like the talk of blind children. They declare these four cessations as mutually destructive. But it should not be so by having mutually contradictory diverse natures; rather, they are of a single nature. Therefore, it is said, "By this..." and so on. "By another way" means it should be in a manner different from what has been stated by them. The repeated phrase, "This is cessation, this is cessation," is spoken by the Teacher to display, through the elegance of his teaching, that cessation is of manifold aspects. Here, "aho" expresses wonder, and "nūna" is a particle indicating recollection. Therefore, the meaning is: "Ah, surely the Blessed One, due to his unparalleled teaching, would speak of cessation in a way that makes it seem marvelous." Similarly, in the phrase, "Ah, surely the Sugata..." the same principle applies. Because of the emphasis on wonder, the expression is repeated twice here, and the word "aho" also conveys the sense of wonder. Since it is grasped through the door of recollection, it is said, "‘aho nūna’ means in the sense of recollection." Due to the many distinctions of time, persons, and so on, these cessation phenomena are spoken of in the plural. The genitive case connected with the word 'kusala' should be understood in the locative sense of abundance. "Because of practiced mastery" means because mastery of the attainment of cessation has been practiced. "He knows the true nature" means he knows the true nature of cessation as it really is.

Ahetukasaññuppādanirodhakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discourse on the Arising and Cessation of Perception Without Cause

412. Gharamajjheyeva [P 1.0478] pakkhalitāti gharato bahi gantukāmā purisā maggaṃ anotaritvā gharājirena samatale vivaṭaṅgaṇe eva pakkhalanaṃ pattā, evaṃ sampadamidanti attho. Asādhāraṇo hetu, sādhāraṇo paccayoti evamādi vibhāgena idha payojanaṃ natthi saññāya akāraṇabhāvapaṭikkhepattā codanāyāti vuttaṃ “kāraṇasseva nāma”nti.

412. "They slipped right in the middle of the house": this means that men wanting to go outside the house, without stepping onto the road, slipped right on the even ground of the open courtyard adjacent to the house. This is the meaning of "this is what happened." There is no need here for a distinction such as "uncommon cause" and "common condition," because the objection that perception is uncaused is rejected by the statement: "It is indeed for a reason."

Pāḷiyaṃ “uppajjantipi nirujjhantipī”ti vuttaṃ, tattha “sahetū sappaccayā saññā uppajjanti, uppannā pana nirujjhantiyeva, na tiṭṭhantī”ti dassanatthaṃ “nirujjhantī”ti vacanaṃ, na nirodhassa sahetusappaccayabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Uppādo hi sahetuko[M 1.0366], na nirodho. Yadi hi nirodhopi sahetuko siyā, tassa nirodhenāpi bhavitabbaṃ aṅkurādīnaṃ viya, na ca tassa nirodho atthi. Tasmā vuttanayeneva pāḷiyā attho veditabbo. Ayañca nayo khaṇanirodhavasena vutto. Yo pana yathāparicchinnakālavasena sabbasova anuppādanirodho, so “sahetuko”ti veditabbo tathārūpāya paṭipattiyā vinā abhāvato. Tenāha bhagavā “sikkhā ekā saññā nirujjhatī”ti. (Dī. ni. 1.412) tato eva ca idhāpi vuttaṃ “saññāya sahetukaṃ uppādanirodhaṃ dīpetu”nti.

In the Pāḷi it is said: "They arise and they cease." Here, the statement "they cease" is for the purpose of showing that "perceptions arise with a cause and a condition, and having arisen, they indeed cease; they do not persist"—it is not for the purpose of showing that cessation has a cause and a condition. For arising is caused, not cessation. If cessation, too, were caused, then it would have to have a cessation of its own, like sprouts and so on; but there is no cessation of that cessation. Therefore, the meaning of the Pāḷi should be understood in the way stated. This principle is stated in terms of momentary cessation. However, that complete non-arising and cessation which is defined by a specific period of time should be understood as "caused," because it does not occur without such a practice. Hence the Blessed One said: "Through training, one perception ceases." For this very reason it is also said here: "to illustrate the caused arising and cessation of perception."

Sikkhā ekāti ettha sikkhāti karaṇe paccattavacanaṃ, eka-saddo aññapariyāyo “ittheke abhivadanti sato vā pana sattassā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.85 ādayo; ma. ni. 3.21) viya, na saṅkhyāvācīti āha “sikkhā ekā saññā uppajjantīti sikkhāya ekaccā saññā jāyantī”ti. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

In the phrase "Through training, one," the word "training" (sikkhā) is a singular noun in the instrumental sense. The word "one" (ekā) is a synonym for "some" or "a certain," as in such passages as "some assert this concerning a being that exists..." (DN 1.85, etc.; MN 3.21); it is not a numeral. Thus it is said: "'Through training, one perception arises' means 'through training, certain perceptions arise.'" This same principle applies to the other terms.

413. Tatthāti tassaṃ uparidesanāyaṃ. Sammādiṭṭhisammāsaṅkappavasena pariyāpannattā āgatāti sabhāvato upakārato ca paññākkhandhe pariyāpannattā saṅgahitattā tatiyā adhipaññāsikkhā sammādiṭṭhisammāsaṅkappavasena [P 1.0479] āgatā. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “yā cāvuso visākha sammādiṭṭhi, yo ca sammāsaṅkappo, ime dhammā paññākkhandhe saṅgahitā”ti (ma. ni. 1.462) kāmañcettha vuttanayena [V 1.0325] tissopi sikkhā āgatā eva, tathāpi adhicittasikkhāya eva abhisaññānirodho dassito, itarā tassa sambhārabhāvena ānītā.

413. "Therein" means in that teaching above. It is said to be "included" because it is comprised by way of right view and right intention. Because it is included and comprised in the aggregate of wisdom by its nature and by its supportive function, the third training, the higher wisdom, is included by way of right view and right intention. For it is said: "Friend Visākha, whatever is right view and whatever is right intention—these states are included in the aggregate of wisdom" (MN 1.462). And although here, in the manner described, all three trainings are indeed included, still, the cessation of higher perception is shown specifically by means of the higher training in mind, while the others are brought in as its requisites.

Pañcakāmaguṇikarāgoti pañcakāmakoṭṭhāse ārabbha uppajjanakarāgo. Asamuppannakāmacāroti vattamānuppannatāvasena asamuppanno yo koci kāmacāro yā kāci lobhuppatti. Purimo visayavasena niyamitattā kāmaguṇārammaṇova lobho daṭṭhabbo, itaro pana jhānanikantibhavarāgādippabhedo sabbopi lobhacāro kāmanaṭṭhena kāmesu pavattanato. Sabbepi hi tebhūmakā dhammā kāmanīyaṭṭhena kāmāti. Ubhayesampi kāmasaññātināmatā sahacaraṇañāyenāti “kāmasaññā”ti paduddhāraṃ katvā tadubhayaṃ niddiṭṭhaṃ.

"Lust connected with the five strands of sensual pleasure" is lust that arises in relation to the five kinds of sensual pleasures. "Unarisen indulgence in sensual desire" is any indulgence in sensual desire, any occurrence of greed, that has not arisen in the sense of being presently arisen. The former, being restricted by way of its object, should be understood as greed that has only the strands of sensual pleasure as its object. The latter, however, is any indulgence in greed of any kind, such as delight in jhāna and craving for existence, because it proceeds within the sensual sphere in the sense of desiring. For all phenomena of the three planes are called "sensual" in the sense of being desirable. Both are designated by the term "perception of sensuality" by the principle of association. Thus, having extracted the term "perception of sensuality," both are explained.

“Tatthā”tiādi [M 1.0367] asamuppannakāmacārato pañcakāmaguṇikarāgassa visesadassanaṃ. Kāmaṃ pañcakāmaguṇikarāgopi asamuppanno eva maggena samugghāṭīyati, tasmiṃ pana samugghāṭitepi na sabbo rāgo samugghāṭaṃ gacchati, tasmā pañcakāmaguṇikarāgaggahaṇena na itarassa sabbassa rāgassa gahaṇaṃ hotīti ubhayasādhāraṇena pariyāyena ubhayaṃ saṅgahetvā dassetuṃ pāḷiyaṃ kāmasaññāggahaṇaṃ katanti tadubhayaṃ sarūpato visesato ca dassetvā sabbasaṅgāhikabhāvato “asamuppannakāmacāro [P 1.0480] pana imasmiṃ ṭhāne vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ.

The passage beginning "Therein" shows the distinction of lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure from unarisen indulgence in sensual desire. Although lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure, being itself unarisen, is uprooted by the path, yet even when that is uprooted, not all lust is uprooted. Therefore, the inclusion of lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure does not entail the inclusion of all other lust. Thus, in the Pāḷi, the term "perception of sensuality" is used to include and show both by a method common to both. Having shown both in terms of their own nature and their distinction, because of its all-inclusive nature, it is said: "But unarisen indulgence in sensual desire applies in this place."

Sadisattāti kāmasaññādibhāvena samānattā, etena pāḷiyaṃ “purimā”ti sadisakappanāvasena vuttanti dasseti. Anāgatā hi idha “nirujjhatī”ti vuttā anuppādassa adhippetattā, tenāha “anuppannāva nuppajjatī”ti.

"Because of similarity" means because of being the same in being perception of sensuality and so on. This shows that in the Pāḷi, the word "former" is used by way of a similar designation. For here future perceptions are said to "cease" because non-arising is intended. Hence it is said: "What is unarisen does not arise."

Nīvaraṇavivekato jātattā vivekajehi paṭhamajjhānapītisukhehi saha akkhātabbā, taṃkoṭṭhāsikā vāti vivekajaṃ pītisukhasaṅkhātā. Nānattasaññāpaṭighasaññāhi nipuṇatāya sukhumabhūtatāya sukhumasaññā bhūtā sukhumabhāvena, paramatthabhāvena aviparītasabhāvā. Jhānaṃ taṃsampayuttadhammānaṃ bhāvanāsiddhā saṇhasukhumatā nīvaraṇavikkhambhanavasena viññāyatīti āha “kāmacchandādioḷārikaṅgappahānavasena sukhumā”ti. Bhūtatāyāti vijjamānatāya. Sabbatthāti sabbavāresu.

Because it is born from seclusion from the hindrances, it should be spoken of together with the joy and happiness of the first jhāna, which are born of seclusion; or, since it is a component of them, it is designated as "born of seclusion, with joy and happiness." It is a subtle perception because it is more refined and subtle than the perceptions of diversity and resistance. It is a real perception because of its subtlety, its ultimate nature, and its undistorted essence. The gentleness and subtlety of the jhāna and its associated states, which are accomplished through development, are known through the suppression of the hindrances; thus it is said: "subtle by way of the abandonment of coarse factors such as sensual desire." "Because it is real" means because it is existent. "In all" means in all cases.

Samāpajjanādhiṭṭhānāni viya vuṭṭhānaṃ jhāne pariyāpannampi hoti yathā taṃ dhammānaṃ bhaṅgakkhaṇo dhammesu, na āvajjanapaccavekkhaṇānīti “paṭhamajjhānaṃ samāpajjanto adhiṭṭhahanto vuṭṭhahanto [V 1.0326] ca sikkhatī”ti vuttaṃ, na “āvajjanto paccavekkhanto”ti. Tanti paṭhamajjhānaṃ. Tenāti hetumhi karaṇavacanaṃ, tasmā paṭhamajjhānena hetubhūtenāti attho. Hetubhāvo cettha jhānassa yathāvuttasaññāya uppattiyā sahajātādipaccayabhāvo kāmasaññāya nirodhassa upanissayatāva, tañca kho suttantapariyāyena. Tathā ceva saṃvaṇṇitaṃ “tathārūpāya paṭipattiyā vinā abhāvato”ti. Etenupāyenāti yvāyaṃ paṭhamajjhānatappaṭipakkhasaññāvasena “sikkhā ekā saññā uppajjati, sikkhā ekā saññā nirujjhatī”ti [M 1.0368] ettha attho vutto, etena nayena. Sabbatthāti sabbavāresu.

Like attaining and resolving, emerging is also included in the jhāna—just as the moment of dissolution of phenomena is included in the phenomena—but adverting and reviewing are not. Thus it is said: "one trains by attaining, resolving, and emerging from the first jhāna," not "by adverting and reviewing." "That" is the first jhāna. "Thereby" is the instrumental case in the sense of cause; therefore the meaning is "by means of the first jhāna which has become the cause." Here, the causal nature of the jhāna is its being a condition of co-arising, etc., for the arising of the aforesaid perception, and its being a decisive support condition for the cessation of the perception of sensuality; and this is according to the sutta method. And it is described thus: "because it is absent without such a practice." "By this method" means by this principle whereby the meaning of "through training, one perception arises; through training, one perception ceases" is stated in terms of the first jhāna and the perception that is its opposite. "In all" means in all cases.

414. Yasmā panettha samāpattivasena taṃtaṃsaññānaṃ [P 1.0481] uppādanirodhe vuccamāne aṅgavasena so vuttoti āha “yasmā panā”tiādi. “Aṅgato sammasana”nti anupadadhammavipassanāya lakkhaṇavacanaṃ. Anupadadhammavipassanañhi karonto samāpattiṃ patvā aṅgato sammasanaṃ karoti, na ca saññā samāpattiyā kiñci aṅgaṃ hoti. Vuttañca “idañca saññā saññāti evaṃ aṅgato sammasanaṃ uddhaṭa”nti. Aṅgatoti vā avayavatoti attho, anupadadhammatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Tadevāti ākiñcaññāyatanameva.

414. Because here, when the arising and cessation of the various perceptions is spoken of by way of attainment, it is spoken of by way of its factors; thus it says, "Moreover, because..." and so on. "Contemplation by way of factors" is a term for the characteristic of insight into phenomena one by one. For one practicing insight into phenomena one by one, having reached the attainment, contemplates by way of its factors; but perception is not any factor of the attainment. And it is said: "And this perception is perception—thus the contemplation by way of factors is set forth." "By way of factors" means by way of components; this is what is meant by "phenomena one by one." "That very thing" is the base of nothingness itself.

Yato khoti paccatte nissakkavacananti āha “yo nāmā”ti yathā “ādimhī”ti etasmiṃ atthe “ādito”ti vuccati itaravibhattitopi to-saddassa labbhanato. Sakasmiṃ attanā adhigate saññā sakasaññā, sā etassa atthīti sakasaññī, tenāha “attano paṭhamajjhānasaññāya saññavā”ti. Sakasaññīti cettha upari vuccamānanirodhapādakatāya sātisayāya jhānasaññāya atthibhāvajotako ī-kāro daṭṭhabbo, tenevāha “anupubbena saññaggaṃ phusatī”tiādi. Tasmā tattha tattha sakasaññitāggahaṇena tasmiṃ tasmiṃ jhāne sabbaso suciṇṇavasībhāvo dīpitoti veditabbaṃ.

The phrase "From which, indeed" is a statement of certainty regarding the individual; thus it says, "Whoever, indeed..." This is just as "ādito" (from the beginning) is used in the sense of "ādimhi" (at the beginning), because the suffix "-to" can be derived from other case endings as well. "One's own perception" (sakasaññā) is the perception one has attained oneself; one who possesses this is a "possessor of one's own perception" (sakasaññī). Hence it says, "one who has the perception of one's own first jhāna." Here, in "possessor of one's own perception," the "-ī" suffix should be understood as indicating the existence of a superior jhāna perception that serves as a basis for the cessation to be discussed below. For that very reason it says: "He gradually touches the peak of perception," and so on. Therefore, it should be understood that by the inclusion of "possessing one's own perception" in each case, complete mastery through thorough practice in each respective jhāna is shown.

Lokiyānanti niddhāraṇe sāmivacanaṃ, sāmiatthe eva vā. Yadaggena hi taṃ tesu seṭṭhaṃ, tadaggena tesampi seṭṭhanti. “Lokiyāna”nti visesanaṃ lokuttarasamāpattīhi tassa aseṭṭhabhāvato. “Kiccakārakasamāpattīna”nti visesanaṃ akiccakārakasamāpattito tassa aseṭṭhabhāvato. Akiccakārakatā cassā paṭusaññākiccābhāvavacanato viññāyati. Yatheva hi tattha saññā, evaṃ phassādayo pīti. Yadaggena hi tattha saṅkhārāvasesasukhumabhāvappattiyā pakativipassakānaṃ sammasituṃ asakkuṇeyyarūpena ṭhitā, tadaggena heṭṭhimasamāpattidhammā viya paṭukiccakaraṇasamatthāpi na hontīti. Svāyamattho paramatthamañjusāyaṃ visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ āruppakathāyaṃ [V 1.0327] (visuddhi. ṭī. 1.286) savisesaṃ vutto, tasmā tattha vuttanayena [M 1.0369][P 1.0482] veditabbo. Keci pana “yathā heṭṭhimā heṭṭhimā samāpattiyo uparimānaṃ uparimānaṃ adhiṭṭhānakiccaṃ sādhenti, na evaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpatti kassacipi adhiṭṭhānakiccaṃ sādheti, tasmā sā akiccakārikā, itarā kiccakārikā vuttā”ti vadanti, tadayuttaṃ tassāpi vipassanācittaparidamanādīnaṃ adhiṭṭhānakiccasādhanato. Tasmā purimoyeva attho yutto.

"Lokiyānaṃ" is the genitive case in the sense of determination, or in the sense of possession. For whatever reason it is the best among them, by that same reason it is also the best among those. "Lokiyānaṃ" is a qualifier because, compared to supramundane attainments, it is not the best. "Kiccakārakasamāpattīnaṃ" is a qualifier because of its non-supremacy (among functional attainments), due to its non-functional aspect. Its non-functionality is understood from the absence of strong perception-related functions. Just as perception is present there, so too are contact and other factors. For whatever reason the remaining formations there, due to their attainment of an extremely subtle state, remain in a form that cannot be discerned by ordinary insight meditators, by that same reason they are not capable of performing strong functions like the lower attainments. This meaning is fully explained in the Paramatthamañjūsā, the commentary on the Visuddhimagga, in the section on the formless attainments (Visuddhi. Ṭī. 1.286), so it should be understood according to the explanation given there. Some, however, say: "Just as the lower attainments fulfill the preparatory functions for the higher ones, the nevasaññānāsaññāyatana attainment does not fulfill any preparatory function for anyone. Therefore, it is non-functional, while the others are called functional." This is incorrect because even it fulfills preparatory functions such as subduing the mind for insight. Thus, the former explanation is the correct one.

Pakappetīti saṃvidahati. Jhānaṃ samāpajjanto hi jhānasukhaṃ attani saṃvidahati nāma. Abhisaṅkharotīti āyūhati, sampiṇḍetīti attho. Sampiṇḍanattho hi samudayaṭṭho. Yasmā nikantivasena cetanākiccassa matthakappatti, tasmā phalūpacārena kāraṇaṃ dassento “nikantiṃ kurumāno abhisaṅkharoti nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Imā idāni me labbhamānā ākiñcaññāyatanasaññā nirujjheyyuṃ taṃsamatikkameneva uparijhānatthāya cetanābhisaṅkharaṇasambhavato. Aññāti ākiñcaññāyatanasaññāhi aññā. Tato thūlatarabhāvato oḷārikā. Kā pana tāti āha “bhavaṅgasaññā”ti. Ākiñcaññāyatanato vuṭṭhāya eva hi uparijhānatthāya cetanābhisaṅkharaṇāni bhaveyyuṃ, vuṭṭhānañca bhavaṅgavasena hoti. Yāva ca upari jhānasamāpajjanaṃ, tāva antarantarā bhavaṅgappavattīti āha “bhavaṅgasaññā uppajjeyyu”nti.

He prepares, that is, he arranges. For one attaining jhāna arranges the bliss of jhāna within oneself, so it is said. He constructs, that is, he exerts; the meaning is he compiles. For the meaning of compiling is the meaning of origination. Since the function of volition reaches its peak through delight, therefore, showing the cause by way of a metaphor of the result, it is said: "One who delights constructs." Now, these perceptions of the base of nothingness that are being attained by me might cease; for by transcending that very state, the construction of volition for the sake of the higher jhāna is possible. Other, that is, other than the perceptions of the base of nothingness. Then, because of being coarser than that, they are gross. But what are they? He says: "the bhavaṅga perception." For only upon emerging from the base of nothingness would the constructions of volition for the sake of the higher jhāna occur, and the emergence occurs by way of the bhavaṅga. And as long as there is the attainment of the higher jhāna, until then the bhavaṅga occurs intermittently. Therefore, he says: "the bhavaṅga perception might arise."

Cetentovāti nevasaññānāsaññāyatanajjhānaṃ ekaṃ dve cittavāre samāpajjanto eva. Na ceteti tathā heṭṭhimajjhānesu viya vā pubbābhogābhāvato pubbābhogavasena hi jhānaṃ pakappento idha “cetetī”ti vutto. Yasmā “ahametaṃ jhānaṃ nibbattemi upasampādemi samāpajjāmī”ti evaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇaṃ tattha sālayasseva [P 1.0483] hoti, na anālayassa, tasmā ekaṃ cittakkhaṇikampi jhānaṃ pavattento tattha appahīnanikantikatāya abhisaṅkharonto evāti attho. Yasmā panassa tathā heṭṭhimajjhānesu viya vā tattha pubbābhogo natthi, tasmā “na abhisaṅkharotī”ti vuttaṃ. “Imassa bhikkhuno”tiādi vuttassevatthassa vivaraṇaṃ. “Svāyamattho”tiādinā tamevatthaṃ upamāya paṭipādeti.

"He intends it" refers to one who enters the jhāna of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception for one or two mind-moments. He does not intend it as in the lower jhānas, due to the absence of prior preoccupation. For here, one who prepares the jhāna by way of prior preoccupation is said to 'intend'. Because the act of volitional formation there—'I produce this jhāna, attain it, enter it'—occurs only for one who has attachment, not for one who is without attachment, therefore, even when causing the jhāna to arise for a single mind-moment, he is still volitionally forming due to unabandoned delight—this is the meaning. However, because there is no such prior preoccupation for him there as in the lower jhānas, it is said, 'he does not form volitionally.' 'For this monk,' etc., is an explanation of the meaning already stated. 'This is the meaning,' etc., illustrates that very meaning by way of a simile.

Pacchābhāgeti [M 1.0370] pitugharassa pacchābhāge. Tato puttagharato. Laddhagharamevāti yato anena bhikkhā laddhā, tameva gharaṃ puttagehameva. Āsanasālā viya ākiñcaññāyatanasamāpatti tato pitugharaputtagharaṭṭhāniyānaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatananirodhasamāpattīnaṃ upagantabbato. Pitugharaṃ amanasikaritvāti pavisitvā samatikkantampi pitugharaṃ na manasi katvā. Puttagharasseva ācikkhanaṃ viya ekaṃ dve cittavāre samāpajjitabbampi nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ na manasi katvā [V 1.0328] parato nirodhasamāpattiatthāya eva manasikāro. Evaṃ amanasikārasāmaññena, manasikārasāmaññena ca upamupameyyatā veditabbā ācikkhanenapi manasikārasseva jotitattā. Na hi manasikārena vinā ācikkhanaṃ sambhavati.

"Later part" means the back part of the father's house. Then, from the son's house. "The very house obtained" means that since alms were obtained by him there, that very house is the son's house. The attainment of the base of nothingness is like an assembly hall, because from there the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the attainment of cessation, which stand in the place of the father's house and the son's house respectively, are to be approached. "Not attending to the father's house" means not attending to the father's house even after entering and passing beyond it. Just as one might only be pointing out the son's house, so too, even though the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception must be attained for one or two mind-moments, one does not attend to it, but attention is solely for the purpose of the attainment of cessation beyond it. Thus, the relationship between the simile and its subject should be understood through the commonality of non-attention and the commonality of attention, since even by the act of pointing out, attention itself is revealed. For without attention, pointing out is not possible.

Tā jhānasaññāti tā ekaṃ dve cittavāre pavattā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasaññā. Nirujjhantīti padeseneva nirujjhanti, pubbābhisaṅkhāravasena pana upari anuppādo. Yathā ca jhānasaññānaṃ, evaṃ itarasaññānaṃ pīti āha “aññā ca oḷārikā bhavaṅgasaññā nuppajjantī”ti, yathāparicchinnakālanti adhippāyo. So evaṃ paṭipanno bhikkhūti so evaṃ yathāvutte saññāgge ṭhito arahatte, anāgāmiphale vā patiṭṭhito bhikkhu [P 1.0484] dvīhi phalehi samannāgamo, tiṇṇaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ paṭippassaddhi, soḷasavidhā ñāṇacariyā, navavidhā samādhicariyāti imesaṃ vasena nirodhapaṭipādanapaṭipattiṃ paṭipanno. Phusatīti ettha phusanaṃ nāma vindanaṃ paṭiladdhīti āha “vindati paṭilabhatī”ti. Atthato pana yathāparicchinnakālaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ sabbaso appavatti eva.

Those perceptions of jhāna are the perceptions of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception that occur for one or two mind-moments. 'They cease' means they cease in that area, but due to previous volitional formations, there is no further arising. And just as with the perceptions of jhāna, so too with other perceptions, it is said, 'No other gross life-continuum perceptions arise,' meaning for that defined period. A monk who practices thus—that is, a monk established in arahantship or the fruit of non-returning, standing in the highest perception as described—is endowed with two fruits, the pacification of three formations, the sixteenfold knowledge-conduct, and the ninefold concentration-conduct. By these means, he practices the path leading to cessation. 'Attains' (phusati) here means experiencing and acquiring, thus it is said, 'He experiences, he acquires.' In essence, it refers to the complete non-occurrence of mind and mental factors for that defined period.

Abhīti upasaggamattaṃ niratthakaṃ, tasmā “saññā” icceva attho. Nirodhapadena anantarikaṃ katvā samāpattipade vattabbe tesaṃ dvinnaṃ antare sampajānapadaṃ ṭhapitanti āha “nirodhapadena anantarikaṃ katvā vutta”nti, tenāha “anupaṭi…pe… attho”ti. Tatrāpīti tasmimpi tathā padānupubbiṭhapanepi ayaṃ visesatthoti yojanā. Sampajānantassāti taṃ taṃ samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya tattha tattha saṅkhārānaṃ sammasanavasena pajānantassa. Anteti yathāvuttāya nirodhapaṭipattiyā pariyosāne. Dutiyavikappe sampajānantassāti sampajānakārinoti attho, tena nirodhasamāpajjanakassa [M 1.0371] bhikkhuno ādito paṭṭhāya sabbapāṭihārikapaññāya saddhiṃ atthasādhikā paññā kiccato dassitā hoti, tenāha “paṇḍitassa bhikkhuno”ti.

'Abhī' is merely a meaningless prefix; therefore, the meaning is simply 'perception.' When the term 'attainment' should have been stated immediately after the term 'cessation,' the term 'clearly knowing' was placed between those two. Thus, it is said, 'It is stated having made it immediate with the term cessation,' and therefore, he says, 'anupaṭi...pe... is the meaning.' Here too, even in that establishment of the sequence of terms, this is a distinct meaning—this is the connection. 'Of one who clearly knows' refers to one who, having entered and emerged from each attainment, comprehends by way of reflecting on the formations in each place. 'The end' means at the conclusion of the cessation practice as described. In the second alternative explanation, 'of one who clearly knows' means one who acts with clear knowledge. Thus, from the beginning, the wisdom of the monk who attains cessation, along with all miraculous wisdom, is shown as wisdom that accomplishes the purpose. Hence, it is said, 'of the wise monk'.

Sabbākārenāti “samāpattiyā sarūpaviseso, samāpajjanako, samāpajjanassa ṭhānaṃ, kāraṇaṃ, samāpajjanākāro”ti evamādi sabbappakārena. Tatthāti visuddhimagge. (Visuddhī. 2.867) kathitatovāti kathitaṭṭhānato eva gahetabbā, na idha taṃ vadāma punaruttibhāvatoti adhippāyo.

'In every way' means 'the specific nature of the attainment, the one who attains, the basis for attainment, the cause, the manner of attainment,' and so on—in every possible way. 'There,' in the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhi. 2.867), 'as previously explained' means it should be understood from the place where it was explained; we are not stating it here due to redundancy—this is the intended meaning.

Evaṃ kho ahanti ettha ākārattho evaṃ-saddo uggahitākāradassananti katvā. Evaṃ poṭṭhapādāti ettha pana sampaṭicchanattho, tenāha “suuggahitaṃ tayāti anujānanto”ti.

In 'Thus, indeed, I,' the word 'thus' has the meaning of 'in this manner,' indicating the form grasped. But here, in 'Poṭṭhapāda, thus,' the meaning is acceptance; therefore, he said, 'Well grasped by you,' thus assenting.

415. Saññā [V 1.0329][P 1.0485] aggā etthāti saññāggaṃ, ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ. Aṭṭhasu samāpattīsupi saññāggaṃ atthi upalabbhatīti cintetvā. “Puthū”ti pāḷiyaṃ liṅgavipallāsaṃ dassento āha “bahūnipī”ti. “Yathā”ti iminā pakāraviseso karaṇappakāro gahito, na pakārasāmaññanti āha “yena yena kasiṇenā”ti, pathavīkasiṇena karaṇabhūtenā”ti ca. Jhānaṃ tāva yutto karaṇabhāvo saññānirodhaphusanassa sādhakatamabhāvato, kathaṃ kasiṇānanti? Tesampi so yutto eva. Yadaggena hi jhānānaṃ nirodhaphusanassa sādhakataṃ abhāvo, tadaggena kasiṇānampi tadavinābhāvato. Anekakaraṇāpi kiriyā hotiyeva yathā “assena yānena dīpikāya gacchatī”ti.

415. 'Perception is pre-eminent here,' thus it is called 'pre-eminent perception,' the base of nothingness. Considering that pre-eminent perception is also found in all eight attainments. Pointing out the gender inversion in the Pāli word 'Puthū,' he said, 'many indeed.' With 'yathā' (as), a specific mode, the way of doing, is taken, not a general mode; therefore, he said, 'by whichever kasiṇa,' and 'by the earth kasiṇa as the instrument.' Now, jhāna is suitable as the instrument because it is the most efficient in attaining the touching of the cessation of perception. How about the kasiṇas? They too are suitable in the same way. For to the extent that jhāna is efficient in attaining the touching of cessation, to that extent the kasiṇas are also efficient, due to their inseparability. An action can certainly have multiple instruments, just as in 'going by horse, vehicle, or torch.'

Ekavāranti sakiṃ. Purimasaññānirodhanti kāmasaññādipurimasaññāya nirodhaṃ, na nirodhasamāpattisaññitaṃ saññānirodhaṃ. Ekaṃ saññāgganti ekaṃ saññābhūtaṃ aggaṃ seṭṭhanti attho heṭṭhimasaññāya ukkaṭṭhabhāvato. Saññā ca sā aggañcāti saññāggaṃ, na saññāsu agganti. Dve vāreti dvikkhattuṃ. Sesakasiṇesūti kasiṇānaṃyeva gahaṇaṃ nirodhakathāya adhikatattā. Tato eva cettha jhānaggahaṇena kasiṇajjhānāni eva gahitānīti veditabbaṃ. “Paṭhamajjhānena karaṇabhūtenā”ti ārammaṇaṃ anāmasitvā vadati yathā “yena yena kasiṇenā”ti ettha jhānaṃ anāmasitvā [M 1.0372] vuttaṃ. “Itī”tiādinā vuttamevatthaṃ saṅgahetvā nigamanavasena vadati. Sabbampīti sabbaṃ ekavāraṃ samāpannajhānaṃ. Saṅgahetvāti sañjānanalakkhaṇena taṃsabhāvāvisesato ekajjhaṃ saṅgahetvā. Aparāparanti punappunaṃ.

'Once' means a single time. 'The cessation of previous perceptions' refers to the cessation of earlier perceptions such as sensual perception, not the cessation of perception designated as the attainment of cessation. 'One supreme perception' means one perception that is supreme, excellent, because it surpasses the lower perceptions; it is called 'supreme perception' because it is perception and supreme, not supreme among perceptions. 'Twice' means two times. 'The remaining kasiṇas' refers specifically to the kasiṇas, as they are more relevant to the discussion of cessation. From this, it should be understood that the jhānas mentioned here refer specifically to the kasiṇa jhānas. 'By the first jhāna as the means' is said without specifying the object, just as 'by whichever kasiṇa' is said without specifying the jhāna. 'Thus,' and so on, summarizes the meaning and concludes the discussion. 'All' refers to all the jhānas attained a single time. 'Summarized' means bringing them together as one, since they share the characteristic of perception without distinction of essence. 'Again and again' means repeatedly.

416. Jhānapadaṭṭhānaṃ vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhentassa puggalassa vasena saññāñāṇāni dassitāni paṭhamanaye[P 1.0486]. Dutiyanaye pana yasmā vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā maggena ghaṭentassa maggañāṇaṃ uppajjati, tasmā vipassanāmaggavasena saññāñāṇāni dassitāni. Yasmā pana paṭhamanayo lokiyattā oḷāriko, dutiyanayo missako tasmā tadubhayaṃ asambhāvetvā accantasukhumaṃ subhaṃ thiraṃ nibbattitalokuttarameva dassetuṃ maggaphalavasena saññāñāṇāni dassitāni tatiyanaye. Tayopete nayā maggasodhanavasena dassitā.

416. In the first method, perceptions and knowledges are shown based on the person who develops insight with jhāna as the foundation. In the second method, because insight is aroused and path-knowledge arises through striving with the path, perceptions and knowledges are shown based on insight and the path. Since the first method is mundane and coarse, and the second method is mixed, therefore, without considering both of these, the utterly subtle, auspicious, stable, and resultant supramundane alone is shown through the path and fruition in the third method, where perceptions and knowledges are presented. These three methods are shown by way of purification of the path.

“Ayaṃ panettha sāro”ti vibhāvetuṃ tipiṭakamahāsivattheravādo ābhato. Nirodhaṃ pucchitvā tasmiṃ kathite tadanantaraṃ saññāñāṇuppattiṃ pucchanto atthato nirodhato vuṭṭhānaṃ pucchati nāma, nirodhato ca vuṭṭhānaṃ arahattaphaluppattiyā vā siyā anāgāmiphaluppattiyā vā, tattha saññā padhānā, tadanantarañca paccavekkhaṇañāṇanti tadubhayaṃ niddhārento thero “kiṃ ime bhikkhū bhaṇantī”tiādimāha[V 1.0330]. Tattha “kiṃ ime bhikkhū bhaṇantī”ti tadā dīghanikāyatantiṃ parivattante imaṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā yathāvuttena paṭipāṭiyā tayo naye kathente bhikkhū sandhāya vadati.

To clarify that 'here is the essence,' the statement of the great elder Mahāsīva of the Tipiṭaka is cited. Having asked about cessation, and when that was explained, by asking about the arising of perception-knowledge immediately afterwards, he is in effect asking about emergence from cessation. Now, emergence from cessation might occur through the arising of the fruit of arahantship or the fruit of non-returning, and in that, perception is pre-eminent, and immediately after that comes reviewing knowledge. The elder, determining both of these, said, 'What are these monks saying?' Here, 'What are these monks saying?' refers to the monks who, at that time, were reciting the Dīghanikāya, and having reached this point, he speaks with reference to the monks who explain the three methods in the order stated.

Yassa yathā maggavīthiyaṃ maggaphalañāṇesu uppannesu niyamato maggaphalapaccavekkhaṇañāṇāni honti, evaṃ phalasamāpattiyaṃ phalapaccavekkhaṇañāṇanti āha “pacchā paccavekkhaṇañāṇa”nti. “Idaṃ arahattaphala”nti idaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇassa pavattiākāradassanaṃ. Phalasamādhisaññāpaccayāti phalasamādhisahagatasaññāpaccayā. Kira-saddo anussaraṇattho. Yathādhigatadhammānussaraṇapakkhiyā hi paccavekkhaṇā. Samādhisīsena cettha sabbaṃ arahattaphalaṃ gahitaṃ sahacaraṇañāyena, tasmiṃ asati paccavekkhaṇāya asambhavo evāti āha “idappaccayā”ti.

For one in whom the path-and-fruit knowledges have arisen in the path-process, there are invariably knowledges of reviewing the path and fruit. Similarly, in fruition-attainment, there is knowledge of reviewing the fruit—hence, he says, "afterward, the reviewing knowledge." "This is the fruit of arahantship"—this shows the manner of occurrence of the reviewing knowledge. "Conditioned by the perception of fruition-attainment" means conditioned by the perception associated with the concentration of fruition. The word "kira" conveys the sense of recollection. For reviewing belongs to the category of recollecting the Dhamma as it has been realized. Here, the entire fruit of arahantship is included under the heading of concentration, by way of associated knowledge. Because without it, reviewing is impossible—hence, he says, "because of this condition."

Saññāattakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on Perception and Self

417. Desanāya [M 1.0373] saṇhabhāvena sārambhamakkhissādimalavisodhanato [P 1.0487] sutamayañāṇaṃ nhāpitaṃ viya, sukhumabhāvena tanulepanavilittaṃ viya, tilakkhaṇabbhāhatatāya kuṇḍalādialaṅkāravibhūsitaṃ viya ca hoti, tadanupasevato ñāṇassa ca tathābhāvo taṃsamaṅgino puggalassa tathābhāvāpatti, nirodhakathāya nivesanañcassa sirisayanappavesanasadisanti āha “saṇhasukhuma…pe… āropitopī”ti. Tatthāti tassaṃ nirodhakathāyaṃ. Sukhaṃ avindanto mandabuddhitāya alabhanto. Malavidūsitatāya gūthaṭṭhānasadisaṃ. Attano laddhiṃ attadiṭṭhiṃ. Anumatiṃ gahetvāti anuññaṃ gahetvā “ediso me attā”ti anujānāpetvā, attano laddhiyaṃ patiṭṭhapetvāti attho. Kaṃ panāti oḷāriko, manomayo, arūpīti tiṇṇaṃ attavādānaṃ vasena tividhesu katamanti attho. Pariharantoti viddhaṃsanato pariharanto, nigūhantoti adhippāyo. Yasmā catusantatirūpappabandhaṃ ekattavasena gahetvā rūpībhāvato “oḷāriko attā”ti pacceti attavādī, annapānopadhānatañcassa parikappetvā “sassato”ti maññati, rūpībhāvato eva ca saññāya aññattaṃ ñāyāgatameva, yaṃ vedavādino “annamayo, pānamayo”ti ca dvidhā voharanti, tasmā paribbājako taṃ sandhāyā “oḷārikaṃ kho”ti āha.

417. The knowledge derived from learning is like being bathed, due to the cleansing of defilements such as agitation, denigration, and envy through the gentleness of the teaching; it is like being anointed with a subtle ointment, due to its refined nature; and it is like being adorned with ornaments such as earrings, due to being stamped with the three characteristics. For one who does not cultivate it, the knowledge is not in such a state, and the person endowed with it does not attain such a state. The settling in the discourse on cessation is comparable to entering a divine resting place—thus it is said: "gentle, subtle... even when placed upon." There, in that discourse on cessation, one not finding happiness due to dullness of intellect, not obtaining it. Due to being tainted by impurities, it is like a cesspit. Holding onto one’s own view, one’s own opinion—this means having taken approval, that is, having obtained permission and having had it acknowledged, "such is my self," one establishes oneself in one’s own belief. But which one? Coarse, mind-made, or formless—this means among the three kinds based on the three theories of self. 'Avoiding' means protecting from destruction; the intention is 'hiding.' Because the proponent of the self-theory grasps the thirty-fourfold material aggregation as a unity due to its material nature and asserts, "the self is coarse," and having conceived of it as sustained by food and drink, regards it as eternal—and due to its material nature, the otherness of perception is indeed logically inferred—which the adherents of the Vedas speak of in two ways as "made of food" and "made of drink." Therefore, the wanderer, referring to this, said, "indeed, the coarse..."

Tattha yadi attā rūpī, na saññī, saññāya arūpabhāvattā, rūpadhammānañca asañjānanasabhāvattā, rūpī ca samāno yadi tava matena nicco, saññā aparāparaṃ pavattanato tattha tattha bhijjatīti bhedasabbhāvato aniccā, evampi “aññā saññā, añño attā”ti [V 1.0331] saññāya abhāvato acetanoti na kammassa kārako, phalassa ca na upabhuñjakoti āpannameva, tenāha “oḷāriko ca hi te”tiādi. Paccāgacchatoti paccāgacchantassa[P 1.0488], jānatoti attho. “Aññā ca saññā uppajjanti, aññā ca saññā nirujjhantī”ti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu uppādapubbako nirodho, na ca uppannaṃ anirujjhakaṃ nāma atthīti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “catunnañca khandhāna”ntiādi.

Here, if the self is material but not percipient—because perception is immaterial and because material phenomena are by nature incapable of perceiving—then even if the self is material, according to your view it would be permanent. But perception, arising and ceasing repeatedly, is impermanent because, given its nature to break up here and there, it has the characteristic of disintegration. Thus, since 'perception is one thing, the self another,' it follows that due to the absence of perception, the self is non-sentient. Therefore, it cannot be the doer of actions nor the experiencer of results—this is the inevitable conclusion. Hence it is said, "For yours is gross," etc. The term 'returns' (paccāgacchati) means 'for one who returns,' which implies 'knowing.' Why is it said, "Some perceptions arise, and other perceptions cease"? Is not cessation preceded by arising, and is there anything that has arisen that does not cease? Anticipating this objection, it is said, "Of the four aggregates," etc.

418-420. Manomayanti [M 1.0374] jhānamanaso vasena manomayaṃ. Yo hi bāhirapaccayanirapekkho, so manasāva nibbattoti manomayo. Rūpaloke nibbattasarīraṃ sandhāya vadati, yaṃ vedavādino ānandamayo, viññāṇamayoti ca dvidhā voharanti. Tatrāpīti “manomayo attā”ti imasmimpi pakkhe. Dose dinneti “aññāva saññā bhavissatī”tiādinā dose dinne. Idhāpi purimavāde vuttanayeneva dosadassanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ pana viseso – yadi attā manomayo, sabbaṅgapaccaṅgī, ahīnindriyo ca bhaveyya, evaṃ sati “rūpaṃ attā siyā, na ca saññī”ti pubbe viya vattabbaṃ. Tenāha – “manomayo ca hi te”tiādi. Kasmā panāyaṃ paribbājako paṭhamaṃ oḷārikaṃ attānaṃ paṭijānitvā taṃ laddhiṃ vissajjetvā puna manomayaṃ attānaṃ paṭijānāti, tañca vissajjetvā arūpiṃ attānaṃ paṭijānātīti? Kāmañcettha kāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva, tathāpi ime titthiyā nāma anavaṭṭhitacittā thusarāsimhi nikhātakhāṇuko viya cañcalāti dassetuṃ “yathā nāma ummattako”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha saññāyāti pakatisaññāya. Uppādanirodhaṃ icchati aparāparaṃ pavattāya saññāya udayavayadassanato. Tathāpi “saññā saññā”ti pavattasamaññaṃ “attā”ti gahetvā tassa ca avicchedaṃ parikappento sassataṃ maññati, tenāha “attānaṃ pana sassataṃ maññatī”ti.

418-420. "Mind-made" (manomaya) means mind-made by way of the mind of jhāna. For one who is independent of external conditions is produced by the mind alone; thus, "mind-made." This refers to the body produced in the form realm, which the adherents of the Vedas speak of in two ways as "made of bliss" and "made of consciousness." Even in this case—in this view that "the self is mind-made"—when faults are pointed out, such as "there will be another perception," etc. Here too, the showing of faults should be understood in the same way as explained in the previous argument. However, there is this distinction: if the self were mind-made, complete with all major and minor limbs, and with unimpaired faculties, then it should be said, as before, that "form could be the self, but it is not sentient." Therefore, it is stated: "For yours is mind-made," etc. But why does this wanderer first claim a gross self, then abandon that belief and declare a mind-made self, and after abandoning that, claim a formless self? Though the reason for this has already been explained below, still, to show that these sectarians are fickle-minded, unstable like a post planted in a heap of chaff, it is said: "Just like a madman," etc. Here, "perception" refers to natural perception. He accepts the arising and cessation, seeing the rise and fall of perception in its continuous flux. Yet, grasping the conventional term "perception" as "self," and imagining its non-interruption, he believes it to be eternal. Hence it is said: "But he imagines the self as eternal."

Tathevāti yathā “rūpī attā”ti, “manomayo attā”ti ca vādadvaye saññāya attato aññatā, tathā cassa acetanatādidosappasaṅgo dunnivāro[P 1.0489], tatheva imasmiṃ vāde doso. Tenāha “tathevassa dosaṃ dassento”ti. Micchādassanenāti attadiṭṭhisaṅkhātena micchābhinivesena. Abhibhūtattāti anādikālabhāvitabhāvena ajjhotthaṭattā nivāritañāṇacārattā. Taṃ nānattaṃ ajānantoti yena santatighanena, samūhaghanena ca vañcito bālo pabandhavasena pavattamānaṃ dhammasamūhaṃ micchāgāhavasena “attā”ti, “nicco”ti ca abhinivissa voharati, taṃ ekattasaññitaṃ ghanaggahaṇaṃ vinibhujja yāthāvato jānanaṃ ghanavinibbhogo, sabbena sabbaṃ titthiyānaṃ so natthīti ayampi paribbājako tādisassa ñāṇassa paripākassa abhāvato vuccamānampi [V 1.0332] nāññāsi. Tena vuttaṃ “bhagavatā vuccamānampi taṃ nānattaṃ ajānanto”ti. Saññā nāmāyaṃ nānārammaṇā nānākkhaṇe uppajjati, veti cāti saññāya [M 1.0375] uppādanirodhaṃ passantopi saññāmayaṃ saññābhūtaṃ attānaṃ parikappetvā yathāvuttaghanavinibbhogābhāvato niccameva katvā maññati diṭṭhimaññanāya. Tathābhūtassa ca tassa saṇhasukhumaparamagambhīradhammatā na ñāyatevāti vuttaṃ “dujjānaṃ kho”tiādi.

Just as in the two doctrines 'the self is material' and 'the self is mind-made,' perception is different from the self, and thus the implication of flaws such as being without consciousness is unavoidable, so too there is a flaw in this doctrine. Hence it is said: 'showing the flaw in that as well.' 'By wrong view' means: by the wrong adherence designated as the view of self. 'Being overwhelmed' means: being submerged because it has been cultivated since beginningless time, and because the range of knowledge is obstructed. 'Not understanding that diversity' means: The fool, deceived by the compactness of continuity and the compactness of the aggregate, through wrong grasping adheres to the mass of phenomena that proceeds as a continuum, asserting 'this is self,' 'this is permanent.' The analysis of compactness is to break up that compact grasping, which is perceived as a unity, and to know it as it really is. This is entirely absent for the sectarians, and thus this wanderer too, lacking the maturity of such knowledge, did not understand that diversity even when it was being stated by the Blessed One. Therefore it is said: 'though it was being stated by the Blessed One, he did not understand that diversity.' This thing called perception arises with various objects at various moments and ceases. Even while seeing the arising and passing away of perception, because of the absence of the aforesaid analysis of compactness, one conceives a self that is made of perception, that consists of perception, and through the conceit of view, one regards it as permanent. For one who is like that, the subtle, fine, and extremely profound nature of the Dhamma is not known. Hence it is said: 'It is difficult to know,' etc.

Diṭṭhiādīsu “evameta”nti dassanaṃ abhinivisanaṃ diṭṭhi. Tassā eva pubbabhāgabhūtaṃ “evameta”nti nijjhānavasena khamanaṃ khanti. Tathā rocanaṃ ruci. “Aññathā”tiādi tesaṃ diṭṭhiādīnaṃ vibhajitvā dassanaṃ. Tattha aññathāti yathā ariyavinaye antadvayaṃ anupaggamma majjhimā paṭipadāvasena dassanaṃ hoti, tato aññathāyeva. Aññadevāti yaṃ paramatthato vijjati khandhāyatanādi, tassa ca aniccatādi, tato aññadeva paramatthato avijjamānaṃ attānaṃ sassatādi te khamati ceva ruccati ca. Āyuñjanaṃ anuyuñjanaṃ āyogo, tenāha “yuttapayuttatā”ti. Paṭipattiyāti paramattacintanādiparibbājakapaṭipattiyā[P 1.0490]. Dujjānametaṃ dhammataṃ tvaṃ “ayaṃ paramattho, ayaṃ sammutī”ti imassa vibhāgassa dubbibhāgattā. “Yadi etaṃ dujjānaṃ, taṃ tāva tiṭṭhatu, imaṃ panatthaṃ bhagavantaṃ pucchissāmī”ti cintetvā yathā paṭipajji, taṃ dassetuṃ “atha paribbājako”tiādi vuttaṃ. Añño vā saññatoti saññāsabhāvato añño sabhāvo vā attā hotūti attho. Assāti attano.

In matters of views and so on, the seeing and adherence 'this is just so' is a view. The preliminary stage of this, the acceptance 'this is just so' by way of reflection, is approval (khanti). Similarly, finding pleasure in it is delight (ruci). 'Otherwise,' etc., is the exposition distinguishing these views and so on. Herein, 'otherwise' means in a way other than how, in the Noble Discipline, the exposition proceeds by way of the middle path, without approaching the two extremes. 'Something else' means: what exists in an ultimate sense are the aggregates, sense bases, etc., and their impermanence, etc.; but they approve of and delight in something else, a permanent self, etc., which does not exist in an ultimate sense. Applying and engaging is application (āyoga); hence it is said 'being yoked and applied.' 'By practice' means: by the practice of the wanderers, such as contemplation on a supreme self. This principle is difficult to understand because of the difficulty of making the distinction 'this is ultimate, this is conventional.' To show how he proceeded after thinking, 'If this is difficult to understand, let it be for now; I will ask the Blessed One about this matter,' it is said: 'Then the wanderer,' etc. 'Or another from perception' means: or is the self of a nature other than the nature of perception? 'Assa' means 'of the self.'

Lokīyati dissati ettha puññapāpaṃ, tabbipāko cāti loko, attā. So hissa kārako, vedako cāti icchito. Diṭṭhigatanti “sassato attā ca loko cā”tiādi (dī. ni. 1.31; udā. 55) nayappavattaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ. Na hesa diṭṭhābhiniveso diṭṭhadhammikādiatthanissito tadasaṃvattanato. Yo hi tadāvaho, so taṃnissitoti vattabbataṃ labheyya yathā taṃ puññañāṇasambhāro. Eteneva tassa na dhammanissitatāpi saṃvaṇṇitā daṭṭhabbā. Ādibrahmacariyassāti ādibrahmacariyaṃ, tadeva ādibrahmacariyakaṃ yathā “vinayo eva venayiko”ti, (pārā. aṭṭha. 21) tenāha “sikkhattayasaṅkhātassā”tiādi. Diṭṭhābhinivesassa saṃsāravaṭṭe nibbidāvirāganirodhupasamāsaṃvattanaṃ vaṭṭantogadhattā, tassa vaṭṭasambandhanato ca. Tathā abhiññāsambodhanibbānāsaṃvattanañca [M 1.0376] daṭṭhabbaṃ. Abhijānanāyāti ñātapariññāvasena abhijānanatthāya. Sambujjhanatthāyāti tīraṇapahānapariññāvasena sambodhanatthāyāti vadanti. Abhijānanāyāti abhiññāpaññāvasena jānanāya, taṃ pana vaṭṭassa paccakkhakaraṇameva [V 1.0333][P 1.0491] hotīti āha “paccakkhakiriyāyā”ti. Sambujjhanatthāyāti pariññābhisamayavasena paṭivedhāya.

The world (loko) is so called because merit, demerit, and their results are seen (lokīyati) therein; this is the self. For it is this that is intended as the doer and the experiencer. A tenet of view (diṭṭhigata) is a tenet of view that proceeds in the manner of 'the self and the world are eternal,' etc. This adherence to views is not based on benefit in this present life and so on, because it does not lead to that. For whatever brings that about could be said to be based on it, like the accumulation of merit and knowledge. By this same reasoning, it should be seen that its non-reliance on the Dhamma is also explained. Of the fundamentals of the holy life: this is the fundamental holy life (ādibrahmacariya); the same is ādibrahmacariyaka, just as 'the discipline (vinayo) is itself disciplinary (venayiko)'; hence it is said: 'designated as the threefold training,' etc. Adherence to views does not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, and peace concerning the round of saṃsāra, because it is immersed in the round and connected to the round. Similarly, it should be seen that it does not lead to direct knowledge, full enlightenment, and Nibbāna. For direct knowledge means: for the purpose of directly knowing by way of full understanding as the known. For full enlightenment means: for the purpose of full enlightenment by way of full understanding as investigating and as abandoning—so they say. For direct knowledge means: for knowing by means of the wisdom of direct knowledge; but that is just the direct experience of the round; hence it is said: 'for the sake of direct experience.' For full enlightenment means: for penetration by way of the breakthrough of full understanding.

Kāmaṃ taṇhāpi dukkhasabhāvā, tassā pana samudayabhāvena visuṃ gahitattā “taṇhaṃ ṭhapetvā”ti vuttaṃ. Pabhāvanato uppādanato. Dukkhaṃ pabhāventīpi taṇhā avijjādipaccayantarasahitā eva pabhāveti, na kevalāti āha “sappaccayā”ti. Ubhinnaṃ appavattīti ubhinnaṃ appavattinimittaṃ, nappavattanti ettha dukkhasamudayā etasmiṃ vā adhigateti appavatti. Dukkhanirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ gacchati adhigacchati, tadatthaṃ paṭipadā cāti dukkhanirodhagāminīpaṭipadā. Maggapātubhāvoti aggamaggasamuppādo. Phalasacchikiriyāti asekkhaphalādhigamo. Ākāranti taṃ gamanaliṅgaṃ.

Granted, craving too has the nature of suffering, but because it is taken separately as being the origin, it is said, 'having set craving aside.' Because of originating means: because of producing. Although craving originates suffering, it originates it only in conjunction with other conditions such as ignorance, not alone; hence it is said, 'with its conditions.' The non-occurrence of both means: the cause for the non-occurrence of both. Non-occurrence is that wherein suffering and its origin do not proceed, or it is that in which their non-occurrence is attained. The path leading to the cessation of suffering is so called because one goes to, attains, the cessation of suffering, Nibbāna, and it is the practice for that purpose. The manifestation of the path is the arising of the highest path. The realization of the fruit is the attainment of the fruit of one beyond training. Mode means: the sign of that going.

421. Samantato niggaṇhanavasena todanaṃ vijjhanaṃ sannitodakaṃ, vācāyāti ca paccatte karaṇavacananti āha “vacanapatodenā”ti. Sajjhabbharitanti samantato bhusaṃ aritaṃ akaṃsūti satamattehi tuttakehi viya tiṃsasatamattā paribbājakā vācāpatodanehi tudiṃsu sabhāvato vijjamānanti paramatthasabhāvato upalabbhamānaṃ, napakatiādi viya anupalabbhamānaṃ. Tacchanti saccaṃ. Tathanti aviparītaṃ lokuttaradhammesūti visaye bhummaṃ te dhamme visayaṃ katvā. Ṭhitasabhāvanti avaṭṭhitasabhāvaṃ, taduppādakanti attho. Lokuttaradhammaniyāmatanti lokuttaradhammasampāpananiyāmena niyataṃ, tenāha “buddhānañhī”tiādi. Edisāti “dhammaṭṭhitata”ntiādinā vuttappakārā.

421. A thorough goading (sannitodaka) is a goading, a piercing, by way of completely restraining. And vācāya ('by speech') is the instrumental case in the sense of the agent; hence it is said 'with a verbal goad' (vacanapatodena). They were thoroughly assailed means: they assailed them severely from all sides; it is as if about three thousand wanderers goaded them with verbal goads as with about a hundred physical goads. Because it exists by its own nature means: because it is found to exist by its ultimate nature, not unfound like primeval nature (pakati), etc. Taccha means true. Tatha means not distorted. The locative case in 'in the supramundane states' (lokuttaradhammesu) has the sense of 'with regard to,' that is, having made those states the object. Having an established nature means: having a stable nature; the meaning is 'that which produces it.' The fixed nature of the supramundane states means: the fixed nature that brings about the attainment of the supramundane states; hence it is said: 'For of the Buddhas…,' etc. Of such a kind means: of the kind stated by 'the stability of the Dhamma,' etc.

Cittahatthisāriputtapoṭṭhapādavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of Citta Hatthisāriputta and Poṭṭhapāda

422. Sukhumesu atthantaresūti khandhāyatanādīsu sukhumañāṇagocaresu [P 1.0492] dhammesu. Kusaloti pubbe buddhasāsane kataparicayatāya cheko ahosi. Gihibhāve ānisaṃsakathāya kathitattā sīlavantassa [M 1.0377] bhikkhuno tathā kathanena vibbhamane niyojitattā idāni sayampi sīlavā eva hutvā cha vāre (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 37; jā. aṭṭha. 1.1.69) vibbhami. Kammasarikkhakena hi phalena bhavitabbaṃ. Mahāsāvakassa kathiteti mahāsāvakassa mahākoṭṭhikattherassa apasādanakathitanimittaṃ. Patiṭṭhātuṃ asakkontoti sāsane patiṭṭhaṃ laddhuṃ asakkonto.

422. “In subtle matters” refers to the aggregates, sense-bases, and other subtle objects of knowledge accessible to wisdom. “Skillful” means he was adept due to previous familiarity with the Buddha’s Dispensation. Because, in the lay life, he had spoken on its benefits and had thereby caused a virtuous monk to waver, he himself, though now virtuous, went astray six times.
