For results must be commensurate with actions. “Spoken by a great disciple” refers to the occasion of speaking in disparagement of the Elder Mahākoṭṭhita, a great disciple. “Unable to establish himself” means he was unable to gain a firm footing in the Dispensation.

423. Paññācakkhuno natthitāyāti suvuttaduruttasamavisamadassanasamatthapaññācakkhuno abhāvena[V 1.0334]. Cakkhumāti ettha yādisena cakkhunā puriso “cakkhumā”ti vutto, taṃ dassetuṃ “subhāsitā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ekakoṭṭhāsāti ekantikā, nibbānāvahabhāvena nicchitāti adhippāyo. Ṭhapitāti vavatthāpitā. Na ekakoṭṭhāsā na ekantikā, na nibbānāvahabhāvena nicchitā vaṭṭantogadhabhāvatoti adhippāyo.

423. “Because of the absence of the eye of wisdom” means the absence of the eye of wisdom capable of seeing what is well-spoken and ill-spoken, even and uneven. Regarding “one with an eye,” to show by what kind of eye a person is called “one with an eye,” it is said, “well-spoken,” etc. “Categorical” means conclusive; the meaning is that they are determined as leading to Nibbāna. “Established” means defined. “Not categorical” means not conclusive, not determined as leading to Nibbāna because of being immersed in the round of existence—this is the meaning.

Ekaṃsikadhammavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Categorical Teachings

425. “Kasmā ārabhī”ti kāraṇaṃ pucchitvā “aniyyānikabhāvadassanattha”nti payojanaṃ vissajjitaṃ. Sati hi phalasiddhiyaṃ hetusiddhoyeva hotīti. Paññāpitaniṭṭhāyāti paveditavimuttimaggassa, vaṭṭadukkhapariyosānaṃ gacchati etāyāti “niṭṭhā”ti vimutti vuttā. Niṭṭhāmaggo hi idha uttarapadalopena “niṭṭhā”ti vutto. Tassa hi aniyyānikatā, niyyānikatā ca vuccati, na niṭṭhāya. Niyyānaṃ vā niggamanaṃ nissaraṇaṃ, vaṭṭadukkhassa vupasamoti attho. Niyyānameva niyyānikaṃ, na niyyānikaṃ aniyyānikaṃ, so eva bhāvo aniyyānikabhāvo, tassa dassanatthanti yojetabbaṃ. “Eva”nti “nibbānaṃ nibbāna”nti vacanamattasāmaññaṃ gahetvā vadati, na pana paramatthato tesaṃ samaye nibbānapaññāpanassa labbhanato, tena vuttaṃ “sā ca na niyyānikā”tiādi. Lokathūpikādivasenāti [P 1.0493] ettha ādi-saddena “añño puriso, aññā pakatī”ti pakatipurisantarāvabodho mokkho, buddhiādiguṇavinimuttassa attano sakattani avaṭṭhānaṃ mokkho, kāyapavattigatijātibandhānaṃ appamajjanavasena appavatto mokkho, yaññehi jutena parena purisena salokatā mokkho, samīpatā mokkho, sahayogo mokkhoti evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Yathāpaññattāti paññattappakārā hutvā na niyyāti, yenākārena [M 1.0378] “niṭṭhā pāpuṇīyatī”ti tehi paveditā, tenākārena tassā appattabbato na niyyāti. Paṇḍitehi paṭikkhittāti “nāyaṃ niṭṭhā paṭipadā vaṭṭassa anatikkamanato”ti buddhādīhi paṇḍitehi paṭikkhittā. Nivattatīti paṭikkhepassa kāraṇavacanaṃ, tasmā tehi paññattā niṭṭhā paṭipadā na niyyāti, aññadatthu taṃsamaṅginaṃ puggalaṃ saṃsāre eva paribbhamāpentī nivattati.

425. “Why was it undertaken?” Having asked the reason, the purpose was answered as “to show the state of being non-emancipating.” For when the fruit is accomplished, the cause is indeed accomplished. By `paññāpitaniṭṭhāya` is meant of the declared path to consummation. Liberation (`vimutti`) is called `niṭṭhā` (consummation) because by it one reaches the end of the suffering of the round of existence. For here the path to consummation (`niṭṭhāmagga`) is called `niṭṭhā` by eliding the latter word. Of that path, its non-emancipating nature and emancipating nature are spoken, not of the consummation itself. Or, `niyyāna` (emancipation) means escape, release, the cessation of the suffering of the round—this is the meaning. Emancipation itself is 'emancipating'; what is not emancipating is 'non-emancipating.' That very state is the 'non-emancipating state,' and it should be construed as 'for the purpose of showing this.' He speaks thus taking just the verbal similarity 'Nibbāna is Nibbāna,' but not because a designation of Nibbāna in the ultimate sense is obtainable in their doctrine; hence it is said, “And it is not emancipating,” etc. By `lokathūpikādivasena` is meant that here, with the word 'etc.,' the following should be included: the understanding of the distinction between Spirit and Nature—that 'Spirit is one thing and Nature another'—is `mokkha`; the establishment of oneself in one's own self, freed from qualities such as intellect, is `mokkha`; non-activity through non-neglect of bodily conduct, destination, and birth-bonds is `mokkha`; sharing the same world with a supreme person endowed with sacrifice is `mokkha`; proximity is `mokkha`; companionship is `mokkha`—and so on. `Yathāpaññattā` means: being of the kind designated, it does not lead out. The way in which it was declared by them, “the consummation is to be reached,” is a way in which it is unobtainable; therefore it does not lead out. `Paṇḍitehi paṭikkhittā` means: it is rejected by the wise, such as the Buddha, with the words, “This is not the path to consummation, as it does not transcend the round.” `Nivattati` is the statement of the reason for the rejection. Therefore, the path to consummation declared by them does not lead out. On the contrary, it turns back, causing the person endowed with it to wander about right in saṃsāra.

Padhānaṃ jānanaṃ nāma paccakkhato jānanaṃ tassa pamāṇajeṭṭhabhāvato, itarassa saṃsayānubaddhattāti vuttaṃ “jānaṃ passa”nti. Tenettha dassanena jānanaṃ viseseti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tumhākaṃ ekantasukhe loke paccakkhato ñāṇadassanaṃ atthīti. Jānanti vā tassa lokassa [V 1.0335] anumānavisayataṃ pucchati, passanti paccakkhato gocarataṃ. Ayañhettha attho – api tumhākaṃ loko paccakkhato ñāto, udāhu anumānatoti.

Principal knowing is direct knowing, because it is the chief authority, while the other kind is bound up with doubt; hence it is said, 'knowing, seeing.' Thus here he qualifies knowing with seeing. This is what is said: 'Do you have direct knowledge and vision of a world that is exclusively pleasant?' Or, by 'knowing' he asks about that world's status as an object of inference; by 'seeing,' about its status as a directly perceptible domain. This is the meaning here: 'Is that world of yours known directly, or by inference?'

Yasmā loke paccakkhabhūto attho indriyagocarabhāvena pākaṭo, tasmā vuttaṃ “diṭṭhapubbānī”tiādi. Diṭṭhapubbānīti diṭṭhavā, dassanabhūtena, tadanugatena ca ñāṇena gahitapubbānīti attho. Evañca katvā “sarīrasaṇṭhānādīnī”ti vacanaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti. “Appāṭihīraka ta”nti [P 1.0494] anunāsikalopaṃ katvā niddesoti āha “appāṭihīrakaṃ ta”nti “appāṭihīraṃ kata”nti evamettha vaṇṇenti. Paṭipakkhaharaṇato paṭihāriyaṃ, tadeva pāṭihāriyaṃ, uttaravirahitaṃ vacanaṃ. Pāṭihāriyamevettha “pāṭihīraka”nti vā vuttaṃ. Na pāṭihīrakaṃ appāṭihīrakaṃ parehi vuccamānauttarehi sauttarattā, tenāha “paṭiharaṇavirahita”nti. Sauttarañhi vacanaṃ tena uttarena paṭihārīyati ativiparivattīyati. Tato eva niyyānassa paṭiharaṇamaggassa abhāvato “aniyyānika”nti vattabbataṃ labhati.

Because in the world a matter that has become directly perceptible is manifest by being in the range of the sense faculties, it is therefore said, 'things seen before,' etc. 'Things seen before' means seen before, that is, grasped before by vision and by the knowledge that accompanies it. And thus the statement 'bodily form, etc.' is supported. The expression `appāṭihīraka taṃ` is a statement made with the elision of the nasal; some explain it as `appāṭihīraṃ kataṃ`, meaning 'made irrefutable.' A teaching is refutable (`pāṭihāriya`) because it can be countered; it is a statement that admits of a rejoinder. Or else, `pāṭihāriya` is here called `pāṭihīraka`. What is not refutable (`pāṭihīraka`) is irrefutable (`appāṭihīraka`). A teaching is refutable because it admits of a rejoinder from rejoinders spoken by others; therefore he said of the Buddha's teaching that it is 'devoid of being countered.' For a statement that admits of a rejoinder is countered and overturned by that rejoinder. Therefore, because their path is a refutable one, it does not lead to release and comes to be called 'non-emancipating'.

426. Vilāso līḷā. Ākappo kesabandhavatthaggahaṇaṃ ādiākāraviseso, vesasaṃvidhānaṃ vā. Ādi-saddena bhāvādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. “Bhāvo”ti ca cāturiyaṃ veditabbaṃ.

426. `Vilāsa` means grace. `Ākappa` means a particular kind of deportment, such as arranging the hair and putting on garments, or the arrangement of attire. By the word 'etc.,' the inclusion of disposition and so on should be understood. And by 'disposition' (`bhāva`), charm should be understood.

Tayoattapaṭilābhavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Three Acquisitions of Self

428. Āhito ahaṃ māno etthāti attā, attabhāvoti āha “attapaṭilābhoti attabhāvapaṭilābho”ti. Kāmabhavaṃ dasseti tassa itaradvayattabhāvato oḷārikattā. Rūpabhavaṃ dasseti [M 1.0379] jhānamanena nibbattaṃ hutvā rūpībhāvena upalabbhanato. Saṃkilesikā dhammā nāma dvādasa akusalacittuppādā tadabhāve kassaci saṃkilesassāpi asambhavato. Vodāniyā dhammā nāma samathavipassanā tāsaṃ vasena sabbaso cittavodānassa sijjhanato.

428. Self (`attā`) is so called because conceit, ‘I am,’ is placed here; it is individual existence. Thus it is said: ‘Acquisition of self is the acquisition of individual existence.’ It shows sensual existence because it is grosser than the other two existences. It shows form existence because, having been produced by jhāna, it is obtainable as a being with form. Defiling states are the twelve arisings of unwholesome consciousness; in their absence, no defilement whatsoever can arise. Purifying states are serenity and insight; by means of them, the complete purification of mind is accomplished.

429. Paṭipakkhadhammānaṃ asamucchede pana na kadācipi anavajjadhammānaṃ pāripūrī, vepullaṃ vā sambhavati, samucchede pana sati eva sambhavatīti maggapaññāphalapaññā-ggahaṇaṃ. Tā hi sakiṃ paripuṇṇā paripuṇṇā eva aparihānadhammattā. Taruṇapītīti uppannamattā aladdhāsevanā dubbalā pīti. Balavatuṭṭhīti punappunaṃ uppattiyā laddhāsevanā [P 1.0495] uparivisesādhigamassa paccayabhūtā thiratarā pīti. “Yaṃ avocumhā”tiādīsu ayaṃ saṅkhepattho [V 1.0336] – yaṃ vohāraṃ “saṃkilesikavodāniyadhammānaṃ pahānābhivuddhiniṭṭhaṃ paññāya pāripūrivepullabhūtaṃ imasmiṃyeva attabhāve aparappaccayena ñāṇena paccakkhato sampādetvā viharissatī”ti kathayimha. Tattha tasmiṃ vihāre tassa mama ovādakarassa bhikkhuno evaṃ vuttappakārena viharaṇanimittaṃ pamodappabhāvitā pīti ca bhavissati, tassā ca paccayabhūtaṃ passaddhidvayaṃ sammadeva upaṭṭhitā sati ca ukkaṃsagataṃ ñāṇañca tathābhūto ca so vihāro. Santapaṇītatāya atappako anaññasādhāraṇo sukhavihāroti vattabbataṃ arahatīti.

429. But without the eradication of opposing states, the faultless qualities can never reach fulfillment or abundance. Only when they are eradicated can such fulfillment and abundance arise—this is the grasp of path wisdom and fruition wisdom. For once these are fully attained, they remain fully attained, being of a nature that does not decline. ‘Tender joy’ is joy that has just arisen, not yet cultivated, and is thus weak. ‘Strong joy’ is joy that arises repeatedly, has been cultivated, serves as a condition for attaining higher distinctions, and is thus more stable. In the passages beginning with ‘What we have said,’ this is the condensed meaning: The utterance that we spoke was: ‘He will dwell having accomplished by direct knowledge, without dependence on another, in this very life, the fulfillment and abundance of wisdom that culminates in the abandoning of defiling states and the development of purifying states.’ There, in that dwelling, for that monk who follows my advice, joy produced from gladness will arise as a sign of dwelling in the manner thus described. And as its conditions, the twofold tranquility, well-established mindfulness, and exalted knowledge will be present, and that dwelling will be of such a nature. Because of its peacefulness and sublimity, it deserves to be called an untroubled and unequaled dwelling in happiness.

Paṭhamajjhāne paṭiladdhamatte hīnabhāvato pīti dubbalā pāmojjapakkhikā, suvibhāvite pana tasmiṃ paguṇe sā paṇītā balavabhāvato paripuṇṇakiccā pītīti vuttaṃ “paṭhamajjhāne pāmojjādayo chapi dhammā labbhantī”ti. “Sukho vihāro”ti iminā samādhi gahito. Sukhaṃ gahitanti apare, tesaṃ matena santasukhatāya upekkhā catutthajjhāne “sukha”nti icchitā, tenāha “tathā catutthe”tiādi. Pāmojjaṃ nivattatīti dubbalapītisaṅkhātaṃ pāmojjaṃ chasu dhammesu nivattati hāyati. Vitakkavicārakkhobhavirahena dutiyajjhāne sabbadā pīti balavatī eva hoti, na paṭhamajjhāne viya kadāci dubbalā. Suddhavipassanā pādakajjhānamevāti upari maggaṃ akathetvā kevalaṃ vipassanāpādakajjhānaṃ kathitaṃ. Catūhi maggehi saddhiṃ vipassanā kathitāti vipassanāya [M 1.0380] pādakabhāvena jhānāni kathetvā tato paraṃ vipassanāpubbakā cattāropi maggā kathitāti attho. Catutthajjhānikaphalasamāpatti kathitāti paṭhamajjhānikādikā phalasamāpattiyo akathetvā catutthajjhānikā eva phalasamāpatti [P 1.0496] kathitā. Pītivevacanameva katvāti dvinnaṃ pītīnaṃ ekasmiṃ cittuppāde anuppajjanato pāmojjaṃ pītivevacanameva katvā. Pītisukhānaṃ apariccattattā, “sukho ca vihāro”ti sātisayassa sukhavihārassa gahitattā ca dutiyajjhānikaphalasamāpatti nāma kathitā. Kāmaṃ paṭhamajjhānepi pītisukhāni labbhanti, tāni pana vitakkavicārakkhobhena na santapaṇītāni, santapaṇītāni ca idhādhippetāni.

In the first jhāna, when it is just attained, joy is weak due to its inferior state, being an aspect of gladness. But when that jhāna is well-developed and proficient, that joy becomes sublime, strong, and fulfilled in its function—hence it is said: ‘In the first jhāna, gladness and other factors, six in total, are obtained.’ By ‘a happy dwelling,’ concentration is taken. Others say happiness is taken. According to their view, in the fourth jhāna equanimity is intended by ‘happiness’ because of its peaceful happiness. Therefore, it is stated: ‘Similarly in the fourth,’ etc. ‘Gladness ceases’ means that gladness, reckoned as weak joy, ceases and declines among the six factors. In the second jhāna, due to the absence of disturbance from applied and sustained thought, joy is always strong, not sometimes weak as in the first jhāna. ‘Pure insight is only the basic jhāna’ means that without speaking of the higher path, only the jhāna that is the basis for insight is spoken of. ‘Insight is spoken of together with the four paths’ means that after speaking of the jhānas as the basis for insight, the four paths preceded by insight are then spoken of. ‘The attainment of fruition pertaining to the fourth jhāna is spoken of’ means that without speaking of the fruition attainments of the first jhāna and so on, only the fruition attainment of the fourth jhāna is spoken of. By treating gladness as merely a synonym for joy: since two kinds of joy do not arise in a single mind-moment, gladness is treated merely as a synonym for joy. Because joy and happiness are not abandoned, and because ‘and a happy dwelling’ implies a superior happy dwelling, the fruition attainment of the second jhāna is spoken of. Although joy and happiness are obtainable in the first jhāna, they are not peaceful and sublime due to the disturbance of applied and sustained thought. Here, what is intended are the peaceful and sublime states.

432-437. Vibhāvanatthoti pakāsanattho sarūpato nirūpanattho, tenāha “ayaṃ so”tiādi. Nanti oḷārikaṃ attapaṭilābhaṃ. Sappaṭiharaṇanti parena coditavacanena saparihāraṃ sauttaraṃ. Tucchoti musā abhūto. Svevāti so eva attapaṭilābho. Tasmiṃ samaye hotīti tasmiṃ paccuppannasamaye vijjamāno hoti. Attapaṭilābhotveva niyyātesi, na naṃ sarūpato nīharitvā dassesi. Rūpādayo cettha dhammāti rūpavedanādayo eva ettha loke sabhāvadhammā. Attapaṭilābhoti pana te rūpādike pañcakkhandhe upādāya paññatti, tenāha “nāmamattameta”nti. Nāmapaṇṇattivasenāti nāmabhūtapaññattimattatāvasena.

432-437. ‘For the purpose of clarification’ means for the purpose of revealing, for the purpose of defining according to its own nature; therefore, he said, ‘This is that,’ and so on. ‘It’ (`naṃ`) means the gross acquisition of self. ‘Refutable’ (`sappaṭiharaṇaṃ`) means admitting of a defense, of a reply, when challenged by another’s words. ‘Empty’ (`tuccho`) means false, unreal. ‘That very’ (`sveva`) refers to that very acquisition of self. ‘Exists at that time’ means it exists in that present moment. ‘Phenomena such as form, etc., here’ means that form, feeling, and so on are the real phenomena with their own nature in this world. But ‘acquisition of self’ is a designation dependent on those five aggregates, such as form, etc.; therefore, he said, ‘This is merely a name.’ ‘By way of nominal designation’ means by way of being merely a designation that has become a name.

438. Evañca [V 1.0337] pana vatvāti “attapaṭilābhoti rūpādike upādāya paññattimatta”nti imamatthaṃ “yasmiṃ citta samaye”tiādinā vatvā. Paṭipucchitvā vinayanatthanti yathā pare puccheyyuṃ, tenākārena [P 1.0497] kālavibhāgato paṭipadāni pucchitvā tassa atthassa ñāpanavasena vinayanatthaṃ. Tasmiṃ samaye sacco ahosīti tasmiṃ atītasamaye upādānassa vijjamānatāya saccabhūto vijjamāno viya vattabbo ahosi, na pana anāgato idāni paccuppanno vā attapaṭilābho tadupādānassa tadā avijjamānattā. Ye te atītā dhammā atītasamaye atītattapaṭilābhassa upādānabhūtā rūpādayo. Te etarahi natthi niruddhattā. Tato eva ahesunti saṅkhyaṃ gatā. Tasmāti tasmiṃyeva samaye labbhanato. Sopi tadupādāno [M 1.0381] me attapaṭilābho tasmiṃyeva atītasamaye sacco bhūto vijjamāno viya ahosi. Anāgatapaccuppannānanti anāgatānañceva paccuppannānañca rūpadhammānaṃ upādānabhūtānaṃ tadā tasmiṃ atītasamaye abhāvā tadupādāno anāgato paccuppanno ca attapaṭilābho tasmiṃ atītasamaye mogho tuccho musā natthīti attho. Nāmamattamevāti samaññāmattameva. Attapaṭilābhaṃ paṭijānāti paramatthato anupalabbhamānattā.

438. And having said this: having stated with the words, ‘at whatever time the mind…,’ the meaning that ‘the acquisition of self is merely a designation dependent on form, etc.’ For the purpose of instruction, having questioned: for the purpose of instructing by making that meaning known, having questioned about the practices according to the divisions of time in the way that others might ask. ‘At that time, it was true’: at that past time, due to the existence of its basis, it was spoken of as if it were truly existing. However, the future or present acquisition of self was not, since its basis did not exist then. Those past phenomena—form, etc.—which were the basis for the past acquisition of self at that past time, do not exist now, for they have ceased. For that very reason they are reckoned as ‘they were.’ Therefore, because it is obtainable only at that time, that acquisition of self of mine, which had that as its basis, was as if true, real, and existing at that past time. As for the future and present: because future and present phenomena that could be its basis did not exist at that past time, the future and present acquisition of self was, at that past time, void, empty, false, and non-existent. ‘Merely a name’ means merely a convention. He acknowledges the acquisition of self, although in an ultimate sense it is not found.

“Eseva nayo”ti iminā ye te anāgatā dhammā, te etarahi natthi, “bhavissantī”ti pana saṅkhyaṃ gamissanti, tasmā sopi me attapaṭilābho tasmiṃyeva samaye sacco bhavissati. Atītapaccuppannānaṃ pana dhammānaṃ tadā abhāvā tasmiṃ samaye mogho atīto mogho paccuppanno. Ye ime paccuppannā dhammā, te etarahi atthi, tasmā yoyaṃ me attapaṭilābho, so idāni sacco. Atītānāgatānaṃ pana dhammānaṃ idāni abhāvā tasmiṃ samaye mogho atīto mogho anāgatoti evaṃ atthato nāmamattameva attapaṭilābhaṃ paṭijānātīti imamatthaṃ atidisati.

By ‘This is the same method,’ he indicates the following: Those future phenomena do not exist now, but they will be reckoned as ‘they will be’; therefore that acquisition of self of mine will be true at that very time. But since past and present phenomena do not exist then, at that time the past is void and the present is void. These present phenomena exist now; therefore this acquisition of self of mine is true now. But since past and future phenomena do not exist now, at this time the past is void and the future is void. Thus he indicates this meaning: that in this sense, he acknowledges the acquisition of self as being merely a name.

439-443. Saṃsanditunti samānetuṃ. Yasmiṃ samaye khīraṃ hotīti yasmiṃ kāle bhūtupādāyasaññitaṃ [P 1.0498] upādānavisesaṃ upādāya khīrapaññatti hoti. Na tasmiṃ…pe… gacchati khīrapaññattiupādānassa dadhiādipaññattiyā anupādānato. Paṭiniyatavatthukā hi ekā lokasamaññā, tenāha “ye dhamme upādāyā”tiādi. Tattha saṅkhāyati etāyāti saṅkhā, paññatti. Niddhāretvā vacanti vadanti etāyāti nirutti. Namanti etenāti nāmaṃ. Voharanti etenāti vohāro, paññattiyeva. Esa nayo sabbatthāti “yasmiṃ samaye”tiādinā khīre vuttanayaṃ dadhiādīsu atidisati.

439-443. ‘To connect’ means to bring together. ‘At the time when it is milk’ means: at the time when, dependent on a particular basis known as primary and derived matter, the designation ‘milk’ occurs. At that time… it does not apply… because the designation ‘curd,’ etc., is not based on the basis for the designation ‘milk.’ For a worldly convention has a specific object as its ground; therefore, it is said: ‘dependent on which phenomena,’ and so on. Here, ‘reckoning’ (saṅkhā) is that by which something is reckoned; it is a designation. ‘Expression’ (nirutti) is that by which one defines and speaks. ‘Name’ (nāma) is that by which the mind inclines. ‘Usage’ (vohāro) is that by which one engages in worldly transaction; it is just a designation. ‘This is the method in all cases’ means that with the phrase ‘at the time when,’ etc., the principle explained for milk is extended to curd and so on.

Samanujānanamattakānīti “idaṃ khīraṃ, idaṃ dadhī”tiādinā tādise bhūtupādāyarūpavisese loke [V 1.0338] paramparābhataṃ paññattiṃ appaṭikkhipitvā samanujānanaṃ viya paccayavisesavisiṭṭhaṃ rūpādikhandhasamūhaṃ upādāya “oḷāriko attapaṭilābho”ti ca “manomayo attapaṭilābho”ti ca “arūpo [M 1.0382] attapaṭilābho”ti ca tathā tathā samanujānanamattakāni, na ca tabbinimutto upādānato añño koci attho atthīti attho. Niruttimattakānīti saddaniruttiyā gahaṇūpāyamattakāni. “Satto phassoti hi saddaggahaṇuttarakālaṃ tadanuviddhapaṇṇattiggahaṇamukheneva tadatthāvabodho. Vacanapathamattakānīti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Vohāramattakānīti tathā tathā vohāramattakāni. Nāmapaṇṇattimattakānīti tasseva vevacanaṃ, taṃtaṃnāmapaññāpanamattakāni. Sabbametanti “attapaṭilābho”ti vā “satto”ti vā “poso”ti vā sabbametaṃ vohāramattakaṃ paramatthato anupalabbhanato, tenāha “yasmā paramatthato satto nāma natthī”tiādi.

“Mere approvals” means not rejecting a conventional designation handed down by tradition in the world regarding specific kinds of primary and derived matter, such as “this is milk, this is curd,” but merely approving it. Similarly, with reference to the collection of aggregates such as form, distinguished by specific conditions, terms like “the coarse acquired self,” “the mind-made acquired self,” and “the formless acquired self” are also mere approvals. The meaning is that there is no other entity whatsoever apart from this, distinct from what is clung to. “Mere terms of language” means they are mere means for grasping by way of the term of language. For after grasping the sound “a being, contact,” the understanding of its meaning occurs only by way of grasping the designation connected with it. “Mere paths of speech” is a synonym for the same. “Mere conventional usage” refers to such conventional expressions. “Mere name-designations” is another synonym for the same—it means merely designating names. All this—whether called “acquired self,” “a being,” or “a person”—is merely conventional usage, as it is not found in an ultimate sense. Hence it is said: “Because in an ultimate sense, there is no such thing as a being,” etc.

Yadi evaṃ kasmā taṃ buddhehipi vuccatīti āha “buddhānaṃ pana dve kathā”tiādi. Sammutiyā vohārassa kathanaṃ sammutikathā. Paramatthassa sabhāvadhammassa kathanaṃ paramatthakathā. Aniccādikathāpi paramatthasannissitakathā paramatthakathāti katvā paramatthakathā. Paramatthadhammo hi “anicco, dukkho, anattā”ti ca vuccati[P 1.0499], na sammutidhammo. Kasmā panevaṃ duvidhā buddhānaṃ kathāpavattīti tattha kāraṇamāha “tattha yo”tiādinā. Yasmā paramatthakathāya saccasampaṭivedho, ariyasaccakathā ca sikhāppattā desanā, tasmā vineyyapuggalavasena sammutikathaṃ kathentopi bhagavā paramatthakathaṃyeva kathetīti āha “tassa bhagavā āditova…pe… kathetī”ti, tenāha “tathā”tiādi, tenassa katthaci sammutikathāpubbikā paramatthakathā hoti puggalajjhāsayavasena, katthaci paramatthakathāpubbikā sammutikathā. Iti vineyyadamanakusalassa satthu vineyyajjhāsayavasena tathā tathā desanāpavattīti dasseti. Sabbattha pana bhagavā dhammataṃ avijahanto eva sammutiṃ anuvattati, sammutiṃ apariccajantoyeva dhammataṃ vibhāveti, na tattha abhinivesātidhāvanāni. Vuttañhetaṃ “janapadaniruttiṃ nābhiniviseyya, samaññaṃ nātidhāveyyā”ti.

If so, why is this also said by the Buddhas? He says: “But the Buddhas have two kinds of discourse,” etc. A discourse that is a statement of convention is a conventional discourse. A discourse that is a statement of the ultimate, of things in their intrinsic nature, is an ultimate discourse. A discourse on impermanence, etc., being a discourse based on the ultimate, is also considered an ultimate discourse. For it is ultimate reality that is called “impermanent, suffering, non-self,” not conventional reality. But why do the Buddhas’ teachings proceed in these two ways? The reason is stated with the words: “In this regard, whoever,” etc. Because the penetration of the truths comes through ultimate discourse, and the teaching of the Noble Truths is the foremost instruction, therefore, even when the Blessed One speaks conventional discourse, having regard for the person to be trained, he is in fact teaching ultimate discourse. Hence it is said: “From the very beginning, the Blessed One… teaches,” and therefore it is said: “Thus,” etc. Thus, in some cases, ultimate discourse is preceded by conventional discourse, depending on the disposition of the person; in other cases, conventional discourse is preceded by ultimate discourse. In this way, it is shown that the teaching of the Teacher, skilled in taming those to be trained, proceeds in such a way according to the dispositions of the trainees. Yet in all cases, the Blessed One, without abandoning the true nature of things, follows convention; without forsaking convention, he elucidates the true nature, without adherence or transgression therein. As it is said: “One should not insist on a regional dialect, nor should one transgress a common term.”

Paṭhamaṃ sammutiṃ katvā kathanaṃ pana veneyyavasena yebhuyyena buddhānaṃ āciṇṇanti taṃ kāraṇena saddhiṃ dassento “pakatiyā panā”tiādimāha. Nanu ca sammuti nāma paramatthato avijjamānattā abhūtā, taṃ kathaṃ buddhā kathentīti āha “sammutikathaṃ kathentāpī”tiādi. Saccamevāti [M 1.0383] tathameva. Sabhāvamevāti sammutibhāvena taṃsabhāvameva, tenāha “amusāvā”ti. Paramatthassa pana saccādibhāve vattabbameva natthi.

But that speaking after first establishing a convention is, for the most part, the practice of the Buddhas according to the capacity of those to be trained—showing this with its reason, he said: “But by nature…” etc. Now, is it not the case that convention, since it does not exist in an ultimate sense, is unreal? How then do the Buddhas speak it? He says: “Although speaking conventionally…” etc. “It is truly so” means it is just so. “It is its own nature” means it is its own nature in the sense of being a convention. Therefore he said, “it is not false.” But concerning the ultimate, there is nothing at all to be said about its being true and so on.

Imesaṃ [V 1.0339] pana sammutiparamatthānaṃ ko viseso? Yasmiṃ bhinne, buddhiyā vā avayavavinibbhoge kate na taṃsaññā, so ghaṭapaṭādippabhedo sammuti, tabbipariyāyato paramattho. Na hi kakkhaḷaphusanādisabhāve ayaṃ nayo labbhati. Evaṃ santepi vuttanayena sammutipi [P 1.0500] saccasabhāvā evāti āha “duve saccāni akkhāsī”tiādi.

What, then, is the distinction between these conventional and ultimate truths? That which, when it is broken, or when its parts are mentally separated, is no longer perceived as such—such as things like a pot or a cloth—is conventional. The ultimate is the opposite of this. For this principle does not apply to the intrinsic nature of things like hardness, contact, and so on. This being so, according to the method stated, convention too has a true nature. Hence he said: “He declared two truths,” etc.

Idāni nesaṃ saccasabhāvaṃ kāraṇena dassento “saṅketavacanaṃ saccanti gāthamāha. Tattha saṅketavacanaṃ saccaṃ visaṃvādanābhāvato. Tattha hetumāha “lokasammutikāraṇa”nti. Lokasiddhā hi sammuti saṅketavacanassa avisaṃvādanatāya kāraṇaṃ. Paramo uttamo attho paramattho, dhammānaṃ yathābhūtasabhāvo. Tassa vacanaṃ saccaṃ yāthāvato avisaṃvādanavasena ca pavattanato. Tattha kāraṇamāha “dhammānaṃ bhūtalakkhaṇa”nti, sabhāvadhammānaṃ yo bhūto aviparīto sabhāvo, tassa lakkhaṇaṃ aṅganaṃ ñāpananti katvā.

Now, showing the true nature of these with a reason, he speaks the verse: “Conventional speech is true.” Therein, conventional speech is true because of the absence of deception. As to that, he states the reason: “because of worldly convention.” For convention established in the world is the reason for the non-deceptive nature of conventional speech. The ultimate, the supreme meaning, is the ultimate meaning—the real nature of phenomena. The statement of that is true because it proceeds in accordance with reality and without deception. As to that, he states the reason: “the true characteristic of phenomena,” because it is the characteristic, the mark, for making known the real, unperverted intrinsic nature of things.

Yadi tathāgato paramatthasaccaṃ sammadeva abhisambujjhitvā ṭhitopi lokasamaññaṃ gahetvāva vadati, ko ettha lokiyamahājanehi visesoti āha. “Yāhi tathāgato voharati aparāmāsa”ntiādi. Lokiyamahājano appahīnaparāmāsattā “etaṃ mamā”tiādinā parāmasanto voharati, tathāgato pana sabbaso pahīnaparāmāsattā aparāmasanto yasmā lokasamaññāhi vinā lokiyo attho loke kenaci duviññeyyo, tasmā tāhi taṃ voharati. Tathā voharanto eva ca attano desanāvilāsena veneyyasatte paramatthasacce patiṭṭhapeti. Desanaṃ vinivaṭṭetvāti heṭṭhā pavattitakathāya vinivaṭṭetvā vivecetvā desanaṃ “aparāmāsa”nti taṇhāmānaparāmāsappahānakittanena arahattanikūṭena niṭṭhāpesi. Yaṃ yaṃ panettha atthato na vibhattaṃ, taṃ suviññeyyameva.

If the Tathāgata, though he abides having perfectly awakened to the ultimate truth, still speaks by adopting worldly conventions, what is the difference here from the great mass of worldlings? He says: “The Tathāgata speaks without clinging,” etc. The great mass of worldlings, because they have not abandoned clinging, speak while clinging with thoughts like “this is mine.” But the Tathāgata, because he has completely abandoned clinging, speaks without clinging. Since without worldly conventions the worldly meaning would be difficult for anyone in the world to understand, he therefore speaks with them. And by speaking thus, through the grace of his teaching, he establishes the beings to be trained in the ultimate truth. “Having concluded the teaching” means: having concluded and distinguished the teaching from the discourse that was previously occurring, he brought it to a conclusion with “without clinging”—by praising the abandonment of craving, conceit, and clinging—with the peak of arahantship. Whatever herein has not been analyzed as to its meaning is nevertheless quite easy to understand.

Poṭṭhapādasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

The Elucidation of the Concealed Meaning in the Commentary on the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta.

10. Subhasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Subha Sutta

Subhamāṇavakavatthuvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Story of the Young Man Subha

444. “Aciraparinibbute”ti [P 1.0501][V 1.0340][M 1.0384] satthu parinibbutabhāvassa cirakālatāpaṭikkhepena āsannatā dassitā, kālaparicchedo na dassitoti taṃ paricchedato dassetuṃ “parinibbānato uddhaṃ māsamatte kāle”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha matta-ggahaṇena kālassa asampuṇṇataṃ joteti. Tudisaññito gāmo nivāso etassāti todeyyo. Taṃ panesa yasmā soṇadaṇḍo viya campaṃ, kūṭadanto viya ca khāṇumataṃ ajjhāvasati, tasmā vuttaṃ “tassa adhipatittā”ti issarabhāvatoti attho. Samāhāranti sannicayaṃ. Paṇḍito gharamāvaseti yasmā appatarappatarepi vayamāne bhogā khiyanti, appatarappatarepi sañciyamāne vaḍḍhanti, tasmā viññujātiko kiñci vayaṃ akatvā āyameva uppādento gharāvāsaṃ anutiṭṭheyyāti lobhādesitaṃ paṭipattiṃ upadisati.

444. By 'not long after he was finally extinguished': by denying that a long time had passed since the Teacher’s final passing, its nearness is shown. Since the specific time period is not indicated, to indicate it specifically it is said: 'about a month after the final passing.' There, the word 'matta' indicates the incompleteness of the time. One whose residence is the village named Tudi is a Todeyya. But since he, like Soṇadaṇḍa in Campā and Kūṭadanta in Khāṇumata, resided there as its lord, it is therefore said 'because of his overlordship,' meaning because of his sovereignty. 'Accumulation' means gathering. He advises a practice taught out of greed, saying: 'Because wealth diminishes even with very little expenditure and increases even with very little accumulation, a person of understanding should maintain the household life by making no expenditure and only generating income.'

Adānameva sikkhāpetvā lobhābhibhūtatāya tasmiṃyeva ghare sunakho hutvā nibbatti. Lobhavasikassa hi duggati pāṭikaṅkhā. Ativiya piyāyati pubbaparicayena. Piṇḍāya pāvisi subhaṃ māṇavaṃ anuggaṇhitukāmo. Niraye nibbattissasi katokāsassa kammassa paṭibāhituṃ asakkuṇeyyabhāvato.

Having been taught only non-giving, and being overcome by greed, he was reborn as a dog in that very house. For one under the sway of greed, a bad destination is to be expected. He was extremely dear on account of past acquaintance. Desiring to favor the young man Subha, he entered for alms. 'You will be reborn in hell, because it is impossible to ward off the kamma that has found its opportunity.'

Brāhmaṇacārittassa bhāvitataṃ sandhāya, tathā pitaraṃ ukkaṃsento ca “brahmaloke nibbatto”ti āha. Taṃ pavattiṃ pucchīti sutametaṃ mayā “mayhaṃ pitā sunakho hutvā nibbatto”ti tumhehi vuttaṃ, kimidaṃ saccanti pucchi. Tatheva [P 1.0502] vatvāti yathā pubbe sunakhassa vuttaṃ, tatheva vatvā. Avisaṃvādanatthanti saccāpanatthaṃ “todeyyabrāhmaṇo sunakho hutvā nibbatto”ti attano vacanassa avisaṃvādanatthaṃ avisaṃvādabhāvassa dassanatthanti attho. Sabbaṃ dassesīti [V 1.0341] buddhānubhāvena so sunakho taṃ sabbaṃ netvā dassesi, na jātissaratāya. Bhagavantaṃ disvā bhukkaraṇaṃ pana purimajātisiddhavāsanāvasena. Cuddasa pañhe pucchitvāti “dissanti hi bho [M 1.0385] gotama manussā appāyukā, dissanti dīghāyukā. Dissanti bavhābādhā, dissanti appābādhā. Dissanti dubbaṇṇā, dissanti vaṇṇavanto. Dissanti appesakkhā, dissanti mahesakkhā. Dissanti appabhogā, dissanti mahābhogā. Dissanti nīcakulīnā, dissanti uccākulīnā. Dissanti duppaññā, dissanti paññāvanto”ti (ma. ni. 3.289). Ime cuddasa pañhe pucchitvā, aṅgasubhatāya kiresa “subho”ti nāmaṃ labhi.

With reference to the cultivation of the Brahmin's conduct, and also praising his father, he said, 'He was reborn in the Brahma world.' He asked about this occurrence: 'I have heard it said by you, “My father was reborn as a dog.” Is this true?' The phrase 'having spoken just as before' means having spoken just as was previously said about the dog. The phrase 'for the sake of non-deception' means for the sake of establishing the truth; that is, for the purpose of demonstrating the non-contradictory nature of his own statement, 'The Brahmin Todeyya was reborn as a dog.' The phrase 'he showed him everything' means that by the Buddha's power, that dog led him and showed him everything, not through recollection of past lives. The dog's barking upon seeing the Blessed One, however, was due to the habitual tendency from its previous existence. The phrase 'having asked fourteen questions' refers to these: 'Indeed, Master Gotama, people are seen to be short-lived, and long-lived. People are seen with many ailments, and with few ailments. People are seen to be ugly, and beautiful. People are seen to be of little influence, and of great influence. People are seen to be poor, and wealthy. People are seen to be of low birth, and of high birth. People are seen to be unwise, and wise.' Having asked these fourteen questions, it is said he obtained the name 'Subha' due to the beauty of his limbs.

445. “Ekā ca me kaṅkhā atthī”ti iminā upari pucchiyamānassa pañhassa pageva tena abhisaṅkhatabhāvaṃ dasseti. Visabhāgavedanāti dukkhavedanā. Sā hi kusalakammanibbatte attabhāve uppajjanakasukhavedanāpaṭipakkhabhāvato “visabhāgavedanā”ti. Kāyaṃ gāḷhā hutvā bādhati pīḷetīti “ābādho”ti ca vuccati. Ekadese uppajjitvāti sarīrassa ekadese uṭṭhitāpi ayapaṭṭena ābandhitvā viya gaṇhāti aparivattabhāvakaraṇato, etena balavarogo ābādho nāmāti dasseti. Kicchajīvitakaroti asukhajīvitāvaho, etena dubbalo appamattako rogo ātaṅkoti dasseti. Uṭṭhānanti sayananisajjādito uṭṭhahanaṃ, tena yathā tathā aparāparaṃ sarīrassa parivattanaṃ vadati. Garukanti bhāriyaṃ kicchasiddhikaṃ[P 1.0503]. Kāye balaṃ na hotīti etthāpi “gilānassevā”ti padaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Heṭṭhā catūhi padehi aphāsuvihārābhāvaṃ pucchitvā idāni phāsuvihārasabbhāvaṃ pucchati, tena saviseso phāsuvihāro pucchitoti daṭṭhabbo, asatipi atisayatthajotane sadde atisayatthassa labbhanato yathā “abhirūpāya deyyaṃ dātabba”nti.

445. By 'And I have one doubt,' this shows that the question to be asked later had already been formulated by him. 'Dissimilar feeling' is painful feeling. For it is the opposite of the pleasant feeling that arises in an existence produced by wholesome kamma, thus it is called 'dissimilar feeling.' It is called an 'affliction' because, having become severe, it harms and oppresses the body. 'Arisen in one part': even when it has arisen in one part of the body, it grips as if one were bound with an iron band, making one unable to turn; by this it is shown that a strong disease is called an affliction. 'It makes life difficult': it brings an uncomfortable life. By this it is shown that a weak, minor disease is called a disorder. 'Rising' means getting up from lying or sitting, thereby repeatedly turning the body in various ways. 'Severe' means burdensome and difficult to cure. 'There is no strength in the body': here too the words 'of one who is sick' should be brought in and connected. Previously, having asked with four phrases about the absence of a comfortable dwelling, he now asks about the existence of a comfortable dwelling. Thus it should be understood that he asks about a comfortable dwelling with a special quality, since a superlative sense can be obtained even when there is no word indicating a superlative, as in 'a gift should be given to a very beautiful person.'

447. Kālañca samayañca upādāyāti. Ettha kālo nāma upasaṅkamanassa yuttapattakālo. Samayo nāma tasseva paccayasāmaggī, atthato tajjaṃ sarīrabalañceva tappaccayaparissayābhāvo ca. Upādānaṃ nāma ñāṇena tesaṃ gahaṇaṃ sallakkhaṇanti dassetuṃ “kālañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pharissatīti vaḍḍhissati.

447. By 'depending on time and occasion': Here, 'time' means the fitting and opportune time for approaching. 'Occasion' means the concurrence of conditions for that very time—in essence, appropriate bodily strength and the absence of attendant hindrances. 'Depending' means taking hold of these with knowledge and discernment; to show this, 'time and occasion' etc. was said. 'Will pervade' means it will increase.

448. Cetiyaraṭṭheti cetiraṭṭhe. Ya-kārena hi padaṃ vaḍḍhetvā vuttaṃ. Cetiraṭṭhato aññaṃ visuṃyevekaṃ raṭṭhanti ca vadanti. Maraṇapaṭisaṃyuttanti maraṇaṃ [M 1.0386] nāma tādisānaṃ roga vaseneva hotīti yena rogena taṃ jātaṃ, tassa sarūpapucchā, kāraṇapucchā, maraṇahetukacittasantāpapucchā, tassa ca santāpassa sabbalokasādhāraṇatā, tathā maraṇassa ca appatikāratāti evaṃ ādinā maraṇapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ [V 1.0342] sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ kathesīti dassetuṃ “bho ānandā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Na randhagavesī māro viya, na vīmaṃsanādhippāyo uttaramāṇavo viyāti adhippāyo. Yesu dhammesūti vimokkhupāyesu niyyānadhammesu. Dharantīti tiṭṭhanti, pavattantīti attho.

448. 'In the Cetiya country' means in the Ceti country; for the word is spoken expanded with the letter 'ya'. Some also say that the Cetiya country is another, quite separate country from the Ceti country. 'Connected with death': To show that he spoke a friendly talk connected with death—concerning such topics as how death occurs for such beings by way of disease, the nature and cause of that disease, the mental affliction caused by death, the universality of that affliction for all the world, and the irremediability of death—to show this, 'Friend Ānanda,' etc., was said. The intention is not like Māra seeking a weakness, nor like the young man Uttara with an investigative intent. 'In those states' means in the means to liberation, the states leading to emancipation. 'They maintain' means they stand, they continue; this is the meaning.

449. Atthappayuttatāya saddapayogassa saddappabandhalakkhaṇāni tīṇi piṭakāni tadatthabhūtehi sīlādīhi dhammakkhandhehi saṅgayhantīti vuttaṃ “tīṇi piṭakāni tīhi khandhehi saṅgahetvā”ti. Saṅkhittena kathitanti “tiṇṇaṃ khandhāna”nti evaṃ gahaṇato sāmaññato cāti saṅkhepeneva kathitaṃ. “Katamesaṃ tiṇṇa”nti [P 1.0504] ayaṃ adiṭṭhajotanā pucchā, na kathetukamyatā pucchāti vuttaṃ “vitthārato pucchissāmī ‘ti cintetvā ‘katamesaṃ tiṇṇa’nti āhā”ti. Kathetukamyatābhāve panassa therassa vacanatā siyā.

449. The three Piṭakas, which are characterized by a composition of words whose usage is connected with meaning, are summarized by the Dhamma aggregates such as virtue, which constitute their meaning. Thus it was said: 'having summarized the three Piṭakas by the three aggregates.' It was stated briefly: because it is taken generally as 'of the three aggregates,' it is stated concisely. 'Which three?': this is a question to illuminate what has not been seen, not a question from a desire to speak. Thus it is said: 'Thinking, "I will ask in detail," he said, "Which three?"' But if there were a desire to speak, it would be the elder's turn to speak.

Sīlakkhandhavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Aggregate of Morality

450-453. Sīlakkhandhassāti ettha iti-saddo ādiattho, pakārattho vā, tena “ariyassa samādhikkhandhassa…pe… patiṭṭhāpesī”ti ayaṃ ettako pāṭho dassitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ tenāha “tesu dassitesū”ti, uddesavasenāti adhippāyo. Bhagavatā vuttanayenevāti sāmaññaphaladesanādīsu bhagavatā desitanayeneva, tenassa suttassa satthubhāsitabhāvaṃ jinavacanabhāvaṃ dasseti. Sāsane na sīlameva sāroti ariyamaggasāre bhagavato sāsane yathā dassitaṃ sīlaṃ sāro eva na hoti sāravato mahato rukkhassa papaṭikaṭṭhāniyattā. Yadi evaṃ kasmā idha gahitanti āha “kevalañhetaṃ patiṭṭhāmattakamevā”ti. Jhānādiuttarimanussadhamme adhigantukāmassa adhiṭṭhānamattaṃ tattha appatiṭṭhitassa tesaṃ asambhavato. Atha vā na sīlameva sāroti kāmañcettha sāsane “maggasīlaṃ, phalasīla”nti idaṃ lokuttarasīlampi sārameva, tathāpi na sīlakkhandho eva sāro atha kho samādhikkhandhopi paññākkhandhopi [M 1.0387] sāro evāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Purimo eva sāro, tenāha “ito uttarī”tiādi.

450-453. Herein, in the phrase sīlakkhandhassa, the word iti has the sense of 'beginning' or the sense of 'manner.' Therefore, it should be understood that this much of the text is shown: '…he established the noble aggregate of concentration…' Hence it is said, 'among those shown,' the intention being 'by way of a summary statement.' 'In the way spoken by the Blessed One' means in the way taught by the Blessed One in discourses such as the Discourse on the Fruits of Recluseship; thereby he shows that this sutta is spoken by the Teacher, the word of the Victor. In the Dispensation, morality alone is not the essence: in the Blessed One’s Dispensation, of which the noble path is the essence, morality as shown is not the essence, being like the bark of a great tree with a substantial core. If so, why is it taken up here? He says: 'For this is merely a foundation.' For one who wishes to attain the higher human states such as the jhānas, it is a mere basis, since for one not established in it, their attainment is impossible. Alternatively, it is not that morality alone is the essence; for although in this Dispensation this supramundane morality, namely 'path morality and fruition morality,' is indeed essential, still, the aggregate of morality is not the sole essence; rather, the aggregate of concentration and the aggregate of wisdom are also essential. Thus the meaning here should be understood. The former explanation is the essential one; hence it is said, 'beyond this,' and so on.

Samādhikkhandhavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Aggregate of Concentration

454. Kasmā panettha thero samādhikkhandhaṃ puṭṭho indriyasaṃvarādike vissajjesi, nanu evaṃ sante aññaṃ puṭṭho aññaṃ byākaronto ambaṃ puṭṭho labujaṃ byākaronto viya hotīti īdisī codanā idha anokāsāti dassento “kathañca māṇava bhikkhu…pe… samādhikkhandhaṃ dassetukāmo [V 1.0343] ārabhī”ti āha, tenettha indriyasaṃvarādayopi samādhiupakārataṃ upādāya samādhikkhandhapakkhikāni uddiṭṭhānīti dasseti rūpajjhānāneva āgatāni, na arūpajjhānāni rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānadesanānantaraṃ abhiññādesanāya avasaroti katvā. Rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānapādikā hi saparibhaṇḍā chapi abhiññāyo. Lokiyā abhiññā [P 1.0505] pana sijjhamānā yasmā aṭṭhasu samāpattīsu cuddasavidhena cittaparidamanena vinā na ijjhanti, tasmā abhiññāsu desiyamānāsu arūpajjhānānipi desitāneva honti nānantariyabhāvato, tenāha “ānetvā pana dīpetabbānī”ti. Vuttanayena desitāneva katvā saṃvaṇṇakehi pakāsetabbānīti attho. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “catutthajjhānaṃ upasampajja viharatī”ti imināva arūpajjhānampi saṅgahitanti dassetuṃ “catutthajjhānena hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Catutthajjhānañhi rūpavirāgabhāvanāvasena pavattaṃ “arūpajjhāna”nti vuccatīti.

454. Why did the elder, when asked about the aggregate of concentration, answer with restraint of the senses and the like? Is it not the case that in doing so, by answering about one thing when asked about another, he becomes like one who answers about a breadfruit when asked about a mango? To show that such an objection has no place here, he said: 'And how, young man, does a bhikkhu… wishing to show the aggregate of concentration, begin?' Thereby he shows that restraint of the senses and the like are pointed out as belonging to the side of the aggregate of concentration on account of their being supportive of concentration. Only the form jhānas are included, not the formless jhānas, because the occasion for teaching the higher knowledges arises immediately after the teaching on the fourth form-realm jhāna. For the six higher knowledges with their equipment have the fourth form-realm jhāna as their basis. However, since the mundane higher knowledges are not accomplished without the fourteen kinds of mind-taming in the eight attainments, when the higher knowledges are being taught, the formless jhānas are also taught because of their immediate sequence. Hence he said: 'But they should be brought in and explained.' The meaning is that, having been taught in the way stated, they should be elucidated by the commentators. In the commentary, however, to show that the formless jhānas are also included by the phrase 'he enters and abides in the fourth jhāna,' the passage beginning 'for by the fourth jhāna' was stated. For the fourth jhāna, when it proceeds by way of developing dispassion towards form, is called a 'formless jhāna.'

471-480. Na cittekaggatāmattakenevāti ettha heṭṭhā vuttanayānusārena attho veditabbo. Lokiyassa samādhikkhandhassa adhippetattā “na citte…pe… atthī”ti vuttaṃ. Ariya-saddo cettha suddhapariyāyo, na lokuttarapariyāyo. Tathā heṭṭhāpi lokiyābhiññāpaṭisambhidāhi vināva arahatte adhigate nattheva uttariṃkaraṇīyanti sakkā vattuṃ yadatthaṃ bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati, tassa siddhattā. Idha pana lokiyābhiññāpi āgatā eva. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

471-480. Here, in the phrase 'not by mere one-pointedness of mind alone,' the meaning should be understood in accordance with the method stated below. Because the mundane aggregate of concentration is intended, it is said: 'Not by mere one-pointedness… is there…' Here the word ariya is a term for 'pure,' not a term for 'supramundane.' Similarly, below also, it can be said that when arahantship has been attained even without the mundane higher knowledges and analytical knowledges, there is nothing further to be done, since that for the sake of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One has been accomplished. Here, however, the mundane higher knowledges are also included. The rest is easy to understand.

Subhasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Subha Sutta

11. Kevaṭṭasuttavaṇṇanā

11. Commentary on the Kevaṭṭa Sutta

Kevaṭṭagahapatiputtavatthuvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Story of Kevaṭṭa, the Householder's Son

481. Pāvārikambavaneti [M 1.0388][V 1.0344][P 1.0506] pāvārikaseṭṭhino ambabahule upavane. Taṃ kira so seṭṭhī bhagavato anucchavikaṃ gandhakuṭiṃ, bhikkhusaṅghassa ca rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānakuṭimaṇḍapādīni sampādetvā pākāraparikkhittaṃ dvārakoṭṭhakasampannaṃ katvā buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa niyyātesi, purimavohārena pana “pāvārikambavana”nti vuccati, tasmiṃ pāvārikambavane. Kevaṭṭoti idaṃ tassa nāmaṃ kevaṭṭehi saṃrakkhitattā, tesaṃ vā santike saṃvaḍḍhitattāti keci. “Gahapatiputtassā”ti ettha kāmaṃ tadā so gahapatiṭṭhāne ṭhito, pitu panassa acirakālaṃkatatāya purimasamaññāya “gahapatiputto” tveva voharīyati, tenāha “gahapati mahāsālo”ti. Mahāvibhavatāya mahāsāro, gahapatīti attho ra-kārassa la-kāraṃ katvā “mahāsālo sukhumālo aha”ntiādīsu (a. ni. 3.39) viya. Saddhāsampannoti pothujjanikāya saddhāya vasena saddhā samannāgato.

481. At Pāvārika's Mango Grove means in the park of the banker Pāvārika, which was full of mango trees. It is said that this banker, having prepared a perfumed chamber suitable for the Blessed One, and huts, pavilions, and so forth for the Sangha of bhikkhus to stay in by day and by night, and having enclosed it with a wall and furnished it with gatehouses, dedicated it to the Sangha with the Buddha at its head. But by its former designation it is called 'Pāvārika's Mango Grove'; thus, at Pāvārika's Mango Grove. Kevaṭṭa: this was his name, some say, either because he was protected by fishermen or because he was raised in their vicinity. Of the householder's son: Here, although at that time he was established in the position of a householder, because his father had passed away not long before, he was still referred to by his former designation, 'householder's son.' Hence it is said, 'a householder of great wealth.' Mahāsālo: on account of his great wealth, he is one of great substance (mahāsāro), which means 'a householder'; the 'l' is a change from 'r', as in such passages as 'I was a man of great substance, delicate' (AN 3.39). Endowed with faith means possessed of faith by way of the faith of an ordinary person.

Samiddhāti sammadeva iddhā, iddhiyā vibhavasampattiyā vepullappattāti attho. “Ehi tvaṃ bhikkhu anvaddhamāsaṃ, anumāsaṃ, anusaṃvaccharaṃ vā manussānaṃ pasādāya iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ karohī”ti ekassa bhikkhuno āṇāpanaṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne tassa ṭhapanaṃ nāma hotīti āha “ṭhānantare ṭhapetū”ti. Uttarimanussānaṃ [P 1.0507] dhammatoti uttarimanussānaṃ buddhādīnaṃ adhigamadhammato. Niddhāraṇe cetaṃ nissakkaṃ. Iddhipāṭihāriyañhi tato niddhāreti. Manussadhammato uttarīti pakatimanussadhammato upari. Pajjalitapadīpoti pajjalanto padīpo.

Prosperous (samiddha) means rightly prosperous (sammadeva iddhā); the meaning is having attained abundance through the accomplishment of spiritual power and wealth. The command given to a single bhikkhu, 'Come, bhikkhu, every half-month, every month, or every year, perform a miracle of psychic power for the confidence of the people,' and the establishing of him in that position, is called 'appointment' (ṭhapanaṃ). Hence he says, 'let him appoint him to another position.' From a superhuman state means from the state of attainment of superhuman beings such as the Buddhas. This is doubtless in the sense of a specification, for he specifies the miracle of psychic power from that. Superior to the human state means above the ordinary human state. A blazing lamp means a lamp that is blazing.

482. Na dhaṃsemīti guṇasampattito na cāvemi, tenāha “sīlabheda”ntiādi. Vissāsaṃ vaḍḍhetvā bhagavati attano vissatthabhāvaṃ brūhetvā vibhūtaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā.

482. I do not destroy means I do not cause to fall from the accomplishment of virtue; hence he says, 'a breach of morality,' etc. Having increased his confidence in the Blessed One, having augmented his own state of trust, having made it manifest and evident.

Iddhipāṭihāriyavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Miracle of Psychic Power

483-4. Ādīnavanti [V 1.0345][M 1.0389] dosaṃ. Gandhārīti cūḷagandhārī, mahāgandhārīti dve gandhārīvijjā. Tattha cūḷagandhārī nāma tivassato oraṃ matānaṃ sattānaṃ upapannaṭṭhānajānanavijjā. Mahāgandhārī tampi jānāti tato uttaripi iddhividhañāṇakappaṃ yebhuyyena iddhividhakiccaṃ sādheti. Tassā kira vijjāya sādhako puggalo tādise desakāle mantaṃ parijappitvā bahudhāpi attānaṃ dasseti, hatthiādīnipi dasseti, dassanīyopi hoti, aggithambhampi karoti, jalathambhampi karoti, ākāsepi attānaṃ dasseti. Sabbaṃ indajālasadisaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aṭṭoti dukkhito bādhito, tenāha “pīḷito”ti.

483-4. 'Danger' means fault. Gandhārī—the Lesser Gandhārī and the Greater Gandhārī—are two Gandhārī sciences. Herein, the Lesser Gandhārī is the science of knowing the place of rebirth of beings who have died within three years. The Greater Gandhārī knows that and even more; for the most part, being comparable to the knowledge of the kinds of psychic power, it accomplishes the tasks of psychic power. It is said that a practitioner of this science, having recited the mantra at such a place and time, can manifest himself in many ways, show elephants and the like, become visible, create a pillar of fire, create a pillar of water, and display himself in the sky. All this should be seen as similar to a magical illusion. 'Afflicted' means distressed, oppressed—hence it is said 'tormented.'

Ādesanāpāṭihāriyavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Miracle of Telepathy

485. Kāmaṃ “cetasika”nti padaṃ ye cetasi niyuttā cittena sampayuttā, tesaṃ sādhāraṇavacanaṃ, sādhāraṇe pana gahite cittaviseso gahitova hoti, sāmaññajotanā ca visese avatiṭṭhatīti cetasikaggahaṇassa adhippāyaṃ vivaranto “somanassadomanassaṃ adhippeta”nti āha. Somanassaggahaṇena cettha tadekaṭṭhā rāgādayo, saddhādayo ca dassitā honti, domanassaggahaṇena dosādayo. Vitakkavicārā pana sarūpeneva dassitā. Evaṃ tava manoti iminā ākārena tava mano pavattoti attho[P 1.0508]. Kena pakārena pavattoti āha “somanassito vā”tiādi. “Evaṃ tava mano”ti idaṃ pana somanassitatādimattadassanaṃ, na pana yena yena somanassito vā domanassito vā, taṃ taṃ dassanaṃ. Dutiyanti “itthampi te mano”ti idaṃ. Itipīti ettha iti-saddo nidassanattho “atthīti kho, kaccāna, ayameko anto”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.15; 3.90) viya, tenāha “imañca imañca atthaṃ cintayamāna”nti pi-saddo vuttatthasampiṇḍanattho. Parassa cintaṃ manati jānāti etenāti cintāmaṇi. Tassā kira vijjāya sādhako puggalo tādise desakāle mantaṃ parijappitvā yassa cittaṃ jānitukāmo, tassa diṭṭhasutādivisesasañjānanamukhena cittācāraṃ [M 1.0390] anuminanto kathetīti keci. Apare “vācaṃ niccharāpetvā tattha akkharasallakkhaṇavasenā”ti vadanti.

485. Granted that the word 'mental' is a general term for what is engaged in the mind and associated with consciousness, when the general is taken, a specific aspect of consciousness is also taken, and the illumination of the general rests on the particular. Thus, explaining the intention behind taking up 'mental,' he says that 'joy and sorrow are intended.' Here, by taking up joy, states that share its basis, such as lust and faith, are shown; by taking up sorrow, states such as hatred are shown. But initial and sustained thought are shown by their own nature. 'Thus is your mind' means your mind proceeds in this manner. In what manner does it proceed? He says: 'accompanied by joy, or…' etc. 'Thus is your mind' is a statement showing merely the presence of joy and so on, not that by which one is joyful or sorrowful. The second phrase is 'in this way too, is your mind.' Herein, in 'in this way too,' the word 'thus' (iti) is for the purpose of illustration, as in such passages as 'This, Kaccāna, is one extreme' (SN 12.15). Therefore he says, 'thinking of this and that matter.' The word 'too' (pi) serves to summarize what has been said. 'Thought-jewel' (cintāmaṇi): because by this one knows (manati) another's thought (cintaṃ). It is said that a practitioner of this science, having recited the mantra at a suitable time and place, when he wants to know another's mind, infers the behavior of the mind by way of recognizing the particulars of what has been seen, heard, etc., and then speaks—so some say. Others say, 'by having him utter speech and then by way of discerning the syllables therein.'

Anusāsanīpāṭihāriyavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Miracle of Instruction

486. Pavattentāti pavattanakā hutvā, pavattanavasenāti attho. “Eva”nti hi padaṃ yathānusiṭṭhāya [V 1.0346] anusāsaniyā vidhivasena, paṭisedhavasena ca pavattiākāraparāmasanaṃ, sā ca sammāvitakkānaṃ micchāvitakkānañca pavattiākāradassanavasena pavattati tattha ānisaṃsassa ādīnavassa ca vibhāvanatthaṃ. Aniccasaññameva na niccasaññanti attho. Paṭiyogīnivattanatthañhi eva-kāraggahaṇaṃ. Idhāpi evaṃ saddaggahaṇassa attho, payojanañca vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Idaṃgahaṇepi eseva nayo. Pañcakāmaguṇikarāganti nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, tadaññarāgassa, dosādīnañca pahānassa icchitattā, tappahānassa ca tadaññarāgādikhepanassa upāyabhāvato tathā vuttaṃ duṭṭhalohitavimocanassa [P 1.0509] pubbaduṭṭhamaṃsakhepanūpāyatā viya. Lokuttaradhammamevāti avadhāraṇaṃ paṭipakkhabhāvato sāvajjadhammanivattanaparaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ tassādhigamūpāyānisaṃsabhūtānaṃ tadaññesaṃ anavajjadhammānaṃ nānantariyabhāvato. Iddhividhaṃ iddhipāṭihāriyanti dasseti iddhidassanena parasantāne pasādādīnaṃ paṭipakkhassa haraṇato. Iminā nayena sesapadadvayepi attho veditabbo. Satataṃ dhammadesanāti sabbakālaṃ desetabbadhammadesanā.

486. 'They cause to occur' means: being agents of occurrence; that is, in the sense of causing to occur. The word 'thus' (evaṃ) refers to the mode of occurrence in accordance with the instruction and guidance given, both by way of injunction and prohibition. And this proceeds by way of showing the mode of occurrence of right thoughts and wrong thoughts, for the purpose of clarifying their benefits and drawbacks. 'Only the perception of impermanence' means not the perception of permanence. The taking up of the particle 'only' (eva) is for the purpose of excluding its opposite. Here too, the meaning and purpose of taking up the word 'thus' (evaṃ) should be understood in the way stated. The same method applies to the taking up of 'this' (idaṃ). 'Lust connected with the five cords of sensual pleasure' should be seen as a mere illustration, for the abandonment of other kinds of lust, hatred, etc., is intended; and it is stated thus because the abandonment of this is a means for dispelling other kinds of lust, etc., just as the removal of corrupted blood is a means for dispelling previously corrupted flesh. 'Only the supramundane Dhamma' is an emphasis; it should be seen as being for the purpose of removing blameworthy states, since it is opposed to them, and because other blameless states, which are the means for its attainment and its benefits, are immediately connected. 'The kinds of psychic power' indicates the miracle of psychic power, because by the display of psychic power one removes what is opposed to faith, etc., in the mental continuities of others. The meaning of the remaining two phrases should be understood in this way. 'Constant teaching of the Dhamma' means the teaching of the Dhamma that should be taught at all times.

Iddhipāṭihāriyenāti sahayoge karaṇavacanaṃ, iddhipāṭihāriyena saddhinti attho. Ādesanāpāṭihāriyenāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Dhammasenāpatissa āciṇṇanti yojanā. “Cittācāraṃ ñatvā”ti iminā ādesanāpāṭihāriyaṃ dasseti. “Dhammaṃ desesī”ti iminā anusāsanīpāṭihāriyaṃ “buddhānaṃ satataṃ dhammadesanā”ti anusāsanīpāṭihāriyassa tattha sātisayatāya vuttaṃ. Saupārambhāni patirūpena upārambhitabbato. Sadosāni dosasamucchindanassa anupāyabhāvato. Sadosattā eva addhānaṃ na tiṭṭhanti cirakālaṭṭhāyīni na honti. Addhānaṃ atiṭṭhanato na niyyantīti phalena hetuno anumānaṃ. Aniyyānikatāya hi tāni anaddhaniyāni. Anusāsanīpāṭihāriyaṃ anupārambhaṃ visuddhippabhavato, visuddhinissayato [M 1.0391] ca. Tato eva niddosaṃ. Na hi tattha pubbāparavirodhādidosasambhavo. Niddosattā eva addhānaṃ tiṭṭhati paravādavātehi, kilesavātehi ca anupahantabbato. Tasmāti yathāvuttakāraṇato, tena saupārambhādiṃ, anupārambhādiṃ cāti ubhayaṃ ubhayattha yathākkamaṃ gārayhapāsaṃsabhāvānaṃ hetubhāvena paccāmasati.

'By the miracle of psychic power': this is the instrumental case in the sense of accompaniment; the meaning is 'together with the miracle of psychic power.' 'By the miracle of telepathy': here too the same method applies. 'Practiced by the General of the Dhamma' is the connection. 'Having known the behavior of the mind' shows the miracle of telepathy. 'He taught the Dhamma' indicates the miracle of instruction. It is said 'the constant teaching of the Dhamma by the Buddhas' because the miracle of instruction is especially excellent in that case. They are censurable because they are to be reproached in a fitting manner. They are faulty because they are not a means for eradicating faults. Because they are faulty, they do not endure; they are not long-lasting. Because they do not endure, they are not liberating—this is an inference of the cause from the effect. Indeed, because they are non-liberating, they are not long-lasting. The miracle of instruction is irreproachable because it originates from purity and is founded on purity. For that very reason it is faultless. For in it there is no possibility of such faults as contradiction between what comes before and what comes after. Because it is faultless, it endures, since it cannot be assailed by the winds of others' doctrines or by the winds of the defilements. 'Therefore' means for the reason stated. By this he considers both sets of qualities—the censurable, etc., and the irreproachable, etc.—each in its own place and in sequence, as the cause for their being reprehensible and praiseworthy.

Bhūtanirodhesakavatthuvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Story of Seeking the Cessation of the Elements

487. Aniyyānikabhāvadassanatthanti [P 1.0510] yasmā mahābhūtapariyesako bhikkhu purimesu dvīsu pāṭihāriyesu vasippatto kusalopi samāno mahābhūtānaṃ aparisesanirodhasaṅkhātaṃ nibbānaṃ nāvabujjhi[V 1.0347], tasmā tāni niyyānāvahatābhāvato aniyyānikānīti tesaṃ aniyyānikabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Tatiyaṃ pana takkarassa ekantato niyyānāvahanti tasseva niyyānikabhāvadassanatthaṃ.

487. For the purpose of showing their non-leading-out nature: Since a bhikkhu seeking the great elements, although skilled and having attained mastery in the first two miracles, did not understand Nibbāna—designated as the cessation without remainder of the great elements—therefore, because those miracles do not bring about an escape, they are non-leading-out. The third miracle, however, certainly brings about an escape for such a person; thus its leading-out nature is shown.

Evametissā desanāya mukhyapayojanaṃ dassetvā idāni anusaṅgikampi dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Mahābhūte pariyesantoti aparisesaṃ nirujjhanavasena mahābhūte gavesanto, tesaṃ anavasesanirodhaṃ vīmaṃsantoti attho. Vicaritvāti dhammatāya codiyamāno vicaritvā. Dhammatāsiddhaṃ kiretaṃ, yadidaṃ tassa bhikkhuno tathā vicaraṇaṃ, yathā abhijātiyaṃ mahāpathavikampādi. Mahantabhāvappakāsanatthanti sadevake loke anaññasādhāraṇassa buddhānaṃ mahantabhāvassa mahānubhāvatāya dīpanatthaṃ. Idañca kāraṇanti sabbesampi buddhānaṃ sāsane īdiso eko bhikkhu tadānubhāvappakāsano hotīti idampi kāraṇaṃ dassento.

Having thus shown the primary purpose of this teaching, now, to indicate a secondary purpose as well, the text beginning with “Moreover” is stated. “Seeking the great elements” means searching for the great elements by way of their cessation without remainder; the meaning is investigating their cessation without remainder. “Having wandered” means having wandered, being impelled by the nature of things. This, it seems, was accomplished by the nature of things—that is, that bhikkhu’s wandering in such a way, just as the great earth trembles and so on at a noble birth. For the purpose of revealing greatness: for the purpose of illuminating the greatness and great power of the Buddhas, which is not shared by others in the world with its devas. “And this reason”: showing this reason too, that in the dispensation of all Buddhas there is one such bhikkhu who makes that power manifest.

Katthāti nimitte bhummaṃ, tasmā katthāti kismiṃ ṭhāne kāraṇabhūte. Kiṃ āgammāti kiṃ ārammaṇaṃ paccayabhūtaṃ adhigantvā, tenāha “kiṃ pattassā”ti. Teti mahābhūtā. Appavattivasenāti anuppajjanavasena. Sabbākārenāti vacanatthalakkhaṇādisamuṭṭhānakalāpacuṇṇanānattekattavinibbhogāvinibbhoga- sabhāgavisabhāgaajjhattikabāhirasaṅgahapaccayasamannāhārapaccayavibhāgākārato, sasambhārasaṅkhepasasambhāravibhattisalakkhaṇasaṅkhepasalakkhaṇavibhattiākārato cāti sabbena ākārena.

As to “where?”: this is a locative of sphere. Therefore, “where?” means in what place that is a causal ground. As to “relying on what?”: this means having attained what as an object and condition. Therefore it is said: “What has one attained?” “They” refers to the great elements. As to “by way of non-occurrence”: by way of non-arising. As to “in every way”: in all ways, that is, from the perspective of the characteristics of the term’s meaning, etc.; from the perspective of origin, group, fine particles, diversity and unity, distinction and non-distinction, homogeneous and heterogeneous, internal and external, inclusion, combination of conditions, and analysis of conditions; and from the perspective of a summary with components, an analysis with components, a summary with characteristics, and an analysis with characteristics.

488. Dibbanti [M 1.0392] ettha pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samaṅgībhūtā hutvā vicaranti, kīḷanti, jotanti cāti devo, devaloko. Taṃ yanti upagacchanti etenāti devayāniyo. Vasaṃ vattentoti [P 1.0511] ettha vasavattanaṃ nāma yathicchitaṭṭhānagamanaṃ. Cattāro mahārājāno etesaṃ issarāti cātumahārājikā yā devatā maggaphalalābhino tā tamatthaṃ ekadesena jāneyyuṃ buddhavisayo panāyaṃ pañhoti cintetvā “na jānāmā”ti āhaṃsu, tenāha “buddhavisaye”tiādi. Ajjhottharaṇaṃ nāmettha nippīḷananti āha “punappunaṃ pucchatī”ti. Abhikkantatarāti rūpasampattiyā ceva paññāpaṭibhānādiguṇehi ca amhe abhibhuyya paresaṃ kāmanīyatarā. Paṇītatarāti uḷāratarā, tenāha “uttamatarā”ti.

488. As to “divine”: here, because they wander, play, and shine, being endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, they are devas, and it is the deva world. That by which one goes to it, approaches it, is a “deva-vehicle.” As to “exercising control”: here, exercising control means going to any desired place. The Four Great Kings are lords over these deities, thus they are of the realm of the Four Great Kings. Those deities who are attainers of the path and fruit might know that matter in part, but thinking, “This question is the domain of a Buddha,” they said, “We do not know.” Hence it is said, “in the domain of a Buddha,” etc. Here, “overwhelming” means pressing; thus it is said, “he asks again and again.” As to “far more excellent”: surpassing us in accomplishment of form and in qualities such as wisdom and ready wit, they are more desirable to others. As to “more sublime”: more lofty; hence it is said, “more supreme.”

491-3. Devayāniyasadiso iddhividhañāṇasseva adhippetattā. “Devayāniyamaggoti vā [V 1.0348] …pe… sabbametaṃ iddhividhañāṇasseva nāma”nti idaṃ pāḷiyaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu ca tattha tattha āgataruḷhivasena vuttaṃ.

491-3. Because it is similar to a deva-vehicle, it is intended as precisely the knowledge of the kinds of psychic power. The statement, “The deva-vehicle path… all this is a name for the knowledge of the kinds of psychic power,” is said in the Pāli Canon and the commentaries according to the established usage found in various places.

494. Āgamanapubbabhāge nimittanti brahmuno āgamanassa pubbabhāge uppajjananimittaṃ. Pāturahosīti āvi bhavi. Pākaṭo ahosīti pakāso ahosi.

494. “The sign in the preliminary stage of arrival” means the sign that arises in the preliminary stage of Brahmā’s arrival. “Appeared” means became visible. “Became evident” means became manifest.

497. Padesenāti ekadesena, upādinnakavasena, sattasantānapariyāpannenāti attho. Anupādinnakepīti anindriyabaddhepi. Nippadesato anavasesato. Pucchāmūḷhassāti pucchituṃ ajānantassa. Pucchāya dosaṃ dassetvāti tena katapucchāya pucchitākāre dosaṃ vibhāvetvā. Yasmā vissajjanaṃ nāma pucchānurūpaṃ pucchāsabhāgena vissajjetabbato, na ca tathāgatā virajjhitvā katapucchānurūpaṃ vissajjenti, atthasabhāgatāya ca vissajjanassa pucchakā tadatthaṃ anavabujjhantā sammuyhanti, tasmā pucchāya sikkhāpanaṃ buddhāciṇṇaṃ, tenāha “pucchaṃ sikkhāpetvā”tiādi.

497. “Partially” means in one aspect, by way of what is clung to, that is, as included in the continuum of a being. “Even in what is not clung to” means even in what is not bound to the faculties. “Completely” means without remainder. “Of one bewildered in questioning” means of one not knowing how to ask. “Having shown the fault in the question” means having pointed out the fault in the way the question was asked. Because an answer should be given in a way that is appropriate to the question and corresponds to its nature, and the Tathāgatas do not give an answer that conforms to a wrongly formulated question. Rather, since their answer corresponds to the real meaning, the questioners, not understanding that meaning, become bewildered. Therefore, instructing on how to question is a practice of the Buddhas. Hence it is said, “having instructed in questioning,” etc.

498. Appatiṭṭhāti appaccayā, sabbaso samucchinnakāraṇāti attho. Upādinnaṃ yevāti indriyabaddhameva. Yasmā ekadisābhimukhaṃ santānavasena saṇṭhite rūpappabandhe dīghasamaññā taṃ upādāya tato appake rassasamaññā tadubhayañca visesato rūpaggahaṇamukhena [P 1.0512] gayhati, tasmā āha [M 1.0393] “dīghañca rassañcāti saṇṭhānavasena upādārūpaṃ vutta”nti. Appaparimāṇe rūpasaṅghāte aṇusamaññā, taṃ upādāya tato mahati thūlasamaññā. Idampi dvayaṃ visesato rūpaggahaṇamukhena gayhati, tenāha “imināpī”tiādi. Pi-saddena cettha “saṇṭhānavasena upādārūpaṃ vutta”nti etthāpi vaṇṇamattameva kathitanti imamatthaṃ samuccinatīti vadanti. Subhanti sundaraṃ, iṭṭhanti attho. Asubhanti asundaraṃ, aniṭṭhanti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenevāha “iṭṭhāniṭṭhārammaṇaṃ panevaṃ kathita”nti. Dīghaṃ rassaṃ, aṇuṃ thūlaṃ, subhāsubhanti tīsu ṭhānesu upādārūpasseva gahaṇaṃ, bhūtarūpānaṃ visuṃ gahitattā. Nāmanti vedanādikkhandhacatukkaṃ tañhi ārammaṇābhimukhaṃ namanato, nāmakaraṇato ca “nāma”nti vuccati. Heṭṭhā “dīghaṃ rassa”ntiādinā vuttameva idha ruppanaṭṭhena “rūpa”nti gahitanti āha “dīghādibhedaṃ rūpañcā”ti. Dīghādīti ca ādi-saddena āpādīnañca saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Yasmā vā dīghādisamaññā na rūpāyatanavatthukāva, atha kho bhūtarūpavatthukāpi. Tathā hi saṇṭhānaṃ phusanamukhenapi gayhati, tasmā dīgharassādiggahaṇena bhūtarūpampi gayhatevāti “dīghādibhedaṃ rūpa”micceva vuttaṃ. Kiṃ āgammāti kiṃ adhigantvā kissa [V 1.0349] adhigamahetu. “Uparujjhatī”ti idaṃ anuppādanirodhaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na khaṇanirodhanti āha “asesametaṃ nappavattatī”ti.

498. “Unestablished” means without a condition; the meaning is that its cause is entirely cut off. “Clung to” means precisely what is bound to the faculties. Because in a continuum of form established in one direction, the designation “long” arises, and based on that, the designation “short” arises for what is smaller, and both are grasped specifically by way of the apprehension of form, therefore it is said: “‘Long and short’ are spoken of as derived form based on dimension.” In a small aggregate of form, the designation “subtle” arises; based on that, in a large one, the designation “gross” arises. This pair is also grasped specifically by way of the apprehension of form; hence it is said: “by this as well,” etc. They say that by the word “pi” (also), this meaning is summarized: that here too, in the statement “derived form based on dimension is spoken of,” only color is mentioned. “Beautiful” means lovely; the meaning is desirable. “Ugly” means unlovely; it means undesirable. Therefore it is said: “Desirable and undesirable objects are thus spoken of.” In the three cases—long and short, subtle and gross, beautiful and ugly—it is only derived form that is grasped, since the primary elements are grasped separately. “Name” refers to the four aggregates beginning with feeling; it is called “name” because it bends toward an object and because it performs the function of naming. What was stated previously as “long and short,” etc., is here taken as “form” in the sense of “being afflicted.” Thus it is said: “and form with its divisions of long, etc.” And by “long, etc.,” the inclusion of the water element, etc., should be understood by the word “etc.” Or, because the designations “long,” etc., are not based only on the form-base, but also on the primary elements. For dimension is also grasped by way of touch. Therefore, by the grasping of “long, short,” etc., the primary elements are also grasped. Thus it is stated simply as “form with its divisions of long, etc.” “Relying on what?” means having attained what, for the sake of what attainment? “It ceases” is said with reference to the cessation that is non-arising, not momentary cessation. Hence it is said: “This entirely does not occur.”

499. Viññātabbanti visiṭṭhena ñātabbaṃ, ñāṇuttamena ariyamaggañāṇena paccakkhato jānitabbanti attho, tenāha “nibbānassetaṃ nāma”nti. Nidissatīti nidassanaṃ, cakkhuviññeyyaṃ. Na nidassanaṃ anidassanaṃ, acakkhuviññeyyanti etamatthaṃ vadanti. Nidassanaṃ [P 1.0513] vā upamā, taṃ etassa natthīti anidassanaṃ. Na hi nibbānassa niccassa ekassa accantasantapaṇītasabhāvassa sadisaṃ nidassanaṃ kutoci labbhatīti. Yaṃ ahutvā sambhoti, hutvā paṭiveti taṃ saṅkhataṃ udayavayantehi saantaṃ, asaṅkhatassa pana nibbānassa niccassa te ubhopi antā na santi, tato eva navabhāvāpagamasaṅkhāto jarantopi tassa natthīti āha “uppādanto…pe… ananta”nti. “Titthassa nāma”nti vatvā tattha nibbacanaṃ dassetuṃ “papanti etthāti papa”nti vuttaṃ. Ettha hi papanti pānatitthaṃ. Bha-kāro kato niruttinayena. Visuddhaṭṭhena vā sabbatopabhaṃ, kenaci anupakkiliṭṭhatāya samantato pabhassaranti attho[M 1.0394]. Yena nibbānaṃ adhigataṃ, taṃ santatipariyāpannānaṃyeva idha anuppādanirodho adhippetoti vuttaṃ “upādinnakadhammajātaṃ nirujjhati appavattaṃ hotī”ti.

499. “To be cognized” means to be known in a special way; the meaning is to be known directly by the supreme knowledge, the knowledge of the noble path. Hence it is said, “This is a name for Nibbāna.” “Pointed out” means an illustration, something cognizable by the eye. “Not pointed out” means not an illustration, not cognizable by the eye—this is the meaning they convey. Or, an illustration is a simile; this it does not have, thus it is “not pointed out.” For no illustration comparable to Nibbāna—which is permanent, single, and has a nature of ultimate peace and sublimity—can be found anywhere. That which, not having been, comes to be, and having been, passes away, that is conditioned, possessing the ends of arising and passing away. But for the unconditioned Nibbāna, which is permanent, both those ends do not exist. For that very reason, aging, which is designated as the departure from a new state, also does not exist for it. Thus it is said: “without an end of arising… without end.” Having stated, “is a name for a ford,” to show the etymology there, it is said: “They go down (papanti) here, hence it is papa.” Here, ‘they go down’ refers to a ford for drinking. The letter “bh” is formed according to etymological method. Or, in the sense of purity, “radiant on all sides” means “luminous all around” because of being untainted by anything. For that by which Nibbāna is attained, the cessation as non-arising is here intended only for those things included in the continuity. Thus it is said: “The collection of clung-to phenomena ceases; it does not occur.”

Tatthāti “viññāṇassa nirodhenā”ti yaṃ padaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmiṃ. “Viññāṇa”nti viññāṇaṃ uddharati vibhattabbattā etthetaṃ uparujjhatīti etasmiṃ nibbāne etaṃ nāmarūpaṃ carimakaviññāṇanirodhena anuppādavasena nirujjhati anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā, tenāha “vijjhātadīpasikhā viya apaṇṇattikabhāvaṃ yātī”ti. “Carimakaviññāṇa”nti hi arahato cuticittaṃ adhippetaṃ. “Abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassāpī”tiādināpi saupādisesanibbānamukhena anupādisesanibbānameva vadati nāmarūpassa anavasesato uparujjhanassa adhippetattā, tenāha “anuppādavasena uparujjhatī”ti. Sotāpattimaggañāṇenāti kattari, karaṇe vā karaṇavacanaṃ. Nirodhenāti pana hetumhi. Etthāti etasmiṃ nibbāne. Sesamettha yaṃ atthato na vibhattaṃ, taṃ suviññeyyameva.

Therein: in that phrase which was stated, 'with the cessation of consciousness.' The word 'consciousness' is singled out. Because it is to be analyzed, it is said, 'here it ceases.' In this Nibbāna, this name-and-form ceases with the cessation of the final consciousness, by way of non-arising, in the Nibbāna-element without residue. Hence it is said: 'Like the flame of an extinguished lamp, it goes to a state beyond designation.' 'Final consciousness' here refers to the death-consciousness of an arahant. Also by the words beginning 'also of formational consciousness,' he speaks of the Nibbāna without residue by way of the Nibbāna with residue, since the cessation of name-and-form without remainder is intended. Therefore, it is said: 'It ceases by way of non-arising.' 'By the knowledge of the path of stream-entry' is in the agentive or instrumental case. 'With cessation' is in the causal sense. 'Here' means in this Nibbāna. The rest here that is not analyzed as to its meaning is easy to understand.

Kevaṭṭasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

The Elucidation of the Concealed Meaning in the Commentary on the Kevaṭṭa Sutta.

12. Lohiccasuttavaṇṇanā

12. Commentary on the Lohicca Sutta

Lohiccabrāhmaṇavatthuvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Story of the Brahmin Lohicca

501. Sālavatikāti [V 1.0350][M 1.0395][P 1.0514] itthiliṅgavasena tassa gāmassa nāmaṃ. Gāmaṇikābhāvenāti keci. Lohito nāma tassa kule pubbapuriso, tassa vasena lohiccoti tassa brāhmaṇassa gottato āgataṃ nāmaṃ.

501. 'Sālavatikā' is the name of that village, in the feminine gender. Some say it is so called because it was a headman's village. There was an ancestor in his clan named Lohita; because of him, 'Lohicca' is the name that came from that brahmin's clan name.

502. “Diṭṭhigata”nti laddhimattaṃ adhippetanti āha “na pana ucchedasassatānaṃ aññatara”nti. Na hi ucchedasassatagāhavinimutto koci diṭṭhigāho atthi. “Bhāsati yevā”ti tassā laddhiyā loke pākaṭabhāvaṃ dasseti. Attato añño paroti yathā anusāsakato anusāsitabbo paro, evaṃ anusāsitabbatopi anusāsako paroti vuttaṃ “paro parassāti paro yo”tiādi. Kiṃ-saddāpekkhāya cettha “karissatī”ti anāgatakālavacanaṃ, anāgatepi vā tena tassa kātabbaṃ natthīti dassanatthaṃ. Kusalaṃ dhammanti anavajjadhammaṃ nikkilesadhammaṃ vimokkhadhammanti attho. “Paresaṃ dhammaṃ kathessāmī”ti tehi attānaṃ parivārāpetvā vicaraṇaṃ kiṃ atthiyaṃ āsayabuddhassāpi anurodhena vinā taṃ na hotīti tasmā attanā paṭiladdhaṃ…pe… vihātabbanti vadati. Tenāha “evaṃ sampadamidaṃ pāpakaṃ lobhadhammaṃ vadāmī”ti.

502. 'A view' is intended to mean a mere tenet, therefore he says 'but not one of annihilationism or eternalism.'
