For there is no holding of a view that is free from the grasp of annihilationism or eternalism. 'He speaks thus' shows that this tenet is well-known in the world. 'Another is different from oneself' means: just as the one to be instructed is different from the instructor, so the instructor is different from the one to be instructed. Thus it is said, 'another to another, that is, one who is another,' etc. Here, with reference to the word 'what,' the future tense 'will do' is used, or it is used to show that even in the future there is nothing to be done by him for that one. 'A wholesome state' means a blameless state, a stainless state, a state of liberation. He says: 'Wandering about having oneself surrounded by them with the thought, "I will teach the Dhamma to others"—what is the purpose? Since this does not happen without complying even with the intention of one who understands one's disposition, therefore what one has attained for oneself...pe... should be abided in.' Therefore he says: 'Thus I say this attainment is an evil, greedy state.'

504. Soti lohicco brāhmaṇo.

504. He is the brahmin Lohicca.

508. Kathāphāsukatthanti kathāsukhatthaṃ, sukhena kathaṃ kathetuñceva sotuñcāti attho. Appeva nāma siyāti ettha pītivasena āmeḍitaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā hi taṃ “buddhagajjita”nti vuccati[V 1.0351]. Bhagavā hi [P 1.0515] īdisesu ṭhānesu visesato pītisomanassajāto hoti. Tenāha “ayaṃ kirettha adhippāyo”tiādi.

508. 'For the sake of a pleasant conversation' means for the sake of ease in conversation, that is, in order to speak and listen with ease. In the phrase 'Perhaps there might be,' the repetition should be seen as due to joy. For that is called 'the Buddha's roar.' For in such instances the Blessed One is especially filled with joy and gladness. Therefore he says: 'This, it seems, is the intention here,' etc.

Lohiccabrāhmaṇānuyogavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Questioning of the Brahmin Lohicca

509. Samudayasañjātīti āyuppādo. Anupubbo kampī-saddo ākaṅkhanattho hotīti “icchatīti attho”ti vuttaṃ. Sātisayena vā [M 1.0396] hitena anukampako anuggaṇhanako hitānukampī. Sampajjatīti āsevanalābhena nippajjati balavatī hoti, avaggahāti attho, tenāha “niyatā hotī”ti. Niraye nibbattati micchādiṭṭhiko.

509. 'Arising and birth' means the production of the life-span. The word 'kampī' has the meaning of longing; hence it is said, 'it means he wishes.' Or, one who is compassionate and helpful for the welfare with excellence is 'one compassionate for the welfare' (hitānukampī). 'It is accomplished' means it is produced through the gain of cultivation, it becomes strong; the meaning is it is taken up. Therefore it is said, 'it becomes fixed.' One with wrong view is reborn in hell.

510-11. Dutiyaṃ upapattinti “nanu rājā pasenadī kosalo”tiādinā dutiyaṃ upapattiṃ sādhanayuttiṃ. Kāraṇañhi bhagavā upamāmukhena dasseti. Ye cimeti ye ca ime kulaputtā dibbā gabbhā paripācentīti yojanā. Asakkuṇantā upanissayasampattiyā, ñāṇaparipākassa vā abhāvena. Ye pana “paripaccantī”ti paṭhanti, tesaṃ “dibbe gabbhe”ti vacanavipallāsena payojanaṃ natthi. Attho ca dutiyavikappe vuttanayena veditabbo. Ahitānukampitā ca taṃsamaṅgisattavasena. Divi bhavāti dibbā. Gabbhenti paripaccanavasena santānaṃ pabandhentīti gabbhā. “Channaṃ devalokāna”nti nidassanavacanametaṃ. Brahmalokassāpi hi dibbagabbhabhāvo labbhateva dibbavihārahetukattā. Evañca katvā “bhāvanaṃ bhāvayamānā”ti idampi vacanaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti. Bhavanti ettha yathāruci sukhasamappitāti bhavā, vimānāni. Devabhāvāvahattā dibbā. Vuttanayeneva gabbhā. Dānādayo devalokasaṃvattaniyapuññavisesā. Dibbā bhavāti devalokapariyāpannā upapattibhavā. Tadāvaho hi kammabhavo pubbe gahito.

510-11. The second ground: by the words 'Is not King Pasenadi of Kosala...' etc., this is the reasoning that establishes the second ground. For the Blessed One shows the reason by way of a simile. 'Ye cime' means 'and these clansmen who bring divine wombs to maturity.' This is the connection. Being unable, owing to a lack of the accomplishment of supporting conditions or of the maturing of knowledge. But for those who read 'paripaccantī' (they mature), the alteration of the expression to 'dibbe gabbhe' serves no purpose. And the meaning should be understood in the way stated in the second alternative. And compassion for what is unbeneficial is in the sense of beings endowed with that. 'Existing in heaven' (divi bhava), thus 'divine' (dibbā). Because they bind together the continuity by way of maturing, they are 'wombs' (gabbhā). 'Of the six deva worlds' is an illustrative statement. For the state of a divine womb is indeed obtained even for the Brahma-world, because it is a cause for a divine abiding. And having established this, this statement 'developing a development' is also supported. Because beings endowed with happiness exist here as they wish, they are 'existences' (bhavā), that is, mansions. Because they bring about the state of a deva, they are 'divine' (dibbā). 'Wombs' (gabbhā) is in the way already stated. Generosity and so on are the specific kinds of merit that lead to the deva world. 'Divine existences' are rebirth-existences included in the deva world. For the kamma-existence that brings that about has been previously taken up.

Tayocodanārahavaṇṇanā

The Description of Three Grounds for Reproach

513. Aniyamitenevāti aniyameneva “tvaṃ evaṃdiṭṭhiko evaṃ sattānaṃ anatthassa kārako”ti evaṃ anuddesikeneva[P 1.0516]. Mānanti “ahametaṃ jānāmi, ahametaṃ passāmī”ti evaṃ paṇḍitamānaṃ. Bhinditvāti vidhametvā, jahāpetvāti attho. Tayo satthāreti asampāditaattahito anovādakarasāvako, asampāditaattahito ovādakarasāvako, sampāditaattahito anovādakarasāvakoti ime tayo satthāre. Catuttho pana sammāsambuddho na codanāraho hotīti “tena pucchite eva kathessāmī”ti codanārahe tayo satthāre paṭhamaṃ dassesi[V 1.0352], pacchā catutthaṃsatthāraṃ. Kāmañcettha catuttho satthā eko adutiyo anaññasādhāraṇo, tathāpi so yesaṃ uttarimanussadhammānaṃ [M 1.0397] vasena “dhammamayo kāyo”ti vuccati, tesaṃ samudāyabhūtopi te guṇāvayave satthuṭṭhāniye katvā dassento bhagavā “ayampi kho, lohicca, satthā”ti abhāsi.

513. By ‘without certainty’ (aniyamiteneva) is meant without certainty, as in ‘You, holding such a view, are the cause of harm to beings in this way,’ thus without specific designation. By ‘conceit’ (māna) is meant the conceit of thinking, ‘I know this, I see this,’ thus the conceit of a wise person. By ‘having shattered’ (bhinditvā) is meant having destroyed, having caused to be abandoned—that is the meaning. By ‘three teachers’ (tayo satthāre) are meant these three teachers: a teacher who has not accomplished his own welfare and whose disciple is disobedient to advice; a teacher who has not accomplished his own welfare but whose disciple is obedient to advice; and a teacher who has accomplished his own welfare but whose disciple is disobedient to advice. The fourth, however, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is not worthy of reproach. Therefore, he first presented the three teachers worthy of reproach, and afterwards the fourth teacher. And though the fourth teacher here is unique, without a second, incomparable, yet because of those supreme human qualities by virtue of which he is called ‘the body of Dhamma,’ even though he is the collection of those qualities, the Blessed One, showing those qualities as components occupying the place of a teacher, said, ‘This too, Lohicca, is a teacher.’

Aññāti ya-kāralopena niddeso “sayaṃ abhiññā”ti ādīsu (dī. ni. 1.28, 37, 52; ma. ni. 1.284; 2.341; a. ni. 2.5; 10.11; mahāva. 11; dha. pa. 353; kathā. 405) viya. Aññāyāti ca tadatthiye sampadānavacananti āha “ājānanatthāyā”ti. Sāvakattaṃ paṭijānitvā ṭhitattā ekadesenassa sāsanaṃ karontīti āha “nirantaraṃ tassa sāsanaṃ akatvā”ti. Ukkamitvā vattantīti yathicchitaṃ karontīti attho. Paṭikkamantiyāti anabhiratiyā agāravena apagacchantiyā, tenāha “anicchantiyā”tiādi. Ekāyāti ekāya itthiyā. Eko iccheyyāti eko puriso tāya anicchantiyā sampayogaṃ kāmeyya. Osakkanādimukhena [P 1.0517] itthipurisasambandhanidassanaṃ gehasitaapekkhāvasena tassa satthuno sāvakesu paṭipattīti dasseti. Ativiya virattabhāvato daṭṭhumpi anicchamānaṃ. Lobhenāti parivāravasena uppajjanakalābhasakkāralobhena. Tattha sampādehīti tasmiṃ paṭipattidhamme patiṭṭhitaṃ katvā sampādehi. Ujuṃ karohi kāyavaṅkādivigamena.

By ‘aññā’ is a designation made by the elision of the letter ‘ya’, as in ‘sayaṃ abhiññā’ and so forth. And ‘aññāya’ is a word in the dative case for that purpose; thus it is said, ‘for the purpose of knowing’ (ājānanatthāya). Because, having declared discipleship, they remain so, yet carry out his teaching only partially, it is said, ‘without continuously fulfilling his teaching.’ By ‘acting presumptuously’ (ukkamitvā vattanti) is meant acting as one pleases. By ‘turning away’ (paṭikkamantiyā) is meant turning away out of dissatisfaction and disrespect; hence it is said, ‘not desiring,’ and so forth. By ‘with one’ (ekāya) is meant with one woman. By ‘one might desire’ (eko iccheyya) is meant one man might desire union with her who does not desire it. The illustration of the relationship between a man and a woman, by way of her shrinking away, etc., shows the conduct of that teacher's disciples with regard to their worldly attachments. She is unwilling even to see him, due to her extreme aversion. By ‘through greed’ (lobhena) is meant greed for the gain and honor that arise by way of having a retinue. By ‘Establish him there’ (Tattha sampādehi) is meant: having established him in that practice of the Dhamma, bring it to accomplishment. By ‘Make him straight’ (ujuṃ karohi) is meant to straighten him by removing bodily crookedness and so on.

515. Evaṃ codanaṃ arahatīti evaṃ vuttanayena sāvakesu appossukkabhāvāpādane niyojanavasena codanaṃ arahati, na paṭhamo viya “evarūpo tava lobhadhammo”tiādinā, na ca dutiyo viya “attānameva tāva tattha sampādehī”tiādinā. Kasmā? Sampāditaattahitatāya tatiyassa.

515. He is worthy of reproach in this way: in the manner stated, he is worthy of reproach for causing a state of indifference in his disciples; not like the first one, with ‘Such is your greedy nature,’ and so forth, nor like the second one, with ‘First, establish yourself in that,’ and so forth. Why? Because the third one has accomplished his own welfare.

Nacodanārahasatthuvaṇṇanā

The Description of the Teacher Not Worthy of Reproach.

516. “Na codanāraho”ti ettha yasmā codanārahatā nāma satthuvippaṭipattiyā vā sāvakavippaṭipattiyā vā ubhayavippaṭipattiyā vā, tayidaṃ sabbampi imasmiṃ satthari natthi, tasmā na codanārahoti imamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “ayañhī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

516. Here, regarding ‘not worthy of reproach’ (na codanāraho), since the quality of being worthy of reproach arises from wrong practice on the part of the teacher, or wrong practice on the part of the disciples, or wrong practice on the part of both, and all of this is absent in this teacher, therefore, to show this meaning that he is not worthy of reproach, ‘for this one…’ and so forth, was stated.

517. Mayā [M 1.0398] gahitāya diṭṭhiyāti sabbaso anavajje sammāpaṭipanne paresaṃ sammadeva sammāpaṭipattiṃ dessente satthari abhūtadosāropanavasena micchāgahitāya nirayagāminiyā pāpadiṭṭhiyā[V 1.0353]. Narakapapātanti narakasaṅkhātaṃ mahāpapātaṃ. Papatanti tatthāti hi papāto. Saggamaggathaleti saggagāmimaggabhūte puññadhammathale. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

517. By ‘the view grasped by me’ (mayā gahitāya diṭṭhiyā) is meant the evil view, wrongly grasped, leading to hell, by way of falsely accusing the teacher—who is utterly blameless, rightly practiced, and teaches others right practice—of faults. By ‘the pit of hell’ (narakapapāta) is meant the great abyss termed hell. For ‘a pit’ (papāta) is where one falls. By ‘the ground of the path to heaven’ (saggamaggathale) is meant the ground of meritorious qualities that constitute the path leading to heaven. The rest is easily understood.

Lohiccasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meanings in the Commentary on the Lohicca Sutta.

13. Tevijjasuttavaṇṇanā

13. The Commentary on the Tevijja Sutta.

518. Uttarenāti [V 1.0354][M 1.0399][P 1.0518] ettha ena-saddo disāvācīsaddato pañcamīantato adūrattho icchito, tasmā uttarena-saddena adūratthajotanaṃ dassento “adūre uttarapasse”ti āha. Akkharacintakā pana ena-saddayoge avadhivācini pade upayogavacanaṃ icchanti. Attho pana sāmivaseneva icchitoti idha sāmivacanavaseneva vuttaṃ.

518. Here, regarding ‘uttarena’ (to the north), the word ‘ena’ is desired to convey the meaning of ‘not far’ when it is the fifth case ending from a word indicating direction. Therefore, showing the indication of ‘not far’ by the word ‘uttarena,’ it is said, ‘not far to the north.’ However, grammarians desire the word ‘ena’ to be a term of usage in a word denoting a boundary. But the meaning here is desired solely as a term of proximity, hence it is stated here specifically as a term of proximity.

519. Kulacārittādīti ādi-saddena mantajjhenābhirūpatādisampattiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Mantasajjhāyakaraṇatthanti āthabbaṇamantānaṃ sajjhāyakaraṇatthaṃ, tenāha “aññesaṃ bahūnaṃ pavesanaṃ nivāretvā”ti.

519. By ‘lineage, conduct, etc.’ (kulacārittādi), the word ‘etc.’ (ādi) includes accomplishments such as mastery of mantras, study, and beauty. By ‘for the purpose of reciting mantras’ (mantasajjhāyakaraṇattha) is meant for the purpose of reciting the Atharva mantras, hence it is said, ‘having prevented the entry of many others.’

Maggāmaggakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discussion of the Path and the Non-Path.

520. “Jaṅghacāra”nti caṅkamato ito cito ca caraṇamāha. So hi jaṅghāsu kilamathavinodanattho cāroti tathā vutto. Tenāha “anucaṅkamantānaṃ anuvicarantāna”nti. Tenāti ubhosupi anucaṅkamanānuvicāraṇānaṃ labbhanato. Sahāyā hi te aññamañña sabhāgavuttikā. “Maggo”ti icchitaṭṭhānaṃ ujukaṃ maggati upagacchati etenāti maggo, ujumaggo. Tadañño amaggo, tasmiṃ magge ca amagge ca. Paṭipadanti brahmalokagāmimaggassa pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ.

520. The word 'jaṅghacāra' means walking, moving here and there. It is called so because it is a walk for relieving fatigue in the legs. Hence it is said, 'for those who walk back and forth, for those who wander about.' This is said because both walking back and forth and wandering about are found in both of them. For they are companions, sharing similar conduct with each other. The word 'maggo' (path) means that by which one goes straight to the desired place; thus it is the path, the straight path. That which is other than this is the non-path; and in that path and non-path... The word 'paṭipadā' (practice) refers to the preliminary practice for the path leading to the Brahma-world.

Niyyātīti niyyānīyo, so eva “niyyāniko”ti vuttoti āha “niyyāyanto”ti. Yasmā niyyātapuggalavasenassa niyyānikabhāvo[P 1.0519], tasmā “niyyāyanto”ti puggalassa yoniso paṭipajjanavasena niyyāyanto maggo “niyyātī”ti vutto. Karotīti attano santāne uppādeti. Uppādentoyeva hi tattha paṭipajjati nāma. Saha byeti vattatīti sahabyo, sahavattanako[V 1.0355]. Tassa bhāvo sahabyatāti āha “sahabhāvāyā”tiādi. Sahabhāvoti ca salokatā, samīpatā vā veditabbā, tenāha “ekaṭṭhāne pātubhāvāyā”ti. Sakameva ācariyavādanti attano ācariyena pokkharasātinā kathitameva ācariyavādaṃ. Thometvā paggaṇhitvā “ayameva ujumaggo ayamañjasāyano”ti pasaṃsitvā ukkaṃsitvā. Bhāradvājopi [M 1.0400] sakamevāti bhāradvājopi māṇavo attano ācariyena tārukkhena kathitameva ācariyavādaṃ thometvā paggaṇhitvā vicaratīti yojanā. Tena vuttanti tena yathā tathā vā abhiniviṭṭhabhāvena vuttaṃ pāḷiyaṃ.

That which leads out (niyyāti) is what is to be led out by (niyyānīyo); that same thing is called 'leading out' (niyyāniko), hence it is said 'leading out' (niyyāyanto). Since its quality of leading out is dependent on the person who goes forth, the path that leads out by way of a person's wise practice is therefore called 'that which leads out' (niyyāti). The word 'does' (karoti) means one produces it in one's own continuum. For it is only by producing it that one is said to practice it. The phrase 'goes along with' (saha byeti vattati) means 'companion' (sahabyo), 'one who lives together' (sahavattanako). Its state is 'companionship' (sahabyatā), hence it is said 'for companionship' (sahabhāvāyā), and so on. And 'companionship' (sahabhāvo) should be understood as 'living in the same world' (salokatā) or 'proximity' (samīpatā); therefore it is said 'for appearing in one place' (ekaṭṭhāne pātubhāvāyā). The phrase 'his own teacher's doctrine' (sakameva ācariyavādaṃ) refers to the very doctrine spoken by his own teacher, Pokkharasāti. 'Having praised and grasped it' means having lauded and extolled it, saying, 'This indeed is the straight path, this is the direct way.' The phrase 'Bhāradvāja also his own' (Bhāradvājopi sakameva) is to be connected thus: Bhāradvāja the youth also wanders, having praised and grasped the very doctrine spoken by his teacher, Tārukkha. The phrase 'spoken by him' (tena vuttaṃ) refers to what is spoken in the Pāli with a state of fixed conviction, whether rightly or wrongly.

521-2. Aniyyānikā vāti appāṭihāriyāva aññamaññassa vāde dosaṃ dassetvā aviparītatthadassanatthaṃ uttararahitā eva. Aññamaññassa vādassa ādito viruddhaggahaṇaṃ viggaho, sveva vivadanavasena aparāparaṃ uppanno vivādoti āha “pubbuppattiko viggaho aparabhāge vivādo”ti. Duvidhopi eso viggaho, vivādoti dvidhā vuttopi virodho. Nānāācariyānaṃ vādatoti nānārucikānaṃ ācariyānaṃ vādabhāvato. Nānāvādo nānāvidho vādoti katvā.

521-2. The word 'not leading out' (aniyyānikā) means those who are without any special attainment, merely pointing out faults in each other's doctrines, lacking any conclusive answer, for the sake of showing the correct meaning. Grasping opposing views in each other's doctrines from the very beginning is a 'dispute' (viggaha); and this very dispute, arising successively as a debate, is called a 'debate' (vivāda), hence it is said, 'a dispute arising earlier, a debate arising later.' This opposition is twofold, spoken of as 'dispute' and 'debate'. The phrase 'from the doctrines of various teachers' (nānāācariyānaṃ vādato) means from the doctrines being held by teachers of diverse inclinations. This is because 'various doctrines' (nānāvādo) means 'doctrines of diverse kinds'.

523. Ekassāpīti tumhesu dvīsu ekassāpi. Ekasminti sakavādaparavādesu ekasmimpi. Saṃsayo natthīti “maggo nu kho, na maggo nu kho”ti saṃsayo vicikicchā natthi. Añjasāyanabhāve pana saṃsayo. Tenāha “esa [P 1.0520] kirā”tiādi. Bhagavā pana yadi sabbattha maggasaññino, evaṃ sati “kismiṃ vo viggaho”ti pucchati.

523. 'Ekassāpi' means: even of one of you two. 'Ekasmiṃ' means: even in one of either one's own or another's doctrines. 'Saṃsayo natthi' means: there is no doubt or uncertainty, such as, 'Is this the path, or is it not the path?' But regarding the absence of a direct way, there is doubt. Therefore he said, 'This indeed,' and so on. But if the Blessed One perceived the path everywhere, then he would ask, 'In what is your disagreement?'

524. “Icchitaṭṭhānaṃ ujukaṃ maggati upagacchati etenāti maggo, ujumaggo. Tadañño amaggo”ti vutto vāyamattho. Sabbe teti sabbepi te nānāācariyehi vuttamaggā.

524. 'The path is that by which one goes straight to the desired place; it is the straight path. That which is other than this is the non-path'—this is the intended meaning of the statement. 'Sabbe te' means: all those paths stated by various teachers.

Ye pāḷiyaṃ “addhariyā brāhmaṇā”tiādinā vuttā. Addharo nāma yaññaviseso, tadupayogibhāvato “addhariyā” tveva vuccanti yajūni, tāni sajjhāyantīti addhariyā, yajubbedino. Ye ca tittiriisinā kate mante sajjhāyanti, te tittiriyā, yajubbedino eva. Yajubbedasākhā hesā, yadidaṃ tittiraṃ. Chando vuccati visesato sāmavedo, taṃ sarena kāyantīti chandokā, sāmavedino. “Chandogā”tipi paṭhanti, so evattho. Bahavo irayo etthāti bavhāri, irubbedo. Taṃ adhīyantīti bavhārijjhā.

These are those mentioned in the Pāli as 'addhariyā brāhmaṇā,' and so on. 'Addhara' is a particular sacrifice; because of its use, the Yajur verses are called 'addhariyā.' Those who recite them are 'addhariyā,' the Yajurvedins. Those who recite the mantras composed by the sage Tittiri are called 'tittiriyā,' who are also Yajurvedins. This is a branch of the Yajurveda, namely the Tittira. 'Chando' specifically refers to the Sāmaveda; those who chant it with a tone are called 'chandokā,' the Sāmavedins. Some read it as 'chandogā,' but the meaning is the same. 'Bavhāri' means 'many verses are in it,' referring to the Ṛgveda. Those who study it are called 'bavhārijjhā.'

“Bahūnī”ti [M 1.0401][V 1.0356] etthāyaṃ upamāsaṃsandanā – yathā te nānāmaggā ekaṃsato tassa gāmassa vā nigamassa vā pavesāya honti, evaṃ brāhmaṇehi paññāpiyamānāpi nānāmaggā brahmalokūpagamanāya brahmunā sahabyatāya ekaṃseneva hontīti.

'Bahūnī': here is the comparison—just as those various paths are certainly for entering that village or town, so too the various paths declared by the brahmins are certainly for reaching the Brahma-world, for companionship with Brahmā.

527-529. Va-kāro āgamasandhimattanti anatthako va-kāro, tena vaṇṇāgamena padantarasandhimattaṃ katanti attho. Andhapaveṇīti andhapanti. “Paññāsasaṭṭhi andhā”ti idaṃ tassā andhapaveṇiyā mahato gacchagumbassa anuparigamanayogyatādassanaṃ. Evañhi te “suciraṃ velaṃ maggaṃ gacchāmā”ti evaṃ saññino honti. Nāmakaṃyevāti [P 1.0521] atthābhāvato nāmamattaṃyeva, taṃ pana bhāsitaṃ tehi sārasaññitampi nāmamattatāya asārabhāvato nihīnamevāti āha “lāmakaṃyevā”ti.

527-529. The letter 'va' is merely an augmentative euphonic combination; the 'va' is meaningless. By that letter augment, merely a juncture between words is created—this is the meaning. 'Andhapaveṇī' means a line of blind people. The phrase 'fifty or sixty blind people' shows the fitness of that great thicket-like group, that line of blind people, for following one after another. Thus, they have the perception, 'We have been traveling this path for a very long time.' 'Nāmakaṃyeva' means: merely a name, because of the absence of substance. But that which is spoken, though perceived by them as substantial, is indeed inferior because it is merely a name and without substance; thus he says, 'lāmakaṃyeva'—utterly base.

530. Yatoti bhummatthe nissakkavacanaṃ, sāmaññajotanā ca visese avatiṭṭhatīti āha “yasmiṃ kāle”ti. Āyācantīti patthenti. Uggamanaṃ lokassa bahukārabhāvato tathā thomanāti. Ayaṃ kira brāhmaṇānaṃ laddhi “brāhmaṇānaṃ āyācanāya candimasūriyā gantvā loke obhāsaṃ karontī”ti.

530. 'Yato' is an ablative used in the sense of the locative, and because a general indication settles on a particular, he says 'yasmiṃ kāle' (at which time). 'Āyācanti' means they wish for. The rising is praised thus because it is of great benefit to the world. This, it seems, is the belief of the brahmins: 'At the request of the brahmins, the sun and moon go forth and illuminate the world.'

532. Idha pana kiṃ vattabbanti imasmiṃ pana appaccakkhabhūtassa brahmuno sahabyatāya maggadesane tevijjānaṃ kiṃ vattabbaṃ atthi, ye paccakkhabhūtānampi candimasūriyānaṃ sahabyatāya maggaṃ desetuṃ na sakkontīti adhippāyo. “Yatthā”ti “idha panā”ti vuttamevatthaṃ paccāmasati.

532. 'Idha pana kiṃ vattabbaṃ' (but here, what is to be said?)—the intention is: In this case, regarding the teaching of the path to companionship with Brahmā, who is not directly perceptible, what is there to be said by those with threefold knowledge, who are unable to teach the path to companionship even with the sun and moon, who are directly perceptible? 'Yatthā' refers back to the very meaning spoken by 'idha pana.'

Aciravatīnadīupamākathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discourse on the Simile of the Aciravatī River

542. Samabharitāti sampuṇṇā. Tato eva kākapeyyā. Pārāti paratīraṃ. Apāranti orimatīraṃ. Ehīti āgaccha.

542. 'Samabharitā' means completely full. Therefore, it is 'kākapeyyā' (drinkable by crows). 'Pāra' means the far shore. 'Apāra' means the near shore. 'Ehi' means come.

544. Pañcasīla…pe… veditabbā yamaniyamādibrāhmaṇadhammānaṃ tadantogadhabhāvato. Tabbiparītāti pañcasīlādiviparītā pañca verādayo. “Punapī”ti vatvā “aparampī”ti vacanaṃ itarāyapi nadi upamāya saṅgaṇhanatthaṃ.

544. The five precepts… should be understood as being included within the brahminical duties such as the restraints and observances (yama and niyama). 'Tabbiparītā' means the five enmities and so on, which are the opposite of the five precepts. Having said 'punapi' (again), the statement 'aparampi' (furthermore) is for the purpose of including the other simile of the river as well.

546. Kāmayitabbaṭṭhenāti [V 1.0357] kāmanīyabhāvena. Bandhanaṭṭhenāti teneva kāmetabbabhāvena sattānaṃ cittassa ābandhanabhāvena. Kāmañcāyaṃ guṇa-saddo [M 1.0402] atthantaresupi diṭṭhappayogo, tesaṃ panettha asambhavato pārisesañāyena bandhanaṭṭheyeva yuttoti dassetuṃ “anujānāmī”tiādinā atthuddhāro āraddho, esevāti bandhanaṭṭho eva. Na hi rūpādīnaṃ kāmetabbabhāve vuccamāne paṭalaṭṭho yujjati tathā kāmetabbatāya anadhippetattā. Rāsaṭṭhaānisaṃsaṭṭhesupi eseva [P 1.0522] nayo tathāpi kāmetabbatāya anadhippetattā. Pārisesato pana bandhanaṭṭho gahito. Yadaggena hi nesaṃ kāmetabbatā, tadaggena bandhanabhāvo cāti.

546. 'Kāmayitabbaṭṭhena' means: by way of being desirable. 'Bandhanaṭṭhena' means: by that very desirability, by way of binding the minds of beings. Now, this word 'guṇa' is also seen used in other senses, but since those are impossible here, it is appropriate only in the sense of 'binding' by the method of elimination. To show this, an explanation of the meaning is undertaken with the words 'anujānāmi,' and so on. This is indeed just the sense of binding. For when the desirability of forms and so on is spoken of, the sense of 'covering' is not fitting, as desirability is not intended in that way. The same principle applies to the meanings of 'taste' and 'benefit,' as desirability is not intended in that way either. By elimination, therefore, the sense of 'binding' is taken. For to the extent that they are desirable, to that extent there is also the state of binding.

Koṭṭhāsaṭṭhopi tesu yujjateva cakkhuviññeyyādikoṭṭhāsabhāvena nesaṃ kāmetabbato. Koṭṭhāse ca guṇa-saddo dissati “diguṇaṃ vaḍḍhetabba”ntiādīsu, sampadāṭṭhopi –

The meaning 'portion' is also indeed suitable in their case, because they are desirable as portions cognizable by the eye, and so on. And in the sense of 'portion', the word 'guṇa' is seen in phrases like 'diguṇaṃ vaḍḍhetabbaṃ' (should be increased twofold), etc.; also in the sense of 'accomplishment'—

“Asaṅkhyeyyāni nāmāni, saguṇena mahesino;

Guṇena nāmamuddheyyaṃ, api nāmasahassato”ti. (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1313; udā. aṭṭha. 53; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 76);

'Countless are the names of the Great Sage, who is endowed with virtues; by a virtue a name may be designated, even from a thousand names.'

Ādīsu sopi idha na yujjatīti anuddhaṭo.

Since that meaning is also not suitable here, it is not cited.

Cakkhuviññeyyāti cakkhuviññāṇena vijānitabbā, tena pana vijānanaṃ dassanamevāti āha “passitabbā”ti. “Sotaviññāṇena sotabbā”ti evamādi etenupāyenāti atidisati. Gavesitampi “iṭṭha”nti vuccati, taṃ idha nādhippetanti āha “pariyiṭṭhā vā hontu mā vā”ti. Iṭṭhārammaṇabhūtāti sukhārammaṇabhūtā. Kāmanīyāti kāmetabbā. Iṭṭhabhāvena manaṃ appāyantīti manāpā. Piyajātikāti piyasabhāvā.

'Cakkhuviññeyya' means to be known by eye-consciousness, but that knowing is simply seeing—hence it is said, 'passitabbā' (to be seen). 'To be heard by ear-consciousness,' and so on—this is extended by this method. Even what is sought after is called 'iṭṭha' (desirable), but that is not intended here—hence it is said, 'pariyiṭṭhā vā hontu mā vā' (whether sought after or not). 'Iṭṭhārammaṇabhūtā' means being an object of pleasure. 'Kāmanīya' means to be desired. Because they please the mind through their desirable nature, they are 'manāpā' (agreeable). 'Piyajātika' means having a pleasing nature.

Gedhenāti lobhena abhibhūtā hutvā pañcakāmaguṇe paribhuñjantīti yojanā. Mucchākāranti mohanākāraṃ. Adhiosannāti adhiggayha ajjhosāya avasannā, tenāha “ogāḷhā”ti. Pariniṭṭhānappattāti gilitvā pariniṭṭhāpanavasena pariniṭṭhānaṃ upagatā. Ādīnavanti kāmaparibhoge sampati, āyatiñca dosaṃ apassantā. Ghāsacchādanādisambhoganimittasaṃkilesato nissaranti apagacchanti etenāti nissaraṇaṃ, yoniso paccavekkhitvā tesaṃ paribhogapaññā. Tadabhāvato anissaraṇapaññāti imamatthaṃ dassento “idametthā”tiādimāha.

'Gedhena': the construction is that, having been overcome by greed, they indulge in the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Mucchākāraṃ' means the state of delusion. 'Adhiosannā' means having seized, clung to, and sunk down; therefore, he said, 'ogāḷhā' (engulfed). 'Pariniṭṭhānappattā' means having swallowed, they have reached consummation by way of bringing it to completion. 'Ādīnavaṃ' means not seeing the fault in the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, either in the present or in the future. 'Nissaraṇaṃ' is that by which one escapes, one departs from the defilement caused by the sign of enjoying things like food and clothing; this escape is the wisdom of using them with proper reflection. To show this meaning—that in the absence of that, there is no wisdom of escape—he said, 'idamettha,' and so on.

548-9. Āvarantīti [M 1.0403][V 1.0358][P 1.0523] kusalappavattiṃ āditova nivārenti. Nivārentīti niravasesato vārayanti. Onandhantīti ogāhantā viya chādenti. Pariyonandhantīti sabbaso chādenti. Āvaraṇādīnaṃ vasenāti āvaraṇādiatthānaṃ vasena. Te hi āsevanabalavatāya purimapurimehi pacchimapacchimā daḷhataratamādibhāvappattā vuttā.

548-9. 'Āvaranti' means they prevent the arising of wholesome states from the very beginning. 'Nivārenti' means they block without remainder. 'Onandhanti' means they cover as if submerging. 'Pariyonandhanti' means they cover completely. 'Āvaraṇādīnaṃ vasena' means by way of the meanings of obstruction, and so on. For they, because of the strength of cultivation, are said to have attained states of being progressively stronger, the later ones than the earlier ones.

Saṃsandanakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discourse on Comparison

550. Itthipariggahe sati purisassa pañcakāmaguṇapariggaho paripuṇṇo eva hotīti vuttaṃ “sapariggahoti itthipariggahena sapariggaho”ti. “Itthipariggahena apariggaho”ti ca idaṃ tevijjabrāhmaṇesu dissamānapariggahānaṃ duṭṭhullatamapariggahābhāvadassanaṃ. Evaṃbhūtānaṃ tevijjānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ kā brahmunā saṃsandanā, brahmā pana sabbena sabbaṃ apariggahoti. Veracittena avero, kuto etassa verappayogoti adhippāyo. Cittagelaññasaṅkhātenāti cittuppādagelaññasaññitena, tenassa sabbarūpakāyagelaññabhāvo vutto hoti. Byāpajjhenāti dukkhena. Uddhaccakukkuccādīhīti ādi-saddena tadekaṭṭhā saṃkilesadhammā saṅgayhanti. Appaṭipattihetubhūtāya vicikicchāya sati na kadāci cittaṃ purisassa vase vattati, pahīnāya pana siyā vasavattananti āha “vicikicchāya abhāvato cittaṃ vase vattetī”ti. Cittagatikāti cittavasikā, tenāha cittassa vase vattantī”ti. Na tādisoti brāhmaṇā viya cittavasiko na hoti, atha kho vasībhūtajjhānābhiññatāya cittaṃ attano vase vattetīti vasavattī.

550. When there is possession of a woman, it is said that a man’s possession of the five strands of sensual pleasure is complete; thus it is said: 'sapariggaho' (he is possessed) means 'possessed through the possession of a woman.' And 'unpossessed through the possession of a woman'—this shows the absence of the grossest possession among the possessions seen in the Brahmins versed in the three Vedas. How then could such Brahmins versed in the three Vedas be united with Brahmā? For Brahmā is entirely free from possession. The meaning is: with a mind free from enmity, how could there be any application of enmity in him? 'Cittagelaññasaṅkhātena' means 'designated as a sickness of thought-production,' thereby indicating that his entire physical body is in a state of sickness. 'Byāpajjhena' means 'through suffering.' 'Uddhaccakukkuccādīhi' (by restlessness and remorse, etc.)—the word 'etc.' includes other defilements of a similar nature. When doubt, the cause of non-practice, is present, a man’s mind never comes under his control. But when it is abandoned, it may come under control—hence it is said: 'vicikicchāya abhāvato cittaṃ vase vatteti' (because doubt is absent, the mind comes under control). 'Cittagatika' means 'controlled by the mind'; therefore, it is said: 'cittassa vase vattanti' (it comes under the control of the mind). 'Na tādiso' (not like them)—he is not controlled by the mind like the Brahmins; rather, through mastery of jhāna and higher knowledge, he brings the mind under his own control—thus, he is 'vasavattī' (one who wields control).

552. Brahmalokamaggeti brahmalokagāmimagge paṭipajjitabbe, paññapetabbe vā, taṃ paññapentāti adhippāyo. Upagantvāti amaggameva “maggo”ti micchāpaṭipajjanena upagantvā, paṭijānitvā vā. Paṅkaṃ otiṇṇā viyāti matthake ekaṅgulaṃ vā upaḍḍhaṅgulaṃ vā sukkhatāya “samatala”nti saññāya anekaporisaṃ mahāpaṅkaṃ [P 1.0524] otiṇṇā viya. Anuppavisantīti apāyamaggaṃ brahmalokamaggasaññāya ogāhayanti. Tato eva saṃsīditvā visādaṃ pāpuṇanti. Evanti “samatala”ntiādinā vuttanayena. Saṃsīditvāti nimmujjitvā. Sukkhataraṇaṃ maññe tarantīti sukkhanaditaraṇaṃ taranti maññe. Tasmāti yasmā tevijjā amaggameva “maggo”ti upagantvā saṃsīdanti, tasmā. Yathā [M 1.0404] teti yathā te “samatala”nti saññāya paṅkaṃ otiṇṇā. Idheva cāti imasmiñca attabhāve. Sukhaṃ vā sātaṃ vā na labhantīti jhānasukhaṃ vā vipassanāsātaṃ vā na labhanti, kuto maggasukhaṃ vā nibbānasātaṃ vāti adhippāyo. Maggadīpakanti maggadīpakābhimataṃ. “Iriṇa”nti araññāniyā idaṃ adhivacananti āha “agāmakaṃ mahārañña”nti[V 1.0359]. Migaruruādīnampi anupabhogarukkhehi. Parivattitumpi na sakkā honti mahākaṇṭakatāya. Ñātīnaṃ byasanaṃ vināso ñātibyasanaṃ. Evaṃ bhogasīlabyasanāni veditabbāni. Rogo eva byasati vibādhatīti rogabyasanaṃ. Evaṃ diṭṭhibyasanampi daṭṭhabbaṃ.

552. 'Brahmalokamagga' means 'on the path leading to the Brahma-world, which should be practiced or taught'; the meaning is that they teach it. 'Upagantvā' means 'approaching by wrongly practicing what is not the path as if it were the path, or by claiming it to be so.' 'Paṅkaṃ otiṇṇā viya' is like having stepped into a great swamp many fathoms deep, mistaking it for level ground due to its surface being dry for an inch or half an inch at the top. 'Anuppavisanti' means 'they plunge into the path to the lower realms, believing it to be the path to the Brahma-world.' From this very act, they sink and come to despair. 'Evaṃ' refers to the manner described by 'samatala' (level ground) and so on. 'Saṃsīditvā' means 'having sunk.' 'Sukkhataraṇaṃ maññe taranti' means 'they imagine they are crossing a dry riverbed.' 'Tasmā' means 'because those versed in the three Vedas, having wrongly approached what is not the path as if it were, sink.' 'Yathā te' means 'just as they, under the perception of 'samatala' (level ground), step into the swamp.' 'Idheva ca' means 'and in this very existence.' 'Sukhaṃ vā sātaṃ vā na labhanti' means 'they do not attain the bliss of jhāna or the delight of insight; how much less the bliss of the path or the delight of Nibbāna'—this is the meaning. 'Maggadīpaka' refers to 'one who is regarded as a lamp of the path.' 'Iriṇa' is another term for wilderness; hence he says, 'agāmakaṃ mahāraññaṃ' (an uninhabited great forest), because of trees unsuitable for enjoyment even by animals like deer and antelopes. They cannot even turn around because of the great thorns. 'Ñātīnaṃ byasanaṃ' means 'the destruction of relatives.' Similarly, the ruin of wealth and virtue should be understood. 'Rogo eva byasati vibādhatīti rogabyasanaṃ' means 'disease itself destroys, it afflicts—this is the ruin by disease.' Likewise, the ruin by wrong view should be seen.

554. Jātasaṃvaḍḍhoti jāto hutvā saṃvaḍḍhito. Na sabbaso paccakkhā honti paricayābhāvato. Ciranikkhantoti nikkhanto hutvā cirakālo. Dandhāyitattanti vissajjane mandattaṃ saṇikavutti, taṃ pana saṃsayavasena cirāyanaṃ nāma [P 1.0525] hotīti āha “kaṅkhāvasena cirāyitatta”nti. Vitthāyitattanti sārajjitattaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana vitthāyitattaṃ nāma chambhitattanti adhippāyena “thaddhabhāvaggahaṇa”nti vuttaṃ.

554. 'Jātasaṃvaḍḍho' means 'born and fully grown.' They are not entirely manifest because of unfamiliarity. 'Ciranikkhanto' means 'having left a long time ago.' 'Dandhāyitatta' refers to 'slowness in responding, sluggishness'; that slowness, however, due to doubt is called 'delaying,' hence it is said, 'kaṅkhāvasena cirāyitatta' (delayed by doubt). 'Vitthāyitatta' means 'being infatuated.' In the commentary, however, 'vitthāyitatta' is explained as being stunned; with this meaning it is said to be 'thaddhabhāvaggahaṇa' (the taking on of a rigid state).

555. U-iti upasaggayoge lumpa-saddo uddharaṇattho hotīti “ullumpatū”ti padassa uddharatūti atthamāha. Upasaggavasena hi dhātu-saddā atthavisesavuttino honti yathā “uddharatū”ti.

555. 'U-' as a prefix in conjunction with the root 'lumpa' means 'lifting out'; thus, for the word 'ullumpatu,' he states the meaning as 'uddharatu' (let him lift out). Indeed, verbal roots, influenced by prefixes, express specific meanings, as with 'uddharatu'.

Brahmalokamaggadesanāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Teaching on the Path to the Brahma World.

556. Yassa atisayena balaṃ atthi, so “balavā”ti vuttoti āha “balasampanno”ti. Saṅkhaṃ dhamayatīti saṅkhadhamako, taṃ dhamayitvā tato saddapavattako. Appanāva vaṭṭati paṭipakkhato sammadeva cetaso vimuttibhāvato.

556. He who has surpassing strength is called 'strong,' thus it is said, 'endowed with strength.' He who blows the conch is a conch-blower; having blown it, he then generates the sound. Absorption alone is fitting, because of the mind being perfectly liberated from opposition.

Pamāṇakataṃ kammaṃ nāma kāmāvacaraṃ pamāṇakarānaṃ saṃkilesadhammānaṃ avikkhambhanato. Tathā hi taṃ brahmavihārapubbabhāgabhūtaṃ pamāṇaṃ atikkamitvā odissakaanodissakadisāpharaṇavasena vaḍḍhetuṃ na sakkā. Vuttavipariyāyato pana appamāṇakataṃ kammaṃ nāma rūpārūpāvacaraṃ, tenāha “tañhī”tiādi. Tattha arūpāvacare odissakānodissakavasena pharaṇaṃ na labbhati, tathā disāpharaṇaṃ.

Kamma that is made limited is kamma of the sensual sphere, because of the non-suppression of the defiling states that make for limitation. Indeed, that which is the preliminary part of the divine abidings cannot be expanded beyond its measure by way of pervading directions specifically and unspecifically. Conversely, kamma that is made measureless is kamma of the form and formless spheres; hence it is said, 'for that…' and so forth. There, in the formless sphere, pervasion by way of specific and unspecific objects is not found, nor is directional pervasion.

Keci [M 1.0405] pana taṃ āgamanavasena labbhatīti vadanti, tadayuttaṃ. Na hi brahmavihāranissando āruppaṃ, atha kho kasiṇanissando, tasmā yaṃ suvibhāvitaṃ vasībhāvaṃ pāpitaṃ āruppaṃ, taṃ “appamāṇakata”nti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yaṃ vā sātisayaṃ brahmavihārabhāvanāya abhisaṅkhatena santānena nibbattitaṃ, yañca brahmavihārasamāpattito vuṭṭhāya samāpannaṃ arūpāvacarajjhānaṃ, taṃ iminā [V 1.0360] pariyāyena pharaṇappamāṇavasena [P 1.0526] appamāṇakatanti vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti apare. Vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ.

Some, however, say that it is attainable by way of arrival, but this is not fitting. For the formless attainment is not the outflow of the divine abidings, but rather the outflow of the kasiṇas. Therefore, it should be understood that the formless attainment which is well-developed and brought to mastery is what is called 'made measureless.' Alternatively, others say that what is produced by a continuum fabricated with an exceeding cultivation of the divine abidings, and the formless-sphere jhāna which is attained after emerging from the attainment of the divine abidings—this, by this method, can be appropriately said to be 'made measureless' in the sense of the extent of pervasion. This should be investigated and adopted.

Rūpāvacarārūpāvacarakammeti rūpāvacarakamme, arūpāvacarakamme ca sati. Na ohīyati na tiṭṭhatīti katūpacitampi kāmāvacarakammaṃ yathādhigate mahaggatajjhāne aparihīne taṃ abhibhavitvā paṭibāhitvā sayaṃ ohīyakaṃ hutvā paṭisandhiṃ dātuṃ samatthabhāve na tiṭṭhati. Laggitunti āvarituṃ nisedhetuṃ. Ṭhātunti paṭibalo hutvā ṭhātuṃ. Pharitvāti paṭippharitvā. Pariyādiyitvāti tassa sāmatthiyaṃ khepetvā. Kammassa pariyādiyanaṃ nāma tassa vipākuppādanaṃ nisedhetvā attano vipākuppādananti āha “tassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā”tiādi. Evaṃ mettādivihārīti evaṃ vuttānaṃ mettādīnaṃ brahmavihārānaṃ vasena mettādivihārī.

'When there is kamma of the form and formless spheres' means when kamma of the form sphere and kamma of the formless sphere are present. 'It does not decline, it does not persist' means that even kamma of the sensual sphere that has been done and accumulated, when the exalted jhāna that has been attained has not declined, is overpowered and obstructed; becoming itself liable to decline, it is unable to persist in a state capable of giving rebirth. 'Laggituṃ' means to obstruct, to prohibit. 'Ṭhātuṃ' means to stand, having become capable. 'Pharitvā' means having pervaded against. 'Pariyādiyitvā' means having exhausted its capacity. The exhaustion of kamma means preventing its result from arising and causing one's own result to arise; hence it is said, 'having obstructed its result,' and so forth. Thus, 'a dweller in loving-kindness and so forth' means one who dwells by way of the divine abidings of loving-kindness and the like, as described.

559. Aggaññasutte…pe… alatthunti aggaññasutte āgatanayena upasampadañceva arahattañca alatthuṃ paṭilabhiṃsu. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

559. In the Aggañña Sutta...and so on...they attained: by the method that comes in the Aggañña Sutta, they attained, they received, both higher ordination and arahantship. The rest is indeed easily understood.

Tevijjasuttavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā.

The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Tevijja Sutta.

Niṭṭhitā ca terasasuttapaṭimaṇḍitassa sīlakkhandhavaggassa atthavaṇṇanāya

The exposition of the meaning of the Sīlakkhandha Vagga, adorned with thirteen discourses, is completed.

Līnatthappakāsanāti.

Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning.

Sīlakkhandhavaggaṭīkā niṭṭhitā.

The Subcommentary on the Sīlakkhandha Vagga is concluded.
